Theophylact follows Chrysostom according to his custom, namely that the Spirit brings forth the fruit of goodness, which opposes bitterness and wrath; justice, which attacks avarice itself; and truth, which stands against the deceptive pleasures of uncleanness.

Latin:

Vers. 9. Ὁ γὰρ καρπὸς τοῦ πνεύματος) In manuscripto ὁ γὰρ καρπὸς τοῦ φωτὸς, quod cum praecedentibus melius co- haeret. Hi opponuntur mox ἔργα σκότους. Ebraeorum mos est, fructuum nomine appellare opera, Matth. 3, 8. Joh. 15, 16. Galat. 5, 22. ex quo loco haec lectio a scribis male mu- tata est. Hoc autem comma totum per παρένθεσιν legen- dum est.

Non hae causae sat praegnantes sunt deserendi receptam lectionem, etsi non MS. tantum Grotii, sed & Claromont. Bezae, Vulgatus etiam & Syrus τοῦ φωτὸς habuerint, idque retineat Hieronymus. Caeteri enim omnes Codices habent τοῦ πνεύματος. Et cur id reprobemus? An novum est, ab una Me- taphora ad aliam transire scripturam? Fructus Spiritus nominari receptum est. At fructus lucis nuspiam leguntur.

ἐν πάσῃ ἀγαθωσύνῃ) Rom. 15, 14. Gal. 5, 21.

καὶ δικαιοσύνῃ) Quae opponitur τῇ πλεονεξίᾳ, quam supra damnavit.

καὶ ἀληθείᾳ) Quae opponitur mendacio, quod itidem damnavit supra 2, 25.

Sic Chrysostomus ἀγαθωσύνην duci πρὸς τὴν πι- κρίαν, δικαιοσύνην, πρὸς τὰς πλεονεξίας ait, (ubi justum in contradistinctione a bono significat id, quo suum cuique tribuitur) ἀλήθειαν πρὸς τὴν ψευδῆ ἡδονὴν, ut opponatur fictae voluptati & men- dacio, uti hypocrisi omnique simulationi & dissi- mulationi opponi dici potest. Chrysostomum Theophylactus sequitur pro more suo, Spiritum nempe fructus proferre bonitatem, quae amaritu- dini & iracundiae adversetur; justitiam, quae avari- tiam ipsam impugnet, & veritatem, quae fallacibus obstet immunditiae voluptatibus.

## 5:10
Ver. 10. Proving what is acceptable to the Lord) This depends on the verb 'walk.' For with the parenthesis finished, one returns to the discourse begun. What he says here is the same as that which is said in Rom. 12, 1. 2.

Latin:

Vers. 10. Δοκιμάζοντες τί ἐστιν εὐάρεστον τῷ κυρίῳ) Pendet hoc a verbo περιπατεῖτε. Nam absoluta παρενθέσει reditur ad coeptum sermonem. Quod hic dicit, idem est cum eo, quod dicitur Rom. 12, 1. 2.

## 5:11
Ver. 11. and have no fellowship with the unfruitful works of darkness) They also make themselves participants who praise such things, or approve of them, Rom. 1, 32. where see the things said. The works of darkness are truly unfruitful. For they bear no fruit, except destruction, Rom. 6, 21. Gal. 6, 8. above 4, 22.

But rather also reprove) According to the prescription of Lev. 19, 17. where in the Greek 'you shall surely reprove your neighbor' הוֹכֵחַ תּוֹכִיחַ, which is the two hundred and fifth among the laws commanding the Hebrews.

Thus it is taught how we may walk as children of light, namely by proving what is pleasing and acceptable to the Lord, Rom. 13, 2. Phil. 1, 10. Let us indeed flee the works of darkness. He calls sins thus, because the Author of them is the Spirit of darkness, Eph. 6, 12. 1 John 3, and they are those of the impious, who are darkness, Eph. 5. Acts 26, 17. and those who commit them love darkness, John 3, 10. and they finally plunge into eternal and outer darkness, 2 Pet. 2. They are, however, truly unfruitful, as they can neither bring utility, nor a good conscience, nor be pleasing to God. Indeed, they are harmful. For they contaminate the soul, and alienate it from God, the true light, and provoke his wrath. They bear no fruit, says Theophylact, except death and ignominy, Gal. 6, 8. Therefore they ought to be reproved both by word and deed, so that by a contrary manner of life, as if by light, those things which had lain hidden in darkness may be manifested, as Photius interprets in the Greek scholia, conf. 1 Pet. 3, 1. 2.

Latin:

Vers. 11. καὶ μὴ συγκοινωνεῖτε τοῖς ἔργοις τοῖς ἀκάρποις τοῦ σκότους) Participes se faciunt etiam, qui laudant talia, aut approbant, Rom. 1, 32. ubi dicta vide. Opera tenebrarum vere ἄκαρπα. Nullum enim fructum ferunt, nisi exitium, Rom. 6, 21. Gal. 6, 8. supra 4, 22.

Μᾶλλον δὲ καὶ ἐλέγχετε) Ex praescripto Levit. 19, 17. ubi in Graeco ἔλεγμῷ ἐλέγξεις τὸν πλησίον σου הוֹכֵחַ תּוֹכִיחַ, quae est Ebraeis inter leges jubentes ducentesima & quinta.

Ita docetur, quomodo tanquam filii lucis am- bulare possimus, probando nempe, quod sit gra- tum & placens Domino, Rom. 13, 2. Phil. 1, 10. Fugiamus vero opera tenebrarum. Ita vocat pec- cata, quia Autor illorum est Spiritus tenebra- rum, Ephes. 6, 12. 1. Johan. 3. & impiorum illa sunt, qui tenebrae Ephes. 5. Actor. 26, 17. & qui ea pa- trant, amant tenebras, Johan. 3, 10. & praecipitant tandem in aeternas & extimas tenebras, 2. Petr. 2. Sunt autem vere infrugifera, utpote quae nec uti- litatem possunt afferre, nec bonam conscientiam, nec Deo grata esse possunt. Imo noxia sunt. Nam contaminant animam, & alienant a Deo, vera luce, iramque ejus provocant. Nihil fructus fe- runt, inquit Theophylactus, praeter mortem & ignominiam, Gal. 6, 8. Redargui ergo debent ii & verbo & facto, ut contraria vitae conversatione, tanquam luce, quae in tenebris latuerant, manife- stentur, interprete in scholiis Graecis Photio, conf. 1. Petr. 3, 1. 2.

## 5:12
Vers. 12. For the things done by them in secret it is a shame even to speak of) I rightly said that those who speak or do shameful things are to be reproved. For unless that is done, they will even dare to do more shameful things in secret. Those things do not stop where they begin, and night takes away shame, as Tacitus also testifies.

The elenctic use is more appropriately referred to avoiding future shameful acts than, as is explained with Musculus and Crocius, to things already done in secret. For how can those things which have been done in secret be reproved? The Church does not judge concerning secret things.

Latin:

Vers. 12. Τὰ γὰρ κρυφῆ γινόμενα ὑπ’ αὐτῶν αἰσχρόν ἐστι καὶ λέγειν) Merito dixi reprehendendos esse illos, qui turpia loquuntur aut faciunt. Nam nisi id fiat, aude- bunt etiam clam turpiora. Non stant ista, ubi incipiunt, & nox pudorem adimit, teste etiam Tacito.

Convenientius ita ad futura turpiora decli- nanda usus elencticus refertur, quam cum Musculo & Crocio explicatur de occulte jam fa- ctis. Quomodo enim ea, quæ occulte facta sunt, reprehendi possunt? de occultis non judi- cat Ecclesia.

## 5:13
Vers. 13. But all things that are reproved are made manifest by the Light) When those things are reproved by a man imbued with divine light, then it appears how shameful they are.

On the contrary, all those things which are reproved by the light of the Divine Word, or by those who are light in the Lord through the Word, which is truly light, are then manifested in the conscience, things which had been hidden, so that they may be acknowledged by the guilty for what they are in themselves, and be changed for the better.

For everything that makes manifest is light) I think πᾶν here is the Accusative: And φανερώμενον is an Attic form, in an Active sense, such as we also had above, 1, 23. Light, that is, that which uncovers any thing whatsoever. Thus, he who is imbued with divine light both sees what the actions of each person are, and makes it so that others see them. Such transpositions of words are frequent in Paul, as is also below 27.

The Vulgate rendered it in a Passive sense. For everything that is manifested is light. Thus the use of reproof is shown, because light arises in the conscience, once manifestation has taken place; just as Bullinger says that sins, once reproved, begin to become light through repentance. And B. Osiander: When sins and crimes are argued by the Word of God, then they become known to those by whom they were perpetrated, so that they may repent and be saved. And when sinners, if they are brought into the light so that they may repent, are illuminated, so that they are no longer darkness or dark; the Greek scholia agree, that sins, when they are manifested, become light, that is, they are turned into righteousness from repentance. But this outcome of reproof does not always follow. Chrysostom also understood it otherwise in a passive signification in this way: Our life, when it has been manifested, is light; no one hides life among those who are irreproachable. Which explanation Coccejus prefers. That which rejoices to be manifested, that at last is light, John 3, 21. positing an ἀνανάκλασιν in the words of the Apostle, that φανερῦται is first, is drawn into the light. Then φανερώμενον, that it is in the light, either rejoices in the testimony of the light, or is in the middle form, that it manifests itself. To which sense the Greek scholia agree, that a virtuous life cannot be hidden, as if it were explained who can be called light, and what works are light. But this sense does not fit or cohere with the preceding. Nor does it appear how the causal particle γάρ fits in that way. Whence the Active sense seems to fit better, that light is that which manifests all things: which Aretius understands concerning the light of truth, which will uncover all things in the final judgment, but the Apostle here deals rather with manifestation in this life. Calvin, Beza, Zanchius, and Crocius explain it concerning the converted Ephesians or the life of the pious, that they themselves, as light in the Lord, ought to uncover the depraved works of others by the splendor of their own most upright life, so that they may understand that they are depraved. Grotius explains it similarly concerning those who are imbued with divine light, but he takes it as a gnome, not as a parenesis pertaining to the Ephesians. It can be taken concerning the light of the Word, through which all things are manifested in the consciences of men, which is effective and penetrating, reaching even to the division of soul and Spirit, Heb. 4, 12. For they are not manifested in the hearts of men, when they are argued by the light, in any other way than that the light of the Word has that power may have that which can manifest all things, or convince the hearts and consciences of men concerning all things. The holy examples of others are not that light which manifests all things. That eulogy is proper to the Word of God. But if this interpretation seems harsh, let these things be understood according to the interpretation of the Vinarions with the blessed Luther: For everything that is made manifest (is publicly reproved) that is light, that is manifested by the light of the Divine Word.

Latin:

Vers. 13. Τὰ δὲ πάντα ἐλεγχόμενα ὑπὸ τῦ Φωτὸς φανερῦ- ται) Cum ista reprehendantur ab homine luce divina per- fuso, tunc apparet, quam sint turpia.

Ex adverso omnia ista, quæ reprehenduntur à luce Verbi Divini, vel ab iis, qui sunt lux in Do- mino per Verbum, quod vere lux est, tum in conscientia manifestantur, quæ latuere, ut agno- scantur à reis, qualia in se sint, & in melius muten- tur.

πᾶν γὰρ τὸ φανερώμενον, φῶς ἐστι) πᾶν puto hîc esse Ac- cusativum: Et φανερώμενον Attica forma, sensu Acti- vo, qualem & supra habuimus, 1, 23. Lux, id est, quod rem quamvis detegit. Sic quales sint cujusque actiones, is qui luce divina perfusus est, & videt, & ut alii videant, facit. Trajectiones vocum tales frequentes Paulo, qualis & in- fra 27.

Vulgatus sensu Passivo reddidit. Omne enim, quod manifestatur, lumen est. Ita usus reprehen- sionis ostenditur, quod lumen oriatur in con- scientia, facta manifestatione; quomodo Bullin- gerus peccata reprehensa dicit lumen fieri icipe- re per pœnitentiam. Et B. Osiander: Cum Verbo Dei peccata & scelera arguuntur, tum ea nota fiunt iis, à quibus sunt perpetrata, ut pœnitentiam agant & salventur. Et cum peccatores, si in lucem pro- ducuntur, ut resipiscant, illuminantur, ne amplius sint tenebræ seu tenebricosi; Congruunt Græca scholia, ὅτι τὰ ἁμαρτήματα, ἐπὰν φανερωθῇ, φῶς γίνεται, τέτἐστιν εἰς δικαιοσύνην τρέπεται ἐκ μετανοίας. Sed hic reprehensionis eventus non semper se- quitur. Aliter etiam passiva significatione intel- lexit Chrysostomus hoc modo: Vita nostra, cum ma- nifestata est, lux est; Vitam in irreprehensibilibus nemo abscondit. Quam explicationem præfert Coccejus. Id quod gaudet manifestari, id demum lux est, Joh. 3, 21. ἀνανάκλασιν statuens in verbis Apostoli, quod φανερῦται primo sit, in lucem pro- trahitur. Deinde φανερώμενον, quod in luce sit, vel lucis testimonio gaudet, vel in forma media, quod ma- nifestat se. Cui sensui congruunt Græca scholia, ὅτι ἐνάρετος βίος ὐ δύναται κρυβῆναι, quasi explicetur, quis dici possit lux, & quæ opera sint lux. Sed hic sensus non convenit aut cohæret cum præceden- tibus. Nec apparet, quomodo ita congruat par- ticula causalis γάρ. Unde videtur Activus sensus magis convenire, lucem esse id, quod omnia manife- stat: quam de luce veritatis intelligit Aretius, omnia retectura in extremo judicio, at de manife- statione in hac vita agit potius Apostolus hic. De Ephesiis conversis vel piorum vita explicant Cal- vinus, Beza, Zanchius, Crocius, quod ipsi ceu lux in Domino vitæ suæ integerrimæ splendore pra- va cæterorum opera detegere debeant, ut intelli- gant, esse prava. Grotius de iis pariter exponit, qui luce divina perfusi sunt, sed pro gnoma ha- bet, non pro parænesi, ad Ephesios pertinente. Potest de luce Verbi accipi, per quod omnia ma- nifestantur in conscientiis hominum, quod efficax & penetrans est, pertingens usque ad discrimen animæ & Spiritus, Ebr. 4, 12. Nam non aliter ma- nifestantur in cordibus hominum, cum arguun- tur à lumine, quam quod lumen Verbi vim eam habeat, quod omnia manifestare possit, vel de omnibus corda & conscientias hominum convin- cere. Sancta aliorum exempla non sunt lux illa, quae manifestat omnia. Elogium id Verbo DEI proprium. Quod si dura videatur trajectio cum B. Luthero secundum interpretationem Vinarien- sium haec intelligantur: Denn alles, was offenbar (öffentlich gestraffet wird) das ist Licht, das wird durch das Licht des Göttlichen Wortes geoffen- baret.

## 5:14
Ver. 14. Wherefore he says) Therefore that light, that is, a man imbued with light, says to another: Awake, you who sleep, and arise from the dead, and Christ shall shine upon you) Epiphanius and others say this is from the Apocrypha of Jeremiah: And it is possible that it was, but without the added word Christ, which in those times does not fit in this sense. They are not the same words, but the sense is nearly the same as in 26:19 and Is. 60:1, 2. But it does not seem to me that Paul is citing any place, but giving to the light, that is, to the man imbued with light, words that are worthy of him. Life in sins and sleep is compared to death, Rom. 13:11, and above 2:1. The sleepy do nothing good; the dead even cause harm by their odor. To those who have been purified, Christ gives the illumination. Concerning which see above 1:18 and Matt. 28:17. Other codices here had you shall touch Christ, but less correctly, if I am not mistaken.

There is no need that one should either have recourse to the Apocrypha or that a speaking light should be feigned. But who is ignorant that Scripture is thus alleged, or the Holy Spirit introduced speaking with the word he says. It is not, however, to Is. 26:19 (which place Grotius wished to be indicated) but to Is. 60:1, as has been observed by most, that it refers. The words and the sentiment agree perfectly. The Prophet was exciting there: Arise, shine, with the reason added, because your light comes, and the glory of the Lord has risen upon you. The Apostle explains and adapts it. Since the true light has come into the world, as Cocceius comments here, arise, you who sleep, it is no longer the time for snoring. Indeed, arise from the dead, and thus your light, that is, Christ, will shine upon you. Which light has now risen, and not only comes, but also comes to excite. And therefore it is preached, and all the sleeping, sluggish, dead, and hard-hearted are compelled, so that they may be excited, and arise, and suffer themselves to be filled with rays. By which instigation and the Spirit of God they are now quickened. But those who do not hear, and close their eyes all the more, and take their sleep for watchfulness, and death for life, are inexcusable, and testify that they are not children of light. This makes for the Apostle's purpose, that men are as if dead and sleeping, until Christ is announced to them, and the glory of the Lord, conspicuous in the faithful, becomes known to them, by which they are convicted of their death and sluggishness, so that they may awaken, and contemplate Christ, and be turned by him into the light. Thus Cocceius. Osiander agrees: Paul explains the words of Isaiah with a very brief and very clear paraphrase, which has this meaning: Arise, you sinners, from the sleep of impiety, and shake off the lethargy of carnal security: indeed arise (excited by the ministry of the Gospel) from the death of sins; and Christ by his word and Spirit will illuminate you, so that recognizing the most benign will of the heavenly Father toward you, and learning what is well-pleasing to him, you may lead a life worthy of illuminated men. Therefore this passage does not support free will. For those who are in the Church, and who have already been converted to Christ, are compelled. Nor do they excite themselves or arise by their own power: For who would grant to the dead the strength to excite themselves? But by the power of this Word, by which they are excited with efficacy and effect, provided they suffer themselves to be excited by the power of the approaching light, which both can and wills to illuminate and excite all, John 1:9, not immediately, but through the command of the Word, by which he excites us, crying out: Awake, you who sleep, and arise from the dead. For this Word is not ineffectual, but the power of God, Rom. 1:16, powerful and efficacious, Heb. 4:12. Furthermore, those things which are commanded cannot be done by us and our own power just because they are commanded by God: From the divine precept we certainly gather our duty; but we certainly cannot conclude the ability to perform it.

Latin:

Vers. 14. Διὸ λέγει) Propterea lux illa, id est, homo lu- ce perfusus dicit alteri: Ἔγειραι ὁ καθεύδων, καὶ ἀνάστα ἐκ τῶν νεκρῶν, καὶ ἐπιφαύσει σοι ὁ Χριστός) Epiphanius & alii dicunt, hoc esse ex Apocryphis Jeremiae: Et fieri potest, ut fuerit, sed non addita voce χρι- στός, qui illis temporibus in hoc sensu non congruit. Sunt non eadem verba, sed sensus prope idem 26, 19. & Es. 60, 1. 2. Sed mihi non videtur Paulus locum aliquem adducere, sed dare luci, id est, homini luce perfuso, verba, quae eo digna sunt. Vita in peccatis & somno comparatur, Rom. 13, 11. & morti, supra 2, 1. Somnolenti nihil boni agunt, mortui etiam nocent odore. Iis, qui purgati sunt, dat Christus τὸν φωτισμόν. De quo supra 1, 18. & Matth. 28, 17. Alii Codi- ces hic habuere ἐπιψαύσεις τοῦ Χριστοῦ, sed minus recte, ni fallor.

Non opus est, ut vel ad Apocrypha recurratur, vel lux loquens fingatur. Ecquis vero ignorat, ita allegari scripturam, vel introduci Spiritum San- ctum loquentem voce λέγει. Non autem ad Es. 26, 19. (quem locum indigitari voluit Grotius) sed ad Es. 60, 1. ut a plerisque observatum respicitur. Verba & sententia optime congruunt. Excitabat ibi Propheta: Surge, luce, addita ratione, quia ve- nit lux tua, & gloria Domini super te exorta est. Explicat Apostolus & accommodat. Quandoqui- dem vera lux venit in mundum, ut hic Coccejus commentatur, surge, qui dormis, non est amplius stertendi tempus. Imo surge ex mortuis, & sic illu- cescet tibi lux tua, hoc est, Christus. Quae lux jam exorta est, nec venit tantum, sed etiam venit ad ex- citandum. Ideoque praedicatur, & omnes dormientes, socordes, mortui, & duri corde compellantur, ut ex- citentur, & surgant, & patiantur se compleri radiis. Per quam instigationem & Spiritum Dei jam vivifi- cantur. Qui vero non audiunt, & oculos suos magis claudunt, & suum somnum habent pro vigiliis, & mortem pro vita, inexcusabiles sunt, & testantur, se non esse filios lucis. Ad propositum Apostoli hoc fa- cit, quod homines sint tanquam mortui & dormien- tes, donec Christus ipsis annuntiatur, & gloria Do- mini in fidelibus conspicua illis innotescat, per quam arguuntur de sua morte & socordia, ut evigilent, & Christum contemplentur, & ab eo in lucem conver- tantur. Haec Coccejus. Osiander consonat: Pau- lus verba Esaiae brevissima & luculentissima para- phrasi explicat, quae hanc habet sententiam: Surgite vos peccatores a somno impietatis, & excutite veter- num securitatis carnalis: imo surgite (ministerio Evangelii excitati) a morte peccatorum; & Chri- stus suo verbo & Spiritu vos illuminabit, ut volun- tatem benignissimam Patris caelestis erga vos agno- scentes, & quid ipsi beneplaceat, discentes, vitam ho- minibus illuminatis dignam ducatis. Non ergo hic locus patrocinatur libero arbitrio. Nam compel- lantur, qui in Ecclesia sunt, & qui conversi jam fuere ad Christum. Nec virtute propria excitant sese, aut surgunt: Nam mortuis quis tribuat vim seipsos excitandi? Sed virtute hujusce Verbi, quo excitantur cum efficacia & effectu, modo se pa- tiantur excitari virtute adventantis lucis, quae omnes illuminare atque excitare & valet & vult, Joh. 1, 9. non immediate, sed per Verbi κέλευσμα, quo nos excitat, acclamans: Excitare, qui dor- mis, & surge a mortuis. Verbum enim hoc non inefficax, sed potentia Dei, Rom. 1, 16. potens & efficax, Ebr. 4, 12. De cætero non ideo à nobis propriaque nostra virtute fieri possunt, quæ man- dantur, quod à Deo mandentur: E præcepto di- vino debitum nostrum certe colligimus; facul- tatem autem id præstandi certe concludere non possumus.

## 5:15
Ver. 15. See then, how you walk accurately) See how you may institute an exact life. For that is what accurately means. See Dan. 7:16, Wis. 19:17, Matt. 2:8, Luke 1:3, 1 Thess. 5:2. And here it is an indicative for a potential, in the Hebrew manner.

Not as unwise, but as wise) He calls philosophers unwise by an allusion of the name, as elsewhere circumcision, concision; they are wise in vain things: you in certain things, since they are revealed by God, and will be profitable for eternity. Moses gives contrary names to the Israelites in Deuteronomy 32:6, namely, looking back to the times of idolatry.

Latin:

Vers. 15. Βλέπετε ὖν, πῶς ἀκριβῶς περιπατεῖτε) Videte, quomodo possitis instituere vitam exactam. Id enim est ἀκριβῶς. Vid. Dan. 7, 16. Sap. 19, 17. Matth. 2, 8. Luc. 1, 3. 1. Thess. 5, 2. Et est hîc Indicativus pro potentiali more Ebræo.

Μὴ ὡς ἄσοφοι, ἀλλ᾽ ὡς σοφοὶ) Philosophos per allusionem nominis ἀσόφυς vocat, ut alibi περιτομὴ, κατατομὴ; illi ina- nia sapiunt: vos & certa, quippe à Deo revelata, & in æter- num profutura. Contraria nomina dat Israelitis Moses Deuteronom. 32, 6. nempe respiciens ad tempora idolola- triæ.

## 5:16
Ver. 16. redeeming the time, because the days are evil) So also Col. 4:5, the times are full of dangers, because of the hatreds of men toward you. This expression is from Gen. 47:9, the same in Ps. 49:6, therefore redeem the time, that is, by any labor and honest compliance of words, avoid dangers, and lead day by day. This expression is in Dan. 2:8. Where in the Greek, because you redeem the time. He does not only look to the dangers of the times. Therefore Crocius is more correct: To redeem the opportunity, he says, is to be intent upon it with the keenest zeal, and as if by a given price to claim it for oneself as one's own. A form of speaking transferred from merchants. They are accustomed to observe the opportunity of time most diligently in buying and selling, so that they may increase their wealth. Thus the Ephesians ought not to neglect the opportunity divinely offered for preserving their innocence, and for reproving evil works, and thus for winning over the unfaithful, but rather they should redeem it. Cocceius is even fuller: Τὸ ἐξ denotes fullness, as in ἐξιλάσκεσθαι, ἐξικνεῖσθαι, ἐκτελεῖν, ἐκπονεῖν. The same in Col. 4:5, where he restricts this to a special end: 'Walk in wisdom toward them that are without, redeeming the time.' He notes it means to buy up for oneself time and opportunity, that is, to neglect no opportunity and no time, even if the opportunity and use of time seem to us to cost a price, as if he were saying, by the omission of our own convenience and pleasure, which must be postponed to utility. In both, however, we must be greedy for time, whether so that we ourselves may work good and progress toward hope, or so that we may benefit the public and, as the situation requires, any neighbor whatsoever. Scripture also warns that we should not neglect the time of finding, Ps. 32:6, Is. 55:9. Thus Paul, 2 Cor. 6:1, 2, 3. The Scholiast: 'One must let go of everything and buy that one may not suffer shipwreck concerning the faith,' Ps. 1:2, day and night. 'In season and out of season,' 2 Tim. 4:2. Hagg. 1:2, 4. Therefore all time must be bought up. That scholion is of Chrysostom and Theophylact: To bestow everything, whatever is asked, provided that you preserve the head, I mean the faith. For this also pertains to redeeming the opportunity, whereas one addicted to the flesh and the world easily allows every occasion for increasing the Christian cause to slip away. Augustine, Book II of Homilies, hom. 1, Vol. X, col. 412: What is it to redeem the time, except when there is need, even to compare the detriments of temporal conveniences to the spaces of time for seeking and seizing eternal things. Homily X: To redeem the time, this is, when someone forces a lawsuit upon you, lose something so that you may have leisure for God, do not lose it to lawsuits. From that which you lose, is the price of time.

Latin:

Vers. 16. ἐξαγοραζόμενοι τὸν καιρὸν, ὅτι αἱ ἡμέραι πονηραί εἰσι) Sic & Col. 4, 5. tempora sunt plena periculis, ob ho- minum in vos odia. Hæc locutio est ex Gen. 47, 9. eadem in Ps. 49, 6. ideo redimite tempus, id est, quovis labore, ac verborum honestis obsequiis vitate pericula, & diem de die ducite. Hæc locutio est Dan. 2, 8. Ubi in Græco, ὅτι καιρὸν ὑμεῖς ἐξαγοράζετε. Non tantum pericula temporum respicit Re- ctius itaque Crocius: Redimere occasionem, inquit, est acerrimo in eam intentum esse studio, & quasi da- to pretio sibi vendicare propriam. Forma loquendi à mercatoribus traducta. Solent illi temporis op- portunitatem diligentissime observare emendo & vendendo, ut rem augeant suam. Ita Ephesii adeo non debent innocentiæ suæ conservandæ, & pravo- rum operum redarguendorum, adeoque infidelium lucrandorum occasionem negligere divinitus obla- tam, ut potius redimant. Plenius adhuc Coccejos: Τὸ ἐξ notat plenitudinem, ut in ἐξιλάσκεσθαι, ἐξι- κνεῖσθαι, ἐκτελεῖν, ἐκπονεῖν. Idem Col. 4, 5. ubi ad specialem finem hoc restringit: Ἐν σοφίᾳ περιπατεῖτε πρὸς ἔξω, ἐξαγοραζόμενοι τὸν καιρόν. Notat sibi coëmere tempus & opportunitatem, hoc est, nullam opportunitatem, nec ullum tempus negligere, etiamsi videatur nobis opportunitas & usus temporis constare pretio, quasi dicat, omissione nostri commodi & volu- ptatis, quæ posthabenda sunt utilitati. In utroque autem temporis avari esse debemus, sive ut operemur ipsi bonum, & proficiamus ad spem, sive ut publico prosimus, &, pro re nata, cuilibet proximo. Scri- ptura monet etiam, ut tempus inveniendi non negli- gamus, Ps. 32, 6. Es. 55, 9. Ita Paulus 2. Cor. 6, 1. 2. 3. Scholiastes: Πάντα δεῖ προῗεσθαι κὶ ἀγοράζειν τὸ μὴ περὶ τὴν πίσιν ναυαγῆσαι, Ps. 1, 2. die & no- cte. Ἀκαίρως & εὐκαίρως, 2. Tim. 4, 2. Hagg. 1, 2. 4. Ergo tempus omne coëmendum. Scholion illud Chrysostomi est & Theophylacti: Largiri omnia, quicquid petatur, duntaxat caput, fidem, dico, conserves. Hoc enim etiam ad opportunitatem redimendam pertinet, cum contra carni & mun- do addictus omnem rei Christianæ augendæ oc- casionem facile elabi patiatur. Augustinus lib. II. Homiliar. hom. 1. T. X. col. 412. Quid est redime- re tempus, nisi cum opus est, etiam detrimenta tem- poralium commodorum ad æterna quærenda & ca- pessenda spatia temporis comparare. Homil. X. Re- dimere tempus, hoc est, quando aliquis tibi inge- rit litem, perde aliquid, ut Deo vaces, non liti- bus perde. Ex eo, quod perdis, pretium est tem- poris.

## 5:17
Vers. 17. 'Wherefore be ye not unwise' (Be as serpents, Matt. 10:16). 'But understanding what the will of the Lord is,' yet so that you always attend to what Christ has commanded. See above 10. It is more to understand (συνιέναι) than to know (γινώσκειν), as appears from this passage compared with Luke 12:47. To know (γινώσκειν) is to be acquainted with; to understand (συνιέναι) is to weigh attentively; the will of God is our sanctification, 1 Thess. 4:13.

Latin:

Vers. 17. Διὰ τῦτο μὴ γίνεσθε ἄφρονες) Estote ut serpen- tes, Matth. 10, 16. Ἀλλὰ συνιέντες, τί τὸ θέλημα τῦ κυρίε) ita tamen, ut sem- per attendatis, quid Christus jusserit. Vide supra 10. Plus est συνιέναι, quam γινώσκειν, ut apparet ex hoc loco col- lato cum Luc. 12, 47. Γινώσκειν est nosse: συνιέναι attente expendere; voluntas Dei est sanctificatio nostra, 1. Thess. 4, 13.

## 5:18
Vers. 18. And be not drunk with wine) Greater temperance is required in this matter from Christians than from the Jews in former times: grace has increased: virtues ought to increase as well: It is a bad custom to let go to waste, even for a time, that which God has given us as best.

In which is debauchery) The Greeks call him ἄσωτον, whom the Latins call a lost man. Which words specifically denote him who squanders his paternal and ancestral property. For Martial said that this is to perish quickly. But they are also transferred to every kind of person, so immersed in vices that their salvation is despaired of, which usually happens to drunkards. For drunkenness is both the mother and nurse of all vices, Gellius VII. 11. translates a wicked man into Greek as ἄσωτον, and with other words ἀκόλαστον, ἄχρειον, ἄχρηστον. The Syrian preserved the Greek word, and placed the same in 1 Pet. IV. 13. and the Chaldeans translate the word זלל in Proverbs XXIII. 20. as סבא, and the noun זולל in Prov. XXIII. 21. they translate as אסרן. Alexis: Is not drunkenness the greatest evil of all for men, and the most harmful? Crobylus: For what pleasure is there in being constantly drunk? Depriving oneself while alive of the ability to think, which is the greatest good that nature has given us.

Thus also for Cocceius, σώφρων and ἄσωτος are opposed, the former is he who has a sound mind: ἄσωτος is insane, who has no soundness or salvation. Clement of Alexandria, book II, Pædag. c. 2, calls ἄσωτον as if it were ἄσωστον, which cannot be saved. This sense agrees with the previous ones, 'not as unwise,' and 'do not be foolish.' The dehortation from drunkenness seems to be added for this reason, because in it there is insanity, and the exhortation to be filled with the Spirit, from whom comes wisdom and understanding. We would not believe, however, that insanity is referred to here, but rather luxury, and lasciviousness of every kind, or generally 'an unorderly being.' B. Luther rendered it: 'We see that drunkards are wild, bold, shameless, and altogether ill-mannered, with words, shouting, gestures, and the like,' he has in the marginal gloss. Therefore Grotius assigns a sense of this kind, that this is the effect of drunkenness, that drunkards dissolve into every immodesty, and are held by no shame. Erasmus on this passage: 'Aσωτία, he says, that is luxury. He warned of this, lest anyone here take luxury for lust, as the common people do. Nor do I see why Faber prefers unhealthiness instead of luxury, as if Paul were acting here like a physician, so that we might be of a healthy body, abstaining from drunkenness. For even if we grant that they are called ἀσώτως from the verb σέσωσαι, that is, 'he has been saved,' with the privative particle α added, and the σ inserted, it still cannot signify unhealthiness, nor is it ever found used in this sense among Greek writers: rather, a person is called ἄσωτος by the Greeks because they were lost in luxury, so constantly engaged in drinking bouts that they never saw the sun sober, neither rising nor setting, of whom Plato makes mention, besides countless others: Hence also the verb is derived, ἀσωτεύουσι, 'I dissolve in luxury,' which Athenaeus used in the eighth book of the Deipnosophists. Now the expression, 'in which,' in my opinion, does not simply refer to wine, but to the whole part of the sentence which preceded. 'Do not be drunk with wine, in which,' that is, in which thing, and in which drunkenness of wine, there is luxury. Furthermore, what he called ἀσωτίαν here, elsewhere he calls ἀσέλγειαν.

Latin:

Vers. 18. Καὶ μὴ μεθύσκεσθε οἴνῳ) Major hac in re tempe- rantia a Christianis exigitur, quam a Judæis priori tempo- re: crevit gratia: crescere debent & virtutes: Malus mos perditum ire vel ad tempus, id quod Deus nobis optimum dedit.

Ἐν ᾧ ἐστιν ἀσωτία) Græci ἄσωτον vocant, quem Latini perditum. Quæ verba specialiter quidem eum denotant, qui rem patriam avitamque prodigit. Nam hoc esse cito perire dixit Martialis. Verum etiam transferuntur ad o- mne genus hominum, ita immersorum vitiis, ut eorum salus deplorata sit, quod plerumque evenire solet ebriosis. Est enim ebrietas omnium vitiorum & mater & nutrix, Gel- lius VII. 11. nequam hominem Græce vertit ἄσωτον, & aliis vocibus ἀκόλαστον, ἄχρειον, ἄχρηστον. Servavit vocem Græ- cam Syrus, eandemque posuit 1. Petr. IV. 13. & Chaldæi verbum זלל Proverb. XXIII. 20. vertunt סבא, & no- men זולל Prov. XXIII. 21. vertunt אסרן. Alexis: Εἶτ’ ὄχ ἁπάντων ἐστὶ τὸ μεθύειν κακὸν, Μέγιστον ἀνθρώποισι κὶ βλαβερώτατον. Crobylus: Tὸ γὰρ ἐνδελεχῶς μεθύειν τίν’ ἡδονὴν ἔχει; ᾿Αποστεροῦντα ζῶνθ’ ἑαυτὸν τοῦ φρονεῖν, Ὃ μέγιστον ἡμῖν ἀγαθὸν ἔσχεν ἡ φύσις.

Ita & Coccejo σώφρων & ἄσωτος opponuntur, ille cui sana mens est: ἄσωτος insanus, cui nulla sa- nitas vel salus est. Clemens Alexandr. lib. II. Pædag. c. 2. ἄσωτον dicit qs. ἄσωστον, quod servari non pos- sit. Convenit hic sensus cum prioribus μὴ ὡς ἄσο- φοι, & μὴ γίνεσθε ἄφρονες. Adjuncta ideo videtur dehortatio ab ebrietate, quia in ea insania & ad- hortatio ut Spiritu impleantur, a quo σοφία κὶ σύ- νεσις. Non tamen insaniam hic respici credideri- mus, sed luxuriam potius, & omnis generis lascivi- am, vel generatim ein unordentlich Wesen, B. Lu- therus reddidit: Wir sehen, daß die Trunckenbolde wilde, freche, unverschämbte, und allerdinge unge- zogen sind, mit Worten, Schreyen, Gebärden und dergleichen, habet in glossa marginali. Ideo sensum Grotius ejusmodi assignat, ebrietatis hunc esse ef- fectum, ut ebrii disfluant in omnem immode- stiam, nec ullo pudore teneantur. Erasmi in hunc locum: 'Aσωτία, inquit, id est luxus. Hoc admonuit, ne quis hic luxuriam accipiat pro libidine, ut vulgus facit. Nec video, cur Faber malit pro luxuria insalu- britatem, quasi hoc agat Paulus ceu medicus, ut si- mus salubri corpore, temperantes ab ebrietate. Nam ut donemus, ἀσώτως dictos a verbo σέσωσαι id est, servatus est, addita particula privativa α, & subjecto σ, non potest tamen significare insalubritatem, nec us- qua apud scriptores Græcos hoc sensu reperitur usur- patum: imo populus ἄσωτος sic dictus est Græcis, quod essent luxu perditi, sic assidue versantes in commessa- tionibus, ut nunquam sobrii viderent Solem nec orien- tem nec occidentem, quorum meminit & Plato præter alios innumeros: Hinc & verbum deductum ἀσω- τεύουσι, luxu dissluo, quo usus est Athenæus libro Di- pnosophistarum octavo. Jam dictio, quo mea sententia non simpliciter refert vinum, sed totam orationis parti- culam, quæ præcessit. Nolite inebriari vino, in quo, hoc est in quare, & in qua vini temulentia est luxus. Porro quod hic dixit ἀσωτίαν, alibi vocat ἀσέλγειαν.

## 5:19
Vers. 19. But be filled with the Spirit) He opposes things that are in some way similar: They are filled with wine, you with the Spirit; that brings joy to them, but this, how much more justly to you? See a similar antithesis in Acts II. 15, 16.

Do you wish, he says, to be affected with pleasantness? Flee the excessive satiety of wine. Do you wish, moreover, to be filled with the Holy Spirit? You will certainly attain that if you are accustomed to sing to the Lord. For those who sing are filled with the Holy Spirit, as opposed to the impure, who sing the songs of Satan, as Theophylact says here.

Speaking to yourselves) Among yourselves, and above IV. 32.

Such singing, therefore, ought to be, as much as it can possibly be, for the understanding of those present, so that they may either sing along or add their Amen, 1 Cor. XIV. 15, 16. Grotius rightly compares these things with the preceding ones in this way: He had noted the effect of bodily drunkenness, so as to deter minds from it: to that he opposes the effect of spiritual filling or drunkenness. Those full of wine are accustomed to chatter among themselves, to sing, and to play musical instruments, where, however, the words themselves are almost profane, often obscene and filthy; all designed for carnal pleasure, not for the glory of God. In their place, the Apostle substitutes exercises of piety proceeding from the filling and joy of the Holy Spirit. The Ephesians, therefore, ought to confer among themselves, full of the Holy Spirit, not walk or sit mute, and with all their senses called to lower things, speak only to themselves, not to others. That pertains to private and public gatherings.

Psalms) תהלים to the Hebrews, in Greek they are called psalms, those excellent songs of David and others, which were accustomed to be adapted to citharas and nabliums in the temple. In these there are many things which Christians can usefully recite among Christians. Moreover, that the ancient Christians sang with the voice alone, not with instruments, is taught by the response to the orthodox CVII, whoever that writer is, who is accustomed to be added to Justin.

Johannes Cocceius, however, corrects that writer here in the Reformed school: But the same man, he says, disapproves of instrumental music, as childish, which served infants in the Old Testament. Let us say, therefore, that David was also a child, and Elisha. We are of like passions with them, and they with us. If there was any typical significance in the instruments, that ceases: but insofar as they are aids and testimonies of spiritual joy, they can be used, provided that it is done for edification. To this end serves the common distinction of these words among the Reformed, which Crocius brings forward: Our people generally agree on this, that psalms are those in which, besides the tongue, a musical instrument is used: hymns, which contain the praises and encomiums of God: odes or songs, which not only contain praises, but also exhortations, doctrines, dehortations, and reproofs. From which it is evident, as Grotius notes, that the ancient Christians in their assemblies (he had said previously that private and public ones are referred to here) employed music. He also praises the opinion of Clement of Alexandria, p. 516: 'Even if you know how to sing and play to the lyre or cithara, no reproach will fall upon you. You will imitate the righteous Hebrew King, who is pleasing and acceptable to God. Rejoice in the Lord, O you righteous. Praise becomes the upright, says the Prophet. And confess to the Lord on the cithara, and sing to him on the ten-stringed psaltery.' These things are to be noted against those of the Reformed who contend that instrumental music belonged to the Levitical worship, which is now abolished, and that musical organs were introduced into the Church against the law of Paul, and indeed even against Grotius himself, since afterwards (p. 517) he says that it is not consistent, in a self-contradiction, that the Apostles and their immediate successors used musical instruments in public assemblies.

κὶ ὕμνοις) Hymns seem to be called extemporaneous praises of God, born from the occasion. Acts 16:25. Add what we said on Matt. 26:30.

κὶ ᾠδαῖς πνευματικαῖς( שירים Odes are premeditated songs, not without some art, such as those in Exod. 14:32, Deut. 31:19, Judg. 5:12, 2 Sam. 22:1, 1 Kings 4:32. But he added 'spiritual' well, for there are also other odes, about which Amos 8:10; thus also Col. 3:16, similar above f. 3.

There is not sufficient reason why hymns should be distinguished from odes in such a way that the former are extemporaneous and the latter are premeditated songs. Basil the Great in Ps. 29 distinguishes them thus: 'A psalm is a musical prayer as to its kind according to metrical principles, and is played on an instrument. A hymn is a sonorous voice, produced for hymns without the harmony of an instrument. Odes, finally, or a canticle, comprise a concise contemplation and discourse about God, even if it is not expressed by singing or by a musical organ.' Jerome says that hymns in general are those which proclaim the strength of God and always admire either His benefits or His deeds. That psalms properly belong to the ethical place, so that through the organ of the body we may know what is to be done and what is to be avoided. But he who disputes about higher things, and the harmony of the world and the order and harmony of all creatures, the subtle Disputant explains, is to sing that spiritual song, he says, but that this distinction is not even perpetual, since there are also Eucharistic and Prophetic Psalms, not only Parenetic. Whence Coccejus, having dismissed that exquisite distinction of terms, says it is enough to know that the Apostle wished to include all types. Which, however, he distinguishes rather by reason of the mode than the matter, namely, that the speech and song may be either bound, or also sung with a modulated voice, or an instrument may be added. In this, however, Coccejus does not deserve assent, in that he wishes those to be called spiritual odes which were inspired by the Holy Spirit; who nevertheless says that songs made by the faithful can have a place in private homes. But why not also in public assemblies? Crocius explained spiritual odes more correctly: He says he distinguishes them from the psalms, hymns, and odes of profane men and shows that they ought to respond to the Spirit by which they are filled, that is, they are spiritual both by reason of their matter and by reason of their end, so that the mind may be edified by them.

ᾄδοντες καὶ ψάλλοντες) Whether reciting your own or another's. Tertullian in the Apologeticus: Everyone is challenged to come forward and sing to God from the holy scriptures or from his own talent. In the Manuscript it is, ἐν χάριτι, ᾄδοντες, not badly, as also in Col. III. 16.

ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ ὑμῶν) With the heart consenting to the sound of the mouth, Hosea VII. 2. see 1 Corinthians XIV. 15. this is משכיל in the psalms. For even if someone, says Jerome, in the manner of tragedians, clears his throat and gullet with sweet modulation, but does not prepare his heart, he is not a singer pleasing to God. Conversely, a bad-toned person, if he has good works, is a sweet singer to God: To sing in the heart, says Theophylact, is to sing with both sense and mind, not with a twisted and restless heart. He, I say, sings with his heart who, by singing, meditates more intently on God and turns it over in his mind.

Τῷ κυρίῳ) In honor of Christ, and to sing a song to Christ as if to God among yourselves. Pliny in his letter about the Christians.

Latin:

Vers. 19. ᾿Αλλὰ πληροῦσθε ἐν πνεύματι) Opponit res in aliquo similes: Illi vino implentur, vos Spiritu; illud illis gaudium parit, hoc vero quanto justius vobis? Vide ἀντίθε- τον simile Act. II. 15. 16.

Vis, inquit, affici jucunditate? fuge nimiam vini satietatem. Vis præterea Spiritu Sancto expleri? Af- sequeris id utique, si psallere Domino consuestes. Psal- lentes namque S. S. opplentur, ut contra impuro, qui Satanæ cantiones emodulantur, ut hic Theophylactus.

Λαλοῦντες ἑαυτοῖς) Inter vos, & supra IV. 32.

Debet igitur talis esse cantus maxime, quantum ejus fieri potest, ut sit ad intellectum præsentium, ut possint vel una canere, vel Amen suum adjicere, 1.Cor. XIV. 15.16. Recte autem hæc cum anteceden- tibus ita confert Grotius: Effectum ebrietatis corpo- ralis notaverat, ut ab ea deterreret animos: illi oppo- nit effectum repletionis seu ebrietatis spiritualis. Vino pleni solent inter se garrire, canere, ac instrumentis Musicis ludere, ubi tamen verba ipsa fere sunt pro- fana, sæpe obscæna turpiaque;omnia ad carnalem vo- luptatem non ad Dei gloriam comparata. Pro iis sub- stituit Apostolus exercitia pietatis a repletione ac gaudio Spiritus Sancti procedentia. Debent igitur E- phesii inter se conferre, Sancto Spiritu pleni, non muti incedere, aut sedere, & sensibus omnibus ad inferiora vocatis sibi ipsis tantum loqui, non aliis. Id pertinet ad congressus privatos & publicos.

Ψαλμοῖς) תהלים Ebræis, græce ψαλμοὶ vocantur exi- mia carmina illa Davidis & aliorum, quæ in templo citharis & nabliis aptari solebant. In his multa sunt, quæ Christiani apud Christianos utiliter recitare possunt. Cæterum Chri- stianos veteres assa voce cecinisse, non μέτ’ ὀργάνων docet re- sponso ad orthodoxos CVII. quisque ille scriptor est, Justi- no addi solitus.

Corrigit tamen hic scriptorem illum in schola Reformata Johannes Coccejus: At idem, inquit, ὀργανικὴν ἀποδοκιμάζει, ut νηπιώδη, quæ infantibus inservierit in Veteri Testamento. Dicamus igitur, & Davidem νήπιον fuisse & Eliseum. Nos ὁμοιοπαθεῖς illis, & illi nobis. Si qua significatio typica in organis fuit, ea cessat: quatenus autem lætitiæ spiritualis adju- menta & testimonia sunt, possunt adhiberi, dummodo id fiat μετ’ οἰκοδομῆς. Huc facit communis harum vocum penes Reformatos, quam affert Crocius, di- stinctio: Communiter in id nostrates consentiunt, quod psalmi sint, in quibus præter linguam adhibetur instrumentum Musicum: hymni, qui continent lau- des & encomia Dei: odæ seu cantiones, quæ non solum continent laudes, verum etiam adhortationes, doctri- nas, dehortationes, reprehensiones. Ex quo patere no- tat Grotius, Christianos veteres in suis congressi- bus (privatos & publicos hic respici antea dixe- rat) Musicam adhibuisse, Laudat & Clementis Ale- xandrini sententiam p. 516. Etsi ad lyram vel citha- ram canere & psallere noveris, nulla in te cadet re- prehensio. Ebræum justum Regem imitaberis, qui Deo est gratus & acceptus. Exultate justi in Domino. Justos decet collaudatio, inquit Propheta. Et consi- temini Domino in cithara, & psalterio decachordo ei psallite. Quæ notanda contra illos e Reformatis, qui contendunt, Musicam instrumentalem ad cultum Leviticum pertinuisse, qui nunc est abolitus,& or- gana Musica contra Pauli legem invecta esse in Ec- clesiam,imo etiam contra ipsummet Grotium, cum postmodum (pag.517.) καθ’ ἑαυτομαχίαν non con- stare ait, Apostolos, illorumque proximos successores instrumentis Musicis esse usos in publicis congressibus.

κὶ ὕμνοις) ὕμνοι dici videntur extemporales Dei laudes, ex occasione natæ. Act. 16, 25. Adde, quæ diximus Matt. 26, 30.

κὶ ᾠδαῖς πνευματικαῖς( שירים ᾠδαὶ sunt carmina præme- ditata, non sine arte aliqua, qualia illa Exod. XIV. 32. Deut. XXXI. 19. Jud. V. 12. 2. Sam. XXII. 1. 1. Reg. IV. 32. Bene au- tem addidit πνευματικαὶ, nam sunt & aliæ odæ, de qui- bus Amos. VIII. 10. sic & Coloss. III. 16. simile supra f. 3.

Non satis causæ est, cur hymni ab odis ita distin- guantur, quod illi extemporales sint, hæ carmina præmeditata. Basilius M. in Ps. XXIX. sic distinguit: Psalmus est oratio Musica quoad genus juxta ra- tiones metricas, & ad instrumentum pulsatur. Hymnus est vox sonora, ad hymnos edita abs- que instrumenti concentu. Odæ denique seu canticum succinctam complectitur contempla- tionem, & de Deo sermonem, licet neque cantu, neque organo musicali exprimatur. Hieronymus hymnos in genere dicit, esse eos, qui fortitudinem prædicant Dei & ejusdem semper vel beneficia vel facta mirantur. Psalmos proprie ad Ethicum lo- cum pertinere, ut per organum corporis, quid fa- ciendum & quid vitandum sit, noverimus. Qui ve- ro de superioribus disputat, & concentum mundi, omniumque creaturarum ordinem atque concor- diam, subtilis Disputator edisserit, istum spiritua- le canticum canere, ait, sed nec hoc perpetuum es- se discrimen, quum & Psalmi sint Eucharastici, & Prophetici, non solum Pærenetici. Unde Coccejus missa exquisita ista vocum distinctione, sufficit, in- quit, scire, Apostolum voluisse omnes species compre- hendere. Quas tamen potius ratione modi, quam materiæ distinguit, quod nempe vel ligata sit ora- tio, & carmen; vel etiam voce modulata canatur, vel addatur instrumentum. In eo autem Coccejus non meretur assensum, quod odas spirituales eas dici velit, quæ a Spiritu Sancto inspiratæ sunt; qui tamen carmina a fidelibus facta in privatis ædibus locum habere posse ait. Cur vero non etiam in pu- blicis cœtibus? Rectius odas spirituales exposuit Crocius: A profanorum hominum, inquit, psal- mis, hymnis & odis discernit ac ostendit, debere respondere Spiritui, quo impleantur, id est, tum ra- tione materiæ esse spirituales, tum ratione finis, ut animus iis ædificetur.

ᾄδοντες καὶ ψάλλοντες) Sive vestra, sive aliena recitantes. Tertullianus Apologetico: Ut quisque de scripturis san- ctis, vel de proprio ingenio potest, provocatur in medium Deo canere. In Manuscripto est, ἐν χάριτι, ᾄδοντες, non male, ut & Col. III. 16.

ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ ὑμῶν) Corde consentiente cum oris sono, Oseæ VII. 2. vide 1. Corinth. XIV. 15. hoc est משכיל in psalmis. Etsi enim quis, inquit Hieronymus, Tragœdo- rum more guttur & fauces dulci modulamine col- linat, non autem cor paret, non est cantor Deo gra- tus. Contra κακότονος, si bona opera habuerit, dulcis Deo cantor est: Psallere in corde est, ait Theophylactus, & sensu & mente decantare, non corde obtorto & inquieto. Ille, inquam, corde ca- nit, qui canendo Deum intentior meditatur, & men- te versat.

Τῷ κυρίῳ) In honorem Christi, carmenque Christo qua- si Deo dicere secum invicem. Plinius epistola de Christia- nis.

## 5:20
Vers. 20. Εὐχαριστοῦντες πάντοτε ὑπὲρ πάντων) Always giving thanks for all good things received to God the Father, as the principal cause, Is. LXIII. 7.

Ἐν ὀνόματι τοῦ κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ χριστοῦ) above III. 21. God the Father is not correctly called the principal cause in relation to the remaining persons of the most holy Trinity, the Son and the Holy Spirit: For these three are one, 1 John V. 7. The name of Christ, who is viewed here as Mediator, brings in not only his command and promise, but also his merit and intercession. Conf. Coloss. III. 17. They observe here, Jerome especially, that we ought to give thanks to God at all times and for all things that happen to us, so that not only for those things which we think are good, but also for those which constrain us and come against our will, the joyful mind may break forth into the praise of God, Job I. 21.

SECTION II. OF THE LATTER PART OF THE PARENETIC EPISTLE, DELIVERING SPECIAL PRECEPTS PERTAINING TO DIVERSE STATES.

PART II. OF THE FIFTH CHAPTER,

On the duties of spouses.

Latin:

Vers. 20. Εὐχαριστοῦντες πάντοτε ὑπὲρ πάντων) De o- mnibus bonis acceptis semper gratias habentes Deo Patri, ut causæ principi, Es. LXIII. 7.

Ἐν ὀνόματι τοῦ κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ χριστοῦ) supra III. 21. Deus Pater non recte dicitur causa princeps in ordine ad reliquas sacrosanctæ Trinitatis per- sonas, Filium, & Spiritum Sanctum: Hi enim tres unum sunt, 1. Johan. V. 7. Nomen Christi, qui hic ut Mediator spectatur, non solum man- datum & promissionem, sed etiam meritum & in- tercessionem ejus infert. Conf. Coloss. III. 17. Ob- servant hic, Hieronymus imprimis, quod in omni tempore, & pro omnibus, quæ nobis accidunt, Deo gratias referre debemus, ut non tantum pro his, quæ bona putamus, sed etiam, quæ nos co- arctant, & contra nostram veniunt voluntatem, in Dei præconium mens læta prorumpat Job. I. 21.

SECTIO II. PARTIS POSTERIORIS EPISTOLÆ PARÆNETICÆ, SPECIALIA PRÆCEPTA, AD DIVER- SOS STATUS PERTINENTIA, TRADENS.

PARS II. CAPITIS QUINTI,

De Officiis conjugum.

## 5:21
Vers. 21. ὑποτασσόμενοι ἀλλήλοις ἐν φόβῳ χριστοῦ) Namely according to the natural, civil, and ecclesiastical order, all of which are to be observed by us for the sake of Christ, lest we lose his favor. Other books have ἐν φόβῳ Θεῦ. But our Manuscript, which we use so often, also has ἐν φόβῳ χριστοῦ, and the Syriac and Arabic are no different. But the learned have rightly noted here that ὑποτασσόμενοι is Passive in sound, but reciprocal in sense: just as verbs of the Niphal form are very often used among the Hebrews. Moreover, this is most frequent in the verb τάσσεσθαι, and those derived from it. So also in the following.

This is set forth as pertaining to all states before the rules prescribed for individual states separately. This precept, says Hemmingius, pertains to all states of all men. For there is no one who ought not to serve others out of the duty of charity. Thus Kings and Princes serve their subjects. For wherever truth occupies the mind, there a prompt will to perform duties is also present. Moreover, the rule of mutual subjection is the fear of Christ. This fear removes all arrogance, by which men look down upon one another as if from on high. This fear causes us, denying ourselves, to renounce all things which Christ cannot bear in his own. Finally, this fear brings it about that we serve all by the example of Christ, and that by our obedience God may be glorified, and we may perform the duties of charity among ourselves mutually, etc. Ἐν φόβῳ Θεῦ does not refer to the cause which moves one to subjection, as Calvin and Musculus maintain, but to the manner, because that subjection is pious only which regards God in all things, or of which God himself is the bond, as Crocius explains with Beza and Aretius.

Latin:

Vers. 21. ὑποτασσόμενοι ἀλλήλοις ἐν φόβῳ χριστοῦ) Nem- pe secundum ordinem naturalem, civilem, Ecclesiasti- um, quæ omnia nobis servanda propter Christum, ne ejus favorem amittamus. Alii libri habent ἐν φόβῳ Θεῦ. Sed ἐν φόβῳ χριστῦ habet & noster ille, quo tam sæpe uti- mur, Manuscriptus, nec aliter Syrus & Arabs. Recte au- tem hic notarunt eruditi ὑποτασσόμενοι, esse sono Passi- vum, sensu reciprocum: quomodo verba formæ Niphal sæpissime usurpantur apud Ebræos. Est autem id frequen- tissimum in verbo τάσσεσθαι, & inde deductis. Sic & in se- quentibus.

Hoc tanquam ad omnes status pertinens præ- mittitur regulis singulis statibus seorsim præscri- ptis. Hoc præceptum, inquit Hemmingius, ad o- mnes omnium hominum status pertinet. Nemo e- nim est, qui non debeat ex officio charitatis aliis servire. Sic Reges & Principes suis serviunt sub- ditis. Nam ubicunque veritas mentem occupat, ibi prompta quoque voluntas ad præstanda officia adest. Regula autem mutua subjectionis est timor Christi. Hic timor tollit omnem arrogantiam, quæ homines se invicem tanquam ex alto despiciant. Hic timor facit, ut nos ipsos abnegantes renunciemus o- mnibus, quæ Christus in suis ferre non potest. De- nique hic timor efficit, ut exemplo Christi omnibus serviamus, idque ut nostra obedientia glorificetur Deus, & inter nos mutuo charitatis officiis funga- mur &c. Ἐν φόβῳ Θεῦ non causam refert, quæ moveat ad subjectionem, ut Calvinus & Muscu- lus volunt, sed modum, quod ea demum pia sit subjectio, quæ Deum in omnibus respicit, vel cujus vinculum ipse Deus est, ut cum Beza & A- retio Crocius explicat.

## 5:22
Vers. 22. Αἱ γυναῖκες τοῖς ἰδίοις ἀνδράσιν ὑποτάσσεσθε) Man was created for this, that he might rule. That was natural in the beginning, 1 Cor. XI. 8, 1 Tim. II. 13. Afterwards, because of the vice of men, it became penal, Gen. III. 16, and again in the Gospel it was rendered sweet on account of the image of Christ and the Church. The same sense is in Col. III. 18, 1 Tim. II. 12, Tit. II. 5, 1 Petr. III. 13.

Coccejus says these things are inept. For natural obedience was never penal, nor is God and Christ named the bridegroom and husband of the Church more in the Gospel than in the Old Testament. See Os. II, Es. LIV and LXII, and Psal. XLV, and in the whole Song of Songs. Nevertheless, it proceeds from sin that the woman is compelled to bear the σκολιότητα of the husband.

Ὡς τῷ κυρίῳ) Just as you wives obey Christ, so also for Christ's sake obey your husbands. For the husband is the image of Christ.

By 'the Lord' Thomas understands the husband. But the Apostle would have spoken in the plural, as 'to the Lords'. Jerome, Lombard, Hugo, as also the Syriac Interpreter, and most others understand Christ, from a comparison with chapter VI. 5, both because the subjection which is rendered for the Lord's sake is rendered to the Lord himself, and because they ought to be subject to their husbands with the same faith and simplicity with which they are to the Lord. The cause of the subjection is finally explained in the following words.

Latin:

Vers. 22. Αἱ γυναῖκες τοῖς ἰδίοις ἀνδράσιν ὑποτάσσεσθε) Vir in id conditus, ut imperet. Id initio fuit naturale, 1. Co- rinth. XI. 8. 1. Tim. II. 13. Postea ob vitium hominum fa- ctum pœnale, Gen. III. 16. rursum in Evangelio suave red- ditum propter imaginem Christi & Ecclesiæ. Idem sensus Col. III. 18. 1. Tim. II. 12. Tit. II. 5. 1. Petr. III. 13.

Hæc inepta dicit esse Coccejus. Nam obedien- tia naturalis nunquam fuit pœnalis, neque magis in Evangelio Deus & Christus nominatur sponsus & vir Ecclesiæ, quam in Veteri Testamento. Vid. Os. II. Es. LIV. & LXII. & Psal. XLV. & in cantico to- to. Attamen ex peccato provenit, quod mulier cogi- tur ferre viri σκολιότητα.

Ὡς τῷ κυρίῳ) Sicut vos mulieres Christo paretis, sic & ob Christum viris parete. Nam vir Christi imago.

Per Dominum Thomas virum intelligit. Sed ita in plurali dixisset Apostolus, ut Dominis. Hie- ronymus, Lombardus, Hugo, ut & Syrus Interpres, ac plerique alii Christum intelligunt, e collatione cap. VI. 5. tum quod Domino ipsi præstetur sub- jectio, quæ propter Dominum præstatur, tum quod ea fide ac simplicitate subjici maritis suis de- beant, qua Domino. Causa subjectionis verbis sequentibus demum exposita est.

## 5:23
Vers. 23. Ὅτι ὁ ἀνήρ ἐστι κεφαλὴ τῆς γυναικός) 1 Cor. XI. 3. The husband has authority over the wife by the privilege of nature and the law of nations. Menander: 'The woman must speak second; the man must have the leadership of all things.' Philemon: 'It is the mark of a good woman, O Nicostrate, not to be better than her husband, but submissive. A woman who overcomes her husband is a great evil.' Euripides: 'The house in which a woman is supreme in all things is not one that has ever prospered.' Josephus against Apion II, describing the institutions of Moses: 'The woman is inferior to the man in all things.' Then: 'Therefore let her obey, not considering these things an insult, but so that she may be ruled; for God gave the power to the man.'

Ὡς κὴ ὁ χριστός κεφαλὴ τῆς ἐκκλησίας) supra I. 22, IV. 15, Coloss. I. 18, II. 19.

Καὶ αὐτός ἐστι σωτὴρ τῦ σώματος) Christ does everything for the salvation of the Church, which is called his body, 1 Corinth. XII. 27, supra I. 23, IV. 1. So also husbands ought to do everything to protect their wives here and lead them to eternal salvation. The ᾿Ανταπόδοτον follows below in 25. For the Apostle wishes to infer first that which corresponds to the former part of this clause, intending then to come to the other part,

Latin:

Vers. 23. Ὅτι ὁ ἀνήρ ἐστι κεφαλὴ τῆς γυναικός) 1. Cor. XI. 3. Imperium in uxorem vir habet naturæ privilegio & gen- tium jure. Menander. Τὰ δευτερεῖα τὴν γυναῖκα δεῖ λέγειν· Τὴν δ’ ἡγεμονίαν τῶν ὅλων τὸν ἄνδρ’ ἔχειν. Philemon: Ἀγαθῆς γυναικός ἐστιν, ὦ Νικόστράτη, Μὴ κρείττον’ εἶναι τ’ ἀνδρὸς, ἀλλ’ ὑπήκοον. Γυνὴ κὴ νικῶσ’ ἀνδρὶ, κακόν ἐστι μέγα. Euripides: Ἡ δ’ οἰκία, ἐν ᾗ πάντα πρωτεύει γυνὴ Οὐκ ἔστιν, ἥτις πώποτ’ ἐκάπώλετο. Josephus adversus Appionem II. instituta Mosis descri- bens : γυνὴ κὴ χείρων φύσει ἀνδρὸς εἰς τὰ πάντα. Deinde: Τοι- γαρῦν ὑπακουέτω, μὴ πρὸς ὕβριν ταῦτ’ ἡγυμένη, ἀλλ’ ἵν’ ἄρχη- ται· Θεὸς γὰρ ἀνδρὶ τὸ κράτος ἔδωκε.

Ὡς κὴ ὁ χριστός κεφαλὴ τῆς ἐκκλησίας) supra I. 22. IV. 15. Coloss. I. 18. II. 19.

Καὶ αὐτός ἐστι σωτὴρ τῦ σώματος) Nihil non facit Chri- stus pro salute Ecclesiæ, quæ dicitur corpus ipsius, 1. Corinth. XII. 27. supra I. 23. IV. 1. Sic & viri nihil non facere debent, ut uxores & hic protegant, & ad salutem perducant æter- nam. ᾿Ανταπόδοτον sequitur infra 25. Nam prius vult Apo- stolus id inferre, quod priori parti hujus commatis respon- det, venturus deinde ad partem alteram,

## 5:24
Verse 24. But just as the church is subject to Christ) 'But' here is, as Corinthus Grammaticus often says it is, hortatory, just as אָכֵן is often so for the Hebrews. The church willingly subjects itself to Christ.

So also wives to their own husbands in everything) Namely, in the Lord, Colossians 3:18, within the limits of discipline, as Tertullian says; Clement, Stromata VII: 'Obeying her husband in all things, so as never to do anything against his will, except for those things which are considered to pertain to virtue and wisdom.'

The husband is the head of the wife by divine institution, but a moral one, on account of the authority of governance. Christ, however, is here the head of the Church, so that He not only rules externally, but also bestows all life and sense. And therefore the particle 'as' is one of similarity, not of equality. Christ is the Savior, who gives salvation to the mystical body by merit and efficacy. Which name 'Savior' Bullinger, Beza, and Aretius wrongly explain here as referring to the husband. Whence Crocius rightly departs from them, along with Jerome, Calvin, Musculus, Zanchius, and Piscatus, referring it immediately to Christ, even though, consequently, by virtue of the similarity, it also applies to husbands in a certain way. We add here also the Cocceian censure of the Grotian explanation: 'But Grotius wants it to be hortatory.' I say it is the Hebrew אָכֵן. He implies, if this is not enough to move the wife to obey and please her husband, 1 Corinthians 7:34, that the husband is the head, as Christ is of the Church; surely this ought to move her, because the Church obeys Christ, and it is compared to a bride or matron who loves her husband alone entirely, honors him alone and entirely, reveres him, desires to please him, is ready for him, Genesis 3:16, suffers with him, rejoices with him, does good to him, Proverbs 31:12, so that Scripture loves to take the parable of the love of the Church toward Christ from the love of a bride. Which parable is elegantly explained in the aforementioned chapter of Proverbs. Wherefore a wife ought to think that she is then finally assimilated to God, and bears His image, when she shows herself to be an example and pattern of the obedience, reverence, and desire to please which the Church renders to Christ.

Latin:

Verf. 24. Ἀλλ' ὥσπερ ἡ ἐκκλησία ὑποτάσσεται τῷ χριστῷ) Ἀλλὰ hic est, ut Corinthus Grammaticus sæpe esse ait παρακελευματικόν, quomodo & אָכֵן sæpe Ebræis. Eccleseia libenter se Christo subjicit.

Οὕτω καὶ γυναῖκες τοῖς ἰδίοις ἀνδράσιν ἐν παντί) Nempe ἐν Κυρίῳ Coloss. III. 18. intra limites disciplinæ, ut loquitur Tertullianus, Clemens Strom. VII. Πάντα μὲν τῷ ἀνδρὶ πειθομένη, ὡς μηδὲν ἄκοντος ἐκείνῳ πρᾶξαί ποτε, πλὴν ὅσα εἰς ἀρετήν τε καὶ σοφίαν διαφέρειν νομίζεται.

Vir est caput uxoris ex divina institutione, sed morale, ob regiminis autoritatem. Christus autem hic est caput Ecclesiæ, ut non tantum regat externe, sed etiam omnem vitam & sensum lar- giatur. Ideoque particula ὡς similitudinis est, non æqualitatis. Christus est σωτὴρ, qui dat salutem corpori mystico merito & efficacia. Quod σωτῆ- ρος nomen perperam Bullingerus, Beza, Aretius hic de marito explicant. Unde ab illis merito dis- cedit Crocius cum Hieronymo, Calvino, Mu- sculo, Zanchio, Piscatore, id immediate ad Chri- stum referens, etsi consequenter vi similitudinis maritis etiam conveniat certa ratione. Addimus & hic censuram Grotianæ explicationis Cocceja- nam: Ἀλλὰ Grotius vult esse παρακελευσματικὸν. Ego esse Ebræum אָכֵן. Innuit, si hoc non satis sit, ut uxorem moveat ad obediendum & placendum marito, 1. Corinth. VII, 34. quod vir est caput, ut Christus Ecclesiæ; certe hoc movere debere, quia Ecclesia obedit Christo, & ea comparatur sponsæ si- ve matronæ, quæ virum suum solum integre dili- git, eum solum & integre honorat, eum reveretur, ei placere cupit, ei præsto est, Gen. III. 16. ei com- patitur, cum eo lætatur, ei bene facit, Prov. XXXI. 12. ita ut amet scriptura ex amore sponsæ sumere pa- rabolam amoris Ecclesiæ erga Christum. Quæ para- bola eleganter explicatur in proverbiis dicto capite. Quare uxor debet putare, se tunc demum assimila- ri Deo, & ejus imaginem ferre, quando se præbet instar, & exemplar obedientiæ, reverentiæ, ἀρεσκεί- ας, quam Ecclesia Christo præstat.

## 5:25
Verse 25. Husbands, love your own wives, just as Christ also loved the church, and gave Himself for it) That is, He loved it so much that He gave Himself to death for its good, than which there is no greater testimony of love. See above, verse 5. Tiberius Gracchus preferred the safety of his wife, Valerius Maximus 6.1. The Greeks use the word 'their own' for all persons.

The explanation of Theophylact is worthy of note here: 'You see how he compels the wife here to submit herself to her husband, and no differently than the Church is subject to Christ. Hear, moreover, how he urges you to love this spouse of yours, not so that you may have power over her in the manner of a tyrant, but so that you may cherish her, just as Christ also did the Church: nay, even that you may have such pity on her as Christ had pity on the Church itself, or if anything must be endured by you, or if for her sake you must die, you will not reject her, or esteem her lightly, since you are joined to her by such a great bond. You yourself perhaps would do that. But Christ behaved in such a way toward an adulterous and malevolent one, and just as He enticed to Himself one who was defying and turning away from Him, not with quarreling and insults or threats, so you yourself, even if you have seen your wife to be hostile to you and given to luxury, prudently, benevolently, and gently entice her, reproaching nothing if you have suffered anything.' For Christ did the same, who for the sake of the Church, which was stubborn toward Him, underwent death.

Latin:

Verf. 25. Οἱ ἄνδρες ἀγαπᾶτε τὰς γυναῖκας ἑαυτῶν, κα- θὼς καὶ ὁ χριστὸς ἠγάπησε τὴν ἐκκλησίαν, καὶ ἑαυτὸν παρέδω- κεν ὑπὲρ αὐτῆς) Id est, ita eam amavit, ut ejus bono mor- ti se traderet, quo nullum amoris testimonium majus. Vi- de supra v. 5. Tiberius Gracchus salutem uxoris suæ præ- tulit, Valerius Maximus VI. 1. Vocem ἑαυτῶν Græci de omnibus personis usurpant.

Observatu digna hic est Theophylacti expli- catio; Vides, quemadmodum uxorem hic cogit, ut viro se subdat, nec secus, quam Christo subest Eccle- sia. Audi præterea, ut conjugem hanc tuam ames, compellat, non ut in Tyranni morem in hanc imperium habeas, sed ita ut colas, quemadmodum & Christus Ecclesiam: quin etiam sic te illius misereat, ut Chri- stus est Ecclesiam ipsam commiseratus, vel si quid fuerit per te tolerandum, vel ejus si sit gratia morien- dum, non illam rejeceris, aut parvi æstimabis, quip- pe cui tanta sis necessitudine copulatus. Id ipse for- sitan feceris. At Christus talem se in adulteratam & malevolam gessit, utque is eandem, quæ se defi- geret & aversaretur ad se non jurgio & convitiis vel minis pellexit, sic ipse, etsi uxorem tibi infensam prospexeris & luxuria deditam, prudenter benevo- leque illam & blande pellicito, nihil exprobrans, si quid fueris perpessus. Idem namque & Christus fecit, qui Ecclesiæ in se contumacis ob gratiam mor- tem subivit.

## 5:26
That He might sanctify it) That He might give the Holy Spirit to it, as a conjugal gift.

Verse 26. Having cleansed it by the washing of water in the word) 'As' is to be understood. After He had cleansed it by His word, as if by a bath. Just as in a bath, which is 'rachzah' in Canticles 4:2, or in the bronze sea of the temple (for both this and that are called a 'washing' exegetically, as the clay of mud to the Hebrews, and similar things), the filth of the body is put away, so through the word of the Gospel, namely perceived by faith, the filth of the soul. See what was said on John 3:5. There is, however, in these words an allusion to the rite of baptism, as also in Titus 3:5-6, 1 Peter 3:21, such allusions as we have already had in many places.

Thus a notable passage concerning water-baptism is perverted in the Socinian manner. The Apostle is not dealing with the cleansing that happens through the Word, but that which happens through the washing of water, that is, baptism. The particle 'as' is not added in the text. Therefore, it is wrongly thrust upon it or understood. Nowhere is the washing of water understood as the Word; nor does that similarity appear in Scripture. On the contrary, baptism is called the washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit, Titus 3:21. Nor is there only an allusion here to baptism; but baptism is constituted as the medium of cleansing, just as in Titus 3:5 it is not only alluded to the rite of baptism, or 1 Peter 3:21, but baptism is designated as the medium of regeneration and salvation. The necessity of which medium Christ explained, John 3:5, concerning which it was dealt with there at greater length. That spiritual cleansing and washing from sins happens in baptism is taught in Zechariah 13:1. Acts 22:16, and its figure was in the bronze sea. The same is called the sea of glass, Revelation 4:6, water, 1 John 5:6, clean water, Hebrews 10:23, a cleansing, John 3:25. In it we are reborn of water and the Spirit, John 3:5, we are baptized for the remission of sins, Acts 2:38. It is called the washing of water in the Word, because on account of the word of command and promise it is a medium of cleansing, Mark 16:16, insofar as it is dispensed in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit according to Christ's institution: According to that of Augustine, Tractate 80 on John: 'Let the Word be added to the element, and it becomes a sacrament.' Therefore, Crocius rightly noted here a certain one of his associates, who interpreted water metaphorically either as the Holy Spirit or as doctrine. For where the literal sense has a place, one must not pass over to the figurative. Would that the Reformed observed this axiom in other matters as well; thus the controversies that exist between them and us could be made of less account. He adds that besides almost all the old Reformed, Calvin, Bullinger, Musculus, Beza, Aretius, Zanchius, Piscator, and others accept [it] concerning baptism. Crocius also notes another of his own [party], who understands the water that flowed from the opened side of Christ as referring to baptism, however, explaining it as consisting of that water and the Spirit or the soul of Christ, the refutation of which may be read in his work.

As to the order and force of the words, Aretius understands sanctification as the remission of sins, Piscator as the obtaining of remission. To Calvin, Hemmingius, Zanchius, and Beza, to sanctify is to set apart for oneself and to consecrate to God. But that translation of the participle καθαρίσας, 'after he had cleansed it with the washing of water,' does not suit the former. Coccejus, therefore, in order to satisfy the emphasis of the words, thinks it better to construe it so that he might both purify it and sanctify it further. To this we agree: although many things in the explanation which he subjoins would need to be noted, if that were our purpose. Concerning sanctification through the Word, see John 17:17.

Latin:

Ἵνα αὐτὴν ἁγιάσῃ) Ut ei Spiritum Sanctum daret, velut conjugale munus.

Verf. 26. Καθαρίσας τῷ λουτρῷ τοῦ ὕδατος ἐν ῥήματι) Subintelligendum ὡς. Postquam eam mundasset verbo suo, tanquam balneo. Sicut in lavacro, quod רַחְצָה, Cant. IV. 2. aut in mari æneo templi, (nam & hoc & illud λυ- τρὸν dicitur ἐξηγητικῶς, ut lutum cœni Ebræis, & similia) sordes corporis deponuntur, ita per verbum Evangelii, nempe fide perceptum, sordes animi. Vide, quæ dicta ad Johan. III. 5. Est autem in his verbis allusio ad ritum baptismi, ut & Tit. III. 5. 6. 1. Petr. III. 21. quales allusio- nes jam pluribus locis habuimus.

Pervertitur ita insignis locus de ὑδατοβαπ- τισμῷ more Sociniano. Non de mundatione, quae fit per Verbum, sed quae fit per aquae lavacrum, hoc est, baptismum, agit Apostolus. Particula ὡς non adjecta est in textu. Perperam ergo ei in- geritur, aut subintelligitur. Nuspiam lavacrum aquae Verbum intelligitur; nec ea similitudo in scriptura comparet. Contra baptismus lavacrum dicitur regenerationis & renovationis Spiritus Sancti Tit. III. 21. Neque allusio tantum hic fit ad baptismum; sed baptismus medium mundationis constituitur, quemadmodum nec Tit. III. 5. allu- ditur tantum ad ritum baptismi, aut 1. Petr. III. 21. sed baptismus medium regenerationis & salu- tis designatur. Cujus medii necessitatem exposuit Christus, Johan. III. 5. de quo illic pluribus actum. Mundationem spiritualem & ablutionem a pec- catis in baptismo fieri docetur Zach. XIII. 1. Act. XXII. 16. ejusque figura fuit in mari aeneo. Voca- tur idem mare vitreum, Apoc. IV. 6. aqua, 1. Jo- han. V. 6. aqua munda, Ebr. X. 23. καθαρισμὸς, Johan. III. 25. In eo ex aqua & Spiritu renascimur, Joh. III. 5. baptizamur ad remissionem peccatorum, Act. II. 38. Dicitur autem lavacrum aquae in Ver- bo, quia ob verbum mandati, & promissi medium est mundationis, Marci XVI. 16. quatenus in no- mine Patris, Filii, & Spiritus Sancti dispensatur secundum Christi institutionem: Juxta illud Au- gustini tract. XXC. in Johannem: Accedat Ver- bum ad elementum, & fiet sacramentum. Ideo merito hic quemdam e sociis notavit Crocius, qui aquam Metaphorice interpretatus vel de Spiritu Sancto, vel de doctrina. Ubi enim literalis sensus locum habet, ad figuratum non est transeundum. Quod axioma utinam alias etiam observarent Re- formati, sic minoris fieri possent controversiae, quae cum ipsis intercedunt. Addit de baptismo praeter veteres fere omnes Reformatos accipere Calvinum, Bullingerum, Musculum, Bezam, Aretium, Zanchium, Piscatorem, alios. Notat & alium Crocius e suis, qui aquam, quae fluxit ex aperto Christi latere intelligat, de baptismo ta- men explicans, qui ex aqua illa & Spiritu vel ani- ma Christi constet, cujus refutatio apud eum legi poterit.

Quod ad ordinem & vim verborum, Aretius per sanctificationem remissionem peccatorum, Piscator impetrationem remissionis intelligit. Calvino, Hemmingio, Zanchio, Beza, sanctifi- care est segregare sibi, ac consecrare Deo. Sed prioribus non convenit illa Participii καθαρίσας translatio, postquam eam purgasset lavacro aquae. Coccejus ergo, ut emphasi vocum satisfiat, melius putat esse, sic construere, ut eam & purificaret & sanctificaret porro. Cui annuimus: Etsi multa in explicatione, quam subjungit, notanda essent, si nostri id instituti foret. De sanctificatione per Verbum, vid. Joh. XVII. 17.

## 5:27
Verse 27. Ἵνα παραστήσῃ αὐτὴν ἑαυτῷ ἔνδοξον τὴν Ἐκκλησίαν) A transposition again for ἵνα παραστήσῃ ἑαυτῷ αὐτὴν Ἐκκλησίαν (that one, namely, which has now begun to be discussed) ἔνδοξον. In the manuscript, perhaps αὐτὸς ἑαυτῷ παραστήσῃ, 'he might present to himself,' is more correct, which verb is similarly attributed to Christ, Colossians 1:22; to the Apostles, 2 Corinthians 11:2; to individual Christians concerning themselves, Romans 6:13. ἔνδοξον, that is, magnificent, such as Solomon's wife, כְּבוּדָה Psalm 45:14.

Μὴ ἔχουσαν σπῖλον ἢ ῥυτίδα) σπῖλος, or σπίλωμα are stains חֹנֶף, Isaiah 28:28, where the LXX [use] the old σπιλωμάτων. Theodotion [uses] δυσπαλίας.

Ἢ ῥυτίδα) A similar wrinkle. The former signifies that Christians ought to be free from vices: the latter that they ought always to be vigorous for doing those things which are right.

Or anything of such a kind)

But that it might be holy and without blemish) Such as the victims were required to be in the old law, that is, solemnly offered to God by the Priests, and without those defects which are called מום, that is μῶμος, Levit. XXI. 16 and following, XXII. 20. Exod. XXIX. 2 and Levit. I. 3. תמים is translated ἄμωμος: Let him who has leisure for it see those places of the law which we have noted. Solomon to his bride, who represented the image of the Church, ומום אין בך μῶμος οὐκ ἔστιν ἐν σοί.

Coccejus recognizes no hyperbaton here, but an antanaclasis in the repetition, or rather a πλοκή. For the name repeated in the repetition signifies something more than it did the first time. The Apostle, he says, implies that the name of the Church is something great, and that it belongs to the faithful, then at last perfectly, when they shall be presented alongside Christ in the sight of the Father, with all the saints gathered together, and looking upon one another, without the fellowship and commerce of sins, so that they may be satisfied with the appearance of God, Psalm XVII. 15. This presentation of the Church, however, is referred by some to the kingdom of grace, by others to the kingdom of glory. The Pelagians said that the Church is presented here as glorious, not having a spot or wrinkle, which is also the explanation of the Donatists, and the Anabaptists, as well as the Papists. Thus Bullinger also interprets it. But he refers this to justification, not to sanctification. But Jerome explains it concerning the state of the Church in the kingdom of glory in Jerem. ch. XXXI. You hear how that Apostolic saying, that it might be without spot and wrinkle in the future and be preserved in the heavens. Augustine, book I. Retract. ch. 7. Since the whole Church says: Forgive us our debts, it is certainly not here without spot and wrinkle or anything of that kind: Yet from that which it receives here, it is led to that glory, which is not here, and to perfection. Which interpretation is confirmed, (1.) because the Apostle had already dealt with the purification and sanctification of this life, now he deals with the end of purification and sanctification, which is eternal glory; (2.) because he excludes every spot, every wrinkle: But in this life the Church is not without every spot, and without a wrinkle. Some, as Antonio Scayna reports, refer the spot to recent sins, the wrinkle to original sin: But neither is original sin extirpated here, nor do actual sins cease entirely. Cornelius a Lapide wishes only mortal sins to be indicated, not venial ones. But all sins by their nature are mortal, and the Apostle removes every spot. But where there is sin, whatever it may be, there is a spot, because every sin is ἀνομία, 1 John III. 4. There is no sin that does not spot: Nor is there any man who does not sin, or who does not have sin, 1 Kings VIII. 46. James III. 2. 1 John I. 8. Nor does the Apostle remove only every spot: But also every wrinkle of the old Adam, every trace of sin, which might in any way render the Church deformed. Now the heavenly bridegroom Solomon indeed says to the bride Church, there is no spot in you, because he grants her his own righteousness, covering every spot of sin, Cant. IV. 7. but there, neither will any spot inhere in her (subjectively), nor will any wrinkle, or any trace of sin remain, with the original stain itself being entirely eliminated. (3.) because the Church is to be presented absolutely glorious. But in this life it is not ἁπλῶς ἔνδοξος, inasmuch as it is still defiled with sins, and exposed to reproaches and afflictions, which obscure its glory in many ways: therefore its glory is hidden with God, Coloss. III. 1. Here the glory of the King's daughter, who is not Solomon's wife, but Christ's bride, the daughter of the King of Kings, is within, Psalm XLV. 14. but then indeed it will be glorious not only internally, but also externally. (4.) because it is to be presented holy and blameless, which holiness must needs be altogether ἄμωμος, most absolute. But here holiness is only begun, not consummated.
