(5.) because Christ will then truly present the Church to himself, when it shall be intimately joined to him, so that it may always be most present, John XVII. 24. 2 Corinth. V. 8. 1 Thess. IV. 17. and therefore he is about to bring the bride, so that the marriage may be celebrated with her, Rev. XIX. 7. ch. XXI. 9.

Latin:

Vers. 27. Ἵνα παραστήσῃ αὐτὴν ἑαυτῷ ἔνδοξον τὴν Ἐκκλη- σίαν) Trajectio rursus pro ἵνα παραστήσῃ ἑαυτῷ αὐτὴν Ἐκ- κλησίαν (illam nempe, de qua jam agi coepit) ἔνδοξον. In Manuscripto forte rectius αὐτὸς ἑαυτῷ παραστήσῃ sibi admo- veat, quod verbum Christo similiter tribuitur, Coloss. I. 22. Apostolis, 2. Cor. XI. 2. singulis Christianis de se Rom. VI. 13. ἔνδοξον, id est, magnificam, qualis Salomonis uxor, כְּבוּדָה Psal. XLV. 14.

Μὴ ἔχουσαν σπῖλον ἢ ῥυτίδα) σπῖλος, vel σπίλωμα sunt sor- des חֹנֶף, Esa. XXVIII. 28. ubi LXX. vetere σπιλωμάτων. Theodotion δυσπαλίας.

Ἢ ῥυτίδα) Rugam similem. Prius illud significat Chri- stianos carere debere vitiis: alterum vegetos semper esse de- bere ad agenda ea, quae recta sunt.

Ἤ τι τῶν τοιούτων) Non cæcam, non claudam, quæ omnia hîc ad animum referenda.

Ἀλλ᾿ ἵνα ᾖ ἁγία καὶ ἄμωμος) Quales victimæ esse debe- bant in veteri lege sanctæ, id est, solenniter Deo oblatæ per Sacerdotes, & sine illis vitiis, quæ מום, id est μῶμος dicuntur Levit. XXI. 16. & sequentibus, XXII. 20. Exod. XXIX. 2. & Levit. I. 3. תמים vertitur ἄμωμος: Videat, cui id vacat, illa legis loca, quæ notavimus. Salomon spon- sæ suæ, quæ Ecclesiæ referebat imaginem ומום אין בך μῶμος οὐκ ἔστιν ἐν σοί.

Coccejus nullam hîc agnoscit trajectionem, sed Antanaclasin in repetitione, vel potius πλο- κήν. Nomen enim repetitum in repetitione signi- ficare quid amplius, quam prima vice. Apostolus, inquit, innuit nomen ἐκκλησίας esse aliquid ma- gnum, & id fidelibus competere, tum demum per- fecte, quando sistentur juxta Christum in conspectu Patris, congregatis omnibus sanctis, & se invi- cem conspicientibus, sine peccatorum consortio & commercio, ut satientur specie Dei Psal. XVII. 15. Præsentatio autem hæc Ecclesiæ ab aliis refertur ad regnum gratiæ, ab aliis ad regnum gloriæ. Pe- lagiani Ecclesiam hic sisti gloriosam, non haben- tem maculam, aut rugam ajebant, quæ etiam Do- natistarum, & Anabaptistarum, ut & Pontificio- rum est explicatio. Sic Bullingerus quoque inter- pretatur. Sed ad justificationem hoc refert, non ad sanctificationem. At de Ecclesiæ statu in regno gloriæ explicat Hieronymus in Jerem. cap. XXXI. Audis, quomodo illud Apostolicum, ut sit sine ma- cula & ruga in futuro & in cœlestibus servetur. Augustinus libr. I. Retract. cap. 7. Cum tota dicat Ecclesia: Dimitte nobis debita nostra, non uti- que hic est sine macula & ruga aut aliquo ejusmo- di: Ex eo tamen, quod hic accipit, ad illam glo- riam, quæ hic non est, perfectionemque perducitur. Quæ interpretatio confirmatur, (1.) quia de puri- ficatione & sanctificatione hujus vitæ jam egerat Apostolus, nunc de fine purificationis & sanctifi- cationis agit, qui est æterna gloria; (2.) quia omnem maculam, omnem rugam excludit: In hac vita autem non est Ecclesia sine omni macula, & sine ruga. Nonnulli, referente Antonio Scayna, maculam ad peccata recentia, rugam ad originale referunt: At nec originale peccatum hic extir- patur, nec actualia cessant penitus. Cornelius a Lapide indigitari tantum vult peccata mortalia, non venialia. Sed omnia peccata natura sua mor- talia sunt, & Apostolus omnem removet macu- lam. Ubi autem peccatum, qualecunque illud sit, ibi macula, quia omne peccatum ἀνομία est, 1. Joh. III. 4. Nullum peccatum est, quod non macu- let: Nec ullus homo, qui non peccet, aut pecca- tum non habeat, 1. Reg. VIII. 46. Jac. III. 2. 1. Jo- han. I. 8. Nec maculam tantum omnem removet Apostolus: Sed & omnem veteris Adami rugam, omne vestigium peccati, quod deformem ulla- tenus reddat Ecclesiam. Jam sponsus cœlestis Sa- lomo dicit quidem Ecclesiæ sponsæ, non est ma- cula in te, quia donat ipsi justitiam suam, omnem maculam peccati tegentem, Cant. IV. 7. sed ibi nec ulla ipsi inerit macula (subjective,) nec ruga, vel ullum supererit peccati vestigium, labe ipsa originali penitus eliminata. (3.) quia absolute glo- riosa sistenda est Ecclesia. In hac autem vita non est ἁπλῶς ἔνδοξος, utpote cum peccatis adhuc defœdata, tum opprobriis & afflictionibus, quæ gloriam ejus obscurant multis modis obnoxia: ideo gloria ejus abscondita est apud Deum, Coloss. III. 1. Hic gloria filiæ Regis, quæ non Salomonis uxor est, sed Christi sponsa, Regis Regum filia interius est, Psal. XLV. 14. tum vero non interne tantum, sed etiam externe gloriosa erit. (4.) quia sancta & inculpata est sistenda, quæ sanctitas prorsus ἄμωμος, absolutissima sit oportet. Hic autem sanctitas tantum est inchoata, non consummata. (5.) quia ἑαυτῷ sibi Ecclesiam tum vere sistet Christus, cum sibi intime eadem conjungetur, ut semper præsentissima sit, Johan. XVII. 24. 2. Corinth. V. 8. 1. Thess. IV. 17. atque ideo adducturus est sponsam, ut nuptiæ cum ea celebrentur, Apoc. XIX. 7. cap. XXI. 9.

## 5:28
Vers. 28. So ought men to love their own wives, as their own bodies) As one flesh, Genesis II. 24. The same words which are here are extant in the Hebrew book Arbaa Turim, as has been noted by others. Just as the body is the instrument of the mind; so the wife is the instrument of the husband for domestic affairs, for seeking children; they ought indeed to love in such a way that they lead their wives not only by admonitions, but also by the example of a holy life, just as Christ led his own.

Theophylactus applies it thus: Just as therefore Christ is the Author of the Church's goods, so I would have you behave toward your wife: and just as he claimed the beauty of the soul, so you yourself shall devote effort to the beauty of the mind of such a kind, not the comeliness of the body. Which beauty of soul if you shall require from your wife, you will most quickly procure it for her, if you shall so instruct and form her, that you may present her to God glorious in Spirit. Some explain "as their own bodies" comparatively, with Lombard, just as that saying, you shall love your neighbor as yourself. But it is more correctly explained causally, because they are their own bodies, namely, morally. For here the discourse is not about a natural, but a moral body, as the Apostle will admonish that each one should love his wife as himself, verse 33. They ought, says Theophylactus, to love, that is, it is not thanks, but a debt, and a certain necessity. For a wife is your body. Coccejus, from the fact that the Apostle says the wife is the husband's body, not unskillfully concludes that a man cannot rightly have several wives. It is a monster, he says, for anyone to have several bodies. Indeed, it cannot be done. If the head becomes the head of another body, it will be taken away from the former. You will say, several wives can be one body of the husband, just as the body of Christ is constituted of many members. But the matter is evident, that Christ, when he is the head of individual believers, does not leave other believers, but at the same time supplies them with the same Spirit, and binds them into one, which a husband cannot do, which is also manifest from the house of Jacob.

He who loves his own wife, loves himself) For spouses are a certain one thing through an inseparable partnership of life.

Indeed, because a wife is another self, and as it were one individual with her husband, just as the body and head constitute one human being.

Latin:

Vers. 28. Οὕτως ὀφείλουσιν οἱ ἄνδρες ἀγαπᾷν τὰς ἑαυτῶν γυναῖκας, ὡς τὰ ἑαυτῶν σώματα) Ut unam carnem, Genes. II. 24. extant eadem, quæ hic sunt verba in libro Ebræo Arbaa Turim, ut ab aliis notatum. Sicut corpus est instrumentum animi; ita uxor instrumentum viri ad res domesticas, ad quærendos liberos; amare nempe debent eo modo, ut non monitis tantum, sed & exemplo sanctæ vitæ uxoribus præeant, sicut Christus suis præivit.

Theophylactus ita applicat: Quemadmodum igitur Christus bonorum Ecclesiæ Autor est, sic ipse velim erga uxorem te gesseris: utquè ille animæ pulchritudinem vendicabat, sic ipse circa istiusmodi animi decorem, non corporis formositatem vacabis. Quam animæ venustatem si ab uxore exegeris, celerrime illi hanc comparabis, si eam ita institues atque formabis, Deo sistes Spiritu gloriosam. Illa ut sua ipsorum corpora nonnulli comparative exponunt, cum Lombardo, quemadmodum illud, diliges proximum, sicut teipsum. Sed rectius exponitur causaliter, quia sunt ipsorum corpora, scilicet moralia. Hic enim non de naturali, sed morali corpore sermo est, ut diligat quisque uxorem suam, sicut seipsum, vers. 33. monebit Apostolus. Debent, inquit Theophylactus, amare, hoc est, non gratia est, sed debitum, & necessitas quædam. Nam uxor tuum est corpus. Coccejus ex eo, quod uxorem Apostolus dicit esse viri corpus non inscite concludit, non posse recte virum unum habere plures uxores. Monstrum est, inquit, habere quem plura corpora. Imo id fieri non potest. Si caput fiat alterius corporis caput, a priori auferetur. Dices, plures uxores posse esse unum corpus viri, quemadmodum Christi corpus constituitur ex multis membris. Sed res evidens est, Christum, quando caput est singulorum fidelium, non relinquere alios fideles, sed simul illis suppeditare eundem Spiritum, & eos compingere in unum, quod maritus facere non potest, quod & ex domo Jacobi manifestum est.

Ὁ ἀγαπῶν τὴν ἑαυτοῦ γυναῖκα, ἑαυτὸν ἀγαπᾷ) Sunt enim conjuges unum quid per individuam vitæ societatem.

Imo quia uxor est alter ego, & unum quasi individuum cum suo viro, sicut corpus & caput unum hominem constituit.

## 5:29
Vers. 29. For no one ever hated his own flesh) Curtius, book VII: our bodies, which we certainly do not hate. Seneca, epistle XIV: I confess that a love for our own body is implanted in us: And from this Seneca seeks an argument similar to this Apostolic one in his book On Clemency, book 5, where he speaks thus to the Prince: If, as is gathered thus far, you are the soul of the Republic and it is your body, you see, I think, how necessary clemency is. For you spare yourself when you seem to spare another.

Paul indeed bruised his body, 1 Cor. 9:27, but not out of hatred, but out of love for the body, so that it might not perish. All the faithful crucify their flesh, Gal. 5:24. But that is not their own proper flesh, which they received from God, but the corruption of nature, the old man, who must be entirely mortified, so that our flesh may not perish.

But he nourishes and cherishes it) He takes care of the body, so that it may be fed and clothed. For thalpein, as also thermainein, is to clothe, Job 31:20, James 2:16. Thalpo is the same as thermaino, and thus chamam is translated in either way. It is granted by nature to every kind of living creature that it should protect itself, its life, and its body, says Cicero in On Duties, book Thus also Musculus, with Zanchius, explains it. But Crocius rightly judges that these things have a wider application. Namely, θάλπειν, which some think is properly said of a hen warming the eggs upon which she sits, is not only to clothe, but also to bear and cure infirmities, to raise up from a fall, to warn one exposed to danger, and to follow up with other offices of love.

As also the Lord the Church) He nourishes it with Word and Spirit, He clothes it with mighty works.

Coccejus is right here: This does not only pertain to the word and Spirit (as Grotius wishes, if indeed he distinguishes them) but also to the provision of every good thing in this life and the future, although this happens not without struggle and affliction, through which he himself is glorified, and the old man is restrained, and the Church receives δοκιμήν. Which nourishment proceeds as far as edification in the likeness of a temple and a city, Eph. 2:21, 4:16. But the warming, as far as the subjection of the Devil under his feet, Rom. 16:20, and peace and the kingdom.

Latin:

Vers. 29. Οὐδεὶς γάρ ποτε τὴν ἑαυτοῦ σάρκα ἐμίσησεν) Curtius libr. VII. corporibus nostris quæ utique non odimus. Seneca epistola XIV. Fateor insitam nobis esse corporis nostri charitatem: Et hinc argumentum petit Seneca simile, plane huic Apostolico libro de Clementia l. 5. ubi Principi sic loquitur: Si quod adhuc colligitur, animus Reipublicæ tu es, illa corpus tuum, vides, ut puto, quam necessaria clementia sit. Tibi enim parcis, cum videris alteri parcere.

Paulus contudit quidem corpus suum, 1. Corinth. IX. 27. ast non odio, sed amore corporis, ne periret. Carnem suam crucifigunt omnes fideles, Galat. V. 24. Sed ea non caro ipsorum est propria, quam a Deo accepere, sed naturæ corruptio, vetus homo, qui omnino mortificandus, ne caro nostra intereat.

Ἀλλ’ ἐκτρέφει κὶ θάλπει ἀυτήν) Curam gerit corporis, ut alatur & vestiatur. Nam θάλπειν ut & θερμαίνειν est vestire, Job. XXXI. 20. Jacob. II. 16. θάλπω idem quod θερμαίνω, itaque חמם utrovis modo vertitur. Generi animantium omni a natura tributum, ut se, vitam, corpusque tueatur, ait Cicero de officiis l. Sic & Musculus cum Zanchio exponit. At Crocius recte censet, haec latius patere. Nempe θάλπειν, quod quidam proprie dici putant de gallina, ova fovente, quibus incubat, non tan- tum esse vestire, sed & infirmitates ferre & curare, a lapsu erigere, periculo expositam praemonere, aliisque amoris officiis prosequi.

Καθὼς καὶ ὁ Κύριος τὴν Ἐκκλησίαν) Nutrit eam Verbo & Spiritu, vestit virtutibus.

Recte hic Coccejus: Id non tantum pertinet ad verbum & Spiritum (ut Grotius vult, si modo ea distinguit) sed & ad suppeditationem omnis bo- ni in hac & futura vita, licet hoc fiat non sine cer- tamine & afflictione, per quam & ipse glorifica- tur, & vetus homo coercetur, & Ecclesia accipit δοκιμήν. Quae enutritio procedit usque ad aedifica- tionem in speciem templi & urbis, Ephes. II. 21. IV. vers. 16. Fotus autem, usque ad subjectionem Diaboli sub pedes, Roman. XVI. 20. & pacem & re- gnum.

## 5:30
Verse 30. For we are members of his body) Individually, 1 Cor. 12:27.

Of his flesh, and of his bones) A Hebrew and Punic expression, about which we spoke at Gen. 2:24, ch. 29:14, 2 Sam. 5:2. The sense in this place is that the Church had its origin from his crucified flesh and bones, that is, from his passion preached and believed. And just as he alluded to baptism a moment ago, so here to the Eucharist, in which the body and blood of the Lord are taken in a sacramental manner. In the manuscript, however, these words are absent, and it could have happened that someone added them to the margin.

And the woman had her flesh from the man, and was bone of his bones: Thus we are from Christ, not because we have a body and soul from Christ the Creator, as Coccejus explains, but since the Church, the bride of Christ, is here compared to Eve, because through Christ's merit we have it that we are spiritually constructed from his flesh and his bones from his side, opened for our sake. Therefore, it is not a matter of our ὁμοουσία with Christ, on account of the assumption of our flesh, which took place in the ἐνσαρκώσει of the Son of God, as Thomas, Aretius, and Coccejus wish, which is also true of unbelievers, and according to which we are not so much flesh from the flesh of Christ, as Christ is flesh from our flesh, Rom. 1:3, 9:5, Heb. 2:14. Thus he himself entered into commerce with us, as Chrysostom says, not we with him; but the matter concerns a mystical kinship with Christ: since we are not only from Christ through regeneration, as Eve was from Adam through creation, flesh of his flesh, but we are also rendered participants and partners of Christ, not indeed in a carnal but in a spiritual manner, Ps. 45:8, and communicating in his flesh and blood, we coalesce with him into one body, which communication happens by the eating of his flesh and the drinking of his blood, both spiritually, John 6, and sacramentally, 1 Cor. 10:15. If it is applied with Grotius to the crucifixion of Christ, it is rightly said that the Church had its origin from the crucified flesh and bones of Christ, or from his passion preached and believed, provided that it is rightly understood. Undoubtedly the Church has its origin from the passion, crucifixion, and death itself, as far as merit is concerned; but as for actual procreation, from the word of the cross and baptism. Also through faith, as they are believers: so also the Church, which is the communion of believers. Faith is of the essence of believers; yet it is the means of justification. It is not only an allusion to the sacrament of the Eucharist: For by that very thing we are rendered participants of the body of Christ, since the bread which we break, or distribute and receive distributed, becomes the κοινωνία of the body of Christ: He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood, he remains in me, and I in him, says Christ, John 6:56.

Latin:

Vers. 30. Ὅτι μέλη ἐσμὲν τοῦ σώματος αὐτοῦ) Singuli 1. Cor. XII. 27.

Ἐκ τῆς σαρκὸς αὐτοῦ, καὶ ἐκ τῶν ὀστέων αὐτοῦ) Locutio E- braea & Punica, de qua diximus ad Genes. II. 24. cap. XXIX. 14. 2. Sam. V. 2. Sensus hoc loco ex carne ejus & ossibus crucifixis, id est, ex passione ejus praedicata & credita ortum habuit Ecclesia. Sicut autem modo allu- sit ad baptismum, ita hic ad Eucharistiam, in qua corpus & sanguis Domini sumuntur Sacramentali modo. In Manuscripto tamen absunt haec voces, & potuit fieri, ut ali- quis ad marginem adscripserit.

Et mulier ex viro habebat carnem suam, & os erat de ossibus ejus: Sic nos ex Christo, non quia a Christo Creatore corpus habemus, & ani- mam, ut Coccejus exponit, sed quum Ecclesia, Christi sponsa, hic conferatur Evae, quia per Christi meritum habemus, quod simus ex carne ejus & ossibus ejus spiritualiter extructi e latere ejus, nostri causa aperto. Non ergo de ὁμοουσία no- stra cum Christo, ob carnis nostrae assumptio- nem, in ἐνσαρκώσει Filii Dei factam, agitur, ut Tho- mas, Aretius, Coccejus volunt, quae etiam infide- lium est, & juxta quam non tam nos sumus caro ex carne Christi, quam Christus caro ex carne nostra, Rom. I. 3. c. IX. 5. Ebr. II. 14. Sic ipse nobiscum com- mercium, dicente Chrysostomo, traxit, non nos cum illo; sed de mystica cum Christo cognatione res est: quum non tantum ex Christo simus per rege- nerationem, uti Eva ex Adamo erat per creationem, caro de carne ejus, sed etiam participes Christi reddamur, & consortes, non carnali quidem sed spirituali ratione, Psal. XLV. 8. & communicantes carni & sanguini ejus, cum eo in unum corpus co- alescamus, quae communicatio fit manducatione carnis & bibitione sanguinis ejus cum spirituali Jo- han. VI. tum sacramentali, 1. Cor. X. 15. Si cum Gro- tio applicetur ad crucifixionem Christi, ex carne & ossibus Christi crucifixis, vel passione praedicata & credita recte dicitur ortum habuisse Ecclesia, mo- do id recte intelligatur. Nimirum ex ipsa passio- ne, crucifixione & morte ortum habet Ecclesia, quantum ad meritum; quoad actualem vero pro- creationem ex verbo crucis & baptismo. Per fidem etiam uti fideles sunt: ita & Ecclesia, quae est com- munio fidelium. Fides est de essentia fidelium; ea tamen medium est justificationis. Non allusio tan- tum fit ad sacramentum Eucharistiae: Nam per ean- dem omnino participes reddimur corporis Chri- sti, quum panis, quem frangimus, vel distribui- mus & distributum accipimus, fit κοινωνία corpo- ris Christi: Qui autem carnem meam edit, & bi- bit sanguinem meum, ille in me manet, & ego in ipso, inquit Christus Joh. VI. 56.

## 5:31
Verse 31. For this cause shall a man leave his father

his, and his mother, and shall be joined to his wife, and they two shall be one flesh) That is, just as Christ held nothing so dear that he did not renounce it for our sake, so we also ought to be glued to him as if by the faith of marriage, John 17:21. In the manuscript: he shall be joined to his wife, as in Matt. 19:5.

Although a comparison of this kind can be made, the literal sense of these Apostolic words is not situated in it, but the preceding verse 30 deals with the mutual love of spouses, and is to be read as if in a parenthesis, as almost all interpreters have commonly accepted. The interpretation of Estius is forced, and savors of the Origenistic genius of allegorizing, that the Son of God left Father and mother, because, as if having left Father and mother, that is, the heavenly Synagogue, he descended to earth. Such an allegory is indeed handed down here even by Jerome; yet he praises the confession of Gregory of Nazianzus, that all things which have been said here by Moses about Adam and Eve cannot be applied to Christ, and he acknowledges that Adam and Eve are proposed here as an example of spouses. Whence we cannot, having abandoned the opinion of the blessed Hunnius, the blessed Balduinus, and others of our own, understand these words about Christ, that he adheres to his Church, and is with it in one flesh: For how could the preceding words, a man shall leave father and mother, and shall adhere to his wife, befit Christ, I confess I cannot understand. Does Christ, having left the Father, adhere to the Church, or does he so adhere to the Church that he puts the fellowship of the Father second? And what is the mother of Christ, whom he himself left for the sake of the Church? Therefore, there is no reason why we should say with Augustine, book 9 of De Genesi ad litteram, that this prophecy is about Christ, from which Andreas Osiander further inferred that Christ would have come in the flesh, even if Adam had not sinned. There is nothing of prophecy here, even if the Apostle also applied these words to Christ and the Church, which, however, was not done at least. The duty of a husband is described, which is the proper subject of this Apostolic treatment, that he ought to leave his parents, not regarding due love, honor, and obedience, but by not associating himself with them, having left the house of his parents, by establishing a new family with her, by loving his wife more than his parents, by withdrawing from them rather than from her: and to cleave to his wife with love, benevolence, fidelity, and all marital duties, and that by an indissoluble bond. He did not say, says Theophylactus, he shall cohabit, but he shall be glued, signifying a union which cannot be torn apart. Compare what has been said about this matrimonial law in the Commentary on Genesis.

Latin:

Vers. 31. Ἀντὶ τούτου καταλείψει ἄνθρωπος τὸν πατέρα

αὐτῦ, κὲ τὴν μητέρα, κὲ προσκολληθήσεται πρὸς τὴν γυναῖκα αὐτῦ, κὲ ἔσονται οἱ δύο εἰς σάρκα μίαν) Id est, sicut Christus nihil tam carum habuit, quod non nostri causa abdicave- rit, ita nos quoque tanquam conjugii fide ipsi conglutinari debemus, Joh. XVII. 21. In Manuscripto: προσκολληθήσεται τῇ γυναικὶ, quomodo Matth. XIX. 5.

Quamvis collatio ejusmodi fieri possit, non tamen horum Apostolicorum verborum sensus literalis in ea situs, sed versus praecedens 30. de con- jugum agit amore mutuo, & veluti in parenthesi le- gendus est, ut communiter omnes fere interpre- tes accepere. Coacta est interpretatio Estii, & O- rigenicum allegorizandi genium resipit, Filium Dei reliquisse Patrem & matrem, quod quasi relicto Patre & matre, id est, Synagoga caelesti, in terram descenderit. Qualem allegoriam hic quidem etiam Hieronymus tradit; laudat tamen Gregorii Nazian- zeni confessionem, quod omnia, quae de Adamo & Eva hic dicta sunt a Mose, non possint Christo ap- plicari, & agnoscit, Adamum & Evam hic in ex- emplum conjugum proponi. Unde non possumus, relicta B. Hunnii, B. Balduini, & aliorum nostro- ru sententia, haec verba de Christo intelligere, quod ille adhaereat Ecclesiae suae, & cum ea sit in unam carnem: Quomodo enim antecedentia, relinquet homo Patrem & matrem, & adhaerebit uxori suae, Christo conveniant, fateor me intelligere non posse. Num Christus relicto Patre adhaerescit Ec- clesiae, aut ita Ecclesiae adhaerescit, ut Patris post- habeat consortium? & quae est mater Christi, quam ipse propter Ecclesiam reliquit? Non ergo est, quod cum Augustino libr. IX. de Genes. ad lit. hanc prophetiam de Christo dicamus, ex quo Andr. Osiander porro inferebat, Christum adven- turum fuisse in carnem, etsi Adam non peccasset. Ni- hil hic Prophetiae, etsi applicaret haec quoque ver- ba Apostolus Christo & Ecclesiae, quod tamen non factum saltim. Officium mariti describitur, quod hic argumentum proprium tractationis A- postolicae, quod relinquere debeat parentes, non quoad debitum amorem, honorem, obsequium, sed uxori, non illis sese sociando, relicta domo parentum, novam cum illa familiam instituendo, uxorem plus, quam parentes diligendo, ab illis potius, quam ab hac recedendo:& adhaerere uxori suae amore, benevolentia, fide, omnibus maritali- bus officiis,idque nexu indissolubili. Non dixit,in- quit Theophylactus, cohabitabit, sed agglutinabitur, unionem, quae divelli non possit, significans. Confer quae de lege hac matrimoniali in Comment. ad Gen. dicta.

## 5:32
Vers. 32. Τὸ μυστήριον τῦτο μέγα ἐσὶν) That is, those words which exist in Moses, I have explained to you not literally, but in a more mystical sense, כמררש. Thus also the Hebrews say that the woman was taken from the side of the man to signify the marriage of the supreme blessed man. But those things which in the Old Testament are applied to God, those are applied to Christ in the New. But Paul said here, α̉ντὦ τέτυ, for that which is in the Greek of Genesis ἕνεκεν τότυ. על כן. Thus we often have διὰ ὧν for because.

Ἐγὼ δὲ λέγω εἰς χρισὸν κὲ Ἐκκλησίαν) These words, he says, I have used concerning Christ and the Church.

Concerning the former words of Moses, flesh of my flesh and bone of my bones, we concede them, but not the latter. For the Apostle did not apply those to the Church, but proposed them to spouses for exhortation. If, however, anyone wishes to apply the latter also, along with Theodoret, Chrysostom, and Theophylactus, it ought to be done skillfully, and not with the intention as if these things had been indicated by Adam, or by the Holy Spirit when He spoke through Adam, who at least prescribed the matrimonial law there, but that afterwards, when Christ deigned to become the bridegroom of the Church, they could consequently be employed in their own way by explaining the mystery of the union of Christ with the Church, which, however, he ap- that an explanation was expressly made here by the Apostle regarding those very words in verse 31 is by no means to be established. But Cocceius is correct: Since God after the fall signified that Christ is the bridegroom of the Church, it is clear that the words which were spoken through Adam concerning the marriage of a husband and wife were spoken at the dictation of the Holy Spirit for this purpose also, that in His own time they might show us how Christ was the bridegroom of the Church, and what the Church might ask and expect from Him. For the conjunction of a man with a woman does not of itself signify and promise the conjunction of Christ and the Church and the faithful, but because Christ is called the bridegroom of the Church, therefore it is necessary to transfer these words to this mystery. Moreover, since τὸ μυστήριον is rendered as sacramentum in the Vulgate, foolish monks have made marriage a sacrament from that, and the conventicle of Trent sanctioned that this must be believed under anathema. Which are truly laughable things. The Apostle says that that mystery is great, which he had brought forward to explain the love of a spouse, namely that we are of His flesh and of His bones. Matrimony does not have a sacramental institution from Christ, nor form, nor matter, nor a sacramental end. See Matæologia Papistica. By the word sacramentum, the Vulgate understood not some medium of grace and salvation, but in general a sacred secret. Nor did the Apostle call marriage a mystery here: But that spiritual union of Christ and the Church, which is shadowed forth in our marriage, if we act in it according to the matrimonial law: and from which Christian spouses ought to seek the form of love and of connubial faith: For the Apostle added a clear interpretation of what he meant by this name. I speak, he says, of Christ and the Church. Truly this is a great mystery: Because it could neither be found by man, how the Vivifier could become the bridegroom of any Church, which was a multitude of men sinful in themselves and deserving of wrath: nor can it be known by him, that He wills this; nor comprehended, how He is both united with it, and He lives in the Church, and completes it, as Cocceius says here.

Latin:

Vers. 32. Τὸ μυστήριον τῦτο μέγα ἐσὶν) Id est, verba ista, quae apud Mosen extant, explicavi vobis non κατά πόδας, sed sensu μυστικωτέρῳ, כמררש. Sic & Ebraei ajunt mulierem de latere viri desumptam ad significandum conjugium viri supremi benedicti. Quae autem in Veteri Testamento ap- plicantur Deo, ea Christo applicantur in novo. Dixit au- tem hic Paulus, α̉ντὦ τέτυ, pro eo, quod in Graeco Geneseos est ἕνεκεν τότυ. על כן. Sic διὰ ὧν, saepe habemus pro quia.

Ἐγὼ δὲ λέγω εἰς χρισὸν κὲ Ἐκκλησίαν) Verba ista, inquit, ego usurpavi de Christo & Ecclesia.

De prioribus verbis Mosis caro ex carne & os ex ossibus meis concedimus, non de posterioribus. Ea enim non applicavit Apostolus Ecclesiae, sed ad paraenesin proposuit conjugibus. Si tamen poste- riora quis etiam cum Theodoreto, Chrysostomo, & Theophylacto applicare velit, dextre id debet fieri, nec ea mente, quasi vel ab Adamo,aut Spiritu San- cto, cum per Adamum loqueretur, haec indicata fuerint, qui legem saltem matrimonialem ibi prae- scripsit, sed quod deinde, cum Christus dignatus est, fieri sponsus Ecclesiae, illa consequenter suo modo adhiberi possint explicando mysterio unionis Christi cum Ecclesia, quam tamen ap- plicationem expresse ab Apostolo hic quoad ipsa illa verba v. 31. factam esse minime statuendum est. Recte autem Coccejus: Quandoquidem Deus post lapsum significavit, Christum esse sponsum Eccle- siæ, patet, quæ verba per Adamum de conjugio vi- ri & uxoris dicta sunt, Spiritu Sancto dictante di- cta esse eo etiam fine, ut suo tempore nobis ostende- rent, quomodo Christus esset sponsus Ecclesiæ, & quid Ecclesia ab ipso possit petere atque expectare. Neque enim per se conjunctio viri cum muliere si- gnificat & promittit conjunctionem Christi & Ec- clesiæ ac fidelium, sed quia Christus sponsus Eccle- siæ dictus est, ideo oportet hæc verba ad mysterium hoc transferre. Cæterum quum τὸ μυστήριον in Vulgata reddatur sacramentum, monachi insul- si inde matrimonium fecerunt sacramentum, id- que sub anathemate conciliabulum Tridentinum credendum sancivit. Quæ vere sunt jocularia. Apostolus mysterium illud magnum esse dicit, quod ad explicandam dilectionem conjugis addu- xerat, quod nempe nos de carne ejus & ex ossibus ejus sumus. Matrimonium non habet a Christo institu- tionem sacramentalem, non formam, non ma- teriam, non finem sacramentalem. Vid. Matæo- logia Papistica. Per sacramentum Vulgatus non medium aliquod gratiæ & salutis, sed in genere sacrum secretum intellexit. Nec conjugium hic Apostolus mysterium dixit: Sed unionem illam spiritualem Christi & Ecclesiæ, quæ in conjugio nostro adumbratur, si juxta legem matrimonialem in eo agamus: & ex quo formam amoris, & fidei connubialis petere debent conjuges Christiani: Addidit enim interpretationem Apostolus lucu- lentam, quid hoc nomine nuncuparit. Loquor autem, inquit, de Christo & Ecclesia. Vere hoc ma- gnum mysterium: Quia id neque potuit ab homine inveniri, quomodo Vivificator possit fieri sponsus Ec- clesiæ alicujus, quæ esset multitudo hominum in se peccatorum & iram promerentium: neque potest ab eo sciri, quod id velit; neque comprehendi, quo- modo & uniatur cum ipso, & is vivat in Ecclesia, & eam compleat, ut hic Coccejus.

## 5:33
Verse 33.

Πλὴν) Although this passage is correctly explained mystically in this way, nevertheless it ought also to be fulfilled by you κατὰ πόδας (to the letter). Πλὴν here is DEN, nevertheless. That little word does not demand that paraphrase. The Apostle had brought forward no mystical sense expressly. He only teaches that this matter, which he had proposed on the occasion, concerning the spiritual union of Christ and the Church, is a huge mystery. Beza rendered the word πλὴν as 'therefore', because he applies it to individuals, concerning whom he had warned in general. Καὶ ὑμεῖς οἱ καθ᾽ ἕνα) You individuals. Ἕκαστος τὴν ἑαυτῦ γυναῖκα ὅτως ἀγαπάτω ὡς ἑαυτὸν) Let each one so love his wife as himself, as above in 28. Η δε γυνὴ ἵνα φοβῆται τὸν ἄνδρα) And here the word ἵνα is transposed, and ἵνα φοβῆται is for φοβείτω: But to fear here signifies to obey, in the way the Hebrew ירא is accustomed to be taken. And this admonition is also in the book Musar. We add the explanation of Theophylact: Since equality of honors produces inconsistency, for that reason he enjoins that the wife be urged by fear, so that the husband alone may hold the primacy and govern the wife. But understand fear in this place as a certain more intense reverence. Therefore the wife will love the husband as a member, she will revere him as a head: What then if the wife does not revere you at all? But you yourself pursue this with love, do what is in your interest: Just so let the wife also act, even if she is less loved, and let her revere the husband. Afterwards he added these things: Nor would I have said these things as if it were necessary that the wife should fear the husband, from which hatred is produced rather than benevolence: But so that she may be compelled neither to contradict, nor to rise up against the husband, nor to covet the primacy. For if she has been allotted the same flesh as the husband, she will not be inferior to the husband in primacy, nor in honors. Yet after the husband, to whom far more is granted, the wife also is to have authority. Chrysostom, whose these words also are, had preceded: For this reason God subjected the woman, but set the man over her, so that there might be peace. For where there is equality of honor, or where the family dominates, or all hold the primacy, there peace can never be able to exist.

Latin:

Vers. 33.

Πλὴν) Quanquam iste locus μυσικῶς sic recte explice- tur, tamen & κατὰ πόδας a vobis impleri debet. Πλὴν hic est DEN attamen. Vocula illa eam paraphrasin non postulat. Nullum expresse attulerat sensum mysticum A- postolus. Solum rem hanc, quam occasione pro- posuerat, de unione Christi & Ecclesiæ spiritua- li ingens esse mysterium docet. Verbum πλὴν Beza reddidit itaque, quia applicat singulis, de quibus in genere monuerat. Καὶ ὑμεῖς οἱ καθ᾽ ἕνα) Vos singuli. Ἕκαστος τὴν ἑαυτῦ γυναῖκα ὅτως ἀγαπάτω ὡς ἑαυτὸν) Suam quisque sic diligat, ut se, ut supra 28. Η δε γυνὴ ἵνα φοβῆται τὸν ἄνδρα) Et hic trajecta est vox ἵνα, & ἵνα φοβῆται est pro φοβείτω: Timere autem hic obe- dire significat, quomodo ירא Ebræum sumi solet. Et est hoc monitum & in libro Musar. Addimus explicationem Theophylacti: Quo- niam inconstantiam parit honorum æqualitas, pro- pterea timore urgeri uxorem injungit, ut vir dun- taxat teneat principatum & moderetur uxorem. Timorem vero hoc loco reverentiam quandam in- tensiorem intellige. Amabit itaque uxor virum ut membrum, ut caput verebitur: Quid ergo si nihil uxor te vereatur? At ipse hanc amore prosequere, quod tuæ interest, facito: Haud secus & uxor, vel si minus ametur, agat, vereaturque virum. Postea hæc adjecit: Neque eo hæc dixerim, quasi necesse sit, ut uxor virum formidet, unde potius odium quam benevolentia paritur: Sed ut cogatur nec contradicere, nec insurgere viro, nec primatum appetere. Nam si eandem cum viro sortita est hæc carnem, non erit cum in principatu, tum in hono- ribus viro inferior. Post virum tamen, cui plus longe conceditur, & uxor habitura est imperium. Præiverat, cujus & hæc sunt, Chrysostomus : Præ- pterea mulierem Deus subjecit, virum vero illi præfecit, ut pax sit. Nam ubi honoris est æquali- tas, aut ubi familia dominatur, vel omnes prin- cipatum gerunt, ibi nunquam poterit esse pax.

## 6:1 Argument
CHAPTER VI.

ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

He exhorts children to obedience and to honor by bringing in the commandment of the Decalogue (Exod. XX. 12.): But he warns parents not to provoke their children, and to bring them up in the fear of the Lord. He also prescribes the obedience owed by servants, and reminds masters what kind of people they ought to show themselves to be to their servants, and he instructs everyone concerning fortitude and the spiritual armor against demons, and seeking the prayers of the Ephesians for the παῤῥησία (boldness) of his office even in his chains, and explaining to them the cause of Tychicus being sent, he concludes the epistle with a vow.

There are three parts: The first pertains to the duty of children and parents, of masters and servants, up to verse 9. The second deals with the spiritual panoply up to verse 20. The third explains the causes of Tychicus being sent, and contains the final vow.

PART I.

On the duties of children and parents, of servants and masters.

Verse 1.

Τὰ τέκνα) This is said in this way, just as αἱ γυναῖκες just before. ὑπακούετε τοῖς γονεῦσιν ὑμῶν ἐν Κυρίῳ) See above V. 24. Jerome rightly says on this passage: It is the sin of children not to obey their parents: And because parents could command something perverse, he added, in the Lord. See what has been said by us on this matter and on the commands of masters in II. de jure belli ac pacis XXVI. 3.

Τῦτο γάρ ἐστι δίκαιον) כָּשֵׁר. For what is more equitable than that you should comply with those through whom you were introduced into the nature of things, to whom you can never render equal thanks. Antiphanes rightly says: Τῷ γὰρ πατρὶς κρατεῖν μὲν αἰσχύνην φέρει Ἡττωμένῳ, δὲ δόξα νικητήριον. And the Latin: Love your parent, if he is fair; if not, endure him.

From spouses it descends to the household, in which there are both children and servants. He instructs the children first, who are the proper parts of the family, as servants are accessory. The fruits of marriage are children, by generating whom spouses become parents. Τέκνα are properly those born, sons, daughters, grandsons, granddaughters, others in the descending line. Yet by analogy, those who are held in the place of children, are fed and educated, stepchildren, adopted children, wards, also pertain to this. Thus also the name of parents is properly from generation, to whom ancestors, grandfather, grandmother, great-grandparents etc. pertain. But the things that are advised concerning the obedience to be shown to parents also concern those who have that name from adoption, education, guardianship, or care. Grotius rightly refers that ἐν Κυρίῳ to the manner of obedience. But it is less conveniently alleged at the same time as a cause by Musculus and Zanchius. For the cause is then brought forward from a divine mandate. For that is not only called just according to the law of God and nature, but it is also confirmed by an express precept of God.

Latin:

CAPUT VI.

ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

Liberos ad obsequium, & ad honorem adducto Decalogi præcepto (Exod. XX. 12.) horta- tur: Parentes vero, ne irritent liberos, & in timore Domini educent, monet. Servis etiam obsequium debitum præscribit, & Dominos, quales se præbere servis debeant, commonefacit, universos autem instruit de fortitudine & armatura spirituali adver- sus Dæmonas, & preces Ephesiorum pro of- ficii sui παῤῥησία etiam in vinculis suis ex- petens, & causam missi Tychici iisdem ex- ponens, voto concludit epistolam.

Partes tres sunt: Prima pertinet ad officium liberorum & parentum, Dominorum & servo- rum, ad v. 9. Altera de panoplia spirituali agit ad v. 20. Tertia causas missi Tychici explicat, & votum finale continet.

PARS I.

De officiis liberorum & Parentum, servorum & Dominorum.

Vers. 1.

Τὰ τέκνα) Hoc sic dictum, ut modo αἱ γυναῖκες. ὑπακούετε τοῖς γονεῦσιν ὑμῶν ἐν Κυρίῳ) Vide supra V. 24. Recte ad hunc locum Hieronymus: Peccatum filiorum est, non obedire parentibus: Et quia poterant parentes aliquid im- perare perversum, adjunxit, in Domino. Vide quæ de hac re & de Dominorum imperiis dicta a nobis II. de jure belli ac pacis XXVI. 3.

Τῦτο γάρ ἐστι δίκαιον) כָּשֵׁר. Quid enim æquius, quam ut eis obsequare, per quos in rerum naturam introductus es, quibus parem gratiam nunquam possis reddere. Recte Antiphanes: Τῷ γὰρ πατρὶς κρατεῖν μὲν αἰσχύνην φέρει Ἡττωμένῳ, δὲ δόξα νικητήριον. Et Latinus: Ames parentem, si æquus est; si non, feras.

A conjugibus ad familiam descendit, in qua & liberi sunt, & servi. Liberos primum informat, qui partes propriæ familiæ, uti servi accessoriæ. Conjugii fructus sunt liberi, quos generando conjuges fiunt parentes. Τέκνα proprie geniti sunt, filii, filiæ, nepotes, neptes, alii in linea de- scendente. Ad analogiam tamen hanc etiam per- tinent, qui liberorum loco habentur, aluntur & educantur, privigni, adoptivi, pupilli. Sic & Pa- rentum nomen proprie a generatione est, ad quos majores, avus, avia, proavi &c. pertinent. Sed quæ de obedientia Parentibus præstanda monen- tur, concernunt etiam illos, qui nomen illud ha- bent ab adoptione, educatione, tutela, vel cura. Illud ἐν Κυρίῳ recte ad modum obedientiæ refert Grotius. Minus autem convenienter simul ut causa allegatur a Musculo & Zanchio. Nam causa a mandato divino deinde adducitur. Nam id non tantum justum dicitur secundum Dei & na- turæ legem, sed diserto Dei præcepto etiam con- firmatur.

## 6:2
Verse 2.

Honor your father and your mother) Thus also the LXX in the Decalogue; we have said in our more extensive commentary on the Decalogue that under the word τιμᾷν (to honor) is also comprehended the care that they lack nothing necessary: to which those Greek maxims point: You will live sufficiently by feeding your parents in their old age. So also, Hope that by honoring your parents you will fare well. Add Proverbs XIII. v. 1.

Although the word honor, if taken strictly, implies an estimation of eminence and a right judgment concerning the duty toward parents, attested even by external signs of reverence; yet here it also comprehends love, observance, and worship, as well as aid in relieving their necessities. For to a judgment of this kind, there should follow in the will a propensity to love and honor parents; in speech, that we speak honorably with them and about them; in gestures, modesty in their presence; in deeds, obedience, service, and aid, as well as the tolerance of their infirmities, Sirach III. 9. Matthew XV. 4, 5. Leviticus XX. 9. Deuteronomy XXI. v. 18.

Which is the first commandment with a promise) It is true; for what precedes: And showing mercy to thousands of those who love me and keep my commandments, is general and pertains to the whole law, and besides, it is opposed to the preceding threats: but this is special, and wisely, speaking as if to children who do not yet conceive of heavenly and eternal things in their minds, he shows that by this deed is promised that which men, as soon as they begin to use reason in some way, love most, that is, a long and at the same time happy life. In the whole Decalogue, this is the one commanding commandment, the others being prohibitive. The Hebrews note, however, that threats are added to the prohibitive commandments, and promises to the commanding ones.

How is that the one commanding or affirmative commandment? Is not the third commandment also an affirmative one? Remember, that you may keep the Sabbath day holy.

Latin:

Vers. 2.

Τίμα τὸν πατέρα συ κὶ τὴν μητέρα) Sic & LXX. in De- calogo, diximus in fusiore nostro ad Decalogum commen- tario, sub verbo τιμᾷν comprehendi & curam, ne quid eis necessariorum desit: quo spectant illæ Græcorum senten- tiæ: Ἱκανῶς βιώσεις γηροβοσκῶν τὺς γονεῖς. Ita & Ἔλπιζε τιμῶν τὺς γονῇς πράξειν καλῶς. Adde Proverb. XIII. v. 1.

Honoris vox etsi stricte accepta eminentiæ æsti- mationem, & rectum de parentum officio judi- cium, externis etiam reverentiæ signis contesta- tum inferat; hic tamen comprehendit etiam amo- rem, observantiam, & cultum, nec non auxilium in necessitatibus ipsorum sublevandis. Ad judi- cium enim ejusmodi intellectus sequi debet in voluntate propensio ad amandos & colendos pa- rentes; in sermonibus, ut cum iis & de iis hono- rifice loquamur; in gestibus modestia in eorum conspectu, in factis obsequium, servitium, & au- xilium, nec non infirmitatum tolerantia, Sirac. III. 9. Matth. XV. 4. 5. Levit. XX. 9. Deuter. XXI. v. 18.

Ἥτις ἐσὶ πρώτη ἐντολὴ ἐν ἐπαγγελίᾳ) Verum est; nam quod præcedit: Et faciens misericordiam in millia his, qui diligunt me, & custodiunt præcepta mea, generale est, & ad totam legem pertinet, & præterea opponitur minis præcedentibus: hoc vero speciale, ac sapienter, loquens quasi pueris, qui cœlestia & æterna nondum concipiunt animo, ostendit ex hoc facto promitti id, quod homines simul aliqua ratione uti cœpere, maxime amant, id est, vi- tam longam & simul felicem. In omni decalogo id unum præceptum est jubens, cætera vetantia. Notant autem E- bræi vetantibus præceptis minas addi, promissa jubenti- bus.

Quomodo id unum præceptum jubens vel af- firmativum est? Nonne præceptum tertium etiam est affirmans? Memento, ut diem sabbathi san- ctifices.

## 6:3
Verse 3.

That it may be well with you, and you may be long-lived upon the earth) These are the very words of the LXX Interpreters. At the same time, Paul wishes it to be understood that what was promised then in that land is the same as what is now provided in other lands, and from this and elsewhere it appears that something is placed in the power of man, from which he may arrive at longevity.

But how does it happen that obedient children are sometimes not long-lived? Are temporal promises to be understood with a condition? Namely, insofar as God has judged those temporal things to be salutary for us. See Wisdom IV. v. 10. For whom the gods love, dies young, said Menander.

Latin:

Vers. 3.

Ἵνα εὖ σοι γένηται, κὶ ἔσῃ μακροχρόνιος ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς) Sunt ipsa verba LXX. Interpretum. Simul vult intelligi Paulus, quod tunc promissum est in terra illa, idem & nunc præstari in terris aliis, & hinc & aliunde apparet, aliquid in pote- state hominis situm, unde ad longævitatem perveniat.

Qui vero fit, quod obedientes etiam liberi quandoque non sint longævi? Promissiones tem- porales cum conditione intelligendæ? quantum scilicet temporalia illa nobis salutaria fore Deus censuerit. Vid. Sap. IV. v. 10. ὃν γὰρ θεοὶ φιλῶσιν, ἀποθνήσκει νέος, dixit Menander.

## 6:4
Verse 4.

And you fathers, do not provoke your children) Beware, lest you treat them badly without cause: For thus you would not even make a horse docile.

But bring them up in the discipline and instruction of the Lord) Παιδεία (discipline) is indeed often extended more broadly, but here it seems to signify instruction through punishments, which are to be applied to children as soon as they can grasp some knowledge of the permitted and the forbidden. Thus the writer to the Hebrews XII. 7 and Sirach VII. 4, ch. XXXII. 12 use παιδεύειν (to discipline). The Latins sometimes say to chastise, sometimes to correct. Νυθεσία (instruction), however, is that instruction which is done by words, formerly indeed of the law, Deut. VI. 7, Prov. XXII. 5, but now of the Gospel: whence is added here κυρίε (of the Lord), that is, of Christ.

There are two frequent vices of parents: excessive severity and excessive indulgence. The Apostle meets both, and recalls from the former, and calls to actions opposite to the latter. Excessive severity inflicts a servile fear upon children, not a filial one: Conf. Col. III, v. 21. He did not say 'love', says Theophylact, for nature demands that even from the unwilling; but 'do not provoke to anger', that is, do not disinherit them, or banish them anywhere, or otherwise coerce and harass them more grievously in the manner of servants, not children. That there be not too much indulgence toward children, he requires in education both discipline, lest they be corrupted by indulgence, and instruction, so that they may be informed about necessary and useful things. Which institution ought to be done no less from the Law than from the Gospel, just as in the Old Testament also, not only the Law had to be proposed to children, but also the Evangelical promises, Isa. VIII. v. 18. And from childhood Timothy had known the holy scripture, which instructed him unto salvation through faith in Christ, 2 Tim. III. verse 15. Theophylact joins and explains these things to the preceding as follows: If you wish, he says, that your children obey you, add them to divine things, and accustom them to the scriptures. And do not say that it is for monks to apply the mind to sacred letters, for it is indeed the duty of any Christian man, and especially of him who is occupied in the affairs of this age: and all the more so, who needs greater help, as one who is tossed by the waves of the world. Do therefore most especially for your own interest, that your children both hear and read the sacred scriptures. For from these they will learn that: Honor your father and mother. But you, on the contrary, nourish your children in the disciplines of the Gentiles, from which they will learn all the worst things, which certainly does not happen when they are imbued with divine things.

Latin:

Vers. 4.

Καὶ οἱ πατέρες μὴ παροργίζετε τὰ τέκνα ὑμῶν) Cavete, ne sine causa eos male tractetis: Nam sic ne equum quidem reddas docilem.

Ἀλλ’ ἐκτρέφετε αὐτὰ ἐν παιδείᾳ κὶ νυθεσίᾳ Κυρίου) Παιδεία sæpe quidem latius extenditur, sed hic significare videtur institutionem per pœnas, quæ adhibendæ sunt filiis, simul- atque aliquam liciti & illiciti cognitionem haurire possunt. Sic παιδεύειν usurpat scriptor ad Ebræos XII. 7. & Siracides VII. 4. c. XXXII. 12. Latini modo castigare dicunt, modo emendare. Νυθεσία autem est ea institutio, quæ fit verbis, olim quidem legis, Deut. VI. 7. Prov. XXII. 5. nunc vero Evangelii: unde additur hic κυρίε, id est, Christi,

Duo sunt Parentum vitia frequentia, nimia se- veritas, & nimia indulgentia. Utrique occurrit Apostolus, & ab illa revocat, ad actiones huic op- positas vocat. Severitas nimia timorem liberis injicit servilem, non filialem: Conf. Col. III, v. 21. Non dixit amate, inquit Theophylactus, id namque vel ab ipsis invitis deposcit natura; sed nolite ad ira- cundiam concitare, hoc est, nolite hos aut exhæred a- re, vel quopiam relegare, vel alias gravius in servo- rum morem non liberorum & coercere & moleste incessere. Ne indulgeatur nimium liberis, requirit in educatione tum disciplinam, ne indulgentia corrumpantur, tum eruditionem, ut de necessa- riis & utilibus informentur. Quæ institutio non minus e lege fieri debet, quam ex Evangelio, quemadmodum in Veteri etiam Testamento non solum lex proponenda fuerat liberis, sed promissiones etiam Evangelicæ, Esi. VIII. v. 18. & a puero noverat Timotheus scripturam sacram, quæ instruebat ipsum ad salutem per fidem in Christum, 2. Timoth. III. vers. 15. Theophylactus hæc ita superioribus jungit & explicat: Si vis, inquit, tibi ut liberi obsequantur, divinis hos ad- de, & assuesce sermonibus. Nec dixeris monacho- rum esse sacris literis intendere animum, quin po- tius Christiani cujusvis hominis id sane officium est, & ejus præcipue, qui in rebus hujus seculi versatur: & eo magis, qui majore indiget ope, ut qui mundi fluctibus agitetur. Facie igitur in rem tuam vel maxime, ut sacra scripta tui & audiant & lectitent liberi. Ex his namque illud per- discent: Honora patrem & matrem tuam. At ipse contra in gentilium disciplinis liberos tuos enutris, ex quibus pessima quæque perdiscent, quod utique non evenit cum imbuuntur divinis.

## 6:5
Vers. 5.

Oi δῦλοι) He does not abolish the custom then received of using servants. For it has its advantages, and it is permitted to use it rightly.

He understands slaves, whose servitude was perpetual, unless they were manumitted by their masters, and that by the law of nations either from captivity or from birth. However, these things no less bind modern servants, who are for the most part mercenaries.

Ὑπακύετε τοῖς κυρίοις κατὰ σάρκα) that is, to those who according to human laws have authority over you. So also Col. III. 22. Servitude does not descend into the whole man, says Seneca, the mind is excepted. God commands the mind of masters as well as of servants, and now under God Christ, below VI. 9. Col. III, 24. IV. 1.

Cocceius notes here a sore in the phrase UNDER GOD Christ. Which must be understood according to human nature. For as regards the divine, to the Apostle Christ is that one Lord, through whom all things 1 Cor. VIII. v. 6. God blessed forever, Rom. IX. v. 6. Chrysostom and Theophylact say that 'carnal masters' is said for consolation, because they are temporary, and will possess this lordship for a short time. Therefore he calls them masters according to the flesh, who are masters of bodies and earthly things, just as those who begat us are called Fathers of the flesh, Heb. XII. v. 9. and have the power of commanding in external things, and that temporal. But he absurdly wishes carnal masters to be opposed to spiritual Prelates or other Ecclesiastics. For Paul does not so call himself with his colleagues, but they profess themselves ministers of the Church, 1 Cor. III. v. 5. 2 Cor. III. v. 5. Furthermore, he requires two things from servants: 1. τὸ ὑπακέειν, which he had also prescribed for children. Since children are therefore bound to that, why should servants be burdened? 2. δελεύειν, which he defines, as to how both ought to be done, not perfunctorily.

With fear and trembling) With obedience and fear of displeasing them: the same words are also used regarding our duties toward God, Phil. II. 12.

However, the fear to be understood regarding our service toward God is not servile, but filial, joined with confidence in the affection of God externally. Fear denotes reverence, trembling denotes dread and solicitude, lest any sin be committed in service. Theophylact says, he reminded the wife to revere her husband simply, but now he has increased this fear in servants, when he said trembling. For trembling exceeds fear in the magnitude of the dread.

In the simplicity of your heart as to Christ) with unfeigned faith, how we serve Christ, see 2 Corinthians I. 12. and above chapter V. v. 22. in the place 2 Chronicles XXIX. v. 17. ישר לבבי is translated in the simplicity of the heart, the Wise Man also uses this expression I. 1.

All hypocrisy, deceit, and fraud are removed. Therefore, simplicity is commended, not of speech, not of gestures, but of the heart, such as we exhibit to Christ who searches the hearts in the service owed to Him.

Vers. 6.

Not by way of eye-service as men-pleasers) like Gehazi, who was one person in his master's sight, and another outside his sight, 2 Kings V. or like the courtiers of Saul, who flattered him in wicked matters. Paul sometimes has elegantly composed words, such as these two, eye-service and men-pleasers. 'In the eyes' is frequent in Cicero for 'in the sight'. The word men-pleasers is also in Colossians III. verse 22, taken from the Greek of Psalm LIII. verse 6. It signifies those who do not think of what their duty is, but how they may capture thanks by fair means or foul. 'Pleasing is an approach not for the best, productive of pleasure.' Such servants you may see in comedies among the lesser heroes. Such were the courtiers of Saul.

But as servants of Christ) Christ commanded that Caesar be obeyed. The principle is the same in the Republic and in the family, nor does it matter at all for our salvation in what part of human affairs we are placed, it is permitted to play any role well, as servants of God, says Peter 1. II. 16.

Doing the will of God from the soul) בכל לבב, Psalm CXI. v. 1. that is, not only because of wrath but also because of conscience, as the Apostle speaks in a similar matter in Romans XIII. v. 5. in some copies that 'from the soul' is referred to the following sense.

We add the explanation of Theophylact: Since it is permitted to serve with simplicity of heart and without deceit, yet not with all one's strength, but only to execute that work which has been prescribed. Therefore he now adds 'from the soul', that is, with all effort and promptness. Furthermore, 'with good will', that is, willingly and not by compulsion. Thus all ignobility of servitude will be removed if those who serve do good things willingly. Chrysostom says, make your service not one of necessity, but of servitude. Regarding that which God wills, Jerome says: Since the Lord of the flesh does not command things different from the Lord of the Spirit.

Latin:

Vers. 5.

Oi δῦλοι) Non tollit morem tunc receptum servis utendi. Habet enim sua commoda, & licet eo recte uti.

Mancipia intelligit, quorum servitus erat per- petua, nisi manumitterentur a dominis, idque jure gentium vel ex captivitate vel ex nativitate. Non minus autem modernos hæc obstringunt servos, qui plerique mercenarii.

Ὑπακύετε τοῖς κυρίοις κατὰ σάρκα) id est, eis, qui secun- dum leges humanas jus in vos habent. Sic & Col. III. 22. Servitus non in totum hominem descendit, ait Seneca, ex- cipitur animus. Animo tam herorum quam & servorum Deus imperat, & nunc sub Deo Christus, infra VI. 9. Col. III, 24. IV. 1.

Notat hic ulcus in voce SUB DEO Chri- stus Coccejus. Quod secundum humanam natu- ram intelligendum. Nam quoad divinam Apo- stolo Christus est Dominus ille unus, per quem omnia 1. Corinth. VIII. v. 6. Deus benedictus in secula, Roman. IX. v. 6. carnales dominos Chry- sostomus & Theophylactus ad consolationem dici ajunt, quod temporarii, & brevi tempore hoc dominatu potituri. Dominos itaque secundum carnem vocat, qui sunt corporum & rerum ter- renarum domini, sicut qui nos genuerunt, di- cuntur Patres carnis, Ebr. XII. v. 9. & habent po- testatem imperandi in rebus externis, eamque temporalem. Inepte autem carnales dominos spiritualibus Prælatis seu aliis Ecclesiasticis op- poni vult. Non enim ita vocat se Paulus eum collegis, sed ministros Ecclesiæ se profitentur, 1. Corinth. III. v. 5. 2. Corinth. III. v. 5. Cæterum duo a servis requirit 1. τὸ ὑπακέειν, quod etiam liberis præscripserat. Id ergo quum liberi tene- antur, quid graventur servi? 2. δελεύειν, quod utrumque, quomodo fieri debeat, non perfun- ctorie definit.

Μετὰ φόβυ κῂ τρόμυ ) Cum obedientia & metu ipsis displicendi: etiam de nostris adversus Deum officiis eadem vocabula usurpantur Phil. II. 12.

De nostro tamen erga Deum servitio intel- ligendus timor non servilis, sed filialis cum fidu- cia de affectu Dei externo conjunctus. Timor reverentiam notat, tremor pavorem & solicitu- dinem, ne qua in servitio peccetur. Uxorem, in- quit Theophylactus, simpliciter ut virum vereatur, commonefecit, nunc vero in servis timorem hunc auxit, cum dixit tremorem. Tremor namque timo- rem excedit formidinis magnitudine.

Ἐν ἁπλότητι τῆς καρδίας ὑμῶν ὡς τῷ χρισῷ) fide non ficta, quomodo Christo servimus, vide 2. Corinth. I. 12. & supra cap. V. v. 22. loco 2. Paral. XXIX. v. 17. ישר לבבי vertitur ἐν ἁπλότητι τῆς καρδίας, utitur hac locutione & Sa- piens I. 1.

Removetur omnis hypocrisis, dolus, & fraus. Simplicitas itaque commendatur non sermonis, non gestuum, sed cordis, qualem Christo cor- da scrutanti exhibemus in servitute ipsi de- bita.

'Vers. 6.

Μὴ κατ' ὀφθαλμοδωλείαν ὡς ἀνθρωπάρεσκοι) ut Giezi, qui alius erat in heri conspectu, alius extra conspectum, 2. Regum V. aut ut aulici Saulis, qui in rebus improbis ipsi adulabantur. Habet interdum voces eleganter composi- tas Paulus, quales sunt hæ duæ ὀφθαλμοδωλεία & ἀνθρω- πάρεσκοι. In oculis frequens, Ciceroni, pro in conspectu. Vox ἀνθρωπαρέσκων est & Coloff. III. vers. 22. desumpta ex Græco Psalm. LIII. vers. 6. Significat eos, qui non cogi- tant, quod sui sit officii, sed quomodo per fas aut nefas gratias captent. Ἀρέσκεια ἕντευξις ἐκ ἐπὶ τῷ βελτίσῳ ἡδο- νῆς παρασκευαστική. Tales videas servos comicos apud he- ros minores. Tales erant aulici Saulis.

'Ἀλλ' ὡς δῦλοι τῦ χρισῦ) Jussit Christus Cæsari pareri. Eadem autem est ratio in Republica, & in familia, nec ad salutem nostram quicquam refert, qua parte in humana re locati simus, licet quamvis personam bene agere, ὡς δῦλοι Θεῦ, ait Petrus 1. II. 16.

Ποιῦντες τὸ θέλημα τῦ Θεῦ ἐκ ψυχῆς) בכל לבב , Psal. CXI. v. 1. id est, ὐ μόνον διὰ τὴν ὀργὴν ἀλλὰ κῂ διὰ τὴν συνείδησιν, ut in re simili loquitur Apostolus Roman. XIII. v. 5. in quibusdam exemplaribus illud ἐκ ψυχῆς refertur ad sensum sequentem.

Addimus Theophylacti ἐξήγησιν: Cum liceat cordis simplicitate & sine dolo, non tamen totis viri- bus inservire, sed solum id operis exequi, quod sit præstitutum. Propterea nunc ex animo addit, hoc est, omni nisu & promptitudine. Quin & bona cum voluntate, hoc est, ultro, & non invite. Sic servitutis tolletur ignobilitas omnis, si volentes bo- na, qui serviunt, fustitent. Chrysostomus, fac, inquit, servitutem tuam non necessitatis esse, sed servitutis. Ad illud, quæ vult Deus, Hieronymus: Cum Dominus carnis a Domino Spiritus diversa non imperat.

## 6:7
Vers. 7.

With good will serving as to the Lord, and not to men) that is, looking primarily not to those men under whom you are placed, but to Christ, who demands this and who renders the reward: But he added 'with good will' well: for there can be a certain friendship between master and servant, although in unequal fortune. Servants are humble friends, says Seneca. See what we said in III. of the Law of War and Peace XIV. 2. and so Euripides also said 'servants well-disposed to the house', and

Of servants as many as love their masters, such were those who spoke in banquets but were silent in torments, as Seneca says in epistle XLVII. 'stubborn, even against torments, is the loyalty of servants,' says Tacitus in his Histories I. see examples in Valerius VI. 8.

Others say rather that a benevolent affection is commended, so that servants may perform their duty promptly, and that out of zeal for their master, by which they may not only burn inwardly, but also demonstrate it outwardly, nay, out of zeal for the Lord, whom they serve, since He has willed them to serve. For God, as Theophylact says, accepts the gratitude of servants toward their masters, as one who has rightly arranged and provided for all things. Whence it happens that he who has served these less than is fitting, has resisted the divine law.

Latin:

Vers. 7.

Μετ' ἐυνοίας δυλεύοντες ὡς τῷ κυρίῳ, κῂ ἐκ ἀνθρώποις) id est, respicientes præcipue non illos homines, sub quibus positi estis, sed Christum, qui id exigit, & qui præmium reddit: Bene autem addidit μετ' ἐυνοίας: esse enim potest inter dominum & servum, quanquam in dispare fortuna, amicitia quædam. Servi, humiles amici, Senecæ. Vide quæ diximus III. de jure belli ac pacis XIV. 2. itaque & δῦ- λοι ἐυμενῆ δόμοις dixit Euripides, &

Δύλων ὅσοι φιλῦσι δεσποτῶν γέν tales illi, qui in conviviis loquebantur, sed in tormentis tacebant, ut ait Seneca epist. XLVII. contumax, etiam adversus tormenta, servorum fides, ait Tacitus historia- rum I. exempla vide apud Valerium VI. 8.

Alii potius affectum benevolum commendari, ajunt, ut prompte servi faciant officium, idque heri studio, quo non tantum flagrent interius, sed etiam id foris demonstrent, imo studio Do- mini, cui serviunt, quum eos servire voluerit. Deus namque dicente Theophylacto, acceptam habet servorum in Dominos gratitudinem, ut qui recte omnia disposuerit, caveritque. Quo fit, ut qui minus, quam decet, his inservierit, divina legi obstiterit.

## 6:8
Vers. 8.

Εἰδότες, ὅτι ὃ ἐάν τι ἕκαστος ποιήσῃ ἀγαθὸν, τοῦτο κομιεῖται παρὰ τοῦ κυρίου) He refers this, that is, the reward of this, by a metonymy, which is frequent enough. A similar expression is in 2 Cor. V. 10. Εἴτε δοῦλος, εἴτε ἐλεύθερος) For Christ neither regards these distinctions now, nor will He regard them in judgment, 1 Cor. VII. 22. XII. 13. Gal. III. 28. Coloss. III. 11. Even if you have received nothing of reward from carnal masters for your benefits toward them, wait for Him to render this, who presides over all. Thus the paraphrase of Theophylact has it.

Latin:

Vers. 8.

Εἰδότες, ὅτι ὃ ἐάν τι ἕκαστος ποιήσῃ ἀγαθὸν, τοῦτο κομιεῖται παρὰ τοῦ κυρίου) Hoc refert, id est hujus præmium, κατὰ μετωνυμίαν, satis frequentem. Similis locutio 2. Cor. V. 10. Εἴτε δοῦλος, εἴτε ἐλεύθερος) Neque enim Christus hæc discrimina aut nunc respicit, aut in judicio respiciet, 1. Cor. VII. 22. XII. 13. Gal. III. 28. Coloss. III. 11. Etsi a carnalibus Dominis pro tuis in eos beneficiis præmii nihil acceperis, opperire, ut ille hoc reddat, qui præsidet cunctis. Ita habet paraphrasis Theophylacti.

## 6:9
Vers. 9.

Καὶ οἱ κύριοι τὰ αὐτὰ ποιεῖτε πρὸς αὐτοὺς) that is, in turn show benevolence toward them. See the admonitions of Pliny and others in the stated place on the law of war and peace: Ὅταν τύχῃ τις εὐνοοῦντος οἰκέτου Οὐκ ἔστιν οὐδὲν κτῆμα κάλλιον βίῳ. Christians are brothers to all Christians: therefore they ought to show equal, nay, greater kindness to Christian servants than the Hebrews once did to Hebrews. See Deut. XV. 12. Jer. XXXIV. 14.

Therefore τὰ αὐτὰ is not to be referred to services to be rendered to God, as Chrysostom, or by which in some way masters serve their servants by taking care of them, etc., as Theophylact, but rather to simplicity, benevolence, and the observance of the Lord's will, so that as Christians are brothers to all Christians: so also Hebrews to all Hebrews. There is no disparity here either in the law or in brotherhood.

Ἀνιέντες τὴν ἀπειλήν) Do not act wrathfully, where you can maintain your right otherwise. Do not be an Antiphates of a trembling household, or a Polyphemus. See Levit. XXV. 43. I said wrathfully. For פֶּרֶךְ which signifies wrath, is translated into Greek as ἀπειλή. Clement of Rome said in the same sense: Οὐκ ἐπιτάξεις δούλῳ σου, ἢ παιδίσκῃ σου ἐν πικρίᾳ ψυχῆς.

He does not prohibit all threats simply, Prov. XXIX. 19. Sir. XXIII. 25. 26. He calls to moderation. See Coloss. IV. 1. There was once a right of life and death for a master. Hence they easily acted cruelly. He commands to remit threats as to time, manner, and execution. As to time, that they may not threaten too quickly, frequently, or perpetually. As to manner, that they may not threaten too atrociously. As to execution, that they may not cruelly and too violently punish delinquent servants, but grant a place for thanks, as Grotius with Zanchius holds in this place.

Εἰδότες, ὅτι καὶ ὑμῶν καὶ αὐτῶν ὁ κύριός ἐστιν ἐν οὐρανοῖς) He commands the same to them and to you. You are men: גם בני אדם גם בני איש Every kingdom is under a heavier kingdom. Barnabas in his epistle: Οὐ μὴ ἐπιτάξῃς παιδίσκῃ ἢ δούλῳ σου ἐν πικρίᾳ τοῖς ἐπὶ τὸν αὐτὸν ἐλπίζουσι, μήποτε οὐ φοβηθήσῃ τὸν ἐπʼ ἀμφοτέροις Θεόν. In the manuscript, καὶ αὐτῶν, καὶ ὑμῶν, it matters little. If in the old law servants were treated gently, because God had acquired them for Himself by leading them out of Egypt, Lev. XXV. v. 42, how much more now, when the same Lord has freed both masters and servants from a much harsher servitude. Lactantius: Although the condition of bodies is different, yet they are not servants to us, but we both have and call them brothers in Spirit, fellow-servants in religion.

Καὶ προσωποληψία οὐκ ἔστι παρʼ αὐτῷ) Christ does not care, as we have already said, for those stage-properties of human fable. See what was said in Acts X. 34. Rom. II. 11. Gal. II. 6. Add Coloss. III. 25. The expression is taken from Deut. X. 17. and 2 Par. XIX. 7.

Theophylact: Do not by any means, he says, think, if you have shown yourself harsher toward a servant, that God will not inquire into that because of the servant's vileness. Perhaps human laws observe these things, which distinguish nobility from servitude and ignobility. For these men established. In heaven, however, it is far otherwise. Indeed, you yourself are bound by servitude to the same Lord, and you rage against a fellow servant. For God did not institute servitude from the beginning, but the greed for possession invented it, so that those who had conquered in war might carry off captives, and frequent injuries might be inflicted upon our ancestors, and many things might happen to the Hebrews and Canaanites; although these things were permitted by God, He nevertheless instituted this very obedience here, so that the order of things might be preserved, and this life might not overflow with blood.

PART II. OF THE SIXTH CHAPTER,

Which presents

THE THIRD SECTION OF THE LATTER PART OF THIS EPISTLE.

Admonitions concerning the spiritual armor.

Latin:

Vers. 9.

Καὶ οἱ κύριοι τὰ αὐτὰ ποιεῖτε πρὸς αὐτοὺς) id est, vicissim in eos benevolentiam ostendite. Vide Plinii & aliorum monita dicto loco de jure belli & pacis: Ὅταν τύχῃ τις εὐνοοῦντος οἰκέτου Οὐκ ἔστιν οὐδὲν κτῆμα κάλλιον βίῳ. Christiani omnibus Christianis fratres: itaque parem, imo majorem bonitatem ostendere debent in servos Christianos, quam olim Ebræi in Ebræos. Vid. Deut. XV. 12. Jer. XXXIV. 14.

Non ergo τὰ αὐτὰ ad servitia Deo præstanda, ut Chrysostomus, vel quibus quodammodo Domini serviunt suis servis curam eorum gerendo &c. ut Theophylactus, sed potius ad simplicitatem, benevolentiam & observationem Dominicæ voluntatis referenda, ut Christiani omnibus Christianis fratres: ita etiam Ebræi omnibus Ebræis. Nulla hic vel in lege, vel in fraternitate disparitas.

Ἀνιέντες τὴν ἀπειλήν) Nolite iracunde agere, ubi aliter jus vestrum tenere potestis. Noli esse Antiphates trepidi laris, aut Polyphemus. Vid. Levit. XXV. 43. dixi iracunde. Nam פֶּרֶךְ quod iracundiam significat, Græce vertitur ἀπειλή. Clemens Romanus eodem sensu dixit: Οὐκ ἐπιτάξεις δούλῳ σου, ἢ παιδίσκῃ σου ἐν πικρίᾳ ψυχῆς.

Non prohibet omnes minas simpliciter, Prov. XXIX. 19. Sir. XXIII. 25. 26. ad moderationem vocat. Vid. Coloss. IV. 1. Erat olim Domino jus vitæ & necis. Inde facile sæviebant. Remittere jubet minas quoad tempus, modum & executionem. Quoad tempus, ne nimis celeriter, crebro aut perpetuo minentur. Quoad modum, ne nimis atrociter minentur. Quoad executionem, ne crudeliter & nimis violenter multent servos delinquentes, sed gratiæ concedant locum, ut cum Zanchio Grotius hoc loco habet.

Εἰδότες, ὅτι καὶ ὑμῶν καὶ αὐτῶν ὁ κύριός ἐστιν ἐν οὐρανοῖς) & ipsis & vobis idem imperat. Homines estis: גם בני אדם גם בני איש Omne sub regno graviore regnum est. Barnabas in epistola: Οὐ μὴ ἐπιτάξῃς παιδίσκῃ ἢ δούλῳ σου ἐν πικρίᾳ τοῖς ἐπὶ τὸν αὐτὸν ἐλπίζουσι, μήποτε οὐ φοβηθήσῃ τὸν ἐπʼ ἀμφοτέροις Θεόν. In Manuscripto, καὶ αὐτῶν, καὶ ὑμῶν, parum refert. Si in lege veteri servi molliter tractati fuere, quia Deus eos sibi acquisiverat, educendo ex Ægypto Lev. XXV. v. 42. quanto nunc magis cum idem Dominus & dominos & servos a servitute multo duriore liberaverit. Lactantius: Tametsi corporum sit diversa conditio, nobis tamen servi non sunt, sed eos & habemus & dicimus Spiritu fratres, religione conservos.

Καὶ προσωποληψία οὐκ ἔστι παρʼ αὐτῷ) Non curat, ut jam diximus, Christus ista fabulæ humanæ choragia. Vide quæ dicta Act. X. 34. Rom. II. 11. Gal. II. 6. Adde Coloss. III. 25. Sumpta locutio ex Deut. X. 17. & 2. Par. XIX. 7.

Theophylactus: Nequaquam, inquit, existimes, si acerbiorem te in servum præstiteris servi ob vilitatem haudquaquam id secus Deum inquisiturum. Id forsitan humanæ leges observant, quæ a servitute & ignobilitate nobilitatem discernunt. Has enim homines condidere. In cœlo autem longe secus se ha- bet. Quin ipse eidem Domino es servitute obstri- ctus, & in conservum desævis. Nullam enim a prin- cipio servitutem instituit Deus, sed habendi cupi- ditas hanc adinvenit, ut captivos abducerent hi, qui bello vicissent, & frequentes injuriæ majoribus nostris inferrentur, Ebræique & Canaan multa acci- derent; tametsi hæc sint a Deo permissa, hic tamen obedientiam hanc ipsam instituit, ut rerum series ser- varetur, nec redundaret vita hæc sanguine.

PARS II. CAPITIS SEXTI,

Quæ exhibet

SECTIONEM TERTIAM PARTIS POSTERIORIS HUJUS EPISTOLÆ.

Monita de Panoplia spirituali.

## 6:10
Ver. 10.

Τὸ λοιπὸν ἀδελφοί με ) An expression of one hastening to the end. In the Manuscript τὸ λοιπῆ, as in Gal. VI. 17. Ἐνδυναμῦσθε ἐν Κυρίῳ ) And here is a passive for a reciprocal, as also 2 Tim. II. 1. and in the Greek, Ps. LII. 7. Καὶ ἐν τῷ κράτει τῆς ἰσχύος ἀυτῦ ) An explanatory genitive as above IV. 26. You have this doubling also above I. 19. The passage in Isa. LII. 1 seems to be regarded.

Since Satan does not cease to attack with various temptations those who strive to perform the duty of their calling, whether in general to Christianity or in a specific state, it remained for him to instruct the Ephesians concerning the battle against the same, which he does by exhorting them to fortitude, to the assumption of spiritual armor, and to constant prayer. Since they do not find fortitude and strength in themselves, he commands them to seek it in the Lord, whose power is perfected even in the weak, 2 Cor. XIII. 9, with true confidence placed in Him, Isa. XLVI. 25. For this is ἐνδύσασθε ἐν Κυρίῳ κὶ ἐν τῷ κράτει τῆς ἰσχύος ἀυτῦ, be strengthened in the Lord, that is, in the might of His fortitude. For in Him we are able to do all things, Phil. IV. v. 13. He is stronger than he who, coming upon the strong man armed, is able to overcome the same and take away his armor in which he trusts, Luke XI. 21, 22. Therefore, by that ἐν Κυρίῳ he hints at the weakness of our own powers, and asserts that spiritual strength is obtained from the Lord Jesus alone, who dwells in us through faith, Eph. III. 15. And lest we doubt His sufficient strength, he sets forth τὸ κράτος τῆς ἰσχύος ἀυτῦ, the might of His fortitude, that is, the most powerful strength, as if he were saying, He who is in us is stronger and more powerful than he who is in the world, 1 John IV. v. 4. Therefore Chrysostom says, in the Lord, that is, through hope in Him, through His help, as if he were saying, do not fear, cast your hope upon Him, He will make all things easy. Theodoret: Expel all fear, fortified by the protection of God's power. Theophylact: Trust in the power of the Lord. By which very thing he simultaneously exhorts to true repentance, since sin is the languor, disease, and death of the soul, Rom. V. 6. But once the remission of sins has been obtained through repentance, that weakness may yield, Isa. XXIII. 24, to the constancy of faith, by which we are rendered robust, Rom. IV. 20, 1 Tim. I. 22, Ps. XXVII. v. 1, Ps. LXXI. 16, to new obedience, and we may be strengthened according to the inner man, Eph. III. v. 16, to the tolerance of the cross, 1 Tim. II. v. 1, 3, Col. I. 11, Isa. XXX. 15, and to the vigilance of prayers, Ps. CXXXVIII. v. 3. All of which he now explains with metaphorical speech, with which reasoning we are comforted in the Lord, namely, by men putting on spiritual armor. Which he then both commends in general and explains in detail by parts.

Latin:

Vers. 10.

Τὸ λοιπὸν ἀδελφοί με ) Locutio ad finem festinantis. In Manuscripto τὸ λοιπῆ, ut Gal. VI. 17. Ἐνδυναμῦσθε ἐν Κυρίῳ ) Et hic est passivum pro Reci- proco, ut & 2. Tim. II. 1. & in Græco, Psal. LII. 7. Καὶ ἐν τῷ κράτει τῆς ἰσχύος ἀυτῦ ) Genitivus ἐξηγητικὸς ut supra IV. 26. Habes hanc geminationem & supra I. 19. respici videtur locus Esa. LII. 1.

Quum illos qui officium vocationis sive in gene- re ad Christianismum, sive in certo statu exequi nituntur, Satanas variis tentationibus aggredi non intermittat, hoc reliquum erat, ut Ephesios de pugna adversus eundem instrueret, quod facit exhortando ad fortitudinem, ad armaturæ spiri- tualis assumptionem, & ad jugem precationem. Fortitudinem & robur, quum in se non inveniant, in Domino, cujus virtus etiam in infirmis perfici- tur, 2. Cor. XIII. 9. vera in ipsum collocata fiducia quærere jubet Esa. XLVI. 25. Hoc enim est ἐνδύ- σασθε ἐν Κυρίῳ κὶ ἐν τῷ κράτει τῆς ἰσχύος ἀυτῦ, corro- boramini in Domino, hoc est, in robore fortitu- dinis ejus. In illo enim omnia valemus, Phil. IV. v. 13. Is est fortior illo, qui τῷ ἰσχυρῷ καθωπλισμέ- νῳ forti armato superveniens vincere eundem po- test, & πανοπλίαν ejus auferre, in qua confidit, Luc. XI. 21. 22. Per illud ergo ἐν Κυρίῳ virium pro- priarum imbecillitatem innuit, & a solo Domino Jesu, qui in nobis per fidem habitat, Eph. III. 15. robur spirituale obtineri asserit. Ac ne de ejus- dem sufficienti robore ambigamus, τὸ κράτος τῆς ἰσχύος ἀυτῦ, robur fortitudinis, id est, robur for- tissimum sistit, quasi dicat, fortior & potentior est, qui in nobis, quam qui in mundo est, 1. Joh. IV. v. 4. Ideo Chrysostomus, in Domino, inquit, est per spem in ipsum, per auxilium ejus, quasi dicat, ne metuatis, spem in illum projicite, ille omnia reddet facilia. Theodoretius: Omnem ti- morem expellite, Dei potentiæ præsidio muniti. Theophylactus: In potentia Domini confidite. Quo ipso simul hortatur ad veram pœnitentiam, siqui- dem peccatum animæ languor, morbus & mors sit, Rom. V. 6. Obtenta autem per pœnitentiam re- missione peccatorum debilitas illa cedat Esa. XXIII. 24. ad fidei constantiam, qua robusti red- dimur, Rom. IV. 20. 1. Tim. I. 22. Psal. XXVII. v. 1. Psal. LXXI. 16. ad novam obedientiam, & corro- boremur secundum interiorem hominem, Ephes. III. v. 16. ad crucis tolerantiam, 1. Tim. II. v. 1. 3. Coloss. I. 11. Esa. XXX. 15. & ad precum vigilantiam, Psal. CXXXVIII. v. 3. Quæ omnia Metaphorica oratione jam explicat, cum qua ratione in Domi- no confortemur homines induendo nempe arma- ma- turam spiritualem. Quam tum generatim com- mendat, tum in specie per partes explicat.

## 6:11
Ver. 11.

Put on the whole armor of God) He begins now to draw figures from military matters. A parallel passage to this is 2 Cor. 10:4, and another 1 Thess. 5:8. Similar is that in Isa. 61:10, 'He has clothed me with the garment of salvation and the robe of gladness.' You have the word πανοπλίας in the Greek of Job 31:20 and 2 Sam. 2:21, where in the Hebrew it is מַעֲטָה, and in the Glossary πανοπλία is armor. Ambrose called it the totality of arms; a pair of armor is also attributed to God in Wisd. 5:18, 19, etc.

That you may be able to stand against the crafty ways of acting of the Devil תַהְכָּרִים See above 4:14. ὁ διάβολος, as elsewhere, ὁ Σατανᾶς signifies the whole totality of evil demons. Compare the passage in Rev. 12:7.

Latin:

Vers. 11.

Ἐνδύσασθε τὴν πανοπλίαν τῦ Θεῦ) Incipit jam a re militari figuras ducere. Locus huic geminus 2. Cor. X. 4. & alter 1. Thess. V. 8. Simile illud Esa. LXI. v. 10. ἐνέδυσέ με ἱμάτιον σωτηρία κὶ χιτῶνα ἐυφροσύνης. Habes πανοπλίας vocem in Graeco Job. XXXI. 20 & 2. Sam. II. v. 21. ubi in Ebraeo מַעֲטָה, in Glossario πανοπλία armatura. Uni- versitatem armorum dixit Ambrosius, par armatura etiam Deo tribuitur Sap. V. 18. 19. seqq.

Πρὸς τὸ δύνασθαι ὑμᾶς στῆναι πρὸς τὰς μεθοδείας τῦ διαβόλυ) adversus Diaboli vias agendi astutas תַהְכָּרִים Vide supra IV. 14. ὁ διάβολος, ut alibi, ὁ Σατανᾶς totam universitatem malorum Daemonum significat. Conf. lo- cum Apoc. XII. 7.

## 6:12
Vers. 12.

For our wrestling is not against blood and flesh) That is, 'only,' which little word is often understood. בָּשָׂר וָדָם are called men, where they are compared to God or the Angels.

But against principalities, against powers) The same names of ranks are used of demons as of angels. For the empire of Satan also consists in order, Matt. 12:26. You have ἀρχάς and ἐξουσίας concerning holy angels also above 1:21, 3:10. Col. 1:6 concerning evil angels, 1 Cor. 15:24, Col. 2:15, ἀρχάς and δυνάμεις concerning the same evil angels Rom. 8:38.

Against the world-rulers of this darkness) In the Manuscript 'of this darkness,' just as both the Latin and the Syrian read. He speaks of those who have power in this dark world, that is, a great part of the human race, who are 'sons of disobedience' above, Eph. 2:2. In a similar way the Prince of that totality, ὁ ἄρχων τῦ κόσμυ, John 12; ὁ Θεὸς τῦ αἰῶνος τύτυ, 2 Cor. 4:4. κοσμοκράτορας τῦ σκότυς is the same as if he had said, 'the rulers of the world of darkness.'
