He opposes 'the world of darkness' to the children of light, of whom above 5:8, where they are likewise said to have previously been 'darkness'; we had 'works of darkness' above 5:11.

Against the spiritual things of wickedness in the heavenly places.) It appears the Syrian read 'against the spirits of wickedness in the heavenly places.' Rightly. Πνέυματα πονηρίας in the Hebrew manner, which are 'evil spirits,' Matt. 12:45. The 'heavenly' places are the aerial places above 2:2, where we reported the opinion of the Hebrews, that everything from the earth to the heaven, namely the starry one, is full of such spirits: 'Clad in air,' Hesiod concerning demons.

Therefore take up the whole armor of God) He repeats what he had said, in order to describe for us an armor far different from that which either Homer does in the affairs of Achilles, or Virgil in the affairs of Aeneas.

Latin:

Vers. 12.

Ὅτι ἐκ ἔστιν ἡμῖν ἡ πάλη πρὸς αἷμα κὶ σάρκα) Tan- tum scilicet, quae vocula saepe subauditur. בָּשָׂר וָדָם dicuntur homines, ubi comparantur Deo aut Angelis.

Ἀλλὰ πρὸς τὰς ἀρχὰς πρὸς τὰς ἐξουσίας) Eadem gra- duum nomina usurpantur de Daemonibus, quae de Angelis. Nam & Satanae imperium ordine constat, Matth. XII. 26. Ἀρχας & ἐξουσίας de sanctis Angelis habes & supra I. v. 21. III. 10. Coloss. I. 6. de malis Angelis, 1. Corinth. XV. 24. Coloss. II. v. 15. ἀρχάς & δυνάμεις de iisdem malis Angelis Rom. VIII. 38.

Πρὸς τὺς κοσμοκράτορας τῦ σκότυς τῦ αἰῶνος τύτυ) In Manuscripto τῦ σκότυς τύτυ, quomodo legerunt & La- tinus & Syrus. Illos dicit, qui imperium habent in mun- dum hunc tenebricosum, id est, magnam partem humani generis, qui ὑιὸι ἀπειθείας supra, Ephes. II. v. 2. Simili modo Princeps ejus universitatis, ὁ ἄρχων τῦ κόσμυ, Johan. XII. ὁ Θεὸς τῦ αἰῶνος τύτυ, 2. Corinth. IV. v. 4. κοσμοκράτορας τῦ σκότυς, idem est, quasi dixisset, τὺς κρατῦντας τῦ κόσμυ τῦ σκότυς. Opponit τὸν κόσμον τῦ σκότυς filiis lucis, de qui- bus supra V. 8. ubi itidem dicuntur illi antea fuisse σκότος; ἔργα σκότυς habuimus supra V. 11.

Πρὸς τὰ πνευματικὰ τῆς πονηρίας ἐν τοῖς ἐπουρανίοις.) Apparet Syrum legisse πρὸς τὰ πνέυματα τῇ πονηρίας ἐν τοῖς ἐπουρανίοις. Recte. Πνέυματα πονηρίας Ebræo more, quae πνέυματα πονηρὰ, Matth. XII. v. 45. loca ἐπουράνια sunt loca aeria supra II. v. 2. ubi retulimus Ebræorum sententiam, omnia a terra ad coelum nempe astriferum plena esse ta- lium Spirituum: Ἡέρα ἑσσάμενοι Hesiodus de Daemoni- bus.

Διὰ τῦτο ἀναλάβετε τὴν πανοπλίαν τῦ Θεῦ) repetit quod dixerat, ut armaturam nobis describat longe aliam, quam aut Homerus in rebus Achillis, aut in rebus Aeneae Virgilius.

## 6:13
That you may be able to withstand in the evil day) That is, even then when men, stirred up by the art of demons, will threaten you with the greatest evils, above 5:16.

And having done all, to stand) It is the duty of a soldier not to be weary, but to stand in battle.

He warns generally concerning the armor: I. What is to be assumed? By the word πανοπλίας, embracing the entire armor, or the totality of arms, whatever pertains to arming the Christian soldier, the perfect armor; such as all the faithful ought to be, 1 Cor. 9:26, 2 Tim. 2:3, Heb. 12:1. Moreover, he requires not human armor, by which nothing is gained in this fight, but the armor of God, not carnal, but spiritual, 2 Cor. 10:4, weapons 'mighty through God.'

II. How are they to be taken up? By putting on, Romans 13:12, by which, as bodily weapons are fitted to the body, so spiritual weapons are to be applied to the soul.

III. Against whom? The enemy is expressed by the word διαβόλε, and who, what kind, and how great he is, is designated here: 1. The abundance of our enemies, which is indeed also insinuated by the word Διαβόλε, inasmuch as it is often used to denote the whole sink of devils, John 8:46, Revelation 12:12. But afterwards it is signified more expressly when they are named indefinitely and in the plural number: Principalities, Powers, rulers of the world, spiritual wickedness. 2. By τὰ πνευματικὰ τῆς πονηρίας, Heinsius wishes to indicate not a personal object, but a real one, πνευματικὰς πονηρίας, that is, perverse doctrines, sects, schisms, etc. but the Apostolic manner of speaking sufficiently teaches that τὰ πονηρὰ πνέυματα [the wicked spirits] are to be understood, as the Syrian, not indeed having another reading in itself, but explaining the sense, has interpreted: And Theophylact says of τὰ πνευματικὰ τῆς πονηρίας [the spiritual things of wickedness], that he himself calls them demons. For since the Angels are spirits, he added of wickedness, against the spiritual things of wickedness: Thus he calls the Demons themselves. For because they are also Angels, he added of wickedness. And also the Scholiast [says] πρὸς τὰ πνευματικὰ [against the spiritual things], that is, demons. For the Apostle repeats the preposition πρὸς [against] for the same reason, against the principalities, against the powers, against the world-rulers, against the spiritual things of wickedness. And the Heinsian interpretation is new, by which they refer all those things from the opposite to a personal object, or to an enemy, and wish τὰ πονηρὰ πνέυματα [the wicked spirits] to be understood. Camerarius has it thus: Ἐναλλαγὴ [a change], already often indicated, is Hebraizing, that is, πρὸς πνευματικὰ πονηρεύματα [against spiritual wickednesses], which will be πνέυματα πονηρά [wicked spirits]. But why shall we not say that the abstract is placed thus for the concrete, so that it may indicate those who are full of spiritual wickednesses in the highest degree, or the chief authors of them and most wicked parties: and through this gradation may finally ascend to that highest degree: Such as are those among the demons, who exercise their wickednesses ἐν τοῖς ἐπυρανίοις [in the heavenly places]. For not just any wickedness, but that which is ἐν τοῖς ἐπυρανίοις, exercising its wickednesses in the heavenly places, is designated. Which word does not denote a place here, much less an airy place, as Grotius opines, who has not yet been proven, but an object, in which they are occupied, exercising their τὰς πονηρίας [wickednesses], namely divine and supercelestial things: in which sense the Greek Interpreters have referred this word καθ' ὑσέρεθατον [by hysteron proteron] to the things above, our wrestling is in the heavenly places, not against flesh: But there is no need for that transposition, if with Camerarius and others it is established that there is an ἐναλλαγὴ τῆς προθέσεως [change of preposition], ἐν τοῖς ἐπυρανίοις for διὰ τὰ ἐπυράνια [on account of the heavenly] things, namely, we are struggling about heavenly things. The Greek Scholiast [says] not about some small things, but about those things which are in the heavenly places, the struggle is. Chrysostom: For the [expression] in the heavenly places is instead of the heavenly things, not that they might happen to win, but that they might deprive us. It means, namely, that those impure Spirits are perpetually struggling with us about divine and heavenly things, not that they themselves might obtain something, but that they might deprive us. Coccejus says of these things thus: We also, he says, while we are on earth, have certain heavenly things, which have descended to us from heaven, peace, liberty, justice, joy, hope, communion with the spirits of the just made perfect. We have an open heaven, into which Christ the forerunner has entered, Heb. VI. 20. We have the Holy Spirit, who has been poured out by Christ upon all flesh. We have the most clear and most absolute word: the treasure of all wisdom and prudence. Satan mixes himself into these through his πονηρίας [wickednesses], that is, wickednesses, sophisms, fallacious reasonings, rash sayings, fraud, imposture. And he does it spiritually, subtly, ingeniously, and in such a way as befits a most crafty Spirit and a master of ten thousand arts. 2. Craftiness, which is designated by τὰς μεθοδείας [the wiles]. Heinsius wishes a crafty circumvention to be indicated. That it is a methodia, he says, and why the Devil is said to methoduein [to use wiles], the learned have striven in vain to know from profane authors: He methodueis who wanders, who goes around, but intent. As one who craftily lies in wait for prey by circling: How this may suit the malignant Spirit is to be sought from Job: With whom in the first chapter: And on a certain day, when the sons of God had come to stand before the Lord, Satan was also present among them. To whom he said

the Lord: Whence do you come? who answering says: I have circled the earth and walked through it. The Hellenist: Having circled the earth, and walked through that which is under heaven, I am present, where having circled is having used wiles, which you may also rightly call having walked through. The Chaldeans have used the word משמש or to search. Hesychius: He uses wiles, he goes among, or he goes through. Other glossators: He uses wiles, he uses artifice, he goes among, he deceives. Nor did D. Peter understand anything other than to use wiles, when he said, That your adversary the devil as a roaring lion walks about, seeking whom he may devour. For to walk about with snares is to use wiles. Which the Hellenists use, when they interpret the word רגל, which you may call to lie in wait by circling, just as מרגל is a spy, a lier in wait. Which they are also accustomed to use instead of to slander, which is proper to the Devil, and also to accuse, which they also call to use wiles. As in that: and he used wiles in deceit against the Lord. He therefore uses wiles, who goes around, so that he may circumvent, just as the Latins also use the word to circumvent regarding snares and harm. Aretius explains it as insults from snares, which interpretation can be joined with the former. A wile is an assault, a snare, an insult from snares, such as crafty enemies are accustomed to devise. The word is formed from the expression methodos, by which he signifies a compendium of teaching arts rightly and briefly. And because methodists are ingenious, therefore a wile has been transferred to crafty traps and arts of deceiving, in which matter the Devil is easily the Prince, he is the best Methodist for deceiving, he deceives and overthrows by a compendium, which others would scarcely accomplish with many circumlocutions. For hence to use wiles signifies not only to treat arts by a compendium, but to deceive and to act with all craft, as if he were to say, to deceive briefly by a compendium. 3. Power, which is expressed by negation and by affirmation. We do not have the wrestling against flesh and blood. Our struggle is not against blood and flesh. Grotius understands ONLY a particle, others wish these words to be taken comparatively. Thus Hemmingius: He does not deny that we must struggle against men and our own flesh, but he speaks comparatively, as if he were saying, if we look at the spiritual enemies we have, the conflict we have with flesh and blood will be judged to be no struggle at all. Therefore, by this formula of speaking, the magnitude of the danger, the kind of war, and the quality of the enemies are signified. But Flacius's explanation is especially pleasing: The discourse is almost as if some General, rousing his men to a most valiant fight, were to say: The contest for them will not be with camp-followers and sutlers, nor even with recruits or common soldiers: But with the strongest veterans, nay, with mere centurions and tribunes, and with the most excellent Generals, and invincible heroes and giants. There are indeed, without doubt, even among those depraved Spirits some more powerful and more cunning than the rest, as Christ himself testifies, and ruling over those and other impious ones, who all conspire against the little ones of Christ, and take up the fight most valiantly. Therefore, he describes the power of these enemies κατὰ θέσιν, when he names the principalities, the powers, the world-rulers; also with the spiritual things. For with spiritual enemies the war is most difficult, especially when they attack divine things, and those spiritual wickednesses tempt us concerning the mysteries of the faith, or those things which are to be believed. Concerning the rulers of the world, Theophylact says: He does not call them rulers of the world because they have command of this machine, but asserts that they preside over depraved deeds. For the sacred letters are accustomed to call wicked works, and those who practice them, the world, as in that saying, you are not of this world, that is, of the order of those who handle worldly things. Therefore, Demons rule over those who have voluntarily subjected themselves to Demons. Similarly, through the world Hemmingius wishes worldly men sleeping in sin, and indeed the very sins themselves, to be signified, when the Apostle defines the world of this age as darkness.

IV. For what purpose? That you may be able 1. στῆναι to stand, to take a stand, against so many, so cunning, so powerful enemies, their assaults and ambushes. In battle, one is said to stand as a victor, to fall or flee as one defeated. They ought to put on the armor and enter the fight, not so that they may flee, but so that they may stand. They can stand in the strength of the Lord. In Him, therefore, they will be confident and will stand firm, Isa. XXVIII. 16, chap. XXX. 5. 2. ἀντιστῆναι to resist, which is done by defending oneself and repelling the enemy. Therefore, weapons of a different kind, both for acting defensively and offensively, must be assumed, so that we may indeed protect ourselves, and drive away the enemy, and crush him under our feet. Moreover, it is added ἐν τῇ ἡμέρᾳ τῇ πονηρᾷ, in the evil day, which Hyperius indeed understands as any time, since the Devil never ceases to lay ambushes; but this day or time of temptation is noted here, when indeed the Devil attacks us in act, which, although he always wishes to do, is not always permitted to him by God. 3. Κατεργάζεσθαι to finish or to lay low, as Xenophon used this word in Cyropaedia IV. Κατειργάσατο τὸν λέοντα, he finished off the lion: And Thucydides IV. Πειρασόμεθα κατεργάζεσθαι αὐτούς: We shall attempt to overthrow them. It is therefore more correctly translated: That you may be able to stand after all have been killed, than in the Vulgate: To stand perfect in all things. He added τὸ στῆναι: Since most have fallen after victory, one must stand, he says, especially when we have emerged as victors, lest that defeated one attack us again. For the enemy, even if struck by death, will revive here and recover his strength if we ourselves are too slow and relapse into disgrace, as Theophylact says here.

Latin:

Ἵνα δυνηθῆτε ἀντιστῆναι ἐν τῇ ἡμέρᾳ τῇ πονηρᾷ) id est, tunc etiam cum Daemonum arte homines suscitati vobis mala maxima minabuntur supra V. 16.

Καὶ ἅπαντα κατεργασάμενοι στῆναι) Militis est non fa- tigari, sed stare in praelio.

Generatim de armatura monet I. Quaenam assumenda sit? Voce πανοπλίας universam ar- maturam complectens, vel armorum universi- tatem, quicquid ad armandum militem Christia- num pertinet, armaturam perfectam; quales omnes fideles esse debent, 1. Corinth. IX. v. 26. 2. Tim. II. 3. Ebr. XII. 1. Armaturam autem non humanam, qua nihil in hac pugna proficitur, sed armaturam Dei, non carnalem, sed spiritualem requirit, 2. Corinth. X. v. 4. arma δυνατὰ τῷ Θεῷ.

II. Quomodo assumenda? Per induitionem, Ro- man. XIII. v. 12. qua ut arma corporalia aptantur corpori; sic arma spiritualia animae applicentur.

III. Adversus quem? Hostis voce διαβόλε expri- mitur, & ut quis, qualis, quantus sit, designatur hic 1. hostium nostrorum copia, quae insinuatur quidem etiam voce Διαβόλε, utpote, qua tota quandoque Diabolorum colluvies notari solet, Joh. VIII. 46. Apoc. XII. 12. Sed postmodum ex- pressius significatur, cum nominantur indefinite & in plurali numero, Principatus, Potestates, mun- di rectores, malitiae spirituales. 2. Per τὰ πνευμα- τικὰ τῆς πονηρίας Heinsius non objectum persona- le, sed reale indigitari vult πνευματικὰς πονηρίας, id est perversas doctrinas, sectas, schismata, &c. Sed modus loquendi Apostolicus satis docet, τὰ πο- νηρὰ πνέυματα intelligi, ut Syrus, non quidem aliam lectionem per se habens, sed sensum expli- cans, interpretatus est: Et Theophylactus τὰ πνευ- ματικὰ τῆς πονηρίας, ἤτω αὐτὸς τὰς δαίμονάς Φη- σιν. Ἐπειδὴ γάρ εἰσικὰ οἱ Ἄγγελοι πνέυματα, προσ- έθηκε τῆς πονηρίας, adversus spiritualia nequitiae: Ita ipsos Daemones vocat. Quia enim & Angeli sunt Spiritus, addidit nequitiae. Nec non Scholiastes πρὸς τὰ πνευματικὰ, τυτέσι δαιμόνια. Nam Apostolus Praepositionem πρὸς eadem ratione repetit, πρὸς τὰς ἀρχὰς, πρὸς τὰς ἐξυσίας, πρὸς τὺς κοσμοκρά- τορας, προς τὰ πνευματικὰ τῆς πονηρίας. Et nova est Heinsiana interpretatio, qua ex adverso omnes ad objectum personale, vel ad hostem ea omnia referant, & τὰ πονηρὰ πνέυματα intelligi velint. Camerarius ita habet: Ἐναλλαγὴ saepe jam indicata ἑβραΐζυσα, id est, πρὸς πνευματικὰ πονηρεύματα, quae erunt πνέυματα πονηρά. Cur vero non abstra- ctum ita pro concreto dicemus positum, ut in sum- mo gradu spiritualium nequitiarum plenos, vel autores earum praecipuos & maxime πονηρᾶ κόμ- ματα, indigitet: atque per hanc gradationem a- scendat demum ad supremum istum gradum: Qua- les sunt illi inter daemones, qui ἐν τοῖς ἐπυρανίοις in supracoelestibus suas exercent nequitias. Non e- nim πονηρία quaevis, sed ea, quae ἐν τοῖς ἐπυρανίοις est, in supracoelestibus suas exercens nequitias de- signatur. Quae vox non locum hic notat, nedum aereum locum, ut Grotius opinatur, qui nondum probatus est, sed objectum, in quo occupantur, τὰς πονηρίας suas exercendo, res nempe divinas & supercaelestes: quo sensu καθ' ὑσέρεθατον hanc vo- cem Interpretes Graeci ad superiora retulerunt, ἡ πάλη ἡμῖν ἐστιν ἐν τοῖς ἐπυρανίοις ὢ πρὸς αἷμα: Sed ea transpositione non est opus, si cum Camerario aliisque statuatur ἐναλλαγὴ τῆς προθέσεως, ἐν τοῖς ἐπυρανίοις pro διὰ τὰ ἐπυράνια scil. πράγματα, nos de caelestibus rebus dimicamus. Scholiasta Graeci ὢ περὶ μικρῶν τινων, ἀλλ' ὑπὲρ τῶν ἐν τοῖς ἐπυρανίοις πραγμάτων, non de exiguis quibusdam, sed de iis, quae in caelo sunt, sive caelestibus, certamen est. Chryso- stomus: Τὸ γὰρ ἐν τοῖς ἐπυρανίοις ἀντὶ τῶν ἐπυρανί- ων ἐσὶν, ἐχ' ἵν αὐτοί τινω τύχωσι νικήσαντες, ἀλλ' ἵνα ἡμᾶς ἀποσερήσωσιν. Id nempe vult, perpetuo impuros illos Spiritus de divinis ac coelestibus cer- tare nobiscum, non ut ipsi consequantur aliquid, sed ut nos privent. Coccejus de his ita: Nos etiam, inquit, dum in terris sumus, habemus ἐπυράνια qua- dam, quae ad nos ex caelo descenderunt, pacem, liber- tatem, justitiam, laetitiam, spem, communionem cum Spiritibus justorum consummatis. Habemus coelum apertum, in quod praecursor intravit Christus, Ebr. VI. 20. Habemus Spiritum Sanctum, qui effusus est a Christo in omnem carnem. Habemus verbum cla- rissimum & absolutissimum: thesaurum omnis sa- pientia ac prudentia. Hisce miscet sese Satanas per πονηρίας suas, hoc est, nequitias, sophismata, ratio- cinationes fallaces, dicta temeraria, fraudem, im- posturam. Et id facit πνευματικῶς, subtiliter inge- niose, & ita, ut decet Spiritum versutissimum & μυριοτέχνην. 2. Versutia, quae per τὰς μεθοδείας designatur. Heinsius circumvagationem callidam indicari vult. Quod μεθοδεία sit, inquit, & quare μεθοδέυειν Diabolus dicatur, frustra ex autoribus profanis scire sategerunt eruditi: Μεθοδέυει qui vagatur, qui circumit, sed intentus. Ut qui praedae circulando callide insidiatur: Quod quo pacto Spiritui maligno conveniat, e Jobo peten- dum: Apud quem primo capite: Quodam autem die, cum venissent filii Dei, ut adsisterent coram Domino, adfuit inter eos etiam Satan. Cui dixit

Dominus: Unde venis? qui respondens ait: Circuivi terram & perambulavi eam. Hellenista: Περιελθὼν τὴν γῆν, καὶ περιπατήσας τὴν ὑπ' οὐρανὸν, πάρειμι, u- bi περιελθὼν est μεθοδεύσας, quod & περιπατήσας recte dicas. Chaldaei voce משמש sive scrutandi usi sunt. Hesychius: Μεθοδεύσῃ, μετέρχεται, ἢ διέρχεται. Glossatores alii: Μεθοδεύῃ, τεχνάζεται μετέρχεται, ἀπατᾷ. Neq; aliud quam τὸ μεθοδεύειν intellexit D. Petrus, cum dixit, Ὅτι ὁ ἀντίδικος ὑμῶν ὁ διάβολος ὡς λέων ὠρυόμενος περιπατεῖ, ζητῶν, τίνα καταπίῃ. Obambulare enim cum insidiis μεθοδεύειν est. Quo u- tuntur Hellenistae, cum τὸ רגל interpretantur, quod circulando insidiari dicas, quemadmodum מרגל κατάσκοπος speculator, insidiator. Quo & ἀντὶ τοῦ διαβάλλειν, quod proprium est Diaboli, τοῦ κατηγο- ρεῖν item uti solent, quod & μεθοδεύειν dicunt. Ut in illo: καὶ μεθώδευσεν ἐν τῷ δόλῳ συ πρὸς τὸν Κύριον. Μεθοδεύῃ ergo, qui circumit, ut circumveniat, quem- admodum & circumveniendi verbo de insidiis & no- xa Latini utuntur. Aretius de insultib. ex insidiis explicat, quae interpretatio cum priori conjungi potest. Μεθοδεία est ἐπιβουλὴ, ἐνέδρα insultus ex insi- diis, quales astuti hostes solent machinari. Vox for- mata est ex dictione μέθοδος, qua significat compen- dium recte & breviter tradendi artes. Et quia inge- niosi sunt methodici, ideo translata est μεθοδεία ad captiones astutas & artes fallendi, in qua re facile Princeps est Diabolus, optimus est Methodicus ad fal- lendum, compendio fallit & evertit, quod alii multis ambagibus vix conficerent. Hinc enim μεθοδεύειν non solum compendio tractare artes, sed ἀπατᾷν & πανεργεῖν significat, quasi dicat, συντόμως ἐξαπα- τᾷν compendio fallere. 3. Potentia, quae exprimitur κατ' ἄρσιν & κατὰ θέσιν. Οὐκ ἔστιν ἡμῖν ἡ πάλη πρὸς αἷμα καὶ σάρκα. Non est nobis pugna ad- versus sanguinem & carnem. Grotius particu- lam TANTUM subaudit, alii dicta haec com- parative volunt. Ita Hemmingius: Non negat, nobis adversus homines & propriam carnem certandum esse, sed comparative loquitur, qua- si dicat, si respicimus hostes spirituales, quos habemus, nulla plane pugna judicabitur, ea con- flictatio, quae nobis est cum carne & sanguine. Significatur igitur hac loquendi formula periculi magnitudo, belli genus, & hostium qualitas. Pla- cet autem imprimis Flacii explicatio: Sermo fere talis est, ac si Dux quispiam excitans suos ad for- tissimam pugnam diceret: Certamen illis fore non cum calonibus & lixis, non etiam cum tironibus aut gregariis militibus: Sed cum fortissimis veteranis, imo cum meris centurionibus ac tribunis, cumque praestantissimis Ducibus, invictisque heroibus & gi- gantibus. Sunt vero haud dubie etiam inter illos pra- vos Spiritus aliqui caeteris ac potentiores ac astutio- res, teste Christo ipso, & illis aliisque impiis impe- ritantes, qui omnes contra pusillos Christi conjurant, & fortissime pugnam capessunt. κατὰ θέσιν ergo potentiam istorum hostium describit, cum τὰς ἀρχὰς τὰς ἐξουσίας, τοὺς κοσμοκράτορας nominat; etiam cum τὰ πνευματικὰ. Cum spiritualibus enim hostibus difficillimum est bellum, maxime cum illi adoriuntur res divinas, & nos circa fidei mysteria, vel ea, quae credenda sunt, tentant spi- rituales illae malitiae. De mundi rectoribus Theo- phylactus: Non hos mundi dicit rectores, quia ha- beant machina hujus imperium, sed pravis asserit facinoribus praesidere. Consuevere namque litera sacra iniqua opera, & qui hac facitarent, mun- dum dicere, ut illud, non estis de hoc mundo, hoc est, ex ordine eorum, qui mundana pertractant. His igitur Daemones imperant, qui ultro se Daemonibus subdidere. Similiter per mundum Hemmingius homines mundanos peccato indor- mientes, atque adeo ipsa peccata significari vult, quum mundum hujus seculi tenebras definiat Apostolus.

IV. Quo fine? Ut possitis 1. στῆναι stare, con- sistere, adversus tot, tam callidos, tam potentes hostes, eorum insultus & insidias. In prælio vi- ctor stare, victus cadere vel fugere dicitur. Ar- maturam induere, pugnam inire debent, non ut fugiant, sed ut stent. In robore Domini stare possunt. Huic ergo confident & consistent, Esa. XXVIII. 16. cap. XXX. 5. 2. ἀντιστῆναι resistere, quod fit sese defendendo, & hostem repellendo. Ideo diversi generis arma & defensive & offensive agendi, ut nempe nos tueamur, & hostem abiga- mus, & sub pedes nostros conteramus, assumenda. Additur autem ἐν τῇ ἡμέρᾳ τῇ πονηρᾷ, in die mala, quem Hyperius quidem intelligit de quovis tem- pore, siquidem Diabolus nunquam cessat insidia- ri; sed notatur hic dies vel tempus tentationis, cum nempe actu nos aggreditur Diabolus, quod etsi semper velit, non tamen semper eidem a Deo permittitur. 3. Κατεργάζεσθαι conficere vel ster- nere, quomodo usus est hoc verbo Xenophon παιδείας IV. Κατειργάσατο τὸν λέοντα, confecit leonem: Et Thucydides IV. Πειρασόμεθα κατεργά- ζεσθαι αὐτούς: Conabimur ipsos evertere. Rectius ergo vertitur: Ut possitis interfectis omnibus sta- re, quam in Vulgata: In omnibus perfecti stare. Addidit τὸ στῆναι: Quoniam plerique post victoriam cecidere, standum est, inquit, vel maxime, cum vi- ctores evasimus, ne victus ille nos rursum oppugnet. Hostis namque vel a morte infectus reviviscet hic, & vires recuperabit, si erimus ipsi tardiores, & in turpitudinem relabemur, ut hic Theophylactus.

## 6:14
Vers. 14.

Στῆτε οὖν περιζωσάμενοι τὴν ὀσφὺν ὑμῶν ἐν ἀληθείᾳ) Soldiers have a ζωστῆρα, that is, a belt, such as Ajax gave to Hector. In the Glossary, ζωστὴρ is a girdle, a belt, a cincture: and truth or sincerity is rightly compared to a belt. There is great looseness in lies. Truth binds a man, האמונה אזור חלציו, Isa. XI. 5, good faith shall be the belt of his loins.

Καὶ ἐνδυσάμενοι τὸν θώρακα τῆς δικαιοσύνης) From Isa. LIX. 7. וילבש צרקה כשרין ἐνεδύσατο δικαιοσύνην ὡς θώρακα. Θώραξ is so called because it covers the chest, a breastplate to the Latins: concerning which Martial has an epigram: The breastplate impenetrable to Sarmatian arrows of the master. In the chest is the heart, which is safe against temptations through the habit of acting rightly.

Latin:

Vers. 14.

Στῆτε οὖν περιζωσάμενοι τὴν ὀσφὺν ὑμῶν ἐν ἀληθείᾳ) Milites ζωστῆρα habent, id est baltheum, qualem Hectori dedit Ajax. In Glossario ζωστὴρ cingula, baltheum, cingu- lum: & recte baltheo comparatur veritas sive sinceritas. Mendaciorum magna est laxitas. Veritas adstringit homi- nem, האמונה אזור חלציו, Esa. XI. 5. bona fides e- rit baltheus lumborum ejus.

Καὶ ἐνδυσάμενοι τὸν θώρακα τῆς δικαιοσύνης) Ex Esa. LIX. 7. וילבש צרקה כשרין ἐνεδύσατο δικαιοσύνην ὡς θώρακα. Θώραξ inde dicitur, quod pectus tegat, lorica Latinis: de qua habet Epigramma Martialis: Invia Sarmaticis domini lorica sagittis. In pectore cor, quod adversus tentationes tutum est con- suetudine recte agendi.

## 6:15
Καὶ ὑποδησάμενοι τοὺς πόδας ἐν ἑτοιμασίᾳ τοῦ Εὐαγγελίου τῆς εἰρήνης) Soldiers are shod. The feet signify daily actions, as we said regarding John XIII, 10, they do not become dirty if they always persist in thoughts of executing and propagating the Gospel. He said, however, the Gospel of peace, alluding to that in Isa. LII. 7, which Paul uses in Rom. X. 15. Ἑτοιμασία in Greek, Dan. XI. 20, 21, is כן, that is, a station.

Now in species he prescribes weapons, which are both φυλακτήρια and ἀμυντήρια. Of the former kind are the belt, the breastplate, the greaves, the shield, the helmet: Of the latter kind is the sword. Others enjoy a trichotomy, because there are coverings, the belt, the breastplate, the greaves; defenses, the shield, the helmet; and repellents, the sword, to which class the darts of prayers can also be referred.

Weapons of the former kind regard the principal parts of the body. For the belt joins tight garments; the breastplate protects the chest especially; the greaves the feet and legs, the shield defends the whole body; the helmet especially the head; the shield is given to the left hand, the sword to the right, and from both, darts and arrows are also used. A soldier girded with a belt handles his weapons nimbly, and leans more powerfully into the enemy, and plants his foot more firmly, just as workers were girded with a belt for labor, runners for running, soldiers for standing in battle, 2 Kings IV. 29, chap. IV. 1, Prov. XXXI. 17.

Truth, with Chrysostom and Theophylact, is to be understood as divine both in faith and in life, with which belt the loins of the mind are to be girded, 1 Pet. 1:13, against the lies and seduction of the Devil, lest it be hindered by hesitation or slip in the battle. As the loins, says Hemmingius, in which are the greatest strengths of the body, are strengthened by a belt, lest the soldier slip while fighting: So the soul is to be strengthened by the truth of God, lest the Devil more easily overthrow and slaughter us as we doubt and hesitate, conf. Luke 12:35. The breastplate is primarily a protection for the chest. Such for us is the righteousness of Christ, which we put on through faith, Gal. 3:27, Jer. 23:6, Isa. 45:23, with which the chest is to be protected against spiritual enemies, conf. Prov. 4:23. We have here Cocceius agreeing: By that through which we are justified, by that we put on righteousness. Through faith we are justified, and we put on Christ. And so through it we put on righteousness, that is, the right of sons to seek and expect eternal life. That righteousness is for us instead of a θώραξ (breastplate). For it is the righteousness of life, Rom. 5:18. Nothing, therefore, can separate us from eternal life. But that righteousness is to be retained, like a breastplate, Isa. 54:14. Be stable in righteousness, or a stabilizer. And because faith, through which the righteousness of Christ becomes ours and protects us, is not without love, therefore in 1 Thess. 5:8 the Apostle calls it the breastplate of faith and love. The shoes of the feet are required for the readiness of the Gospel of peace in its preaching and confession. The Apostle does not teach that we ought to be shod for the Gospel, but the putting on of shoes is the very ἑτοιμασία τοῦ εὐαγγελίου (preparation of the Gospel). The metaphor fits beautifully: One girding himself for a journey protects his feet with shoes; there is need of the Gospel of peace, that we may be protected, if feet must walk in the course of the calling. For one must often walk through thorns, briars, and thistles, Acts 14:11. Cocceius understands the readiness of announcing peace: Among the Apostle, he says, in many places εὐαγγέλιον (Gospel) is εὐαγγελισμός (evangelization). He compares that readiness with shoes or greaves, namely so that the way may be as it were flat for going through the whole world, just as to him who is greaved and shod, every way is soft and easy. For God through the Gospel of peace wishes to subdue the world, and wishes all towns to be open to it. Nor is there anything that is sweeter to the mind and εὐαρεστότερον (more pleasing) to every conscience and ἑλκυστικώτερον (more attractive), and more effective for unlocking and opening the heart of the hearer. Certainly by no other speech are hard hearts crushed, and rocks turned into pools of water, Jer. 22:29, Heb. 4:12, Ps. 114:8, and God wishes to bless it, Rom. 1:17, Isa. 55:10, 11. Crocius has it thus in this place: The Vulgate version has 'in the preparation of the Gospel.' Erasmus, 'that you may be prepared for the Gospel of peace,' as if Paul wishes to teach for what they ought to be shod. But Beza, rightly following Calvin, observes that he also provides the shoes. Soldiers protected their shins with greaves, which they called κνημίδες, against the cold and other harms, and the feet themselves, if they wished. Similarly, Paul does not want the Ephesians to go forth to the struggle barefoot. Nay rather, just as Greek soldiers wore their κνημίδες, and the Israelites, about to set out from Egypt through the desert into Canaan, ate the lamb with shod feet, Exod. 12. Thus he provides shoes with which the Ephesians may protect their feet, namely the preparation of the Gospel. Thus also Calvin alludes, if I am not mistaken, to military boots. For these also were counted among the weapons, of which there was no use at home. The sense is: Just as soldiers covered their legs and feet against the cold and other harms: So we ought to be shod with the Gospel, by which we may pass through this world unharmed. Nor is this commentary of Grotius inappropriate here.

Latin:

Καὶ ὑποδησάμενοι τοὺς πόδας ἐν ἑτοιμασίᾳ τοῦ Εὐαγγελίου τῆς εἰρήνης) Milites caligati sunt. Pedes significant quoti- dianas actiones, ut diximus ad Joh. XIII, 10. ex non sor- descent, si semper insistant cogitationibus exequendi & propagandi Evangelii. Dixit autem Evangelium pacis, al- ludens ad illud Esa. LII. 7. quo Paulus utitur Rom. X. 15. Ἑτοιμασία Græce Dan. XI. 20. 21. est כן, id est, statio.

Jam in specie arma præscribit, quæ tum φυλα- κτήρια sunt, tum ἀμυντήρια. Illius generis sunt cingulum, thorax, ocreæ, clypeus, galea: Hujus generis est gladius. Alii τριχοτομίᾳ gaudent, quod sint tegumenta, cingulus, thorax, ocreæ; muni- menta clypeus, galea; & amolimenta, gladius, ad quam classem etiam jacula precum referri pos- sunt.

Prioris generis arma respiciunt præcipuas corporis partes. Cingulum enim vestes arctæ con- jungit; thorax pectus præcipue munit; ocreæ pe- des & crura, clypeus totum corpus defendit; ga- lea maxime caput; clypeus sinistræ datur, gladius dextræ, ab utraque etiam jacula & sagittæ adhi- bentur. Miles baltheo cinctus expeditus arma tractat, & validius in hostem incumbit, & firmius pedem figit, uti baltheo operarii ad laborem cin- gebantur, cursores ad cursum, milites ad standum in pugna, 2. Reg. IV. 29. cap. IV. 1. Prov. XXXI. 17.

Veritas cum Chrysostomo & Theophylacto intelli- genda est divina tum in fide, tum in vita, quo bal- theo cingendi sunt mentis lumbi, 1. Petr. I. 13. ad- versus mendacia & seductionem Diaboli, ne per hæsitationem impediatur aut labatur in pugna. Ut lumbi, inquit Hemmingius, in quibus potissi- mæ corporis vires sunt, cingulo firmantur, ne in- ter pugnandum miles labatur: Ita animus veritate Dei firmandus est, ne Diabolus nos dubitantes ac hæsitantes facilius prosternat ac trucidet, Conf. Luc. XII. 35. Thorax imprimis pectoris est munimentum. Tale est nobis justitia Christi, quam per fidem induimus, Gal. III. 27. Jer. XXIII. v. 6. Esa. XLV. 23. qua pectus adversus hostes spi- rituales muniendum est, conf. Prov. IV. v. 23. Habemus hic consentientem Coccejum: Per quod justificamur, per id induimus justitiam. Per fidem justificamur, & Christum induimus. Itaque per eam induimus justitiam, hoc est, jus filiorum ad peten- dam & expectandam vitam æternam. Ea justitia nobis est pro θώρακι. Est enim justitia vitæ, Rom. V. v. 18. Nihil igitur potest nos a vita æterna sepa- rare. Sed ea justitia retinenda est, ut thorax, Esa. LIV. 14. In justitia stabilis esto, vel stabilitor. Et quia fides, per quam Christi justitia nostra sit, nosque munit, non est fine charitate, idcirco 1. Thess. V. 8. thoracem fidei & charitatis nuncupat Apostolus. Calcei pedum requiruntur, ad prom- ptitudinem Evangelii pacis in ejus prædicatione & confessione. Non docet Apostolus, calceatos nos esse debere ad Evangelium, sed calceorum in- duitio est ipsa ἑτοιμασία τοῦ εὐαγγελίου. Metaphora pulchre convenit: Ad iter se accingens calceis pe- des munit, Evangelio pacis opus est, ut muniamur, si ambulare pedes in cursu vocationis debent. Ambulandum enim sæpius per spinas, sentes & tribulos, Act. XIV. 11. Coccejus promptitudinem annunciandi pacem intelligit: Apud Apostolum, inquit, multis in locis εὐαγγέλιον est εὐαγγελισμός. Eam promptitudinem comparat cum calceis vel ocreis, nempe ut quasi plana sit via ad eundum per totum mundum, quemadmodum ei, qui ocrea- tus & calceatus est, omnis via mollis & facilis est. Deus enim per Evangelium pacis vult mundum subigere, & ei vult oppida omnia patere. Neque est quicquam, quod sit suavius animo & εὐαρεστότερον apud omnem conscientiam & ἑλκυστικώτερον, atque efficacius ad reserandum & aperiendum cor au- dientis. Certe per nullum alium sermonem corda dura conteruntur, & petræ convertuntur in stagna aquarum, Jerem. XXII. 29. Ebr. IV. 12. Ps. CXIV. v. 8. & ei vult Deus benedicere, Rom. I. v. 17. Esa. LV. v. 10. 11. Crocius ita habet hoc loco: Vulgata versio habet in præparationem Evangelii. Erasmus ut parati sitis ad Evangelium pacis, quasi Paulus docere velit, ad quid debeant esse calceati. Sed recte post Calvinum observat Beza, etiam præbere cal- ceos. Milites ocreis, quas κνημῖδας vocabant, ad- versus frigus & alias noxas tuebantur tibias, & ipsos pedes, si vellent. Similiter Paulus Ephesios non vult nudipedes prodire ad luctam. Quin imo, sicut suas κνημῖδας milites Græci gerebant, & Israëlitæ ex Ægypto per Eremum in Cananæam profecturi, cal- ceatis pedibus vescebantur agno, Exod. XII. Sic cal- ceos præbet, quibus pedes muniant Ephesii, nempe præparationem Evangelii. Sic & Calvinus alludit, ni fallor, ad caligas militares. Nam hæ quoque inter arma censebantur, quorum nullus domi usus erat. Sensus est: Quemadmodum milites adver- sus frigus & alias noxas crura tegebant ac pedes: Sic Evangelio nos oportere esse calceatos, quo illæsi per hunc mundum transeamus. Nec in- conveniens est hic Grotii commentarius.

## 6:16
Verse 16.

In all things taking up the shield of faith, in which you will be able to quench all the fiery darts of the wicked one) It was customary for leaden bullets to be sent by slingers, which would grow hot by their very motion: when repelled by a firm shield, they would lose their force, no less than fire, which is extinguished. Such a σάκος ἐπὶλέβετος, a true מגן דויר, which name the Jews foolishly apply to their phylacteries, is faith in Christ, repelling all lusts, which are the fiery darts of the Devil; faith overcomes the world, 1 John V. 4.

Others understand by the shield of faith the Word of God, Prov. XXX. 5, Psalm XCI. 4; it is so called, just as God is also called the shield of the pious, Deut. XXXIII. v. 29, Psalm III. 4, Psalm XXVIII. 7, Psalm CXIX. 114. Yet the Word of God is a shield to us insofar as it is apprehended by faith: nor is God our shield otherwise than when we trust in God. And therefore faith is rightly called a shield, but by reason of its correlate, insofar as it relies upon God in the revealed Word or the Word of God. For it is not a shield and a protection of the soul insofar as it is a quality or virtue in us, but insofar as it apprehends God and His promises, and acquiesces in them. As therefore a shield is held out to the whole body, which indeed protects and encompasses it like a gate: so a more ardent and undoubted faith guards and protects the soul on every side, says Theophylact, who understands by fiery darts absurd desires and thoughts of distrust, and explains 'fiery' thus: He said 'fiery', not only because those burning desires inflame us to fouler deeds, but because we feel the heat of these even in the conscience itself. Furthermore, it happens that the Demon burns us even with these thoughts of distrust, when he suggests perfidy to us, all of which faith finally extinguishes. Therefore, if it prostrates the demons themselves, it will much more subdue vices. Crocius more fully: He calls them 'fiery' because they are not only carried very swiftly, penetrate easily, harm easily when admitted, and inflame minds to base works: for we are full of depraved desires, like cannons with powder: but also they are extinguished with difficulty, unless they are extinguished immediately from the beginning, and they inflict mortal wounds. Nor indeed can we resist Satan otherwise than through faith, 1 Pet. V. v. 8, 9. Cocceius not incorrectly: Indeed, let it always be in memory, I know whom I have believed, I know in whom I have believed, in whose faith I live: I know what I hope for and why I have believed. Let it always be ready to consider, whether this, to which we are tempted, is from faith? And whatever is not from faith is sin, Rom. XIV. 23. This shield is to be taken up for all things. For through faith we stand girded with truth, through faith we are righteous, through faith, proficient and exercised, we are shod with the readiness of the proclamation of peace. Through it the salvation is safe for us. Through it we use the sword of the Spirit rightly and unimpeded. Thus he explains that 'in all things'.

Latin:

Verf. 16.

Ἐπὶ πᾶσιν ἀναλαβόντες τὸν θυρεὸν τῆς πίστεως, ἐν ὧ δυνήσε- σθε πάντα τὰ βέλη τῦ πονηρῦ τὰ πεπυρωμένα σβέσαι) Sole- bant a funditoribus mitti glandes, quæ ipso motu ardesce- bant: Ex scuto firmo repulsæ vim suam perdebent, non minus, quam ignis, qui extinguitur. Tale σάκος ἐπὶλέβε- τος verum מגן דויר, quod nomen Judæi stulte indunt suis φυλακτηρίοις, est fides in Christum, repellens libidi- nes omnes, quæ tela sunt Diaboli ignita, fides vincit mun- dum, 1. Joh. V. 4.

Alii per fcutum fidei Verbum Dei intelligunt, Prov. XXX. 5. Pfal. XCI. 4. id ita vocetur, sicut etiam Deus piorum scutum dicitur, Deut. XXXIII. v. 29. Psal. III. 4. Psal. XXVIII. 7. Psal. CXIX. 114. Verbum tamen Dei scutum nobis est, quatenus fide apprehenditur: nec aliter Deus scutum no- strum, nisi cum in Deo confidimus. Ideoque fi- des recte scutum dicitur, sed ratione correlati, quatenus Deo in Verbo revelato vel Verbo Dei nititur. Non enim fcutum est, & animæ muni- mentum, quatenus qualitas vel virtus in nobis, sed quatenus apprehendit Deum, ejusque pro- missiones, iisque acquiescit. Ut itaque toti corpori scutum obtenditur, quod utique illud tanquam por- ta tutatur & circumcludit: Sic fides ardentior & indubitata animam undiquaque custodit & prote- git, inquit Theophylactus, qui per tela ignea ab- surdas cupiditates & diffidentiæ cogitatus intelli- git, & ignea ita explicat: Ignea autem dixit, non modo, quia ad fœdiora incendunt facinora flagran- tes illæ cupiditates, sed quia vel in conscientia ipsa harum sentimus ardorem. Accedit præterea, quod vel ex istius diffidentia cogitationibus exurit nos Dæmon, cum nobis perfidiam suggerit, quæ omnia tandem fides extinguit. Hæc itaque, si Dæmones ipsos prosternit, longe magis & vitia subjugabit. Plenius Crocius: Ignita vocat, quia non tantum fe- runtur celerrime, facile penetrant, admissa nocent facile, ad turpia opera animos incendunt: Sumus enim pravis cupiditatibus pleni, ut bombardæ pul- vere: sed etiam difficulter extinguuntur, nisi mox ab initio extinguantur, & mortalia vulnera infli- gunt. Nec vero aliter, quam per fidem resistere possumus Satanæ, 1. Petr. V. v 8. 9. Non inrecte Coccejus: Nempe semper in memoria versetur, scio cui crediderim, scio in quem crediderim, in cujus fide vivo: Scio quid sperem & cur crediderim. Semper sit in promptu, considerare, an hoc, ad quod tentamur, sit ex fide? Et quicquid non fit in fide, peccatum est, Rom. XIV. 23. Hic clypeus assumen- dus ad omnia. Nam per fidem veritate accincti sta- mus, per fidem justi sumus, per fidem proficientem & exercitatam sumus calceati promptitudine an- nunciationis pacis. Per eam τὸ σωτήριον nobis tutum est. Per eam gladio Spiritus recte utimur & im- pæpedite. Ita illud ἐπὶ πᾶσιν explicat.

## 6:17
Verse 17.

And take the helmet of salvation) And this is in the already mentioned place of Isaiah, 'and a helmet of salvation upon his head', he put on a helmet of salvation. By 'salvation' here is understood metonymically the hope of eternal salvation conceived from the Gospel; the same appears from 1 Thess. V. 8, where it is, 'and a helmet, the hope of salvation'. The head is among the principal parts to be protected for a soldier, both because the blows that fall on that part are almost lethal, and because the head commands the whole body. In our head is the mind, which that hope of eternal life, which is solidly revealed in no other doctrine except in the Gospel, does not allow to be seduced by false doctrines.

Bullinger, Gualther, and Cocceius understand Christ by 'the salvation' from Luke II. v. 30, but the explanation from 1 Thess. V. 8 is more certain. For this parallel passage compares the hope of salvation to a helmet, by which the head is covered, because hope always makes one upright in battle, constant in dangers, by promising the help of God and the crown of righteousness to those who strive lawfully, says B. Balduinus on 1 Thess. V. 8. Take the helmet of salvation, says B. Osiander on this passage. But they place the helmet of salvation on the head who have a firm HOPE, that the Lord is not going to tempt us beyond what we are able to bear, 1 Corinth. X., and that the Lord is most certainly going to deliver us at last from every evil, and adorn us with eternal glory. And this hope does not disappoint, Rom. V.

And the sword of the Spirit, which is the Word of God) A spiritual sword, that is, spiritual. Such things are accustomed to be added for softening translations, as we said at Matt. XXVI. v. 29. A two-edged sword, or a two-edged blade (for these two words are placed in the same sense in these books, and among the interpreters of the Old Testament) is every doctrine which proceeds from God, because it penetrates the innermost parts, and separates evil affections from good; see Heb. IV. 12, Rev. XVI. 11, 12. But this similitude is taken from Isa. XLIX. 2, and at the same time the words of Psalm CXLIX. 5 are mystically explained.

From the preceding things, says Theophylact, Paul has armed us, and in such a way that the enemies can harm us in nothing. But now he also bestows arms, with which we will be able to offend more. It is little for a soldier to defend himself, unless he goes against the enemy and routs him. Therefore, as a soldier seeks, strikes, and prostrates the enemy with a sword: So Paul arms the Christian soldier with a sword, but of the Spirit, or the spiritual word of God, cf. Heb. IV. 12. Rev. I. 16. Matt. IV.

Latin:

Verf. 17.

Καὶ τὴν περικεφαλαίαν τῦ σωτηρίυ δέξασθε) Et hoc est dicto jam Esaiæ loco וכובע ישועה בראשה, περιέθε- το περικεφαλαίαν σωτηρίε. Per σωτήριον hic intelligitur με- τωνυμικῶς spes de salute æterna ex Evangelio concepta, appa- ret idem ex 1. Thessal. V. 8. ubi est, κὲ περικεφαλαίαν, ἐλπίδα σωτηρίας. Caput inter præcipua tuendum militi, tum quia lethales ferme sunt ictus, qui in eam partem cadunt, tum quia toti corpori caput imperat. In capite nostro mens est, quam falsis doctrinis seduci non patitur spes illa vitæ æ- ternæ, quæ solide in nulla alia doctrina, præterquam in Evangelio, revelatur.

Per τὸ σωτήριον Christum intelligunt Bullin- gerus, Gualtherus, Coccejus ex Luc. II. v. 30. sed explicatio e 1. Thess. V. 8. certior est. Hic enim locus parallelus spem salutis confert galeæ, qua caput tegitur, quia spes semper facit erectos in pugna, constanter in periculis, pollicendo auxi- lium Dei & coronam justitiæ legitime certanti- bus, ait B. Balduinus ad 1. Thess. V. 8. Galeam salutis, ait B. Osiander in hunc locum, assumite. Galeam autem salutis capiti imponunt, qui firmam habent SPEM, quod Dominus non sit tentaturus nos ultra, quam sufferre valeamus, 1. Corinth. X. & quod nos Dominus certissime tandem sit ab omni malo liberaturus, & aeterna gloria ornaturus. Et haec spes non confundit, Rom. V.

Καὶ τὴν μάχαιραν τοῦ πνεύματος, ὅ ἐστι ῥῆμα Θεοῦ) Μά- χαιραν πνευματικὴν, id est, πνευματικήν. Solent talia addi translationibus molliendis, ut diximus ad Matth. XXVI. v. 29. μάχαιρα δίστομος, sive ῥομφαία δίστομος (nam hae duae voces eodem sensu ponuntur in his libris, & apud ve- teris Testamenti interpretes) est doctrina omnis, quae a Deo procedit, quia intima penetrat, separatque affectus malos a bonis; Vid. Ebr. IV. 12. Apoc. XVI. 11. 12. Sumpta autem haec similitudo ex Esa. XLIX. 2. & simul mystice ex- plicantur verba Psal. CXLIX. 5.

Ex superioribus, inquit Theophylactus, dictis ar- mavit nos Paulus, & ita, ut hostes obesse nobis nihil queant. Nunc vero & armis donat, quibus offende- re bos magis poterimus. Parum est, militem se tue- ri, nisi in hostem eat, eumque profligat. Ergo ut miles gladio hostem petit, caedit, prosternit: Ita armat militem Christianum Paulus gladio, sed Spi- ritus, vel spirituali verbo Dei, conf. Ebr. IV. 12. Apoc. I. 16. Matth. IV.

## 6:18
Ver. 18.

Διὰ πάσης προσευχῆς καὶ δεήσεως) προσευχὴ is indeed a general word, in which sense we shall also have the word προσεύχεσθαι immediately, but when δέησις is opposed to it, as here, and 1 Tim. II. 1: Προσευχὴ signifies prayers for obtaining good things, δέησις deprecation for warding off evils which we fear. For the name is derived ἀπὸ τοῦ δέος. In the Glossary δέησις is deprecation. δέησις is usually placed in Greek where in Hebrew there is תְּחִנָּה or תַּחֲנוּנִים, which words signify the imploring of mercy.

Ἐν παντὶ καιρῷ) always, Luke XVIII. v. 1. Without ceasing, 1 Thess. V. 17.

Ἐν πνεύματι) not with the voice only, but also with the mind. See above V. 19.

Καὶ εἰς αὐτὸ τοῦτο ἀγρυπνοῦντες) שׁוֹקְדִים. It is a military saying: Soldier, keep watch. Prayers and vigils are accustomed to be joined, Matt. XXVI. 41. Ps. V. 4. LXXXVIII. v. 14. In the temple there was always a vigil for some. Εἰς αὐτὸ τοῦτο refers to the whole preceding matter.

Ἐν πάσῃ προσκαρτερήσει) In the sacred rites of the gentiles it was said: Hoc age (Do this). Plutarch teaches us this in Numa, and says that by these words men are commanded προσέχειν τοῖς ἱεροῖς, καὶ μηδὲν ἔργον ἐμβαλεῖν μεταξὺ μηδὲ χρείαν ἀσχολίας.

The primary, as Flacius says, and our final armor is assiduous and ardent prayer, by which we obtain all help and victory from God, and overcome enemies. For unless He assists us everywhere, and rules us with His Spirit, giving counsel, help, and outcome, and powerfully represses Satan himself, and strengthens us, it is clearly all over for us. Theophylact beautifully: Thus, therefore, Paul leads those who are so armed and instructed by themselves to the Emperor, whose help they both need, and that he might stretch out his hand, and be an aid. For when he had said that it will be permitted for us to extinguish the fire that has been thrown, lest they should attribute it to glory, or become proud, he says, you have need of God, by whose help you will accomplish all things. προσευχὴ is that by which good things are sought from God, spiritual fortitude, truth, justice, readiness to announce the Gospel, faith, hope, the use of the word; δέησις, by which we deprecate evils, both temptation and the impediments and damages of the armor and spiritual warfare. For he warns that prayers should be made 1. incessantly, at all times, not that nothing else is to be done than to pray, or that one must pray assiduously, on every occasion and opportunity day and night, as much in favorable as in adverse circumstances, and that our heart ought always to be directed to GOD, to whom one must sigh even among labors, in whose name all things are to be undertaken and dispatched.

The Devil never ceases to tempt us, 1 Pet. 5:7, therefore we must never cease in praying. 2. Devoutly & ardently ἐν πνεύματι, which Beza understands of the Holy Spirit: But it is more correctly understood as the spirit of those praying, because prayer ought to be made from the heart with the attention, devotion, and fervor of our spirit. Prayers ought not to be born in the mouth, but in the heart, Ps. 27:8, Ps. 62:9. Against the fiery darts of the Demon are required the fiery darts of prayer, with which we may strike the heart of GOD, that He may have mercy on us. 3. Soberly & vigilantly: Καὶ εἰς ἀυτὸ τῦτο ἀγρυπνῶντες, which can be referred both to the fight and the armor, because one must be vigilant in spiritual warfare, so that we may be able to resist the enemy and rightly use spiritual weapons, or to the prayers, of which the Apostle has treated and continues to treat hereafter. Therefore it is better to refer this to the whole preceding matter. For in prayers there is need of vigilance, Matt. 26:4; but if one must be vigilant, one must certainly live soberly, therefore sobriety is joined with vigils, Luke 21:36, 1 Pet. 5:5, 1 Thess. 5:6, and we are warned that we should be sober for prayers, 1 Pet. 4:7. 4. Perseveringly: Ἐν πάσῃ προσκαρτερήσει: In all perseverance, Ambrosiaster rendered it; with all constancy, the Vulgate. Theophylact explained the word in the same sense as Chrysostom: Just as that Canaanite woman and that widow persisted in prayer with the utmost patience. For that is true supplication, which is persevering and assiduous. So also Crocius, Cocceius, and others; that we may not lose heart, Luke 18:1, but always press on, Isa. 62:6-7, let us ask, seek, knock, Matt. 7:7-8, that confidence, hope, and patience may not waver. 5. Humbly: which the word δέησις implies, descending from δέομαι, which is to be in need.

And supplication for all the saints) He does not want everyone to pray only for himself, but also for others, which he calls ἐντεύξεις, 1 Tim. 2:1.

Latin:

Vers. 18.

Διὰ πάσης προσευχῆς καὶ δεήσεως) προσευχῆς vox est qui- dem generalis, quo sensu & verbum προσεύχεσθαι illico habebimus, sed cum opponitur ei δέησις, ut hic, & 1. Ti- moth. II. 1: Προσευχὴ significat preces ad bona impetran- da, δέησις deprecationem arcendis malis, quae metuimus. Est enim ἀπὸ τοῦ δέος deductum nomen. In Glossario δέησις deprecatio. Solet plerumque δέησις in Graeco poni, ubi in Ebraeo est תְּחִנָּה aut תַּחֲנוּנִים, quae voces imploratio- nem misericordiae significant.

Ἐν παντὶ καιρῷ) πάντοτε Luc. XVIII. v. 1. Ἀδιαλείπτως, 1. Thess. V. 17.

Ἐν πνεύματι) non voce tantum, sed & animo. Vide su- pra V. 19.

Καὶ εἰς αὐτὸ τοῦτο ἀγρυπνοῦντες) שׁוֹקְדִים. Militare di- ctum est: Mars vigila. Conjungi solent preces & vigiliae, Matth. XXVI. 41. Psal. V. 4. LXXXVIII. v. 14. In templo semper aliquibus erat pervigilium. Εἰς αὐτὸ τοῦτο ad rem to- tam praecedentem refertur.

Ἐν πάσῃ προσκαρτερήσει) In sacris gentium dicebatur: Hoc age. Docet nos hoc Plutarchus in Numa, aitque eis verbis homines juberi προσέχειν τοῖς ἱεροῖς, καὶ μηδὲν ἔργον ἐμβαλεῖν μεταξὺ μηδὲ χρείαν ἀσχολίας.

Primaria, dicente Flacio, & postrema nostra armatura est assidua, ardensque precatio, quae omnem opem ac victoriam a Deo impetramus, & hostes superamus. Nisi enim ille ubique nobis assi- stat, nosque suo Spiritu regat, dans consilium, auxi- lium, ac eventum, & Satanam ipsum potenter re- primat, nosque corroboret, actum plane est de nobis. Pulchre Theophylactus: Hos itaque ita per se Pau- lus armis munitos instructosque ad Imperatorem de- ducit, cujus & ope indigeant, & manum ut porri- gat, & auxilio sit. Cum enim dixisset, restinguere nobis licebit injectum incendium, ne id gloriae duce- rent, vel superbirent, Deo, inquit, vobis est opus, quo adjuvante cuncta perficietis. προσευχὴ est, qua petuntur a Deo bona, fortitudo spiritualis, veri- tas, justitia, promptitudo annunciandi Evange- lium, fides, spes, usus verbi; δέησις, qua mala de- precamur tum tentationem, tum armaturae & mi- litiae spiritualis impedimenta & damna. Monet enim, ut preces fiant 1. indesinenter, omni tem- pore, non quod nihil aliud agendum sit, quam precandum, seu quod orandum sit assidue, omni occasione & opportunitate die ac nocte, tam in secundis, quam adversis, quodque semper cor nostrum ad DEUM directum esse debeat, ad quem etiam inter labores suspirandum, in cujus nomine omnia suscipienda & expedienda.

Nunquam cessat Diabolus nos tentare, 1. Petr. V. 7. nunquam ergo nos debemus cessare oran- do. 2. Devote & ardenter ἐν πνεύματι, quod de Spiritu Sancto intelligit Beza: Sed rectius Spi- ritus precantium intelligitur, quod ex animo cum attentione, devotione ac fervore Spiritus nostri fieri debeat oratio. Preces non nasci debent in ore, sed in corde, Psal. XXVII. 8. Psal. LXII. 9. Adversus ignita jacula Daemonis requiruntur ignea jacula orationis, quibus cor DEI feriamus, ut nostri misereatur. 3. Sobrie & vigilanter: Καὶ εἰς ἀυτὸ τῦτο ἀγρυπνῶντες, quod referri potest tum ad pugnam & armaturam, quod vigilandum sit in militia spirituali, ut resistere hosti, & armis spiritualibus recte uti possimus, vel ad preces, de quibus egit, & agere deinceps adhuc pergit Apo- stolus. Ideo praestat, hoc ad rem totam praece- dentem referre. Nam in precibus opus est vigi- lantia, Matth. XXVI. 4. si autem vigilandum, so- brie utique vivendum, ideo cum vigiliis sobrie- tas conjungitur, Luc. XXI. 36. 1. Petr. V. 5. 1. Thessal. V. 6. & monemur, ut sobrii ad preces simus, 1. Petr. VI. 7. 4. Perseveranter: Ἐν πάσῃ προσκαρτερήσει: In omni perseverantia reddidit Ambrosiasler; cum omni constantia, Vulgatus. Eodem sensu exposuit vocem cum Chrysostomo Theophylactus: Quemadmodum Cananaea & vi- dua illa orantes summa in patientia perstiterunt. Illa namque est vera deprecatio, quae perseverans sit, & assidua. Ita & Crocius, Coccejus, alii; ne ἐκκακῶμεν Luc. XVIII. 1. sed semper instemus, Esa. LXII. 6. 7. petamus, quaeramus, pulsemus, Matth. VII. 7. 8. ne vacillet fiducia, spes & pa- tientia. 5. Humiliter: quod vox δέησις infert, à δέομαι, quod est indigeo, descendens.

Καὶ δέησει περὶ πάντων τῶν ἁγίων) Non pro se tantum o- rare vult unumquemque, sed & pro aliis, quod ἐντεύξεις vo- cat 1. Tim. II. 1.

## 6:19
Ver. 19. And for me) Behold how much Paul values the prayers of the pious, when he, who has such great grace before God, hopes that he can be helped by the prayers of others, and shall we think that the prayers of Paul, who reigns with Christ, are of no benefit to us?

That utterance may be given to me in the opening of my mouth, to make known with boldness the mystery of the Gospel) that is, that I, free from this military guard, may be able to carry the word of the Gospel through the whole city, the things of which were hitherto hidden, that speech may be given to me, that is, that it may be permitted to me to speak; in the opening of the mouth, that is, an occasion being given. For the occasion of speaking is פתחון פה to the Rabbis. Thus God is said to open lips, when He supplies matter for giving thanks to Himself, Ps. 51:15, and παῤῥησία here signifies not so much the confidence of Paul as the removal of impediments coming from without, a word indeed of Greek origin, but a Syrian idiom. For the Rabbis use בפרהסיא for publicly and openly. So also John 11:54.

Latin:

Vers. 19. Καὶ ὑπὲρ ἐμῦ) Ecce quanti Paulus preces pio- rum faciat, cum ille tantae apud Deum gratiae speret, se aliorum precibus posse adjuvari, & nos existimabimus, Pau- li cum Christo regnantis preces nihil nobis prodesse?

Ἵνα μοι δοθῇ λόγος ἐν ἀνοίξει τῦ σόματός μυ, ἐν παῤ- ῥησίᾳ γνωρίσαι τό μυσήριον τῦ Εὐαγγελίου) id est, ut ab hac custodia militari liber per omnem urbem perfer- re possim sermonem Evangelii eum, cujus res antehac oc- cultae fuere, ut detur mihi sermo, id est, ut loqui mihi li- ceat; in apertione oris, id est, occasione data. Nam oc- casio loquendi Rabbinis פתחון פה. Sic Deus labia ape- rire dicitur, ubi materiam suppeditat sibi gratias agendi, Psal. LI. 17. & παῤῥησία hic non tam fiduciam Pauli, quam impedimentorum extrinsecus advenientium remotionem significat, vocabulo quidem Graecae originis, sed Syra lo- cutione. Nam בפרהסיא pro palam & aperte usurpant Rabbini. Sic & Joh. XI. 54.

## 6:20
Ver. 20. For which I am an ambassador in a chain) Now also I do not cease to perform the embassy entrusted to me, but with great troubles and difficulties, since the same chain holds me and the guard assigned to me. See what we said at the end of Acts, where you have the very name ἄλυσιν, 28:20, as also 2 Tim. 1:16, for which he said δεσμὰ in Col. 4:18, Phil. 1:7, 13, 14, 16, 2 Tim. 2:9, Philem. v. 10, 13.

That in it I may speak boldly, as I ought to speak) that I may freely declare everywhere the things that must be said by me.

The object of the prayer is expressed, which generally are all the saints, not the deceased, as Papists pray for the dead without scripture, and specifically here it was Paul, who seeks the prayers of the Ephesians primarily for the success of his office. Grotius here seems to favor the Papists, who believe that the saints in heaven pray for our needs, and therefore invoke them; although indeed there is no doubt that the saints in heaven pray generally for the necessity of the Church, yet that they know the special necessity of the faithful, or hear prayers, is foreign to the scriptures. Abraham was the Father of believers: And Israel or Jacob was easily the chief among believers: And of them the Israelitic people confessed, Isa. 63:16, Abraham does not know us, and Israel does not recognize us: You, O Lord, are our Father. Furthermore, our prayers ought not to be solitary, therefore we are commanded to pray as a group: Our Father, etc. In the opening of the mouth is nowhere an occasion given, and here it is explained by the added word in boldness, which is wrongly understood as the external removal of impediments, without an example from scripture, since it denotes confidence in speaking, see Acts 4:29, 31, as John 11:54, the confidence of conversing publicly. That Paul sought prayers for liberation from chains, it occurs to no one here, nor are the words of the Apostle dragged to that except by force. More convenient is the observation of the Greeks, that God opened the mouth for the Apostles, by putting words into them. Nothing, therefore, says Theophylact, did the Apostle premeditate that he was about to say. For he followed the Lord's saying, do not premeditate what you are to speak: For it will be given to you in that hour what you ought to speak. Not otherwise did he himself, opening his mouth, bring forth what was suggested by the Lord. Thus he performed all things by divine grace. The opening of the mouth, however, also hints at our inability, that the mouth is closed for bringing forth divine things, and that we are not able to open it, or dare to do so in dangers, unless the Lord opens it for us. To open the mouth is a Hebrew phrase, and signifies to speak, Judg. 11:35, 36, Prov. 31, Acts 13:14. But here it is taken passively. He wants the mouth to be opened for him by God; which, even if it was opened for him before with great fruit, he asks that it be opened for him further even in chains. Concerning the confidence of speaking, Theophylact says: To make known the mystery of the Gospel with confidence, that is, that I may answer as it behooves, more confidently or manfully and very wisely. The chains are enjoined upon me so that they may obstruct my liberty of speaking. Yet the Spirit will open my mouth, so that I may be more confident in declaring those things which have been enjoined upon me by Him who sent me. Cf. Col. 4:4. What he asks does not pertain to himself, but to their good. He asks that speech be given to him, not that chains be loosed. He asks for the opening of his mouth, not of his bonds. He asks for παῤῥησία of speech in his very bonds, not for liberation from the same. With the opening of the mouth, to speak is not only to speak promptly and readily, but also openly, and so that we may be understood, and also without fear, or with singular confidence. The bonds were not burdensome to the Apostle, but he shows that for his speech to be bound would be burdensome to him. Nor is he so solicitous about his own life as about the good of the Church, desiring all things to be filled with the Gospel, and not only that some fame of it might be spread through the world, but that the word, pronounced in the opening of the mouth without covering, without enigma, without circumlocutions, might stand forth in clear explanation of the truth for every memory. Therefore he was commanding the Ephesians to ask that a door of speech might be opened to him, and an occasion for speaking might be given, and that ears and hearts might be opened through the Spirit of the love and fear of GOD, and that in those occasions God might be present with him, and might give him open speech, veiled by no wrappings, and that he might be commanded to speak a clear explanation of the truth, as this Coccejus: Who explains the word ἐν παῤῥησίᾳ as ἀκωλύτως openly, publicly, so that there is no need to mutter, or to act secretly, from a comparison of Mark 8:32, John 7:4, 13, 26, chapter 11:14, 54. But the passage Acts 4:29 seems to be more to the point, in which the confidence of speech is noted by this word, by force of comparison, verse 31, which is also the proper signification of the word. See Aeschines in the oration against Timarchus in Suidas. But why should one depart from the proper signification, when this conveniently by way of epexegesis can the word be taken in the present tense? Finally, the Apostle commands that it be requested of GOD that there be granted to him παῤρησιάζε- θαι ε̐ν αὐτω̃, with the addition of ὡς δει̃ με λαλη̃σαι. Παῤρησιά- ζεθαι ε̐ν τω̃ Εὐαγγελίω is to preach freely, so that even if he himself is not free, but in chains, yet the Gospel is not chained, 2 Tim. II. 9, as Cocceius himself explains. Meanwhile, we do not wrongly admit, as the same author observes regarding that παῤρησιάζεθαι of the Apostle, that it also pertains to speaking before all, and concealing nothing from anyone wishing to hear. Which he notes against Bellarmine, who contends that the Apostle did not teach all things openly. Let Coloss. I. 28 be compared. The mystery of the Gospel is not that discourse of the Gospel whose matters were hitherto hidden, but the whole Gospel unknown to nature, and hidden from the ages, Ephes. I. 9, 13, chap. III. 4, 9. Whether that chain, of which Acts XXIX. 20 speaks, that is, of the former Roman captivity, or indeed the latter, is referred to in this place, is doubtful. From the former he was liberated after two years had passed, not so from the latter, which Pareus in the Prolegomena to the Epistle to the Romans thinks is to be understood, and Crocius judges that the collation of the text 2 Tim. IV. 12 makes for this: The envoys of princes are accustomed to be held in honor. But the envoy of Christ, who had been sent to assert into liberty men loosened from the bonds of sins, was cast into chains. But what are you yourself now delegated to, asks Theophylact? To men, indeed, that I may reconcile them to God. These, however, have cast me into chains and bonds, although it is provided by the law of nations that Orators and Nuncios should be unpunished, as they are those who carry the mandates of their Lords.

PART III. OF CHAPTER VI. CONCLUSION OF THE EPISTLE. The reason for Tychicus being sent and the final wish.

Latin:

Vers. 20. Ὑπὲρ ὗ πρεσβεύω ἐν ἀλύσει) Nunc quoque non desino obire legationem mihi mandatam, sed cum magnis molestiis ac difficultatibus, quippe eadem catena me & appositum mihi custodem tenente. Vide quae di- ximus ad finem Actorum, ubi ipsum nomen habes ἄλυσιν, XXVIII. 20. ut & 2. Timoth. I. 16. pro quo δεσμὰ dixit Coloss. IV. 18. Philipp. I. 7. 13. 14. 16. 2. Timoth. II. 9. Philem. v. 10. 13.

Ἵνα ἐν ἀυτῷ παῤῥησιάσωμαι, ὡς δεῖ με λαλῆσαι) ut libere ubique enuntiem, quae mihi dicenda sunt.

Objectum precationis exprimitur, quod ge- neratim sunt omnes sancti, non defuncti, ceu Papistae pro mortuis orant ἄτερ γραφῆς, & sigilla- tim hic erat Paulus, qui preces Ephesiorum ex- petit imprimis pro successu muneris sui. Favere hic videtur Grotius Pontificiis, qui credunt sanctos in caelis pro necessitatibus nostris orare, atque ideo eos invocant; Quanquam vero generatim pro Ecclesiae necessitate orare sanctos in caelis nullum sit dubium, specialem tamen necessitatem fidelium eosdem novisse, aut preces audire, à scri- pturis alienum est. Abraham Pater credentium erat : Et Israel vel Jacob inter credentes facile præcipuus : Et de illis populus Israeliticus fate- batur, Efa. LXIV. 16. Abraham nescit nos, & Ifrael ignorat nos : Tu Domine Pater noster. De cætero non debent preces nostræ esse solitariæ, ideo ju- bemur, ut plures, orare : Pater noster &c. Ev ἀνοί- ξει τῶ στόμα[τος] nuspiam est occasione data, & hic exponitur per vocem adjectam ἐν παῤῥησίᾳ, quæ perperam de externa remotione impedimento- rum, sine scripturæ exemplo intelligitur, quum fiduciam in dicendo notet, vid. Actor. IV. 29. 31. uti Joh. XI. 54. fiduciam palam conversandi. Pro liberatione à vinculis Paulum preces expetiisse, hic nulli in mentem venit, nec nisi coacte verba Apostoli eo abripiuntur. Convenientior Græco- rum est observatio, quod Deus aperuerit Aposto- lis os, verba ipsis indendo. Nihil ergo, inquit Theo- phylactus, quod esset dicturus, præmeditabatur Apo- stolus. Sequebatur enim Domini dictum, nolite præ- meditari, quid loquamini : Dabitur enim vobis in illa hora, quid vobis loquendum sit. Haud secus & ipse os suum aperiens proferebat, quæ à Domino sug- gerebantur. Sic cuncta divina gratia exequabatur. Innuit tamen apertio oris etiam nostram ἀδυνα- μίαν, quod os clausum sit ad proferendas res di- vinas, quodque id aperire non valeamus, vel in periculis audeamus, nisi aperiat id nobis Domi- nus. Aperire os phrasis est Ebræa, & significat loqui Jud. XI. 35. 36. Prov. XXXI. Actor. XIII. 14. Sed hic passive accipitur. Vult ut à Deo sibi os aperiatur; Quod etsi antea apertum ipsi magno cum fructu fuerit, ut porro etiam in vinculis sibi aperiatur petit. De fiducia loquendi sic Theophy- lactus : Cum fiducia notum facere mysterium Ev- angelii, hoc est, ut quemadmodum oportet respon- deam, fidentius seu viriliter & sapienter admo- dum. Catenæ eo mihi injunctæ sunt, ut meam ob- struant loquendi licentiam. Animus tamen os mi- hi aperiet, ut fidentior sim ea enarrans, quæ mihi sunt per eum injuncta, qui me legavit. Conf. Col. IV. 4. Quod petit, non ad ipsum, sed ad bonum ipsorum pertinet. Petit sibi sermonem dari, non catenas solvi. Petit apertionem oris, non vincu- lorum. Petit sermonis παῤῥησίαν in ipsis vincu- lis, non liberationem ab iisdem. Cum apertio- ne oris loqui est non tantum prompte & expe- dite loqui, sed etiam aperte, & ut intelligi possi- mus, nec non sine pavore, vel cum singulari fidu- cia. Vincula Apostolo non erant gravia, sed ser- monem vinci ri grave sibi futurum ostendit. Neque tam est de vita sua solicitus, quam de bono Eccle- siæ, cupiens omnia impleri Evangelio, neque ut tan- tum ejus fama aliqua spargeretur per orbem, sed ut sermo in apertione oris pronuntiatus sine tegmi- ne, sine ænigmate, sine ambagibus, in clara expli- catione veritatis in omnem memoriam extaret. Id igitur jubebat Ephesios petere, ut sibi aperiretur ostium sermonis, & daretur loquendi occasio, & au- res ac corda aperta per Spiritum amoris & timoris DEI, & ut in illis occasionibus Deus sibi adsit, & sibi det sermonem apertum, nullis involucris vela- tum, & claram explicationem veritatis jubiret lo- qui, ut hic Coccejus : Qui vocem ἐν παῤῥησίᾳ ex- plicat ἀκωλύτως palam, publice, ut non opus sit mussare, aut clam agere è collatione Marc. IIX. 32. Joh. VII. 4. 13. 26. cap. XI. 14. 54. Sed magis ad rem facere videtur locus Act. IV. 29. in quo fiducia sermonis notatur hac voce, vi collationis, vers. 31. quæ etiam propria est vocis significatio. Vid. Æschin. in orat. contra Timarch. apud Sui- dam. Cur autem à propria significatione disce- dendum, quum commode κατ' ἐπεξήγησιν hæc vox accipi in Præsenti possit? Denique jubet Apo- stolus peti à DEO, ut sibi concedatur παῤρησιάζε- θαι ε̐ν αὐτω̃, addito, ὡς δει̃ με λαλη̃σαι. Παῤρησιά- ζεθαι ε̐ν τω̃ Εὐαγγελίω est prædicare libere, ut et- iamsi ipse non sit liber, sed vinctus, tamen Evange- lium non vinciatur, 2. Tim. II. 9. ut explicat Cocce- jus ipse. Interim non male fatemur, ut idem obser- vat ad illud Apostoli παῤρησιάζεθαι pertinere etiam coram omnibus loqui, & neminem, quic- quam audire volentem, celare. Quod contra Bellarminum, Apostolum non omnia palam do- cuisse, contendentem notat. Conferatur Coloss. I. 28. Evangelii mysterium non est ille Evangelii sermo, cujus res occultæ antehac fuere, sed Ev- angelium totum naturæ ignotum, & à seculo absconditum, Ephes. I. 9. 13. cap. III. 4. 9. An catena illa, de qua Actor. XXIX. 20. hoc est, prioris captivitatis Romanæ, an vero posterio- ris hoc loco respiciatur, dubium est. E priori liberatus est, elapso biennio, non item è poste- riori, quam vero intelligi censet Pareus in Pro- legom. epist. ad Rom. eoque facere collationem textus 2. Tim. IV. 12. judicat Crocius: Principum legati honorifice haberi solent. At Christi lega- tus in vincula conjectus, qui missus erat, ut ho- mines peccatorum nexibus solutos in libertatem assereret. Verum ad quod es ipse nunc delegatus, quærit Theophylactus? Ad homines quidem, ut eos Deo conciliem. Hi vero me in catenas & vincu- la conjecere, tametsi jure gentium caveatur, impu- nes esse Oratores & Nuntios, quippe qui Domi- norum mandata jam deferunt.

PARS III. CAPITIS VI. CONCLUSIO EPISTOLÆ. Causa missi Tychici & votum finale.

## 6:21
Ver. 21. That you also may know the things concerning me) Those things which pertain to me.

What I am doing, Tychicus will make known to you all) The Syriac does not read 'all': and the discourse coheres more correctly without it. It has also been noted in certain books that this word does not exist. This Tychicus was from Asia, Acts XX. 4, and perhaps an Ephesian. Thus Titus was sent to the Corinthians, himself a Corinthian.

The beloved brother) By this title the same Tychicus is distinguished in Col. IV. 7. It is credible that he was more advanced in age. For Paul calls younger men 'children' more often. More advanced men are called 'Haverim' by the Rabbis.

And a faithful minister in the Lord) The word 'minister' is taken here to include all who devote effort to the Gospel, such as were the Evangelists, and the Apostles themselves in particular. See 1 Cor. III. 5, 2 Cor. III. 6, VI. 4, XI. 23, above III. 7; when he says 'faithful', he shows that he is to be trusted safely.

Latin:

Vers. 21. Ἱνα δὲ εἰδη̃τε κἁι ὑμει̃ς τὰ κατ̓ ε̐μὲ) Ea quæ ad me pertinent.

Τί πράσσω, πάντα ὑμι̃ν γνωρίσει Τυχικὸς) πάντα non legit Syrus: & rectius sine eo cohæret oratio. Notatum etiam in quibusdam libris eam vocem non extare. Ex Asia erat hic Tychicus, Act. XX. 4. & forte Ephesius. Sic ad Corinthios missus Titus, Corinthius & ipse.

Ὁ ἀγαπητπ̀ς ἀδελφὸς) Hoc titulo idem Tychicus insi- gnitur Col. IV. 7. Credibile est, provectiorem fuisse ætate. Juniores enim τέκνα magis appellat Paulus. Provectiores Rabbinis dicuntur חבירים.

Καὶ πιστὸς Διάκονο̂ς ε̐ν Κυρίω) Διακόνου vox hic sumitur, ut comprehendat omnes, qui Evangelio navant operam, quales erant Evangelistæ, ipsique imprimis Apostoli. Vi. de 1. Cor. III. 5. 2. Cor. III. 6. VI. 4. XI. 23. supra III. 7. cum dicit fidelem, ostendit tuto ei credi.

## 6:22
V. 22. Whom I have sent to you for this very thing, that you may know the things concerning us, and that he may comfort your hearts) A brief expression for 'and that he himself may comfort', etc.

The reason for Tychicus being sent is twofold: 1. Information concerning the state of Paul, which was also done for others from his chains, and the particle 'and' indicates this, by which he wished to testify his love to them. This declared how much he loved them, and how much they loved him. For it was no small journey. Ephesus was distant from Rome by 249 miles. There appears no reason why the word 'all', which is read in almost all codices, should be omitted. For the discourse does not cohere badly with that retained. The Ephesians were anxious, and not without cause, about the chains of Paul, perhaps also troubled by various errors. Therefore, that they might be fully informed, it seemed that Tychicus should be sent, from whom they could know all things most excellently. If he was cherished by Paul as a most dear brother, there was surely nothing more welcome to all: If he was a faithful (minister), he could not be a liar, as Theophylact says. All things, how I am, how the case is being conducted before Caesar, in what frame of mind I am in chains, what my zeal is, what my works. Which he did not wish them to be ignorant of, so that they might have a type and example of patience, constancy, hope, prudence, and a cause for condoling, for giving thanks to GOD, and for praying. He calls him a minister, not a private person, but of the Gospel, Ephes. III. 7, because he calls him a fellow-servant, Coloss. IV. 7, even though he also performed ministries for them; cf. 2 Tim. IV. 12. 2. Consolation, both because of the sadness concerning the chains of Paul, and because they were dismayed by various rumors and whispers of Pseudo-Apostles. There will be great consolation if they hear Paul in Rome, in the mistress of cities and the citadel of the Roman empire, comforting them from prison and chains, says Jerome.

Latin:

V. 22. Ὀ̔ν ἔπεμψα πρὸς ὑμα̃ς εἰς αὐτὸ τυ̃το, ἵνα γνω̃τε τὰ περὶ ἡμω̃ν, καὶ παρακαλέση τὰς καρδίας ὑμω̃ν) Brevis loquutio pro καὶ ίνα αὐτὸς παρακαλέση &c.

Causa missi Tychici gemina est, 1. informatio de statu Pauli, quæ & aliis è vinculis facta est, idque particula καὶ indicat, quibus ea ratione amorem suum testari voluit. Hoc declarabat, quam eos diligeret, quam eum ipsi. Non enim parvum iter erat. Ephesus Romæ 249. milliaribus distabat. Cur vox πάντα, quæ in omnibus fere codicibus legitur, omittenda sit, ratio apparet nulla. Nec enim oratio male cohæret illa reten- ta. Soliciti nec immerito erant Ephesii de vin- culis Pauli, forte etiam erroribus variis turbati. Ut ergo plene informentur, mittendus videba- tur Tychicus, ex quo omnia optime cognoscere poterant. Qui si à Paulo colebatur ceu frater charissimus, omnium profecto nihil erat gratius: Si fidus (minister) mendax esse non poterat, Theo- phylacto dicente. Omnia, quomodo habear, quo- modo agatur causa coram Cæsare, quo in vincu- lis sim animo, quodnam meum studium, quæ ope- ra. Quæ ipsos non voluit ignorare, ut typum & exemplar haberent patientiæ, constantiæ, spei, prudentiæ, & causam condolendi, gratias DEO agendi, orandi. Ministrum dicit, non privatum, sed Evangelii, Ephes. III. 7. quia conservum vo- cat, Coloss. IV. 7. etsi etiam ipsi ministeria præsti- terit; conf. 2. Tim. IV. 12. 2. Consolatio, tum ob tristitiam de vinculis Pauli, tum quod consternati rumoribus variis ac susurris Pseudo-Apostolo- rum fuerint. Futura grandis consolatio, si audi- rent Paulum Romæ in Domina urbium & arce Romani imperii de carcere & vinculis consolan- tem, inquit Hieronymus.

## 6:23
Ver. 23. Peace to the brethren) Prosperous things. And love with faith) Which two joined together have the promise of eternal life; in the Manuscript 'and mercy with faith'.

Most take these as a wish. To Cocceius it seems to be an admonition, but done through prayer and a vow, who renders this paraphrase: I have nothing more in my wishes, there is nothing that I desire more, than that the brethren may have peace and charity with faith, and that God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ may grant these to them. Wherefore I pour out my prayers to God, hoping that God will give this to them, as a most kind Father for the sake of his Son Jesus Christ, and that Christ will give it to them, because he is Lord. Beza added the particle 'to you'. But it is not held in the text, therefore it should not have been added. Although the name of peace in the manner of the Hebrews embraces all good things, especially however spiritual goods, in which the peace of GOD stands out, or with GOD ἡ ὑπερέχουσα πάντα νοῦν, inasmuch as it is a certain serenity and tranquility of the soul resting, putting to flight the entire storm and whirlwind of perturbations, and guards the hearts of the saints like some rampart, Phil. IV. 7. Charity is understood both as that by which they love GOD, and that by which they love their neighbor according to the first and second table of the Decalogue μετὰ πίστεως. True charity cannot exist without faith, 2. Pet. I. 5, nor faith without charity, Gal. V. 6. Although salvation is attributed to faith alone, and not truly to both faith and charity; yet faith does not exist alone, nay rather it is dead if it be without charity, James II.

From God the Father, and the Lord Jesus Christ) He has joined the principal cause with the secondary cause, so that we may always remember that we are obligated to both.

Cocceius has already touched upon this jurisdiction of Grotius, in whose refutation we acquiesce: Wrongly, he says, is Christ the Lord of glory, 1. Cor. II. 8. Ἀρχηγὸς τῆς σωτηρίας, Heb. II. 10.
