He is the first and the last, Rev. I. 17. He who calls Christ a secondary cause denies that He is God, or that He is a divine person, Rom. I. 4. For insofar as He is a person, He is a cause. For persons are actions. If a person is dependent and not primary, He is not God. Wherefore, as it is unscriptural, so it is of evil sound to call Christ a secondary cause. Furthermore, if Christ is a secondary cause, we cannot glorify Him, nor give Him thanks, nor believe in Him, nor invoke Him. For He does not have an independent will or authority, He does not have life in Himself, nor does He give life to whom He wills, John V. 21, nor is He the Lord, through whom are all things, 1. Cor. VIII. 6.

Latin:

Vers. 23. Εἰρήνη τοῖς ἀδελφοῖς) Res prosperæ. Καὶ ἀγάπη μετὰ πίστεως) Quæ duo juncta promissum habent vitæ æternæ, in Manuscripto καὶ ἔλεος μετὰ πί- στεως.

Plerique hæc ut votum accipiunt. Coccejo vi- detur monitum esse, sed per precationem & εὐ- χὴν factum, qui hanc reddit paraphrasin: Nihil magis in votis habeo, nihil est, quod magis deside- rem, quam ut fratres cum fide habeant pacem & charitatem, atque ut Deus Pater & Dominus Jesus Christus hæc ipsis largiantur. Quapropter preces meas ad Deum effundo, sperans, Deum hoc ipsis daturum, ut benignissimum Patrem propter Fili- um suum Jesum Christum, & Christum id illis da- turum, quia est Dominus. Beza addidit particu- lam vobis. Sed ea in textu non habetur, ideo addenda non fuit. Pacis nomen quamvis Ebræ- orum more omnia complectatur bona, imprimis tamen bona spiritualia, in quibus eminet pax DEI, vel cum DEO ἡ ὑπερέχουσα πάντα νοῦν, ut- pote quæ serenitas quædam est, & tranquillitas animæ quiescentis, universam tempestatem & tur- binem perturbationum fugans, & corda sancto- rum custodit instar valli alicujus, Phil. IV. 7. Cha- ritas intelligitur tum illa, qua DEUM, tum qua proximum diligunt secundum primam & secun- dam Decalogi tabulam μετὰ πίστεως. Non po- test sine fide esse vera charitas, 2. Petr. I. 5. nec sine charitate fides, Gal. V. 6. Etsi fidei soli tri- buatur salus, non vero & fidei & charitati; fides tamen sola non existit, imo mortua est, si sine charitate sit, Jac. II.

Ἀπὸ Θεῦ Πατρὸς, καὶ Κυρίου ἰησοῦ χριστοῦ) Conjunxit causam principem cum causa secunda, ut semper memine- rimus, nos utrique obligatos.

Perstrinxit hanc Grotii δικαιοδοξίαν jam Cocce- jus, cujus elencho acquiescimus: Prave, inquit, Christus est Dominus gloriæ, 1. Cor. II. 8. Ἀρχη- γὸς τῆς σωτηρίας, Ebr. II. 10. est primus & ulti- mus, Apoc. I. 17. Qui Christum dicit causam se- cundam, negat esse Deum, sive esse personam di- vinam, Roman. I. 4. Nam quatenus persona est, causa est. Personæ enim sunt actiones. Si persona est dependens & non prima, non est Deus. Quare ut ἄγραφον, ita κακέμφατον est dicere Christum causam secundam. Porro, si Christus causa secun- da est, non possumus ipsum glorificare, neque ipsi gratias agere, neque in ipsum credere, neque eum invocare. Nam non habet voluntatem indepen- dentem sive αὐτοκρατορικὸν, non habet vitam in se- ipso, neque dat vitam, cui vult, Joh. V. 21. neque est Dominus, per quem sunt omnia, 1. Cor. VIII. 6.

## 6:24
Ver. 24. Grace be with all them that love our Lord Jesus Christ in sincerity) He greets not only the Ephesians, but also all Christians in Asia. The word for sincerity (incorruption) related to the mind is read also in Tit. II. 7, where however it is absent in some Codices, because a word of the same meaning, ἀδιαφθορίαν, preceded it. In the Glossary, Plato and Demosthenes use the word ἀδιάφθορος, incorrupt. Plato also uses the word ἀδιαφθόρως in the same sense. He is signified who, by no force, no entreaties, no allurements, suffers himself to be corrupted, that is, to be led away from what is right. Such a state of mind is here called ἀφθαρσία, and this can be consistently translated as ἀφθαρσία. Just as a virgin is corrupted by defilement, so is the mind by any sin whatsoever. Thus Chrysostom here, and other Greeks after him.

We do not disapprove of this sense, which is favored by the version of B. Luther, unverrückt, which Emser also followed as unverrücklich. Among the Reformed, Bullinger, Calvin, Aretius, Coccejus, and Crocius agree, namely that the sincerity of love is being noted: even though Beza rendered it as 'unto immortality.' Doubtless they saw that in the Greek it is not εἰς ἀφθαρσίαν but ἐν ἀφθαρσίᾳ, which is not 'unto immortality,' nor 'with immortality,' but 'in incorruption,' as the Vulgate rendered it. However, that ἐν is placed for εἰς or σὺν could not be proven; one must not rashly depart from its proper meaning. Jerome notes that some have taken the word to refer to the chastity of the body; but he rejects that. Erasmus admits that it signifies the sincerity and integrity of a mind free from every corruption of vices: And this word coheres not with the first χάρις, but with the verb τῶν ἀγαπώντων. Thus, therefore, he commends at the end, and in the votive clause to the Ephesians, again the sincere love of Jesus Christ, and promises to those who love him the grace of GOD; It is of the grace of GOD that we are both able and willing to love the Lord, and God further grants grace to those who love; which the Apostle prays for them, and bids them be certain of it, adding the customary seal of the word Amen. May God the Father of all grace grant that we may embrace the Lord Jesus with both a sincere and constant true faith, and love him with our whole heart, in the power of the Holy Spirit: To Him be glory in Christ Jesus through the Holy Spirit now and for evermore. Amen!

Latin:

Vers. 24. Ἡ χάρις μετὰ πάντων τῶν ἀγαπώντων τὸν Κύ- ριον ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦν χριστὸν ἐν ἀφθαρσίᾳ) Non Ephesios tan- tum salutat, sed & omnes in Asia Christianos. Ἀφθαρσίας vox ad animum relata legitur & Tit. II. 7. ubi tamen ab- est ea in nonnullis Codicibus, quia præcessit vox idem va- lens ἀδιαφθορίαν. In Glossario ἀδιάφθορος, incorruptus, utuntur Plato & Demosthenes. Plato & ἀδιαφθόρως voce sensu eodem. Significatur is, qui nulla vi, nullis precibus, nullis illecebris se corrumpi, id est, à recto abduci patitur. Talis animi status hic dicitur ἀφθαρσία, potestque hoc is ἀφθαρσία verti constanter. Sicut virgo stupro corrum- pitur, sic peccato quovis animus. Ita hic Chrysostomus, & ex illo Græci alii.

Non improbamus hunc sensum, cui favet B. Lutheri versio, unverrückt, quam Emserus etiam sequutus unverrücklich. Annuunt è Reformatis Bullingerus, Calvinus, Aretius, Coccejus, Crocius, quod nempe notetur dilectionis sinceritas: etsi Beza reddiderit ad immortalitatem: Nimirum viderunt illi in Græco non haberi εἰς ἀφθαρσίαν sed ἐν ἀφθαρσίᾳ, quod non est ad immortalita- tem, nec cum immortalitate, sed in incorruptio- ne, ut Vulgatus reddidit. Quod autem ἐν pro εἰς vel σὺν ponatur, probari non potuit; à cujus pro- pria significatione temere recedendum non est. Hieronymus notat quosdam, qui de castimonia corporis vocem accepere; sed reprobat illud. Era- smus sinceritatem ac integritatem animi vacantis omni corruptela vitiorum significari fatetur: Et cohæret vox hæc non cum prima χάρις, sed cum verbo τῶν ἀγαπώντων. Ita ergo commendat sub finem, & in clausula votiva Ephesiis iterum dile- ctionem sinceram Jesu Christi, & pollicetur dili- gentibus gratiam DEI; Gratiæ DEI est, quod di- ligere & valeamus & velimus Dominum, & iis, qui diligunt, porro præstat Deus gratiam: quam pre- catur iisdem Apostolus, deque ea certos esse jubet, addens signaculum consuetum vocis Amen. Lar- giatur Deus Pater omnis gratiæ, ut & sincere & constanter veræ fidei amplectamur Dominum Jesum, eumque diligamus toto pectore, in virtute Spiritus Sancti: Ei sit gloria in Christo Jesu per Spi- ritum Sanctum nunc & in seculo- rum secula. Amen!

# Philippians

## 1:1 Introduction
[Abraham Calov, Biblia Novi Testamenti Illustrata (Vol. 2, Part 1). English: machine translation, The Faith Received (Mere Orthodoxy); the original follows each comment.]
I. N. I. TO THE EPISTLE OF ST. PAUL TO THE PHILIPPIANS.

Latin:

I. N. I. AD EPISTOLAM S. PAULI AD PHILIPPENSES.

## 1:1 Introduction: Prologue of Grotius
PROLOGUE OF GROTIUS.

This epistle, although it was itself written at Rome in chains, is more joyful, more cheerful, and more gentle than the others, for the reason that Paul had been twice at Philippi, which is the chief city of Macedonia, and a Colony, Acts 16 and 20, and Paul's preaching had succeeded well there, with the purple-seller woman converted, the Pythonic spirit cast out, the jailer converted by a miracle, and satisfaction received from the magistrates for the injury received. After which times, most of the Philippians had faithfully kept those things which they had received from Paul, and had testified their love and reverence for so good a teacher in many ways. Yet the discourse sometimes rises into a certain harshness against men similar to those whom he notes to the Galatians, who, although they were not Jews themselves, nevertheless persuaded those whom Paul had converted from the Gentiles to Judaism, taking the opportunity from Paul's chains and the evils which seemed to threaten Christians who were not Judaizing. Against this design, which proceeded from nothing but care for the flesh, Paul inveighs with the fortitude that is required.

that he might bring back a strong report, that the Apostle had diligently investigated the state of that Church, and having known the faith and piety of the saints in it, but the insidious machinations of the Pseudo-Apostles, he had wished to accompany Epaphroditus, who was returning to his own people, with a letter. Salmasius indeed denies, under the name of Walo Messalinus, diff. I. against Petavius on Bishops and Presbyters, cap. II. p. 117, that Epaphroditus was sent by the Bishops of the Philippians to Paul, but in this he rashly opposes himself to the Greeks and Latins, and indeed to the Apostle himself, out of the fervor, as it appears, of the dispute. For the Apostle himself clearly indicates this, Phil. 4:18, 'having received from Epaphroditus the things from you.' Whence Chrysostom in the preface: But that Epaphroditus was sent by them, hear him saying: 'I have all things and abound, I am filled, having received from Epaphroditus the things which you sent.' For this reason, therefore, they had sent him, that they might both comfort him and learn of his affairs. For that they also sent to learn this, he shows immediately at the very beginning of the epistle, writing and saying concerning his own state: 'But I want you to know, brethren, that the things which happened to me have fallen out rather unto the progress of the gospel.' And again: 'But I hope to send Timothy shortly unto you, that I also may be of good comfort, when I know your state.' That 'that I also' clearly signifies this, that just as you, in order to satisfy your mind, sent to learn of my affairs: So also I may be of good comfort when your affairs are known. Since, therefore, when they had not sent for a long interval (for he indicates that with those words, 'that at last you have flourished again to think of me') and were hearing that he was in chains (for if they had heard of the ill health of Epaphroditus, a man not very famous, such as Paul was, it was much more consistent that they should be troubled about Paul;) Therefore, in the very prologue of the epistle, he introduces consolation for his own chains, so far from it being the case that one ought to be troubled by them, that one should rather rejoice. This, therefore, was entirely the occasion and cause of the writing for Paul, which Theophylact also, according to his custom, handed down with Chrysostom: But the Philippians had sent to Paul through Epaphroditus the things that were necessary for his life, and at the same time they also wished to know,

OBSERVATIONS.

The city of Philippi in the first part of Macedonia, which was formerly called κρηνίδες, that is, fountain-like, as Artemidorus testifies in Volaterranus, book 8 of his Geography, on account of the very abundant springs flowing forth around the hill upon which it is situated, received its name from Philip of Macedon, who restored and enlarged it. It was a colony, as Luke testifies in Acts 16:12, and indeed not so much of the Thracians, from the neighboring island, as of the Romans, as appears from verse 21. For there the Philippians call themselves Romans. However, Paul having been called into Macedonia by a notable vision shown in Troas, Acts 16:9, in this city, at his first sermon, with Lydia, a seller of purple, being converted with her household, the first beginnings of the Church indeed commenced. But the Church, through the miracles by which the Spirit of Python was cast out of the slave girl, and Paul and Silas were freed from prison, and also the subsequent conversion of the jailer with his family, soon obtained notable growth, so much so that it grew into an entire Church, over which several bishops with deacons were to be set.

They make this the occasion of the epistle, when the Philippians sent Epaphroditus, who might bring aid to Paul, who was established in bonds at Rome, and his were, just as he was being treated at that time. And since it was right that they, when they understood that their Teacher was in chains, should be distressed in spirit not a little, writing to them he reminds them that they ought not on that account to be affected by grief or overwhelmed by perturbation, but rather to rejoice greatly and be glad, since he suffers these things for Christ. But what the Apostle does in this epistle besides that consolation, Chrysostom explains further: Then he gives them counsel that they should cultivate concord and humility, teaching that this is the safest protection for them, and that by this means they can easily become superior to their enemies. For it is not troublesome to your Teachers to be in chains, but to see the disciples not at all in concord among themselves. For the former makes for the advancement of the Gospel, but the latter for its disturbance. When, therefore, he had exhorted them to concord, and had taught that concord proceeds from humility, and had inveighed against the Jews, who, pretending Christianity, were in every way hindering the doctrine, calling them dogs and evil workers, and had persuaded them that they must abstain from them, and had admonished them as to what things they should study, and had discoursed much about matters pertaining to morals, and had composed and refreshed them with those words, The Lord is near, then indeed, with the prudence that became him, he also makes mention of the things sent to him, and thus brings great consolation. Similarly Theophylact: He advises them besides to pursue concord and humility. He carps, moreover, at the Jews, who under the pretext of the Christian name were devastating the doctrines of Christ, and he calls these dogs and wicked workers. He discourses also to the Philippians about the honesty of life and morals: He also prudently makes mention of the necessities transmitted to him.

Moreover, although this epistle is so adorned that it may seem more hortatory than didactic, since it treats of doctrines while almost doing something else, yet the Apostolic exhortation to constancy in faith, and also to concord and obedience, is filled with various dogmas of faith not perfunctorily expounded, so that these make, as it is said, both pages almost in the same. For he taught briefly, but clearly, about the blessed state of souls after death concerning the declaration of his confidence, and about the vivification of Christ in his body, whether through life or through death, chap. I: he treated the sublime article concerning the emptying and exaltation expressly, as nowhere else, in chap. II, although on the occasion of an exhortation to the study of charity and humility. Furthermore, when he was warning them to beware of Pseudo-Apostles, he elucidated very clearly the chief head of that faith concerning the imputed righteousness of Christ, and proposing the end of the enemies of the cross of Christ, he treated clearly of the mystery of the transfiguration of our body, chap. III. Finally, he expounded the peace of God, which guards our hearts in Christ Jesus, indeed by way of a wish, but in very emphatic words, chap. IV, so that Flacius seems to have hit the mark more than others when he judged that the whole body of Christian doctrine is treated in this epistle, inasmuch as it first highly commends the Christian religion, and exhorts all most ardently to it, then discourses about Christ and his emptying and passion and the acquisition of immense merits, and finally proposes the mode of apprehending the merits, and refutes the false method of justification by works.

B. Luther proposed the argument and summary thus: In this epistle St. Paul praises and exhorts the Philippians to remain and proceed in the true faith, and to make progress in charity. But since false Apostles and workers always harm the faith, he warns them to beware of them, and rejects righteousness that is devoid of faith and human, and finally exhorts them to peace and honest conversation, and gives thanks for the gift transmitted. His piety toward the Philippians having thus been declared, in that he perpetually gives thanks and prays for them, and the fruit of his chains having been set forth, as well as his confidence and παῥῥησίἀ of glorifying Christ both in life and in death, which he did in chap. I. Then indeed he exhorts them pathetically to unanimity and humility, by the example of Christ, who was emptied for our sake, and also to the continuation and sincerity of obedience, promising the mission of Timothy, whom he commends significantly along with Epaphroditus, who was sent back to them now after the restoration of his health: And all these things in chap. II. Afterwards he also commands them to beware of those workers from the Jews, and opposes to their vain boasting and perverse doctrine concerning justification his own true glory and righteousness, which is obtained not from the law but through faith in Christ, and proposes himself as an example to those striving for the goal of salvation, by which he completes the rule of faith and life, as well as the hope of future glorification, with which chap. III is concluded. Finally, he excites all the brethren, and some by name, to perseverance, joy in the Lord, and gentleness toward others, and prayers, with a wish for the peace of God, inflames them to whatever is worthy of praise and honest, and for a sacrifice of gratitude with a pious wish and celebration of divine remuneration gives thanks to GOD, greets the saints, and prays for the grace of GOD for them, which are the contents of chap. IV and the last.

The parts of the epistle, besides the inscription and the votive conclusion, can be constituted as two: I. Παθητικὴ, the declaration of pious affection toward the Philippians, chap. I, which is a preparation for the following exhortation: II. Παραινετικὴ or exhortation, both to unanimity, the adjuncts of which are humility, by the example of Christ, and the observation of true teachers, Timothy and Epaphroditus, chap. II, with the avoidance of false teachers, with whom the Apostle compares himself as to origin, faith, course, and end, chap. III, and also to other studies of piety and honesty, with a signification of joy perceived from their liberality, chap. IV.

PART I. OF THE EPISTLE, THE PATHETIC.

Latin:

PROOEMIUM GROTII.

ESt hæc epistola quanquam & ipsa Romæ in vin- culis scripta, lætior, alacriorque, & blandior cæ- teris, ideo, quod Philippis, quæ urbs præcipua est Macedoniæ, & Colonia, bis fuisset Paulus Act. XVI. & XX. & bene successisset ibi Pauli prædicatio, con- versa muliere purpuraria, ejecto Spiritu Pythonico, con- verso & per miraculum commentariensi, accepta à magi- stratibus ob injuriam acceptam satisfactione. Post quæ tempora Philippenses plerique fideliter custodierant ea, quæ à Paulo acceperant, amoremque in tam bonum ma- gistrum & reverentiam multis modis erant testati. Insur- git tamen nonnunquam in asperitatem aliquam oratio ad- versus homines similes illis, quos ad Galatas notat, qui cum Judæi ipsi non essent, illis tamen, quos Paulus ex gentibus converterat, suadebant Judaismum, occasione capta ex vinculis Pauli & malis, quæ Christianis non Ju- daizantibus imminere videbantur. In quod consilium ex sola carnis cura profectum, qua debet fortitudine, de- spuit Paulus.

fortem referret, indagasse Apostolum sedulo Ec- clesiæ istius statum, & cognitâ sanctorum in ea- dem fide ac pietate, Pseudo-Apostolorum vero insidiosa molitione literis Epaphroditum ad suos revertentem comitari voluisse. Negat quidem Salmasius, sub nomine Walonis Messalini diff. I. contra Petav. de Episc. & Presbyt. cap. II. p. 117. temere ne- Epaphroditum à Philippensium Episcopis ad Pau- gat Epa- lum missum, sed in eo temere se Græcis Latinisque imo Apostolo ipsi opponit, ex fervore, ut appa- ret, disputationis. Nam clare id indicat Aposto- lus ipse, Phil. IV. 18. δεξάμενος παρὰ Ἐπαφροδί- του τὰ παρ᾽ ὑμῶν. Unde Chrysostomus in præloquio: Quod autem missus ab illis fuerit Epaphroditus, audi ipsum dicentem: Habeo autem omnia & abun- do, repletus sum acceptis ab Epaphrodito, quæ misi- stis. Ob hanc igitur causam miserant, ut & illum consolarentur, & res illius cognoscerent. Nam quod & hoc cognituri miserint, in ipso statim epistolæ ini- tio ostendit de suo statu scribens ac dicens: Scire autem vos volo, quia quæ circa me sunt, magis ad profectum venerunt Evangelii. Et rursus: Spero autem Timotheum me cito mittere ad vos, ut & ego bono animo sim cognitis quæ circa vos sunt. Illud, ut & ego, perspicue significat hoc, ut quemadmo- dum vos, quo vobis animum expleretis, misistis ad mea cognoscenda: Ita & ego bono animo sim rebus vestris cognitis. Quoniam igitur quum longo in- tervallo jam non misissent (id enim indicat illis verbis, quoniam tandem aliquando refloruistis pro me sentire) audiebantque ipsum in vinculis esse (nam si de Epaphroditi mala valetudine audierant, homi- nis non valde clari, qualis quidem Paulus erat, mul- to magis consentaneum erat, de Paulo ipsos contur- bari;) Idcirco in ipso epistolæ proæmio inducit con- solationem pro ipsis suis vinculis, tantum abesse, ut inde perturbari oporteat, ut gaudendum potius sit. Hæc ergo Paulo omnino occasio fuit, & causa scriptionis, quam etiam cum Chrysostomo pro mo- re suo tradidit Theophylactus: Philippenses vero per Epaphroditum transmiserant Paulo, quæ ipsi ad vitam erant necessaria, simul etiam rescire opta- bant,

OBSERVATIONES.

Philippi urbs in prima Macedoniæ parte, quæ κρηνίδες, hoc est fontana, teste Artemidoro apud Volateranum libr. IIX. Geogr. ob fontes uberri- mos circa collem, cui imposita est, promanantes, quondam vocata est, à Philippo Macedone, qui eam instauravit & amplificavit, nomen accepit. Colonia fuit, teste Luca Act. XVI. 12. & quidem non tam Thaciorum, ex insula vicina, quam Ro- manorum, ut è v. 21. apparet. Ibi enim Philippen- ses se Romanos appellant. Vocato autem insigni visione Paulo in Macedoniam, in Troada exhibi- ta, Act. XVI. 19. in hac urbe, ad primam ejus con- cionem, è Lydia purpurarum venditrice,cum do- mo suâ, conversa, prima quidem cœperunt Ec- clesiæ auspicia. Quæ vero per miracula ejecti ex ancilla Spiritus Pythonis, & liberati ex carcere Pauli & Silæ, nec non subsequutam commentari- ensis cum familia ejus conversionem, insignia mox nacta est incrementa, adeo ut integrum Ec- clesia eorum, cui plures Episcopi cum Diaconis præficiendi fuerint, excreverit.

Occasionem epistolæ hanc faciunt, quum Phi- lippenses Epaphroditum mitterent, qui subsidium Paulo in vinculis Romæ constituto afferret, ejusq; bant, quemadmodum tunc cum eo ageretur. Et quo- niam par erat, illos, cum Præceptorem vinctum in- tellexissent, animo haud mediocriter angi, ad eos scribens commonefacit, nihil propterea hos vel mœ- rore affici, vel offundi perturbatione debere, quin potius lætari magnopere & gaudere, quandoquidem pro Christo hæc patiatur. Quid vero præter con- solationem istam in hac epistola agat Apostolus, sic exponit porro Chrysostomus: Deinde consilium illis dat, ut concordiam atque humilitatem colant, hoc illis tutissimum esse præsidium docens, atque hac ratione illos facile inimicis suis superiores fieri posse. Non enim Doctoribus vestris molestum est in vin- culis esse, sed discipulos inter se minime concordes videre. Illud enim vel ad provehendum Evange- lium facit, hoc vero ad disturbandum. Quum igi- tur illos ad concordiam esset cohortatus, concordiam vero ab humilitate proficisci docuisset, atque adver- sus Judæos, qui Christianismum prætendentes omni- bus modis dogmati officiebant, invectus esset, canes eos vocans, ac malos operarios, atque ab illis abstinen- dum esse suasisset, & quibus rebus studendum esset, admonuisset, multaque disseruisset de rebus ad mores pertinentibus, eosque composuisset, ac recreasset ver- bis illis, Dominus prope est, tum vero ea, quæ ipsum decebat, prudentia, rerum etiam ad se missarum mentionem facit, atque ita magnam affert conso- lationem. Similiter Theophylactus: Consulit præ- terea his, ut concordiam & humilitatem sectentur. Carpit insuper & Judæos, qui sub prætextu nominis Christiani Christi dogmata devastarent, & canes hos nuncupat, & pravos operatores. Edisserit & Philippensibus de vitæ honestate & moribus: Pru- denter etiam facit de transmissis ad se necessariis mentionem.

Cæterum quamvis epistola hæc ita adornata sit, ut parænetica magis, quam didactica videri queat, siquidem fere aliud agendo doctrinas tra- ctet, adhortatio tamen Apostolica ad constantiam in fide, nec non ad concordiam & obedientiam di- versis dogmatibus fidei non perfunctorie expo- sitis referta est, ut hæc utramque, quod dicitur, paginam propemodum in eadem faciant. Nam de statu animarum post mortem beato circa decla- rationem fiduciæ suæ, de Christi vivificatione in corpore suo, sive per vitam, sive per mortem cap. I. breviter, sed perspicue docuit: articulum subli- mem de exinanitione, & exaltatione ex professo, ut nuspiam alias pertractavit cap. II. licet ex occa- sione paræneseos ad charitatis, & humilitatis studi- um. Porro cum de cavendis Pseudo-Apostolis mo- neret, præcipuum illius fidei caput de justitia im- putata Christi admodum præclare dilucidavit, ho- stiumque crucis Christi exitum proponens, de mysterio transfigurationis corporis nostri luculen- ter egit, cap. III. Pacem denique Dei, quæ corda nostra custodit, in Christo Jesu, per modum qui- dem voti, sed verbis perquam emphaticis expo- suit, cap. IV. ut præ aliis rem acu tetigisse videa- tur Flacius, cum totum corpus doctrinæ Christianæ in hac epistola pertractari censuit, utpote quod valde primum commendat Christianam religio- nem, ad eamque omnes hortatur ardentissime, de- inde de Christo ejusque exinanitione ac passione & in- gentium meritorum acquisitione disserit, denique modum apprehendendi merita proponit, & falsam rationem justificationis per opera redarguit.

Argumentum & summam B. Lutherus ita pro- posuit: In hac epistola laudat & hortatur S. Pau- lus Philippenses, ut permaneant & pergant in vera fide, ac proficiant in charitate. Quum vero fidei semper noceant falsi Apostoli, & operarii; de illis cavendis monet, ac rejicit justitiam, fidei expertem, & humanam, ac postremo hortatur ad pacem, & honestam conversationem, gratiasque agit pro trans-misso munere. Declarata itaque pietate sua in Phi-lippenses, quod perpetuo gratias agat, oretque pro ipsis, & exposito fructu vinculorum suorum, nec non omine ac παῥῥησίἀ, Christum cum in vita, tum in morte glorificandi, quæ egit cap. I. Tum vero pathetice ad unanimitatem & humilitatem, exemplo Christi, qui nostri causa exinanitus est, nec non ad obedientiæ continuationem, ac sin-ceritatem hortatur promittens Timothei missio-nem, quem cum Epaphrodito jam post restitutio-nem sanitatis ad ipsos ablegato insigniter com-mendat: Atque hæc omnia cap. II. Postea etiam illos operarios è Judæis caveri jubet, eorumque glo-riationi vanæ & doctrinæ perversæ de justificatio-ne veram suam gloriam & justitiam, quæ non ex lege, sed per fidem in Christum obtinetur, oppo-nit, seque in exemplum contendentibus ad salu-tis metam proponit, qua regulam fidei & vitæ, nec non spem glorificationis futuræ, quibus absolvitur cap. III. Tandem fratres universos, & nominatim quosdam ad perseverantiam, gaudium in Domino, & lenitatem erga alios, ac preces, cum voto pacis Dei excitat, ad quævis laude digna & honesta in-flammat, & pro sacrificio gratitudinis cum pio remunerationis divinæ voto ac celebratione DEI gratias agit, sanctos salutat, & gratiam DEI ipsis precatur, quæ sunt contenta cap. IV. & ultimo.

Partes epistolæ præter inscriptionem & conclu-sionem votivam constitui possunt duæ I. Παθητικὴ, affectus pii erga Philippenses declaratio cap. I. quæ est παρασκευὴ ad sequentem exhortationem: II. Παραινετικὴ vel exhortatio tum ad unanimitatem, cujus προσκείμενα sunt humilitas, exemplo Christi, & observatio verorum doctorum, Timothei & Epa-phroditi cap. II. cum vitatione falsorum doctorum, cum quibus se comparat Apostolus qua ortum, fidem, cursum, & exitum, cap. III. tum ad alia pie-tatis & honestatis studia, cum significatione gaudii è liberalitate ipsorum percepti, cap. IV.

PARS I. EPISTOLÆ ΠΑΘΗΤΙΚΉ. Affectus erga Philippenses declaratio.

## 1:1 Argument
CHAPTER I.

ARGUMENT & PARTITION.

The inscription having been premised, with a prayer the Apostle testifies that he perpetually gives thanks to God for them in his prayers, for their fellowship in the Gospel, and he sets forth his good confidence concerning the completion of the good work begun in them, as well as his desire for them, and the sum of his prayers, and the clear fruit of his bonds in the propagation of the Gospel, preached partly out of contention, partly out of good intention, and his hope of glorifying Christ both in his life and in his death, by the choice of either of which he professes himself to be distressed: hoping nevertheless that for their sake he will be preserved, so that they may rejoice at his coming, provided they have walked worthily of the Gospel, and have not hesitated to fight with one mind with him for the faith, and to suffer.

The parts of the chapter, with the title and prayer preceding, are three: I. It contains the thanksgiving and prayer of the Apostle to v. 11. II. It explains the fruit of the bonds of the death and life of the Apostle to v. 14. III. His confidence of his preservation in life and of his visitation of them, with good omen, that it will come to pass that it may result in their joy and glory, at v. 30.

PART I. Eucharist, and the Apostle's prayer for the Philippians.

Ver. 1. Paul and Timothy) He adds the name of Timothy for the reason that, since he had accompanied Paul on both journeys to Philippi, he was for that reason known and dear to the Philippians.

He also seems to be joined for the reason that they might not doubt concerning the arrival of Timothy, whom Paul promises, and that he might procure for himself greater authority among the same. He also joined the same man to himself in other inscriptions, 2 Cor. I. 1. Coloss. I. 1. 1. Thessal. I. 1. 2. Thessal. I. 1.

Servants of Jesus Christ) He modestly sought that title in which he might associate Timothy with himself. He has no need here to assert apostolic authority for himself, since it was not being called into question at Philippi.

Theophylact had handed these things down more clearly with Chrysostom: In this place the Apostle makes no mention of the dignity of his Apostleship, but subscribes himself a servant of Jesus Christ, which indeed, although it is great, is nevertheless common to many. But writing to Timothy and the Corinthians, he names himself an Apostle. Why that? Because, since he was about to enjoin many things upon them for correction, he assumed the dignity of the Apostleship. But since he is about to enjoin nothing of this kind upon these, but rather deems them all worthy of equal honor, he by no means needed the title of Apostle.

To all the saints in Christ Jesus)

From Chrysostom and the Greek scholia, as also Zanchius and Cornelius à Lapide, Crocius observes that those alone are saints who are in Christ, who is the holy of holies, and holiness itself, and the root of all true holiness, so that unless one is grafted into him, as a branch to a tree, or a shoot to a vine, and sucks and draws holiness from him, he is not a saint, but profane, whence also the unbelieving Jews are henceforth profane.

To those who are in Philippi with the Bishops and Deacons) So most Codices and the Syriac, not as Chrysostom and the Greeks who followed him read, with-bishops. It is not new for the principal persons to be named in the last place, concerning which matter we spoke at Mark XVI. 7. The word Bishops in the Greek versions corresponds to the Hebrew pakidim, by which all who have the care and inspection of any matter are accustomed to be called. In the New Testament all Presbyters were so called, because they had inspection over the flock, Acts XX. 28, which inspection is episkope, Acts I. 20. But he who held the first place in that order was called by excellence the Bishop, whence it came about that this name remained to him by a certain proper right, just as the name of Elders [remained] to the Bishops in Africa. The head of this Philippian presbytery, however, seems to have been Epaphroditus himself, who went from Philippi to Paul, whom Paul will soon call fellow-worker and fellow-soldier.

That is clear from this place, that the name of Episcopate does not imply a preeminence of jurisdiction, such as the Papists dream of, since here in one city several Bishops were established, nor could Grotius deny that (although he gladly wishes to help the Papists), all Presbyters are called Bishops, Acts XX. 28. These things, therefore, are certain. But that he who obtained the first place in the order of Presbyters is called by excellence the Bishop in the New Testament, is evident from no place. For the word is used for any Presbyters whatever, not only in that very place of the Acts, and here, but also 1 Tim. III. 2, Tit. I. 7. Nor is the verb exercising oversight, 1 Pet. V. 2, or the name of oversight, 1 Tim. III. 1, Acts I. 20, used otherwise, outside of which places none of these occur, except that Christ is called Bishop antonomastically and with the addition of our souls by Saint Peter, 1 Epist. II. 25. Therefore the distinction of the Papist schools between Bishop and Presbyter, by which the former is constituted superior to the latter by a certain power of jurisdiction of ordaining and consecrating, has no foundation in the sacred writings. Does not Saint Peter also, exhorting the presbyters of those to whom he had directed his first epistle, namely the sojourners of the dispersion of Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia, chap. V., sufficiently testify that there was no episcopal order in the churches of those places at that time, but only a presbyteral one; of whom he also calls himself a fellow-presbyter. Acts 12:30. Only Presbyters are named who administered the Jerusalem Church, no Bishops; indeed there was no Bishop in the primitive Church, except the Presbyter, who were themselves also Bishops, and several in one city: as in chapter 14:23 it is said of Paul and Barnabas that in the cities of Cilicia they appointed and ordained Presbyters throughout every Church: who had no Bishop set over them, because they themselves were and were called Bishops, they appointed. Furthermore, chapter 15, the Apostles together with the Presbyters are mentioned in the Jerusalem Church as the leaders of that Church, v. 11, with no mention made of Bishops among them, because those Presbyters were also Bishops: nor in the Council were there any others besides the Apostles, than the Presbyters, with the whole Church, or the assembly of the faithful v. 6, none v. 21, none v. 23, Bishops are mentioned, because they were included under the name of Presbyters. But neither is any single Bishop listed among these, because at that time there existed no such person who alone had authority over the rest. Therefore Theodoret himself, to whom Papists otherwise appeal in this cause in his Commentary on chapter 1 of the first to Timothy: τὲς ἀυτὲς ἐκάλεν ποτὲ Πρεσβυτέρους κὴ Ἐπισκόπως. They formerly called the same men Presbyters and Bishops, which Theodoret gathers from Acts 20 and Titus 1. Concerning which passage, see if you please, against Dionysius Petavius who argues at length, Walo Messalinus in his dissertation on Bishops and Presbyters, book 1, chapter 1. On this text Theodoret has it thus: He joined Deacons to Bishops, when he had made no mention of Presbyters. Otherwise it could not even happen that many Bishops were pastors of one city. Whence it is that they were, namely, Presbyters, whom he named Bishops. Nor could the Jesuit Petavius deny this against Salmasius, page 44. That Presbyters were sometimes called true Bishops, and that there were several in the same city. Indeed he confessed, as cited by Walo Messalinus in the aforementioned place, p. 377, that it was not decreed by divine law that there should be one Bishop in individual cities and Churches, but by the authority of the Church and the sanctions of councils. And Cornelius à Lapide acknowledges from Jerome on Titus 1, that formerly before the schism, Churches were governed not so much by distinct authority and jurisdiction as by the common counsel, labor, and Spirit of the Presbyters. Why therefore have the Papists diverged from this Apostolic custom, or why do they impudently assert that that distinction was already in use in the age of the Apostles and ought to be considered of divine law? If there had been an ὁ Ἐπίσκοπος among the Philippians so called by way of excellence, certainly the Apostle would not have passed him over here.

Nor indeed is there any reason why it should be said with Cornelius à Lapide that Epaphroditus the letter-bearer was that Bishop, which Grotius, playing the Papist, similarly hints here. For that will have to be proven. Dorotheus certainly testifies that Epaphroditus was Bishop in Adriana in Syria. Chrysostom, however, in the argument of the epistle calls Epaphroditus a man and σφόδρα ἐπίσημον not very famous. St. Jerome certainly appeals to this place as very clear in the aforementioned Commentary on the epistle to Titus. Let someone think that it is not the opinion of the scriptures but our own, that Bishop and Presbyter are one, and that one is a name of age, the other of office, let him read the words of the Apostle writing to the Philippians: Paul and

Timothy, servant of Jesus Christ, who are at Philippi, with the Bishops & Presbyters, grace to you and peace, and the rest. Philippi is one city of Macedonia. And certainly in one city there could not be many, as they are called, Bishops, but because he called those same persons Bishops at that time whom he also called Presbyters, for that reason he spoke indifferently of Bishops and Presbyters. We add from the Greek Scholiasts on 1 Tim. III: Τί δήποτε τὰς πρεσβυτέρους παρέλιπεν; ὅτι ἐνέμιξεν αὐτὰς τοῖς Ἐπισκόποις. Ἃ γὰρ περὶ Ἐπισκόπων εἶπε, ταῦτα καὶ περὶ τῶν πρεσβυτέρων ἁρμόζει. Ὁμοίως γὰρ καὶ αὐτοὶ ἱερεῖς τέ εἰσι, καὶ διδασκαλίαν εἰσὶ πεπιστευμένοι. Why indeed did he pass over the Presbyters? Because he mixed them with the Bishops. For what he said concerning Bishops, these same things also suit the Presbyters. For they are likewise priests, and the duty of teaching is entrusted to them at the same time. As Paul does in 1 Tim. III. 17. assigned only two different orders in the Church, of Bishops and Deacons, including the Presbyters under them, so the same is observed in the first epistle of Clement to the Corinthians (which Grotius highly esteems) when he says concerning the Apostles, that they, preaching the Word of God through provinces and cities, appointed their first-fruits, having tested them by the Spirit, as Bishops and Deacons of those who were to believe.

Latin:

CAPUT I.

ARGUMENTUM & PARTITIO.

Præmissa inscriptione, cum voto testatur Apo-stolus, se Deo perpetuo pro ipsis gratias age-re in precibus, pro communione Evangelii, bonamque fiduciam de operis boni in ipsis cœpti consummatione, nec non desiderium suum de ipsis, precumque suarum summam, & fructum luculentum vinculorum in Ev-angelii propagatione, partim ex contentio-ne, partim bona intentione prædicati, ac spem de Christo & vita & morte sua glori-ficando, cujus alterutrius optione se angi profitetur, exponit: sperans tamen ipsorum causa se conservatum iri, ut gaudeant de ipsius adventu, dummodo digne Evange-lio ambularint, & una mente cum ipso pro fide militare, ac pati non dubitarint.

Partes capitis, prævio titulo & voto tres sunt, I. Eucharistiam & precationem Apostoli con- tinet ad v. 11. II. Fructum vinculorum mortis & vita Apostoli explicat ad v. 14. III. Fiduciam sua in vita conservationis & visitationis ipsorum, cum omine bono, fore, ut illa gaudio & gloriæ ipso- rum cedat, ad v. 30.

PARS I. Eucharistia, & precatio Apostoli pro Philippensibus.

Vers. 1. Παῦλος καὶ Τιμόθεος) Timothei nomen ideo addit, quod cum in utroque Philippos itinere Paulum esset comitatus, notus ob id, charusque esset Philippensibus.

Junctus etiam ideo videtur, ut de adventu Timothei, quem promittit Paulus, ne dubitarent, utque ipsi autoritatem majorem apud eosdem conciliaret. Adjunxit eundem etiam sibi in aliis inscriptionibus, 2. Cor. I. 1. Coloss. I. 1. 1. Thessal. I. 1. 2. Thessal. I. 1.

Δοῦλοι Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ) Modeste eum quæsivit titulum, in quo Timotheum secum sociaret. Apostolicam autorita- tem hic opus non habet sibi adstruere, quando ea Philip- pis in controversiam non vocabatur.

Luculentius hæc cum Chrysostomo tradiderat Theophylactus: Hoc loco nullam facit sui Aposto- latus dignitate mentionem Apostolus, sed servum se Jesu Christi subscribit, quod sane etsi magnum est, commune tamen est multis. Ad Timotheum autem & Corinthios scribens sese Apostolum nominat. Cur illud? Quia cum illis esset ad castigationem injun- cturus multa, Apostolatus ad se dignitatem rece- pit. His vero cum nihil hujusmodi sit indicturus, quin potius pari omnes in honore dignetur futurum, nequaquam Apostoli appellatione indiguit.

Πᾶσι τοῖς ἁγίοις ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ)

E Chrysostomo & scholiis Græcis, ut & Zanchio & Cornelio à Lapide observat Crocius, eos duntaxat esse sanctos, qui sunt in Christo, qui est sanctus san- ctorum, ipsaque sanctitas, & radix omnis veræ san- ctitatis, ut nisi quis illi inseratur, tanquam ramus arbori, seu palmes viti, ab eaque sanctitatem sugat & hauriat, sanctus non sit, sed profanus, unde & Judæi infideles deinceps profani.

Τοῖς οὖσιν ἐν Φιλίπποις σὺν Ἐπισκόποις καὶ Διακόνοις) Ita plerique Codices & Syrus, non ut Chrysostomus & secuti eum Græci legunt συνεπισκόποις. Non novum est, præci- puas personas postremo loco nominari, qua de re dixi- mus ad Marcum XVI. 7. Ἐπισκόπων vox in Græcis ver- sionibus respondet Ebræis מפקדים, פקידים, quibus quomodo vocari solent omnes, qui cujuslibet rei curam & inspectionem habent. In novo Testamento vocati sic Presbyteri omnes, quia in gregem habebant inspectionem, Act. XX. 28. quæ inspectio ἐπισκοπὴ, Actor. I. 20. At is, qui in eo ordine primas habebat, dicebatur per excellen- tiam ὁ Ἐπίσκοπος, unde factum, ut id ei nomen proprio quodam jure manserit, sicut Senum nomen Episcoporum primis in Africa. Princeps autem hujus presbyterii Philip- pensis videtur fuisse ipse Epaphroditus, qui Philippis ad Pau- lum ivit, quem mox Paulus vocabit συνεργὸν & συστρατιώτην.

Id luculentum ex hoc loco, Episcopatus nomen non inferre jurisdictionis ἐξοχὴν, qualem Papistæ somniant, quum in una civitate hic plures con- stituti fuerint Episcopi, nec diffiteri id potuit Gro- tius, (etsi lubenter juvare Papistas cupiat) Pres- byteros omnes Episcopos vocari, Act. XX. 28. Hæc ergo certa sunt. At quod is, qui primas in ordi- ne Presbyterorum obtinuit, per excellentiam, ὁ Ἐπίσκοπος in Novo Testamento dicatur, è nullo loco patet. De Presbyteris enim quibusvis non modo in ipso Actorum loco, & hic, sed etiam 1. Tim. III. 2. Tit. I. 7. vox illa accipitur. Nec aliter verbum ἐπισκοποῦντες, 1. Petr. V. 2. aut nomen ἐπι- σκοπῆς, 1. Tim. III. 1. Act. I. 20. extra quæ loca nihil horum occurrit, nisi quod Christus ἐπίσκοπος ἀν- τονομαστικῶς & cum addito τῶν ψυχῶν ἡμῶν à san- cto Petro, 1. Epist. II. 25. vocetur. Non ergo Papi- scolarum distinctio Episcopi & Presbyteri, qua ille hoc superior jurisdictionis ordinandi & conse- crandi quadam potestate constituitur, ullum in sacris literis fundamentum habet. Sanctus Petrus etiam πρεσβυτέρους eorum, ad quos primam episto- lam direxerat, nempe παρεπιδήμων διαπορᾶς Pon- ti, Galatiæ, Cappadociæ, Asiæ & Bithyniæ exhortans, cap. V. annon satis testatur, nullum eo tempore in Ecclesiis istorum locorum fuisse ordinem Episco- palem, sed tantum presbyteralem; quorum etiam ipse se συμπρεσβύτερον appellat. Act. XII. 30. soli Presbyteri nominantur, qui Hierosolymitanam Ecclesiam dispensarint, nulli Episcopi; imo nul- lus Episcopus fuit in primitiva Ecclesia, præter Presbyterum, qui & ipsi Episcopi, & plures in una civitate: uti cap. XIV. 23. de Paulo & Barnaba di- citur, quod in urbibus Ciliciæ per singulas Ecclesias constituerint & ordinarint Presbyteros: qui nul- lum sibi superpositum habuere Episcopum, quo- niam & ipsi erant ac dicebantur Episcopi, consti- tuebant. Porro cap. XV. Apostoli cum Presbyte- ris in Ecclesia Hierosolymitana junctim memo- rantur illius Ecclesiæ præpositi, v. 11. nulla Epi- scoporum inter eos mentione facta, quia illi Pres- byteri etiam fuere Episcopi: nec in Concilio præ- ter Apostolos alii erant, quam Presbyteri, cum Ecclesia tota, vel cœtu fidelium v. 6. nulli v. 21. nulli v. 23. commemorantur Episcopi, quia Presbytero- rum nomine comprehensi. Sed nec ullus in his singularis recensetur Episcopus, quia eo tempore nullus extitit talis, qui unus in reliquos haberet imperium. Ideo Theodoretius ipse, ad quem pro- vocant alias Papistæ in hac causa in Comment. ad cap. I. prioris ad Timotheum: τὲς ἀυτὲς ἐκάλεν ποτὲ Πρεσβυτέρους κὴ Ἐπισκόπως. Eosdem olim Pres- byteros appellabant & Episcopos, quod ex Act. XX. & Tit. I. colligit Theodoretus. De quo loco vide sis adversus Dionys. Petavium fuse differentem Wa- lonem Messalinum de Episcopis & Presbyteris dis- sert. I. cap. I. In hunc textum ita habet Theo- doretus: Episcopis conjunxit Diaconos, cum de Presbyteris nullam fecisset mentionem. Alioquin nec fieri quidem poterat, ut multi Episcopi essent unius civitatis Pastores. Quo sit, ut essent scil. Pres- byteri, quos nominavit Episcopos. Nec diffiteri po- tuit Jesuita Petavius contra Salmasium pag. 44. Presbyteros nonnunquam Episcopos veros dictos esse, & in eadem civitate plures extitisse. Imo profes- sus est, citante Walone Messalino l. c. p. 377. Di- vino jure decretum non esse, ut unus in singulis ci- vitatibus & Ecclesiis esset Episcopus, sed Ecclesiæ au- toritate, conciliorumque sanctionibus. Et agnoscit ex Hieronymo ad Tit. I. Cornelius à Lapide, quod olim ante schisma non tam autoritate & jurisdi- ctione distincta, quam communi Presbyterorum con- silio, labore, & Spiritu gubernatæ fuerint Ecclesiæ. Cur ergo Papistæ ab hac consuetudine Apostolica divaricati sunt, aut illam distinctionem jam Apo- stolorum ætate in usu fuisse, jurisque divini censeri debere, impudenter asseverant. Si fuissent Philip- pensibus ὁ Ἐπίσκοπος secundum excellentiam ita dictus, certe Apostolus hic eum non præteriisset.

Nec vero est, quod cum Cornelio à Lapide di- catur, Epaphroditum τὸν γραμματοφόρον Episco- pum illum fuisse, quod hic Grotius Papizans simi- liter innuit. Probandum enim id erit. Dorotheus certe Epaphroditum Hadriana in Syria Episco- pum fuisse testatur. Chrysostomus vero in argu- mento epistolæ Epaphroditum vocat hominem & σφόδρα ἐπίσημον non admodum clarum. Provocat utique ad hunc locum ceu admodum luculentum S. Hieronymus Comm. laudato in epist. ad Tit. Putet aliquis, non scripturarum, sed nostram esse sententiam, Episcopum & Presbyterum unum esse, & aliud ætatis, aliud nomen esse officii, relegat Apo- stoli ad Philippenses scribentis verba: Paulus &

Timotheus servi Jesu Christi, qui sunt Philippis, cum Episcopis & Presbyteris gratia vobis & pax, & reliqua. Philippi una est urbs Macedoniæ. Et certe una in civitate plures ut nuncupantur Episcopi esse non poterant, sed quia eosdem Episcopos illo tempore, quos & Presbyteros appellabant, ideo indifferenter de Episcopis & Presbyteris est loquutus. E Græcis addimus Scholiastas in 1. Tim. III. Τί δήποτε τὰς πρεσβυτέρους παρέλιπεν; ὅτι ἐνέμιξεν αὐτὰς τοῖς Ἐ- πισκόποις. Ἃ γὰρ περὶ Ἐπισκόπων εἶπε, ταῦτα καὶ περὶ τῶν πρεσβυτέρων ἁρμόζει. Ὁμοίως γὰρ καὶ αὐ- τοὶ ἱερεῖς τέ εἰσι, καὶ διδασκαλίαν εἰσὶ πεπιστευμένοι. Cur vero Presbyteros prætermisit? Quia immiscuit eos Episcopis. Quæ enim de Episcopis dixit, hæc eadem & conveniunt Presbyteris. Pariter quippe Sacerdotes sunt, & docendi munus eis simul concreditum est. Ut autem Paulus 1. Tim. III. 17. duos tantum diversos ordines assignavit in Ecclesia Ἐπισκόπων καὶ Διακό- νων, Presbyteros sub illis comprehendens, ita idem observatur in epistola Clementis ad Cor. 1. (quam magnifacit Grotius) cum de Apostolis ait, eosdem κατὰ χώρας καὶ πόλεις κηρύσσοντας καθισᾶναι τὰς ἀπαρχὰς αὐτῶν δοκιμάσαντας τῷ πνεύματι εἰς Ἐ- πισκόπους καὶ Διακόνους τῶν μελλόντων πισέυειν, per provincias ac civitates Verbum DEI prædicantes con- stituisse primitias ipsorum probantes Spiritu in Episco- pos & Diaconos eorum, qui erant credituri.

## 1:2
Verse 2. Grace to you and peace) Rom. I. 7. 1 Cor. I. 3. 2 Cor. I. 2. Gal. I. 3. Eph. I. 2.

Lyranus refers grace to the present life, and peace to the future life. But more correctly, by grace is understood the fountain of all good things and the Paternal benevolence of God, and by peace, spiritual and heavenly happiness; embracing the peace and tranquility of heart on account of the grace of God and reconciliation with God through faith in Christ, Rom. V. 1.

Latin:

Vers. 2. Χάρις ὑμῖν καὶ εἰρήνη) Roman. I. 7. 1. Cor. I. 3. 2. Cor. I. 2. Gal. I. 3. Eph. I. 2.

Lyranus gratiam ad præsentem, pacem ad futu- ram vitam refert. Sed rectius per gratiam fons omnium bonorum & Paterna Dei εὐδοκία, per pa- cem vero felicitas spiritualis, & cælestis; comple- ctens pacem & tranquillitatem cordis ob gratiam DEI & reconciliationem cum DEO per fidem in Christum, Rom. V. 1. intelligitur.

## 1:3
Verse 3. I thank my God upon every remembrance of you) As often as I remember you, I give thanks to God. Similar to Rom. I. 8. 1 Cor. I. 4. Eph. I. 16.

Maldonatus, in Cornelius à Lapide, understands the memory of the Philippians actively, that is, that the Apostle was mindful of them. But all other interpreters explain it passively concerning the memory by which the Apostle was mindful of them, because the object of the thanksgiving is not the memory of the Philippians, but the fellowship, which is expressed in verse 5.

Latin:

Vers. 3. Εὐχαριστῶ τῷ Θεῷ ἐπὶ πάσῃ τῇ μνείᾳ ὑμῶν) Quo- tiescunque vestri memini, Deo gratias ago. Simile Rom. I. 8. 1. Cor. I. 4. Eph. I. 16.

Maldonatus apud Cornelium à Lapide memo- riam Philippensium activè intelligit, quod nempe memores fuerint Apostoli. Sed omnes alii Inter- pretes explicant Passivè de memoria, qua Apo- stolus ipsorum memor erat, quia objectum εὐ- χαρισίας non est memoria Philippensium, sed κοινωνία, quæ v. 5. exprimitur.

## 1:4
Verse 4. Always in every prayer of mine for you all making request with joy.) A testimony of truly great affection, to intermix prayers for them in all his prayers. And it is a great praise that he adds, with joy. For he was hearing about most of them what he wished.

Calvin refers the joy to the thanksgiving and the past time, and the prayer to the future: Zanchius refers the joy to both. But it coheres with the prayer, and the prayers are said to be made with joy. For the Corinthians they were not made without sadness on account of schisms, 2 Cor. II. 4, nor for the Galatians, on account of their bewitchment, Gal. III. 1. But for the Philippians they were performed with joy, which joy he desires to be fulfilled, Phil. II. 2, and calls them by the sweetest name, his joy, Phil. IV. 1. Compare Heb. XIII. 17.

Latin:

Vers. 4. Πάντοτε ἐν πάσῃ δεήσει με ὑπὲρ πάντων ὑμῶν μετὰ χαρᾶς τὴν δέησιν ποιούμενος.) Magni sane affectus te- stimonium omnibus suis precibus pro ipsis preces admi- scere. Et laus magna, quod addit, cum gaudio. Audie- bat enim de plerisque eorum, quæ vellet.

Gaudium ad εὐχαρισίαν & præteritum tempus refert Calvinus, δέησιν ad futurum: Zanchius gau- dium refert ad utrumque. Sed cohæret id cum δεήσει, & preces cum gaudio fieri dicuntur. Pro Corinthiis non sine tristitia fiebant ob schismata, 2. Cor. II. 4. nec pro Galatis, ob fascinationem eorum, Gal. III. 1. Pro Philippensibus autem μετὰ χαρᾶς peragebantur, quod gaudium impleri o- ptat, Phil. II. 2. vocatque ipsos suavissimo nomine gaudium suum Phil. IV. 1. Conf. Ebr. XIII. 17.

## 1:5
V. 5. For your fellowship in the Gospel) I rejoice in this, that you have been made participants of the Gospel, 'in the Gospel' instead of 'in the Gospel'. The same is the fellowship of the Son, 1 Cor. I. 9, and the fellowship of the mystery, Eph. III. 9, the fellowship with the Father, and the Son, 1 John I. 3.

From the first day until now) He praises also their constancy in the faith received.

Cornelius à Lapide and Justinianus explain the communion concerning alms with Chrysostom, Theophylact, the Greek scholia, the Glossa Ordinaria, and Lyranus; Joh. Crocius wishes for the same to be understood at the same time, but how can the same word obtain different meanings at once, if indeed he interprets communion in the Gospel concerning the society of faith and the assembly, and

the Church of the faithful with Bullinger, Crocius, nor does he deny Piscator explaining that participation in the Gospel as an efficacious calling to the Gospel. Which explanation, however, presupposes that there is also given some inefficacious calling, by which God calls most people only by the will of the sign, not by the will of good pleasure, just as that mind of Piscator was not unknown to Crocius, by which it is certain that God is impiously posited as a hypocrite. Therefore, Zanchius interprets more simply that they were brought to the communion of the Gospel, so that they might be participants of it, and through its reception have communion with the Church. For there is no doubt that there were also hypocrites in that Church: yet he gives thanks for all, because grace was made to all of the communion of the Gospel and the Church, through which an approach to salvation was open to all. For he did not wish anyone, whom God calls to salvation through the Word, to be excluded from salvation by an absolute decree or good pleasure.

Latin:

V. 5. Ἐπὶ τῇ κοινωνίᾳ ὑμῶν εἰς τὸ Εὐαγγέλιον) id gaudeo, quod Evangelii participes facti estis, εἰς τὸ Εὐαγγέλιον, pro ἐν τῷ Εὐαγγελίῳ. Eadem κοινωνία τοῦ υἱοῦ, 1. Cor. I. 9. & κοινωνία τοῦ μυστηρίου, Ephes. III. 9. κοινωνία μετὰ τοῦ Πα- τρὸς, καὶ τοῦ υἱοῦ, 1. Cor. I. 3.

Ἀπὸ πρώτης ἡμέρας ἄχρι τοῦ νῦν) Laudat & constantiam in accepta fide.

Communionem de Eleemosyna explicat cum Chrysostomo, Theophylacto, scholiis Græcis, glossa or- dinaria & Lyrano Salmero, Cornelius à Lapide, & Justinianus, eandem simul comprehendi vult Joh. Crocius, sed quomodo eadem vox diversa signifi- cata simul obtinere potest, siquidem communio- nem in Evangelio, de societate fidei ac cœtus, &

Ecclesiæ fidelium cum Bullingero interpreterur , Crocius, nec abnuat Piscatori explicanti illam in Evangelio participationem de efficaci ad Evange- lium vocatione. Quæ vero explicatio præsuppo- nit, dari etiam vocationem aliquam inefficacem, qua Deus voluntate figni plerosque tantum vo- cet, non voluntate beneplaciti, uti Piscatoris mens illa non ignota fuit Crocio, qua Deum hypocritam impie statui, certum est. Simplicius itaque Zan- chius interpretatur, quod sint adducti ad commu- nionem Evangelii, ut ejus essent participes, & per ejus receptionem communionem cum Ecclesia haberent. Nam & hypocritas fuisse in illa Eccle- sia dubium non est: Pro omnibus tamen gratias agit, quod omnibus gratia facta esset communionis Evangelii, & Ecclesiæ, per quam omnibus patebat aditus ad salutem. Neminem enim, quem vocat Deus ad salutem per Verbum, à salute exclusum voluit per absolutum decretum vel beneplacitum.

## 1:6
V. 6. Πεποιθώς αὐτὸ τῦτο) בטח hoping, see Eph. III. 12. and what is said there. Ὄτι ὁ ἐναρξάμενος ἐν ὑμῖν ἔργον ἀγαθὸν, ἐπιτελέση ἄχρι ἡμέρας χριστῦ Ἰησῦ) Namely, with you cooperating, which the following things indicate. But he preferred to name the principal and more worthy cause. Similar is that of Philo in the Allegories: Πολλοὶ ἀσκηταὶ γενόμενοι τῆς ἀρετῆς, ἐπὶ τὸ τέλος μετέβαλον, ὧ δὲ παρέσχεν ὁ Θεὸς ἐπισήμην βεβαίαν, τύτῳ δίδωσιν ἀμφότερα τό ἐργάζεσθαι τὰς ἀρετάς καὶ μηδέποτε αὐτῶν ἀφί- σασθαι, ἀλλ’ ἀεὶ ταμιεύειν καὶ φυλάττειν ἑκάστην. There is no συνέργεια here of the powers of free will, or of the converted Philippians toward the perfection of a good work, as it is something he claims for God alone in verse 29, chapter II. 13, and which must be claimed for the power of GOD, 1 Pet. I. 5, and for divine grace and faithfulness, 1 Cor. I. 8, 9. Conf. Heb. XII. 11, 1 Thess. V. 23, Jude v. 24, nor indeed do those following things imply συνέργειαν. It was fitting to hope that concerning them, not because of their own holiness, but because of the ἐνέργειαν of divine grace in them, and this persuasion can be joined with the ἐυχαριστίᾳ in v. 3, nor incorrectly does Calvin say: he did not gather this confidence from the powers of the Philippians, but only from the fact that God had declared His love toward them. Lombard himself, to the word 'I am confident,' which the Vulgate has, adds 'not in you, but in God.' Therefore, the gloss of Grotius is not to be approved, much less that of Cornelius: 'I am confident that just as you have begun a good work, so through God's grace you will persevere in the same until the end.' The Apostle says not that they themselves began, but that God began in them, nor does he pray that they themselves, but that God may perfect it. The good work is their faith, charity, and hope, which were from God, and were to be preserved and perfected by God. Yet God did not work in them as if in logs, which Chrysostom and Theophylact object, but a log does not resist the operation, whereas man can resist grace: nor did He work in them and not in others out of an absolute good pleasure, which the Calvinists wish, but when the Gospel was announced to all with the same divine saving intention, it had its efficacy in the very act only in those who did not repudiate grace, nor resist the Holy Spirit. Conf. the parable of the seed, Luke VIII.

One may understand the day of Christ either as the day on which Christ appears to each of the faithful for his μετάστασιν regarding the soul, which Bullinger understood here, or on which He is about to appear to all to render to us the plenary reward of heavenly glory regarding body and soul, concerning which most interpreters explain, Theophylact, Haymo, Lombard, and others, from whom some not rashly observe that Paul speaks here, as also in 1 Thess. IV. 15, about the final day, as if it were already then imminent, so that individuals might have it before their eyes, and think that it is already at hand, as the beginning of eternity, in respect to which not only our present life, but the duration of the whole world is scarcely to be reckoned like a moment: and yet God does not for that reason work in the dead: for he is said to perfect until the day of redemption, not that a continuity up to that day is noted, but that the limit and complement of perfection, which we shall have on that day, may be designated. For progress belongs to this life, not another. Perfection is not obtained in this life, but in the other.

Latin:

V. 6. Πεποιθώς αὐτὸ τῦτο) בטח sperans, vid. Eph. III. 12. & ibi dicta. Ὄτι ὁ ἐναρξάμενος ἐν ὑμῖν ἔργον ἀγαθὸν, ἐπιτελέση ἄχρι ἡμέρας χριστῦ Ἰησῦ) Nempe vobis cooperantibus, quod sequentia indicant. Sed maluit nominare causam princi- pem ac digniorem. Simile Philonis illud in Allegoriis: Πολλοὶ ἀσκηταὶ γενόμενοι τῆς ἀρετῆς, ἐπὶ τὸ τέλος μετέβα- λον, ὧ δὲ παρέσχεν ὁ Θεὸς ἐπισήμην βεβαίαν, τύτῳ δίδωσιν ἀμφότερα τό ἐργάζεσθαι τὰς ἀρετάς καὶ μηδέποτε αὐτῶν ἀφί- σασθαι, ἀλλ’ ἀεὶ ταμιεύειν καὶ φυλάττειν ἑκάστην. Non hic συνέργεια virium liberi arbitrii, aut Philippensium conversorum ad operis boni perfe- Žtionem, utpote quam soli Deo vendicat vers. 29. cap. II. 13. quæque potentiæ DEI vindicanda est, 1. Petr. I. 5. ac gratiæ & fidelitati divinæ 1. Cor. I. 8. 9. Conf. Ebr. XII. 11. 1. Thess. V. 23. Jud. v. 24. nec ve- ro sequentia illa συνέργειαν innuunt. Par erat id de ipfis sperare non ob ipsorum sanctitatem, sed ob gratiæ divinæ in ipsis ἐνέργειαν, & conjungi potest hæc persuasio cum ἐυχαριστίᾳ v. 3. neque inrecte Calvinus: non de Philippensium viribus hanc fidu- ciam colligebat, sed tantum ex eo, quod Deus amo- rem suum erga eos declaraverat. Lombardus ipse ad verbum confido, quod habet Vulgatus, addit non in vobis, sed Deo. Probanda ergo non est glossa Grotii, multo minus illa Cornelii: Confido, quod sic- ut cœpistis bonum opus, ita per Dei gratiam in eo- dem perseverabitis in finem. Non ipsos cœpisse, sed Deum in ipsis dicit Apostolus, nec ut ipsi sed ut Deus id perficiat, precatur. Bonum opus est fides, charitas, & spes ipsorum, quæ à Deo erant, & à Deo confer- vanda erant ac perficienda. Nec tamen Deus in ipsis, tanquam in truncis operatus est, quod ob- jicit Chrysostomus & Theophylactus, sed truncus non resistit operationi, homo autem potest resi- stere gratiæ: neque etiam ex absoluto beneplacito in iis, non in aliis operatus est, quod Calviniani volunt, sed quum omnibus annunciaretur Evange- lium eàdem intentione divina salutifera, in iis tan- tum, qui gratiam non repudiarunt, nec Spiritui Sancto restiterunt, efficaciam suam actu ipso ha- buit. Conf. parabola de semine, Luc. IIX.

Diem Christi intelligere licet, vel de die, qua christus apparet unicuiq; fidelium ad ejus μετάστα- σιν quoad animam, quem hic intellexit Bullingerus, vel qua appariturus est universis ad reddendum nobis quoad corpus & animu plenarium cœlestis gloriæ præmium, de quo pleriq; Interpretes expli- cant, Theophylactus, Haymo, Lombardus alii, è qui- bus nonnulli haud temere observant, Paulum hic, ut & 1. Thess. IV. 15. de die extremo, ac si jam tum in- stitisset, loqui, ut singuli illum ante oculos habe- ant, & jamjam imminere cogitent, tanquam initium æternitatis, cujus respectu non tantum vita præ- sens nostra, sed totius mundi duratio vix instar mo- menti æstimanda : Nec tamen ideo Deus operatur in mortuis : nam perficere dicitur in diem redemptio- nis, non ut continuitas usque ad illum diem notetur, sed ut terminus & complementum perfectionis, quod habituri isto die erimus; tantum designetur. Profectus enim est hujus, non alterius seculi. Per- fectio non in hac vita obtinetur, sed in altera.

## 1:7
Vers. 7. Just as it is right for me to think this of you all) You have conducted yourselves so well heretofore, that I ought to hope the best of you for the future. But as you continue in this way, God also will continue to heap gifts upon you. Δίκαιόν ἐστι is right, as in Acts IV. 19. ישר.

Grotius makes the past life the cause of the Apostle's persuasion. But Erasmus and Aretius think that the cause not of the Apostolic persuasion, but of the gift of perseverance, is being brought forward. Furthermore, they interpret τὸ Φρονεῖν ὑπὲρ πάντων as to care for you, which explanation Zanchius says is not to be despised. With this agrees that which is in διὰ τὸ ἔχειν με ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ ὑμῶν, therefore we also add our vote to the same. The love of Paul is not the cause why God is about to give perseverance, but it is the cause for the Apostle why he should care for them and pray for them solicitously. The ordinary sense of the particle ὑπὲρ also favors this. For it is not DE, but PRO. The Apostle says ὑπὲρ, not περὶ ὑμῶν. Let Flacius be compared in his gloss, whom we have here agreeing. Furthermore, even if the prior life of the Ephesians is established as the cause why the Apostle hoped well of them for the future: yet it must be explained in such a way, according to how he hoped. For he hoped that God would perfect in them what He had begun. He does not attribute this to their piety, but to God. But he is confident concerning them, according to how they had conducted themselves thus far, that they would not give cause for GOD to withdraw His grace from them, or that they would render themselves unworthy of divine grace and eternal life by their unbelief and sins. That Δίκαιον is right is also evident from Col. IV. 1 and 2 Pet. I. 13. The reason which Calvin brings forward for the equity of this φρονήσεως: For we are malignant interpreters of the gifts of God, unless we hold them for children of God in whom the signs of true piety shine forth, by which marks the Spirit of adoption shows itself, rests upon a false hypothesis concerning the inamissible character of the children of God, or the absolute perseverance of the children of God.

Because I have you in my heart, both in my bonds, and in the defense and confirmation of the Gospel, you all being partakers with me of grace) There are ancients who think this was written in his second bonds after the first pleading of his case before Nero, at which time no one had stood by Paul, 2 Tim. IV. 16, and at that very time Timothy had not been in Rome, as appears from the same passage. But it seems to me that ἀπολογία can be understood as that before the Jews who were in Rome, about which it was spoken in the Acts. But in all these evils which Paul was bearing, he consoled himself in this, that the Philippian Christians, not for the same reason, but in a like manner, with the Jews inciting the Roman magistrates, had endured and were enduring many evils, as can be seen below in verse 29. But he calls this very thing grace, to suffer for Christ, as also below ἐχαρίσθη. Great is the honor in this matter, great are the rewards. The defense and confirmation of the Gospel is said by way of epexegesis, which is more briefly the defense of the Gospel below in verse 17. Confirmation is קים.

That 'and in my bonds' does not cohere with the preceding, as if he were saying, even in my bonds I have you in my mind, as Theophylact, Bullinger, and Aretius do with Chrysostom, but with the following, namely, you who are partakers of grace with me both in bonds and in the defense and confirmation of the Gospel. He does not so much explain to them that he has them in his mind, namely that they were partakers of grace, as the cause why he has the Philippians in his mind, when as partakers with him of the same, not of joy, as the Vulgate translates, which is χαρᾶς, but of χάριτος or grace, as all the codices have, and the ancient Greeks rendered, and indeed not of the grace of election, which pleased Vatablus, but of the passions, which the Apostle held as a benefit in verse 29. Which interpretation of grace is generally that of Theodoret, Theophylact, and others. And therefore most people wish to give such an honorable name to his bonds, Theodoret, Theophylact, and the Greek scholiasts; others, because he called them the defense and confirmation of the Gospel. The confirmation of the Gospel, says Theophylact, and the defense, he calls his bonds and the pressures by which he himself was afflicted. For it is clear that if the Apostle had not been persuaded and had not held it as a known fact that those ineffable rewards and heavenly goods are of such value that they cannot be explained in words, he would not have endured bonds at all, nor would he have resisted the savage Nero more pertinaciously, unless he had predicted another Emperor who would be firmer and incomparably more powerful than him. Therefore the pressures and evils which we suffer will confirm the Gospel. But that the Philippians joined their helping efforts to the defenses, which Zanchius and Crocius also wish to be expressed by the name of the confirmation of the Gospel, because defense and confirmation are governed by one article, and Grotius does not interpret it badly by way of epexegesis, whether before the tribunal of Nero, or before the Romans and Jews perhaps appearing in custody, is rashly asserted by some and without foundation. Indeed, Paul affirms in his first defense that no one stood by him except God, 2 Tim. IV. 16, and therefore he is not only speaking of those who were present in Rome, as Crocius thinks, but he excludes all men; who would believe that assistants were sent to him from elsewhere? Nor in the Acts is there anything to be read about the assistance of anyone provided in the defense of Paul in his bonds.

However, we do not deny that those first bonds are to be understood here. This was rightly proven by Chrysostom in the ὑποθέσει τῆς ἐπιςολῆς, not indeed from the presence of Timothy, which he himself signifies, that at the time of that defense no one stood by him: But at this time, when he wrote this to the Philippians, Timothy was present with him, whom he joins to himself at the threshold of the letter. For that reasoning is less binding. For he would not have announced through a letter what he knew to be known to him. He does not so much announce it to Timothy as call it to his memory, and celebrates the grace of God, because ten years before, when he was deserted by all, He stood by him. Therefore, the Apostle speaks of those bonds both there, 2 Tim. IV. 16, and here, namely of the first captivity, from which he was released; who nevertheless, after he had seen the Philippians, was cast into bonds again at Rome in his final captivity. That the prior captivity is altogether to be understood in the present passage, Chrysostom proves more correctly from the hope and confidence of liberation. For what he says (c. II.) 'but even if I am poured out as a drink offering upon the sacrifice and service of your faith,' he does not say so as if it were happening now, but since if that should happen, and whenever it should happen, I rejoice, he says, relieving them of the sorrow which they had conceived from his bonds, for it is clear from those words that he was by no means about to die then, 'But I trust in the Lord that I myself shall also come to you shortly,' and again: 'And being confident of this, I know that I shall remain and continue with you all.'

Latin:

Vers. 7. Καθώς ἐστι δίκαιον ἐμοὶ τῦτο φρονεῖν ὑπὲρ πάντων ὑμῶν) Ita antehac vos gessistis, ut optima sperare in po- sterum de vobis debeam. Vobis autem sic pergentibus Deus quoque sic perget vos cumulare donis. Δίκαιόν ἐστ par est, ut Actor. IV. 19. ישר.

Causam persuasionis Apostoli facit Grotius vitam anteactam. At Erasmus & Aretius non persuasio- nis Apostolicæ, sed doni perseverantiæ causam afferri putant. Porro τὸ Φρονεῖν ὑπὲρ πάντων interpretan- tur pro vobis curare, quam explicationem non contemnendam esse dicit Zanchius. Cui consonat illud διὰ τὸ ἔχειν με ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ ὑμῶν, ideo & nos eidem calculum addimus. Amor Pauli non est causa, cur Deus sit daturus perseverantiam, causa autem est Apostolo, cur illorum curam gereret, ac pro illis oraret solicite. Particulæ etiam ὑπὲρ sensus ordinarius favet. Nam ea est non DE, sed PRO. Apostolus ait ὑπὲρ non περὶ ὑμῶν. Confe- ratur Flacius in glossa, quem hic consentientem habemus. Porro etsi vita Ephesiorum prior cau- sa, cur bene sperarit porro de ipsis Apostolus, sta- tuatur : Ita tamen ea explicanda, prout speravit. Speravit vero Deum, quod cœpit, in ipsis perfectu- rum. Non ipsorum id tribuit pietati, sed Deo. Id autem de ipsis, prout hactenus se gesserant, confi- dit, eos non daturos causam, ut DEUS gratiam ipsis suam subtrahat, aut incredulitate ac peccatis suis sese indignos reddituros divina gratia & æterna vi- ta. Δίκαιον æquum esse etiam è Col. IV. 1. 2. Pet. I. 13. patet. Ratio, quam pro æquitate istius φρονή- σεως Calvinus affert : Maligni enim sumus dono- rum Dei interpretes, nisi eos habeamus pro filiis Dei, in quibus veræ pietatis signa emicant, quibus notis Spiritus adoptionis se profert, fallâ nititur hypothesi de charactere filiorum Dei inamissibili, vel abso- luta filiorum Dei perseverantiâ.

Διὰ τὸ ἔχειν με ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ ὑμᾶς ἔν τε τοῖς δεσμοῖς με, καὶ ἐν τῇ ἀπολογίᾳ καὶ βεβαιώσει τῦ Εὐαγγελίυ συγκοινωνός με τῆς χάριτος πάντας ὑμᾶς ὄντας) Sunt veteres, qui pu- tant hoc scriptum in secundis vinculis post primam causæ dictionem apud Neronem, quo tempore nemo Paulo ad- fuerat 2. Tim. IV. 16. atque eo ipso tempore Timotheus Romæ non fuerat, ut ex eodem loco apparet. At mihi vi- detur ἀπολογία posse intelligi illa apud Judæos, qui Romæ erant, de qua dictum in Actis. In omnibus autem his malis, quæ Paulus ferebat, in eo se solabatur, quod Philippenses Christiani non eadem modo de causa, sed pari modo, susci- tantibus Romanos magistratus Judæis, multa mala tolera- verant ac tolerabant, ut videre est infra 29. Gratiam au- tem hoc ipsum vocat, pati pro Christo, ut & infra ἐχαρίσθη. Magnus in hac re honos, magna præmia. Ἀπολογία καὶ βε- βαίωσις Εὐαγγελίε dictum per ἑπεξήγησιν, quod brevius ἀπολογία Εὐαγγελίε infra 17. Βεβαίωσις est קים.

Illud & in vinculis meis non cohæret cum præ- cedentibus, quasi dicat, etiam in vinculis meis vos in mente mea habeo, ut cum Chrysostomo Theo- phylactus, Bullingerus, & Aretius, sed cum conse- quentibus, vos nempe qui & in vinculis & in defen- sione & confirmatione Evangelii una mecum gratiæ participes. Non tam quod in mente habeat, scilicet quod fuerint participes gratiæ, quam causam, cur Philippenses in mente habeat, illis exponit verbis, cum ceu participes ejusdem secum non gaudii, ut Vulgatus vertit, quod est χαρᾶς, sed χάριτος vel gratiæ, ut Codices omnes habent, & veteres Græ- ci reddiderunt, & quidem non electionis gratiæ, quod Vatablo placuit, sed passionum, quas pro be- neficio habebat Apostolus v. 29. Quæ interpreta- tio gratiæ fere communis est Theodoreti, Theophy- lacti aliorum. Ideoque vinculis suis tam honorifi- cum ipsum nomen dare plerique volunt, Theodo- retus, Theophylactus, Græci Scholiastæ; alii, quod ea vocarit defensionem & confirmationem Evangelii. Confirmationem Evangelii, inquit Theophylactus, & defensionem vincula dicit & pressuras, quibus ipse afflictabatur. Est namque perspicuum, quod si persua- sum Apostolus ac pro re comperta non habuisset, re- munerationes ineffabiles illas & bona cælestia tanti esse, ut explicari verbis non possint, non prorsus vin- cula fuisset perpessus, nec efferato Neroni pertinacius obstitisset, nisi Imperatorem alium prædixisset, qui fir- mior esset, & illo incomparabiliter longe potentior. Pressuræ ergo & mala, quæ patimur, Evangelium confirmabunt. At apologias, quas etiam βεβαιώσεως τῶ εὐαγγελίε nomine exprimi vult Zanchius & Crocius, quod defensio & confirmatio ab uno regatur articulo, & per ἐπεξήγησιν non male interpretatur Grotius, sive coram tribunali Neronis, sive coram Romanis & Judæis in custodia forte comparenti- bus, operas socias conjunxisse Philippenses, missis viris, qui Paulo assisterent, temere à quibusdam as- seritur & citra fundamentum. Imo Paulus in prima sua defensione neminem nisi Deum sibi adstitisse affir- mat, 2. Tim. IV. 16. ideoque non solum de iis, qui Romæ præsentes erant, loquitur, ut Crocius putat, sed omnes excludit homines, aliunde missos ipsi parastatas, quis credat? Nec in Actis de παραςά- σει cujuspiam in apologia Pauli in vinculis præsti- ta quicquam legere est.

Cæterum prima illa vincula hic intelligi non ab- nuimus. Quod recte à Chrysostomo probatum est in ὑποθέσει τῆς ἐπιςολῆς, non quidem à præsentia Timothei, quod ipse significet, tempore istius defen- sionis neminem sibi adstitisse: Hoc autem tempore, quo ad Philippenses hæc scripsit, Timotheus ipsi præsto fuerit, quem in limine literarum sibi jungit. Nam ratio ista minus stringit. Non enim illi per li- teras nunciaffet, quod notum ipsi esse sciret. Non tam nunciat Timotheo, quam in memoriam ipsi revo- cat, & gratiam Dei celebrat, quod ipsi ante decen- nium ab omnibus deserto adstiterit. De illis ergo vinculis & illic, 2. Tim. IV. 16. & hic loquitur Apo- stolus, nempe captivitatis primæ, è quibus est di- missus; qui tamen, postquam vidisset Philippenses, denuo Romæ in postrema captivitate in vincula conjectus est. Quod omnino prior captivitas in præsenti loco intelligatur, rectius è spe ac confiden- tia liberationis probat Chrysostomus. Quod enim inquit (c. II.) sed etsi immolor supra sacrificium, & obsequium fidei vestræ, non ita dicit, quasi nunc fie- ret, sed quoniam si id eveniat, & quandocunq; eveniat, gaudeo, inquit, relevans illos mœrore, quem ex ipsius vinculis conceperant, nunc enim mortem minime obiturum fuisse, ex illis verbis perspicuum est, Con- fido autem in Domino, quoniam & ipse veniam ad vos cito, & rursus: Et hoc confidens scio, quia ma- nebo, & permanebo omnibus vobis.

## 1:8
Vers. 8. Μάρτυς γάρ μοί ἐστιν ὁ Θεὸς) An oath as in Rom. I. 9. 2. Cor. I. 23. 1. Thessal. II. v. 5. 10. אלהים עד Gen. XXXII. 50. בשמים עדי ושהדי במרומים, Job. XVI. 18.

Ὡς ἐπιποθῶ πάντας ὑμᾶς ἐν σπλάγχνοις ἰησοῦ χριστοῦ) that is, I love you with a love, not that common one, but truly Christian. σπλάγχνα means every affection, 2. Cor. VI. 12. Philem. v. 11. 12. 20. 1. Joh. III. 17.

The words ἐν σπλάγχνοις Ἰησοῦ χριστοῦ Anselm explains regarding the love of Christ, as if he were saying, I desire you to be in the inmost heart of Christ, so that you may be cast as it were into the bowels of Christ, and Christ may love you as his own bowels, he explains. To which also returns the sense of Vatablus: How much I desire Christ to pour out his mercy upon you. Cornelius à Lapide [explains it as] with that love with which Christ loves us, as if we were established in his own bowels.

Others [speak] of the bowels of Paul, or of the affection of truly Christian love, because by bowels is figuratively denoted the innermost affection of love and as it were maternal, as the Hebrew רחם he loved from the innermost bowels, so that that love of Christ may be called [his], because it is not carnal, or worldly, but spiritual and Christian love. Perhaps it could be said that he desires them and longs for them, and loves the Apostles in his bowels, which bowels were Christ's, because Paul was Christ's, and lived in Christ; or even in his own bowels dedicated to Christ, full of Christ, burning with the love of Christ, for the sake of whom he also embraced all who are Christ's.

Latin:

Vers. 8. Μάρτυς γάρ μοί ἐστιν ὁ Θεὸς) Juramentum ut Rom. I. 9. 2. Cor. I. 23. 1. Thessal. II. v. 5. 10. אלהים עד Gen. XXXII. 50. בשמים עדי ושהדי במרומים, Job. XVI. 18.

Ὡς ἐπιποθῶ πάντας ὑμᾶς ἐν σπλάγχνοις ἰησοῦ χριστοῦ) id est, amo vos amore, non illo communi, sed vere Chri- stiano. σπλάγχνα omnis affectus, 2. Cor. VI. 12. Philem. v. 11. 12. 20. 1. Joh. III. 17.

Verba ἐν σπλάγχνοις Ἰησοῦ χριστοῦ Anshelmus de in σπλάγ- amore Christi explicat, quasi dicat, cupio vos esse χνοις Ἰησοῦ. in intimo corde Christi, ut trajiciamini quasi in vi- scera Christi, & Christus vos ceu viscera sua dili- gat, explicat. Quo redit etiam Vatabli sensus: Quantum cupiam, Christum suam misericordiam in vos effundere. Cornelius à Lapide eo amore, quo Christus nos amat, quasi in visceribus suis constitutos.

Alii de visceribus Pauli, vel de affectu amoris ve- re Christiani, quia per viscera figurate intimus amoris affectus ac veluti maternus denotatur, ut Ebræum רחם dilexit ex intimis visceribus, ut Christi amor ille dicatur, quia non carnalis, vel mundanus, sed spiritualis, & Christianus amor est.
