Forte dici possit, quod cupiat ipsos ac desideret, ametque Apostolos in visceribus suis, quæ viscera erant Christi, quia Paulus Christi erat, & in Chri- sto vivebat; vel etiam in visceribus suis Christo di- catis, Christo plenis, Christi amore flagrantibus, ob quem etiam omnes, qui Christi sunt, complecte- batur.

## 1:9
V. 9. That your love may abound yet more and more) It is a metonymy. For he wishes to say this: I pray that this love of yours toward me may receive greater gifts from God day by day. For from receiving that, the abounding will follow.

There is no need for a metonymical sense, since the proper one has a place, that the love and affection of the Philippians may abound more and more (not gifts, as the cause of a richer love). He does not pray for a common increase of charity, says Crocius, but an excellent one, and such that, like a living fountain, waters gush forth, which in full streams may both leap upward into heaven and flow far and wide into every field, especially of the faithful. However, he rightly rejects with Calvin the interpretation of his own Bullinger, 'your charity,' that is, 'you yourselves,' because such formulas, which modern custom uses, e.g., 'your reverence,' 'your paternity,' nowhere exist in Paul, nor were they accepted at that time.

In knowledge) Thus is called a greater cognition of divine things, as Rom. III. 20, Eph. I. 17, IV. 17.

And in all discernment) that is, experience. Thus the LXX translate דעת as discernment in Prov. I. 4, and often elsewhere in the same book: which elsewhere [they translate as] understanding, knowledge, and in other ways.

The version of Blessed Luther also tends toward that, which we here and deservedly prefer to the interpretation of Beza, Theophylact, and Chrysostom, who explain it not of the knowledge and experience of divine things, but of those who are loved, in knowledge and all discernment, that is, that you should not simply love just anyone, but with testing and judgment.

Latin:

V. 9. Ἵνα ἡ ἀγάπη ὑμῶν ἔτι μᾶλλον καὶ μᾶλλον περισσεύη) Est μετωνυμία. Hoc enim vult dicere, oro, ut iste vester in me amor à Deo majora indies dona accipiat. Ex illo enim accipere sequetur τὸ περισσεύειν.

Non opus est sensu Metonymico, quum proprius locum habeat, ut magis magisque abundent (non do- na, ceu causa uberioris amoris, sed) amor & affe- ctus Philippensium. Non vulgare incrementum cha- ritatis, inquit Crocius, precatur, sed excellens & ta- le, ut instar fontis vivi aquas scaturiunt, quæ plenis rivulis tum sursum saliant in cœlum, tum longe la- teque in omnem agrum imprimis fidelium dimanent. Bullingeri autem sui interpretamentum charitas vestra, id est, vos ipsi, merito cum Calvino rejicit, quod ejusmodi formulæ, quibus hodierna con- suetudo utitur, v. g. vestra reverentia, vestra pater- nitas, nusquam in Paulo extet, nec tum receptæ fuerint.

Ἐν ἐπιγνώσει) Sic vocatur major rerum divinarum co- gnitio, ut Rom. III. 20. Eph. I. 17. IV. 17.

Καὶ πάσῃ αἰσθήσει) id est experientia. Sic דעת LXX. vertunt αἴσθησιν Prov. I. 4. & sæpe alibi in eodem libro: quod alibi σύνεσιν, ἐπιστήμην, & aliis modis.

Eo etiam abit B. Lutheri versio, quam hic & merito interpretationi Bezæ, Theophylacti, & Chrysostomi de agnitione atque experientia non rerum divinarum, sed eorum, qui diliguntur, expli- cantium, in agnitione & omni sensu, id est ut non simpliciter quosvis diligatis, sed cum probatione & judicio, præferimus.

## 1:10
Vers. 10. To the end that you may test the things that are different) that is, that in every circumstance of things, you may understand what is right and what is not, as we explained this expression in Romans II. verse 18.

Thus also Cornelius à Lapide and Crocius, that you may discern true, necessary, and useful dogmas from false, unnecessary, and useless ones as things that are especially different: Here, however, he adds, and that you may compare good examples with bad: 1 Thess. V. 21, nor does he disapprove of the version of Blessed Luther, approved by Bullinger and Piscator, which is 'the things that are excellent,' because the word διαφέρω is often the same as to excel and to surpass, as Matt. VI. 26, ch. X. 31, ch. XII. 12, Luke XII. 7, Gal. II. 6. With which the Vulgate also agrees, nor does Theophylact depart from that explanation: that you may approve the better things, that is, the conducive ones.

That you may be sincere) that is, that you may clearly perceive all things. Thus Peter called it a sincere mind, 1 Pet. III. 1.

Not so much that they may clearly perceive, as that they may be sincere, and not only in faith or doctrine, but also in life and charity: as Theodoret understands the sincerity of faith: Haymo, however, explains it more fully thus: That you may be perfect (I would prefer sincere) both in faith and in all goodness. To this end, says Crocius, he asks for a perennial redundancy of charity and of all cognition and discernment, that they may be incorrupt in all things, that the mind and thought may be sincere, 2 Pet. III. 1, the will sincere, the affections pure, charity from a pure heart and a good conscience and faith unfeigned, 1 Tim. I. 5. Without the leaven of the Pharisees, Matt. XVI. 11, and malice and wickedness, 1 Cor. V. verse 8.

And blameless) See 1 Cor. X. 32, Acts XXIV. 16.

Εἰς ἡμέραν χριστῦ) That is, always. See above 6. That they may not offend others, namely men, as Theophylact, Thomas, Erasmus, and others do with Chrysostom, 1 Cor. 10:32. To Calvin, Musculus, and Beza, however, the passive meaning was pleasing, so that they might not be offended by scandals. Crocius joins both senses, but that hardly has a place in the same word.

Latin:

Vers. 10. Εἰς τὸ δοκιμάζειν ὑμᾶς τὰ διαφέροντα) id est, ut in quaque rerum circumstantia, quid rectum, quid non sit, intelligatis, quomodo hanc locutionem explicavimus Ro- man. II. vers. 18.

Sic etiam Cornelius à Lapide, & Crocius, ut dog- mata vera, necessaria, & utilia à falsis, non ne- cessariis, & inutilibus ceu διαφέροντα maxime dis- cernatis: Hic tamen addit, & exempla bona cum malis conferatis: 1. Thessal. V. 21. nec improbat B. Lutheri versionem, Bullingero & Piscatori pro- batam, quæ sunt præstantia, quod verbum διαφέρω sæpe idem sit, quod præsto & antecello, ut Matth. VI. 26. cap. X. 31. cap. XII. 12. Luc. XII. 7. Galat. II. 6. Quibus etiam consentit Vulgata, nec abit ab eâ explicatione Theophylactus: ut probetis potiora, hoc est, conducentia.

Ἵνα ἦτε εἰλικρινεῖς) id est, ut clare omnia perspiciatis. Sic τὴν εἰλικρινῆ διάνοιαν dixit Petrus 1. Petr. III. 1.

Non tam ut clare perspiciant, quam ut sinceri sint, nec in fide tantum vel doctrina, sed etiam in vita & charitate: uti Theodoreus sinceritatem fidei intelligit: Haymo vero plenius ita exponit: Ut si- tis perfecti (malim sinceri) & fide & omni boni- tate. Hoc fine, inquit Crocius, petit charitatis, omnis que cognitionis & sensus redundantiam perennem, ut sint in omnibus incorrupti, sincera sit mens & co- gitatio, 2. Petr. III. 1. voluntas sincera, affectus pu- ri, charitas ex puro corde & conscientia bona & fide non simulata, 1. Tim. I. 5. Absque fermento Pharisæo- rum, Matth. XVI. 11. & malitia nequitiaque, 1. Cor. V. vers. 8.

Καὶ ἀπρόσκοποι) Vide 1. Cor. X. 32. Actor. XXIV. 16.

Εἰς ἡμέραν χριστῦ) Id est semper. Vide supra 6. Ne offendant alios scilicet homines, ut cum Chrysostomo Theophylactus, Thomas, Erasmus alii- que 1. Cor. X. 32. Calvino tamen, Musculo & Bezae passiva significatio placuit, ne scandalis offendan- tur. Utrumque sensum conjungit Crocius, sed vix ille in eadem voce locum habet.

## 1:11
Vers. 11. Πεπληρωμένοι καρπῶν δικαιοσύνης) Thus you have כרב פריו in Hosea 10:1. The sense is that you may bear fruit abundantly of good works, all of which come under the name of righteousness. In which most interpreters agree; compare Gal. 5:22, Eph. 5:9. Anselm, however, takes it of the reward in heaven, but contrary to the mind of the Apostle. For he is dealing with the fruits of which they ought to be full here until the day of Jesus Christ, and not indeed on the day of Jesus Christ.

Τῶν διὰ ἰησοῦ χριστῦ) which ought to be more perfect than the works of the law.

Works more perfect than the law prescribes, neither Christ nor the Apostle ever demanded. But the fruits of righteousness are said to be done through Jesus Christ, because faith in Christ is the cause of them, and from Christ as the principle, since we are grafted into Him through faith, good works as fruits of righteousness overflow, John 15:1 ff., fruits which Christ produces in you, not which you bear by native and proper strengths. For by nature we are unfruitful trees.

Εἰς δόξαν καὶ ἔπαινον Θεῦ) For all those pious works of men, formerly impious, redound to the great praise of divine grace, Eph. 1:6, 12, 14. Theophylact: This will result in the glory of God, not in mine, the teacher's. Wherefore there is no reason why you should stand in the way of the glory of God. Less correctly, Lombard explains that through these they are to pass into eternal glory. Compare Matt. 5:16.

PART II. Explanation of the fruit of the Apostle's bonds.

Latin:

Vers. 11. Πεπληρωμένοι καρπῶν δικαιοσύνης) Sic כרב פריו habes Osea X. 1. Sensus est, ut large fructum feratis bonorum operum, quae omnia veniunt δικαιοσύνης nomine. In quo conveniunt plerique Interpretes; Conf. Gal. V. 22. Eph. V. 9. Anshelmus tamen de mercede in coelo accipit, sed praeter mentem Apostoli. Agit enim de fructibus, quibus hic pleni esse debeant usque ad diem Jesu Christi, non vero in die J. C.

Τῶν διὰ ἰησοῦ χριστῦ) quae consummatiora esse debent, quam legis opera.

Opera consummatiora, quam lex praescribat, nec Christus postulavit unquam, nec Apostolus. Per Jesum Christum autem fieri dicuntur fructus justi- tiae, quia fides in Christum est causa eorum, & à Christo tanquam principio, cum illi per fidem in- siti simus, opera bona ceu fructus justitiae redun- dant, Joh. XV. 1. seqq. fructus quos Christus in vobis producit, non quos viribus nativis & propriis fer- tis. Natura enim sumus arbores infrugiferae.

Εἰς δόξαν καὶ ἔπαινον Θεῦ) Omnia enim illa hominum, ante impiorum, pia opera ad magnam redundant laudem divinae gratiae Eph. I. 6. 12. 14. Theophylactus: In gloriam Dei hoc cedet, non in meam docentis. Quare non est, quod obsistatis gloriae Dei. Minus recte Lombardus exponit, quod per haec transituri sint in aeternam gloriam. Conf. Matth. V. v. 16.

PARS II. Fructus vinculorum Apostoli explicatio.

## 1:12
V. 12. Γινώσκειν δὲ ὑμᾶς βέλομαι.

Since he has called the Philippians partners in his bonds and in the confirmation of the same Gospel of grace, not so much by reason of compassions as of afflictions and the spirit of enduring the same, he now shows them the fruit of his own afflictions or bonds, so that they may be confirmed by his example and with him glorify Christ. Now these fruits were 1. the progress and propagation of the Gospel, v. 12, both in that some in the Praetorian guard and others, and in that the brothers in the Lord, having become more confident by the bonds and the boldness of the Apostle, preached the Gospel without fear, although there were not lacking those who announced it with not good intention, v. 13, 14, 15, 16, 17. 2. The Apostle's joy, which followed from that, v. 18, the cause of which is rendered both by the announcement of Christ, v. 18, and by the promotion of the Apostle's salvation, v. 19, which also happens through his bonds, whether those things result in life or in death, since he is certain, and relies on that hope, that Christ will be glorified in his body in either way, inasmuch as he has both surrendered his life to Christ, and in death he is not about to lose Christ and eternal life, but to gain them, whence he is in doubt as to which he ought to choose; since indeed death is better for him, but preservation in life is more necessary for them, v. 20 to 24. The apology for the bonds is also instituted in this way, whether on account of detractors, who by injecting fear into the Philippians tried to deter them from the profession of the Gospel, as it seemed to some, or on account of the proper perturbation of the Philippians themselves, which is Theophylact's reason. It was fitting, he says, that the Philippians should be perturbed in mind when they had learned that Paul had been bound in chains, just as if the proclamation of Christ had been cut off. Intending therefore to remove from them the suspicion conceived in their minds, he says thus: For not only have these my bonds not hindered the Gospel at all, but they have rather profited it.

That my affairs) My affairs, as Eph. VI. 21.

Rather for the progress of the Gospel) You do well that you are not terrified by these my bonds. For they themselves serve the Gospel. We have the word progress also below 25. and 1 Tim. IV. 15. It is also found in Sirach.

Zanchius also refers these things to Paul's voyage, but it is manifest that he is speaking of his captivity and his bonds.

Latin:

V. 12. Γινώσκειν δὲ ὑμᾶς βέλομαι.

Quum consortes in vinculis, & confirmatione Evangelii ejusdem secum gratiae non tam ratione compassionum, quam afflictionum, animique eas- dem sustinendi dixerit Philippenses, jam afflictio- num suarum vel vinculorum fructum ipsis exhibet, ut suo exemplo confirmentur, secumque Christum glorificent. Fructus autem hi erant 1. profectus & propagatio Evangelii v. 12. tum qua nonnullos in pre- torio Caesareo, aliosque, tum qua fratres in Domino, qui confidentiores vinculis & παῤῥησία Apostoli facti Evangelium sine metu praedicarunt, licet non defuerint, qui intentione non bona id annuncia- rint, v. 13. 14. 15. 16. 17. 2. Gaudium Apostoli, quod inde consequutum est v. 18. cujus causa redditur tum Christi annunciatio v. 18. tum salutis Apostoli promotio v. 19. quae etiam per vincula ejus fiat, sive ad vitam, sive ad mortem illa cedant, quum certus sit, ac spe illa nitatur, Christum in corpore suo utro- vis modo glorificatum iri, siquidem & vitam suam Christo manciparit, & in morte Christum ac vi- tam aeternam haud perditurus, sed lucraturus sit, unde ambigit, utrum eligere debeat; quum sibi qui- dem melior sit mors, ipsis vero conservatio in vita sit magis neceffaria v. 20. ad 24. Apologia etiam vinculorum ita instituitur, sive propter obtrecta- tores, qui metu Philippensibus injecto eosdem absterrere conabantur à professione Evangelii, ut nonnullis visum, sive propter ipsorummet Philip- pensium propriam perturbationem, quae Theophy- lacti ratio est. Decens, inquit, erat, ut animo pertur- barentur Philippenses, cum Paulum didicissent vin- culis fuisse constrictum, perinde ac intercisum fuisset Christi praeconium. Dempturus itaque his conceptam animo suspicionem sic inquit: Neque enim solum nil prorsus mea haec vincula Evangelium interceperunt, sed illi potius profuere.

Ὄτι τὰ κατ᾽ ἐμὲ) Res meæ, ut Eph. VI. 21.

Μᾶλλον εἰς προκοπὴν τῦ Εὐαγγελία ἐλήλυθεν) Recte fa- citis, quod non terremini his vinculis meis. Nam ea ipfa Evangelio serviunt. Vocem προκοπῆς habemus & infra 25. & 1. Tim. IV. 15. Est & apud Sirachidem.

Hæc ad navigationem Pauli etiam refert Zan- chius, sed manifestum est ipsum loqui de captivita- te, & vinculis suis.

## 1:13
Verse 13. So that my bonds in Christ have become manifest in the whole praetorium) Metonymy. My bonds in Christ have been made known: that is, it has become known that I am bound only for the sake of Christ. Which rumor, flowing wider and wider, had even reached the court, so that even there some of the servants and freedmen of Caesar had become Christians, below IV. 22. A praetor was once called he who went before the army, as Varro explains, hence the praetorian cohort, the praetorian ship. Hence the Emperor's tent began to be called the praetorium: thence also the house of the governor of a province: two praetoria are mentioned by Tacitus. At Rome the house of the Caesars was called the palace: But provincials accustomed to the term praetorium called this also a praetorium.

And to all the rest) Among the Roman populace.

Theophylact notes another sense, by which that 'in Christ' is not referred to the bonds, which he was suffering in Christ or because of Christ, but to the fame or manifestation of the bonds, because it happened in Christ, that is, by the power of Christ. But the former sense, because of similar passages where he calls himself a prisoner in the Lord, seems more agreeable, because it became known not only in the praetorium that Paul was sustaining those bonds because of the preaching of Christ, and not indeed because of some crime, but also among all others, whom it is by no means to be believed were converted by the power of the Lord, or at least even knew Christ: yet all had from thence an occasion of recognizing the Gospel concerning Christ. Although indeed the name of praetorium also signifies the court, and is so understood by Chrysostom, yet that signification is more famous by which the place of judgment is denoted, which is approved here by the blessed Luther. That it became known in the whole Imperial court that Paul was bound in the name of Christ, and that Paul's bonds were thus made manifest, is not to be denied, since the Apostle adds: and to all the rest. For as the Senators in the praetorium, when the Apostle was pleading his cause, understood that it was not a crime, and by that occasion the Gospel of Christ was also made manifest to them, for whose sake the Apostle was suffering those things: So the fame flowed from there to the whole court, nay, penetrated through the entire city, to all places, or to all men existing in them, just as is wont to happen when some notable prisoner is brought in. Chrysostom and Theophylact understand this of all places in the city, the blessed Luther, Piscator, and Musculus understand it of persons, or those who are at Rome, so that the preposition 'in' is not repeated from the common, but the Dative case is that the bonds had become known to all the rest dwelling at Rome, both citizens and foreigners, they explained. The matter comes to the same thing, because it became known not to the places by themselves, but to the men in the places: From whom without doubt some were brought to Christ.

Latin:

Vers. 13. Ὡστε τὺς δεσμύς με φανερὺς ἐν χριστῷ γενέσθαι ἐν ὅλῳ τῷ πραιτωρίῳ) Μετωνυμία. Vincula mea in Christo no- ta facta sunt : id est, innotuit, me vinctum esse tantum Christi causa. Qui rumor latius latiusque manans etiam in aulam pervenerat, ita ut & ibi quidam servorum & li- bertorum Cæsaris facti essent Christiani, infra IV. 22. Præ- tor olim dictus is, qui præiret exercitui, ut Varro explicat, hinc cohors prætoria, navis prætoria. Hinc prætorium dici cœpit tentorium Imperatoris : inde etiam Præsidis pro- vinciæ domus : duo prætoria coli apud Tacitum. Romæ Cæsarum domus palatium dicebatur : Sed provinciales assueti vocabulo prætorii appellabant & hanc πραιτώριον.

Καὶ τοῖς λοιποῖς πᾶσι) Apud plebem Romanam.

Theophylactus notat & alium sensum, quo illud ἐν χρισῷ non ad vincula referatur, quæ in Christo vel propter Christum patiebatur, sed ad celebri- tatem, vel manifestationem vinculorum, quod ea in Christo, id est, Christi virtute contigerit. Prior autem sensus ob loca similia, cum se captivum in Domino vocat, magis consentaneus videtur, quod non modo in prætorio id innotuerit, Paulum ob Christi præconium, non vero ob scelus quoddam vincula ista sustinere, sed etiam apud omnes alios, quos virtute Domini conversos esse, aut saltem etiam Christum cognovisse, minime credendum : omnes tamen inde occasionem habuere Evange- lium de Christo agnoscendi. Quanquam vero prætorii nomine etiam aula veniat, & ita à Chryso- stomo intelligatur, famosior tamen illa significatio est, qua locus judicii notatur, quæ B. Luthero hic probata. In tota aula Imperatoria id innotuisse, quod Paulus Christi nomine vinctus sit, adeoque manifesta facta esse Pauli vincula, negandum non est, quum addat Apostolus: καὶ τοῖς λοιποῖς πᾶσι. Nam ut Senatores in prætorio, cum causam suam ageret Apostolus, intellexêre, non esse ma- leficium, eaque occasione Evangelium Christi etiam manifestum factum est iisdem, cujus causa patiebatur Apostolus ista: Ita fama inde dimana- vit ad totam aulam, imo penetravit per universam urbem, ad omnia loca, vel ad omnes homines, in illis existentes, quemadmodum fieri solet, cum in- signis aliquis captivus adductus est. De locis omni- bus in urbe Chrysostomus & Theophylactus, de per- sonis, vel iis, qui Romæ sunt B. Lutherus, Piscator, Musculus intelligunt, ut præpositio ἐν non repe- tatur ἀπὸ τῦ κοινῦ, sed casus Dativus sit innotuisse vincula τοῖς λοιποῖς πᾶσι reliquis omnibus Romæ versantibus tum civibus tum peregrinis, exposue- re. Res eodem recidit, quia non locis per se, sed hominibus in locis innotuit: E quibus sine dubio nonnulli ad Christum adducti sunt.

## 1:14
Verse 14. And the majority of the brethren in the Lord) such as those who are greeted in Rom. XVI.

Confident in my bonds) excited, he says, by the example of my patience.

To speak the word of God more abundantly) more abundantly, fearlessly, that is, more fearlessly.

Another fruit is noted, according to the interpretation of B. Hunnius, which arose beyond the expectation of the enemies from the captivity of Paul, namely that most of the brothers, or Christians, who were staying in Rome, whom the adversaries of Paul hoped would be deterred from the Gospel by the chains of the Apostle, were by this rendered more courageous to profess it fearlessly, and to spread the name of Christ far and wide, being indeed confirmed by the invincible constancy of their Apostle, who does not hesitate to approach prisons, nay, to meet death and shed his blood for this doctrine concerning the crucified and risen-from-the-dead JESUS. The former fruit was thus the more ample propagation of the sound doctrine concerning Christ: the latter, however, is the more confident confession of the name of Christ. For indeed, says Theophylact, although they dared to preach more confidently before, now they are going to dare it even more zealously, because they see me, even bound and cast into prison, proclaiming the Word of God with greater confidence. And they were truly rendered stronger when they had seen me detained in chains, and were incited to imitate me. If, therefore, those who are closer to my chains do not lose heart at all, but dare more, then you also ought to be so much the more confident, the further you are from these chains. They are brothers faithful in the Lord. But those who disseminated the doctrine concerning Christ out of envy did not pertain to them. For the μερισμὸς, which follows, is not of those who would announce Christ more confidently, but, on the occasion of both the fame concerning Christ being propagated by many and everywhere, and the more confident confession of Christ made by the brothers in the Lord, the Apostle explains the diverse causes and the men of diverse kinds who spread the doctrine or the fame concerning Christ, and he teaches how all those things are nevertheless directed by GOD to the glorifying of the name of Christ.

Latin:

Vers. 14. Καὶ τὺς πλείονας τῶν ἀδελφῶν ἐν κυρίῳ) quales illi, qui salutantur Rom. XVI.

Πεποιθότας τοῖς δεσμοῖς με) excitati, inquit, meæ pa- tientiæ exemplo.

Περισσοτέρως τολμᾷν τὸν τῦ Θεῦ λόγον λαλεῖν) περισσοτέ- ρως, ἀφόβως, id est ἀφοβωτέρως.

Alius, interprete B. Hunnio, notatur fructus, qui præter expectationem hostium ex captivitate Pauli enatus est, quod plerique fratres, sive Christia- ni, qui Romæ versabantur, quos adversarii Pauli sperabant deterritum iri ab Evangelio vinculis A- postoli, hinc animosiores sunt redditi ad profitendum intrepide, & longe lateque spargendum nomen Chri- sti, quippe confirmati invicta Apostoli sui constan- tia, qui non dubitet adire carceres, quin mortem oppetere & sanguinem profundere ob hanc de cru- cifixo & ex mortuis resuscitato JESU doctrinam. Prior fructus ita fuit amplior fanæ de Christo do- ctrinæ propagatio: Alter vero est, confidentior no- minis Christi confessio. Enimvero, inquit Theophy- lactus, etsi antea prædicare confidentius sunt ausi, nunc vero eo enixius id sunt ausuri, quia & me vel vinctum & conjectum in carcerem majori fiducia Verbum Dei enuntiare conspiciunt. Et fortiores profecto sunt redditi, cum me vidissent in vinculis detineri, & ad me imitandum sunt incitati. Si ita- que qui sunt vinculis meis propinquiores, nihil ani- mo concidunt, sed audent magis, ergo & vos tanto fidentiores esse debetis, quanto à vinculis hisce abestis. Fratres in Domino fideles sunt. Ad quos vero non spectabant illi, qui ex invidia doctrinam de Chri- sto disseminarunt. Nam μερισμὸς, qui sequitur, non est illorum, qui confidentius Christum an- nunciarent, sed occasione tum famæ de Christo per plurimos, & passim propagatæ, tum confiden- tioris Christi confessionis à fratribus in Domino factæ, exponit Apostolus diversas causas & diversi generis homines, qui doctrinam vel famam de Christo spargunt, ac quomodo omnia tamen illa dirigantur à DEO ad glorificandum nomen Christi, docet.

## 1:15
Vers. 15. Some indeed out of envy and strife) He indicates the Jews, who, in order to impede the progress of Christianity, were everywhere spreading rumors about what that doctrine was, and by what arguments it supported itself, which thing caused many to run to Paul, to understand the whole matter from him himself.

But some also out of good will preach Christ) Some were also spreading the Christian dogma for the reason that they themselves approved of it, because they were well-pleased in it, which kind of expression is in 2 Corinthians 12:10. And the good will in Romans 10:1 is not much different.

Latin:

Vers. 15. Τινὲς μὲν καὶ διὰ φθόνον καὶ ἔριν) Judæos indi- cat, qui ut progressum Christianismi impedirent, ubique rumoribus differebant, qualis esset illa doctrina, quibus se argumentis fulciret, quæ res efficiebat, ut multi ad Pau- lum concurrerent, ex ipso rem totam intellecturi.

Τινὲς δὲ καὶ δι' εὐδοκίαν τὸν χριστὸν κηρύσσουσι) Quidam etiam vulgabant Christianum dogma, ideo quod ipsi id probarent, ὅτι ἐν αὐτῷ εὐδόκησαν, qualis loquutio 2. Corinth. XII. 10. Nec multo aliter εὐδοκία Rom. X. 1.

## 1:16
Vers. 16. Some indeed out of faction) that is, out of strifes. And the 'out of' in this place is in place of an adjective, as in Romans 4:12, and with the same word 'faction' in Romans 2:6.

They announce Christ not sincerely) not with a pious and pure mind.

Thinking to bring affliction to my bonds) They seek this, that they might bring me into stricter custody, for that is why they speak everywhere about the dogma, because they hope that they will stir up hatred against both me and the dogma. In the Manuscript, instead of 'to bring' there is 'to raise up,' as the Latin also appears to have read.

Latin:

Vers. 16. Οἱ μὲν ἐξ ἐριθείας) id est ἐξ ἐρίδων. Et ἐξ hoc loco est vice Adjectivi, ut Rom. IV. 12. & cum eadem voce ἐριθείας Rom. II. 6.

Τὸν χριστὸν καταγγέλλουσιν οὐχ ἁγνῶς) non pio, puroque animo.

Οἰόμενοι θλίψιν ἐπιφέρειν τοῖς δεσμοῖς μου) Hoc quæ- runt, ut in arctiorem der custodiam, ideo enim ubique de dogmate loquuntur, quod sperent se & mihi & dogmati odium concitaturos. In Manuscripto pro ἐπιφέρειν est ἐγείρειν, quomodo & Latinum legisse apparet.

## 1:17
Vers. 17. But others out of love) Because they love me, they say what things they are that I teach, namely those pertaining to the amending of morals, not at all seditious.

Thus also B. Hunnius understands this concerning the Jews: The Apostle uses 'division' to explain the variety of the manner in which the fame of the Gospel concerning Christ is spread. He shows, however, that there are two main kinds of men by whose speeches the name of Christ becomes famous. Some, he says, preach Christ through contention and envy. He strikes at the Jews, among whom there was much talk in Rome about the Gospel being divulged into the whole world by the Apostles, to which they did not fear to brand with the mark of heresy, saying: concerning this heresy it is known to us that it is spoken against everywhere, Acts 28. Although they were indeed carping at and blaspheming the doctrine of the Gospel, by this very fact they were speaking about it, and beyond their own intent they were making that fame concerning CHRIST more celebrated, and they were providing an opportunity for others to inquire into this doctrine, whether it was from GOD or not. Which thing was, as it were, paving the way for the conversion of many. That does not please Crocius. He prefers with Zanchius to explain it concerning the brothers: who, when they were contending with Paul about fame and reputation, evangelized only when inflamed by envy and driven by that emulation. But were those brothers in the Lord? By name, says Crocius, they were brothers, but in deed they were enemies. But the Apostle did not say brothers simply, but brothers in the Lord: he furthermore proclaimed those brothers, because they dared to speak the word fearlessly, having become more courageous by the bonds of the Apostle, which do not befit those rivals. Nor could the Apostle have praised such contention. However, there is no doubt that the Apostle himself provided the cause for the enemies of the Gospel to be heard and for the truth to be known. The blessed Hunnius adds contained false teachers, who, although they had embraced Christianity, nevertheless mixed in Judaism. And therefore, for whatever reason, they desired to cause trouble for Paul the Apostle. Nor is that inconvenience [a problem], namely that those classes are adequate for all who announce Christ. Not that he rejoiced because of the proclamation of the Pseudo-Apostles, whom he wishes to be guarded against like dogs, ch. III, but because he believed that it could be turned by divine goodness to a good end and contribute to his own salvation. Furthermore, although the objections of Crocius against the opinion of the blessed Hunnius—which was also that of the blessed Balduinus—can be satisfied in this way: nevertheless, that explanation of Crocius does not seem inconsistent, provided that those preachers are not reckoned among the brothers in the Lord, by which he thinks are noted the rivals who were envious, who, grieving that they and their own preaching were being obscured by Paul, tried to depress him so that they alone might stand out; who, while they increased his preaching and equally with him made disciples, sharpened the anger of the King against Paul, as Chrysostom notes. For by the proclamation of these, Nero could easily be more incited against Paul, as against the primary leader of a sect whom everyone followed, even a prisoner, so that he might constrain him with prison and tighter bonds, prohibit everyone from access, and thus restrain the progress of the Pauline proclamation both in his praetorium and in the whole city, or even remove him from the midst. Since they hoped that, with him removed, they alone would triumph as the chief masters of the faith. Crocius therefore wishes to note those who indeed taught the truth, but with an evil mind, that is, vitiated by envy, hatred, and the desire for empty glory, bringing in Augustine for that matter from book II, Quæst. Evang. cap. 33, who, he says, did not announce anything else, like heretics, but this, which the Apostle [did], yet not with the same mind with which the Apostle Paul [did]. Whence they are rightly called mercenaries, indeed handling the same bread of the Word in the same house, yet not called to the eternal inheritance, but hired for a temporal wage. The words ἔρις and ἐρίθεια are distinguished here in the ascetics ascribed to Basil: Ἔρις μέν ἐσιν, ὅταν τις ὑπὲρ τῶν μὴ ἐλάττων φανῆναί τινῷ σπεδάζῃ ποιεῖν τι. Ἐρίθεια δὲ τὸ ἐξ ὧν ποιεῖ τις ἐπιδεικτικῶς ἢ κενοδόξως προκαλεῖσθαι καὶ ἐριθίζειν ἄλλως εἰς τὰ ὅμοια.

Εἰδότες ὅτι εἰς ἀπολογίαν τῦ Εὐαγγελίυ κεῖμαι) κεῖμαι, that is, τίθεμαι. Thus we had κεῖται in Luke II. 34. Thus also κείμεθα, 1 Thess. III. 3. Thus שימה is translated ᾧ κείμεθα, 2 Sam. XIII. 32. Therefore they love me and pity me, because they know that I did not come to the duty of preaching this Gospel of my own accord, but was called by God. Ἀνάγκη μοι ἐπίκειται, he himself says in 1 Cor. IX, 16. In the manuscript, οἱ μὲν ἐξ ἀγάπης &c. precedes, but οἱ δὲ ἐξ ἐριθείας follows. The Latin interpreter used a similar codex.

Theodoret also explained it concerning divine selection and vocation, about which [he wrote] in Rom. I. 1, 1 Cor. I. v. 1, Eph. I. 1. Lombard and Piscator understand it concerning the bonds. The blessed Hunnius combines both: that I was appointed for the defense of the Gospel, and because of its assertion was cast into bonds. The bonds can be implied. But primarily and directly, the appointment is understood in the vocation, in this sense: knowing that I have been appointed and called divinely for this, that I should defend the Gospel, even if I must undergo bonds and death, cf. Acts IX. 15, 16.

Latin:

Vers. 17. Οἱ δὲ ἐξ ἀγάπης) Ideo quod me ament, dicunt quæ sint, quæ doceam, spectantia scilicet ad emendandos mores, minime seditiosa.

Ita & B. Hunnius de Judæis hoc intelligit: Με- ρισμῷ utitur Apostolus ad explicandam varieta- tem modi, quo spargatur fama Evangelii de Chri- sto. Ostendit autem, duo potissimum esse genera ho- minum, quorum sermonibus inclarescat nomen Christi. Quidam inquit per contentionem & invi- diam Christum prædicant. Pervringit vero Judæos, inter quos multus erat Romæ sermo de Evangelio per Apostolos in orbem terrarum divulgato, cui non verebantur hæreseos notam inurere dicentes; de hac hæresi notum est nobis, quod ubique contra- dicitur ei, Actor. XXVIII. Quanquam vero do- ctrinam Evangelii carpebant & blasphemabant, hoc ipso tamen de ea loquebantur, & præter insti- tutum suum illam de CHRISTO famam redde- bant celebriorem, qui & ansam subministrabant aliis inquirendi in hanc doctrinam, num ex DEO esset vel non. Quæ res ad conversionem multorum quasi viam sternebat. Non placet id Crocio. Ma- vult cum Zanchio de fratribus exponere: qui cum Paulo de fama & existimatione contendebant, non nisi invidia accensi, & impellente eos illa æmulatione evangelizarunt. Sed num illi fratres erant in Domino? Nominetenus, inquit Crocius, erant fratres, sed facto erant inimici. At Apostolus non fratres dixit simpliciter, sed fratres in Domi- no: Prædicavit insuper fratres illos, quod ausint impavide sermonem loqui animosiores facti vin- culis Apostoli, quæ æmulis istis non conveniunt. Nec talem contentionem laudare potuisset Apo- stolus. Hostium autem Evangelii insectationem & calumnias causam præbuisse Apostolum ipsum audiendi & veritatem cognoscendi dubium nul- lum est. Addit B. Hunnius sub hac prædicantium Christum classe contineri etiam falsos Doctores, qui cum Christianismum amplexi essent, nihilo- minus Judaismum admiscebant. Ideoque Paulo Apostolo quacunque ratione cupiebant ægre fa- cere. Nec id incommodum, ut scilicet classes il- læ adæquatæ sint omnibus annuntiantibus Chri- stum. Non quod ob Pseudo-Apostolorum præ- conium gauderet, quos ceu canes caveri vult, c. III. sed quod in bonum finem divina bonitate etiam converti, suæque saluti cedere crederet. Cæterum quamvis ita Crocii objectionibus, adversus B. Hunnii, quæ etiam B. Balduini fuit, sententiam, satisfieri possit: Non inconcinna tamen videtur illa Crocii explicatio, dummodo ne fratribus in Domino præcones illi accenseantur, qua notari pu- tat æmulos, qui invidebant, qui se suamque prædi- cationem à Paulo obscurari dolentes ipsum depri- mere conati sunt, ut soli eminerent, qui cum præ- dicationem illius augebant, & pariter cum illo di- scipulos faciebant, acuebant iram Regis in Pau- lum, notante Chrysostomo. Horum enim præco- nio magis concitari in Paulum facile poterat Ne- ro, tanquam in sectæ Ducem primarium, quem omnes sequerentur, etiam captivum, ut eum car- cere ac vinculis arctioribus constringeret, accessu omnes prohiberet, ac ita profectum præconii Paulini tum in prætorio suo, tum in urbe tota co- hiberet, aut etiam è medio ipsum tolleret. Siqui- dem isti sperarint, illo sublato se solos triumpha- turos, tanquam præcipuos fidei Magistros. Nota- ri ergo eos vult Crocius, qui verum quidem doce- bant, sed malo animo, id est, invidia, odio, & ina- nis gloriæ cupiditate vitiato, Augustinum eam in rem adducens è libr. II. Quæst. Evang. cap. 33. qui non aliud annunciabant, inquit, sicut hæretici, sed hoc, quod Apostolus, non tamen eo animo, quo Apo- stolus Paulus. Unde & mercenarii recte appellan- tur, in eadem quidem domo eundem panem Ver- bi tractantes, non tamen in hæreditatem æternam vocati, sed temporali mercede conducti. Voces ἔρις & ἐρίθεια hic distinguuntur in asceticis, adscri- ptis Basilio: Ἔρις μέν ἐσιν, ὅταν τις ὑπὲρ τῶν μὴ ἐ- λάττων φανῆναί τινῷ σπεδάζῃ ποιεῖν τι. Ἐρίθεια δὲ τὸ ἐξ ὧν ποιεῖ τις ἐπιδεικτικῶς ἢ κενοδόξως προ- καλεῖσθαι καὶ ἐριθίζειν ἄλλως εἰς τὰ ὅμοια.

Εἰδότες ὅτι εἰς ἀπολογίαν τῦ Εὐαγγελίυ κεῖμαι) κεῖμαι, id est τίθεμαι. Sic κεῖται habuimus Luc. II. 34. Sic & κεί- μεθα, 1. Thessal. III. 3. Sic שימה vertitur ᾧ κείμεθα, 2. Sam. XIII. 32. Ideo me amant & me miserantur, quia sciunt me ad munus prædicandi Evangelii hujus non spon- te venisse, sed à Deo vocatum. Ἀνάγκη μοι ἐπίκειται dicit ipse 1. Cor. IX, 16. In Manuscripto præcedit, οἱ μὲν ἐξ ἀγά- πης &c. sequitur vero, οἱ δὲ ἐξ ἐριθείας. Simili codice usus est Latinus interpres.

De divina selectione & vocatione etiam Theo- doretus exposuit, de qua Roman. I. 1. 1. Cor. I. v. 1. Eph. I. 1. Lombardus & Piscator de vinculis intelli- gunt. B. Hunnius conjungit utrumque: Me in de- fensionem Evangelii constitutum, & propter as- sertionem ejus in vincula conjectum esse. Subin- nui vincula possunt. Primo autem & directe con- stitutio in vocatione intelligitur, hoc sensu, scientes, quod ego ad id constitutus & vocatus sim divi- nitus, ut defendam Evangelium, etsi vincula & mortem subire debeam, conf. Act. IX. 15. 16.

## 1:18
Vers. 18. Τί γάρ;) It is an idiomatic expression. This is what it means: What follows from this? Nothing except &c.

Πλὴν παντὶ τρόπῳ εἴτε προφάσει εἴτε ἀληθείᾳ Χριστὸς καταγγέλλεται) In the manuscript, πλὴν ὅτι is not bad. Προφάσει here does not signify pretext, but occasion. For from the occasion, those Jews, while they study to harm Paul, were drawing many to the Gospel. Thus Prov. XVIII. 1, Προφάσεις ζητεῖ, the Latin translates: he seeks occasions. Thus ἐν προφάσει πλεονεξίας, the Latin: in the occasion of avarice. In the glossary, πρόφασις is occasion. Thus πρόφασιν λαμβάνειν in Plato: to seize an occasion. Thus also Euripides: Ἐπεὶ βραχείας προφάσεως ἔδει μόνον. Conversely, ἀληθείᾳ here is with a sincere mind.

If ἀλήθεια denotes a sincere mind, why should πρόφασις not signify a mere pretext of sincere zeal for the glory of God and heavenly truth, rather than an occasion by way of opposition? So that Christ or the true doctrine of Christ is said to be announced either in appearance, when the name and glory of Christ are used as a pretext for envy and contention, and in reality one's own glory and private advantage are sought: or truly, not from the heart, without simulation, when the glory of Christ is sincerely intended. Simulation is not approved, nor is the pretext, but the announcement of Christ, even if simulated, is not deprived of its utility, since what is announced by the preachers with an insincere mind can be received by the hearers with a sincere mind.

Καὶ ἐν τούτῳ χαίρω ἀλλὰ καὶ χαρήσομαι) In the good outcome even of evil counsels.

These things, says Theophylact, [they do] so that they may affect him with grief. But I myself rejoice, because by this the name of Christ will be the more spread abroad. And the more they have done this, the more I shall be filled with joy.

Latin:

Vers. 18. Τί γάρ;) Est oratio ἰδιωτική. Hoc vult: Quid hinc sequitur? Nihil nisi &c.

Πλὴν παντὶ τρόπῳ εἴτε προφάσει εἴτε ἀληθείᾳ Χριστὸς καταγ- γέλλεται) In Manuscripto πλὴν ὅτι non male. Προφά- σει hic non significat prætextu, sed occasione. Nam ex occa- sione isti Judæi, dum nocere Paulo student multos pertrahe- bant ad Evangelium. Sic Prov. XVIII. 1. Προφάσεις ζητεῖ Latinus vertit, occasiones quærit. Sic ἐν προφάσει πλεονε- ξίας, Latinus in occasione avaritiæ. In Glossario πρόφασις occasio. Sic πρόφασιν λαμβάνειν apud Platonem occasionem arripere. Sic & Euripides: Ἐπεὶ βραχείας προφάσεως ἔδει μόνον. Contra ἀληθείᾳ hic est animo sincero.

Si ἀλήθεια animum sincerum notat, quidni πρό- φασις nudum prætextum sinceri studii gloriæ Dei & veritatis cœlestis potius, quam occasionem vi oppositionis significet? Ut Christus vel vera Chri- sti doctrina annunciari dicatur vel in speciem, cum invidiæ ac contentioni prætexitur Christi nomen & gloria, & revera gloria propria, accom- modum privatum quæritur: vel vere id, non ex animo, citra simulationem, cum Christi gloria, sincere intenditur. Non probatur simulatio, non prætextus, sed Christi annunciatio, etsi simulata, utilitate sua non destituitur, quum sincero animo recipi possit ab Auditoribus, quod animo non sin- cero annunciatur à præconibus.

Καὶ ἐν τούτῳ χαίρω ἀλλὰ καὶ χαρήσομαι) In bono eventu etiam malorum consiliorum.

Hæc quidem, inquit Theophylactus, illi ut mœ- rore afficiant. At ipse lætor, quia eo amplius Christi nomen vulgabitur. Et quo id maxime egerint, eo & maxime explebor jucunditate.

## 1:19
Vers. 19. Οἶδα γὰρ ὅτι τοῦτό μοι ἀποβήσεται εἰς σωτηρίαν) This will turn out for salvation, namely of many men.

Διὰ τῆς ὑμῶν δεήσεως καὶ ἐπιχορηγίας τοῦ πνεύματος Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ) With you praying, and at your prayers, Christ supplying to me the perpetual strength of His Spirit. Χορηγία is supply.

The Apostle speaks of his own salvation, not that of others. Τοῦτό μοι ἀποβήσεται εἰς σωτηρίαν, this will turn out for me for salvation. For that pronoun of the first person is not added rashly. And the Apostle treats later of Christ being glorified in his body, by his death, or by his life. But how did the feigned preaching of others result in the salvation of the Apostle? The Apostle knew that, however much his rivals or enemies might intend to harm him, nothing would be taken away from his salvation; nay, that through patience, if afflictions should be increased, and death itself should finally have to be undergone, he would overcome all things, and would bring back the glorious crown of the constancy of faith, Apoc. II. 10. But Paul knew this not from an insuperable faith, as Crocius speaks, or absolutely, from the certainty of perseverance, but from faith in the divine promises, that all things work together for good to those who love God, and that provided we do not desert God, He would by no means wish to desert us with His grace, 1. Cor. I. 1. 1. Petr. I. & V. Therefore he joins prayers with the supply of the Spirit, because by assiduous prayers, both our own and those of others, that is obtained, for which reason he tacitly seeks the intercession of the Philippians for himself, and commends the efficacy of the prayers of the Church.

Latin:

Vers. 19. Οἶδα γὰρ ὅτι τοῦτό μοι ἀποβήσεται εἰς σωτηρίαν) Exibit hoc ad salutem, nempe multorum hominum.

Διὰ τῆς ὑμῶν δεήσεως καὶ ἐπιχορηγίας τοῦ πνεύματος Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ) Vobis precantibus & ad vestras preces Christo mihi suppeditante vim perpetuam Spiritus sui. Χορηγία ספק.

De sua salute loquitur Apostolus, non aliorum. Τοῦτό μοι ἀποβήσεται εἰς σωτηρίαν, hoc mihi exibit ad salutem. Non enim temere illud Pronomen primæ personæ additum. Et de Christo glorifican- do in corpore suo, morte sua, aut vita sua, agit Apo- stolus postea. Quomodo autem aliorum simulata prædicatio saluti cedebat Apostoli? Sciebat Apo- stolus, quantumcunque nocere ipsi intendant æ- muli aut hostes, saluti suæ nihil decessurum, imo per patientiam, si afflictiones augeantur, ac mors denique ipsa subeunda sit, sese omnia superaturum, & constantiæ fidei coronam gloriosam reportatu- rum, Apoc. II. 10. sciebat autem id Paulus non ex insuperabili fide, ut Crocius loquitur, vel absolute, ex perseverantiæ certitudine, sed ex fide promisso- rum divinorum, quod Deum diligentibus omnia cooperantur in bonum, quodque modo ipsi non deseramus Deum, nos gratia sua deserere haud ve- lit, 1. Cor. I. 1. 1. Petr. I. & V. Ideo preces cum subministratione Spiritus conjungit, quod assiduis precibus tum nostris, tum aliorum ea obtineatur, quo nomine tacite Philippensium intercessionem pro se expetit, & efficaciam precum Ecclesiæ com- mendat.

## 1:20
Vers. 20. Κατὰ τὴν ἀποκαραδοκίαν καὶ τὴν ἐλπίδα μου) Concerning the word ἀποκαραδοκίας see Rom. VIII. 19. Ps. XXXVII. 7. התחולל is translated by Aquila ἀποκαραδόκει.

It is indicated by this word that he is constantly panting, with his head and mouth as it were stretched toward heaven, expecting salvation from God: because κάρα signifies head. Whence ἀποκαραδοκία is a vehement desire, which is not only included in the mind, but also reveals itself through the gestures of the body, when someone, in the manner of those who are vehemently gasping and with the whole head bent, looks around here and there, whether that appears which he desires in his mind. Ἀποκαραδοκίαν, says Theophyl., the Greeks say, which the interpreter called expectation, from κάρα, which designates the head, and δοκεῖν, which is to nod, just as if the whole head nods and inclines toward that which is firmly and certainly hoped for.

that I shall not be ashamed in anything) That it will not be a vain labor. It is a Metonymy, such as 2 Cor. X. 8. לא אבוש Psalm CXIX. 80. Is. XLIX. 23.

There is no need for a Metonymy. The literal sense is clear. For he implies that his hope is such that it will not be put to shame in any matter concerning the glory of God or his own salvation. Just as the prayers of the Church will not be ineffectual; so he testifies that his hope also will not be put to shame: but he is not dealing here with the success of his own labors. Theophylact says at this point that he reminds us that not everything is to be entrusted to the prayers of others, but that we must also hope for what we desire through ourselves, and must ask for it in our prayers, as Paul infers, and the Prophet affirms when he says, let thy mercy be upon us, O Lord, according as we have hoped in thee. And elsewhere: Who has hoped in the Lord, and was confounded? And Paul the same: Hope does not confound.

But in all boldness) Through the free profession of believers, as Acts IV. 13, 29, 31.

As always and now Christ shall be magnified) As before, so also now he will obtain a great name. Concerning the word μεγαλύνεσθαι see Luke I. 46, 58. Acts X. 46, XIX. 17. Psalm CIV. 1, and often elsewhere.

In my body, whether by life, or by death) He rightly referred the word body to both. For the body speaks, and the body is killed. Martyrs are said by their death to glorify God, as we have seen at John XXI. 19.

Therefore he does not designate the boldness of others but his own: Hence the Hunnian paraphrase is more correct: Therefore I have a certain and undoubted confidence that it will come to pass that, just as always before in the whole course of my ministry, so also henceforth CHRIST will be glorified in my body, whether by life or by death. If it is granted to live further, I will gladly carry around the treasure of the Gospel entrusted to me in the earthen vessel of my body. But if I must die, and this body must be sacrificed for the testimony of the Lord JESUS: be it so, also through a glorious martyrdom my Lord will be glorified in my body.

Latin:

Vers. 20. Κατὰ τὴν ἀποκαραδοκίαν καὶ τὴν ἐλπίδα μου) De voce ἀποκαραδοκίας vide Rom. VIII. 19. Ps. XXXVII. 7. התחולל vertitur ab Aquila ἀποκαραδόκει.

Indicatur hac voce, quod jugiter anhelus exer- to quasi in cœlum capite & ore salutem à Deo ex- pectet: quia κάρα significat caput. Unde ἀποκα- ραδοκία vehemens desiderium, quod non solum in- cluditur animo, sed etiam per gestus corporis se prodit, cum quis vehementer inhiantium more totoque inflexo capite huc illuc circumspicit, num id appareat, quod animo concupiscit. Ἀπο- καραδοκίαν, inquit Theophyl. dicunt Græci, quam expectationem dixit interpres, ex κάρα, quod caput designat, & δοκεῖν, quod annuere est, perinde ac si ca- put totum nutet, & vergat ad id, quod firmiter & cer- to speratur.

ὅτι ἐν ὀὐδενὶ αἰσχυνθήσομαι) Fore ut non in vanum labo- rem. Est Μετωνυμία, quales 2. Corinth. X. 8. לא אבוש Pfal. CXIX. 80. Ef. XLIX. 23.

Non opus Metonymia est. Senfus proprius est luculentus. Spem enim suam talem esse innuit, quæ nulla in re gloriam Dei aut salutem suam concer- nente pudefiat. Ut preces Ecclesiæ non irritas fore; Ita spem suam etiam non pudefieri testatur: non autem de laborum suorum successu hic agit. Commonefacit hoc loco, inquit Theophylactus, non omnia esse alienis precibus commendanda, quin etiam sperandum per nos erit, quod cupimus, & vo- tis id deposcendum, ut Paulus infert, & Propheta affirmat, cum inquit, fiat misericordia tua Domine, quemadmodum speravimus in te. Et alibi: Quis speravit in Domino, & confusus est? Et Paulus idem: Spes non confundit.

Ἀλλ' ἐν πάσῃ παῥῥησίᾳ) Per liberam professionem creden- tium, ut Actor. IV. 13. 29. 31.

Ὡς πάντοτε καὶ νῦν μεγαλυνθήσεται χριστὸς) Sicut ante, ita & nunc magnum confequetur nomen. De voce μεγα- λύνεσθαι vide Luc. I. 46. 58. Actor. X. 46. XIX. 17. Pfalm. CIV. 1. & alibi sæpe.

Ἐν τῷ σώματί μου, εἴτε διὰ ζωῆς, εἴτε διὰ θανάτου) Bene corporis vocem ad utrumque retulit. Nam & corpus loquitur, & corpus occiditur. Dicuntur martyres morte sua δοξάζειν τὸν Θεὸν, ut vidimus ad Joh. XXI. 19.

Non ergo aliorum παῥῥησίαν sed propriam de- signat: Rectius proinde habet sese paraphrasis Hunniana: Ideo certam indubiamque fiduciam ha- beo, futurum, ut quemadmodum antehac semper toto cursu ministerii mei, sic etiam porro glorifice- tur CHRISTUS in corpore meo, sive per vitam, sive per mortem. Si dabitur porro vivere, libenter concreditum mihi thesaurum Evangelii circumfe- ram in vase testaceo corporis mei. Sin moriendum erit, & hoc corpus ad testimonium Domini JESU immolandum: age sic quoque per gloriosum marty- rium in corpore meo glorificabitur Dominus meus.

## 1:21
Verse 21. For to me to live is Christ) that is, if I live, I serve Christ. My life is occupied with nothing but the things of Christ. Gregory Nazianzen: A life that has drunk up gain day by day.

And to die is gain) And if I die, by my death I will gain some for Christ. Thus we have κερδαίνειν in 1 Cor. IX. 19, 20, 21, 22. 1 Pet. III. 1. This is the opposite of that which is in Psalm XXX. 18. מה־בצע בדמי.

He is not dealing so much with the gain of the salvation of others as with the gain of his own salvation. Furthermore, to live to me, says the Apostle (or my life), is Christ, and to die (TO ME, or my death) is gain. Christ here is the predicate, my living or my life is the subject. To which corresponds in the other clause the word to die in the place of the subject, and indeed the word gain as the predicate. Therefore that proposition is not to be inverted in this way: Christ is life to me, which is done by those who explain how Christ is to us natural, spiritual, heavenly life, because he is its author; thus Thomas explained it actively, as if he were professing Christ to be the whole principle of his life and operation: for he is not dealing with the origin of life, but the Apostle explains how Christ may be glorified in his body while he lives, because, namely, he esteems this living of his, and has determined to do this through his life, and does it, so that Christ may be uniquely glorified, so that his life is not so much the union of soul and body, or a vital act, as Christ himself, whom he had instead of his soul and his life, for the life of his soul and of his body; just as he reckons his dying not for the destruction of life, but for the gain of a better and eternal life, not for the loss of any good, but for the attainment of every good. Where does the interpretation of Theophylact go: But to me to live is Christ, that is, I lead a certain new life, and Christ is to me for all things. For spirit, I say, life and light. For in this place the Apostle does not deny that he will live a natural life, but that which is bound by sins and is intent upon the deceptions of this age. Moreover, he confesses that CHRIST is to him for life, just as he also says elsewhere: I live in the faith of the Son of God. With which also the commentary of Chrysostom agrees: In this life, what I live, is not life to me, but CHRIST. Nor is the explanation of Lombard foreign: As if he were to say: I live for the sake of Christ, that I may magnify Christ, and for no other reason: There is also added the exegesis of Zanchius and Piscator: The scope of my whole life is CHRIST, and his glory: And also John Crocius: as if he were saying: I am certain that Christ will be magnified with the greatest freedom in my fragile body, whether I live or die, for this reason, because every power, faculty, endeavor, study, action, and suffering of my life is directed by me to nothing other than to illustrate the glory of Christ. He attempts to excuse Beza's interpretation, although it is also that of Calvin and Musculus, which is also approved by Erasmus Schmid, yet he hardly dares to approve it, which Piscator indeed expressly disapproves, because he rendered it: For to me Christ is gain both in life and in death.

Piscator says that this transposition is harsh and foreign to the simplicity of the Pauline style, both because he would have placed the words thus: Ἐμοὶ γὰρ χριστὸς κὴ τὸ ζῆν, καὶ τὸ ἀποθανεῖν κέρδος, and because that sentence does not cohere as a reason with the preceding one, which the conjunction γὰρ nevertheless demands, because the glory of CHRIST is one thing, and the salvation of Paul, which he understands by the name of gain, is another. Crocius therefore prefers the version of Blessed Luther with this praise from Piscator and the Vulgate: The other version is more common, and has the consensus of all antiquity, as far as I have been able to examine it, and it presses the letter of the Apostle, and fits the text beautifully. You may also hear Daniel Heinsius here at length acting the tragedian concerning Beza's version: It is sometimes a source of grief to me that men, even the greatest, could not approve the simplicity of the ancients in those places too, which had no difficulty at all. For what else did the Apostle say here, except what he proclaims everywhere? Namely, that his life is in Christ, and that death also will be gain for him on account of Him: he who lives in Him, who excites spiritual motions in Him, by whom he is enlivened and excited to preach Him. Just as at Galatians 2:20: ζῶ δὲ ὀκέτι ἐγὼ, ζῇ δὲ ἐν ἐμοὶ χριστός. Since Christ lived in him, however, it is not a wonder if it happens, as he says, that he who lives thus, namely, cannot die: or if he is said to die, that death is gain to him, by which that which can die is laid aside, and that which cannot die is put on. But what need was there to interpret this as if the Apostle had said: Ἐμοὶ γὰρ τὸ ζῆν καὶ τὸ ἀποθανεῖν χριστός ἐστι κέρδος, so that τὸ κατὰ might be understood in both places, as if he were saying, ἐμοὶ γὰρ κατὰ τὸ ζῆν καὶ κατὰ ἀποθανεῖν χριστός ἐστι κέρδος. That this is troublesome cannot be denied, unless we are greatly deceived: since the other is plain and straightforward. See therefore the highest simplicity: To me, he says, life is Christ, and to die is gain. We have Flacius as of the same opinion. He says that this earthly living is Christ to him, that is, the preaching and glorification of Christ, but that to die is his own proper gain. Others wish the sense to be that Christ lives in him: Others that Christ is gain to him both in life and in death. But the former opinion seems to me to agree better both with the words of this very verse, and with the following comparison or explanation of this verse. Therefore he calls Christ here the promotion of the kingdom of Christ. These are the words of Flacius. This therefore is the proper sense of the words of the Apostle, that his life, every thought, every intention, every action of his life is directed to the glory of Christ, that his living is to glorify Christ. Thus the word ζῆν is accepted in no other than its proper sense, just as death is also to be understood concerning natural death; and in the preceding and following parts, the bonds and death, and so also life, through which the Apostle properly understood Christ to be glorified in his body, v. 20 and 22. Death, therefore, is called gain, as it pertains to Paul, and those like him, all the faithful dying in Christ, not that the Apostle is to gain by his death by constantly professing Christ, others for Christ, and others salvation, who will be excited to equal constancy by this example, although this has actually followed, and the Apostolic admonition tends to this, Heb. XIII. 7. For the Apostle here judges that life is to be chosen rather than death for the sake of the utility of the salvation of others, but that τὸ ἀποθανεῖν will be gain, because he is to gain for animal life the heavenly, for temporal goods the eternal, for the earthly dwelling of the body God his eternal dwelling, for sin righteousness, for captivity liberty, for spiritual thoughts, counsels, actions, and studies in human life still various and exposed to defects on account of the remnants of the flesh, heavenly thoughts, intentions, and actions free from every defect, dedicated solely to the knowledge, love, and glorification of God, for labor rest, for struggles triumph, for miseries beatitude, for ignominy glory, for a tomb of evils a heap of all goods, for sadness and pain joy and gladness to be terminated by no ages, for the kingdom of grace the kingdom of glory, for faith sight, for the preaching of Christ the blessed vision of the same. It is gain to have escaped the increments of sin, it is gain to have fled worse things, it is gain to pass to better things, as someone from the Ancients says. It is the greatest gain, says St. Cyprian, serm. IV. de mortal., that (the faithful) computes that he is no longer held by the snares of the age, that he is no longer made subject to any sins and vices of the flesh, removed from pressing burdens, and liberated from the poisonous jaws of the Devil, he proceeds to the joy of eternal salvation as GOD calls. Let us hear Chrysostom elucidating this passage more fully, but let us hear him through a summary of words: To me, he says, to live is Christ, and to die is gain. For even by dying, he says, I shall not die, having life in myself; then they would have taken me away, if they could have driven faith from my soul through fear. But as long as Christ is with me, even if death should rush in, I shall live. And even in this life, this is not living for me, but Christ. But if while I live here, this is not living for me, what will it be in the other age? But that now, he says, I live in the flesh, I live in faith. He says this also there: I live now not I, but Christ lives in me. It behooves a Christian to be such; I do not live, he says, a common life. He does not deny that he lives a natural life, but also that which is of sinners, which all men live. And indeed he rightly denies it. For he who is not desirous of the present life, how does he live this? He who hastens to the other, how does he live this? He who despises death, how does he live this? He who loves nothing of those things which are in the world, how does he live this? Thus he who does nothing for the sake of food, nothing for clothes, nothing for the sake of any present thing, how does he live here? He is surely not to be said to live even a natural life. He who cares for nothing of those things which pertain to life, he does not even live. We live this life, who do everything for this life, but he did not live, nor was he occupied in any inferior things: How therefore did he live? Thus also we say of some: He is not present to me, where he does nothing that pertains to me. Thus also again, he does not live for me. For that he does not reject this natural life, he shows elsewhere in these words: But that I now live in the flesh, I live in the faith of the Son of God, who loved me, and delivered himself for me, that is, I live a certain new life, and different from the customary law. He says all these things indeed for the consolation of the Philippians. Do not think, he says, that it will be that I am despoiled of this life, since not even living did I live this life. For tell me, he who despises money, who food, who hunger and thirst, who dangers, who health, who safety, does he live this life? He who has nothing on earth, who often desires to pour it out, if there be need, and does not struggle, does he live this life? By no means. To me, he says, to live is Christ, if you trace my life, that is it, and to die is gain: Why? Because there will be a greater knowledge of him for me, and I shall converse more familiarly with him. Wherefore this is nothing else than to arrive at life by dying. They will do nothing harder to me, those who shall kill me, sending me forth to my life, and liberating me from this, which is not suitable for me.

Latin:

Verf. 21. Ἐμοὶ γὰρ τὸ ζῆν χριστὸς) id est, si vivo, Christo servio. Vita mea non nisi in Christi rebus occupatur. Gre- gorius Nazianzenus. Βίος τὸ κέρδος ἐκπιὼν καθ' ἡμέραν.

Καὶ τὸ ἀποθανεῖν κέρδος) Et si moriar, morte mea ali- quos Christo lucrabor. Sic κερδαίνειν habemus 1. Cor. IX. 19. 20. 21. 22. 1. Petr. III. 1. Est hoc oppositum ei, quod est in Pfal. XXX. 18. מה־בצע בדמי.

Non tam de lucro salutis aliorum, quam de lu- cro salutis propriæ agit. Porro vivere mihi, inquit Apostolus (vel vita mea) Christus, & mori (MIHI, vel mors mea) lucrum. Christus hic prædicatum est, subjectum vivere meum vel vita mea. Cui re- spondet in altero commate subjecti loco τὸ mori, prædicati verò τὸ κέρδος vel lucrum. Non ergo invertenda propositio illa hoc modo: Christus est vita mihi, quod ab illis fit, qui exponunt, quomo- do Christus nobis sit vita naturalis, spiritualis, cælestis, quia autor ejus est; ita Thomas active ex- posuit, quasi Christum profiteatur totum princi- pium vitæ & operationis suæ: non enim de origine vitæ agit, sed quomodo glorificetur Christus in cor- pore suo, dum vivit, exponit Apostolus, quia scili- cet hoc vivere suum æstimet, hoc per vitam suam agere constituerit, & agat, ut Christus unice glo- rificetur, ut adeo vita sua sit non tam unio animæ ac corporis, vel actus vitalis, quam Christus ipse, quem pro anima & pro vita sua habebat, pro vita animæ suæ, & corporis sui; uti mori suum non pro destructione vitæ, sed pro lucro melioris & æternæ vitæ, non pro jactura alicujus boni, sed pro con- secutione omnis boni reputet. Quo abit Theo- phylacti interpretatio: Mihi autem vivere Chri- stus est, hoc est, novam quandam dego vitam, & mihi pro universis Christus est rebus. Pro spiritu inquam, vita & luce. Hoc enim loco non naturalem negat se vitam victurum Apostolus, sed eam, quæ sit peccatis obstricta, & seculi hujus sit intenta de- ceptionibus. Cæterum sibi CHRISTUM ad vitam esse fatetur, sicut & alibi dicit: In fide vivo Filii Dei. Cui etiam consonat Chrysostomi commen- tarius: In hac vita, quod vivo, non est vita mihi, sed CHRISTUS. Nec aliena est Lombardi ex- plicatio: Quasi dicat: Christi causa vivo, ut Chri- stum magnificem, non ob aliud: Accedit etiam ἐξήγησις Zanchii & Piscatoris: Scopus totius vi- tæ meæ est CHRISTUS, ejusque gloria: Nec non Johan. Crocii: quasi dicat: Certus sum, Chri- stum summa cum libertate magnificatum iri in fra- gili corpore meo, sive vivam, sive moriar, ex eo est, quia vitæ meæ omnis vis, facultates, conatus, studia, actiones, perpessiones non alio quam ad Christi glo- riam illustrandam à me diriguntur. Qui perinde Bezæ interpretationem, etsi Calvini ea etiam sit & Musculi, quæ etiam Erasmo Schmidio proba- ta, excusare quidem nititur, probare tamen vix ausus est, quam vero diserte improbat Piscator, quod reddiderit: Mihi enim est Christus & in vita & in morte lucrum.

Piscator dicit, trajectionem hanc duram esse, & à styli Paulini simplicitate alienam, tum quod sic potius collocasset verba: Ἐμοὶ γὰρ χριστὸς κὴ τὸ ζῆν, καὶ τὸ ἀποθανεῖν κέρδος, tum quod ista sen- tentia non cohæreat, ut ratio cum præcedente, quod tamen postulet conjunctio γὰρ, quia aliud sit gloria CHRISTI, aliud salus Pauli, quam lu- cri nomine intelligit. Præfert itaque B. Lutheri versionem Crocius ex Piscatoris & Vulgati hoc elogio: Altera versio communior est, & habet consensum totius antiquitatis, quantum mihi qui- dem inspicere licuit, & premit literam Apostoli, & textui pulchre convenit. Prolixe etiam paratragœ- diari hic audias Danielem Heinsium de Bezæ ver- sione: Mihi dolere interdum solet, maximis in- terdum viros in iis quoque locis, quæ difficultatis nihil admodum haberent, veterum simplicitatem appro- bari non potuisse. Quid enim aliud hic, nisi quod ubique prædicat, Apostolus dixit? Vitam nempe suam esse in Christo, lucrumque propter hunc etiam mor- tem sibi fore: qui in eo vivat, qui in eo motus exci- tet spirituales, à quo vegetetur atque ad prædican- dum eum excitetur. Quemadmodum ad Galat. II. vers. 20. ζῶ δὲ ὀκέτι ἐγὼ, ζῇ δὲ ἐν ἐμοὶ χριστός. Cum in eo autem viveret Christus, mirum non est, si eveniat, quod dicit, eum, qui sic vivit nempe, mo- ri non posse: aut si mori dicatur, mortem ei lucrum esse, qua deponitur, quod mori potest, induitur, quod mori non potest. Quid autem opus fuit, hoc interpretari, ac si Apostolus dixisset: Ἐμοὶ γὰρ τὸ ζῆν καὶ τὸ ἀποθανεῖν χριστός ἐστι κέρδος, ut τὸ κατὰ utrobique intelligatur, ac si dicat, ἐμοὶ γὰρ κατὰ τὸ ζῆν καὶ κατὰ ἀποθανεῖν χριστός ἐστι κέρδος. Quod quam molestum sit negari, nisi vehementer fallimur, non potest: cum expositum sit alterum atque expedi- tum. Vide igitur simplicitatem summam: Mihi vita, inquit, Christus est, & mori lucrum. Ὁμόψηφον ha- bemus & Flacium. Dicit sibi terrenum istud vivere esse Christum, id est Christi prædicationem & glori- ficationem, mori autem esse ei proprium lucrum. Alii volunt esse sensum, Christum in sese vivere: Alii quod Christus sibi sit & in vita & in morte lucrum. Sed mihi prior sententia melius videtur convenire & verbis hujus ipsius versus, & sequenti collationi aut explicationi hujus versus. Christum ergo hic vocat promotionem regni Christi. Hæc Flacius. Hic ergo sensus verborum Apostoli proprius est, quod vita sua, omnis cogitatio, omnis intentio, omnis actio vi- tæ suæ in Christi gloriam directa sit, quod vivere suum sit Christum glorificare. Ita verbum ζῆν non alio quam proprio sensu accipitur, quemadmodum mors etiam de morte naturali est intelligenda; & in antecedentibus ac consequentibus vincula & mortem, ita & vitam, per quæ in corpore suo Christus glorificandus proprie intellexit Apostolus, v. 20. & 22. Mors itaque lucrum dicitur, quod ad Paulum, eique similes, omnes fideles, in Christo decedentes, non quod lucraturus morte sua Apostolus sit constanter Christum profitendo, alios Christo, aliisque salutem, qui hoc exemplo ad parilem constantiam excitabuntur, etsi hoc reapse consequutum sit, eoque tendat Apostolicum monitum, Ebr. XIII. 7. nam utilitatis salutis aliorum causa vitam potius eligendam hic censet Apostolus, quam mortem, sed quod lucrum futurum sit τὸ ἀποθανεῖν, quod pro vita animali cœlestem, pro bonis temporalibus æterna, pro terreno corporis habitaculo Deum habitaculum suum æternum, pro peccato justitiam, pro captivitate libertatem, pro spiritualibus cogitationibus, consiliis, actionibus, & studiis in hominis vita variis adhuc obnoxiis, ob carnis reliquias, defectibus, cœlestes, ab omni defectu liberas cogitationes, intentiones, actiones, unice Dei cognitioni, amori, glorificationi deditas, pro labore requiem, pro certaminibus triumphum, pro miseriis beatitudinem, pro ignominia gloriam, pro malorum tumulo, omnium bonorum cumulum, pro tristitia & dolore gaudium & lætitiam, nullis seculis terminandam, pro regno gratiæ regnum gloriæ, pro fide speciem, pro Christi prædicatione visionem ejusdem beatam lucraturus sit. Lucrum est, evasisse incrementa peccati, lucrum fugisse deteriora, lucrum ad meliora transire, ut nonnemo è Veteribus. Lucrum maximum, inquit S. Cyprianus serm. IV. de mortal. computat (fidelis) jam seculi laqueis non teneri, jam nullis peccatis & vitiis carnis obnoxium fieri, exemptum pressuris angentibus, & venenatis Diaboli faucibus liberatum ad lætitiam salutis æternæ DEO vocante proficisci. Audiamus plenius hunc locum dilucidantem Chrysostomum, sed audiamus per verborum compendia: Mihi, inquit, vivere Christus, & mori lucrum. Nam & moriendo, inquit, non moriar, vitam habens in meipso; tunc me sustulissent, si per metum potuissent ex anima mea fidem exturbare. Quamdiu vero Christus mecum fuerit, etiamsi mors ingruerit, vivam. Atque in hac etiam vita non hoc mihi vivere est, sed Christus. Quod si dum hic vivo, non hoc mihi vivere, quod in altero seculo futurum est? Quod vero nunc, inquit, in carne vivo, in fide vivo. Hoc & ibi dicit: Vivo jam non ego, vivit vero in me Christus. Talem oportet Christianum esse, non vivo, inquit, communem vitam. Non negat naturalem se vitam vivere, sed etiam, quæ peccatorum est, quam vivunt omnes homines. Et merito quidem negat. Nam qui præsentis vitæ cupidus non est, quomodo hanc vivit? Qui ad alteram festinat, quomodo hanc vivit? Qui mortem contemnit, quomodo hanc vivit? Qui nihil ex iis, quæ in mundo sunt, amat, quomodo hanc vivit? Ita qui nihil alimenti, nihil vestium, nihil ullius rei præsentis causa facit, quomodo hic vivit? Hic profecto ne naturalem quidem vitam vivere dicendus est. Qui nihil eorum, quæ ad vitam faciunt, curat, is nec vivit. Nos hanc vitam vivimus, qui pro hac vita omnia facimus, ille vero non vivebat, neque in rebus ullis inferioribus versabatur: Quomodo igitur vivebat? Ita etiam de quibusdam dicimus: Ille mihi non adest, ubi agat nihil, quod ad me pertineat. Ita etiam rursus, ille mihi non vivit. Quod enim naturalem hanc vitam non rejiciat, alibi r his verbis ostendit: Quod autem nunc vivo in carne, vivo in fide Filii Dei, qui dilexit me, & tradidit se- metipsum pro me, id est novam quandam vitam vi- vo, atque ab usitata lege diversam. Hæc sane omnia ad Philippensium consolationem dicit. Ne putetis, inquit, fore, ut hac vita spolier, quandoquidem ne vivens quidem hanc vivebam vitam. Dic enim mihi, qui pecunias contemnit, qui cibum, qui fa- mem & sitim, qui pericula, qui sanitatem, qui salu- tem, is hanc vitam vivit? Qui nihil in terris habet, qui sæpe profundere ipsam cupit, si opus sit, neque re- luctatur, is hanc vivit vitam? Neutiquam. Mihi inquit vivere Christus, si meam vestigas vitam, ille est, & mori lucrum: Cur? quoniam major mihi il- lius notitia erit, & familiarius cum ipso versabor. Quare hoc nihil aliud est, quam moriendo ad vitam pervenire. Nihil mihi durius facient, qui interfe- cerint, ad meam me emittentes vitam, & ab hac, quæ mihi apta non est, liberantes.

## 1:22
Vers. 22. Εἰ δὲ τὸ ζῇν ἐν σαρκὶ) Thus also Gal. II. v. 20, this life subject to death is designated.

Τῦτό μοι καρπὸς ἔργε) A Latin idiom, operæ pretium (worth the effort): Such as ἐρωτᾷν for to ask: ἱκανὸν λαμβάνειν to accept enough, διδοναι ἐργασίαν, to devote effort.

Καὶ τί αἱρήσομαι) Τί for πότερον, just as Latin writers also place quis for uter.

Οὐ γνωρίζω) it is not sufficiently clear to me.

Heinsius labors at length over these words. He observes especially that the particle καὶ here does not perform the function of a Copulative. Τὸ καὶ does not connect, as the learned have thought, but only introduces. For it serves an interrogation, it increases doubt, so that it is used ἐν πάθει and effectively, as the ancients speak. Just as in that καὶ τίς δύναται σωθῆναι; A most well-known place, οἱ δὲ περισσοτέρως ἐξεπλήσσοντο, λέγοντες πρὸς ἑαυτὰς, κ͵ τίς δύναται σωθῆναι; Mark X. 26. Likewise εἶπον δὲ οἱ ἀκύσαντες, κ͵ τίς δύναται σωθῆναι; Luke XVIII. 26. And who then will be able to be saved? Thus here: But if to live in the flesh is worth the effort, and what then shall I choose? I certainly do not know. For I am urged on both sides. For as for me; I desire and long to be dissolved, and to be with Christ. For that is far better for me. But that I should still remain in the flesh, is more necessary for your sake: and thus also the 'natus' is removed, of which our Interpreter complains. Heinsius says this: Crocius praises this observation and our translation by the force of the same: Luther's explanation would be very clear, were the copula not neglected, unless you say that here it does not have the force of connecting, but of inferring: just as elsewhere it serves for interrogation, and increases doubt, it does not connect, Mark X. 26. Luke XVIII. 26. We acquiesce to Luther's version: Thus there will be no need to employ another distinction with Heinsius. But whoever desires the various versions compared more laboriously, let him approach Crocius here. A similar observation occurs regarding the particle καὶ in Camerarius: ὁ κ͵ συλλογιστικὸς in this place, that is, indeed. Theophylact: Lest you perchance think that Paul is accusing this life, just as if it were superfluous and clearly useless. If, he says, to live in the flesh is fruit of work for me, that is, I have indeed said that I would consider this death as gain; nevertheless, since this life of mine is by no means useless to me in the flesh, inasmuch as I instruct others and enlighten them to the faith, I do not know what I should choose, death or life. However, the phrase of the Apostle must be noted here, as the blessed Hunnius warns. For it is one thing to live in the flesh, another to live according to the flesh. Those who live according to the flesh, that is, who obey the desires of the flesh, cannot please God, Romans VIII. But to live in the flesh is to live in this mortal body, just as Paul himself distinguishes both locutions, 2 Corinthians X: walking in the flesh we do not war according to the flesh.

Latin:

Vers. 22. Εἰ δὲ τὸ ζῇν ἐν σαρκὶ) Sic & Gal. II. v. 20. desi- gnatur vita hæc morti obnoxia.

Τῦτό μοι καρπὸς ἔργε) Latina locutio, operæ pretium: Qualia ἐρωτᾷν pro rogare: ἱκανὸν λαμβάνειν satis accipere, διδοναι ἐργασίαν, dare operam.

Καὶ τί αἱρήσομαι) Τί pro πότερον, quomodo & Latini scriptores quis ponunt pro uter.

Οὐ γνωρίζω) non satis mihi liquet.

De verbis his prolixe laborat Heinsius. Id im- primis observat, particulam καὶ hic non fungi Co- pulativæ munere. Τὸ καὶ non connectit, quod existi- marunt eruditi, sed infert tantum. Interrogationi enim servit, dubitationem auget, ita ut ἐν πάθει ac efficaciter, ut veteres loquuntur, adhibeatur. Quem- admodum in illo καὶ τίς δύναται σωθῆναι; Locus no- tissimus, οἱ δὲ περισσοτέρως ἐξεπλήσσοντο, λέγοντες πρὸς ἑαυτὰς, κ͵ τίς δύναται σωθῆναι; Marc. X. 26. Item εἶπον δὲ οἱ ἀκύσαντες, κ͵ τίς δύναται σωθῆναι; Luc. XVIII. 26. Et quis tandem poterit servari? Ita hic: Quod si vivere in carne operæ pretium est, & quid tandem eligam? Ignoro certe. Utrinque enim urgeor. Quod ad me enim; plane dissolvi, & cum Christo esse opto ac desidero. Longe enim melius id mihi. Ut adhuc autem permaneam in carne, magis propter vos necessarium: atque ita & natus tollitur, de quo conqueritur Interpres noster. Hæc Heinsius: Hanc observationem & vi ejusdem translationem no- stram laudat Crocius: Lutheri explicatio esset valde perspicua, nisi negligeretur copula, nisi dicas, hic non habere vim connectendi, sed inferendi: quemadmo- dum alias interrogationi servit, & dubitationem auget, non connectit, Marc. X. 26. Luc. XVIII. 26. Acquiescimus versioni Lutheri: Ita nec aliam di- stinctionem cum Heinsio opus erit adhibere. Qui vero operosius collatas diversas versiones desi- derat, Crocium hic adeat. De particula καὶ similis occurrit apud Camerarium observatio: ὁ κ͵ συλλο- γιστικὸς hoc loco, id est, sane. Theophylactus: Ne forte existimes, Paulum vitam hanc criminari, perinde ac supervacaneam & plane inutilem. Si in carne inquit vivere mihi fructus est operis, hoc est, dixi equidem, pro lucro me habiturum hanc mortem; veruntamen cum vita hæc mea nequa- quam mihi in carne inutilis sit, quippe, qui alios instruo, & ad fidem illumino, ignoro, quid eligam, mortemne, an vitam. Attendenda autem hic, mo- nente B. Hunnio, est phrasis Apostoli. Nam aliud est in carne vivere, aliud secundum carnem. Qui secundum carnem vivunt, hoc est, carnis cupidita- tibus obsequuntur, Deo placere non possunt, Roman. VIII. At in carne vivere, est vivere in hoc mortali corpore, quemadmodum Paulus ipse utramque locu- tionem discernit, 2. Corinth. X. in carne ambulantes non secundum carnem militamus.

## 1:23
Vers. 23. I am hard pressed between the two) That is, I am constrained on both sides. Thus we have συνέχεσθαι in Luke 12:50, Acts 17:5, 2 Cor. 5:14, that is, there are grave causes which compel me to prefer this, and which compel me to prefer that. Thus David 2 Sam. 24:14, צַר לִי מְאֹד, I am in a great strait on every side. After the word δύο a punctuation mark should be placed here, as Augustine rightly advises in De doctrina Christiana 3.3.

Having a desire to depart) that is, נִפְטַר, which is frequent among the Hebrews, as is also the noun פְּטִירָה, to signify the death of the pious. The Syrian used the same word here. But ἀναλύειν properly is to return; Tertullian translates it to be received. The spirit is from God, and returns to God. Eccles. 12:7. Philostratus speaks thus in the life of Apollonius, and Cicero in the first book of De divinatione, explaining the dream of Eudemus, that when the soul of Eudemus had departed from the body, then at last it seemed to have returned. Jerome also, citing this passage in his first apology against Rufinus, translates ἀναλύειν as to return.

Others say the word ἀναλῦσαι is taken from sailors, who, when about to sail, first loosen the tied ships, because Paul desires to sail out of this evil age, and through temporal death to cross the vast sea of all miseries, and to arrive at the port of eternal rest and happiness, and furthermore to be in all eternity with Christ. For the holy heart of the Apostle was burning with an incredible desire to see Him and to contemplate Him face to face, and to reign with Him. And he confirms that this is indeed much and far better for himself, as the blessed Hunnius says here. Erasmus Schmid explains it: To make a loosening, to unyoke, as if from a yoke which I have drawn. Others commonly think the loosening of the soul from the body is meant. For the body is a tabernacle for the soul, 2 Cor. 5:1, 4, and because of sin, as it were a certain prison, Ps. 142:8. Crocius approves of that version by which ἀναλῦσαι is rendered to return, as in Luke 12:36, just as it pleased Beza above others, insofar as it is judged that the metaphor is drawn from sailors. But for that reason this word should not be rendered to return, or by remigration, which pleased Beza, but rather with the Vulgate to be dissolved, so that the formal sense is expressed, even if the end of this dissolution is to return, or rather to migrate, as Chrysostom rendered it, and the Hunnius interpretation is to be preferred. The consequence of the dissolution is that migration, which is tacitly comprehended by the subsequent words, to be with Christ.

However, one must be careful not only that no one concludes from the word to return, with Sandius, the return of the soul into heaven, in which it had been created from the beginning of creation, but also that one does not maintain with the Calvinists that souls are created by God when we are born and are infused from heaven.
