Certainly no mention of any remigration is made here, nor is the spirit said to return to God, Eccles. 12:7, otherwise than because in the first creation the body of Adam, who represented the whole human species and had it in his loins, was taken from the dust of the earth, which, as it cannot be said of the other bodies of the descendants of Adam, so neither is it necessary to affirm it of their souls by the force of that statement.

However, the emphasis is on the word ἐπιθυμίαν ἔχω. For here it is more than to desire, namely, to be held by an ardent and constant desire.

And to be with Christ) that is, in the custody of Christ as regards the better part, Acts 7:59. Nothing can be defined from this concerning the place. Polycarp in the epistle likewise inscribed to the Philippians: That they are in the place owed to them beside the Lord. Jerome in the epitaph of Nepotianus: We know that our Nepotianus is with Christ, and mixed with the choirs of the saints.

The passage is to be considered as spoken in a crude manner, or that the place is already defined by these words. For the Apostle does not say in the custody of Christ, but to be with Christ. From which is inferred presence with Christ in the heavens, in the bosom of Christ, into which Abraham, the Father of believers, was also received, Luke 16:22, where also the converted thief began to be after death by the force of the promise of Christ, today you will be with me in Paradise, Luke 23:43. However, one must not, with the Calvinists, understand some place in heaven above the ether, circumscribed by definite spaces; for just as the soul is with Christ as soon as it is dissolved from the body, so it has no need of intervals of place and spaces of time, so that it might perhaps only after many years be carried up above the firmament into the crystalline or empyrean heaven, or whatever is more sublime, in order to be with Christ; such childish thoughts ought to be banished from here, since it is not right to confine Christ to heaven, who, when seen by the dying Stephen on earth, present and not departing, received his spirit. Where Christ is, there is heaven and heavenly blessedness.

Πολλῷ μᾶλλον κρεῖσσον) This is said by way of apposition concerning the whole of what preceded, as if he were saying: which indeed is much better for me, because it was destined to happen in this way, namely, that Paul should rest from so many labors, Rev. 14:13.

Latin:

Vers. 23. Συνέχομαι δὲ ἐκ τῶν δύο) Id est, utrinque cogor. | Sic συνέχεσθαι habemus Luc. XII. 50. Act. XVII. 5. 2. Cor. | V. 14. id est, causæ sunt graves, quæ me hoc, & quæ me il- | lud præoptare compellunt. Sic David 2. Sam. XXIV. v. 14. | צַר לִי מְאֹד, τινά μοι πάντοθεν σφόδρα ἐσὶ· Post vocem | δύο ponenda hîc διαστολὴ, ut recte monet Augustinus de do- | ctrina Christiana III. 3.

Τὴν ἐπιθυμίαν ἔχων εἰς τὸ ἀναλῦσαι) id est, נִפְטַר, quod | Ebræis frequens, ut & nomen פְּטִירָה, ad significandam | piorum mortem. Syrus eadem voce hic usus. Sed ἀναλύειν | proprie est redire, recipi vertit Tertullianus. Spiritus à Deo | est, & ad Deum redit. Ecclef. XII. 7. Loquitur sic & Phi- | lostratus in vita Apollonii, & Cicero de divinatione primo, | Eudemi somnium exponens, ut cum animus Eudemi ex cor- | pore excesserit, tum demum revertisse videatur. Hieronymus | quoque hunc locum citans priore apologia contra Ruffi- | num ἀναλύειν vertit, reverti.

Alii verbum ἀναλῦσαι à nautis sumptum dicunt, | qui navigaturi naves prius alligatas solvunt, quod | navigare Paulus cupiat ex hoc malo seculo, & per | temporalem mortem vastissimum ac omnium mise- | riarum pelagus trajicere, & ad portum sempiternæ | quietis ac felicitatis appellere, & porro in omni æter- | nitate cum Christo esse. Hujus enim videndi & de fa- | cie ad faciem contemplandi, & cum ipso regnandi | desiderio incredibili flagrabat sanctum pectus Apo- | stoli. Et hoc sibi quidem multo longeque melius esse | confirmat, ut hic B. Hunnius. Erasmus Schmidius | explicat: Ad exsolutionem faciendam, auszuspann- | nen, tanquam ex jugo, quod traxi. Alii communi- | ter solutionem animæ à corpore notari putant. Cor- | pus enim animæ est tabernaculum, 2. Cor. V, 1. 4. & | propter peccatũ veluti carcer quidam, Psal. CXLII. | vers. 8. Crocius ita probat illam versionem, qua | ἀναλῦσαι redditur reverti, ut Luc. XII. 36. quem- | admodum ea placuit præ aliis Bezæ, quatenus np. | à nautis metaphora ducta judicatur. Sed ea ratione | non reddendum erit hoc verbum reverti, vel per | remigrationem, quod Bezæ placuit, sed potius | cum Vulgato dissolvi, ut formalis exprimatur sen- | sus, etsi hujus dissolutionis finis sit τὸ reverti, vel | potius τὸ μεθίστασθαι migrare, ut reddidit Chrysosto- | mus, & præferenda Hunniana interpretatio. Con- | sequens dissolutionis est illa migratio, quæ tacite | comprehenditur vocibus subsequentibus, esse cum | Christo.

Cavendum autem non tantum, ne quis ex | τῷ reverti cum Sandio reditum animæ in cælum, in | quo condita ab initio creationis fuerit, concludat, | sed etiam ne cum Calvinianis animas à Deo, cum | nascimur, creari ac cœlitus infundi, statuat. Nul- | lius sane remigrationis mentio hîc facta, nec aliter | redire ad Deum Spiritus dicitur, Eccl. XII. 7. quam | quia in prima creatione corpus Adami, qui totam | speciem humanam repræsentabat, & in lumbis | suis habebat, è pulvere terræ desumptum est, quod | ut de aliis Adamigenarum corporibus dici nequit, | ita nec de animabus eorum, vi dicti istius affirmari | necessum est.

Emphasis autem est in verbo ἐπιθυ- | μίαν ἔχω. Hic enim plus est, quam ἐπιθυμεῖν, | scilicet ardenti & jugi desiderio teneri.

Καὶ σὺν χρισῷ εἶναι) id est, in Christi custodia quoad | partem potiorem, Actor. VII. 59. Nihil hinc de loco de- | finiri potest. Polycarpus in epistola itidem Philippensibus | inscripta : Ὅτι εἰς τὸν ὀφειλόμενον αὐτοῖς τόπον εἰσὶ παρὰ κυ- | ρίῳ. Hieronymus in epitaphio Nepotiani : Scimus Nepo- | tianum nostrum esse cum Christo, & sanctorum mixtum | choris.

Locum παχυλῶς dictum, vel τὸ, ubi jam defini- | tum istis verbis esse, censendum est. Non enim di- | cit Apostolus in Christi custodia, sed cum Christo | esse. Quo infertur præsentia penes Christum in | cælis, in sinu Christi, in quem etiam receptus Abra- | ham, Pater credentium, Luc, XVI. 22. ubi & latro | conversus esse cœpit post mortem vi promissio- | nis Christi, hodie mecum eris in Paradiso, Luc. | XXIII. 43. Non tamen cum Calvinistis locus ali- | quis in cælo super æthera, spatiis definitis circum- scriptus intelligendus; nam ut cum Christo anima est, quam primum dissolvitur à corpore; ita non opus habet locorum intervallis, & temporum spatiis, ut multis forte annis demum evehatur supra firmamentum in cœlum crystallinum, empyræum, aut quodcunq; sublimius, ut cum Christo esse possit; quæ pueriles cogitationes hîc exulare debent, cum nec Christum cœlo compescere fas sit, qui Stephano morituro in terris visus præsens, non abiens, spiritum ejus suscepit. Ubi Christus, ibi cœlum & beatitudo cœlestis.

Πολλῷ μᾶλλον κρεῖσσον) Hoc dicitur per appositionem de toto eo, quod præcessit quasi diceret, quod quidem mihi multo est melius, quia sic scilicet futurum erat, ut Paulus requiesceret à tot laboribus, Apoc. XIV. 13.

## 1:24
Vers. 24. Τὸ δὲ ἐπιμένειν ἐν τῇ σαρκὶ) In this mortal body, as above in 21.

Ἀναγκαιότερον δι' ὑμᾶς) He includes not only the Philippians but also other Christians under this name.

It is helpful to add the whole commentary of Theophylact: By these words the Apostle renders the Philippians more prepared to endure his future death manfully. For why should you think that my death is to be lamented, which I myself have long since desired above all things? And this will turn out for the better for me, since it grants me the license to converse with Christ. Therefore, you ought not to be affected by any grief when I undergo death, otherwise it is more necessary that I remain in this flesh for your benefit, for I do not seek what is my own, but yours. But if the choice were given, whether I would prefer to depart from human affairs or to lead this life, I am indeed hard-pressed, that is, I am in doubt and uncertain: and so, that I do not easily know which of these I should choose. I would, however, consider it more necessary that, living and breathing, I should be of service to you. Is there, therefore, anyone so great or exalted whose mind can be compared with this mind of Paul? Since he prefers the utility of others to the conversation of Christ in such a way that he is more joined to Christ when he rejects the conversation of Christ, so that he may be of benefit to others.

PART III. Confidence of the Apostle's liberation and of his visitation of the Philippians.

Latin:

Vers. 24. Τὸ δὲ ἐπιμένειν ἐν τῇ σαρκὶ) In hoc mortali corpore, ut supra 21.

Ἀναγκαιότερον δι' ὑμᾶς) Non Philippenses tantum, sed & alios Christianos, hoc nomine complectitur.

Juvat addere totum Theophylacti commentarium: Philippenses his dictis Apostolus reddit paratiores, ut suum obitum futurum proxime viriliter tolerent. Cur enim mea de morte dolendum censebitis, quam ipse summopere jampridem concupivi? Idq; & mihi in melius sit concessurum, quippe quod mihi licentiam præbeat cum Christo conversandi. Non itaque dolore affici ullo debetis cum mortem obiero, alioquin in carne hac me permanere ob vestram utilitatem magis est necessarium, non enim quæ mea sunt quæro, sed vestra. Quod si optio detur, utrum ex humanis abscedere, an vitam hanc ducere malim, coarctor equidem, hoc est, in ancipiti sum subdubius: & ita, ut non facile sciam, quid horum sim electurus. Duxerim tamen præcipue id necessarium magis, ut vivens & spirans vobis conducam. Estne igitur quispiam ingens adeo aut excelsum, quod cum hac Pauli mente possit æquari? Quandoquidem aliorum utilitatem Christi conversationi sic præfert, ut Christo conjunctior sit, cum Christi conversationem rejiciat, ut aliis prosit.

PARS III. Fiducia liberationis Apostoli, & visitationis Philippensium.

## 1:25
Vers. 25. Καὶ τῦτο πεποιθὼς οἶδα) He does not say that he knows he will remain for a long time, but he says that he is so conscious of himself that, because he sees his life is still necessary for many Christians, he therefore hopes all the more that he will remain in life, however troublesome, and will return to them. Οἶδα πεποιθὼς, I know that I hope for this, that is, I prefer it. See above 6.

Οἶδα πεποιθὼς does not mean, I know that I hope for this, that is, I prefer it. For what would that saying mean? But I know with certain persuasion, or, being certain of this, I know. For this conviction was not from vain presumption but from divine revelation. Therefore, there is no doubt that Paul attained in actual fact what he testified to by divine inspiration. For he did not write these things from his last, but from his first imprisonment, which Chrysostom and most others affirm. But how does this harmonize with the words of the Apostle in the valedictory address delivered at Ephesus, Acts 20:25: And now behold, I know that you all, among whom I have gone about preaching the kingdom of God, will see my face no more. Resp. That Paul did not deny that anyone from the Ephesians would see him. For it is not at all likely that, having been liberated from the first Roman imprisonment, Paul never came to the East. Baronius, indeed, was rendered doubtful by these words in his annals for the year of Christ 61, no. 1. Whether Paul set out again for the East, since it could not have happened, if he had returned to Asia and the East, that he would not have visited the most desired Ephesian Church, the metropolis of all Asia! But he did not only promise his arrival here to the Philippians, or at least was persuaded of it, which he also promised in chapter 2:24: I trust in the Lord, that I myself am to come shortly; but he also, writing to Philemon, ordered that a lodging be prepared for him: At the same time also prepare me a lodging: For I hope that through your prayers I shall be granted to you. And in the Epistle to the Hebrews ch. XIII. 23. know, he says, our brother Timothy, with whom, if he comes sooner, I will see you. And at least eight years intervened until the final captivity, at which time who would believe that any believers in the East were completely neglected and not visited? The words cited concerning the Ephesians do not even prove that, because not even from those did he see any of them afterwards, but they only mean this, that the Apostle knew that all those before whom he delivered his farewell speech would not see his face again in the future, since many of them would die in the meantime, until he could arrange his return. The Grotian gloss on that passage therefore is not to be admitted, because it is a Hebraism, and the speech ought to be extended to all Asians: You will not see, all of you, that is, none of you. Nor does Erasmus Schmidius deny this here, explaining, not all of you will see, this is, he says, some of you will not see again. For it could have happened that, although not all, yet some might have seen him again. Just as Luke, having accompanied him as far as Rome, saw him frequently thereafter. And could it not easily have happened that some of the Presbyters saw Paul elsewhere? That none of the Asians saw his face thereafter, Grotius affirms quite rashly. As for the present passage of the Apostle, we have Crocius as a fellow-voter, who also defends our sense against Calvin and Beza. I do not yet understand, he says, that Paul's hope was only probable. For why, from the suggestion of the Holy Spirit, was he not clearly certain? As to what he says in v. 25: Whether I come and see you, or am absent, that does not detract: For it is clear from the following words that absence does not pertain to death: I will hear of your affairs. For he was no longer going to hear from death. He speaks therefore of that which they ought to do in his absence, while he was staying either at Rome or elsewhere, ch. II. 17. he says that he will rejoice if he is offered as a drink offering: he does not say that the present captivity is going to end in an offering. He also cites Bullinger, Musculus, Zanchius, Dan. Tossanus, Aretius, Piscator, who conclude from this passage that the Apostle was liberated from these bonds. With Tossanus even saying that this passage has something prophetic. Finally, Crocius adds, since it is not obscure, nor do we know that it happened differently from what he says he knows for certain will be, I do not see why we should depart from the common opinion of the ancients.

That I will remain and continue with you all) To all who believe in Christ.

For your greater progress. See above 12. and 1. Tim. IV. 15.

So that your faith may be joined with greater joy.

Latin:

Vers. 25. Καὶ τῦτο πεποιθὼς οἶδα) Non dicit, scire se diu mansurum, sed dicit, se ita sibi esse conscium, ut quia videat suam vitam Christianis multis adhuc necessariam, ideo magis speret se in vita, quamvis molesta, mansurum, & ad ipsos rediturum. Οἶδα πεποιθὼς, scio me hoc sperare, id est malle. Vide supra 6.

Οἶδα πεποιθὼς non est, scio, me hoc sperare, id est, malle. Quid enim hoc dictum foret? Sed scio certa persuasione, vel de hoc certo persuasus scio. Nam πεποίθησις hἘc erat non ex vana præsumptione sed divina revelatione. Ideo dubium non est, Paulum, quod divinitus testabatur, actu ipso consecutum esse. Neq; enim hæc scripsit è postrema, sed prima captivitate, quod Chrysostomus & pleriq; alii affirmant. Sed quomodo hoc consonat verbis Apostoli in oratione valedictoria Ephesi habita, Act. XX. 25. Et nunc ecce ego scio, quia amplius non videbitis faciem meam vos omnes, per quos transivi, prædicans regnum Dei. Resp. Paulum non negasse, quenquam ipsum visurum ex Ephesinis. Nam à prima captivitate Romana liberatum non venisse unquam Paulum in Orientem, haud fit verisimile. Baronius equidem ex his verbis ambiguus redditus est in annalibus suis ad ann. Christi LXI. n. 1. Anne profectus Paulus iterum sit in Orientem, quum contingere baud potuerit, si in Asiam & Orientem rediisset, quin optatissimam Ecclesiam Ephesinam Asiæ totius metropolin concessisset! Sed non tantum hic promisit adventum suum Philippensibus, vel certe de eo persuasus fuit, quem pollicitus est quoque cap. II. 24. Confido in Domino, quod ipse brevi venturus sim; sed etiam ad Philemonem scri- bens hospitium sibi parari jussit: Simul autem & para mihi hospitium: Nam spero per orationes ve- stras donari me vobis. Et in Epistola ad Ebræos cap. XIII. 23. cognoscite, inquit, fratrem nostrum Timo- theum, cum quo, si celerius venerit, videbo vos. Et octo ad minimum anni intercessere usque ad postremam captivitatem, quo tempore toto ne- glectos plane, nec visitatos fideles ullos in Orien- te, ecquis crediderit? Verba utique de Ephesinis allegata ne id quidem evincunt, quod nec ex illis quidem ullum viderit deinceps, sed hoc tantum si- bi volunt, scire Apostolum, quod omnes illi, coram quibus orationem valedictoriam habuit, imposte- rum non visituri teram sint faciem suam, quum mul- ti ipsorum interea decessuri sint, donec ille rever- sionem parare possit. Glossa ergo Grotiana ad illū locum admittenda non est, quod Ebraismus sit, & oratio extendi debeat ad omnes Asiaticos: Non videbitis vos omnes, id est, nemo vestrum. Nec dif- fitetur hic Erasmus Schmidius, exponens, non omnes vos videbitis, hoc est, inquit, quidam ve- strum non videbunt rursus. Potuisset enim fieri, ut licet non omnes, tamen aliqui rursus eum vidis- sent. Sicut Lucas eum Romam usque comitatus posthac eum frequenter vidit. Et annon fieri fa- cile potuit, ut aliquis Presbyterorum illorum Pau- lum alibi locorum videret? Nullum certe Asiati- corum faciem ejus deinceps vidisse, admodum te- mere affirmat Grotius. Quod ad præsentem Apo- stoli locum, habemus Crocium ὁμόψηφον, qui etiam adversus Calvinum & Bezam nostrum sensum tue- tur. Nondum, inquit, intelligo, Pauli spem fuisse tantum probabilem. Cur enim ex Spiritus Sancti sug- gestione non fuerit plane certus? Quod v. 25. ait: Si- ve venero & videro vos, sive absens fuero, id non de- rogat: Absentiam enim ad mortem non pertinere pa- tet ex verbis sequentibus: Audiam de rebus vestris. A morte enim non amplius erat auditurus. Loqui- tur igitur de eo, quod agere debeant ipso absente, dum vel Romæ, vel alibi versaretur, cap. II. 17. dicit, se gavisurum esse, si pro libamento offeratur: non dicit, præsentem captivitatem in oblationem exituram esse. Adducit etiam Bullingerum, Musculum, Zanchium, Dan. Tossanum, Aretium, Piscatorem, qui ex hoc loco colligunt, Apostolum ex his vin- culis liberatum esse. Tossano etiam dicente habere hunc locum aliquid Prophetici. Denique addit Crocius, cum obscurum non sit, nec sciamus, diver- sum accidisse ab eo, quod futurum esse, hoc certo se scire dicit, non video, cur à communi veterum sententia discedere debeamus.

Ὄτι μενῶ κ̓ συμπαραμενιῶ πᾶσιν ὑμῖν) Omnibus in Chri- stum credentibus.

Εἰς τὴν ὑμῶν προκοπὴν) Ad profectum vestrum majo- rem. Vide supra 12. & 1. Tim. IV. 15.

Καὶ χαρὰν τῆς πίσεως) Quo majori cum gaudio sit con- juncta fides vestra.

## 1:26
Vers. 26. That your boasting may abound in Christ Jesus in me) Boasting here, as elsewhere, is exultation: In Christ Jesus, through Christ Jesus, as the author of this good. In me, that is, because of me, for my sake.

What he says, with you all, is to be understood of most, or of the whole Church. For it should by no means be said with Zanchius that none of the Philippians will die before he sees them.

Latin:

Vers. 26. Ἱνα τὸ καύχημα ὑμῶν περισσεύη ἐν Χρισῷ Ἰησῦ ἐν ἐμοὶ) Καύχημα hîc, ut & alibi, est ἀγαλλίαμα exulta- tio: Ἐν Χρισῷ Ἰησῦ, per Christum Jesum, tanquam boni hu- jus autorem. Ἐν ἐμοὶ id est, propter me, mea causa.

Quod dicit, cum vobis omnibus, de plerisque in- telligendum, vel de tota Ecclesia. Nam neminem Philippensium moriturum, priusquam ipsos vide- rit, cum Zanchio minime dicendum.

## 1:27
V. 27. Only conduct yourselves worthily of the Gospel of Christ) By a very Greek expression, to conduct oneself signifies a manner of living, as in Acts XXIII, 1. Hence citizenship is a frequent word for Chrysostom and others for a way of life. It is a translation taken from citizens who live according to the laws of their city.

Whether I come and see you) which I would like.

Or am absent) which may happen.

By what reason their joy can be rendered more abundant, if, namely, they conduct themselves worthily of the Gospel, to which he urges them. That one thing, he says,

With Theophylact as interpreter, I demand of you that you study virtue more zealously. Yet he acts in accordance with the dignity of the Gospel who renounces himself and, having taken up his cross, follows Christ. He does not say these things, whether I come or am absent, to render doubtful the arrival about which he had said he was certain, but, as Hyperius notes and Crocius approves, so that he may shake off all sloth from them, and that he may not want them to defer their due duty until his liberation and return, but to fulfill it with the same diligence no less while he is held captive than when he is present to inspect everything.

I will hear the things concerning you) τὰ, that is, ταῦτα. These things, which will follow. A similar manner of speaking in Rom. XI. 29.

That you stand in one spirit) equally affected. For πνεῦμα signifies affection, 1 Cor. IV. 21 and often elsewhere.

Some interpret it as the mind itself, with Calvin and Aretius; others as the Holy Spirit, with Beza and Zanchius. Why should it not be accepted as the regenerated part of man, as in Gal. V. 17, so that in one Spirit, as one spiritual man, one soul, they may contend through concord against any enemies whatsoever? For the unity of the Spirit is required above all for this spiritual fight; cf. 1 Cor. XII. 13, 1 Thess. V. 23.

With one soul) loving one another.

Striving together for the faith of the Gospel) Contending as if in a formed battle line against the enemies of the Gospel, and that through the faith held and kept for the Gospel itself. Συναθλεῖν. התחזק יחד

Latin:

V. 27. Μόνον ἀξίως τῦ Εὐαγγελίε τῦ Χρισῶ πολιτεύεσθε) Πολιτεύεσθαι locutione bene Græca fignificat vivendi ratio- nem התהלך, ut Actor. XXIII, 1. Hinc πολιτέια frequens vox Chrysostomo, & aliis pro vitæ instituto. Est translatio ducta à civibus, qui secundum civitatis suæ leges vivunt.

Ἱνα εἴτε ἐλθὼν καὶ ἰδὼν ὑμᾶς) quod velim.

Εἴτε ἀπὼν) quod fieri potest.

Qua ratione gaudium ipsorum abundantius reddi possit, si scilicet dignos sese gesserint Evan- gelio, ad quod eosdem incitat. Id unum, inquit,

Theophylacto interprete, à vobis deposco, ut virtuti enixius studeatis. Atqui pro Evangelii dignitate ille agit, qui sibi ipsi renuntiat, & cruce sublata Chri- stum sectatur. Non autem hæc, sive venero, sive absens fuero, dicit, ut dubium reddat adventum, de quo se certum esse dixerat, sed quod Hyperius no- tat, approbatque Crocius, ut ita segnitiem omnem illis excutiat, & nolit eos in liberationem & reditum differre officium debitum, sed eadem diligentia im- plere non minus, dum captivus tenetur, quam cum præsens inspecturus est omnia.

Ἀκούσω τὰ περὶ ὑμῶν) τὰ, id est, ταῦτα. Hæc, quæ se- quentur. Simile loquendi genus Rom. XI. 29.

Ὅτι στήκετε ἐν ἑνὶ πνεύματι) pariter affecti. Nam πνεῦμα affectum significat 1. Cor. IV. 21. & alibi sæpe.

Alii de mente ipsa interpretantur cum Calvino & Aretio; alii de Spiritu Sancto cum Beza & Zan- chio. Quidni accipiatur de parte hominis regenita, ut Gal. V. 17. ut uno Spiritu, ceu unus homo spiri- tualis, una anima per concordiam decertent con- tra hostes quoscunque. Requiritur enim impri- mis Spiritus unitas ad hanc spiritualem pugnam, conf. 1. Cor. XII. 13. 1. Thess. V. 23.

Μιᾷ ψυχῇ) amantes vos mutuo.

Συναθλοῦντες τῇ πίστει τοῦ Εὐαγγελίου) Certantes quasi fa- cto agmine contra hostes Evangelii, idque per fidem habi- tam & servatam ipsi Evangelio. Συναθλεῖν. התחזק יחד

## 1:28
Verse 28. And in nothing terrified by your adversaries.) Not at all frightened by the threats of those enemies. In the Glossary, πτύρομαι means to tremble, to be terrified. Plutarch uses this word regarding a startled horse.

As the word στήκετε was athletic, belonging to those whose duty it is to hold their ground and not retreat: so now it requires a common fight without any terror. For he does not say, 'lest you collapse,' as Theophylact warns, but 'lest you be terrified,' that is, do not be perturbed in any matter. For if dangers are threatened or deaths are inflicted, these men will have achieved nothing, but they only terrify, to such an extent that they are proven both weak and impotent. But it was necessary for them to contend joined together not only among themselves, but also with the strength of the Apostle, and that τῇ πίστει, through faith, by which word the medium is expressed rather than the object. For it is not said 'for the doctrine of the Gospel,' but 'through the faith of the Gospel.' Although, by all means, the struggle had to be undertaken primarily for the doctrine of the Gospel. In the word συναθλοῦντες, the argument from utility—namely, from the prize which they call ἆθλον, or the reward proposed to those contending—is involved; this is Piscator's observation, cf. 1 Cor. IX. 24, 28.

Which is to them an indication of perdition, but to you of salvation) Ἔνδειξις is an argument. For הראה is translated as δεικνύειν. Hesychius: ἔνδειξις, ἀπόδειξις. When they see that their threats achieve nothing, but that you are sustained by God in the midst of evils, from that they ought to take an argument as to what the outcome for both will be.

And this from God) All these things happen, with God thus dispensing.

The stubborn fury of the enemies and the constancy of the faithful is certainly an indication of the destruction of the former and the salvation of the latter. But both are not to be referred to God, as Zanchius wished, but only the latter—namely, the salvation of the faithful—as most of the Reformed, Calvin, Piscator, Crocius, and others acknowledge with Chrysostom and Theophylact. The Apostle himself certainly refers it to the latter, when he adds, 'because it has been given,' etc. Therefore, that 'this' is not to be referred to all those preceding things.

Latin:

Vers. 28. Καὶ μὴ πτυρόμενοι ἐν μηδενὶ ὑπὸ τῶν ἐναντίων.) Nihil territi illorum hostium minis. In Glossario πτύρομαι trepido, terrefio. Utitur Plutarchus hac voce de equo con- stcrnato.

Ut verbum στήκετε Athleticum erat, quorum est gradum servare, non referre: Ita nunc pugnam requirit communem sine ullo terrore. Non enim, ne collabamini, dicit, monente Theophylacto, sed ne terreamini, hoc est, nulla in re perturbemini. Nam si vel pericula comminentur, vel inferant mortes, nihil profecto hi egerint, sed territant modo, adeo illi & imbecilles coarguuntur & impotentes. Certan- dum autem erat ipsis conjunctis non tantum inter se, sed etiam cum Apostoli viribus, idque τῇ πίστει, per fidem, qua voce medium potius exprimitur, quam objectum. Non enim dicitur pro doctrina Evangelii, sed per fidem Evangelii. Quamvis omnino pro doctrina Evangelii imprimis subeun- dum fuerit certamen. In verbo συναθλοῦντες argu- mentum ab utili, nimirum à præmio, quod ἆθλον dicunt, vel brabejo certantibus proposito invol- vi, Piscatoris est observatio, conf. 1. Cor. IX. 24. 28.

Ἥτις αὐτοῖς μέν ἐστιν ἔνδειξις ἀπωλείας, ὑμῖν δὲ σωτηρίας) Ἔνδειξις argumentum. Nam הראה vertitur δεικνύειν. Hesychius ἔνδειξις, ἀπόδειξις. Cum videant minas suas ni- hil proficere, vos autem in mediis malis à Deo sustentari, inde capere argumentum debent, quis futurus sit utrorum- que exitus.

Καὶ τοῦτο ἀπὸ Θεοῦ) Omnia hæc eveniunt, Deo sic dis- pensante.

Nimirum hostium furor pertinax & fidelium constantia certum est indicium interitus istorum & salutis horum. Ad Deum autem non referri utrumque, prout Zanchius voluit, sed posterius tantum, nimirum salutem fidelium, cum Chrysosto- mo & Theophylacto agnoscunt plerique è Refor- matis, Calvinus, Piscator, Crocius, alii. Ad poste- rius utique refert ipse Apostolus, cum addit, quia verbis datum est, &c. Non ergo ad omnia ista præ- cedentia illud τοῦτο referendum.

## 1:29
Verse 29. For to you it has been granted for Christ's sake not only to believe in him, but also to suffer for his sake) It is a pleonasm, as the Syrian rightly saw. For it would have been enough to have said, 'to you it has been granted not only to believe in Christ, but also to suffer for Christ.' Just as faith is said to be the gift of God, Eph. II. 8. So also are those occasions of suffering hard things for Christ, which is the highest honor to Christ; he believes Christ who believes that he speaks the truth. He believes in Christ who trusts that through Christ he will receive eternal life.

As faith in Christ is ascribed to divine grace; so also is τὸ ὑπὲρ Χριστοῦ πάσχειν: which not by occa- notes "suffering for Christ," as if it is insinuated here that these come from God: For it is said that not only the occasions for believing are given by God, but faith itself is a gift of God, which in John 6:29 is called "the work of God."

Moreover, "to suffer" in this place denotes such a kind of suffering as the Apostle had required, namely, that which consists of faith and perseverance.

For not only is faith given to us by God, but also that we may be able to fight by faith and to overcome all afflictions by the constancy of faith. For that is not placed in human strength.

Theophylact does not hesitate to compare this with the gift of raising the dead, nay, even to prefer it to the same. For we cannot do anything rightly without GOD, since this gift of God will perhaps surpass the grace of raising the dead.

For if I were to raise the dead, I would undoubtedly have been bound to God in the highest degree for such a benefit: But if I have undergone punishments for His sake, I would have had Him bound and a debtor. O admirable thing! He bestows, and is bound to me by a debt.

But there is no need to posit a pleonasm.

For "to" can be taken for "for the sake of Christ," as Grotius had a similar note on v. 27. "For the sake of Christ" is "on account of Christ," so that merit may be excluded all the more strongly, which Crocius praises as having been done here by Luther and Calvin. "For the sake of Christ" can also (if by chance that meaning of the preposition seems less accepted) be explained as "on account of Christ," or for the sake of Christ, or of the kingdom of Christ, or of the glory of Christ.

For God had therefore both converted the Philippians to faith and had given them grace to sustain whatever persecutions for the name of Christ. "For the sake of Christ" can also be conveniently explained as "that which pertains to Christ," as Camerarius interpreted it.

Beza rendered it "in the business of Christ." But the emphasis of the Apostolic locution is rightly observed: By the word "believing" he signifies not only the faculty, but also the act of believing, and shows that, since by their own nature they were not better or more apt for the faith of Christ, God by singular grace had given them both the will and the faculty, and the act of believing itself, or that they might believe by the act itself.

But he does not say: "The grace of faith has been offered to you," but "it has been given," that is, it has been conferred upon you in reality. He does not say, "it is given, that you may be able to believe, if you wish," but "it is given to believe," but in act.

Furthermore, he does not say "to believe" nakedly, but "in Christ." But to believe in Christ is not only to know Christ, as He revealed Himself in the word, and to assent to Him, but also to apprehend Him trustfully as offered in the Gospel.

All this was given to the Philippians, and indeed not only by reason of the beginning, but also of the progress. For he does not say, "that you might at some time believe," or "that you might have believed," but "to believe," namely, even now, not only from the beginning.

But not only that, but also that they might undergo dangers for the name and glory of Christ, and experience adversities, and bear them patiently. For to be afflicted here, as Zanchius rightly warns, is not to be afflicted nakedly, but to bear affliction patiently, and that for the sake of Christ, or out of true faith and love of Christ, and of His doctrine.

All of which things are most correctly situated, provided that irresistible grace is absent. Ver.

Latin:

Vers. 29. Ὅτι ὑμῖν ἐχαρίσθη τὸ ὑπὲρ Χριστοῦ οὐ μόνον τὸ εἰς αὐτὸν πιστεύειν, ἀλλὰ καὶ τὸ ὑπὲρ αὐτοῦ πάσχειν) Est πλεονα- σμὸς, ut recte vidit Syrus. Satis enim fuerat dixisse ὑμῖν ἐχα- ρίσθη οὐ μόνον τὸ εἰς χριστὸν πιστεύειν, ἀλλὰ καὶ τὸ ὑπὲρ χριστοῦ πάσχειν. Sicut fides dicitur Dei donum, Eph. II. 8. Sic etiam occasiones illæ pro Christo dura patiendi, qui honor sum- mus Christo credit, qui eum credit vera dicere. In Chri- stum credit, qui per Christum accepturum se confidit vi- tam æternam.

Ut divinæ gratiæ adscribitur fides in Christum; Ita etiam τὸ ὑπὲρ Χριστοῦ πάσχειν: quod non occa- notat patiendi pro Christo, quasi illas a Deo esse hic insinuatur: Nam nec occasiones tantum credendi a Deo dari dicuntur, sed fides ipsa Dei donum est, quae Joh. VI. 29. ἔργον τοῦ θεοῦ dicitur.

Notat autem τὸ πάσχειν hoc loco ejusmodi pati, quale requiviferat Apostolus, nimirum quod fide & perseverantia constat.

Nam non tantum a Deo nobis donatur fides, sed etiam ut fide pugnare, ac fidei constantia afflictiones omnes superare possimus. Id enim positum non est in humanis viribus.

Theophylactus non dubitat hoc cum dono resuscitationis mortuorum conferre, imo eidem praeferre. Non enim facere fine DEO recte aliquid possumus, siquidem Dei hoc donum forsitan suscitandorum mortuorum gratiam superabit.

Nam si mortuos suscitarem, Deo procul dubio fuerim tanto beneficio maximum in modum obstrictus: Sin vero pro ea paenas subierim, hunc ipsum habuerim obligatum & debitorem. O rem admirandam! largitur ille, & debito mihi obstringitur.

Non autem opus est Pleonasmi statuere.

Nam τὸ accipi potest pro τῷ ὑπὲρ Χριστοῦ, ut simile habuit Grotius ad v. 27. ὑπὲρ Χριστοῦ est propter Christum, ut excludatur tanto fortius meritum, quod a Luthero & Calvino hic factum laudat Crocius. Potest etiam ὑπὲρ Χριστοῦ (si forte illa significatio Praepositionis minus recepta videatur propter Christum) exponi, Christi, vel regni Christi, aut gloriae Christi causa.

Nam ideo Deus & ad fidem Philippenses converterat, & gratiam illis dederat pro Christi nomine persecutiones quas cunque sustinendi. Potest etiam commode exponi τὸ ὑπὲρ Χριστοῦ, quod ad Christum pertinet, ut interpretatus est Camerarius.

Beza reddidit in Christi negotio. Recte autem observata emphasis loquutionis Apostolicae: Verbo credendi non tantum significat facultatem, sed etiam actum credendi, atque ostendit, cum natura sua aliis non essent meliores, aptioresque, ad fidem Christi, Deum singulari gratia illis dedisse & voluntatem & facultatem, & ipsum credendi actum, seu ut ipso actu credant.

Non autem dicit: Oblata est vobis gratia fidei, sed datum est, id est, reipsa vobis collatum. Non ait, datum est, ut possitis credere, si velitis, sed datum est credere, sed actu.

Porro non dicit nude credere, sed in Christum. Credere autem in Christum est non tantum nosse Christum, ut se in verbo revelavit, & ei assentiri, sed etiam fiducialiter apprehendere in Evangelio oblatum.

Hoc totum datum Philippensibus, & quidem non tantum ratione initii, sed etiam progressus. Non enim ait, ut aliquando crederetis, vel ut credideritis, sed credere, nempe etiam nunc, non tantum ab initio.

Non autem id solum, sed ut etiam subeant propter Christi nomen & gloriam pericula, & experiantur adversa, ferantque patienter. Affligi enim hic, ut recte monet Zanchius, non est nude affligi, sed afflictionem patienter ferre, idque propter Christum, seu ex vera fide & amore Christi, ejusdemque doctrina.

Quae omnia rectissime sese habent, modo gratia absit irresistibilis. Vers.

## 1:30
30. The same struggle, which you saw in me. He says "the same struggle," which comes from the same cause.

What you saw in me touches upon the history, which is in Acts 16.

19 and following. There is here a nominative "having" for the dative "to those having," such as there are some also in Homer. And now you hear in me.

And "in me" here is "about me," how the Syrian and Latin take it. He understands his bonds.

Nay, it is gathered from these things that, besides those which are commemorated in the Acts, the Philippians had suffered not a few things, since he makes them his equals, or similar not only in the cause of the passions, but also in the passions themselves, which could not be commemorated in the Acts. For these reach only as far as the Roman captivity of the Apostle.

But those which are touched upon here by the Apostle seem to be more recent. He shows that they are in the same struggle with him, fighting in the same things, which thing provides them with a great testimony of virtue, as Theophylact says.

PART II.

OF THE EPISTLE, EXHORTATORY. Exhortation to unanimity, piety, and honesty. SECTION I. Exhortation to unanimity. CHAP. II. ARGUMENT AND PARTITION. He exhorts very pathetically to unanimity and concord, for the sake of which ambition is to be avoided, humility is to be followed, with a zeal for helping one's neighbor, and that by the example of Christ, who willed to be emptied for us, to be humbled, and to become obedient even unto the death of the cross; exalted afterwards by God, and having obtained a name above every name, so that they may proceed to obey similarly, and strive for salvation with fear and trembling, God working in them both to will and to do, and that they may perform all things without murmuring and doubting, without spot and offense, or as sincere children of God, holding fast the word of life. He also teaches that joy arises for him from thence, however much he may have to undergo death on account of the gift of their faith, and excites them similarly to joy, and trusts that he will be refreshed by the news of Timothy, who is to be sent to them shortly, whom he commends for his unanimity and care for them, as well as for his filial observance in the sacred office, and testifies that he himself will come to them shortly, but now he is sending Epaphroditus, as it were a remainder, so that they may be cheered by the sight of him, whom he therefore warns them to receive in the Lord. There are two parts: I.

It is exhortatory to unanimity, and to the humility and obedience connected with it, to v. 16.

II. Testificatory concerning the joy which Paul has in them, and which he desires them in turn to have in Paul, whence he also desires to be refreshed through Timothy, and they may now be cheered through Epaphroditus, to v. 30. PART I. EXHORTATORY To unanimity, and to the humility and obedience connected with it. V. 1. If there is any consolation. A very bland and pathetic speech. "If" sometimes affirms vehemently. For great are the consolations which we have from Christ. If there is any fellowship of the Spirit. Were they once called pagans, who drank from the same Spirit?

1 Cor. 12:4. If there are any bowels and mercies. "Bowels" are any affections whatsoever.

"Mercies" are affections toward the calamitous. Thus these are to be explained, where they are placed equally. Otherwise, that general term is also taken in the meaning of the species.

But these are great among true Christians. He had warned in chap. 1:27, but tacitly, and as if in passing, that if the arrival of the Apostle should yield to their joy, they should walk worthily of the Gospel, and especially stand in the unity of the Spirit, and strive together with one soul against the enemies. Now he pursues that exhortation professionally, exhorting especially to unanimity, and humility, and obedience, and thus to the observation of true Teachers, such as Timothy and Epaphroditus were, and the visitation of false ones, and to the pursuits of piety and honesty whatsoever; and that both with words and affections most pious and wonderfully full, and with arguments very effective: And thus he promises himself and for himself exceptional joy. But let the present adjuration be in the name of the most holy Trinity, if any exhortation in Christ, or any that is in the name and by the command of Christ, is of any value, fulfill, I beseech you, my joy, that you may be of one mind and humble, and intent upon the comforts and salvation of others. Which inference is for repeating the individual arguments of the Apostolic persuasion. παράκλησις denotes exhortation, Acts 13:15, Rom. 12:8, 1 Cor. 14:3, 1 Thess. 2:3, 1 Tim. 4:13, and in that sense it is accepted by Ambrose, B. Luther, B. Hunnius, Piscator, and others. And since παραμύθιον, consolation, follows here, the present noun παράκλησις, since it does not say the same thing twice, but establishes a different reason in such a vigorous and argumentative discourse, is more correctly rendered here by exhortation than by consolation, even though this pleased Chrysostom and the Greek Scholiasts, to whom Calvin, Zanchius, Tossanus, and Crocius also subscribe. 2. If any consolation of the love of God the Father is of value, than which no greater argument for vivifying consolation, or more effective incitement for obtaining anything can be conceived, fulfill my joy, that you may cultivate unanimity and cherish mutual charity. In which manner the κοινωνία of the Holy Spirit and the love of God are joined, 2 Cor. 13:13. παραμύθιον is properly an address by which the sad are raised up and confirmed. παραμυθεῖσθαι to console, Job 11:29, 1 Thess. 2:11, ch. 5:14. What kind of internal address of vivifying consolation the faithful feel in their heart when they experience the power of the Fatherly love of God, who therefore warns in Is. 40:1, Comfort ye, comfort ye my people, speak to the heart of Jerusalem, for her warfare is accomplished, her iniquity is pardoned. Ps. 34:9, Taste and see how sweet the Lord is. Bullinger, Calvin, Zanchius, Tossanus, along with Chrysostom, understand it concerning mutual charity. But the argument from mutual charity follows then, and in the last place. However, it does not fit with τῇ παρακλήσει in Christ, and τῇ κοινωνίᾳ of the Holy Spirit, for our charity to be interposed. And it is a far more effective ὁρμητήριον, sought from the immense love of God, which he had already prayed for the Philippians at the very threshold, v. 2, and concerning which he had made them more certain, ch. 1:28, and was about to confirm them further in ch. 2:13, under the name of χάριτος and εὐδοκίας. Concerning which Aretius also understands this ἀγάπην. 3. If any communion of the Spirit! B. Hunnius thus: If you acknowledge that you have received one and the same Spirit of Christ, certainly this communion of the Spirit ought to provoke you to nourish mutual concord and to cultivate humility. Chrysostom is almost similar: If you wish to exhibit any communion, which is in the Spirit. To which the sense of Theophylact is akin. Bullinger: If the Spirit, who binds the whole assembly of the faithful into one body, has any power in you. Which Crocius acknowledges as piously and well said. However, it seems to him a more effective argument if it is founded not in the consideration or demonstration of communion, but in the very existence of communion. Above he had said that they had arrived into the communion of the Gospel, which is called the communion of the Spirit, because the communion of the members with the head and among themselves in the natural body is no otherwise than from the vital spirit; so from the Holy Spirit is the communion of the saints with Christ, and among themselves in the mystical body. Now to persist in that communion is life-saving, but to fall from it is joined with the danger of salvation. If that has not entirely expired, but survives in any part of itself, through it he asks that they fulfill his joy with a zeal for concord. But the κοινωνία of the Spirit brings even more ample gifts and goods, for through it is had not only mystical union, but whatever solace can redound from the fatherly grace and love of God, all that is applied to us through the Spirit when we have his κοινωνία; or if you prefer to take κοινωνία actively, as in 2 Cor. 13:13, the Spirit communicates all that to us, whatever παρακλήσεως in Christ comes to us with effect, all that is to be credited to the gracious communication of the Holy Spirit, 1 Cor. 12:3. Therefore the Apostle wants this: if the communication of the Holy Spirit is of any value, by which he graciously gave himself and heavenly gifts to you, so that you lack nothing in any grace, 1 Cor. 1:7. What could be a more effective adjuration than by the exhortation in Christ, by the consolation of the love of God the Father, by the communication of the Holy Spirit. The Apostle exhorted the Corinthians to unanimity through the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, 1 Cor. 1:10; here he exhorts the Philippians in the name not only of Christ, but also of God the Father and the Holy Spirit. He adds, however, 4. if any bowels and mercies, that is, bowels of mercies by hendiadys, so that he might not pass over the love of the Philippians, by which they then embraced him as their Teacher, if they are touched by any affection of mercy; he strikes their heart, and moves the most tender affection of love, such as is wont to be not only of mothers toward their children, 1 Kings 3:26, but also of brothers toward each other, Gen. 43:10.

For thus σπλάγχνα & רחמים are understood among the Hebrews, and they designate such an inmost and most tender affection, even of God towards us, Deut. XIII. v. 17. nor is the word σπλαγχνίζομαι otherwise applied to Christ, Matth. IX. 36. XIV. 14. &c. The general sense here does not suffice nor exhaust the force of the Apostolic argument: And the word οἰκτιρμοὶ is added for its greater efficacy, just as also σπλάγχνα οἰκτιρμῶν are read, Col. III. 12. & σπλάγχνα ἐλέες, Luke I. 78. He had already spoken of his own affection towards them in the bowels of Jesus Christ, ch. I. 8. and had testified to the same at length throughout the whole first chapter, now he strikes their own bowels, as if he were to say, if there is any affection of love towards me and sense of reciprocal charity, by which we are accustomed to be moved towards those whom nature has joined to us, if there is any commiseration towards my bonds and towards the afflicted Church, fulfill my joy &c.

Latin:

30. Τὸν αὐτὸν ἀγῶνα ἔχοντες, ὃν εἴδετε ἐν ἐμοὶ. Idem certamen dicit, quod ex eadem venit causa.

Quod vidistis in me, tangit historiam, quae est Act. XVI.

19 & sequentibus. Est hic nominativus ἔχοντες pro Dativo ἔχουσι, qualia & apud Homerum nonnulla. Καὶ νῦν ἀκούετε ἐν ἐμοὶ.

Et ἐμοὶ hic est, de me, quomodo accipere Syrus & Latinus. Vincula sua intelligit.

Imo colligitur ex hisce, praeter illa, quae in actis commemorantur, fuintuiffe non pauca Philippenses, quum eos sibi pares faciat, aut similes non solum in causa passionum, sed etiam in ipsis passionibus, quae in actis commemorari non potuere. Haec enim pertingunt tantum usque ad captivitatem Apostoli Romanam.

Recentiora autem videntur, quae hic attinguntur ab Apostolo. Ostendit, quod in eodem sint secum certamine, in iisdem pugnantes, quae res magna ipsis virtutis testimonium praebent, dicente Theophylactum.

PARS II.

EPISTOLAE ΠΑΡΑΙΝΕΤΙΚΗ. Exhortatio ad unanimitatem, pietatem & honestatem. SECTIO I. Paranesis ad unanimitatem. CAP. II. ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO. Adhortatur valde pathetice ad unanimitatem & concordiam, cujus causa vitanda ambitio, sectanda humilitas, cum studio juvandi proximum, idque exemplo Christi, qui pro nobis exinaniri, humiliari, & ad mortem crucis usque obediens fieri voluit; exaltatus postmodum a Deo, nomeng, supra omne nomen consequutus, ut similiter obsequi pergant, & cum timore, ac tremore ad salutem contendant, Deo in ipsis & velle & posse operante, utque omnia sine murmure, & dubitatione peragant, sine macula & offensa, seu sinceri Dei filii, verbum vitae servantes. Gaudium etiam sibi inde, quantumvis ob fidei ipsorum munus mortem subire debeat, oriri docet, ipsosque similiter ad gaudium excitat, & confidit, se Timothei, brevi ad ipsos mittendi, nuncio recreatum iri, quem ab ὁμοψυχία & cura pro ipsis, necnon filiali observantia in sacro munere, commendat, seque brevi ad ipsos venturum, nunc autem Epaphroditum, veluti residuum, mittere testatur, ut per ejusdem conspectum exhilarentur, quem proinde in Domino suscipiant, monet. Partes duae sunt: I.

Exhortatoria est ad unanimitatem, eique connexam humilitatem & obedientiam ad v. 16.

II. Testificatoria de gaudio, quod Paulus in ipsis habet, quodque ipsi vicissim in Paulo habere desideret, unde & ille per Timotheum recreari desideret, & ipsi per Epaphroditum exhilarari jam queant, ad v. 30. PARS I. EXHORTATORIA Ad unanimitatem, eique connexam humilitatem & obedientiam. V. 1. Εἴ τις ἐν παράκλησις Valde & blanda & παθητική oratio. Si interdum vehementer affirmat. Magna enim sunt, quae a Christo habemus solatia. Εἴ τις κοινωνία πνεύματος Olim pagani dicti, qui de eodem bibebant Spiritu?

1. Cor. XII. 4. Εἴ τινα σπλάγχνα καὶ οἰκτιρμοὶ σπλάγχνα sunt affectus quivis.

Oἰκτιρμοὶ affectus circa calamitosos. Ita haec explicanda, ubi pariter ponuntur. Alioqui & generale illud in significatione speciei sumitur.

Magna autem haec sunt inter vere Christianos. Monuerat cap. I. 27. sed tacite, & ὡς ἐν παρόδῳ, ut si gaudio ipsis adventus Apostoli cedere debeat, digne Evangelio ambulent, & imprimis stent in unitate Spiritus, unaque animadcertent adversus hostes. Jam persequitur illam paranesin ex professo, exhortans imprimis ad unanimitatem, & humilitatem, & obedientiam, adeoque verorum Doctorum, quales Timotheus & Epaphroditus erant, observationem, ac falsorum visitationem, & ad pietatis & honestatis studia quæcunque; idque & verbis affectibus pientissimis mirifice plenis, & ar- gumentis valde efficacibus: Et gaudium ita sibi ipsique pollicetur eximium. Præsens autem ob- testatio sit in nomine sacrosanctæ Trinitatis, si quæ exhortatio in Christo, vel quæ nomine ac mandato Christi sit, quicquam valet, implete, obsecro, gau- dium meum, ut unanimes sitis atque humiles, & aliorum commodis ac saluti intenti. Quæ illatio ad singula Apostolicæ suasionis argumenta repeten- da. παράκλησις adhortationem notat, Act.XIII.15. Rom.XII.8. 1.Cor. XIV.3. 1.Thess. II.3. 1.Tim. IV.13. eoque sensu accipitur ab Ambrosio, B. Luthero, B. Hunnio, Piscatore, aliis. Et quum hic sequatur παραμύθιον consolatio, præsens nomen παράκλη- σις, quum non eadem bis dicat, sed diversam ratio- nem in tam nervosa & argumentosa oratione con- stituat, rectius per exhortationem, quam conso- lationem hic redditur, etsi hoc Chrysostomo & Scholiastis Græcis placuerit, quibus etiam Calvi- nus, Zanchius, Tossanus, Crocius suffragantur. 2. Si quid valet consolatio dilectionis Dei Patris, qua nul- lum vel majus consolationis vivificæ argumen- tum, vel efficacius ad aliquid impetrandum incita- mentum cogitari potest, gaudium meum implete, ut unanimitatem colatis & charitatem mutuam foveatis. Quo pacto κοινωνία Spiritus Sancti & di- lectio Dei conjungitur, 2. Cor. XIII. 13. παραμύ- θιον proprie est alloquium, quo tristes eriguntur & confirmantur. παραμυθεῖσθαι consolari, Job. XI. 29. 1.Thess. II. 11. cap. V.14. Quale internum con- solationis vivificæ alloquium sentiunt fideles in corde suo, cum vim amoris Paterni Dei experi- untur, qui propterea monet Es. XL. 1. Consolami- ni, consolamini populum meum, loquimini ad cor Jerusalem, quoniam impleta est militia ejus, di- missa iniquitas illius. Ps. XXXIV. 9. Gustate & vi- dete, quam suavis est Dominus. Bullingerus, Cal- vinus, Zanchius, Tossanus cum Chrysostomo de cha- ritate mutua intelligunt. Sed argumentum à mu- tua charitate sequitur deinde, ac loco postremo. Non convenit autem τῇ παρακλήσει in Christo, & τῇ κοινωνίᾳ Spiritus Sancti, charitatem nostram in- terponi. Et longe efficacius est ὁρμητήριον, à dile- ctione Dei immensa petitum, quam in ipso limi- ne precatus statim est Philippensibus v. 2. & de qua ipsos certiores reddidit, cap.I. 28. ac porro eos confirmaturus erat c. II.13. sub χάριτος & εὐδοκίας nomine. De qua etiam Aretius hanc ἀγάπην in- telligit. 3. Siqua communio Spiritus! B. Hunnius ita: Si agnoscitis, vos unum eundemq́; accepisse Spi- ritum Christi, certe hæc communio Spiritus vos ad mutuam concordiam alendam, humilitatem colen- dam provocare debet. Similiter fere Chrysostomus: Si quam communionem exhibere volueritis, quæ sit in Spiritu. Cui affinis est Theophylacti sensus. Bullingerus: Si quam vim in vobis habet Spiritus, qui omnem fidelium cœtum in unum corpus compingit. Quæ pie & bene dicta agnoscit Cro- cius. Efficacius tamen ipsi videtur esse argumen- tum, si non vel in consideratione vel demonstratione communionis, sed in ipsa communionis existentia fundetur. Supra dixerat, eos pervenisse in commu- nionem Evangelii, quæ communio Spiritus appella- tur, quia non aliter ac à spiritu vitali est communio membrorum cum capite & inter sese in corpore na- turali; ita à Spiritu Sancto est communio sanctorum cum Christo, & inter se in corpore mystico. Jam in illa communione persistere est salutiferum, at cum sa- lutis periculo conjunctum ea excidere. Si illa non prorsus expirarit, sed ulla sui parte supersit, per eam rogat, ut expleant suum gaudium concordiæ studio. Sed ampliora adhuc dona & bona impor- tat κοινωνία Spiritus, nam per eam habetur non tantum mystica unio, sed quicquid solatii à pater- na Dei gratia & dilectione redundare potest, id omne applicatur nobis per Spiritum, cum ejus κοινωνίαν habemus; vel si Active malis κοινωνίαν ac- cipere, ut 2. Cor. XIII. 13. id omne communicat nobis Spiritus, quicquid παρακλήσεως in Christo cum effectu nobis obtingit, id omne communica- tioni gratiosæ Spiritus Sancti acceptum ferendum est, 1. Cor. XII. 3. Id ergo vult Apostolus, si quid valet communicatio Spiritus Sancti, qua semetipsum & cælestia dona vobis gratiose donavit, ut nihil vobis desit in ulla gratia, 1. Cor. I. 7. Quæ potuit ef- ficacior esse obtestatio, quam per exhortationem in Christo, per consolationem amoris Dei Patris, per communicationem Spiritus Sancti. Hortatus est Apostolus Corinthios ad unanimitatem per nomen Domini Jesu Christi, 1. Cor. I. 10. hic Phi- lippenses hortatur in nomine non Christi tantum, sed etiam Dei Patris & Spiritus Sancti. Addit au- tem 4. si quæ viscera ac miserationes, id est, viscera miserationum per hendyaden, ne prætereat amo- rem Philippensium, quo tum ipsum ceu Docto- rem suum complectebantur, si ullo misericordiæ affectu tangantur; Cor ipsorum pulsat, & affectum amoris tenerrimum, qualis non tantum matrum esse solet erga liberos, 1. Reg. III. 26. sed etiam fra- trum erga se mutuo, Gen. XLIII. 10. commovet.

Nam ita σπλάγχνα & רחמים apud Hebræos acci- piuntur, talemque intimum ac tenerrimum etiam Dei erga nos affectum designant, Deut. XIII. v. 17. nec aliter verbum σπλαγχνίζομαι de Christo ad- hibetur, Matth. IX. 36. XIV. 14. &c. Sensus gene- ralis hic non sufficit nec exhaurit vim argumenti Apostolici: Et additur ad majorem ejus efficaciam vox οἰκτιρμοὶ, uti etiã σπλάγχνα οἰκτιρμῶν legun- tur, Col. III. 12. & σπλάγχνα ἐλέες, Luc. I. 78. Jam dixerat de suo in visceribus Jesu Christi erga ipsos affectu, c. I. 8. eundemq; prolixe testatus erat toto capite primo, nunc pulsat propria ipsorum visce- ra, quasi dicat, si ullus amoris erga me affectus & charitatis reciprocæ sensus, quo erga eos, quos na- tura nobis conjunxit, commoveri solemus, si quic- quam commiserationis erga vincula mea & erga Ecclesiam afflictam, implete gaudium meum &c.

## 2:2
V. 2. Πληρώσατέ με τὴν χαρὰν) The same expression in John III. verse 29. Ἵνα τὸ ἀυτὸ φρονῆτε) Rom. XII. 16. XV. 5. 2. Cor. XIII. 1. that you may have the same purpose. See below III. 15. Τὴν ἀυτὴν ἀγάπην ἔχοντες) Equals in mutual love. Σύμψυχοι) The same as above I. 27. μιᾷ ψυχῇ. Τὸ ἓν φρονῦντες, μηδὲν κατ' ἐρίθειαν, ἢ κενοδοξίαν) supply to do. Striving for this one thing, especially of course, that you do nothing contentiously or ambitiously. The same as Gal. V. 26. μὴ γεινώμεθα κενόδοξοι, ἀλλήλες προκαλέμενοι. Add 2. Cor. XII. 20. James III. 16. In the Manuscript here is τὸ ἀυτὸ φρονῦντες. V. 3. Ἀλλὰ τῇ ταπεινοφροσύνῃ ἀλλήλες ἡγύμενοι ὑπερέ- χοντας ἑαυτῶν) This is a modest disposition, always to think more magnificently of others than of oneself. V. 4. Μὴ τὰ ἑαυτῦ ἕκαστος σκοπείτω) which is most natural, I am nearest to myself. Ἀλλὰ κὶ τὰ τῶν ἑτέρων ἕκαστος) which indeed to some extent agrees with human society: But in the Gospel it is commanded in a certain highest degree, especially in those things in which the eternal salvation of others turns, with which all earthly goods cannot be compared. In the Manuscript it is: ἀλλὰ κὶ τὰ ἑτέρων ἕκαστοι τῦτο φρονείτω.

We see how much the Apostle valued unanimity. For he testifies that this is his only joy, for this reason he so greatly adjures the faithful. He requires, however, first a unanimous opinion in the doctrine of faith. By that τὸ ἀυτὸ φρονῆτε, not so much the same purpose of will, as the same opinion of mind, so that in one Spirit and one soul they may be able to stand for the doctrine of faith. Therefore he warns so diligently about observing sincere Teachers, and avoiding Pseudo-Apostles, lest from heavenly truth be led away to pernicious errors.

Unanimous love; because faith is never without love, nor does the parity of love have a place, except where there is unity of faith. But it is not the same charity, by reason of degrees, for thus the subjects vary greatly, although they ought to tend toward the same mode of perfection, but by reason of vicissitude, or reciprocation, by which they embrace one another in turn , as well as parity in sincerity. Chrysostom: Having the same charity, that is, studying equally both to love and to be loved. Do not you indeed wish much to be loved, but return little love in turn; so that you may abound in this matter also. Theophylact not dissimilarly: Having the same charity, not, if anyone is vehemently loved, that he should love back remissly and sluggishly, but that he should love back in the same measure. Which is to be understood concerning the measure of sincerity and ardor, not precisely of the work. For although one does not declare charity by an equally manifold work, he can nevertheless have the same measure of integrity and zeal, and therefore the same charity.

Unanimity of every kind, so that they may be of one mind, nay, one soul, as regards the consent of minds not only in faith and mutual charity, but in counsels, institutions, actions, directed by one mind in the unity of the Spirit to the glory of God, and mutual edification. Unanimous, says Chrysostom, that is, accommodating the one soul of all bodies as if it were their own, not indeed in substance itself, for that cannot be, but in choice and sentiment, so that all things may proceed as if from one soul. And to this also tends the Grotian interpretation of the remaining words: That you may think nothing through strife or vainglory, studying this one thing, most especially, that you do nothing contentiously or ambitiously. Ambition is joined to contention, because these are connected, and ambition is for the most part the mother of contention.

Whence the Apostle proceeds further to commend the study of humility, which is opposed to ambition, and that we should not seek only those things which are each our own, but also not neglect to look to the salvation of our neighbor (which particle the Vulgate rashly omits). For the law of charity requires this, that we love our neighbor as ourselves, without which concord cannot consist.

It appears from so pathetic and laborious an exhortation, to which a twin hardly occurs in the sacred writings, that contentions had arisen among the Philippians, without doubt through those dogs and the faction, against whom he warned in chapter III, which were to be stifled in the bud, and with such an apparatus of words he exhorts them, and is already sending Epaphroditus to them, and was shortly to send Timothy, like-minded to himself in all things, whom he deigned to join to himself in this literary colloquy, nay, he himself was shortly to come to them, if, as he hoped, he had been released from prison. The words of the Apostle here are to be observed. He does not say: Let him say, but let him esteem. It is not base-speaking, which is often wont to be feigned, but humility that is required. We ought not, says Augustine in book LXXXIII of questions, no. 71, to esteem in such a way that we do not esteem, or that we esteem by feigning, but that we truly esteem.

He also piously warns that it should be considered that there is no man who cannot have some good which you do not yet have, although it lies hidden, in which without doubt he can be your superior. Which thought is valid for convincing and subduing pride, lest you judge, because your goods indeed stand out and appear, that therefore another has none which lie hidden, and perhaps goods of greater weight, in which he surpasses you, unknown to you.

The middle voice φρονέω is taken either actively, let (each) think, or passively, let it be thought, which is more agreeable. But thus the sentence is complete: Let this be thought, (or let the very sense and affection be in you) which was thought in Christ, or rather, what kind of affection was in Christ.

Grotius more correctly takes it concerning the affection of the will, not however excluding the judgment of the mind, as most do, because by this illustrious example the Apostle exhorts us both to humility and to the care of our neighbor's salvation, which if it be rendered with the Vulgate, for think this, or with Jerome, everyone among you will understand this. Meanwhile, it requires a consideration of the mystery that is not perfunctory, although not merely theoretical, but practical, which he executes with care. Namely, concerning the emptying and exaltation of Christ.

For it is nowhere else so exquisitely proposed by the Holy Spirit. And Flacius rightly observes that the Apostle does not only do this in this treatment, that he may recall the Philippians and us to charity, modesty, and helping our neighbor, but also much more, that he may propose and inculcate before the eyes of all that far more noble and useful doctrine, namely, the very emptying of Christ, or his whole obedience and passion, by which the human race has been redeemed and saved, so that, all confidence in the law and works and virtues and merits being utterly put aside, they may hang upon Christ alone.

Which B. Luther, as he is wont, has excellently explained in Tom. I. Jen. Lat. de libert. Christ. fol. 392. Because it makes for the application of the same, which is perplexed not so much by the Apostolic phrase as by the variety of interpretations, it is worth bringing it in whole: Here we clearly see the life of Christians to have been placed by the Apostle upon this rule, that all our works should be ordered for the convenience of others, since through his own faith each one so abounds that all other works are superfluous to his life, by which he may serve and benefit his neighbor with spontaneous benevolence.

To this he induces Christ as an example, saying: Think this, etc. For this most wholesome word of the Apostle is obscured for us by those who have not understood at all the Apostolic terms form of God, form of a servant, habit, likeness of men, and have transferred them to the natures of divinity and humanity, when Paul intends this, that Christ, when he was full of the form of God, and abounding in all goods, so that he needed no work, no passion, that he might be just and saved. For he has all these things immediately from his beginning. Yet he was not puffed up, nor was he elevated above us, and he did not arrogate to himself a certain power over us, although he could have done so by right. But on the contrary, he acts thus, laboring, working, suffering, dying, so that he might be like other men, and in habit and gesture nothing other than a man; as if he needed all those things, and had nothing of the forms of God, which nevertheless he did entirely for our sake, that he might serve us, and all things might become ours, which he might work by this form of a servant.

Which is the simplest interpretation flowing from the scope, context, and Apostolic phrase, as will soon appear, which Megalander applies thus: Thus the Christian, just as his head Christ, through his own faith full and satisfied, ought to be content with this form of God, obtained through faith, except that, as I said, he ought to increase this very faith, until it is perfected.

For this life, justice, and his salvation is the person himself saving and making acceptable, and bestowing all things, which Christ has, as was said above, and Paul confirms in Gal. I,... saying: But that I live in the flesh, I live in the faith of the Son of God: And although he is thus free from all works, he ought nevertheless again to empty himself, in this liberty to take the form of a servant, in to be made in the likeness of men, and to be found in habit as a man, to serve, to assist, and in every way to act with his neighbor, just as he sees that it has been acted with him and that he is acted upon by God through Christ, and this very thing freely, and for no regard, except for the divine pleasure, and thus to think: Behold, for me, an unworthy... and damned little man, without any merit, my GOD has given in Christ, by mere and gratuitous mercy, all the riches of righteousness and salvation, so that I am in need of nothing at all anymore, except faith, by which he may believe that this is so.

To such a Father, therefore, who overwhelms me with his twice-inestimable riches, why should I not liberally, cheerfully, with my whole heart and spontaneous zeal, do everything that I know to be pleasing and acceptable before him? And so I will give myself as a certain Christ to my neighbor, just as Christ offered himself to me, intending to do nothing in this life except what I see will be necessary, convenient, and salutary for my neighbor, since through faith I am abundant in all good things in Christ. Behold, thus charity and joy in the Lord flow from faith, and from charity a cheerful, willing, free spirit, for serving one's neighbor spontaneously, so that it has no regard for gratitude, ingratitude, praise and blame, gain or loss. For he does not do this to win men over to himself, nor does he distinguish between friends and enemies, nor does he accept the grateful or the ungrateful, but most freely, most willingly, he scatters himself and his own, whether he loses them on the ungrateful or trades them.

V. 2. Πληρώσατέ με τὴν χαρὰν) Eadem locutio Joh. III. vers. 29. Ἵνα τὸ ἀυτὸ φρονῆτε) Rom. XII. 16. XV. 5. 2. Cor. XIII. 1. ut idem habeatis propositum. Vide infra III. 15. Τὴν ἀυτὴν ἀγάπην ἔχοντες) Pares in mutua dilectione. Σύμψυχοι) Idem quod supra I. 27. μιᾷ ψυχῇ. Τὸ ἓν φρονῦντες, μηδὲν κατ' ἐρίθειαν, ἢ κενοδοξίαν) supple facere. Hoc unum studentes, maxime scilicet, ne quid con- tentiose aut ambitiose agatis. Idem quod Gal. V. 26. μὴ γεινώμεθα κενόδοξοι, ἀλλήλες προκαλέμενοι. Adde 2. Cor. XII. 20. Jac. III. 16. In Manuscripto hic est τὸ ἀυτὸ φρονῦντες. V. 3. Ἀλλὰ τῇ ταπεινοφροσύνῃ ἀλλήλες ἡγύμενοι ὑπερέ- χοντας ἑαυτῶν) Hoc est modestia ingenium, de aliis ma- gnificentius semper, quam de se opinari. V. 4. Μὴ τὰ ἑαυτῦ ἕκαστος σκοπείτω) quod maxime est naturale, egomet mihi proximus. Ἀλλὰ κὶ τὰ τῶν ἑτέρων ἕκαστος) quod societati quidem humanæ aliquatenus congruit: Sed in Evangelio in summo quodam gradu præcipitur, præsertim in rebus illis, in qui- bus salus aliorum æterna vertitur, cum qua omnia bona terrena comparari nequeunt. In Manuscripto est: ἀλλὰ κὶ τὰ ἑτέρων ἕκαστοι τῦτο φρονείτω.

Videmus, quanti unanimitatem fecerit Aposto- lus. Hanc enim unicum suum gaudium testatur, ob eam tantopere obtestatur fideles. Requirit au- tem primo sententiam unanimem in doctrina fidei. Per illud τὸ ἀυτὸ φρονῆτε, non tam idem propositum voluntatis, quam eadem mentis sententia, ut in uno Spiritu, unaque anima stare pro doctrina fidei possint. Ideo de observandis sinceris Doctoribus, vitandis Pseudo-Apostolis tam sedulo monet, ne à veritate cœlesti abducantur ad errores pernitiosos.

Unanimem dilectionem; quia fides nunquam est fine dilectione, nec paritas dilectionis locum habet, nisi ubi unitas est fidei. Non autem eadem charitas est, ratione graduum, sic enim variant subjecta maximopere, licet ad eundem modum perfectionis tendere debeant, sed ratione vicissitudinis, vel reciprocationis, qua se κατ’ ἀμοιϐὴν complectuntur, ut & paritatis in sinceritate. Chrysostomus: Eandem charitatem habentes, id est, pariter & amare & amari studentes. Noli tu quidem multum velle diligi, parum vero dilectionis vicissim rependere; ut & in hac re abundes. Theophylactus non absimiliter: Eandem charitatem habentes, non, si qui vehementer amatur, remisse ac pigre redamet, sed si eadem mensura redamet. Quod de mensura sinceritatis & ardoris, non operis præcise accipiendum. Etsi enim quis non æque multiplici opere declarat charitatem, potest tamen eandem habere mensuram integritatis & studii, proinde eandem charitatem.

Unanimitatem omnimodam, ut σύμψυχοι coanimes, imò μία ψυχὴ, una anima, sint, quoad consensum animorum non in fide tantum & charitate mutua, sed in consiliis, institutis, actionibus, una mente in unitate Spiritus ad gloriam Dei, mutuamque ædificationem dirigendis. Unanimes, inquit Chrysostomus, id est, uni animæ omnium corporum quasi propria accommodantes, non quidem substantia ipsa, nam id fieri non potest, sed electione & sententia, ut quasi ex una anima omnia, proficiscantur. Atque eo etiam tendit Grotiana reliquorum verborum interpretatio: Τὸ ἐν φρονῆτες μηδὲν κατ’ ἐρίθειαν ἢ κενοδοξίαν, hoc unum studentes, maxime scilicet, ne quid contentiose aut ambitiose agatis. Jungitur contentioni ambitio, quia hæc conjuncta sunt, & ambitionis contentionis mater est plerumque.

Unde ad commendandum humilitatis studium porro digreditur Apostolus, quæ ambitioni opponitur, & ut non ea, quæ nostra uniuscujusque sunt, quaramus unice, sed salutem proximi etiam (quam particulamtemere prætermittit Vulgata) spectare non negligamus. Hoc enim charitatis lex requirit, ut proximum diligamus sicut nosipsos, fine qua concordia consistere nequit.

Apparet ex tam pathetica & operosa exhortatione, cui vix gemina occurrit in sacris, contentiones Philippis exortas esse, fine dubio per canes illos & concionem, de quibus virandis monuit cap. III. ad quas in herba suffocandas & tanto verborum apparatu eosdem exhortatur, & Epaphroditum ad eosdem jam mittit, ac brevi missurus erat Timotheum, fibi per omnia ὁμόψυχον, quem dignatus est in hoc colloquio literario sibi adjungere, imo ipse propediem ad ipsos venturus erat, si, quod sperabat, ex carcere dimissus fuerit. Verba Apostoli hic observanda. Non ait: Dicat, sed existimet. Non ταπεινολογὴν, quæ sæpe simulata esse solet, sed ταπεινοφροσύνην requiritur. Non nos, inquit Augustinus libr. LXXXIII. quæstion. num. 71. ita debemus existimare, ut non existimemus, seu existimemus fingamus, sed vere existimemus.

Pie etiam monet, cogitandum, nullum esse hominem, qui non possit habere aliquod bonum, quod tu nondum habes, quamvis lateat, in quo fine dubio te possit esse superior. Quæ cogitatio ad convincendam edomandamque superbiam valet, ne arbitreris, quoniam bona tua quident eminent & apparent, ideo alterum nulla habere, quæ lateant, & fortassis majoris ponderis bona, quibus te superat nescientem.

Vox mediaφρονέω vel active accipitur, sentiat, (quisque) vel passive, sentiatur, quod magis consentaneum. Sic autem completa est oratio: Hoc sentiatur, (vel ipse sensus & affectus sit in vobis) quod in Christo sentiebatur, vel potius, qualis affectus in Christo fuit.

Rectius Grotius de affectu voluntatis, non exclusa tamen judicio mentis, cum plerisque accipit, quia exemplo hoc illustri Apostolus tum ad humilitatem, tum ad salutis proximi curam nos exhortatur, quam si cum Vulgata reddatur, hoc enim sentite, vel cum Hieronymo, hoc intelliget unusquisque in vobis. Interim considerationem mysterii non perfunctoriam, etsi nec mere theoreticam, sed practicam requirit, quod cum cura exequitur. De Christi nempe exinanitione & exaltatione.

Nam id nuspiam alias à Spiritu Sancto tam exquisite propositum est. Et recte observat Flacius, hac tractatione non illud tantum agere Apostolum, ut Philippenses & nos ad charitatem, modestiam juvandumque proximum revocet, sed etiam multo magis, ut illam longe nobiliorem utilioremque doctrinam, nempe ipsam Christi exinanitionem, aut totam ejus obedientiam ac passionem, qua genus humanum redemptum servatumque est, et omnibus ante oculos proponat & inculcet, quo prorsus feposita omni fiducia legis ac operum virtutumque ac meritorum distant à folo Christo pendere.

Quod præclare, ut solet, exposuit B. Lutherus Tom. I. Jen. Lat. de libert. Christ. fol. 392. Locum, quia ad illustrandum textum non tam phrasi Apostolicæ, quam varietate interpretationum perplexum, ejusdem applicationem facit, integrum adducere juvat: Hic clare videmus, vitam Christianorum ab Apostolo in hanc regulam esse positam, ut omnia opera nostra ad aliorum commoditatem ordinentur, cum per fidem suam quisque sic abundet, ut omnia alia opera totas vitæ ei superfluant, quibus proximo spontanea benevolentia serviat & benefaciat.

Ad hoc inducit Christum pro exemplo, dicens: Hoc sentite &c. Hoc enim verbum Apostoli faluberrimum nobis obscurrunt ii, qui vocabula Apostolica formam Dei, formam servi, habitum, similitudinem hominum, prorsus non intellexererunt, & ad naturas divinitatis & humanitatis transtulerunt, cum Paulus id velit, Christum, cum esset plenus forma Dei, & omnibus bonis abundans, ita ut nullo opere, nullo passione indiguerit, ut justus & salvus fieret. Habeat enim hæc omnia statim ab initio sui. Non tamen is inflabatur, nec super nos elevabatur, & quandam potentiam super nos sibi arrogabat, licet id jure potuisset. Sed contra sic agit labornans, operans, patiens, moriens, ut similis esset cæteris hominibus, & habitu & gestu non aliud quam homo; quasi iis omnibus egeret, & nihil haberet formarum Dei, quod tamen totum propter nos fecit, ut nobis serviret, & nostrum fierent omnia, quæ hac forma servi operaretur.

Quæ est simplicissima ex scopo, contextu & phrasi Apostolica, ut mox apparebit, fluens interpretatio, quam sic applicat Megalander: Ita Christianus, quemadmodum caput suum Christus, per fidem suam plenus & fatur, contentus esse debet hac forma Dei, per fidem obtenta, nisi quod, ut dixi, ipsam hanc fidem augere debet, donec perficiatur.

Hac enim vita, justitia, & salus ejus est personam ipsam servans & gratam faciens, omniaque tribuens, qua Christus habet, ut supra dictum est, & Paulus Gal. I. confirmat dicens: Quod autem in carne vivo, in fide vivo Filii Dei: Et quanquam sic liber est ab omnibus operibus, debet samen rursus se exinanire, hac in libertate formam servi accipere, in familitudine hominum fieri, & habitu inveniri ut homo, servire, adjuvare, & omnimodo cum proximo suo agere, sicut videt secum actum & agi a Deo per Christum, & hoc ipsum gratis, nulloque respectu, nisi divini placiti, & ita cogitare: En mihi indigno... damnatoque homuncioni citra omne meritum, mera gratuitaque misericordia dedit DEUS meus in Christo omnes divitias justitiae & salutis, ut amplius nulla re prorsus indigeam, nisi fide, qua credat, hoc se sic habere.

Huic ergo tali Patri, qui me suis bis inestimabilibus divitiis obruit, cur non liberaliter, hilariter, toto corde spontaneoque studio omnia faciam, quaecunque scivero placita & grata esse coram illo? Dabo iraq; me quendam Christum proximo meo, quemadmodum Christus sese praebuit mihi, nihil facturus in hac vita, nisi quod videro proximo meo necessarium, commodum, & salutare fore, quandoquidem per fidem omnium bonorum in Christo abundans sum. Ecce sic fluit ex fide charitas & gaudium in Domino, & ex charitate hilaris, libens, liber animus, ad sponte serviendum proximo, ita ut nullam habeat rationem gratitudinis, ingratitudinis, laudis & vituperii, lucri aut damni. Neque enim agit hoc, ut homines sibi demercatur, nec inter amices inimicosque discernit, nec gratos, nec ingratos suscipit, sed liberrime, libentissime dispergit se & sua, sive ea perdat in ingratu, sive mercatur.

## 2:6
Vers. 6. ὃς ἐν μορφῇ Θεῦ ὑπάρχων) Μορφὴ in our books does not signify something internal and hidden, but that which strikes the eyes, such as was the extraordinary power in Christ of healing all diseases, casting out demons, raising the dead, changing the natures of things, which are truly divine, so that Moses, because he did not do such great things, was for that reason called the God of Pharaoh.

You have the word μορφῆς in the sense I mentioned in Mark XVI. verse 12. ἑτέρα, Dan. IV. 33. V. 6. 10. VI.

28. where in the Chaldean,

Job IV. 16. where in the Hebrew. Does Μορφὴ Θεῦ denote the essence itself?

It is not poorly explained thus as form, and the form of God.

Bellarminus book I. de Christo chap. IV., contending that by μορφὴν Θεῦ the essence of God itself is noted here, says that that word is nowhere in scripture taken for an external form or work, and that this is evident to one running through all the passages. But the contrary is rather evident, if we run through the passages.

It is not read outside of this place, this noun, except in Mark XVI. verse 12. ἑφα-νερώθη ἐν ἑτέρᾳ μορφῇ, where another form of substance cannot be understood, but accidental, and the same external one with even extrinsic acts.

The verb μορφῆσθαι, Gal. IV. verse 9. concerning Christ in the Galatians, who had turned back to God, is used in no other way. Certainly not through a reformation, or μεταμόρφωσιν of the essential form of Christ, as if they had lost what they had received from baptism, and had taken on the form of the Pseudo-Apostles.

The form of Christ was true righteousness applied to them by faith for salvation, Galat. III. verse

26. 27. who was made for us by God as righteousness, so that we might be rendered the righteousness of GOD in him, 1. Corinth. I. verse 29. 2. Cor. V. verse 21. The form of the Pseudo-Apostles was the righteousness of their own works, which they had impressed upon themselves as perfect and sufficient for obtaining salvation, or had required alongside some kind of faith in Christ for salvation.

Similarly μορφωσις Rom. II. 20. and 2. Tim. III. 5. denotes not a substantial form, but an accidental one, and an appearance, and an external image.

The compound verb μεταμορφῶσθαι, Matth. XVII. 2. and συμμορφῶσθαι, Phil. III. 20. 21. and the noun σύμμορφος, Rom. IX. v. 29. Phil. III. 21. do not imply any substantial transformation or conformation, it is certain.

Although μορφὴν does not directly and immediately denote the internal essence of GOD here, but that power and Majesty which struck the senses, yet that was truly the divine power and Majesty proper to the Only-Begotten Son of GOD, and thus consequently and mediately it connotes or presupposes the divine nature or essence, from which that is inseparable; and in this sense the explanation of some of the Fathers, especially when they conclude the Deity of Christ from this passage, is not disapproved, provided the immediate sense is not neglected.

Therefore the commentary ascribed to Ambrose teaches that μορφὴν Θεῦ and the divine substance are to be distinguished in such a way that, nevertheless, because of the connotation or consequence, it asserts that the form of GOD differs nothing from GOD, just as the power of God does not differ from the divine essence, and the latter is firmly concluded from the former.
