For here is understood not a false μορφὴ Θεῦ, but a true one: But it cannot be a true μορφὴ Θεῦ unless it truly embraces the Θεότητα itself, since that is its foundation.

Which B. Feuerbornius neatly illustrates from B. Luther on Palm Sunday, fascic. III. disp. Theol. disp. II. th. 33. 34. observing that three modes obtain in the form of GOD, 1.

The divine essence is found (by us men) without the essence of GOD, as when GOD hides himself, and offers himself as angry, and withdraws his grace from us. See Psalm XIII. v. 2. Psalm XXV. v. 8. Jer. XIV. v. 8. 9. 10. &c. 2.

The form of God is found (but fictitious) without the essence of GOD, as when Satan and the Protoplasts attempted to seize the form of God, Gen. I. 9. Matth. IV. v. 9. and the King of Tyre, Ezech. XXVIII. v. 2. the Anti-Christ, 2. Thess. II. v. 4. 3. Both μορφὴ and ὐσία are found joined together, as when God behaves propitiously toward us, and offers his kindness for us to taste. Since, therefore, Christ existed in the form of GOD ὄντως &amp; ἀληθῶς, hence his eternal Deity is concluded indubitably and immovably.

For it is impossible that a true form of GOD can exist without a true Deity. For it is the nature of blaspheming men and the Devil to sell μορφὴν Θεῦ without the divine essence, since they are destitute of it.

D. Luther says: When GOD shows himself with grace, that is both the essence and the gesture.

But the other he cannot do, that he should gesture like GOD, and yet not be so, or not have the essence, but that belongs to the Devil and his own, who set themselves in the place of GOD, and present themselves as GOD, when they are not GOD, &amp;c. When, therefore, the question is about the proper and immediate sense of the word μορφὴ Θεῦ, and the phrase ὑπάρχειν ἐν μορφῇ Θεῦ, the Calvinists, along with Bellarmine and other Papists, maintain that the divine nature and essence of Christ are indicated by the form of GOD; our people, however, either understand τὸ ἔχειν the external form of GOD, the appearance and demonstration of divine glory, which shone forth in divine works, or they explain τὸ ἐν μορφῇ Θεῦ ὑπάρχειν in such a way that it is not to be God by nature, but to demonstrate oneself gloriously, and to act AS GOD, by truly divine words and deeds through a communicated divine power and Majesty: concerning which whole phrase the matter is mostly how B.

Aegydius Hunnius concedes, that the Word by reason of his divine nature is the form of God the Father himself, but according to his humanity he is in the form of God; for the flesh assumed is in the unity of him who is the form and image of GOD.

Although it can be said without violating orthodoxy that Christ according to his human nature ὑπάρχειν exists in the form of God, because he subsists in the person or ὐπάρξα of the Son of God, this communication of the divine hypostasis of the Son of God also becomes the foundation of the communicated divine glory and power: Yet that ὐπάρξις is not directly viewed here; but as through the form of a servant the servile condition of the flesh, through the assumption of the form of a servant, the assumption of a servile status, not the human nature itself, is what is being criticized, thus by the form of God is noted not the divine nature, but the divine status, and by ὑπάρχειν μορφῇ θεοῦ [existing in the form of God], not the subsistence in the person, or the divine nature of the Son of GOD, but the existence in the state of the divine condition, by virtue of which Christ, according to his human nature, not only possessed the divine Majesty, because the whole fullness of divinity dwelt in him bodily, but also had in his own hand the plenary use of it, which he indeed freely deigned to empty himself of for the sake of our redemption.

To be in the form of GOD absolutely and simply is not to be God by nature, but to bear oneself as God, to declare oneself as GOD, to exert divine Majesty by performing divine works, as rightly the Blessed Gerhard in Exeg. Loc. IV. §. 295. says of ὑπάρχειν ἐν μορφῇ θεοῦ [existing in the form of God], Feuerborn says in the cited place §. 52. it immediately denotes being in a state, honor, and divine glory, and thus in the splendor and brightness of divine Majesty. He observes, however, that this divine glory is not understood here only in real use, but rather in the use itself, and indeed not only particular, but universal.

The Blessed

Luther in Postill. on the Epistle

Sunday

Palm

Thus we have this text, I think, almost clearly, that the divine form is nothing else than to show oneself with words and works toward others as a GOD and Lord, and that Christ did such with miracle-signs and wholesome words, as the Gospels hold, not like the other saints, who did not have the essence, but he had besides that also the divine essence and nature in the divine form, which he leads, &c.

But this is to be accepted regarding the whole phrase, that Christ Jesus exists in the form of GOD, primarily.

Furthermore, the Blessed

Glassius in Epistle

Sun.

Palm. page

944. thinks that, as regards the simple denomination of μορφῆς θεοῦ [form of God], it seems to fall into the same scope, whether μορφὴν θεοῦ [form of God] is said to be the very Majesty and essence of GOD, (which, however, we think Dan. Heinsius in Aristarchus proved more laboriously than solidly, page 348. (in the edition of exerc. sacr. page

873.)) or an external form of GOD, as it were, and appearance, which shines forth in the government of the world and the demonstration of divine power and Majesty, as Mr.

Menzerus speaks in this way: because these two, the essence of GOD and his glory exerting itself, are inseparable, and from the latter to the former a most firm argument is drawn. Moreover, that the whole phrase χριστὸν ἰησοῦν ἐν μορφῇ θεοῦ ὑπάρχειν [that Christ Jesus exists in the form of God] does not denote only the same as being God by nature, which some Fathers wish, but is to be explained from the mystery of the personal union, that Christ according to his humanity, or the human nature of Christ, exists in the form of GOD, that is, in glory and divine Majesty, and is filled with the whole fullness of divine Majesty, just as the Blessed Chemnitz in the book on the two natures in Christ, chap. XXIV. page 352. explains: Paul says that Christ not only was the very form of GOD, according to his divinity, but was also in the form of GOD, that is, in the highest glory, majesty, and power of divinity, as true God, equal to the Father, as most of the ancients interpret, or as Ambrose, Erasmus, and Luther interpret, (which interpretations come to the same thing) that the whole fullness of the Deity dwelt in the assumed nature personally, just as through union iron ignited is said to be in the fire.

Ambrose on this place, whose opinion Erasmus approves, has it thus: The Son of GOD born man was thus in the form of GOD, because while he was seen as a man, he did the works of GOD, so that it might appear in the deeds done that he was God, who was thought to be only a man.

For the works signified the form, so that because his works were not at all the works of a man (a mere or pure one), he who was in the work or form of GOD might be understood as God. For what is the form of GOD, if not the example by which God might appear, while he raises the dead, restores hearing to the deaf, cleanses lepers, and other things.

The Blessed

Luther in the cited place has it thus: The form of God is called therefore, that one places himself as God, and also behaves as such, or takes upon himself and undertakes the Godhead, which happens not secretly by himself alone, but toward others, who perceive that same behavior or form.

Therefore one could not speak it more clearly than in the way, he behaves divinely, or places himself as a God, when he proves himself, and thus speaks and does what belongs to GOD or well befits him &c.

We add also the assent of Calvin: Just as a man is known from his form and appearance: So the Majesty, which shines back in GOD, is his figure.

And of Piscator, who says, through the form of GOD, I do not think Aristotle in his Philosophy understands by the word μορφῆς [form] the nature and essence of a thing.

Nor is it probable that the Apostle uses this word in that meaning which was known only to Philosophers, but unknown to the people.

Then it appears from the coherence of the sentence, verses 7 and 8, that the Apostle signifies one and the same thing by these three words μορφῇ [form], ὁμοιώμα [likeness], σχῆμα [fashion]. Furthermore, if he understands the divine nature by the form of GOD, it follows that by equal reason in v. 7 seq. he understands the human nature by the form of a servant. For the antithesis demands this. But he does not seem to understand the human nature by the form of a servant, since Christ did not lay aside the human nature, nor is he ever going to lay it aside: But he did not lay aside the form of a servant through exaltation.

For who would say that he, who perpetually declares himself as the Lord of lords, is endowed with the form of a servant?

Since therefore the Apostle does not understand the human nature itself by the form of a servant, but a servile status or condition, as he declares by the following words: it follows that by equal reason he does not understand the divine nature by the form of GOD, but a divine status or divine condition, namely, the divine glory or Majesty.

Which glory indeed depends on nature, and necessarily coheres with it.

Nevertheless it is distinguished from it by reason. Nor is Zanchius anywhere entirely alien to this, in book I. de Incarn. p. 14. saying: the μορφῇ [form] which he seems to be is his immense glory, Majesty, divine splendor &c. That indeed is the chief thing in this case, according to which nature Christ is said to be in the form of God, which the Reformed and Papists contend is attributed to him according to his divine nature, asserting that the divine dignity and Majesty before the incarnation is described.

Yet Joh. Piscator opposes them in their own school with Calvin, since the most firm arguments from the text convince that the discourse here is not about the λόγῳ ἀσάρκῳ [Word without flesh], but ἐνσάρκῳ [in flesh], not about the humiliation of the incarnation, which is asserted by certain Fathers, but about the humiliation of the incarnate one.

The Blessed produced most of our arguments

Hunnius, which Joh. Crocius tried to refute in vain. It is helpful to weigh those things which are disputed on both sides.

The Blessed

Hunnius's thesis is: that Paul's discourse looks indeed to the λόγον [Word], but now incarnate, and made man, and deals with the humiliation and emptying of Christ, which befell him in the flesh and according to the flesh.

His first argument is: Paul in this place does not record how the Son of God or λόγος [Word] assumed humanity and became man it is done, but how Jesus Christ, who was already God & man, assumed the form of a servant in his humanity, that is, the habit and servile condition, and together with all human infirmities (sin excepted) was clothed with affections and passions. It is therefore one thing to speak of that condescension λόγῳ, by which he did not disdain to join our nature to himself by a hypostatic union, which we indeed do not deny in its proper place, but we say that nothing is treated here by the Apostle concerning it: It is another thing, again, to preach of the humiliation of Jesus Christ, who, it is agreed, was called Jesus among men after he was made man, and called Christ from the anointing not of his Deity, but of his flesh. For he was not anointed by his divinity, so that he might be called Christ from this, since the Deity anoints rather than is anointed, and the anointing proceeds from this in eternity.

But he was anointed in the flesh, which Hilary lib. II. de Trin., Athanasius in his salutary sermon, Epiphanius, Augustine epist. CLXXIV., Ambrose lib. I. de fide, Cyril lib. VIII. thesauri cap. I., Theophylact in epist. ad Roman. cap. I., and Damascene lib. IV. orthod. fidei capite sexto, clearly testify. Crocius objects two things: 1. that there is no consequence. After the incarnation he is called Jesus. Therefore, what is enunciated concerning him must be understood of the flesh, not of the Deity; which negation of consequence he confirms by the brought-in instances from 1. Joh.

IV. 2. 3. Resp. The force of the Hunnian argument is this: Wherever it is not mentioned how the Son of God assumed humanity, but how Jesus Christ, who was already God & man, assumed the form of a servant in his humanity, that is, the habit and servile condition, there it is a question of the humiliation, not which happened to him according to his divinity, but which happened to him according to the flesh. Let him now apply the instance, or let anyone from the flock of the Reformers deny the consequence, if he can. That

That Jesus Christ came in the flesh, 1. Joh. IV. 2. is a far different thing, when Jesus Christ, who came in the flesh, is said to have emptied himself and assumed the form of a servant. The former denotes the incarnation, as will be said later. 2. He objects that the name of Christ is derived from the anointing not of the Deity but of the humanity, in respect of gifts, and that the sayings of the Fathers hint at this, but when it is said thus, by reason of the ordination to an office, that it concerns the whole person, and is sometimes attributed to Christ named, which belongs to him not by reason of the flesh, but of the Deity, as 1. Cor. X. 9. Resp. That Christ is said to be anointed in respect of gifts, although the end of that anointing is the office committed to Christ, is evident from Psal. XLV. 7. Es. LXI. 1. Dan. IX. 24. Nor indeed is it affirmed by us that wherever Christ is named, that which is attributed to him is always attributed to him by reason of the flesh.

But now the anointing of Christ imports by reason of gifts, that those things which are said of Christ done after the anointing, such as the κένωσις of Christ, belong to Christ according to the flesh. And it is one thing when it is manifest that he is so called concerning the pre-existence λόγον ἄσαρκον, another when in the New Testament after the incarnation he is set forth to Christians in those virtues as an example, which do not befit the λόγῳ simply, such as in modesty, humility, the zeal of obeying, and the like. The Apostle proposes to the Philippians the example of Christ, as a rule of life. Therefore he designates those things which occur to the senses, and are imitable, such as the incarnation is not. Ambrose uses this argument: Before the incarnation, either Christ or Jesus can be said, because both names together signify both the Son of man and the Son of GOD. For before the birth, what does he say among other things: The Rock was Christ, and let us not tempt Christ, as some tempted him. Where therefore scripture wishes to signify either God or man, it puts one of the two, either Jesus or Christ: for the Son of GOD born a man was thus in the form of GOD, because while he seemed a man, he did the works of GOD, so that he might appear to be God who was thought to be only a man. For works signify the form, so that because his works are certainly not the works of a man, he who was in the work or form of GOD might be understood to be God. Let us hear Piscator: This passage, he says, most expound of the incarnation of the Son of GOD, and accordingly understand by the form of GOD his very divine nature, and likewise by the form of a servant the human nature. I indeed confess that both natures of Christ are firmly gathered from those things which are here said by Paul: nevertheless I judge that those very words are not to be expounded of the natures, nor do I judge that the Apostle speaks here of the incarnation of the Son of GOD, but of the humiliation of him already incarnate. Which will become manifest from the following exposition. Therefore let this affection be in you, which was also in Christ Jesus, τοῦτο γὰρ Φρονείσθω ἐν ὑμῖν, ὃ καὶ ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ. By these words the Apostle intimates that he considers here the Son of GOD as already manifested in the flesh. For on this account these two names agree to him: Christ Jesus: Likewise the word Φρονεῖν, to be an affection, gefinnet seyn. Of the same consideration the institution of the Apostle seems to demand. For he institutes to propose to the Philippians the example of Christ to be imitated, as a rule of life. Therefore let him consider the deeds of Christ, which run into the eyes, and among whose number the incarnation is not. Thirdly it appears that the Apostle speaks here of that humiliation of Christ, which was taken away through his exaltation: but the incarnation (that is, the human nature assumed through incarnation) was not taken away, since by it he remains into eternity. The second argument, drawn from the words, who being in the form of GOD, B.

Hunnius proposed it thus: This particle of the Calvinians they command to be the same as that by which Christ is said to be God by nature. And although in itself this is true, that Christ is God by nature, nevertheless that the interpretation of the Adversaries is alien from the present text and scope of D. Paul is evident even from this, that the λόγος, which is simply λόγος and God, is said to be in the form of GOD only absurdly, then he himself becomes GOD. The absurdity is evident by comparison with the other persons. For if to be in the form of GOD is the same as to be God by nature: then because the Father & the Holy Spirit also are God by nature, no less must be said of the Father, that he becomes in the form of God; and likewise of the Holy Spirit. But since it is much less fitting to become constituted in the form of God than to be God himself: certainly this manner of speaking concerning the Father & the Holy Spirit, and consequently also concerning the Son, qua he is God, cannot be tolerated in the Church. If you urge that this phrase is fitted rather to the Son according to his Deity than to the Father or the Holy Spirit, because the Son becomes the image of God the Father, you will accomplish nothing: nay, you will plainly refute yourself. For that ὁ λόγος becomes the very image of the invisible God is known from scripture, Col. I. Hebr. I. But that it is said, ὁ λόγος by reason of his Deity is in the image of God, is taught nowhere. Therefore so far is it asserted that the divine nature with respect to the λόγος is in the form of God, as it is not affirmed that he becomes in the image of God, when rather he becomes the very image OF GOD, the very form of GOD the Father. According to his humanity, however, he is in the λόγος, in the Son of GOD, in the image of GOD, in the form of GOD. For flesh was assumed into the unity of him who is the form & image of GOD, & elevated personally into the κοινωνία of his Majesty. What does Crocius say to these things? If it is not absurd for the image of GOD to be spoken of, when he is God himself, why is it said absurdly that he is in the form of God, when he is God himself? But thus the terms are changed. For it is one thing to be the image of God, another to exist in the image of God, as it is said here in the form of God ὑπάρχειν (to exist).

Crocius replies: That the ancients held these for the same. But he could not prove this from the ancients. He brought forward one Athanasius from orat. IV. against the Arians, in which, however, it is not read that to be the image of God is the same thing; he becomes the image of the Father, it is gathered that he has the essence of the Father, and the same is proved from the present passage, because he is said to be in the form of God, which argument for the Deity of Christ is not denied by us. Finally, Crocius acknowledges that it is nowhere said in the scriptures that the λόγος (Word) is in the image of God, by reason of Deity: He wishes, however, that it be rightly said that he is in the form of God of the Deity. But this is a mere begging of the question, nor is it proved from Chemnitius, but the contrary, inasmuch as he affirms that Christ not only was the very form of God according to his divinity, but also in the form of God according to his humanity.

Nor do the words of Hilary in book II. on the Trinity demand anything else than that Christ, who is in the form of God, becomes God: which far be it from being denied by anyone. The other arguments, which are taken from the following words of the text, will have their defenses concerning the same.

Now it seems to remain that we examine Crocius's contrary arguments looking to this.

First, he urges that Christ according to the flesh was not in the form of God before the emptying, because the emptying coheres with the beginning of the incarnation. Which, brought forward in other words in place of a new argument, he urges here later: According to which nature he is said to have been in the form of God, that was before the emptying, v. 5. 6. But the human nature was not before the emptying, but the emptying begins with its assumption. I respond. Christ according to the flesh was in the form of God before the emptying, and in the emptying itself. For the Apostle uses the word ὑπάρχειν (existing) in the form of God he emptied himself, and he did not so empty himself that he ceased to be in the form of God entirely, but that he did not show himself to be in it openly, everywhere, and always, because the splendor of Majesty did not shine everywhere or always in the flesh. Furthermore, he was entirely before the emptying human nature not as to moments of time: For thus the emptying entirely coheres with the beginning of the incarnation, but as to moments of nature.

For in the order of nature, the assumption of the servile form and state is prior to human nature, and existence in the form of God is prior to κένωσις (emptying) or inanition. For it is neither fitting, nor is it necessary, with Enjedini to imagine in this place three states of Christ, and to establish the first, in which he was in the form of God before his birth, which fiction we have refuted in the Socinianism refuted sect. II. artic. III. tit. 2. controv. 1.

Secondly, Crocius urges, if the form of God pertained to the flesh, it should certainly not have been said, ὃς ἐν μορφῇ Θεῦ ὑπάρχων (who existing in the form of God), but ὃς λαβὼν μορφὴν Θεῦ (who having taken the form of God), or made in the form of God. But here we deny the consequence: because it was the Apostle's purpose to set forth the humility of Christ as an example: Therefore it was not now to be said what dignity he had received, but how, when he was in dignity, he humbled himself, just as it had to be said how, when he was rich, he deigned to become poor for our sake, 2. Cor. VIII. 9. how existing in the form of God he willed the human nature to be emptied according to the same.

You say: That which pertains to him by reason of the flesh alone, that was not, but he received it in time. Resp. That was not from eternity.

But it is falsely supposed that Christ is here said to have been in the form of God from eternity; He was God from eternity, it is said, Job I. 3; that he was in the form of God from eternity is said nowhere. We do not say that he received the flesh as the form of God, but that he began to be in the form of God; which the flesh could not owe to itself, but received through the grace of communication by the force of the personal union.

Furthermore, Crocius also urges this: If that ὃς ἐν μορφῇ Θεῦ ὑπάρχων (who existing in the form of God) is said of Christ with respect to the flesh already assumed, then emptied, finally exalted again. But the text or the whole scripture has nothing of the sort.

Resp. The exaltation of Christ, according to the Biblical phrase, is consequent upon the emptying, not antecedent. But it is one thing ὑπαρξις ἐν μορφῇ Θεῦ (existence in the form of God), another ὑπερύψωσις (superexaltation). That the former is prior in the order of nature to the emptying Paul says: but he makes this emptying posterior not only in the order of nature, but also in the order of time. Indeed that ὑπάρχων ἐν μορφῇ Θεῦ (existing in the form of God) implies a communication of Majesty, yet not that superexaltation which followed the humiliation. And does not Paul clearly teach 2. Cor. IX. 9. that Christ was first rich, before he was made poor for our sake. But who would deny that after poverty he was exalted? Hence just as that πλάσιος ὢν (being rich) by no means implies exaltation taken in the biblical style, so neither does that ὑπάρχων ἐν μορφῇ Θεῦ (existing in the form of God) imply it.

That which 4. Hebr. I. 3. χαρακτὴρ ὑποστάσεως (the express image of the substance) of God the Father is said of the Son, is far different from τῷ ὑπάρχειν ἐν μορφῇ Θεῦ (existing in the form of God).

For the form of God and being in the form of God differ most greatly. Nor is it necessary that the name of God, when he is said to be in the form of God, be taken personally, since it can be taken essentially by an Hebraism, Christ to have been in the form of God, that is, divine, just as μορφῇ δούλου is explained as of the servile form, and therefore on this account the passage Ebr. I. 3. is not parallel. As to what 5. to the Fathers produced by Crocius, Theophilus Alexandr. adv. serm. I. Paschat. does nothing for the Calvinian. The Son of God himself, he says, when he was in the form of God, and equal to God, emptied himself, taking the form of a servant. But who denies this? Leo I. in epist. ad Flacian. understands by form nature, but does not apply the phrase in the form of God to the divine nature. Athanasius in epistola de Dionysii sententia deduces Deity from this passage, yet does not attribute being in the form of God to the divine nature. The judgment is the same concerning most of the others.

The judgment is the same concerning most of the others. But Ambrose is openly ὁμόφυλον (of the same nature) to us on this passage: The Apostle, he says, treats of the Son of God, when he was made incarnate man, saying: Feel this in yourselves, which also in Christ Jesus, that is, of God and man, who when he was in the form of God, was conversing among men and by his deeds and works appeared to be God. Οὐκ ἁρπαγμὸν ἡγήσατο τὸ εἶναι ἴσα Θεῷ (He did not count it robbery to be equal to God) Ἁρπαγμὸν ἴσα Θεῷ (robbery equal to God) is the Syriac reading. In the Syriac liturgy John the Baptist says to Christ who is seeking baptism from him, לא תסב אליך גזלנא (I will not take robbery upon myself). Those who have produced something by Hellenic virtue are accustomed to show it to everyone, as the Romans were accustomed to do in a triumph. Not much otherwise Plutarch in Timoleon, ὡς ἁρπαγμὸν ἡγήσατο (as he counted it robbery). The sense is: Christ did not sell, did not boast of that power, because he often even commanded that what he had done should not be published: ita (so) here is an Adverb. Thus Odyssey O: Τῶ ὧν ἵνα Θεῷ ἰδανήκου ἁρπαγέσιν. ἰδανήκου Θεῷ (equal to God) the writer said 2. Macc. IX. 12. ἴσα Θεῷ (equal to God) is to be looked upon as God. See the excellent use of this passage in Eusebius V. 2. The phrase ἁρπαγμὸν ἡγήσατο (he counted it robbery) is rightly explained thus. ἁρπαγμὸν (robbery) is the same ἐξήγησις (explanation) in the place of B. Chemnitius cited: That form of God without robbery, when according to it he was equal to God, nor would there have been need that he should snatch it as if it were alien, which as God he had by nature, to be able by his divine majesty, glory and power in the assumed nature and through it, so magnificently to conduct himself, and so to exert himself, that all might manifestly see. they might feel, that he is truly God, and that he might powerfully repel all infirmities, injuries, insults, and passions from his own flesh.

B. Osiander has it thus: Although Christ (who is God and man) according to his humanity (on account of the personal union) had received divine Majesty and omnipotence: so that he might also have power equal to God according to his humanity, yet he did not proudly display it, as those are wont to display plunder, who have despoiled the conquered. And so also Christians (who are true members of Christ) ought not to be proud of their gifts.

B. Ægidius Hunnius explains it not dissimilarly: He did not ambitiously display this equality, as they do, who have invaded and acquired something through plunder.

B. Balduini’s paraphrase is this, p.

981: Let everyone imitate the example of Christ, who, although according to the flesh he was personally united with him who is the form or image of God, and adorned with divine majesty and power: yet he did not wish to be proud of this eminence, like those who have stripped spoils from enemies, and on that account walk about pompously.

B. Dannhauerus, Hodosoph. p. 699: ἐξ ἁρπαγμὸν ἡγήσατο, he did not boast of his Majesty.

B. Glassius, who in Grae. S. p. 269 approved the opinion of B. Chemnitius: he did not wish, beyond his calling and before the time, to seize the usurpation and display of divine power and operation in the assumed nature and through the assumed nature.

Of Chemnitz: he did not wish, beyond his calling and before the time, to seize the usurpation and manifestation of divine power and operation in the assumed nature and through the assumed nature. B. D.

B. D. Georg. Konig in Vindic. sacr. disp. XX. th. 8. p. 359: Christ, since on account of the hypostatic union and the true and real communication flowing from it, he had divine power and glory, did not consider it plunder to be equal with God, i.e., he did not openly hold, or continuously usurp, in any way (for he alludes to robbers, who possess what they take away, or obtain in any way, as their own most tenaciously, and show it to others as their own) but he was made as a man.

Which explanation is also approved in the Weimar Pamphlets, nor does B. D. Dorcheus seem alien to the same in diff. Pendad. de rapin. majest. th. 26. This, therefore, Paul says: Christ, by usurping plenary divine Majesty, would not be usurping some thing violently snatched from elsewhere, but his own, and yet he did not wish to usurp it incessantly from the moment of conception through the whole state of exinanition, and by usurping, to display it.

Add also B. D.

Cluverus in Orthotomia, etc. Although some of our own, not so much insisting on B.

Luther’s Vulgate version, or because ἡγήσατο is elsewhere certainly and undoubtedly established, Phil. II. 3. 25. c. III. 7. 8. explain that Christ did not doubt, but was certainly persuaded that this was by no means alien to him, nor plunder, but that this was his own by nature, so that he is ἴσος to God, as B. Gerhardus interpreted it in Exeg., understanding it of the divine nature of Christ, and B. Feuerbornius l. c. §.

59. who indeed explains it of Christ according to human nature: he hints here that he did not consider it plunder, that Christ certainly and solidly and by best right knew and determined that it was intact for him ἴσα Θεῷ, to conduct himself equally to God, and thus to remain perpetually in supreme and infinite glory, and with equal splendor of divine Majesty without his own emptying and diminution, and without injury to anyone, and to appear totally in that to men. The devil, indeed, and those like him, who wish to be equal to God, do not indeed consider that plunder, but not certainly and irrefragably, but fallaciously and mendaciously.

For their own conscience, at least in the end, refutes them. But Christ certainly and truly knew that he was equal.

This is B. Feuerbornius, who, however, lest the sense should seem gaping, assumed the former reason in the text as a supplement. Which explanation, he says §.

78. p. 82, that it may shine forth more, the words are to be supplemented thus: Christ Jesus existing in the form of God, did not consider it plunder to be equal to God, therefore if he had wished, he could always have remained in that quality without injury to anyone, but he did not wish to use this right of his.

Or in this way: Christ Jesus when he was in the form of God, did not consider it plunder to be equal to God, and therefore he was not humbled as a robber by another, nor were they precipitated into hell like Satan and the fallen angels, or out of Paradise into the dungeon of various tribulations like the Protoplasts, and indeed as a punishment for their pride and sacrilege, by which they attempted to snatch equality with God, so also he, as if he had committed plunder, was cast down into this vile condition of men and the cross, but he spontaneously and willingly emptied and made himself nothing. But there is no need for that supplement, if the words οὐχ ἁρπαγμὸν ἡγήσατο are accepted according to the reception of the explanation.

Which Job. Piscator also made his own from the Reformed: Christ therefore although he was in the form of God, i.e., endowed with divine glory, as the Lord of glory or glorious Jehovah: yet he did not consider it plunder to be equal to God, namely the Father: that is, he did not display that divine glory of his, just as victors are wont to display spoils stripped from enemies in a triumph, but he hid that glory, which is to be understood of the greatest part of his life.

For sometimes he manifested that glory of his through miracles, as through the conversion of water into wine at the wedding, John II. 11. and other miracles. Whence also John says that he and the rest of the Apostles and disciples had beheld his glory as of the Only-begotten who came forth from the Father, John I.

14. This exposition of this verse is confirmed both from the phrase itself, which has a metaphor drawn from those who triumph, and from the antithesis which is had in the following verse, where he says, but he emptied himself.

Which is also praised in the Bibles of Luther glossed by Toffanus, but enriched by more recent Reformed from the Belgian notes, and other authors. Others give it thus: He did not consider it plunder, that is, he did not boast with his Divine Majesty, as the victors boast and triumph with the plunder which they have snatched from the enemy.

Most Reformed, however, to whom the Pontificians are added in accumulation, because of their Latin version, take the word ἡγήσατο in the sense of estimation or knowledge, from whom indeed Calvin interpreted these things concerning Christ according to human nature, rendering it in the subjunctive, that he might have considered.

He judges, however, that the series of the text requires the subjunctive mood, and that it is sufficiently customary for the Apostle to take the Past Indicative for the Subjunctive, by subauditing the potential particle ἂν, as Rom. IX. 3. 1 Cor. II. 8. and thus he refers the words to the manifestation in the flesh in this way: when he was in the form of God, he would not have considered it illicit for himself to conduct himself in the same form, and to appear equal to God. But others, and among these Crocius, and others of his great interpreter, as they call him, by his authority, retain the indicative, and draw these things also to the pristine glory of Christ, which he had from eternity.

Therefore Bullinger, Zanchius, Beza, Artetius, Crocius prefer the Greek scholia: He knew that he did not have by plunder that he is equal to the Father, but that this is a natural dignity. But truly what shall we deem this saying to be, concerning Christ, as God, that he should have rightly known that he is equal to the Father: Could it in any way be even a doubt to those believing the Deity of Christ, that he knew his own Deity, or is it fitting to speak thus concerning God the Father, with whom Christ is of the same Deity, God the Father knows best that he is God.

Therefore Erasmus, although here more unjust to the Fathers, who assert the Deity of Christ from this place, which is altogether solidly asserted from it, asks, what great thing does Paul attribute to Christ, if when he was God by nature he understood that it was not plunder, that is, he knew himself? Beza certainly seeks mysteries here, as does Flacius, using the same methods and words as Beza; what mystery can there be in the fact that Christ, as true God by nature, knew for certain that He did not possess divinity by robbery? That indication of thought or knowledge must certainly be admitted here in no other way than that Christ, as a man, did not consider it robbery, or that He knew for certain that it was not robbery that things equal to God were His, or that He did not have or consider it as robbery, understanding this not as theoretical knowledge, but practical—that is, He did not consider the Majesty He possessed as something to be displayed like robbery, just as Cluverus explains: "Who, when He was in the form of God (possessing divine splendor and Majesty, and subsisting in it in His flesh), did not consider it robbery (which He would consider for display) to be equal to GOD (to be things equal to Him, or to be able to be equal to God, i.e., to be able to act equally to God)."

Not as if He wished to show Himself off with stolen divinity, and use it according to human will.) To this also tends the explanation of Erasmus Schmid: Who proves from Greek writers that ἁρπαγμὸν ἡγεῖσθαι is to most greedily seize an opportunity offered for obtaining a thing vehemently desired and loved, and not to suffer it to slip away in any way, to interpose no delay, but immediately to pursue the desired thing, and to occupy it most studiously with the greatest joy and gladness, and to enjoy the same; rendering this sense: "Who, when He was in the form of GOD, did not consider it robbery, that is, He did not greedily seize, or refuse to defer for some time without delay, the plenary usurpation of the Deity equal in part with God, but He emptied Himself of it at some point, having awaited the just time, when the Father exalted Him."

Thus also we, even if we happen to have opportunities for exaltations, must not, out of a zeal for humility, greedily and without delay, like a prey that is exposed to the first comer and which, once taken, is not wont to return, rush to seize them, but we must use them moderately, relying on the hope that God will make those exaltations all the more illustrious in His own time.

From these things, therefore, it is clear that these things are said of Christ according to His human nature.

For the argument is immovable: According to whichever nature it is fitting for Christ to be an example of humility in "not considering it robbery to be equal to God," according to that same nature it must be understood in the present Apostolic exhortation.

But this does not befit Christ according to His divine, but according to His human nature, whether it be explained as the divine Majesty not being displayed like robbery, or as that knowledge and science by which He knew it was not robbery.

For how can the Son of GOD be proposed as an example of humility by reason of His divine nature?

Crocius replied: Who would not be astonished that the Son of GOD, when He knew that He was in all things equal to GOD His Father, should cast Himself down to the lowest lot, not for any good of His own, but only for the sake of our salvation?

But it is shown that this is ineptly said of the Son of GOD by reason of His divine nature, that He did not believe His divine nature, or equality with His Father, to be robbery; nor does that abjection to the lowest lot befit the divine nature, even if it be explained concerning the incarnation, which the ancients sometimes describe as a humiliation (but improperly and by rhetorical exaggeration); how can either the incarnation be proposed to us as an example of humility, or that which is called humiliation only improperly be drawn into an example of true humiliation?

For who would say that the divine nature of the Son of GOD was truly humiliated when He was incarnated?

As for what Crocius objects to us, that Christ, as a man, was never equal to God, to that we respond that it is not said here that Christ was ἴσα θεῷ, equal to God, in the way Christ speaks of Himself when He vindicates His divine nature, John V.

But that τὸ εἶναι ἴσα θεῷ is attributed to Him, which, whether it be taken adverbially for ἴσως (not as robbery did He display it to be, equally to God), or explained by ellipsis, with τὸ εἶναι (ἑαυτῷ) retaining the nominal sense (to be things equal to GOD [for Himself]), befits the human nature; and the matter comes back to the same thing, namely, that Christ, through the divine majesty communicated to Him, could display τὸ εἶναι ἴsa-liter DEO, or act equally to God; or openly testify and demonstrate by the very work that things equal to God the Father were His—equal power, equal glory.

In this way, the example of humility remains consistent, nor does anything depart from the argument usually brought forward by the ancients for divinity from this passage.

Regarding the latter, so that it may not be further objected to us, as was done by Crocius, and so that against those two arguments which are sought from the deity of Christ from this oracle, they may be solidly brought forward, and the present text more richly illustrated, it is helpful to bring here what we committed to paper on that matter twenty-eight years ago in the ἀπόδειξις (demonstration) of the Deity of Christ.

The first argument is as follows: Whoever truly exists in the form of the Son of GOD, he is true God by nature.

But Christ truly exists in the form of GOD.

Therefore.

Christ is true God.

We prove the major: Because ἐν μορφῇ Θεῦ ὑπάρχειν (to exist in the form of God) presupposes true and essential Deity: since it brings with it Majesty and glory that is truly divine, which is altogether inseparable from the divine essence.

What else is it to exist in the form of God, than to enjoy divine Majesty and glory, and to be able to exercise it?

Whoever, however, enjoys glory and majesty that is truly divine, and therefore infinite, and can exercise it at will, and offer it to be seen publicly, so that He may be acknowledged to exist in the form of the most high GOD Himself, he is certainly true and most high God.

But this must be explained a little more fully.

The words of the Apostle are taken in two main ways by the orthodox.

Some, with certain ancients like Chrysostom, Theodoret, and Oecumenius, wish the Deity or divine essence of the Son of GOD to be designated here immediately: which can again be understood in two ways: Either as implying the pre-existence of the Son of GOD before the incarnation, which they judge to be inferred by the emptying and the assumption of the form of a servant: Or as designating the divine essence of the Son of God in the person of Christ after the ἐνσαρκωσις (incarnation) had taken place, namely, that Christ was then in the form of God, i.e., endowed with divine essence and nature, and thus the truth of the divine essence is immediately inferred.

Daniel Heinsius is prolix on this in Ex. Sacr. p. 873 seq., to demonstrate from the ancients that μορφὴν θεῦ (form of God) is ἴσαν θεῷ (equal to God), when they are used in this way by Basil, Nyssen, Photius, Ephraim, Cyril, Leo, Anastasius, and Damascene.

From Basil he brings forward τὸ ἐν μορφῇ, ἐν οὐσίᾳ (that "in the form" is "in the essence"), for "form of God" is one thing, and "essence of God" is another.

Anastasius said: "Nature and essence and form are the same thing in the subject."

Whence Psellus says of the Holy Fathers: "The holy fathers place the name of essence and nature and form on the same thing." Therefore, μορφὴν (form) is the same as τὸ εἶναι τινος (to be something), and these, from the usage of the sacred language, are equivalent to Μορφὴν, ὁμοίωμα, ἰσότητα, κτῆμα (form, likeness, equality, possession); that "like" among the Hellenists is the same as "to be made equal," nay, "to be made like" among the Hebrews is "to be," and "likeness of God" is God Himself; and from this he gathers the force and efficacy of the singular words in this place; that they demonstrate, as a true man, so God, καὶ ἰσότητα (and equality).

Moreover, we do not deny that the opinion of those who do not interpret the form of God immediately as the divine essence, but as the Majesty and glory of God shining forth in the works of divine power and wisdom, is more approved by us: which they wish to be as it were external.

the form and appearance of God, shining forth in the government of the world and the demonstration of divine power and majesty. In which manner the blessed Luther explains it (T. I. Latin. Jen. f. 470), denying that the word here is to be transferred to the divine nature; that Paul means that Christ was full of the form of God, and abounding in all good things, so that he stood in need of no work, no passion, etc.

On the contrary, B. Chemnitius compares this phrase, in the form of God, with Col. 2:9, and observes that this is also the opinion of Ambrose, Erasmus, and B. Luther, that Christ was in the form of GOD, because the whole fullness of the Deity dwelt in the assumed nature personally, just as through union iron ignited is said to be in the fire, and that he could exercise that form of God without robbery (since according to it he was equal to God, and there was no need that he should snatch it as if it were another's, which he had by nature as God) by his divine Majesty, glory, and power in the assumed nature, and through it so magnificently conduct himself that all might manifestly see and feel that he was truly God himself, and might powerfully repel all infirmities, injuries, insults, and passions from his flesh, etc.

See his book on the two natures in Christ, c. 24, p. 351. Most Orthodox follow B. Luther and Chemnitius: and Dn. D. Glassius adds in Observ. Philolog. ad med. sacr. p. 776, that the word μορφὴ among the LXX interpreters corresponds to the Chaldean word splendor, which denotes the external appearance of a man rightly comporting himself, Dan. 5:6, 10; 7:28. For just as a man is recognized by his form and appearance; so the majesty which shines in God is his image, which are the words of Calvin in this place.

To illustrate the phrase itself, D. Glassius brings forward examples analogous to it, Christ is in the form of GOD, ἀλλ᾽ ἡ κατὰ πάντα, as it is said in Apoc. 1:10, ἐγενόμην ἐν πνεύματι, I was in the Spirit, i.e., endowed with a peculiar gift and manifestation of the Holy Spirit, and as it were caught up into an ecstasy of the Spirit; Rom. 8:9, You are in the Spirit, i.e., as the explanation is immediately subjoined, the Spirit of God dwells in you. Also Mark 5:25, a certain woman ὅσα ἐν ῥύσει αἵματος, existing in a flux of blood, i.e., seized and intimately affected by a flux. Mark 5:2, ἄνθρωπος ἐν πνεύματι ἀκαθάρτῳ, a man is said to be in an unclean spirit, who has an unclean spirit in himself, or is obsessed and filled by that Spirit (which two examples, however, are compared only as to the phrase, not as to the thing itself, which differs as much as heaven from earth). On the contrary, a man is said to be in Christ, 2 Cor. 5:17, 12:2, who has Christ dwelling in his heart by faith; Eph. 2:17, who lives in Christ, and Christ in him; Gal. 2:20, who is filled into all the fullness of God; Eph. 3:19, θείας Φύσεως κοινωνὸς, made a partaker of the divine nature by faith, 2 Pet. 1:1, from which mystical union the personal union is excellently illustrated, by the power of which the Son of God dwells in the assumed humanity with all his fullness of Deity. The Son of GOD lives in the assumed flesh, and the assumed flesh lives in the Son of God, it being filled with that whole fullness of divine Majesty, and made a partaker of the divine nature through the unity of the person.

According to this comparison, he was in the form of God in Christ, as believers are said to be in the Spirit of God, because the Spirit dwells in them: or that Christ was endowed with the form of God, and could exercise the same at his pleasure, i.e., the divine Majesty and glory, divine omnipotence, omniscience, and the dignity of religious adoration: that he was thus in the height of the glory, majesty, and power of divinity: and consequently, since this cannot be without the divine essence, he truly existed as God by nature.

For they call it μορφὴν, as Dn. Chemnitius again rightly observes, i.e., when some nature or essence is so considered, as if it were endowed with, and as it were clothed and adorned with, an idiom, attributes, and properties, whether divine or human, just as Augustine says to Peter: One must understand the form of God as the natural fullness of God. In which manner the interpretations of the ancients, for the most part, and those of Ambrose, Erasmus, and Luther, who understand the divine Majesty and glory, seem almost to coincide; both certainly contribute to establishing the true Deity of Christ, which the former asserts literally, the latter by way of meaning: since divine majesty, glory, and power presuppose the divine essence, and cannot be separated from it.

Nor is Socinus altogether a stranger to this development of our phrase in his refutation of Wujeck, p. 27, etc., asserting that Christ being in the form of God signifies nothing else than that he had that divine appearance, or divine external form. God, he says, commands all things, and restrains the demons themselves, so that they obey his nod; he has the same everywhere, that they should adore him, and humbly implore his aid, as human powers are of no avail. Thus Christ, before he humbled himself, by his word alone commanding the seas, winds, diseases, and the demons themselves, had them obedient to him, and there were those everywhere who would prostrate themselves before him, and prostrate implore his aid, and that in things which could in no way be done by human powers. Therefore he is deservedly said by Paul to have been in the form of God.

Thus Socinus. Who indeed differs in this, that he interprets being in the form of God as an external appearance, as it were, of works and the likeness of divine worship: but it is indubitable that such divine works can proceed from nothing but divine power, nor should the worship of invocation be rendered except on account of the divine majesty and glory, worthy of adoration and invocation.

We judge that this divine majesty, glory, and power is designated by that very phrase, when Christ is said ὑπάρχως to be in the form of GOD: since that phrase denotes not the second act but rather the first act, namely that, being a partaker of divine glory, majesty, and power, he was able on every side to exercise its rays: such power and authority as permanently residing in Christ Socinus also was compelled to admit. l. c. p. 279. For when he was pressed by the objection that Christ is not said to be in the form of God on account of those outward works and miracles, since also the Apostles performed very great miracles, whom nevertheless no one could, or would dare, to say were in the form of God, Socinus explained the distinction which intervenes in this respect between Christ and the Apostles thus: that Christ performed many miracles by a power and authority permanently residing in himself, after the example of God: which the Apostles never did, nor could do: forasmuch as they did not have the power with which they were endowed in working miracles permanently residing in themselves, nor did they work them by their own authority, but by that of Christ himself, whose name also, in performing them, they always invoked either openly or tacitly without doubt.

Whence we conclude: In whomever divine power, authority, and might perpetually reside, by virtue of which he himself performs miracles, and executes other divine works by his own authority, and on account of which he is rightly invoked by others with religious and divine adoration, and finally by whose power others also perform miracles, in him the divine essence, the infinite Deity, must perpetually reside.

Because virtue, infinite power, such as that by which miracles are wrought, is not without the infinite essence: divine power and authority presuppose the divine essence, nor can it be given without it.

Because virtue, infinite power, such as that by which miracles are performed, is not without an infinite essence: divine power and authority presuppose the divine essence, and cannot be given without it.

The majesty of religious adoration cannot be established outside of the true and essential Deity without sacrilege. But Socinus acknowledges that this resides in Christ by the power of the phrase, by which it is said that Christ ὑπάρχων ἐν μορφῇ Θεῷ.

It is therefore necessary that he confess, by the power of that phrase, that the divine essence, the infinite Deity, resides in Christ, which the Church altogether professes, when it asserts that the human and divine nature of Christ are united, which it believes constitute one Christ, joined perpetually and inseparably after the union was made.

Another argument holds thus: He who does not count it robbery τὸ εἶναι ἴσα Θεῷ (to be equal to God), he is truly equal to the most high GOD, and therefore is truly the most high God.

But Christ did not count it robbery τὸ εἶναι ἴσα Θεῷ. Therefore.

The prior and immediate consequence is gathered from the Apostolic phrase, the sense of which, that it may be elicited, must be observed (1.) That some make this sentence affirmative, he did not count it robbery: and they refer the negative particle not to the verb ἡγήσατο (he counted), but to the noun ἁρπαγμὸν (robbery); that Christ possessed that τὸ εἶναι ἴσα Θεῷ not as a robbery, but as his own, the particle 8x, they say, removes ἄρπαγμος, but on the contrary ἴδιον (his own) is placed, which is not ἁρπαγμός, for if you were to say a purely negative proposition, the Apostle's speech would not be full, because it would bring forward nothing certain, in what place, namely, Christ at the time of his exinanition had that τὸ εἶναι ἴσα Θεῷ. See B. Gerhard, Exeg. on the Person and Office of Christ, § 296. B. Feuerborn, Fascic. III, disp. II. Furthermore, they think that ἡγήσατο ἁρπαγμὸν placed there stands for ἁρπάζειν (to snatch), to usurp to himself like a robbery, at will, and to abuse rashly, just as a similar locution is read in Heb. X. v. 26. κοινὸν ἡγησάμενος (counting common) for κοινώσας (having made common), or κοινωσάμενος, since the verb frequently signifies that which the noun joined to it signifies, by which they also refer to similar phrases, count the longsuffering of the Lord salvation, that is, be of one mind in that for your salvation, 2 Pet. III. v. 16. to count worthy of honor, for to honor, 1 Tim. VI. 1. 1 Thess. V. 13. count it all joy for to rejoice, James I. 2, etc. Thus Flacius in Clavis Scripturae under the word 'arbitrari' (to count). Giving this reason for this locution: that we abuse rashly and at will those things which we obtain by robbery: but on the contrary, those things which we obtain with great price or sweat, are to be enjoyed sparingly, just as if it were not in our power. Conf. also D. Glaffius, Gramm. S. p. 269. (3.) Again, others wish that ἡγήσατο, used by the Apostle elsewhere, and especially five times in this Epistle to the Philippians, signifies the same thing, which is to determine certainly, to know indubitably, Phil. II. v. 6, 25, III. 7, 8, so that the sense is, he knew certainly and indubitably that τὸ εἶναι ἴσα Θεῷ was not a robbery, that this was by no means alien to him, nor snatched, but by nature this was his own ἴσα Θεῷ, that he bore himself equally to GOD, and therefore rendered himself conspicuous in supreme and infinite glory without his own emptying and diminution: Thus most of the ancient interpreters, Chrysostom, Theodoret, Oecumenius, Theophylact, and B. Augustine, Epist. 66. (4.) Others interpret the phrase he did not count it robbery in this way: he did not ambitiously display the majesty and glory received from the union, as is accustomed to be done with spoils, which are carried around in a triumph for the sake of ostentation. To which it seems to favor that from the verb ἡγῆσθαι descends the noun ἡγέμενος (leader) designating a leader: that he did not display, boast, and carry around everywhere like a leader, victor, or some tyrant as a robbery, but rather wished to hide and conceal the divine glory and majesty for the sake of our redemption, and for a time emptied himself of the same. (5.) There are those who explain this phrase more fully. They say the Apostle looks (1.) to the pride of the Devil, as well as of the first parents, who through robbery wished to become equal to GOD, and thus they wish to point a finger to Ps. LXIX. 6, where Christ says of himself, I restored that which I took not away. That Christ did not wish to usurp as a robbery at the time of humiliation what the first parents wished to usurp through robbery, concerning whom Augustine in the Comment. on this Psalm. The first parents wished to snatch divinity, and lost felicity, and Chrysost. hom. 60, on cap. 18. Matth. teaches, that the first man hoped for equality with God by false thinking. (2.) to the savagery of tyrants; that not as tyrants tenaciously hold the snatched goods of rapacity, which they most greedily coveted, and which they seized most avidly, and fear to lay down, so Christ held the divine majesty, since he neither seized it by violence, nor feared in a certain way to strip it off through exinanition, when he knew certainly that it was proper to himself. Chrysostom & Theophylact in h. l. (3.) to the victory and glory of those triumphing: that Christ in the days of his flesh did not count the divine glory and majesty as a robbery, nor displayed it everywhere in public triumph after the manner of the victors triumphing. (6.) that as to the word εἶναι ἴσα Θεῷ, some wish the word ἴσα to be placed for the adverb ἴσως, to bear oneself equally to God or equally and alike to God in the full splendor of the divine Majesty, when the neuter plural adjective ἴσα is accustomed to be used adverbially, as examples prove Hen. Stephani in thesaur. p. 727. Others think it placed for ἴνισω, to be in equal and like Majesty and glory with God, others judge it used for ἴσον, that he is equal to God, as Job V. v. 17. he is said to be equal to God, others think that sentence τὸ εἶναι ἴσα Θεῷ is placed for the noun ἰσότητα (equality), according to the Grammatical Rule: the article of the neuter gender also transforms the whole infinitive sentence into a noun. Others take the article τὸ δεικτικῶς (demonstratively), that which would be, as ἔλλειψις occurs, and τὰ ἑαυτῦ falls short, and so this becomes the full sentence τὸ εἶναι τὰ ἑαυτῦ ἴσα Θεῷ non rapinam duxit, he did not count it robbery that they themselves should be equal to GOD, or that their own things should be equal to GOD, or that he himself (for it is a Grecism, τὰ ἑαυτῦ for ipse) should be in all things equal and like to GOD. See Camer. in notat. figur. sermon. ad h. l. p. 11. These things concerning the Grammatical sense of the word. (2.) As to the matter itself: some wish less to be intimated by this phrase τὸ εἶναι ἴσα Θεῷ than when it is said ἴσα Θεῷ, because the prior infers ταὐτότητα (identity), the posterior ποιότητα (quality), the prior ποιαῦθ, the posterior a certain ταὐτὸ; the prior to be equal or equally to GOD, the posterior to be equal to GOD. But others wish a greater emphasis to be brought into the phrase τὸ εἶναι ἴσα Θεῷ: among ours D. Christianus Sledanus, who illustrated this excellent testimony Ps. II. 6. 7. 8. with exegesis th. 26. Thus truly, he says, the speech of Paul would have been less emphatic (if namely the plural adjective in the neuter gender is supposed to be placed συνθετικῶς, either for the adverb ἴσως, or for the noun of the masculine gender ἴσον seu ἐν ἴσῳ. For ἴσον εἶναι is, to be parem ὁμότιμον, & ὁμο-δύναμον equal to God the Father. ἴσα δὲ εἶναι is to be equal to GOD in all things and in everything. The thing indeed is the same, but the latter speech is more full. To which Dan. Heinsius gives suffrage, a man most versed in Greek literature l. c. This has been said so efficaciously, τὸ εἶναι ἴσα Θεῷ, that no tongue occurs which sufficiently represents its force. For he did not say ἴσον Θεῷ, but ἴσα, that he might manifestly represent τὴν ὠσιώδη ἰσότητα (the reverent equality). (8.) Of the Apostolic sentence ἁρπαγμὸν ἡγήσατο τὸ εἶναι ἴσα Θεῷ, there is a twofold declaration in the Church. Some wish it to infer immediately the divine nature, because indeed he did not assume it to himself through robbery, but had it by nature, that he might be equal to God, or might be able to bear himself equally to God. Theodoret thus παραφράζει (paraphrases): Since he was God, and God by Nature, and equal to the Father, he did not esteem this great: for this is proper to those who have obtained some honor beyond merit; but with the highest dignity concealed he chose humility. Theophyl. following Chrysostom: When anyone, he says, receives something, lest that lest he lose that, he fears, because what is alien, he easily despises, being certain indeed that he has obtained it in such a way that he cannot lay it aside, and is immediately about to receive it back, if there were need to have laid it aside. Oecumenius: He did not think equality with God a robbery, i.e., he knew indeed that he did not have it by robbery, so as to be equal to the Father, but by natural dignity, κατὰ φύσιν ἀξίωμα. August. Ep. 66. For Christ to be equal to GOD in the form of God was not robbery, but nature: since he assumed it by being born, he did not presume it by being proud. The Greek Scholia oppose here τὸ ἔχειν τὴν θεότητα κατ' ἁρπαγήν, τῷ ἔχειν κατὰ φύσιν, to have Deity by robbery, and to have the same by nature. Not a few of the more recent interpreters follow in their footsteps: But others say these things are spoken of Christ according to his human nature, that by the power of the divine majesty communicated to him, he could conduct himself equally and in the same manner as GOD, or that the things which were communicated to him were equal to God, that is, that he was instructed, enriched, and endowed with the divine majesty and glory of the Son of GOD, by which he himself is equal to God the Father, and that he did not have the same by seizure, nor did he ever display it publicly as a robbery, but obtained it through the communication of the person, at least when, as often as, and where he had laid aside his life. Which opinion most of the orthodox recent doctors of the Church embrace.

But whichever is assumed, our thesis is invincibly established; since according to the former it is inferred that Christ as God was equal to God by nature: according to the latter, that Christ according to his human nature obtained majesty equal with GOD through personal union. In short: However one may receive the words of the Apostle, he will certainly be forced to confess that Christ did not have it by robbery, but truly and properly, so that he was equal to GOD, or could conduct himself equally to GOD in majesty and glory. What of the fact that Socinus teaches that not only did equality with GOD truly belong to Christ, but that this equality is in reality the same thing as the form of GOD, which he had: and he interprets these words thus against Wujek, p. 274. He did not tenaciously retain his equality with GOD, as some robber is accustomed to do with a thing he has stolen. For he acknowledged that he had not indeed stolen it, but had it by the gratuitous gift of GOD.

Therefore he confesses that Christ was truly equal to the supreme GOD.

Now as to the latter consequence: He who is truly equal to the supreme GOD, he is truly the supreme God: we prove the same by the following documents: (1.) Because Scripture openly denies that any creature can be held equal to GOD 2. Sam. VII. ver. 22. There is no peer, or equal to Jehovah. Conf. 1. Chron. XXIX, 20. If therefore the Son of God is truly equal to the Father, he must be not a mere creature, but Jehovah himself. (2.) While Scripture asks: Who is a peer to Jehovah our God? Ps. CXIII. 5. Who is the strong God a peer or equal to you? Mich. 6, 18. by asking it denies that there can be any of the gods, men, or creatures, who is a peer and equal to Jehovah the supreme GOD. Conf. Jer. XLIX. ver. 19. L. 44. Ps. XXXV. 10. as also LXXI. 19. & LXXXIX. 9. & c. For it is known that questions of this kind are equivalent to negatives. If therefore no creature is equal to GOD, then certainly the Son of God, who is equal to the Father, will not be a creature, but true God by nature.

(3.) The comparison of creatures with GOD is denied, namely that no creature can be compared or conferred with GOD. Is. XL. 18. 25. c. XLVI. 5. it is also taught that no creature is equal to God: But the Son of God is equal to the supreme GOD. Who therefore is the Son of God a creature!

(4.) He who is truly equal to the supreme God by reason of wisdom, power, majesty, and glory of God, to him divine essence cannot be denied. For those axioms are the same in reality as the divine essence, and are altogether inseparable from it, and therefore necessarily suppose the essence of God. But the former is true of Christ. Therefore also the latter.

(5.) He who is truly equal to God the Father, he must be of the same essence with God the Father. Because a creature cannot be set as simply equal to God, the finite to the infinite. Nor indeed is there but one only God in essence.

(6.) If God does not wish to give his glory to another, it is necessary that Christ, who is equal to God in glory and Majesty, is not alien from the essence of God.

(7.) There is added the fact that this equality is here vindicated to Christ in such a way that it supposes, or infers, the form of God, since the Apostle joins these together. Now the form of God infers the divine essence, if not ἀμέσως & immediately, certainly ἐμμέσως mediately & consequently. (8.) What need of many words? Oforodus acknowledges in instit. c. 19. He who is absolutely and perfectly equal to the supreme God is not a creature, but plainly identical in essence with God the Father, and therefore true God by nature.

The opponents here object: Socinus indeed l. c. (1.) That the form of God, or equality with God, which Paul attributes to Christ in this place, cannot be the divine nature and essence itself, because he is said to have laid aside the form of God, or that equality with God, for a time. (2.) Because it by no means falls to God himself not to think that he had seized the divine nature, nor can it be said of God that he was able to retain his divine essence mordicus. (3.) That likewise emptying does not fall to God, since God could not lower or cast down himself without ceasing to be the Most High. (4.) That being exalted does not fall to God (otherwise he would not be Most High), much less so exalted that adoration and divine worship follow from it. (5.) That Paul wishes to persuade self-abasement by the example of Christ; whence Socinus judges it follows that in Christ his own abasement must have been seen and beheld, so also Smalcius de incarn. verbi 0. 20. (6.) Enjedinus moreover urges these things besides, pag. 307. that neither the appellation of Jesus nor of Christ befits anyone other than a begotten man, and therefore this status of the Messiah, that he was in the form of God and equal to God, cannot be referred to that time when he had not yet been begotten of his Mother. (7.) That it is far different to be in the form of someone than to be something. (8.) That never in the New Testament is either the very word μορφῆς, or others derived from it, applied to substance, but always with the signification of accidents. (9.) That the humility to which the Apostle exhorts by the example of Christ requires not a mutation of substance, not an essential transfiguration, but only a mutation of morals and a state of life. Furthermore (10.) Enjedinus also denies that those qualities are here enumerated which draw substance with them and are inseparable from essence, pag. 312. because also equality with God. (11.) That the form of God and equality with God do not signify supreme glory, because Christ afterwards attained greater glory. (12.) That the form of God marks here royal majesty, dignity and authority, right and power of commanding, and that Paul signifies that Christ was King of the Jews designated. (13.) That some interpret the words of the Apostle here thus, that although Christ was in the form of God, yet he did not seize, nor attribute to himself, equality with God, nor did he say or think himself equal. (14.) That the word ἴσα often signifies the same as ὅμοιον, similar, the same Smalcius urges contra nova monstra cap. 9. (15.) Equa-

(15.) That equality is also said in respect of accidents. But many things agree in accidents, which are most diverse in substances. (16.) That equality with GOD signifies miraculous works, power, and forces above human nature. (17.) That ἴσα θεῷ [equal to God] is a proverbial form of speaking, which we use as often as we wish to signify that someone is constituted above the common and vulgar lot, which he proves from Homer and Horace. For here, by the word God, not substance, and much less the individual, i.e., the Father God, is signified, which that also seems to persuade, because the article is not applied to it.

That the Father is signified as God is also suggested by the fact that the article is not applied to him.

(18.) He explains 'to count it a robbery' from Heliodorus, as to seize most greedily the opportunity offered for a thing vehemently desired and loved to be obtained, when the opportunity of occupying royal majesty and Jewish empire had been offered to Christ.

(19.) What great thing, Enjedinus grumbles along with him, would Paul say of Christ, if he affirmed that he, when he was God by nature, understood that he did not have this by robbery?

(20.) That someone can have something, which he has neither by nature, nor by theft, but either by succession, or by the donation of someone. Thus Christ had equality with God neither by nature, nor by robbery, but by the munificence of God the Father, the Apostle testifying, he gave him a name above every name: that Christ could also refer this received [name] to his own labors, patience, and obedience.

All of which Enjedinus pursues.

1. 1. Resp. ad 1.

To (1.) Resp.

Although we concede that it is not immediately designated by τὸ ὑπάρχειν ἐν μορφῇ θεοῦ [being in the form of God], and τὸ εἶναι ἴσα θεῷ [being equal to God] the divine essence and nature, especially as the same is attributed to the Son of GOD before he assumed human nature.

But rather the communion of majesty and divine glory, and the equal power with GOD of exercising the same, which befell Christ in the days of his flesh: Yet it is not to be admitted that the form of God itself, and the equality with GOD itself, by no means infer a divine nature or essence: nor do the reasons brought by Socinus or Enjedinus prove this.

The form of God, and equality with GOD, belongs to him as he is God, and the Son of God. But did he cease to be God for a time, did he cease to be the Son of God?

The Apostle does not commemorate the deposition of the form of God and equality with GOD, but rather hinted that he remained in the form of GOD when he says that he emptied himself, ὑπάρχων ἐν μορφῇ θεοῦ [being in the form of God], existing in the form of God: that he likewise retained equality with God, even if he did not count it a robbery; he did not hold it for robbery, nor did he publicly display the τὸ εἶναι ἴσα θεῷ [being equal to God] as a robbery on all sides.

Enjedinus confesses [p. 309] that the Apostle demonstrates quite openly that at the very same time Christ was in the form of God, he was humble and emptied. For these, he says, are the words of the Apostle: ὃς ἐν μορΦῇ θεοῦ ὑπάρχων, ἑαυτὸν ἐκένωσε [who being in the form of God, emptied himself].

This is, of GOD, which the participle of the present tense ὑπάρχων [being] indicates. If therefore he was in the form of God at the very time he was humbling and emptying himself, he certainly did not lay aside the form of God by that evacuation and humiliation.

Nor indeed is it said he emptied the form of God; but ἑαυτὸν ἐκένωσε [he emptied himself]. Which was done not by the deposition, abjection, and abdication of power, majesty, and glory, but by the use of retraction, and the intermission of the exercise of the same, so that the divine glory and power seemed as it were empty and void, when he assumed the form of a servant, and humbled himself for our sake.

Since in the midst of the state of emptying, the rays of power, majesty, and glory shone forth, even in the time of his passion, as in the miraculous healing of the cut-off ear, in the divine institution of the Eucharist, etc.

All the fullness of the Deity dwelling in Christ did not cease at the time of the emptying, col.

II. 9. Nor did Christ cease to be God blessed above all things forever, Rom. IX. 5.

IX. 5.

Nazianzen tract. de fid. it.

Ambrose libr. de fid. c. 8. declare this in similar words, whose brightness is covered with a cloud, is compressed, not blinded.

Bede in h. l. from Augustine, he says, he emptied himself, not losing the form of GOD, but assuming the form of a servant, and Fulgent. l. de incarnat. c.

2. The emptying of the only-begotten GOD was the acceptance of the servile form, not the loss or diminution of the Deity.

What of the fact that Socinus himself confesses that Christ had power and authority, residing in him perpetually [p. 279]? How therefore did he lay aside the same at the time of the emptying, if he had the same residing in him perpetually?

Add moreover, that that emptying is not to be restricted only to the time of the great passion, which Socinus wrongly thinks, but looks to the whole curriculum of Christ's life, even if the supreme degree of emptying is in the time of the great passion, and the last term of humiliation is the death of the cross, of which matter elsewhere.

Therefore, as to the phrase, he did not count it a robbery, we deny that the same is signified which Socinus wants: he did not tenaciously retain the equality which he had with GOD, as some robber is accustomed to do with a thing he has stolen, he laid himself down at the nod of GOD.

Because Socinus did not give proof of this, that this is not another signification, he merely asserted it, and we showed above that that phrase admits another sense.

Finally, if the discourse is about the divine majesty and power of Christ, viewed as to the second act, or his plenary use and exercise, we can indeed admit that it was abdicated in the days of his flesh, but from the cessation and intermission of the second act, the consequence does not hold for the negation or abdication of the first act.

Resp. ad 2.

To (2.) Those who explain it concerning Christ as GOD before the incarnation, respond:

It is not repugnant, nor is it inconvenient, if it is said that the Word or Son of God knew for certain that he had equality with God, not by robbery, but by nature: Nor will they grant place to that Socinian gloss, that he did not tenaciously retain that equality, which never even entered the mind of them or others in that sense.

Moreover, it is better to take the present text concerning the incarnate Son of God, since the state of emptying and exaltation agree with him according to human nature. But according to this, who does not see that Christ knew for certain that the things of God were equal to him, or that he could conduct himself equally to God, and indeed even that he did not tenaciously retain the use of divine glory and power, without any inconvenience being said.

Resp. ad 3.

To (3.) Those who wish the emptying of the incarnation to be designated, respond, that it is not repugnant to GOD to have such a κένωσιν [emptying] & ταπείνωσιν [humiliation], as that which changes nothing in God, nor casts God down from his height, but only infers a change to the outside, as God was not changed when in the O.T. an external visible form was assumed, and he willed to be manifested by it, so he was not changed when he was manifested in the flesh 1.

Tim. III. verf. 16. For although he assumed our humble flesh, and thus the most high was made humble, yet that was not done by the depression or change of the most high God, but by the assumption of our humility.

Some also distinguish between emptying ἑτικὴν [habitually] and relatively accepted, and ἁπλῶς [simply] or absolutely. They confess that this does not agree with God, but they say that the former is rightly attributed to GOD, as GOD is also said to be exalted ἑτικῶς [habitually], and by reason of us.

Others Chri- They say that Christ, according to his divine nature, lowered himself, partly by a voluntary subjection of his person, partly as he submitted himself to the Father as mediator: partly by the concealment of his divine glory for a time, while he did not exert the same in the assumed human nature. But it is better to refer the kenosis and tapeinosis to the human nature of Christ, since those things are either not said without danger, or finally return to this, that the exact divine glory is not made in the human nature in the state of emptying.

To (4.) Resp.

That exaltation does not fall upon the most high God, insofar as he is viewed by reason of his divine nature, is confessed by all the orthodox. But we deny that it follows from this that he who is the most high God, or above all things, can in no way be said to be exalted. Therefore, we believe without contradiction that Christ is both God above all or the most high, and that he was exalted by reason of his assumed human nature. Socinus’s argument, which he urges on p. 276: "He who emptied himself is also the same one who was exalted. But Christ emptied himself according to his divine nature, according to the opinion of those who understand the emptying as the incarnation. Therefore, Christ was exalted according to his divine nature," is faulty in form; since it labors under a quaternity of terms, and confuses absolute and reduplicative propositions. But if it is reduced to another form: "According to the same nature that Christ emptied himself, according to the same he was also exalted," then the authors of the said opinion will not concede that that proposition is true. Therefore, they will indeed say that the same person who had lowered himself was clearly exalted, although not according to the same nature. But what Socinus retorts: "That it is the same thing, that the eternal Son of God was exalted only according to his human nature, which is that the eternal Son of God was not truly exalted, but only through the communication of idioms": this they will thoroughly and deservedly deny. Because what is brought forth through the communication of idioms, that he truly and really had: since the communication of idioms is not verbal and improper, but true and real. As truly as his flesh is proper to the Son of God, so truly and properly was the Son of God exalted, with his flesh being exalted. Concerning which, elsewhere.

To (5.) Resp.

Examples are not only sought from things seen or beheld for teaching and persuading, as Socinus contends, but also from those things which have never been seen or beheld and are only to be believed; such as when divine Holiness, divine perfection, etc., are proposed to us as an example. Lev. XIX. 2. 1. Pet. I. 16. Matt. V. last.
