Si ergo Filius Dei vere aequalis est Patri, oportet eum esse non meram creaturam, sed ipsum Jehovam. (2.) Dum Scriptura quaerit: Quis par Jehovah Deo nostro? Ps. CXIII. 5. Quis est Deus fortis tibi par vel aequalis? Mich. 6, 18. quaerendo negat, quenquam dari posse Deorum, hominum, aut creaturarum, qui sit Jehovah summo DEO par & aequalis. Conf. Jer. XLIX. vers. 19. L. 44. Ps. XXXV. 10. ut & LXXI. 19. & LXXXIX. 9. & c. Notum enim est, quod quaestiones ejusmodi negativis aequipolleant. Si ergo creatura nulla aequalis est DEO, utique Filius Dei, qui aequalis est Patri, creatura non erit, sed verus natura Deus.

(3.) Comparatio creaturarum cum DEO negatur, nullam scilicet creaturarum DEO comparari vel conferri posse. Es. XL. 18. 25. c. XLVI. 5. docetur etiam, nullam creaturam Deo aequalem esse: At Filius Dei aequalis est DEO summo. Qui ergo Filius Dei creatura!

(4.) Qui summo Deo vere aequalis est ratione sapientiae, potentiae, majestatis & gloriae Dei, ei denegari non potest essentia divina. Axiomata enim illa idem sunt realiter cum essentia divina, & ab ea prorsus sunt inseparabilia, adeoque necessario supponunt essentiam Dei. At de Christo verum est prius. Ergo & posterius.

(5.) Qui vere aequalis est Deo Patri, eum oportet ejusdem essentiae esse cum Deo Patre. Quia creatura nequit Deo simpliciter aequalis statui, finitum infinito. Nec vero est nisi unus tantum essentia Deus.

(6.) Si Deus gloriam suam alteri dare non vult, necessum est, Christum, qui gloria & Majestate Deo aequalis est, non esse alienum ab essentia Dei.

(7.) Accedit, quod hic ita aequalitas Christo vindicetur, ut forma Dei eadem supponat, vel inferat, cum Apostolus haec conjungat. Forma autem Dei infert essentiam divinam, si non ἀμέσως & immediate, certe ἐμμέσως mediate & consequenter. (8.) Quid multis? Agnoscit Oforodus in instit. c. 19. Qui Deo summo absolute, & perfecte aequalis est, cum non esse creaturam, sed essentia plane idem cum Deo Patre, adeoque verum natura Deum.

Excipiunt hic adversarii: Socinus quidem l. c. . (1.) Dei formam, seu, cum Deo aequalitatem, quam Paulus Christo hoc in loco tribuit, non posse esse ipsam naturam & essentiam divinam, quia formam Dei, seu aequalitatem istam cum Deo ad tempus deposuisse dicitur. (2.) Quia neutiquam in Deum ipsum cadit, non arbitrari se rapuisse naturam divinam, nec dici potest de Deo, eum mordicus suam essentiam divinam retinere potuisse. (3.) Quod similiter in Deum non cadat exinanitio, quam Deus sese demittere, aut dejicere non possit, quin altissimus esse desinat. (4.) Quod non cadat in Deum exaltari (alioquin non esset altissimus) nedum ita exaltari, ut adoratio, & divinus cultus inde consequatur. (5.) Quod Paulus exemplo Christi sui ipsius demissionem velle persuade: unde consequi censet Socinus, necesse esse, ut in Christo bet sui ipsius demissio fuerit visa, atque conspecta, sic etiam Smalcius de incarn. verbi 0. 20. (6.) Enjedinus vero haec insuper urget pag. 307. neque Jesu, neque Christi appellatio ulli, quam genito homini conveniat, ac proinde hic Messiae status, quod fuerit in forma Dei, & aequalis Deo referri ad tempus illud non possit, quo nondum a Matre genitus erat. (7.) Longe aliud esse, in forma alicujus esse, quam esse aliquid. (8.) Nunquam in Novo Testamento, vel ipsam vocem μορφῆς, vel ab ea deductas alias ad substantiam, sed semper ad accidentium adhiberi folderi significationem. (9.) Humilitatem, ad quam exemplo Christi hortatur Apostolus, non substantiae mutationem, non essentialem transfigurationem, sed mutationem tantum morum, & statum vitae requirere. Porro (10.) negat etiam Enjedinus, eas hic recenseri qualitates, quae secum substantiam trahant, & ab essentia inseparabiles sint, pag. 312. eo quod & aequalitatem cum Deo. (11.) Formam Dei, & aequalitatem cum Deo non significare summam gloriam, quia majorem postea Christus gloriam consecutus sit. (12.) Formam Dei notare hic regiam majestatem, dignitatem & auctoritatem, jus & potestatem imperandi, Paulumque id significare, quod Christus Rex fuerit Judaeorum designatus. (13.) Nonnullos verba Apostoli hic interpretari, quod licet Christus fuerit in forma Dei, tamen non rapuerit, neque sibi attribuerit aequalitatem cum Deo, neque se aequalem esse dixerit, existimaverit. (14.) Vocem ἴσα sape idem significare, quod ὅμοιον simile, idem urget Smalcius contra nova monstra cap. 9. (15.) Equa-

(15.) Aequalitatem etiam accidentium respectu dici. Multa autem convenire in accidentibus, quae substantiis diversissima sunt. (16.) Aequalitatem cum DEO significare mirifica opera, potentiam, & vires supra naturam humanam. (17.) ἴσα θεῷ esse formulam loquendi proverbialem, qua utimur, quoties aliquem supra communem & vulgarem sortem esse constitutum significare volumus, quod ex Homero & Horatio probat. Nam hic per vocabulum Dei, non substantiam, & multo minus individuum, h.e.

Patrem Deum significari, illud quoque suadere videri, quod ei articulus appositus non est.

(18.) Rapinam ducere ex Heliodoro explicat, esse rei vehementer desideratae, & amate potiunde occasionem oblatam avidissime arripere, quum Christo oblata fuerit occasio regiae maiestatis & imperii Judaici occupandi.

(19.) Quid magni, oggannit cum Enjedinus, diceret de Christo Paulus, si affirmaret, illum cum esset natura Deus, intellexisse, hoc se non ex rapina habere?

(20.) Posse aliquem habere quodpiam, quod nec natura habeat, nec raptu, sed aut ex successione, aut ex donatione alicuius. Sic Christum aequalitatem cum Deo nec natura habuisse, nec ex rapina, sed ex munificentia Dei Patris, teste Apostolo, donavit illi nomen supra omne nomen: posse etiam hoc acceptum referre Christum suis laboribus, patientia & obedientia.

Quae omnia fuisse prosequitur Enjedinus.

Resp. ad 1.

Ad (1.) Resp.

Quanquam concedamus, immediate non designari per τὸ ὑπάρχειν ἐν μορφῇ θεοῦ, & τὸ εἶναι ἴσα θεῷ essentiam & naturam divinam, praesertim, qua eadem Filio DEI tribuitur, antequam humanam assumeret naturam.

Sed maiestatis potius, & gloriae divinae communionem, eiusdemque exercendae aequalem cum DEO potestatem, quae Christo in diebus carnis convenerit: Non tamen admittendum, ipsam Dei formam, ipsamque cum DEO aequalitatem haudquaquam inferre naturam seu essentiam divinam: nec id probant a Socino, vel Enjedino allatae rationes.

Formam Dei, & aequalitatem cum DEO ipsi convenit, qua Deus est, & Filius Dei. Num vero ad tempus desiit esse Deus, num desiit esse Filius Dei?

Apostolus non depositionem formae Dei & aequalitatis cum DEO commemorat, sed manifeste potius in forma DEI mansit cum dicit, quod seipsum evacuarit, ὑπάρχων ἐν μορφῇ θεοῦ, existens in forma Dei: retinuisse itidem aequalitatem cum Deo, etsi non rapinam duxerit; non pro rapina habuerit, neque seu rapinam publice ostentaris undique τὸ εἶναι ἴσα θεῷ.

Fatetur id Enjedinus p. 309. satis aperte demonstrare Apostolum, eodem ipso tempore fuisse Christum in forma Dei, quo fuit humilis, & exinanitus. Hec enim, inquit, verba sunt Apostoli: ὃς ἐν μορΦῇ θεοῦ ὑπάρχων, ἑαυτὸν ἐκένωσε.

Hoc est, DEI, quod indicat participium presentis temporis ὑπάρχων, Si ergo eo ipso tempore in forma Dei erat, quo sese humiliabat & evacuabat, utique formam Dei non deposuit illa evacuatione & humiliatione.

Neu vero dicitur μορφὴν θεοῦ ἐκένωσε; sed ἑαυτὸν ἐκένωσε, seipsum exinanivit. Id quod non potentiae, maiestatis & gloriae depositione, abjectione & abdicatione factum, sed retractione usus, & exercitii ejusdem intermissione, ut quasi vacua, & inanis videretur gloria & potentia divina, cum formam servi assumeret, & nostri causa sese humiliaret.

Quandoquidem in medio exinanitionis statu radii potentiae, maiestatis & gloriae emicuerint, ipso etiam passionis tempore, utpote in miraculosa auris abscissae sanatione, in divina Eucharistiae institutione &c.

Omnis plenitudo Deitatis in Christo habitans tempore exinanitionis non cessavit, col.

II. 9. Nec Christus desiit esse Deus super omnia benedictus in secula, Rom.

IX. 5.

Nazianzenus tract. de fid. it.

Ambrol. libr. de fid. c. 8. declarant id similibus verbis, cujus claritas cum nube tegitur, comprimitur, non caecatur.

Beda in h. l. ex Augustino, semetipsum, inquit, exinanivit, non formans DEI amittens, sed formam servi suscipiens, & Fulgent. l. de incarnat. c.

2. Exinanitio unigeniti DEI acceptio fuit formae servilis, non amissio vel diminutio Deitatis.

Quid quod Socinus ipse fateatur potestatem & autoritatem Christum habuisse, in se perpetuo residentem p. 279. Quî ergo eandem deposuit tempore exinanitionis, si perpetuo eandem in se residentem habuit?

Adde insuper, quod exinanitio illa non restringenda fit tantum ad tempus passionis magnae, quod perperam censet Socinus, sed ad totum vitae Christi curriculum spectet, etsi supremus exinanitionis gradus fit in tempore passionis magnae, ultimusque terminus humiliationis fit mors crucis, qua de re alias.

Quod ergo ad phrasin, non rapinam duxit, negamus eandem id significari, quod vult Socinus: non mordicus retinuit quam cum DEO aequalitatem, ut raptor aliquis rem, quam rapuerit, solet, se ad DEU nutum deposuit.

Quia nec id probatum dedit Socinus, hanc non aliam esse significationem, nude saltim afferuit, & alium admittere phrasin istam sensum, supra ostendimus.

Denique si de maiestate & potentia Christi divina, quoad actum se cundum spectata, vel plenario ejus usu & exercitio sermo fit, admittere quidem possumus, abdicatum fuisse in diebus carnis, a cessatione vero & intermissione actus secundi, ad negationem vel abdicationem actus primi non valet consequentia.

Resp. ad 2.

Ad (2.) Qui de Christo qua DEO ante incarnationem explicant, respondent:

Non repugnare, nec inconveniens esse, si dicatur, λόγῳ or Filium Dei certo scivisse, non rapinam, sed naturam sese habere aequalitatem cum Deo: Nec glossae isti Socinianae, quod non retinuerit mordicus eam aequalitatem, locum concedent, quae ipsis aut aliis nunquam etiam eo sensu in mentem venit.

Caeterum praestat textum praesentem de Filio Dei incarnato accipere, quum status exinanitionis & exaltationis conveniant ei secundum humanam naturam. At juxta hanc Christum certo scivisse, sibi esse aequalia Dei, aut sese aequaliter Deo gerere posse, imo etiam usum gloriae & potentiae divinae non retinuisse mordicus, quis non videt, citra ullum dici incommodum.

Resp. ad 3.

Ad (3.) Qui exinanitionem incarnationis designari volunt, respondent, DEO non repugnare ejusmodi κένωσιν & ταπείνωσιν, ut quae in Deo nihil mutet, nec Deum de altitudine sua dejiciat, sed ad extra solum mutationem inferat, ut Deus mutatus non fuit, cum in V.T. externa vitibili forma assumpta, e ea manifestari voluit, ita nihil mutatus fuit, cum manifestatus est in carne 1.

Tim. III. vers. 16. Quanquam enim humilem nostram carnem assumsit, & ita altissimus humilis factus fit, non tamen id factum Dei altissimi depressione, aut mutatione, sed humilitatis nostrae susceptione.

Distinguunt etiam nonnulli inter exinanitionem ἑτικὴν ac relative acceptam, & ἁπλῶς vel absolute. Hanc Deo non convenire fatentur, illam vero DEO recte tribui ajunt, ut DEUS etiam ἑτικῶς, & ratione nostri exaltari dicitur.

Alii Christum secundum divinam naturam dicunt sese demisisse, partim voluntaria personae subjectione, partim qua Patri tanquam mediator se submisit: partim gloriae suae divinae ad tempus occultatione, dum eandem in assumpta humana natura non exseruit. Sed praestat κένωσιν & ταπείνωσιν referre ad humanam Christi naturam, cum illa aut non dicantur fine periculo, aut tandem huc redeant, quod in humana natura non fit exacta gloria divina in statu exinanitionis.

Ad (4.) Resp.

Exaltationem in Deum altissimum, quatenus ratione divinae naturae spectatur, non cadere, apud omnes orthodoxos in confesso est. Sed inde negamus consequi, exaltari cum nullo pacto dici posse, qui Deus est altissimus, vel super omnia. Christum ergo & Deum super omnia vel altissimum esse, & exaltatum ratione assumptae humanae naturae, citra contradictionem credimus. Socini argumentum, quod p. 276. urget: Qui sese exinanivit idem etiam exaltatus est. At Christus sese exinanivit secundum divinam naturam, juxta eorum sententiam, qui exinanitionem de incarnatione intelligunt. Ergo exaltatus fuit Christus secundum divinam naturam, vitiosum est in forma; quandoquidem terminorum laborat quaternitate, ac propositiones permutet absolutam & reduplicativam. Quod si in aliam redigatur formam: Secundum quam naturam Christus sese exinanivit, secundum eandem etiam exaltatus est, tunc Autores sententiae dictae propositionem istam veram esse non concedent. Proinde eundem quidem plane fuisse exaltatum dicent, qui se demiserat, licet non secundum eandem naturam. Quod vero regerit Socinus: Idem esse, aeternum Dei Filium secundum humanam naturam tantum exaltatum fuisse, quod ipsum, aeternum Dei Filium revera non fuisse exaltatum, sed tantum per communicationem idiomatum: Id penitus & merito inficiabuntur. Quia quod per communicationem idiomatum affertur, id vere & reapse habuit: quum idiomatum communicatio non verbalis & impropria sit, sed vera & realis. Quam vere propria est Filio Dei caro sua, vare proprieque Filius Dei exaltatus est, exaltata carne sua. De quo alias.

Ad (5.) Resp.

Non tantum a rebus visis aut conspectis exempla petuntur ad docendum & persuadendum, quemadmodum contendit Socinus, sed ab iis etiam, quae nunquam visa, aut conspecta tantum credenda sunt; qualia sunt, cum divina Sanctitas, divina perfectio &c. in exemplo nobis proponuntur. Lev. XIX. 2. 1. Pet. I. 16. Matt. V. ult. Qui ergo Filium Dei in uterum virginis humanam assumendo naturam sese demittentem, humilitatis exemplum nobis praebere afferunt, minime eo urgeri possunt, quod nemo id viderit: Sufficit, quod id testatum sit in scripturis, & oculis mentis vel fidei apprehendatur. Quid? quod nec nostrum quisquam viderit Christi humiliationem in diebus carnis, fide saltem eandem suscipimus, quae tamen omnino nobis in exemplum humilitatis sistitur. Ad id porro, quod Enjedinus objicit: Exempla quibus alios docere volumus, ea adferenda esse, quae imitari possint, neminem autem posse se humiliare ut homo fiat: Responsio facilis est: exemplum praeberi non incarnationis, sed humilitatis: non speciem, vel modum, ut nempe humiliemur incarnatione. Sufficit, si affectus humiliationis in nobis respondeat humiliationis affectui, ut Apostolus loquitur, in Christo, quemadmodum sufficit, quod sanctitati studeamus, ut Deus sanctus est, etsi sancti essentiali sanctitate, ut Deus est, fieri non possimus. Ad (6.) Quod est Enjedini, responderi potest, Jesu, ut & Christi nomen non inrecte tribui Filio Dei etiam ante assumptam carnem, quum ipse & salvator fuerit in Veteri Testamento, & ab aeterno unus vel destinatus in Sacerdotem & Regem justum.

Quod vero Christo nomen Jesu ab angelo assignatum fuerit, Matt.

I. vers. 21. Luc. I. 31. exinde minime sequitur, Filium DEI antea in V. Test. non potuisse hoc nomine nuncupari; imo ut Filio Dei nato ex Maria virgine in Nov. Test. id nomen solenniter imponebatur, ita ante nativitatem temporalem jam eodem & similibus designatus legitur nominibus in Vet. Test. Gen. XLIX. vers. 18. Es. XXV. vers. 7. XLIX. v. 9. LI. 10. LXIII. 11. Deinde, ut Christus fuisse dicitur antequam Abraham esset, Job. VIII. 59. ita de Jesu Christo juxta hanc veterum sententiam pariter dici poterat, quod in forma Dei fuerit, antequam carnem assumeret: nimirum ob identitatem personae, & communicationem idiomatum: cum eadem sit persona Filius Dei ὃς ἄσαρκῳ, & ipse Jesus Christus. Ad (7.) Fatetur equidem nos, aliud esse in forma Dei existere, aliud Deum esse, illud de Christo dici secundum humanam naturam: Sed qui e veteribus afferunt, illa etiam phrasi divinam essentiam immediate inferri, reponere poterunt, Christum ita in forma DEI esse dici, ut etiam Deus sit, quemadmodum & imago DEI, patris scilicet, dicitur, & ipse Deus est, idque citra ullam ἀντίφασιν.

Ad (8.) Negari potest consequentia; quum ab aliis locis, utpote disparibus, non videatur ad hunc firmiter concludi: praeprimis, cum nisi semel adhuc ipsa vox μορφῆς in Nov.

Test. occurrat

Marc. XVI. apparuit ἑτέρᾳ μορφῇ alia forma, editam apud Vulgatos interpretes, ut & apud DD. Ecclesiae passim, nec non apud Theologos creberrimus & frequentissimus ejus fit usus pro essentia vel natura rei.

Ad (9.) Responsio patet e praecedentibus, quod in exemplum proponitur Christi humiliatio, non autem modus humiliationis.

Etsi ergo toto genere diversus ac prorsus immutabilis fit ille humiliationis modus, quod nobis praescribi non potuit, sufficiat tamen, quod exemplum praebeat Christus praeclarissimum humiliationis, quod humilitate, qua possumus, imitari debeamus. Atque haec pro defensione eorum reponi possunt, ad exceptiones adversariorum, qui statuunt humiliationem incarnationis hic proponi ab Apostolo. Cui sententiae etsi omnino praeferamus eam, quae humiliationem Christo vindicat secundum humanam naturam, satis tamen infirma fuisse Adversariorum tela, quibus istam petitam voluere, jam manifestum esse arbitramur. Ideoque nunc reliquas eorum exceptiones, nostram quoque sub sententiam revocabimus.

*Ad (10.) Resp.

Certum est τὸ ὑπάρχων ἐν μορφῇ Θεοῦ, Et τὸ εἶναι ἴσα Θεῷ Christo tribui ratione Majestatis, gloriae, ac potentiae divinae.* Ea autem vel est eadem numero cum potentia & gloria Dei Patris, vel diversa ab eadem. At diversa non est: quia sic plures forent potentiae, & gloriae, ut ita dicam, divinae, quod absurdum. Adhac illa potentia & gloria, vel est infinita, vel finita. Si infinita, ergo plura dabuntur actu infinita numero distincta, quod impossibile. Si finita, non erit vere divina potentia, & gloria, nec causa erit miraculorum, quae non nisi ab infinita procedunt virtute, nec ratio & fundamentum adorationis & invocationis. religiosae, quae omnia de majestate, gloria & potentia Christi etiam in diebus carnis exerta e Scripturis constant. Ideoque ita concludimus: Quaecunque gloria, majestas & potentia (1.) vere divina est, (2.) sese exerit per miracula vere divina, (3.) cultum meretur & requirit adorationis divinae & invocationis religiosae, ea inseparabilis est ab essentia DEI, & talis est majestas, gloria & potentia Christi.

Enjedini argumentum, quod formam DEI, & aequalitatem cum DEO deposuerit Christus, ψευδερμηνεία laborat verborum Apostoli, & supra jam profligatum est.

Ad 11.

Ad (11.) Resp.

Falsum est, quod ait Enjedinus, Christum majorem postea gloriam forma Dei, & aequalitate cum Deo consequutum esse. Falsum: τὸ ὑπερύψωσε superexaltavit, idem esse, quod majori, quam antea, cum in forma DEI esset, honore, gloria & potentia ornavit. Praepositio ὑπὲρ sublimitatem gloriae infert, non autem comparationem cum forma DEI: Falsum, Christum desiisse in forma DEI esse, eamque abjecisse, spe majoris gloriae. Nam eodem ipso tempore, quo humiliabat sese, erat in forma DEI, quod supra pag. 309. professus erat Enjedinus. Mansit semper in forma Dei, nec unquam abjecit τὸ εἶναι ἴσα θεῷ. Nec ὑπερύψωσις vel opponitur, vel confertur τῇ μορφῇ θεοῦ, sed opponitur τῇ ταπεινώσει, & κενώσει, ut ergo illa per collocationem ad dexteram DEI, vel evectionem ad plenarium & universale Dominium super omnia consistit, ita hanc inferre Dominii ejusmodi plenarii, incessantis & universalis evacuationem ad tempus factam non diffitemur; sed ab ejusmodi evacuatione, & intermissione Dominii, ad formae Dei, & aequalitatis cum Deo, vel etiam ad majestatis, gloriae & potentiae abdicationem non valet consequentia; tum non ratione Deitatis illa evacuatio fit intelligenda, sed ratione humanitatis Christi, quod fecit.

Majestas & potentia divina per eam sese non exuerit, quod tum a negatione actus secundi ad negationem actus primi, ab intermissione usurpationis, ad inficiationem possessionis, a negata χρήσει ad negandam κλῆσιν nulla fit ἀκόλουθα.

Quod ergo Christus Luc. XXIV. vers. 26. post passionem dicitur ingressus in gloriam: quod Johan. XVII. vers. 5. petit summa illa gloria, quam ante mundi constitutionem habuit, coronari, non de prima gloriae & majestatis divinae communicatione, sed de plenaria ejusdem usurpatione, ad quam non nisi post passionem admissus fuit, accipiendum.

Quandoquidem habitarit in ipso jam omnis plenitudo Deitatis,

Col. II. vers. 9. viderantque Apostoli gloriam ejus tanquam gloriam unigeniti Johan. I. vers. 14. et qui poterat carere gloria & majestate divina, cum esset in forma DEI, nec rapinam duceret esse ἴσα θεῷ, si ad id gloria & majestate divina, quod fatetur Socinus, pertinebat: quomodo poterat miracula patrare, αὐτεξουσίως peccata remittere, mortuos vivificare, ac potestatem miracula patrandi & peccata remittendi Apostolis concedere, quomodo poterat cogitata cordis inspicere, omnia novisse, si prorsus caruit summa gloria, & potentia in diebus carnis suae?

Quandoquidem illa pertinebat ad summam DEI gloriam & potentiam, ad ἀξιώματα & ἰδιώματα DEO uni propria.

Psal. LXXII. vers. 18. 1. Reg. VIII. vers. 39. Marc. II. 7. &c. Ad 12.

Ad (12.) Regia dignitas intelligitur vel de regimine seculari, mundano, & terreno; vel de regimine spirituali, caelesti & divino.

Prioris respectu neque designatione, neque actuali gubernatione Christus Rex fuit, dum in terris ageret. Quia regnum ejus non erat de hoc mundo, Johan. XIIX. vers. 36. Posteriori autem respectu, non designatione tantum nuda Rex erat, sed actuali etiam administratione, nec Judaeorum solum, sed omnium populorum, imo omne judicium, omne regnum sibi datum testabatur Joh. V. vers. 22. Pater meus, dicebat, operatur & ego operor vers. 17. &, quaecunque facit Pater, ea similiter & Filius facit, v. 19. Ad plenam vero regiminis universalis in coelo & in terra, & incessantem administrationem admissus fuit Christus demum per exaltationem ad dexteram DEI, sed ratione humanae naturae, quod nihil derogat perpetuo Deitatis regimini.

Caeterum falsum est, & ἀδύνατον, quod ostendit adversarius, formam Dei hic nihil aliud significare, quam Regiam dignitatem.

Falsum, inquam, id est, quia longe sublimius est nomen formae Dei, & aequalitatis cum Deo, quae fere eadem esse censet ipse Enjedinus, quam dignitatis Regiae: quod adeo manifestum, ut prolixe id concedat Enjedinus. Quis enim, regia qui gaudent dignitate dixerit esse in forma Dei, & aequales Deo, stylo Apostolico? Ἀσύσατον, quia forma Dei juxta Enjedinum deposita est humiliatione Christi. At regiam dignitatem depositam esse dicere non potest, quam cum ne habeat quidem adhuc, nisi designatione tantum, secundum Enjedinum. Porro impietate haud caret, quod Enjedinus ita differat de Regia Enjedinus Christi dignitate, ac si Judaeorum Rex ac Monar- cha terrenus designatione fuerit: ac regnum Judaeorum occupare poruisse, idque recte, seu ex gratuito Dei beneficio oblatum pag. 325. Respiunt haec impia Judaeorum dogmata, somniantium, nescio quam terrenam monarchiam Messiae promissam. Penes Christianos autem extra controversiam positum est (esse certe debebat) Christo nec oblatum fuisse, nec promissum divinitus regnum terrenum, Christum nec designatione divina regem fuisse secularem Israelis, nec debuisse Magistratum inire, aut occupare regnum Judaeorum, cum eo fine missus non fuerit, sed venerit, ut ministraret, non ut sibi ministraret, Matth.

XX. vers. 28. Denique si de Spirituali sermo fit regno Christi, falsissimum est, Judaeorum Regem tantum fuisse Christum, designatum a conceptione, & nativitate.

Quia eorum fine dubio Rex divina fuit designatione, quorum reipsa deinde factus est, nisi quis dicere velit, divinam designationem mutabilem, & revera mutatam fuisse quod ἄτοπον. At Christus reipsa non Judaeorum tantum, sed & gentium regem factum esse, non diffitetur Enjedinus.

Dictum Matth. XV. 24. non de regio, sed prophetico Christi officio agit. Aliis quibus Rex Israel vel Judaeorum dicitur, partim sensu exclusivo accipienda non sunt de solo populo Judaico, partim non de Israelitis agunt secundum carnem, sed secundum Spiritum.

Ad (13.) Impium est glossema, & Ariano veteris spiritu dignum, quo id negatur, quod a Paulo affirmatur.

Hic enim ut in forma Dei existentem Christum introduxit, ita etiam τὸ εἶναι ἴσα θεῷ ipsi non derogavit, sed attribuit, etsi hoc negarit, rapinam ei fuisse, vel instar rapinae ab ipso habitum. Illo vero prorsus negatur, Christum sibi id attribuisse.

Nec Paulus saltem id ei attribuit, sed aequalitatem etiam cum Deo Christum ipsum sibi vindicasse & Joh.

V. vers. 18. liquet, unde refellit ipse Enjedinus glossam istam suorum complicum (quamquam sibi ipsi non constet, quamnam interpretationem per se ratam esse afferat, & ambigat, an verba ista Apostolica hic eum sensum habeant, imo argumentis etiam refutet:) quod æqualem esse DEO, & in forma DEI esse, aut idem sint, aut certe illud non plus significet, quam hoc. Si ergo hoc Christo tribuitur, cur non etiam illud possit? Accidit, quod simile quid alibi quoque de Christo legimus Joh. V. 19. æqualem se faciens Deo. Vid. expl. loc. adh. l. p. 318. Enjedini.

Ad (14.) Resp. Apud Græcos in prosa passim ἴσος est æqualis, & par, ut ἰσότης æqualitatem notat, ἰσόω, æquo, ἰσόκωλος, ubi paria membra, eaque si- gnificatio prima & maxime propria est. At a pro- pria significatione citra causas graves discedendũ non est. (2.) in sacris itidem accipitur pro æquali, & pari, Matth. XX. 12. Marc. XIV. 16. (3.) Aposto- lum non loqui de aliqua solum similitudine, sed exquisita æqualitate vox addita μορφῆς confirmat, eam nempe ἰσότητα indigitare, quæ supponat, vel inferat μορφὴν θεῤ: Idemque modus loquendi emphaticus comprobat, quod τὸ εἶναι ἶσα θεῶ di- xerit, de quo supra. Denique locus parallelus Joh. V. 18. statuminat, non similitudinem tantum, sed æqualitatem cum Deo inferre. Tandem quænam hæc est consequentia: Vox ἴσος quandoque & ra- rius quidem (usuatiorem enim esse significationem æqualitatis, fatetur Enjed. p. 319.) apud propha- nos adhibetur pro simili: E. hic etiam ita accipi- tur in oraculo Paulino? Invalida, nulla.

Ad (15.) Resp. Æqualitas ratione quantitatis nihil ad æqualitatem cum Deo facit. Qui omnis quantitatis expers est. Inepta ergo est probatio Enjedini, nihil aliud voce ἶσα quam accidens hic notari, quia Philosophus æqualia dicat propter quantitatem. Porro quũ nec accidentia in Deum cadant, sed attributa Dei a parte rei sunt ipsa ejus essentia, qui Deo æqualis est, ratione attributo- rum, utpote majestatis & potentiæ divinæ, illi ef- sentia divina denegari nequit.

Ad (16.) Si æqualitas cum Deo hic notat po- tentiam miracula patrandi, utique non ipsa opera mirifica denotat. Aliud enim est potentia, aliud sunt opera ab illa profecta, quæ imperite permiscet & confundit Enjedinus. At fatetur adversarius notare potentiam & vires supra naturam huma- nam. Atque hæc est prima contradictio. Altera in eo sita est, quod formam Dei idem fere esse cum æqualitate, nec magis hanc significare dicat, quam illam. At illa notabat regiam dignitatem, quod Christus designatione Judæorum Rex esset, juxta Enjedinum. Nihil ergo amplius etiam hæc signi- ficabit, adeoque nec miracula, nec potentiam ea patrandi significabit. Ita sibi constant Sophistæ! Ulterius: Si Christus non tantum inanem titulum Dei gessit, verum reipsa potestatem faciendi quid- vis habuit, quam quoties opus fuit, & voluit, exe- ruit, usurpavit, & reipsa declaravit, quod asserit Enjedinus, eoque æqualitatem cum Deo declara- vit, p. 311. utique potentiam divinam & infinitam habuit, vereque summus Deus fuit, idque insuper æqualitate cum Deo infertur. Ratio consequutio- nis est, quia reipsa potestatem habere QUIDVIS faciendi, cumque quoties opus, pro voluntate li- bera exercere, usurpare, & reipsa declarare, non nisi summi Dei, qui solus potentia infinita pollet, proprium est.

Ad (17.) Resp. Eo sensu Christo tribui τὸ εἶναι ἶσα θεῶ temere & non sine impietate dicitur, quo sensu Homerus aliique Poetæ heroes suos ἰσοθέες di- xere æquales Diis: quorum etiam Diis, vel quos pro Diis venerabantur, facile æquales esse pote- rant hæroes, ut non opus sit ullam in illis poeta- rum dictis proverbialem loquendi formulam fin- gere. Et quid illa ad præsentem Apostoli locum? Quomodo probabitur Paulum hic proverbiali loquutione Christo vindicare τὸ εἶναι ἶσα θεῷ, qui etiam ipsi ὕπαρξιν ἐν μορφῇ θεῦ vindicat? Annon e Joh. V. 18. constat, vere, non proverbiali solum locutione æqualem fuisse Christum Deo Patri, ceu proprium ejus Filium. Porro quis non videt, quam jejuna hæc sit tanti elogii Christi detorsio, verius, quam explicatio, qua τὸ εἶναι ἶσα θεῷ nihil aliud inferre docetur, quam eminentiam aliquam supra communem sortem; ea certe ratione & Jo- hanni Baptistæ, & Paulo, ac Apostolis cæteris tri- bueretur τὸ εἶναι ἶσα θεῷ, quos supra communem sortem aliorum hominum eminuisse quis nega- bit! Denique inepte negatur voce θεῦ notari hoc loco Deum Patrem. Is enim voce θεῦ notatur in phrasi εἶναι ἶσα θεῷ, qui voce θεῷ exponitur in præcedenti phrasi ὑπάρχων ἐν μορφῇ θεῦ. At hic denotari Patrem, certo certius est, nec diffitetur Enjedinus, etsi pariter ibi non addatur articulus. Sine quo etiam summum designari Deum exem- plis longe plurimis & extra omnem controver- siam positis suo loco evicimus. Adde quod nus- piam vox θεῦ absolute posita, & sine articulo in N. T. occurrat, nisi de uno summo Deo. Et cuinam Deo alii, quam Patri par & æqualis, aut æqualia gessisse dicetur Christus? Edisserant adversarii, sed non possunt, ideoque commentum illud Enjedini missum facere coacti sunt cæteri, Socinus, Smal- cius, professi voce Dei hic Deum Patrem designari.

Ad (18.) Resp. Nimis jejuna est explicatio illa, quod Christus non rapinam duxerit τὸ εἶναι ἶσα θεῷ, id est, non arripuerit avide occasionem regnandi sibi oblatam. Longe eminentius ἀξίωμα inferri, su- pra ostensum fuit. Aliud esse æqualitatem cum Deo, aliud regnum, vel occasionem regnandi, nemo non videt. Et quis admittet, solum occasionem regnandi habuisse Christum, dum in terris ageret, nec alia ratione τὸ εἶναι ἶσα θεῷ tum habuisse? Quandoquidem omnia data fuerint Filio in ma- nus, Joh. III. 35. XIII. 3. Omnia, inquit Christus Matth. XI. 27. data mihi sunt a Patre. Quid? quod testatus fuerit Christus se juxta cum Patre operari, se æqualem Patri esse, se unum esse cum Patre Joh. V. vers. 17. 18. X. vers. 30. Imperii etiam Judaici occupandi oblatam fuisse Christo occa- sionem nuspiam in Scripturis docetur, sed affine potius est commentis Judaicis de terreno Messiæ imperio. Et quid terrenum ejusmodi regnum ad τὸ εἶναι ἶσα θεῷ? Num qui acceptant imperii ter- reni sceptrum, obtinent τὸ εἶναι ἶσα θεῷ? Sic de Regibus quibusvis id dicendum, non vero Chri- sto proprium erit ἀξίωμα, imo aliis monarchis terrenis tanto eminentius id conveniet, quanto augustiora sunt eorum imperia, quam regnum e- rat judaicum: quod absurdum.

Ad (19.) Magnum omnino est humilitatis ex- emplum; quod cum Christus in forma Dei esset, adeoque natura Deus, non tanquam rapinam hoc undique ostentarit, sibi scilicet esse æqualia Deo, vel τὸ εἶναι ἶσα θεῷ, sed ea majestate semetipsum evacuavit. Quis non obstupescat hanc humilita- tem æterni Dei? Tum vero annon & hoc vere magnum & stupendum est, hominem illum, qui tam abjectus fuit, ut de se diceret, vermis ego, non homo, Psal. XXII. nihil dubitasse, non ex rapina se habere, quod Deus sit, vel se esse verum natura Deum? Imo annon id magnum est, quod homo Deus sit, cujus certe mysterii magnitudo tanta est, ut superet omnem creatum intellectum, atque ideo a Socinianis, qui nihil quod intellectum excedit, credunt, negetur. Est enim ὁμολογημένως μέγα μυστήριον. 1. Tim. III. 16.

Ad (20.) Æqualitas cum Deo per raptum proprie haberi non potest, etsi homo a Satana dementatus per raptum eandem affectaret. Cui rapinæ affectatæ hac loquendi forma, non rapinam duxit, opponi censent nonnulli, quod hoc ἴδιον vere proprium fuerit Christo (quia hæc sibi ἀμέσως opponuntur, aliquid habere ceu rapinam, & habere aliquid non ut rapinam, sed ut naturale, atque proprium) ut sensus sit, secundum explicationem B. Gerhardi: Christum, etsi in statu exinanitionis fuerit novissimus vivorum, non tamen dubitasse, a se hoc minime esse alienum, nec raptum, sed a natura hoc sibi esse proprium, ut sit Deo ἴσ⊕ ἰσοτέρως καὶ ὁμοάσιος. Porro quamvis per communicationis gratiam Christo, qua homo est, conveniat εἶναι αὐτῷ τὰ ἴσα Θεῷ quod ipsi sint æqualia Deo, quod vero citra rationem meriti ei tribuendum, utpote qui sibi nihil, nobis omnia meruit. Id tamen ad illam, quæ jam adducta, interpretationem nihil facit, ideoque eos qui sic explicant, haud ferit: utpote qui de divina natura hæc accipiunt, non vero de communicatione Christo facta secundum humanam naturam. Confer B. Feuerborn. fascic. III. disputat. II. §. 59. sequ. Atque hæc de isto loco classico.

## 2:7
Verse 7. But he emptied himself (Ἀλλὰ ἑαυτὸν ἐκένωσε) הריק. Clearly the same sense as 2 Cor. VIII. 9: "that for your sakes he became poor, being rich" (ὅτι δι᾽ ὑμᾶς ἐπτώχευσε πλούσιος ὤν).

For the needy are called ‎רוקנים (empty) Gen. XXXI. 42, Luke I. 53, Judges XI. 3, where in the Hebrew it is ‎אנשים רוקים, in the Greek, "empty men" (ἄνδρες κενοί), the Latin translates "needy men."

Therefore "he emptied himself" (ἑαυτὸν ἐκένωσεν) is: he willingly led a needy life, Matt. VIII. 20. Grotius explains the emptying (κένωσιν) as referring to external poverty, as it appears; but from the hypothesis, that he was in the form of God, and the antithesis, that he did not count "being equal to God" (τὸ εἶναι ἴσα Θεῷ) as robbery, it is sufficiently clear that this thesis, "he emptied himself" (ἑαυτὸν ἐκένωσεν), implies far greater things. For it refers to those things which pertain to "being in the form of God" (τὸ εἶναι in forma DEI) and "being equal to God" (τὸ εἶναι ἴσα Θεῷ), to the evacuation of divine power and Majesty, by which Christ could have conducted himself as equal to God, as a man in the days of his flesh, which he abdicated by the use of the same, so that he did not wish to openly display it as a robbery.

In order that this may be understood more fully, it must be examined: (1.) According to which nature is the emptying (κένωσις) attributed to Christ? (2.) What kind of emptying (κένωσις) is it? (3.) Of what thing? As to the first question, it must be believed that it is attributed to Christ entirely according to the Human nature. For according to the divine nature the Son of God is entirely unchangeable (ἀναλλοίωτος) and immutable, and therefore a true emptying (κένωσις) does not fall upon him. Calvin and Piscator from the Reformed side acknowledged this, who, as Crocius admits, refer this emptying to the humanity alone. But this does not please Crocius. Why, indeed? Because they make this emptying entirely the same as the humiliation which follows in verse 8, which he says all antiquity distinguishes, and that it is more convenient to the thing itself and to the text. But it is not necessary that we make them entirely the same, even if we attribute both to the Human nature. For the emptying (κένωσις) imports an emptying or evacuation of divine Majesty, but the humiliation (ταπείνωσις) imports a humiliation, which is something divine (Θεϊκόν), just as the former is something privative (ςερητικόν). Nor does Piscator hold these to be entirely the same; rather, he wishes that evacuation to be declared by the Apostle not only through humiliation, but also through the assumption of the form of a servant, and what is connected to it: and in that he appealed not only to Calvin, but also to Wolfgang Musculus and the Genevans, and also in antiquity to Cyprian, and he sufficiently elucidated the convenience of the text.

But he emptied himself, or (if you prefer) he made himself empty. For in the Greek it is not "he out-emptied" (ἐξεκένωσε), but "he emptied" (ἐκένωσε): namely from "to empty" (κενόω), not from "to out-empty" (ἐκκενόω), although by these words, both simple and compound, the same is signified both among the Greeks and among the Latins. But what is "he emptied himself"? That is, he as it were evacuated himself of that divine glory of his, he laid it aside as it were: insofar, namely, as he did not perpetually manifest and exert it. Which the Apostle himself declares in the following words, where he says that Christ emptied himself insofar as he took the form of a servant, that is, a servile, humble, and abject condition. In the margin he has these things: The gloss of the Genevans is interpreted similarly, on Isaiah LII. verse 14. Likewise Cyprian in his sermon on the resurrection of Christ with these words: "The Angelic Spirits perform these paschal joys in the heavens, and admire the glory of the rising Lord, they rejoice and delight in the fact that the form of a servant has returned into the form of GOD, and the emptying of humility has returned to the majesty of the deposited height."

To our argument, that evacuation does not befit an immutable nature, Crocius objects: Certainly an evacuation, which denotes alteration, change, conversion, does not fall upon an immutable nature. What then does it denote here? He answers: The acceptance of the form of a servant. But this is distinguished by the Apostle insofar as the former denotes the emptying of divine Majesty and glory, but the latter denotes the assumption of a servile condition, which are distinguished as a privative and a positive act. And is the assumption of human nature, which Crocius understands through the form of a servant, not one thing, and the emptying of divine Majesty another? He says from his Aretius: "He covered the divine glory as with a garment, and as it were laid it aside": And from Elias of Crete, this emptying of Christ is called the abjection of himself lowering himself to a viler garment, which would befit his Majesty, yet done without any change of it, and the putting on of a human form; And from Leo the Great in his epistle to Flavian, chapter III: "That emptying, by which the invisible made himself visible, and the Creator and Lord of all things willed to be one of the mortals, was an inclination of mercy, not a failure of power."

But the discussion here is not about such an emptying, improperly so called, but about that to which an exaltation properly so called is opposed. Which therefore is also a true and proper emptying. Not about the incarnation, but about the emptying of the incarnate one, not about the covering of the glory of GOD, but about a true emptying (κένωσι) and evacuation, not as if he set it aside, as Aretius says, but Christ truly emptied (ἐκένωσε) himself: just as he was also truly exalted; Which cannot happen without a true change: Since therefore all antiquity understands a true exaltation, and for that reason ascribes it to the human, not the divine nature, a proper emptying cannot be understood in this place, and according to the same nature that the exaltation was made, according to the same must the emptying necessarily be attributed to Christ; Crocius says that Christ did not lay aside his glory by diminishing it, but by suppressing it in the sight of men, having indeed sometimes exerted sparks of Majesty, yet not fully, nor always. But is the assumption of human nature and incarnation one thing, and the suppression of glory in the sight of men and the not full nor perpetual exertion of Majesty another? And does the divine nature of the Son suppress and not always exert its Majesty? Must not the same be said of the Father, and of the Holy Spirit, whose works ad extra are common with the Son of GOD? Therefore this emptying (κένωσις) is to be attributed not to the divine nature, which cannot be changed, but to the Human, which did not always exert its Majesty, which he possessed not indeed as transfused, as Piscator, accusing our opinion, falsely imputes heresy to us, but communicated by the power of the personal union, Col. II, ver. 9.

That the inclination of mercy is one thing, and the κένωσις or emptying of Majesty is another, is too clear. Crocius rashly appeals here to our blessed Gesner, who, on page 253 concerning the person of Christ, admits indeed some improper emptying of the Word, especially because he rested in the passion of the flesh, as Irenaeus and Theodorus speak, but immediately adds that the Humanity of Christ is emptied and evacuated in a far different way, and explains the present κένωσις concerning it, since the divine nature is ἄτρεπτος, and thus can in no way admit such an evacuation.

What properly is this κένωσις?

If, therefore, II. it be asked, What properly is this κένωσις, it is not (1.) ἀδένωσις, annihilation: For the Apostle does not say he annihilated, but he emptied. (2.) Nor is it the incarnation itself, because the emptying ceased through exaltation, which cannot be said of the incarnation or manifestation in the flesh. (3.) Nor is it that condescension by which the Son of GOD lowered himself to the vileness of our body, for by that reason he did not lay aside his Majesty, nor diminish it in any way.

That inclination was, we say with Leo, one of mercy, not a defect or κένωσις of power. (4.) It is not a dissolution or breaking of the union, or a cessation, or abdication, or removal of the communication of Majesty: For the union could never be dissolved, nor exist without the communication of Majesty.

The fullness of divine Majesty remained, whose rays often appeared even in the state of emptying.

(5.) It is not a hiding or mere concealment of Majesty, as if he had used his Majesty indeed but secretly, but a true emptying, just as the humiliation is true, not merely such κατὰ δόκησιν (according to appearance). (6.) It is not a simulation, but a most profound and most real emptying, which the most real and profound humiliation of Christ absolutely required.

(7.) It is not a removal of all use or exercise whatsoever, but it is a spontaneous and free abdication and evacuation of the plenary, perpetual, and incessant use of divine Majesty.

And thus Ambrose explains this passage: Christ, that he might teach the law of humility, not only did not resist the Jews who were seizing him, but emptied himself, that is, he withdrew his power from the work, so that it might seem to be weakened by the idleness of humility.

The blessed Chemnitius, in the cited place, explained this word with the preceding phrase thus: Because he was sent, that he might become a victim for the human race in infirmities, passions, and death, therefore he did not wish, contrary to his calling, to display his Majesty in the flesh and through the flesh, and to seize its use contrary to the will and mission of God, as if by robbery and force, but he yielded and emptied himself of his own accord by his own right; that is, he concealed, withdrew, and caused to rest the usurpation and effusion of his divine glory and power in the flesh and through the flesh. But lest there be introduced here, in place of the evacuation of the plenary use of Majesty, only a concealment of the same, as if Majesty indeed had stripped itself in the flesh always and everywhere, especially in incessant dominion but secretly, the emphasis of the word κένωσις stands in the way.

For he did not say he hid, but he emptied; and indeed himself, so that that emptying might obtain in Christ himself, not only by reason of us, not κατὰ δόκησιν, according to the opinion of men, but κατ' ἀλήθειαν, according to the truth of the matter.

The comparison of exaltation stands in the way. For even in that state he keeps the plenary acts of divine Majesty hidden, while we still await his appearing. The scope of the Apostle stands in the way, because one could thus humble himself apparently and secretly, who nevertheless would truly rule over others and exalt himself.

The truth of the emptying stands in the way, for he had to be emptied not apparently and only in our eyes, but truly and in the eyes of GOD; whereas, according to that concealment, he would have been glorious in the state of emptying in the eyes of God, and obscure only to men. The end of the emptying stands in the way, because he himself did not seize, but man seized, or attempted to seize, which in divine judgment, in which the will is taken for the act, is considered to have been seized, since even in human judgment the attempt at robbery is sometimes held as robbery.

Therefore, the true work of emptying was that which he could have held as a prize, but for our sake he did not wish to: a true impoverishment and deposition of the riches of his glory, as far as the plenary use is concerned, an evacuation of all his opulence. For Christ, the second Adam, had to abdicate himself from all that for our sake, which the first Adam (and we in him) seized.

But he seized and wished to rob the use of divine Majesty. If you say, he should have also abdicated himself from the possession of Majesty itself: I answer, he had to abdicate himself from all that he could abdicate. But he could not abdicate the possession without the dissolution of the union, Col. II, ver. 9. Which, that he might abdicate, the office of Mediator and the propitiation required, but the office did not permit the abdication of Majesty itself; for thus it would not have sufficed for expiating sins, for paying for our robbery, for conquering Satan, for satisfying divine justice, for which works divine power was needed, and he had to remain always King and Priest, even if he did not always exercise these offices.

As to the third question: Of what thing is the κένωσις designated here? As to the third question: Of what thing is the κένωσις designated here? The answer is clear from the text: in one word: The plenary use of Deiformity and Majesty (ἰσοθεότης). For as far as the possession is concerned, because the communication of that Majesty is a consequence of the personal union, by which the Human nature of Christ was in the form of GOD, and was not indeed in no way GOD, yet there were to him things equal, that is, equal to GOD: because of the breath of humility and the business of our redemption, he did not use that Majesty, and it is said that Christ emptied himself regarding this use, to the full exercise of which he had emptied himself.

That this Majesty is truly divine and infinite, we prove in the Examination of Reformed Doctrine concerning the person of Christ, and we show that divine omnipotence, omniscience, omnipresence, and the glory of adoration pertain to the same.

Wherefore the blessed Dannhaver, in the cited place, answers not unaptly: Why did he empty himself?

Not by the mere repulsion of enemies. For thus God also rested: But by Deiformity (not of the fullness of deity, but) of the fullness (Eph. IV, ver.

10), which is properly of the emptying, that is, of the plenary, universal, constant, and incessant use of Deiformity, not that he never used it, but that he did not use it always, but only then, as often as it was expedient by reason of his offices. Which he proves both from the connection of the context in this way: He who emptied himself of the most plenary state and gesture of divine glory, he withdrew the plenary and catholic use of his glory.

But Christ emptied himself in this manner; and from the end of the union, which is his propitiatory or restorative work, which Christ did not seize, but which the first parents attempted to seize. Whence he concludes thus on page 706: He who solves all Adamic robbery by the fulfillment of the contrary, he expiates the affected omniscience, omnipotence, omnipresence, dominion, worship, by contrary retribution, the wisdom of Catholic usage through voluntary ignorance; power through contrary infirmity; presence through local circumscription; opulence through contrary poverty; dominion through servitude; the worship of adoration through abjection below the Angels: Yet thus stands the solution and payment of Christ. Furthermore, the blessed Dannhauer argues thus on page 707. Christ had emptied himself of all that could impede the end of the incarnation. Thus, many men often abdicate rights due to them, lest they be frustrated in their intention. Now, not only the repulsion of enemies and injuries inflicted in the passion could impede our Savior Christ (if this were enough for the emptying, it is little short of saying that the very Deity itself, resting, could have been emptied), but everything which, while it remained, would not have been fully satisfied for us, nor the Adamic rapine fully expiated, if, however secretly, yet truly and in the second act, he had vibrated the Catholic rays of his glory. Μορφὴ δούλου λαβὼν)

made similar to servants, who possess nothing of their own. Here a διαστολὴ (distinction) must be placed: for now he has begun to [speak of] other things that are ἀντίθετοι (opposed). Ἐν ὁμοιώματι ἀνθρώπων γενόμενος) Since he was similar to men, namely to those first ones, that is, devoid of sin, 2 Cor. 5, verse 21. Καὶ σχήματι εὑρεθεὶς ὡς ἄνθρωπος) σχῆμα here is ἀξίωμα, a conspicuous dignity, as often among the Greeks, which word the Syrian here preserved, and ἐγεεῖ: it is אדםם he was seen, ὡς ἄνθρωπος כָּאָדָם as Adam, who is the first man.

In dignity he appeared such as Adam, that is, in dominion over all creatures, in the sea, winds, bread, water; for which reason, that which had been said of Adam in Psalm 8 is applied mystically to Christ. Ἑαυτὸν ἐκένωσε) he did not conduct himself according to that dignity, but very humbly, so that he even washed the feet of the disciples, John 13, 12, 13. As he emptied himself, so he humbled himself; they are forms of Hiphil, but they signify to exhibit or show oneself as such. Thus also the Latins say: To make oneself common. Γενόμενος ὑπήκοος μέχρι θανάτου) he was made obedient, namely to men, as much to Jews as to Romans.

He did not oppose that divine force to those seizing him, condemning him, killing him. He willingly endured such injuries for the good of the human race. Θανάτου δὲ σταυροῦ)

Which punishment is both extremely atrocious (for thence also to torture and torture) and most despised. Appian, Civil Wars, book 1: they were hanged to death. A servant in Plautus: I know that the cross will be my sepulcher.

This is a new distinction, and a new gloss, which easily comes to no one's mind, except Grotius.

It means this: that there are two opposites; the first, that he was in the form of GOD, and emptied himself, made similar to servants, who possess nothing of their own; the second, that he did not boast of divine power, that is, to be looked upon as God, when he was similar to the Protoplasts, he did not conduct himself according to that dignity, but very humbly, whence he was also made in the form of an obedient one. But whence will such a distinction, whence those two opposites be proven? Whence will faith be reconciled to those newly invented glosses? For that αὐτὸς ἒφα (he himself said it) has no place here, nor does the idia ἐπίλυσις (private interpretation). Furthermore, that first opposition is vain.

For to the 'being in the form of God' is not opposed that poverty, through which, made a humble servant, he possesses nothing of his own, since that first member of the opposition infers divine power in Christ according to Grotius, which is not opposed by the emptying of possessions and of one's own faculties, and the poverty of servants, but the emptying of that divine power and of the fullness of all power, and thus is inferred the evacuation of the public and plenary use of 'being equal to God,' and also the assumption of the servile form.

For in two ways the opposite member is described . ἐπητικῶς (in a way of addition) through the emptying already explained. θετικῶς (in a way of position) and that (1) generally through the taking of the servile form, by which form of a servant, not human nature, as such, is immediately understood. For this pertains to the subject, which is Christ Jesus, which name brings in the 'both together,' but that is to be referred to the predicate; and therefore the servile status and condition is noted. Just as by the form of God, not the divine nature is immediately designated, but the divine status, in which Christ was according to human nature: So also by the form of a servant, the form of a servant is the servile status, not indeed the human nature itself immediately understood, although it is entirely presupposed, since that servile status falls upon nothing but human nature. This is understood by the form of a servant, which befits the status of emptying, and in the status of exaltation no longer has a place.

For through it Christ was made Lord, Acts 2, 36, and receives a name above every name, with which servitude and the name of a servant cannot consist. That assumption is designated here, which could be for us an example of the humility of the son, that we might imitate it.

But the assumption of human nature, how can it be imitable for us? Add that the Apostle refers the form of a servant to the status of emptying.

For after he names the emptying, he adds the assumption of the servile form. (6.) Crocius has it thus here: How did he accept the form of a servant?

Made similar to men, and found in habit as a man, v. 7 and 8. But these do not pertain to the incarnation, but to the status of emptying, as will be said later. Ambrose interprets the form of a servant thus: Accepting the form of a servant, while he is held and bound, and driven by lashes even to the cross, made obedient to the Father, to whom he made himself equal.

He does not defend equality for himself, but subjected himself. He teaches us this patience and humility, that we not only do not prefer ourselves to our equals, but even incline ourselves, having followed the example of our author.

But he is not said to have accepted the form of God, but to be in the form of God.

But he is said to have accepted the form of a servant, while he is humbled as if a sinner. But servants are made from sin, just as Cham, the daughter of Noah, who first deservedly accepted the name of servant.

For it does not seem to me, as it seems to some, that he thus accepted the form of a servant, while he was born a man. For see what he says: Think this in yourselves, which is also in Christ Jesus, that is, God and man.

Thus St. Cyprian expounded it, cited above. So also Calvin, Musculus, the Genevan, and Piscator interpret: His words will be these: The Apostle says that Christ emptied himself insofar as he took the form of a servant, that is, a servile, humble and abject condition: as he further declares with the following words, that he was made in the likeness of men, that is, similar to common men, subject indeed to all the infirmities of the human race, sin alone excepted, so that he hungered, thirsted, slept, was grieved; and which he himself further declares v. 8, saying: And σχήματι, that is, figure or habit (Luber. or Gebärden) found as a man. There it is to be noted, that the Apostle takes these words μορφῇ, ὁμοιώματι, σχήματι in the same signification.

Whence it is clearly perceived that by 'form' here, nature or essence is not to be understood. Add Matth. Martini in Spicil. p. 164. What is said of the form, he says, of a servant, I do not understand simply as human nature, but his vile condition, which was for a time.

For the rest, we do not deny that human nature is mediately inferred, because unless Christ were true man, the form of a servant would not befit him. For that form of a servant was not an idea of some sort, fluttering in the air, but required a true man. as the subject, in which it truly was. Whence Blessed Feurbornius notes that three modes of the servile form are found. 1. When someone is a servant, yet does not conduct himself as a servant, but as Lord or God. Such are all the sons of Adam, who all ought to be servants of GOD, but wish to be GODS, Gen. II. & III. 2. When someone is a servant, and conducts himself as a servant. Just as good servants do in the world, but before God all the pious, who are subject to God, serve as servants. 3. When someone is not indeed a servant, yet conducts himself as a servant, as if a King were to minister to his own in the world. Before God no one did this, except Christ. Conf. Job XIII. 4. These things Feurbornius and Blessed Luther l. c. p. 110. What Crocius objects, with Eph. LIII. that Christ is called a servant, not only to indicate status, but also nature, helps nothing. For it is one thing to assume the form of a servant, another to come in the name of a servant. There the servile condition is assumed, here indeed he is called a servant from the servile condition, but it is held not as an abstract but as a concrete name.

Nor is the same true of the passages in Isaiah ch. LIII. v. 13. ch. XLII. 1. 4. Ezek. XXXII. v. 23. & Zech. III. v. 8. with the present reasoning. For this name is sometimes that of the office of Mediator, for the accomplishing of which the Son of God was sent, which he executed in the days of his flesh, which befits Christ by reason of both natures; conf. Job X. 18. ch. XVII. v. 4. Ps. XL. 9. Is. XLIII. v. 24. Matt. XX. 28. but when it is of the servile condition, humble & abject, it is significant, and is attributed to Christ by reason of human nature in the state of exinanition.

Nor does the received song of Blessed Luther help at all: 30g ein eins Knechtes leib gering, because it means nothing else than that in the incarnation the form & condition of a servant immediately began, but not that the assumption of the form of a servant is the incarnation itself. For it is one thing to be a body of servile condition and status in general, another to assume the form of a servant. There the body, which was assumed, is described both by reason of substance, and by reason of status and condition, and it is intimated that the servile status began immediately with the incarnation itself, and that that humble form and condition is not separated from it at any moment of time, but here only the vile condition is expressed, even if the body or human nature is necessarily supposed, as that which assumed that form of a servant, so that nevertheless formally and by moments of nature the incarnation and the assumption of the form of a servant are distinguished.

The mind of Blessed Luther is sufficiently understood from other places. And Crocius himself acknowledges that Blessed Luther explains somewhere, as Hunnius, Menzer, and most other Lutherans do, concerning the mere servile condition which Christ the man had already assumed; nor does he himself deny that the servile condition which Christ underwent is noted; but he denies that the mere servile condition is noted in such a way that the human nature itself is not simultaneously comprehended by the same word, and thus he understands the essence and human nature as whole, namely consisting of a true soul and a true body, not naked, however, but clothed with all its essential and natural properties, and subject to all common blameless defects.

But human nature clothed with essential properties, and those common blameless defects do not necessarily cohere. For that was without these in our first Parents; but these were freely assumed by Christ for the sake of our salvation: Nor is it permitted to attribute the form of a servant to Christ in the state of glory, where he nevertheless retains a true human nature.

Wiederumb knechtisch oder dienstlich gestalt seyn, ist, says Blessed Luther, the best interpreter of his own words, to show oneself with words and deeds toward others as a servant. Which Christ did, when he served among the disciples, and gave himself for us, yet also not like other Saints, who are servants by nature, but it was an assumed thing with him, for our good and as an example, that we also ought to do likewise toward others, and to divest ourselves of our Divine Form.

Nor do Philippus or Blessed Simon Pauli, to whom Crocius rashly appeals, understand it otherwise. Furthermore, whether by servant here a slave is understood, Blessed Feurbornius discusses against Oforodus who affirms it, l. c. p. 113. (2.) Specifically the form of a servant is explained both by ὁμοίωμα the likeness of other men, understand, as regards all the infirmities of the body, yet devoid of sin; and by σχῆμα the figure or habit of men as regards common conversation and familiar association, where all things were servile, abject & vile, except that sometimes certain rays of divine Majesty shone forth. For if you ask, how he assumed the form of a servant? Paul replies, γενόμενον ἐν ὁμοιώματι ἀνθρώπων, made in the likeness of men, καὶ σχῆματι εὑρεθεὶς ὡς ἄνθρωπος, and in habit found as a man. Therefore, by this likeness and figure (1.) the Human nature of Christ itself is not understood, as the Calvinists wish, for he is not only like men, or assumed an ὁμοίαν nature with us; nor was he only found ὡς ἄνθρωπος, as a man, or in the schema and figure of a man, but he was a true man like us in all things.

That is not the Apostle's purpose, what Christ was by reason of essence, but how he conducted himself at the time of exinanition, namely that of his own accord and most free will he was made ὁμοιοπαθής to us, and in the conversation of his life, he provided an example of humility, patience, gentleness, mercy, obedience. Conf. Heb. II. 17. ch. IV. v. 15. Nor (2.) is ὁμοίωμα & σχῆμα to be twisted with Marcion, so that in place of the truth of nature a mere figure and phantasm is introduced.

For this destroys the work of redemption, and likeness denotes not appearance only, but a true and real likeness Gen. I. v. 26. when Adam was created in the image and likeness of GOD; ch. V. v. 3. when he is said to have begotten Seth in his own image and likeness. Nor (3.) was Christ made in the likeness of men, because he was like the first parents.

For here it is indicated by no word that the first parents are referred to. By what right then can they be foisted upon the text, which are insinuated by no iota in the whole context: The discourse is about men in general, to whom he is said to have been made like.

No one can gather from this mode of speaking that Christ is intimated to be without sin, and by that reason designated as similar to the Protoplasts, nor is he said in the figure to have been found as Adam the first man, but indefinitely, as any man whatever. It is not a matter of the dignity of a Lord, but rather of servile condition. Deiformity & ἰσοτιμία with GOD, asserted already before, vers. 6., there is no cause why it should here be brought forward anew; moreover the Apostle uses the word ὁμοιώματι ἀνθρώπων, to signify the likeness with men of any other kind, with whom he is said not to be the same but similar, because it is not a matter of identity of nature, but of similarity with respect to accidental infirmities of the body, with respect to which he is similar to us.

For although they seem to be of the same genus, they ought rather to be considered similar; since the syntajilla (disgrace) , not from nature, as it is now after the fall, corrupted by sin, in necessity, redounded in Christ, but were assumed by the freedom of the oikonomia (dispensation); in which manner he was not similar, but dissimilar to the first Parents; For they contracted those infirmities through sin, of which Christ was clearly devoid. Furthermore, that Adam had dominion over all creatures, over the sea, the winds, etc., and that this is said of Adam according to the letter of Psalm 8, and mystically applied to Christ, Grotius falsely assumes, the contrary of which has been shown at Psalm 8.

Therefore, the Grotian gloss is merely precarious, and altogether alien to the mind of the Holy Spirit, that he was found in the schema (form) as a man, that is, in the dignity of the lord Adam; Which also has no place for this reason, that the dominion of Christ is far more sublime, and embraces all power in heaven and on earth, and that Christ was exalted to that not before his humiliation, but after it.

To say nothing of the fact that a common and ordinary man is sometimes called simply 'man' not without emphasis, as Psalm 22, verse 7;

Judges 16, verse 2, 15; whereas, on the contrary, an eminent man is not only called 'man', but 'man of God'; see Deut. 23, verse 1; 1 Kings 13, verse 4; 1 Tim. 3, verse 11. Nor did the ancients note without reason that Paul said, 'in the likeness of men', to indicate that Christ was not a mere man, that not all things of Christ and ours are equal, but that Christ had certain singular things, such as that he is theotetos (God-begotten), that he was not born from the cohabitation of man and woman, that he is anamartetos (sinless).

That these things pertain to expressing the state of emptying is beyond doubt among all Interpreters.

Therefore, by schema (form), in which Christ was found as a man, most of our people understand habit and gesture, and the common manner of living, because he ate, drank, slept, hungered, walked, etc., after the manner of other men, and in all things was found in such an external habit as another man.

That schema (form) is neglected and despised, which Heinsius in the New Testament observes to be noted among the LXX Interpreters from Isaiah 3, verse 17. The schema (form) of this world, 1 Cor. 7, verse 31, is called the external appearance of the world, empty and vain, offering no solid happiness; it is agreed that schema (form) in general denotes habit, gesture, appearance. But he is said to have been 'found', and it is not added by whom he was found: namely, by all who saw him in the days of his flesh.

Whence also he was held by most as a common man, even though by sermons and miracles he showed himself as the only-begotten Son of God and true God.

And Calvin confesses that Paul here commemorates that he was as an abject man and of common lot in habit.

Piscator notes that the Apostle takes these words morphe (form), homoioma (likeness), schema (form) in the same signification, and hence concludes that by morphe (form) one should not understand nature and essence, and proves Luther's interpretation of schema (form), as 'Gebärden' (gestures).

From which it is clear that the particle 'as' is not taken here in a bebaiotiko (confirmatory) sense, as Grotius wishes with others like Bullinger, Beza, and Zanchius, but that it retains its more usual signification, which the word schema (form) and homoioma (likeness) altogether demand.

There succeeds therefore in order the third degree of emptying.

The first was the form of God, kenosis (emptying) or evacuation. The second was the form of a servant, lepsis (taking) or assumption, which the Apostle has just explained. The third is tapeinosis (humiliation) or that extreme humiliation, by which Christ humbled himself especially in his passion, which is here specially regarded. For it is added, 'becoming obedient unto death' .

But that obedience is not designated by which he subjected himself as much to the Jews as to the Romans, as Grotius wishes, but he is understood as having been made obedient to GOD the Father, which happened both in the active obedience, by which he subjected himself to the law and fulfilled it for us, and in the passive obedience, by which he willed to subject himself to passions and to death itself.

This twofold obedience shone forth in Christ throughout his whole life, but most especially in his passion, in the painful week.

Where indeed he subjected himself to both Jews and Romans willingly and freely;

But by these words directly, 'he was made obedient', it is not hinted as if it refers consequently to the obedience which he had to perform not to men but to the Father, because, forsooth, the Father had given this command to him, John 10, verse 19, and this was the will of the Father, Psalm 40, verse 7; John 5, verse 39; chap. 6, verse 38; chap. 8, verse 54, 55; chap. 12, verse 49; chap. 14, verse 31; chap. 17, verse 4; Luke 22, verse 41. Nor did he subject himself to men only by the will of the Father, but as the blessed Luther warned in the cited place, even to sin, death, and Satan.

He says 'unto death', not because obedience was not performed when he willed to be buried and to remain in the sepulchre and in the state of death for three days, but because the death of the cross is the extreme degree of humiliation, in which he was made a curse, and complained of desertion by GOD, and was liable to infernal punishments, and because death also embraces the state of death, or at least brings it on.

Concerning that extreme degree of obedience unto the death of the cross, Chrysostom exclaims in this place: 'Papa! how great and vehemently ineffable it is that he was made a servant!

But that he also endured death is much more. But there is also something else greater than this and much more admirable; Wherefore?

Because not every death is like this one. For this one seemed the most shameful of all, that one full of honor, this one cursed. For cursed is everyone who hangs on a cross, Deut. 21, verse 23.' But the extreme degree is called that external death, which the added determination of 'the death of the cross' indicates, even if the deepest humiliation was situated in the sense of infernal pains, because here the Apostle deals with external things, and did not touch upon the internal passions of the soul, although they are comprehended in the scope of the same general word etapeinosen (he humbled himself), and that he was made hypekoos (obedient), nay, as we have said, are designated by the death of the cross.

They pertain indeed most especially to tapeinosis (humiliation) and also to hypakoen (obedience), Psalm 40, verse 3;

Psalm 69, verse 1, 2, 16; and in the punishment of the cross they are comprehended on account of the curse added to it, because by undergoing that he was made for us katara (a curse), Gal. 3, verse 13. This obedience befits Christ according to his Human nature, concerning which Damascenus, book 3, de orthod. fide, chap.

14: 'He was made obedient to the Father as Lord, not according to what he is GOD, but according to what he is man.

For according to what he is GOD, he is neither obedient nor disobedient. For these are things of subjects.'

Latin:

Vers. 7. Ἀλλὰ ἑαυτὸν ἐκένωσε) הריק Plane idem sensus, qui 2. Cor. VIII. 9. ὅτι δι᾽ ὑμᾶς ἐπτώχευσε πλούσιος ὤν.

Nam inopes dicuntur ‎רוקנים‏ Gen. XXXI. 42. Luc. I. 53. Jud. XI. 3. ubi in Ebræo est ‎אנשים רוקים‏ Græco, ἄνδρες κενοί, Latinus vertit viri inopes.

Itaque ἑαυτὸν ἐκένωσιν est, libenter duxit vitam inopem, Matth. VIII. 20. De externa, ut apparet, paupertate κένωσιν explicat Grotius, at ex ὑποθέσει, quod fuerit in forma Dei, & ἀντιθέσει, quod non rapinam duxerit τὸ εἶναι ἴσα Θεῷ, satis liquet, longe majora hanc Θέσιν, ἑαυτὸν ἐκένωσεν, inferre. Respicit enim ea, quæ spectant ad τὸ εἶναι in forma DEI, & τὸ εἶναι ἴσα Θεῷ, ad evacuationem divinæ potentiæ & Majestatis, qua se Deo æqualiter gerere poterat Christus, ut homo in diebus carnis, quod usu ejusdem sese abdicaret, ita ut palam eandem instar rapinæ ostentui ducere noluerit.

Quod ut intelligatur plenius dispiciendum (1.) Secundum quam naturam κένωσις Christo tribuatur? (2.) Qualis κένωσις sit? (3.) Cujus rei? Quod ad primum quæsitum, secundum Humanam naturam eam Christo omnino tribui credendum est. Nam secundum divinam naturam Filius Dei prorsus est ἀναλλοίωτος & immutabilis, ideoque vera κένωσις in eum non cadit. Agnovere id e Reformatis Calvinus & Piscator, qui hanc inanitionem, fatente Crocio, ad solam humanitatem referunt. Non autem id placet Crocio. Cur vero? Quod illi hanc inanitionem prorsus eandem faciant cum humiliatione, quæ sequitur v.8. quam totam antiquitatem distinguere ait, idque rei ipsi, & textui convenientius. Sed non est, ut plane eandem faciamus, etsi utramque naturæ Humanæ tribuamus. Nam κένωσις divina Majestatis inanitionem, vel evacuationem, ταπείνωσις vero humiliationem, quæ Θεϊκόν quid, ut illa ςερητικόν quid importat. Neque Piscator hæc pro iisdem prorsus habet; imo evacuationem illam non modo per humiliationem, sed etiam per formæ servi assumptionem, & quæ illi connexa sunt, ab Apostolo declarari vult: Et in eo non ad Calvinum tantum, sed etiam ad Wolffgangum Musculum & Genevenses, nec non in antiquitate ad Cyprianum provocavit, ac convenientiam textus satis dilucidavit.

Sed seipsum exinanivit, vel (si mavis) inanivit. Nam in Græco non est ἐξεκένωσε, sed ἐκένωσε: Nempe a κενόω, non ab ἐκκενόω, quanquam istis verbis & simplici & composito tum apud Græcos, tum apud Latinos idem significatur. Quid autem est exinanivit se? id est, gloria illa sua divina se quasi evacuavit, illam veluti deposuit: quatenus scilicet eam non perpetuo manifestavit atque exeruit. Quod ipsum verbis sequentibus declarat Apostolus, ubi ait, Christum se exinanivisse, quatenus formam servi suscepit, id est, conditionem servilem, humilem & abjectam. Ad marginem hæc habet: Similiter interpretatur glossa Genevensium, ad Es. LII. vers. 14. Item Cyprianus sermone de resurrectione Christi his verbis: Agunt in cœlestibus hæc paschalia gaudia Angelici Spiritus, & resurgentis Domini gloriam admirantur, latantur & delectantur in eo, quod forma servi reversa sit in formam DEI, & exinanitio humilitatis ad depositæ altitudinis redierit majestatem.

Ad argumentum nostrum, evacuatio non competit naturæ immutabili, excipit Crocius: Certe evacuatio, quæ alterationem, immutationem, conversionem notet, in naturam immutabilem non cadit. Quid ergo hic notat? Respondet: Acceptionem formæ servi. Sed hæc distinguitur ab Apostolo hactenus, quod illa Majestatis & gloriæ divinæ inanitionem, hæc autem servilis conditionis assumptionem notet, quæ ut actus privativus & positivus discriminantur. Et annon aliud est naturæ humanæ assumptio, quam per formam servi intelligit Crocius, aliud Majestatis divinæ inanitio. Dicit ex Aretio suo: Carne velut veste texit divinam gloriam, & quasi deposuit: Et ex Elia Cretensi, appellatur hæc inanitio Christi abjectio se demittentis ad indumentum vilius, quæ ipsius Majestati conveniret, citra tamen mutationem ejus ullam facta humanæque formæ indutio; Et ex Leone M. in epist. ad Flavian. cap. III. Exinanitio illa, qua se invisibilis visibilem præbuit, & Creator ac Dominus omnium rerum unus voluit esse mortalium, inclinatio fuit miserationis, non defectio potestatis.

Verum de exinanitione tali improprie ita dicta hic sermo non est, sed de ea, cui opponitur exaltatio proprie dicta. Quæ proinde etiam vera & propria est exinanitio. Non de incarnatione, sed de incarnati exinanitione, non de tegumento gloriæ DEI, sed de vera κένωσι & evacuatione, non quasi seposuit, ut Aretius, sed vere ἐκένωσε Christus: quemadmodum vere etiam exaltatus est; Quod sine mutatione vera fieri non potest: Quum ergo tota antiquitas exaltationem veram intelligat, eamque ideo humanæ, non divinæ naturæ adscribat, non potest exinanitio propria hoc loco intelligi, & secundum quam naturam exaltatio facta, secundum eandem exinanitio Christo necessario tribuenda est; Dicit Crocius, Christum gloriam suam non minuendo, sed supprimendo in hominum conspectu deposuisse, scintillas Majestatis quidem interdum exeruisse, non tamen plene, nec semper. Sed annon aliud est humana naturæ assumptio, & incarnatio, aliud gloriæ in hominum conspectu suppressio, & Majestatis non plena nec perpetua exertio. Et num divina natura Filii supprimit nec semper exerit Majestatem suam? Annon idem de Patre, & Spiritu sancto dicendum erit, cujus utriusque opera ad extra cum Filio DEI sunt communia? Ideo non divinæ naturæ, quæ mutari nequit, sed Humanæ ista κένωσις tribuenda, quæ nö exeruit semper Majestatem suam, quam non quidem transfusam, ut Piscator nostram criminator sententiam, haeresin nobis affingens, sed vi unionis personalis communicatam possidebat, Col. II, vers. 9.

Aliud esse inclinationem miserationis, aliud κένωσιν vel inanitionem Majestatis, nimis luculentum est. Ad Beat. Gesnerum nostrum temere hic provocat Crocius, qui de persona Christi pagin. 253. impropriam quidem aliquam λόγῳ exinanitionem, maxime quod in passione carnis quieverit, ut ex Irenaeo, Theodor. loquitur, admittit, sed actutum subjicit, Humanitatem Christi longe aliter exinaniri & evacuari, ac de ea praesentem κένωσιν explicat, siquidem divina natura ἄτρεπτος sit, adeoque evacuationem ejusmodi nullo modo admittere possit.

Quidnam proprie fit haec κένωσις? Si ergo II.

Quidnam proprie fit haec κένωσιν, quaeratur, non est illa (1.) ἀδένωσις, annihilatio: Non enim dicit Apostolus ἀδένωσε, sed ἐκένωσε. (2.) Nec est ipsa ἐνσάρκωσις, quia exinanitio cessavit per exaltationem, quod de incarnatione vel Φανερώσει in carne dici nequit. (3.) Nec est συγκατάβασις illa, qua sese Filius DEI ad vilitatem corporis nostri demisit, nam ea ratione Majestatem suam non deposuit, nec ulla ratione imminuit.

Inclinatio illa fuit, dicimus cum Leone, miserationis, non defectio vel κένωσις potestatis. (4.) Non est λύσις vel solutio unionis, vel cessatio, aut abdicatio, vel ἀφαίρεσις communicationis Majestatis: Nam nec unio solvi umquam potuit, nec esse fine communicatione Majestatis.

Maufit τὸ πλήρωμα divinae Majestatis, cujus radii saepe in ipso exinanitionis statu apparuerunt.

(5.) Non est κρύψις vel mera Majestatis occultatio, quasi plane quidem sed latenter Majestatem suam usurparit, sed vera inanitio, aeque uti vera est humiliatio, non κατὰ δόκησιν tantum talis. (6.) Non est simulatio quadam, sed profundissima & realissima inanitio, quam requirebat omnino realissima & profundissima Christi humiliatio.

(7.) Non est remotio omnis omnino usus vel χρήσεως, sed est, spontanea & libera usus plenarii, perpetui & incessantis Majestatis divinae abdicatio, & evacuatio.

Atque ita explicat Ambrosius hunc locum: Christus ut humilitatis legem doceres, Judaeis se comprehendentibus non solum non repugnavit, sed semetipsum exinanivit, hoc est, potestatem suam ab opere retraxit, ut humilitatis otiose virtute infirmari videretur. Beat.

Chemnitius loco citato hanc vocem cum phrasi praecedenti sic exposuit: Quia missus erat, ut infirmatibus, passionibus, ac morte fieret victima pro genere humano, ideo non voluit contra vocationem Majestatem suam in carne ac per carnem ostentare, & ejus usurpationem contra Dei voluntatem & missionem, quasi per rapinam & vim arripere, sed sponte jure suo cessit ac exinanivit, se, hoc est, usurpationem & effusionem divinae suae gloriae & potentiae in carne & per carnem occultavit, retraxit, & quiescere fecit. Ne autem ingeratur hic loco evacuationis usus plenarii Majestatis occultatio tantum ejusdem, quasi exuerit se quidem Majestas in carne semper & ubique, imprimis in dominio incessanti sed occulte, obstat vocis κένωσις emphasis.

Non enim dixit ἔκρυψεν occultavit, sed ἐκένωσεν inanivit; & quidem ἑαυτὸν, ut in ipso Christo, non ratione nostri tantum inanitio illa obtineat, non κατὰ δόκησιν, secundum opinionem hominum, sed κατ' ἀλήθειαν, secundum rei veritatem. Obstat exaltationis collatio.

Nam etiam in illa actus divinae Majestatis plenarios clam habet, nobis adhucejus ἐπιφάνειαν expectantibus. Obstat scopus Apostoli, quia sic humiliare sese quis posset apparenter & latenter, qui tamen vere super alios dominaretur, seque exaltaret.

Obstat veritas inanitionis, non enim apparenter, & in oculis tantum nostris, sed vere & in oculis DEI debuit inaniri; quum contra juxta κρύψιν illam in statu κενώσεως in oculis Dei gloriosus fuisset, nec nisi hominibus obscurus. Obstat finis κενώσεως, quod non rapuit ipse, sed quod rapuit homo, vel rapere attentavit, quod in judicio divino, in quo voluntas habetur pro actu, rapuisse censetur, quum etiam in judicio humano captatio ad raptum raptus quandoque habeatur.

Vera ergo κενώσεως opus fuit ejus, quod poterat ceu ἁρπαγμὸν ἡγῆσαι, nostri autem causa noluit: vera depauperatione ac divitiarum gloriae suae, quantum ad usum plenarium, depositione, omni opulentiae suae evacuatione. Omni enim illo sese abdicare debuit Christus, secundus Adam, nostri causa, quod primus Adam (& nos in ipso) captavit.

Captavit autem & rapere voluit Majestatis divinae usum. Si dicas, ita etiam abdicare se debuisset possessione ipsa Majestatis: Resp. omni illo se abdicare debuit, quod potuit abdicare. Κτῆσιν autem non potuit fine solutione unionis, Coloss. II, vers. 9.
