Quod ut abdicaret, requisivit officium Mediatorum & ἱλασικὸν, at Majestatis ipsius abdicationen non permittebat officium; ita enim non suffecisset expiandis peccatis, luendae rapinae nostrae, vincendo Satane, satisfaciendo justitiae divinae, ad quae opus erat divina virtute, ac manere semper debuit Rex & Sacerdos, etsi non semper fungeretur hisce muneribus. Quod ergo ad III. quaesitum: Cujusnam rei κένωσις hic designetur?

Quod ergo ad III. quaesitum: Cujusnam rei κένωσις hic designetur? e textu responsio patet: uno verbo: Usus Deiformitatis & Majestatis ἰσοθεότητος plenarii. Nam quod ad κτῆσιν attinet, quia consequens unionis personalis est communicatio Majestatis illius, qua Humana Christi natura erat in forma DEI, & nequaquam quidem DEO fuit, erant tamen ipsi τὰ ἴσα, hoc est, aequalia DEO: ob statum humilitatis, & negotium redemptionis nostrae ea Majestate usa non est, quod ad plenum ejus exercitium hunc inaniisse seipsum, quoad hunc usum, dicitur Christus.

Quam Majestatem vere divinam & infinitam esse in exam. Doctr. Reform. de persona Christi probamus, & ad eandem pertinere divinam omnipotentiam, omniscientiam, omnipraesentiam, & adorationis gloriam ostendimus.

Quapropter non inconcinne respondet Beat. Dannhaverus Hodosoph. loc. cit. Quare exinanivit?

Non sola propulsatione hostium. Nam sic etiam Deus quievit: Sed Deiformitate (non πληρώματι θεότητος, sed) πληρώσεως. Eph.

IV. vers. 10. quae proprie κενώσεως, hoc est, Deiformitatis plenario, universali, jugi ac indefinenti usu, non quod numquam uteretur, sed quod non semper, sed tum solum, quoties ex officiis ratione expediret. Quod probat tum ex contextus συναφεία hoc modo: Qui se inanivit plenissimo gloriae divinae statu ac gestu, is retraxit plenarium & catholicum suae gloriae usum.

At Christus hunc in modum seipsum exinanivit; tum ex fine unionis, qui est ἱλασικὸς sive solutorius ejus, quod Christus non rapuit, sed quod rapere attentarunt primi Parentes. Unde ita concludit p. 706. Qui solvit omnem rapinam Adamicam per contrarii adimpletionem, is expiat affectatam omniscientiam, omnipotentiam, omnipraesentiam, dominium, cultum, contraria retributione catholici usus sapientia per voluntariam ignorantiam; potentia per contrariam infirmitatem; praesentia per localem circumscriptionem; opulentie per contrariam paupertatem; dominii per servitutem; cultus adorationis per abjectionem infra Angelos: Atqui sic se habet solutio & luitio Christi. Porro etiam ita argumentatur Beat. Dannbauerus pag. 707. Omni eo se exinaniverat Christus, quod finem incarnationis poterat impedire. Sic multi saepe homines jure ipsis debito se abdicant, ne intentione sua frustrentur. Jam Salvatorem nostrum Christum poterat impedire non sola propulsatio hostium ac injuriarum in passione irrogatarum, (id insuper si ad exinanitionem satis esset, parum abest, quin & ipsa Deitas quiescens disi exinanita posset) sed omne id, quo stante non pleno pro nobis fuisset satisfactum, non plene expiata rapina Adamica, si quamvis occulte, tamen vere & actu secundo radios suae gloriae catholicos evibrasset. Μορφὴ δούλου λαβὼν)

similis factus servis, qui nihil proprium possident. Hic ponenda διαστολὴ: incepit enim jam ἀντίθετοι aliud. Quod supplicium & summe atrox (nam inde & cruciare & cruciatus) & maxime despectum. Appianus Civilium ll. ἐκρεμάσθησαν δὲ θάνατον ἑταυ-Servus apud Plautum: Scio ego crucem mihi fore sepulchrum.

Nova haec est distinctio, & nova glossa, quae nemini facile, nisi Grotio, in mentem venit.

Nimirum hoc vult: Duo esse ἀντίθετα, prius, quod in forma DEI fuerit, & seipsum inanierit, similis factus servis, qui nihil proprium possident; posterius, quod non jactarit potestatem divinam, hoc est, spectari tanquam Deus, cum similis esset Protoplastis, non pro ea dignitate se gessit, sed humiliter admodum, unde & formae obedientis factus. Sed unde talis διαστολὴ, unde illa duo ἀντίθετα probabuntur? Unde glossis illis noviter inventis fides conciliabitur? Illud enim αὐτὸς ἒφα tam non locum hic habet, quam nec idia ἐπίλυσις.

Porro prima illa oppositio vana est. Nam τῷ elle in forma Dei non opponitur illa inopia, per quam humilis factus servis nihil proprii possidentibus, quum istud prius oppositionis membrum divinam in Christo potestatem secundum Grotium inferat, qui non κένωσις possessionum, & facultatum propriarum, & inopia fervorum opponitur, sed inanitio illig divinae potestatis & πλήρωσεως omnis potestatis, adeoque infertur evacuatio publicae ac plenariae χρήσεως τῆς εἶναι ἴσα θεῷ, nec non formae servilis assumptio.

Duobus enim modis oppositum membrum describitur. ἐπητικῶς per κένωσιν jam explicatam. θετικῶς idque (r.) generatim per λῆψιν μορφῆς δουλικῆς, per quam formam servi non natura humana, qua tali, immediate intelligitur. Haec enim ad fubjectum pertinet, quod est Christus Jesus, quod nomen τὸ συναμφότερον infert, illa autem ad praedicatum referenda; ideoque status & conditio servilis notatur. Quemadmodum per formam Dei non immediate designata divina natura, sed divinus status, in quo erat Christus secundum humanam naturam: Ita etiam per formam servi, forma servi status servilis, non vero ipsa humana natura immediate intelligitur, quamvis ea supponatur omnino, siquidem status ille servilis non nisi in humanam naturam cadat. Id intelligitur per formam servi, quod statui exinanitionis convenit, & in statu exaltationis non amplius locum habet.

Per eam enim Christus Dominus factus est, II. 36. & nomen supra omne nomen accipit, cum quo servitus & nomen servi consistere non potest. Ea assumptio hic designatur, quae nobis in exemplum humilitatis filii poterat, quod imitemur.

At assumptio naturae humanae quomodo imitabilis nobis esse potest? Adde quod Apostolus referat formam servi ad statum exinanitionis.

Nam postquam κένωσιν nominat, addit assumptionem formae servilis. (6.) Crocius ita hic habet: Quomodo formam servi accepit?

Similis factus hominibus, & habitu repertus ut homo v. 7. & 8. At haec non ad incarnationem, sed ad statum exinanitionis pertinent, ut postea dicetur. Ambrosius formam servi sic interpretatur: Formam servi accipiens, dum tenetur & ligatur, & verberibus agitur usque ad crucem, factus obediens Patri, cui se aequalem faciebat.

Non sibi defendit aequalitatem, sed subjecit se. Hanc patientiam & humilitatem nos docet, ut non solum aequalibus nos non anteponamus, verum etiam inclinemus nos, auctoris nostri secuti exemplum.

Formam autem Dei non accepisse dicitur, sed esse in forma Dei.

Servè autem formam accepisse, dum quasi peccator humiliatur. Servui autem ex peccato fiunt, sicut Cham filiae Noe, qui primus merito nomen servi accepit.

Non enim mibi, sicut quibusdam videtur sic servè formam accepisse, dum homo natus est. Vide enim quid dicat: Hoc sentite in vobis, quod & in Christo Jesu, id est, Deo & homine.

Sic exposuit S. Cyprianus antea adductus. Ita & Calvinus, Musculus, Genevensis, Piscator interpretantur: Hujus verba fichabent: Apostolus ait, Christum se exinanivisse, quatenus formam servi suscepit, id est, conditionem servilem, humilem & abjectam: sicut amplius declarat verbis sequentibus, quod factus fuerit in similitudine hominum, id est, similis vulgaribus hominibus, subjectus nimirum omnes generis infirmitatibus humanis, peccato solo excepto, ut quod esurit, sitivit, dormivit, contristatus est & quod ipsum adhus amplius declarat v. 8. inquiens: Et σχήματι, id est, figura seu habitu (Luber. an Gebärden) comperius ut homo. Ibi notandum, Apostolum in eadem significatione accipere has voces μορφῇ, ὁμοιώμα, σχήμα.

Unde scilicet percipitur, per μορφὴν hic non intelligendam naturam seu essentiam. Adde Matth. Martinium in fpicil. p. 164. Quod dicitur de forma, inquit, servi, non simpliciter intelligo humanam naturam, sed vilem ejus conditionem, que fuit ad tempus.

De caetero non negamus, mediate inferri humanam naturam, quia nisi Christus verus homo esset, servi forma eidem non conveniret. Nam ista μορφὴ δούλου non fuit idea quadam, in aere volitans, sed requisivit verum homine ceu subiectum, in quo vere fuit. Unde B. Feurbornius notat, tres modos formae servilis reperiri. 1. quando aliquis est servus, veruntamen se non gerit ut servum, sed ut Dominum vel Deum. Tales sunt omnes Adae filii, qui omnes debebant esse DEI servi, sed volunt DII esse, Genes. II. & III. 2. Quando quis servus est, & se gerit ut servum. Sicut in mundo faciunt probi servi, coram Deo vero omnes pii, qui Deo subiecti uti serviunt. 3. Quando quis servus quidem non est, veruntamen se ut servum gerit, ut si Rex suis ministraret in mundo. Coram Deo nemo id fecit, nisi Christus. Conf. Iob. XIII. 4. Haec Feurbornius et Beat. Lutherus l. c. pag. 110. Quae obiicit Crocius, cum Es. LIII. Christus dicitur servus, non tantum statum, sed & naturam indicari, nihil iuvant. Aliud enim est formam servi assumere, aliud nomine servi venire. Ibi conditio servilis assumitur, hic vero servus a conditione quidem servili vocatur, non autem abstractum sed concretum nomen habetur.

Nec eadem est locorum apud Esaiam cap. LIII. vers. 13. cap. XLII. 1. 4. Ezech. XXXII. vers. 23. & Zach. III. v. 8. cum praesenti ratio. Nam nomen istud quandoque est officii Mediatoris, ad quod expediundum missus est Filius Dei, quod in diebus carnis executus est, quod competit Christo ratione utriusque naturae; conf. Iob. X. 18. c. XVII. v. 4. Psal. XL. 9. Es. XLIII. vers. 24. Matth. XX. 28. quando vero est conditionis servilis, humilis & abiectae σημαίνικον, & Christo tribuitur ratione humanae naturae in statu exinanitionis.

Nec quicquam iuvat cantio recepta Beat. Lutheri: 30g ein eins Knechtes leib gering, quia nihil aliud ea vult, quam quod in incarnatione statim forma & conditio servilis coeperit, non vero quod assumptio formae servilis sit ipsa incarnatio. Aliud enim est corpus servilis conditionis & status in genere, aliud formam servi assumere. Ibi corpus, quod assumptum est, tum ratione substantiae, tum ratione status & conditionis describitur, & cum ipsa statim incarnatione statum servilem coepisse, nec ullo temporis momento humilem illam fortem & conditionem ab eadem disseparari innuitur, hic vero sola vilis conditio exprimitur, etsi corpus vel natura humana necessario supponatur, utpote quae illam formam servi assumpsit, ut formaliter tamen & momentis naturae distinguantur incarnatio, & formae servi assumptio.

Beati Lutheri mens satis ex aliis locis perspecta est. Et agnoscit Crocius ipse, de mera servili conditione, quam Christus homo iam factus susceperit, Lutherum alicubi explicare, ut Hunnium, Menzerum & alios plerosque Lutheranos, neque negat ipse, notari conditionem servilem, quam Christus subiit; sed meram servilem conditionem notari, ut non simul voce eadem ipsa natura humana comprehendatur, pernegat, adeoque intelligit essentiam & naturam humanam integram, anima scilicet vera & corpore vero constantem, non nudam tamen, sed omnibus suis essentialibus & naturalibus proprietatibus vestitam, ac omnibus defectibus inculpabilibus communibus obnoxiam.

At humana natura essentialibus proprietatibus vestita, & defectus isti inculpabiles communes non necessario cohaerent. Fuit enim illa fine hisce in primis nostris Parentibus; sed hi libere assumpti sunt a Christo nostrae salutis causa: Neque formam servi tribuere licet Christo in statu gloriae, ubi tamen veram humanam naturam retinet.

Wiederumb knechtisch oder dienstlich gestalt seyn, ist, ait Beat. Lutherus, optimus verborum suorum interpres, sich erzeigen mit Worten und Wercken gegen andere als ein Diener. Welches hat Christus gethan, da er unter den Jüngern gedienet, und sich für uns gegeben hat, doch auch nicht wie andere Heilgen, welche von natur Knechte sind, sondern ist eine angenommene Sache mit ihm gewest, uns zu gut und zum Exempel, dass wir auch also thun sollen gegen andere, und unser Göttlichen Gestalt uns äussern.

Nec aliter intelligunt vel Philippus, vel Beat. Simon Pauli, ad quos temere provocat Crocius. Caeterum an per servum hic mancipium intelligatur, contra Oforodum id affirmantem disquirit Beat. Feurbornius l. c. pag. 113. (2.) Speciatim explicatur forma servi tum per ὁμοίωμα similitudinem aliorum hominum, intellige, quoad omnes corporis infirmitates, expertes tamen peccati; tum per σχῆμα figuram vel habitum hominum quoad communem conversationem & convictum familiarem, ubi omnia fuere servilia, abiecta & vilia, nisi quod interdum effulgerent radii quidam Majestatis divinae. Nam si quaeras, quomodo formam servi assumpserit? Resp. Paulus, γενόμενον ἐν ὁμοιώματι ἀνθρώπων, factus in similitudine hominum, καὶ σχῆματι εὑρεθεὶς ὡς ἄνθρωπος, & habitu inventus sicut homo. Non ergo per hanc similitudinem & figuram (1.) ipsa Humana Christi natura intelligitur, quod Calvinianae volunt, non enim similis tantum hominibus est, aut ὁμοίαν nobiscum naturam assumpsit; nec tantum inventus est ὡς ἄνθρωπος, instar hominis, vel in schemate & figura hominis, sed verus homo fuit per omnia nobis similis.

Non id propositum Apostolo, qualis fuerit Christus ratione essentiae, sed qualem se gesserit tempore exinanitionis, quod nempe sponte sua & voluntate liberrima factus nobis sit ὁμοιοπαθής, & in vitae suae conversatione, humilitatis, patientiae, mansuetudinis, misericordiae, obedientiae exemplum praebuerit. Conf. Ebr. II. 17. cap. IV. vers. 15. Neque (2.) eo torquendum cum Marcione ὁμοίωμα & σχῆμα, ut loco veritatis natura mera figura & phantasma introducatur.

Hoc enim tollit opus redemptionis, & similitudo non apparentiam tantum, sed veram & realem similitudinem notat Gen. I. vers. 26. cum ad imaginem & similitudinem DEI Adam conditus; cap. V. vers. 3. cum Sethum ad imaginem & similitudinem suam genuisse dicitur. Neque (3.) factus Christus in similitudine hominum, quod primis parentibus similis fuerit.

Nam hic nullo verbo indicatur, primos parentes respici. Quo jure ergo textui possunt ingeri, qui nullo apice in toto contextu insinuantur: De hominibus in communi sermo est, quibus similis factus dicitur.

Nemo etiam ex hoc loquendi modo colligere potest, quod Christus innuatur expers esse peccati, eaque ratione similis Protoplastis designetur, neque schemate dicitur inventus ut Adam homo primus, sed indefinite, ut homo quicunque. Non de dignitate domini, sed servili conditione potius agitur. Deiformitas & ἰσοτιμία cum DEO jain ante asserta, vers. 6. hic cur denuo afferretur, causa nulla est; Utitur autem Apostolus voce ὁμοιώματι ἀνθρώπων, ad significandam similitudinem cum hominibus quibusvis aliis, quibus non idem sed similis dicitur, quia non de identitate naturae, sed similitudine quoad accidentales corporis infirmitates, quarum respectu nobis similis est.

Nam quamvis generis ejusdem videantur esse, similes tamen potius censeri debent; siquidem syn-tajilla δυσγενεία , non ex natura, qualis nunc post lapsum est, per peccatum scilicet corrupta, necessitate, in Christo redundarint, sed ex οἰκονομία libertate susceptae sint; quo pacto primis Parentibus non similis, sed dissimilis fuit; Hi enim infirmitates illas per peccatum contraxerunt, cujus plane expers fuit Christus. Porro Adamum in omnes creaturas, in mare, ventos &c. dominium habuisse, idque, de Adamo quod literam Psal.

IIX. dici, & mystice Christo applicari, falso assumit Grotius, cujus contrarium ad Psal. IIX. ostensum. Mere ergo precaria, & a mente Spiritus sancti prorsus aliena est glossa Grotiana, quod schemate inventus sit ceu ἄνθρωπος, hoc est, in dignitate domini Adami; Quae etiam ideo locum non habet, quod dominium Christi longe sublimius fit, omnemque potestatem in coelo & in terra complectatur, quodque ad illud non ante humiliationem, sed post eandem, evectus sit Christus.

Ut taceam, quod vulgaris & communis homo non fine emphasi simpliciter homo quandoque dicatur, ut Psalm.

XXII. vers. 7. Jud. XVI. vers. 2. 15. cum contra homo eximius non modo homo dicatur, sed homo Dei; Vid. Deut. XXIII. vers. 1. 1. Reg. XIII. vers. 4. 1. Tim. III. vers. 11. Nec abs re notarunt veteres quod Paulus dixerit, in similitudine hominum, ut indicaret, Christum non esse nudum hominem, non omnia Christi & nostra aequalia esse, sed habere Christum quaedam singularia, utpote quod θεόθετος fit, quod non natus ex cohabitatione viri & foeminae, quod ἀναμάρτητος.

Ad exinanitionis statum exprimendum haec pertinere penes omnes Interpretes extra dubium est.

Per schema itaque, in quo ut homo inventus est Christus, plerique nostrates intelligunt habitum & gestum, ac communem vivendi rationem, quod aliorum hominum more ederit, biberit, dormiverit, esuriverit, ambularit, &c. & per omnia inventus habitu ejusmodi externo fuerit ut alius homo. σχῆμα neglectum ac contemptum quod notare apud LXX.

Interpretes ex Es. III. vers. 17. observat Heinsius in Nov. Testam. σχῆμα mundi hujus 1. Cor. VII. vers. 31. dicitur species mundi externa, inanis & vana, nullam solidam felicitatem praestans, alias in genere σχῆμα habitum, gestum, speciem notare constat. Inventus autem dicitur, nec a quo inventus fit, additur: nimirum ab omnibus, qui in diebus carnis ipsum viderunt.

Unde etiam pro vulgari homine habitus est a plerisque, utut & concionibus & miraculis sese ut Filium Dei unigenitum verumque Deum demonstravit.

Et fatetur Calvinus, Paulum hic commemorare, tanquam hominem abjectum & communis sortis habitum fuisse.

Piscator notat, Apostolum in eadem significatione accipere has voces μορφή, ὁμοίωμα, σχῆμα, & hinc concludit per μορφήν non intelligendam naturam & essentiam, probatque Lutheri σχῆμα interpretationem, an Gebärden.

Ex quibus liquet, non accipi hic particulam ὡς sensu βεβαιωτικῷ, ut cum aliis Bullingero, Beza, Zanchio Crocius vult, sed usitatiorem suam significationem retiuere, quam vox σχῆμα & ὁμοίωμα omnino postulat.

Succedit itaque ordine tertius exinanitionis gradus.

Primus erat forma Dei κένωσις vel evacuatio. Alter formae servi λῆψις vel assumptio, quam modo exposuit Apostolus. Tertius est ταπείνωσις vel extrema illa humiliatio, qua semetipsum Christus imprimis in passione magna humiliavit, quae hic specialiter respicitur. Additur enim γενόμενος ὑπήκοος μέχρι θανάτου , factus obediens usque ad mortem.

Non autem obedientia illa, qua sese tam Judaeis, quam Romanis subjecit, ut Grotius vult, designatur, sed obediens factus DEO Patri, intelligitur, quod tum in obedientia activa, qua legi sese subjecit, eandemque implevit pro nobis, tum in obedientia passiva, qua passionibus ipsique morti subjicere se voluit, accidit.

Haec utraque obedientia per totam vitam effulsit in Christo, sed maxime in passione mea, in hebdomade poenosa.

Ubi sane & Judaeis & Romanis sese submisit sponte ac libere; Sed hoc directe verbis illis, obediens factus est, non innuitur, quasi ad obedientiam, quam non hominibus sed Patri praestare debuit, consequenter id referatur, quia scilicet Pater hoc mandatum ei dederat, Johan.

X. vers. 19. & hae Patris fuit voluntas, Psalm. XL. vers. 7. Johan. V. vers. 39. cap. VI. vers. 38. cap. IIX. vers. 54. 55. cap. XII. vers. 49. cap. XIV. vers. 31. cap. XVII. vers. 4. Luc. XXII. vers. 41. Nec hominibus tantum ex voluntate Patris se subjecit, sed ut Beat.

Lutherus loco citato monuit, etiam peccato, morti, & Satanae. Dicit usque ad mortem, non quod obedientia haud praestita fit, cum sepeliri, & in sepulchro ac statu mortis per triduum manere voluit, sed quod mors crucis extremus fit humiliationis gradus, in qua maledictum factus est, & de DEI desertione questus, poenis infernalibus obnoxius fuit, quodque mors etiam complectatur statum mortis, vel saltem subinferat.

De extremo illo gradu obedientiae usque ad mortem crucis exclamat Chrysostomus hoc loco: Papa quam magnum & vehementer ineffabile est, quod servus factus est!

Quod vero quoque mortem sustinuit, multo plus est. Sed est & aliud majus quiddam isto & multo admirabilius; Quamobrem?

Quia non quevis mors isti similis est. Ista namque omnium videbatur probrosissima, illa plena decore, ista maledicta. Maledictus enim omnis, qui pendet in cruce, Deut. XXI. vers. 23. Gradus autem extremus mors illa externa dicitur, quam intelligi determinatio addita mortis crucis indicat, etsi profundissima humiliatio in sensu dolorum infernalium sita fuerit, quia hic de externis agit Apostolus, non autem passiones animi interiores attigit, licet eadem generali vocis ἐταπείνωσεν, & quod factus fit ὑπήκοος, comprehendantur ambitu, imo ut diximus morte crucis designentur.

Pertinent utique maxime ad ταπείνωσιν necnon ad ὑπακοήν, Psal.

XL. vers. 3. Psal. LXIX. vers. 1. 2. 16. & in supplicio crucis comprehenduntur ob maledictionem illi additam, quod illud subeundo factus sit pro nobis κατάρα execratio, Gal. III. vers. 13. Obedientia haec Christo convenit secundum Humanam naturam, de quo Damascenus libr.

III. de orthod. fide cap. 14. Obediens Patri factus est Dominus, non secundum quod DEUS, sed secundum quod homo.

Secundum enim DEUS, neque obediens, neque inobediens. Nam subjectorum haec sunt.

## 2:9
Verf. 9. Therefore also God highly exalted him) he allowed himself to be brought low . Therefore God made him much more sublime than he was before. Conf. Heb. XII. 2. highly exalted, exalted, Dan. IV. verf. 34. And gave him a name which is above every name) Name here is dignity, as Eph. I. 21. Thus Deut. 26, verf. 19. who made you famous and a boast. Verf. 10. That in the name of Jesus every knee should bow of those in heaven, and of those on earth, and of those under the earth) to bow the knee is a sign of reverence, Gen.

XLI. 43. in Latin: But it is a great honor not only to show such signs to someone present, but even to one absent, by calling upon his name. But this distribution is threefold, and in Rev. V. 13. where it is said under the earth, which is here those under the earth.

But by those under the earth here it seems that the dead ought to be understood, as the word is accustomed to be used by the Greeks, so that those are understood who are now dead, and hidden under the earth, about to show signs of reverence to Christ, where indeed they will be awakened by him. Verf. 11. And every tongue) Not only of men, but also of Angels, 1. Cor. XIII.

Latin:

Vers. 9. Διὸ καὶ αὐτὸν ὁ Θεὸς ὑπερύψωσε) ipse deprimi se passus est. Ideo Deus eum multo sublimiorem fecit, quam erat antea. Conf. Ebr. XII. 2. ὑπερύψωσε, מרום, Dan. IV. vers. 34. Καὶ ἐχαρίσατο αὐτῷ ὄνομα τὸ ὑπὲρ πᾶν ὄνομα) Nomen hic est dignitas, ut Eph. I. 21. Sic Deut. 26, vers. 19. ὃς ἐποίησέ σε ὀνομαστὸν καὶ καύχημα. Vers. 10. Ἵνα ἐν τῷ ὀνόματι Ἰησοῦ πᾶν γόνυ κάμψῃ τῶν ἐπουρανίων, καὶ ἐπιγείων, καὶ καταχθονίων) genu flectere signum reverentiæ, Gen.

XLI. 43. in Latino: Magnus autem honos non præfenti tantum alicui exhibere signa talia, sed etiam absenti, nomine ejus nuncupato. Distributio autem ista triplex est, & in Apoc. V. 13. ubi ὑποκάτω τῆς γῆς dicitur, quod hic καταχθόνιος.

Videntur autem per καταχθονίους hic intelligi debere mortui, quomodo Græcis se vox usurpari solet, ut intelligantur ii qui nunc mortui, & sub terras abditi sunt, reverentiæ signa exhibituri Christo, ubi nempe per eum excitabuntur. Vers. 11. Καὶ πᾶσα γλῶσσα) Non hominum tantum, sed & Angelorum, 1. Cor. XIII.

## 2:11
1. Should confess, that the Lord Jesus Christ) Let them acknowledge Jesus to be the Lord of all things, Acts II. 26. In Isaiah, from whence both these and the preceding are taken, it is: Every tongue shall swear, chap. XLV. 23. To the glory of God the Father) For the honor of Christ returns to the honor of the Father. For this honor was given to him by the Father, for the reason that he had honored the Father more than anyone, John XVII.

5, 6. This was the consequence of the emptying; because exaltation followed the emptying, the donation of a name above every name followed humiliation: By which reason at the same time a new argument for commending humility is insinuated: Since indeed exaltation certainly follows it. For since the same affection ought to be in us, which is in Christ, whose humility has been proposed thus far, Christians ought to imitate it, and now they are also excited to the pursuit of the same through exaltation, which is taught by the example of Christ to certainly follow humility.

Confer. Heb. XII. verf. 1, 2. Rom. VIII. 17. 29. 2. Tim. II. verf. 11. 1. Pet. V. 5. But that 'therefore' is not to be taken causally and meritoriously, as if the emptying of Christ were the meritorious cause of his exaltation, which the Socinians and Papists wish, to which Zanchius does not dissent, nor Matth.

Martinius in his summary of faith disp. XXII. sometimes affirming that Christ merited for himself not indeed salvation, but a higher degree in salvation, notwithstanding that Calvin accused him of the foolish curiosity and rashness of the Sorbonists, book II. instit. chap. 2. §.

6. Particles of this kind are certainly not rarely taken not causally but syllogistically, not in a causal sense, but of mere consequence. Indeed that 'therefore' is a mere inference, wherefore, consequently. But how it may be allowed to proceed from inference to inference to a cause or meritorious cause, when an inference can be sought from various Dialectical places.

Conf. Luc. VII. verf. 2. Acts XIII. verf. 35. chap. XX. verf. 26. chap. XXV. v. 3. Heb. XIII. verf. 12. 1. Cor. VIII. verf. 13. chap. X. v. 13. chap. XII. verf. 3. etc. Nor did Christ merit anything for himself, but whatever he merited, he merited it all for us, Therefore Athanasius orat. II. against the Arians. They are mistaken, he says, the Arians rely on the conjunction therefore, while it is said by Paul: Therefore also God exalted him.

For he did not signify the reward of virtue, nor excellence in progressing by those words, but the cause of sublimation redounding IN US. Humiliation was the way, through which Christ arrived at glory, but not the meritorious cause, Luc. XXIV. 26. and our sufferings are the way of the kingdom, not the cause of reigning. Erasmus renders 'highly exalted' periphrastically, he raised to the highest sublimity, which is certainly ineffable to us, Eph. 1. verf. 19. seqq. But that is opposed to 'to be emptied', and by the force of opposition, instead of the evacuation of the form of GOD, it introduces the plenary execution of the form of GOD, instead of the concealment of those things which were equal to GOD, the public manifestation of them, instead of the assumption of the servile form, the deposition of the same, and to the administration of the universal dominion of all things, the admission, or solemn enthronement, and to the right hand of God the exaltation.

That name which GOD gave to Christ according to his Human nature, that at the name of Jesus every knee of those in heaven, of those on earth and of those under the earth should bow, is opposed to that extreme humiliation, not only did he humble himself below all heavenly things, and wished to be brought low for the sake of our salvation, because he was made lower than the Angels, Ps.

VIII. but also below earthly things, because he was held as the lowest of men, or even like a worm, by any earth-born and mortal men whatsoever, who ought to have bowed their knees to him, so that also below those under the earth, the Devils themselves, together with the damned in hell, by whom he was tempted in the desert, mocked through their instruments, and agitated by terrors and infernal torments in his agony, in the garden of Gethsemane, and in his passion on the cross, so that he exclaimed: My God, my GOD, why have you forsaken me?

All of which, when he was made obedient to the Father even unto death, even the death of the cross, he sustained, and suffered, but because glory, eminence and supreme pleasure succeeded to ignominy, humiliation and extreme affliction: Glory, a name above every name, than which none more sublime can be given or named, majesty indeed infinite and truly divine, conferred upon him as to its fullest use, imports: The eminence of supreme dominion, that eminence, by which he commands all creatures in heaven, on earth, in hell, and is to be worshipped and adored by all as the supreme Lord through submission and genuflection and also public confession, and most submissive celebration:

Will, by which he rejoices, that all things yield to the glory of GOD the Father, brings supreme happiness and joy to him; since indeed all things are subject to him, and now enemies are placed as a footstool for his feet, Ps. CX.

110.

1. Cor. XV. Heb. II. By those under the earth not so much the dead, who are either blessed, and thus look to the heavenly ones, or damned, and thus are to be referred to the society of Demons, are to be understood, so that the distribution may be adequate.

For even Demons believe, that Christ is born, and they tremble, James II. verf. 19. and therefore they are held to bow their knees to him. But that honor is not shown to one absent, because he is nowhere absent, but fills all things with his present dominion over all, Eph.

IV. verf. 10. Concerning the Isaianic passage, which is looked to here, we have spoken in its place and Rom.

XIV. 6. Furthermore, that which some interpret as 'the Lord Jesus Christ' being the subject, so that it is the predicate, which is 'in the glory of God the Father', such as Lombard, Hugo Cardinalis, Thomas etc., just as it is sometimes used for 'ev' and rendered by the Vulgate 'in the glory of God the Father', others make it the matter of confession, that Jesus Christ is Lord, the end, to the glory of GOD the Father, or they assign the glory of the Father as the end of that dignity of Christ.

Both explanations are convenient. But because the usual signification of the particle 'eis' is to denote 'To', it does not appear to be a cause why one should depart from it.

Moreover, Reformed interpreters refer the exaltation to both natures of CHRIST, nor do they admit that the glory and eminence which the Apostle testifies was given to CHRIST should be understood as the infinite and immense glory and eminence of GOD.

But that Christ was exalted only according to his human nature, not according to his Divine nature, is certain, 1. because the Divine nature cannot be exalted, being the highest; He had the name above every name from eternity, he did not receive it in time.

Whatever things, however, were given to Christ in time, according to the rule of antiquity, they were given to him as a man.

The name above every name was given to Christ out of grace, which the word ἐχαρίσατο (he graciously bestowed) imports, descending from the noun χάρις (grace).

Whence by unanimous consent antiquity referred this exaltation to the Human nature of Christ, and judged those who referred it to the Divine nature to be swept into the company of Arius.

Athanasius, orat.

II. against the Arians.

For our sake GOD was made flesh, and that which we now say, "he exalted him," does not signify that the substance of the Word was exalted.

For he was God: and is always equal to God, but it looks to his Humanity.

Nor were these things said before they were done, when the Word had already been made flesh, so that it might be made plain that "he humbled" and "he exalted" were said of the man.

Likewise: Now also that (he bestowed upon him) was not written for the sake of the Word himself: For he was, before he became Man, to be worshipped both by the Angels and by the whole creation according to his property from the paternal substance: But for our sake and for us it was written concerning him.

For just as the man died and was superexalted: So also he is said to receive as man that which he always had as GOD.

Concerning the name above every name, St.

Athanasius writes on the nature

of the Humanity assumed, he speaks of the temple, which is his body.

For it is not he who is the Highest, but his flesh that is exalted, and to his flesh he gave the highest name, which is above every name.

Jerome on this passage: Because, he says, the assumed man deigned to humble himself, the divinity, which cannot be humbled, exalted him who had been humbled: But also a name was given to him, because he did not have it before.

Whence this passage is more rightly to be understood according to the Human nature than the Divine.

Leo the Great comments on this passage thus, epist.

Although in him there is one and the same person of Deity and Humanity, we understand the exaltation and the name above every name to pertain to that form by which he was to be endowed with such a great increase of glorification.

For nothing had departed from the Word through the incarnation, which would be restored to him by the Father's gift.

The FORM of a SERVANT, however, is human humility, which was raised into the glory of Divine power, so that neither without the Man were Divine things done, nor without GOD were Human things done.

The same, when the Roman Bishop Leo the Great, epist.

Let the adversaries of the truth say, he says, when the almighty Father, or according to which nature, raised his Son above all things, or to which substance he subjected all things?

For they were always subject to the Deity as Creator.

If power was added to this, if the exalted sublimity was less than the one promoting it, and it did not have the riches of that nature whose bounty it needed, then Arius sweeps the one thinking such things into his company.

of Concord.

That, however, a truly infinite glory and eminence is to be understood here, the very weight of the words proves.

For that ὑπερύψωσις (superexaltation) denotes a superexaltation; so it was done, the Apostle himself being the interpreter, "far above all rule and authority, and power, and dominion, and every name that is named, not only in this age, but also in the coming one"; and he infers the subjection of all things under the feet of Christ, Ephes.

I. 21, 22. which is not a finite, but an infinite eminence.

For it is not of finite virtue to subject all things to itself.

For that "above every name" imports an infinite dignity, than which none is higher, for if a higher one were given, it would not be that name above every name.

The glory of the adoration of all creatures is an infinite and truly Divine dignity, since religious adoration presupposes an infinite eminence and is the acknowledgment of the same, concerning which, against the Socinians, it was spoken professedly in Theol.

679. who, even if he judges that Zanchius truly and orthodoxly explained that name given, in that it was revealed to the whole world by God.

And, that this whole crucified Jesus is the Only-begotten Son, and it was brought about that he is everywhere preached, and named, and acknowledged, and invoked as true God: He confesses, however, that it pleases him more that by that name above every name there is noted here the power, dignity, and glory which far transcends every power, dignity, and glory of all creatures, which are from God, who gave the name, and he says that this is the opinion of Calvin, Beza, Bullinger, Aretius, Piscator, Hyperius, Toffanus, and of the Ancients according to Theodoret, and (which is the chief thing) of scripture, which sometimes signifies by "name" dignity, Majesty, and glory, Psal.

12. it is fitting. And although he does not reject even that Zanchian interpretation, by which the exaltation of Christ is taken so generally that it embraces the resuscitation from the dead, the ascension into heaven, and the placement at the right hand of God, whence glory accrued to the whole Christ, which he had not had before according to the flesh: Inasmuch as he received the impassibility and immortality of the flesh in the resurrection, with the most exquisite gifts that can fall to a glorified body: Yet he sides more with Toffanus, that the Apostle used the word ὑπερύψωσεν (he superexalted), that is, he exalted beyond measure, so that we may know that that supreme sublimity is to be considered only after the resurrection and ascension into heaven in the glory of the Father.

For the discourse is about an excellence which does not belong to any other creature, since we too are to rise again, and to ascend into the heavens; but we are not to attain that name which he attained.

Moreover, the Zanchian explanation can in no way be proven, since in it the revelation that Jesus is the Son of GOD is not that ὑπερύψωσις (superexaltation) of which the Apostle treats; which is clear even from this, that in the state of humiliation also that was revealed, although not so universally throughout the world (thus, therefore, the state of exaltation would be confused with the state of humiliation) and especially from this, that this exaltation is not to be explained only relatively and by reason of us, for thus an exaltation could also be uttered concerning the Father and the Holy Spirit, when they manifest the Divine glory more fully, and that they bring about a true change, and a βελτίωσιν (improvement) or betterment, and it belongs only to the human nature.

But impassibility and immortality and other gifts belong not only to the body of Christ, but also to the glorified bodies of the Elect, Phil.

III. 21.

Sed quod Christus secundum humanam tantum naturam, non secundum Divinam exaltatus sit, ita constat, 1. quia Divina natura exaltari non potest, utpote altissima; Nomen supra omne nomen ab æterno habuit, non in tempore accepit.

Quæcunque vero in tempore Christo data sunt, secundum regulam antiquitatis, quum ad illa ut homini data sunt.

Nomen supra omne nomen Christo datum est ex gratia, quod vox ἐχαρίσατο importat, à nomine χάρις gratia descendens.

Unde unanimi consensu antiquitas hanc exaltationem ad Humanam Christi naturam retulit, & ad Divinam naturam eam referentes in societatem Arii rapi censuit.

In gratiam nostri DEUS caro factus est, & illud, quod nunc dicimus, exaltavit eum, non substantiam Verbi exaltatam significat.

Neque ista prius dicta fuere, quam actum, cum jam Verbum caro esset factum, ut palam fieret, illud humiliavit & illud exaltavit de homine dictum esse.

Sicut enim homo mortuus est & superexaltatus: Ita quoque id ut homo accipere dicitur, quod ut DEUS semper habuit.

Hum. suscepta, de templo loquitur, quod corpus ejus.

Unde rectius hic locus secundum Humanam naturam intelligendus est, quam Divinam.

12. conveniat. Et quamvis non rejiciat etiam illam Zanchianam interpretationem, qua exaltatio Christi tam generaliter accipitur, ut complectatur resuscitationem ex de mortuis, ascensionem in cœlum, & collocationem ad dextram Dei, unde toti Christo gloria accesserit, quam antea secundum carnem non habuerit: Siquidem impassibilitatem & immortalitatem carnis in resurrectione acceperit, cum exquisitissimis dotibus, quæ in corpus glorificatum possunt cadere: Magis tamen facit cum Toffano, quod Apostolus verbo ὑπερύψωσεν usus sit, id est, supra modum exaltavit, ut sciamus summam illam sublimitatem post resurrectionem demum & ascensum in cœlum in gloria Patris considerandam.

Sermonem enim esse de excelsitate, quæ non alii creaturæ competit, cum & nos resurrecturi simus, & ascenduri in cœlos; at illud nomen non consecuturi, quod ille consequutus est.

Cæterum nullo modo probari potest Zanchiana explicatio, quum in illa patefactio, quod Jesus sit Filius DEI, non sit ὑπερύψωσις ista, de qua Apostolus agit; quod vel ex eo liquet, quod in statu etiam exinanitionis illud patefactum sit, etsi non ita universaliter per orbem (ita ergo status exaltationis confundetur cum statu exinanitionis) & imprimis ex eo, quod hæc exaltatio non σχετικῶς tantum & ratione nostri sit explicanda, sic enim & de Patre ac Spiritu sancto exaltatio efferri posset, quando gloriam Divinam plenius manifestant, & quod veram mutationem inferant, ac βελτίωσιν vel meliorationem, ac humanæ naturæ tantum competat.

Impassibilitas vero & immortalitas aliæque dotes non soli corpori Christi, sed etiam corporibus glorificatis Electorum, Phil.

III. 21.

Num vero Electorum, ais ideo hæc ὑπερύψωσις tribuenda?

Quod autem Crocius nomen hoc super omne nomen datum esse toti personæ, secundum utramque naturam cum plerisque Reformatis asserit, quod Filius DEI ut Mediator & caput Ecclesiæ in carne gloriose regnet, ejusque gloria Divina palam à mundo agnoscatur, id ἀσύσατον est.

Nam nomen supra omine nomen ex gratia datum est Christo: Quomodo ergo juxta utramque naturam? Num Divinæ naturæ quicquam ex gratia datum? Quod Mediator est, & caput Ecclesiæ, quod regnat gloriose, hoc CHRISTO secundum utramque naturam convenit: Sed hoc Filio DEI, aut Christo secundum Divinam naturam ex gratia datum esse à Patre exquis dixerit!

Illud, regnare gloriose in carne Filii DEI si est ipsa Filii DEI exaltatio, aut exaltatio ejus est quod Divinam, aut quod utramque naturam.

Non quoad Divinam, hæc enim exaltari non potest. Proinde nec quoad utramque naturam. Restat ergo, ut exaltatio CHRISTI fit tantum quoad Humanam naturam, quod secundum illam CHRISTUS jam gloriose regnet, ejusque Divina gloria palam agnoscatur & celebretur.

## 2:12
A name above every name was given to Christ by grace: How, therefore, according to both natures? Was anything given to the Divine nature by grace? That He is Mediator, and head of the Church, that He reigns gloriously, this pertains to CHRIST according to both natures: But that this was given to the Son of GOD, or to Christ according to the Divine nature, by grace from the Father, who would say! That, to reign gloriously in the flesh of the Son of GOD, if it is the very exaltation of the Son of God, either it is His exaltation according to the Divine, or according to both natures. Not according to the Divine, for this cannot be exalted. Therefore, neither according to both natures. It remains, therefore, that the exaltation of CHRIST is only according to the Human nature, because according to that, CHRIST now reigns gloriously, and His Divine glory is openly acknowledged and celebrated.

Ver. 12.

[a] Since Christ gave us in Himself a specimen of those things which we ought to expect.

This *mê* is not in most codices. Therefore, understand *tô euangeliô* [the Gospel], as in 1 Thess. 1:8, or *tô logô* [the Word], as in 2 Thess. 3:14.

He had proposed Christ as an example not only of humility, but also of obedience. Now, therefore, he applies this, so that the Philippians may prove their obedience, with the addition of a commendation of their past life. He commends, therefore, their past obedience, so as to entice and incite them to future obedience, as if he were saying, in the interpretation of Chrysostom: Imitate, I beseech you, not others, but yourselves: And according to Theophylact, who connects these things: I have shown you that the Son of God was made obedient: Imitate Him, therefore; but imitate also yourselves.

These things are to be read thus in one Spirit. It is the mark of true friends to retain the commands of those who are absent with a mindful heart and to fulfill them faithfully. The working of salvation, as also conversion and faith, are now ascribed to God, now to men, sometimes in one place to both—to God, as the Principal Cause; to men, as those whose own labor is also required for this, 1 Cor. 5:7, 2 Tim. 2:21, James 4:8, Eph. 4:22, 23, 24, Col. 3:9, 10. *Phobô* signifies obedience; *tromô* the fear of offending, which are said regarding the duty of servants toward mortal masters, as we saw in Eph. 6:5. Much more justly are they adapted to that which we owe to GOD, as in 2 Cor. 7:15. Add 1 Pet. 1:17, ch. 3:2, Rom. 10:20, Heb. 4:1, ch. 12:28. Macarius, homil. XXVII: *alla kan tên toiautên charan paraklêsin echontes hypo phobou kai tromou eisi* [but even having such joy and consolation, they are in fear and trembling]. But he did not simply say *ergazesthai* [to work], but *katergazesthai* [to accomplish/work out]. The Syrian: "more work." The Arab: "increase in work."

We deny that conversion is ascribed to men when the discourse is about the first conversion. That work is of God alone. Man in conversion behaves passively. He is the subject of conversion, not the cause of it. But we are commanded to work out our salvation, so that we may take care not to lose it through sins against conscience and disobedience against salvation; so that we may do those things which God requires of the reborn, hear the Word of God, use the Sacraments, and pray incessantly, through which means, by the power of His promises, God wills to be effective in us unto salvation. By the word "working," as the blessed Hunnius rightly warns, he takes it in a broader sense, in which way in John 6 we are said to work the works of God when we believe in Him whom He sent. He warns the Philippians, therefore, by this formula of speech, so that they may constantly persevere in the faith once begun, and in the new obedience which follows it, lest they be secure, as if

the battle were already entirely won, and full victory gained against Satan, but with fear and trembling, with all contention of soul, they should labor toward this, that they may flee the sins by which faith is extinguished and eternal salvation is shaken off. Give diligence, therefore, that they may retain faith and a good conscience, by asking of God the increase of faith, by nourishing faith with continuous meditation on the Word and the use of the Sacraments, by strengthening it with a strong struggle against the temptations of the Devil, the seduction of the world, and the lusts of the flesh: Finally, by exercising it with new obedience and worship, so that by the means ordained by God, with faith legitimately retained, consequently through faith preserved, salvation also may be preserved. The blessed Dositheus in *Exeg. Epist. ad Ebr.* on ch. 2:14, explains *katergazesthai tên sôtêrian* [to work out salvation] as *ergazesthai kata tên sôtêrian* [to work according to salvation]. For *kata*, he says, is often omitted, as in Eph. 6:6, Heb. 10:7, 13, 21, Gal. 5:5, Eph. 2:3, Rom. 2:5. For salvation is not our work, but a *charisma tô theô* [gift of God], Rom. 6:23. Nor are our actions or sufferings worthy of the glory to be revealed, Rom. 8:18. Nor is salvation from works, Eph. 2:8 & 9. Therefore, one must work *kata tên sôtêrian* [according to salvation], as befits those who hope for such an inheritance, or *axiôs tês sôtêrias* [worthily of salvation], just as we are also commanded to live or *politeuesthai axiôs tou euangeliou* [to conduct ourselves worthily of the Gospel], Phil. 1:27. Therefore, it is not to be concluded from these words that we work out salvation by our actions or works, as the Papists wish, whom Grotius seems to gratify here, just as Bellarmine in book IV *de Justif.* ch. 6, gathers from this place that good works are necessary for salvation. Lombard, however, proceeds further, and says that "work" is the same as "merit by works," and "prepare your salvation." The Apostle exhorts to modesty and humility. How, therefore, could he teach that salvation is obtained by one's own works or merits? Thus they would rather have cause for boasting before God, which the Apostle excludes elsewhere, Eph. 2:8, lest anyone should boast, and he will teach in ch. 3 how much our works are valued by the Apostle. The Apostle excludes everywhere not only any merits, but even our works from the article of justification and salvation—merits through the unique merit of Christ, works through faith, or the apprehension of the merit of Christ, by which alone we are justified and saved. Therefore, to work out our salvation cannot mean or imply that we effect or merit salvation by our works. Nor are we simply commanded *katergazesthai*: but *meta phobou kai tromou*, which is not "with obedience and offensive movement," but "with fear and trembling." What else, therefore, can this precept require, saving the analogy of faith, than that we ought to conduct ourselves with fear and trembling in the cause of salvation, lest we shake off or lose faith, which happens through the neglect of the means of faith, carnal security, and mortal sins, when we do not walk according to the Spirit, but according to the flesh, do not mortify the works of the flesh through the Spirit, and do not present our members as servants of righteousness unto sanctification. "With fear," says Jerome on this place, that is, not with negligence, but as Job, "I feared all my works because of GOD," knowing that He would not spare the delinquent, and that the Holy Spirit of God seeks one who honors and fears His words. Therefore, neither is diffidence commanded, nor doubt about grace, nor is filial confidence and trust excluded by *phobou kai tromou*, as the Papists affirm; for they cannot do otherwise than hope for salvation from works, and thus, being imperfect, unclean, and polluted with sins, if they do not despair, they must necessarily doubt about salvation, since even those who have done all that they ought are required to profess that they are unprofitable servants, Luke 17:10.

Servile fear and trembling is excluded, but filial fear is not, which can consist with confidence in the grace of GOD and eternal salvation. The scope of the Apostle is to be observed, who is so far from wishing anything to be attributed to us here, that he rather acts so that pride may be suppressed in every way, and all things attributed to GOD, requiring obedience, but with due humility, so that we attribute nothing to ourselves, but all things to GOD.

Moreover, says S. Augustine on nature and grace against Pelagius, ch. XXVII, vices only prevail in evil deeds, but pride alone is to be guarded against in right deeds. Whence they are admonished, lest by attributing the gifts of God to their own piety, and by exalting themselves, they sin more gravely than if they performed no good works, to whom it is said, work out your salvation with fear and trembling. For it is GOD who works in you both to will and to perform for his good pleasure. Why therefore with fear and trembling, and not rather with security, if God works, unless because on account of our will, without which we cannot work well, it can quickly creep into the human mind that it should esteem what it works well as only its own, and say in its abundance, I shall not be moved forever.

Add Augustine Sermon on the Words of the Apostle, ch. III. Teaching us humility, Scripture leads us through the Apostle, work out your salvation with fear and trembling, and lest they should then attribute anything to themselves, because he said work out, he immediately added: For it is GOD who works in you both to will and to perform for his good pleasure: It is God who works in you, therefore with fear and trembling, make a valley, receive the rain: the depressed are filled, the high are dried up, grace is rain.

Why therefore do you wonder if GOD resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble? Therefore with fear and trembling, that is, with humility. Do not be wise in your own conceit, but fear. Fear that you may be filled. Do not be wise in your own conceit, lest you be dried up. Thus therefore the Apostle subjoins this, God is he who works both to will and to perform, partly lest anyone should think that it is in our power to work out salvation, partly lest we should despair, when we are commanded to work out salvation with fear and trembling, and lose heart, so that we may be raised up by the grace of GOD εὐδοκία, in which way Chrysostom explains the connection of the words.

For what does he say? It is God who works in you, do not fear what I said, with fear and trembling. I did not say that for this reason, that you should despair, that you should think virtue incomprehensible, but that you should take heed, lest you dissolve and relax yourself. If this happens, God will work all things. Be of good courage. Verf. 13. Θεὸς γάρ ἐστιν ὁ ἐνεργῶν καὶ τὸ θέλειν, καὶ τὸ ἐνεργεῖν ὑπὲρ τῆς εὐδοκίας) As if he were to say: Do not despair, as if through lack of strength you could not fulfill that which I teach, for GOD through the revelation of his promises will cause that we should will what is right, and through his Spirit he will cause that we should also constantly perform such things.

In the Manuscript it is: Θεὸς γάρ ἐστιν ὁ ἐνεργῶν δύναμιν ἐν ὑμῖν. That ὑπὲρ τῆς εὐδοκίας can indeed be rightly explained as for his supreme benevolence toward us, but not badly by those who explain it as for our desire, and that from the passage of Ps. 145:19, where it is רצון. We have already given the reason for the connection, that he wished not only to persuade humility in this way, but at the same time also to remove diffidence, which, if the matter were committed to our own powers, would most certainly arise: But now because GOD for his own εὐδοκία also wishes to work τὸ ἐνεργεῖν, who works τὸ θέλειν, we safely rely both on divine power and grace.

Some also refer the present aphorism to humility and modesty. For since man does not have from himself, as if from himself, either to will or to perform, who therefore would dare to exalt himself, unless he wishes to hear: What have you, O man, that you did not receive? 1 Cor. 4: 7. Nor indeed does the Apostle say: It is GOD who wills that you should will, and that you should perform. Not he who persuades and exhorts, but he who effects, both that you should will, and that you should perform. This was the opinion of Pelagius, that GOD works in us to will, while he inflames us with the promise of rewards, whom Augustine refutes everywhere: See book I on the grace of Christ against Pelagius and Caelestius, ch. 20. Nor does the Apostle say, that you may be able to will, nor that you may be able to perform, but that you should will, and perform.

That you should will, for example, to believe in act, to love, to hope, to pray, to strive, to persevere, and that you should believe, love, hope, pray, strive, persevere in act. He does not effect what we previously will; but when we did not will before, from those who do not will he makes those who will, and that having been made those who will, we should further will. Nor are the Semi-Pelagians, Arminians, Innovators, Latermann, Dreier, and their followers to be heard here, who contend that it is in man's power for a man to be able to believe, if he wishes to believe, and to will to believe.

See what we have said in Harmonia Calixtina, Heretical Sections, etc., III, ch. V, p. 1010, seqq.

To will indeed, insofar as it is an act of the will, is ours, from creation; to will well is also ours, but insofar as having been made those who will through conversion, we will well. Not that the beginning is from us, or even the perfection itself, whether of conversion or of a good action. Not that we do not will well, but that from ourselves we do not will well. Nor is obedience therefore commanded to us in vain, nor do we not obey. For the precept shows, not what we can or will from ourselves, but what we ought to will to do, and with GOD giving, can do. Although indeed GOD effects obedience in us, we nevertheless obey, GOD does not obey.

For we act by GOD himself, just as Augustine said: It is GOD who works in us both to will and to perform. We therefore will. But GOD works in us to will. We therefore perform, but God works in us to perform for his good pleasure.

It is profitable for us both to believe and to say this, this is pious, this is true, so that you may be humble, and the confession submissive, and all things be given to GOD, book on the gift of perseverance, ch. 13. Therefore, in order that we may will what is right, the relation of Divine promises does not suffice, but the efficacious operation of the Spirit of GOD is required, and the conversion and regeneration of our heart. That revelation alone suffices, Pelagianism rejects. Nor is τὸ ἐνεργεῖν ἐνεργεῖν to work in us to work, to effect through his Spirit that we should constantly perform what is right, but also to work those things in us, for although we who are reborn also work through the grace of the Holy Spirit, that nevertheless, so that we may be able to perform what is right, and the very performing of what is right arises in us from the Holy Spirit. Nor does the Holy Spirit produce only good works in us, but also faith, which is the mother of good works, and he produces and preserves it by his infinite power. But this εὐδοκία is not ours, as Pelagius interprets, but God's. For it is predicated even in that, that GOD works the willing in us; where certainly it cannot be said that GOD works for his own εὐδοκία.

If anyone, it is said in the Council of Orange II, chapter III, contends that our will is anticipated by GOD so that we may be purged from sin, but does not confess that even our willing to be purged comes to pass through the infusion and operation of the Holy Spirit in us, he resists the Holy Spirit himself, by through Solomon saying: The will is prepared by the Lord, and the Apostle, wholesomely preaching: It is God who works in us both to will and to perform for his good pleasure: And chap. XXVI. from August. Tractat. XIX. on John and Prosper Sentent. CCCXXXVIII. Men do their own will, not God's, when they do that which displeases God. But when they so do what they will, that they serve the Divine will, although they do what they do willingly, yet it is the will of Him by whom that which they will is prepared and commanded.

Latin:

Vers. 12. (Sre) Cum Christus in se specimen nobis dederit eorum, quæ expectare debemus.

(Καθὼς πάντοτε ὑπηκέσατέ με) Hoc μὴ non est in codicibus plerisque.

Itaque subintel. lige τῇ Εὐαγγελίῳ, ut 1.

Thessal. 1, 8. aut τῷ λόγῳ, ut 2. Thess. 3, 14. Christum exemplum proposuerat non solum humilitatis, sed etiam obedientiæ.

Nunc itaque hoc applicat, ut obedientiam suam probent Philippenses, addito elogio anteactæ vitæ.

Commendat ergo ipsorum obedientiam præteritam, ut alliciat & instiget ad futuram, quali dicat, interprete Chrysostomo: Imitemini, obsecro, non alios; sed vos ipsos: Et juxta Theophylactum, qui hæc connectit: Ostendi vobis, quod Filius Dei obediens factus est: Imitamini igitur illum; Imitamini autem vos ipsos.

(Μὴ ἐν τῇ παρουσίᾳ μου μόνον, ἀλλὰ νῦν πολλῷ μᾶλλον ἐν τῇ ἀπουσίᾳ με, μετὰ φόβου καὶ τρόμου τὴν ἑαυτῶν σωτηρίαν κατεργάζεσθε.) Hæc ita uno Spiritu legenda.

Verorum amicorum est, etiam absentium mandata meinore animo retinere & fideliter implere.

Salutis operatio, ut & conversio, & familia, nunc Deo adferibuntur, nunc hominibus, interdum uno loco utrisque Deo, ut Causæ Principi: Hominibus, ut quorum etiam aliqua ad hoc opera requiritur, 1.

Cor. 5, 7. 2. Tim. 2, 21. Jacob. 4, 8. Ephes. 4, 22. 23. 24. Coloss. 3, 9. 10. significat obedientiam: τρόμῳ metum offendendi, quæ de fervorum erga mortales heros officio dicuntur, ut vidimus Ephes. 6, 5. Multo justius aptantur ad id, quod nos DEO debemus, ut 2.

Corinth.

7, 15. Adde 1. Petr. 1, 17. cap. 3, 2. Rom. 10, 20. Ebr. 4, 1. c. 12, 28. Macarius hom. XXVII. (ἀλλὰ κἀν τῇ τοιαύτῃ χαρᾷ παράκλησιν ἔχοντες φόβον καὶ τρόμον εἰσὶ) Non autem simpliciter dicit κατεργάζεσθαι, sed κατεργάζεσθαι peragite.

Syrus: magis operamuni. Arabs: augecite in opere. Conversionem hominibus adscribi, cum de conversione prima sermo est, negamus.

Opus ea solius Dei est. Homo in conversione se passive habet. Subjectum conversionis est, non causa ejusdem. Salutem autem operari jubemur, ut caveamus, ne peccatis contra conscientiam, & inobedientia contra salutem deperdamus, ut ea agamus, quæ requirit Deus à renatis, Verbum Dei audiamus, Sacramentis utamur, indesinenter oremus, per quæ media, vi promissionum suarum, Deus in nobis efficax elle vult ad salutem.

Operandi etiam voce, ut recte B.

Hunnius monet, in lationi sumit significatione, quo pacto Johannis 6. operari dicimur opera Dei, quando credimus in illum, quem misit ipse. Admonet ergo Philippenses hac locutionis formula, ut in fide semel inchoata, & quæ hanc sequitur, nova obedientia constanter perseverent, ne sint securi, quasi penitus jam debellatum sit, & plena adversus Satanam parata victoria, sed cum timore & tremore omni animi contentione huc laborent, ut fugiant peccata, quibus extinguitur fides, & æterna salus excutitur.

Denet igitur operam, ut retineant fidem, & bonam conscientiam, petendo à Deo augmentum fidei, alendo fidem continua meditatione Verbi & Sacramentorum usu, corroborando illam forti dimicatione adversus Diaboli tentationes, mundi seductionem, & carnis concupiscentias: Denique exercendo eam nova obedientia cultu, ut mediis à Deo ordinatis, legitime retenta fide, consequenter per fidem servatam servetur & salus.

B.

Dorfiheus in Exeg. Epist. ad Ebr. ad cap. 2, 14. (Κατεργάζεσθαι τὴν σωτηρίαν exponit ἐργάζεσθαι κατὰ τὴν σωτηρίαν. Κατὰ enim, inquit, sæpius omittitur, ut Epb.

6, 6. Ebr. 10, 7. 13. 21. Galat. 5, 5. Ephes. 2, 5. Rom. 2, 5. Salus enim non est opus nostrum, sed χάρισμα τῷ θεῷ, Rom. 6, 23. Nec condignæ sunt sive actiones, sive passiones gloria manifestanda Rom. 8, 18. Nec salus est ex operibus Ephes.

2, 8. & 9. Itaque operandum κατὰ τὴν σωτηρίαν, ut decet eos, qui tantam hæreditatem sperant, seu ἀξίως τῆς σωτηρίας, uti etiam jubemur vivere seu πολιτεύειν ἀξίως τῷ εὐαγγελίῳ Phil. 1, 27. Non ergo ex his verbis concludendum, quod actionibus vel operibus nostris salutem operemur, ut Papistæ volunt, quibus hic gratificari videtur Grotius, quemadmodum Bellarminus libr.

IV. de justif. cap. 6. ex hoc loco colligit, bona operatione efficientia necessaria esse ad salutem. Lombardus vero ulterius progreditur, & operamini idem esse ait, quod mercamini operibus, & preparate vestram salutem.

Hortatur Apostolus ad modestiam & humilitatem.

Quomodo ergo salutem propriis operibus aut meritis obtineri doceret? Ita potius causam haberent superbiendi coram Deo, quam prorsus excludit alias Apostolus, Epb.

2, 8. ne quis glorietur, ac quanti opera nostra fiant ab Apostolo cap. 3. docebit. Excludit passim Apostolus non modo merita quævis, sed opera etiam nostra ab articulo justificationis & salutis, merita per unicum Christi meritum, opera per fidem, vel apprehensionem meriti Christi, qua sola justificamur & salvamur.

Non ergo operari salutem nostram, id velle aut inferre potest, quod nos efficiamus aut mereamur operibus nostris salutem.

Neque simpliciter jubemur κατεργάζεσθαι, sed μετὰ φόβου καὶ τρόμου, quod non est cum obedientia & offensa metu, sed cum timore ac tremore. Quid ergo hoc præceptum aliud falva fidei analogia requirere potest, quam quod cum timore & tremore versari debemus in causa salutis, ne fidem excuriamus vel deperdamus, quod fit per neglectum medium fidei, securitatem carnalem, & peccata mortalia, cum non ambulamus secundum Spiritum, sed secundum carnem, non mortificamus opera carnis per Spiritum, non sislimus membra serva justitiæ ad sanctificationem.

Cum timore, ait Hieronymus in hunc locum, id est, non cum negligentia, sed sicut Job, verebar omnia opera mea propter DEUM, tantem & timentem verba tua Dei Spiritus sanctus requificit.

Neque ergo diffidentia jubetur, dubitatio de gratia, vel confidentia & fiducia filialis excluditur per φόβον καὶ τρόμον, quod Papistæ firmant; non enim aliter ipsi possunt, quam salutem ex operibus sperent, adeoque iis imperfectis, immundis, ac peccatis pollutis, ut non desperare, dubitare certe de salute necessum habeant, siquidem etiam illos, qui omnia quæ debuere, fecerunt, profiteri oporteat, se servos inutiles esse, Luc. 17, 10.

Excluditur timor & tremor servilis, non autem excluditur filialis, qui cum confidentia de gratia DEI & salute æterna posse consistere potest. Scopus aspiciendus Apostoli, qui tantum abest, ut hic quicquam nobis tribui velit, ut potius id agat, ut omnibus modis deprimatur superbia, & omnia DEO tribuantur, obedientiam requirens, sed cum humilitate debita, ut non nobis quicquam, sed omnia DEO tribuamus.

Cæterum, inquit S. Augustinus de natur. & grat. contra Pelag. cap. XXVII. vitia tantum in malefactis valent, sola autem superbia in recte factis cavenda est. Unde admonentur illi, ne dona Dei suæ pietati tribuendo, sese extollendo gravius peccent, quam si nihil operentur boni, quibus dicitur, cum timore & tremore salutem vestram operamini. DEUS enim est, qui operatur in vobis & velle & perficere pro bona voluntate. Quare ergo cum timore & tremore, & non potius cum securitate, si Deus operatur, nisi quia propter voluntatem nostram, sine qua bene non possumus operari, cito potest subrepere animo humano, ut quod bonum operatur, suum tantummodo existimet, & dicat in abundantia sua, non movebor in æternum.

Adde Augustinus Serm. de Verb. Apost. cap. III. Humilitatem nos docens fastigia scriptura ducit per Apostolum, cum timore & tremore salutem vestram operamini, & ne sibi deinde aliquid darent, quia dixit operamini, continuo subjunxit: DEUS enim est, qui operatur in vobis & velle & operari pro bona voluntate: Deus est, qui operatur in vobis, ideo cum timore & tremore, vallem facite, imbrem suscipite: depressa implentur, alta siccantur, gratia pluvia est.

Quid ergo miraris, si DEUS superbe resistit, humilibus vero dat gratiam? Ideo cum timore & tremore, id est, cum humilitate. Noli altum sapere, sed time. Time ut implearis. Noli altum sapere, nec ficceris. Ita ergo hoc subjicit Apostolus, Deus est, qui operatur & velle & perficere, partim ne quis arbitretur, in nostra facultate esse, operari salutem, partim ne diffidamus, quum jubeamur cum timore & tremore salutem perficere, animumque despondeamus, ut gratia DEI εὐδοκία erigamur, quo pacto συνέχειαν verborum explicat Chrysostomus.

Quid enim dicit? Deus est, qui operatur in vobis, ne timeas, quod dixi, cum timore ac tremore. Non ideo istud dixi, ut desperet, ut virtutem incomprehensibilem putes, sed ut attendas, ne te ipsum dissolvas ac remittas. Hoc si fuerit, Deus omnia operabitur. Tu bono fis animo. Vers. 13. Θεὸς γάρ ἐστιν ὁ ἐνεργῶν καὶ τὸ θέλειν, καὶ τὸ ἐνεργεῖν ὑπὲρ τῆς εὐδοκίας) Quasi dicat: Nolite diffidere, ac si virium inopia non possitis id, quod doce, implere, DEUS enim per revelationem promissorum suorum faciet ut recta velimus, & per Spiritum suum faciet, ut etiam constanter talia operemur.

In Manuscripto est: Θεὸς γάρ ἐστιν ὁ ἐνεργῶν δύναμιν ἐν ὑμῖν. Illud ὑπὲρ τῆς εὐδοκίας potest quidem recte exponi, pro summa sua in nos benevolentia, sed nec male illi, qui exponunt, pro desiderio nostro, idque ex loco Psal. 145, 19. ubi est רצון. Nexus rationem jam dedimus, quod non modo humilitatem ita suadere, sed simul etiam diffidentiam removere voluerit, quæ, si nostris res committeretur viribus, certo certius oriretur: Jam autem quia DEUS pro εὐδοκία sua etiam operari vult τὸ ἐνεργεῖν, qui operatur τὸ θέλειν, divinæ tum potentiæ, tum gratiæ tuto innitimur.

Ad humilitatem & modestiam etiam præsentem aphorismum referunt nonnulli. Quum enim homo non habeat ex seipso, tanquam ex seipso, vel velle, vel operari, quis ergo ausit, sese efferre, nisi audire velit: Quid habes homo, quod non accepisti? 1. Corint. 4, 7. Nec vero dicit Apostolus: DEUS est, qui vult, ut velitis, & efficiatis. Non, qui suadet & hortatur, sed qui efficit, tum ut velitis, tum ut perficiatis. Pelagii hæc sententia erat, DEUM in nobis operari velle, dum nos præmiorum pollicitatione succendit, quem refellit passim Augustinus: Vid. libr. I. de grat. Christ. contra Pelag. & Cœlest. cap. 20. Nec dicit Apostolus, ut possitis velle, nec ut possitis efficere, sed ut velitis, & efficiatis.

Ut velitis, verbi gratia, actu credere, diligere, sperare, orare, certare, perseverare, & ut allu credatis, diligatis, speretis, oretis, certetis, perseveretis. Non efficit, quod ante volumus; sed cum nollemus antea, ex nolentibus facit volentes, & ut volentes facti porro velimus. Neque audiendi hic Semi-Pelagiani, Arminiani, Novatores, Latermannus, Dreierus, affeclæ, qui contendunt, in hominis potestate esse, credere hominem posse, si credere velit, & velle credere.

Vide quæ diximus Harmon. Calixt. Hæret. Sect. &c. III, cap. V. pag. 1010. seqq.

Velle quidem, quatenus est actus voluntatis, nostrum est, ex creatione; bene velle etiam nostrum est, sed quatenus volentes facti per conversionem bene volumus. Non quod a nobis initium fit, vel etiam ipsa perfectio, sive conversionis, sive bonæ actionis. Non quod nos non bene velimus, sed quod ex nobis non velimus bene. Nec ideo vel frustra nobis præcipitur obedientia, vel nos non obedimus. Præceptum enim ostendit, non quid a nobis vel possimus vel velimus, sed quid velle facere debeamus, & DEO dante possimus. Etsi vero DEUS efficit in nobis obedientiam, nos tamen obedimus, DEUS non obedit.

Ati enim à DEO ipsi agimus, sicut Augustinus dixit: DEUS est, qui operatur in nobis & velle & operari. Nos ergo volumus. Sed DEUS operatur in nobis & velle. Nos ergo operamur, sed Deus in nobis operatur & operari pro bona voluntate. Hoc nobis expedit & credere & dicere, hoc est pium, hoc est verum, ut sis humilis, & submissa confessio, & totum detur DEO, libr. de dono persever. cap.

13. Ut ergo recta velimus, non sufficit relatio promissorum Divinorum, sed requiritur Spiritus DEI efficax operatio, & gratia cordis nostri conversio, ac regeneratio. Solam revelationem sufficere, Pelagianismum resipit. Nec τὸ ἐνεργεῖν ἐνεργεῖν operari in nobis operari est efficere per Spiritum suum, ut constanter recta operemur, sed ea etiam in nobis operari, nam quamvis operemur etiam renati per Spiritus sancti gratiam, id tamen, ut possimus recta operari, & ipsum τὸ operari recta à Spiritu sancto in nobis oritur. Nec tantum opera bona in nobis producit Spiritus sanctus, sed etiam fidem, quæ bonorum operum genitrix est, & producit & conservat infinita sua virtute. Εὐδοκία autem ista non nostra est, ut Pelagius interpretatur, sed Dei. Nam ea prædicatur etiam in illo, quod DEUS velle in nobis operetur; ubi certe operari DEUM pro εὐδοκία sua, dici nequit.

Si quis, dicitur in Concil. Araufican. II. capitulo III. ita ut à peccato purgemur, voluntatem nostram DEUM expellare, contendit, non autem etiam, ut purgari velimus, per sancti Spiritus infusionem & operationem in nobis fieri confitetur, resistit ipsi Spiritui sancto, per Salomonem dicenti: Præparatur voluntas à Domino, & Apostolo, salubriter prædicanti: Deus est, qui operatur in nobis & velle & perfice- re pro bona voluntate: Et cap. XXVI. ex August. Tractat. XIX. in Johannem & Prospero Sentent. CCCXXXVIII. Suam voluntatem homines faciunt, non Dei, quando id agunt, quod Deo displicet. Quan- do autem ita faciunt, quod volunt, ut Divinæ serviant voluntati, quamvis volentes agant, quod agunt, illius tamen voluntas est, à quo præparatur & jubetur, quod volunt.

## 2:14
Vers. 14.

Do all things without murmurings and disputings) Most codices have Without murmurings and disputings, and so the Syriac and Latin read. Moreover, γογγυσμὸς or γόγγυσις is תְּלֻנּוֹת, Exod. 16, 7. 8. 9. 12. Num. 14, 27. c. 17, 10. that which the Greeks call μεμψιμοιρίαν, where one does not acquiesce in the Divine dispensation concerning himself. But disputings here seem to be bitter quarrels about things that contribute nothing to piety, such as were many among the Philosophers, especially the Aristotelians, of whom there were many in Macedonia.

Murmurings for the most part accompany arrogance and pride. Since, therefore, the Apostle is now exhorting to humility, he wishes them to be banished here. They accompany impatience most of all. But he commended humility in such a way that he simultaneously exhibited an example of patience in Christ. See Luc. 5, 20. Johan. 6, 41. Act. 6, 1. 1. Petr. 4, 9. Disputings, however, are prohibited, not only such as were among the Philosophers, but any others whatsoever, because the unity of the Spirit, to which the Apostle had exhorted, is immediately disturbed. Compare Luc. 9, 46. Matth. 18, 1. Rom. 14, 1. And since disputings arise most of all from arrogance and κενοδοξίᾳ, he deservedly excludes them here, where he has proposed the highest example of humility. Compare Matth. 11, 29.

Latin:

Vers. 14.

Πάντα ποιεῖτε χωρὶς ὀργῆς καὶ διαλογισμῶν) Codices plerique habent Χωρὶς γογγυσμῶν καὶ διαλογισμῶν, & ita legerunt Syrus & Latinus. Est autem γογγυσμὸς sive γόγ- γυσις תְּלֻנּוֹת, Exod. 16, 7. 8. 9. 12. Num. 14, 27. c. 17, 10. id quod Græci dicunt μεμψιμοιρίαν, ubi quis Divinæ de se dispensationi non acquiescit. Διαλογισμοὶ vero videntur hic esse rixæ acerbæ de rebus ad pietatem nihil facientibus, quales multæ erant inter Philosophos maxime Aristotelicos, quales in Macedonia multi.

Murmurationes plerumque arrogantiam & su- perbiam comitantur. Cum ergo ad humilitatem jam hortetur Apostolus, easdem hic exulare vult. Comitantur maxime impatientiam. At humilita- tem ita commendavit, ut patientiæ exemplum si- mul in Christo exhibuerit. Vid. Luc. 5, 20. Johan. 6, 41. Act. 6, 1. 1. Petr. 4, 9. Disceptationes au- tem non tantum quales inter Philosophos erant, sed quæcunque aliæ prohibentur, quia illico turbatur unitas Spiritus, ad quam hortatus erat Apostolus. Conf. Luc. 9, 46. Matth. 18, 1. Rom. 14, 1. Et quum oriantur disceptationes quam maxime ex arro- gantia, & κενοδοξίᾳ, merito hic eas excludit, ubi summum humilitatis exemplum proposuit. Conf. Matth. 11, 29.

## 2:15
Vers. 15.

That you may be blameless and harmless) Blameless before men, harmless before God. תְּמִימִים וִישָׁרִים. Children of God) Rom. 8, 16. 21. chap. 9, 8. Gal. 4, 28. Without fault) Eph. 4, 4. chap. 5, 27. Coloff. 1, 22. 1. Petr. 3. 34. Jude v. 24. Apoc. 14, 5.

The Pelagians and their modern followers draw these things to the perfection of man in this life. To whom Augustine replies in the book on the perfection of righteousness against Caelestius, chap. 17. This is the point, that we may be this, if the immaculate are to be understood as those who are altogether without sin: But if the immaculate are those who are without crime, we cannot deny that they have been and are even in this life; because someone is not therefore without any sin, because he does not have the stain of crime. Therefore the passage Apoc. 14, 5 does not apply here, except that we ought to strive for it in this life, although we may only attain it in the next.

In the midst of a crooked and perverse generation) So also Acts 2, 40. deservedly. For the customs of the Jews and of the nations not converted to Christ were most corrupt at that time. The words are taken from Deut. 32. 20. where in the Greek: that it is a perverse generation. Add also Es. 59, 8.

Theophylact thus handed down the connection. I know, he says, that there are many who attack you and compel you to complaints. But that is of great praise, when even though provoked, someone complains of nothing. Therefore he means this, that the greater the occasion for sinning is given, the more the sin of murmuring because of impatience, of contentions because of provocations, and of other vices because of the examples of a wicked and διεστραμμένης generation, that is, thoroughly tortuous, distorted, and in every way perverse, in the midst of which it was necessary to live, must be avoided.

Among whom you shine as lights in the world) It is accepted among the Hebrews that the works of external creation have in themselves an image of internal, that is, new creation. They are also accustomed to say: what the luminaries are in heaven, that the wise are on earth: Lights מְאֹרֹת, Gen. 1, 14. sun and moon, to which those who are truly Christians are rightly compared, Matth. 5, 14. Eph.

from 5, 8. 1. Thess. 5, 5. Compare also what was said long ago in Dan. 12, 3. to which the Apostle looks in Rom. 2, 19. Many take shine here in the Imperative. I would prefer it in the Indicative: See how you live. All look to you.

The commentary inscribed to Jerome reads it in the Imperative, so that the duty of the reborn may be designated. Erasmus also translates it thus, lucete; but B. Luther preferred the Indicative, as did Beza and Piscator. Theophylact brings forward both senses: For just as torches shine in the darkness, so you yourselves are among the crooked and perverse, inasmuch as you both stand upright and strive for light. Holding forth the word of life, that is, you have already obtained the seed of life. Or because just as torches shine together; and as if by the warmth of their own brightness they restore life to bodies, so you must strive with all zeal, that you may be in the place of virtue to men, which can provide life from itself. The Indicative is pleasing, so that the dignity of the children of God may be commended, who shine among the children of the world, Matth. 5. and the faithful are excited by this eulogy, so that they may strive to shine more and more, and by the splendor of wisdom may dispel the darkness of ignorance and errors, and by the brightness of virtue the gloom of vices, as lights of the world. The faithful were shining in the darkness of the world not with some native light, but illuminated by Christ the true light, enlightening all men, that sun of justice, Joh. 1. 9. Malach. 4, 1. Which dignity the Apostle had also proposed to the Ephesians, Eph. 5, 8. They are excited, however, to scatter the brightness of faith and holiness in the midst of the darkness of the world, both so that it may appear the more illustrious, and so that others may be converted by that light, Matth. 5, 14. For even stars, as Chrysostom says, shine at night, and appear in the darkness, and yet their beauty is not harmed at all, but they even appear more splendid: So also you, if you remain upright among the crooked, will shine more.

Latin:

Vers. 15.

Ἵνα γένησθε ἄμεμπτοι καὶ ἀκέραιοι) Ἄμεμπτοι apud ho- mines, ἀκέραιοι apud Deum. תְּמִימִים וִישָׁרִים. Τέκνα Θεῶ) Rom. 8, 16. 21. cap. 9, 8. Gal. 4, 28. Ἀμώμητα) Eph. 4, 4. cap. 5, 27. Coloff. 1, 22. 1. Petr. 3. 34. Judæ v. 24. Apoc. 14, 5.

Ad perfectionem hominis in hac vita hæc trahunt Pelagiani, & eorum sectatores moderni. Quibus respondet Augustinus libr. de perfect. justit. contra Cœlest. cap. 17. Hoc agitur, ut hoc simus, si immacu- lati intelligendi, qui omnino sine peccato sunt: Sin au- tem immaculati sunt, qui sunt sine crimine, etiam in hac vita fuisse atq; esse, negare non possumus; quia non ideo sine ullo peccato est aliquis, quoniam non habet maculam criminis. Idcirco locus Apoc. 14, 5. huc non facit, nisi quod eo contendere debeamus in hac vita, licet id demum consequamur in altera.

Ἐν μέσῳ γενεᾶς σκολιᾶς καὶ διεστραμμένης) Sic & Actor. 2, 40. merito. Erant enim eo tempore mores Judæorum & gentium non conversarum ad Christum corruptissimi. Sunt verba desumpta ex Deut. 32. 20. ubi in Græco: ὅτι γενεὰ ἀπεστραμμένη ἐστι. Adde & Es. 59, 8.

Connexionem ita tradidit Theophylactus. No- vi, inquit, esse plerosque, qui vos impugnent & ad que- rimonias cogant. At illud ingentis est laudis, cum vel percitus quispiam nil conqueritur. Id ergo vult, quo amplior datur occasio peccandi, eo magis vi- tandum esse peccatum murmurationis ob impa- tientiam, contentionum ob provocationes, vitio- rum aliorum ob exempla generationis pravæ & διεστραμμένης, id est, penitus tortuosæ, distortæ, at- que omnibus modis perversæ, in cujus medio ver- sari oportebat.

Ἐν οἷς φαίνεσθε ὡς φωστῆρες ἐν κόσμῳ) Receptum apud Ebræos, opera creationis externæ habere in se imagi- nem creationis internæ, id est, novæ. Dicere etiam so- lent: quod luminaria in cœlo, id sapientes in terra: Φωστῆρες מְאֹרֹת, Gen. 1, 14. sol & luna, quibus recte com- parantur ii, qui vere sunt Christiani, Matth. 5, 14. Eph.

à 5, 8. 1. Thess. 5, 5. Confer & quod olim dictum Dan. 12, 3. quo Apostolus respicit Rom. 2, 19. Φαίνεσθε multi hic su- munt in Imperativo. Ego in Indicativo malim: Vide quomodo vivatis. Omnes vos respiciunt.

In Imperativo legit Hieronymo inscriptus com- mentarius, ut designetur renatorum officium. Sic etiam vertit Erasmus lucete; Indicativum autem prætulit B. Lutherus, ut & Beza ac Piscator. Utrum- que sensum affert Theophylactus: Ut enim faces in tenebris splendent, sic ipsi estis inter obliquos & tortuo- sos, quippe qui & erecti consistitis, & luci studetis. Ser- monem autem vitæ habentes, hoc est, vitæ semen ad- epti jam estis.
