Vel quia quemadmodum faces collu- cent; & quasi sui fulgoris fomento vitam corporibus reddunt, sic vobis omni studio est enitendum, ut virtu- tis loco hominibus sitis, quæ vitam de se possit præstare. Placet Indicativus, ut commendetur dignitas fi- liorum Dei, qui lucent inter filios mundi, Matth. 5: & excitentur hoc elogio fideles, ut magis magis- que lucere nitantur, & sapientiæ splendore te- nebras ignorantiæ & errorum, virtutis fulgore ca- liginem vitiorum discutiant, ceu mundi lumina. Lucebant fideles in tenebris mundi non nativa quadam luce, sed collustrati à Christo vera luce, omnes homines illuminante, sole illo justitiæ, Joh. 1. 9. Malach. 4, 1. Quam dignitatem etiam proposue- rat Ephesiis Apostolus, Eph. 5, 8. Excitantur au- tem ad spargendum fulgorem fidei, & sanctitatis in medio tenebrarum mundi, tum ut eo illustrior ille appareat, tum ut alii luce illa convertantur, Matth. 5, 14. Nam & stellæ, dicente Chrysostomo, noctu lu- cent, & in tenebris comparent, & tamen nihilo læditur illorum venustas, sed & splendidiores apparent: Ita & tu si apud tortuosos rectus manseris, magis splendesces.

## 2:16
V. 16. Λόγον ζωῆς ἐπέχοντες) It is an ἀπόδοσις mixed with a comparison. Just as those celestial lights give life to living creatures, so you lift up a life-giving light to all nations. Thus the Greeks say ἐπέσχειν ἡμέρᾳ. Barnabas says: Τῷ λόγῳ ζωοποιούμενοι.

Those also go in that direction who, with Beza, translate the word of life as 'holding forth' (luminaries), because they communicate the word of life to others by a purer confession and holy examples, Rom. 15, 17, which explanation of Zanchius is preferred by Crocius. But because that had already been indicated by the name of luminaries of the world, according to B. Luther as interpreter, to whom Bullinger agrees, the reason is rendered here as to how they thus shine before the world like luminaries, namely, in so far as, or because they retain the word of life. However, because of the more common meaning of the word ἐπέχω, and its construction with the Accusative, and also because of the force of the Metaphor, since they are compared to luminaries, because they provide light, I do not disagree with Grotius. That word is not found with the Accusative case in the meaning of attending to, or even retaining. Erasmus Schmidius: Λόγον ζωῆς ἐπέχοντες, exhibiting the word of life, namely to others, to whom you shine forth ἄμεμπτοι κἀκέραιοι ὡς Φωστήρες ἐν κόσμῳ. Just as a nurse is said μασὸν ἐπέχειν to an infant.

Εἰς καύχημα ἐμοὶ εἰς ἡμέραν Χριστῦ) So that in that great day I may rejoice over you. For we have often said already that this is what it means to καυχᾶσθαι and καύχημα.

Why the more common meaning of boasting should not be retained does not appear. Conf. 2. Cor. 1, 14. 1. Thess. 2, 29. 30. Concerning joy, it will be spoken of next in v. 17.

Ὅτι ἐκ εἰς κενὸν ἔδραμον, ἐδὲ εἰς κενὸν ἐκοπίασα) εἰς κενὸν, that is, without fruit, 2. Corinth. 6, 1. Galat. 2, 2. There is, however, a λιτότης here. For he wishes to say, not without copious fruit of the Gospel. Preaching is rightly compared both to a race, as in the cited place to the Galatians, Act. 20, 24. 2. Tim. 4, 7. and to laborious work, Actor. 20, 35. 1. Cor. 15, 10. Gal. 4, 11. 1. Tim. 4, 10. chap. 5, 17. Apoc. 2, 3.

It seems to some that the word for running alludes to the race in the stadium from 1. Cor. 9, 24. 2. Tim. 4, 8. But here it is not so much the contention, which was customary in running in the stadium, as the zeal, promptness, and alacrity, just as the difficulty in duty is noted by the word for laboring.

Concerning the mutual joy of Paul and the Philippians.

Latin:

V. 16. Λόγον ζωῆς ἐπέχοντες) Est ἀπόδοσις mixta compara- tioni. Sicut illa lumina cœlestia vitam dant animalibus, ita vos attollitis lumen omnibus gentibus vivificum. Sic ἐπέσχειν ἡμέρᾳ dicunt Græci. Barnabas ait: Τῷ λόγῳ ζωοποιούμενοι.

Eo etiam abeunt, qui cum Beza reddunt verbum vitæ prætendentiæ (luminaria) quod aliis verbum vitæ communicent, puriori confessione, & sanctis exemplis, Rom. 15, 17. quæ Zanchii explicatio præ- fertur à Crocio. Sed quia illud jam indicatum erat, luminarium mundi nomine, B. Luthero interprete, cui adstipulatur Bullingerus, redditur hic ratio, quo pacto ita præluceant mundo instar luminarium, quatenus nempe, vel quia verbum vitæ retinent. Ob usitatiorem tamen verbi ἐπέχω significationem, & cum Accusativo constructionem, tum etiam ob Metaphoræ vim, siquidem luminaribus comparen- tur, quod præbeant lumen, non abnuo Grotio. Non invenitur verbum istud cum Accusativo casu signi- ficationi attendendi, vel etiam retinendi. Erasmus Schmidius: Λόγον ζωῆς ἐπέχοντες sermonem vitæ exhibentes, aliis scilicet, quibus ἄμεμπτοι κἀκέραιοι ὡς Φωστήρες ἐν κόσμῳ prælucetis. Sicut μασὸν ἐπέ- χειν infanti nutrix dicitur.

Εἰς καύχημα ἐμοὶ εἰς ἡμέραν Χριστῦ) Ut in die illo ma- gno de vobis gaudeam. Id enim esse καυχᾶσθαι & καύχη- μα sæpe jam diximus.

Cur non sit retinenda significatio usitatior glo- riationis, non apparet. Conf. 2. Cor. 1, 14. 1. Thess. 2, 29. 30. De gaudio deinceps dicetur v. 17.

Ὅτι ἐκ εἰς κενὸν ἔδραμον, ἐδὲ εἰς κενὸν ἐκοπίασα) εἰς κενὸν, id est, sine fructu, 2. Corinth. 6, 1. Galat. 2, 2. Est autem hic λιτότης. Vult enim dicere, non sine copioso fructu Evangelii. Prædicatio recte comparatur & cursui, ut dicto ad Galatas loco, Act. 20, 24. 2. Tim. 4, 7. & operæ labo- riosæ, Actor. 20, 35. 1. Cor. 15, 10. Gal. 4, 11. 1. Tim. 4, 10. cap. 5, 17. Apoc. 2, 3.

Verbo currendi ad cursum in stadio alludi non- nullis videtur è 1. Cor. 9, 24. 2. Tim. 4, 8. Sed hic non tam contentio, quæ in stadio decurrendo usitata e- rat, quam studium, promptitudo, & alacritas, uti ver- bo laborandi difficultas in officio, notatur.

e gaudio amoebaeo Pauli & Philippensium.

## 2:17
Verse 17. Ἀλλ' εἰ καὶ σπένδομαι ἐπὶ τῇ θυσίᾳ καὶ λειτουργίᾳ τῆς πίστεως ὑμῶν) A libation Ammonius says is the pouring of wine alongside the sacred rites. In sacred things there was a victim, θυσία, which was prepared by the Levites and Priests with a solemn rite.

It was בערבה. There followed a libation of wine, σπονδὴ, Judges 9:13. Paul had made the Philippians victims to God, Rom. 12:1, ch. 15:16, Eph. 5:2. He had so prepared them by his doctrine and example that they might be pleasing to God. He saw that it could easily happen that he might confirm the faith of both the Philippians and others with his own blood.

This he calls here σπένδεσθαι, to be poured out as a libation. Blood is compared to wine, and in sacred things wine is in the place of blood. See what we have said at Matt. 26:27. Thrasea dying in Dio: Σοὶ τὸ αἷμα ζῶ ἐλευθέριος σπένδω. Χαίρω) I will rejoice in such honor. The present for the future. Καὶ συγχαίρω πᾶσιν ὑμῖν) I will also congratulate you and the other faithful, to whom the fruit of my death will reach. Τὸ δὲ αὐτὸ καὶ ὑμεῖς χαίρετε καὶ συγχαίρετέ μοι) Thus we also say in Latin: I rejoice in this. He means this: For this reason rejoice, and congratulate me.

We add the paraphrase of Theophylact: If I should die, he says, (for he calls death an immolation) for I am immolated upon the sacrifice and service of your faith, that is, when I had previously offered you as a sacrifice to God and a service, and had made you faithful, not that I should be finished as a dead man, but I am a bringer of joy, and I am affected with joy together with you. I rejoice indeed, because I am offered to be immolated: but I congratulate you, because I have offered your faith no otherwise than some sacrifice to God himself. But rejoice also in this same thing; that is, because you have been offered through me in this manner. And congratulate me; because when I am to be immolated, I am affected with incredible joy.

The Commentary of Jerome has it thus: Congratulate me, because it is a great reward for me to be killed for you. Friends are accustomed to congratulate one who is triumphing. Paul will triumph when he is poured out over you. Therefore they congratulate him deservedly. Verse 19. Ἐλπίζω δὲ ἐν Κυρίῳ Ἰησοῦ) that is, I hope that I, with Christ helping, will obtain this, which follows. Τιμόθεον ταχέως πέμψαι) He promises much. For he wishes to send him, whom he calls genuine, 1

Tim. 3:2. Ἵνα κἀγὼ εὐψυχῶ κἀγὼ τὰ περὶ ὑμῶν) Others have ἐνψυχῶ. But this reading is not to be despised. For ἐμψυχον, which is also ἀνάψυχον, is active for the reciprocal, to refresh oneself, which the Hebrews say in Psalm 39:14. They compare calamities to heat, and consolations to refrigeration, hence also παραψυχή. Verse 20. Οὐδένα γάρ εἰμι ἰσόψυχον) from Psalm 55:14, where in Hebrew בערכי אנוש ואתה . In Greek: οὐ δὲ ἄνθρωπε ἰσόψυχε. I have no other so dear to me, and faithful to me. The Syriac: As my soul. Ὅτις γνώσε τὰ περὶ ὑμῶν μεριμνήσει) who will be about to take care of you with such faith. Freoins sincere in the glossary. You have that word in 2 Maccab. 14:8. Calvin and Beza think that others are compared with Timothy regarding affection for the Philippians. But St. Luther with Theophylact and the Greeks more correctly thinks that Timothy is compared with Paul, because he is of an equal mind with him in caring with singular zeal and industry, which word μεριμνήσει implies, for the Philippians. Whom Aretius and Piscator follow.

Latin:

Vers. 17. Ἀλλ' εἰ καὶ σπένδομαι ἐπὶ τῇ θυσίᾳ καὶ λειτουργίᾳ τῆς πίστεως ὑμῶν) Σπονδὴ Ammonio ἡ τῷ οἴνῳ ἔγχυσις παρὰ τὰ ἱερουργήματα. In sacris erat victima, θυσία ea solemni ritu per Levitas ac Sacerdotes praeparabatur.

Id erat בערבה Accedebat vini libatio, σπονδὴ Judic. 9, 13. Paulus Philippenses fecerat Deo victimas Rom. 12, 1. cap. 15, 16. Eph. 5, 2. Eos doctrina & exemplo suo ita paraverat, ut Deo grati essent. Videbat facile fieri posse, ut ipso suo sanguine fidem & Philippensium & aliorum confirmaret.

Id hic vocat σπένδεσθαι libari. Sanguis vino comparatur, & in sacris vinum est vice sanguinis. Vide quae diximus ad Matth. 26, 27. Thrafea moriens apud Dionem: Σοὶ τὸ αἷμα ζῶ ἐλευθέριος σπένδω. Χαίρω) Gaudebo tanto honore. Praesens pro futuro. Καὶ συγχαίρω πᾶσιν ὑμῖν) Gratulabor etiam vobis & fidelibus aliis, ad quos fructus mortis meae perveniet. Τὸ δὲ αὐτὸ καὶ ὑμεῖς χαίρετε καὶ συγχαίρετέ μοι) Sic & Latine dicimus: Hoc gaudeo. Hoc vult: Ob hanc rem gaudete & vos, & mihi gratulamini.

Addimus Theophylacti paraphrasin: Etfimoriar, inquit, (mortem enim immolationem appellat) immolor namque supra sacrificium & obsequium fidei vestrae, hoc est, cum antea vos in sacrificium Deo & obsequium obtulissem, & fideles effecerim, nequaquam ut mortuus mare conficiar, sed lator equidem, & vobiscum una afficior gaudio. Gaudeo quidem, quia offeror immolandus: gratulor vero, quia fidem vestram non secus ac sacrificium aliquod Deo ipsi obtulerim. Idipsum autem & vos gaudete; id scilicet, quia estis per me hunc in modum oblati. Et congratulamini mihi; quia cum sim immolandus, incredibili jucunditate afficior.

Hieronymi Commentarius ita habet: Gratulamini, quia mihi grande premium est, pro vobis occidi. Triumphanti solent amici gratulari. Paulus triumphabit, cum libabitur de vobis. Merito igitur gratulantur. Vers. 19. Ἐλπίζω δὲ ἐν Κυρίῳ Ἰησοῦ) id est, spero me, Christo adjuvante hoc consecuturum, quod sequitur. Τιμόθεον ταχέως πέμψαι) Multum promittit.

Eum enim vult mittere, quem γνήσιον vocat, 1. Timoth. 3, 2. Ἵνα κἀγὼ εὐψυχῶ κἀγὼ τὰ περὶ ὑμῶν) Alii habent ἐνψυχῶ. Sed non spernenda haec lectio. Nam ἐμψυχον, quod & ἀνάψυχον, est activum pro reciproco, refrige rare semet, quod Ebraei dicunt Psalm. 39, 14. calamitates aestui comparant, solatia refrigeratione, inde & παραψυχή. Vers. 20. Οὐδένα γάρ εἰμι ἰσόψυχον) ex Psal. 55, 14. ubi in Ebraeo בערכי אנוש ואתה In Graeco: οὐ δὲ ἄνθρωπε ἰσόψυχε. Non alium habeo tam charum mihi, mihique fidum. Syrus: Ut anima mea. Ὅτις γνώσε τὰ περὶ ὑμῶν μεριμνήσει) qui tanta fide vestri curam fit gesturus. Freoins sincere in glossario. Habes eam vocem 2. Maccab. 14, 8. Alios comparari cum Timotheo quoad affectum in Philippenses, Calvinus & Beza censent. Sed rectius S. Lutherus cum Theophylacto & Gracis fibus comparari Timotheum cum Paulo, quod pari secum fit animo in curandis singulari studio & industria, quod verbum μεριμνήσει infert, Philippensibus. Quem sequuntur Aretius & Piscator.

## 2:21
Verse 21. Οἱ πάντες γὰρ τὰ ἑαυτῶν ζητοῦσιν, ἃ τὰ τοῦ χρισοῦ) All is put here for many, as in Rom. 3:2. Most men seek their own things. Verse 22. Τὴν δὲ δοκιμὴν αὐτοῦ γινώσκετε) You know what proofs of his faith he has given. We have had this word in Rom. 2:4, 2 Cor. 2:9, ch. 8:20, ch. 9:13, ch. 13:3. Ὅτι ὡς Πατρὶ τέκνον σὺν ἐμοὶ ἐδούλευσεν εἰς τὸ Εὐαγγέλιον) He served me for the advancement of the Gospel no less than children are accustomed to serve their father, 1 Tim. 1:1, 2 Tim. 1:1. V. 23. Τῦτον μὲν οὖν) such and so great a man. Ἐλπίζω πέμψαι, ὡς ἂν ἀπίδω τὰ περὶ ἐμὲ) When I shall have seen what will become of me.

Latin:

Vers. 21. Οἱ πάντες γὰρ τὰ ἑαυτῶν ζητοῦσιν, ἃ τὰ τοῦ χρισοῦ) Πάντες hic positum pro multi, ut Rom. 3, 2. Sua agunt plerique hominum. Vers. 22. Τὴν δὲ δοκιμὴν αὐτοῦ γινώσκετε) Scitis quanta fidei suae documenta dederit. Habuimus vocem hanc de Rom. 2. 4. 2. Cor. 2, 9. c. 8, 20. c. 9, 13. c. 13, 3. Ὅτι ὡς Πατρὶ τέκνον σὺν ἐμοὶ ἐδούλευσεν εἰς τὸ Εὐαγγέλιον) Ad Evangelium promovendum non minus mihi inserviit, quam filii Patri solent, 1. Tim. 1, 1. 2. Tim. 1, 1. V. 23. Τῦτον μὲν οὖν) tantum ac talem virum. Ἐλπίζω πέμψαι, ὡς ἂν ἀπίδω τὰ περὶ ἐμὲ) Ubi videro quid me futurum sit.

## 2:24
Verf. 24. Πέποιθα δὲ ἐν Κυρίῳ) That I will obtain this from the Lord, as above ἐλπίζω ἐν Κυρίῳ. For πέποιθα is the same as ἐλπίζω, above ch. 1:6. Ὅτι καὶ αὐτὸς ταχέως ἐλεύσομαι) The same sense as above ch. 1:26. In the Manuscript πρὸς ὑμᾶς is added.

Latin:

Vers. 24. Πέποιθα δὲ ἐν Κυρίῳ) A Domino me hoc consecuturum esse, ut supra ἐλπίζω ἐν Κυρίῳ. Nam πέποιθα idem est quod ἐλπίζω, supra cap. 1, 6. Ὅτι καὶ αὐτὸς ταχέως ἐλεύσομαι) Idem sensus, qui supra cap. 1, 26. In Manuscripto additur πρὸς ὑμᾶς.

## 2:25
V. 25. Ἀναγκαῖον δὲ ἡγησάμην) I judged it necessary. Thus we had ἀναγκαῖότερον above at ch. 1, 24. Ἐπαφρόδιτον τὸν ἀδελφὸν) Of whom he also makes mention below at ch. 4, 18. I think he is the same as the one called ἐπαφρᾶς in contracted form, Coloss. 1, 7. ch. 4, 12. For we said at the beginning of the commentary on Luke that names were accustomed to be contracted in this manner. The name Epaphroditus is also found in the orations of Lyfiz. Καὶ συνεργὸν) A partaker of labor in announcing the Gospel, Rom. 16, 3. 9, 21. 2. Cor. 8, 23. below ch. 5, 3. Coloss. 4, 11. 1. Thess. 3, 2. Phil. v. 24. Καὶ συστρατιώτην μου) Also a partaker of dangers: which is excellently signified by a metaphor taken from military affairs. Thus also Philem. v. 2. A similar metaphor in 2. Corinth. 10, 14. 1. Tim. 1, 18. Ὑμῶν δὲ ἀπόστολον) that is; for those speaking Hebrew, while those speaking Greek called ἀπόστολους those who collected and carried sacred moneys, as we said at Matt. 11. Ὁ θεόδομος said Ignatius, and ἱεροκήρυξ and ἱερόπομπος. Epaphroditus and Epaphras are different persons, as we shall say in the preface to the epistle to the Colossians. Moreover Walo Messalinus de Episc. & Presbyt. p. 40. makes Apostles of two kinds, first and second. The first, who had received their mission from Christ, sent immediately by him himself: the second, who were sent by the Apostles themselves. As Christ, he says, sent his Apostles to preach the word to me, and to announce the Gospel: so the Apostles further sent others to establish presbyters, that is, bishops in those Churches whose foundations they themselves had laid. These second Apostles were as it were coadjutors and συνεργοὶ of the Apostles in building up the Churches, in which, by the precept and command of those by whom they were sent, they established presbyters, the same as bishops. Such were for Paul Timothy, Titus, Linus, also Clement, Phil. 4. he twice mentions Epaphroditus. These συνεργοὶ of the Apostles, who were also in a certain way their Apostles, were attached and fixed to no city, but at the discretion of the Apostles, whom they served in this office, they were sent to various cities.

"The Apostles (to whom the most learned man also adds Luke and Silas)," he says on page 44, "or the vicars of the Apostles and *synergoi* [co-workers], were also called bishops of those churches which they had received to administer from the Apostle, although they were not the special curators of them, and were sent to several churches with the same authority. These are the Apostles," he continues, p. 53, "whom Paul commemorates along with the Prophets, Evangelists, Pastors, and Teachers as having served the Church for the complete perfection of the saints, for the work of the ministry, and for the edification of the body of Christ in the epistle to the Ephesians, chapter 4, 11. For those Apostles of the churches are not to be understood as only the twelve, but also of those who had this function delegated to them by the true and greater Apostles. Such as Mark, Clement, Titus, Timothy, Epaphroditus, and many others. Therefore, Paul himself, who had used his ministry for this purpose in building and establishing the Church of the Philippians, calls Epaphroditus the Apostle of the Philippians, chapter 2. There the Vulgate rightly translates, 'and your Apostle.' For although our own [scholars] and even the Greeks take the word *apostolon* to refer to a secular ministry, and wish for Epaphroditus to have been sent by the Philippians themselves to Paul as a kind of legate, so that he might deliver what was necessary for them, I cannot, however, concede to this opinion. 'For they were the ones who sent to him,' say the Greek commentators, 'the things for his need. Therefore he calls him an Apostle and a minister of his own need.' For through him, that is, Epaphroditus, the Philippians had sent to Paul what was necessary for him. For that reason he calls him an Apostle and a minister of his own necessity. This does not seem likely to me, as if I knew that the word *apostolo* is never used by Paul nor by other Apostles and Evangelists except for the holy ministry. And although they seem to be called Apostles properly of those by whom they are sent, nonetheless they can also be called [Apostles] of those to whom they are sent, and whom they serve by instructing, teaching, and governing. Thus Paul said that God had placed in the Church first Apostles, then Prophets, in the third place Teachers and Pastors. Just as they are called prophets of that church in which they prophesy, and pastors of that whose flock they feed, so also the Apostles, who had established some particular church, whether they did so by themselves, as the greater ones, or by the mission and mandate of the greater ones, as those of whom we have spoken, were called Apostles of that church which had been established by them. Thus, therefore, Epaphroditus may be called by Paul the Apostle of the Philippians, because he had sent him to the Philippians to confirm their Church and to establish Presbyters and Bishops in it." Thus Messalinus, by his true name Claudius Salmasius. The Polyhistor brings forward here the passage of Theodoret on this place: "He called Epaphroditus their Apostle, as one to whom their care had been entrusted, so that it is clear that those who were called bishops in the beginning were under him, as they were in the order of Presbyters." With the added testimony of Clement in the Epistle to the Corinthians, he concludes: "Therefore they are and are called Apostles of those to whom they are sent, and whom they teach and direct." Regarding Timothy, page 64, he has this: "Those whom we called Apostles, who set bishops over the Church, either by the mandate of the greater Apostles or by their own, as the greater ones, did not establish a fixed seat in one place, not even in those cities or churches which they had established, except for a time, until they were fully constituted. Thus Paul sent Timothy to Ephesus and ordered him to remain there for a while. He also directed the same to Thessalonica. But he sent him to the Corinthians, as is evident from the first to the Corinthians, chapter 4. Later he recalled him to Rome. Timothy, therefore, was traveling through the churches. Which task is properly an Apostolic duty. Certainly, he never undertook the administration of one church."

"For in this way he would have been the bishop of several churches: of Corinth, Thessalonica, Philippi, Ephesus, and even Rome." It pleased me to bring forward the opinion of the most celebrated man: "Which indeed does not seem to be rejected, provided the matter had been defined a little more clearly in antiquity. In general, it is understood as a Minister of the Gospel, and in that way others wish for Andronicus and Junia also to be called Apostles. But that meaning of 'Minister of the Gospel' is too general. Nor does it seem that Andronicus and Junia are called Apostles only in such a *genikos* [general] way. Musculus, Beza, Tremellius, Zanchius, and Piscator understand it as a special duty of legation, that he went to Paul as ordered by the Philippians, and for that reason they are called Apostles who had been sent by the churches to collect aid for the Jerusalem Church, 2 Cor. 8:23. But this is not evident from that passage. And the name 'Apostle' is more illustrious here than to denote merely one sent for the sake of some thing, which would be an acceptance not more special than the former, but even more general. Grotius indeed refers himself to this opinion, favoring it at Matt. 11, but there he has by no means proven it from the scriptures of the New Testament or ecclesiastical antiquity in such a way that we can acquiesce. But it will perhaps be spoken of more fully at the beginning of the epistle of James, God willing. Something more or more sublime seems to be imported by that name than *synergos* [co-worker] and *systratiotes* [fellow soldier]: and that *leitourgia* [ministry] is expressed thereafter."

"And minister of the need": The Philippians had sent money to Paul through Epaphroditus, which he accepted, both because, being placed in chains, he could not labor with his hands as before, and so that he might relieve the poor Christians who were at Rome from that [money]. This is called *chreia* [need] in Acts 2:45, ch. 4:35, ch. 6:3, ch. 20:34, ch. 28:10, Romans 12:13, Eph. 4:28, below ch. 4:16. "I will send to you": He said 'to send' for 'to send back.' The simple for the compound. Verse 26. "Since he was longing for you all": In the manuscript, 'to see' is rightly added, just as the Apostle speaks in Rom. 1:11, 2 Tim. 1:4. And thus it appears the Syrian read here. "And was anxious": He was distressed. See Matt. 26:37, Mark 14:33. Aquila also uses it in Job 18:21. The Syrian here [has] *me'aq*: Well. "He was sick near to death": *chalah lamut*, Isaiah 38:1, where some Greeks [have] *emalakisthe heos thanatou* [he was sick unto death]: others *heos tou apothanein* [until dying], others *eis thanaton* [unto death]. "Lest he should have sorrow upon sorrow": Namely, if the loss of a friend had been added to the chains. That would have been *tsarah 'al tsarah* [trouble upon trouble]. Verse 28. "More eagerly": More hastily, as the Latin has it. For this is the genuine meaning of this word from *speudo*. From there the other [meaning] was transferred, which signifies diligence. "That seeing him again you may rejoice": The punctuation must be changed in this way: *hina idontes auton palin*, so that seeing him again, you may rejoice on that account. "And I may be less sorrowful": Namely, when I shall have learned that he has come safe to his own. For we do not rejoice so much, says Chrysostom, hearing that those whom we desire are healthy, as when we see them, and especially if that happens beyond expectation, which is what happened in the case of Epaphroditus. Verse 29. "With all joy": Rom 15:32. "And hold such men in honor": 1 Tim. 5:17. Verse 30. "Because for the work of Christ he drew near unto death": *charav lamut*, Job 33:22. He calls it the work of Christ, the labor expended for the sake of Christ. "Risking his life": It must be read entirely as *paraboleusamenoi te psyche*, that is, exposing his life to dangers, as the great men Scaliger and Salmasius have warned. Pliny in his letters: "Dangerous," and as the Greeks better explain, *parabola*. The Latin interpreter, older than the received one, had here: "he was parabolized in his soul." For in Latin also they are called *parabolani* who attend to the sick with danger to their life. The Syrian here placed *besar 'al napsheh*: he despised his life.

Latin:

V. 25. Ἀναγκαῖον δὲ ἡγησάμην) E re esse judicavi. Sic ἀναγκαῖότερον habuimus supra cap. 1, 24. Ἐπαφρόδιτον τὸν ἀδελφὸν) Cujus & infra meminit cap. 4, 18. Puto eumdem esse, qui ἐπαφρᾶς contracte, Coloss. 1, 7. c. 4, 12. Nam in eum modum contrahi solita nomina diximus initio ad Lucam. Nomen Epaphroditi est & in orationibus Lyfiz. Καὶ συνεργὸν) Participem laboris in annuntiando Evangelio, Rom. 16, 3. 9, 21. 2. Cor. 8, 23. infra cap. 5, 3. Coloss. 4, 11. 1. Thess. 3, 2. Phil. v. 24. Καὶ συστρατιώτην μου) Participem etiam periculorum: quod egregie significatur tralatione sumpta à re militari. Sic & Philem. v. 2. Similis tralatio 2. Corinth. 10, 14. 1. Tim. 1, 18. Ὑμῶν δὲ ἀπόστολον) id est, Sic enim Ebraice loquentes, Grace vero loquentes ἀπόστολους vocabant eos, qui sacras pecunias colligebant atque portabant, ut diximus ad Matth. 11. Ὁ θεόδομος dixit Ignatius & ἱεροκήρυξ & ἱερόπομπος. Diversi sunt Epaphroditus & Epaphras, ut in prooemio epistolae ad Colossenses dicturi sumus. Caeterum Walo Messalinus de Episc. & Presbyt. p. 40. duorum generum facit Apostolos, primi & secundi. Primi, qui à Christo missionem suam acceperant, immediate ab ipso missi: Secundi, qui ab ipsis Apostolis. Ut Christus Apostolos suos, inquit, misit ad predicandum verbum sum, & annuntiandum Evangelium: Ita Apostoli alios porro miserunt ad constituendos Episcopos sive Presbyteros in illis Ecclesiis, quas fundamenta ipsi jecerant. Hi secundi Apostoli quasi coadjutores & συνεργοὶ fuere Apostolorum in edificandis Ecclesiis, in quibus ex praecepto & mandato eorum, à quibus mittebantur, Presbyteros, eosdemq; Episcopos constituebant. Tales fuere Paulo Timotheus, Titus, Linum, etiam Clemens, Phil. 4. bis accenset Epaphroditum. Hi συνεργοὶ Apostolorum, qui & Apostoli quodammodo eorum nulli civitati erant affixi & additi, sed pro arbitrio Apostolorum, quibus ad hoc munus subserviebant, in varias civitates mittebantur.

Ifti Apoftoli, (quibus Lucam & Silam etiam accen-fet Vir Doctiffimus) inquit pag. 44. five Apoftolo rum vicarii & συνεργοὶ etiam Epifcopi vocabantur earum Ecclefiarum, quas ab Apoftolo adminiftran-das acceperant, quamvis fpeciales non effent earum curatores, & ad plures Ecclefias eam eadem pote-ftate mitterentur. Hi funt Apoftoli, pergit, p. 53. quos Paulus commemorat cum Prophetis, Evangeli-ftis, Paftoribus, & Doctoribus inferviiffe Ecclefia ad confummationem integram fanctorum, ad opus mini-fterii, & ad aedificationem corporis Chrifti in epiftola ad Ephefios cap. 4, 11. Non enim illi Apoftoli Eccle-fiarum de folis tantum duodecim intelligendi, fed de il-lu etiam, qui hanc functionem à veris & majoribus Apoftolis demandatam habuerant. Ut Marcus, Clemens, Titus, Timotheus, Epaphroditus, & alii mul-ti. Ideo & Epaphroditum ipfe Paulus, qui ejus mi-nifterio ad hoc ufus fuerat, in Ecclefia Philippenfium ftruenda & conftituenda, Apoftolum Philippenfium appellat, cap. 2. Ibi recte Vulgata vertit, & Apofto-lum veftrum. Quamvis enim noftri atque etiam Grati vocem ἀπόστολον accipiant de profano minifterio, ve-lintque Epaphroditum ab ipfis Philippenfibus ad Pau-lum quafi legatum miffum, ut, quae ipfi neceffaria ef-fent, deferret, non poffum tamen in hanc fententiam concedere. Διὰυτὰ γὰρ ἦσαν αὐτῷ, inquiunt Graeci commentatores, τὰ πρὸς χρείαν πέμψαντες. Διὸ Ἀπόστολον ἐκεῖνον καὶ τῆς οἰκείας χρείας λειτουργὸν αὐτὸν καλεῖ. Per illum enim, id eft, Epaphroditum, Philippenfes ad Paulum miferant, quae ipfi erant necef-faria. Ea gratia Apoftolum eum vocat, & admini-ftrum propriae neceffitatis. Hac mibi verifimilis non vi-detur, quafi fciam, vocem ἀποστόλῳ nunquam à Paulo nec ab aliis Apoftolis & Evangeliftis ufurpari nifi de fancto minifterio. Etfi autem proprie dici videantur Apoftoli eorum, à quibus mittuntur, nihilo fecius eo-rum etiam dici poffunt, ad quos miffi funt, & quibus inftruendis ac docendis regendisque infervium. Sic Paulus dixit, Deum pofuiffe in Ecclefia Apoftolos primum, deinde Prophetas, tertio loco Doctores & Pa-ftores. Ut Propheta illius Ecclefia dicuntur, in qua illi prophetant, paftores etiam illius, cujus gregem pafcunt, ita & Apoftoli, qui aliquam Ecclefiam pecu-liarem conftituerant, five ipfi per fe, ut majores, five majorum miffu & mandato, ut illi, de quibus dixi-mus, Apoftoli illius Ecclefia dicebantur, quae ab ipfis conftituta fuerat. Sic ergo Epaphroditus Paulo di-catur Apoftolus Philippenfium, quia ad Philippen-fes eum miferat ad Ecclefiam eorum confirmandam, & conftituendos in ea Presbyteros & Epifcopos. Hac Meffalinus, vero nomine Claudius Salmafius. Af-fert Polybiftor huc locum Theodoreti in hunc lo-cum: Epaphroditum autem vocavit Apoftolum ipfo-rum, utpote cui effet eorum cura credita, ut clarum fit, fub eo fuiffe, qui in Principio dicti funt Epifcopi, utpote qui in Presbyterorum ordine effent. Addito tefti-monio Clementis in Epift. ad Corinthios conclu-dit: Ergo Apoftoli eorum funt & vocantur, ad quos mittuntur, & quos docent, & dirigunt. De Timotheo pag. 64. ita habet: Illi, quos diximus Apoftoli, qui Ecclefia praeponebant Epifcopos, vel mandato majorum Apoftolorum, vel fuo proprio, ut majores, non uno in loco fixam fedem ftatuebant, ne in illis quidem urbibus vel Ecclefiis, quas conftituerant, ni-fi ad tempus, donec plena conftituta effent. Ita Pau-lus Timotheum Ephefum mifit & aliquantifper per-manere ibi juffit. Theffalonicen quoque eundem dire-xit. Sed ad Corinthios legavit, ut conftat ex priore ad Corinthios cap. 4. Romam poftea revocavit. Ti-motheus igitur Ecclefias peragrabat. Quod munus pro-prie eft & officium Apoftolicum. Nusquam certe unius

Ecclefiae adminiftrationem fufcepit. Hoc enim modo plurium Ecclefiarum fuiffet Epifcopus, Corinthi, Theffalonica, Philipporum, Ephefi atque etiam Roma. Libuit plane adducere fententiam Viri Celeberri-mi: Quae fane non videtur reprobanda, modo pau-lo clarius res definita effet in antiquitate. In gene-re intelligi Evangelii Miniftrum, atque eo pacto Andronicum, & Juniam etiam dici Apoftolos alii volunt. Sed illa fignificatio Miniftri Evangelii ni-mi generalis eft. Neque tantum ita γενικῶς Andro-nicus & Junia Apoftoli dici videntur. Mufculus, Beza, Tremellius, Zanchius, Pifcator de fpeciali le-gationis munere intelligunt, quod à Philippenfi-bus juffus abiit apud Paulum, eaque ratione Apo-ftolos dictos effe, qui ad fubfidium pro Ecclefia Hierofolymitana colligendum miffi ab Ecclefiis erant, 2. Cor. 8, 23. Sed hoc è loco illo non patet. Et Apoftoli nomen illuftrius hic eft, quam ut tan-tum miffum alicujus rei caufa notet, quae priori non fpecialior, fed adhuc generalior foret acceptio. Refert fefe quidem Grotius huic fententiae favens ad Matth. 11. fed illic eam è fcripturis N. Teftam. aut antiquitate Ecclefiaftica ita minime probavit, ut acquiefcere poffimus. Dicetur autem de eo for-fan uberius in limine epiftolae Jacobee, cum Deo. A-liquid amplius vel fublimius id nominis importare videtur, quam sunerγὸ & συστρατιώτη: & illa λει-τουργία deinde exprimitur.

Καὶ λουτουργὸν τῆς χρείας με) Miferant Philippenfes pe-cunias ad Paulum per Epaphroditum, quas accepit, tum quia in vinculis conftitutus laborare, ut ante, manibus fuis non poterat, tum ut inde pauperes Chriftianos, qui Romae erant, fublevaret. Hoc dicitur χρεία Actor. 2, 45. cap. 4, 35. c. 6, 3. c. 20, 34. c. 28, 10. Romanor. 12, 13. Eph. 4, 28. infra c. 4, 16. Πέμψω πρὸς ὑμᾶς) Mittere dixit pro remittere. Sim-plex pro Compofito. Verf. 26. Ἐπειδὴ ἐπιποθῶν ἦν πάντας ὑμᾶς) In Manufcripto recte additur ἰδεῖν, quomodo loquitur Apoftolus Rom. 1, 11. 2. Tim. 1, 4. Et ita apparet hic Syrum legiffe, Καὶ ἀδημονῶν) Anxius erat. Vide Matth. 26, 37. Marc. 14, 33. Utitur & Aquila Job. 18, 21. Syrus hic מְעַק : Bene. Ἡδύνετο παραπλησίον θανάτῳ) חָלָה לָמוּת Efa. 38, 1. ubi Graci quidam ἐμαλακίσθη ἕως θανάτου: alii ἕως τοῦ ἀπο-θανεῖν, alii εἰς θάνατον. ἵνα μὴ λύπῃ ἐπὶ λύπῃ σχῇ) Nempe fi ad vincula acces-fiffet jactura amici. Id fuiffet צָרָה עַל צָרָה. Verf. 28. Σπουδατοτέρως) feftinantius, ut habet Latinus. Eft enim haec genuina hujus vocis fignificatio à σπεύδω. Inde trans-lata altera, quae diligentiam fignificat. ἵνα ἰδόντες αὐτὸν πάλιν χαρῆτε) mutanda diftinctio in hunc modum, ἵνα ἰδόντες αὐτὸν πάλιν, ut ipfum itetum con-fpicientes, ob id gaudeatis. Κἀγὼ ἀλυπότερος ὦ) Nempe ubi eum falvum ad fuos ve-niffe cognovero. Non enim ita gaudemus, dicente Chryfoftomo, au-dientes eos effe fanos, quos defideramus, ut quando eos videmus, & maxime, fi quando iftud praeter fpem ac-ciderit, id quod in Epaphrodito factum eft. Verf. 29. Μιτὰ πάσης χαρᾶς) Rom 15, 32. Καὶ τοὺς τοιύτους ἐντίμους ἔχετε) 1. Tim. 5, 17. Verf. 30. Ὅτι διὰ τὸ ἔργον τοῦ χρισοῦ μέχρι θανάτου ἤγγισε) חָרַב לָמוּת Job. 33, 22. Chrifti opus vocat, operam pofi-tam Chrifti caufa. Παραβουλευσάμενοι τῇ ψυχῇ) Omnino legendum eft παραβολευσάμενοι τῇ ψυχῇ, id eft, vitam objectantes pericu-lis, quomodo viri magni Scaliger & Salmafius monuere. Plinius in epiftolis: Periculofa utque Graeci melius expo-nunt παράβολα. Latinus interpres recepto vetuftior po-fuerat hic: parabolatum eft animam fuam. Nam & Lati-ne parabolani dicuntur, qui cum vitae periculo aegrotis adfunt. Syrus hic pofuit בְּסַר עַל נַפְשֵׁהּ : fprevit vi-tam fuam.

## 2:30
in order that he might supply your lack of service toward me. That he might himself supply the services which you could not render to me by reason of your absence.

A similar sense is found in Philem. v. 13. The manner of speaking is not difficult; see 2 Cor. 11:9. Chrysostom infers from this that it was not permitted for Paul to approach or be ministered to without danger: which does not quite harmonize with the passage in Acts 28:30.

Others, therefore, refer it to an illness which he had contracted through excessive labor and anxiety. The words of the Apostle certainly seem to imply this: in order that he might supply your lack, etc.

Latin:

ἵνα ἀναπληρώσῃ τὸ ὑμῶν ὑστέρημα τῆς πρός με λειτουργίας ) Ut quæ obsequia vos per absentiam mihi præstare non potestis, ipse suppleret.

Similis sensus Philem. v. 13. Loquendi genus non difficile 2. Cor. 11, 9. Confectat inde Chrysostomus, non licuisse absque periculo Paulum accedere aut ei ministrare: Quod non adeo consonat loco Actor.

28, 30. Alii ergo ad morbum referunt, quem nimio labore ac sollicitudine contraxerit.

Id certe verba Apostoli innuere videntur: ἵνα ἀναπληρώσῃ τὸ ὑμῶν ὑστέρημα &c.

## 3:1 Argument
CHAPTER III.

ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

He exhorts them to joy in the Lord; and that this may be solid, he testifies that it is not at all burdensome for him to repeat the same things.

He warns, however, that the Pseudo-Apostles must be guarded against in this matter, and, beating back their vain boasting in carnal prerogatives, he contrasts the righteousness of faith with the righteousness of the law, pronouncing the latter to be mere loss in comparison, and teaches that true righteousness is obtained only through faith in Christ, and [teaches] the communion of the sufferings of Christ, even though one must still strive toward the proposed goal. He exhorts the brethren to imitate him, deploring the enemies of the cross of Christ and their unhappy end, and proposing his own politeuma (citizenship) in heaven, with the expectation of Jesus from the heavens and the transfiguration of our body into the likeness of the glorified body of Christ. There are two parts: the first is didactic, concerning imputed righteousness—a doctrine which the Pseudo-Apostles were perverting by mixing the righteousness of the law with the righteousness of faith—up to v. 16. The second is parenetic, concerning homopsychia (oneness of mind) and the imitation of himself, up to v. 21. B.

Hunnius assigns these two parts thus: I. An exhortation that righteousness and salvation are to be sought not in legal ceremonies and works, but in Christ. II. Concerning the completion of the begun course of faith and piety. B.

Balduinus exhibits the synecheia (continuity) of the preceding chapters and the distribution of the present one as follows: Paul proposed to himself in this epistle to exhort the Philippians to perseverance in faith and charity, as the principal parts of our Christianity. In these they could have been hindered partly by the persecutions of the Church, which had cast the Apostle himself into chains; partly by internal contentions and disputes; and partly also by the blandishments and deceit of the Pseudo-Apostles.

He removed the first impediment in the first chapter, teaching that his chains had profited the Church rather than harmed it. He removed the second in the preceding chapter, where he exhorted them to humility, as the mother of concord, by the example of Christ. Now, in the third chapter, he writes against the Pseudo-Apostles, whose errors in the article of our justification before GOD he refutes, and he exhorts them to beware of these very seducers: he opposes the true doctrine concerning justification to their errors, and adds an exhortation to the pursuit of good works, as the fruits of righteousness.

There are, therefore, two parts to the chapter: the first deals with the righteousness of faith against the Pseudo-Apostles up to verse 13. The second [deals] with the pursuit of new obedience against the Epicureans, up to the end of the chapter.

PART I. DIDACTIC

Concerning imputed righteousness, which doctrine the Pseudo-Apostles were perverting, mixing the righteousness of the law with the righteousness of faith.

Verse 1. Finally, my brethren, rejoice in the Lord. The Apostle seems to have wished to finish the epistle here, as he is accustomed to do by the word to loipon, or loipon, or to loipō, as in 2 Cor. 13:11, Gal. 6:17, Eph. 6:10, 2 Thess. 3:1, and by the verb chairete, 2 Cor. 13:11, below c. 4:4, 1 Thess. 5:16; but afterward, when he had received a little more time, he added those things which follow: something of which kind happened to him also when he was writing the epistle to the Romans, as we noted there. There is no need to imagine an appendix or an addendum tacked on unexpectedly, which also in no way befits Divine inspiration.

B. Hunnius has grasped the connection and sense not unsuitably: After you have been called to the fellowship of the Gospel, you stand in it by the grace of the Lord: it is fitting to both rejoice always and give thanks for so great a benefit of God, with all confidence of your hope and boasting placed not in yourselves, but solely in the acknowledged CHRIST JESUS, from which that joy of the Holy Spirit immediately flourishes. To Johannes Crocius, it seems that the foundation of the admonition to beware of dogs and evil workers, who mix the righteousness of the law with the righteousness of faith, is exhibited here.

That which is joy in the Lord cannot certainly be solid if that mixture is admitted. For he who wishes to boast or rejoice solidly must boast and rejoice solely in the Lord, 1 Cor. 1, v. last. He had delivered the mystery of the emptying and exaltation of CHRIST, which is the matter of joy, primarily because the obedience of CHRIST, undertaken for us even to the death of the cross, is imputed to us by faith for salvation, upon which, as it is the sole [foundation], so the certainty of obtaining the prize of the heavenly calling most firmly rests.

This warning concerning joy in the Lord is therefore deduced from the preceding doctrine concerning CHRIST humbled for us, and his obedience, both active and passive, and his exaltation for our sake, in whom alone one must rejoice; and a preparation is made for the practical use and application of how we may enjoy CHRIST and possess solid joy in him: namely, by the apprehension of his righteousness and the acknowledgment of the fruit of his passion and resurrection: yet so that, having been apprehended by CHRIST, we may strive to apprehend the prize of the heavenly calling in Christ Jesus. To write the same things to you) To repeat often those things which are of great use. It is not burdensome to me) Here oknēron is placed in a passive sense, as in Proverbs 31:27; it is not grievous to me, it does not irk me. But for you it is safe).

For things repeated often stick better in the mind; so that you may be more cautious, the Syriac [version] not badly [renders].

It may appear that the Apostle had already written the same things to the Philippians in another epistle, which B.

Ægidius Hunnius gathered from these words. However, by ta auta (the same things) can be understood those things which he had delivered by word of mouth, which pleases B.

Balduinus. He therefore calls to memory the doctrine which he had proposed to them while present at Philippi, for the preservation of which he had given thanks to God above, c.

1:3, for which he had warned them to contend, v. 27, and from which, lest the Philippians be seduced by evil workers, he wished the same to be repeated in the present letter against the depravation of the Pseudo-Apostles: which is the same.

 The repetition of the same doctrine contributes much to the ἀσφάλειαν (security) and certainty of faith, and becomes most necessary in the danger of seduction. Furthermore, since Paul writes the same things (τὰ αὐτά) which he had taught by word of mouth, it is clear that there is no distinction by the Papists between the written and unwritten Word. Since they pretend that something else was preached by the Apostles, which is to be believed, which is not read in scripture, which indeed the Papists will never prove.

Latin:

CAPUT III.

ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

Excitat ad gaudium in Domino, quod ut solidum sit, eadem repetere sibi minime grave esse testatur, monet autem, cavendos esse in eo Pseudo-Apostolos, ac retundens vanam eorum in carnalibus prærogativis jactantiam, justitiam fidei cum justitia legis contendit, ejusque respectu merum damnum esse pronunciat, nec nisi per fidem in Christum veram justitiam obtineri, & communionem passionum Christi docet, etsi contendendum adhuc sit ad metam propositam, ac fratres ad sui imitationem hortatur, deplorans crucis Christi hostes, atque infelicem eorum exitum, ac proponens πολίτευμα suum in cælo, cum expectatione Jesu è cœlis, & transfigurationis corporis nostri ad similitudinem glorificati corporis Christi.

Partes sunt duæ; prior didactica de justitia imputata, quam doctrinam pervertebant Pseudo-A- postoli miscentes justitiam legis cum fidei justitia, ad v. 16. Altera paranetica ad ὁμοψυχίαν, suique imitationem ad v. 21. B.

Hunnius hasce duas partes assignat: I. est exhortatio de justitia & salute non in legalibus ceremoniis & operibus, sed in Christo quærenda. II. De consummando inchoato fidei pietatisque cursu. B.

Balduinus συνέχeιαν capitum præcedentium & distributionem præsentis ita exhibet: Proposuit sibi Paulus in hac epistola hortari Philippenses ad perseverantiam in fide & charitate, tanquam præcipuis Christianismi nostri partibus. In his impediri potuissent partim persecutionibus Ecclesiæ, qua Apostolum ipsum in vincula conjecerant; partim contentionibus & litibus intestinis; partim etiam blanditiis & fallacia Pseudo-Apostolorum.

Primum impedimentum removit capite primo, docens, vincula sua profuisse potius, quam nocuisse Ecclesiæ. Secundum removit capite præcedente, ubi exemplo Christi ad humilitatem, tanquam concordia matrem exhortatus fuit. Jam in tertio capite contra Pseudo-Apostolos scribit, quorum errores in articulo justificationis nostræ coram DEO redarguit, & ut sibi ab ipsis seductoribus caveant hortatur: verum autem de justificatione doctrinam erroribus illorum opponit, & exhortationem ad studium bonorum operum, tanquam fructus justitiæ, addit.

Dua igitur sunt partes capitis: Prima agit de justitia fidei contra Pseudo-Apostolos usque ad vers. 13. Altera de studio novæ obedientiæ contra Epicuros, usque ad finem capitis.

PARS I. DIDACTICA De iustitia imputata, quam doctrinam Pseudo-Apostoli pervertebant, miscentes iustitiam legis cum fidei iustitia.

Vers. 1. Τὸ λοιπὸν, ἀδελφοί με, χαίρετε ἐν Κυρίῳ.

Videtur hic Apostolus finire epistolam voluisse, ut facere solet per vocem τὸ λοιπὸν, aut λοιπὸν, aut τῷ λοιπῷ, ut 2. Cor. 13, 11. Gal. 6, 17. Eph, 6, 10. 2. Thess. 3, 1. & per verbum χαίρετε, 2. Corinth. 13, 11. infra c. 4, 4. 1. Thessal. 5, 16. sed postea, cum temporis aliquanto plus accepisset, addidisse ea, quæ sequuntur: quale quid ei evenisse etiam, cum epistolam ad Romanos scriberet, ibi notavimus.

Non opus est fingere appendicem vel additamentum ex improviſo ſubjunctum, quod etiam nullatenus convenit inſpirationi Divinæ.

Nexum & sensum non incommode complexus est B. Hunnius: Poſteaquam vocati ad conſortium Evangelii, in eo per Domini gratiam ſtatis: de tanto beneficio Dei merito & gaudere ſemper, & gratias agere convenit, omni fiducia ſpei & gloriationis veſtræ, non in vobis ipſis, ſed in agnito CHRISTO JESU unice repoſita, ex qua gaudium illud Spiritus Sancti protinus effloreſcit.

Johanni Crocio videtur fundamentum admonitionis de cavendis canibus & malis operariis, iustitiam legis cum iustitia fidei commiſcentibus, hic exhiberi. Quod eſt gaudium in Domino, id certe ſolidum eſſe nequit admiſſa illa mixtura.

Nam qui gloriari aut gaudere ſolide velit, eum in Domino gloriari ac gaudere unice oportet, 1. Cor. 1. v. ult. Tradiderat myſterium exinanitionis & exaltationis CHRISTI, quod eſt gaudii materia, imprimis quia obedientia CHRISTI usque ad mortem crucis pro nobis ſuſcepta per fidem nobis imputatur ad ſalutem, qua ut unice, ita firmiſſime nititur certitudo conſequendo clinodio cœleſtis vocationis.

Deducitur ergo hoc monitum de gaudio in Domino è præcedenti doctrina de CHRISTO pro nobis humiliato, & obedientia ejus cum activa tum paſſiva, noſtrique cauſa exaltato, in quo uno gaudendum; & præparatio fit ad uſum & applicationem practicam, quomodo CHRISTO fruamur, & in eo ſolido potiamur gaudio: nimirum apprehenſione iuftitiæ ejus, & agnitione fructus paſſionis ac reſurrectionis ejusdem: Ita tamen ut apprehenſi à CHRISTO apprehendere contendamus clinodium cœleſtis vocationis in Chriſto Jeſu. Τὰ αὐτὰ γράφειν ὑμῖν) Sæpe repetere ea, quæ magno ſunt uſui. Ἐμοὶ μὲν ἐκ ὀκνηρὸν) Hic ὀκνηρὸν ponitur ſenſu Paſſivo, ut Proverb. 31, 27. mihi non grave eſt, me non piget. Ὑμῖν δὲ ἀσφαλὲς).

Sæpe enim repetita eo melius hærent animo; ut vos cautiores sitis, Syrus non male.

Videri poteſt, alia epiſtola jam idem ſcripſiſſe ad Philippenſes Apoſtolum, quod B. Ægidius Hunnius ex hiſce verbis collegit.

Poſſunt tamen per τὰ αὐτὰ ea intelligi, quæ viva voce tradiderat, quod B. Balduino placet.

In memoriam ergo revocat doctrinam, quam præſens Philippis propoſuerat, ob quam ſervatam Deo ſupra gratias egerat cap. 1, 3. pro qua certandum eſſe monuerat, v. 27. à qua ne Philippenſes per malos operarios ſeducantur, eandem præſentibus literis adverſus depravationem Pseudo-Apoſtolorum repetitam voluit: Quod ejusdem. jusdem doctrinae repetitio multum ad ἀσφάλειαν & certitudinem fidei conducat, & in periculo seductionis maxime necessaria fit. Porro cum τὰ αὐτά eadem Paulus scribat, quae viva voce docuerat, patet, nullam esse Papicolarum distinctionem inter Verbum scriptum & non scriptum. Cum fingunt, aliud quicquam ab Apostolis praedicatum esse, quod ad credenda, quod in scriptura non legatur, quod vero nunquam probabunt Papistae.

## 3:2
Verf. 2. Βλέπετε τοὺς κύνας (Beware of dogs)) Here he begins to touch those commendators of Judaism, treating them more harshly, for the reason that he knew their mind thoroughly. I see that it is also used for 'beware'. The Latins use it: But it is more frequently constructed in that sense with ἀπό, as in Mark 8:15, ch. 12:38. But he calls men dogs who are both shameless and greedy from Isaiah 56:10. Βλέπετε τοὺς κακοὺς ἐργάτας (Beware of evil workers)) 'deceitful workers' 2 Cor. 11:13, who are not engaged in the work of the Lord, that is, in the Gospel, in good faith. Βλέπετε τὴν κατατομήν (Beware of the concision)) It was the custom of the Jews, both toward idols and toward evil men, to give some name that would not depart far from their own name, so that they might denote their weakness or vices. Thus Paul calls those who called themselves 'the circumcision' (περιτομήν), namely, with the abstract noun placed in place of the concrete, as in Rom. 3:30, ch. 4:17, ch. 15:8, Gal. 2:7, 8, 9, Eph. 2:11, presently § he calls it 'concision' (κατατομήν), that is, 'those who cut' (τοὺς κατατέμνοντας), the lacerators of the Churches of Christ.

For to lacerate (κατατέμνειν) is to tear into parts, שרט Levit. 21:5, 1 Kings 18:28. Xenophon, Plutarch, and others use it thus.

In the glossary, 'concision' (κατατομή) is 'cut to pieces'. Because a most grave danger was impending from the Pseudo-Apostles, he warns gravely that they must be observed and avoided. That triple repetition 'beware, beware, beware' indicates both the gravity of the danger and the necessity of caution. Cf. James 3:7, Isa. 55:1, Mark 14:33, 35, 37. Concerning the Pseudo-Apostles, the Greek scholia from Chrysostom: 'they were hard to discern, therefore he says beware, that is, keep yourselves, and be on guard.' But it is set before the eyes even more by the titles with which he adorns the seducers.

He calls them dogs, not only because of shamelessness, or rather canine impudence, and because of greed, but also because of filth, 2 Pet. 2:22, and because of cruelty, because they lacerate the flock, and tear the men themselves like rabid dogs, Matt. 7: 6. Cf. Apoc. 22: 15. Add the famous biting of dogs, and the sharp boldness of pursuing and biting, Ps. 22: 17. For they were not only fixing the venomous bites of their doctrine into the minds of the simpler ones, but were also gnawing at the reputation of pious Doctors.

Nor is it added rashly by B. Balduinus that they are called dogs because their doctrine is not pleasant or full of consolation, but is like the barking of dogs, which bites consciences while it sends sinners back from Christ to their own works. He calls them evil workers because of the dangerous and destructive mixture of legal and Evangelical justice, Gal. 1:7, 8, 9, ch. 5:4, 12. He calls them the concision, because they cut, making circumcision and the observation of the law necessary for salvation, the doctrine of the Gospel; they cut the law, taking away its perfection and the complement, to which it leads us like a schoolmaster, having it in addition; they cut the mystical body of the Church through dangerous schism; they cut the souls of the faithful through destructive dogma; they cut the sacrament of circumcision itself, boasting of external circumcision, but neglecting internal circumcision, and rejecting the justice of which circumcision is the seal.

While they were fighting for the truth of the circumcision of the foreskin already performed through Christ, they were in reality betraying that they were not at all circumcised in heart. For if they had been circumcised in heart, they would not have urged the circumcision of the flesh, the obligation of which had ceased upon Christ's death, with baptism substituted in its place. Therefore, their circumcision, used against the will of Christ under the opinion of necessity, was only a cutting of the flesh, as here not badly Crocius.

There is a beautiful marginal gloss here by B. Luther .

Latin:

2. Βλέπετε τοὺς κύνας) Hic tangere incipit illos Judaismi commendatores, durius eos tractans, ideo quod animum ipsorum penitus noverat. Video pro cavere etiam. Latini usurpant: Sed frequentius eo sensu construitur per ἀπό, ut Marc. 8, 15. cap. 12, 38. Κύνας autem vocat homines & invere cundos & avaros ex Es. 56, 10. Βλέπετε τοὺς κακοὺς ἐργάτας) ἐργάτας δολίους 2. Cor. 11, 13. qui in opere Domini, id est, in Evangelio non versantur bona fide. Βλέπετε τὴν κατατομήν) Moris erat Judais, tum idolis, tum hominibus malis nomen aliquod indere, quod ab ipsorum nomine non longe abiret, ut eorum imbecillitatem aut vitia denotarent. Sic Paulus eos, qui se vocabant περιτομήν, nempe abstracti voce posita vice concreti, ut Rom. 3, 30. cap. 4, 17. C. 15, 8. Gal. 2, 7. 8. 9. Ephes. 2, 11. mox §. vocat κατατομήν, id est, τοὺς κατατέμνοντας, scissores Ecclesiarum Christi.

Nam κατατέμνειν est in partes lacerare שרט Levit. 21, 5. 1. Reg. 18. 28. Usurpant sic Xenophon, Plutarchus & alii.

In glossario κατατομή consciso. Quia periculum gravissimum imminebat a Pseudo-Apostolis, eos observandos & cavendos esse graviter monet. Trina illa repetitio βλέπετε, βλέπετε, βλέπετε & periculi gravitatem, & cautionis necessitatem indicat. Conf. Jac. 3, 7. Es. 55, 1. Marc. 14, 33. 35. 37. De Pseudo-Apostolis scholia Graeca è Chrysostomo: ἦσαν δυσδιάγνωστοι, διό φησι βλέπετε, τοῦτ' ἔστι, τηρεῖτε ἑαυτούς, καὶ φυλάττεσθε.

Sed magis ea adhuc ob oculos ponitur titulis, quibus seductores ornat. Vocat canes, non tantum ob invere cundiam, vel potius impudentiam caninam, & ob avaritiam, sed etiam ob immunditiem, 2. Petr. 2, 22. & ob saevitiam, quia dilacerant sara, ipsosque homines instar rabidorum canum dilaniant, Matt. 7, 6. Conf. Apoc. XXII, 15. Adde famam canum mordacitatem, & acrem insectandi noncedique audaciam, Ps. 22, 17. Non enim tantum venenatos morsus doctrinae, & simpliciorum animis dentes infigebant, sed & famam piorum Doctorum arrodebant.

Nec temere à B. Balduino additur, canes vocari, quia doctrina ipsorum non est jucunda aut solatio plena, sed instar latratus canum, qui mordet conscientias, dum peccatores à Christo ad sua remittit opera. Vocat malos operarios ob periculosam & exitiosam mixturam legalis & Evangelica justitia, Gal. 1, 7. 8. 9. cap. 5, 4. 12. Vocat concisionem, quod concidant, circumcisionem, & legis observationem ad salutem necessariam facientes, doctrinam Evangelii; concidant legem, ejus perfectionem tollentes, & complementum, ad quod paedagogi instar nos deducit, insuper habentes; concidant Ecclesiae corpus mysticum per schisma periculosum; concidant fidelium animas per dogma exitiosum, concidant ipsum circumcisionis sacramentum, externam circumcisionem jactantes, at internam circumcisionem negligentes, ac justitiam, cujus sigillum est circumcisio, reprobantes.

Dum pro praeputii circumcisione veritate per Christum jam praestita pugnabant, revera prodebant, se minime circumcisos esse corde. Si enim corde fuissent circumcisi, non urissent carnis circumcisionem, cujus obligatio, Christo mortuo, cessaverat, baptismo in ejus locum surrogato. Circumcisio igitur illorum contra Christi voluntatem sub opinione necessitatis adhibita erat tantum carnis consciso, ut hic non mala le Crocius.

Pulchra hic est marginalis B. Lutheriglossa: Er nennet die falschen Prediger die Zerschneidung, darum, dass sie die Beschneidung nöthig zur Seligkeit lehreten, damit die Herzen vom Glauben abgeschnitten werden.

## 3:3
Verf. 3. Ἡμεῖς γάρ ἐσμεν ἡ περιτομή (For we are the circumcision)) the circumcision of the heart, Rom. 2:29, that is, circumcised in heart: which the Prophets urge as the chief thing. οἱ Πνεύματι Θεῷ λατρεύοντες (who worship God in the Spirit)) With a pure mind, which is the greatest thing, Job 4:24. Καὶ καυχώμενοι ἐν χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ (And rejoice in Christ Jesus)) Rejoicing most in this, that we have perceived Christ, that is, his doctrine. Καὶ ἐν σαρκὶ πεποιθότες (And have no confidence in the flesh)) The Jews had an argument for their confidence in God, because God had commanded them, only his covenanted people, to be circumcised in the skin: But we, because Christ has ratified the covenant with us by his death.

He opposes the antithesis of true glorification and orthodox faith to the vain boasting and false doctrine of the Pseudo-Apostles in four points, so that they may be able to discern evil workers from the upright.

1. To the doctrine of the necessity of external circumcision, he opposes true spiritual circumcision, which is done in the heart, and is far better, and necessary for all, whereas that was instituted for the sake of this, and was only temporary, because the Jewish polity was to last only until then, Gen. 17:12, Deut. 30:6, Jer. 4:4, Rom. 2:29. This therefore is true glorification: 'For we are the circumcision' (Ἡμεῖς γάρ ἐσμεν ἡ περιτομή), proper to those to whom circumcision was the seal of the righteousness of faith, Rom. 4:11, or even to those who had succeeded in its place, baptism or 'circumcision made without hands' (περιτομὴ ἀχειροποίητος), as in Col. 2:11, Gal. 2:8, 9, 12, Rom. 3:30, ch. 4:12, Tit. 1:10. 2. To the doctrine concerning the necessity of ceremonial worship, he opposes the doctrine concerning spiritual worship of God, and does not want the glorification of the faithful to be sought in the observation of the ceremonies of the law, which were already abrogated, after the body had succeeded the shadow, Col. 2:17, Heb. 10:1, but in that which he could truly say: 'For we are those who worship God in the Spirit' (Ἡμεῖς γάρ ἐσμεν ἐν Πνεύματι Θεῷ λατρεύοντες), concerning which spiritual worship Rom. 12:1. They explain the word 'in spirit' (πνεύματι) adverbially as 'spiritually' (πνευματικῶς), Chrysostom, Theophylactus, the Greek Scholiast.

3. To the doctrine and glorification concerning the justice of the law, he opposes the Evangelical doctrine, and glorification in the Lord Jesus, and his justice, Isa. 45:23, 24, 25, Jer. 9:24, 1 Cor. 1:30, 31, which was truly of the faithful. 'For we are those who rejoice in Christ Jesus' (Ἡμεῖς γάρ ἐσμεν καυχώμενοι ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ).

Cf. Gal. 6:14, 15. Rejoicing, he says, not boasting: Although that glorification of the Christian faith was joined with true joy in the Lord, which indeed was not situated in the mere perception of the doctrine of Christ, but in the induction of Christ and his justice, Gal. 3:27, or in fiducial application: as that glorification is described by Isaiah, 'in the Lord is my justice', ch. 45:23. For in the Lord shall be justified, shall glory, says the Prophet, all the seed of Israel, whose profession and glory is Jehovah our justice, Jer. 23:6, ch. 33:15, inasmuch as he himself was made justice for us by God, so that he who glories, may glory in the Lord, 1 Cor. 1:30, 31. 4.

To the glorification and confidence in the flesh or carnal prerogatives, which they sought not only in circumcision, but also in other external things, in singular things, and in the Israelitic people, or the covenanted of God, in their own promises and dignities and privileges, he opposes confidence and glorification in the new covenant, which embraces the remission of sins, and the internal inscription of the divine law, and other gifts and goods promised to the faithful, and covenants ratified through the passion and death of Christ, Jer. 31:31 f., Heb. 8:8 f. Verf. 4. Καίπερ ἐγὼ ἔχων πεποίθησιν καὶ ἐν σαρκί (Though I have confidence also in the flesh)) 'In' is understood before 'itself' according to the Hebrew custom.

'Confidence' (Πεποίθησιν), that is, an argument of confidence. Even in the flesh, if there is any glory in that.

Latin:

Vers. 3. Ἡμεῖς γάρ ἐσμεν ἡ περιτομή) circumcisio cordis, Rom. 2, 29. id est corde circumcisi: quod ut praecipuum urgent Prophetae. οἱ Πνεύματι Θεῷ λατρεύοντες) Puro animo, quod maximum, Job. 4, 24. Καὶ καυχώμενοι ἐν χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ) Hoc maxime gaudentes, quod Christum, id est, doctrinam ejus perceperimus. Καὶ ἐν σαρκὶ πεποιθότες) Judzi suae in Deum fiduciae habebant argumentum, quod Deus ipsis, tantum foederatis suis, praecipisset in cute circumcidi: At nos, quod Christus foedus nobiscum morte sua sanxerit.

Opponit Pseudo-Apostolorum vanae jactantiae & falsae doctrinae in quatuor punctis antithesin verae gloriationis & orthodoxae fidei, ut malos operarios a probis discernere possint.

1. Doctrinae necessitate externae circumcisionis opponit veram spiritualem circumcisionem, quae corde fit, ac longe potior, & omnibus necessaria, quam illa hujus causa instituta, & temporaria tantum fuerit, quod usque duratura erat politia Judaica, Gen. 17, 12. Deut. 30, 6. Jer. 4, 4. Rom. 2, 29. Haec ergo vera est gloriatio: Ἡμεῖς γάρ ἐσμεν ἡ περιτομή, illorum propria, quibus erat circumcisio sigillum fidei justitiae, Rom. 4, 11. vel etiam, qui in locum ejus successerat, baptismus seu περιτομὴ ἀχειροποίητος, ut Ab. 11, 2. Gal. 2, 8. 9. 12. Roman. 3, 30. cap. 4, 12. Coloss. 2, 11. Tit. 1, 10. 2. Doctrinae de cultus ceremonialie necessitate opponit doctrinam de cultu Dei spirituali, & gloriationem fidelium non vult quaeri in observatione ceremoniarum legis, quae jam abrogatae, postquam corpus successerat umbrae, Col. 2, 17. Ebr. 10, 1. sed in eo, quod ex vero dicere poterat: Ἡμεῖς γάρ ἐσμεν ἐν Πνεύματι Θεῷ λατρεύοντες, de quo spirituali cultu Rom. 12, 1. Vocem πνεύματι exponunt Adverbialiter per πνευματικῶς, Chrysostomus, Theophylactus, Scholiastes Graecus.

3. Doctrinae & gloriationi de justitia legis opponit doctrinam Evangelicam, & gloriationem in Domino Jesu, ejusque justitia, Es. 45, 23. 24. 25. Jerem. 9, 24. 1. Cor. 1, 30. 31. quae erat vere fidelium. Ἡμεῖς γάρ ἐσμεν καυχώμενοι ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ.

Conf. Gal. 6, 14. 15. Gloriantes, inquit, non gaudentes: Etsi illa Christianae fidei gloriatio cum vera in Domino laetitia conjuncta erat, quae vero non in sola doctrina Christi perceptione, sed in Christi & justitiae ejus inductione, Gal. 3, 27. vel applicatione fiduciali sita erat: uti gloriatio illa describitur ab Esais, in Domino justitia mea, cap. 45, 23. Nam in Domino justificabitur, glorietur, inquit Propheta, omne semen Israel, cujus professio est & gloria Jehovah justitia nostra, Jer. 23, 6. cap. 33, 15. siquidem ideo factus ipse nobis fit justitia a Deo, ut, qui glorietur, in Domino glorietur, 1. Cor. 1, 30. 31. 4.

Gloriationi & fiduciae in carne vel carnalibus praerogativis, quam non in sola tantum circumcisione quaerebant, sed etiam in aliis externis, in singularibus, populoque Israelitico, seu Dei foederato, propriis promissionibus & dignitatibus ac privilegiis, opponit fiduciam & gloriationem de foedere novo, quod remissionem peccatorum, & legis divinae internae nostra inscriptione, aliaque dona & bona fidelibus promissa, & foedera per Christi passionem & mortem sancita complectitur, Jer. 31, 31. f. Ebr. 8, 8. f. Vers. 4. Καίπερ ἐγὼ ἔχων πεποίθησιν καὶ ἐν σαρκί) Ad ipsum subauditur tum more Ebrzo. Πεποίθησιν, id est, fiduciae argumentum.

Etiam in carne, si qua ea est gloria.

## 3:5
Verf. 5. Circumcised on the eighth day) At that time circumcised, when Isaac and his posterity were. "Eighth day" is said as "third day," [an interval of time]. Of the stock of Israel) He rightly adds this, because both Ishmaelites and Idumeans were circumcised.

Thus "of the stock of the Jews," Esther 6:13. [From the seed]. For "seed" is translated "stock," Leviticus 21:16. Jeremiah 29:32, ch. 31:36, 38, ch. 36:31, ch. 41, verf. 1. Of the tribe of Benjamin) Sprung from him whom Jacob had loved so much, and of whom the same Jacob and Moses had predicted excellent things.

An Hebrew of the Hebrews) Not [a son], that is, born of a proselyte, but through the whole series of ancestors from the Hebrews, Acts 22:3, 2 Corinthians 11:22. As touching the law, a Pharisee) He calls "law" here special institutions, as Numbers 6:13, Proverbs 1:8, ch. 6:20, where the Greeks have "ordinances." And when he says that he was a Pharisee, he means this: of the most exquisite sect, Acts 26:5. Verf. 6. Concerning zeal) That, of which Romans 10:2 speaks.

Latin:

Vers. 5. Περιτομὴ ὀκταήμερος) Eo tempore circumcisus, quo Isaac & posteri ejus. Ὀκταήμερος dicitur ut τριήμερος, διαστήματος. Ἐκ γένους Ἰσραὴλ) Recte hoc addit, quia & Ismaëlita & Idumaei circumcidebantur.

Sic ἐκ γένους Ἰουδαίων, Esther. 6, 13. מזרע. Nam זרע vertitur γένος, Levit. 21, 16. Jerem. 29, 32. cap. 31, 36. 38. cap. 36, 31. cap. 41. vers. 1. Φυλῆς Βενιαμὲν) Ex eo ortus, quem tantopere dilexerat Jacobus, & de quo egregia praedixerant idem Jacobus & Moses. Ἑβραῖος ἐξ Ἑβραίων) Non בַּר, id est, ex proselyto natus, sed tota majorum serie ex Ebraeis, Actor.

22, 3. 2. Cor. 11, 22. Κατὰ νόμον Φαρισαῖος) Nomos hic vocat specialia instituta, ut Num. 6, 13. Prov. 1, 8. cap. 6, 20. ubi Graeci habent θεσμούς. Et cum dicit, Pharisaeum se fuisse, hoc vult, sectae exquisitissimae, Act. 26, 5. Vers. 6. Κατὰ ζῆλον) Illum, de quo Rom.

## 3:6
Persecuting the Church) that is, having persecuted. For the Hebrews use present participles, because they have no others, even for the past. Compare 1 Corinthians 15:9. Touching the righteousness which is in the law, blameless) He accepts the name of "law" here for those precepts according to which judgments were exercised. He says, therefore, that he had done nothing that should be punished by death or stripes. Blameless Job 11:4. The Pseudo-Apostles were very boastful; they not only exalted themselves in doctrine and worship, but also boasted of other merely carnal axioms, as is hinted here, as also in 2 Corinthians 11:22.

The Apostle now teaches that he is in no part inferior to them, nay, even superior to them; but to beat down their boasting, he confirms by his own example that nothing is to be done according to the righteousness of the law itself, and he sets forth and commends to them the true righteousness. There were four things in particular in which the Pseudo-Apostles boasted: circumcision, lineage, profession, life; in all these, the Apostle says, he could have confidence, if those things were of any value in the judgment of God. Therefore, he brings forward not only those external things in which they trusted—circumcision and Israelitish origin—but also religion and the Pharisaic sect and zeal for religion, and even the observance of the whole law according to the tenor of that sect, which were publicly known and most attested. But that Pharisaic righteousness was by no means sufficient, because it stuck only in the external court of the law, Matthew 5:20; wherefore not only the forensic or judicial law is regarded here, but especially the observance of the moral law, which the Pharisees required and the Pseudo-Apostles, together with faith in CHRIST, declared necessary for justification and salvation, Acts 15:5. Justinianus explains concerning the moral law from the Pontifical side, to say nothing of others. Not in the judgment of God, but to man, as far as it is lawful to judge, there was nothing in me that the Jews could deservedly blame. For this is what the Apostle says, "blameless." Verf.

Latin:

10, 2. Διώκων τὴν Ἐκκλησίαν) id est, διώξας. Nam Ebraei participiis praesentibus, quia alia non habent, etiam pro Praeteritis utuntur. Conf. 1, Cor. 15, 9. Κατὰ τὴν δικαιοσύνην τὴν ἐν νόμῳ γενόμενος ἄμεμπτος) Nomen legis hic accipit pro illis praeceptis, secundum quae judicia exercebantur. Dicit ergo nihil se fecisse, quod morte aut verberibus castigandum esset. Ἄμεμπτος Job. 11, 4. Pseudo-Apostoli erant admodum gloriabundi, non tantum doctrina & cultu sese efferebant, sed jactabant etiam alia mere carnalia axiomata, quemadmodum hic innuitur, ut & 2. Corinith.

11, 22. His ergo sese nulla parte inferiorem, imo superiorem ipsis esse jam docet Apostolus, quam vero eorum jactantiam ut retundat, nihil facienda esse juxta cum ipsa etiam legis justitia, exemplo suo confirmat, veramque ipsis justitiam sistit & commendat. Quatuor imprimis erant, in quibus gloriabantur Pseudo-Apostoli, circumcisio, genus, professio, vita; in his omnibus ait Apostolus, se confidere posse, si illa quicquam in judicio Dei valerent. Non ergo ista externa tantum, in quibus confidebant, circumcisionem, & originem Israeliticam, sed etiam religionem ac sectam Pharisaicam & zelum pro religione, imo & observantiam universae legis secundum tenorem istius sectae adducit, quae publice nota erant, & testatissima. Quae vero Pharisaica justitia minime sufficiebat, quia in externo tantum corte legis haerebat, Matth. 5, 20. quapropter non tantum lex forensis, vel judicialis hic respicitur, sed maxime legis moralis observantia, quam Pharisaei requirebant & Pseudo-Apostoli una cum fide in CHRISTUM necessaria ad justificationem & salutem dictitabant, Actor. 15, 5. De lege morali explicat e Pontificiis Justinianus, ut alios taceamus. Non Dei judicio, sed homini quantum fas est judicare, nihil in me erat, quod Judaei merito possint reprehendere. Hoc est enim quod ait Apostolus, γενόμενος ἄμεμπτος. Vers. 7. Ἀλλ' ἅτινα ἦν μοι κέρδη) Quae mihi lucro esse poterant: origo Judaica: secta laudabilis: secunda inter meos fama. Ταῦτα ἤγημαι διὰ τὸν Χριστὸν ζημίαν εἶναι) Postquam Jesum Christum cognovi, vidi in illis nihil esse veri lucri. ἤγημαι. מלתהי Zauias. Ἀλλὰ μενοῦν ἤγημαι πάντα ζημίαν εἶναι) Non illa tantum quae dixi, sed & honores & bona hujus vitae omnia, & ipsam vitam. Διὰ τὸ ὑπερέχον τῆς γνώσεως τοῦ Χριστοῦ Ἰησοῦ τοῦ Κυρίου μου) id est, si comparentur ista cum cognitione Christi, qui mihi super omnia est. Τὸ ὑπερέχον τῆς γνώσεως, Graeca constructio pro τὴν γνῶσιν τὴν ὑπερέχουσαν. Διὰ ὃν πάντα ἐζημιώθην) propter quem libenter rerum aliarum omnium jacturam feci secundum praeceptum Christi, Matth.

## 3:8
7. But what things were gain to me) Which could be gain to me: Jewish origin: a laudable sect: second fame among my own. These I have counted loss for Christ) After I knew Jesus Christ, I saw that there was no true gain in them. "I have counted." [His words] Zauias. But doubtless I count all things but loss) Not only those things which I have said, but also the honors and all the goods of this life, and life itself. For the excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus my Lord) that is, if these things are compared with the knowledge of Christ, who is above all things to me. "The excellency of the knowledge," a Greek construction for "the knowledge which excels." For whom I have suffered the loss of all things) for whom I have willingly made loss of all other things according to the commandment of Christ, Matthew 16:24. And do count them but dung) In the glossary: "dung" is filth, refuse. Charisius explains it as trifles. See Sirach 27:5. The Hebrews would say . That I may win Christ) That I may gain Christ, that is, the favor of Christ, . He says not only that there is no true gain in them, but that they are held by him as loss and damage, since they lead us away from the true knowledge and faith of Christ, without which there is no faith for us, but a certain loss of salvation, in which alone we ought to glory, since there is no other name under heaven in which we may have salvation . He expresses the tribe of Benjamin specifically, lest he be thought to be of the ten tribes, which is the reasoning of Chrysostom, and also because of the dignity of the tribe, which it had, of the kingdom of origin from Rachel, and in respect of the temple, . That he calls himself a Hebrew, Chrysostom explains in this way, that he was not from ancient proselytes, but from ancient illustrious Jews. Nor did it please him to stop at Abraham, but to ascend to Eber, which was also done in 1 Corinthians 11:22. Furthermore, he was not only a Pharisee by profession, but also by birth, . Concerning Paul's zeal, Theodoret says: He did not tear apart the Church because of any other thing, nor moved by envy, as the Jewish leaders, but spurred by emulation for the law. But why does the Apostle add that, which certainly did not make for his praise? He seems to have done it to remove suspicion, as if he were always alien to the law and hated those diverse ceremonies and their observers. says Theophylact, not very much emulators of the law, since they were full of ostentation, and so vehement that they persecuted the Church of Christ. For there were many who were led by such zeal, not for protecting the law and observing the traditions of the fathers, but for the sake of principality or glory; therefore Paul says, because I am free from blame, and am not to be accused according to the righteousness of the law, how can it be that I persecuted the Church for the sake of some human thing rather than for the zeal of God? Jewish origin indeed does not stand in the way of salvation, but boasting of origin with contempt for the Gentiles does. Circumcision also was of no value, which was urged as an external work, and the same, as the Scholastics say, was believed to be profitable for salvation ex opere operato, by which pact it was even harmful, and after Christ brought an end to circumcision, those who received it fell away from Christ, . The zeal of the Pharisees was without knowledge, . Pharisaic righteousness was such that no one could enter the kingdom of heaven through it, as Christ testifies . The Reformed, Calvin, Bullinger, Beza, Hyperius, Zanchius, Aretins, Crocius, etc., deservedly depart into a different view, who take "gains" from merits, in which the confidence of salvation is placed, and "losses" not as less useful things, but as true losses, not that the Apostle thinks the external prerogatives and works of the law are in themselves damnable, but insofar as they had placed the hope of salvation in them as merits, and had allowed himself to be led away from Christ in Judaism by them, and would be led away further if he continued to place the confidence of salvation in them. But what he had before his conversion as a great treasure of merits, these, having been converted to CHRIST, he counted not only useless, but also harmful, and to be joined with the danger of destruction, he acknowledged, on account of the confidence of righteousness and salvation placed in them, from which he was led away by Christ, in whom alone the hope of salvation must be fixed. Rightly, therefore, did Ambrose express the sense: When he spoke earlier of the race of Abraham, and of the law, and of his righteousness and the merits of those who err, counting all these things as loss in comparison with the promises of the Savior: Now he adds, not only these, but also that all things are loss on account of the excellence, he says, of the knowledge of CHRIST JESUS my Lord: After the law and its righteousness, what will all these things be, unless the recognition of CHRIST is preferred to the life of the body and soul itself.

Which things thus rightly touch the scope of the Apostle. Yet those ALL things are more conveniently explained for the present matter and context, and especially for those things which follow further concerning all works done according to the law, whether before conversion or after conversion, which in respect of the eminent knowledge of Christ are to be held as losses.

For he removes his own righteousness v. 9. and requires nothing but the righteousness of CHRIST, in respect of which all our works in the business of salvation are to be estimated as loss and waste, not because they are of no use in themselves; for those things which are done from faith, and have proceeded from the Holy Spirit, have their own utility, as the Apostle testifies, 1 Tim. 4, but because the opinion of merit or necessity for salvation is damnable and destructive. Εζημιώθην

By the verb ἐζημιώθην, which the Vulgate rendered, to be fined, he indicates that he voluntarily made a loss of all things, that he had cast away the confidence of all things outside of Christ, and that he had fined himself of all things, which he himself once held for gains, and which others still hold.

The Apostle adds that he holds all those things as σκύβαλοις. For what are those things, which were judged to be most excellent, but foul-smelling dung, such as the Pharisaic discipline, and the observance of that law from the rigor of that sect. For the religion of this sect was the most exact mere hypocrisy, they themselves were pronounced by CHRIST to be like whitened sepulchres, which from the outside appear beautiful to men, but inside are full of the bones of the dead and all filth, Matt. 23, 27. σκύβαλα Some explain σκύβαλα as if it were κυσκύβαλα, filth thrown to dogs.

To physicians, σκύβαλα are harder excrements, which are passed with difficulty, as if they were δύσβαλα, which meaning is especially clear to Aretius, because it is signified that there is need of sharp purging to purge away the opinion of merit, which tenaciously adheres to us who are sick. To Crocius it is certain that the Apostle signified a sordid thing, which all sane men turn away from.

Thus he shows that he did not cast away the confidence of all legal righteousness, and of whatever prerogatives, with a desire to retain them, which is the confession of the maker.

But he warns with Calvin that it is not a matter of substance, but of quality, that is, of the confidence of merit. He does not count circumcision, the observation of ceremonies, sobriety, chastity, and other virtues in themselves as dung, but the confidence placed in them.

Add also the opinion of necessity for salvation. Nor is the impurity adhering to our virtues or works to be neglected; on account of which they stink before GOD, unless the odor of the death of CHRIST, a sacrifice of sweet fragrance and a scent of rest, is reconciled to them.

The more the carnal Pseudo-Apostles valued these Jewish prerogatives, says B. Hunnius, the more vehemently the Apostle disparages them, not once only calling them loss and detriment, but repeating and inculcating it a second and even a third time.

Moreover, he calls them σκύβαλα, that is, dung and excrement. Doubtless the Apostle wished to compare those most empty safeguards of righteousness to filth, than which nothing can be viler, nothing more abject or contemptible. But all these things are said comparatively and with a hypothesis. With a hypothesis indeed, if the hope of salvation and eternal life is placed in them: But comparatively, if they are all compared together to the excellent knowledge of JESUS CHRIST, who is the only author of all righteousness, and the beginning and end, the alpha and omega of all our salvation.

The Apostle therefore wishes to say, I willingly cast away all things, and I count as nothing what I once held in treasures and gain, provided that I may gain CHRIST and be found in him.

Good works, says B. Balduinus, are in themselves most precious, and as Luther speaks, each one is dearer than heaven and earth: For they are commanded by GOD, they are the effects of the Holy Spirit, they are the fruits of faith and exercises of piety, due to GOD in obedience and gratitude: but that they become harmful and pernicious even in the business of salvation, that they have from an accident, namely from the opinion of merit, which workers attach to them, who place confidence in their works, and by this very thing evacuate the merit of CHRIST, as Paul testifies, Gal.

2, 21. Against which Nicol. Ambsdorf. is to be noted, who in the act of disputation said that good works are pernicious to salvation: which phrase indeed the other colloquutors of Altenburg by no means approved, as is evident from the Acts pag. 338. Good works can be called neither necessary, nor harmful, or pernicious to salvation, because of themselves they have no relation to salvation, as we have shown elsewhere against the Calixtines.

That ἵνα κερδήσω κερδήσω is not, that I may gain the favor of CHRIST, but that I may gain CHRIST, whom alone I hold for my gain, and in whom I have all things, when I make his merit and righteousness my own, and this hidden treasure, this most precious pearl, having dismissed all things which can be esteemed in the eyes of men, I may acquire, Matt. 13, 44. 45.
