Behold, He Himself offers to us with a liberal hand, Apoc. 3, 18. Come, come, come, He cries out with great ardor and desire for our salvation, who has no money: buy without money and gratis, Esa. Thus the Apostle explains himself, that I may gain CHRIST, and be found in him, having not my own righteousness, namely that which is from the law, but that which is through faith in Christ.

He speaks of that which he opposes to the observation of the ceremonial moral law, which the Pseudo-Apostles urged, and by which they exalted themselves, and which the Apostle, imbued with Pharisaic doctrines, had valued as having the greatest momentum in the cause of salvation: in comparison with which he now affirms that he makes all those things as loss and as σκύβαλοις, which is not the favor of Christ, but the righteousness of Christ recognized by faith, which is that excellent knowledge of Christ, and true confidence of the heart received and apprehended. For in this way at last we are found in CHRIST, in this way we have the righteousness which is through faith, of Christ.

Those who are swollen with the opinion of their own merit are not in Christ: Those who place confidence in external things do not rest solely in the righteousness of Christ. It is therefore a great gain to count all those things as loss, and to do nothing.

Latin:

16, 24. Καὶ ἡγοῦμαι σκύβαλα εἶναι) In glossario: σκύβαλον fercus, retrimentum. Charisius exponit quisquilias. Vide Sirac. 27, 5. Ebrzi dicerent . Ἵνα Χριστὸν κερδήσω) Ut lucrifaciam Christum, id est, Christi favorem, . Non tantum nihil in illis veri lucri esse ait, sed ea à se pro damno & jactura haberi, quum vera cognitione, & fide Christi, fine qua nulla nobis fides, sed certa salutis jactura, nos abducant, in quo unice nos gloriari oportet, quum aliud sub caelo non fit nomen, in quo salutem nos habeamus . Tribum Benjamin specialiter exprimit, ne putetur esse ex decem tribubus, quae Chrysostomi est ratio, tum etiam ob dignitatem tribus, quam habebat, originis ex Rachele regni, & templi respectu, . Quod se Ebraeum dicit, Chrysostomus explicat hoc modo, quod non ex antiquis proselytis, sed ex vetustis illustribus Judaeis fuerit. Nec in eo aut Abrahamo subsistere, sed ad Eber ascendere placuit, quod & 1. Cor. 11, 22. factum. Porro Pharisaeus non profellus tantum fuit, sed & natus, . De Zelo Pauli Theodoretus: Non propter aliam, neque invidia motus, ut Judaeorum Principes, sed pro lege aemulatione percitus Ecclesiam diripiebat. Cur autem id addit Apostolus, quod sane ad laudem ejus non faciebat? Id ideo fecisse videtur, ut suspicionem amoliretur, quasi semper à lege alienus atque eas diversas ceremonias, & earum observatores inclaretur. ait Theophylactus, non admodum legis aemulatores, quippe qui ad ostentationem plemarant, & adeo vehementi, ut Christi Ecclesiam inseclarer. Erant enim plerique, qui ejusmodi zelo non pro lege tutanda, & majorum traditionibus observanda, sed principatus vel gloria gratia ducerentur, idcirco Paulus inquit, quia cum culpa vacem, nec sim secundum legis justitiam incufandus, qui fieri potest, ut humana potius rei cujuspiam gratia, non Dei zelo Ecclesiam sim persecutus. Origo Judaica quidem non obstat faluti, sed gloriatio de origine cum contemptu gentium. Circumcisio etiam nihil valebat, qua opus externum urgeabatur, eademque ut Scholastici loquuntur, ex opere operato prodesse ad salutem credebatur, quo pacto etiam noxia erat, ac postquam finem attulit circumcisioni Christus, à Christo excidebant, qui eandem suscipiebant, . Zelus Pharisaeorum fine scientia erat, . Justitia Pharisaica talis, ut per eam in regnum caelorum ingredi nemo potuerit, teste Christo . Merito abeunt in diversum Reformati, Calvinus, Bullinger, Beza, Hyperius, Zanchius, Aretins, Crocius &c. qui lucra de meritis, in quibus fiducia salutis collocatur, & damna non de minus utilibus, sed veris damnis accipiunt, non quod externas prerogativas & opera legis per se damnosa censeat Apostolus, sed quatenus in illis, tanquam meritis, spem salutis collocaverant, & per illa a Christo in Judaismo se abduci passus erat, & porro abduceretur, si in illis fiduciam salutis collocare pergeret. Quae vero ante conversionem pro magno meritorum thesauro habuit, ea ad CHRISTUM conversus non tantum inutilia, sed & noxia, ac cum exitii periculo conjuncta esse, ob fiduciam justitiae, & salutis in illis locatam agnovit, qua à Christo, in quo unico spes salutis figenda abductus fuit. Recte itaque sensum expressit Ambrosius: Cum superius de genere Abrahae, & de lege, & de justitia ejus & meritis oberrantium loqueretur, haec omnia detrimentum deputans ad comparationem promissionum Salvatoris: Nunc addit, non solum haec, sed & omnia damnum esse propter eminentiam, inquit, scientiae CHRISTI JESU Domini mei: Post legem & justitias ejus, quae erunt bae omnia, nisi ut ipsi vita corporis animaque anteponatur agnitio CHRISTI.

Quae sicopum Apostoli probe tangunt. Illa tamen OMNIA convenientius pro materia praesenti & contextu, ac imprimis iis, quae porro sequuntur de operibus omnibus secundum legem factis, sive ante conversionem, sive post conversionem, explicantur, quae respectu agnitionis Christi eminentis pro damnis habenda.

Removet enim propriam justitiam vers. 9. nec nisi justitiam CHRISTI requirit, cujus respectu nostra opera in negotio salutis omnia pro damno, & jactura aestimanda, non quod per se nullius sint usus; ea enim, quae ex fide fiunt, & à Spiritu sancto profecta sunt, omnino suam habent utilitatem teste Apostolo, 1. Timoth. 4. sed quod opinio meriti aut necessitatis ad salutem damnalis & exitiosa est. Εζημιώθην

Verbo ἐζημιώθην, quod Vulgatus reddidit, multari, indicat, se ultro jacturam fecisse omnium, fiduciam omnium rerum extra Christum abjecisse, seque multasse omnibus, quae & ipse olim habuerit pro lucris, & alii adhuc habent. Addit Apostolus se pro σκύβαλοις illa omnia habere.

Nam quid nisi stercora sunt illa male foetentia, etiam quae praestantissima judicabantur, utpote disciplina Pharisaica, & observantia illius legis ex rigore illius sectae. Erat enim sectae istius religio exactissima mera hypocrisis similes ipsi à CHRISTO pronuntiabantur sepulchris dealbatis, quae à foris hominibus apparent speciosa, intus vero plena sunt ossibus mortuorum & omni spurcitia, Matth. 23, 27. σκύβαλα Nonnulli σκύβαλα exponunt, quasi κυσκύβαλα, sordes canibus objectas.

Medicis σκύβαλα sunt duriora excrementa, quae difficulter egeruntur, quasi δύσβαλα, quae significatio imprimis patet Aretio, quod ita significetur, acri purgatione opus esse ad expurgandam opinionem meriti, quae nobis aegris tenaciter adhaeret. Crocio id certum, significasse Apostolum rem sordidam, quam omnes fani aversentur.

Ita ostendit, se non cum retinendi desiderio abjecisse fiduciam omnia justitiae legalis, & quarumcunque prerogativarum, quod fatone factoris.

Monet autem cum Calvino non de substantia, sed de qualitate agi, id est, de fiducia meriti. Non ducit circumcisionem, observationem ceremoniarum, sobrietatem, castitatem & virtutes alias in se pro stercoribus, sed fiduciam in illis positam.

Adde & necessitatis ad salutem opinionem. Neque impuritas adhaerens virtutibus aut operibus nostris negligenda; ob quae foetent com coram DEO, nisi per sacrificium bonae fragrantiae & odorem quietis mortis CHRISTI gratus iisdem odor concilietur.

Quo pluris aestimabant, inquit B. Hunnius, Pseudo-Apostoli carnales has prerogativas Judaicas, eo impensius eas Apostolus extenuat, non semel duntaxat damnum & detrimentum nominans, sed vice altera, quin tertia insuper id repetens & inculcans.

Appellat autem insuper σκύβαλα, hoc est stercora & excrementa. Nimirum voluit Apostolus illa justitiarum inanissima praesidia ita comparare sordibus, quibus nihil vilius, nihil abjectius aut contemptius esse potest. Qua omnia vero comparate dicuntur & cum hypothesi. Cum hypothesi quidem, si in iis spes salutis & vita aeterna reponatur: Comparate vero, si conferantur ea simul omnia ad excellentem cognitionem JESU CHRISTI, qui omnis justitiae autor unicus, omnisque salutis nostrae principium & finis, a & ω est.

Vult ergo dicere Apostolus, libenter abjicia omnia, proque nihilo duco, qua olim habebam in thesauris & lucro, dummodo CHRISTUM meum lucrifaciam & in ipso reperiar.

Bona opera, inquit B. Balduinus, in se sunt pretiosissima, & ut Lutherus loquitur, caelo & terra charius est unumquodvis: Sunt enim à DEO praecepta, sunt Spiritus sancti effecta, sunt fructus fidei & exercitia pietatis, obedientiae ac gratitudinis DEO debita: quod autem noxia & pernitiosa fiunt etiam in salutis negotio, id ex Accidente babent, nimirum ex opinione meriti, quam eis operarii affingunt, qui fiduciam in operibus suis collocant, & hoc ipso meritum CHRISTI evacuant, teste Paulo, Galat.

2, 21. Quod contra Nicol. Ambsdorf. observandum, qui in actu disputationis bona opera pernitiosa ad salutem esse dixit: quam vero phrasin caeteri colloquutores Altenburgi, ut ex Actis pag. 338. patet, minime approbarunt, Bona opera nec necessaria, nec noxia, aut pernitiosa ad salutem dici possunt, quia propria nullam relationem ad salutem habent, ut alias contra Calixtinos ostendimus.

Illud ἵνα κερδήσω κερδήσω, non est, ut CHRISTI favorem lucrifaciam, sed ut CHRISTUM, quem unice pro lucro meo habeo, & in quo habeo omnia, cum merito & justitia sua meum faciam, & hunc absconditum thesaurum, hanc pretiosissimam margaritam, dimissis omnibus, quae aestimari in hominum oculis possunt, comparem, Matth. 13, 44. 45. Quo vero pretio lucari hoc tantum pretium possumus?

Ecce offert nobis ipse liberali manu, Apoc. 3, 18. venite, venite, venite, clamat magno ardore ac desiderio salutis nostrae, qui pecuniam non habetus, emite sine pecunia & gratis, Esa. 55, 1. Sic explicat semetipsum Apostolus, ut CHRISTUM lucrifaciam, & in eo inveniar, habens non meam justitiam, nempe qua est ex lege, sed eam, qua per fidem est Christi.

De eo loquitur, quod observationi legis ceremonalis moralis opponit, quam urgebant, & qua se efferebant Pseudo-Apostoli, & quam aestimaverat, maximum habere momentum in causa salutis, Apostolus, Pharisaicis imbutus doctrinis: prae quo omnia illa sese pro damno nunc facere ac pro σκύβαλοις affirmat, quod non est favor Christi, sed justitia Christi fide agnita, quae est excellens illa Christi agnitio, & vera fiducia cordis suscepta, atque apprehensa. Hac enim demum ratione invenimur in CHRISTO, hoc modo nos habemus justitiam, quae per fidem est, Christi.

Qui proprii meriti opinione turgent, non sunt in Christo: Qui in rebus externis fiduciam collocant, non unice in Christi justitia acquiescunt. Magnum ergo lucrum est, illa omnia pro damno habere, ac nihil facere.

## 3:9
Verf. 9. Και ίυρεθῶ ἐν αὐτῷ]

That I may be found, that is, I am in him, engrafted into him. Thus the Hebrews use Nצמ.

Μὴ ἔχων ἐμὴν δικαιοσύνην τὴν ἐκ νόμου) That innocence which holds weight in judgments according to the law and is obtainable by human aid. Compare Rom. 4:2 and ch. 10:3, where it is thus called "one's own righteousness" (ἰδία δικαιοσύνη). That "from the law" (ἐκ νόμου) here is "according to the law," namely, in the manner in which it was urged by the Pharisees. See Matt. 5:20 and the remarks there.

Διὰ τὴν πίστιν Χρισῦ) That which we obtain through faith in Christ, which is "through faith" (διὰ τῆς πίστεως). The genitive "of Christ" (Χρισῦ) here signifies the object; how that happens, he will now explain more precisely.

Τὴν ἐκ Θεῦ δικαιοσύνην) Which GOD works in us, and therefore approves as His own work. Romans 3:2, 22; ch. 10:3.

Ἐπὶ τῇ πίστει) Thus also Acts 3:16, for "through faith" (διὰ τῆς πίστεως). Through faith both in Christ and in God.

He explains how he gains Christ: namely, while he is found in Him through faith. For we are in no other way in Christ than through faith. He does not say, "so that I may recover those things in Christ which I hold as losses," as Calvin takes the verb actively; because Grotius, following Beza, warns that the verb ἐυρεθῶ can in no way be taken actively according to the usage of the Greek language. But [he says it] "so that I may be found in Christ," whom I have, while reckoning all other things as loss, who alone suffices for me in the cause of salvation, and in whom alone I rest. But those who bring their own righteousness here at the same time, which was done by the Pseudo-Apostles, the Apostle implies that they are not found in Christ. For they are not subject to the righteousness of God who strive to establish their own righteousness, as the Apostle testifies, Rom. 10:3. Christ alone is the "end of the law" (τέλος νόμου) for righteousness to everyone who believes, v. 4. Therefore, he calls it "his own righteousness," not only that external one which is regarded in human judgments, but any [righteousness] whatsoever that is regarded in the law and performed according to the law, however much of it there is in us! For since it is performed by us very imperfectly, that righteousness of ours cannot stand before the tribunal of God. Therefore, the Apostle removes it and opposes to it the righteousness which is not ours. For this is what an *antithesis* requires. Since righteousness according to the law is ours, or inherent, that in which he does not wish to be found before the judgment of GOD, it must be understood in what [righteousness] the Apostle wishes to be found, which is not ours; that is, not inherent, but alien, which is ours, namely, only through faith, through the appropriation of faith, through gracious imputation in the judgment of GOD. Which is the righteousness of Christ Himself. For we apprehend this by faith, and we gain Christ; in comparison to this, all those external things are to be reckoned as mere losses, and because of its preciousness or dignity, as mere dung, because of its purity and holiness. "Lest I have," says Theophylact as interpreter, "my own righteousness, which is compiled from the works of the law, just as if I had obtained this very righteousness from these." For no righteousness proceeds from works, because this cannot consist of these, but [I pray] that I may obtain righteousness through faith in Christ, which is from God. "Not having," says the Blessed Hunnius, "nor boasting of my own righteousness from the law, whether moral or ceremonial, but that righteousness which is through the faith of Christ, that is, which Christ donates and applies to us, acquired by His own obedience, namely, the righteousness which is from God upon faith, that is, which God imputes to our faith, which also holds weight before His judgment." The entire paraphrase of the Blessed Balduinus has it thus: "Formerly indeed, when I was still of the Pharisees, I held these things as gain, but now if I were to add them to the merits of Christ, I would receive great detriment from it. For all things which could seem greatest in the world, in comparison to the righteousness of Christ my Lord, I hold for loss and refuse; for to know the righteousness of Christ, and to wish to apply it to oneself, I hold as the greatest gain, in which alone I desire to be righteous, not seeking righteousness from the law, which consists in my works, but in the Gospel, which commends faith in Christ, which God works in me, so that I may be filled with His power, and understand how effective His resurrection is, so that, as in His passion, so also in His glory I may be made like Him."

But Grotius seems here to "papize" again: Grotius explains the righteousness which is of the faith of Christ, which is of God, and [in a] Papizing [manner], as righteousness in faith. For Bellarmine, book 1, *De Justificatione*, ch. 1, thus explains the mind of the Pontificians: that the righteousness of God is an internal certainty by which a man is rightly ordered toward God and neighbor, and that this alone is simply and absolutely righteousness, and is called the righteousness of faith because it begins from faith, and the righteousness of God because it is donated by God, and that Paul is dealing with this in this place; and he notes that the righteousness from the law, which is opposed to the righteousness from faith, is not the righteousness of the law, that is, the righteousness written in the law, but is righteousness done without the help of grace from the mere knowledge of the law. Furthermore, ch. XIX, § "I respond," he says it is strange that the Apostle here opposes righteousness to righteousness, namely, his own righteousness, that is, his own just works, done from faith, which are truly just before God, and again his own righteousness, that is, his own just works done in the law without faith, which could not be truly just before God, but only outwardly and in the face of men, among whom he had lived without blame in Judaism. But this is mere *skaiotēs* (perversity). For (I.) the righteousness of faith here is not internal rectitude, nor just works done from faith. Which we teach by these [points]: 1. The righteousness of faith is manifested by the word of faith, or the Gospel, Rom. 1:17, ch. 10:8, without the law, Rom. 3:21. But internal rectitude, by which a man is ordered toward God and neighbor, is not from the Gospel, but from the law, and has the law as its norm, nor do good works which are done from faith acknowledge any other norm. 2. The righteousness of faith is not that which begins from faith, but which is apprehended by faith, which is called God's; not because it is infused into us by God, but because it is righteousness also from Christ, inasmuch as He is Jehovah our righteousness, Jerem. 23:6, and has been made righteousness for us by GOD, 1 Cor. 1:29. 3. The righteousness of faith is called ἡ διὰ πίστεως χρισῦ, which is obtained through faith of Christ, or in Christ; but that internal rectitude, whether it be placed in just works or constituted in the heart of man, that infused habit of righteousness, or of charity, or the acts redundant from it, are not obtained through faith in CHRIST. For was not such habitual rectitude in the Protoplasts before the fall, where there was no faith in Christ, nor did it have a place? 4. The righteousness of faith is ἡ ἐκ θεῦ δικαιοσύνη ἐπὶ τῇ πίστει, that righteousness from God in faith, or through faith, which is opposed to our righteousness. Therefore, by the force of opposition, it cannot denote righteousness or rectitude inherent in us. For this, even if it is from God, is truly ours: since good works and rectitude toward God and men are truly of the reborn, even by the admission of the Pontificians themselves. 5. That rectitude and just works pertain to the fruits of our justification, which is merely gratuitous and only through faith, by and because of the merit of CHRIST, [and] can in no way be referred to the causes of justification. Good works follow the justified, they do not precede the justifying [act]. For here it is a matter of righteousness from GOD, through which we are justified.

(II.) Paul does not constitute a twofold righteousness of ours, one which is external and done without the help of grace, from the mere knowledge of the law; another which is internal and done through faith: But he calls "our righteousness" all that righteousness which is according to the law, whether before conversion or after conversion.

For both here refers to the law, and both are distinguished from the righteousness which is by faith, and has been revealed in the Gospel without the law. Which righteousness is not ours, but is distinguished from ours, not being inherent, but imputed to us through faith.

(III.) The righteousness of the law, the law of righteousness, and the works of the law are not different to the Apostle, as is evident from

Rom. IX. 31. Similarly, the righteousness of faith and [that] from faith are synonyms, Rom. III. 22. Phil. III. 9. And thus, since the reason for opposites is the same, the righteousness of the law and the righteousness from the law are also the same. And therefore the Cardinal distinguishes these rashly.

(IV

(IV.) The Apostle did not consider only external righteousness and obedience as loss, but also internal, nay, all obedience to the law, whatever it may be, and EVERYTHING whatsoever outside of Christ.

Not that works done from faith do not please God, but that they cannot stand before the judgment of God on account of their imperfection and native impurity.

Here indeed Bellarmine exclaims: But what blasphemy, I pray, is it to call works done from faith and the grace of Christ dung! But after those declamations, let Kemnitius now go, he says, and let it be sought, because we say that he is an enemy of good works. A less than just accusation, a complaint altogether unjust. Not we, but the Spirit calls all things dung, which, outside of and beyond Christ, with his merit and righteousness, which he alone considers as gain here, are mixed into our sphere of justification and salvation, which was done by the Pseudo-Apostles, and is still done even now by the Papists through the confusion of law and Gospel. Good works are held in esteem, as by Luther, B. Chemnitius, so by any genuine Lutherans, but outside the business of justification and salvation, which is to be attributed solely to the merits of Christ, [and] in no way to our works or merits, which, when that happens, are to be held as loss and dung, not in themselves, but on account of the abomination of merits or necessity for salvation attached to them.

Outside the cause of justification, says B. Luther, in chapter 3 to the Galatians, no one can truly commend good works magnificently enough: But who can sufficiently proclaim the utility and fruit of even one good work, which a Christian does from faith and in faith? For it is more precious than heaven and earth.

But the reason why we do not admit our works into justification is, 1. because they are too imperfect if they are brought into the Divine judgment, Ps. 143, 2. to which passage St. Augustine [says]: However more upright I may seem to myself, you nevertheless produce a rule from your treasury, you adapt me to it, and I am found crooked. And book XIX. of the City of God, ch. XXVII. our righteousness itself, however true it may be on account of the true good to which it is referred, is nevertheless so great in this life that it consists rather in the remission of sins than in the perfection of virtues. 2. Because by our works required for justification, the merit and righteousness of Christ is altogether derogated, to whom alone our salvation is to be ascribed, Rom. VI. last [verse], who alone trod the winepress, Is. 63, alone is our Savior, Is. 65, 22. 23.

To this excellent knowledge of Christ, therefore, let anyone strive [to bring] his own righteousness, whether internal or external, whether before conversion, (where indeed no good works have a place, lest we imagine fruits without a tree, an effect without a cause, and therefore such works are a Papistic fiction;) or after the same: These, not in themselves indeed, but on account of the accompanying imperfection and impurity, and when they are added to the merit and righteousness of Christ, so that they flow into our righteousness and salvation, the holy Apostle considers as losses and dung, so that he may esteem Christ solely as gain, which gain is certainly lost as soon as any work, whatever it may be, is joined to it as necessary for salvation. The Walenburg brothers felt the force of the truth here, therefore to the question, what is that righteousness which we ought to have, so that we may appear before the tribunal of God, be absolved in his judgment, and not be condemned; they say that Catholics answer: It is the righteousness imputed and given to us, and that it is the sole cause why we are not condemned for our sins, but are absolved from them. To the question, whether we are constituted perfectly righteous in the judgment of God by the righteousness of Christ given and imputed to us? [They] answer: that we are constituted, or rather considered and held to be, perfectly righteous by that righteousness which is extrinsic to us and most perfect. They grant that the righteousness inherent in us is imperfect with respect to the righteousness of Christ given and imputed to us. Which without doubt infinitely exceeds our righteousness. Which and many other things of this kind we have adduced in the Exegem.

Latin:

Vers. 9. Και ίυρεθῶ ἐν αὐτῷ]

Ut inveniar, id est, sum in ipso, ipsi insitus. Sic Ebraei usurpant Nצמ.

Μὴ ἔχων ἐμὴν δικαιοσύνην τὴν ἐκ νόμου) Illam innocentiam, quæ in judiciis fecundum legem valet, & humana ope parabilis eft. Simile Rom. 4, 2. & cap. 10, 3. ubi ita juftitia dicitur ἰδία δικαιοσύνη. Illud ἐκ νόμου hic eft fecundum legem, nempe qualiter illa a Pharifæis urgebatur. Vide Matth. 5, 20. & ibi dicta.

Διὰ τὴν πίστιν Χρισῦ) Eam, quam per fidem in Chriftum confequimur, quod eft διὰ τῆς πίστεως. Genitivus Χρισῦ hic objectum fignificat, quomodo id hat, jam exactius explicabit.

Τὴν ἐκ Θεῦ δικαιοσύνην) Quam DEUS in nobis operatur, & propterea ut opus fuum approbat Romanor. 3, 2. 22. cap. 10, 3.

Ἐπὶ τῇ πίστει) Sic & Act. 3, 16. pro διὰ τῆς πίστεως. Per fidem tum in Chriftum, tum in Deum.

Explicatur, quomodo Chriftum lucrifaciat? dum fcilicet in ipfo invenitur per fidem. Non aliter enim in Chrifto fumus, quam per fidem. Non alidicit, ut recuperem ea in Chrifto, quæ pro damnis habeo, ut Calvinus active verbum accipit: quia nullo modo verbum ἐυρεθῶ ex Græcæ quidem linguæ ufu accipi poffe active, è Beza monet Grotius. Sed ut inveniar in Chrifto, quem unice pro lucro, cætera omnia pro damno reputans, habeo, qui unus mihi fufficit in caufa falutis, in quo folo acquiefco. Qui vero propriam juftitiam fimul huc afferunt, quod à Pfeudo-Apoftolis factum, eos in Chrifto non inveniri innuit Apoftolus. Non enim fubjiciuntur juftitiæ Dei, qui fatagunt propriam juftitiam erigere, tefte Apoftolo, Rom. 10, 3. Chriftus de folus eft τέλος νόμου complementum legis ad juftitiam omni credenti, v. 4. Juftitiam ergo fuam vocat non tantum externam illam, quæ in judiciis humanis refpicitur, fed quamvis, quæ refpicitur in lege, & præftatur juxta legem, quanta quanta ea eft in nobis! Quum enim ea valde imperfecte præftetur à nobis, non poteft illa juftitia noftra coram Dei tribunali confiftere. Ideo removet eandem Apoftolus, & opponit ei juftitiam, quæ noftm non eft. Hoc enim ἀντίθεσις requirit. Quum juftitia fecundum legem noftra fit, vel inhærens, ea quam coram judicio DEI non vult inveniri, oportet intelligi, in qua vult inveniri Apoftolus, quæ non fit noftra; hoc eft, non inhærentem, fed alienam, quæ noftra fcilicet tantum fit per fidem, per appropriationem fidei, per imputationem gratiofam in judicio DEI. Quæ eft ipfiusmet Chrifti juftitia. Hanc enim fide apprehendimus, & Chriftum lucrifacimus, præ hoc omnia illa externa mera damna, ob iftius pretiofitatem vel dignitatem, ftercora mera æftimanda funt, ob iftius puritatem & fanctitatem. Ne habeam, inquit Theophylacto interprete, meam juftitiam, quæ ex legis operibus compamtur, perinde ac ex bis fuerim juftitiam hanc ipfam adeptus. Neque enim ex operibus juftitia ulla proficifcitur, quia neque ex his conftari hæc poteft, fed per Chrifti fidem juftitiam adipifcar, quæ ex Deo eft. Non habens, inquit B. Hunnius, neque jactans meam juftitiam ex lege five momli, five ceremoniali, fed juftitiam eam, quæ eft per fidem Chrifti, hoc eft, quam Chriftus obedientia fua nobis acquifitam per fidem donat & applicat, juftitiam nimirum, quæ ex Deo eft fuper fide, hoc eft, quam Deus imputat fidei noftræ, quæ etiam coram judicio fuo valet finit. B. Balduini paraphrafis integra ita habet: Olim quidem, cum adhuc è barifæis effem, ifta in luero babui, nunc autem fi meritis Chrifti ea adjungerem, magnum inde detrimentum caperem. Omnia enim, quæ commundo maxima videri poterant, in collatione juftitiæ Chrifti Domini mei, pro detrimento & quifquiliis habeo, Chrifti enim juftitiam noffe, fibique velle applicare, maximi lucri inftar habeo, in quo folo juftus effe cupio, non ex lege quærens juftitiam, quæ in meo confiftat operibus, fed in Evangelio, quod fidem in Chriftum commendat, quam Deus in me operatur, ut facientia ejus implear, & quam fit efficax ejus refurrectio, intelligam, 5, ut in paffione, ita & in gloria ei fimilis efficiar.

Videtur autem hic Grotius iterum papizare: Hrotius cum juftitiam, quæ ex fide eft Chrifti, quæ ex Deo, & Papizans, juftitia in fide eft, explicat. Nam ita Pontificiorum mentem exponit Bellarminus libr. 1. de Juftif. cap. 1. Juftitiam Dei effe certitudinem internam, qua homo recte ordinatur erga Deum & proximum, eamque folam effe fimpliciter & abfolute juftitiam, & dici juftitiam fidei, quia à fide incipit, & juftitiam Dei, quia donatur à Deo, & de hac hoc loco agere Paulum: notatque juftitiam ex lege, quæ opponitur juftitiæ ex fide, non effe juftitiam legis, id eft, juftitiam fcriptam in lege, fed effe juftitiam factam fine auxilio gratiæ ex fola cognitione legis. Porro cap. XIX. §. refpondeo mirum eft, juftitiam juftitiæ opponere bic Apoftolum, ait, juftitiam nempe fuam, id eft, opera fua jufta, facta ex fide, quæ vere jufta fint coram Deo, & iterum juftitiam fuam, hoc eft, opera fua jufta facta in lege fine fide, quæ non potuerint effe vere jufta coram Deo, fed folum exterius & in facie hominum, apud quos fuerat in Judaismo fine querela verfatus. Sed hæc eft mera σξελότης. Nam (I.) juftitia fidei hic non eft rectitudo interna, nec opens jufta facta ex fide. Quod hifce docemus: 1. Juftitia fidei eft verbo fidei, vel Evangelio, Rom. 1, 17. cap. 10, 8. manifeftata fine lege, Rom. 3, 21. Rectitudo autem interna, qua homo ordinatur erga Deum & proximum, non ex Evangelio, fed ex lege eft, ac pro norma habet legem, neque aliam normam agnofcunt bona opera, quæ fiunt ex fide. 2. Juftitia fidei eft, non quæ à fide incipit, fed quæ à fide apprehenditur, quæ Dei dicitur; non quod à Deo nobis infundatur, fed quod & à Chrifto juftitia fit, utpote qui eft Jehovah juftitia noftra Jerem. 23, 6. & nobis à DEO factus eft juftitia, 1. Cor. 1, 29. 3. Juftitia fidei dicitur ἡ διὰ πίστεως χρισῦ, quæ per fidem Chrifti, vel in Chriftum obtinetur; at rectitudo illa interna, five in operibus juftis pofita dicatur, five in corde hominis conftituatur, habitus ifte infifus juftitiæ, aut charitatis, aut athus inde redundantes non obtinentur per fidem in CHRISTUM. Annon enim ejusmodi rectitudo habitualis fuit in Protoplaftis ante lapfum, ubi nulla fides in Chriftum fuit, nec locum habuit? 4. Juftitia fidei eft ἡ ἐκ θεῦ δικαιοσύνη ἐπὶ τῇ πίστει, illa ex Deo juftitia in fide, vel per fidem, quæ opponitur juftitiæ noftræ. Quare vi oppofitionis non poteft notare juftitiam vel rectitudinem nobis inhærentem. Hæc enim etfi ex Deo fit, vere tamen noftra eft: quum opera bona & rectitudo erga Deum & homines vere fint renatorum Pontificiis ipfis contendentibus. 5. Rectitudo illa & opera jufta pertinent ad fructus juftificationis noftræ, quæ mera gratuita & tantum per fidem eft, per & propter CHRISTI meritum, ad caufas juftificationis nullo modo referri poffunt. Opera bona fequuntur juftificatum, non antecedunt juftificantem. Hic enim agitur de juftitia ex DEO, per quam juftificamur.

(II.) Non conftituit Paulus geminam juftitiam noftram, aliam, quæ externa, & fiat fine auxilio gratiæ, ex fola cognitione legis: aliam quæ interna, & fiat per fidem: Sed noftram juftitiam dicit omnem illam juftitiam, quæ eft fecundum legis five ante converfionem, feu poft converfionem.

Utraque enim hic refertur ad legem, utraque contradistinguitur justitiæ, quæ ex fide est, & in Evangelio patefacta est fine lege. Quæ justitia non nostra, sed nostræ contradistinguitur, non inhærens est, sed imputata nobis per fidem.

(III.) Justitia legis, lex justitia, & opera legis Apostolo non sunt diversa, ut è

Rom. IX. 31. patet. Similiter justitia fidei, & ex fide Synonyma sunt, Rom. III. 22. Phil. III. 9. Atque ita quum oppositorum eadem sit ratio, justitia legis & justitia ex lege etiam eadem sunt. Ideoque temere hæc distinguit Cardinalis.

(IV

.) Non externam solam justitiam & obedientiam pro damno habuit Apostolus, sed etiam internam, imo omnem legis obedientiam, qualiscunque ea sit, & OMNIA prorsus extra Christum.

Non quod opera ex fide facta Deo haud placeant, sed quod coram judicio Dei ob imperfectionem & immunditiem nativam consistere haud valeant.

Hic vero exclamat Bellarminus: At quanta quæso blasphemia est, opera facta ex fide & gratia Christi stercora nominare! Sed post declamationes illas, eat nunc, inquit, Kemnitius, & quæratur, quod cum boftem bonorum operum esse dicamus. Accusatio minus justa, querela prorsus injusta. Non nos, sed Spiritus facta σκύβαλα vocat omnia, quæ extra & præter Christum cum merito & justitia ejus, quem solum pro lucro hic reputat, de nostro sphæræ justificationis & salutis immiscentur, quod fiebat à Pseudo-Apostolis, atque etiamnum fit à Pontificiis per confusionem legis & Evangelii. In pretio habentur opera bona, ut à Luthero, B. Chemnitio, ita à quibusvis γνήσιοις Lutheranis, sed extra justificationis & salvationis negotium, quæ unice Christi meritis tribuenda, nullatenus pro operibus vel meritis nostris, quod cum fit, ea pro ζημία & σκύβαλοις habenda non per se, sed ob affictum iisdem meritorum aut necessitatis ad salutem βδέλυγμα.

Extra causam justificationis, inquit B. Lutherus, in caput 3. ad Gal. nemo potest vere opera bona satis magnifice commendare: Quis vero vel unius boni operis, quod Christianus ex fide & in fide facit utilitatem & fructum satis prædicare potest? Est enim pretiosus quam cœlum & terra.

Causa autem cur in justificationem non admittamus opera nostra est, 1. quod nimis imperfecta sint, si in judicium Divinum adferuntur, Ps. 143, 2. ad quem locum S. Augustinus: Quantumlibet rectius mihi videar, producis tamen de thesauro tuo regulam, coaptas me ad eum, & pravus invenior. Et libr. XIX. de Civit. Dei cap. XXVII. ipse nostra justitia quamvis vera propter veri bonem, ad quem refertur, tanta tamen est in hac vita, ut potius peccatorum remissione constet, quam virtutum perfectione. 2. Quod correquifitis operibus nostris ad justificationem omnino derogetur merito & justitia Christi, cui uni accepta ferenda est salus nostra, Rom. VI. ult. qui solus torcular calcavit, Es. 63. solus est Salvator noster, Esa. 65, 22. 23. Ad hanc ergo Christi excellentem cognitionem se contendat quis propriam justitiam, seu internam, seu externam, sive ante conversionem, (ubi vero nulla bona opera locum habent, ne fructus fingamus fine arbore, effectum fine causa, ideoq; talia opera horum commentum Papisticum sunt;) sive post eandem: Hæc non in se quidem, sed propter accedentem imperfectionem & immunditiem, & cum fuccenturiantur Christi merito & justitiæ, ut confluant in nostram justitiam & salutem, pro damnis & σκύβαλοις reputat S. Apostolus, ut Christum unice pro lucro æstimet, quod utique lucrum perdi necesse est, quamprimum ullum opus, quodcunque illud fuerit, eidem ceu necessarium ad salutem adjungitur.

Vim veritatis hic sensere Walenburgici fratres, ideoad quæstionem, quam fit illa justitia, quam nos habere debemus, ut coram Dei tribunali comparemus, in ejus judicio absolvamur, & non condemnemur; respondere Catholicos ajunt: Esse justitiam nobis imputatam & donatam, utque sola sit causa, cur non condemnemur ob peccata nostra, sed ab iis absolvamur. Ad quæstionem, an in judicio Dei constituamur perfecte justi justitia Christi nobis donata & imputata? Resp. nos justitia illa nobis extrinseca & perfectissima constitui, vel potius censeri, haberique perfecte justos. Largiuntur justitiam nobis inhærentem imperfectam esse respectu justitiæ Christi nobis donatæ & imputatæ. Quæ fine dubio justitiam nostram infinite excedit. Quæ & alia hujusmodi plura adduximus in Exegem. Art. IV. cap. VII. 11. 12. 13.

## 3:10
Art. IV. cap. VII. 11.

Καὶ τὴν κοινωνίαν τῶν παθημάτων αὐτοῦ) That this also be known, that we too, by his example, ought to willingly tolerate the cross, if it should so happen, Matth. 10, 38. cap. 16, 24. Mark 8, 34. Vers. 10. Τῷ γνῶναι αὐτὸν)

Ostendit, quibus in rebus fides ista consistat, nempe primum ut noscatur Christus, id est, doctrina ejus. Καὶ τὴν δύναμιν τῆς ἀναστάσεως αὐτοῦ) Ut noscatur etiam Christus, Divina vi resuscitatus, in testimonium nobis idem eventurum, si ipsum sequamur, Eph. 1. 19. 20. ## 3:11
11. Εἴπως καταντήσω εἰς τὴν ἐξανάστασιν τῶν νεκρῶν)

Manuscript, τὸ ἐκ νεκρῶν. That shows the matter to be uncertain and difficult. Καταντᾶν ὡς τι is to reach some thing, 1. Corinth. 14, 36. Eph. 4, 13. He preferred to say ἐξανάστασιν, rather than ἀνάστασιν, so that that full resurrection may be understood, which no death, no evil follows, which in the Hebrews.

Others make a peculiar doctrine here, another gain of trust and boasting in Christ alone, a richer knowledge of Christ, which is the opinion of Zanchius and Crocius; but it is more correctly referred to the description of faith. For faith consists in the knowledge of Christ, namely, that we know Christ by reason of his person and office; and to these are added those things which are specifically required further for faith, namely, that we know the power of his resurrection, which presupposes the passion, and is the complement of redemption, that Christ was delivered for our sins, and raised for our righteousness, which knowledge the Apostle requires most for saving faith, Rom. 4, 21. As Osiander [says] in his paraphrase: I diligently strive for this, that I may know my most beloved Savior Jesus Christ more and more, and that I may know how great benefits accrue to us from him, because he conquered death, the Devil, and hell, of which victory the glorious resurrection of Christ is the most evident testimony. Which sense Calvin and Zanchius also acknowledged: But although the mention of the passions of CHRIST is made later, which Crocius opposes to this sense, it is nevertheless done for another reason. For here the discourse is about γνῶσις or knowledge, which is the prior act of faith, and at the same time in this place embraces assent. But it follows then concerning the fiducial apprehension of the merit of Christ as the other act of faith.

Annotations on Philippians.

Chap.

III. v. And the fellowship of his sufferings, which we understand as the proper sufferings of Christ, concerning which Heb. 2, 9. chap. 9, 26. not those which he is estimated to sustain in his members, Acts 9, 4. Col. 1, 24. and concerning the practical and experimental knowledge of that communion, by which, namely, those grafted into Christ through faith feel and experience the communion of Christ's sufferings, or that they are participants in his sufferings for the remission of sins, and the imputation of Christ's satisfaction.

For that Christ died for all is the same as if all men had died, 2 Cor. 5, 19. by which reasoning we are also rendered συμμορφούμενοι τῷ θανάτῳ αὐτοῦ, conformed to his death, provided that in the judgment of God it is reckoned as if we ourselves had satisfied for our sins, and the satisfaction of Christ is as truly imputed to us as if it had been performed by ourselves. For thus, finally, the error of the Pseudo-Apostles is thoroughly overturned, so that no place is left for it.

For if justifying faith is the apprehension of Christ's satisfaction, which is imputed to us in the judgment of God through faith, our own righteousness or any good work cannot in any way concur in our justification. For just as we obtain the remission of sins by the power of the appropriation of Christ's satisfaction: so there is no need for any satisfaction, nor for any of our merits or works. For those who obtain the remission of sins are absolved from sins and justified. If, therefore, we are justified through faith and the application of Christ's satisfaction, our works are required for justification, unless we believe that Christ's satisfaction is sufficient, and detract from it.

If righteousness is through the law, Christ died in vain, Gal. 2, 21. Thus also the cause of the resurrection is best established, which is not the mortification of the old man, or even the enduring of sufferings similar to the external sufferings of Christ, for these are not worthy of the future glory, Rom. 8, 17. but the communion of the sufferings and death of Christ, which occurs through faith.

Some indeed explain the communion of Christ's sufferings as the tolerance of those things which must be sustained for Christ's sake following his example. But the Apostle here is occupied with refuting the Pseudo-Apostles, bringing forward the righteousness of faith, and therefore explaining the nature of justifying faith. The consequences of justification follow thereafter.

The cause of the encounter in the resurrection of the dead is also faith in Christ, and the apprehension of his merits, not the killing of vicious affections. For through that conformation with the death of Christ, by which through faith we are grafted into Christ, who died for us, and are rendered participants in his sufferings and satisfaction, each of the faithful is so conformed to his death as if he himself had died in Christ, just as we put on Christ with all those things which he suffered for us, and when he puts on our person in the expiatory and satisfactory death of Christ, we in turn put on his person before the judgment of God, and by that reason are conformed to his death.

If we are rendered conformed to Christ's sufferings and death, when we suffer and sustain death, just as he himself suffered and died, why should we not be rendered conformed when, in true contrition and the sense of divine wrath, we are led with Christ into the judgment of God, and there are compelled to be sorrowful and troubled, to experience the horrors of death and hell, just as Christ was taken from judgment, freed from the death which he sustained for us, and drawn out of the pit into which he descended: So we are rendered conformed to his sufferings and death through the communion of his sufferings and death, we are likewise taken from judgment with him, freed from the guilt of death, and sent forth from the pit of hell in the blood of his Testament. If the communion of sufferings and the internal conformation of death consists in the crucifixion and mortification of the old man, Gal. 5, 34. why should not the communion and conformation consist in the passion before judgment and divine absolution, just as Christ stood in divine judgment and was absolved, although he himself as alien sin, we as our own sin, so that a double sense is implied through communion and conformation, and a similar absolution; By which through faith we apprehend the absolution of Christ, having been vivified and resurrected on account of our righteousness.

Whence the Apostle says in Col. 3, 3: You have died and your life is hidden with Christ in God. This explanation we commit to the judgments of the orthodox, but we force it upon no one morosely; indeed, we here subjoin the interpretation of one or another interpreter, so that the reader may discern which he should consider following.

For me, to find my Jesus here was the goal, that I might be found in him. And I rejoice that I have been apprehended by Jesus, so that I may finally apprehend my Jesus, and I strive solely toward the fullness of that joy, or the ultimate end.

Flacius has it thus here: He explains still more fully true faith and the righteousness of Christ: He says faith is the knowledge of Christ and the efficacy of his resurrection: At the same time, however, he shows that righteousness is the gift of Christ, the consequence of which is regeneration, by which, with the old Adam mortified, we are both co-crucified and co-buried with him, and at the same time rise again, as is had copiously in Rom. 6. B.

These are the words of Balduinus, which follow: Lest anyone boast of faith in vain, the Apostle describes justifying faith by reason of its object, v. 10, and at the same time by this description indicates the final cause of our justification, v. 11, namely, the escape from death and the resurrection from sins. The object of faith is Christ with all his merit; This object is broken down into parts thus: 1. faith acknowledges Christ himself with respect to his person in two natures, 2. the virtue of his resurrection, that is, the merit of Christ, which is noted here by its final completion, 3. the fellowship of Christ's sufferings and the configuration of his death, that is, faith believes that the pious man suffers together with Christ in this world, and therefore includes all his miseries in the sufferings of Christ, by which they are sanctified, not indeed that they are meritorious, as the sufferings of Christ, but that they are symbols of the truly faithful, of whom Paul writes elsewhere, that they are conformed to the image of Christ, Rom. 8, 29.

Yet I would not easily accept these things concerning the resurrection from the death of sin, since the resurrection of the dead can be understood properly, and the comparison of v. 10 and 11 is understood more correctly here, as the paraphrase in Osiander has it: And I die daily, it cannot happen otherwise than that we suffer adversities together with him, if we wish to become participants in the heavenly glory, Rom. 8.

And so I desire to be conformed to Christ also in sufferings (according to my measure) and thus may the old Adam in me be mortified again and again, so that at some time in that blessed resurrection of Christ I may be caught up in the clouds in the air to meet my Savior, and thus always be able to be with the Lord, 1 Thess. 4.

To which the paraphrase of the blessed Balduinus himself also seems to tend: That I may be filled with the knowledge of him, and understand how effective his resurrection is, and, as in passion, so also in glory I may be made like unto him.

To that point entirely goes B. Hunnius: It also achieves this, (faith) that I may know the communion of his afflictions, namely, that it is necessary that I be made a participant in his sufferings through faith, and through patience bear afflictions in this age according to his example, so that I may be made conformed to his death, and thus having omitted this from the evil age, that I may contend and attain to the resurrection of the dead, which is the set goal, that at some time, having been raised and perfectly blessed, he may live forever. I would indeed, says Theophylact, that you understand the resurrection in this place as that which is to happen with glory and will be lifted into the air. For all are to be resurrected, yet not all will be lifted up in a cloud, but will await the coming of the Judge on earth. But the saints will be taken into the air, about to go to meet the Lord. Understand, however, from the consequence of things, what has been done. Dead, he says, is Christ, and he himself first, he rose again with the highest glory; I myself also strive, and I struggle most, that I may attain this most glorious resurrection.

But that this conformation with the death of Christ is the killing of vices and affections can hardly be admitted: For since there were no vicious affections in Christ, which he needed to kill, how shall we be conformed to Christ in the killing of vices and affections? The particle ὅπως is not a sign of uncertainty in every way, but can well consist with hypothetical certainty, and is used at least to shake off security.

Compare what we said on Joel 2: 21. Salmero acknowledges this in Tom. XV, disp. 6, when he says: "If by any means I may attain," is not the word of one doubting, but of one speaking modestly of himself. For it should be doubtful to no one that he who is conformed to the death of Christ will be conformed to his life, which is eternal.

Latin:

Vers. 11. Εἴπως καταντήσω εἰς τὴν ἐξανάστασιν τῶν νεκρῶν)

Manuseriptus, τὸ ἐκ νεκρῶν. Illud ostendit rem incertam & difficilem. Καταντᾶν ὡς τι est ad rem aliquam pertingere, 1. Corinth. 14, 36. Eph. 4, 13. ἐξανάστασιν maluit dicere, quam ἀνάστασιν, ut intelligatur illa plena resurrectio, quam nulla mors, nihil mali sequitur, quæ Ebrais.

Alii faciunt hic peculiarem doctrinam, alterum lucrum fiducia & gloriationis in solo Christo, uberiorem Christi cognitionem, quæ Zanchii & Crocii est sententia; sed rectius refertur ad fidei descriptionem. Nam fides in cognitione Christi consistit, ut nempe Christum cognoscamus ratione personæ & officii; & adduntur his, quæ speciatim porro ad fidem requiruntur, ut nempe vim resurrectionis ipsius, quæ passionem præsupponit, & complementum redemptionis est, cognoscamus, quod Christus traditus sit propter peccata nostra, & resuscitatus propter justitiam nostram, quam cognitionem maxime ad fidem salvificam requirit Apostolus Rom. 4, 21. Quomodo Osiander in παραφράσει: In id sedulo incumbo, ut magis magisque dilectissimum Salvatorem meum Jesum Christum agnoscam, & ut cognoscam, quanta nobis beneficia ex eo contingant, quod mortem, Diabolum & infernum devicerit, cujus victoria evidentissimum testimonium est gloriosa Christi resurrectio. Quem sensum Calvinus & Zanchius etiam agnoverunt: Etsi autem postea passionum CHRISTI mentio fiat, quod obvertit isti sensui Crocius, id tamen alia ratione fit. Nam hic de γνώσει vel cognitione, quæ prior actus est fidei, & simul hoc loco assensum complectitur, sermo est. Sequitur autem deinde de apprehensione fiduali meriti Christi altero fidei actu.

Annotata ad Philipp.

Cap.

III. v. Καὶ τὴν κοινωνίαν τῶν παθημάτων αὐτοῦ, quod intelligimus de passionibus Christi propriis, de quibus Ebr. 2, 9. cap. 9, 26. non quas in membris suis sustinere aestimatur, Actor. 9, 4. Col. 1, 24. & de cognitione illius communionis practica, & experimentali, qua nempe Christo infiti per fidem sentiunt & experiuntur communionem passionum Christi, vel se participes esse passionum ejus in remissionem peccatorum, & imputationis satisfactionis Christi.

Quod enim Christus pro omnibus mortuus est, idem est, ac si mortui essent omnes homines, 2. Cor. 5, 19. qua ratione etiam nos reddimur συμμορφούμενοι τῷ θανάτῳ αὐτοῦ, conformes morti ejus, siquidem in judicio Dei reputetur, ac si ipsi satisfecissemus pro peccatis nostris, & satisfactio Christi nobis tam vere imputetur, ac si nobismetipsis praestita esset. Sic enim demum funditus evertitur Pseudo-Apostolorum error, ut nullus ei locus relinquatur.

Nam si fides justificans est apprehensio satisfactionis Christi, quae nobis in judicio Dei imputatur per fidem, non potest ullatenus ad justificationem nostram concurrere rectitudo nostra, vel ullum bonum opus. Uti enim vi appropriationis satisfactionis Christi remissionem peccatorum consequimur: Ita nulla opus est satisfactione, nullis nostris meritis aut operibus. Qui enim remissionem peccatorum consequuntur, absolvuntur a peccatis & justificantur. Si ergo justificamur per fidem & applicationem satisfactionis Christi, opera nostra ad justificationem requiruntur, nisi Christi satisfactione sufficere credamus, eique derogemus.

Si per legem est justitia, Christus frustra mortuus est, Gal. 2, 21. Sic etiam causa resurrectionis optime constat, quae non est veteris hominis mortificatio, vel etiam passionum similium passionibus Christi externis exantlatio, hae enim non sunt condignae futura gloria, Rom. 8, 17. sed κοινωνία passionum & mortis Christi, quae fit per fidem.

Explicant sane nonnulli de κοινωνίᾳ passionum Christi qua tolerantiam eorum, quae propter Christum exemplo ejus sustinenda. Sed Apostolus hic occupatus est in retundendis Pseudo-Apostolis, afferenda justitia fidei, & explicanda ideo natura fidei justificae. De consequentibus justificationis deinceps sequitur.

Causa etiam occursus in resurrectionem mortuorum est fides in Christum, & apprehensio meritorum ejus, non interfectio vitiorum affectuum. Nam per illam conformationem cum morte Christi, qua per fidem Christo, qui pro nobis mortuus est, infiti, participes passionum & satisfactionis ejusdem reddimur, quisque fidelium ita conformatur morti ejus, ac si ipse in Christo mortuus esset, quemadmodum induimus nos Christum cum omnibus illis, quae pro nobis passus est, & quum ille persone nostram in morte Christi expiatoriae, & satisfactoriae personam ejus vicillim induimus coram Dei judicio, eaque ratione conformamur morti ipsius.

Si conformes reddimur Christi passionibus & morti, cum patimur, mortemque sustinemus, quemadmodum ipse passus & mortuus est, quidni conformes reddamur, cum in feria contritione ac sensu irae divinae cum Christo in judicium Dei deducimur, atque ibi cogimur λυπεῖσθαι καὶ ἀδημονεῖν, horrores mortis & inferni experiri, ut Christus de judicio sublatus est, a morte liberatus, quam pro nobis sustinuit, e lacu, in quem descendit, extractus est: Ita nos conformes reddimur passionibus & morti ejus per communionem passionum & mortis ipsius, pariter cum ipso de judicio tollimur, a morte reatu liberamur, e lacu inferni in sanguine Testamenti ejus emittimur. Si communio passionum, & conformatio mortis interna in veteris hominis crucifixionem & mortificationem consistit, Gal. 5, 34. quidni communio & conformatio consistat in passione coram judicio & absolutione divina, quemadmodum Christus in judicio divino stetit & absolutus, quamvis ipse qua peccatum alienum, nos qua peccatum proprium, ut sensus geminus per communionem & conformationem innuatur, similisque absolutio; Qua per fidem absolutionem Christi apprehendimus, vivificati & resuscitati propter justitiam nostram.

Unde Apostolus Col. 3, 3. inquit: Mortui estis & vita vestra abscondita est cum Christo in Deo. Quam explicationem judiciis orthodoxorum committimus, neminem autem morose obtrudimus; imo interpretationem unius atque alterius interpretis hic subjicimus, ut utrum sequendum duxerit lector, dispiciat.

Mihi hic invenire meum Jesum probulium fuit, ut inveniar in ipso. Quid & apprehensum me a Jesu, ut Jesum meum tandem apprehendam, gaudeo, & ad plenitudinem istius gaudii, seu finem ultimum unice contendo.

Flacius hic ita habet: Explicat adhuc plenius veram fidem & justitiam Christi: Fidem dicit esse cognitionem Christi & efficaciae resurrectionis: Simul vero ostendit, justitiam esse donationem Christi, cujus consequens est regeneratio, qua mortificato vetere Adamo & concrucifigimur, & consepelimur cum eo, & simul consurgimus, ut habetur copiose Rom. 6. B.

Balduini haec sunt, quae sequuntur: Ne quis frustra fidem jactet, describit Apostolus fidem justificantem ratione sui objecti, v. 10. simulque hac descriptione causam finalem nostrae justificationis indicat, v. 11. nimirum evasionem ex morte & resurrectionem a peccatis. Objectum fidei Christus est cum omni suo merito; In partes hoc objectum ita disfecitur, 1. fides agnoscit ipsum Christum respectu suae personae in duabus naturis, 2. virtutem resurrectionis ejus, hoc est, meritum Christi, quod hic a postremo complemento ejus notatur, 3. societatem passionum Christi & configurationem mortis ejus, hoc est, fides credit, hominem pium una cum Christo pati in hoc mundo, ac proinde omnes suas aerumnas passionibus Christi includit, a quibus sanctificatae sint, non quidem ut sint meritoria, ut passiones Christi, sed ut sint symbola vere fidelium, de quibus Paulus alibi scribit, quod sint conformes imagini Christi, Rom. 8, 29.

De resurrectione tamen a morte peccati haec non facile acceperim, cum resurrectio mortuorum proprie intelligi possit, & collationis v. 10. & 11. rectius hic intelligitur, ut apud Osiandrum paraphrasis habet: Et disto quotidie, fieri aliter non posse, quam ut una cum ipso patiamur adversa, si glorie caelestis fieri participes velimus, Rom. 8.

Itaque Christo etiam in passionibus (pro meo modulo) conformis fieri cupio, & sic semper nes subinde vetus Adam in me mortificetur, ut aliquando in beata illa resurrectione Christi Servatori meo obviam in nubibus rapiar in aere, & sic semper cum Domino esse possim, 1. Thess. 4.

Quo & abire videtur ipsius B. Balduini paraphrasis: Ut scientia ejus implear, & quam sit efficax resurrectio ejus intelligam, &, ut in passione, ita & in gloria ipsi similis efficiar.

Eo omnino abit B. Hunnius: Praestat & hoc, (fides) ut cognoscam communionem afflictionum ejus, oportere scilicet me per fidem participem reddi passionum ipsius, & per patientiam ad ipsius exemplum ferre afflictiones in hoc seculo, ut conformis fiam morti ejus, atque sic omisso hoc seculo malo contendam et pertingam ad resurrectionem mortuorum, quae prefixa meta est, ut aliquando resuscitatus et perfecte beatus vivat in eternum. Velim equidem, inquit Theophylactus, resurrectionem hoc loco eam intelligas, quae et cum gloria fit futura et in aerem sublevet. Sunt namque omnes resurrecturi, haud tamen in nube omnes sublevabuntur, sed in terris judicis adventum opperientur. Sancti vero tollentur in aera, obviam Domino processuri. Intelligas autem ex rerum consequentia, quod gestum est. Mortuus, inquit, est Christus, et ipse prior, resurrexit ille summa cum gloria, studeo et ipse, et maxime nitor, ut resurrectionem hanc consequar gloriosissimam.

Conformationem autem istam cum morte Christi esse interfectionem vitiorum, affectuum, admitti vix potest: Nam quum in Christo nulli affectus vitiosi fuerint, quos interficere necessum habuerit, quomodo in interfectione vitiorum affectuum Christo conformabimur? Particula ὅπως non est omnimode incertitudinis σιμαντική, sed cum certitudine hypothetica probe potest consistere, et adhibita saltem ad excutiendam securitatem.

Conf. quae ad Joel. 2, 21. diximus. Agnoscit id Salmero Tom. XV. disp. 6. cum ait: Si quo modo occurram, non est verbum dubitantis, sed modeste de se loquentis. Nemini enim esse dubium debet, configuratum morti Christi configurandum iri vita ejus, quae est aeterna.

## 3:12
Verf. 12. οὐκ ἤδη ἔλαβον) He indeed had, such as he was now, a right to the blessed resurrection: But that right could still be lost, as he himself says in 1 Cor. 9: 27. And so ἤδη here is understood of that reception which cannot be lost in the future. ἡ ἤδη τετελείωμαι) Paul was indeed perfect in some way, as can be understood from Matt. 5:48, and soon v. 15, but he was not placed outside of danger, like those who have finished their course, such as he says he is in 2 Tim. 4:6, 7, declaring the thing about to happen very soon with a verb of the present tense.

Chrysostom aptly says on this passage: "If he persuades himself of these things, he who is disposed thus, if he who has already obtained the victory should fear concerning that resurrection, what should we say?" חתם τετελείωμαι is said of a finished work, 1 Kings 7:22. Διώκω δὲ, εἰ καταλάβω) A simile taken from runners, to whom a palm is proposed at the end of the stadium. See 1 Cor. 9:24. διώκω is that which I pursue, I reach for, as in Rom. 9:30, 31, ch. 12, 13, 1 Cor. 14:1. ἐφ' ᾧ καὶ κατελήφθην ἀπὸ τοῦ κυρίου Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ) That I might be able to reach this, Christ first led me, as if taken by his own hand, into this pursuit.

There is a ploce in the verb καταλαμβάνω and καταλαμβάνεσθαι, such as in 1 Cor. 13:12. καταλαμβάνειν is to apprehend, as it is translated in the Greek-Latin Glossary. How are we said to be apprehended by Christ?

We are said to be apprehended by Christ, not as we are led into the stadium of the race, but as he draws us to himself, of which gracious drawing see John 6:44, ch. 12: 32. Christ must indeed first apprehend us by the hand of grace in conversion, so that we may apprehend him himself with his merit by the hand of faith unto justification, John 1:12, and in him apprehend the right to the blessed resurrection, nay, salvation itself and eternal life, 1 John 5:11, 12. Osiander connects these with the preceding in this way: But lest anyone (especially from the Pseudo-Apostles) should object to Paul, as if he were boasting of his own supreme perfection in Christianity, as one who could not progress further, he adds (to avoid calumnies) a correction, by which he shows that he aspires and contends for greater perfection.

I do not (says the Apostle) write these things in the sense that I have already received all things which are required for the fullest knowledge of Christ, or that I am already perfect, in such a way that I cannot make greater progress in true piety. Because Christ apprehended me, that he might snatch a miserable sinner from destruction, I strive to apprehend that deliverer of mine more and more with firm faith. Theophylact speaks thus of the sense of the words: "I am still," he says, "in the contest and I struggle, I am still, I say, pursued, perhaps the prize and the end may escape me": And soon, arguing that he does this by duty, he introduces this: "Since I also have been apprehended by Christ," that is, Christ apprehended me, who once existed from the number of the lost, and of those to whom all hope of salvation had been taken away, and he drew back me who was fleeing.

I am bound, therefore, and I myself to pursue him for so long, that I may hold fast what has been apprehended. But he said "I follow" more significantly. For he who pursues another, even passing by all things more dear, strives for nothing else than to apprehend him, for whose sake he accelerates his journey. We ought therefore with all effort and without any interruption to contend toward Christ.

For he who pursues, says Chrysostom, you know with what contention he pursues. He looks at no one, drives off with great force those who impede him in any way, contracts mind and eyes and strength and spirit and body into one, stretching toward nothing else but the prize alone. Calvin expresses the sense in this way: He had said that he strives and labors for the resurrection of the dead through the proclamation of the cross of Christ. He adds: That he had not yet attained this: What then? Namely that he may communicate fully in the sufferings of Christ, that he may have a perfect taste of the power of the resurrection, that he may know him fully. Crocius observes that Hyperius and Zanchius also embrace this sense, and to them he adds his own reckoning: To embrace this sense moves me first, because it was manifest to all that he had not yet apprehended the prize; therefore there was no need for him to remove it from himself with such great zeal. Then in v. 14 he distinguishes the goal and the prize from other things which are behind, toward which he contends. But this confession of imperfection could strongly repress the boasting of the Pseudo-Apostles, and fortify the Philippians against presumption. The Pseudo-Apostles arrogated to themselves full knowledge of Christ, contending that it was enough for Christ to be known, since no one is ignorant that Christ is the true Messiah, the expiator of past sins, but that now one must apply oneself to the knowledge and fulfillment of the law, so that from this full salvation may result. Now indeed Paul knew Christ excellently, yet he denies that he knows him perfectly as yet, so that there would be no need of progress. But if so great an Apostle confesses his own imperfection, who would presume that he has reached the goal?

PART II. PARENETICA On the ὁμόνοιαν in faith, and the imitation of the Apostle.

Latin:

Vers. 12. οὐκ ἤδη ἔλαβον) Habebat quidem talis, qualis nunc erat, jus ad resurrectionem beatam: Sed illud jus adhuc amitti poterat, ut ipse dicit 1. Cor. 9, 27. Itaque ἤδη hoc hic intelligitur de ea acceptione, quae in futurum amitti nequit. ἡ ἤδη τετελείωμαι) Erat quidem τέλειον aliquo modo Paulus, ut intelligere est ex Matth. 5, 48. mox v. 15. sed non erat extra periculum constitutus, ut illi, qui cursum suum absolverunt, qualem se esse dicit 2. Tim. 4, 6, 7. rem proximam futuram praesentis temporis verbo enuntians.

Apte ad hunc locum Chrysostomus: Εἰ δὲ ἑαυτὸν ταῦτα πεπείθει, ἃ δέ ὁ διακείμενος, εἰ δὲ ὁ τὴν νίκωσιν ἔχων ἤδη ἰδάρξῃ περὶ τῆς ἀναστάσεως ἐκείνης, τί ἂν εἴποιμεν ἡμεῖς; חתם τετελείωμαι dicitur de opere consummato, 1. Reg. 7, 22. Διώκω δὲ, εἰ καταλάβω) A cursoribus sumpta similitudo, quibus palma proposita in fine stadii. Vide 1. Cor. 9, 24. διώκω est, id quod ro, eo tendo, ut Rom. 9, 30. 31. cap. 12, 13. 1. Cor. 14, 1. ἐφ' ᾧ καὶ κατελήφθην ἀπὸ τοῦ κυρίου Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ) Quo ut pervenire possem, Christus prior me velut manu sua prehensum deduxit in hoc studium.

Est πλοκὴ in verbo καταλαμβάνω et καταλαμβάνεσθαι, qualis in ἰτιγ: ὠσκεν et ἰτιγ: ἰώσκεν, 1. Cor. 13, 12. καταλαμβάνειν est apprehendere, quomodo vertitur in Glossario Graeco-Latino. Apprehendi a Christo quomodo dicamur?

Apprehendi a Christo dicimur, non qua deducimur in stadium cursus, sed qua nos ad se trahit, de quo tractu gratioso Joh. 6, 44, cap. 12, 32. Nimirum Christus primum manu gratiae nos apprehendere debet in conversione, ut nos ipsum cum merito suo manu fidei apprehendamus ad justificationem, Joh. 1, 12. et in ipso apprehendamus jus ad beatam resurrectionem, imo salutem ipsam et aeternam vitam, 1. Joh. 5, 11, 12. Connectit haec cum superioribus hoc modo Osiander: Ne vero quis (praesertim ex Pseudo-Apostolis) objiceret Paulo, quasi de summa sua perfectione in Christianismo gloriaretur, ut qui in majus proficere non posset, addit (propter vitandas calumnias) correctionem, qua ostendit, se ad majorem perfectionem adspirare et contendere.

Non (inquit Apostolus) haec scribo in eam sententiam, quod jam omnia acceperim, qua ad plenissimam Christi agnitionem requiruntur, aut quod jam perfectus sim, ita quidem, ut in vera pietate majores progressus facere non possim. Quia Christus me apprehendit, ut miserum peccatorem ab interitu eriperet, ego liberatorem illum meum magis magisque firma fide apprehendere studeo. De sensu verborum ita Theophylactus: Adhuc, inquit, in agone sum et decerto, adhuc inquam infector, silueat forsitan mihi et brabeum et finem comprehendere: Moxque arguens ex debito se id agere, infert hujusmodi: Quoniam et a Christo comprehensus sum, hoc est, ipsum me, qui olim ex numero perditorum existerem, et eorum, quibus fuisset salutis spes omnis sublata, infestatus est Christus, comprehenditque se fugientem et retraxit.

Obstringor itaque, et ipse tamdiu hunc persequi, quod comprehensum detineam. Significantius autem sequor dixit. Nam qui alium insectatur, vel chariora quaeque praeteriens, nihil aliud studet, quam cum prehenfare, cujus gratia iter accelerat. Debemus igitur omni nisu et fine interpellatione ulla ad Christum contendere.

Qui enim persequitur, inquit Chrysostomus, scitis, quanta contentione persequatur. Neminem adspicit, quosvis impedientes magno impetu abigit, mentem, et oculos, et robur, et animum, et corpus in unum contrahit, ad aliud nihil nisi ad solum brabeum pertendens. Calvinus sensum hoc modo exprimit: Dixerat se contendere et eniti ad resurrectionem mortuorum per annuntiationem crucis Christi. Addit: Se nondum id esse affectum: Quid? Nempe ut in solidum communicet Christi passionibus, ut perfectum habeat gustum potentiae resurrectionis, ut ipsum plene cognoscat. Hunc sensum etiam amplecti Hyperium et Zanchium observat Crocius, illique ita calculum suum adjicit: Ut amplectar hunc sensum, me movet primo, quia omnibus erat manifestum, nondum apprehendisse brabeum, non opus igitur erat, ut id a se tanto removeret studio. Deinde v. 14. scopum et brabeum ab aliis, quae a fronte sunt, distinguit, ad quae contendit. Hac vero imperfectionis confessio fortiter poterat reprimere Pseudo-Apostolorum jactantiam, et Philippenses munire adversus praesumptionem. Pseudo-Apostoli sibi plenam Christi cognitionem arrogabant, contendentes, satis esse Christum cognitum, cum nemo nesciat, Christum esse verum Messiam, praeteritorum peccatorum expiatorem, nunc vero legis notitia et impletione incumbendum esse, ut inde plena constet salus. Jam quidem Paulus egregie noverat Christum, negat tamen, se adhuc perfecte cognoscere, ut profectu non sit opus. Si vero tantus Apostolus suam fatetur imperfectionem, quis praesumeret, se attigisse metam?

PARS II. PARÆNETICA Ad ὁμόνοιαν in fide, ac imitationem Apostoli.

## 3:13
Verf. 13. Ἀδελφοὶ, ἐγὼ ἐμαυτὸν οὐ λογίζομαι κατειληφέναι) In the Manuscript: οὔ, rightly. Because although I am certain of the reward of perseverance, I am not certain of perseverance itself, as Augustine says. These things do not tend to the point as if he were doubting about perseverance . For even if the faithful do not have absolute certainty of perseverance, they do have hypothetical certainty. He repeats only his former confession, that he had not yet attained perfection. But he tacitly notes the vain boasting of the Pseudo-Apostles, who did not hesitate to sell themselves as perfect. If anyone opposes that 2 Tim. 4:7, "I have finished the course," let him know that the past is used for the imminent future, and so these things were said at a different time. For he was saying this latter when he already understood his immolation. But in his first captivity he was still hoping for liberation. Nor does the Apostle boast of his own perfection in those words, but indicates the apostolic course and the end and consummation of the Christian life now imminent.

He adds, moreover, these things to the doctrine of justification, which he claimed against the Pseudo-Apostles, and illustrated by his own example, so that he might teach more fully that there is no absolute certainty of perseverance (such as the Calvinists imagine), but that we must be careful with diligence lest we fall from the grace of justification, and that we must strive with the greatest zeal to aspire to the perfection which is obtained in the other life. Where Blessed Balduinus notes that four precepts have been handed down: 1. The recognition of native weakness, for this is the first step of the perfect recognition of God, "brethren, I do not consider that I have apprehended." 2. The forgetting of past things, which, namely, draw us back in the race; such things among those which are behind Blessed Balduinus judges the chief to be: first all the sins with which our life has been polluted, then all the good things which we have done, and finally carnal desires. 3. The desire and contention to progress. 4. The communion of the Christian rule. Inasmuch as he wishes us to be of the same mind and to remain in the same rule.

Latin:

Vers. 13. Ἀδελφοὶ, ἐγὼ ἐμαυτὸν οὐ λογίζομαι κατειληφέναι) In Manuscripto: οὔ, recte. Quia quanquam de praemio perseverantiae certus sum, de ipsa perseverantia certus non sum, ut loquitur Augustinus. Hae non eo tendunt, ac si dubitet de perseverantia. Nam etsi absolutam certitudinem perseverantiae non habeant fideles, habent tamen hypotheticam. Repetit solum confessionem pristinam, se nondum adeptum esse perfectionem. Notat autem tacite Pseudo-Apostolorum vanam jactantiam, qui se pro perfectis venditare non dubitabant. Si quis opponat illud 2. Tim. 4, 7. Cursum consummavi, sciat, praeteritum adhiberi pro imminente futuro, adeoque diverso ista dicta esse tempore. Hoc enim posterius dicebat, cum jam immolationem infare intelligeret. Jam vero in prima captivitate adhuc liberationem sperabat. Neque suam perfectionem illis verbis jactat Apostolus, sed cursum apostolicum et Christianae vitae exitum et consummationem jamjam imminentem indicat.

Addit autem hæc doctrinæ de justificatione, quam contra Pseudo-Apostolos vendicavit, suoque exemplo illustravit, ut doceat uberius nullam esse absolutam certitudinem perseverantiæ, (qualem fingunt Calviniani) sed cavendum fedulo esse, ne justificationis gratia excidamus, & annitendum studio maximo, ut ad perfectionem, quæ in seculo altero obtinetur, adspiremus. Ubi B. Balduinus notat, quatuor tradita esse præcepta, 1. nativæ imbecillitatis agnitionem, hic enim primus gradus est perfectæ agnitionis Dei, fratres, ego me non arbitror comprehendisse. 2. Præteritorum oblivionem, quæ scilicet in curriculo nos retrahunt, qualia ex iis, quæ à tergo sunt, præcipua hæc esse censet B. Balduinus, primum omnia peccata, quibus vita nostra fuit polluta, tum bona omnia, quæ fecimus, denique carnalia desideria. 3. Proficiendi desiderium & contentionem. 4. Regulæ Christianæ communionem. Siquidem velit nos idem sapere & in eadem regula permanere.

## 3:14
V. 14. (But those things which are behind, forgetting, and reaching forth unto those things which are before; I press toward the mark for the prize of the high calling of God in Christ Jesus) As in military matters, Czerat is always reaching toward things further on: And thinking nothing high, while anything remained to be done, he did not think about what he had already done, but was intent on this, that he might add more and greater things to what had been done; so also in this spiritual warfare, Paul, when he had performed great things, did not rest in them. (in this only. This is referred not to one word, but to the whole sense. He uses Oríw for that which has passed, as Homer, Odyssey σ. ἐπεκτεινόμενος; the passive here is for the reciprocal in the Hebrew manner, "myself," as the Latin translates here, that is, extending my own self, namely to things further on. Διώκω here is "I run" by Metonymy. In that κατὰ σκοπὸν is a Metaphor. Σκοπὸς is the mark, at which the javelin is directed, Job 6:12, Lamentations 3:12. Pindar: ἵπεχς τῶι σκοπῶι τόξον. To this corresponds in ἁρυ the palm-branch. The βραβεῖυαι or ἀγωνοθέται were accustomed to sit in a high place, and from there to summon the individual runners by a herald. To these he compares God, who calls us from the highest place, that is, from heaven, through Christ. Not alien to this passage is that of Plutarch: "The soul struggles like an athlete throughout life, but when it has finished the struggle, then it attains the things that are appropriate.")

Those things which are behind, Augustine understands as sins in Psalm 39. This does not please Crocius, because here those respects are condemned which either break or diminish alacrity: but the remembrance of sins and infirmities should not make us sluggish, but should impel us to strive for the goal more alacritously. But how sins are to be forgotten, so that they may not be a hindrance to us in the race, Blessed Antecessor has already taught: They are to be forgotten in such a way, he says, 1. that we do not delight our minds with an impure recollection. For there is no heavier crime, says Augustine, than to rejoice in the recollection of a sin already forgiven. 2. That we do not despair on account of admitted faults, but hide them in the wounds of Christ, that is, to put sins behind us into Him, who was wounded for our sins: so that we do not fall again into similar sins. For those things which have been deleted among us by oblivion are no longer a care to us, much less do we have any further business with them. He adds that carnal desires must also be forgotten, which war against the soul, and retard many in the race of piety, whence often from the best Christians they become Epicureans and carnal men, who, immersed in the pleasures and honors of the world, rarely think of heavenly goods, and therefore remain excluded by their own fault from the prize of eternal happiness. Conf. Col. 3:1. Meanwhile, not only sins, but also good deeds must be forgotten, which we have ever done, lest they become a matter of vain glory, ambition, and merit, all of which easily block the way for those who have even rightly begun to run: Just as Theodoret refers to those things which are behind as the life lived according to the institution of the law: Chrysostom and Theophylact, those things which were rightly done, of all of which the Apostle strips the memory, so far is he from placing in them any confidence of merit or justice.

The prize of the high calling (He calls it Brabejon not from the place, Crocius acknowledges, even though a Calvinist, because God is not local, or is above (of vocation. by reason of essence rather than below, not without ἑαυτομαχία: He adds, that He dwells above, and immediately manifests His glory to the Angels and blessed Spirits. For God to have a palace or some dwelling place above the firmament of the heavens like a King, dwelling in a local palace, is a Calvinian fantasy. What then? τὸ ἄνω is taken not only by reason of place, but also by reason of status and eminence. It is added, however, in Christ Jesus, so that our works and merits may be excluded again. For the divine high or heavenly calling, which is purely gracious, does not propose to us a prize to be obtained by our merits, but solely by the merit of Christ. For eternal life is χάρισμα, a gift of God in Christ Jesus, Rom. 6, v. ult. Verf.

Latin:

V. 14. ἡ δὲ, τὰ μὲν ὀπίσω ἐπιλανθανόμενος, τοῖς δὲ ἔμπροσθεν ἐπεκτεινόμενος· κατὰ σκοπὸν διώκω ἐπὶ τὸ βραβεῖον τῆς ἄνω κλήσεως τοῦ Θεοῦ ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ) Sicut in re bellica Czerat ad ulteriora tendens semper: Nilque putans altum, dum quid superesset agendum, non cogitabat, quid jam fecisset, sed in id intentus erat, ut actis plura & majora adjiceret, ita & in hac spirituali militia Paulus, cum magna præstitisset, iis non acquiescebat. (in hoc tantum. Refertur hoc non ad verbum unum, sed ad sensum totum. Oríw pro eo, quod præteriit, usurpat, ut Homer. Odyssex σ. ἐπεκτεινόμενος· passivum hic est pro reciproco more Ebræo, meipsum, ut hic vertit Latinus, id est, corsum meum extendens, nempe ad ulteriora. Διώκω hic est curro per Metonymiam. In illo κατὰ σκοπὸν est Metaphora. Σκοπὸς est signum, ad quod dirigitur jaculum, Job. 6, 12. Lament. 3, 12. Pindarus: ἵπεχς τῶι σκοπῶι τόξον. Huic respondet in ἁρυ voc pæ palmæ. Solebant oi βραβεῖυαι sive ἀγωνοθέται ledere in sublimi loco, atque inde per præconem citare curfores fingulos. His Deum comparat, qui ex loco fublimiffimo, id est, ex cœlo nos per Christum vocat. Non alienum ab hoc loco illud Plutarchi: Ἀγωνίζεται ἡ ψυχὴ ὥσπερ ἀθλητὴς κατά τὸν βίον, ὅταν δὲ διαγωνίσηται, τότε τυγχάνει τῶν προσσηκόντων.)

Ea, quæ à tergo sunt, de peccatis intelligit Augustinus in Psal. 39. Non placet id Crocio, quod hic respectus damnentur, qui alacritatem vel frangunt vel minuunt: Peccatorum autem & infirmitatum recordatio non reddat segnes, sed impellat, ut ad metam contendamus alacrius. Sed quomodo peccatorum obliviscendum fit, ne illa nobis remora sint in curriculo, docuit jam B. Antecessor: Eorum ita obliviscendum est, inquit, 1. ne impura recordatione animi nostri sensa oblectemus. Nullum enim est gravius feelus, inquit Augustinus, quam de peccato jam remisso recordando gaudere. 2. Ne propter admissa delicta desperemus, sed in vulneribus Christi ea abscondamus, hoc est peccata retro ponere in eum, qui propter peccata nostra vulneratus est: ita in similia peccata denuo incidamus. Nam quæ oblitione apud nos deleta sunt, ea non amplius cure nobis sunt, multo minus amplius quicquam cum illis nobis est negotii. Addit obliviscendum etiam esse carnalium desideriorum, quæ contra animam militant, & multos in curriculo pietatis retardant, unde fæpe ex optimis Christianis fiunt Epicurei & carnales homines, qui voluptatibus & honoribus seculi immersi raro cogitant de cœlestibus bonis, ideo ab æternæ felicitatis brabeo sua culpa manent exclusi. Conf. Col. 3, 1. Interim non peccatorum tantum, sed etiam bonorum obliviscendum, quæ unquam fecimus, ne fiant materia vanæ gloriæ, ambitionis & meriti, quæ omnia facile viam intercludunt iis, qui etiam recte inceperunt currere: Quomodo Theodoretus ad ea, quæ à tergo sunt, refert vitam ex legis institutione actam: Chrysostomus & Theophylactus, quæ recte facta sunt, quorum omnium memoriam exuit Apostolus, tantum abest, ut iis meriti aut justitiæ fiduciam collocet.

Brabejon superna vocationis (Brabejon vocat non a loco, agnoscit Crocius, etsi Calvinianus, quod Deus non fit localis, aut sursum fit (focationis. ratione essentiæ magis, quam infra est, non fine ἑαυτομαχία: Addit, quod sursum habitet, ac immediate gloriam suam manifestet Angelis & beatis Spiritibus. Deum enim in loco aliquo supra cœlorum firmamenti palatium vel habitaculum quoddam habere instar Regis, in locali quodam palatio habitantis, phantasia est Calviniana.
