Quid ergo τὸ ἄνω non tantum ratione loci accipi solet, sed etiam ratione status & eminentie. Additur autem in Christo Jesu, ut iterum excludantur nostra opera & merita. Non enim proponit nobis vocatio divina superna vel cœlestis, quæ mere gratiosa est, brabejum nostris meritis, sed unice merito Christi obtinendum. Vita enim æterna χάρισμα, donum Dei est in Christo Jesu, Rom. 6. v. ult.

## 3:15
15. (Let us therefore, as many as be perfect, be thus minded) He returns to that which he had begun to say above v. 3. Thus, he says, let us be affected, even if we have confidence not in the flesh, but in the Spirit. He calls those perfect here who are best versed in divine matters, as 1 Cor. 2:6, ch. 14:20.

(And if in anything ye be otherwise minded) If any of you have been led away by those new teachers. (God shall reveal even this unto you)

God will reveal this to you, namely that you are deceived.

He speaks on behalf of the hope which he had conceived from his former piety. So also Gal. 5, 10. These things are not said indiscriminately to those who, carried away by the Pseudo-Apostles, thought otherwise. For they disagreed in the fundamental article of faith, namely concerning justification, against whom the Apostle pronounced anathema, Gal. 1, 8. Some refer these things to the perfect, that is, those not confirmed in doctrine or life; for no one is such in this imperfection, 1. Cor. 13, 10. but the sincere and instructed in the doctrine of the Gospel, 1. Cor. 2, 6. Which he exhorts, with Blessed Balduinus as interpreter, so that they may be of the same mind with him, that they do not acquiesce in this progress of piety, but desire from every side consummated perfection, and therefore desire daily to make progress. Therefore he adds, if they think anything otherwise, that is, if perhaps they err in some things, or if they have fallen into any human frailty, from which they will not easily be able to extricate themselves, God will reveal this to them. He understands revelation, however, not secret through dreams, visions, or Enthusiasms, but such as is made in the usual manner through the Word: therefore a little later he adds, all ought to remain in the same canon, namely the canon of the revealed word.

B. Hunnius explains the perfect in the present passage thus: He calls those perfect here, not those who have attained an absolute recognition of God and Christ, or who are no longer surrounded by any infirmity of sin at all (for such perfection, complete in all its ways and numbers, he denied to himself in the preceding) but the word of perfection in this place is opposed partly to hypocrisy and the ostentation of feigned piety, and partly (and indeed according to the subject matter, principally) it is opposed to the infirmity of those who still wavered concerning Jewish ceremonies and rites, and were not yet sufficiently instructed in the article of Christian liberty. These, although Christians by profession, and not alien to true piety, he nevertheless calls imperfect, still wavering concerning the doctrine of circumcision and other Levitical rites and shadows. The perfect, on the contrary, are those who, concerning the abrogation of circumcision and the Levitical law from Christian liberty, are... were sufficiently instructed in the article.

He wishes, therefore, that these perfect ones should conform to his example in the same sentiment regarding circumcision and the other shadows of the Mosaic law. Regarding the imperfect, however, it is not wrongly understood here that those who think otherwise, the infirm, and those who, if they were seduced by the Pseudo-Apostles, did not understand their sermons correctly, but were not stubbornly persisting in error, but allowed themselves to be informed, just as the blessed Hunnius says that these things pertain to Christians who are still infirm, whom the Pseudo-Apostles had disturbed not a little in adiaphora, while they were otherwise thinking correctly about the faith of Jesus Christ, by urging circumcision and other things: So that the sense is: If any of you have allowed yourselves to be persuaded otherwise by false Doctors, as if circumcision and other Levitical things were required for Christianity: God will reveal this also to these infirm ones in his own time through the institution of the Gospel, and what they are not yet able to attain because they are preoccupied with their own opinion. Cf. Augustine in Psalm. CXXX. Calvin refers Τὸ Φρονῶμεν, and not wrongly, to the preceding. Others also agree with this, Hyperius, Aretius, &c.

For the Apostle requires this above all, that we renounce confidence in all things, and glory in the righteousness of Christ alone, and, having put all things behind us, aspire to the communion of his sufferings, which may lead us to a blessed resurrection.

Latin:

Vers. 15. ὅσοι οὖν τέλειοι, τοῦτο φρονῶμεν) Redit ad id, quod cœperat dicere supra v. 3. Ita, inquit, affecti fimus, etsi fiduciam habeamus non in carne, sed in Spiritu. Τέλειους hic vocat in rebus divinis optime versatos, ut 1. Cor. 2, 6. cap. 14, 20. Καὶ εἴ τι ἑτέρως φρονεῖτε)

Si qui vestrum à novis illis magistris abrepti estis. Καὶ τοῦτο ὑμῖν ὁ Θεὸς ἀποκαλύψει)

Hoc vobis Deus aperiet, nempe vos esse deceptos.

Loquitur pro spe, quam ex priore pietate conceperat. Sic & Gal. 5, 10. Non hæc promiscue ad eos, qui à Pseudo-Apostolis abrepti aliud sentiebant, dicta. Nam illi dissentiebant in articulo fidei fundamentali, nimirum de justificatione, qualibus anathema dixit Apostolus, Gal. 1, 8. Ad perfectos ea nonnulli referunt, hoc est, non in doctrina aut vita confirmati sunt, talis enim nemo in hac imperfectione, 1. Cor. 13, 10. sed sinceros & eruditos in doctrina Evangelii, 1. Cor. 2, 6. Quca hortatur, interprete B. Balduino, ut idem secum sentiant, non in isto pietatis profectu acquiescant, sed undiquaque consummatam perfectionem desiderent, ac proinde quotidie proficere cupiant. Idcirco addit, si quid aliter sentiant, hoc est, si forte in aliquibus aberrent, aut si quibus inciderint in humanita, ex quibus seipsos facile extricare non poterunt, id Deum ipsis revelaturum. Intelligit autem revelationem non arcanam per somnia, visiones aut Entusiasmos, sed qua usitato more fit per Verbum: ideo paulo post addit, omnes permanere debere in eodem canone, canone nempe verbi revelati.

B. Hunnius perfectos in præfenti loco ita explicat: Perfectos hic nominat, non eos, qui vel absolutam agnitionem Dei & Christi sint affecti, vel nulla amplius prorsus infirmitate peccati circumdati (talem enim perfectionem omnibus suis modis & numeris completam ipsomet sibi in præcedentibus derogavit) sed opponitur vox perfectionis hoc loco partim hypocrisi & ostentationi fucatæ pietatis, partim (& quidem secundum subjectam materiam præcipue) opponitur infirmitati eorum, qui de Judaicis ceremoniis atque ritibus adhuc ambigebant, necdum satis instituti in articulo libertatis Christianæ. Hos licet professione Christianos, & à vera pietate non alienos, adhuc tamen circa doctrinam circumcisionis aliorumque rituum Leviticorum umbras titubantes imperfectos nominat. Perfectos econtra eos, qui de abrogatione circumcisionis, & legis Levitica ex Christiana libertate articulo satis edocti erant.

Hos igitur perfectos vult ad suum exemplum in eadem de circumcisione, caterisque umbris legis Mosaicae sententia perfiare. De imperfectis vero non male hic intelligi possunt aliter sentientes, infirmi, & si quibus a Pseudo-Apostolis seducti minus recte eorum conciones intelligebant, non autem praefracte in errore haerebant, sed informari sese patiebantur, quemadmodum B. Hunnius haec ad Christianos adhuc infirmos pertinere ait, quos alias de fide Jesu Christi recte sentientes, in adiaphoris tamen non nihil turbaverant Pseudo-Apostoli, urgendo circumcisionem & alia: Ut sensus fit: Si qui vestrum a falsis Doctoribus aliter sibi persuaderi sunt passi, quasi circumcisio aliaque Levitica requirantur ad Christianismum: His quoque infirmis Deus suo tempore revelabit per Evangelii institutionem, et quod opinione sua praeoccupati jam quidem assequi nondum valent. Conf. Augustinus in Psalm. CXXX. Τὸ Φρονῶμεν refert Calvinus nec male ad antecedentia. Cui annuunt etiam alii Hyperius, Aretius, &c.

Id enim imprimis requirit Apostolus, ut abdicemus omnium rerum fiduciam, ac in sola Christi justitia gloriemur, & posthabitis omnibus adpiremus ad communicationem passionum ejus, quae nos ad beatam resurrectionem ducat.

## 3:16
Vers. 16. πλὴν εἰς ὃ ἐφθάσαμεν, τῷ αὐτῷ στοιχῶμεν Even those who think otherwise about circumcision and other rites should meanwhile know that the precepts of the Gospel, which they are persuaded are divine, must be followed by them. Φάσειν here is to arrive, as in Matt. 12:28, Luke 11:20, Rom. 9:31, 2 Cor. 10:14, 7:13. We have said what Στοιχεῖν κανών is, Gal. 6:16. But in the Manuscript it is κανόνι, so that τῷ αὐτῷ στοιχῶ may be referred to that εἰς ὃ. הלך signifies a perpetual tenor of life: so also God reveals future things to those who well fulfill the open [way] of walking.

Moreover, here, in what follows, the Infinitive is used for the Imperative in the Attic style. By that to which they had attained, is understood the heavenly doctrine, especially concerning Christ, which he had proposed in the preceding and this chapter, which he had also delivered to them by word of mouth, and which they had received ὁμοθυμαδὸν (with one mind). He wishes them, therefore, to walk by that same rule of heavenly doctrine, according to the canon of the divine Word, not according to the dictate of human reason, both regarding faith and the Christian life.

The word στοιχῶεν requires an ordered walk, such as must be accurately observed in an army and militia; but walking is done not with the feet of the body, but with the affections of the mind and the morals of life, as St. Augustine has it in lib. II. de peccat. merit. & remiss. cap.

13. Τὸ αὐτὸ Φρονεῖν requires the same sentiment, and in the doctrine of religion ὁμοψυφίαν (unanimity of soul).

Which is necessary for avoiding schism in the Church and preserving unity. For without consensus in faith there is no spiritual unity.

SECTION II.

PARTIS POSTERIORIS EPISTOLAE.

Exhortation to piety and honesty.

Latin:

Vers. 16. πλὴν εἰς ὃ ἐφθάσαμεν, τῷ αὐτῷ στοιχῶμεν Etiam qui de circumcisione & aliis ritibus sentiunt aliter, interim sciant Evangelii praecepta, quae divina esse persuasi sunt, sibi esse sequenda. Φάσειν hic est pervenire, ut Matth. 12, 28. Luc. 11, 20. Rom. 9, 31. 2. Corinth. 10, 14. 7, 13. Στοιχεῖν κανών quid sit, diximus Galat. 6, 16. Sed in Manuscripto est κανόνι, ut τῷ αὐτῷ στοιχῶ referatur ad illud εἰς ὃ. הלך vitae perpetuum tenorem significat: ita & στοιχῶν Deus aperta bene implentibus revelat futura.

Est autem hic in eo, quod sequitur, Infinitivus pro Imperativo Attice. Per id, ad quod pervenerant, intelligitur doctrina coelestis, imprimis de Christo, quam praecedente & hoc capite proposuerat, quam ipsis viva voce etiam tradiderat, quamque ὁμοθυμαδὸν ipsi susceperant. Eadem ergo illa coelestis doctrina regula ipsos incedere vult, secundum canonem Verbi divini, non secundum rationis humanae: dictamen, tum quoad fidem, tum quoad vitam Christianam.

Verbum στοιχῶεν incessum requirit ordinatum, qualis in exercitu & militia accurate observandus; ambulatio autem fit non corporis pedibus, sed mentis affectibus & vitae moribus, ut habet S. Augustinus lib. II. de peccat. merit. & remiss. cap.

13. Τὸ αὐτὸ Φρονεῖν eandem requirit sententiam, & in doctrina religionis ὁμοψυφίαν.

Quod necessarium est ad evitandum schisma in Ecclesia & conservandam unitatem. Sine consensu enim in fide nulla est spiritualis unitas.

SECTIO II.

PARTIS POSTERIORIS EPISTOLAE.

Exhortatio ad pietatem & honestatem.

## 3:17
Vers. 17. Συμμιμηταί μου γίνεσθε ἀδελφοί He said Μιμηταί με γίνεσθε in 1 Cor. 4:16, Eph. 5:1, 1 Thess. 1:16, cap. 2:14. But here συμμιμηταί, that is, all of you imitate me with equal zeal. Καὶ σκοπεῖτε τοὺς ὕτω περιπατοῦντας, καθὼς ἔχετε τύπον ὑμᾶς here it means consider attentively, as we are accustomed to do with those things which we wish to imitate. Τύπον here is an exemplar, as in Acts 7:44. In the Rabbis צור. He commands all to imitate him equally in doctrine and life, and requires this of all, that all may look upon one idea, with eyes fixed upon him, and strive to express it, so that thus ὁμόνοια (concord) and ὁμοψυφία (unanimity) may be preserved among all.

The blessed Glassius otherwise: imitate together with me: But whom does Paul imitate, and whom must the Philippians imitate together with him?

He responds: Christ Jesus, from whose faith righteousness had hitherto flowed excellently, and who had finally constituted the canon and rule of the whole course of piety, v. 16. He expresses this exhortation more clearly in 1

Cor. 11:1. Be imitators of me, just as I also am of Christ.

But lest they lack more ideas or types, he also sets forth others, walking or proceeding in the same way with him, such as Timothy, whom he had joined to himself at the front of the epistle, and Epaphroditus, whom he had notably commended along with Timothy in chapter 2. He had ordered that the false Apostles, or dogs, evil workers, and the concision, be avoided: Now he commands them to imitate sincere Doctors, approved in doctrine and life, twins to himself. Vers. 18.

Latin:

Vers. 17. Συμμιμηταί μου γίνεσθε ἀδελφοί Μιμηταί με γίνεσθε dixit 1. Cor. 4, 16. Eph. 5, 1. 1. Thess. 1, 16. cap. 2, 14. Hic vero συμμιμηταί, id est, omnes pari studio me imitamini. Καὶ σκοπεῖτε τοὺς ὕτω περιπατοῦντας, καθὼς ἔχετε τύπον ὑμᾶς hic valet attente considerate, ut solemus ea, quae imitari volumus. Τύπον hic est exemplar, ut Act. 7, 44. Rabbinis צור. Imitari se jubet omnes in doctrina pariter & vita, & ab omnibus id requirit, ut omnes unam ideam, defixis in ipsum oculis intueantur, & exprimere annitantur, quo ita ὁμόνοια & ὁμοψυφία inter omnes conservetur.

B. Glassius aliter: una mecum imitamini: At quem imitatur Paulus, & quem una cum ipso Philippenses imitari debent?

Respond. Christum Jesum, de cujus fide justitia hactenus praeclare diffuererat, tandemque canonem & regulam totius curriculi pietatis constituerat, v. 16. Clarius hanc exhortationem exprimit 1.

Corinth. 11. v. 1. Imitatores mei estote, sicut & ego Christi.

Ne autem plures ipsis desint ideae aut typi, alios etiam sistit, eadem secum ratione ambulantes vel incedentes, utpote Timotheum, quem sibi in fronte epistolae conjunxerat, & Epaphroditum, quem juxta cum Timotheo insigniter cap. 2. commendarat. Falsos Apostolos seu canes, malos operarios & concisionem vitari jusserat: Nunc imitari praecipit Doctores sinceros, doctrina & vita probatos, sibi geminos.

## 3:18
πολλοὶ γὰρ περιπατοῦσι Namely, far otherwise, which is understood from the nature of the antithesis. ὡς πολλάκις ἔλεγον ὑμῖν, νῦν δὲ κλαίων λέγω, τοὺς ἐχθροὺς τοῦ σταυροῦ τοῦ χριστοῦ λέγειν here is to call. I have called, he says, heretofore, and now I call you with tears, the enemies of the cross of Christ, that is, such men who say that nothing must be done so that the cross may be avoided, Gal. 6:12. These are the false Apostles, whose malice and destruction he deplores with intense grief of heart. Such is his compassion, as Chrysostom says, and he is solicitous for all men.

Lest he be thought to speak against the Pseudo-Apostles out of envy, says Hyperius, he says that he weeps and deplores their lot, and wishes miserably that, if it be possible, they might repent. And this is of charity, at least to grieve for the blindness and ignorance of others, whom you cannot otherwise lead to the knowledge of God: Truly such men are to be deplored more than to be attacked with insults, or, what is more bitter, to be afflicted with punishments and tortures, to which, however, arrogant and impious men are inclined more than can be said.

He calls them enemies of the cross of Christ because of the doctrine, of which he himself has treated here primarily; because they were overturning the doctrine that salvation must be sought in the cross of Christ alone: Which was a scandal to the Jews, and foolishness to the Gentiles, 1 Cor. 1. Thus Theodoret: He called them enemies of the cross, as those who taught that no one could obtain salvation without the legal institution of life; similarly Lombard, the ordinary gloss, Aquinas, and most others, except that some, with Hyperius and Zanchius, join this and the Grotian explanation: Which does not conflict with the unity of the sense of scripture.

He calls them enemies of the cross of Christ in verse 18, says the blessed Glassius, that is, corrupters and deniers of the salutary doctrine of righteousness and life, and that it is to be expected and obtained from the cross or passion and death of Christ alone.

This is the most terrible perfidy against Christ, who by this reasoning is rendered a Minister of sin, Gal. 2:7, where the notable annotation of the blessed Luther is in the margin: He who wants to become pious through works, does exactly as if he makes Christ, through his service, office, preaching, and suffering, first of all a sinner, who must become pious through the Law, that is, he has denied, crucified, slandered Christ, and rebuilds the sin which was previously abolished through the preaching of faith.

It is a spiritual fascination, Gal. 3:1, by which Jesus Christ crucified is depicted before the eyes, and, with a glaucoma as it were placed before them, and the eyes of the heart fascinated and blinded by the Devil, he is plainly ignored and rejected.

It is a nefarious sacrilege, by which Christ is entirely taken away, and lost, cap. 5:4, and with Christ, life and eternal salvation.

It is a spiritual abscission from saving faith, Phil. 3:2.

Latin:

Vers. 18. πολλοὶ γὰρ περιπατοῦσι Neimpe longe aliter, quod ex natura ἀντιθέτα intelligitur. ὡς πολλάκις ἔλεγον ὑμῖν, νῦν δὲ κλαίων λέγω, τοὺς ἐχθροὺς τοῦ σταυροῦ τοῦ χριστοῦ λέγειν hic est appellare. Appellavi, inquit, antehac, & nunc doletis appello hostes crucis Christi, id est, tales homines, qui nihil non faciendum dicunt, ut crux defugiatur, Gal. 6, 12.

Indigitantur falsi Apostoli, quorum malitiam & interitum deplorat prae ferio cordis dolore.

Tanta scilicet compassionis est, dicente Chrysost. & solicitus pro omnibus hominibus. Ne invidiae, inquit Hyperius, asiro percitus crederetur sic loqui contra Pseudo-Apostolos, ait se flere ac deplorare illorum vicem, misireque optare, ut, si fieri possit, resipiscant. Et hoc charitatis est, saltem dolere aliorum caecitatem & ignorantiam, quos aliter non potes ad agnitionem Dei adducere: Sane deplorandi sunt ejusmodi homines magis, quam exagidandi convitiis, vel, quod acerbius est, afficiendi panis & cruciatibus, quas tamen ad res quidum arrogantes & parum pii, supra quam dici potest, sunt proclives.

Hostes autem crucis Christi vocat ob doctrinam, de qua ipse imprimis hic egit; quia doctrinam de salute in sola Christi cruce quaerendam evertebant: Quae Judais scandalum, gentibus stultitia erat, 1. Corinth. 1. Ita Theodoretus: Es crucis inimicos vocavit, ut qui docerent, quod fine legali vitae institutione non posset quisquam salutem consequi; similiter Lombardus, glossa ordinaria, Aquinas, alii plerique, nisi quod nonnulli cum Hyperio & Zanchio hanc & Grotianam explicationem conjungant: Quod non repugnat unitati sensus scripturae.

Inimicos crucis Christi vocat vers. 18. inquit B. Glassius, hoc est, corruptores & abnegatores doctrinae salutiferae de justitia & vita, & sola Christi cruce seu passione & morte expectanda obtinendaque.

Haec teterrima est perfidia adversus Christum, qui hac ratione Minister peccati redditur, Gal. 2, 7. ubi notabilis B. Lutheri annotatio est in margine: Wer durch Werck will fromm werden, der thut eben, als macht uns Christus durch seinen Dienst, Ampt, Predigen und leiden allererst zu Sünder, die durch das Gesetz müssen fromm werden, das ist Christum verlaugnet, gecreutziget, verlästert, und die Sünde wieder bauet, die zuvor durch des Glaubens Predigt abgethan war.

Est spiritualis fascinatio, Gal. 3, 1. qua Jesus Christus crucifixus ante oculos depictus, glaucomate quasi objecto, & oculis cordu per Diabolum fascinatis & excaecatis plane ignoratur abjiciturque.

Est nefarium sacrilegium, quo Christus in solidum aufertur, amittiturque cap. 5, 4. & cum Christo vita & salus aeterna.

Est spiritualis abscissio a fide salvifica, Phil. 3, 2.

## 3:19
Vers. 19. whose end is destruction Gal. 6, 8. Rom. 6, 21. 2. Cor. 11, 15.

A phrase taken from Num. 24, 20. where it speaks of Amalek אַחֲרִיתוֹ עֲדֵי אֹבֵד. whose god is the belly For we hold that as God, for whom we do all things.

See Eph. 5, 5. Homer: "The belly, which is eager to be filled, and which gives much to men." Euripides: "Need conquers the ill-managed belly, from which all evils arise."

The curse of the serpent comes upon them, Gen. 3, 15. Athenaeus calls such people "belly-demons." - Thus, seducers in the Roman Church are also said to serve the belly, not God, Rom. 16, 18.

False Prophets feeding themselves, Ezech. 34. lovers of pleasure rather than lovers of God, 2. Tim. 3, 4.

Which fits those fat dogs, Is. 56. those false Apostles, especially well, because for the sake of their belly, so that they might be more pleasing to the Jews, they mixed Judaism with Christianity, Gal. 6, 12.

But their glory is said to be in their shame, not because they boasted of things that are least becoming, or because they attended banquets daily, or because they committed shameful acts, as Chrysostom explains, of which they ought rather to be ashamed; but because the glory which they seek here must be exchanged for their perpetual ignominy, as Thomas, Lyra, B. Luther, and most others explain.

Cf. Rom. 2, 8. Dan. 12, 1. They may indeed excel in wealth, says Scneccerus in his explanation of this passage, in honors, in pleasures, and in all earthly and bodily goods.

What then? In the end, however, they will be confounded and perish with all those things in which they swelled with pride and were magnified before the world.

Cf. 2. Petr. 2, 1.

2. 13. 14. 16. 17. - Those who set their minds on earthly things, satiety, wealth, glories.

See Jac. 3, 15. They are souls curved toward the earth.

And this is from the curse of the serpent, to lick the dust.

Latin:

Vers. 19. ὧ τὸ τέλος ἀπώλεια Gal. 6, 8. Rom. 6, 21. 2. Cor. 11, 15.

Loquutio desumpta ex Num. 24, 20. ubi de Amaleco אַחֲרִיתוֹ עֲדֵי אֹבֵד. ὧ ὁ θεὸς ἡ κοιλία Id enim pro Deo habemus, cujus omnia facimus.

Vide Eph. 5, 5. Homerus: Γαστέρα δ' ἄτης ἦν ἀποπλήτῃ μεμαυῖα. ἐλομένη, ἡ πολλὰ καὶ ἀνθρώποισι δίδωσι. Euripides: Νικᾷ δὲ χρεία τὴν κακῶς οἰκουμένην Γαστέρα, ἅς τὰ πάντα γίνεται κακά.

Venit super eos maledictio serpentis, Gen. 3, 15. Athenaeus tales vocat κοιλιοδαίμονας. - Sic ventri etiam servire dicuntur, non Deo, seductores in Romana Ecclesia, Rom. 16, 18.

Semetipsos pascere falsi Prophetae, Ezech. 34. φιλήδονοι μᾶλλον, ἢ Φιλόθεοι, 2. Tim. 3, 4.

Quod canibus illis pinguibus, Es. 56. falsis Apostolis apprime convenit, quia ventris causa, ut Judaeis gratiores essent, Judaismum cum Christianismo miscebant, Gal. 6, 12.

Gloria autem in confusione ipsorum fore dicitur, non quod de iis, quae minime decent, gloriarentur, sive quod conviviis quotidie interessent, sive quod flagitia, ut Chrysostomus explicat, committerent, quorum eis potius debebat puderi; sed quod gloriae, quam hic captant, cum perpetua ipsorum ignominia, commutanda fit, ut Thomas, Lyra, B. Lutherus, alii plerique explicant.

Conf. Rom. 2, 8. Dan. 12, 1. Emineant sane opibus, inquit Scneccerus in explic. h. l. honoribus, voluptatibus, & omnibus bonis terrenis & corporalibus.

Quid tum? Ad extremum tamen confundentur & pereant cam omnibus, quibus tumuerunt, & coram mundo magnifuerunt.

Conf. 2. Petr. 2, 1.

2. 13. 14. 16. 17. - Οἱ τὰ ἐπίγεια φροντῶντες Satietatem, opes, glorias.

Vide Jac. 3, 15. Sunt curvae in terras animae.

Et hoc ex maledictione serpentis, pulverem lingere.

## 3:20
Vers. 20. for our citizenship is in heaven. This is the opposite of what preceded, "setting their minds on earthly things."

We, he says, are already in spirit in heaven, we think of heavenly things: we care for those things which lead thither, we are ruled by heavenly laws.

We are here as if we were pilgrims, which Jacob said of himself, Gen. 47, 9. and the divine writer to the Hebrews explains musically 11, 9. 10. 13. 14. 15. The same says that we approach the heavenly Jerusalem, that we seek a future city 12, 22. etc.

13. 14. Philo in his book on rewards: "To be removed far from God is the race. They say that some are always of the ethereal [realm], and [are] led by virtue."

Add Apoc. 4. and what is to be said there. Anaxagoras used to say that heaven was his fatherland. And Tertullian translated "politeuma" in this passage as "municipality" several times.

You could also translate it as "conversation" [way of life]. For we had "politeuesthe" [conduct yourselves as citizens] above 1, 27.

Seneca ep. 41. on the wise man: "The greater part of him is there, whence he descended."

The same, epist. LXVI: "Do you forbid me to be concerned with heaven, and order me to live with my head bowed down?" Porphyry: "On Abstinence," book one: [Greek text provided in source].

And what follows. The soul is there where it loves.

Thus the prophecy of Dan. 2, 44 is fulfilled. Thus let both explanations be joined, which pleases some, both this one about "conversation" [way of life], approved by Ambrose, Lombard, Thomas, B. Luther, and that one about the right of citizenship, of Photius, Balduinus; perhaps it can be admitted in this way, namely that "conversation" is understood in heaven not as in a foreign place, but as in a city proper to us, so that the origin of the word "politeuma" is not neglected, and different interpreters are brought back to harmony.

In what way "our citizenship is in heaven," let us not therefore seek rest here: we are glorious there, where we also exercise our citizenship. Our conversation is in heaven.

Let us not therefore seek rest here. But we wish to be there, where we also cultivate life.

Theophylactus: These indeed were born for the belly instead of God, who meditate on nothing spiritual or heavenly. But our conversation is in heaven. We ought therefore to feel and savor heavenly things, and strive toward that higher fatherland of ours, where it is ordained for us to dwell and live. Beza: We indeed conduct ourselves as citizens of heaven; and Justinianus: We, as if citizens of a heavenly fatherland, thinking assiduously of that senate and assembly of the blessed, thus conduct ourselves; and examples of imitation are set forth, and to wait for what outcome they have, seems to require both the precept of imitation, which had to be explained in some way, and the opposition of the Pseudo-Apostles, of whose doctrine and life and its outcome he had spoken before.

Therefore, care for earthly things is opposed to conversation in heaven: And since they serve only the belly, and seek glory in worldly things, the Apostle with his fellow-mystics is implied to be intent on those things which please the Lord of the heavenly city, and on heavenly things, as befits citizens of heaven. Therefore their end is destruction and confusion: But theirs is eternal salvation and heavenly glory. Cornel. a Lapide explains similarly that our conversation is in heaven through heavenly hope: The earthly and worldly savor, love, and care for earthly things: we Christians savor, love, and care for heavenly things: the earthly are like moles moving on the earth, digging the earth, panting for the earth, delighting in earthly wealth: we Christians are fed by heavenly things, we tend toward the heights, we pant for heavenly things, our heart and all our goods are in heaven, therefore we are in heaven, not on earth, because the soul is more where it loves than where it animates.

Just as a house, says St. Gregory, lib. VIII. moral. cap. 31. is the building of the exterior life, which the body inhabits: So our house is any matter of thought, which the soul inhabits through love. Whence Paul, who had fixed his heart on things above, though placed on earth, yet being a stranger to the earth, said: Our conversation is in heaven.

Cornelius indeed brings forward a triple explanation: But in truth it falls back into one meaning, namely that "politeuma" denotes the manner and institution of life according to Budaeus, and that is to act in heaven: Secondly, that "politeuma" signifies occupation, and conversation in heaven, and is opposed to conversation on earth in the stated way; thirdly, that our city is in heaven, in this sense, that we conduct ourselves as citizens of heaven, that the kingdom of heaven is our city, by whose municipal law all the saints are ruled, which government is spiritual and heavenly, not carnal and earthly, as if he were saying, we conduct ourselves as citizens of heaven, who are ruled by and live by the laws, custom, polity, right, and goods of the heavenly city and kingdom. Who does not see that all these coincide? "From whence we await a Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ") It is no wonder that we look thither, whence our redemption is to come. "Ex hou" [from whence] looks to the thing, not to the word that preceded.

From that, however, it cannot be gathered that heaven is a certain place above the firmament. For cannot Christ be expected from the heavens, even if he were not to come from some material place, in which he might now be confined above the firmament? Did he not descend from the heavens to these lands, when he assumed our flesh, John. 3, 13. c. 6. etc. But shall we judge that the Son of God, having left heaven, came to these lands, having left a place above the firmament to this lower part of the world, which we inhabit, having come through the material heavens and the air itself?

Latin:

Vers. 20. ἡμῶν γὰρ τὸ πολίτευμα ἐν οὐρανοῖς ὑπάρχει Oppositum est ei, quod praecessit, τὰ ἐπίγεια φροντῶντες.

Nos vero, inquit, animo jam in coelo sumus, coelestia cogitamus: curamus ea, quae illuc ducunt, coelestibus legibus regimur.

Sumus hic quasi peregrini, quod de se Jacob dicebat, Gen. 47, 9. & μουσικῶς explicat divinus ad Ebraeos scriptor 11, 9. 10. 13. 14. 15. Idem dicit nos accedere ad Jerusalem coelestem, quaeri a nobis civitatem futura 12, 22. c.

13. 14. Philo libro de praemiis: Τὸ τὸ γένος ἐ μακρῷ ἀπώκισαι θεῦ. Φασὶν οἵ μεν ἀεὶ τὰ αἴθερια καί, τὰ ποδαγώμενον ὑπ' ἀρετῆς ὑρῶν.

Adde Apoc. 4. & ibi dicenda, Anaxagoras coelu patria esse dicebat τεθελαέρτιο. Et πολίτευμα hoc loco municipatu, transtulit aliquoties Tertullian.

Posses & conversatione vertere. Sic enim πολιτεύεσθε habuimus supra 1, 27.

Seneca ep. 41. de sapiente: Majore fui parte illic est, unde descendit.

Idem epist. LXVI: Vetas me coelo interesse, & jubes me vivere capite demisso? Porphyrius: Περὶ ἀποχῆς primo: ξένοιμεν γὰρ τοῖς εἰς ἀσφάλου ἰδόντων ἔχουσι ἀπεληλυθόσι, κὴ μὴ μόνον τοῖς οἰκείοις ἐξεθέσεως, ἀλλὰ κὴ ἐκ τῆς ξένης ἐμπληθῶσι πᾶσι πάντων κὴ ἀπὸ ἰδίων νομίμων ἐμφύλων, κὴ πρὸς ταῦτα ἐστὶ ἐσχηκόσι. Οἷς ἐπὶ πρέπον ὁ ἐκθεῖσαι εἰς ξένα μέλλον ἱκανῶς, κὴ μόνον προθυμοῦνται οὐδέν, ἀλλὰ κὴ ἵνα παραδεχθῶ, μελλὰ μὲν ἀποτίθεσθαι πᾶν, ἐπὶ προσελαῖεν ἀλλοφύλου. Επαταμμηκέναι δὲ ἑαυτὸν, ἂν ἔχων ἐπὶ ἀλλοθύων, ἂν εἶεν παραδεχθῆναι ἦν οὐχ οἷον τε πρὸς τῶν οἰκείων τῷ αὐτὸν τρόπον κὴ μᾶς δὲ ἐλευθεῶν, εἰπερ πρὸς τοὺς οἰκείους μεῖναι μελοικει ἐπαιτέων, ὡς κὴ ἐκ τῆς θηλῆς ὑπαλλοφαμεν Φύσεως, κὴ πρὸς τὸ ἀρχέωλον κὴ ἀποιοῦνπεῦδοιθας ἐπανελθεῖν.

Et quae sequuntur. Animus ibi est, ubi amat.

Sic impletur vaticinium Dan. 2, 44. Sic utraque conjungatur explicatio, quod nonnullis placet, & haec de conversatione, Ambrosio, Lombardo, Thoma, B. Luthera probata, & illa de jure civitatis, Photii, Balduini, ita forte id admitti poterit, nimirum ut conversatio intelligatur in coelis non ut in peregrino loco, sed ut civitate nobis propria, ut vocis πολίτευμα origo non negligatur, & diversi interpretes ad consonantiam revocentur.

Quo pacto τὸ πολίτευμα ἐν οὐρανοῖς ὑπάρχει, μὴ τοίνυν ἐνταῦθα ζήλωμεν ἄνεσιν: ἐκεῖ ἐσμεν λαμπροῖ, ἔνθα κὴ πολιτευόμεθα. Nostra conversatio est in coelis.

Non igitur hic quaeramus requiem. Sed ibi volumus dari esse, ubi & vitam colimus.

Theophylactus: Hi quidem pro Deo ventrem sunt nati, qui spirituale nihil aut celeste meditantur. Nostra autem conversatio in caelis est. Debemus itaque, coelestia sunt, sentire & sapere, & ad nostram superiorem illam patriam contendere, ubi nobis est versari & vivere constitutum. Beza: Nos vero ut municipes coelorum gerimus; & Justinianus: Nos quasi coelestis patriae municipes de illo senatu & beatorum coetu assidue cogitantes itaque; nos gerimus inpos & exemplaria imitationis sistuntur, & quem exitum habeant, expectare, videtur requirere tum imitationis praeceptum, quod aliquo modo erat explicandum, tum oppositio Pseudo-Apostolorum, de quorum doctrina & vita ejusque exito ante dixerat.

Cura itaque; terrenorum opponitur conversatio in coelis: Et quum illi ventri tantum serviant, & in rebus mundanis gloriam quaerant, Apostolus cum Symmystis suis innuitur iis intentus esse, quae Domino superna civitatis placent, & rebus coelestibus, ut municipes coeli decet. Ideo illorum exitus est interitus & confusio: Eorum vero aeterna salus & coelestis gloria. Similiter explicat Cornel. a Lapide, quod nostra conversatio in coelis fit per spem coeleste: Terreni & mundani sapiunt, amant, curant terrena: nos Christiani sapimus, amamus, curamus caelestia: terreni quasi talpe in terra versantur, terram fodicant, terra inhiant, terra opibus delectantur: nos Christiani coelestibus pascimur, ad altum tendimus, coelestibus inhiamus, in caelis est cor nostrum & bona omnia, in caelis ergo sumus, non in terra, quia anima magis est, ubi amat, quam ubi animat.

Sicut domus, inquit S. Gregor. lib. VIII. moral. cap. 31. exterioris conversationis est edificium, quod inhabitat corpus: Ita domus nostra e cogitationis est res qualibet, quam per dilectionem inhabitat animus. Unde Paulus, qui in supernis cor fixerat, in terra quidem positus, sed tamen a terra extraneus, dicebat: Conversatio nostra in caelis est.

Adfert quidem Cornelius triplicem explicationem: Sed revera in unum fensum illa recidit, utpote quod πολίτευμα notet vitam rationem & institutum juxta Budaeum, idq; fit in coelis agere: Secundo quod πολίτευμα significet occupationem, & conversationem in caelis, conversationem in term dicto modo opponatur; tertio, quod nostra civitas in coelo fit, hoc sensu, quod nos geramus, ut municipes coelorum, quod regnum coelorum fit civitas nostra, cujus municipali jure sancti omnes reguntur, quod regimen est spirituale & coeleste, non carnale & terrestre, quasi dicat, conversamur, ut cives coelorum, qui scilicet legibus, consuetudine, politia, jure ac bonis civitatis & regni coelestis reguntur & vivunt. Quis non videt, haec omnia coincidere? Ἐξ οὗ σωτῆρα ἀπεκδεχόμεθα κύριον Ἰησοῦν Χριστὸν) Non mirum est, nos eo respicere, unde ventura est redemptio nostra. Ἐξ ὧ rem spectat, non quod praecessit vocabulum.

Ex eo autem colligi nequit, coelum esse locum quendam supra firmamentum. Annon enim e coelis potest expectari Christus, etiam si non adventurus e loco aliquo materiali, in quo jam supra firmamentum conclusus haereat? Annon e coelis descendit in has terras, cum carnem nostram assumpsit, Job. 3, 13. c. 6. &c. Num autem Filium Dei relicto coelo in hasce terras venisse, relicto loco supra firmamentum ad inferiorem hanc mundi partem, quam nos colimus, per coelos materiales, ipsumque aerem venisse censebimus.

## 3:21
Vers. 21. who will transform the body of our humiliation) "tapeinosis" in this place is the very "tapeinotes," a vile condition, as also Luc. 1, 48. Jac. 1, 10. אַחֲרִיתוֹ עֲדֵי אֹבֵד.

He called the same "atimian" [dishonor], 1. Cor. 15, 43.

Eis τὸ γενέσθαι αὐτὸ σύμμορφον τῷ σώματι τῆς δόξης αὐτοῦ) to be acknowledged: According to which all things are delivered into his hands, Matth. 11. Job. 3. c. 13. Thus he is crowned with glory after his passion & death, so that he may subject all things to himself, not indeed by his own innate virtue, but by faith c. 6. you have learned, that he can subject all things to himself, according to the operation of the Deity. Learn now, that he receives all things as subject according to the flesh. Chrysostom attributes adoration and Majesty to the body of Christ. This very body (of ours) becomes conformed to that which is adored by the Angels, to that which incorporeal powers attend, to that which is above every principality & virtue & power, to that very thing it becomes conformed. And further: He has the power of subjecting all things to himself. Therefore also destruction and death. But rather, he does this even from that same power. For tell me, what greater work is it in power, to subject Angels & Archangels & Cherubim & Seraphim, and demons, or to make the body immortal, and not subject to corruption? That is certainly much greater. He shows that the power is for greater works, so that you may believe these things also.

Latin:

Vers. 21. ὃς μετασχηματίσει τὸ σῶμα τῆς ταπεινώσεως ἡμῶν) ταπείνωσις hoc loco est ipsa ταπεινότης, vilis conditio, ut & Luc. 1, 48. Jac. 1, 10. אַחֲרִיתוֹ עֲדֵי אֹבֵד.

Idem ἀτιμίαν dixit, 1. Cor. 15, 43.

Eis τὸ γενέσθαι αὐτὸ σύμμορφον τῷ σώματι τῆς δόξης αὐτοῦ) agnoscendum: Secundum quam omnia ipsi tradita sunt in manus, Matth. 11. Job. 3. c. 13. Ita gloria est coronatus post passionem & mortem, ut possit omnia sibi subjicere, non quidem virtute sua nata, sed fide c. 6. didicisti, quod omnia sibi subjicere possit, secundum operationem utique Deitatis. Disce nunc, quod secundum carnem omnia subjecta accipiat. Chrysost. corpori Christi adorationem & Majestatem tribuit. Hoc ipsum, corpus (nostrum) conforme illi fit, quod adoratur ab Angelis, illi cui assistunt incorporea potestates, illi, quod est supra omnem principatum & virtutem & potestatem, illi ipsi conforme fit. Et porro: Potestatem habet omnia sibi subjiciendi. Ergo & interitum & mortem. Potius autem ex eadem ipsa potestate hoc etiam facit. Quod enim, dic mihi, potentia majus opus est, Angelos & Archangelos & Cherubim & Seraphim subjicere, ac damonas, an corpus facere immortale, & corruptela non obnoxium? Illud sane multo majus. Ostendit majora opera potentia ut, ut haec etiam credas.

## 4:1 Argument
CAPUT IV. ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

He admonishes with most sweet words, that they may persist in the Lord, & be one, namely Evodia, Syntyche, Clemens, & others, that they may rejoice in the Lord, that they may strive for gentleness toward others, that they may place their trust in God, with the addition of a prayer for peace that transcends all understanding. He also exhorts that they may follow by his example what is true, what is just, what is honest, what is pure, and he testifies to his joy concerning their provident solicitude, he commends them exceptionally above others for their liberality, and having properly rendered the praise of all to Epaphroditus, he concludes with a prayer for divine retribution, a loving salutation, and the seal of the epistle.

There are two parts: The former still pertains to the imitation of the Apostle in piety & honesty, to v. 9. The latter presents the conclusion, consisting of eulogies, salutations & prayers to v. 23. & the last.

PARS I. Continuation of the exhortation to the constant imitation of the Apostle.

Verf. 1. ὅτε ἀδελφοί μου) Since such great rewards are proposed to us, of which I have already spoken. Ἀγαπητοὶ καὶ ἐπιπόθητοι) Whom I love & desire to see, יקיריי ונחמדי) Thus also the Latins call him their joy, for which they rejoice. ἐπιποθής) That is, my sweet ornament. For עטרת signifies ornament, a genus from a species, Job 19, 9. Prov. 4, 9. c. 12, 4. c. 14, 26. c. 16, 31. c. 17, 6. He expresses not only the desire of seeing, but also the intensity & ardor of love, because he holds them in his delights, & desires all the best things for them. Theophylact says thus of these epithets: See with what various praises he pursues them: For he calls them brothers, and says they are most dear, and most desired, that is, at one time sought by me, and finally found and seen. And he affirms that they are not only a joy to him, but a crown, than which nothing is more glorious to one struggling: For he says, I cannot but be filled with joy, when I contemplate the faith and foresee the palm, which I have obtained for your sake.

Before he could admonish them, he praised them, and heaped praises upon those who had been admonished, and others. So much did Paul value them. Compare Proverbs ch. XVII, v. 6, where children are the crown of their parents, and 1 Thessalonians ch. II, v. 18, where the Thessalonians (the faithful) are called the crown of Paul even on the last day. Οὕτω στήκετε ἐν Κυρίῳ Persist in life according to CHRIST, 1 Cor. ch. XV, v. 1. 2 Cor. ch. I, v. 24. 1 Peter ch. V, 12. Ἀγαπητοί having been turned around, this is the difference of this word.

I do not deny that the Apostle is exhorting, or rather, by exhorting, is praying that they persist in the well-instituted life, concerning which he had already warned them by his own proposed example, but especially also that they persist in the faith, he prays, as the Greek Scholia explain.

See Job XV, 4, 7. 1 Cor. XVI, 3. Therefore, the blessed Hunnius fully expressed the matter: Stand in the LORD, that is, persist with a constant purpose in the sincere doctrine of the Gospel, and in that integrity of morals by which you may adorn and honor that doctrine of the Savior GOD in all things. In the power of the LORD act manfully, and do not allow any adverse event to easily cast you down from your faith or piety.

For it is not enough to have begun in the course of faith and piety, but there is need of perseverance even to the end, Matthew X, v. 22. ch. XXIV, v. 13. Hebrews III, v. 14. And this is the first exhortation of the Apostle, namely, to perseverance; the second follows, to unanimity and concord.

Latin:

CAPUT IV. ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

Suavissimis verbis monet, ut in Domino persistant, & unum sint, nominatim Evodia Syntyche, Clemens, & alii, in Domino gaudeant, lenitati erga alios studeant, fiduciam in Deum collocent, addito voto pacis omnem intellectum transscendentis. Hortatur etiam, ut qua vera, qua justa, qua honesta, qua casta, suo exemplo sectentur, & gaudium suum de provida ipsorum solicitudine testatur, eos eximie commendat prae aliis ob liberalitatem, ac omnium probe reddito, rum laudem Epaphrodito tribuit, cum voto retributionis divinae, salutatione amaba, & signaculo epistola confecto.

Partes sunt duae: Prior adhuc pertinet ad imitationem Apostoli in pietate & honestate, ad v. 9. Posterior conclusionem exhibet, elogiis, salutationibus & votis constantem ad v. 23. & ultimum.

PARS I. Continuatio adhortationis ad Apostoli constantem imitationem.

Vers. 1. ὅτε ἀδελφοί μου) Cum tanta nobis proposita sint præmia, de quibus jam egi. Ἀγαπητοὶ καὶ ἐπιπόθητοι) Quos amo & videre desidero, יקיריי ונחמדי) Sic & Latini gaudium suum vocant eum, ob quae gaudent. ἐπιποθής) Id est, dulce decus meum. Nam עטרת ornamentum significat, genus ex specie, Job. 19, 9. Prov. 4, 9. c. 12, 4. c. 14, 26. c. 16, 31. c. 17, 6. Non tantum desiderium videndi, sed & intensionem & ardorem amoris exprimit, quod in delitiis eos habeat, & ipsis optima quæque cupiat. Theophylactus de his epithetis ita habet: Vide quam variis laudibus hos prosequatur: Nam & fratres appellat, & charissimos dicit, desideratissimosque, hoc est, aliquando per me conquisitos, inventos demum & visos. Nec gaudio solum esse hos sibi, sed corona affirmat, qua nihil gloriosius est decertanti: Non enim (inquit) possum non jucunditate expleri, cum fidem contemplor & palmam prospicio, quam vestri gratia sum consecutus.

Hos itaque priusquam commonefaceret, laudavit, & commonefactis laudes ingessit & alias. Tanti hos faciebat Paulus. Conf. Proverb. cap. XVII. vers. 6. ubi liberi corona parentum, & 1. Thessal. cap. II. vers. 18. ubi Thessalonicenses (fideles) corona Pauli etiam in novissimo die dicuntur. Οὕτω στήκετε ἐν Κυρίῳ Persistate in vita secundum CHRISTUM, 1 Cor. c.

XV. v. 1. 2 Cor. c. I. v. 24. 1 Petr. c. V, 12. Ἀγαπητοί περιταθεὶς hæc vocis hujus διαφορά. Non nego, hortari, vel potius hortando precari Apostolum, ut persistant in vita bene instituta, de qua exemplo suo proposito jam monuerat, sed imprimis etiam, ut in fide persistant, precatur, ut Scholia Græca explicant.

Vide Job. XV. 4. 7. 1. Cor. XVI. 3. Plene ergo rem expressit B. Hunnius: State in DOMINO, id est, constanti proposito persistite in doctrina Evangelii sincera, & morum integritate ea, qua doctrinam illam Salvatoris DEI ornet & cohonestet in omnibus. In virtute DOMINI viriliter agite, neque facile quemvis casum adversum vos de fide vel pietate vestra dejicere patiamini.

Non enim satis est, in fide ac pietatis cursu cœpisse, sed opus est perseverantia usque ad finem, Matth. X. vers. 22. cap. XXIV. v. 13. Ebr. III. v. 14. Et hæc prima est exhortatio Apostoli, nimirum ad perseverantiam; sequitur altera ad unanimitatem & concordiam.

## 4:1
Cf. Rom. 5: 1. Col. 3: 15. Which, because it arises from the fact that we have been reconciled to God through Christ, and enjoy his grace, brings solid joy, Rom. 16: 17. John 14:27, 28; 16: 33. The argument, says Hunnius, leads from the effect of prayer, so as to stimulate one to make prayers diligently and without ceasing.

That effect is the peace of conscience and tranquility of heart, born from the sense of the Fatherly clemency of God. For while praying, that filial love and trust of the elect is excited, by which they uniquely acquiesce in the most clement will, kindness, and Fatherly favor of God, and with respect to him, with prepared minds, they undergo and tolerate any adversities.

This peace of God, he says, will guard your hearts, and your senses or thoughts will thus gather, thus rule, thus stabilize, that no anxiety or adversity can cast you from the right state, or separate you from the love of God. He amplifies the sweetness of this ineffable gift, showing that this tranquility of a peaceful heart resting in God surpasses every intellect, so that no one can express it in prayer, or grasp in thought the magnitude of this so great and so divine a benefit.

B. Luther: It surpasses, he says, every sense, or intellect, or mind, it is not understood in such a way that the peace of God does not end in the soul, but that it is incomprehensible in the mind, for it is peace in faith, which is of things not appearing, as much in the sense of the flesh as of the mind.

Understand this thus: when we are disturbed by tribulations, then those who are anxious, and do not know how to flee to God with prayers, seek peace with great and many efforts, but that which they themselves grasp, that is, the removal and flight of evil.

For this the mind and sense of man desires peace, which does not surpass any sense, and is the peace of man, which is prepared or preparable by the force or industry of man, for thus, he who is wounded or sick, certainly both understands and desires the health contrary to it.

But those who ordain their refuge to their Lord, they do not flee evil, but stand and sustain it manfully in the will of God; nor do they affect the peace which sense or intellect suggests, (that is, the removal of evil) they expect rather the internal strengthening of the Word through faith, by which they may conquer evil, being entirely uncertain how long it will last, and with what end the evil is to be terminated, and therefore they understand nothing about peace, nor do they grasp what kind it will be, who if they persist, and have passed a little while with the bride, soon find him whom the souls of them love.

Behold, this is the peace of God being superior to every intellect.

For faith captures every intellect into obedience to itself. But after they have persevered and received peace, they feel such as they could not have imagined with all their thoughts, much less hoped for.

For his right hand leads his own wonderfully, and makes his own holy, while it thus terminates their evils, and with such fruit, that no man could have hoped or foreseen it. Nor does he speak only of this peace of finished evil, but also, and especially of that which is, in the midst of evil, strongly sustaining, so that the Spirit of man is not disturbed.

For a man to be in peace under the cross, and not to be disturbed, while he is being disturbed, nay rather to rejoice in tribulations, no intellect grasps, but it is the work of God, known to none except the experienced. Augustine also extends it to the Angels, but doubtfully: Whom except ours, or perhaps even of the Angels themselves, lib. 22 de Civ. Dei c. 29. Φρουρήσει τὰς καρδίας ὑμῶν καὶ τὰ νοήματα ὑμῶν ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ) If you act thus, the goodness of God will guard through Christ both your mind and your affections, namely, that you may not sin through fear and anxiety.

A place clearly similar to 1 Pet. 1:5, where the same word is used. The similarity is drawn from military matters, for Φρουρὰ is a military garrison. With another word Col. 3:15, the Apostle uses in a similar way, whether as a wish or an admonition: Let the peace of God βραβευέτω reign in your hearts, that is, let it be Prince and Director in you, and in any temptations whatsoever preserve you, that you may not murmur against God, but strongly trust in God according to that of Christ in John 16:33, as the marginal gloss of Luther has it, but in Christ Jesus it may guard.

The Greek Scholia among the Oecumenians have it thus: Φρουρήσει, ῥησά τὰς καρδίας ὑμῶν, ὥστε μὴ ὑπὸ πειρασμῶν καταπαλίζεσθαι, μήτε ὑπὸ ἀπάτης περιφέρεσθαι, that is, that you may not be submerged under temptations, or be carried about and err under fraud.

B. Luther explains it clearly: But the peace of God guards hearts and intelligences, or senses, or minds, that is, the affection and intellect, which is in Christ, or in the knowledge of Christ, that they may persevere to the end and be saved.

For perturbation and tribulation quickly subverts those who otherwise think very well of Christ (if they have not been strengthened by the peace of God and patience in the Lord), so that they do and think something far different than what is worthy of a Christian. Nor is there any other guardian of piety begun in Christ than the very peace of faith and patience, without which guardianship the fall to the peace of man and the world (that is, the removal of evil) is easy, in which the doctrines of men are most to be avoided, which teach one to be offended by the word of the cross and to flee. But then immediately the true opinion of God and trust in Him perishes, and his heart and senses are already depraved, seeking this from himself and men, which is to be expected from God alone.

Concerning the distinction of the terms τὰς καρδίας and τὰ νοήματα, the interlinear gloss is not bad: Your hearts and your intelligences, that is, the will and the intellect, so that you may desire or understand nothing outside of Christ. For man is accustomed to divide his soul, as Calvin does here, into two parts regarding its faculties, the mind and the heart: the mind signifies the intelligence; the heart, however, all affections and wills. Therefore these two names comprehend the whole soul in this sense: The peace of God will guard you, lest you fall away from God by perverse thoughts or desires. But where the heart is kept whole and the mind is whole, there the body itself is kept blameless for the coming of Christ, and no passions harm it, but rather profit it.

Verf.

8. Τὰ λοιπὰ ἀδελφοὶ) Having drawn out the discourse longer than he had intended, he returns to the epilogue.

See above III. v. 1. The Hebrews would say את סוף דבר, as in Ecclesiastes XII. 13. It is not to be presumed that a discourse drawn out longer than expected is from a God-breathed writer.

But he reduces to a summary all the precepts for governing life, which he could have pursued with more prolix admonitions, prescribed by a universal rule, so that they might know, above all, how they ought to live among the nations and in the midst of a perverse generation.

The passage in Ecclesiastes XII. 13 is not incorrectly compared. B. Hunnius: Since it is too long to admonish about each virtue separately, Paul gathers them as if into a bundle, and illustrates by kinds the duties to be cultivated by Christians.

He adorns his speech, moreover, with the anaphora of one and the same diction with an elegant resumption: The sense, therefore, is: It is of no use to designate specifically each virtue by its own names and to illustrate them with descriptions. It is enough to point the finger to those things which are appropriate to your profession.

I would wish, therefore, in summary, that you think upon, nay, and also do (for the text has both words) whatsoever things are true, whatsoever things are honest, etc. ὅσα ἐστὶν ἀληθῆ) Removed from bad faith and lying. את אשר נאמנים. This first directs the mind or intellect, which is devoted to truth and ought to embrace nothing but what is true; nor should it allow itself to be snatched away from the truth of faith to the errors of seducers, or by extending these things more broadly, that whatsoever things are truly true in religion, or in common life, they should approve, hold, speak, do, and keep the faith given, not only among Christians, but even among infidels.

First, says B. Hunnius, he commends to the Philippians the study of truth to be observed in words and deeds. In words, that they speak what is true.

In deeds, that they be alien to all hypocrisy and simulation. ὅσα σεμνὰ) Full of gravity, 1. Tim. III. 8, 11. Tit. II. 2. Add 1. Tim. II.

2, III. 4. Tit. II. 7. Σεμνὰ Prov. VIII. 6. In the Glossary, σεμνὸς is venerable.

The Vulgate translates it as chaste, Ambrose as magnificent, B. Luther as honest, in which sense Crocius acknowledges the word is often taken, and thus he wishes the study of gravity in morals to be commanded, so that, on the contrary, those things which argue for levity of mind are avoided in speech, habit, gestures, deeds, and the whole conversation, as interpreted by Oecumenius. ὅσα δίκαια) Which are far removed from greed .

Παρελάβετε a more exact doctrine: Ἡρελάβετε refers to familiar discourses, adapting the doctrine to the things that have arisen. Εἴδετε, however, refers to Paul's own actions. Theophylactus has it thus: Because it would have been long to repeat everything, he now concludes the whole briefly and in summary, saying thus: Whatsoever you have learned or heard, or received from me preaching, you have undoubtedly seen in me in reality and in deeds. Latin:

V. 1. Col. III. 15. Quæ quia inde oritur, quod Deo reconciliati simus per Christum, ejusque gratia fruamur, solidum affert gaudium, Rom. XVI. 17. Joh. XIV. 27. 28. cap. XVI. 33. Argumentum, inquit Hunnius, ducit ab effectu precationis, ut ad preces sedulo & fine intermissione faciendas extimulet.

Effectus ille est pax conscientiæ & tranquillitas cordis, orta ex sensu Paterna Dei clementia. Nam inter precandum excitatur ille filialis amor, & fiducia electorum, qua in clementissima Dei voluntate, benignitate, Paternoque favore unice acquiescunt, ejusque respectu paratis animis adversa quævis subeunt & tolerant.

Hæc pax Dei, inquit, custodiet corda vestra, & sensus seu cogitationes vestras ita colliget, ita reget, ita stabiliet, ut nulla vos anxietas vel adversitas è recto statu dejicere, aut à Dei dilectione separare queat. Amplificat autem dulcedinem inenarrabilis istius doni, perhibens, hanc pacati cordis tranquillitatem in Deo requietem superare omnem intellectum, ut nemo quisquam vel oratione exprimere, vel cogitatione complecti valeat hujus tanti tamque divini beneficii magnitudinem.

B. Lutherus: Superat, inquit, omnem sensum, seu intellectum, seu mentem, non sic intelligitur, quod pax Dei non finiatur in anima, sed quod in mente sit incomprehensibilis, cura sit pax in fide, quæ est rerum non apparentium, tam in sensu carnis quam animi.

Hoc sic intellige, quando tribulationibus turbamur, tunc hi, qui soliciti sunt, & ad Deum orationibus fugere nesciunt, magnis & multis studiis quærunt pacem, sed eam, quam ipsi capiunt, hoc est, remotionem & fugam mali.

Hæc enim pacem cupit mens sensusque hominis, quæ non superat ullum sensum, & est pax hominis, qui vi vel industria hominis parata vel parabilis, sic enim, qui vulneratur vel æger est, certe sanitatem illi contrariam & intelligit & appetit.

Sed qui ad Dominum suum refugium ordinant, hi non fugiunt malum, sed perstant & sustinent viriliter in voluntate Dei; nec affectant pacem, quam sensus aut intellectus suggerit, (id est, remotionem mali) expectant potius internam roborationem Verbi per fidem, qua vincant malum, prorsus incerti, quamdiu duraturum, & quo fine terminandum sit malum, ideoque nihil intelligunt de pace, nec qualia futura sit, capiunt, qui si perstent, & cum sponsa paululum transierint, mox inveniunt quem diligunt animæ eorum.

Ecce hoc est pacem Dei superiorem esse omni intellectu.

Capti-pat enim fides in obsequium sui omnem intellectum. Postquam autem perseveraverunt & pacem acceperunt, talem sentiunt, qualem non possuissent omnibus cogitationibus fingere nedum optare.

Deducit enim dextra ejus mirabiliter, & mirificat finctos suos, dum mala eorum sic terminat, & tanto cum fructu, ut nullus hominum potuisset id sperare aut providere. Nec solum de hac pace finiti mali loquitur, sed etiam, & maxime de ea, quæ est, in medio mali fortiter sustinens, ne turbetur Spiritus hominis.

Esse enim hominem in pace sub cruce, & non turbari, dum turbatur, imo gaudere in tribulationibus, non capit ullus intellectus, sed est opus Dei, nulli nisi experto cognitum. Augustinus etiam ad Angelos extendit, sed dubitanter: Quem nisi nostrum, aut fortasse etiam ipsorum Angelorum lib. XXII. de Civ. Dei cap. 29. B. Lutherus id explicat præclare: Custodit autem Dei corda & intelligentias, seu sensus, seu mentes, hoc est, Affectum & intellectum, qui est in Christo seu in cognitione Christi, ut perseverent in finem & salvi fiant.

Nam perturbatio & tribulatio cito subvertit, alioqui optime de Christo sentientes, (si non fuerint pace Dei & patientia in Domino firmati) ut faciant & sentiant longe aliud, quam Christiano dignum est. Neque est alius custos pietatis in Christo cœpta, quam ipsa pax fidei & patientia, sine qua custodia facilis est lapsus ad pacem hominis & mundi (id est, remotionem mali) in quare maxime fugiende sunt hominum doctrinæ, qua verbo crucis offendi docent & fugere. At tunc mox perit vera opinio Dei & fiducia in cum, depravatumque est jam cor & sensus ejus, quærens hoc apud se & homines, quod expectandum est a solo Deo.

De distinctione vocum τὰς καρδίας & τὰ νοήματα non mala glossa interlinearis: Corda vestra & intelligentias vestras, hoc est, voluntatem & intellectus, ut nihil extra Christum appetatis vel intelligatis. Suam enim, ut hic Calvinus, animam homo quoad facultates in duas partes solet dividere, mentem & cor: mens intelligentiam significat: Cor autem omnes affectus & voluntates. Ergo hæc duo nomina totam animam comprehendunt hoc sensu: Pax Dei vos custodiet, ne pravis cogitationibus aut desideriis deficiatis a Deo. Ubi autem integrum servatur cor & mens integra, ibi corpus ipsum servatur in adventum Christi inculpate, nec ullæ passiones illi nocent, sed potius prosunt.

PARS II. ΕΠΙΛΟΓΙΚΗ.

## 4:2
Verse 2. Εὐοδίαν παρακαλῶ καὶ Συντύχην παρακαλῶ τὸ αὐτὸ φρονεῖν ἐν Κυρίῳ Other codices more correctly have ἐυοδίαν. There were dissensions among them, which he urges them to settle in the Lord, that is, for the sake of the Lord. Syntyche, like Eutyche, is a masculine name.

Instead of women, the Interpreters have men, both Syntyche and Evodia: to which the text fully agrees, because in verse 2 it is added, help them, and those who labored with me in the Gospel. Thus Chrysostom, Theophylactus, and others among the Ancients. Thus among our own, B. Hunnius, B. Balduinus, and others. Nor do most of the Reformed think otherwise.

Whom, therefore, Justinianus notes here, who in certain Circean cups change women into men, escapes me, unless Grotius attempted the same. But whether there was some peculiar dissension in faith among those women is not sufficiently clear. It seems probable, however, that he has now particularly exhorted them to τὸ αὐτὸ φρονεῖν ἐν τῷ Κυρίῳ, after he had generally excited all of them until now to unanimity, and had diligently warned them that false Doctors were to be avoided, and had inculcated perseverance in the faith, and wished to use the work of some distinguished person in helping them.

It appears entirely that much depended on these two women in the Church of the Philippians, for whose unanimity the Apostle labors.

These two women, says Theodoret (with the agreement of Theophylactus and Anselm), were primary among the Christians of Philippi, who were busy promoting the Christian cause. Verse 3. Καὶ ἐρωτῶ καὶ σε, σύζυγε γνήσιε, συλλαμβάνου αὐταῖς, αἵτινες ἐν τῷ ἐυαγγελίῳ συνήθλησάν μοι In the Manuscript: Ναὶ ἐρωτῶ σε, where ναὶ is an admonition of one praying of the Hebrews, as in Revelation ch. XXII, v. 20. ἰοῦ ἐπὶ I pray. The locution is fashioned after the Latin manner, as in John XIV, 16. XVI, 26. XVII, 9. 1 Thessalonians IV, 1. ch. V, 12. 2 Thessalonians II, 1. 1 John V, 16. 2 John 5. σύζυγε, which in Hebrew is not only said of those joined in marriage, but also of colleagues.

But whom would Paul rather call a colleague at Philippi than the τὸν συνεργὸν of the Gospel, whose authority was also great in the distribution of money? Therefore, the speech turns to Epaphroditus by way of apostrophe, as if he were present, where this Epistle would be read in the Church of the Philippians.

And this σύζυγος is nothing other than the συνεργός mentioned above. To him, therefore, he commends the πρεσβυτέρας, or the τὰς προκαθημένας, namely, the elder widows, as Ferrandus Diaconus calls them, who had labored much in converting other women to Christ. He commends them, however, in this, that they might have the means to support themselves and their own honestly.

In Judea there had been no need for such προφῆται or even for deaconesses, because there the access to women was freer. In Greece, the women's quarters were closed. Therefore, women had to be imbued with the first knowledge of Christianity through women, and thus be drawn to the Churches. These same πρεσβύτιδες were the σωφρονίστριαι to the converted women, and the inspectors and teachers of their morals.

Concerning whom see the Laodicean canon XI and Epiphanius, Heresy LXXIX. Whom the Apostle is addressing here is doubtful. Chrysostom wishes a famous man to be designated, to whom he was accustomed to commend others, who was either the brother of one of them, or her husband.

Theophylactus, Vatablus, and Toffanus follow him, saying that perhaps Epaphroditus is hinted at. Nor is that explanation of Grotius concerning Epaphroditus improbable. For if you say that these persons could have been commended to Epaphroditus in person and orally by Paul, when he was being sent to the Philippians: the answer is ready, that the Apostle preferred to address him in the epistle itself, so that those persons might also understand how much care he has, and that the Church might hold them in greater esteem, and that Epaphroditus might have that written commendation the more before his eyes.

Oecumenius takes σύζυγον as a proper name, and wishes them to be commended to him. And so also some already in the time of Chrysostom thought.

But Lynus and Lombard think it is called genuine or german. However, the opinion of those who wish Paul's wife to be noted should not be agitated, which pleased Clement of Alexandria, lib. III, Strom., Eusebius, lib. III, Hist. Eccles., ch. 27, Bullinger, Hypetrius, Flacius, Erasmus, Cajetan, and did not displease Zanchius, Aretius, Martyr, or our B.

Luther, Tom. III, Jenenf. Germ., fol. 303. b. Nor does Justinianus deny that the Masculine gender is frequently used for the Feminine in Attic Greek. It seems little probable, however, that Paul's wife lived at Philippi, and not rather in Judea, or in Tarsus of Cilicia: nor is it certain that Paul had a wife when he was writing this epistle, and no necessity compels one to admit an enallage of gender, or to recur to Atticisms.

But as far as the commended persons are concerned, they had already been named before, namely Evodia and Syntyche: whom he therefore recognizes here as women, and indeed as elder widows, concerning which, however, he brings forward no certain document, as he seemed before to understand men by those names.

The end of the commendation, which Grotius designates, can easily be admitted. Μετὰ γὰρ Κλήμεντὸς, καὶ λοιπῶν συνεργῶν μου Clemens here seems to have been some Roman doing business in Macedonia. He, and those whom Paul designates here under a general name, were Presbyters of the Church of Philippi.

Therefore, this does not agree with the Papists, among whom Cornelius says: This is, he says, Clement of Rome, a disciple of SS. Peter and Paul, who succeeded Peter in the Pontificate after Linus and Cletus. That the Pontificate at that time was still a mere non-entity, and that there were classes of preachers in the primitive Church, Eph.

IV and 1 Cor. XII, is clear, in which there is no, and not even an obscure, trace of a Pontificate, but rather the exclusion of the same through the designation of one head of the Church of Christ. That Peter was the Bishop of the Roman Church is a Papist fable. Nor does Eusebius make Clement, to whom the decretal epistles are falsely attributed, the fourth, but the third Roman Bishop, l.

III, Histor. eccles., ch. 4 and 19, to whom Linus is the first, Anacletus the second. In which order, however, writers vary greatly. But this is not the place for this. Zanchius makes this Philippian Clement a Presbyter of that Church. Clement of Rome-

…that he lived among the Philippians is supported by no sufficient document. (τὰ ὀνόματα ἐν βίβλῳ ζωῆς) A figurative way of speaking: It is taken from the custom of the best cities, of writing citizens in a public register, so that if they become rebels, they can even erase their names.

See what we have said at Dan. ch. XII. v. 2, at Luke ch. X. v. 20, and at Apocalypse ch. XIII. v. 8. While the pious are such, they have a certain right to eternal life. They can also lose it, as Demas lost it, who in the epistle to Philemon is adorned with this same title, fellow-worker, v. 24, but yet afterwards fell away, 2. Tim. IV. 10. The Hebrews say, כתוּב בסֵפֶר חַיִים. Concerning the book of life Lombard understands the book of life as concerning predestination, by which all who are to be saved are prescribed; Thomas understands it as concerning the knowledge of God, concerning the predestined; and Calvin explains it in almost the same sense as a catalogue of those who are predestined to eternal life.

For it is certain that the book is attributed to God only anthropopathically, just as we are accustomed to register names in a book, e.g., of citizens, soldiers, or friends, so that they may be kept in memory, and the knowledge of them may not fade; So when GOD keeps the faithful in perpetual memory, for He knows who are His, 2.

Tim. II. 19, and by their faith foreseen from eternity, those who were to depart in Christ through faith, He chose or predestined them to eternal life, therefore He inscribed them into the book of life as a register and catalogue of His heavenly ones or heavenly citizens, whose citizenship indeed πολίτευμα ἐν ὀρανοῖς ὑπάρχει exists in heaven.

Which opinion is received by most interpreters, but explained differently by others, according to how they feel about the dogma of predestination, since the Calvinists reject election from foreseen faith, and wish it to have been done according to absolute good pleasure.

The Papists assert it was done from the foresight of works and merits. But our people believe that God chose according to the foreknowledge of faith in Christ, and inscribed His own in the book of life.

And to this refers that which was spoken by Christ to the disciples, Luke X. v. 20, Rejoice, because your names are written in heaven.

By Moses it is also called the book of God, Exod. XXXII. v. 37, by David the book of the living, Psalm. LXIX. vers. 29. By Daniel it is called absolutely the book, ch. XII. v. 1, it is called the book of life of the Lamb, Apoc. XIII. v. 8, because through and on account of the blood of the Lamb the Elect are inscribed.

The book of life simply, as here, Apoc. XIII. vers. 8. How Paul brings in Clement and others written in the book of life Yet it is not ill observed here by Crocius, that this is not an assertion of faith, but of charity, concerning Clement and the fellow-workers, that they were chosen by God; and that it relies not on revelation, but on signs, from which the Apostle was gathering this.

But that it is to be understood in such a way that these words were not dictated by God to the Apostle, but that God did not wish to open and reveal to him the book of life and the secret of election by that inspiration, which God reveals to no one immediately, lest they neglect to work out their salvation with vigilance, fear, and trembling, only by willing His own judgment, which he had conceived in his mind out of charity concerning them, so that it was manifested to them, that they might continue to persist in faith and piety, and likewise render themselves more certain in their own heart, and also the Apostle in his judgment concerning their election, just as Peter warns those who had received faith ἰσότιμον in justice, 2.

Petr.

I.

10. The blessed Balduinus counts seven pages of this book of life, which he bids those to read through who wish to be certain of the inscription of their names, which I would wish to be said not so much concerning the catalogue of the Elect, as concerning the Holy Scripture, that book of life, insofar as it is the rule of obtaining eternal life; as for instance 1. Of the universal will, 1. Tim. II. v. 4, 2.

Petr. III. v. 9. 2. Of the gracious goodness of GOD, which does not regard our merits, Rom. ch. IX. v. 11. 3. Of universal redemption, 1. Johann. ch. II. v. 2. 4. Of universal vocation, Matth. ch. XI. v. 28. 5. Of divine patience and long-suffering, Roman. ch. II. vers. 4. 6. Of the faithful consummation of GOD, 1. Cor. I. vers. 9, 1. Petr. I. v. 5, ch. VI. v. 10. 7. Of divine protestation, Es. ch. V. v. 4, Of. ch. XIII. v. 9. The Holy Scripture knows nothing of a mutable book of life. It is vain, therefore, what Grotius thinks, that the inscribed can be erased in turn.

For as they perish eternally who are not inscribed, Apocal. ch. XIII. vers. 8, So they are saved eternally who are inscribed from eternity, Ephes. ch. I. v. 4. Whom GOD predestines, these He also glorifies, Rom. ch. VIII. v. 9. Those who are inscribed in the book are saved, Dan. ch. XII. v. 1, conf.

Job. ch. X. v. 27, seqq. And this also concerning the other exhortation to concord: There follows now the third to spiritual joy in Christ. Verf. 4. Χαίρετε ἐν Κυρίῳ πάντοτε, πάλιν ἐρῶ χαίρετε For he had said χαίρετε, that is, rejoice, above ch. III. v. 1. Now he repeats it, and indeed with the word placed twice, to signify an exceptional affection. Such is that: Vale, Sale, says Isola. Therefore he repeats it with a triple voice, so that he may excite them more effectively to joy.

For the joy of those benefits which we have in the kingdom of grace is the highest and chief. Therefore let us act with all contention, that that joy may be our own, and perpetual. But what joy? Not joy in contention or other carnal things, which is damnable: not in fleeting things, for that is momentary: But joy in the Lord.

Joy in the vocation and conversion of the Lord, which he preached in chapter I: Joy in the redemption of Christ, and all the gifts which we obtain through Christ emptied and exalted for us, according to chapter II. Joy in justification, which we obtain through faith in Christ, chapter III. Joy in the hope of the promised heavenly prize, and the clarity of our body, which is here humbled to the conformity of the glorified body of Christ, according to the same chapter III. Joy in perseverance, in the justice of faith and true holiness.

Joy finally in peace and tranquility of soul, since the kingdom of God consists in these, in justice, in peace, in joy in the Holy Spirit, Rom. ch.

XIV. v. 17. He had called them his joy. Now he warns them to rejoice in the Lord, and so, filled with true joy, to fulfill their joy, just as he had excited them to it with the sweetest words, Phil. ch. II. v. 2. But joy requires 1. true joy in the Lord Christ Jesus, outside of whom there is no joy, Es. ch. IX. v. 3, Luc. ch. II. v. 12, Es. ch. LXI. v. 10, Psalm. LXIII. v. 4, Pf. XCVII. v. 1, & 8, 11. Conf. Ebr. ch. I. v. 6. Ordinary Gloss: Rejoice in the Lord, that is, in truth, not in iniquity: In the hope of eternity, not in the flower of vanity.

Establish every good, from which one must rejoice, in the Lord, not outside. The blessed Luther, Tom. II. Jen. Lat. fol. 340, beautifully on this matter: He commands to rejoice, but in the Lord, and always, defining most briefly and beautifully the joy of a Christian man, which is heavenly and perpetual.

Heavenly, because in the LORD, perpetual or continuous, because always. Therefore, those who rejoice in riches, powers, honors, pleasures, rejoice with a gentile and worldly joy, for those joys are not of Christians.

Nor do they rejoice in the Lord who rejoice in wisdom, science, arts, virtues, benefits, or whatever spiritual gifts, for when he says, to rejoice in the Lord, he shows that whatever is not the Lord,

even if it be an excellent gift and creature of God, is not that in which a Christian can and ought to rejoice. For in other things, to rejoice otherwise than in the Lord is either to take pleasure, or to be proud and to please oneself, all of which are sins.

But how is one to rejoice in the Lord?

Namely, if the Lord be known, as in Jer. ch. IX: let him who glories, glory in this, that he knows and understands me; 1 Cor. I: He who glories, let him glory in the Lord; and Ps. XXXII:

Rejoice in the Lord and exult, you just, etc. But this happens when one believes in Christ, and presumes the remission of sins from his mercy in a joyful and pleasant conscience.

Pure joy, because it is in the Lord: there is no sadness here. There is joy even in tribulations, Rom. V. 3, James I. v. 2, because Christ drives away all sadness and brings solid joy, Is. XXXV. ver.

10. Therefore rejoice; rejoice, says the Apostle.

Constant and perpetual joy.

Rejoice πάντοτε (always), as if those who are sad are always rejoicing, 2 Cor. VI. ver. 10; he does not forbid sadness in private or public mourning, because one must weep with those who weep, Rom. ch. XII. ver. 15. But that sadness is of the flesh or of the world: here we are dealing with spiritual joy, which is not extinguished by that, but is kindled more and more in those who truly believe.

For when one rejoices in the Lord, what does he care for the accidents of the world? He believes that the right hand of the Most High can change all things, Psalm LXXVII. 11; he knows that all things turn to good, Rom. VIII. 31; he is certain that mourning is to be converted into joy, Job ch. XVI. v. 20.

And although spiritual joy may sometimes waver even in the faithful, which is a weakness of the flesh, yet the Spirit helps our weakness and confirms our minds through the Word, so that joy in the Lord may be perennial and not taken from us, John XVI. 22. Therefore the Holy Spirit admonishes: rejoice in the Lord, and exult, you just, and glory, all you of upright heart, Psalm XXXII.

11, cf. Jer. XV. 16. Regarding spiritual temptations, lest they disturb the joy of the faithful, we add the passage of Blessed Luther in the cited place: For this exhortation to rejoice in the Lord is vehemently necessary, because as in the midst of tribulations, so also the smoke of sins, where we are tempted to sadness of spirit as much by guilt as by the enemy, against which one must diligently resist through joy and a good conscience in the goodness of God.

For we are not at any time without sin, but sin necessarily carries with it the disturbance of conscience from the face of future judgment. Therefore, against this disturbance, he teaches that we are to be prepared and firm with joy in the Lord.

Augustine, Serm. XXXVII on the Words of the Lord in the Gospel: The Apostle commands us to rejoice, but in the Lord, not in the world. For whoever wishes to be a friend of this world, as the scripture says, will be reckoned an enemy of God. But just as a man cannot serve two masters, so no one in this world can rejoice and [also] in the Lord.

These two joys differ greatly from each other, and are entirely contrary. When one rejoices in the world, one does not rejoice in the Lord. Let joy in the Lord prevail, until joy in the world ends. Joy in the LORD is always increased, joy in the world is always diminished, until it ends.

Latin:

Vers. 2. Εὐοδίαν παρακαλῶ καὶ Συντύχην παρακαλῶ τὸ αὐτὸ φρονεῖν ἐν Κυρίῳ Rectius alii Codices ἐυοδίαν. Erant inter hos orra dissidia, quæ hortatur eos, ut concordes sint in Domino, id est, propter Dominum. Συντυχὴς ut Εὐτυχὴς virile est nomen.

Pro fœminis non pro viris habent Interpretes & Syntychen & Evodiam: Quibus textus omnino adstipulatur, quia vers. 2. additur, adjuva illas, & qui in Evangelio mecum certarunt. Sic Chrysostomus, Theophylactus alii è Veteribus. Sic è nostris B. Hunnius, B. Balduinus alii. Nec aliter plerique è Reformatis.

Quos ergo hic notet Justinianus, qui Circais quibusdam poculis fœminas in viros commutent, me fugit, nisi quod idem tentarit Grotius. An vero inter illas fœminas peculiaris quidam dissensus in fide fuerit, non satis liquet. Probabile tamen videtur, quod easdem nunc peculiariter hortatus fit ad τὸ αὐτὸ φρονεῖν ἐν τῷ Κυρίῳ, postquam communiter omnes hactenus ad unanimitatem excitavit, & falsos Doctores vitandos esse sedulo monuit, ac perseverantiam in fide inculcavit, operaque insignis alicujus personæ in iis juvandis uti voluit.

Id omnino apparet, multum situm fuisse in istis duabus fœminis in Ecclesia Philippensium, quod pro earum unanimitate laborat Apostolus.

Dua hæ fœminæ, inquit Theodoretus, (annuente Theophylacto & Anselmo) primariæ erant inter Christianos Philippi, quæ rem Christianam promovere fatagebant. Vers. 3. Καὶ ἐρωτῶ καὶ σε, σύζυγε γνήσιε, συλλαμβάνου αὐταῖς, αἵτινες ἐν τῷ ἐυαγγελίῳ συνήθλησάν μοι In Manuscripto: Ναὶ ἐρωτῶ σε, ubi ναὶ est precantis admonitum Ebræi, ut Apoc. cap. XXII. vers. 20. ἰοῦ ἐπὶ precor. Locutione efficta ad Latinum sermonem, ut Joh. XIV. 16. XVI. 26. XVII. 9. 1. Thessal. IV. 1. cap. V. 12. 2. Thessal. II. 1. 1. Joh. V. 16. 2. Joh. 5. σύζυγε, qui Ebraico non tantum dicitur de junctis matrimonio, verum etiam de collegis.

Quem autem Philippis potius collegam vocaret Paulus, quam τὸν συνεργὸν ἐυαγγελίου, cujus summa erat etiam in pecuniis elargiendis auctoritas? Ad Epaphroditum ergo per ἀποστροφὴν se vertit oratio, tanquam præsentem futurum, ubi Epistola hæc in Ecclesia Philippensium legeretur.

Nec aliud hic σύζυγος, quam supra συνεργός. Ei igitur commendat τὰς πρεσβυτέρας, sive τὰς προκαθημένας, viduas nempe seniores, ut eas vocat Ferrandus Diaconus, quæ in convertendis ad Christum fœminis aliis plurimum laboraverant. Commendat autem in hoc, ut habeant, unde se & suos honeste sustentent.

In Judæa non fuerant necessariæ aut προφῆται fides tales, aut etiam fœminæ διάκονοι, quia liberior ibi vis erat aditus ad fœminas. In Græcia clausa gynæconitis.
