Itaque fœminæ per fœminas prima Christianismi cognitione imbui, & sic ad Ecclesias pertrahi debebant. Eadem πρεσβύτιδες mulieribus conversis erant σωφρονίστριαι, morumque inspectrices & magistræ.

De quibus vide Laodicenum canonem XI. & Epiphanium Hæref. LXXIX. Quemnam hic compellet Apostolus, dubium est. Virum celebrem, cui consueverit alios commendare, Chrysostomus designari vult, qui aut frater fuerit alterius ipsarum, aut maritus.

Quem sequitur Theophylactus, Vatablus & Tossanus, Epaphroditum fortassis innui ajunt. Nec improbabilis illa Grotii de Epaphrodito explicatio. Nam si dicas, potuisse has personas Epaphrodito coram & oretenus commendari à Paulo, cum ad Philippenses mitteretur: Responsio parata est, maluisse Apostolum in ipsa epistola eum compellare, ut & personæ illæ intelligant, quantam curam habeat, & Ecclesia in majori eas pretio haberet, & Epaphroditus scriptam illam commendationem eo magis ob oculos haberet.

Oecumenius σύζυγον pro nomine proprio habet, eique illas commendatas vult. Atque ita etiam aliqui jam tempore Chrysostomi senserunt.

Lynus vero & Lombardus putant, γνήσιον nuncupatum vel germanum. Non tamen exagitanda eorum opinio, qui uxorem Pauli notari volunt, quæ Clementi Alexandrino lib. III. Strom. Eusebio lib. III. Hist. Eccles. cap. 27. Bullingero, Hypetrio, Flacio, Erasmo, Cajetano placuit, nec displicuit Zanchio, Aretio, Martyri, aut B.

Lutheri nostro Tom. III. Jenenf. Germ. fol. 303. b. Neque diffitetur Justinianus, Artice frequenter genus Masculinum pro Fœminino usurpari. Parum tamen probabile videtur, Pauli uxorem Philippis habitasse, & non potius in Judæa, vel in Tarso Ciliciæ: nec constat, uxorem tunc habuisse Paulum, cum hanc epistolam exararet, & Enallage generis admittere, vel ad Atticissimum recurrere nulla cogit necessitas.

Quod autem ad commendatas personas attinet, illæ jam nominatæ erant antea, nimirum Evodia & Syntyche: quas proinde hic agnoscit fœminas, & quidem viduas feriores, quo de tamen certum non profert documentum, ut antevisus est viros per illa nomina intelligere.

Finis commendationis, quem designat Grotius, facile admitti potest. Μετὰ γὰρ Κλήμεντὸς, καὶ λοιπῶν συνεργῶν μου Clemens hic videtur fuisse Romanus aliquis in Macedonia negotians. Is, & ii, quos sub generali nomine hic designat Paulus, fuere Presbyteri Ecclesiæ Philippensis.

Non annuit ergo hic Pontificiis, e quibus Cornelius: Hic est, inquit, Clemens Romanus, discipulus SS. Petri & Pauli, qui Petro post Linum & Cletam in Pontificatu successit. Pontificatum isto tempore adhuc merum non-Ens fuisse, & classibus præconum in Ecclesia primitiva, Eph.

IV. & 1. Cor. XII. liquet, in quibus nullum, ac ne quidem obscurum Pontificatus vestigium, imo exclusio ejusdem per unius capitis Ecclesiæ Christi designationem. Petrum Ecclesiæ Romanæ Episcopum fuisse, fabula est Papistica. Nec Clementem, cui affinguntur epistolæ decretales, quartum, sed tertium Episcopum Romanum facit Eusebius l.

III. Histor. eccles. cap. 4. & 19. cui Linus primus, Anacletus secundus est. In quo ordine tamen valde variant Scriptores. Sed hoc non est hujus loci. Clementem hunc Philippensem Zanchius Ecclesiæ istius Presbyterum facit. Clementem

Romanum Philippis vixisse nullo sufficienti documento liquet. (τὰ ὀνόματα ἐν βίβλῳ ζωῆς) Loquendi genus figuratum: Sumitur enim à more optimarum civitatum, scribendi in albo publico cives, ita ut si perduelles fiant, etiam delere possint eorum nomina.

Vide, quæ diximus ad Dan. c. XII. v. 2. ad Lucam c. X. v. 20. & ad Apocalypsin c. XIII. v. 8. Pii dum tales sunt, certum habent jus ad vitam æternam. Possunt & perdere, ut Demas perdidit, qui in epistola ad Philemonem eodem hoc titulo συνεργὸς decoratur, v. 24. at postea tamen defecit, 2. Tim. IV. 10. Ebræi dicunt, כתוּב בסֵפֶר חַיִים. De libro vitæ Librum vitæ Lombardus de prædestinatione, qua omnes salvandi præscripti sunt, Thomas de notitia Dei, de prædestinatis intelligit, ac eodem fere sensu Calvinus de catalogo eorum, qui prædestinati sunt ad vitam æternam, explicat.

Nam certum est, librum non nisi ἀνθρωποπαθῶς Deo tribui, quod veluti nos in libro nomina, v.g. civium, militum aut amicorum consignare solemus, ut in memoria habeantur, & notitia eorum non excidat; Ita quum DEUS in memoria perpetuo habeat fideles, novit enim, qui sint sui, 2.

Tim. II. 19. & fide eorum ab æterno prævisa, qui in Christo per fidem decessuri sint, illos ad vitam æternam elegerit aut prædestinarit, ideo in librum vitæ ceu matriculam & catalogum cœlitum suorum vel civium cœlestium, quorum nempe πολίτευμα ἐν ὀρανοῖς ὑπάρχει ipsos inscripserit.

Quæ sententia à plerisque interpretibus recepta, sed ab aliis aliter, prout nempe de dogmate de prædestinatione sentiunt, explicatur, siquidem Calviniani electionem ex prævisa fide reprobent, eamque secundum absolutum beneplacitum factam velint.

Papistæ ex prævisione operum & meritorum factam afferunt. Nostri autem κατὰ πρόγνωσιν fidei in Christum elegisse Deum, libroque vitæ inscripsisse suos credant.

Atque eo refertur illud Christi ad discipulos prolatum, Luc. X. v. 20. Gaudete, quod nomina vestra in cœlis scripta sint. A Mose etiam nominatur liber Dei, Exod.

XXXII. v. 37. à Davide liber viventium, Psalm. LXIX. vers. 29. A Daniele absolute vocatur liber, cap. XII. v. 1. liber vitæ agni dicitur Apoc. XIII. v. 8. quia per & propter sanguinem Agni inscripti sunt Electi. Liber vitæ simpliciter, ut hic, Apoc.

XIII. vers. 8. Quomodo afferat Paulus Clementem & alios in libro vitæ scriptos Id tamen non male hic observatur à Crocio, non esse hanc fidei assertionem, sed charitatis, de Clemente & συνεργοῖς, quod à Deo electi sint; ac niti non revelatione, sed signis, è quibus id colligebat Apostolus.

Quod vero ita intelligendum, quod verba hæc à Deo haud dictata sint Apostolo, sed quod Deus ea inspiratione ipsi non librum vitæ & arcanum electionis aperire ac revelare voluerit, quod nemini immediate Deus aperit, ne cum vigilantia timore ac tremore salutem operari negligant, solum voluendo judicium suum, quod de ipsis ex charitate animo suo conceperat, ita illis manifestari, ut pergant in fide ac pietate persistere, ac sese pariter in corde proprio, nec non Apostolum in judicio suo de sui electione certiores reddere, quemadmodum Petrus monet eos, qui fidem ἰσότιμον acceperant in justitia, 2.

Petr.

I. 10. Libri hujus vitæ septem paginas numerat B.

Balduinus, quas perlegere jubet eos, qui inscriptione nominum fuorum certi esse volunt, quod non tam de catalogo Electorum, quam de Scriptura Sacra, libro illo vitæ, quatenus regula est vitæ æternæ consequendæ, dictum velim; utpote 1. Universalis voluntatis, 1.

Tim. II. v. 4. 2. Petr. III. v. 9. 2. Gratiosae DEI bonitatis, quæ non respicit merita nostra, Rom. c. IX. v. 11. 3. Universalis redemptionis, 1. Johann. cap. II. v. 2. 4. Universalis vocationis, Matth. cap. XI. v. 28. 5. Divina patientia & longanimitatis, Roman. cap. II. vers. 4. 6. Fidelis DEI consummationis, 1. Cor. I. vers. 9. 1. Petr. I. v. 5. cap. VI. v. 10. 7. Divina protestationis, Es. cap. V. v. 4. Of. c. XIII. v. 9. De libro vitæ mutabili nihil novit Scriptura Sacra. Vanum ergo est, quod Grotius putat, deleri vicissim posse inscriptos.

Nam ut æternum pereunt, qui non inscripti sunt, Apocal. cap. XIII. vers. 8. Ita æternum salvantur, qui inscripti sunt ab æterno, Ephes. cap. I. v. 4. Quos DEUS prædestinat, hos etiam glorificat, Rom. c.

VIII. v. 9. Qui inscripti in libro sunt, salvantur, Dan. c. XII. v. 1. conf. Job. c. X. v. 27. seqq. Atque hæc etiam de altera exhortatione ad concordiam: Sequitur jam tertia ad gaudium spirituale in Christo. Vers. 4. Χαίρετε ἐν Κυρίῳ πάντοτε, πάλιν ἐρῶ χαίρετε Nam dixerat χαίρετε, id est, gaudete, supra cap. III. v. 1. Nunc id repetit, & quidem voce bis posita, ad significandum affectum eximium. Tale illud: Vale, Sale, inquit Isola. Trina ergo voce repetit, ut eo efficacius ad gaudium excitet.

Gaudium enim eorum, quæ in regno gratiæ habemus beneficia, summum est & præcipuum. Id itaque agamus omn contentione, ut gaudium illud nobis proprium sit, & perpetuum. Quodnam vero gaudium? Non gaudium in contentione aut aliis carnalibus, quod est damnabile: non in rebus caducis, id enim momentaneum est: Sed gaudium in Domino.

Gaudium in vocatione ac conversione Domini, quam capite I. prædicavit: Gaudium in Christi redemptione, omnibusque, quæ per Christum pro nobis exinanitum et exaltatum obtinemus muneribus, secundum cap. II. Gaudium in justificatione, quam per fidem consequimur in Christum, cap. III. Gaudium in spe promissi cœlestis brabei, & claritate corporis nostri, quod hic humiliatur ad conformitatem glorificati corporis Christi, juxta idem caput III.

Gaudium in perseverantia, in justitia fidei & sanctitate vera. Gaudium denique in pace & tranquillitate animæ, siquidem in hisce regnum Dei consistat, in justitia, in pace, in gaudium in Spiritu Sancto, Rom. cap.

XIV. v. 17. Vocarat eos suum gaudium. Nunc monet, ut in Domino gaudeant, & ita ipsi gaudio vero repleti gaudium suum adimpleant, quemadmodum dulcissimis verbis ad id excitarat eosdem, Phil. c. II. v. 2. Gaudium vero requirit 1. verum in Domino Christo Jesu, extra quem nullum est gaudium, Es. cap. IX. v. 3. Luc. cap. II. v. 12. Es. c. LXI. v. 10. Psalm. LXIII. v. 4. Ps. XCVII. v. 1. & 8. 11. Conf. Ebr. c. I. v. 6. Glossæ ordinaria: Gaudete in Domino, id est, in veritate, non in iniquitate: In spe æternitatis, non in flore vanitatis.

Omne bonum, unde gaudendum est, statuite in Domino, non extra. B. Lutherus Tom. II. Jen. Lat. fol. 340. pulchre hac de re: Gaudete præcipit, sed in Domino, & semper, brevissime & pulcherrime Christiani hominis gaudium definiens, quod est cœleste & perpetuum.

Cœleste, quia in DOMINO, perpetuum seu continuum, quia semper. Proinde, qui vel in divitiis, potestatibus, honoribus, voluptatibus gaudent, gentili & mundano gaudio gaudent, non enim ea gaudia sunt Christianorum.

Nec illi in Domino gaudent, qui in sapientia, scientia, artibus, virtutibus, beneficiis, aut quibuscunque spiritualibus donis gaudent, nam cum dicit, in Domino gaudere, ostendit, quicquid non est

Dominus, quantumlibet excellens donum & creatura Dei, non est, in quo Christianus gaudere possit & debeat. Nam in aliis rebus, quam in Domino gaudere est aut voluptari, aut superbe & sibi placere, quae omnia peccata sunt.

Quomodo autem gaudetur in Domino?

Nempe, si cognoscatur Dominus, ut Jerem. cap. IX. in hoc glorietur, qui gloriatur, scire & nosse me, 1. Cor. I. Qui gloriatur, in Domino glorietur; & Ps.

Laetamini in Domino & exultate justi &c. Hoc autem fit, quando in Christum creditur, & de misericordia ejus praesumitur remissio peccatorum in laeta jucundaque conscientia.

2. Gaudium merum, quia in Domino: Nulla hic tristitia. Etiam in tribulationibus gaudium, Roman. V. 3. Jacob.

I. v. 2. quia Christus omnem pellit tristitiam, solidam affert laetitiam, Es. XXXV. vers. 10. Ideo gaudete; gaudere, inquit Apostolus.

3. Gaudium juge ac perpetuum.

Gaudete πάντοτε, quasi tristes semper gaudentes, 2. Cor. VI. vers. 10. non prohibet in luctu sive privato, sive publico tristitiam, quia lugendum cum lugentibus, Rom. cap. XII. vers. 15. Sed ea tristitia est carnis vel mundi: Hic agitur de gaudio spirituali, quod per illam non extinguitur, sed in vere credentibus magis magisque accenditur.

Cum enim in Domino quis gaudet, quid curat mundi casus? Dextram excelsi mutare posse omnia credit, Psalm. LXXVII. 11. omnia in bonum vertere novit, Rom. VIII. 31. luctum in gaudium convertendum certus est, Job. cap. XVI. v. 20.

Etsi autem spirituale gaudium quandoque etiam in fidelibus vacillet, quae carnis est infirmitas, nostrae tamen infirmitati opitulatur Spiritus, & confirmat mentes nostras per Verbum, ut gaudium in Domino perenne sit, nec auferatur a nobis, Johann. XVI. 22.

Ideo monet Spiritus Sanctus, laetamini in Domino, & exultate justi, & gloriamini omnes recto corde, Psalm. XXXII. 11. conf. Jer. XV. 16. Quod ad tentationes spirituales, ne illae turbent fidelium gaudium, adjicimus locum B. Lutheri loco citato: Vehementer enim necessaria est ista exhortatio ad gaudendum in Domino, quia ut in medio tribulationum, ita & peccatorum sumus, ubi nos tam culpa quam affidae tentat ad tristitiam spiritus, quibus per gaudium & bonam conscientiam in Dei bonitate affidue resistendum est.

Non enim fine peccato sumus aliquando, at peccatum necessario secum habet turbationem conscientiae a facie judicii futuri. Idco contra hanc turbationem docet, nos gaudio in Domino paratos esse & firmos.

Augustinus Serm. XXXVII. de Verb. Dom. in Evangel. Gaudere nos Apostolus praecipit, sed in Domino, non in seculo. Quicunque enim voluerit amicus esse hujus seculi, sicut scriptura dicit, inimicibus Dei reputabitur. Sicut autem non potest homo duobus Domino servire, sic & nemo in hoc seculo potest gaudere & in Domino.

Multum inter se haec duo gaudia differunt, suntque omnino contraria. Quando gaudetur in seculo, non gaudetur in Domino. Vincat gaudium in Domino, donec finiatur gaudium in seculo. Gaudium in DOMINO semper augetur, gaudium in seculo semper minuatur, donec finiatur.

## 4:5
Verf. 5. Τὸ ἐπιεικὲς ὑμῶν γνωσθήτω πᾶσιν ἀνθρώποις (Let your moderation be known to all men), that is, ἐπιείκεια (moderation), Acts XXIV. 4, 2 Cor. X. 1. In the Glossary: ἐπιείκεια, gentleness, clemency, modesty.

For this word is not taken here in the narrow sense in which Aristotle takes it, but denotes goodness, partly yielding much of one's own right, partly seeking occasions for doing good to others. Ὁ Κύριος ἐγγύς, ὃς (The Lord is near, who) Thus indeed they thought, because Christ had kept that time of his advent in secret, 1 Thess. IV. v. 6, 1 Cor. XV. 22, 2 Cor. V. 11 and following. Compare Apocalypse ch. I. v. 3, ch. XXII. v. 10. The speech is taken from Ps.

XLV. 11. Verf. 6. Μηδὲν μεριμνᾶτε (Be anxious for nothing) Do not be anxious about the things of this fleeting life.

The same sense as Matt. VI. 34, where see what is said. Ἀπ' ἐπιεικεῖ (By moderation) At all times, as the Syriac.

Elsewhere διαπαντός (always). Τῇ προσευχῇ καὶ δεήσει (By prayer and supplication) Concerning the distinction of these words, see what we have said in Eph. VI. 18. Μετὰ ἐυχαριστίας (With thanksgiving) For these must be joined: grace for things given, prayer for things to be given, 1 Cor. XIV. 16, Eph. V. 4. Εὐχαριστία (thanksgiving) שֶׁבַח הַהוֹדָיָה (praise of thanksgiving). Τὰ αἰτήματα ὑμῶν γνωρίζεσθω πρὸς τὸν θεόν (Let your requests be made known to God) You have the word αἴτημα (request) in this sense in 1 John V.

15, αἴτημα (request) שְׁאֵלָה (petition) 1 Samuel I, 17, 27, Ps. XX. 6, XXXVI. 4. Cast your cares upon God.

Either he will give what is necessary for this life, or he will free you from this sorrowful life. We have the word γνωρίζεσθω (be made known) in Roman.

XVI. 26, Ephes. III. 5, 10, נוֹדַע (made known) Exod. XXI. 36 and elsewhere. Πρὸς τὸν θεόν (to God) here is אֶל הָאֱלֹהִים (to God).

That joy in the Lord may be kept unblemished, one must take care that it is not violated or contaminated by us ourselves; and for this to happen, there is need of gentleness toward men, since spiritual joy is easily disturbed by vehemence, bitterness, anger, hatred, impatience, and similar affections, toward which the fourth exhortation is directed: let your gentleness be known to all men, the Lord is near.

Regarding that gentleness, Blessed Selneccer says thus: Spiritual joy extinguishes all frauds of hatred, envy, ἐπιχαιρεκακίας (rejoicing in evil), and leads men to gentleness.

But gentleness is that part of piety which restrains and represses anger and the desire for vengeance, and forgives offenses and even true injuries, according to the command of God: Forgive and it will be forgiven you, Luke VI. 37. Likewise, learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart, Matt. XI. 29. Therefore, the daily prayer of all the pious ought to be this, which was that of a certain Doctor of the Church: Repress and restrain in me, O JESU CHRISTE, whatever is proud, turgid, ambitious, irascible, and arrogant, and bend me to the consideration and some imitation of your voice: Learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart.

Blessed Luther in the cited place: You see, therefore, that modesty or ἐπιεικὲς (gentleness) in this place is equability, convenience, and the tempering of ourselves to the weakness, or foolishness, or iniquity of others, and the remission of our own rigor and right, so that it may be known or recognized, so that all men may perceive it.

Whence Ambrose not ineptly calls modesty in this place a reasonable conversation, where he beautifully expressed the force of the word. For it is not enough to speak of it, to think, to dispute subtly, and to preach, but to prove and show it by life itself.

Where see the diligence of the Apostle, who says to all men—who is the one who commands this to all men—that the modesty of us all may be notified to all.

Then, does he command this, that we should boast and glory in our modesty, making it known to men through fame? Far be it.

For he does not say, boast of it, but let it be known or recognized, namely, that it may be done outwardly in the eyes of men, and without our own striving, that men may recognize it, exposed to all for their utility, as in Matt. ch. V: Let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father, who is in heaven.

Then, because it is not in our power that our modesty should please men, we have done this, we have done, because we have exhibited it to all, and made it known by the example of our own life.

Furthermore, there is need of ἀμεριμνίᾳ, so that we do not stifle it with anxiety, or vain and useless care, and with diffidence joined toward GOD, to which the fifth exhortation looks, THE LORD is near, be not anxious, see Matt. ch.

VI. v. 25. and that then by prayer and supplication in every business and cause we may commit the whole matter to God, μετὰ παρρησίας, and then by thanksgiving of the divine name we may testify our εὐδοκίαν and acquiescence in God, calm our heart, and whatever remains of τῶν αἰτημάτων, that is, whether it be a petition or of our desires, we may piously commend to God, הִוא יַעֲשֶׂה, HE SHALL DO IT, Ps. XXXVII. v. 5. which pertain to the sixth exhortation. Moreover, the nearness of the Lord, and his gracious presence, by which he is near to all who place their trust in him, and call upon him, Psalm

CXLVI. 18. and it can be understood concerning glorious nearness. For the presence of God, who beholds all things, recalls us from anger and bitterness, as does the imminent arrival of the judgment of the Lord, James

Latin:

Vers. 5. Τὸ ἐπιεικὲς ὑμῶν γνωσθήτω πᾶσιν ἀνθρώποις, id est, ἐπιείκεια, Actor. XXIV. 4. 2. Cor. X. 1. In Glossario: ἐπιείκεια, mansuetudo, clementia, modestia.

Non enim hic sumitur arto significato hac vox, quam cum sumit Aristoteles, sed bonitatem denotat, partim cedentem multum de suo jure, partim occasiones quaerentem benefaciendi aliis. Ὁ Κύριος ἐγγύς, ὃς) Ita sane arbitrabantur, quia Christus tempus illud sui adventus in occulto tenuerat, 1. Thess. IV. v. 6. 1. Cor. XV. 22. 2. Cor. V. 11. & sequentibus. Confer Apocalypsin c. I. v. 3. c. XXII. v. 10. Loquitio sumpta ex Ps.

XLV. 11. Vers. 6. Μηδὲν μεριμνᾶτε) Ne anxii estote de rebus vitae hujus caducae.

Idem sensus, qui Matth. VI. 34. ubi dicta vide. Ἀπ' ἐπιεικεῖ) In omni tempore, ut Syrus.

Id alibi διαπαντός. Τῇ προσευχῇ καὶ δεήσει) De discrimine harum vocum vide, quae diximus Eph. VI. 18. Μετὰ ἐυχαριστίας) Debent enim haec jungi, gratia pro datis, precatio pro dandis, 1. Cor. XIV. 16. Eph. V. 4. Εὐχαριστία שֶׁבַח הַהוֹדָיָה. Τὰ αἰτήματα ὑμῶν γνωρίζεσθω πρὸς τὸν θεόν) Vocabulum αἴτημα habes hoc sensu 1.

Joh. V. 15. αἴτημα שְׁאֵלָה 1. Samuel I, 17, 27. Ps. XX. 6. XXXVI. 4. In Deum rejicite curas vestras.

Aut dabit, quod huic vitae necessarium est, aut vos a moesta hac vita liberabit. Verbum γνωρίζεσθω habemus Roman.

XVI. 26. Ephes. III. 5. 10. נוֹדַע Exod. XXI. 36. & alibi. Πρὸς τὸν θεόν hic est אֶל הָאֱלֹהִים.

Ut illibatum sit gaudium in Domino, cavendum, ne a nobis ipsis temeretur, aut contaminetur, quod ut fiat, lenitate opus est erga homines, quum vehementia, acerbitate, ira, odio, impatientia ac similibus affectibus facile gaudium spirituale turbetur, ad quam directa est quarta exhortatio, lenitas vestra nota sit omnibus, Domino prope est.

De illa lenitate B. Selneccerus ita: Gaudium spirituale extinguit omnes fraudes odii, invidiae, ἐπιχαιρεκακίας, & mansuetudinem homines adducit.

Est autem mansuetudo pars illa pietatis, quae iracundiam & cupiditatem vindictae cohibet & reprimit & condonat offensiones & injurias etiam veras, juxta mandatum Dei: Remitte & remittetur vobis, Luc. VI. 37. Item, discite à me, quia mitis sum & humilis corde, Matth. XI. 29. Omnium ergo piorum quotidiana precatio debet esse haec, quae fuit piicujusdam Doctoris Ecclesiae: Reprime & cohibe in me, O JESU CHRISTE, quicquid superbum, turgidum, ambitiosum, iracundum & arrogans, & flecte me ad considerationem & imitationem aliquam vocis tuae: Discite à me, quia mitis sum & humilis corde.

B. Lutherus loco citato: Vides ergo, quod modestia seu ἐπιεικὲς hoc loco sit, aequabilitas, commoditas, & attemperatio nostri, ad aliorum sive imbecillitatem, sive stultitiam, sive iniquitatem, & nostri rigoris & juris remissio, ut nota sit seu cognoscatur, ut sentiant cam omnes homines.

Unde Ambrosius non inepte modestiam vocat hoc loco rationabilem conversationem, ubi vim vocabulo pulchre expressit. Non enim satis est, de ea loqui, cogitare, subtiliter disputare, & praedicare, sed vita ipsa probare & ostendere.

Ubi vide Apostoli diligentiam, qui dicit omnibus hominibus, quis unus omnibus hominibus hoc precipit, ut omnium nostrum modestia omnibus notificetur.

Deinde numquid hoc jubet, ut jactemus & gloriemur de nostra modestia, facientes eam notam hominibus per famam? Absit.

Non enim dicit, jactate eam, sed nota sit seu cognoscatur, scilicet, ut foris fiat in oculis hominum, & fine nostro studio cam homines agnoscant, omnibus ad utilitatem expositam, sicut Matth. cap. V. Sic luceat lux vestram coram hominibus, ut videant opera bona vestra, & vestrum Patrem glorificent, qui in caelis est.

Deinde quia non in nostra est potestate, ut hominibus placeat modestia nostra, hoc satisfecimus, fecimus, quod eam omnibus exhibuimus, & cognitam fecimus, exemplo ipsius vitae nostrae.

Opus porro est ἀμεριμνίᾳ, ne sollicitudine, aut cura vana & inutili ac cum diffidentia coniuncta erga DEUM id suffocemus, quo spectat quinta adhortatio, DOMINUS prope est, ne soliciti sitis, vid.

Matth. c. VI. v. 25. utque tum precatione, ac obsecratione in omni negotio, & causa Deo rem committamus omnem, μετὰ παρρησίας, tum εὐχαρισίᾳ nominis divini nostram in Deo εὐδοκίαν & acquiescentiam testemur, cor nostrum tranquillemus, & quicquid superest τῶν αἰτημάτων, hoc est, sive postulatum, sive desideriorum nostrorum, pie Deo commendemus, הִוא יַעֲשֶׂה, IPSE FACIET, Ps. XXXVII. v. 5. quae ad sextam paraenesin pertinent. Caeterum propinquitas Domini, & praesentia ejus gratiosa, qua prope est omnibus, fiduciam in ipsum collocantibus, eumque invocantibus, Psalm.

CXLVI. 18. & de propinquitate gloriosa intelligi potest. Nam & praesentia Dei omnia intuentis nos revocat ab ira & acerbitate, ut & adventus instans judicii Domini, Jac.

## 4:7
Vers. 7. Καὶ ἡ εἰρήνη τοῦ Θεοῦ) If you do this, which I have said, if you cast your cares upon God. Εἰρήνη Θεοῦ here is the favor of God. See Ps. 28:11. Rom. 1:7, 10; 5:1. 1 Cor. 1:3. 2 Cor. 1:2. It is, however, a metonymy, because those who have peace among themselves are accustomed or ought to wish well to others.

The sense is the same in Num. 6:24. But in the Manuscript it is εἰρήνη τοῦ Χριστοῦ. Ἡ ὑπερέχουσα πάντα νοῦν) Which favor is greater than can be thought. These things, B. Luther connects and explains with the preceding as follows: See the beautiful order of the Apostle: He taught how we ought to be toward God, namely, that we should always rejoice in the Lord, creeping to him in joy.

Then if you ask: But what shall I do toward men? He says: Be equitable to all, forgetting yourself and yours, trusting in what is theirs. But how can I? The Lord, he says, is near. What if adversity presses?

How shall I always rejoice? Or what shall I do? Be anxious for nothing, refer all things to God through prayer and praise of God. But shall I be disturbed? By no means, but the peace of God will guard you in all things. And further: It is to be noted indeed, he says, that no one should rashly presume that in adversities he can arrive at this patience or peace by his own powers, either by despising or neglecting adversities, or as some are accustomed to say, by simply committing the cause to GOD, but with prayers, supplications, petitions, and thanksgivings added, one must be submissive, and thus nothing is to be worried about, with trust placed in the nearness of God.

For the Apostle does not assign the peace of God as a guardian of hearts, except to those who have first made themselves known to God by prayers and praises of God.

Although it does not matter much whether these are put forward in the manner of a wish or of a promise, there is no reason, however, why they should not be taken as a wish with B.

Luther. For the future is accustomed to be put for the Optative, and a similar example occurs in Rom. 16:20. And the Apostle is accustomed to include promises as well as exhortations in a wish, for the sake of testifying affection, Rom. 15:13. Eph. 3:16. Phil. 1:9, 3:5, 16. Col. 1:9. 1 Thess. 3:12, 13; 5:23. 2 Thess. 1:11, 12; 2:16, 17; 3:5, 16. Heb. 13:20, 21. 1 Pet. 5:10. By the peace of God is understood not the favor of God, but the best and greatest gift overflowing from the favor and grace of God, the peace and tranquility of conscience. Ambrose and B. Luther take it concerning the peace of conscience.

Latin:

Vers. 7. Καὶ ἡ εἰρήνη τοῦ Θεοῦ) Si hoc faciatis, quod dixi, si curas vestras in Deum rejicitis. Εἰρήνη Θεοῦ hic est Dei favor. Vide Ps. XXVIII. 11. Rom. I. 7. II. 10. V. 1. 1. Cor. I. v. 3. 2. Cor. I. 2. Est autem μεταωνυμία, quia qui pacem inter se habent, solent aut debent aliis bene velle.

Sensus idem Num. VI. 24. At in Manuscripto est εἰρήνη τοῦ Χριστοῦ. Ἡ ὑπερέχουσα πάντα νοῦν) Qui favor major est, quam cogitari possit. Hæc, cum superioribus ita & conne&it & explicat B. Lutherus: Vide ordinem pulchrum Apostoli: Docuit, quomodo nos habere debemus erga Deum, nempe ut gaudeamus semper in Domino, serpientes ei in lætitia.

Deinde si queras: Quid autem faciam erga homines? Dicit: Esto omnibus æquus, cui tuorumque oblitus, qua illorum sunt, confidens. At quomodo possum? Dominus, inquit, prope est. Quid si inslet adversitas?

Quomodo semper gaudebo? Aut quid faciam? De nulla re sis solicitus, omnia per orationem & laudem Dei ad Deum refer. At interturbabor? Nequaquam, sed pax Dei custodiet te in omnibus. Et porro: Notandum sane, inquit, ut ne quis temere præsumat in adversitatibus ad hanc patientiam vel pacem pervenire suis viribus se posse, aut contemnendo, aut negligendo adversitates, aut ut solent quidam dicere, DEO causam simpliciter committendo, sed additis orationibus, obsecrationibus, petitionibus, gratiarum actionibus, insubdendum est, & sic nihil curandum, in Dei propinquitatem fiducia posita.

Non enim pacem Dei custodem cordium Apostolus assignat, nisi iis, qui orationibus & laudibus Dei primum innotuerint Deo.

Quanquam vero non multum intersit, an in modum voti, an vero promissi hæc subjiciantur, nulla tamen causa est, cur non cum B.

Luthero pro voto habeantur. Futurum enim pro Optativo poni solet, & occurrit simile exemplum Rom. XVI. 20. Et consuevit Apostolus promissiones ut & adhortationationes voto includere, affectus testandi gratia, Rom. XV. 1. 13. Eph. III. v. 16. Phil. I. 9. cap. III. 5. 16. Col. I. 9. 1. Thess. III. v. 12. 13. cap. V. 23. 2. Thess. I. 11. 12. cap. II. 16. 17. cap. III. 5. 16. Ebr. XIII. 20. 21. 1. Petr. V. 10. Per pacem Dei non favor Dei, sed redundans è favore & gratia Dei donum optimum maximum, pax & tranquillitas conscientiæ, intelligitur. De pace conscientiæ Ambrosius accipit, & B. Lutherus. Conf. Rom.

## 4:9
V. 9. Matt. V. 5. Concerning which Aretius has it thus: As if he were to say, live modestly, as if the Lord himself were the inspector, who is not so far away.

And as if you were to say to a family: Be modest: The master of the family is present. Thus, for the disciples, the presence of the Teacher would have been an argument for tranquility.

B. Luther on the word: THE LORD is near: he says this, so that he may confirm joy in the Lord, and render them secure, and make them more eager for ease or equity of manners and conversation. For to a Christian man this ought to be enough, that the Lord is near him, that is, prompt, propitious, prepared to do all things which he may have desired. And with this knowledge of the Lord, he ought to be joyful and secure, to fear nothing, to seek nothing, to care for nothing, except that he himself may also be near to all men by a similar example, accommodating himself to be easy in their wishes, and showing himself to them such as he feels GOD is toward him, who certainly seeks nothing else than how he may be profitable to men and show himself easy in their conditions, forgiving them all sins, which by his right he could demand and avenge.

For unless he holds such an opinion of God toward himself, he will never be able to be joyful or secure.

But he who is sad and restless will not be easy and humane or equitable to all men.

Megalander exhibits the connection of the text thus: While he takes away one anxiety, he establishes another.

For he commends modesty to be exhibited to men, and as he says elsewhere: Being anxious to keep the unity of the Spirit, in the bond of peace, we ought not to be anxious for ourselves, as we have the Lord near and easy for all things, And as Eph. V. teaches, each one considering not what is his own, but what is of others. For that anxiety of keeping spiritual unity is the very modesty, equity, and ease which he teaches in this place.

After this he teaches how anxiety (which he forbids) toward God, since he is near to us, is to be rejected, saying: But in everything, etc.

For here a distinction must be made, and it is not to be connected with prayer, and it would be better rendered thus: But in any matter or in any thing, through prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your petitions be made known before God. So that the sense becomes: Let no anxiety take hold of you, but if anything attempts to make you anxious, do not care for it with your anxiety, but act thus, having laid aside anxiety, flee to God, pray, and ask, whatever you may have need of, let him be anxious for you.

And as Peter teaches, casting all your anxiety upon him, knowing that he cares for you, when saying in Psalm XL: THE LORD is anxious for me, for he involves himself in great questions, who, when any necessity comes, struggles first to extricate himself by his own prudence and his own strength, rather than to flee to God in prayer, indeed he also takes upon himself a fleeting and most vain business, since he cannot extricate himself, but involves himself all the more, the more stubbornly he labors to extricate himself while neglecting prayer, as we see in daily examples, both in our own life and in the lives of others in most unhappy turmoil.

And see how beautifully the Apostle opposes no thing and every thing. Be anxious for nothing, he says, but in everything, be anxious for no thing, but in any matter flee to GOD, sufficiently indicating that there are many things which attempt to make us anxious and restless, such as various tribulations and adversities, but they ought not to prevail over those who have the Lord near, with whom they can do all things by prayer and supplication, if only they ask.

Beautifully B. Hunnius: He names modesty or τὸ ἐπιεικές, as it is read in the Greek, when in any matters a convenient measure is kept, but especially when in human conversation one conducts himself so moderately and gently, that he is not too rigid toward others, nor is accustomed to mark the words and deeds of others with a censorious rod at his pleasure, or to demand them to the plumb-line of his own sense, but knows how to concede something to his neighbor, to indulge, to forgive, and to accommodate himself to him, as much as the reasons of duty and conscience allow. He wishes this lovable virtue to be made manifest toward all, not that each one ought to be a herald of his own virtue, but that by deeds toward everyone, ἐπιείκεια or lenity should be proclaimed, so that men may feel it, and perceive its pleasant and wide fruits. THE LORD is near.

This can be the reason for the Apostolic admonition, why our right is not to be urged so strictly in all things, but τὸ ἐπιεικές is to be embraced, because indeed THE LORD is near, because he beholds all evils at once, which are brought upon us by others, with a vindicating eye, and is accustomed to provide his divine help to the oppressed and afflicted.

Those four words, δέησις, προσευχή, αἴτημα (1 Tim. ch. II. ver. 1. there is ἐντευξις) εὐχαρισία, precation, prayer or supplication, petition, thanksgiving, are thus distinguished by Hilary, in his explanation of Psalm CXL. It is of our humility to deprecate, it is of the magnificence of God to be prayed to, it is of faith to petition, it is of confession and praise to glory.

Theodoret on 1 Tim. II. has it thus concerning this: Petition is indeed supplication, so that we may be freed from some evils and troubles.

But deprecation is the asking for good things.

Interpellation, however, is the accusation of those who affect us with injury.

Eph. ch. VI. Our wrestling is not against flesh and blood, but against Principalities, against powers, against the Princes of this world, against spiritual wickedness in heavenly places. Against them we interpellate the just Judge, and ask for just help. But thanksgiving is offered to GOD for the good things which have previously come to us.

Which explanation is approved by B. Balduinus, nor is it disapproved by us.

B. Luther, prayer is strong, he says, through supplication, but pleasing, and sweet, and exaudible through gratitude, so that thus by its fortitude and sweetness it may at the same time deserve to receive what is asked.

That, however, made known before God is said ἀνθρωποπαθῶς it is said, as very often in the Psalms such things, e.g. to perceive prayer with the ears, my prayer has reached his ears, etc. B. Luther beautifully: As smoke carries scent upward from the censer: so faith carries into the sight of God the petitions of believers, by which we certainly believe that our petitions will reach God, and that we will undoubtedly obtain what we ask.

Latin:

V. 9. Matth. V. 5. De quo Aretius ita habet: Quasi dicat, modeste vivite, tanquam inspectore ipso Domino, qui non ita procul abest.

Ac si familiae dicas: Modesti sitis: Adest herus familias. Sic discipulis praesentia Praeceptoris fuisset argumenti ad tranquillitatem.

B. Lutherus ad Verbum: DOMINUS prope est: hoc dicit, ut confirmet gaudium in Domino, securosque reddat, & ad facilitatem seu aequitatem morum & conversationis alacriores faciat. Christiano enim homini hoc satis esse debet, quod Dominus ei prope est, hoc est promptus, propitius, paratus ad faciendum omnia, quae desideraverit. Et hac scientia Domini laetus securusque nihil metuere, nihil quaerere, nihil curare debet, nisi ut simili exemplo & ipse prope sit omnibus hominibus, sese accommodans facilem in eorum vota, talemque se iis praebens, qualem sentit DEUM erga se, qui utique aliud non quaerit, quam quomodo profit hominibus & eorum conditionibus se facilem praebeat, donans eis omnia peccata, quae pro jure suo poterat exigere & ulcisci.

Nisi enim talem de Deo erga se opinionem tenuerit, nec latus nec securus esse poterit unquam.

Tristis autem & inquietus non erit facilis & humanus seu aequus omnibus hominibus.

Connexionem autem textus sic exhibet Megalander: Dum unam aufert sollicitudinem, alteram statuit.

Commendat enim modestiam hominibus exhibendam, & sicut alibi dicit: Soliciti servare unitatem Spiritus, in vinculo pacis, pro nobis soliciti esse non debemus, ut habemus Dominum prope & facilem ad omnia, Et ut Eph. V. docet, unusquisque non quae sua sunt, sed quae aliorum considerantes. Sollicitudo enim ista fervande unitatis spiritualis, est ipsa modestia, aequitas, & facilitas, quam hoc loco docet.

Post hoc docet, quomodo sollicitudo, (quam probibet) in Deum, quum prope sit nobis, rejicienda sit, dicens: Sed in omni &c.

Hic enim distinctio facienda est, & non connectendum cum oratione, & melius sic redderetur: Sed in quoliber seu in qualibet re, per orationem & obsecrationem cum gratiarum actione petitiones vestrae innotescant apud Deum. Ut fit sensus: Nullius rei vos capiat sollicitudo, quod si qua vos solicitos reddere tentat, nolite eam folicitudine vestra curare, sed sic agite, posita sollicitudine ad Deum confugite, orate, & petite, quodcunque vobis opus fuerit, finite illum sollicitum esse pro vobis.

Et sicut Petrus docet, projicientes in eum omnem sollicitudinem vestram, ficientes, quoniam ipsi cura est de vobis, cum Psalm. XL. dicendo: DOMINUS solicitus est mei, magnis enim quaestionibus sese miscets, qui veniente quacunque necessitate prius sua prudentia suisque viribus satagit sese evolvere, quam oratione ad DEUM confugere, quin fluitune quoque & vanissimum negotium sibi desumit, cum non possit se evolvere, sed eo magis involvat, quo pertinacius neglecta oratione laborat sese evolvere, sicuti videmus quotidiana exempla, tam in nostra quam aliorum vita tumultu infelicissimo.

Et vide, quam pulchre opponat Apostolus nullam rem & omnem rem. Nibil inquit soliciti sitis, sed in omni, de nulla re soliciti sitis, sed in qualibet ad DEUM confugite, satis indicans, multa esse, qua nos conentur solicitos & inquietos facere, utpote, varie tribulationes & adversitates, sed non debent praevalere iis, qui Dominum prope habent, apud quem oratione & obsecratione omnia possunt, si modo petant.

Pulchre B. Hunnius: Modestiam sive τὸ ἐπιεικές, ut in Graeco legitur, nominat, cum quibusvis in rebus conveniens servatur modus, maxime autem, quando in humana conversatione quis sese ita moderatum gerit & mansuetum, ut non nimis rigidus sit in alios, nec aliorum dicta & facta pro libitu censoria virgula notare, aut ad sui sensus amussim exigere consuevit, sed novit proximo aliquid concedere, indulgere, condonare, seque illi accommodare, quantum per rationes officii & conscientia licet. Hanc amabilem virtutem vult manifestam fieri erga omnes, non quod fue quisque virtutis praeco esse debeat, sed quod factis erga quosvis declamda sit ἐπιείκεια sive lenitas, quo sentiant eam homines, ejusque jucundos & latos fructus percipiant.

DOMINUS prope est. Potest hec esse ratio commonefactionis Apostolicae, cur non ita stricte in omnibus urgendum sit nostrum jus, sed ampledendum τὸ ἐπιεικές, quia nimirum DOMINUS prope fit, quia mala simul omnia, que nobis ab aliis inferuntur, vindice oculo adficiat, & afflictis oppressis divinam opem suam praestare soleat.

Quatuor illas voces, δέησις, προσευχή, αἴτημα (1. Timoth. cap. II. vers. 1. habetur ἐντευξις) εὐχαρισία, precatio, oratio seu obsecratio, postulatio, gratiarum actio, ita distinguit Hilarius, in explicat. Psalm. CXL. Humilitatis nostrae est deprecari, magnificentiae Dei est orari, fidei est postulare, confessionis est & laudis gloriari.

Theodoretus in 1. Timoth. II. de hoc ita habet: Postulatio est quidem supplicatio, ut a malis aliquibus & molestiis liberemur.

Deprecatio autem est bonorum petitio.

Interpellatio autem est accusatio eorum, qui nos injuria afficiunt.

Eph. cap. VI. Est nobis colluctatio non adversus carnem & sanguinem, sed adversus Principatus, adversus potestates, adversus Principes hujus seculi, adversus spiritualia nequitia in caelestibus. Adversus eos justum Judicem interpellamus, & justum auxilium petimus. Gratiarum autem actio DEO offertur pro bonis, que nobis prius obtigerunt.

Quae explicatio probata B. Balduino, nec nobis improbatur.

B. Lutherus, fortis est oratio, inquit, per obsecrationem, sed grata, & dulcis & exaudibilis per gratitudinem, ut sic fortitudine & dulcedine sua simul mereatur petita accipere.

Illud autem innotescans apud Deum ἀνθρωποπαθῶς dicitur, ut sæpius in Psalmis talia, v. g. auribus percipere orationem, pervenit in aures ejus oratio mea, &c. Pulchre B. Lutherus: Ut sumus odorem sursum fert à thuribulo: ita fert in conspectum Dei petitiones credentium fides, qua certo credimus, petitiones nostras ad Deum perventuras, nosque, quæ petimus, indubie impetraturos.

## 4:10
10. But I rejoiced in the Lord greatly.

That word μεγάλως (greatly) is often read among the interpreters of the Old Testament, the writers of Tobit and the Maccabees; he says he did not rejoice ὀχάρην μεγάλως (with great joy) for his own sake, but for the sake of the Gospel.

Greatly, says Chrysostom, because it was not a bodily joy; nor for his own recreation, but for their progress.

The pseudo-Apostles rejoiced because of gifts, for they served their bellies, Phil. III. The Apostle rejoiced because of the spirit, faith, charity, and gratitude of the givers.

He had received nothing from the Corinthians, although he could have, because of the pseudo-Apostles, who wanted to appear to receive nothing, 2 Cor. XI. 10, 20. But here he does receive, as Theophylact speaks, having found lovable and most desired givers, whom he would have undoubtedly offended if he had rejected their gifts. Ὅτι ἤδη ποτὲ ἀνεθάλετε τὸ ὑπὲρ ἐμοῦ φρονεῖν.

You have long since caused care for me to spring up in your mind. Ἀνάθαλεν here is transitive.

So also Ezech.

XVII. 24. it is used for the Hebrew הפרח. Sirach also uses it thus I.

15. XI. 22. Vulgate: For you have at length flourished again to think for me.

Beza and Schmidius: At length you revive in your care for me, in a much different sense: To which the Greek interpreters agree. But he silently reproves them too, says Theophylact, for the negligence of the past time, just as if he were reminding them of continuous giving.

Yet he hints at this and keeps silent, nor does he explain it more openly. But by saying "at length," he pretends a long duration of time, as if they had come to their senses after a long time. He drew "flourished again" from the metaphor of trees, which, although they may have seemed to have dried up for the most part, nevertheless sprout and flourish again, as if he were saying: You indeed, when you were flourishing by giving to those in need and doing what is right, have finally become drier, because you were sluggish in bestowing alms.

Yet you have flourished again now at last, because you have resumed that former and best custom of giving. And so, just as it results in their reproach, so it also results in their praise.

For it should not be considered a small thing to have flourished again at last, for those who have once withered. But lest anyone perhaps think that they had also behaved imprudently in other matters, he added, "to think for me," that is, in undertaking care for me and satisfying my needs. Ἐφ' ᾧ καὶ ἐφρονεῖτε) that is, and after that you always retained that affection in your mind.

"Exi" (for) after, as Heb. IX. v. 17. Thus the best Greek writers also often use it with the dative. Ηκαιρεῖσθε δὲ) No opportunity was given to you before this to show your affection, because there was no one suitable and prepared to undertake the journey whom you might send.

More correctly, as in the preceding comma, so here the Greeks, with the Vulgate, express the mind of the Apostle. Just as you were thinking, that is, says Theophylact, as you indeed held me in your heart: so you also undertook the care, and it was in your mind to provide for my needs.

For that is not unusual for you, that you should take care of me. But you were occupied, and it is not to be ascribed to your negligence, but to necessity, that some interruption of your benefit toward me and others occurred.

That "you were occupied" does not please the Vulgate, Beza, nor Crocius; who notes that Chrysostom and Theophylact interpret ἀκαιρίαν (lack of opportunity) as opportunity, which the word implies: but that he gives the cause of it, that they were in need.

Therefore, the interpretation is to be preferred: You were destitute of opportunity, whether because of poverty or because of a delaying messenger. Ver. 11. Οὐχ ὅτι καθ' ὑστέρησιν λέγω) I do not say this because I have had need of your liberality. Ὑστέρημα or ὑστέρησις, see above II.

30. Ὑστέρησις occurs regarding penury in Mark.

XII. 44. Tom. II. He does not deny that he was in penury before the gift was sent, as the Syrian, Cornelius à Lapide, and here Grotius [say]: but that he was anxious about it, as Theophylact explained: I do not complain about you because I am tormented by penury and look to my own affairs.

For thus the Apostle says later: I know how to be abased, I know also how to abound, v. 12. Ἐγὼ γὰρ ἔμαθον, ἐν οἷς εἰμι, αὐτάρκης εἶναι) I have learned to be content in whatever circumstances I am. Ἐν οἷς εἰμι, in those things which I find. Αὐτάρκης is said both of a thing which suffices, and of a man who is content with what he has.

Hence the virtue αὐτάρκεια (self-sufficiency), 1.

Cor. IX. 8. 1. Tim. VI. 6. "Content with the least," "content with a little" is often found in Cicero. Οἶδα κὶ ταπεινοῦσθαι) To bear myself patiently in meager circumstances. Οἶδα κὶ περισσεύειν) To use abundance with moderation.

For there is a metonymy in both verbs. Someone might say, what kind of virtue is it to know how to abound?

Theophylact answers with Chrysostom: A great one. For the luxury of things drives far more people to ruin than poverty itself, and it directs the mind to manifold desires and is much more absurd.

But how was the Apostle skilled in this abundance? Because what he had received, he consumed by imparting it to others.

Nor did he rejoice in the excessive abundance of things, but he held himself equally in satiety as in poverty: nor was he dissolved into luxury by the former, nor oppressed by the latter. Ἐν παντὶ κὶ πᾶσι) At any time and in any matter. Μεμύημαι) I have been initiated, that is, instructed.

The Apostle did not fear to transfer the word of Greek superstition to better uses.

For the word μυηθεὶς also comes from this. In the Glossary, μύω, to initiate, to imbue.

And here Ambrose placed "imbutus sum" (I have been imbued). Diodorus Siculus, "μυεῖν τὰς ἀνθρώπους τοῦτο δέ ἐστι διδάσκειν τὰ καλά" (to initiate men, this is to teach good things).

Whence he also wishes "μύσας" to be said, as if "μυέας." Note: this word [is from] the Macedonians, who had received the mysteries from the Thracians.

See Plutarch in Alexander. Καὶ χορτάζεσθαι) To take from a great abundance of things as much as is enough.

See Matth.

XIV. 20. chap. XV. 37. Mark VI. 42. VIII. 42. Luke IX. 17. John VI. 26. James II. 16. Καὶ πεινᾶν) Not only to be fed, but also to suffer hunger with an even mind, see 1.

Cor. IV. 11. Καὶ περισσεύειν) He repeats what he had said. Καὶ ὑστερεῖσθαι) The same meaning as just now in the word ταπεινοῦσθαι.

You have this word in Luke.

XV. 24. chap. XXII. 35. John II. 3. 2. Cor. XI. 9. 707 Deut. XV. 8. Compare here Gregor. M. homil. XIX. in Ezech. Thus the Apostle shows from these things that he was neither affected by sadness when the Philippians contributed nothing to him, nor that he rejoiced now that they were contributing, as the mind of mortals goes, but that he rejoiced greatly from their progress, as Theophylact [says] in this place.

Ver.

Latin:

10. Ἐχάρην δὲ ἐν κυρίῳ μεγάλως.

Illud μεγάλως saepe legitur apud Interpretes veteris Testamenti, scriptores Tobiz & Maccabaicorum, ὀχάρην μεγάλως (רב ששון) gauisum se ait non fui, sed Evangelii causa.

Magnopere, inquit Chrysostomus, quoniam non erat corporale gaudium; nec propter suum ipsius recreationem, sed propter illorum profectum.

Pleu-do-Apostoli gaudebant ob dona, ventri enim serviebant, Phil. III. Apostolus ob animum, fidem, charitatem & gratitudinem donantium.

A Corinthiis nihil acceperat, quum posset, ob Pseudo-Apostolos, qui volebant videri nihil accipere, 2. Cor. XI. 10. 20. Hic vero accipit, ut Theophylactus loquitur, amabiles nactus, & desideratissimos largitores, quos procul dubio offendisset, si eorum dona repudiasset. Ὅτι ἤδη ποτὲ ἀνεθάλετε τὸ ὑπὲρ ἐμοῦ φρονεῖν.

Pridem fecistis in animo vestro oriri curam pro me. Ἀνάθαλεν hic est Transitivum.

Sic & Ezech.

XVII. 24. ponitur pro Ebræo הפרח. Utitur sic & Siracides I.

15. XI. 22. Vulgatus: Quoniam aliquando refloruistis pro me sentire.

Beza & Schmidius: Tandem reviretis in vestra pro me cura, sensu multum diverso: Cui Græci Interpretes annuunt. Tacite autem & hos arguit, inquit Theophylactus, præteriti temporis negligentie, perinde ac si ad continuam largitionem commonefaciat.

Id tamen adumbrans reticet, nec apertius explicat. Tandem vero aliquando sum dicit, temporis diuturnitatem prætendit, quasi longo post tempore resipuisent. Refloruistis autem ex arborum metaphora traxit, qua etsi plerumque, exaruisse sint visæ, pullulant tamen & reflorent, tanquam id inquiat: Vos quidem florentes cum essetis, vestra egentibus largiendo, & quæ recta sunt, operando, aridiores estis tandem effecti, quia eleemosynas impertiri desides eratis.

Refloruistis tamen nunc demum, quia pristinam illam & optimam donandi recepistis consuetudinem. Ita itaque, ut sicut in eorum vituperationem id cedat, ita & laudem.

Neque enim parvi debet existimari, refloruisse tandem, qui semel aruerint. Sed ne quis forsitan hos arbitretur vel cæteris item in rebus se imprudentia gessisse, adiecit, pro me sentire, hoc est, in mei cura suscipienda, & necessitatibus meis satisfaciendo. Ἐφ' ᾧ καὶ ἐφρονεῖτε) id est, & post id semper eum affectum in animo retinuistis.

Exi post, ut Ebr. IX. v. 17. Sic cum dativo fæpe usurpant & optimi Græci scriptores. Ηκαιρεῖσθε δὲ) Non data est vobis antehac occasio ostendendi affectum, quia nemo erat idoneus & paratus suscipiendo itineri, quem mitteretis.

Rectius ut in præcedenti comate, ita hic Græci cum Vulgata mentem Apostoli exprimere. Sicut & sentiebatis, hoc est, inquit Theophylactus, ut cordi quidem me habebatis: ita suscepistis & curam, & menti erat, necessitatibus meis prospicere.

Id namque vobis est non insuetum, ut mei curam geratis. Occupati autem eratis, neque enim vestra est negligentia, sed necessitati est adscribendum, quod intermissio aliqua vestri in me & in cæteris beneficii facta sit.

Illud occupati eratis Vulgari Beza non placet, nec Crocio; qui notat, Chrysostomum & Theophylactum ἀκαιρίαν de opportunitate interpretari, quam verbum importat: Causam autem ejus reddere, quod inopes fuerint.

Ideo præferendam esse interpretationem: Opportunitate destituebamini, sive ob paupertatem, sive ob deferentem legati. Vers. 11. Οὐχ ὅτι καθ' ὑστέρησιν λέγω) Non ideo ego hoc dico, quod opus habuerim vestra liberalitate. Ὑστέρημα vel ὑστέρησις, vide supra II.

30. De penuria occurrit ὑστέρησις Marc.

XII. 44. Tom. II. Non negat, quod in penuria fuerit ante missum donum, ut Syrus, Cornelius à Lapide, & hic Grotius: sed quod de eo anxius fuerit, ut Theophylactus exposuit: Non propterea de vobis conqueror, quod penuria angar, atque meam ipsius rem spectem.

Sic enim postea Apostolus: Novi deprimi, novi etiam abundare, v. 12. Ἐγὼ γὰρ ἔμαθον, ἐν οἷς εἰμι, αὐτάρκης εἶναι) Didici contentus esse rebus quamvis arctis. Ἐν οἷς εἰμι, in iis, quæ reperio. Αὐτάρκης & res dicitur, quæ sufficit, & homo, qui eo, quod habet, contentus est.

Hinc virtus αὐτάρκεια, 1.

Cor. IX. 8. 1. Tim. VI. 6. minimo contentus, parvo contentus fæpe est apud Ciceronem. Οἶδα κὶ ταπεινοῦσθαι) In rebus exiguis patienter me gerere. Οἶδα κὶ περισσεύειν) Rebus abundantibus cum modo uti.

Est enim in utroque verbo μετωνυμία. Dicat aliquis, quænam illa est virtus, ut abundare quis sciat?

Respondet cum Chrysostomo Theophylactus: Ingens. Nam longe plures rerum luxuries agit praecipites, quam ipsa egestas, & ad multiplices animum intendit cupiditates & multo absurdiorem est.

Verum quo pacto hanc copiam callebat Apostolus? quia quod ille susceperat, impertiendo aliis confumebat.

Neque in nimia rerum abundantia giebiebat lætitia, sed aque se ut in satietate, ita & in egestate habebat: neque ex hac solvebatur in luxum, aut ex illa opprimebatur. Ἐν παντὶ κὶ πᾶσι) In quovis tempore & in quavis re. Μεμύημαι) Initiatus sum, id est, institutus.

Non formidavit Apostolus vocem Græcæ superstitionis ad meliores usus transferre.

Nam & μυηθεὶς vox hinc venit. In Glossa-rio μύω, initio, imbuo.

Et hic Ambrosius posuit, imbutus sunt. Diodorus Siculus, μυεῖν τὰς ἀνθρώπους τοῦτο δέ ἐστι διδάσκειν τὰ καλά.

Unde & dictas vult μύσας, quasi μυέας. Nota: hæc vox Macedonibus, qui à Thracibus mysteria acceperant.

Vide Plutarchum in Alexandro. Καὶ χορτάζεσθαι) Ex magna rerum copia sumere, quantum satis est.

Vide Matth.

XIV. 20. cap. XV. 37. Marc. VI. 42. VIII. 42. Luc. IX. 17. Joh. VI. 26. Jac. II. 16. Καὶ πεινᾶν) Non tenuitur tantum pasci, sed & famem pati æquo animo, vide 1.

Cor. IV. 11. Καὶ περισσεύειν) Repetit, quod dixerat. Καὶ ὑστερεῖσθαι) Eadem significatio, quæ modo in verba ταπεινοῦσθαι.

Habes hoc verbum Luc.

XV. 24. cap. XXII. 35. Joh. II. 3. 2. Cor. XI. 9. 707 Deut. XV. 8. Conf. hic Gregor. M. homil. XIX. in Ezech. Ostendit itaque ex his Apostolus, neq; mærore se fuisse affectum, cum nihil sibi Philippenses conferrent, neque illius nunc conferentibus, ut fert mortalium animus, gaudere, sed ex eorum profectu lætari magnopere, ut hoc loco Theophylactus.

Vers.

## 4:13
13. Πάντα ἰσχύω ἐν τῷ ἐνδυναμοῦντί με Χριστῷ) Paul had great strength, but he had received it from Christ.

Paul's merits were great, as Augustine says, but that they were in him, the grace of God had brought about, 2 Cor. III. 5. In the manuscript, the word χριστῷ is missing, so that τῷ ἐνδυναμοῦντί με becomes an antonomasia.

Becanus ignorantly concludes from this place in his manual that we can keep the law, and Salmero on this place, that we can resist in temptations, others [conclude] that priests could contain themselves.

It is not about priests, nor about continence, or resistance against all temptations, or the fulfillment of the law, but about αὐτάρκεια (self-sufficiency) in prosperous and adverse circumstances, which the Apostle attributes not to his own strength, but to divine power, and he says he can do all things not of himself, but in Christ.

And for that reason, Bernard extends this to other things as well in sermon LXXXV. in Cant.

Why should not all things be possible to one leaning on Him who can do all things? What a voice of confidence, "I can do all things in Him who strengthens me!" Nothing renders the omnipotence of the glorious Word more [glorious] than that He makes all who hope in Him omnipotent.

Finally, all things are possible to the believer.

Is he not omnipotent to whom all things are possible? Thus the mind should not presume of itself, but if it were strengthened by the Word, it would certainly be able to master itself, so that all injustice might not master it: Thus, I say, leaning on the Word. supported and clothed with virtue from on high, no force, no fraud, no allurement now, will be able either to cast down or to depress one who is standing.

Latin:

13. Πάντα ἰσχύω ἐν τῷ ἐνδυναμοῦντί με Χριστῷ) Habebat vires magnas Paulus, sed à Christo eas acceperat.

Magna erant Pauli merita, ut ait Augustinus, sed ut ea in ipso essent, fecerat gratia Dei, 2. Cor. III. 5. In Manuscripto deest vox χριστῷ, ita ut τῷ ἐνδυναμοῦντί με fit αὐτονομασία.

Imperite ex hoc loco in manuali Becanus colligit, legem nos servare posse, ac Salmero in hunc locum, quod resistere possimus in tentationibus, alii, tur, legem quod Sacerdotes continere possent.

Non de Sacer- à nobis servari posse. dotibus, nec de continentia, vel resistentia adversus omnes tentationes, aut de legis impletione, sed de αὐτάρκεια in rebus prosperis, & adversis agitur, quam non propterea suis viribus, sed divinæ virtuti tribuit Apostolus, nec de se, sed in Christo omnia se valere ait.

Atque ea ratione ad alia etiam hæc extendit Bernhardus sermone LXXXV. in Cant.

Quidni omnia possibilia sint innitenti ei, qui omnia potest? Quante fiducia vox, omnia possum in eo, qui me confortat? Nil omnipotentiam verbi gloriosiorem reddit, quam quod omnipotentes facit omnes, qui in se sperant.

Deniq; omnia possibilia sunt credenti.

Annon omnipotentes, cui omnia possibilia sunt? Ita animus non præsumat de se, sed si conforteretur à verbo, poterit utique dominari sui, ut dominetur non ei omnis injustitia: Ita inquam verbo innixum. & indutum virtute ex alto, nulla vis, nulla fraus, nulla jam illecebra, poterit vel stantem subjicere, vel deprimere.

## 4:14
Verf. 14. Nevertheless you have done well He does not say this to mean that I give you thanks. You have done well is a formula of one giving thanks. Concerning this expression we have spoken in Acts X, 33. Having communicated with my affliction that is, because you showed that you were touched by the sense of my calamities. Elsewhere this expression signifies the very fellowship of adverse things, as in Apoc. I, 9. partakers in the affliction. See also 2 Cor. I, 7. More convenient here is the commentary of Theophylact: He had said that he had enough: but lest the Philippians should take offense, just as if he were not accepting with a willing mind what was offered by them, or as if he considered what they had contributed to be less necessary (for those who confer benefits are wont to be offended when they have contributed something, while the recipients assert that they are not in need), he moderates and corrects these things, saying thus: Nevertheless you have done well, that is, even if I myself am in no need, yet the things which were sent to me as a gift by you were welcome.

He continues: Note, how prudently he extols the matter itself, when he says, communicating with my tribulation. For he also makes them equal to himself, as if he were saying, I indeed am the superior, but since care for me has been undertaken by you, God is not going to count you as unequal to me in the contest. But from the things said above, he has enticed their benevolence toward himself. And from these present things, he confirms both their dedication in giving and their readiness.

Latin:

14. Πλὴν καλῶς ἐποιήσατε Non hæc ait eo dico, ut vobis gratias agam. Καλῶς ἐποιήσατε formula gratias agentis. De hac locutione diximus Act. X, 33. Συγκοινωνήσαντές με τῇ θλίψει id est, quod ostendistis tangi vos sensu calamitatum mearum. Alibi hæc loquutio ipsam rerum aduerfarum societatem significat, ut Apoc. I, 9. συγκοινωνοὶ ἐν τῇ θλίψει. Vide & 2. Cor. I, 7. Commodior hic est commentarius Theophylacti: Dixerat se satis habere: verum ne Philippenses se se offendantur, perinde ac si animo non libenti ab his oblata acciperet, vel ut minus necessaria duceret, qua illi contulerant (solent enim offendi, qui beneficia conferunt, cum aliquid, afferentibus se non egere, contulerint) dicta hæc, sic inquiens, moderatur castigatque: Verumtamen bene fecistis, hoc est, vel si nihil ipse indigeam, fuere tamen per vos, qua mihi dono transmissa sunt, grata.

Pergit: Adverte, prudenter rem ipsam ut extollat, cum inquit, tribulationi meæ communicantes. Nam & pares sibi hos facit, tanquam inquiat, ipse equidem potior, verum cum mei fit per vos cura suscepta, nequaquam vos impares mihi in me certamine deputaturus est Deus. Ex superioribus autem dictis illorum in se pellexit benevolentiam. Ex iis verò præsentibus eorundem indectum in largiendo & voluntatem, & roborat promptitudinem.

## 4:15
Verf. 15. But you Philippians also know in order to praise them more, he says that they did this by custom, not by command. You also know, he says, implying that both they and others know, namely the companions of the journey, the partners of the labor, and the Church of Macedonia. that in the beginning of the Gospel when I first sowed the Gospel in Macedonia, the history of which matter is in Acts XVI and XVII. when I departed from Macedonia When also I was heading toward Attica, Acts XVII. 14, 15. No Church communicated with me in the matter of giving and receiving, but you only Since I had no accounts of expenditure or receipt with any Church, except with you. Benefits are not indeed wont to be entered into a calendar: but yet we often speak thus, as if they were entered into ledgers. I am in your ledgers of expenditure, you in mine of receipt. They had been the first to whom he had preached the Gospel in Macedonia; the first to receive it, the first to declare themselves grateful. This is indeed a huge praise, says Theophylact, and because in the very beginnings of the Gospel, and when you were not only providing for me the things necessary for my stay among you, but even when I was departing from Macedonia, that is, when I had crossed the boundaries of your region. For no Church gave to me, he says, but none communicated: for that reason, that he might exchange, receiving spiritual things for carnal ones.

Verf. 16. that even in Thessalonica both once and twice you sent to my need in Thessalonica for into Thessalonica. For that was, except for Beroea, the furthest of the cities of Macedonia which Paul saw. When he says, to my need, he understands for the uses of the poor, who were in other cities.

Once and twice, that is, more often, 1 Sam. XXVI. 8. 2 Kings VI. 10. Nehem. XIII, 20. 1 Macc. III. 30. Not only in the city, not only in the vicinity, but even in furthest Macedonia they helped him.

Theophylact adds: This redounds to their great praise, that Paul, residing in the metropolis and a larger city, was supported by a smaller one and with such great zeal. But why should we not understand the necessity of the Apostle himself, as the words sound: To my need. Thus the Greeks understood it entirely. But he calls the expenses necessary for use, says Theophylact, for he was not asking for delicacies and luxury.

Latin:

Vers. 15. Οἴδατε δὲ καὶ ὑμεῖς Φιλιππήσιοι ut magis eos laudet, dicit eos fecisse hoc more, non imperio. Nostis & vos, inquit, innuens, & ipsos, & alios nosse, nempe comites itineris, socios laboris, & Ecclesiæ Macedoniæ. ὅτι ἐν ἀρχῇ τοῦ Εὐαγγελίου cum primum Evangelium fevi in Macedonia, cujus rei historia est Act. XVI. & XVII. ὅτε ἐξῆλθον ἐκ Μακεδονίας Cum item Atticam versus, Act. XVII. 14. 15. Οὐδεμία μοί Ἐκκλησία ἐκοινώνησεν εἰς λόγον δόσεως καὶ λήψεως, εἰ μὴ ὑμεῖς μόνοι Cum nulla Ecclesia rationes habui expensi aut accepti, nisi vobiscum. Non solent quidem beneficia in calendarium referri: sed tamen sæpe ita loquimur, quasi ea in tabulas referrentur. Ego sum in vestris expensi tabulis, vos in meis accepti. Primi fuerant, quibus Evangelium in Macedonia prædicarat; primi qui reciperent, primi qui se gratos declararent. Ingens sane hæc laus, inquit Theophylactus, & quia in Evangelii ipsius primordiis, & cum non modo apud vos permanenti necessaria mihi subministratis, sed etiam ex Macedonia abeunti, hoc est, ubi vestræ regionis excessi confinia.

Non enim ulla Ecclesia mihi dedit, inquit, sed nulla communicavit: Ea ratione, ut pro carnalibus spiritualia capiens commutaret. Vers. 16. ὅτι καὶ ἐν Θεσσαλονίκῃ καὶ ἅπαξ καὶ δὶς εἰς τὴν χρείαν μου ἐπέμψατε ἐν Θεσσαλονίκῃ pro εἰς Θεσσαλονίκην. Nam ea fuit, excepta Berœa, extrema urbium Macedoniæ, quam vidit Paulus.

Cum dicit, εἰς χρείαν μου, intelligit ad usus pauperum, qui in aliis erant urbibus. ἅπαξ καὶ δὶς, id est, sæpius, 1 Sam. XXVI. 8. 2. Reg. VI. 10. Nehem. XIII, 20. 1. Macc. III. 30. Non tantum in urbe, non tantum in vicinia, sed etiam in extrema Macedonia ei fuccurrerunt.

Addit Theophylactus: In magnam hoc illis vel laudem cedit, quod in metropoli residens Paulus & urbe majori à minori & tanto studio aleretur. Cur vero non intelligamus necessitatem Apostoli ipsius, uti verba sonant: Εἰς χρείαν μου. Ita omnino intellexere Græci. In usum autem necessarias, inquit Theophylactus, dicit impensas, non enim delitias depofcebat & luxum.

## 4:17
Verf. 17. Not that I seek the gift, but I seek the fruit that abounds to your account I do not rejoice so much in these things given, as that from that liberality a huge fruit will return to you, God of course repaying it. Again he said, to your account, continuing the metaphor taken from merchants. Referring many things under this name as interest into the ledgers of receipt.

Piscator understands it of the fruit of faith. But most Interpreters more correctly with Grotius understand it of the fruit of the labor bestowed, of the Evangelical preaching, which redounds to their accounts. He teaches that this fruit is so compacted, that nothing at all from this expenditure of theirs departs from their own accounts, but rather it yields to them themselves before God as a profit entirely inestimable, as here B. Hunnius. Chrysostom: I do not say this for my own sake, but for yours, for your salvation. For I, while I receive, gain nothing. For the reward is laid up for those who give, but for those who receive, the things which they receive are consumed here. Such ledgers the Philippians had before God. For He was consigning all their expenses, as if they were credits, to be paid back both here and hereafter in heaven, and that with the greatest interest.

This therefore he wants: I look to this one thing, that I may provide for your affairs, that your ledgers may not be empty, but full of names, which you credit here to God, before whom there are no evils, and from the same you may receive with most ample interest, as Crocius well says here.

Latin:

Vers. 17. Οὐχ ὅτι ἐπιζητῶ τὸ δόμα, ἀλλ’ ἐπιζητῶ τὸν καρπὸν τὸν πλεονάζοντα εἰς τὸν λόγον ὑμῶν Non tam istis datis gaudeo, quam quod ex ista liberalitate ingens ad vos fructus redibit, Deo scilicet eam repensante. Rursum dixit, εἰς τὸν λόγον continuans tralationem à mercatoribus sumptam. Multos hoc nomine usuras referens in tabulas accepti.

De fructu fidei intelligit Piscator. Sed plerique Interpretes rectius cum Grotio de fructu collati laboris prædicationis Evangelicæ redundante in rationes ipsorum. Hunc fructum sic esse compactum docet, ut nihil quicquam ex hac erogatione illorum decedat ipsorum rationibus, sed potius ipsismet apud Deum in lucrum prorsus inestimabile cedat, ut hic B. Hunnius. Chrysostomus: Non mea causa hoc dico, sed vestra ad vestram salutem. Ego enim dum accipio, nihil lucror. Gratia dantibus enim illis est reposita merces, accipientibus vero hic consumuntur, quæ accipiunt. Tales tabulas habebant Philippenses apud Deum. Is enim consignabat omnia illorum expensa, tanquam credita, soluturus tum hic, tum olim in cælo, idque cum maximo fænore.

Hoc ergo vult: Hoc unum specto, ut vestris rebus consulam, ut codicilli vestri non sint vacui, sed nominum pleni, quæ Deo, apud quem nulla sunt mala, hic credatis, & ab eodem recipiatis cum fænore amplissimo, ut bene hic Crocius.

## 4:18
Verf. 18. But I have all I have rightly received all things. See Matth. VI. v. 2. This is I have, which clears Epaphroditus of faithlessness.

This does not only pertain to this, says B. Hunnius, that it signifies the gift entrusted to Epaphroditus, rightly cared for, and faithfully delivered, but also that it renders his own gratitude testified, for this timely and excellent benefit, by which he refers his own need as abundantly compensated. And I abound I have more than I desire. I am filled namely with joy, as 2 Tim. I. 4. or with consolation, as 2 Cor. VII. 4. There is no need for a supplement sought from elsewhere, the sense is clear by itself, I have been filled: namely, so that I desire nothing more, nay, that I may even be able to bring help to others.

Having received from Epaphroditus the things from you above II. 25. That from Epaphroditus is not placed here in the Manuscript. An odor of sweetness Whence the kind of speaking comes, we have said at Ephes. V. 2. There that expression is mystically adapted to the sacrifice of Christ: Here to the works of mercy, which themselves also are sacrifices, as will now be said. A sacrifice acceptable, well-pleasing to God we have said at Roman. XII. v. 1. There the expression is mystically adapted to the bodies of the pious, here truly to their works. Here is added acceptable, that is רָצוֹן without blemish.

For those victims which had a blemish, were not acceptable, Levit. XXII. v. 20.

Alas, to what height of dignity, exclaims Theophylact, did their gift raise them? For he did not, (he says) receive what was transmitted through you, but God did for me. Wherefore even if I myself am less in need twice over, it is by no means a loss to us. For God also was in no need at all of these, yet He receives and keeps them. Doubtless, having received by faith the victim of Christ, which is of the odor of a good fragrance, He makes it before God, that those things which are offered out of charity arising from faith, as sacrifices of gratitude toward God, and of beneficence toward one's neighbor, may be for Christ's sake also a good odor to God.

Latin:

Vers. 18. Ἀπέχω δὲ πάντα Recte omnia accepi. Vide Matth. VI. v. 2. Hæc est ἀπέχω, quæ Epaphrodito fidem liberat.

Hoc non tantum eò pertinet, dicente B. Hunnius, ut munus Epaphrodito concreditum, rectè curatum, fideliterque traditum significet, sed etiam ut animi sui gratitudinem testatam reddat, pro tempestivo hoc & eximio beneficio, quo indigentiam suam abunde pensatam refert. Καὶ περισσεύω plus habeo, quam desiderem. Πεπλήρωμαι nempe χαρᾶς, ut 2. Tim. I. 4. aut παρακλήσεως, ut 2. Cor. VII. 4. Non est opus supplemento aliunde petito, sensus per se luculentus est, expletus sum: scilicet, ut nihil amplius desiderem, imo aliis etiam opem ferre possim. Δεξάμενος παρ’ Ἐπαφροδίτου τὰ παρ’ ὑμῶν supra II.

25. Illud παρ’ Ἐπαφροδίτου hic in Manuscripto non ponitur. Ὀσμὴν εὐωδίας Unde fit loquendi genus veniat, diximus ad Ephes. V. 2. Ibi ad sacrificium Christi perfecti mum ea locutio mysticè aptatur: Hic ad opera misericordiæ, quæ & ipsa sacrificia sunt, ut jam dicetur. Θυσίαν δεκτὴν, εὐάρεστον τῷ Θεῷ diximus ad Roman. XII. v. 1. Ibi mystice aptatur locutio corporibus piorum, hic vero eorum operibus. Additur hic δεκτὴν, id est רָצוֹן fine vitio.

Nam quæ victimæ vitium habebant, non erant δεκταὶ, Levit. XXII. v. 20. Vah quo celsitudinis, exclamat Theophylactus, illorum munus evexit?

Non enim ipse, (inquit) per vos transmissa suscepi, sed prome Deus. Quocirca etsi bis ipse minus indigeam, haudquaquam nobis fit. His namque & Deus nihil prorsus indiguit, accipit tamen & servat. Nimirum fide suscepta Christi victima, quæ est odoris bonæ fragrantiæ, coram Deo facit, ut quæ ex charitate à fide oriunda offeruntur gratitudinis erga Deum, & beneficentiæ erga proximum sacrificia, propter Christum Deo etiam bonus odor sint.

## 4:19
Verf. 19. But my God God who holds as accepted what you have spent on me. This is emphatic, as Crocius notes, because he says my God, who sent me, who dedicated Himself entirely to me, who sustains, cherishes, consoles, defends me, to whom I have consecrated myself entirely in obedience of faith, who received the gift from your hand through me. Πληρώσει πᾶσαν χρείαν ὑμῶν) He shall provide all that which is necessary for you.

Thus Job 22. If God promises great things to those who feed the Levites, how much more to those who feed the Apostles? Κατὰ τὸν πλοῦτον αὐτοῦ ἐν δόξῃ) that is, according to His supreme power.

For πλοῦτον, as we have often said, signifies to Paul the abundance of anything whatsoever. And δόξα is used metonymically for power . See Eph. 3:16. In the manuscript here, as elsewhere, it is always κατὰ τὸ πλοῦτον in the neuter. Ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ) through Christ Jesus, as the giver and dispenser of all spiritual gifts; and so also of eternal life.

Why should we not understand πλοῦτον, as it properly sounds, of the opulence of the riches of the Lord, as Theophylact [does] according to His riches, that is, He who can equally and abundantly bestow necessary things upon you; why should we not accept δόξαν as 'in glory', that is, gloriously? B. Hunnius therefore renders the sense well: to the praise of liberality he adds the sweet promise of a reward laid up with God, promising that it will come to pass, as God (whom he calls his God from the nature of true faith) will in turn, out of the opulence of His riches and the most generous fountain of His kindness, abundantly pour out and dispense to them all those things at once, which they need both for the use of this life and for the attainment of future eternal things, and that through Christ Jesus, as it were the channel of God's temporal and heavenly goods and gifts.

Moreover, B. Luther and others, following Chrysostom and Theophylact, as well as Theodoret, take these not as a promise, but as a wish. Crocius judges that it does not matter much which way you translate it. For a wish contains a promise, because it is not empty; nor is it doubtful that whatever the Apostle promises in the name of God, he prays for that from the heart.

Latin:

Vers. 19. ὁ δέ Θεός μου Deus qui acceptum habet, quod in me impendistis. Emphaticum hoc est, notante Crocio, quod ait Deus meus, qui me misit, qui se totum mihi addixit, qui me sustentat, fovet, consolatur, defendit, cui me totum consecravi fidei obsequio, qui à manu vestra per me munus accepit. Πληρώσει πᾶσαν χρείαν ὑμῶν) Praestabit omne id, que est opus vobis.

Sic Iob. XXII. Si Deus magna promittit alentibus Levitas, quanto magis alentibus Apostolos? Κατὰ τὸν πλοῦτον αὐτοῦ ἐν δόξῃ) id est, pro summa sua potestate.

Nam πλοῦτον, ut sæpe diximus, Paulo abundantiam rei cujusvis significat. Et δόξα ponitur Metonymice pro potestate . Vide Ephes. III. 16. In Manuscripto hic, ut alibi semper est κατὰ τὸ πλοῦτον neutraliter. Ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ) per Christum Jesum, ut donorum omnium spiritualium; Ita & vitæ æternæ datorem & dispensatorem.

Cur non πλοῦτον, ut proprie sonat, intelligamus de opulentia divitiarum Domini, ut Theophylactus secundum divitias suas, id est, qui æque vobis abunde potest necessaria impertiri, cur non accipiamus δόξαν de gloria, in gloria, id est, gloriose? B. Hunnius itaque sensum probe reddit: Laudationi liberalitatis adjungit dulcem promissionem repositæ apud Deum retributionis, spondens futurum, ut Deus, (quem ex natura vere fidei suum Deum nominat) vicissim ex opulentia divitiarum suarum, largissimeque fonte benignitatis suæ illis ubertim fundat & eroget ea simul omnia, quibus & ad hujus vitæ usum, & ad futura perpetua consecutionem indigent, idque per Christum Jesum, veluti canalem bonorum & donorum Dei temporalium & cœlestium.

Cæterum non ut promissum hæc, sed ut votum accipiunt B. Lutherus & alii præeunte Chrysostomo & Theophylacto, ut & Theodoreto. Non multum referre judicat Crocius, utro modo reddas. Nam votum continet promissionem, quia non inane; nec dubium, quicquid Apostolus promittit nomine Dei, id ex animo precari.

## 4:20
Verf. 20. Τῷ δὲ Θεῷ καὶ Πατρὶ ἡμῶν) To God who is also our Father, so also Eph.

5:20. Καὶ δόξα εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων) that is, praise, Rom. 11:36, 16:27, Gal. 1:5, Eph. 3:21. Greek scholia take this doxology specifically, because thanks are given to God for the liberality bestowed by the Philippians.

But it is a general act of thanksgiving, with which the Apostle customarily concludes his epistle, which nevertheless can be referred at the same time to the preceding, as if, having certainly been heard, he now gives thanks to God for the wish previously expressed.

Latin:

Vers. 20. Τῷ δὲ Θεῷ καὶ Πατρὶ ἡμῶν) Deo qui idem Pater est noster, sic & Eph.

V. 20. Καὶ δόξα εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων) id est, laus, Rom. XI. 36. XVI. 27. Gal. I. 5. Eph. III. 21. Δοξολογίαν hanc Græcæ scholia specialiter accipiunt, quod Deo gratiæ agantur pro liberalitate à Philippensibus impensa.

Sed est generalis gratiarum actio, qua pro more concludit Apostolus epistolam, quæ tamen referri simul potest ad Antecedentia, quasi certe exauditus quod votum præmissum gratias jam de eo agat Deo.

## 4:21
Verf. 21. Ἀσπάσασθε πάντα ἅγιον ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ) That is, all those who have attained holiness through Christ.

The Syriac accepts it thus. Justinian's doubt, since the epistle was written to the Church of the Philippians alone, as to how he commands them to salute all the saints, is easily resolved, if indeed the Apostle could have deemed other saints in the vicinity or in all of Macedonia worthy of that salutation.

Latin:

Vers. 21. Ἀσπάσασθε πάντα ἅγιον ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ) Id est, omnes eos, qui per Christum sanctitatem sunt adepti.

Ita accipit Syrus. Justiniani dubium, cum ad solam Philippensium Ecclesiam exarata sit epistola, quomodo omnes sanctos jubeat salutare, facile expeditur, siquidem sanctos alios in vicinia vel in universa Macedonia ea salutatione dignari potuerit Apostolus.

## 4:22
Verf. 22. Ἀσπάζονται ὑμᾶς οἱ σὺν ἐμοὶ ἀδελφοὶ) Suppose Timothy, Linus, Clement of Rome. Ἀσπάζονται ὑμᾶς πάντες οἱ ἅγιοι) The Christians who are at Rome. Μάλιστα δὲ οἱ ἐκ τῆς καίσαρος οἰκίας) Certain freedmen, as is credible.

See above 1:13. Not inappropriately [does] Theophylact [agree] here with Chrysostom. Hence he also confirms them in the faith, showing that even the Emperor's family had reached this preaching, and that it signified that they who were in the Royal Palace, having despised other things, should follow Christ the Lord, how much more then [should] those who were far inferior be bound and compelled to do so?

He indicates furthermore that they [the Philippians] should share with these who were in the Royal Palace, for otherwise they would not share their greetings with those who were in the Royal Palace, unless they had heard that Paul had extolled the good deeds of these men.

Theodoret says he brought them great enough consolation when he taught that the divine Gospel holds sway even in the Royal Palace, and has taken the servants of the impious Emperor alive for life.

Latin:

Vers. 22. Ἀσπάζονται ὑμᾶς οἱ σὺν ἐμοὶ ἀδελφοὶ) Puta Timotheus, Linus, Clemens Romanus. Ἀσπάζονται ὑμᾶς πάντες οἱ ἅγιοι) Christiani, qui Romæ. Μάλιστα δὲ οἱ ἐκ τῆς καίσαρος οἰκίας) Liberti quidam, ut credibile est.

Vide supra I. 13. Non inconvenienter cum Chrysostomo hic Theophylactus. Hinc etiam in fide obfirmat eosdem, ostendens, vel Imperatoris familiam predicationem hanc attigisse, utque sibi, qui in Regia diverterentur, ceteris rebus contemptis, Christum Dominum sectarentur, quanto magis & bos, qui essent longe inferiores, id facere obstringi & cogi significaret?

Indicat præterea se apud hos Philippensium impertirent, qui in Regia essent, Nam alias nec salutem his impertirent, qui in Regia essent, nisi Paulum audissent istorum benefacta laudibus extulisse.

Satis magnam, inquit Theodoretus, eis consolationem attulit, cum docuit, quod etiam in Regia dominatum obtinet divinum Evangelium, & impii Imperatoris domesticos vivos cepit ad vitam.

## 4:23
Verf. 23. Ἡ χάρις τοῦ κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ μετὰ πάντων ὑμῶν, ἀμήν.) Rom.

16:20, 24, 1 Cor. 16:22, Gal. 6:18. In the manuscript: Μετὰ τοῦ πνεύματος ὑμῶν, as the Latin also reads. According to his custom, as Theophylact says, Paul concludes the epistle with a prayer, and reminds the Philippians that whatever virtue was in them, they should consider that they had attained it by the grace of Christ: and that they should not be puffed up with vain glory on account of it, and that it will come to pass that the grace of Christ will remain with them perpetually, if they are not proud.
