The reading of the Greek codices and of the interpreters of one manuscript and the Latin reading cannot make it doubtful, especially because he is accustomed to conceive his wish in this way in other epistles, Rom. 16:24, 1 Cor. 16:23, 1 Thess. 5:28, and he established this as the sign of his letters, 2 Thess. 3:18. THE GRACE OF OUR LORD JESUS CHRIST BE WITH YOU ALL.

AMEN!

Latin:

Vers. 23. Ἡ χάρις τοῦ κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ μετὰ πάντων ὑμῶν, ἀμήν.) Rom.

XVI. v. 20. 24. 1. Corinth. XVI. 22. Gal. VI. 18. In Manuscripto: Μετὰ τοῦ πνεύματος ὑμῶν, quomodo legit & Latinus. Pro sua consuetudine, dicente Theophylacto, Paulus comprecatione concludit epistolam, commonefacitque Philippenses, quicquid in se inesset virtutis, Christi gratia se assecutos fuisse existiment: neve ob id inani gloria efferantur, futurumque, ut perpetuo Christi cum eis maneat gratia, si minus superbiant.

Lectionem Græcorum codicum & Interpretum unius manuscripti & Latini lectio non potest dubiam reddere, imprimis, quia ita votum suum consuevit concipere in aliis epistolis, Rom. XVI. 24. 1. Cor. XVI. 23. 1. Thess. V. 28. & hoc signum literarum suarum constituit, 2. Thess. III. 18. GRATIA DOMINI NOSTRI JESU CHRISTI SIT CUM OMNIBUS VOBIS.

AMEN!

# Colossians

## 1:1 Introduction
[Abraham Calov, Biblia Novi Testamenti Illustrata (Vol. 2, Part 1). English: machine translation, The Faith Received (Mere Orthodoxy); the original follows each comment.]
All of Paul’s Epistles are excellent: but above all, those which were sent from Rome out of bonds. I judge the first of these in chronological order to have been that to Philemon. For at that time Epaphroditus, who is also Epaphras, was still with him: the second to the Philippians, where he sends back Epaphroditus. The third to the Ephesians, and at nearly the same time this one to the Colossians, while the things he had written to the Ephesians still clung to his mind: but the last of all is that which is the later one to Timothy. Colossae was a city of Phrygia, mentioned by Herodotus, and Xenophon, and Strabo, and Pliny, not far from Laodicea, which cities both collapsed due to an earthquake not long after this Epistle was written. Therefore they are not found in Ptolemy. That this Laodicea was near to Colossae is apparent below II. 1. IV. 13. 15. 16.

We admit the comparison of the Pauline Epistles, which were sent from Rome out of bonds, with those which were written before the captivity, which Grotius has from Theophylact, only with a grain of salt. For, not to speak of others before the captivity, does not the Epistle written to the Romans carry off the palm from all? Nor does the order which Grotius assigns deserve approval. For that which was directed to Philemon was transmitted together with this one to the Colossians, namely by Onesimus, as is evident from a comparison of chapter IV. 9 and Philem. v. 17, as well as the subscription of both Epistles. The Epistle to Philemon cannot be placed in the prior position, or preferred to that which was written to the Philippians, if Epaphras, as Grotius maintains at Phil. II. 25, is Epaphroditus. For Epaphroditus was sent from Rome to the Philippians with the Epistle dedicated to them. But when the Epistle to Philemon was given, Epaphras was a prisoner at Rome with Paul, Philem. v. 23. How, therefore, could he have been sent from captivity by Paul to the Philippians as a letter-bearer? Furthermore, Epaphras was still present with Paul at Rome when he wrote to the Colossians, Coloss. IV. 12, which Epistle Grotius acknowledges to be later than that which was written to the Philippians. But otherwise, that hypothesis of Grotius is not sound, that Epaphroditus is the same person as Epaphras. For Epaphroditus was a minister of the Philippian Church. "Leaders of the assembly of the Philippians," as Grotius has it at Phil. IV. 12. But Epaphras was a minister of the Colossian Church, Col. I. 7. Whom most interpreters also make distinct from Epaphroditus. Nor does any reason appear why we should believe the Epistle to the Ephesians to be later than that which was written to the Philippians. Nor is that argument of any weight, that this was destined for the Colossians at nearly the same time the Apostle wrote to the Ephesians, because, forsooth, the things he wrote here were still in his mind. For the Apostle, as a God-inspired writer, had no need to draw from memory what he should write, but received from the Holy Spirit what he ought to write, of whom he was only an amanuensis, receiving those things which the Holy Spirit dictated into his pen. Not to mention that the interpreters of the Epistle to the Ephesians do not compare this one so much with our own, as with the preceding one to the Philippians. Thus certainly Bened. Aretius in the proem to this Epistle: "Just as," he says, "in all others it has a great similarity with the Epistle to the Philippians, so also in the manner of composition. The principal part is hortatory, for he wishes to confirm them in the received doctrine, etc." This, I say, I do not make my own. For I do not disagree with difficulty with the more accurate judgment of B. Luther in the preface to this Epistle: "Just as the Epistle to the Galatians fashions itself and turns out after the Epistle to the Romans, and grasps in a short summary that which the one to the Romans sets forth more broadly and richly: so this one to the Colossians fashions itself after the one to the Ephesians, and also grasps the same content in a short summary." Which B. Hunnius demonstrates by parts in the preface of his Exegesis regarding all the chapters. But Cornelius à Lapide proves from this that this present one and that to the Ephesians were not written at the same time or impulse, because the latter was written in the previous year, when Timothy had not yet come to Rome, but this one later. Furthermore, if Chrysostom does not wish this to the Colossians to have been written at the same time shortly after that which the Apostle, already an old man, wrote to Philemon, as we observed in the proem to the Epistle to the Romans, Sect. 1. "This Epistle," says Matthias Flacius again in the argument of this Epistle, "altogether seems to have been written at the same time as that to Philemon." Wherefore he also greets them in the name of the same people, as also there to Philemon, namely in the name of Luke, Mark, Aristarchus, and Epaphras. He also makes mention in both of Archippus, as existing in another place and function among them. Finally, in both he indicates that he is writing through a certain Onesimus, his intimate. I do not doubt, therefore, that both were written at the same time, namely toward the end of the first captivity, around the fourth year of Nero. Thus Flacius. To whom others concur. B. Hunnius: "There was," he says, "among the Colossian citizens also that Philemon, to whom at the very time when Paul gave this to the Colossians, he wrote a private Epistle, by which he brought Onesimus, a fugitive slave, but converted to the faith of Jesus Christ in the bonds of the Apostle, back into favor with his master Philemon, and in that Epistle he also honorably mentions Archippus of the Church of the Colossians." Just as conversely in this Epistle, in the last chapter, he makes honorable mention of the slave Onesimus, commended and reconciled to Philemon.

Regarding Colossae, we give our assent to Grotius, that it was a city of Phrygia. For that Sebast. Münster makes the Colossians Rhodians, men named from the Colossus, that in no way agrees with ancient writers. For Herodotus, l. VII, calls it a great city of Phrygia. Xenophon, l. I, of the expedition of Cyrus, writes that he, after he had entered Phrygia, marched straight to Colossae, a populous, prosperous, and great city. See also Strabo, l. XII. Pliny, l. V, Hist. natur. c. 32. Whence Chrysostom and Theophylact, as well as Jerome, Oecumenius, and others, report that Colossae was a city of Phrygia in Asia Minor, near Laodicea and the Metropolis. That these cities were neighbors is evident from the Epistle itself, Col. IV. 13, 15, 16. However, it might seem strange that, although the Apostle had traveled through Phrygia, as Luke reports in Acts XVI and XVIII, he made no mention of this city or its neighbors; but regarding this, the following must be held.

In the Apostle's travels, only the lesser Phrygia is mentioned, not the greater, which was also called Pacatiana, in which Colossae was located. That the Apostle did not reach the Colossians is manifest from Col. II, v. 1. And therefore Gentianus Hervetus, the translator of Theodoret, in the argument of the Epistle, asserts otherwise, claiming that Paul had already seen and taught the Colossians before. Regarding what Grotius reports about Colossae and Laodicea, that both those cities collapsed due to an earthquake not long after this Epistle was written, and therefore are not found in Ptolemy, the following must be held: that not only those two, but a third also mentioned by Paul, Hierapolis, fell, as witnessed by Paulus Orosius, book VII, ch. 7, which they refer to the tenth year of Nero, when the Apostle was still among the living.

Laodicea is nevertheless still commemorated in the Apocalypse, ch. III, and it is evident from the annotations to his book on this Epistle that in the time of Theophylact, Colossae was called Chonae. Add to this that Baronius, from the argument of Theodoret, brings forward that in his time the house of Philemon still existed at Colossae. Wherefore it is likely that these cities, while horribly shaken, collapsed for the most part, but were not utterly destroyed. Which is also the opinion of our B. Hunnius.

Regarding the term from which the present Epistle dates, Erasmus, without cause, raises a difficulty with Lombard, opining that it was written not at Rome, but at Ephesus by Paul, who was imprisoned there. For not only from the appendix added to the Greek copies, "sent from Rome by Tychicus and Onesimus," is the place from which it was sent clear; but it is also evident from the Epistle itself, c. IV. 8, 9, that it was sent by them. And Onesimus had not fled from his master to the Apostle at Ephesus, but to Rome: nor was the Apostle imprisoned at Ephesus, but at Rome. From this, however, the wondrous zeal of the Apostle is evident, in that he did not cease in custody to care for such a distant Church. For Colossae is distant from Rome by more than 270 miles, according to the calculation of Bunting in his Itinerary.

As to the status or genus of the Epistle, it is indeed protreptic regarding the retention of the prior doctrine handed down by Epaphras, but because it is mostly occupied in explaining that doctrine which they are ordered to retain, it is properly didactic, and in that it is occupied most of all with that cardinal dogma of faith, that the reconciliation of Christ alone suffices for us for salvation, and that by faith in Christ alone we are righteous, by whose grace he condemns the alien doctrines of the Pseudo-Apostles concerning the reconciliation of the grace of God through mediating angels, concerning circumcision and the observation of Levitical laws, especially regarding the distinction of foods and days necessary for salvation: deducing two things from this porismatically, and subjecting exhortations not only general regarding the duties of the reborn, but also special, by which he admonishes individual orders of their duty. And therefore, after the completed introduction of the Epistle, the inscription and acro-connection, he connects a constant doxology, and also the premia of the Apostolic Epistle, which is completed in two parts primarily, namely the didactic, by which in ch. I and II the principal dogmas of the Christian faith are explained. The former indeed concerning Christ, and the Gospel concerning Christ; the latter, however, concerning the application of the grace of Christ, not through external circumcision, or the observation of ceremonial law, much less through the worship of angels, but through Baptism and faith in Christ: And the admonitory, by which they are reminded of duties worthy of a Christian, ch. III and the beginning of IV to v. 6. For the rest concern private matters and pertain to the Epilogue.

PART I.

Latin:

OMnes Epistolæ Pauli egregiæ funt: fed omnium imprimis, quæ Romæ ex vinculis missæ funt. Harum primam temporis ordine arbitror fuisse illam ad Philemonem. Nam tunc adhuc cum ipso erat Epaphroditus, qui & Epaphras: alteram ad Philippenses, ubi Epaphroditum remittit. Tertiam ad Ephesios, & eodem propè tempore hanc ad Colossenses, cùm adhuc, quæ ad Ephesios scripserat, in animo hærerent: postrema verò omnium ea, quæ posterior est ad Timotheum. Erant Colossæ, urbs Phrygiæ memorata & Herodoto, & Xenophonti, & Straboni, & Plinio, non longè à Laodicea, quæ urbes ambæ non multo post scriptam hanc Epistolam terræ motu corruêre. Ideo apud Ptolomæum non reperiuntur. Laodiceam istam vicinam fuisse Colossis apparet infra II. 1. IV. 13. 15. 16.

Comparisonem Epistolarum Paulinarum, quæ Romæ missæ sunt è vinculis, cum iis, quæ scriptæ sunt ante captivitatem, quam à Theophylacto habet Grotius, nonnifi cum grano salis admittimus. Nam ne de aliis dicamus ante captivitatem, annon palmam omnibus præripit Epistola ad Romanos exarata? Neque ordo, quem assignat Grotius, calculum meretur. Nam illa, quæ ad Philemonem directa, unà cum hac ad Colossenses transmissa fuit, per Onesimum scilicet, ut è collatione cap. IV. 9. & ad Philem. v. 17. nec non subscripione utriusque Epistolæ patet. Priori loco collocari non potest, aut præferri ei, quæ ad Philippenses exarata est Epistola ad Philemonem, si Epaphras, quod Grotius ad Philipp. II. 25. vult, Epaphroditus est. Nam Româ missus est Epaphroditus ad Philippenses, cum Epistola illis dedicata. Quum autem Epistola ad Philemonem daretur, Epaphras captivus fuit Romæ cum Paulo, Philemon. v. 23. Quomodo ergò è captivitate à Paulo ad Philippenses dimitti potuit ceu γεγραμ-τοφόρος? Porro Romæ adhuc adfuit Epaphras Paulo, cum ad Colossenses scriberet, Coloff. IV. 12. quam Epistolam illâ, quæ ad Philippenses exarata est, posteriorem agnoscit Grotius. Cæterum verò affinis non est hypothesis illa Grotiana, quod Epaphroditus item fit, qui Epaphras. Nam Epaphroditus Ecclesiæ Philippensis minister fuit. Principes cœtus Philippensium, ut ad Phil. IV. 12. habet Grotius. Epaphras verò Colossensis Ecclesiæ minister fuit, Col. I. 7. Quem plerique etiam interpretes ab Epaphrodito diversum faciunt. Causa etiam nulla apparet, cur Epistolam ad Ephesios posteriorem credamus eâ, quæ ad Philippenses scripta est. Nec alicujus ponderis argumentum illud est, quod hæc ad Colossenses destinata sit, eodem propè tempore, quo scripsit ad Ephesios Apostolus, quia nempe illa, quæ hic scripsit, adhuc in animo habebant. Nam Apostolus ceu Scriptor θεόπνευσος è memoria depermere opus non habebat, quæ scriberet, sed à Spiritu S. accipiebat, quæ scribere debuit, cujus amanuensis tantum fuit excipiens illa, quæ Spiritus S. dictabat in calamum. Ne de eo dicam, quod non tam Epistolæ ad Ephesios Interpp. comparent hanc nostrâ, quàm præcedenti ad Philippenses. Ita certè Bened. Aretius in procœm. ad hanc Epistolam: Quemadmodum, inquit, in aliis omnibus magnam habet similitudinem cum Epistola ad Philippenses, sic quoq; in genere compositionis. Principale est Protrepticum, vult enim eos confirmare in recepta doctrina, &c. Non hoc, inquam, meum facio. Nam haud ægrè assentior B. Lutheri in præfat. hujus Epistolæ judicio accuratiori: Gletchwie die Epistel an die Galater sich artet, und gerathen ist nach der Epistel an die Römer, und eben dasselbige mit kurzem Begriff fasset, das die an die Römer weiter und reicher ausführet: Also artet sich diese an die Colosser nach der an die Epheser, und fasset auch mit kurzem Begriff denselbigen Inhalt. Quod per partes demonstrat in præfat. Exegef. suæ B. Hunnius quoad omnia capita. Non autem eodem tempore aut impetu hanc præsentem & illam ad Ephesios scriptam esse hinc probat Cornelius à Lapide, quod illa anno priore, cum nondum Romam venisset Timotheus, scripta sit, hæc verò posterius. Porrò si non eodem tempore brevi post eam, quam ad Philemonem jam fenex scripsit Apostolus, hanc ad Colossenses exaratam esse vult Chrysostomus, ut observavimus in proœm. Epistolæ ad Romanos Sect. 1. Hæc Epistola, inquit denuo in argumento hujus Epistolæ Matth. Flacius, omnino videtur esse eodem tempore scripta, quo illa ad Philemonem. Quare etiam nomine eorundem eos salutat, ut & ibi ad Philemonem, nempe nomine Lucæ, Marci, Aristarchi, & Epaphræ. Facit etiam in utraque mentionem Archippi, tanquam alio loco & functione apud eos existentis. Denique in utraque indicat se scribere per Onesimum quendam suum familiarem. Non dubito igitur utramque eodem tempore esse scriptam, nempe sub finem captivitatis prioris circa quartum Neronis annum. Hæc Flacius. Cui suffragantur alii. B. Hunnius: Fuit, inquit, ex Colossensibus civibus etiam ille Philemon, ad quem eo ipso tempore, quo hanc ad Colossenses dedit Paulus, privatam exaravit Epistolam, qua Onesimum servum fugitivum, sed in vinculis Apostoli ad fidem Jesu Christi conversum, cum Philemone bero in gratiam redegit, inque illa Epistola simul Archippi Ecclesiæ Colossensium honorifice meminit. Quemadmodum vicissim in hac Epistola capite ultimo, mentionem honestam facit servi Onesimi, Philemoni commendati & reconciliati.

De Colossis assenfum præbemus Grotio, quod urbs Phrygiæ fuerint. Nam quod Sebast. Münsterus Colossenses Rhodios facit, dictos à Colosso homines, id nullo pacto antiquis scriptoribus convenit. Herodotus enim l. VII. vocat magnam Phrygiæ civitatem. Xenophon l. I. de expeditione Cyri, scribit, illum postquam Phrygiam ingressus est, tendisse rectà εἰς Κολοσσάς πόλιν οἰκουμένην εὐ-δαίμονα κ; μεγάλην. Vid. & Strabo l. XII. Plinius l. V. Hist. natur. c. 32. Unde Chrysostomus & Theo- phylactius, nec non Hieronymus, Oecumenius, alii tradunt, Colossas urbem Phrygiae in minore Asia, vicinam Laodiceae, & Metropoli. Quas urbes vicinas fuisse ab ipsa Epistola patet Col. IV. 13. 15. 16. Mirum autem videri possit, quod cum Apostolus Phrygiam peragrasset, Act. XVI. & XVIII. tradiderit Lucas, nullam hujus civitatis, aut vicinarum mentionem fecerit, sed de eo ita habendum.

In peregrinationibus Apostoli minores tantum Phrygiae mentionem fieri, non majoris, quae & Pacatiana dicta, in qua erant Colossae. Ad Colossenses non pervenisse Apostolum e Col. II. v. 1. manifestum est. Ideoque aliter Gentianus Hervetus, Theodoretis interpres, in Epistolae argumento, Paulum jam ante Colossenses vidisse, & docuisse afferens. Quod de Colossis & Laodicea refert Grotius, ambas illas urbes non multo post scriptam hanc Epistolam terrae motu corruisse, ideo apud Ptolemaeum non reperiri, de eo ita habendum: non duas illas tantum, sed tertiam etiam Paulo memoratam Hierapolin concidisse, teste Paulo Orosio lib. VII. c. 7. quod ad decimun Neronis annum, quum adhuc in vivis esset Apostolus, referunt.

Commemoratur tamen adhuc in Apocalypsi Laodicea cap. III. & Theophylacti tempore Colossas Chonas dictas esse, ex annotationibus ad libr. ejus in hanc Epistolam constat. Adde, quod Baronius ex Theodoreti argumento adferat, quod illius tempore domus Philemonis Colossis extiterit. Quapropter verisimile est, urbes has horribiliter quidem concussas, magna ex parte corruisse, non autem penitus eversas esse. Quae etiam B. Hunnii nostri est sententia.

De termino a quo praesentis Epistolae, citra causam, difficultatem cum Lombardo movet Erasmus, opinatus eandem non Romae, sed Ephesi scriptam esse ab incarcerato ibidem Paulo. Nam non tantum ex appendice Graecis exemplaribus adjecta, missa e Roma per Tychicum & Onesimum, locus unde missa, luculentus est; sed etiam ex ipsa Epistola c. IV. 8. 9. per eosdem missam esse constat. Ac onesimus ab hero suo non Ephesum profugerat ad Apostolum, sed Romam: nec Ephesi, sed Romae vinctus erat Apostolus. Ex eo autem mirificus zelus Apostoli patet, quod in custodia non cessavit curam gerere tam dissitae Ecclesiae. Colossae enim Roma distant plus quam 270. milliaribus, juxta calculum Buntingii in Itinerario.

Quod ad statum vel genus Epistolae attinet, pro Status, vel genus Epistolae. trepticum id quidem est de retinenda priori doctrina ab Epaphra tradita, sed quia maxime occupatur in explicanda illa doctrina, quam retinere jubentur, proprie didacticum est, & in illo maxime adeo, archidinali fidei dogmate occupatur, solius Christi reconciliationem nobis ad salutem sufficere, fideq; in Christum nos unice justos esse, cujus gratia damnat Pseudo-Apostolorum alienas doctrinas de gratia Dei per angelos mediatores concilianda, de circumcisione atq; observatione legum Leviticarum, imprimis quoad discrimen ciborum & dierum ad salutem necessaria: promore duo deducens hinc πορισματικῶς, & subjiciens Paraneses non tantum generales de officiis renatorum, sed etiam speciales, quibus singulos ordines sui officii admonet. Ideoque post confectum ingressum Epistolae ἐπιγραφῇ & acroconnectit constantem δοξολογίαν, nec non prae mia Epist. Apostolica duabus imprimis absolvitur partibus, utpote διδαχικῇ, qua c. I. & II. praecipua dogmata fidei Christianae explicantur. Priori quidem de Christo, & Evangelio de Christo; altero autem de applicatione gratiae Christi, non per circumcisionem externam, aut observationem legis ceremonialis, nedum per angelorum cultum, sed per Baptismum & fidem in Christum: Et νουθετικῇ, qua ad officia Christiani digna commonefiunt, cap. III. & initio IV. ad v. 6. Caetera enim privata concernunt, & ad Epilogum pertinent.

PARS I.

## 1:1 Argument
DIDACTIC OF THE EPISTLE. CHAPTER I. ARGUMENT AND PARTITION. With the subscription, as they call it, and the inscription and prayer having been premised, the Apostle gives thanks to God for the faith of the Colossians received from Epaphras, and explains that he prays perpetually for their sake, and by that reason prepares an approach for himself to the dogma which he has decided to teach primarily: explaining the redemption of Christ, and the eternal Deity of this redeemer and sole head of the Church, and the personal union made to that end, that all things might be reconciled solely through him by his blood and death, through whom they also have been reconciled, formerly to be presented to the same, provided they persist in the faith of the Gospel: Of which he rejoices to be a minister, even in his passion, in which

Occasion of the Epistle. However, the occasion of the Epistle must not be passed over in silence. Seek this in the fact that the Apostle had heard of the faith of the Colossians, primarily from Epaphras and Onesimus, Col. I. 8, ch. IV. v. 12, and also of the danger of seduction through the Philosophy and traditions of certain Pseudo-Apostles, who were spreading Platonic dogmas about the mediation of angels, and who were Judaizing regarding circumcision and the ceremonial law, concerning the necessity of the distinction of foods, days, and feasts, as from chapter

II. 8, 11, 16, 18, c. I. 16, 18, it is clear, concerning which Theophylact in the prologue: For from these some perverse dogma had recently been received. For some were thinking, denying that the way to God and the Father lay through the Son, but through angels, deeming it absurd to believe that the Son of God would come in the fullness of time, since in the Old Testament all things were carried out by the ministry of angels. They were observing, moreover, most Jewish institutions, the customs of the nations, avoiding days and hours and foods: all of which, since they had to be corrected, impelled the Apostle to write this Epistle. Thus, therefore, he deemed it necessary, perhaps also prompted by their faithful teacher Epaphras, to give this Epistle to the Colossians, and from the same, for a not ambiguous cause, he wished it to be communicated to the neighboring Laodiceans, as being subject to a similar danger.

For he repeats, and excellently explains in the same, the principal article of faith concerning Christ, the eternal Son of God, the creator of Angels, the sole Mediator and Reconciler of the human race, against fictitious Mediators, and concerning the un-hand-made Circumcision, which succeeded in place of external circumcision, the same having been abrogated, namely the Sacrament of Baptism, and the evacuation of Levitical ceremonies, which were a shadow of the true body which we have in Christ, whose benefits through death, burial, resurrection, and triumph over our enemies, and liberation from the Law, he describes graphically. Wherefore, Davenant, Bishop of Salisbury, did not poorly establish the scope of the Epistle: that all hope of human salvation is placed in Christ alone; therefore one must acquiesce in the faith of Christ, and live according to the prescription of the Gospel, having rejected Mosaic ceremonies, and whereby the glorious riches may be exhibited, and whereby each one may be perfect in himself in Christ Jesus. There are two parts of the chapter, I. παρασκευαστικὴ, Preparatory, consisting of the inscription at v. 2. Eucharist at v. 8. and the office of prayer at v. 12. II.

Didactic, both concerning the unique Redeemer Christ, at v. 22, and concerning the Gospel, and its ministry at v. 29, and the last.

PART I.

PREPARATORY.

Ver. 1. Paul an Apostle of Jesus Christ by the will of God) The same beginning as to the Ephesians. Theophylact however observes that thus, immediately at the beginning, the dogma scattered among the Colossians is tacitly removed, when he calls himself an Apostle of Christ, not of Angels, and that this is done by the will of God, because he was his Apostle, not of the Angels, and the praise of truth is reconciled to the Apostle, if he performs the office of Apostleship according to the will of God, it is clearly evident that he himself preaches the truth.

The name of Apostle by the primary usage of the Scriptures belongs to those who (1) were called immediately by God, Luke 6, 13. John 20, 21. (2) were immediately inspired by the Holy Spirit, John 16, 13. c. 20, 21. (3) were instructed by a universal command to inform the whole world, Matt. 28, 19. seq. Mark 16, 15. all of which things that are set forth apply to Paul, Acts 15, 23. seq. Gal. 1, 12. Rom. 1, 5. None of the Roman Pontiff: whence he can by no reason be called an Apostle, or an Apostolic Bishop.

And Timothy the brother) He adds his name for this reason, because he was well known to the Colossians, as one who had at some time been sent to them.

Concerning this mission nothing is certain from the Scriptures. Theophylact gives another reason, namely that he wished to insinuate Timothy to the same Apostles in this way. Therefore, since Timothy himself was an Apostle, he was deservedly to be insinuated to their knowledge.

He was an Apostle of another order, as was said at Phil. 2, 25: who therefore also wished to be sent to various Churches. Nor could his fame be unknown. Therefore he wished to reconcile authority both to him and to his Epistle, as being given by two Apostles, and the love and care which he wished to testify, because he also joined Timothy to himself in confirming them in the faith, and in procuring their salvation.

Latin:

EPISTOLAE DIDACTICA. CAP. I. ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO. Pramissa subscriptione, quam vocant, & inscriptionie, ac voto, gratias agit Deo Apostolus pro fide Colossensium ab Epaphra accepta, & quod maxime ipsorum causa perpetuo precetur, exponit, eae, ratione sibi aditu parat ad dogma, quod praecipue tradere constituit: explicans redemptionem Christi, & hujus redemptoris, capitisq; Ecclesiae unici aeternam Deitatem, eoque fine factam unionem personalem, ut unice per ipsum reconciliarentur omnia per sanguinem & mortem ejus, per quem etiam ipsi reconciliati sint, olim eidem sistendi, modd in fide Evangelii persistant: Cujus se ministrum esse, etiam in passione sua, gaudet, in quo

Occasio Epistolae. Non tacenda autem occasio Epistolae. Quaerat haec, quod audierit Apostolus de fide Colossensium, imprimis ex Epaphra, & Onesimo Col. I. 8. cap. IV. v. 12. nec non de periculo seductionis per Philosophiam, & traditiones Pseudo-Apostolorum quorumdam, dogmata Platonica de angelorum mediatione spargentium, & quoad circumcisionis, & legis ceremonialis, de discrimine ciborum, dierum & festorum necessitatem, judaizantium, ut e cap.

II. 8. 11. 16. 18. c. I. 16. 18. luculentum est, de quo Theophylactus in prologo: Ab his namque pravum aliquod dogma erat nuper susceptum. Putabant namque aliqui negantes per filium, sed per angelos ad Deum & Patrem viam patere, absurdum existimantes Dei filium credere utemilis seculis adventurum, quandoquidem in V. Test. angelorum cuncta ministerio gererentur. Servabant praeterea Judaica pleraque instituta, gentium mores, dies cavendo & horas & escas: quae omnia cum corrigenda essent, Apostolum us hanc Epistolam scriberet, impulere. Ita ergo necessarium duxit, forte etiam monente fideli ipsorum Doctore Epaphra, ad Colossenses hanc Epistolam dare, atque ex eadem, prolix ambiguo, causa eandem & Laodicensibus vicinis, utpote simili periculo obnoxiis, communicari voluit.

Repetit enim, & praeclare exponit in eadem articulum fidei praecipuum de Christo, aeterno Dei Filio, de creatore Angelorum, unico Mediatore, ac Conciliatore generis humani, adversus fictitios Mediatores, deq; Circumcisione ἀχειροποιήτῳ, quae in locum externae circumcisionis, eadem abrogata successit, Sacramento nempe Baptismi, & evacuatione Leviticarum ceremoniarum, quae umbra fuerunt veri corporis, quod habemus in Christo, cujus beneficia per mortem, sepulturam, resurrectionem, & triumphum de hostibus nostris, ac liberationem e Lege graphice describit. Quapropter scopum Epistolae non male constituit Davenantius, Episcopus Saresburiensis: in solo Christo repositam esse omnem salutis humanae spem; proinde acquiescendum esse in fide Christi, & vivendum juxta praescriptum Evangelii, rejectis ceremoniis Mosaicis, & speculationibus philosophicis. quo divitiae gloriosae exhibeantur, & per quod unusquisque perfectus sibi possit in Christo Jesu. Partes duae sunt capitis, I. παρασκευαστικὴ, Praeparatoria, constans ἐπιγραφῇ ad v. 2. Eucharistia ad v. 8. & precationis officio ad v. 12. II.

Didactica tum de Redemptore unico Christo, ad v. 22. tum de Evangelio, ejusque ministerio ad v. 29. & ultimum.

PARS I.

PRAEPARATORIA.

Vers. 1. Παῦλος Ἀπόστολος ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ διὰ θελήματος θεοῦ) Idem initium, quod ad Ephesios. Theophylactus tamen observat, ita initio statim, sed tacite dogma tolli apud Colossenses sparsum, cum Christi se dicit, non Angelorum Apostolum, idque voluntate Dei fieri, quod ejus, non Angelorum esset Apostolus, & veritatis laudem Apostolo conciliari, si pro Dei voluntate Apostolatus munere fungatur perspicuum sane ipsum vera praedicare.

Apostoli nomen ex usu Scripturis praecipuo convenit iis, qui (1) immediate a Deo vocati, Luc. 6, 13. Job. 20, 21. (2) per Spiritum S. immediate inspirati, Job. 16, 13. c. 20, 21. (3) universali praecepto ad orbem terrarum informandum instructi fuere, Matt. 28, 19. seq. Marc. 16, 15. quae προσκείμενα omnia Paulo conveniunt, Act. 15, 23. seq. Gal.

1, 12. Rom. 1, 5. Nulla Romani Pontificis: unde hic nulla ratione Apostolus, aut Episcopus Apostolicus dici potest. Καὶ Τιμόθεος ὁ ἀδελφος) Hujus nomen ideo adjungit, quod probe notus esset Colossensibus, ut qui aliquando eo missus fuisset.

De hac missione nihil constat e Scripturis. Aliam causam reddit Theophylactus, nempe quod ita Timotheum insinuare voluerit iisdem Apostolis. Ergo Timotheus ipse cum esset Apostolus, merito istorum cognitioni erat insinuandus.

Apostolus erat alterius ordinis, ut ad Phil. 2, 25. dictum: qui proinde etiam ad varias Ecclesias mitti volebat. Nec fama ejus ignota esse poterat. Auctoritatem ergo & eidem, & Epistolae suae, utpote a duobus Apostolis datae conciliare volebat, amoremque ac curam quam testari, quod etiam Timotheum sibi junxerit in ipsorum fide confirmanda, & salute procuranda.

## 1:2
Ver. 2. To the saints and faithful brethren in Christ who are at Colossae) So to the Ephesians. We add what Theophylact has: But whence have you obtained this holiness? Is it not from Baptism already instituted in the death of Christ? Whence were you made faithful? Is it not because you believe in Christ, and through Christ holy mysteries have been entrusted to you? Therefore we are faithful not only from the faith of Christ, but because mysteries have been entrusted to us by God, which not even the Angels themselves had known.

Whence also are we rendered Brethren? Is it from works and our own offices? By no means, but in Christ. Why therefore do you ascribe to Angels that which they themselves lead to the Father.

Latin:

Vers. 2. Τοῖς ἐν Κολοσσαῖς ἁγίοις καὶ πίστοις ἀδελφοῖς ἐν χριστῷ) Sic ad Ephesios. Addimus, quae habet Theophylactus: Verum unde hanc estis vos sanctitatem adepti? Nonne ex Baptismo in morte Christi jam instituto? Unde fideles effecli? Nonne quia in Christum creditis, & per Christum sancta sunt vobis mysteria credita? Fideles itaque non solum sumus ex fide Christi, sed quia a Deo nobis sunt mysteria demandata, quae nec Angeli ipsi cognorant.

Unde & Fratres nos redditi? num ex operibus & nostris officiis? Minime, sed in Christo. Cur ergo Angelis, quod ad Patrem deducant ipsi, adscribitis.

## 1:3
Ver. 3. Grace to you, and love from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ) Eph. 1, 2. In many Greek and Latin codices this "Lord Jesus Christ" is absent, as also in the Syriac.

That it does not abound in the received [texts], and those which are superior in both number and authority; but that it is lacking in those codices which Grotius praises, the collation of a similar passage in Eph. 1 and the consensus of interpreters teaches. We give thanks to God and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ always praying for you) Eph. 1, 16. But that "always" coheres with "praying," as can be seen in Rom. 1, 10. Phil. 1. Ver. 4. Having heard of your faith in Christ Jesus, and the love which you have to all the saints) Eph. 1, 15. In the Manuscript "the love which you have to all the saints," as the Latin also reads.

Christ, says Theophylact, is our Lord, not the Angels, who are servants. And further: We give thanks, because it has been reported to us through Epaphras that your faith [is], not that which consists in Angels, but which is in Christ. Because Christ is anointed for us, and is Jesus to all, because he also saved the people from their sins. But he names faith before charity, because faith is the root and mother of charity, Gal. 5, 6. Ver. 5.

Because of the hope which is laid up for you in the heavens) He calls that hope which is hoped for, as Eph. 1, 18. Life eternal and heavenly promised by Christ excites both faith and love.

Thus it is called "laid up," because it is kept for someone, as 2 Tim. 4, 8. Deut. 32, 34. Faith and love are not said to be EXCITED by eternal life, or the promise of the same, although that can truly be said, if only the Popish sense is absent, that we merit eternal life through charity: and the Arminian and Socinian [sense], that the word of GOD works only softly, by persuading and promising in our conversion, regeneration, and production. For divine promises excite faith, excite love, but the operation of the Holy Spirit through the word is not to be excluded: we can also work well in view of divine promises, although good works are not the meritorious cause of eternal life.

Theophylact, although he adduces that sense: Cultivate, brothers, not with the hope of human things, but with the expectation of future goods. He adds however another interpretation more congruent: Or we give thanks for this, because you are about to have an inheritance, even if of immortality.

Indeed three causes are brought forward by Paul, for which he has to give thanks to God. First faith, then charity, third the hope of the Colossians. Which sense most Interpreters follow.

Faith in Christ is founded in his propitiatory blood, Rom. 3, 25. Charity is the fruit of faith, and has Christ, who loved us even unto death, as an example, John 13, 12, 13. The hope of salvation arises from the resurrection of Christ from the dead, 1 Pet. 1, 3. But whence could it be certain to the Apostle, either concerning faith in Christ, or concerning charity without hypocrisy, or concerning the hope and certainty of the salvation of others?

I answer: He could be certain from the divine promises concerning the word of God and the grace of the Holy Spirit by intention, that some in the Church of the Colossians were entirely truly faithful and holy: for he could be presumed concerning faith by the judgment of charity from external signs, especially the works of charity, the zeal of the word, of prayers, and other excellent exercises, when he sees the light shine before men, Matt. 5, 16. and the saints shine as lights in a perverse generation, Phil. 2, 15. , Phil. II. 15. (which he set before you in the word of truth) You received the first rudiments.

For those who hear are called Catechumens by Tertullian in On Patience, who in the same place calls them the basic training of hearers.

Cyprian also uses it thus. Moreover, that addition signifies that some time has already passed since then, the word of truth being the most true discourse, 2 Cor. VI. 7, Eph. 1. 13. They are not to be believed to have received only the first rudiments from the faithful teacher Epaphras, whom the Apostle notably commends.

Nor are all who are said to have heard the word of truth catechumens. Indeed, all the more perfect are bound to hear the word of God. Those who are of God hear the word of God, John 8:47. (the Gospel) An apposition.

He did not say "of preaching," says Theophylact, but "of the Gospel," so that he might twice recall God's benefits. For the Gospel discourses about the best things. Since it is a word of truth, there is no falsehood in it. Why then do you accuse it as if of falsehood? Because you believe less, as you have been instructed by him, namely that entrance is given through Christ for salvation.

Moreover, it is called the word of truth by antonomasia, John XVIII. And it is opposed to human traditions and inventions of reason, since hope in heaven is held from the Gospel alone. (which has come to you) So 2 Pet.

1. 12, in the present truth. The Latin translator rightly renders: "which has reached you."

For it is put for "to come," Prov. 1. 27. And it is a present participle put for the past, in the Hebrew manner.

It is for "to."

Phil. Concerning the word παρόντος, Theophylact says: Not otherwise than as if he said the Gospel had arrived to you as some animate thing.

By prosopopoeia. They themselves did not come first to the Gospel. The Gospel had arrived to them, neither sought nor requested. Cf. Is. 65:1. Nor do the Greek Scholia note without cause that the preposition εἰς is used.

But because, as Chrysostom explains, it did not arrive to you and depart again, but remained, and is still among you. ver. 6. καθὼς καὶ ἐν παντὶ τῷ κόσμῳ) A synecdoche signifying the most illustrious parts of the world, as Rom. 1:8. You see from this very thing how true Christ's precepts are, Matt. 24:12. Neither the present passage, nor the parallel passage in Matt.

24:14, admits a synecdoche: for in the present passage, care is taken in many ways, lest, the proper sense being abandoned, one should deflect from the universal to a particular proclamation: besides that it is not fitting to deflect from the letter to a trope without necessity. It is said not simply ἐν κόσμῳ, even if that also implies the whole world, by force of collation with Christ's command in Mark 16:15: but ἐν παντὶ τῷ κόσμῳ, utilizing πορευθέντες εἰς τὸν κόσμον ἅπαντα, for he who says all things, excepts or leaves out nothing, Heb. 2:8. It is said in v. 23 that the Gospel was preached ἐν πάσῃ τῇ κτίσει, as in Mark 16:15. Added besides is τῇ ὑπὸ τὸν οὐρανόν.

Therefore, whatever creature (human, cf. 1 Pet. 2:13) is under the Sun, to it the Gospel has been preached. He says that πάντα ἄνθρωπον is admonished, that πάντα ἄνθρωπον is taught, so that they may present πάντα ἄνθρωπον perfect in Christ.

Therefore, GOD willed not only the elect, but also the reprobate to be admonished and taught; He willed not only those, but all men to be presented perfect in Christ, and for that end He willed the Gospel to be preached not to some only, but to all men throughout the whole world: because He wills all to come to the knowledge of the truth, 1 Tim. 2: 4. He wills that no one should perish, 2 Pet. 3:

9. Luculent also is the passage in Matt.

24:14, concerning the whole world ἐν ὅλῃ οἰκουμένῃ, and concerning all nations εἰς μαρτύριον πᾶσι τοῖς ἔθνεσι. Luculent were other places, especially Rom. 10: 18. Did not (ALL) hear it? For that universal [truth] is evident from v. 6: ἀλλ' ἐπάντες ὑπήκουσαν τῷ εὐαγγελίῳ. How could ALL be able ὑπακούειν, unless ἤκυσαν πᾶτες, indeed εἰς πᾶσαν τὴν γῆν its sound went out into ALL the earth, καὶ εἰς τὰς σαν τὴν οἰκουμένην, into the ends of the UNIVERSE of words: Where in the earth the heaven is seen, wherever the Sun shines, to whom the firmament announces the glory of GOD, Ps. 19. The Fathers agree.

Certainly, says Crusius in this place, among the Greeks Chrysostom, Theophylact, among the Latins Hilary in Matt. 25, Jerome in Matt. 24, that before the destruction of the temple and the city, the light of the Gospel had reached all. Why do I myself, why do other Calvinists deny the universal preaching, and pervert the Apostle's words either by synecdoche or hyperbole, which is done even by Papists, the former by Cornelius à Lapide, the latter by Salmeron and Justinian?

This is Theophylact's observation: Since most people are then most confirmed when they have others who think with them, and he added to the whole world. For the Gospel is diffused there also, and stands everywhere and is firm. καὶ ὄν καρποφορούμενον καὶ αὐξανόμενον) That ὄν is not wrongly absent in the manuscript.

Just as a tree both brings forth fruit and grows at the same time. This is said also of the Gospel, as here and Acts 6:7, 19:29, and of the faithful themselves, below 10. καρποφορούμενον ὅλην αὐξανόμενον Alluding to Gen. 1: 28. That αὐξανόμενον is not present in the Manuscript. Nor is that ὄν wrongly present in other Codices, by which a single MS. cannot be prejudiced; just as that αὐξανόμενον is not wrongly read in some.

For they wish to indicate both the abundance of fruits, and the increase, and the propagation of the Gospel. It bears fruit indeed, according to Theophylact, by works, it grows from the continuous multitude of believers admitted to the faith. For it would not bear fruit, unless it had received strength, and grew stronger daily in power. And trees, when they are strengthened with deeper roots, produce most abundant fruits. Crucius rightly refutes Bellarmine here, even if he favors his own particularity not obscurely: Bellarmine lib. 3, De Pontifice Romano cap. 4, where from the fact that the Gospel had not yet reached the whole world; he excepts against this text, that Augustine ep. 80 to Hesychius says that the Apostle did not wish to say that the Gospel was in act in the whole world, but in virtue, because, forsooth, the seed of the divine word had been cast by the Apostles into the world, which by gradually bearing fruit and growing, the whole world had been filled. Bellarmine is a false witness. Augustine in the cited letter neither praises nor explains this text. The words of the text show that the Apostle is speaking of act, not of virtue alone.

He says, it reached you just as it did the whole world, and bears fruit, it does so among you. To the Colossians it had reached in act, among them it bore fruit in act. καθὼς καὶ ἐν ὑμῖν) No less among you, than among others. ἀφ' ἧς ἡμέρας ἠκούσατε, καὶ ἐπίγνωτε τὴν χάριν τῷ Θεῷ ἐν ἀληθείᾳ) That sum of GOD'S benevolence, which is revealed through the Gospel. ver.

Latin:

Vers. 3. χάρις ὑμῖν, ἡ ἀγάπη καὶ πατρὸς ἡμῶν καὶ κυρίου ἰησοῦ χριστοῦ) Eph. 1, 2. In multis codicibus Graecis & Latinis abest hic κυρίου ἰησοῦ χριστοῦ, ut & in Syriaco.

Non abundare in receptis, iisque & numero & auctoritate potioribus; sed in illis, quos Grotius laudat, codicibus deficere, collatio similis loci Eph. 1. & consensus interpretum docet. Εὐχαριστοῦμεν τῷ θεῷ καὶ πατρὶ τῷ κυρίῳ ἡμῶν ἰησοῦ χριστοῦ πάντοτε περὶ ὑμῶν προσευχόμενοι) Eph. 1, 16. Coharet autem illud πάντοτε οὗ προσευχόμενοι, ut videre est Rom. 1, 10. Phil. 1. Vers. 4. Ἀκούσαντες τὴν πίστιν ὑμῶν ἐν χριστῷ ἰησοῦ, καὶ τὴν ἀγάπην τὴν εἰς πάντας τὰς ἁγίους) Eph. 1, 15. In Manuscripto τὴν ἀγάπην ἣν ἔχετε εἰς πάντας τὰς ἁγίους, quomodo legit & Latinus. Christus, inquit Theophylactus, Dominus noster est, non Angeli, qui sunt servi.

Et porro: Gratiam nos agimus, quia per Epaphram nobis renuntiatum est fides vestra, non que in Angelis constet, sed quae in Christo. Christus quia pro nobis est unctus, & Jesus est omnibus, quia & populum a peccatis salvavit. Fidem autem prius nominat, quam charitatem, quia fides est radix, & mater charitatis, Gal.

5, 6. Vers. 5. Διὰ τὴν ἐλπίδα τὴν ἀποκειμένην ὑμῖν ἐν τοῖς οὐρανοῖς) Spem vocat id, quod speratur, ut Ephes. 1, 18. Vita aeterna & coelestis a Christo promissa excitat & fidem, & dilectionem.

Sic ἀποκειμένη dicitur, quod alicui servatur, ut 2 Tim. 4, 8. Deut. 32, 34. Non dicitur fides, & dilectio EXCITATA per vitam aeternam, vel promissionem ejusdem, etsi vere id dici possit, si modo absit sensus Papisticus, quod per dilectionem vitam aeternam mereamur: ac Arminianus & Socinianus, quod verbum DEI moliter tantum, suadendo & promittendo operetur in nostri conversione, regeneratione, ac ei productione. Nam promissiones divinae excitant fidem, excitant dilectionem, sed excludenda non est Spiritus S. per verbum efficax operatio: possumus etiam intuitu promissionum divinarum bene operari, licet opera bona non sint causa meritoria vitae aeternae.

Theophylactus etsi adducat illum sensum: Colite fratres non humanarum spe rerum, sed futurorum bonorum expectatione. Addit tamen & aliam interpretationem magis congruam: Vel eo gratias agimus, quia hereditatem etsi immortalitatis vos habituri.

Nimirum tres causae adferuntur a Paulo, ob quas Deo gratias agere habeat. Prime fides, deinde charitas, tertid spes Colossensium. Quem sensum plerique Interpretes sequuntur.

Fides in Christum fundatur in sanguine ejus propitiatorio, Rom. 3, 25. Charitas fidei fructus est, & Christum nos ad mortem usque diligentem pro exemplo habet, Job. 13, 12, 13. Spes salutis ex resurrectione Christi ex mortuis oritur, 1 Pet. 1, 3. Sed unde constare poterat Apostolo, vel de fide in Christum, vel de charitate ἀναποκρίτω, vel de spe ac certitudine salutis aliorum?

Respondeo: Poterat e promissionibus divinis de verbo Dei ac gratia Spiritus S. intentione certus esse, quosdam omnino in Ecclesia Colossensium vere fideles & sanctos esse: poterat enim de fide praesumi charitatis judicio e signis externis, charitatis imprimis operibus, zeli verbi, precum, aliisque praeclaris exercitiis, quum luce videat luceat coram hominibus, Matt. 5, 16. & sancti velut luminaria fulgeant in perversa generatione, , Phil. II. 15. ἣν προηκέσαζε ἐν τῷ λόγῳ τῆς ἀληθείας) Prima accepi-ſtis rudimenta.

Nam audientes sunt Catechumeni Tertulliano de patientia, qui ibidem vocat auditorum tirocinia. Utitur sic & Cyprianus.

Illud autem additum, fignificat jam aliquod tempus ex eo transiisse, λόγω αλη deias fermo verissimus, 2. Cor. VI. 7. Eph. 1. 13. Non prima tantùm rudimenta accepiſſe à fideli magistro Epaphra credendi sunt, quem egregie commendatApostolus.

Nec omnes, qui audifle dicuntur verbum veritatis, catechumeni ſunt. Imò tenentur omnes perfectiores audire verbum Dei. Qui ex Deo sunt, verbum Dei audiunt, Job. 8,57. τῷ ὀναγελία) Appositio.

Non pradicationis, inquit Theophylactum, dixit, sed Evangelii, ut bis Dei commemoret beneficia. Evangelium namque de rebus optimis differit. Quod cum fermo fit veritatis, nil in eo inest mendacii. Cur igitur vos quasi mendacii illud arguitis? quia minus creditis, ut estis ab eo instructi, per Christum videlicet dari ad salutem ingreſſum.

Dicitur autem fermo veritatis xαζ᾽ ἀντονομασίαν Job. XVIII. Et opponitur traditionibus humanis, ac inventis rationis, cum non nisi ex uno Evangelio ſpes in cælis habeatur. Τὰ παρόντα εἰς ὑμᾶς) Sic 2.

Petr. 1. 12. ἐν τῇ παρίση ἀληθώ. Recte Latinus interpres: Quod pervenit ad vos.

Nam y ponitur pro אחת venire Prov. 1.27. Est autem participium præfens pro præterito politum, more E- brzo. it is pro ad.

De

Phil. 2, 15. De verbo παρόντος Theophylactus: Non secus, ac animatam rem aliquam ad vos dixit Evangelium pervenisse.

Per prosopopoeiam. Ipsi non venerunt priores ad Evangelium. Evangelium ad ipsos pervenerat, nec quaesitum, nec expetitum. Es. LXV. 1. Nec sine causa praepositionem εἰς adhibitam notant Graeca Scholia.

Sed quia, ut explicat Chrysostomus, non advenit ad vos, & rursus abfiesit, sed mansit, & adhuc apud vos est. vers. 6. καθὼς καὶ ἐν παντὶ τῷ κόσμῳ) Συνεκδοχὴ significans illustrissimas orbis partes, ut Rom. I. 8. Videtis ex hoc ipso, quam vera sint Christi praecepta, Matth. XXIV. 12. Nec locus praesens, nec locus parallelus Matth.

XXIV. 14. admittit Synecdochen: nam praesenti loco multis modis cavetur, ne sensu proprio relicto ab universali deflectatur ad particulare praeconium: praeterquam, quod non conveniat à litera deflectere ad tropum, citra necessitatem. Dicitur non simpliciter ἐν κόσμῳ, etsi etiam id universum mundum, vi collationis cum mandato Christi Marc. XVI. 15. inferat: sed ἐν παντὶ τῷ κόσμῳ, utilic πορευθέντες εἰς τὸν κόσμον ἅπαντα, qui enim omnia dicit, nihil excipit vel relinquit, Ebr. II. 8. Dicitur v. 23. Evangelium praedicatum ἐν πάσῃ τῇ κτίσει, ut Marc. XVI. 15. Additur insuper τῇ ὑπὸ τὸν οὐρανόν.

Quaecunque ergo creatura (humana, conf. 1. Pet. II. 13.) sub Sole est, illi praedicatum est Evangelium. Dicit moneri πάντα ἄνθρωπον, doceri πάντα ἄνθρωπον, ut sistant πάντα ἄνθρωπον perfectum in Christo.

Non ergo tantum electos, sed etiam reprobos moneri & doceri voluit DEUS, non illos tantum, sed omnes homines voluit perfectos sisti in Christo, eoque fini non quibusdam tantum, sed universis per totum orbem hominibus voluit praedicari Evangelium: quia omnes vult ad agnitionem veritatis pervenire, 1. Tim. II. 4. Nemini vult perire, 2.

Petr. III. 9. Luculentum etiam est locus Mateb.

XXIV. 14. de toto mundo ἐν ὅλῃ οἰκουμένῃ, & de omnibus gentibus εἰς μαρτύριον πᾶσι τοῖς ἔθνεσι. Luculenta fuit alia loca imprimis Rom. X. 18. Nonne (OMNES) id audiverunt, illa enim universalis è v. 6. patet: ἀλλ' ἐπάντες ὑπήκουσαν τῷ εὐαγγελίῳ. Quomodo OMNES poterant ὑπακούειν, nisi ἤκυσαν πᾶτες, utique εἰς πᾶσαν τὴν γῆν in OMNEM terram exivit sonus ejus, καὶ εἰς τὰς σαν τὴν οἰκουμένην, in fines UNIVERSI verborum: Ubi in terra coelum conspicitur, quibuscunque Sol lucet, quibus firmamentum gloriam DEI annunciat, Ps.

XIX. Annuunt Patres. Certè, inquit in h. l. Crusius, è Graecis Chrysostomus, Theophylactus, è Latinis Hilarius in Mattb. XXV. Hie- vonymus in Mattb. XXIV. ante templi & urbis destructionem, lucem Evangelii ad omnes pervenisse. Cur ego ipse, cur alii Calviniani negant universalem praedicationem, & Apostoli verba vel per Synecdochen, vel hyperbolem, quod à Papistis etiam fit, illud Cornelio à Lapide, hoc à Salmeriano & Justiniano, pervertunt?

Theophylacti haec est observatio: Quoniam plerique, tunc maxime confirmantur, cum alios habent, qui secum sentiant, & universo mundo adjecit. Est namque Evangelium id quaque diffusum, & perstat ubique & firmum est. καὶ ὄν καρποφορούμενον καὶ αὐξανόμενον) Illud ὄν non male abest in manuscripto.

Tanquam arbor & fructus profert & simul crescit. Dicitur hoc & de Evangelio, ut hic & A&. VI. 7. XIX. 29. & de fide 2. Cor. X. 15. & de ipsis fidelibus, infra 10. καρποφορούμενον ὅλην αὐξανόμενον Allufo ad Gen. I. 28. Illud αὐξανόμενον non adest in Manuscripto. Nec male ὄν illud adest in aliis Codd. quibus unicum MS. praejudicari non potest; quemadmodum nec illud αὐξανόμενον male in quibusdam legitur.

Nam & fructuum copiam, & incrementum, ac propagationem Evangelii indicare volunt. Fructificat quidem, interprete Theophylacto, operibus, crescit ex credentium continua multitudine ad fidem admissa. Non enim fructum deferret, nisi robore accepto, & viribus quotidie invalesceret. Et arbores cum altioribus radicibus obfirmantur, fructus producunt uberrimos. Recte hic refellit Bellarminum Crucius, etsi suae particularitati faveat non obscure: Bellarminus lib. III. De Pontifice Romano cap. 4. ubi ex eo, quod Evangelium nondum fit orbe toto nisse; ad hunc textum excipit, quod Augustinus ep. 80. ad Hesychium dicat, Apostolum non voluisse dicere esse actu Evangelium in toto mundo, sed virtute, quia nimirum jaclum fuerit per Apostolos semen verbi divini in mundum, quod paulatim fructificando & crescendo totum mundum repletum erat. Bellarminus est falsus testis. Augustinus in Epistola citata nec textum hunc laudat, nec explicat. Verba textus ostendunt, Apostolum de actu, non de sola virtute loqui.

Dicit, pervenit ad vos sicut in totum mundum, & fructum profert, ficit apud vos. Ad Colossenses actu pervenerat, apud illos actu fructum ferebat. καθὼς καὶ ἐν ὑμῖν) Non minus apud vos, quam apud alios. ἀφ' ἧς ἡμέρας ἠκούσατε, καὶ ἐπίγνωτε τὴν χάριν τῷ Θεῷ ἐν ἀληθείᾳ) Summam illam DEI benevolentiam, quae per Evangelium revelatur. vers.

## 1:7
7. καθὼς ἐμάθετε ἀπὸ Ἐπαφρᾶ τοῦ ἀγαπητοῦ συνδούλου ἡμῶν) Paul himself was indeed in Phrygia more than once, but he could not visit all the cities of Phrygia, below 2:1. And so he had sent Epaphroditus there, who, having wandered through many places, finally settled at Philippi, and was thence sent to Paul. Epaphras is the same as Epaphroditus, by contraction of pronunciation, concerning which at the beginning of Luke. Thus Δυμᾶς is Δημήτριος. ὃς ἐστι πιστὸς ὑπὲρ ὑμῶν τῷ χριστῷ διάκονος) He is a faithful herald of the Gospel, both for others, and for your own greatest good. Διάκονος is a word taken here as 1 Cor. 3:5, 2 Cor. 3:6, 6:4, 11:23, Eph. 3:7, 6:21.

That Epaphras is Epaphroditus is not certain.

The contrary is rather probable. He was a Minister of the Colossian Church, the latter of the Philippian: He was also Colossian by birth, which is not certain of this one. For he is called a faithful Minister, not only because he went to Paul in matters pertaining to Christ, which seemed so to Chrysostom and Theophylact, and because he performed the duty of the Colossians before Paul at Rome, which Bullinger notes, but especially because he performed the Ministry of the word among them.

Therefore he is also called a faithful fellow-servant of Paul. All of which things contribute both to commending Epaphras to the Colossians, and to confirming them in the doctrine received from him. If he were a faithful minister, it was necessary that he should have handed down the truth. Nor would he have acknowledged Epaphras as his fellow-servant, if he had proposed alien dogmas, Gal. 1:8. If so, Epaphras is Christ's minister, and preached all things, by what pact do you assert that mortals are brought to the Father through Angels? says Theophylact.

That Epaphras settled at Philippi is not to be said, but had to be proven from antiquity. That conjecture from the name Epaphroditus abbreviated, because it is destitute of the authority of the ancients, does not deserve assent. ὃν δηλοῦτε ἐμῖν τὴν ὑμῶν ἀγάπην ἐν πνεύματι) How you love us because of the Holy Spirit given to you.

He signified without doubt the whole state, and among other things also the sincere love of the Colossians. And the particle ὃν tends to this. But he speaks of love in the Spirit, that is, spiritual: not indeed because of the Holy Spirit given. The reason for the love is not rendered, but the principle and quality of the love, which is done by the Spirit and in the Spirit and truth. They loved Paul also (though not others) in the Spirit, whom they had never seen in the flesh.

Rightly Theophylact: In spirit: This is spiritual, the benevolence you have toward me. For here is stable and firmer love, which consists in the spirit. The remaining kind of benevolence, whether it be of nature, as a parent in children, or from friendship and the conjunction of souls, as is wont to be between friends, is unstable and infirm. Concerning which Chrysostom thus: Spiritual love is the supreme of all, as a certain queen, which holds dominion over her own, and is honest in appearance, and beautiful, and in an adorned habit. For nothing earthly brings it forth, as it does that, not custom, not benefit, not nature, not gold, but it descends from above from heaven. And why do you marvel, if it needs no benefit to consist, since even if it receives nothing evil, it is not overturned? But that this is that Major, hear Paul saying: I could wish that I myself were anathema from Christ for my brethren. What Father would have wished this, to be in evils? And again, to be dissolved and to be with Christ is far better, but to remain in the flesh is more necessary for your sakes. What Mother would have wished to say this, that she might despise her own?

Latin:

7. καθὼς ἐμάθετε ἀπὸ Ἐπαφρᾶ τοῦ ἀγαπητοῦ συνδούλου ἡμῶν) Paulus ipse fuit quidem in Phrygia plus semel, sed non potuit adire omnes Phrygiae urbes, infra II. 1. Itaque Epaphroditum eo miserat, qui multis locis oberratis tandem Philippis consedit, atque inde ad Paulum missus est. Epaphras idem, qui Epaphroditus, contractione pronunciationis, de qua ad initium Luc. Sic Δυμᾶς est Δημήτριος. ὅς ἐστι πιστὸς ὑπὲρ ὑμῶν τῷ χριστῷ διάκονος) Fidus est Evangelii praeco, tum & aliorum, tum & vestro maximo bono. Διάκονος vox hic sumitur ut 1.

Cor. III. 5. 2. Cor. III. 6. VI. 4. XI. 23. Eph. III. 7. VI. 21. Epaphram esse Epaphroditum non constat.

Contrarium potius verisimile est. Ille fuit Minister Ecclesiae Colossensis, hic Philippensis: Ille etiam Colossensis ortu fuit, quod de hoc non constat. Fidus enim Minister dicitur, non tantum quod in rebus ad Christum pertinentibus ad Paulum iverit, quod Chrysostomo & Theophylacto visum, quodq; vicem Colossensium penes Paulum Romae obierit, quod Bullingerus monet, sed imprimis, quod Ministerio verbi penes ipsos perfunctus sit.

Ideo dicitur etiam conservus Pauli fidus. Quae omnia faciunt, tum ad Epaphram Colossensibus commendandum, tum ad illos in doctrina ab ipso accepta confirmandos. Si minister fidg, vera oportuit ipsum tradidisse. Nec pro conservo suo agnovisset Epaphram, si aliena dogmata proposuisset, Gal. I. 8. Si ita, Christi minister est Epaphras, & re omnia predicavit, quo pacto ipsi afferitis per Angelos ad Patrem traduci mortales? inquit Theophylactu.

Epaphram Philippis consedisse non dicendum, sed ex antiquitate probandum erat. Illa conjectura è nomine Epaphroditi abbreviato, quia auctoritate veterum destituta, assensum non meretur. ὃν δηλοῦτε ἐμῖν τὴν ὑμῶν ἀγάπην ἐν πνεύματι) Quomodo nos diligatis propter Spiritum Sanctum vobis datum.

Significavit procul dubio statum omnem, & inter alia dilectionem quoque finceram Colossensium. Ed tendit particula ὃν. Amorem autem in Spiritu dicit, hoc est spiritualem: non verò propter datum Spiritum S. Non ratio amoris redditur, sed amoris principium & qualitas, quod à Spiritu & in Spiritu & veritate fit. Diligebant etiam Paulum, (non tamen alios) in Spiritu, quem in carne nunquam viderant.

Recte Theophylactus: In spiritu: Hoc est spiritualem, me estis erga me affecti benevolentiam. Hic namque stabilis est, & firmior amor, qui spiritu constat. Reliquum verò benevolentia genus, sive natura sit illud, ut paren tis in liberos, sive ex amicitia & animorum conjunctione, quale esse inter amicos solet, instabile & infirmum. Quo de ita Chrysostomus: Dilectio spiritualis est omnium suprema, veluti quadam regina, quae in suos dominatum obtinet, honesta-que est specie, pulchroque, & ornato habitu. Nihil enim terrestre eam parit, sicut illam, non consuetudo, non beneficium, non natura, non aurum, sed à superis descendit e caelo. Et quid miraris, si beneficio non eget, ut consistat, quum ne si mali quidem quicquam accipiat, evertatur? Quod autem haec sit illa Major, audi Paulum dicentem: Optarem ego ipse esse anathema à Christo pro fratribus meis. Quis hoc Pater opsaverit, esse in malis? Et rursus, resolvi & esse cum Christo longè est melius, manere autem in carne est magis necessarium propter vos. Quanam Mater hac voluisset dicere, ut sua despiceret?

## 1:9
Verf. 9. διὰ τοῦτο καὶ ἡμεῖς ἀφ' ἧς ἡμέρας ἠκούσαμεν

For so we have it Matth. v. 42. VI. 8. VII. 7. 8. 11. XVIII. 19. XXI. 22. he explains the chief matter of his prayers. ἵνα πληρωθῆτε τὴν ἐπίγνωσιν τοῦ θελήματος αὐτοῦ It is a construction not frequent in Paul: but received among the Greeks, for among them, whatever case active verbs govern, they also govern passive ones. But πληροῦν governs the fourth case, as Philipp. II. 2. and elsewhere. ἐπίγνωσις is a greater and more exact knowledge, as Eph. I. 17. IV. 13. Philipp. I. 9. A good part of it is the knowledge of the mysteries of the Old Testament pertaining to the New Testament, αὐτοῦ of God, namely, from verse 6. ἐν πάσῃ σοφίᾳ Ephes. I. 8. καὶ συνέσει πνευματικῇ That is φρονήσει, as can be seen in the place cited to the Ephesians. He understands the knowledge of things to be done. σύνεσις is one thing, φρόνησις another. The Philosopher makes this in I. VI. Eth. c. 11. ἐπίταξιν, preceptive. But he interprets that as κριτικὴν μόνον, only judicial. Crocius rightly notes this.

The Colossians indeed had some knowledge of divine things: But the Apostle prays that they may be filled with all acknowledgment, namely, necessary and salutary, an acknowledgment of the will, concerning which Job XIV. 39-40. He prays also for wisdom for them, i.e., the habit of heavenly wisdom, 1. Cor. I. 23. Col. II. 6. 7. sometimes of nature, and of the divine essence, Job XVII. 3. Finally, he prays for intelligence, and spiritual perspicacity, or the faculty of judging, so that they may prudently perceive and solidly discern from the truth whatever fallacies and impostures of the Sophists and Pseudo-Apostles there may be, and thus be able to avoid them.

There is noted here by Davenant p. 54. a double fullness, of knowledge and of every grace; the fullness of the fatherland, and the fullness of the way. The fullness of the fatherland is that maximum measure of grace which the mind of each one can contain: this is not had until we are introduced to the state of glory. But the fullness of the way is that maximum measure of grace which He has decreed to bestow upon each of the elect in this world: and this is had by all the elect, before they depart from this life: Of this the Apostle speaks to Eph. IV. 7. To each of us grace is given according to the measure of the gift of Christ. And Augustine in Ps. 38. According to the mode of this life there is a certain perfection and to that perfection it is deputed, that each one knows himself not yet to be perfect. This perfection and fullness of grace he desires for them in this place. This he says not badly, provided the fiction of an absolute decree be absent. περιπατῆσαι ὑμᾶς ἀξίως τοῦ κυρίου περιπατῆσαι here is for ὡς τὸ περιπατῆσαι, which kind of ἴδωμεν we have often had. ἀξίως τοῦ κυρίου, that is, as is due to Christ.

Thus περιπατῆσαι ἀξίως τοῦ 1. Thess. II. 12. that ὑμᾶς is absent in the Manuscript, not badly. There is no need for that Ellipsis, nor that the pronoun ὑμᾶς be expunged. The other object of the prayer, or the good which the Apostle vows to the Colossians, that is, that they may walk worthily of the Lord, namely, in a life truly Christian: just as before it was a fuller knowledge of Christ. For these things follow one another. For he who has learned the kindness of God, and that He delivered His Son for us, by what pact ought he not to strive with all zeal, that he may infuse it into virtue, and himself also take up his own cross. Thus everywhere Theophylactus. Who also notes this, when life is expressed by walking, it is indicated that as the very gait is necessary for us, so also the best mode of living will be most profitable.

Conf. Ps. CXIX. 1. seq. 44. 45. 59. Ps. XV. 2. Eph. IV. 17. Phil. I. 17. εἰς πᾶσαν ἀρέσκειαν That we may please in every way, to God namely. ἀρέσκεια is taken by Aristotle and Theophrastus in a vicious part.

Otherwise the word itself is in itself neutral, as appears Prov. XXXI. 30. in the Glossary it is translated placor, in Apuleius placentia. ἐν παντὶ ἔργῳ ἀγαθῷ καρποφοροῦντες & αὐξανόμενοι ἐν ἐπιγνώσει τοῦ θεοῦ In the Manuscript αὐξανόμενοι τῇ ἐπιγνώσει Bearing fruit of every kind of good works, and in the knowledge of GOD more and more progressing.

What it is to bear fruit, we have seen at Matth. XIII. 25. Marc. IV. 20. Luc. VIII. 15. What αὐξανόμενοι is, 2. Corinth. IX. 15. Ephes. II. 21. Below II. 9. 1. Pet. II. 2. 2. Pet. III. 18. The observation of Theophylact here is not inelegant: Attend, that above he said the divine knowledge would be exceedingly necessary, so that the dignity of walking according to GOD might be preserved, now again he requires the same increased by good works, that he may at once have both a more accurate knowledge of GOD and of life.

For each strengthens the other. ἐν πάσῃ δυνάμει δυναμούμενοι Strengthened with every kind of strength, namely spiritual. δυναμοῦν which also ἐνδυναμοῦν Ath. IX. 22. Rom. IV. 20. Eph. VI. 10. 1. Tim. I. 12. 2. Tim. II. 1. IV. 17. Ebr. I. 34. 119 as is seen Ps. LXVIII. 29. κατὰ τὸ κράτος τῆς δόξης αὐτοῦ It is the same as κράτος ἰσχύος, Eph. I. 19. VI. 10. for also δόξα is taken μετωνυμικῶς for strength, as Ephes. III. 16. and 17 Ebrum is thus sometimes rendered. εἰς πᾶσαν ὑπομονὴν κ μακροθυμίαν So that you may not only bear evils constantly, but also hope better things of your enemies.

See 2. Cor. VI. 6. Gal. V. 22. Eph. IV. 2. μετὰ χαρᾶς This is great and as it were proper to Christians, to rejoice in evils themselves tolerated for Christ's sake, Philipp. II. 17. 18. Act. V. 41. He prays for divine strength for the Colossians, that not only persevering in faith they may patiently sustain any persecutions whatsoever, but also bear enemies with long-suffering, being alien from the desire of vengeance, Gal. V. 22. And all that with joy, as follows. For this coheres with the preceding, as B. Luther renders it, not with the following, as the Vulgate thinks. He commends strength to them in faith, Eph. I. 19. c. III. 17. 1. Petr. I. 5. V. 11. in patience, Phil. I. 23. seq. Rom. VIII. 37. 2. Cor. VI. 4. in long-suffering, or meekness, Matth. XI. 28. 29. Conf. Ps. CXXXII. 3.

PART II. ΔΙΑΚΤΙΚΗ, ON CHRIST.

Latin:

Vers. 9. διὰ τοῦτο καὶ ἡμεῖς ἀφ' ἧς ἡμέρας ἠκούσαμεν

Sic enim habemus Matth. v. 42. VI. 8. VII. 7. 8. 11. XVIII. 19. XXI. 22. explicat precum suarum praecipuam materiam. ἵνα πληρωθῆτε τὴν ἐπίγνωσιν τοῦ θελήματος αὐτοῦ Est con-structio Paulo non frequens: sed apud Graecos recepta, nam apud eos quem casum regunt activa, eundem regunt & passiva. πληροῦν autem quartum casum regit, ut Philipp. II. 2. & alibi. ἐπίγνωσις est major exartiorque cognitio, ut Eph. I. 17. IV. 13. Philipp. I. 9. Ejus bona pars est cognitio mysteriorum Veteris Testamenti ad Novum Testamentum spectantium, αὐτοῦ Dei scilicet, ex commate 6. ἐν πάσῃ σοφίᾳ Ephes. I. 8. καὶ συνέσει πνευματικῇ Id est φρονήσει, ut videre est dicto ad Ephesios loco. Cognitionem rerum agendarum intelligit. Aliud est σύνεσις, aliud φρόνησις. Hanc facit Philosophus I. VI. Eth. c. 11. ἐπίταξιν, praeceptivam. Illam vero κριτικὴν μόνον solùm dijudicatricem interpretatur. Id Crocius recte advertit.

Colossenses quidem notitiam aliquam habuerre rerum divinarum: Sed precatur Apostolus, ut impleantur omni agnitione, necessaria scil. atq; salutari, agnitione voluntatis, de qua Job. XIV. 39-40. precatur etiam ipsis sapientiam, h. e. habitum coelestis sapientiae, 1. Cor. I. 23. Col. II. 6. 7. nonnunquam natura, & essentiae divinae, Job. XVII. 3. precatur deniq; intelligentiam, & perspicaciam spiritualem, seu dijudicandi facultatem, ut fallacias & imposturas Sophistarum & Pseudo-Apostolorum quascunq; prudenter animadvertere & à veritate solidè discernere, adeoque vitare possint.

Notatur hic à Davenantio p. 54. duplex plenitudo, cognitionis & cujuscunque gratiae; plenitudo patriae, & plenitudo viae. Plenitudo patriae est illa maxima gratiae mensura, quam uniuscujusque mens capere potest: bac non habetur priusquam introducamur ad statum gloriae. Sed plenitudo viae est maxima illa gratia mensura, quam Unicuique electorum in hoc mundo impertiri decrevit: atque hac habetur ab omnibus electis, antequam migrent ex hac vita: De hac loquitur Apostolus ad Eph. IV. 7. Unicuique nostrum data est gratia pro mensura donationis Christi. Et Augustinus in Ps. 38. Secundum istius vitae modum est quaedam perfectio eique perfectioni deputatur, ut se quisque noverit nondum esse perfectum. Hanc perfectionem & plenitudinem gratiae illis exoptat in hoc loco. Haec ille non malè, modo absit commentum decreti absoluti. περιπατῆσαι ὑμᾶς ἀξίως τοῦ κυρίου περιπατῆσαι hic est pro ὡς τὸ περιπατῆσαι, qualem ἴδωμεν jam saepe habuimus. ἀξίως τοῦ κυρίου, id est, ut Christo debetur.

Sic περιπατῆσαι ἀξίως τοῦ 1. Thess. II. 12. illud ὑμᾶς abest in Manuscripto non malè. Opus non est illa Ellipsi, nec ut expungatur pronomen ὑμᾶς. Alterum precationis objectum, vel bonum, quod Colossensibus vovet Apostolus, hoc est, ut ambulent dignè Domino, vita nempe vere Christiana: quemadmodum prius erat plenior Christi notitia. Haec enim se consequuntur. Nam qui Dei didicerit benignitatem, & quod Filium pro nobis tradiderit, quo pacto non debet omni studio niti, ut virtuti infudet, suamque & ipse crucem attollat. Ita ubique Theophylactus. Qui etiam id notat, cum per ambulationem vita exprimitur, id indicari, ut nobis necessarius est ipse incessus, sic & optimum vivendi modum maximè profuturum.

Conf. Ps. CXIX. 1. seq. 44. 45. 59. Ps. XV. 2. Eph. IV. 17. Phil. I. 17. εἰς πᾶσαν ἀρέσκειαν Ut omni modo placeamus, Deo scilicet. ἀρέσκεια Aristoteli & Theophrasto in vitiosam partem sumitur.

Est alioqui vox ipsa per se media, ut apparet Prov. XXXI. 30. in Glossario vertitur placor, Apulejo-placentia. ἐν παντὶ ἔργῳ ἀγαθῷ καρποφοροῦντες & αὐξανόμενοι ἐν ἐπιγνώσει τοῦ θεοῦ In Manuscripto αὐξανόμενοι τῇ ἐπιγνώσει Fru-ctum ferentes omnis generis bonorum operum, & in cognitione DEI magis magisque proficientes.

Quid fit καρπο-φορεῖν, vidimus ad Matth. XIII. 25. Marc. IV. 20. Luc. VIII. 15. Quid αὐξανόμενοι 2. Corinth. IX. 15. Ephes. II. 21. Infra II. 9. 1. Pet. II. 2. 2. Pet. III. 18. Non inelegans Theophylacti hic est observatio: Attende, ut superius divinam scientiam dixerit fore admodum necessariam, ut secundum DEUM in-cedendi dignitas servaretur, nunc rursus eandem bonis operibus auctam exigat, ut simul & DEI quia babeat rectiore cum vita cognitionem.

Alterutrum enim se invicem roborant. ἐν πάσῃ δυνάμει δυναμούμενοι Roborati omni genere roboris, nempe spiritualis. δυναμοῦν quod & ἐνδυναμοῦν Αθ. IX. 22. Rom. IV. 20. Eph. VI. 10. 1. Tim. I. 12. 2. Tim. II. 1. IV. 17. Ebr. I. 34. 119 ut videre est Ps. LXVIII. 29. κατὰ τὸ κράτος τῆς δόξης αὐτοῦ Idem est quod κράτος ἰσχύος, Eph. I. 19. VI. 10. nam & δόξα sumitur μετωνυμικῶς pro valentia, ut Ephes. III. 16. & 17 Ebrum sic interdum vertitur. εἰς πᾶσαν ὑπομονὴν κ μακροθυμίαν Ut non tantùm mala constanter feratis, sed & meliora speretis de inimicis vestris.

Vide 2. Cor. VI. 6. Gal. V. 22. Eph. IV. 2. μετὰ χαρᾶς Magnum hoc est & Christianorum velut proprium, ipsis malis ob Christum toleratis laetari, Philipp. II. 17. 18. Aθ. V. 41. Robur divinum precatur Colossensibus, ut non tantum perseverantes in fide patienter per-secutiones quasvis sustineant, sed etiam hostes cum longanimitate ferant à vindictae cupiditate alieni, Gal. V. 22. Idque omne cum gaudio, ut sequitur. Hoc enim cohaeret cum praecedentibus, ut B. Lutherus reddit, non cum sequentibus, uti vulgatus censet. Robur ipsis commendat in fide, Eph. I. 19. c. III. 17. 1. Petr. I. 5. V. 11. in patientia, Phil. I. 23. seq. Rom. VIII. 37. 2. Cor. VI. 4. in longanimitate, sive mansuetudine, Matth. XI. 28. 29. Conf. Ps. CXXXII. 3.

PARS II. ΔΙΑΚΤΙΚΗ, DE CHRISTO.

## 1:12
V. 12. ἰσχυσαμένους τῇ θεῷ, τῷ πατρὶ τῷ ἱκανώσαντι ἡμᾶς εἰς τὴν μερίδα τοῦ κλήρου τῶν ἁγίων ἐν τῷ φωτί. We have had the word ἱκανός at 2. Corinth. III. 8. Answer Ebrzo 116 μέρις κλήρου 117 Deut. XXXII. 9. but so that the distinction of law and Gospel may be shown, here is added ἅγιον ἐν τῷ φωτί, that is, τῷ φωτί with the article understood in τῷ φωτὶ as often, which is expressed Rom. XI. 19. where it is σὺν ἐν σκότῳ. But it is ᾧ φωτὶ who has light for a companion, 1. Joh. II. 19. 10. The thanksgiving is either attributed to the Colossians, namely because the Apostle prays that they themselves, weighing the divine benefits, give thanks to God, or — which we judge more fitting — it belongs to Paul and Timothy, who as at V. 3. gave thanks for the conversion of the Colossians, so now, as they hasten to the principal discussion, again discharge their εὐχαριστίαν, not for them alone, but in common, for all the faithful. by the benefits exhibited to the faithful.

Which are then summarized in this verse, and then more fully executed; and thus the Apostle explains the translation into the kingdom of God, and its meritorious cause, the redemption of Christ and the formal remission of sins, as well as the author of Redemption, the Son of God, the head of the Church, who for this reason inhabits the assumed flesh in the fullness of His Deity, by virtue of the hypostatic union, through whom the ἀποκαταλλαγὴ (reconciliation) of all things was made, and peace was conciliated.

The word ἱκανώσαντι ἡμᾶς, who made us worthy, according to Chrysostom implies two things: both that He deigned us this honor, and that He makes us fit for it, μέρος κλήρου, a portion of the lot, or participation of the inheritance.

Its figure was in the portion of the lot of the land of Canaan, which fell to each tribe.

Cf. Ex. XIX. 6. 1. Pet. II. 9. but there individuals obtained a part, in eternal life individuals will possess the whole, Apoc. XXI. 7. For God will be to them all in all, 1. Cor. XV. 28. In the Church, says Theophylact, we are all by lot, but we obtain different parts; here, however, He made us worthy of both His lot and portion.

By which, however, the degrees of glory are not taken away. But to all, the essential glory is assigned the same in eternal life.

That it is also called a lot, Theophylact observes with Chrysostom, because as a lot falls to no one by human skill, but falls according to the divine will, Prov. XXXIII. so also we, by nothing of our own (as his words have it), neither by office nor by virtue, are worthy of the heavenly kingdom, but by the gift of God, whatever good there is, is brought to us. Therefore the Lord says, say, that we are unprofitable servants, we have done what we ought to have done.

This truth extorted from Cornelius: The inheritance of the saints is called a lot, because no men had a right to it, while yet among men they have a right to an inheritance, of which they are heirs; Whence Ephes. I. 11. the Apostle says, we are called by lot to the faith and grace of Christ. This inheritance of the saints is therefore called a lot, because it happens to men without merit, freely and as if by chance.

It is called the portion of the saints, because, to wit, they are washed, sanctified, and justified through the name of the Lord Jesus, and by the Spirit of God, 1. Cor. VI. Cf. 1. Petr. I. 2. Ebr. XII. 14. Ephes. V. 27. It is called the lot of the saints in light, to wit, heavenly, Is.

LX. 19. 20. Apoc. XXI. 23. XXII. 5. Theophyl. In the present light, to wit, and the future, that is, knowledge.

For revelation provided us with mysteries, and light to the living, that it might bestow a more shining light in the future age. V. 13. ὃς ἐρρύσατο ἡμᾶς ἐκ τῆς ἐξουσίας τοῦ σκότους) ἐξουσία σκότους (power of darkness) are called here darkness most effectively for blinding the minds, ἐξουσία משל (dominion).

He who commits sin is the servant of sin. Joh. VIII. 34. καὶ μετέστησεν) העביר (He transferred). εἰς τὴν βασιλείαν τοῦ υἱοῦ τῆς ἀγάπης αὐτοῦ) That is, τῦ ἀγαπημένου (of the beloved) Ephes. I. 6. It is a Hebraism as when it is said הר קדש (Mount of holiness) and family.

The description here and in the following is more special, how He led us to the lot of the heavenly inheritance, and how He rendered us worthy of the same: He led us partly by liberating us from the power of darkness, partly by transferring us into the kingdom of His Son, which is the kingdom of light, through the darkness not only of vices, but also of ignorance and errors, not only the darkness of guilt, but also, he understands, the darkness of misery, both temporal and eternal.

For all those darknesses arise from the Devil, under whose power we were, before we were translated into the kingdom of the Son of God by divine grace.

The power of darkness can be understood either of the Magistrate and prince of darkness, i.e., the Devil, or of the force and power of that gloom, which is induced to hold us as if we were servants and captives, by prosopopoeia. He did not say from darkness, says Chrysostom, but from power.

For he had great power over us, and obtained dominion over us, for it is grave, even only to be under the Devil, but with power, this is also more grave. Which power no one could destroy, except the Son of God.

But He transferred us into the kingdom of the Son of His love; Not therefore only, says Chrysostom, in the liberation from darkness does He show His kindness. And yet it is a great thing to have liberated from darkness, but to have introduced into the kingdom is much greater.

See therefore, how manifold the gift is. First, that He liberated us lying in the depths. Second, that He not only liberated us, but also transferred us into the kingdom. Which he repeats after his custom, Theophylact, adding: nor did He bring us in vain, but that we might possess the heavenly kingdom with the Son of His love, that is, with His beloved Son, we who were previously hostile to Him, and were wandering in darkness, which he also says elsewhere: If we endure, we shall also reign together. But what Theophylact further adds with Chrysostom: Nor did He transfer (μετήγαγε, or μετέθηκεν) but He transferred (μετήγαγε) so that he does not ascribe that all is transferred, but argues that we also contributed something to that matter, that can neither be drawn from that word, nor is it consonant with Scripture.

For what would they contribute to their own translation, who are under the power of darkness? All that is of God, not of us.

No one comes to me, unless the Father has drawn him, says Christ Joh. VI. 44. Therefore He does not say, He led us across, because we are not led violently, but He transfers, if indeed no good will of ours preceded.

The kingdom of the Son of God is both the kingdom of grace and the kingdom of glory, into the former we are transferred in this age; into the latter, however, in the future.

He calls Him the Son, not Christ, because He was about to speak of the Son's eternal Deity and incarnation. The kingdom of the Son is opposed to the power of darkness or Satan, and so that kingdom is of light, not of darkness.

Therefore, although by nature we are darkness, we are nevertheless made light in the Lord, Eph. V. 8. And although in the kingdom of grace there is not mere light, but the darkness of sin and misery sometimes exists, yet they do not reign and dominate in the faithful, Rom. IX. 15. In the kingdom of glory, however, there will be no place for them anymore.
