The Son of His love, so in whom all complacency and love of God is as it were deposited, Matth. III. 17. In whom alone we enjoy love and grace, Eph. I. 6. and in whom God glorifies His beloved, Is. XLIII. 4. Verf.

Latin:

V. 12. ἰσχυσαμένους τῇ θεῷ, τῷ πατρὶ τῷ ἱκανώσαντι ἡμᾶς εἰς τὴν μερίδα τοῦ κλήρου τῶν ἁγίων ἐν τῷ φωτί Vocem ἱκανὸν habuimus 2. Corinth. III. 8. Responder Ebrzo 116 μέρις κλήρου 117 Deut. XXXII. 9. sed ut ostendatur discrimen legis & Evangelii, additur hic ἅγιον ἐν τῷ φωτί, id est τῷ φωτί ἐν τῷ φωτὶ subaudito articulo ut saepe, qui exprimi-tur Rom. XI. 19. ubi est σὺν ἐν σκότῳ. Est autem ᾧ φωτὶ qui lucem habet comitem, 1. Joh. II. 19. 10. Gratiarum actio vel Colossensibus tribuitur, quod nempe precetur Apostolus, ut ipsi expendentes beneficia divina gratias agant Deo, vel quod magis congruere judicamus, Pauli est & Timothei, qui uti V. 3. pro Colossensium conversione gratias egere, ita, ut ad principalem tractationem nunc accellum parent, iterum εὐχαριστίαν suam exsolvunt, non pro ipsis tantum, sed in communi, pro omnibus fidelibus. exhibitus beneficiis.

Quae tum summatim exhibent hoc versu, tum deinceps plenius exequuntur; atque ita explicat Apostolus translationem in regnum Dei, ejusque causam meritoviam, redemptionem Christi & formalem remissionem peccatorum, nec non autorem Redemptionis Filium Dei, caput Ecclesiae, qui ideo plenitudine Deitatis suae assumptam carnem inhabitat, vi unionis hypostaticae, per quem ἀποκαταλλαγὴ facta est omnium, & pax conciliata.

Verbum ἱκανώσαντι ἡμᾶς, qui nos dignos fecit, juxta Chrysostomum duo infert, tum quod dignatus nos sit hoc honore, tum quod aptos ad eum nos faciat, μέρος κλήρου, portio sortis, vel participatio hereditatis.

Figura ejus erat in portione fortis terrae Canaan, quae cuivis tribui contigit.

Conf. Ex. XIX. 6. 1. Pet. II. 9. sed illic singuli partem adepti, in vita aeterna singuli totum possidebunt, Apoc. XXI. 7. Erit enim Deus ipsis omnia in omnibus, 1. Cor. XV. 28. In Ecclesia, inquit Theophylactus, sumus omnes sorte, sed partibus diversis potimur; hic vero nos & sortis ejusdem, & portionis dignos effecit.

Quo tamen gradus gloriae non tolluntur. Sed omnibus gloria essentialis eadem assignatur in vita aeterna.

Sortem etiam nominari, observat Theophylactus cum Chrysostomo, quod ut fors nulli obvenit humana solertia, sed pro divina voluntate cadit, Prov. XXXIII. ita & nos, nullo nostro, (ut verba ejus habent) vel officio, vel virtute, caelesti digni sumus imperio, sed Dei munere, quodcunque est boni, ad nos defertur. Propterea Dominus inquit, dicite, quoniam inutiles servi sumus, fecimus, quod facere debebamus.

Veritas haec Cornelio extorfit: Hereditas sanctorum vocatur fors, quia nulli homines ad eam jus habebant, cum tamen inter homines jus habeant ad hereditatem, cujus sint heredes; Unde Ephes. I. 11. dicit Apostolus, nos sorte vocatos ad fidem & gratiam Christi. Hereditas ergo haec sanctorum dicitur fors, quia hominibus fine merito, gratis & quasi fortuito obtingit.

Dicitur sanctorum portio, quia scil. abluti, sanctificati, & justificati sunt per nomen Domini Jesu, & per Spiritum Dei, 1. Cor. VI. Conf. 1. Petr. I. 2. Ebr. XII. 14. Ephes. V. 27. Dicitur fors sanctorum in lumine, caelesti scil.

Es. LX. 19. 20. Apoc. XXI. 23. XXII. 5. Theophyl. In lumine praesenti scilicet & futuro, hoc est, scientia.

Nam revelatio nobis mysteriis, & lumen viventibus praebuit, ut futuro in seculo fulgentiorem lucem elargiretur. V. 13. ὃς ἐρρύσατο ἡμᾶς ἐκ τῆς ἐξουσίας τοῦ σκότους) ἐξουσία σκότους dicuntur hic tenebrae efficacissime ad obcoecandos animos, ἐξουσία משל dominatus.

Qui facit peccatum, servus est peccati. Joh. VIII. 34. καὶ μετέστησεν) העביר transtulit. εἰς τὴν βασιλείαν τοῦ υἱοῦ τῆς ἀγάπης αὐτοῦ) Id est, τῦ ἀγαπημένου Ephes. I. 6. Est Ebraismus ut cum dicitur הר קדש Mons sanctitatis & familia.

Descriptio hic & in sequentibus, est specialior, quomodo nos perduxerit ad fortem hereditatis caelestis, & quomodo dignos eadem reddiderit: perduxit partim liberando ex potestate tenebrarum, partim transferendo in regnum Filii sui, quod est regnum lucis, per tenebras non solum vitiorum, sed etiam ignorantiae & errorum, non solum culpae tenebras, sed & pane, tenebras miseriae & temporalis, & aeterna intelligit.

Omnes enim illae tenebrae a Diabolo oriuntur, sub cujus potestate fuimus, antequam in regnum Filii Dei divina gratia, traduceremur.

Potestas tenebrarum intelligi potest vel de Magistratu & principe tenebrarum, h. e. Diabolo, vel de vi & potestate caliginis illius, quae veluti servos & captivos nos tenere inducitur, per prosopopoeiam. Non dixit a tenebris, inquit Chrysostomus, sed a potestate.

In nos enim magnam habuit potestatem, & in nos dominatum obtinuit, est enim grave, vel solum esse sub Diabolo, cum potestate autem, est hoc quoque gravius. Quam potestatem nemo destruere potuit, nisi Dei Filius.

Transtulit autem in regnum Filii dilectionis suae; Non ergo solum, inquit Chrysostomus, in liberatione a tenebris ostendit suam benignitatem. Atqui magna quidem res est liberasse a tenebris, in regnum autem introduxisse, est multo major. Vide ergo, quam multiplex fit donum.

Primum quod in imo jacentes nos liberaverit. Secundum quod non solum liberaverit, sed etiam in regnum transtulerit. Quae pro more suo repetit Theophylactus, addens: nec frustra invexit, sed ut cum Filio suae dilectionis, hoc est, cum Filio suo dilecto, caelesti imperio potiremur, qui sibi antea essemus infensi, & in tenebris versabamur, quod item & alibi dicit: Si sustinemus, & simul regnabimus. Quod vero porro cum Chrysostomo subjicit Theophylactus: Nec transtulit, (μετήγαγε, aut μετέθηκεν) sed transtulit, (μετήγαγε) ut non id omne transferri adscribat, sed arguat nos etia aliquid ad eam rem contulisse, id nec è verbo illo erui potest, nec Scripturae consentaneum est.

Nam quid conferent ad sui translationem, qui sub potestate tenebrarum sunt? Totum id Dei, non nostrum est.

Nemo venit ad me, nisi Pater traxerit eum, ait Christus Joh. VI. 44. Idcirco non ait, traduxit nos, quia non violenter dacimur, sed tranfulit, siquidem nulla nostra bona voluntas praecesserit.

Regnum Filii Dei est tum regnum gratia, tum regnum gloria, in illud transferimur in hoc seculo; in hoc vero in futuro.

Vocat autem Filium, non Christum, quia de Filii aeterna Deitate & incarnatione dicturus erat. Regnum Filii potestati tenebrarum vel Satanae opponitur, adeoque illud regnum lucis est, non tenebrarum.

Etsi ergo natura tenebrae sumus, reddimus tamen lux in Domino, Eph. V. 8. Et quanquam in regno gratiae non mera lux, sed tenebrae peccati, & miseriae quandoque dentur, non tamen regnant & dominantur illae in fideles, Rom. IX. 15. In regno vero gloriae nullus erit iis amplius locus.

Filius dilectionis suae, ita quo omnis complacentia & dilectio Dei velut deposita est, Matth. III. 17. In quo solo dilectione & gratia fruimur, Eph. I. 6. & in quo dilectos suos Deus glorificat, Es. XLIII. 4.

## 1:14
14. ᾧ ἔχομεν τὴν ἀπολύτρωσιν διὰ τοῦ αἵματος αὐτοῦ) Eph. I. 7. that διὰ τοῦ αἵματος αὐτοῦ (through His blood) seems to be ascribed here from that place to the Ephesians.

For that manuscript, which we use so often, does not have it here any more than the Syriac, and the Latin, and Ambrose. τῇ ἀφέσει τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν) & παραπτωμάτων (and trespasses) in the said place to the Ephesians. Now how He renders us worthy of the kingdom of the Son of God is explained, as to the meritorious cause; not by our works, or merits, but solely through ἀπολύτρωσιν (redemption), made by the price of the blood of Christ.

The emphasis of which word Chrysostom notes, because he did not say λύτρωσιν, but ἀπολύτρωσιν, to indicate a full redemption.

But that it is not an entanglement that διὰ τοῦ αἵματος αὐτοῦ (through His blood), the Greek codices agreeing, are a proof to the Greek interpreters. But Crocius rightly warns, (which is to be noted against Piscator) when he names blood, he understands the whole obedience of humiliation, which appeared most in the shedding of blood, 1. Cor. VI. 11. 1. Petr. I. 19. Ebr.

IX. 12. 14. As for the formal cause of the same translation from the power of darkness into the kingdom of the Son of GOD, it does not consist in the infusion of the habit of justice, but in the gratuitous remission of sins.

For our sins are taken away, not so that they do not exist, but so that they are not imputed; and thus we are liberated from the power of sins.

and Satan, since we are redeemed by Christ, through faith we obtain the remission of sins: thus we are transferred into the kingdom of the Son of GOD, when through faith we are rendered participants of the justice of the Son of GOD, and become children of light. In us there is nothing but injustice, but Christ has been made justice for us by GOD, 1. Corinth. I. 30. For those two things, the non-imputation or forgiveness of sins, and the imputation or donation of the justice of Christ, we have spoken of elsewhere in the Scriptures. By the former we are liberated from the power of Satan, who has power over us only on account of sins; by the latter we are rendered worthy of the lot of the saints in light, and the kingdom of the Son of GOD: because there is no dignity in us, all is ours from Christ, by whose light we are irradiated, and by whose justice we shine, 2. Corinth. III. 9. All of which must be attributed to the redemption of Christ: for through it we have been liberated not only from sin, the Devil, and death, but justice and eternal salvation have been acquired for us. Theophylact has it thus here: If we had not been redeemed, and our wicked deeds had not been forgiven us, we would by no means have been transferred to the celestial empire. Since therefore the Son himself has redeemed you, and led you to the Father, why do you boast that the angels themselves perform that duty. ὅς ἐστιν εἰκὼν τοῦ Θεοῦ ἀοράτου, the image of the unaspectable GOD, for so the Latins speak. The same sense is in 2. Cor. IV. 4. & 1. Tim. III. 16. & Heb. I. 3. Adam was the image of GOD, but a very faint one: in Christ it appeared most perfectly, how GOD was wise, powerful, and good. Thus we see the sun in the water. An image is one thing, a shadow is another, such as is in the law, Heb. X. 1.

Concerning Deity.

He now describes the Redeemer, and indeed first from his eternal divinity: that he is the substantial image of the invisible GOD, namely the Father: from whom he is indeed distinguished in person, so that the image is not the same as that of which it is the image, yet it is similar in all things; just as for an image, a likeness to that of which it is the image is required, as well as a configuration according to that subject, so that it may be expressed and fashioned by the same. But because the Son is not an accidental image of the Father, but a substantial one, having his origin from the Father, through generation, of the same essence as the Father, Johan. X. 30. 1. Job. V. 7. therefore he is to be called so similar to the Father, that he is not denied to be ὁμοούσια with the Father, Ebr. I. 3. he is called ἀπαύγασμα τῆς δόξης καὶ χαρακτὴρ τῆς ὑποστάσεως αὐτοῦ. But things which do not agree with Christ according to his human nature: For thus he is neither similar to the Father, nor one of the same essence with him; but according to his divine nature, according to which he is from the Father through eternal generation, who fashioned himself in the Son, and communicated his own essence to him through generation. Wherefore that periphrasis of the image of the unaspectable GOD, which is brought forward by Grotius, does not fit. For the Son is no less unaspectable than the Father, as he is GOD, the invisible image of the invisible GOD. Who is the image of the invisible GOD, says Chrysostomus; whose image then is he? GOD's. He is therefore immutable, who is above all magnitude. Ἡ τοῦ ἀοράτου εἰκὼν καὶ αὕτη ἀοράτου, καὶ ὁμοίως ἀοράτου, ἐπειδὰν αἱ εἰκὼν εἴη. τὴν γὰρ εἰκόνα καθὸ ἐστιν εἰκὼν, καὶ παρ' ἡμῖν ἀπαράλλακτον δεῖ εἶναι. οἷον τῶν χαρακτήρων, καὶ τῆς ὁμοιώσεως. Of him who is invisible, the image is also itself invisible, and similarly invisible. For an image, insofar as it is an image, must also among us be immutable, as being from the characters and likeness. Nor is anything else hinted at in 2. Corinth. IV. 4. But the passage 1. Tim. III. 16. is irrelevant; for there it concerns the manifestation of GOD in the flesh, i.e. the incarnation of the Word of GOD, Johan. I. 14. In the works of Christ there shines forth not only that GOD is wise, powerful & good, but also the wisdom, power & goodness of Christ himself, in whom dwelt all the fullness of Deity bodily, Col. II. 9.; & we have seen, say the Apostles, his glory, the glory as of the only-begotten of the Father, Johan. I. 14. But it is another thing that is said here. For here the argument is concerning the fact that the Son of GOD was before creation, before the Angels were founded & all things visible & invisible, before all creatures. Afterwards however there follows at last concerning the hypostatic union, as Grotius acknowledges on verse 19. If the image of GOD, says Theophylactus, then the Son has been changed in nothing by the Father, or made alien from the very image. And further: Since the image becomes both GOD & the Son of GOD, it will be most similar to that figure which is in GOD & the Father. And invisible, namely because he cannot be seen. Among us, however, because images are fashioned by the art of men, by which they are often deceived, they cannot have conformity, so as to be most similar: but nothing of this sort falls upon GOD, wherefore the similarity with the Son is more certain, & true with the Father. But if the Son were by no means most similar to the Father, what prevents even the angels themselves from bearing the true image of GOD? For these also are invisible, yet they are not asserted to be images of GOD. Chrysostomus had gone before, from whom Calvinus here rashly departs. See B. Hunnius's Calvinus Judaizans. Crocius himself acknowledges it, when he tries to vindicate his own Calvinus. With respect to the Father, he says, he was from eternity a substantial image, & one about to remain, even if men had never been created, to whom he might represent the Father, & indeed he is called the image of the Father, because he is the character of that person, Ebr. I. 3. he has the same essence with the Father through eternal generation in the manner proper to the Son, existing equal to him in all things, excepting only this, that he is not the Father, nor without beginning, nor unbegotten, as the Orthodoxus says in Theodoretus. But what Crocius says, that with respect to us, to whom the Son represents the Father, he is also called an image, does not fit. For that representation is wholly different in kind, namely of manifestation, or revelation of the Father, Joh. I. 18., from that representation by which the Son here is constituted the image of the Father by Paul, for this one is eternal & substantial; that one temporal & accidental. Therefore nothing solid for the defense or exculpation of Calvinus in his corruption of this passage favoring Arianism could be brought forward, whether by Pareus or by Crocius, but they cut down their own vineyards, and destroy themselves. Magister Magnus, whom he calls the interpreter, openly contradicts Calvinus himself, while he says that not what Christ becomes in himself is thus treated, but what he effects in others, This is true, he says, (because in him were created &c.) but concerning these words (the image of GOD inconspicuous, firstborn of every created thing) I do not understand it to be true, nay rather it expresses what becomes in himself, & is proven from what he did in others. πρωτότοκος πάσης κτίσεως First in creation, namely the new one, of which 2.

Cor. V. 17. Apoc. XXI. 5. Heb. II. 5. (In Hebrew it is said both what is first, and what is highest in every genus, as Ps. XXIX. 27. Jer. XXXI. 9. Job. XVIII. 13. and elsewhere. Not first in the new creation, but he is said to be begotten before the creation, and every creature. For Paul does not say πάντων οὐ, nor πρωτόκλισις, says Chrysostomus, and Theophylact note against the Arians; not in the creation, but before every creature, nor is the discourse here about the new creation, but about the creation made in the beginning... of all things, when all things were created, both visible and invisible, for in him they were created, and he is before all things. Nor can the Son of GOD be called first in the new creation. Because creation presupposes; where there is no oldness of the flesh, where there is no renewal of the Spirit, or new creation. If any one is a new creature, he is in Christ, 2 Cor. V. 17. Therefore Christ himself is not a new creature. Grotius received that gloss from the Socinians, which we have refuted professedly in a special Exercise, which has been inserted into the Thirty Exercises.

When a new creature is indicated, it is not called κτίσις (creation) simply and without addition. Which Grotius himself admits at Romans VIII. 19. And therefore Theophylact: Paul wishes to demonstrate this, that before anything was created, the Son existed.

But to exist is because of the genus. Therefore he is also prior to the Angels, and in such a way that he created them. And further: Note the prudence of the Apostle, lest anyone hearing that the Son consists before all created things, might think that he lacks a beginning, he teaches both that he has a Father, and that he was begotten by Him, since it is certain that both he and the rest proceeded from GOD.

Otherwise he shows that this one differs far from the others, since he derives his origin from the Father, as the Son. But those things, as if created through the same Son, were founded, which he reveals more clearly in the following. Therefore Erasmus is not to be heard here, who conjectures that it should be read πρωτότοκον (first-born), so that the sense might be that Christ produced all things first.

But Beza, with Crocius approving, and urging this against Calvin's gloss, rightly rejects the conjecture as one confirmed by the authority of neither codex, nor writer, nor even the Arian, and devised for the sake of destroying this passage, both because it is repugnant to the perpetual consensus of all codices and interpreters, and because it removes the distinction between to beget and to create, which must be observed in this matter. Chrysostom, therefore, Theodoret, and other Fathers first respond that he is not called by the Apostle πρωτόκτιστον (first-created), but πρωτότοκον (first-born), so that he might separate his birth from the creature, as the Commentary inscribed to Ambrose speaks.

Then they urge the heretics. If Christ were a creature, he would have a creature as a sister, but it is impossible that the same one be creator and brother. Since, therefore, he is called by Paul the creator of the creature, he is not therefore a brother.

The same Crocius attributes this version to B. Luther, the first-born among all creatures.

But B. Luther's Version, which appeared here at Wittenberg in the year 1546 by Johann Lufft, has: the first-born before all creatures. Theodoret says most excellently that it is stated here, because he was begotten before every creature, πρότερον τεχθεὶς ἡ πᾶσα κτίσις, ἡ μία κτίσις, so that πρωτότοκον might include the preposition πρὸ, i.e., first-born before every creature.

That it pertains to the Deity, says Grotius, is evident from the fact that he proves the first-born status from creation, verse 16. Thus Bullinger, Beza, Matthias Martinus, lib. 1 de persona Christi tr. 2 c. 12. Before them Zwingli in this place: first-born, that is, the Son of GOD before every creature, yet not to be numbered among creatures.

He brings this reason, because in him all things were created. To be created by another connotes a defect. Therefore it does not befit Christ.

In the same way Tertullian lib. de Trin. But if he is called by the Apostle the first-born of every creature, how could he be the first-born of every creature, unless because according to his divinity he proceeded from the Father of GOD as the Word before every creature? And lib. adversus Praxean. he is called first-born, as begotten before all things, and only-begotten, as begotten alone from GOD. Therefore the Apostle proclaims the eternal generation of the Son.

Therefore, the comparison of the word בכור (first-born) here is foreign, because he is called first-born, which is that which is first and that which is highest in every genus. For the Son of GOD is not the first or highest among those things which were created, but he is their creator. But creator and creature differ in their whole genus. He is not in the order of creatures, but he himself is before all things, and all things were founded through him and in him.

Conf. John I. v. 3. The passage Ps.

XXCIX. 27 (Ps. XXCIX. 27.) makes for the proper signification, that he is called first-born by reason of eternal generation. Concerning which see our notes on the said Psalm. Nor does that comparison of the first-born from the dead make for this.

For Christ was not at all from the number of the dead: but he himself is by no means in the number of creatures as creator. But note, says Theophylact, how in this place he is called first-born as if he were the first-fruits of the dead.

For regeneration (the blessed one of the resurrection (Matt. XIX.)) is the same, but there (in eternal generation) he does not offer the first-fruits of creation, even if he is first-born. For it is not a mode of essence: for he is indeed begotten, but those things are creation. Rightly Tertullian de Trinit.

How could he be first-born, unless because according to his divinity he proceeded from the Father before every creature? And Ambrose lib. 1 de Fid. c. 4. He is called first-born, not first-created, so that he may be believed both begotten according to nature, and first according to eternity.

And here Crocius himself rejected the comparison of v. 18, because those are different passages from the present one.

The very form of speaking, he says, shows that it was from the dead, for which reason the Apostle writes elsewhere that Christ was made ἀπαρχὴν (first-fruits) of those who sleep, 1 Cor. 15. 20. But that form of speaking πρωτότοκος πάσης κτίσεως (first-born of every creature) does not have an expressed signification of order.

Rather, the context clearly proves that he is not in the order of creatures. For the Apostle affirms that all things were founded through him, that he is before all things, and that all things consist through him, which are so many arguments for the divine nature. And therefore Crocius not only departs from Calvin and other Reformers in these matters, but also refutes them at length alongside the Socinians. Conf.

Eam. of the books of Crellius on the one GOD the Father §. 448. pag. 1459. seq. Verse 16. ὅτι ἐν αὐτῷ ἐκτίσθη τὰ πάντα τὰ ἐν τοῖς οὐρανοῖς καὶ τὰ ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς (for in him were created all things that are in heaven and that are on earth) It is certain that all things were created through the Word.

But the things which precede show that this concerns Christ, which is a name of man, just as Chrysostom also accepts this passage. But he understands the world created for the sake of Christ, in a sense not evil, but because of that which excels, it is more correct to interpret ἐκτίσθη here as: they were ordered, they were finished in a certain new state.

Concerning which signification of the word κτίζειν we have spoken in the Prolegomena to the Gospels: And Ephes. II. 10. 13. III. 9. IV. 24. Angels to men, men reconciled among themselves are under Christ.

Since Grotius acknowledges that through the Word: all things were created (II. from the work of creation), Job I. 3. which concerns the first creation; it is described what must be acknowledged by all, just as we have demonstrated professedly against the Socinians in the praised Exercises; Why then does he deny in this place, which even the Arians and Socinians themselves admit to be parallel, that it concerns the first creation: He says that this concerns Christ, which is a name of man.

But neither did the name of Christ precede, but that of the Son of GOD, and of the invisible image of GOD, nor where the name of Christ is held, is Christ always viewed according to human nature. Examples are John IIX. 28. 1 Cor. X. 9. Heb. XIII. 19. What Grotius says about Chrysostom is openly false.

For on the contrary, Chrysostom understands these things not only of the first creation, but also of the divine nature of Christ, according to which he himself is before the Angels. The Apostle, he says, attacks the dogma itself. For lest they might think him to be more recent, for the reason that formerly they were indeed led by Angels: but now through him, he shows that you could do nothing first.

For he himself would not have led them out of darkness. But secondly, because he is before them. But what if he uses this argument before them, that they were created by him. For in him, he says, all things were created. What do the followers of Paul of Samosata say here? And afterwards: And he is before all things. This is fitting for God. Where is Paul of Samosata, And all things... consist in him. That is, they were created into him. Adduce those words, by the continuation of the words, as if with frequent blows, rooting out the pernicious dogma.

For if so many things were said, and after so much time Paul of Samosata arose, much more so if these things had not been predicted. And all things, he says, consist in him. How do they consist in him, who does not exist? Wherefore also those things which are done through the Angels, are his. All these things Chrysostomus. Whom one ought not to have failed to examine here, Grotius.

That gloss κτίση (were created), that they were finished in a certain new state, which we have refuted, having been accepted by the Socinians, from our formal Exercise on the present peculiar saying, and we have given proof by many arguments, that it is treated here of the creation of all things: as from the property of the word κτίση (were created) (2) from the absolute usage of this word, (3) from the repetition of the same word, (4) from the mark of universality, (5) from the subjoined distribution, (6) from the new distribution of created things, which is altogether adequate, (7) from the mention of thrones, powers, etc., (8) from the Apostolic complex, (9) from the sustenance and conservation of all things, (10) from the pre-existence before all things, (11) from the generation before every creature, (12) from the distinct treatment of the Apostle, (13) from the collation of similar places, (14) from the unanimous confession of the Interpreters. Discussed also in the same place is the false interpretation of Enjedinus concerning the reconciliation, or the renovation and reformation of all things, and also concerning the new state of the angels, concerning the whole universe restored through Christ, as also the depravation of Socinus concerning all things endowed with intelligence being reformed.

We do not wish to do what has already been done. τὰ ὁρατὰ, ἀόρατα) Those things which are in the supreme world, which is φῶς ἀπρόσιτον (light unapproachable) 1. Tim. I. 16. Why only those things which are in the supreme world, as he speaks? For not only are there δόξατα (glories) there, namely Angels, but also on earth; for the souls of men are truly invisible. Which Chrysostomus wishes to be hinted at here. For even if we do not admit that they were all created at the beginning, they nevertheless acknowledge GOD as Creator; and thus they are from the Son of GOD, through whom all things were created, and were made, and are contained under the number of creatures, since there is no medium between creator and creature.

And who will concede that τὰ ὁρατὰ (visible things), as the Grotian Paraphrase seems to hint, are all in the supreme world. Nor does Crocius note inconveniently with Zanchius, that these things are opposed to the Pseudo-Apostles converted from Judaism, who were introducing the worship of angels.

For if they are a creature, and Christ is the creator, religious worship is due not to them, but to Christ. εἴτε θρόνοι) That is, Angels confident in thrones, as if they were certain Kings. See what we have said at Gen. XLI. 40. Rom. VIII. 38. and Ephes. I. 21. Such are those in Daniel, who preside over whole kingdoms, of the Chaldeans, Persians, Greeks.

To these correspond the Patriarchs in the Church, whose seats are eminently called thrones. εἴτε κυριότητες) See at the said place Ephes. I. 21. εἴτε ἀρχαὶ) Which are δυνάμεις (powers) in the said place to the Ephesians and Rom. VIII. 38. Ignatius to the Trallians: δυνάμεις τε καὶ κυριότηται διάφοροι θρόνοι τε καὶ ἐξουσίαι παραλλαγαί (different powers and lordships, thrones and authorities, variations). εἴτε ἐξουσίαι) See in the same place. τὰ πάντα δι' αὐτοῦ) δι' ὧν τὰ πάντα ἐποίησε (through whom he made all things), says the writer to the Hebrews I. 2. Understand by τὰ πάντα (all things) all things which pertain to the new creation. κτίσις αὐτοῦ ἔκτισαι) For his sake, that is, that he himself might preside over all those things, Apoc.

V. 13. Ebr. II. 8. He explains the invisible things, omitting the visible, as being those about which there was no doubt; as Chrysostomus and Theophylactus note.

But how do thrones, dominions, principalities, powers pertain to the new creation? If they are understood of good Angels, they had no need of renovation: If of evil ones, they were never renovated. If of both, it is rightly said that they were all created, but it cannot be said that they were renovated or reformed. And the Apostle repeats this so often, that it becomes an impudence to restrict this to a few certain creatures, when the scripture does not restrict it.

Therefore Theophylactus with Chrysostomus compares it with that of John c. I. All things were made through him.

The particles are also to be noted: He says all things were created IN him: all things were created THROUGH him and IN him. In him and THROUGH him as the efficient cause. Into him as the ultimate end. So that in no part of the work of creation is he constituted inferior to GOD the Father.

Conf. Prov. XVI. 4. Rom. XI. 34. Verf. 17. καὶ αὐτός ἐστι πρὸ πάντων) That is, the A & Ω, as the Apocalypse says I.

Latin:

Vers. 14. ᾧ ἔχομεν τὴν ἀπολύτρωσιν διὰ τοῦ αἵματος αὐτοῦ) Eph. I. 7. illa διὰ τοῦ αἵματος αὐτοῦ videntur adscripta hic ex illo ad Ephesios loco.

Manuscriptum enim ille, quo toties utimur, non magis hic habet, quam Syrus, & Latinus, & Ambrosius. τῇ ἀφέσει τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν) & παραπτωμάτων dicto ad Ephesios loco. Jam quomodo dignos nos reddat regno Filii Dei, explicatur, quod ad causam meritoriam; non nostris operibus, aut meritis, sed unice per ἀπολύτρωσιν redemptionem, pretio sanguinis Christi factam.

Cujus vocis emphasin notat Chrysostomus, quod non dixerit λύτρωσιν, sed ἀπολύτρωσιν, ut plenam redemptionem indicaret.

Non autem irretitionem esse illud διὰ τοῦ αἵματος αὐτοῦ, codices Graeci consentientes, interpretibus Graecis docemento sunt. Recte autem monet Crocius, (quod contra Piscatorem notandum) cum nominat sanguinem, totam obedientiam humiliationis intelligit, quae maxime apparuit in effusione sanguinis, 1. Cor. VI. 11. 1. Petr. I. 19. Ebr. IX. 12.

14. Quantum vero ad causam formalem eiusdem traductionis è potestate tenebrarum in regnum Filii DEI, non consistit ea in habitus justitia infusione, sed in gratuita peccatorum remissione.

Peccata enim nostra tolluntur, non ut non sint, sed ut non imputentur; atque ita liberamur à potestate peccatorum.

& Satanae, cum redempti a Christo, per fidem consequimur remissionem peccatorum: ita in regnum Filii DEI transferimur, cum per fidem iustitiae Filii DEI participes reddimur, & filii lucis evadimus. In nobis nil est nisi iniustitia, sed Christus nobis a DEO factus est iustitia, 1. Corinth. I. 30. Illa enim duo, peccatorum non imputationem, seu condonationem, & iustitiae Christi imputationem, vel donationem, in Scripturis idem alias diximus. Illa liberamur a potestate Satanae, qui non nisi ob peccata potestatem in nos habet; hac digni reddimur forte sanctorum in luce, & regno Filii DEI: quia dignitas nulla in nobis est, omnis nobis est a Christo, cuius luce irradiamur, iustitia fulgemus, 2. Corinth. III. 9. Quae accepta ferenda omnia sunt redemptioni Christi: nam per illam non tantum a peccato, Diabolo & morte liberati fumus, sed acquisita est nobis iustitia & salus aeterna. Theophylactus hic ita habet: Si nec redempti essemus, nec remissa nobis prava fuissent facinora, baud quaquam translati ad caeleste imperium fuissemus. Cum itaque vos Filius ipse redemerit, & ad patrem deduxerit, cur angelos ipsos adfruitis id muneris fungi. ὅς ἐστιν εἰκὼν τοῦ Θεοῦ ἀοράτου DEI inaspecti aspectabilis imago, ita enim Latini loquuntur. Idem sensus 2. Cor. IV. 4. & 1. Tim. III. 16. & Ebr. I. 3. Adam imago DEI fuit, sed valde tenuis: in Christo perfectissime apparuit, quam DEUS esset sapiens, potens, bonus. Sic in aqua solem conspicimus. Aliud imago, aliud umbra, qualis in lege, Ebr. X. 1.

Redemptoris descriptio 1. Deitate.

Describit jam Redemptorem, & quidem primum ab aeterna eius divinitate: quod sit imago substantialis DEI invisibilis Patris nempe: a quo persona quidem distinguitur, ut imago non est idem cum illo, cuius est imago, tamen est similis per omnia; quemadmodum ad imaginem similitudo cum eo, cuius imago est, requiritur, nec non effiguratio juxta illud suppositum, ut ab eodem expressa, ac effigiata sit. Quia vero Filius non accidentalis Patris imago est, sed substantialis, a Patre originem habens, per generationem, ejusdem cum Patre essentiae, Johan. X. 30. 1. Job. V. 7. ideo ita similis Patri dicendus est, ut non negetur ὁμοούσια cum Patre, Ebr. I. 3. dicitur ἀπαύγασμα τῆς δόξης καὶ χαρακτὴρ τῆς ὑποστάσεως αὐτοῦ. Quae vero Christo non conveniunt secundum humanam naturam: Sic enim nec similis est Patri, nec unus ejusdem cum ipso essentiae; sed secundum divinam naturam, secundum quam a Patre est per aeternam generationem, qui se effigiavit in Filio, ipsique per generationem essentiam suam communicavit. Quapropter non congruit illa περιφρασις DEI inaspecti aspectabilis imago, quae a Grotio adfertur. Nam non minus Filius est inaspectus, quam Pater, qua DEUS est, invisibilis DEI imago invisibilis. Qui est imago DEI invisibilis, inquit Chrysostomus; Cujus ergo vis eum esse imaginem? DEI. Est ergo immutabilis, qui est supra omnem magnitudinem. Ἡ τοῦ ἀοράτου εἰκὼν καὶ αὕτη ἀοράτου, καὶ ὁμοίως ἀοράτου, ἐπειδὰν αἱ εἰκὼν εἴη. τὴν γὰρ εἰκόνα καθὸ ἐστιν εἰκὼν, καὶ παρ' ἡμῖν ἀπαράλλακτον δεῖ εἶναι. οἷον τῶν χαρακτήρων, καὶ τῆς ὁμοιώσεως. Ejus, qui est invisibilis, imago est ipse quoque invisibilis, & similiter invisibili. Nam imaginem, quatenus est imago, etiam apud nos oportet esse immutabilem, utpote a characteribus, & similitudine. Nec aliud 2. Corinth. IV. 4. innuitur. Locus vero 1. Tim. III. 16. ἀλλότριος est; ibi enim de Φανερώσεως DEI ἐν σαρκὶ, h. e. verbi DEI incarnatione agitur Johan. I. 14. In Christi operibus effulfit, non tantum quod DEUS sit sapiens, potens & bonus, sed etiam ipsius Christi, in quo habitavit tota plenitudo Deitatis corporaliter, Col. II. 9. sapientia, potentia & bonitas; & vidimus, inquiunt Apostoli, gloriam ejus, gloriam velut unigeniti a Patre, Johan. I. 14. Sed aliud est, quod hic dicitur. Hic enim fermo est de eo, quod Filius DEI fuit ante creationem, antequam conderentur Angeli & omnia visibilia & invisibilia ante omnes creaturas. Postmodum autem sequitur demum de ἐνώσει ὑποστατικῇ, ut agnoscit Grotius ad vers. 19. Si DEI imago, inquit Theophylactus, ergò a Patre nihil immutatus est Filius, vel imagine ipsa alienus effectus. Et porro: Cum imago & DEUS fit, & DEI Filius, persimilis erit ei, quae in DEO est & Patre effigies. Et invisibilis, ideo scilicet, quia videri non potest. Apud nos autem, quia hominum arte, qua fallitur saepe, effingantur imagines, habere nequeunt conformitatem, ut persimiles sint: In DEUM vero nihil ejusmodi cadit, eo que certior est Filio, & vera cum Patre similitudo. Quod si nequaquam esset Patri persimilis Filius, quid impedit, quo minus nec angeli ipsi veram DEI imaginem preferant? Sunt namque & hi invisibiles, haud tamen DEI esse imagines adstruuntur. Praiverat Chrysostomus, a quo temere hic deflectit Calvinus. Vid. B. Hunnii Calvinus Judaizans. Agnoscit Crocius ipse, cum vindicare conatur Calvinum suum. Respectu Patris, inquit, ab eterno fuit imago substantialis, & mansurus, etsi nulli unquam conditi fuissent homines, quibus Patrem repraesentaret, & quidem dicitur imago Patris, quia est character personae illius, Ebr. I. 3. eandem habet cum Patre essentiam per aeternam generationem modo filio proprium, eidem per omnia aequalis existens, eo solum excepto, quod non est Pater, nec fine principio, nec ingenitus, ut Orthodoxus ait apud Theodoretum. Quod autem Crocius ait, respectu nostri, quibus repraesentat Filium Patrem, imaginem etiam dici, non congruit. Nam illa repraesentatio toto genere diversa est, nimirum manifestationis, vel revelationis Patris, Joh. I. 18. ab ea repraesentatione, qua Filius hic imago Patris constituitur a Paulo, haec enim aeterna & substantialis est; illa temporalis & accidentalis. Nihil ergo solidi pro defensione vel exculpatione Calvini in depravatione hujus loci Arianizantis adferre potuit, sive Pareus, sive Crocius, sed propria vineta caedunt, seque ipsos conficiunt. Palam contradicit ipsi Calvino Magistro Magno, quem vocat, interpreti, dum ille non quid Christus in seipso fit, sic tractari ait, sed quid in aliis efficiat, Hoc verum est, inquit, (quia in ipso condita &c. at de his verbis (imago DEI inconspicui primogenitus omnis rei creatae) non intelligo, verum esse, immo exprimitur, quid in ipso fit, & probatur ex eo, quod in aliis fecit. πρωτότοκος πάσης κτίσεως Primus in creatione, nova scilicet, de qua 2.

Cor. V. 17. Apoc. XXI. 5. Ebr. II. 5. (Ebraeis dicitur & quod primum, & quod summum est in quoque genere, ut Ps. XXIX. 27. Jer. XXXI. 9. Job. XVIII. 13. & alibi. Non primus in nova creatione, sed genitus ante creationem, omnemque creaturam dicitur. Nam πάντων οὐ non πρωτόκλισις, inquit Paulus, sed πρωτότοκος, quod Chrysostomus, & Theophylactus notant contra Arianos; non in creatione, sed ante omnem creaturam, nec de nova creatione hic fermo est, sed de ...creatione in principio rerum omnium facta, cum omnia conderentur tum visibilia, tum invisibilia, in ipso enim condita sunt, & ipse est ante omnia. Nec primus in nova creatione dici potest Filius DEI. Quia creatio vetustatem praesupponit; ubi nulla est carnis vetustas, ubi Spiritus renovatio, vel nova creatio non est. Si quis nova creatura est, in Christo est, 2. Corinth. V. 17. Non ergo Christus ipse est nova creatura. Glossam illam à Socinianis accepit Grotius, quam ex professo in peculiari Exercitatione, quæ Trige Exercitationum inserta est, profligavimus.

Cum nova creatura indigitatur, non simpliciter, & sine additamento κτίσις vocatur. Quod fatetur Grotius ipse ad Roman. VIII. 19. Ideoque Theophylactus: Id vult demonstrare Paulus, antequam aliquid crearetur, Filium esse.

Esse autem quia genus. Ergo & Angelis prior, & ita ut eos creaverit. Et porro: Adverte Apostoli prudentiam, me filium audiens quispiam ante omnia creata constare, existimet eumdem carere principio, & docet & patrem habere, & ab eo esse progenitum, quandoquidem cum ipse, tum reliqua constet à DEO prodiisse.

Alioqui hunc patefacit à cateris longè differre, siquidem à Patre hic ortum ducat, ut Filius. Illa vero tanquam creata per eumdem sunt Filium condita, quod clarius in sequentibus aperit. Non ergo audiendus hic Erasmus, qui conjecat, legendum esse πρωτότοκον, ut sensus sit, Christum primum omnia produxisse.

Sed Beza, probante Crocio, idque contra Calvini glossam urgente, rectè conjetturam illum nec codicis, nec scriptoris, ne Arriani quidem auctoritate confirmatam, & huic loco elidendo excogitatam, prorsus rejicit, tum quod repugnet perpetuo omnium codicum & interpretum consensui, tum quod discrimen inter gignere & condere, in hac materia observandum tollat. Chrysostomus igitur, Theodoretus, alii Patres primò respondent, non vocari ab Apostolo πρωτόκτιστον primum creatum, sed πρωτότοκον primogenitum ut secerneret nativitatem ejus à creatura factum, ut loquitur Commentarius Ambrosio inscriptus.

Deinde hæreticos urgent. Si Christus esset creatura, haberet creaturam sororem, fieri autem non posse, ut idem sit opifex & frater. Cum igitur Paulo dicatur opifex creaturæ, non ergo frater.

Tribuit idem Crocius B. Lutheri hanc versionem, der Erstgebohrne unter allen Creaturen. Sed B.

Lutheri Versio, quæ hic Wittebergæ Anno 1546. per Johann Lufft prodiit, habet: der Erstgebohrne vor allen Creaturen. Optimè Theodoretus hic dictum ait, quod ante omnem creaturam sit genitus πρότερον τεχθεὶς ἡ πᾶσα κτίσις, ἡ μία κτίσις, ut πρωτότοκον in cludat præpositionem πρὸ, q.d. πρωτότοκον πρὸ πάσης κτίσεως.

Ad Deitatem pertinere, inquit Grotius, patet ex eo, quod probat primogenituram ex creatione, vers. 16. Sic Bullingerus, Beza, Matthias Martinus, lib. 1. de persona Christi tr. 2. c. 12. Ante illos Zwinglius in hoc loco primogenitus, id est, Filius DEI ante omnem creaturam, non tamen inter creaturas numerandus.

Rationem hanc affert, quia in illum sunt creata omnia. Creatum esse ab alio defectum connotat. Christo ergo non convenit. Eodem modo Tertullianus lib. de Trin.

Quod si primogenitus omnis creaturæ ab Apostolo dictus est, quomodo omnis creaturæ primogenitus esse potuit, nisi quoniam secundum divinitatem ante omnem creaturam ex Patre DEI sermo processit? Et lib. adversus Praxean. primogenitus dicitur, ut ante omnia genitus, & unigenitus, ut solus ex DEO genitus. Prædicat ergo Apostolus æternam Filii generationem.

Aliena itaque hic collatio vocis בכור, quod primogenitus dicatur, id quod primum, & quod summum est in quoque genere. Nam non est primus aut summus inter ea, quæ creata sunt, Filius DEI, sed est eorum creator. Creator autem & creatura differunt toto genere. Non est in ordine creaturarum, sed ipse est ante omnia, & omnia per ipsum, & in ipsum condita sunt.

Conf. Johann. I. v. 3. Locus Ps.

XXCIX. 27. pro significatione propria (Ps. XXCIX. 27.) facit, quòd primogenitus dicitur ratione æternæ generationis. Quo de vide annotata nostra ad dictum Psalmum. Neque huc facit illa primogeniti à mortuis collatio.

Nam è mortuorum numero Christus omnind fuit: in creaturarum autem numero ipse creator minimè est. Attende autem, inquit Theophylactus, quemadmodum hoc loco dictus est primogenitus tanquam mortuorum primitia fuerit.

Nam regeneratio (beata resurrectionis (Matth. XIX.)) eadem est, ibi vero (in æterna generatione) non præfert creationis primitias, etsi primogenitus sit. Non enim est essentiæ modus: is quippe genitus est, illa vero creatio sunt. Recte Tertullianus de Trinit.

Quomodo primogenitus esse posuit, nisi quoniam secundum divinitatem ante omnem creaturam se ex Patre processit? Et Ambrosius lib. 1. de Fid. c. 4. Primogenitus dicitur, non primò creatus, ut & genitus pro natura, & primus pro æternitate credatur.

Collationem v. 18. & hic ipse Crocius reprobavit, quod diversa illa loca sint à præsenti.

Ipsa loquendi forma, inquit, ostendit, ex mortuis fuisse, quam ob causam Apostolus alibi scribit, Christum esse factum ἀπαρχὴν primitias obdormientium 1. Cor. 15. 20. At illa loquendi forma πρωτότοκος πάσης κτίσεως non habet expressam ordinis significationem.

Imo contextus evincit clarè, non esse in creaturarum ordine. Affirmat enim Apostolus, per eum omnia esse condita, esse ante omnia, & omnia per eum consistere, quæ naturæ divinæ totidem sunt argumenta. Ideoque Crocius non tantum à Calvino aliisque Reformatis in hisce discedit, sed eos etiam juxta cum Socinianis prolixè refellit.

Conf. Eam. librorum Crellii de uno DEO Patre §. 448. pag. 1459. seq. Vers. 16. ὅτι ἐν αὐτῷ ἐκτίσθη τὰ πάντα τὰ ἐν τοῖς οὐρανοῖς καὶ τὰ ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς) Certum est, per Verbum creata omnia.

Sed quæ præcedunt, ostendunt, hic de Christo agi, quod hominis est nomen, quomodo etiam Chrysostomus hunc accipit locum. Sed ille intelligit mundum creatum propter Christum, sensu non malo, sed propter id, quod præcellit, rectius est ἐκτίσθη hic interpretari, ordinata sunt, novum quendam statum sunt confecta.

De quo significatu vocis κτίζειν diximus in Prolegomenis ad Evangelia: Et Ephes. II. 10. 13. III. 9. IV. 24. Angeli hominibus, homines inter se reconciliati sunt sub Christo.

Quum agnoscit Grotius, per Verbum: creata (II. ab opere creationis) esse omnia, Job. I. 3. quod ad primam creationem; Describitur quod omnino agnoscendum est, quemadmodum Filius DEI adversus Socinianos in laudatis Exercitationibus ex professo demonstravimus; Cur ergò negat in hoc loco, quem parallelum esse fatentur etiam ipsi met Arriani, & Sociniani, de prima creatione agi: Dicit de Christo hic agi, quod hominis est nomen.

At nec Christi nomen præcessit, sed Filii DEI, & imaginis DEI invisibilis, nec ubi Christi habetur nomen, semper Christus secundum humanam naturam spectatur. Exempla sunt Joh. IIX. 28. 1. Cor. X. 9. Ebr. XIII. 19. Quod de Chrysostomo Grotius dicit, apertè falsum est.

Contra enim Chrysostomus hæc non tantum de prima creatione intelligit, sed etiam de divina Christi natura, secundum quam ipse ante Angelos est. Agreditur, inquit, Apostolus ipsum dogma. Nam ne existimarent eum esse recentiorem, eo quod olim quidem adducerentur per Angelos: nunc autem per ipsum, ostendit primum vos nihil potuisse.

Non enim ipse abduxisset è tenebris. Secundo autem, quod fit ante ipsos. Quod autem si ante ipsos hoc utitur argumento, quod ipsi per eum sint creati. Quoniam in ipso inquit, condita sunt omnia. Quid hic dicunt assecla Pauli Samosateni? Et poltmodum: Et ipse est ante omnia. Hoc est Deo conveniens. Ubi est Paulus Samosatenus, Et omnia in ipso constant. Hoc est, in ipsum sunt condita. Adduce eam verba, verborum continuatione, tanquam crebris quibusdam ictibus, perniciosum dogma evertentes radicitus.

Nam si & tam multa dicta sunt, & post tantum tempus exortus est Paulus Samosatenus, multo magis si haec non fuissent praedicta. Et omnia, inquit, in eo constant. Quomodo constant in eo, qui non est? Quamobrem & quae per Angelos fiunt, ejus sunt. Haec omnia Chrysostomus. Quem hic non inspexisse oportet Grotium.

Glossam illamκτίση ordinata sunt, novum quendam statum confecta sunt, à Socinianis acceptam profligavimus ex professo Exercitatione de praesente dicto peculiari, & pluribus argumentis probatum dedimus, hic de creatione omnium rerum agi: utpote è vocis κτίση creata sunt proprietate (2) ex absoluta hujus vocis usurpatione, (3) è verbi ejusdem repetitione, (4) ex universalitatis nota, (5) è subjuncta distributione, (6) è nova creatorum, prorsus adaequata, distributione, (7) è thronorum, potestatum &c. mentione, (8) è complexione Apostolica, (9) ex omnium rerum sustentatione ac conservatione, (10) è praexistentia ante omnia, (11) è generatione ante omnem creaturam, (12) è distincta Apostoli pertractatione, (13) è similium locorum collatione, (14) ex unanimi Interpp. confessione. Discussa etiam ibidem ψευδερμηνεία Enjedini de reconciliatione, vel renovatione omnium & reformatione, nec non de novo statu angelorum, de toto universo per Christum restituto, ut & Socini depravatio de rebus omnibus intelligentia praeditis reformatis.

Nolumus actum agere. τὰ ὁρατὰ, ἀόρατα) Ea, quae sunt in mundo supremo, qui φῶς ἀπρόσιτον 1. Tim. I. 16. Cur tantum ea, quae in Mundo, ut loquitur, supremo sunt? Non tantum enim ibi δόξατα sunt, Angeli scil. sed etiam in terris; nam animae hominum vere sunt invisibiles. Quas hic innui vult Chrysostomus. Etsi enim eas sub initium omnes creatas non admittamus, DEUM tamen Creatorem agnoscunt; atque ita à Filio DEI, per quem omnia condita sunt, & creata sunt, & sub numero creaturarum continentur, quam inter creatorem & creaturam non detur medium.

Et quis concedet τὰ ὁρατὰ, uti innuere Grotiana Paraphrasis videtur, omnia in mundo supremo esse. Nec incommode cum Zanchio notat Crocius, opponi haec Pseudo-Apostolis ex Judaismo conversis, qui angelorum cultum introducebant.

Si enim sunt creatura, Christus creator, non illis, sed Christo religiosus cultus debetur. εἴτε θρόνοι) Id est, Angeli in θρόνοις confidentes, quasi Reges quidam. Vide, quae diximus ad Gen. XLI. 40. Rom. VIII. 38. & Ephes. I. 21. Tales sunt illi in Daniele, qui regnis totis praesident, Chaldaeorum, Persarum, Graecorum.

His respondent in Ecclesia Patriarchae, quorum sedes throni eximie dicti. εἴτε κυριότητες) Vide dicto loco Ephes. I. 21. εἴτε ἀρχαὶ) Quae δυνάμεις dicto ad Ephesios loco & Rom. VIII. 38. Ignatius ad Trallenses: δυνάμεις τε καὶ κυριότηται διάφοροι θρόνοι τε καὶ ἐξουσίαι παραλλαγαί. εἴτε ἐξουσίαι) Vide ibidem. τὰ πάντα δι' αὐτοῦ) δι' ὧν τὰ πάντα ἐποίησε, ait scriptor ad Ebraeos I. 2. τὰ πάντα intellige omnia, quae ad novam creationem pertinent.

κτίσις αὐτοῦ ἔκτισαι) Propter ipsum, id est, ut ipse omnibus illis praeesset, Apoc. V. 13. Ebr. II. 8. Explicat invisibilia, omissis visibilibus, utpote de quibus non dubitabatur; ut Chrysostomus & Theophylactus annotat.

Quomodo vero throni, dominationes, principatus, potestates ad novam pertinent creationem? Si de Angelis bonis intelligantur, illi renovatione opus non habuere: Si de malis, nunquam illi renovati sunt. Si de utrisque, creatos eos esse omnes recte dicitur, renovatos, aut reformatos esse dici non potest. Et toties hoc repetit Apostolus, ut impudentiae fit, hoc restringere ad paucas quasdam creaturas, scriptura non restringente.

Ideo Theophylactus cum Chrysostomo confert cum illo Johannis c. I. Omnia per ipsum facta sunt.

Notandae etiam particulae: Omnia dicit IN ipso creata sunt: omnia PER ipsum & IN ipso condita sunt. In ipso & PER ipsum ceu causam efficientem. In ipsum ceu finem ultimum. Ne ulla parte in opere creationis DEO Patre inferior constituatur.

Conf. Prov. XVI. 4. Rom. XI. 34. Vers.

## 1:17
8. He understands πρὸ πάντων (before all things), as we have already said. καὶ τὰ πάντα ἐν αὐτῷ συνέστηκε) And this word is transferred from the old creation to the new. See 2. Petr. III. 5. Thus among the Philosophers σύστασις Φυσική (natural constitution), that is, κατασκευή (construction). Indeed, that Grotian-Crocian distortion is thus accurately precluded.

For therefore he is said to have been the firstborn of every creature BEFORE ALL THINGS, lest anyone should imagine that it is treated of him, which was done after the creation of things: nor that he should be brought into the order of creatures. Because he is said to have been before all creatures visible and invisible, whatsoever they may be, and thus simply before all things.

Before all things is a description of eternity, which is evident from Ps. XC. 2. Prov. VIII. 23. seq. And that there may be no doubt, that it is treated of the old creation, he says all things consist and are conserved in him.

For what else is conservation, than a certain continuation of creation. Conf. Ebr. I. 2. And not only, says Theophylactus, did he himself create these things, but he himself contains these same things, and so, that if they were led away from this providence of his, it would be necessary that they perish immediately.

He often turns and repeats the same thing, so that by the frequency of words, as if by frequent blows dealt, he might root out that exitial dogma. Note, that he did not say he was made before all things, but he is before all things, which especially befits GOD. Where in the world is that Paul of Samosata, who asserts that Christ took his beginning from Mary, and yet in himself, and as if in some foundation, he consists, and is in this way the firstborn of the other created things, when the Apostle by no means affirms that this firstborn is a created consubstantial being, but that all things are carried and exist in him?

Latin:

17. καὶ αὐτός ἐστι πρὸ πάντων) Id est, A & Ω, ut ait Apocalypsis I. 8. πρὸ πάντων intelligit, ut jam diximus. καὶ τὰ πάντα ἐν αὐτῷ συνέστηκε) Et haec vox de veteri creatione ad novam traducitur. Vide 2. Petr. III. 5. Sic apud Philosophos σύστασις Φυσική, id est, κατασκευή. Imò ita accurate praecluditur illa detorsio Grotiano-Crociana.

Ideo enim ANTE OMNIA dicitur primogenitus omnis creaturae fuisse, ne quis fingat de eo agi, quod post rerum creationem factum: neve creaturarum ordini inferatur. Quia ante omnes creaturas visibiles & invisibiles, quaecunque illae sint, adeoque simpliciter ante omnia fuisse dicitur.

Ante omnia descriptio est aeternitatis, quod è Ps. XC. 2. Prov. VIII. 23. seq. constat. Et ut dubium nullum sit, de veteri creatione agi, omnia dicitur in ipso consistere & conservari.

Quid enim aliud est conservatio, quam creationis quaedam continuatio. Conf. Ebr. I. 2. Nec solum, inquit Theophylactus, haec ipse creavit, sed eadem haec continet, & ita, ut si ab ejus hac providentia abducantur, pereant protinus necesse fit.

Eadem saepe versat & repetit, ut verborum frequentia, tanquam crebris adactis vulneribus radicitus exitiale dogma illud extirpet. Adverte, ut non ante omnia factum est dixerit, sed est ante omnia, quod DEO praecipue convenit. Ubinam gentium est Paulus ille Samosatenus, qui asserit, à Maria Christum duxisse principium, & in se tamen ipso, & tanquam in aliquo fundamento constare, esseque hoc pacto creatis cateris primogenitum, cum Apostolus nequaquam primogenitum hunc consubstantialem creatum esse affirmat, sed universa in ipso deferri, verfarique?

## 1:18
Verf. 18. καὶ αὐτός ἐστι ἡ κεφαλὴ τοῦ σώματος τῆς ἐκκλησίας) He is the head of the body, that is, of the Church, as this locution is presently explained Ephes. I. 22. IV. 15. V. 23. ὃς ἐστι ἀρχὴ) So also Apoc. I. 8. ראשית (beginning) the origin of a better world. πρωτότοκος ἐκ τῶν νεκρῶν) So also Apoc. I. 5. and in the same sense ἀπαρχὴ τῶν κεκοιμημένων (firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep) 1. Cor. XV. 20. Christ rose from the dead to immortal life, Ebr. IX. 28. the writer of the response to the orthodox LXXXV. ὃς γὰρ ἀθάνατος τε καὶ ἄφθαρτον ζωὴν ἄνω γέγονε τῷ ἡ διάτασις πλὴν τὸ σωτήριον Ἰησοῦ Χριστῷ (for he who is immortal and has become life incorruptible above, the arrangement is for the salvation of Jesus Christ).

From the eternal Divinity and the work of Creation, the Apostle, about to descend to the work of redemption, [declares] that the Same, who is the Creator of all things even of the Angels, but not any Angel, or throne, or principality, or whatever is of Angelic dignity, has been constituted the head of the Church: That this befits the one Son of GOD, to whom therefore alone we ought to betake ourselves in our necessities. When he had spoken, says Theophylactus, of the dignity of the Son of GOD, he now makes mention of his benignity and charity: since when he so excelled all things, who created and founded the universe, he nevertheless joined himself to these earthly and humble things. No, he said the complement of the Church, but the head, so that he might demonstrate the highest conjunction which it has with us, and that he might show that the flesh of the same, of which ours also consists, had taken its substance, not from heaven.

Who was made the beginning, and was constituted the highest Lord of the Church, or the causal beginning of the glorious resurrection, as being the firstborn from the dead. Who, since he died for our sins, and was raised for our justification (Rom.

14), was made the firstfruits (ἀπαρχὴ) of those who sleep (1

Cor. XV. v. 20), and therefore he is called the firstborn from the dead, not so much by reason of order; because Moses was raised to immortal life entirely before him (Matt.

XVII), as by reason of causality, because by his resurrection he consecrated that mass like firstfruits (ἀπαρχῆς), and we all have been made alive in him, and he himself was made the cause of resurrection for us all (Job XI. 25, 26).

He who is the firstborn of every creature, begotten from eternity before all creatures, and the cause of the creation of all things by reason of his divinity; the same is the firstborn of all the dead by reason of his human nature, because he was the first to rise from the dead with a glorified body, which perhaps did not happen to Moses, although he could have been raised in a mortal body as were the son of the Sareptan woman, the Shunammite's son, the widow's son in Nain, Lazarus, and others who were raised, and that is to be changed when he was translated into heaven, in the manner of those who are believed to have risen with Christ and to have been translated into heaven with him.

Which, however, we leave in the middle: since it easily suffices for this title that Christ is the cause of the resurrection of all who rise to immortal life: since in him all shall be made alive (1 Cor.

XV). He is the beginning of the resurrection, says Theophylact, because he rose first of all.

And because you dissolve the pains of death, he is deservedly called the firstborn.

For he who offers the firstfruits has those who follow him. For it is necessary that he who offers the firstfruits should have the primacy of some, and just as for one sheaf or another due as firstfruits, the harvest or the rest is blessed, so we all through him have attained holiness: and with the one body of the Lord rising, all human nature was made worthy to be raised as from the dead.

"ἵνα γένηται ἐν πᾶσιν αὐτὸς πρωτεύων" In the holiness of life, in miracles, in doctrine, in the return to life.

To him, not only as God, does the most eminent dignity belong as the creator of all things, but he is also of greater dignity as man, in all things: in the gifts of the Holy Spirit, in office, in word (λόγῳ), in work (ἔργῳ), in honor: and therefore it was fitting that he should be the first in the resurrection from the dead, as the head of the Church, and the beginning (ἀρχὴ) of the resurrection.

Theophylact not inappropriately: In all things which we contemplate around us.

For he was begotten by the Father before all things, and he is the first of all, as the head of the Church, and he rose before the others, because he bestowed immortality as if upon those who are the firstfruits.

For even if you say that some were raised from the dead before him, whom he himself raised, and so that nothing further is perpetual in death.

I would prefer, however, that the word πρωτεύων be referred not to eternal generation, but rather to other things.

For eternal generation does not come into comparison with temporal, as if it preceded by the property of order, and thus these things are reduced to the same order: since he transcends every order. And here Christ is viewed according to his human nature:

For although he is the head of the Church also according to his divine nature, yet he is the firstborn of the dead according to that nature according to which he was raised from the dead, which belongs to Christ by reason of his human nature. But according to which nature he is the firstborn from the dead, according to that nature he is also the head of the Church, and holds the primacy among all things. From which it is firmly concluded that the communication of divine power and Majesty was made to Christ according to his human nature.

For according to which nature Christ is the head of the Church, according to the same he diffuses the Spirit of life and motion into the whole body of the Church and all its members, and rules the universal Church, and is eminent over the universal Church, the Church confessing that he is, as Crocius, who recounts these things among the requirements of the head of the Church, concludes.

But these things imply divine power and Majesty . Crocius concedes: He who is the head of the Church, with the infinite power of vivifying, and that he is omnipotent.

But not necessarily, he says, is he omnipotent according to that nature, according to which Crocius is the head.

Why not?

How would he flow according to that nature with vivifying virtue, unless he were omnipotent according to that nature? He says: But Christ as he is head to us is substantial.

But is he therefore consubstantial with us according to both natures?

I answer: the reason is different:

For the being consubstantial with the members is not required of the head, since the Father is also the head of the Angels, and the head of the Church, and yet he is not consubstantial with the Angels, nor with the members of the Church: nor is he another, or a certain effect (ἀποτέλεσμα) of the head of the Church, as if by vivifying virtue infused into the members of the Church, therefore the blessed Henry Ekkardi rightly argues thus: Christ is truly and most effectively the vivifying head of the Church.

Christ is head according to his human nature.

Therefore. Crotins answers: He concludes thus, with us favoring.

For we, he says, willingly acknowledge the flesh of Christ to be vivifying, and that in four ways: 1. by merit, because by his word (λόγῳ) through the offering of his flesh he restored life to the world (Job VI).

2. by application; because by his word (λόγῳ) through his flesh he bestows eternal life upon believers, as Chemnitius loves to speak, or as Beza writes, because we are nourished by the intervention of his flesh communicated through faith, and finally we shall be glorified both in soul and body.

3. Because he raised the dead in the Gospel by his bodily voice and touch. 4.

Because the universal resurrection of the dead will take place by the voice of the son of man, and through the man of the resurrection (1 Cor.

XV). Chemnitius teaches these ways in his book on the two natures in Christ, c. 24, f. 176. If the Lutherans would stop here, there would be peace.

But if they contend that there is one vivifying power, by which both the divine word (λόγῳ) and the human nature are said to vivify, and that only the mode of attribution is different, we do not assent, nor do they conclude correctly from the reason of the head: For since vivification is an effect (ἀποτέλεσμα), both natures must indeed concur: but with a distinct operation.

They will not deny this: If the operation of the Deity is one, and that of the flesh another, why is the power not distinct?

All these things Crocius: but those are mere results (τελεσίσματα).

If the flesh is truly vivifying, it must be truly endowed with divine virtue: For there is no power of vivifying, unless it is divine and infinite.

It is not of finite power to vivify anyone spiritually. As for merit, certainly to merit life and eternal salvation for the human race is not of finite power.

But Christ merited eternal life for us not only as GOD, but as GOD and man.

As for efficacy, who will deny that to give life is the work of divine power!

But the flesh of Christ gives life to the world (Job VI. v. 33, 51).

The blood of Christ cleanses us from all sin (1 John I. 7). Who will deny, either that it pertains to the truly bodily flesh and touch, by which he healed the incurable diseases of the sick and restored life to the dead, or that these works are also of truly infinite power?

But if there is not one infinite power of vivifying for the divine and human nature, just as there is one and the same infinite hypostasis for each, divine in itself, human agreeing through communication, therefore a twofold virtue must be imagined, the one infinite, the other finite. Which is ἀθεόλογον & ἀφιλόσοφον (atheological and unphilosophical). Each nature acts indeed in the works of the office, which is its own, but with the communication of the other. Therefore, as the communication of the hypostasis cannot be denied, so neither ought the communication of the divine virtue, which does not differ really from the hypostasis, to be denied, unless one wishes to pass into the camp of the Reformers regarding the Person of Christ.

Verf.

Latin:

Vers. 18. καὶ αὐτός ἐστι ἡ κεφαλὴ τοῦ σώματος τῆς ἐκκλησίας) Caput est corporis, id est, Ecclesiae, ut mox haec locutio exponitur Ephes. I. 22. IV. 15. V. 23. ὃς ἐστι ἀρχὴ) Sic & Apoc. I. 8. ראשית origo mundi melioris. πρωτότοκος ἐκ τῶν νεκρῶν) Sic & Apoc. I. 5. & eodem sensu ἀπαρχὴ τῶν κεκοιμημένων 1. Cor. XV. 20. Christus ex mortuis furrexit ad vitam immortalem, Ebr. IX. 28. scriptor responsum ad orthodoxos LXXXV. ὃς γὰρ ἀθάνατος τε καὶ ἄφθαρτον ζωὴν ἄνω γέγονε τῷ ἡ διάτασις πλὴν τὸ σωτήριον Ἰησοῦ Χριστῷ.

Ab aeterna Divinitate & opere Creationis, ad opus redemptionis descensurus Apostolus, Eundem, qui est Creator omnium etiam Angelorum, non autem Angelum ullum, aut thronum, aut principatum, aut quicquid est dignitatis Angelicae, Ecclesiae caput constitutum esse: Id uni Filio DEI convenire, ad quem proinde solum nos in necessitatibus nostris conferre debeamus. Cum de DEI Filii, inquit Theophylactus, dignitate dixisset, de ejus benignitate & charitate nunc meminit: quandoquidem cum adeo cunctis praestaret, qui creavit & condidit universa, terrenis tamen se & humilibus hisce conjunxit. Neg, Ecclesia complementum dixit, sed caput, ut summam ejus, quam nobiscum habet, conjunctionem, demonstret, utque & carnem ejusdem, qua & nostra constat, substantia ceperit, non e caelo.

Qui est principium factus, & summus constitutus Dominus Ecclesiae, vel principium causale resurrectionis gloriosae, utpote primogenitus a mortuis. Qui cum mortuus sit propter peccata nostra, & resuscitatus propter justitiam nostram Roman.

14. ἀπαρχὴ primitiæ factus est dormientium 1.

Cor. XV. v. 20. ideoque primogenitus e mortuis dicitur, non tam ratione ordinis; quia Moses ante ipsum omnino ad vitam immortalem resuscitatus fuit Matth.

XVII. quam ratione causalitatis, quia resurrectione sua istam massam instar ἀπαρχῆς consecravit, nosque omnes in ipso vivificati sumus, nobis omnibus resurrectionis ipse causa factus est, Job. XI.

25. 26. Qui primogenitus est omnis creaturæ, ab æterno ante omnes creaturas genitus, & causa creationis omnium ratione divinitatis; idem primogenitus est omnium mortuorum ratione humanæ naturæ, quia primus e mortuis resurrexit corpore glorificato, quod forte Mosi non contigit, quum potuerit excitari corpore mortali ut filius Sareptanæ, Sunamitidis, viduæ in Nain, Lazarus, aliique resuscitati sunt, idque immutari cum in cœlum traductus est, more illorum, qui cum Christo resurrexisse, & cum ipso in cœlum translati creduntur.

Quod tamen in medio relinquimus: Quum facile ad hunc titulum sufficiat, quod causa sit Christus resurrectionis omnium, qui ad immortalem vitam resurgunt: siquidem in ipso omnes vivificabuntur 1.

Cor. XV. Principium inquit resurrectionis est ille, interprete Theophylacto, quia omnium primus resurrexit.

Et quia dolores mortis dissolvis, merito primogenitus dicitur.

Habet namque qui primitias præfert, qui se subsequantur. Est enim necesse eum qui primitias præferat, nonnullorum habere primatum, utque pro uno manipulo aliquo pro primitiis debito, messi vel reliquæ benedicitur, sic ipsi per eum ad unum omnes sanctitatem famus adepti: & corpore uno Domini resurgente, natura omnis humana ut a mortuis excitaretur digna facta est.

"ἵνα γένηται ἐν πᾶσιν αὐτὸς πρωτεύων" In vitæ sanctitate, in miraculis, in doctrina, in reditu ad vitam.

Ipsi non tantum ut Deo dignitas eminentissima convenit ceu creatori omnium, sed etiam potioris dignitatis est ut homo, in omnibus: donis Spiritus S. officio, λόγῳ, ἔργῳ honore: ideoq; conveniebat, ut primus esset in resurrectione a mortuis, ceu caput Ecclesiæ, & ἀρχὴ principium resurrectionis.

Theophylact. non inconcinne: In omnibus, quæ circum nos contemplamur.

Nam ante omnia a Patre genitus est, & primus est omnium, ut Ecclesiæ caput, surrexitque quam cæteri prior, quia tanquam his qui primitiæ sint, immortalitatem donavit.

Nam etsi nonnullos dixeris ante hunc a mortuis excitatos, quos ipsemet excitabat, et ut nil ultra fit morte perpetuus.

Malim tamen non ad generationem æternam, sed ad alia potius verbum πρωτεύων referri.

Nam æterna generatio non venit in comparationem cum temporali, quasi ordinis proprietate antecedat, atque ita ad eundem ordinem ista redigantur: Siquidem omnem ordinem transcendat. Et spectatur hic Christus secundum humanam naturam: Nam quamvis caput Ecclesiæ fit etiam quoad naturam divinam, primogenitus tamen mortuorum est secundum eam naturam, secundum quam resuscitatus est e mortuis, quod Christo convenit ratione humanæ naturæ.

At secundum quam naturam primogenitus est e mortuis, secundum eam naturam etiam caput Ecclesiæ est, & primas tenet inter omnia. Ex quo firmiter concluditur communicatio divinæ potestatis & Majestatis Christo secundum humanam naturam facta.

Nam secundum quam naturam Christus caput Ecclesiæ, secundum eandem Spiritum vitam lema se diffundit, & motum in totum corpus Ecclesiæ & omnia membra, regitque universam Ecclesiam, et eminet super Ecclesiam universam, fatente Ecclesia est, Crocio, qui inter requisita capitis Ecclesiæ ista concluditur recenfert.

At hæc divinam virtutem & Majestatem inferunt. Concedit Crocius: Qui caput est Ecclesiæ, cum infinitam habere vivificandi potentiam, eaque esse omnipotentem.

At non necessario, inquit, secundum eam naturam est omnipotens, secundum quam Crocii ex-caput est.

Quidni?

Quomodo influeret secundum eam naturam virtute vivifica, nisi omnipotens esset secundum eam naturam? Infat: At Christus qua caput nobis est substantialis.

Num vero ideo secundum utramque naturam consubstantialis nobis est?

Respondeo: disparem esse rationem: Nam τὸ esse consubstantiale membris neq; requisitum est capitis, quum etiam pater caput sit Angelorum, & caput Ecclesiæ, nec tamen Angelis, neque membris Ecclesiæ consubstantialis fit: neque etiam est alius, vel ἀποτέλεσμα quoddam capitis Ecclesiæ, ut virtute vivifica infuse in membra Ecclesiæ, idcirco vere B.

Henricus Ekkardi sic arguit: Caput Ecclesiæ vere & efficacissime est vivificum.

Christus secundum humanam naturam est caput.

E. Respondet Crotins: Sic concludit, nobis faventibus.

Nos n. ultro, inquit, agnoscimus carnem Christi esse vivificam, idque quatuor modis 1. merito, quia λόγῳ per carnis fuæ traditionem mundo vitam restituit Job.

VI. 2. applicatione; quia λόγῳ per carnem credentibus vitam æternam largitur, ut loqui amat Chemnitius, vel ut Beza scribit, quia carnis per fidem spiritualiter communicata interventu alimur, & tandem tum anima, tum corpore glorificabimur.

3. Quia corporali sua voce & contactu mortuos in Evangelio suscitavit.

4. Quia universalis resurrectio mortuorum fiet voce filii hominis, & per hominem resurrectionem 1.

Cor. XV. Hos modos Chemnitius tradit lib. de duabus naturis in Christo c. 24. f. 176. Hic si subsisterent Lutherani, pax esset.

Sed si contendane, unam vim vivificatricem esse, qua & divina λόγῳ & humana natura vivificare dicitur, & tantum attributionis modum diversam esse, non assentimur, nec recte concludunt a ratione capitis: Cum enim vivificatio fit ἀποτέλεσμα, utraque natura quidem debet concurrere: at operatione distincta.

Hoc non negabunt: Si alia est operatio Deitatis, alia carnis, cur non distincta vis?

Hæc omnia Crocius: sed mera illa τελεσίσματα.

Si caro vere est vivifica, oportet ipsam virtute divina vere præditam esse: Nam nulla est vivificandi vis, nisi divina & infinita.

Finitæ virtutis non est, quemquam spiritualiter vivificare. Quod ad meritum, utique vitam & salutem æternam humano generi mereri non est finitæ potentiæ.

Sed Christus non tantum ut DEUS, sed ut DEUS & homo meritus est nobis æternam vitam.

Quod ad efficaciam, æquis negabit, dare vitam opus esse divinæ virtutis!

At caro Christi dat mundo vitam, Job.

VI. v. 33. 51. Sanguis Christi emundat nos ab omni peccato, 1. Joh. I. 7. Quis inficiabitur, aut ad carnem pertinere vere corporalem & contactum, quo morbos sanavit ægrotorum incurabiles, vitam restituit mortuis, aut opera hæc etiam virtutis esse vere infinitæ?

Si autem non una est infinita virtus vivificandi divinæ & humanæ naturæ, quemadmodum una eademque est infinita hypostasis utrique divinæ per se, humanæ per communicationem conveniens, ergo gemina virtus fingenda erit, altera infinita, finita altera. Quod ἀθεόλογον & ἀφιλόσοφον. Agit utiq; in operibus officii unaquæque natura, quod suum est, sed cum communicatione alterius. Ut ergo communicatio hypostaseos negari non potest, ita nec divinæ virtutis, quæ ab hypostasi non differt realiter, communicatio negari debet, nisi in castro ris transire quis velit.

Sed de his ex professo in Examine Reformatorum de Persona Christi.

## 1:19
"Ὅτι ἐν αὐτῷ εὐδόκησε" (For in him it pleased) Namely God: which nominative is often understood. But "Εὐδοκεῖ" (it pleases) is rightly joined with a nominative, as Rom. XV. 26. 1. Cor. I. 26. Gal. I. 15. "Πᾶν τὸ πλήρωμα κατοικῆσαι" (All the fullness to dwell) Namely τῆς θεότητος (of the Godhead), of the divinity, which some Latin codices add here for the sake of interpretation, that is, of the divine virtues, as below II. 9. Thus we have πλήρωμα (fullness) also in John I. 16. where see the things said. And note κατοικῆσαι (to dwell), that is, to be present perpetually and inseparably, not through times, as in the Prophets.

This is the ὑποστατικὴ ἔνωσις (hypostatic union). These things are rightly said, and are evident from the collation of chap. II. v. 9. For the cause is rendered here, that Christ is both the head of the Church, and the causal principle, and the firstborn from the dead, whose infinite virtue does not only flow into all the members of his mystical body, by bestowing spiritual life upon it, but can also vivify the dead to a glorious and immortal life, so that through him alone we may come to the Father.

Namely because this was the εὐδοκία (good pleasure) of God the Father, that we might obtain life through the Son. This is the will of him who sent me, that whoever sees the Son, and believes in him, may have eternal life, and I will raise him up at the last day (namely, to eternal life) John VI. verf. 40. conf. 1. John V. verf. 1. 12. John XIV. verf. 6. And this is the cause of the mission of the Son into the world, and the coming of the Son into the flesh, and thus of the τῆς φανερώσεως ἐν σαρκὶ (manifestation in the flesh), of the incarnation, and of the hypostatic union of the divine and human nature, and of the inhabitation of the whole fullness of the divinity in the human nature, from the εὐδοκία (good pleasure) of God the Father, and his most gracious will, that namely all might be reconciled to the Father through the Son by the delivery of his flesh unto death, and by the shedding of his blood for the life of the world.

Therefore, the mystery of our reconciliation and redemption through the blood of CHRIST is explained in this place, of which he had spoken in verf. 14, through and for whom we are liberated from the power of the Devil, and are transferred into the kingdom of the Son of GOD verf. 13. And his grace is primarily the communication of the fullness of the Deity: because unless the divine virtue had been communicated to the human nature of CHRIST, reconciliation could not have been made through his blood, nor would the blood of CHRIST cleanse us from sin, nor through the body of CHRIST, and through his death, would life have been acquired and reconciled for us mortals, or be able to be conferred upon believers. Chrysostom and Theophylact explain πλήρωμα (fullness) concerning the fullness of the divinity.

That it pleased the λόγον (Word) to inhabit in the human nature, not by operation and act, but by substance. Cyril in defense of Anath. XI. against the Orientals. But because the Word, which is from GOD the Father, is life according to nature, he makes his flesh vivifying.

And again: But because it is the body of life, it is vivifying: Therefore he bestows life upon our mortal bodies, and evacuates the empire of death. Likewise in his book to the Queens. If the flesh of CHRIST were only the flesh of a man, which indeed pertains to his own nature, it would by no means vivify. But neither does the blood of an ordinary man have any power at all of vivifying by itself, and according to itself. But since it belongs to GOD alone to impart life, which is destitute of the spirit of life, but the body of CHRIST, and his precious blood, does vivify, why can there be a doubt that CHRIST is GOD?

For hence his body has it, that it is vivifying. Likewise lib. IV. in John cap. XXIII. Since the flesh is joined to the vivifying Word, it is made entirely VIVIFYING. For he did not drag the Word of GOD down to his own corruptible nature, but it itself was raised to a better virtue.

What does Crocius say here? He professes that if the Brentian effusion of divine properties should depart from here, he would willingly acknowledge what many ancients and moderns accept in this text concerning the inhabitation of the divinity of the Word in the flesh. But he wishes it also to be able to be accepted conveniently with Zwingli, Calvin, Beza, Zanchius, and other Reformers concerning the fullness of habitual graces.

But no effusion is believed by us: it is believed to be hypostatic: yet true and real, not verbal. Nor did the blessed Brentius wish to assert anything against the Calvinists, other than what Cyril asserted in lib. IV. in John cap. XIV. against the Nestorians: that the flesh of CHRIST HAD DRAWN the whole power of vivifying, since it is joined with the Spirit, and his whole body is full of the virtue of the vivifying Spirit. But what is this fullness of habitual graces here, in relation to those truly divine works of reconciliation of the human race, of redemption, of vivification, of the government and conservation and salvation of the Church?

Crocius explains himself, as it having pleased the eternal and best Father, that in Christ all fullness of wisdom, justice, goodness, power, and of all goods should dwell, from which as from an inexhaustible fountain all graces, as rivulets, are sufficiently derived into the whole body, and all its members, according to the measure of each, so that there is no need for other mediators and means of salvation outside of Christ. Which sufficiency of salvation Bullinger and Aretinus name. And that this sense agrees best both with the praises with which Christ is adorned in the preceding verse; and with those things which are said in the following verse.

It does not agree, neither with the words, nor with those praises. The word πᾶν τὸ πλήρωμα (all the fullness) is explained far otherwise by the Apostle, namely by πᾶν τὸ πλήρωμα τῆς θεότητος (all the fullness of the Godhead). In which way also Cyril Alex. in his book on the true faith to the Queens is observed by Crocius to have read it here. The praises of the preceding verse require something far more ample than habitual and finite gifts. For he could not be the head of the universal Church through finite power or wisdom: nor govern it presently, unless he were omnipresent: nor be the cause of resuscitation to eternal life, unless Christ were endowed with the virtue of vivifying according to his human nature.

For that he is the head of the Church, and the principle and firstborn from the dead according to his human nature, is not denied by the Reformers. Habitual graces are by no means sufficient for this: nor is their fountain so inexhaustible that their rivulets could diffuse themselves into the whole body of the Church throughout the entire world. Therefore the Spirit was given to him ἐν ἐκ μέτρῳ (not by measure), not by measure, that is, in an immense and infinite manner.
