The praises also of the following verses are so compared, that habitual graces are by no means sufficient for them: For to reconcile the human race to God the Father, to redeem from the power of Satan, from the hand of death and hell and from sin, to vivify the dead to eternal life, and to present the saints and blameless before himself are not of finite virtue, but that infinite virtue is required, which, since it does not have it by itself with the human nature, it ought to belong to it through the hypostatic communication. And this is what the Apostle says, that the whole fullness of the Godhead dwells in Christ; and therefore Crocius admits that it is possible with Lyranus and Dionysius. Dionys. Carthus. tò pân plḗrōma [the whole fullness], in a fuller sense regarding wisdom, grace, power, and the very Deity itself.

I add that it is not only possible, but necessary, not in a fuller sense only, but in the fullest sense. For where there is fullness, there nothing is lacking, much less where there is tò pân plḗrōma, all or the whole fullness: least of all where there is pân tò plḗrōma tês theótētos, all the fullness of the Deity.

But infinite things would be lacking, if the wisdom, grace, and power communicated to CHRIST according to the flesh were not infinite. For the finite and the infinite are infinitely distant.

The infinite is infinitely more perfect than the finite. Nor can it be called sufficient for salvation where there are only habitual gifts, which differ from ours only according to more and less, that is, by degree.

No vivifying and saving power can be imagined outside the divine. Nor would there have been any need for pân tò plḗrōma to inhabit the flesh, if human and finite gifts of habitual graces had sufficed.

That could have been accomplished through a holy man abundantly instructed by the gifts of the Holy Spirit: such a one as Nestorius finally fashions out of Christ, and Zwingli, Nestorianizing, in his epistle to Nestor. For he says, "We have not received that as common flesh."

Far be this: nor again as that of any sanctified man, or one associated with the Word only by equality of dignity, or one who has obtained a divine indwelling, but as truly VIVIFYING, and proper to the Word himself. For when life becomes, as GOD, according to nature, at the same time as it is made one with his own flesh, HE IMMEDIATELY CONFERRED UPON IT THE VIRTUE OF VIVIFYING. Kaì di' autoû apokataláxai pánta eis autón.

Eis autón [to him], here is to be taken as above 16, under him, or in such a way that they obey him. Regarding the word apokataláxai [to reconcile], see Eph.

II. v. 16. for it Eph.

I. vers. 10. he said anakephalaiṓsasthai [to sum up].

Neither above in verse 16, nor here is di' autoû [through him] "under him," nor elsewhere, as far as is known, anywhere. The proper meaning must be retained entirely.

For there is no reason why it should be abandoned. Furthermore, all things are reconciled to him.

Because the Son was no less offended by sin than the Father, and had become an enemy of the human race. It was necessary, therefore, that the reconciliation should reach even to him.

Nor is the sense of this word the same as that of the word anakephalaiṓsasthai: The meanings of the words differ greatly. For katallagḗ [reconciliation] is one thing, anakephalaíōsis [summing up] is another: in the former, a disagreement has intervened between the parties to be reconciled; the latter can be obtained without a prior disagreement.

And since the reason is given here why CHRIST becomes the head of the Church, it is not so fitting to interpret the present word as anakephalaiṓseōs, lest the same be proved by the same. Furthermore, should the proper sense not be retained?

For it follows immediately about pacification, and through the same, reconciliation is also explained regarding enmity, and katallagḗ is opposed to it. *Eirēnopoiḗsas dià toû haímatos toû stauroû autoû, di' autoû, eíte tà epì tês gês, eíte tà en toîs ouranoîs.* Which Eph.

II. v. 16.

It is attributed to Christ as God, it is attributed here to his Father, as one who accomplished this through CHRIST. Mĕšallēm [reconciling/making peace]. Made to the example of the Hebrew. Mention is made here of blood, because they were accustomed to ratify covenants through blood, as we said at Matth.

XXVI. vers. 28. add also Roman.

III. vers. 25.

V. vers. 9.

Ephes. I. vers.

7. He added, however, toû stauroû [of the cross], so that it may be understood that this death was joined with extreme torments.

Again he adds through him, that is, through his Word, eíte tà epì tês gês, eíte tà en toîs ouranoîs, the same as Ephes. I. vers.

10. tà en toîs ouranoîs kaì tà epì tês gês [those in the heavens and those on the earth] the pious angels and the pious men. The expression would have been full, tà ónta eíte tà epì tês gês, eíte en toîs ouranoîs.

"Through him" is rashly perverted, as if it were "through his WORD": For it is not about the pacification which is made through the Word of the Gospel, but which was made through the blood of his cross and therefore through his death, by which we have been reconciled to GOD, Roman. V. vers.

10. Not only was reconciliation given, says Chrysostom, but also the mode of reconciliation, pacifying through the blood of his cross.

He shows indeed that enmities are reconciled, but war is pacified: Through the blood, he says, of his cross in him, whether those which are on earth, or those which are in the heavens. It is indeed a great thing to reconcile.

Through him, however, is greater, and greater still is, through his blood. And not only blood, but what is greater than that, the cross.

Wherefore there are five admirable things by which he reconciled to God, through himself, through death, through the cross. Through him, says Theophylact, that is, he himself by his own work produced this salvation for us.

But how are those in the heavens and those on the earth reconciled? Those which had need of reconciliation, among which dissension and enmity flourished: understand intellectual natures differing among themselves because of sin: And on earth indeed men who had become enemies to GOD through sin, were reconciled to GOD, through the Mediator of GOD and men JESUS CHRIST, who gave himself a ransom for ALL.

Therefore not for good men only. For he was made a propitiation not for our sins only, but for the sins of the whole world, 1.

Johan. II. vers.

2. therefore he is said to have died for ALL 2. Corinth.

V. vers. 14.

The reconciliation made between all who were differing was perfect. But all were differing from GOD.

There is no diastolḗ [distinction] here, Rom. III.

23. And therefore those who lived before Christ, and those after Christ, without distinction, whether pious or impious.

For outside the reconciliation of Christ all are sinners, all impious are reconciled through the passion of CHRIST. For his passion profited forward and backward.

In the heavens are the Angels, who had no need to be reconciled with GOD. Nor does the Son of GOD take hold of Angels anywhere, but he takes hold of the seed of Abraham, Ebr.

II. vers. 16.

Therefore the Angels were not reconciled to God. The evil Angels remain enemies.

But the good Angels were enemies to men because of sin; just as they warded off the Protoplasts with a hostile sword from Paradise, and from the tree of life, Genes. III. to whom therefore we have been reconciled through CHRIST.

For GOD having been reconciled to us, peace was also established with the Angels: who rejoice together with GOD over the reconciliation, conversion, and salvation Luke 11. vers. 14. cap.

XV. vers. 14.

The earth had been cut off from heaven, says Chrysostom in this place, the Angels were waging war against men, seeing their Lord affected with disgrace and contumely. He says all things are restored in CHRIST, which are in the heavens, and which are on the earth.

How those which are in the heavens? He caused man to migrate thither: but he lifted up the enemy and foe to them.

This is profound peace. The Angels are henceforth seen again on earth, since man also appeared in heaven.

Theophylact repeats these and applies both against the Pseudo-Apostles: Why therefore do you trust in Angels? For they are so far from leading you and providing access, that they even waged war, unless GOD himself had reconciled you to them, and had made peace.

Why therefore do you run to them? Unless JESUS had reconciled us to them, he adds

Theophylact, we would not enjoy this peace. Crocius deduces from the particle τὰ in this verse another reason by which it is proved that CHRIST is the head of the Church; but the Apostle is rather occupied here with the same reason, namely, that it pleased GOD to that end to inhabit the whole fullness of the Divinity in CHRIST, so that all things might be reconciled through his blood. But those τὰ πάντα, all things, are not to be extended even to all creatures, for GOD was not incensed against all creatures on account of sin; nor are they to be drawn, with Origen, to men and Devils.

For as Devils never return into grace with GOD nor can they return: so they are not reconciled to GOD through Christ. See Jude verse 7. Nor is the reconciliation of good Angels with GOD to be imagined with Calvin, as if they were confirmed in grace through CHRIST, and their obedience were not so perfect outside of CHRIST, that it satisfies God in every respect.

Nor, however, is it to be maintained with Sam. Huber (which the Calvinists sometimes cast at our Churches) that all and singular men, without regard to faith, have been restored to the grace of God and placed in the bosom of grace, much less elected to eternal salvation.

For that, in order to be received into grace actually, there is need of faith, Acts X. verse 43. Nor are they elected to salvation, unless they are believers, because God chose us from eternity to salvation in sanctification of the Spirit and belief of the truth, 2 Thessalonians II. verse 13. The grace of God and the remission of sins has been acquired for all through the death of Christ. But for the application and enjoyment of the same, faith is actually required, which is not of all, 2 Thessalonians III. verse 2. Reconciliation, he Crocius refutes this invention of the Patriarch [Cyril Lucaris] in such a way that there is no need for other arguments.

First, he says, there is no need for reconciliation where alienation has not preceded: Pacification is not necessary where there is no discord.

Then, reconciliation was made through the death of CHRIST, Romans V. Therefore, from the very beginning, it is predicted of the heel of the heel, Genesis III. v. 15. and the image of reconciliation is proposed in sacrifices never without the blood of the Mediator, where there was need for the death of CHRIST, there sin preceded, for the wages of sin is death, Romans VI. verse 23. In the Angels there was no sin: Therefore, there was no need for them of reconciliation through the death of Christ. Third: CHRIST is called the Mediator between GOD and men, 1 Timothy II. verse 5. He is not called the Mediator between GOD and Angels.

And he would be the Mediator of the Angels if he had reconciled them to GOD. That he is not, is evident, because a Mediator must be of the same nature as he of whom he is the Mediator, which cannot be said of CHRIST and the Angels. Fourth, CHRIST appeared to destroy the work of the Devil, 1 John III. verse 1. But there was nothing of the sort in the good Angels. He came to save that which was lost, Matthew XVIII. verse 11. Whence they do not say to us and to you, but to you a Savior is born, Luke II. verse 11.

The reasons brought to the contrary are not very firm. Not the first. For although they were not to be outside the danger of falling, unless they had been confirmed by the grace of God, yet there was no need for the grace of a Mediator, otherwise he would also have had to become the Mediator of men, even if they had not sinned. On the contrary, the whole of Scripture refers the necessity of a Mediator to sin, and Paul writes that he came to save sinners, 1 Timothy I. verse 15.

Not the latter: The perfection of Angels is compared either with the law or with the justice by which God himself is just. If with the law, their justice is indeed exquisite, and according to it they are acceptable to GOD, for they fulfill the law given to them most perfectly. But in God there is a higher justice, to which even the created justice of Angels does not in the least correspond.

But GOD, as Calvin correctly warns in his commentary on Job, chapter XV, does not judge the Angels according to his infinite justice, but according to the law. Therefore, there is no need for any pardon for the Angels. For pardon presupposes sin or at least a defect. All these things Crocius [says] against the great Interpreter, as he calls him. Which are also to be noted against Daventianus, who is thrice inept, when he assigns a triple meaning to the word uniche.

It can be said, he says, not inappropriately, that CHRIST reconciled all things to GOD both on earth and in heaven: men properly by taking away their sins and the wrath of GOD arisen from sin: Angels analogically, by taking away the impossibility of sinning and incurring divine wrath: the whole of this fabric metaphorically, by freeing it from the servitude of corruption and restoring it to the integrity and beauty of its own nature, when the fullness of time has arrived according to that 2 Peter III. verse 13.

Only the proper sense holds. For the analogical [sense], having been refuted by Crocius, therefore the metaphorical [sense] is also alien and false. Therefore, the particle all things which is on earth pertains only to men, as all things which are in heaven pertains to the good Angels. But not those [things] to men only, who are actually reconciled, that is, who enjoy the reconciliation of Christ, which the Calvinists want, and also Crocius.

For although not all were truly [reconciled] by the reconciliation, or redemption of CHRIST, yet all were reconciled through CHRIST, all were redeemed. Crocius acknowledges that reconciliation is attributed to CHRIST, both on account of merit, insofar as he shed his blood on the cross, and thereby acquired reconciliation, and on account of efficacy, by which he applies his merit to believers, and actually restores them to the grace of the Father.

He also acknowledges that all pertain to the reconciliation of Christ, insofar as CHRIST satisfied for the sins of the whole world, so that there is no need for another victim to appease God, but by the virtue of that one victim all can return into grace with God, if they repent and believe. Although that hypothetical [proposition] is deceitful, if by an absolute decree that grace is restricted, by which alone faith can be excited in our hearts, namely to the few whom GOD out of mere good pleasure chose for that purpose, that they might believe, and for eternal life.

Concerning which we have spoken laboriously at John III. verse 16. He reconciled the world, according to the Apostle 2 Corinthians V. verse 19. and proposed reconciliation to the world, so that it might enjoy it. Therefore, he did not pass over the greatest part with efficacious grace.

Crocius says that the world of believers is understood, because he reconciles with [himself], not imputing sins: But he does not forgive sins to the incredulous but imputes them. But in this he contradicts Musculus, Copenius, Gerbardo de Neufuille, the Nassovian theologians, Johann Heinrich Alsted, and Georg Fabricius, who understand all men by the world. He contradicts his brother Ludovicus Crocius, who likewise interprets it of all.

He contradicts himself. For how are all commanded to embrace by faith a reconciliation which does not pertain to all by divine intention, so that it may be believed by all? No one is damned, except on account of the neglect of that thing which in some way pertains to him, says Johannes Crocius himself in his Confessio Prutenica, part II, chapter 16, page 476. Concerning the Apostolic passage in its own place. Wolffg. Musculus says in this place: it properly concerns sinners, and thus it pertains to the whole human race. The reason for reconciliation is universal because of the universal sin, which separated the human race from GOD.

The same on 2. Corinthians V. v. 19. observes: To be reconciled is said in two ways: First, it is to be reconciled to one who is unappeased: Then, to embrace with a grateful heart, through repentance and faith in the blood of reconciliation, the reconciliation already made in CHRIST the Son of God, who is now appeased.

The work of reconciliation is prepared for and sufficient for the whole human race. But since reconciliation cannot take place between those who are unwilling, a ministry of reconciliation has been instituted by GOD, by which all are called and invited to embrace this grace eagerly. If the whole world were to embrace this, then indeed the whole world, with all imputation of sins cast away, would be reconciled with GOD and saved.

Latin:

Vers. 19. "Ὅτι ἐν αὐτῷ εὐδόκησε" Nempe Deus: qui nominativus sæpe subauditur. "Εὐδοκεῖ" autem cum nominativo recte jungitur, ut Rom. XV. 26. 1. Cor. I. 26. Gal. I. 15. "Πᾶν τὸ πλήρωμα κατοικῆσαι" Nempe τῆς θεότητος, divinitatis, quod hic interpretandi causa addunt quidam Latini codices, id est divinarum virtutum, ut infra II. 9. Sic πλήρωμα habemus & Johan. I. 16. ubi dicta vide. Et nota κατοικῆσαι, id est, perpetuo & inseparabiliter adesse, non per tempora, ut in Prophetis.

Hæc est ὑποστατικὴ ἔνωσις. Hæc recte dicuntur, & e collatione cap. II. v. 9. patent. Causa nempe hic redditur, quod Christus, & caput Ecclesiæ sit, & principium causale, ac primogenitus e mortuis, cujus infinita virtus non influit tantum in omnia membra corporis sui mystici, vitam spiritualem eidem largiendo, sed etiam mortuos vivificare queat ad gloriosam & immortalem vitam, ut per eum solum ad Patrem veniamus.

Nimirum quia hæc fuit εὐδοκία Dei Patris, ut per Filium vitam consequeremur. Hæc est voluntas ejus, qui misit me, ut qui Filium videt, & credie in eum, vitam æternam habeat, & ego excitabo eum in die novissimo (ad vitam scil. æternam) Johan. VI. vers. 40. conf. 1. Johan. V. vers. 1. 12. Johan. XIV. vers. 6. Atque hæc est causa missionis Filij in mundum, & adventus Filii in carnem, adeoque τῆς φανερώσεως ἐν σαρκὶ τῆς ἐνσαρκώσεως, & τῆς ἑνώσεως ὑποστατικῆς divinæ & humanæ naturæ, ac inhabitationis totius plenitudinis divinæ in humana natura, ex Dei Patris εὐδοκία, & gratiosissima voluntate, ut nempe omnes reconciliarentur Patri per Filium per traditionem carnis in mortem, & per effusionem sanguinis pro mundo vita.

Explicatur ergo hoc loco mysterium nostræ reconciliationis, ac redemptionis per sanguinem CHRISTI, de qua vers. 14. dixerat, per & propter quos nos liberamus e potestate Diaboli, & transferimur in regnum Filii DEI vers. 13. Et ejus gratia primum communicatio plenitudinis Deitatis: quia nisi humanæ CHRISTI naturæ communicata esset divina virtus, non potuisset per sanguinem ejus fieri reconciliatio, nec sanguinis CHRISTI emundaret nos a peccato, neque per corpus CHRISTI, & per mortem ejus nobis vita acquisita & conciliata esset mortalibus, aut conferri potest credentibus. πλήρωμα de plenitudine divinitatis Chrysostomus & Theophylactus explicant.

Quod placuerit λόγον vel verbum inhabitare in humana natura, non operatione & actu, sed substantia. Cyrillus in defens. Anath. XI. contra Oriental. Quia autem vita secundum naturam est verbum, quod ex DEO Patre est, vivificatricem efficit carnem suam.

Et rursus: Quoniam autem est corpus vitæ, vivificum est: Propterea namque mortalibus nostris corporibus largitur vitam, & mortis imperium evacuat. Item in lib. ad Reginas. Si CHRISTI caro tantum hominis caro foret, quod quidem ad propriam illius naturam spectat, nequaquam vivificaret. Sed neque vulgaris quoque hominis sanguis ullam omnino per se, & secundum se vivificandi vim habet. Atqui cum soli DEO conveniat vitam impertiri, quod vitæ spiritu destituitur, corpus autem CHRISTI, & pretiosus illius sanguis vivificat, cur dubium esse potest, quin DEUS sit CHRISTUS?

Hinc namque corpus illius habet, ut sit vivificum. Item lib. IV. in Johan. cap. XXIII. Quoniam vivificanti verbo caro conjuncta est, tota VIVIFICA effecta est. Non enim ad corruptibilem suam naturam junctum DEI verbum detraxit, sed ipsa ad meliorem virtutem elevata est. Quid hic Crocius?

Profitetur, si Brentiana effusio proprietatum divinarum hinc facessat se libenter agnoscere, quod de inhabitatione Deitatis τῦ λόγυ in carne veteres & recentes multi hunc textum accipient. Sed vult commode quoque accipi posse cum Zvinglio, Calvino, Beza, Zanchio & aliis Reformatis de plenitudine gratiarum habitualium.

Sed effusio a nobis nulla creditur: creditur hypostatica: vera tamen & realis, non verbali. Neque aliud Beat. Brentius contra Calvinianos assertum voluit, quam quod Cyrillus lib. IV. in Johan. cap. XIV. contra Nestorianos afferuit: carnem CHRISTI HAUSISSE totam vim vivificandi, quin cum Spiritu conjunctam, totumque ejus corpus vivifica Spiritus virtute plenum esse. Quid vero hic gratiarum habitualium plenitudo, ad opera illa vere divina, reconciliationis generis humani, redemptionis, vivificationis, regiminis & conservationis ac salvationis Ecclesiæ?

Explicat se Crocius, ut æterno placuisse optimo Patri, ut in Christo omnis sapientia, justitiæ, bonitatis, potentiæ, omniumque bonorum plenitudo habitet, ex quo tanquam fonte inexhausto omnes gratia, tanquam rivuli in totum corpus, omniaque membra, pro cujusque modulo sufficienter deriventur, ut alius mediatoribus & medii salutis extra Christum non sit opus. Quam sufficientiam salutis nominent Bullingerus & Aretinus. Atque hunc sensum optime convenire tum elogiis, quibus Christus versu precedente ornatur; tum iis, quæ versu sequente dicuntur.

Non convenit neque verbis, neque elogiis illis. Verbum πᾶν τὸ πλήρωμα longe aliter explicatur ab Apostolo, nimirum per πᾶν τὸ πλήρωμα τῆς θεότητος. Quo pacto etiam hic legisse Cyrillum Alex. lib. de recta fide ad Reginas, observat Crocius. Elogia vers. præced. longe amplius quid requirunt, quam dona habitualia & finita. Nam nec caput Ecclesiæ universæ esse posset per potentiam aut sapientiam finitam: nec præfenter eam regere, nisi omnipræsens esset: nec causa resuscitationis ad vitam æternam, nisi virtute vivificandi præditus esset Christus secundum humanam naturam.

Nam caput Ecclesiæ, & principium ac primogenitus e mortuis secundum humanam naturam est non negantibus id Reformatis. Gratiæ habituales ad id minime sufficiunt: nec tam inexhaustus earum fons est, ut in totum Ecclesiæ corpus per universum orbem rivuli earum sese diffundere possint. Ideo Spiritus ei datus est ἐν ἐκ μέτρῳ non ad mensuram, hoc est, immensa & infinita ratione.

Elogia etiam vers. seqq. ita comparata sunt, ut minime ad ea sufficiant habituales gratiæ: Nam reconciliare Deo Patri genus humanum, redimere e potestate Satanæ, e mortis & inferni manu & a peccato, vivificare mortuos ad æternam vitam, & sistere sanctos & inculpatos coram se non sunt virtutis finitæ, sed ea infinita requiritur virtus, quam cum humana natura non habeat per se, per communicationem hypostaticam convenire eidem oportet. Atque hoc est, quod ait Apostolus, in Christo habitare totam plenitudinem Deitatis; Ideoque admittit Crocius posse cum Lyrano & Diony. Dionys. Carthus. τὸ πᾶν πλήρωμα, pleniore sensu de sapientia, gratia, potestatis & ipsius Deitatis.

Addo quod non possit tantum, sed debeat, non pleniori tantum, sed plenissimo sensu. Ubi enim plenitudo, ibi nihil deficit, multo minus ubi τὸ πᾶν πλήρωμα, omnis vel tota plenitudo: minime omnium, ubi πᾶν τὸ πλήρωμα τῆς θεότη, omnis plenitudo Deitatis.

At infinita deficerent, nisi infinita esset sapientia, gratia, potestas, quæ CHRISTO communicata secundum carnem. Nam finitum & infinitum in infinitum distant.

Infinitum infinities perfectius est finito. Nec potest ad salutem sufficientia dici, ubi tantum sunt habitualia dona, quæ a nostris solum secundum magis, & minus differunt, hoc est, gradu.

Non potest ulla vis vivifica & salvatrix fingi extra divinam. Neque opus fuisset πᾶν τὸ πλήρωμα inhabitare carnem, si humana ac finita dona gratiarum habitualium suffecissent.

Id per hominem sanctum donis Spiritus sancti copiose instructum præstari potuisset: qualem tandem Nestorius e Christo efformat & Nestorianizans Zovinglius in epist. ad Nestor. Neque enim, inquit, illam ut carnem communem suscepimus.

Absit hoc: neque rursum tanquam viri cujuspiam sanctificati, aut dignitatis tantum equalitate Verbo consociati, aut divinam inhabitationem fortiti, sed tanquam vere VIVIFICAM, ipsiusque Verbi propriam. Nam cum vita fit, ut DEUS, secundum naturam, simul atque unum quoddam cum ipsa sua carne factum est, MOX VIVIFICANDI VIRTUTEM IPSI CONTULIT. Καὶ δι' αὐτὰ ἀποκαταλάξαι πάντα εἰς αὐτόν.

'Εἰς αὐτὸν, hic sumendum, ut supra 16. sub ipso, sive ita, ut ipsi pareant. De voce ἀποκαταλάξαι vide Eph.

II. v. 16. pro eo Eph.

I. vers. 10. dixit ἀνακεφαλαιώσασθαι.

Neque supra versu 16. neque hic δι' αὐτὰ est sub ipso, neque alias, quod constet, uspiam. Retinenda omnino propria significatio.

Causa enim nulla cur relinquatur. Porro omnia ad ipsum reconciliata.

Quia non minus Filius quam Pater offensus erat per peccatum, & inimicus factus humani generis. Opus ergo erat, ut ad ipsum reconciliatio etiam pertingeret.

Neque idem hujus verbi sensus, qui verbi ἀνακεφαλαιώσασθαι: Significata verborum maxime discrepant. Aliud enim est καταλλαγὴ reconciliatio, aliud ἀνακεφαλαίωσις: ibi diffidium intercessit inter partes conciliandas; hæc obtinere potest fine prævio diffidio.

Et quum causa hic reddatur, cur CHRISTUS caput Ecclesiæ fit, non adeo convenit de ἀνακεφαλαιώσεως verbum præfens interpretari, ne idem per idem probetur. Porro non retinendus sensus proprius?

Nam sequitur de pacificatione statim, ac per eandem explicatur reconciliatio etiam de inimicitia, eique opponitur καταλλαγή. Εἰρηνοποιήσας διὰ τοῦ αἵματος τοῦ σταυροῦ αὐτοῦ, δι' αὐτοῦ, εἴτε τὰ ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς, εἴτε τὰ ἐν τοῖς οὐρανοῖς. Quod Ephes.

II. v. 16.

Christo tribuitur Deo, id hic tribuitur ejus Patri, ut qui hoc per CHRISTUM effecerit. מְשַׁלֵּם Sanguinoneas factum ad exemplum Ebræi. Sanguinis hic fit mentio, qui per sanguinem sancire fœdera solebant, ut diximus ad Matth.

XXVI. vers. 28. adde & Roman.

III. vers. 25.

V. vers. 9.

Ephes. I. vers.

7. Addidit autem τοῦ σταυροῦ, ut intelligatur mors hæc conjuncta fuisse cum fummis cruciatibus.

Rursum addit per ipsum, id est, per Verbum ipsius, εἴτε τὰ ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς, εἴτε τὰ ἐν τοῖς οὐρανοῖς, idem quod Ephes. I. vers.

10. τὰ ἐν τοῖς οὐρανοῖς καὶ τὰ ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς pios Angelos & pios homines. Locutio plena fuerat, τὰ ὄντα εἴτε τὰ ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς, εἴτε ἐν τοῖς οὐρανοῖς.

Per ipsum temere pervertitur, quasi fit per VERBUM ipsius: Non enim de pacificatione, qua per Verbum Evangelii ea fit, sed qua facta est per sanguinem crucis ipsius adeoque per mortem ejus, qua reconciliati nos sumus DEO, Roman. V. vers.

10. Non data est solum, inquit Chrysostomus, reconciliatio, sed etiam modus reconciliationis, pacificans per sanguinem crucis ejus.

Inimicitias quidem ostendit reconciliare, bellum autem pacificans: Per sanguinem inquit crucis ejus in ipso, sive qua in terris, sive quæ in cælis sunt. Magnum quidem est reconciliare.

Per ipsum autem, majus, & eo majus est, per sanguinem ejus. Et non solum sanguinem, sed quod eo majus est crucem.

Quamobrem quinque sunt admirabilia quæ Deo reconciliavit, per se ipsum, per mortem, per crucem. Per eum, inquit Theophylactus, hoc est, ipse suapte opera hanc nobis peperit salutem.

Sed quomodo reconciliata & quæ in cœlis & quæ in terris? Illa quæ reconciliatione opus habebant, inter quæ vigebat dissensio & inimicitia: naturas intellectuales inter se ob peccatum diffidentes intellige: Et in terris quidem homines inimici facti DEO per peccatum, reconciliati sunt DEO, per Mediatorem DEI & hominum JESUM CHRISTUM, qui dedit semetipsum pretium redemptionis pro OMNIBUS.

Ergo non pro hominibus solum bonis. Propitiatio enim factus est non pro nostris tantum, sed pro totius mundi peccatis, 1.

Johan. II. vers.

2. ideo pro OMNIBUS mortuus dicitur 2. Corinth.

V. vers. 14.

Perfecta fuit reconciliatio inter omnes diffidentes facta. Diffidebant autem omnes a DEO.

Nulla hic διαστολὴ, Rom. III.

23. Ideoque qui vixerunt ante Christum, & qui post Christum, citra discrimen, pii, an impii.

Nam extra reconciliationem Christi omnes peccatores sunt, omnes impii reconciliati sunt per passionem CHRISTI. Nam passio ejus profuit antrorsum, & retrorsum.

In cælis in cælis sunt Angeli, qui cum DEO ut reconciliarentur, opus non habuere. Nec uspiam Angelos assumit Filius DEI, sed assumit semen Abrahæ, Ebr.

II. vers. 16.

Idcirco Angeli Deo reconciliati non sunt. Manent Angeli mali hostes.

Boni autem Angeli inimici erant hominibus propter peccatum; quemadmodum Protoplastos hostili gladio arcebant a Paradiso, & ab arbore vitæ, Genes. III. quibus proinde reconciliati sumus per CHRISTUM.

DEO enim reconciliato nobis, pax etiam constituta est cum Angelis: qui juxta cum DEO lætantur fuper reconciliatione, conversione ac salute Lucæ 11. vers. 14. cap.

XV. vers. 14.

Abscissa erat, inquit Chrysostomus in h. l. terra a cælo, bellum gerebant Angeli adversus homines, videntes suum Dominum probro & contumelia affectum. Dicit omnia restaurari in CHRISTO, quæ sunt in cælis, & quæ sunt in terra.

Quomodo ea, quæ sunt in cælis? Illuc commigrare fecit hominem: sed ad ipsos sustulit hostem & inimicum.

Hoc pax profunda. Angeli de cætero rursus cernuntur in terra, quoniam homo quoque apparuit in cælo.

Repetit hæc Theophylactus & applicat uterque adversus Pseudo-Apostolos: Cut ergo Angelis confiditis? Tantum enim abest, ut illi vos adducant & accessum faciant, ut etiam bellum gefferint, nisi vos DEUS ipse illis reconciliasset, pacem non egisset.

Quid ergo ad illos accurritis? Ni JESUS nos ipsis reconciliasset, addit

Theophylactus, nihil pace hac frueremur. Crocius e particula τὰ in hoc versu alteram rationem, qua probetur, quod CHRISTUS fit caput Ecclesiae, deducit; sed versatur potius ad huc Apostolus in eadem ratione, quod nempe DEO placuerit eo fine inhabitare plenitudinem totam Divinitatis in CHRISTO, ut omnia per sanguinem ipsius reconciliarentur. Quae vero τὰ πάντα omnia non vel ad creaturas omnes extendenda, non enim omnibus creaturis insensus fuit DEUS ob peccatum; vel cum Origene trahenda ad homines et Diabolos.

Nam ut Diaboli cum DEO nunquam in gratiam redeunt nec redire possunt: ita DEO per Christum reconciliati non sunt. Vide Iude vers. 7. Nec cum Calvino reconciliatio Angelorum bonorum cum DEO fingenda, quasi per CHRISTUM in gratia confirmati sint, et obedientia eorum non tam perfecta sit extra CHRISTUM, ut Deo omni ex parte satisfaciat.

Neque tamen cum Sam. Hubero statuendum, (quod nostris Ecclesiis nonnunquam affricant Calviniani) omnes et singulos homines citra fidei respectum esse in gratiam Dei restitutos, et in sinum gratiae repositos, nedum ad salutem aeternam electos. Ad id, ut in gratiam recipiamur actu, opus est fide, Actor.

X. vers. 43. Nec ad salutem electi sunt, nisi credentes, quia elegit nos Deus ab aeterno ad salutem ἐν ἁγιασμῷ πνεύματ, καὶ πίστει ἀληθείας 2. Thessal. II. vers. 13. Gratia Dei et remissio peccatorum acquisita est omnibus per Christi mortem. Sed ad applicationem et fruitionem ejusdem actualiter requiritur fides, quae non est omnium, 2. Thessal. III. vers. 2. Reconciliatio, Quod commentum Patriarchae fui sic refellit Crocius, ut aliis opus non sit argumentis.

Primum, inquit, nulla reconciliatio opus est, ubi non praecessit alienatio: Pacificatio non necessaria, ubi nullum dissidium. Deinde reconciliatio facta est per mortem CHRISTI, Roman. V. ideo mox ab initio praedicitur calcaneo calcanei Gene. III. v. 15. et imago reconciliationis proposita in sacrificiis nunquam sine sanguine Mediator, ubi opus fuit morte CHRISTI, ibi praecessit peccatum, peccati enim stipendium mors, Roman.

VI. vers. 23. In Angelis peccatum non fuit: Non igitur illis opus fuit reconciliatione per mortem Christi. Tertio: CHRISTUS dicitur Mediator inter DEUM et homines, 1. Timoth. II. vers. 5. non dicitur Mediator inter DEUM et Angelos. Ae esset Angelorum Mediator, si eos DEO reconciliasset.

Non esse, inde patet, quia Mediator ejusdem esse natura debet cum eo, cujus est Mediator, quod de CHRISTO et Angelis dici nequit. Quarto CHRISTUS apparuit, ut diruat opus Diaboli, 1. Iohan. III. vers. 1. At nihil tale in Angelis bonis fuit. Ille venit ad servandum quod perierat, Matth. XVIII. vers. 11. Unde non dicunt nobis et vobis, sed vobis natus est Salvator, Luc.

II. vers. 11. Rationes in contrarium allatae non sunt admodum firmae. Non prior. Etsi enim extra lapsus periculum non erant futuri, nisi gratia Dei fuissent confirmati, non tamen ideo opus erat Mediatoris gratia, alioquin debuisset quoque hominum Mediator fieri, quamvis non peccassent. Contra scriptura universa Mediatoris necessitatem ad peccatum refert, et Paulus scribit, venisse ut peccatores salvos faceret, 1.

Timoth. I. vers. 15. Non posterior: Perfectio Angelorum vel cum lege comparatur, vel cum justitia, qua Deus ipse justus est. Si cum lege, exquisita sane est in illis justitia, et secundum illam sunt DEO accepti, perfectissime enim implent legem sibi datam. At in Deo altior est justitia, cui creata etiam Angelorum justitia minime respondet.

DEUS vero, ut Calvinus conc. LVIII. in cap. XV. Iobi optime monet non judicat Angelos secundum infinitam suam justitiam, sed secundum legem. Non igitur opus est Angelis ulla venia. Venia enim praepponit peccatum aut saltem defectum. Haec omnia Crocius adversus magnum, quem vocat, Interpretem. Quae etiam adversus Daventianum notanda, qui ter ineptus est, cum triplicem voci uniche assignat acceptionem.

Non incommode, inquit, dici potest, CHRISTUM reconciliasse DEO omnia tam in terra quam in caelo: homines proprie tollendo illorum peccata, et DEI iram ortam ex peccato: Angelos analogice, tollendo impossibilitatem peccandi et incurrendi iram divinam: Universi hanc fabricam Metaphorice, liberando a servitute corruptionis et restituendo naturae suae integritati et pulchritudini, cum plenitudo semporis advenerit juxta illud 2.

Petr. III. vers. 13. Solus proprius sensus habet. Nam analogicus a Crocio profligatus, ergo Metaphoricus quoque et alienus, et falsus est. Particula ergo omnia quae in terris ad homines tantum pertinet, ut omnia quae in caelis ad Angelos bonos. Non autem illa ad homines tantum eos, qui actu reconciliati, hoc est, reconciliatione Christi fruuntur, quod Calviniani volunt, etiam Crocius.

Etsi enim non omnes fuerunt vere reconciliatione, sive redemptione CHRISTI, omnes tamen per CHRISTUM reconciliati, omnes redempti sunt. Agnoscit Crocius, CHRISTO tribui reconciliationem, tum propter meritum, quatenus ipse sanguinem fudit in cruce, eoque reconciliationem acquisivit, tum propter efficaciam, qua applicat suum meritum credentibus, eosque actu in gratiam Patris restituit.

Agnoscit et omnes pertinere reconciliatione Christi, quatenus CHRISTUS pro peccatis totius mundi satisfecit, ut non fit opus alia ad Deum placandum victima, sed unius illius victimae virtute in gratiam cum Deo redire possint omnes, si resipiscant et credant. Quanquam subdola sit illa hypothetica, si per absolutum decretum restricta fit gratia illa σεμινάδως qua sola excitari potest fides in cordibus nostris, ad paucos nempe, quos ex mero beneplacito DEUS ad id, ut credant, et ad vitam aeternam elegit.

Quo de ad Iohan. III. vers. 16. operose diximus. Reconciliavit mundum, teste Apostolo 2. Corinth. 5. Cor. V. vers. 19. mundoque reconciliationem proposuit, ut ea fruatur. Non ergo maximam partem gratia efficaci praeteriit.

Dicit Crocius, intelligi mundum credentium, quia reconciliat cum, non imputans peccata: At incredulis non condonat peccata sed imputat. Sed eo contradicit Musculo, Copenio, Gerbardo de Neufuille, Theologis Nassovicis, Iohanni Henrico Alfedio, et Georgio Fabricio, qui per mundum omnes homines intelligunt. Contradicit fratri Ludovico Crocio, qui pariter de omnibus interpretatur.

Contradicit sibi ipsi. Quomodo enim omnes jubentur fide amplecti reconciliationem, quae non ad omnes pertinet ex intentione divina, ut credatur ab omnibus. Nemo damnatur, nisi propter ejus rei neglectum, quae aliqua ratione ad ipsum pertinet, inquit ipse Iohannes Crocius Convers. Pruten. part. II. cap. 16. pagin. 476. De loco Apostolico suo loco. inquit Wolffg. Musculus in h. l. proprie concernit peccatores, atque ita pertinet ad totum genus humanum. Catholica est ratio reconciliationis propter catholicum peccatum, quod genus humanum a DEO divisit.

Idem ad 2. Corintb. V. v. 19. observat: Reconciliari duobus modis dici: Primo esse reconciliari implacato: Deinde reconciliationem jam placati in CHRISTO Filio Dei factam grato animo per resipiscentiam ac fidem in sanguinem reconciliationis amplecti.

Reconciliationis opus toti generi humano paratum esse ac sufficiens. Verum quoniam reconciliatio inter invitos locum habere non potest, institutum esse a DEO ministerium reconciliationis, quo cuncti ad hanc gratiam cupide amplexandam vocentur & invitentur. Hanc si totus mundus amplexaretur, utique totus mundus omni peccatorum imputatione rejecta cum DEO reconciliaretur & servaretur.

## 1:21
Verse 21. Καὶ ὑμᾶς ποτε ὄντας ἀπηλλοτριωμένους, namely, from the people of GOD, which is added in Ephesians II. verse 12. Ἀπηλλοτριωμένους Psalm LXIX. verse 9. Καὶ ἐχθροὺς τῇ διανοίᾳ, in mind alienated from GOD, Romans V. verse 10. Ἐν τοῖς ἔργοις τοῖς πονηροῖς, which are wont to accompany impiety, 1 Cor. VI. verse 10.

11. Reconciliation made through the blood of the cross is universal for all men.

Now the application is made to the Colossians, and therefore their status is exhibited, both their former status under Heathenism and their modern status under Christianity. For there they lived ἀπηλλοτριωμένοι (alienated) from the people of God and from GOD Himself without Christ, nay, without GOD in the world, Ephesians II. v. 12. Nay, they lived as enemies altogether to GOD, as being under the state of sin and wrath, Ephesians II. verse 3, and not only alienated from GOD, but even enemies, which is more.

For they can be alienated from one another who do not pursue each other with hostility. Cf. Rom. VIII. verse 7. But they are said to have been enemies, first because they wanted what GOD did not want, and did not want what He wanted, James IV. verse 4. Secondly, because they hated Him as the executioner of the human race, as Aretius loves to speak, and with him Crocius.

They lived in evil works only, because they were alienated from GOD not only in mind, but also in will, not only in thoughts and every figment of the heart, which is only evil, Genesis VI. verse 6, but also in actions and works adverse to GOD: Because whatever is not of faith is sin, Romans XIV. verse 23. Why mention was made particularly of the Διανοίας (mind), Crocius explains more fully: The Apostle wished to show, in the most excellent faculty of the soul, by which we understand, think, reason, and will, the unhappy seat of enmities, from which even all the lower faculties were armed against GOD, and broke out into all kinds of sins.

For while he says that the primary faculty is hostilely opposed to GOD, he testifies quite openly that there was nothing in the Colossians that did not resist GOD, and indeed with hostile impetus. Therefore, not by fate and necessity, as if unwilling and forced, but of their own accord and by deliberate counsel did they act against GOD, which had its beginning not from above, but from themselves, as Theophylact notes with Chrysostom. Regarding evil works: He understands not only external works, but also internal ones, such as false opinions, doubts, incredulity, distrust toward GOD, erroneous judgment about Him, trust in oneself and one's own gifts, idolatry, self-love, ἀσέβεια (impiety), impatience, desire for revenge, hatred of enemies, love of lying, contempt for divine truth and for GOD Himself, sinister suspicions, envy, to which were added the manifest works of the flesh, anger and gross idolatry, carousings, adulteries, drunkenness, quarrels, blasphemy, and thus whatever fights against the law of God: These they could not deny.

These were the fruits and sad testimonies of hostility. When they were committing such things, and not thinking of peace, the grace of peace came to them, of which follows.

Latin:

Vers. 21. Καὶ ὑμᾶς ποτε ὄντας ἀπηλλοτριωμένους Nempe a DEO populo, quod additur Ephes. II. vers. 12. Ἀπηλλοτριωμένους Psalm. LXIX. vers. 9. Καὶ ἐχθροὺς τῇ διανοίᾳ Animo alieno a DEO, Roman. V. vers. 10. Ἐν τοῖς ἔργοις τοῖς πονηροῖς qui impietatem comitari solent, 1. Cor. VI. vers. 10.

11. Reconciliatio per sanguinem crucis facta universalis est omnium hominum.

Jam applicatio fit ad Colossenses, ideoque eorum status tum pristinus sub Ethnicismo, tum modernus sub Christianismo exhibetur. Ibi enim vivebant ἀπηλλοτριωμένοι a populo Dei & ab ipso DEO fine Christo, imo fine DEO in mundo, Ephes. II. v. 12. imo vivebant inimici omnino DEO, utpote sub peccati & iræ statu, Ephes. II. vers. 3. nec alienati tantum a DEO, sed hostes etiam, quod amplius est.

Possunt enim abalienati esse a se invicem, qui se non persequuntur hostiliter. Conf. Rom. IIX. vers. 7. Hostes autem fuisse dicuntur, primo quia volebant, quod DEUS nolebat, & nolebant, quod ille volebat, Jac. IV. vers. 4. Secundo, quia eum oderant tanquam carnificem humani generis, ut loqui amat Aretius, & cum eo Crocius.

Vivebant in malis tantum operibus, quia non tantum mente, sed & voluntate alieni a DEO erant, non tantum cogitatis & figmento omni cordis, quod tantum malum, Genes. VI. vers. 6. sed etiam actionibus & operibus DEO adversis: Quia quicquid non est ex fide, peccatum est, Roman. XIV. vers. 23. Διανοίας cur peculiariter mentio facta, plenius explicat Crocius: Voluit Apostolus in præstantissima animi facultate, qua intelligimus, cogitamus, ratiocinamur & volumus, monstrare inimicitiarum infelicem sedem, unde & inferiores facultates omnes fuerint armatæ contra DEUM, & in omnia genera peccata proruperint.

Dum enim primariam facultatem DEO hostiliter adversam esse dicit, satis aperte testatur in Colossensibus nihil fuisse, quod DEO non repugnarit & quidem hostili impetu. Non igitur fato & necessitate invitos coactosque, sed sua sponte ac deliberato consilio gessisse cum DEO, quod non ex supernis, sed ex ipsis habuerit exordium, ut cum Chrysostomo Theophylactus annotat. De operibus malis: Non solum externa intelligit opera, sed etiam interna, ut sunt falsæ opiniones, dubitationes, incredulitas, diffidentia erga DEUM, judicium de eo erroneum, fiducia fui donorumque suorum, idolatria, philautia, ἀσέβεια, impatientia, vindictæ cupiditas, odium inimicorum, amor mendacii, contemptus divinæ veritatis & ipsius DEI, sinistra suspiciones, invidia, quibus accefferunt manifesta opera carnis, ira & idololatria crassa, comesationes, adulteria, ebrietates, lites, blasphemia, adeoque quicquid pugnat cum lege Dei: Hæc negare non poterant.

Hi fuerunt hostilitatis fructus & testimonia tristia. Cum talia patrarent, nec cogitarent de pace, gratia pacie illis obtigit, de qua sequitur.

## 1:22
Verse 22. Now δὲ ἀποκαταλλάξῃ. This δὲ is redundant here, as in Ephesians II. verse 4. ἀποκαταλλάξῃ, that is, He made them friends to GOD, namely, through conversion. Ἐν τῷ σώματι τῆς σαρκὸς αὐτοῦ, Through the body of Christ similar to ours, consisting of flesh and bones. He accomplished such great things with an instrument so slight. Αὐτοῦ here refers to a name further removed, as does δι' αὐτοῦ, which preceded. Διὰ τοῦ θανάτου, A wondrous thing: Life from death.

The body of CHRIST is indeed said to be similar to ours in flesh, just as he expressed the likeness of sinful flesh, because he assumed a fragile body, such as ours is through sin, Romans III. verse 5, but it is not ὁμοούσιον (consubstantial) or merely similar, but of the same nature as us, as far as substance is concerned, and thus ὁμοούσιον, not only in that it consists of flesh and bones, which Jerome rightly urges against the spiritual, airy, thin body of John of Jerusalem, epistol. LXI. to Pamm., but also as regards the soul, which is of the same substance as ours. For σῶμα (body) is understood not as inanimate, as Apollinarius feigned, but animated. The soul cannot be excluded: For in it, by the grace of our reconciliation, he felt the wrath of GOD and the pains of hell.

In the Old Testament, sacrifices were made from animals, which typically satisfied and reconciled, Leviticus XVII. verse 11.

Num. V. verses 6, 7, 8. Exod. XXII. verse 3. Numer. XV. verses 22, 23. CHRIST accomplished true reconciliation not in the bodies of animals, but in that truly human body, endowed with a rational soul, consubstantial with us, according to that: Sacrifice and offering you did not desire, but a body you have prepared for me, Heb. X. verse 5, from Psalm XL. verse 7, as Crocius rightly says here. Nor indeed a naked body or ψιλὴν ἄψευδῶς (merely bare), but one in which the whole fullness of the Deity dwells, verse. 19. is indicated. For the body, even if ἔμψυχον (ensouled), even if having GOD as an inhabitant, as GOD dwells in the saints by grace, was by no means sufficient to effect such a great thing. Therefore it pleased that the whole fullness of the Deity should dwell in the body of CHRIST, which was to be delivered up for the life of the world. Wherefore the name of instrument is too vile. Christ is not an instrumental cause, but the meritorious cause of reconciliation.

Let the double sense of ἀποκαταλλαγῆς (reconciliation) be noted here.

The first, verse 19, is about the reconciliation by which God is reconciled to us, or as Paul speaks, by which we are reconciled to Him through Christ, so that He might be rendered propitious to us, which was done on the cross and by the death of Christ. The other is about the application of this reconciliation, by which the same is appropriated to us through faith, we enjoy it, and are rendered friends of God, which happens in justification.

Cf. 2. Corinthians V. verses 19, 21. But it is said that this is done also in the body of his flesh and through the death of Christ: Because this is the meritorious cause of our justification.

And in truth there is only one reconciliation, which is viewed in two ways, first universally, by which all men are reconciled to God, and God is appeased toward all men: Then appropriatively, by which each of the faithful makes it his own, believing that he is reconciled through Christ and that God is appeased toward him, and by that faith enjoys that reconciliation, just as the redemption of Christ is not doubled, since for all gave himself as a ransom for all, 1 Tim. II. v. 6. & when each of the believers appropriates this to himself with Paul. For redemption is common & universal for this reason, that it may be made applicable to all, & each one may be able to claim it for himself through faith.

Crocius wishes this reconciliation not to be attributed here to GOD the Father, but to the Son. For thus do Aretius and Tossanus explain it, and it does not say in the body of his flesh, but in the body of his flesh, not through the death of him, but through his own death. For some Codices explicitly add this pronoun. And in the former, they read αὐτοῦ [his] with Jerome in epistle LXI, Ambrose, and Chrysostom, homily IV on this passage. Oecumenius also refers it to Christ, with the agreement of the codices of the best quality in Beza. Theophylact: Again, he says, he introduces the mode of reconciliation, which was done in his body. And afterwards: When he had explained everything that is the duty of the son, as one who had accomplished all these things through death, lest by chance he should say: Therefore we will have nothing to work for, rather he says it is necessary that you be more constant in faith, lest you be rendered even more sluggish, & relapse into former crimes.

Not therefore with Socinus should these things be snatched away from the Father, against whom Theodoret’s paraphrase is to be noted: For you, who lead an impious and wicked life, and were entirely deprived of the light of the knowledge of the truth and were made strangers to GOD, not by this gift given to you by the law, but by your debt paid by CHRIST and his body delivered to death. To present you holy and blameless, and irreproachable— (Founded Matth.

VII. v. 25. Luc. VI. vers. 48. Eph. III. vers. 17. 1. Petr. I. vers. 5. 104 מְיֻסָּדִים Houses well founded endure.

Moreover, it is a metaphor drawn from a temple, 1. Reg. VI. v. 37. And steadfast 1. Cor. VII. 57. XVI. vers. 38. In the Glossary, steadfast means firm, stable. To sit is a durable position. All these things look toward faith.

In it one must persevere until the end, Apoc. II. 7. in it we must be founded upon that unique foundation, which is Christ, 1. Cor. III. 9. In it we must be firm against any temptations: Thus salvation is ascribed to faith alone, which we shall obtain when we are one day set before the sight of God.

Grotius here [understands] a good purpose, while Crocius mixes in charity. But that has nothing to do with salvation, it is a gift of God, not from works, lest anyone should boast, Eph. II. 8. 9. And Crocius himself acknowledges that in both metaphors faith is regarded: There is, he says, a double metaphor in the two words: One taken from a building, whose foundation, if it has been properly laid, does not easily fall, compare Matth.

VII. 24. 25. Luc. VI. 48. The other taken from those who sit firmly in a seat, & are not driven about by the wind: Thus they must be firm in faith, lest they be carried about by various & strange doctrines, Heb. XIII. 9. It denotes the firmness of faith, which it has not from themselves, but from Christ the primary foundation, upon which it is built, Col.

II. 7. from the Word of the Prophets & Apostles, upon which it rests, for they had been built upon the foundation of the Prophets & Apostles. Elsewhere he expresses this matter thus: We have become partakers of Christ, if only we have held fast that beginning, by which we are sustained, firm unto the end, Heb. III. 14. Which are more analogous to faith. And not moved away from the hope of the Gospel, which you heard) moved away מְנֹעָנִים, faith generates hope, hope perseverance, with hope lost, perseverance collapses.

That hope, in which we must be unmoved, is produced solely from faith, and not from works. If it were to rely upon our works, how greatly would it have to waver! Nothing, says Theophylact as interpreter, that is burdensome is laid upon you, except that no one should separate you from Christ. For in him all the hope of the Gospel is situated, & it will be for all who have received the Gospel to hope in him, as one who has pacified all things. Which makes it so that whoever might perhaps ascribe this reconciliation to the Angels themselves, must necessarily be moved away from Christ.

Indeed, it is impossible that one should deviate a little from virtue, but in faith one cannot be changed. And so he does not demand what is burdensome to tolerate. He does not call it the hope of the law, which was also observed by Crocius, but of the Gospel.

For the law makes hope of life only for those who provide perfect obedience; but the Gospel [does so] for all, whoever repent, & embrace Christ by faith. Sinners cannot finally be cast down by the hope of the law: For no one among all fulfills the law absolutely. They can be supported by the hope of the Gospel. PART II.

Concerning the Word & Ministry of the Gospel. The preaching in all creation under heaven) You ought not to doubt about future things, since what you see agrees so well with what was predicted.

See above 6. 4 which you saw earth, Luc. XVII. vers. 24. or what lives on earth, as Acts IV. vers. 12. Thus the Hebrew בְּרִיאָה is translated, Prov. VIII. v. 26, Creation בְּרִיאָה signifies man by way of eminence to the Hebrews. See Mark XVI. v. 15. The Apostle now descends from the reconciliation made through Christ to the Word, and the proclamation of it, through which we are made partakers of the same.

Therefore he made mention of the Gospel, which they had heard: Because from the Gospel alone is faith & hope had: And that through the hearing of the Gospel, for it to be truly heard, there is need of proclamation, Romans X. This therefore is the reason for the connection, which Grotius renders. For there is no reason why they should not doubt about future things, nor even of exhortation the argument of the passage is sought from the testimony of the whole world, which Crocius, along with Chrysostom and Theophylact, desires. He says what was preached, not what was believed, or even what was received, or believed by every creature. But whence faith and hope are had, was to be explained here, so that it might be declared how we are made partakers of such great benefits of Christ, and to whom these pertain, it might be further elucidated. Namely, every creature (human, that is) which is under heaven.

Therefore it was necessary for the Gospel to be preached, and it was preached to every creature; Mark XVI. 15. It is added 'under heaven,' not because it is under every climate of heaven, as Crocius explains, favoring his own particularity, but because the discourse is about any who are wandering on the earth, as Hugo interprets. For it is not for us to imagine a hyperbolic Synecdoche, since there is no necessity for it, and it is not admitted as necessary even in the examples brought by Crocius, Acts II, 24; Deut.

II, 25. As to what is objected concerning the new world, that the Gospel was never known to those peoples in the time of the Apostles, Davenant responds: First, he says, this is uncertain; for Ecclesiastical histories teach that the Gospel had penetrated to the furthest shores of the East Indies, and most learned men, among whom is Arias Montanus in the book Phaleg, opine that the western parts of this India are contiguous to the eastern parts of America or the new world.

Although it can also be answered that those regions were inhabited long after the time of the Apostles: but when the Gospel is said to have reached the whole world, it is understood as those parts of the world which are inhabited by men. 'I, Paul, became a minister' in many places, even in your Phrygia.

Concerning the word 'minister' (diakonos), it was spoken of above, verse 7. In the Manuscript it is more fully 'and I became a minister,' as 1 Tim. II. 7; 2 Tim. I, 11. The word of the Gospel is not dispensed immediately, nor through Angels, but through men, it was sent forth; such as Paul was among many, as Epaphras was among the Colossians. The name of Deacon is taken generally for any Minister of the Word, under which even the Apostles are included. Thus all heralds of the Gospel are called Ministers, in respect to God, by whom they were appointed to the ministry, and to whom they minister and serve.

Thus he professes himself not the author, but only a Minister of the Gospel. He thus conciliates faith and reverence for himself and those like him, the faithful Ministers of the Word, for that reason. He calls himself a Minister of the Gospel, says Theophylact, he compels them the more, that they may obey. For I do not preach what is mine, he says, but I minister to another, namely God.

Wherefore also give faith to my words. Ver. 24. 'Now I rejoice in my sufferings for you.' I rejoice in these evils, which I not only endure for this reason, that I preached the Gospel to the Gentiles, but I also willingly tolerate them for this, that you and others may be the more confirmed in the faith, 2 Tim. II. 10. The Greeks commenting on this passage did not read 'os ante.'

And 'now I rejoice' well begins the sense, as 2 Cor. VII, 9. He testifies that he rejoices in his sufferings on account of the preaching of the Gospel, both to testify that the Gospel is genuine, and because of his affection, that he should also glory among the Colossians, for whose sake he asserts that he also endures sufferings. When he had said, says Theophylact, that he was made a Minister of the Gospel, and prayed that they might not fall away from it, he shows that it is so truthful and certain, that he confesses he suffers for himself, saying thus: I not only suffer, but I also labor in suffering.

And what I suffer, I tolerate also for your sake, so that through tolerance some things of this kind might profit you. 'For you,' that is, for your good, so that you may be edified and confirmed by my patience, constancy, and exultation in sufferings in the faith. Lombard: 'for confirming you in the truth of the Gospel.' So also Hugo and Thomas.

Therefore others rashly distort these things toward satisfactions. 'And I fill up what is lacking of the afflictions of Christ in my flesh.' Christ suffered great things, sufficient for our salvation, for us. But He so loves His own, that He feels the evils which they themselves bear as if they were brought upon Himself, Acts IX. Thus, while Paul bears chains, Christ in a certain way was bearing them. 'What is lacking,' that is, the remaining things, the Syriac here has 'that which is lacking,' or 'His body' for the good of the Church, as we have already said.

'Which is the Church,' above 18. Therefore these things are not to be understood concerning a supplement of the satisfaction or merit of Christ through the satisfactions and merits of the saints, which the Papists desire, Cajetan, Valentinus, Bellarminus, Suarez, Cornelius a Lapide. But concerning those sufferings which are still lacking to the mystical body of Christ, not to the proper body of Christ. For he taught in v. 19, 22 that by that a perfect reconciliation had been made. There would not be a true reconciliation, unless a perfect satisfaction had been performed. The Apostle acts to teach that we have in Christ all things which are required for salvation. But we do not have them, if the satisfactions of others were required, if there were any 'lacking things' in the merits of Christ. Therefore Christ explains the sufferings of Christ in the mystical body.

He not only died for you, but also, besides the fact that He died, He is prepared to be bound for you. Bened. Justinianus acknowledges that this does not pertain to the merit or satisfaction of the Apostle, but that he suffers for the sake of amplifying or propagating the Church to confirm it in its faith, so that he may provoke others to his own imitation. Adam Sasbout also confesses this to be the genuine sense, so that His body, which is the Church, may be perfected.

Not badly, therefore, Lyranus on this passage: The sufferings of Christ, he says, are accepted in two ways: in one way for those which He sustained in His own body, and there is nothing left there to be fulfilled: in another way for those which He will suffer until the end of the age in the mystical body, and thus the remains of many sufferings remain to be fulfilled. Conf. Acts IX. 6; 2 Cor. I. 5; 1 Cor. I. 12. But the Apostle speaks of the singular measure of his own sufferings, when each of the faithful and especially the Ministers of the Word contributes his own 'part' to those things which are still lacking of the afflictions of Christ in the mystical body, which he testifies is also done by himself.

CHRISTUS non in corporibus animalium, sed in corpore illo vere humano, anima rationali prædito, nobis consubstantiali veram reconciliationem perfecit, juxta illud: Sacrificium & oblationem noluisti, corpus vero aptasti mihi, Ebr. X. vers. 5. ex Psalm. LX. vers. 7. ut hic recte Crocius. Nec vero corpus nudum aut ψιλὴν ἄψευδῶς, sed in quo habitat tota plenitudo Deitatis, vers. 19. indigitatur. Nam corpus etsi ἔμψυχον, etsi DEUM habens ἔνοικον, ut in sanctis habitat DEUS per gratiam, ad rem tantam efficiendam minime sufficiebat. Ideo placuit, ut tota plenitudo Deitatis in corpore CHRISTI habitaret, quod pro mundi vita tradendum erat. Quapropter nimis vile est nomen instrumenti. Christus non causa est instrumentalis, sed meritoria reconciliationis.

Notetur hic geminus sensus ἀποκαταλλαγῆς.

Primus vers. 19. de reconciliatione, qua Deus nobis reconciliatus est, vel ut Paulus loquitur, qua per Christum reconciliati sumus in ipsum, ut ipse nobis propitius redderetur, quod factum est in cruce, & morte Christi. Alter est de reconciliationis hujus applicatione, qua nobis per fidem eadem appropriatur, nos fruimur, Dei amici reddimur, quod fit in justificatione.

Conf. 2. Corintb. V. vers. 19. 21. Dicitur autem hoc fieri etiam in corpore carnis ejus & per mortem Christi: Quia hæc est causa meritoria nostræ justificationis.

Et revera unica tantum est reconciliatio, quæ vero duobus modis spectatur, primum universim, qua omnes homines Deo reconciliati est, omnibus hominibus Deus placatus est: Deinde appropriative, qua quisque fidelium eam suam facit, se per Christum reconciliatum, sibi Deum placatum esse credens, eaque fide illius reconciliatione fruitur, quemadmodum non duplicatur redemptio Christi, cum pro omni omnibus semetipsum tradidit in ἀντίλυτρον, 1. Timoth. II. vers. 6. & cum quisque credentium hoc sibi cum Paulo appropriat. Nam ideo communis & universalis est redemptio, ut applicabilis fit omnibus, & quisque eam sibi per fidem vendicare possit.

Crocius hanc reconciliationem non DEO Patri hic tribui, sed Filio vult. Sic enim explicant Aretius & Tossanus, nec ait in corpore carnis ejus, sed in corpore carnis suae, non per mortem ipsius, sed per mortem suam. Hoc enim pronomen differte addunt nonnulli Codices. Et in priori αὐτῦ sua legerunt cum Hieronymo epist. LXI. Ambrosius, Chrysostomus, homil. IV. in h. l. Ad Christum etiam refert Oecumenius, consentientibus codicibus optimae notae apud Bezam. Theophylactus: Rursus, inquit, reconciliationis modum inducit, quae in corpore ejus facta sit. Et postea: Quum omne, quod filii est officium, explicasset, utpote, qui per mortem hec omnia confecisset, ne forte sic inquit: Ergo nihil nobis erit elaborandum, quinimo inquit necesse est, ut in fide sitis constantiores, ne vel reddamini segniores, & in priora facinora relabamini.

Non ergo cum Socino ad Patrem ista abripienda, contra quem Theodoreti notanda paraphrasis: Vos enim, qui impiam & sceleratam vitam agitatis, & luce cognitionis veritatis omnino privati DEO effesti estis familiares, non hoc vobis dono a lege donato, sed vestro debito a CHRISTO exoluto & corpore morti tradito. Haec ergo ratio συνεχέιας est, quam reddit Grotius. Quid prædicatum dicit, non quid creditum, etiam quid receptum est, aut creditum omni creaturæ. Nimirum omnem creaturam (humanam puta) quæ est sub cœlo.

Additur sub cœlo, non quia sub quavis cœli plaga, ut Crocius, fuæ particularitati velificans, explicat, sed quia sermo est de quibusvis in terra peregrinantibus, ut interpretatur Hugo. Quamvis & illud responderi potest, illas regiones captas fuisse habitari longe post Apostolorum tempora: Cum autem Evangelium dicitur pervenisse in totum mundum, intelligitur in illas mundi partes, quæ ab hominibus incoluntur. Tim. II 10. *Οσ αντε non legerunt Græci commentantes ad hunc locum. Et νῦν χαίρω bene sensum inchoat, ut 2.

Cor. VII, 9. De passionibus ob Evangelii præconium gaudere se testatur, tum ut Evangelii certitudinem genuinum esse testatur, tum ob affectum, sibi etiam apud Colossenses gloriandum, quorum causa se quoque passiones tolerare asseverat. Cum dixisset, inquit Theophylactus, Evangelii se Ministrum effectum, à quo ne illi exciderent precaretur, ostendit verax adeo illud esse & certius, ut pro se pati fateatur, sic inquiens: Non solum patior, sed etiam labor perpetiendo.

Quæ autem patitur, vestri etiam causa tolero, ut per tolerantiam vobis hujusmodi quædam prodesse. Pro vobis, id est, bono vestro, ut ædificemini & confirmemini mea patientia, constantia & exultatione in passionibus in fide. Lombardus pro vobis confirmandis in veritate Evangelii. Sic etiam Hugo & Thomas.

Temere itaque ad satisfactiones hæc detorquent alii. Καὶ ἀνταναπληρῶ τὰ ὑστερήματα τῶν θλίψεων τοῦ χριστοῦ ἐν τῇ σαρκί μου Christus magna & saluti nostræ sufficiens pro nobis passus est. Sed ita ainat suos, ut quæ ipsi ferunt mala, tanquam sibi illata sentiat, Act. IX. § Sic Paulo vincula ferente, Christus ea quodammodo ferebat. Τὰ ὑστερήματα, id est, τὰ λοιπά, ἣλ, Syrus hic חסרון, id quod deest, ἣ τὰ σώματὰ αὐτῦ bono Ecclesiæ, ut jam diximus. Ὁ ἐστιν ἡ Ἐκκλησία supra 18.

Non ergo de supplemento satisfactionis aut meriti Christi per satisfactiones & merita sanctorum hæc intelligenda, quod Papistæ volunt, Cajetanus, Valentinus, Bellarminus, Suarez, Cornelius a Lapide. Sed de iis passionibus, quæ corpori Christi mystico adhuc desunt, non corpori Christi proprio. Per illud enim perfectam reconciliationem factam esse v. 19. 22. docuit. Non foret vero reconciliatio, nisi perfecta præstiti esset satisfactio. Id agit Apostolus, ut doceat in Christo nos habere omnia, quæ ad salutem requiruntur. Non habemus autem, si aliorum satisfactiones requirerent, si in meritis Christi ulla essent ὑστερήματα. Ideo Christus fortunius de passionibus Christi in corpore mystico explicat.

Non duntaxat mortuus est pro vobis, sed & præterquam, quod mortuus est, paratus est et iam alligii propter vos, Bened. Justinianus agnoscit non pertinere hoc ad meritum vel satisfactionem Apostoli, sed quod patiatur pro amplificanda seu propagandæ Ecclesiæ ad ejus fidem confirmandam, ut caceros ad jui imitationem provocet. Quem sensum germanum esse fatetur etiam Adamus Sasbout, ut corpus ipsius, quod est Ecclesia, perficiatur.

Non male ergo Lyranus in hunc locum: Passiones, inquit, Christi dupliciter accipiuntur: uno modo pro illis, quas sustinuit in corpore proprio, & fit ibi nihil reflat adimplendum: alio modo pro illis, quas in finem usq; seculi patietur in corpore mystico, & sic restant multarum passionum reliquiæ adimplendæ. Conf. Act. IX. 6. 2. Cor. I. 5. 1. Cor. I. 12. Loquitur autem Apostolus de singulari passionum suarum mensura, quum quisque fidelium & imprimis Ministrorum Verbi suum ἐπιβάλλων μέροσ conferat ad ea, quæ adhuc detunt afflictionum Christi in corpore mystico, quod à se etiam fieri testatur.

## 1:25
V. 25. 'Of which I became a minister,' above 23. He who serves the Gospel, the same serves the Church. For the Gospel was given for the sake of gathering and preserving the Church. 'According to the stewardship of God, which was given to me for you.'

See 1 Cor. IX. 17. We have almost the same words in Eph. III. 6. 'To fulfill the word of God,' that is, 'in order to fulfill.' See above. 'To fulfill the word' is the same locution as Rom. XV. 19. He again professes himself a Minister. Before he had said Minister of the Gospel, now of the Church; a Minister, I say, not the Redeemer of the Church, not the Lord. He refers this ministry of his to God; he says 'from the dispensation of God': which is then in general in this, that through the ministry of men, not of Angels, we are led to God, and it is especially conspicuous in the ministry and vocation of Paul, Acts IX; 1 Cor.

XV; Gal. I. He uses the word 'stewardships' (oeconomias) the more willingly because Ministers are stewards, having been constituted by the divine stewardship of the mysteries of God, 1 Cor. IV. 1, and that this divine dispensation contributes to the stewardship of our salvation, by which it pleased God through the foolishness of preaching to save those who believe, 1 Cor.

I. 21. Whence in the word 'stewardships' Theophylact seeks the grace of God with the merits of men excluded, because God Himself did not seek works or virtues (to obtain salvation) but faith only and Baptism, which is indeed a certain supreme dispensation. For who would ever have attained salvation, if works were lacking to him? To fulfill the word of God, the word namely, of the promise concerning the calling of the Gentiles, as Chrysostom, Theophylact, Vatablus [say], but not indeed for the fulfilling or perfectly delivering of the word of the Gospel, as Bullinger, Hyperius, Zanchius, Toffanus [say]: for this was not delivered imperfectly before Paul. It was promised, says B. Balduinus, to the Gentiles also, the Gospel, which was deferred until the times of Christ, but neither was it necessary then immediately at the first to announce the kingdom of heaven, Acts 13:46.

Therefore, lest the Gentiles be detained too long, behold God through a singular economy bestows the Apostle, who with great speed filled almost the whole world with his Gospel.

For which reason Theodoret wrote concerning Paul, that he himself with the other Apostles had brought not only the Romans, and those who live under the Roman empire, to the Evangelical law, but also the Scythians and Sauromatae, Indians, Ethiopians, Persians, Seres, Hyrcanians, Britons, Cimmerians, Germans, and finally the whole human race and all nations.

If, however, we understand it concerning the doctrine of the Gospel, to which sense the following things favor, he implies not that it was committed to him to be delivered more fully, but to be derived into the Gentiles.

Indeed, the word is thus fulfilled not by reason of itself or as if imperfect, but by reason of men, when it spreads itself to more, in which manner, as far as the thing is concerned, there is no doubt that the promises of God concerning the calling of the Gentiles are also fulfilled.

The word 'to fulfill' is emphatic, as B. Hunnius warns, and it commends the singular zeal of the Apostle, and the faith by which he relied to derive and pour out the doctrine of the Gospel like a certain river into the deserts of the Gentiles by his preaching, and to fill all things everywhere with the Gospel of Christ, and thus to render this ministry of his fully approved.

Add that the Word of God had to be fulfilled, both by others and by the Apostle in the New Testament, in respect to the heralds of the Word in the Old Testament, by whom it was not delivered so clearly and so fully, as is evident from the following verse.

Cor. IX. 17. Verba prope eadem habemus Eph. III. 6. Πληρῶσαι τὸν λόγον τῦ Θεῦ id est εἰσ τὸ πληρῶσαι. Vide fu. Πληρῶσαι τὸν λόγον eadem locutio, quæ Rom. XV. 19. Ministrum se denuo profitetur. Antea Evangelii dexerat Ministrum, jam Ecclesiæ; Ministrum, inquam, non Redemptorem Ecclesiæ, non Dominum. Hoc ministerium suum ad Deum refert; ex dispensatione Dei inquit: quæ tum in genere in eo est, quod per hominum ministerium, non Angelorum nos ad Deum perducamur, tum in ministerio & vocatione Pauli imprimis conspicua est, Act.

IX. 1. Cor. XV. Gal. I. Oeconomias voce eo libentio utitur, quod Ministri œconomi sint per œconomiam divinam constituti mysteriorum Dei, 1. Cor. IV. 1. quodq; hæc divina dispensatio ad œconomiam salutis nostræ faciat, qua placuit Deo per stultitiam prædicationis salvos facere credentes, 1.

Cor. I. 21. Unde in voce œconomias Theophylactus quærit gratiam Dei cum exclusis hominum meritis, quia non opera ipse Deus aut virtutes quasivit (ad consequendam salutem) sed fidem duntaxat & Baptismum, quod sane summa quædam est dispensatio. Nam quis unquam fuisset salutem adeptus, si opera ipsi defosterent? Ad implendum verbum Dei, verbum scilicet promissionis de vocatione gentium, ut Chrysostomus, Theophylactus, Vatablus, non vero ad implendum vel perfecte tradendum verbum Evangelii, ut Bullingerus, Hyperius, Zanchius, Tossanus: id enim ante Paulum non imperfecte fuit traditum. Promissum est, inquit B. Balduinus, gentibus etiam Evangelium, quod usque ad tempora Christi differebatur, sed neque tum statim ad primum oportuit annuntiari regnum caelorum, Act. XIII, 46.

Igitur ne nimis diu detineantur gentes, ecce Deus per singularem οἰκονομίαν largitur Apostolum, qui magna celeritate totum fere orbem terrarum Evangelio suo replevit.

Quam ob causam Theodoretus scripsit de Paulo, quod ipse cum ceteris Apostolis ad legem Evangelicam non Romanos solum, et qui sub Romano vivunt imperio, sed Scythas quoque et Sauromatas, Indos, Aethiopas, Persas, Seres, Hircanos, Britannos, Cimmerios, Germanos, denique omne genus humanum et omnes nationes induxerit.

Si tamen de doctrina Evangelii intelligamus, cui sensui favent sequentia, non id plenius tradendum sibi commissum, sed in gentes derivandum innuit.

Nimirum impletur ita verbum non ratione sui seu imperfectum, sed ratione hominum, cum ad plures sese diffundit, quo pacto, quantum ad rem, promissa Dei de vocatione gentium etiam impleri dubium non est.

Emphaticum, monente B. Hunnio, implendi verbum est, et commendat Apostoli singulare studium, atque fidem, qua nitebatur Evangelii doctrinam ceu flumen quoddam in deserta gentium sua praedicatione derivare et effundere, omniaque implere passim Evangelio Christi, atque adeo ministerium hoc suum ad plenum probatum reddere.

Adde quod impleri etiam Verbum Dei debuerit, cum per alios, tum per Apostolum in Novo Testamento, respectu praeconum Verbi in Veteri Testamento, a quibus tam luculenter et tam plene non fuit traditum, ut e v. seq. constat.

## 1:26
V. 26. The mystery which has been hidden from the ages, Eph.

3:5, 9, where see the sayings. Mystery רז, Dan. 2:18. And from the generations. The same is signified by generations, Acts 15:21, Eph. 3:5, which are ages, and thus all and generations. Generation דור properly the duration of human life.

But now it has been manifested to his saints, Rom. 16:26. 'To him' is understood. To whom God willed to make known.

See Eph. 1:4, 9, 6:19. To make known הודיע. The object and quality of the Word, which the Apostle had to fulfill, he explains, because the mystery is hidden from the ages and from the generations; not absolutely, because this mystery was promulgated in Paradise itself, delivered through the Patriarchs, proposed by the Prophets, Acts 10:43, but relatively, because it was not so delivered that the riches of the glory might appear so fully and clearly.

Indeed, many riches of glory still, not only of power, but also of the riches of grace, reveal themselves in the Apostolic doctrine, which neither appeared so in the Old Testament, nor spread themselves so widely: and therefore this must be referred to the manifestation of the New Testament, both because the more solemn promulgation of the Gospel, which was done in the days not only of the flesh of Christ by Christ himself, but primarily from the feast of Pentecost of the New Testament through the Apostles, with the Holy Spirit poured out upon them, Acts 2, and also by the diffusion of the same through the whole world, even among the Gentiles most alienated from God, who once lived without Christ, without hope of salvation, Eph. 2. The Jews had this mystery, but in promises, types, and figures, and thus in hope and expectation of the fulfillment: but in the New Testament we have it in the sacraments, testimonies, and with the shadows removed, in the very body of Christ, and thus in the undoubted fulfillment. But to the Gentiles it was for a long time in great part hidden.

Add that commonly that part of the mystery concerning the calling of the Gentiles to be admitted without circumcision was unknown, Eph.

3: 9. But it is said to have been manifested to the saints, not because the Gospel had not penetrated to others, for it was preached to every creature, but because the darkness did not comprehend the light, John 1, 2, 3, 4, to whom God willed to do [it], not that he did not will it for others, but because God, moved by no merits of anyone, but solely by his own grace, willed to manifest it; What the riches of grace in Christ are, that 'to whom' is not restrictive or determinative, but indicative and explanatory, how God manifested it, namely, he willed to show these riches through the Gospel.

Latin:

V. 26. Τὸ μυστήριον τὸ ἀποκεκρυμμένον ἀπὸ τῶν αἰώνων Eph.

III, 5, 9. ubi dicta vide. Μυστήριον רז, Dan. II, 18. Καὶ ἀπὸ τῶν γενεῶν. Idem significant γενεαί, Actor. XV, 21, Eph. III, 5. quod αἰῶνες, et sic omnes καὶ γενεαί. γενεὰ דור proprie duratio vitae humanae. Νυνὶ δὲ ἐφανερώθη τοῖς ἁγίοις αὐτοῦ Rom.

XVI, 26. Subintelligitur αὐτῷ. Οἷς ἐθέλησεν ὁ Θεὸς γνωρίσαι.

Vid. Eph. I, 4, 9. VI, 19. Γνωρίσαι הודיע. Objectum et qualitatem Verbi, quod implere debuit Apostolus, explicat, quod mysterium sit absconditum a seculis et a generationibus; non absolute, quia hoc mysterium promulgatum in ipso Paradiso, per Patriarchas traditum, a Prophetis propositum, Act.

X, 43. sed secundum quid, quia non ita traditum, ut tam plene et luculenter ὁ πλοῦτος τῆς δόξης constaret. Nimirum multae adhuc divitiae gloriae, non potentiae tantum, sed et gratiae divitiae sese pandunt in doctrina Apostolica, quae nec ita patebant in Veteri Testamento, nec tam late sese diffundebant: ideoque referendum hoc ad patefactionem Novi Testamenti, tum quia solenniorem Evangelii promulgationem, quae in diebus non tantum carnis Christi ab ipso Christo facta, sed imprimis inde a festo Pentecostes Novi Testamenti per Apostolos, effuso in ipsos Spiritu Sancto, Act. II, tum qua diffusioem ejusdem per totum orbem propagationem, etiam inter gentes maxime a Deo alienas, quae sine Christo, sine spe salutis olim vivebant, Eph. II. Habebant Judaei hoc mysterium, sed in promissionibus, typis et figuris, adeoque in spe et expectatione complementi: sed novo autem Testamento habemus in sacramentis, testimoniis, et remotis umbris, in ipso corpore Christi, adeoque in indubitato complemento.

Gentibus autem magnam partem olim id absconditum fuit. Adde quod communiter pars illa mysterii de vocatione gentium fine circumcisione admittendarum ignota fuerit, Eph.

III, 9. Sanctis autem patefactum dicitur, non quod ad alios non penetrarit Evangelium, id enim omni creaturae praedicatum, sed quod tenebrae non apprehenderint lucem Joh. I, 2, 3, 4. quibus Deus voluit facere, non quod aliis id noluerit, sed quod Deus nullis cujusquam meritis, sed unice gratia sua motus id patefacere voluerit; Quænam sint divitiae gratiae in Christo, illud οἷς non est restrictivum vel determinativum, sed indicativum et explicativum, quomodo id manifestarit Deus, voluit nempe per Evangelium hasce divitias ostendere.

## 1:27
Verf. 27. What is the riches of the glory how abundant the power, Rom. 9:23, Eph. 1:18, see also above II. This mystery among the Gentiles, which is Christ in you, the hope of glory The great secret of God has been revealed, when he placed Christ, that is, the doctrine of Christ, among the Gentiles as the hope of eternal life.

There is therefore here a double mystery: Christ for the doctrine of Christ, and hope for the cause of hope.

In the Manuscript 'which is'.

B. Hunnius explains that Christ is the riches of this mystery in this way: In these words, he says, he again touches upon the majesty and excellence of the Evangelical doctrine, while he declares that inestimable treasures, wealth, and riches of the mystery of God lie hidden under it, which transcends every mode of human wisdom by its sublimity. He points out both the sum and the object of this mystery in one word, writing that the riches of this mystery is Christ, as in whom all mysteries together, and all the treasures of the wisdom and knowledge of God as it were flow together, for instance, the mystery of our election in him unto salvation, the mystery of the counsel of the restoration of the human race, the mystery of the incarnation of the Son of God in time, and thus whatever is admirable in the person of Christ, and in his own sacrosanct office, and in the whole work of redemption and the benefits performed, and exceeds the grasp of human reason.
