Furthermore, he constitutes this Christ as the mystery of mysteries not simply and absolutely, as he is in himself, but also as he is considered in respect to us.

Therefore the Apostle D. adds: Which is Christ in you: Namely, dwelling in you through faith, and acting in you by his power.

HOPE OF GLORY commends Christ to the Colossians with another title besides, calling him the hope of glory, as if he were to say: Outside CHRIST, not glory, but ignominy will be to be expected by you.

But Christ is he who, having recalled [you] from the desperation of all things, has raised and regenerated [you] into this illustrious hope, so that by the benefit of his merit apprehended through faith, eternal life of glory may be prepared for you in heaven. But he calls them riches AMONG THE GENTILES, because these riches, although they appeared in others, yet primarily appeared most clearly among the Gentiles.

Concerning which Chrysostom beautifully: It appears most in the Gentiles, just as you also say elsewhere, that the Gentiles glorify God for his mercy.

For it appears indeed also in others, but much more in these is the great glory of the mystery. For to have suddenly led men less endowed with sense than stones to the dignity of Angels solely through bare words and faith without any operation, is truly the glory and wealth of the mystery.

As if someone were to have suddenly made a dog, lost to hunger and mange, foul and deformed, and which could not even move, but lay there, into a man, and shown him in a Royal seat. They were worshipping stones and ear-

...and they learned that they are better than both heaven and sun, and that the whole world serves them. They were captives and in the chains of the Devil: suddenly they were above his head, and were commanding him and scourging him. When they were captives and slaves of the demons, they were made the body of the Lord, of Angels and Archangels. Those who were not even becoming God, soon sat together on the same throne with God. Theophylact repeats these things, but more succinctly.

Latin:

Vers. 27. Τίς ὁ πλοῦτος τῆς δόξης quam abundans potentia, Rom.

IX, 23. Eph. I, 18. vide et supra II. Τὸ μυστήριον τοῦτο ἐν τοῖς ἔθνεσιν, ὅ ἐστι χριστὸς ἐν ὑμῖν, ἡ ἐλπὶς τῆς δόξης Ingens arcanum Dei patuit, cum Christum, id est doctrina Christi in gentibus sonuit in spem vitae aeternae. Est ergo hic duplex μυστήριον, Christus pro doctrina Christi, et spes pro causa spei.

In Manuscripto ὅ ἐστι. Divitias hujus mysterii Christum esse ita B.

Hunnius explicat: Hisce verbis, inquit, rursum μυστήριον attingit Evangelicae doctrinae majestatem et excellentiam, dum perhibet, sub ea latere inestimabiles thesauros, opes et divitias mysterii Dei, quod omnem humanae sapientiae modum sublimitate sua transcendat. Hujus mysterii cum summam, tum objectum uno verbo indigitat, scribens τὸν πλοῦτον divitias hujus mysterii esse Christum, ut in quo mysteria simul omnia, cunctique thesauri sapientiae et cognitionis Dei quasi confluunt, puta mysterium nostra in ipso electionis ad salutem, mysterium consilii reparatio nis humani generis, mysterium incarnationis Filii Dei in tempore, adeoque quicquid et in persona Christi, et in ipsus sacrosancto officio, totoque opere redemptionis praestitisque beneficiis admirabile est et captum humana ratione excedens.

Hunc porro Christum constituit mysterium mysteriorum non simpliciter et absolute, ut in se est, sed simul ut respectu nostri consideratur.

Proinde subjicit D. Apostolus: Qui est Christus in vobis: Nimirum in vobis per fidem habitans, et in vobis sua virtute agens.

SPES GLORIAE commendat Christum alio insuper elogio Colossensibus, spem gloriae illum appellans, ac si dicat: Extra CHRISTUM non gloria, sed ignominia vobis erit expectanda.

Christus autem est, qui ex rerum omnium desperatione revocatos in hanc praeclaram spem erexit ac regenuit, ut beneficio meriti illius per fidem apprehensa vobis in caelo parata sit vita aeterna gloriae. Divitias autem vocat INTER GENTES, quia hae divitiae etsi in aliis, imprimis tamen in gentibus apparebant clarissime.

Quo de Chrysostomus pulchre: Maxime apparet in gentibus, sicut etiam dicis alibi, gentes pro misericordia glorificare Deum.

Nam apparet quidem etiam in aliis, multo magis autem in his magna gloria mysterii. Homines enim sensu minus praditos quam Lapides repente deduxisse ad dignitatem Angelorum solummodo per nuda verba et fidem absque omni operatione, revera est gloria et divitia mysterii.

Ut si quis canem fame et scabie perditam, turpem et deformem, et sed qui ne moveri quidem posset, sed jaceret, repente et hominem fecerit, et in sede Regia ostenderis. Lapides adorabant et ter-

xam, & didicerunt, quod & cælo & fole fint meliores, & univerfus mundus eis ferviat. Erant captivi & in vinculis Diaboli: repente fuerunt fupra caput ejus, eique imperabant & eum flagellabant. Quum Dæmonum effent captivi & fervi, facti funt corpus Domini, Angelorum & Archangelorum. Qui ne quid effet quidem Deus fiebant, mox in eodem cum Deo throno confederunt. Quæ repetit, fed fuccinctius Theophylactus.

## 1:28
Ver. 28. Whom we proclaim 1 Cor. II. 1. IX. 14. Phil. I. 16. 18.

Crocius is correct: "alone" and "wholly": "Alone," not mixing him either with Moses, which the Pseudo-Apostles were doing, or with human philosophy, which the wise men of the gentiles would have preferred: "Wholly," so that nothing is suppressed, and finally also received from above according to that saying, "I received from the Lord," 1 Corinth. XI. 23. Compare 1 John I. 3.

Admonishing every man Acts XX. 31. Rom. XV. 14.

And teaching Matth. XXVIII. 20.

In all wisdom namely spiritual, 1 Cor. II. 6. 7. XII. 8. Eph. I. 8. 17. above 9. III. 16.

That we may present every man in Christ Jesus namely perfect to God, as Ministers. See above 22. In Christ, that is, through Christ as the reconciler. "Every man perfect in Christ," as Ephes. IV. 3. and thus the Latin reads.

The parts of the Ecclesiastical office are, in general, the announcement of Christ, but in particular, both admonition (whether exhortatory or dehortatory), *nouthesia*, and *didascalia*, the doctrine concerning matters of faith. Which must also be sufficient, and certain, and solid, so that it may be "in all wisdom," which the Spirit of GOD clearly hands down in His word, 2 Timoth. III. 15. 16. The object of the information is every man, that is, not only as many as possible, but universally all and each, Acts XX. 31. For just as God wills all to come to the knowledge of the truth, 1 Timoth. II. ver. 4, so it is the duty of the ministers of GOD to inform all concerning the heavenly truth, which the Apostle teaches primarily by his own example. Moreover, he intends to present everyone perfect, instructed by the saving knowledge of GOD, and prepared for every good work, 2 Timoth. III. 16. He testifies that this perfection is situated in Christ Jesus, and is to be sought in him alone, inasmuch as he also makes them perfect by the knowledge of himself, that is, just before GOD, Isa. LIII. And by his Spirit he advances us from one degree of justification to another in turn, as the blessed Hunnius says here.

Latin:

Verf. 28. Ὁ ἦμᾶς καταγγέλλομεν 1. Cor. II. 1. IX. 14. Phil. I. 16. 18.

Recte Crocius: folum & totum: Solum non mifcentes eum vel cum Moſe, quod faciebant Pfeudo-Apoſtoli, vel cum Philoſophia humana, quod gentilium ſapientes maluiffent: Totum, ut nihil fupprimatur, denique & fupernis acceptum juxta illud, accopi a Domino, 1. Corinth. XI. 23. confer 1. Joban. I. 3.

Νουθετῦντες πάντα ἄνθρωπον Actor. XX, 31. Rom. XV. 14.

Καὶ διδάσκοντες Matth. XXVIII. 20.

Ἐν πάσῃ σοφίᾳ ſpirituali nempe, 1. Cor. II. 6. 7. XII. 8. Eph. I. 8. 17. fupra 9. III. 16.

Ἵνα παραστήσωμεν πάντα ἄνθρωπον ἐν χρισῷ ἰησῦ τελείους nempe Deo, tanquam Miniſtri. Vide fupra 22. In Chriſto, id eſt per Chriſtum tanquam conciliatorem. Πάντα ἄνθρωπον τέλειοι ἐν χρισῷ, ut Epheſ. IV. 3. & fic legit Latinus.

Partes officii Eccleſiaſtici funt in genere quidem annuntiatio Chriſti, in ſpecie vero tum admonitio five exhortatoria five debortatoria, νθεσία, tum didascalia, doctrina de rebus fidei. Quæ & fufficiens eſſe debet, & certa atque folida, ut fit ἐν πάσῃ σοφίᾳ, quam ſcilicet tradit Spiritus DEI in verbo fuo, 2. Timoth. III. 15. 16. Informatio-nis objectum eſt omnis homo, hoc eſt, non tantum quamplurimi, fed in univerfum omnes & finguli, A&or. XX. 31. ut enim Deus omnes vult ad agnitionem veritatis pervenire, 1. Timoth. II. verf. 4. fic miniſtrorum DEI eſt, omnes de cœleſti veritate informare, quod exemplo imprimis fuo docet Apoftolus. Perfectum autem exhibere quemvis intendit, falvifica DEI cognitione inſtructum, & ad omne opus bonum apparatum, 2. Timoth. III. 16. Quam perfectionem in Chriſto Jeſu ſitam, in eo unice quærendam eſſe teſtatur, utpote qui & notitia fui efficit perfectos, id eſt, juſtos coram DEO, Eſa. LIII. Et Spiritu fuo nos ab uno gradu juſtificationis ad alterum fubinde provebit, ut hic B. Hunnius.

## 1:29
Ver. 29. For which I labor (עמלתי), Acts XX. 35. 1 Corinth. XV. 16. XVI. 16. Galat. IV. 11. Philipp. II. 16. 1 Thessal. V. 12. 1 Timoth. V. 17.

Striving (משתדל), Dan. VI. 14. Not without merit did he add this, so that besides labor he might also signify dangers, below II. 1. 1 Cor. IX. 25. Philipp. I. 39. below IV. 12. 1 Timoth. VI. 12. 2 Timoth. IV. 7.

According to his energy which is energized in me in power "Energized" here is in an active sense, as Galat. V. 6. Thus "energy" and "I energize" are joined in Ephes. I. 19. "Energy" shows "power." Hence "energy of power" Ephes. III. 7. God inspired in Paul exceptional strengths for struggling, above II. Phil. IV. 13. 1 Tim. I. 12.

I labor, says Theophylact, not content to have said that, he added "and striving," so that he might show both vigilance, and a certain most sharp abstinence, and that he kept the rest, to which those about to struggle are accustomed to apply themselves. If, therefore, I myself, so that good things may happen to you, expend effort and labor, how much more ought you yourselves to expend just as much, so that by struggling you may carry off the victory. He professes, however, that this is not of his own powers, but of divine virtue, to which he ascribes every "energy," because every blessing, every success in the sacred ministry is of the divine "energy," which works in us and through us in power or effectively. And therefore we have here an entire passage concerning the sacred ministry, concerning its author and efficient cause, GOD, who according to his "economy" calls and appoints ministers, and through them effectively works: Concerning the subject: that they are "deacons," Ministers of the Gospel, and "deacons of the Church," Ministers of the Church: Concerning the object, which is the Word of GOD, but primarily the mystery hidden from eternity, but revealed most especially in the latest times, concerning the glorious riches of divine grace in CHRIST, concerning the parts of the office, which are exhortation and information, concerning the internal end, which is to present a man perfect in Christ Jesus, and the external, which is eternal salvation, the hope of which is designated here; Concerning the adjuncts, labor, struggles, passions, and the tolerance of them.

Latin:

Verf. 29. Eis ὃ ὴ κοπιῶ (עמלתי), A&or. XX. 35. 1. Corinth. XV. 16. XVI. 16. Galat. IV. 11. Philipp. II. 16. 1. Theffal. V. 12. 1. Timoth. V. 17.

Ἀγωνιζόμενος (משתדל), Dan. VI. 14. Non immerito hoc addidit, ut præter laborem etiam pericula fignificaret, infra II. 1. 1. Cor. IX. 25. Philipp. I. 39. infra IV. 12. 1. Timoth. VI. 12. 2. Timoth. IV. 7.

Κατὰ τὴν ἐνέργειαν αὐτῦ τὴν ἐνεργουμένην ἐν ἐμοὶ ἐν δυνάμει Ἐνεργουμένην hic eſt fenfu activum, ut Galat. V. 6. fic ἐνέργεια & ἐνεργῶ junguntur Epheſ. I. 19. Ἐνέργεια oftendit δύναμιν. Hinc ἐνέργεια δυνάμεως Epheſ. III. 7. vires ad certandum eximias Deus Paulo adfpirabat, fupra II. Phil. IV. 13. 1. Tim. I. 12.

Laboro, inquit Theophylactus, dixiffe haud contentus, & certando adjunxit, ut & vigilantiam preferat, & abſtinentiam quandam acerrimam, & reliqua ſe ſervaſſe oftendat, quibus folent certaturi ſtudere. Si itaque ipſe, ut bona vobis contingant, operam & laborem impendo, quanto magis & ipſi tantundem debetis & labores infumere, ut certando viſtoriam referatis. Non autem fuarum virium id eſſe, fed virtutis divinæ profitetur, cui omnem ἐνέργειαν adſcribit, quod omnis benedictio, omnis fucceffus in facro miniſterio divinæ ἐνεργείας, quæ operatur in nobis & per nos in virtute vel efficaciter. Ideoque habemus hic integrum locum de facro miniſterio, de ejus autore & cauſa Efficiente, DEO, qui fecundum οἰκονομίαν fuam vocat, & conſtituit miniſtros, ac per eosdem efficaciter operatur: De ſubjecto: quod funt διάκονοι Miniſtri Evangelii, & διάκονοι τῆς Ἐκκλησίας, Miniſtri Ecclefiæ: De objecto, quod eſt Verbum DEI, imprimis autem myſterium abſconditum ab æterno, fed revelatum maxime noviſſimis temporibus, de divitiis gloriofis divinæ gratiæ in CHRISTO, de partibus officii, quæ funt adhortatio & informatio, de fine interno, qui eſt ſiſtere hominem perfectum in Chriſto Jeſu, & externo, qui eſt æterna falus, cujus ſpes hic deſignata; De adjunctis, labore, certaminibus, paſſionibus & tolerantia eorum.

## 2:1 Argument
CHAPTER II. ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

Having signified the struggle for the fuller faith of the Colossians in Christ, in whom all the treasures of knowledge are hidden, and having declared his joy concerning them, he warns that they should beware of seduction through Philosophy and the doctrines of men according to the traditions of the world, and having repeated the doctrine concerning Christ, in whom the fullness of the Deity dwells bodily, in whom they have true perfection, and true circumcision through baptism, through which they are made participants of the fruits of the death, burial, and resurrection of Christ, of the remission of sins and the victory of Satan through faith, he exhorts that they should not allow themselves to be bound to those external things, circumcision, or the distinction of foods and days as necessary for salvation, nor to be led away by the worship of Angels from Christ, the unique head of the whole mystical body.

There are three parts: I. Exhortation to constancy in the true faith with dehortation from seduction to verse 8. II. Explanation of the doctrine concerning Christ, baptism, and faith to verse 15. III. Admonition that they should not allow their consciences to be bound by external ceremonies and the worship of Angels, since that does not agree with the doctrine handed down, to verse 23.

PART I. Exhortation to constancy in faith: with dehortation from seduction.

Ver. 1. For I want you to know what a great struggle I have for you "What a great struggle" (כמה נלחמתי). He connects this discourse on the occasion of the word "striving." By "struggle," however, he understands not only solicitude, but also assiduous prayers, signified by the wrestling of Jacob.

For you and those in Laodicea Understand the Laodicea of Phrygia.

And as many as have not seen my face in the flesh? The Latins would say: Who have not known me by face. But because פנים (Panim) in Hebrew signifies many things, for the sake of clarity he added "in the flesh." So that the Apostolic admonition concerning the guarding of the Evangelical truth, which places salvation in Christ alone, and the avoiding of seduction toward other things, might penetrate all the more among those who had not seen him in the flesh, he sets forth his struggle for them, and the joy which he has hitherto received from their faith, and that in the most serious and most emphatic words, such as those of which the very exhortation itself consists.

Davenant imagines the exordium here in the first seven verses, of whose artifice he says that nothing written by Aristotle, Cicero, and the remaining masters of eloquence concerning the forming of proems is not observed in it. Contest or struggle.

Per We do not deny, however, that by ἀγῶνα (struggle) both solicitude and the struggle of prayers are implied, in which sense he also used the word ἀγωνιζόμενον (struggling) concerning prayers below in chapter IV. 12. He had said just before in chapter I. 29 that he had struggled by laboring for others; now he testifies that he also struggles and strives for them by praying.

Nec Nor was the struggle completed by these things alone, for he had to struggle in his mind, especially as contrary emotions arose, because he was now rejoicing, now grieving, and fearing, cf.

Rom. XVI. 19. 2 Cor. XI. 29. He had to struggle in his work against all the insults and machinations by which Satan was attacking the Colossians and other Churches.

Certandum He had to struggle with his body, while various adversities had to be endured for that reason. Whence Davenant argues that Erasmus and the Vulgate did not translate it quite conveniently as "solicitude," because, forsooth, one can be solicitous about one's own or another's business, even if there is no one who opposes and resists him; but one is not said to have an ἀγῶνα (struggle) unless he is one who has a struggle and contention with an Adversary, as here with Satan and his impostor members.

Laodicena He makes mention of the Laodicean Church specifically, both because danger was threatening it also from similar or the same impostors, whence he also desired this epistle to be read there, and so that he might render his solicitude testified to the same by the same work.

Non That the solicitude for the Laodiceans was not in vain is evident from the hypocrisy and χλιαρότητι (lukewarmness) which prevailed there in subsequent times, Rev. III. 16. He adds, "and as many as have not seen my face in the flesh," not that he doubts their solid faith, but because the nature of those who love, as Davenant rightly says, is such that they are more solicitous about absent friends than present ones, and so he implies that this absence of his is the cause of this solicitous care, rather than any diffidence regarding their faith; he says he is so affected toward all the rest to whom he could not be present.

Theophylact: When he is about to discuss a dogma, he says, he already reveals his greatest benevolence toward the Colossians, so that he may find favor with them and become more acceptable.

For by that decree (he says), so that I may also protect you, and lest he disturb them, just as if he were weak and in need of foreign help, he added both the Laodiceans and others who had not seen his face in the flesh (that is, corporally) and had never seen it. He teaches what he contends for in his prayers, namely, that their hearts might be filled with solid consolation, which is easily shaken by the dogma of the Pseudo-Apostles concerning the necessity of observing the law: then that they might be knit together and as it were glued together in charity, then that they might progress in the knowledge of GOD and of Christ.

Consolatio Consolation, therefore, does not consist in the fact that the Colossians might see that they are cared for and vehemently loved by the Apostle, as Cornelius wishes, which sense Davenant also brings here, but solely in that which the Apostle intends by these prayers of his, or in the thing itself which he tries to persuade them of, that is, in perseverance in the Evangelical truth, since this doctrine alone concerning salvation to be obtained only through faith in Christ brings tranquility to troubled consciences, and thus solid consolation, Rom. V. 1. 2 Thess. II. 16. But the doctrine of the innovators (by establishing the necessary observation of ceremonies, and introducing the worship of angels, and other vain and empty traditions) harassed the hearts and minds of men with various scruples and anxieties; but to beware of these is a great part of spiritual consolation, as Davenant rightly says. Furthermore, the Apostle intended by his prayers the concord by which minds cohere among themselves with an indissoluble bond, like beams joined by carpenters, so that the faithful might not be distracted from one another by dissensions, animosities, and hatreds, which is then truly solid in the Church when it is founded in the truth.

Nihil For nothing, according to Nazianzen, orat. X. on reconciliation to the Monks, so strongly conciliates concord among those who have the business of GOD at heart as consonance concerning GOD: And nothing makes more for discord than dissonance concerning Him. Therefore, they do not attain the sense of the Apostle, either those who wish to be shown who are capable of true consolation, namely those who are united among themselves by charity, or those who, with Hyperius, think it is taught in what thing consolation consists, namely in charity and the perfect knowledge of the Gospel: or even Davenant, when he judges that the fruit of perseverance in the truth of the doctrine received from Epaphras is noted.

Tertio Thirdly, the Apostle intends the progress of the faithful by his prayers and all his struggle for them in salvific knowledge. The chief thing he could seek is the consolation of the heart: The next thing after that is the conjunction of minds: Finally, there follows a further progress in sacred matters, which they especially needed because of the seduction of false Teachers, ἦ εἰς πάντα πλῶτον τῆς πληροφορίας τῆς συνέσεως, where he retains the proper signification of εἰς (unto), nor is it necessary that it be taken for ἐν (in). For the struggle of prayers looked, among other things, to all that abundance or riches of the πληροφορίας (full assurance) of understanding. Riches which the Apostle desired.

Non The word πληροφορίας (full assurance) introduces not fullness but certainty, which is manifest both from other places and also from that in Romans XIV. verse 5. Let each one be (not filled, but) certain in his own mind. Nor does σύνεσις (understanding) denote science, but intelligence or prudence: which is distinguished here in intelligence from science itself or the knowledge of mysteries, and is required for the same.

For in order that we may have a more exact knowledge of God and the Father and of Christ, and persist firmly in it, there is need (Ἵνα παρακληθῶσιν αἱ καρδίαι αὐτῶν) that the prophecy of Is. XL. 1. 2 might be fulfilled in them. Συμβιβασθέντες ἐν ἀγάπῃ) A likeness taken from the curtains of the temple.

What is םוֹנֵיָהוּ or σύνδεισος (bond) there, is συμβίβασον (knit together) here. See Exod. XXVI. in many places. See Eph.

IV. 16. and here below 19. Καὶ εἰς πάντα πλῶτον τῆς πληροφορίας τῆς συνέσεως) Eis for εἰς, and πλῶτον (riches), as we have often said, signifies abundance: Πληροφορία συνέσεως (full assurance of understanding) is full science, that is, as much as can exist in this age. Πληροφορία ἵνα πληρωθῶσιν (full assurance that they might be filled) we offend at Rom.

XIV. 5. Hence πληροφορία (full assurance) and πληροφορήμα (fullness). Εἰς ἐπίγνωσιν τὸ μυστηρίου τὸ Θεοῦ κὶ Πατρὸς κὶ τοῦ χριστοῦ) A more exact one.

Myisterium He calls that will of GOD which Christ revealed a mystery. Τὸ Θεοῦ κὶ Πατρὸς (of God and the Father), that is, of God who is the same as our Father, as Eph. II. 3. IV. 6. Phil. IV. 20.

Mysterium Dei is a work of the riches of a more certain understanding or certainty in the intellect of divine matters of the holy scriptures. The mystery of God, however, regards not so much the divine essence—just as Anselm explains the mystery of the most holy Trinity, and Ambrose the mystery of the Deity of Christ—as it regards the revealed will of God and the Gospel. For the mystery of God and the Father, as also of Christ, is indicated. What the name of the Father imports in the mystery is known: And Crocius, with Calvin, not wrongly notes that, since the Apostle said the mystery of God and the Father and of Christ with the conjunction interposed, it is taught by a most powerful argument that both the Father and Christ are the same true God. For if the word θεοῦ (God) were to look only to the person of the Father, the conjunction after θεοῦ should have been omitted, and it should have been said, in the acknowledgment of GOD the Father and Christ. Nor does it indicate that Christ is any more other than God than the Father is, but it proclaims that the Father and Christ are one and the same God. He joins Christ with the Father, both because the Father revealed the mystery through the Son, and because neither can the Father be known without the Son, nor the Son without the Father. For the Father is in the Son, and the Son in the Father, The Father alone reveals the Son, and Christ the Father. Verf.

3. 'Ἐν οἷς πάντες οἱ θησαυροὶ τῆς σοφίας καὶ τῆς γνώσεως ἀπόκρυφοι' (In whom are all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge hidden) in which mystery are contained all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge, namely, saving [knowledge].

See above I. 9. Eph. 1. 8. When he says 'Ἀπόκρυφος' (hidden), he takes the similitude from a chest, in which monies are kept, to be drawn from thence when there is need Dan.

XI. 43. 'ἀπόκρυφοι τοῖς χρυσοῖς' (hidden treasures of gold) & 1. Maccab. I. 24. 'ἔλαβε τοὺς θησαυροὺς τοὺς ἀποκρύφους' (he took the hidden treasures).

Wisdom is wont to be compared to treasures, Prov. VIII. 18. 19. Matth. XIII. 44. Pronomen & an Evangelium an v. Christi? These things are to be understood not of the mystery, but of Christ. For 1. the rule of interpretation requires this, that the pronoun should be referred to the immediately preceding noun.

But the noun 'τῆς γνώσεως' (of knowledge) immediately precedes. 2. Because he prays from Christ for them all the riches of the certainty of spiritual understanding, for a more exact knowledge of the divine mystery, he teaches that all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden in Christ. He, therefore, can abundantly confer all certain understanding, and all knowledge of divine mysteries, who is the fountain and foundation of all wisdom and knowledge.

It is therefore, says the Apostle, with Theophylact as interpreter, that wisdom and knowledge are to be sought from him. 3. Not the mystery, but Christ rather is compared to the chest, in which those treasures are stored, and from which those riches overflow into all the faithful, of whose fullness we all receive grace for grace, Whatever wisdom and knowledge is in the Gospel, it is not hidden, but rather revealed in the Gospel and through the Gospel to us, to whom it is proposed.

5. Nowhere in the scriptures is it said of the Gospel that the treasures of wisdom are hidden in it, but the Gospel is called wisdom once hidden, now revealed, Rom. XVI.

26. 6. Nor are ALL treasures of knowledge contained in the mystery, or hidden [there], but in Christ. For although the Gospel may exhibit the treasure of wisdom, yet not all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are exhibited in the same.

There are, moreover, infinite treasures of wisdom and knowledge in God, inasmuch as He is of infinite wisdom, which are not patent or revealed in the Gospel. And σοφία (wisdom) and γνῶσις (knowledge) are joined, with the note of universality added besides, so that whatever pertains to the treasures of wisdom and knowledge may be understood to be implied, as Calvin, Bullinger, and Hyperius note, that the duplication pertains to augmenting the matter. Nor do we suffer this to be restricted by Grotius to the wisdom and knowledge that is saving, which the holy scriptures teach, For although the wisdom and knowledge which is contained in the holy scriptures may suffice for us, and cannot be exhausted by us, yet not ALL the TREASURES of wisdom and knowledge are absolutely recondite in holy scripture.

For many and innumerable and infinite things are held in the arcana of divine wisdom and omniscience, which are not revealed in the holy scriptures. Many treasures of omniscience surpass the divine, which neither the elect, nor the Angels, of whatever order and eminence, can penetrate or grasp. 7. In Him are recondite the treasures of wisdom and knowledge, in whom dwells the whole fullness of the Deity, as is evident from the collation of v. 3 & 9. But that dwells not in the mystery, but in Christ. Therefore the ancients explain this with great consensus concerning Christ, and Crocius acknowledges this, nay, most Calvinists also—Marloratus, Aretius, Gryneus, Perkins, Lubertus—interpret it not of the mystery, but of Christ, whence Crocius confesses that Calvin, and almost all the Reformed, accept it thus, and he follows them entirely.

Which things are therefore to be opposed to Jerome, Zanchius, Piscator, and others who dissent in the Reformed school, who now call these things into doubt οἱ ἐκ τῆς ἐναντίας (those of the contrary part), than that they deny that omniscience agrees with Christ according to his human nature. For the argument is invincible: Second Argument. according to which nature all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden in Christ, according to that human omniscience Christ is truly omniscient. But according to human nature, by the power of the personal union, all those treasures are hidden in CHRIST.

Therefore. Although they may apply other exceptions to elide the demonstration, yet they have been abundantly satisfied in the Exam. de perfon.

Christi controv. VII. membr. II. pag. 347. seqq. Nor is there any reason why Crocius should object that there is no discourse here of infinite wisdom and knowledge, by which God is wise and knows all things, but by which the faithful understand and know the mystery of God and of Christ. For thus diverse things are confounded.

For the discourse was not about the object of prayers in the preceding words. But now it is not a question of the object, what the Apostle intends and contends for in the agony of his prayers, but of the cause and principle of that knowledge and understanding, which he labors to obtain for the Colossians by prayers: which, however, he implies is to be obtained not from Angels but solely from Christ. The fountain of wisdom, therefore, hidden and inexhaustible in Christ, with the rivulets derived thence into all the faithful without decrease or defect of that immense wisdom, ought not to be confounded with the created wisdom granted to us according to the measure of the gift of Christ, with that immense and infinite wisdom in Christ, by which He possesses it ἐκ μέτρος (without measure), The Colossians are recalled from the Angels to Christ, and he wishes them not to doubt, nay, he bids them trust, that in the same, according to human nature, the immense treasures of divine wisdom are recondite, and that those riches will easily be obtained from Christ our brother, who is ὁμοούσῳ (consubstantial) to us, which may suffice for each, inasmuch as he is anointed by the Holy Spirit for his consorts not by measure. But lest they say, who contradict, that wisdom is understood to be finite, which is the comment of Perkins, Pareus, Bergius, and Wendelinus, the proper emphasis of the words is to be noted: He does not say only knowledge is hidden in Christ, but also wisdom; and not only some knowledge and wisdom, but the treasures of knowledge and wisdom: and not only this, but to express divine wisdom, he adds that ALL the treasures of knowledge and wisdom are hidden in Christ. But he who says all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge, what else does he express than the divine treasures of OMNISCIENCE and OMNISAPIENCE? In whom the treasures of at least finite wisdom are hidden, in him ALL the treasures of wisdom cannot truly be said to be hidden; because besides the treasures of knowledge, far richer and more eminent treasures of divine wisdom are given. Which totality of every kind and absolute totality of all treasures of wisdom, which leaves nothing remaining, is emphatically expressed by the Arabic Interpreter with the word גמץ all, whole, universal, from גמץ to gather, to collect, to couple, designating the universality of a thing of every kind, so that it is understood ὅλως, ὅλον τι, totally whole, without any defect, as B. observes.

Mr. Dr. Myslenta, in his first disputation on this passage, th.

18. whence the Fathers ὁμοθυμαδὸν (with one accord) accepted the present passage concerning divine and infinite omniscience, Cyril of Alexandria.

Chrysostom, the Greek scholiast, Theophylact, Damascenus, Isidore of Pelusium, likewise Ambrose, Jerome, Fulgentius, Remigius, Dionysius the Carthusian, Lyranus, Thomas, and others among the Papists, as well as among the Reformed, Bullinger, Sibrandus, Lubbertus, Maresius, and others, who prove the Deity of the Son of GOD from this passage, as we have shown in the cited place.

Latin:

CAPUT II. ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

Significato agone pro Coloſſenfium pleniori fide in Chriſtum, in quo omnes theſauri ſcientiæ reconditi, ac declarato gaudio fuo de iisdem, monet, ut ſeductionem per Philoſophiam, & doctrinas hominum ſecundum traditiones mundi caveant, & repetita doctrina de Chriſto, in quo plenitudo Deitatis habitat corporaliter, in quo perfectionem veram habent, ac circumciſionem veram per baptiſmum, per quem mortis, ſepulturæ ac reſurrectionis Chriſti fructus participes redduntur, remiſſionis peccatorum & victoria Satanæ per fidem, hortatur, ut nec ad externa illa circumciſionem, aut diſcrimen ciborum ac dierum ceu neceſſaria ad ſalutem obligari, nec per Angelorum cultum a Chriſto unico capite totius myſtici corporis abduci ſeſe patiantur.

Partes tres funt I. Adhortatio ad conſtantiam in vera fide cum dehortatione a ſeductione ad verf. 8. II. Explicatio doctrinæ de Chriſto, baptiſmo & fide ad verf. 15. III. Admonitio ne conſcientias obligari patiantur externis ceremoniis, & cultu Angelorum, quum id doctrinæ traditæ non conveniat ad verf. 23.

PARS I. Adhortatio ad conſtantiam in fide: cum debortatione a ſeductione.

Verf. 1. Θέλω γὰρ ὑμᾶς εἰδέναι, ἡλίκον ἀγῶνα ἔχω περὶ ὑμῶν Ἡλίκον ἀγῶνα (כמה נלחמתי) Ex occaſione verbi ἀγωνιζόμενος fermonem hunc nectit. Per ἀγῶνα autem non intelligit folicitudinem tantum, fed & preces affiduas, ſignificatas per luctam Jacobi.

Περὶ ὑμῶν κὶ τῶν ἐν τῇ Λαοδικίᾳ Laodiceam Phrygiæ intellige.

Καὶ ὅσοι οὐχ ἑωράκασι τὸ πρόσωπόν μου ἐν σαρκί; Latini dicerent: Qui me de facie non noverunt. Sed quia פנים Ebrais multa significat, perspicuitatis causa addidit ἐν σαρκί. Ut Apostolica admonitio de custodienda veritate Evangelica, quæ in solo Christo salutem collocat, ac cavenda seductione ad alia apud eos, qui in carne ipsum non viderant, eo magis penetret, luctam suam exponit pro iisdem, & lætitiam, quam hactenus accepit e fide ipsorum, idque verbis gravissimis, maximeque emphaticis, qualibus etiam constat ipsa parænesis.

Exordium hic fingit Davenantius in septem prioribus versibus, de cujus artificio dicit, nihil ab Aristotele, Cicerone, reliquisque eloquentiæ Magistris scriptum de conformandis proœmiis, quod in eo non obfervetur. Certamen vel lucta pretum.

Per ἀγῶνα autem tum solicitudinis tum precum luctam innui non abnuimus, quo sensu de precibus verbum ἀγωνιζόμενον etiam adhibuit infra cap. IV. 12. Proxime dixerat cap. I. 29. se certasse laborando pro aliis; jam se pro ipsis etiam certare ac luctari precando testatur.

Nec hisce solum absolvebatur lucta, nam certandum erat animo, contrariis imprimis affleibus exorientibus, quia modo gaudebat, modo dolebat, & timebat, conf.

Rom. XVI. 19. 2. cor. XI. 29. Certandum erat operæ adversus omnes insultus & machinationes, quibus Colossenses aliasque Ecclesias impetebat Satanas.

Certandum corpore, dum varia ideo sustinenda adversa. Unde Davenantius Erasmum & Vulgatum non satis commode solicitudine vertisse arguit, quia scilicet potest quis solicitus esse de suis vel alienis negotiis, etiam si nemo fit, qui illi obstet & adversetur; at ἀγῶνα ἔχειν non dicitur, nisi ille, cui lucta & contentio est cum Adversario, ut hic cum Satana & membris ejus impostoribus.

Laodicena Ecclesiæ mentionem speciatim facit, tum quæ illi etiam ab impostoribus similibus aut iisdem periculum imminebat, unde etiam in illa hanc epistolam prælegi cupiebat, tum ut eidem suam solicitudinem eadem opera testatam redderet.

Non frustra fuisse solicitudinem de Laodicenis, ex hypocrisi & χλιαρότητι, quæ ibi temporibus sequentibus invaluit, patet, Apoc. III. 16. Addit, & quotquot faciem meam non viderunt in carne, non quod de illorum solida fide dubitet, sed quod natura amantium, ut recte Davenantius, ita ferat, ut magis soliciti sint de amicis absentibus quam præsentibus, ut itaque innuant hanc suam absentiam causam esse potius solicita hujus cure, quam ullam de illorum fide diffidentiam, dicit se ita affectum esse in reliquos omnes, quibus adesse non poterat.

Theophylactus: Cum fit de dogmate, inquit, jam differturus, plurimam in Colossenses aperit ejus benevolentiam, ut apud hos gratiam ineat, & acceptior fit.

Nam eo (inquit) decreto, ut & vos tuear, & ne eos obturbet, perinde ac ut imbecilli & aliena indigeat ope, & Laodicenses adjecit, & alios, qui ejus non viderint faciem in carne (hoc est corporaliter) nunquam vidissent. Quid precibus contendat, docet, nimirum Quid precibus ut corda ipsorum solida consolatione repleantur, quæ per Pseudo-Apostolorum dogma de dat Apost. necessitate observationis legis facile labefactatur: tum ut charitate compingantur ac veluti conglutinentur, tum ut in cognitione DEI & Christi proficiant.

Consolatio ergo non in eo sita, quod viderent Colossenses curari se vehementer amari ab Apostolo, ut vult Cornelius, quem sensum huc affert etiam Davenantius, sed unice in eo, quod his precibus suis intendit Apostolus, vel in reipsa, quam persuadere ipsis conatur, hoc est, in perseverantia in veritate Evangelica, siquidem sola hæc doctrina de salute non nisi per fidem in Christum consequenda, turbatis conscientiis tranquillitatem, adeoque solidam consolationem afferat, Rom. V. 1. 2. Thess. II. 16. doctrina autem novatorum, (stabiliendo necessariam observationem ceremoniarum, & introducendo Angelorum cultum, & alias traditiones inanes & intertas) hominum corda mentesque variis scrupulis & anxietatibus divexabat, bisce autem cavere magna pars est consolationis spiritualis, ut recte Davenantius. Porro concordiam, qua animi nexu indissolubili inter se cohærent, ut trabes a fabris lignariis compactæ, intendebat Apostolus precibus suis, ne fideles distrahantur a se invicem dissensionibus, fimultatibus, odiis, quæ tum demum solida est in Ecclesia, cum in veritate fundata.

Nihil enim, secundum Nazianzenum orat. X. de reconcil. ad Mon. concordiam tam fortiter conciliat inter eos, quibus DEI negotia cordi sunt, quam consonantia de DEO: Et nihil magis ad discordiam facit, quam dissonantia de illo. Non ergo sensum Apostoli assequuntur, vel qui monstrari volunt, quinam sint capaces vera consolationis, scilicet qui charitate inter se coadunentur, vel qui cum Hyperio putant doceri, qua in re sita fit consolatio, nempe in charitate & perfecta cognitione Evangelii: aut etiam Davenantius, cum censet notari fructum perseverantiæ in veritate doctrinæ ab Epaphra acceptæ.

Tertio profectum intendit fidelium Apostolus precibus suis & lucta omni pro ipsis in cognitione salvifica. Præcipuum quod expetere poterat, est consolatio cordis: Proximum ab eo conjunctio animorum: Sequitur demum ulterior profectus in rebus sacris, quo imprimis opus habebant ob seductionem falsorum Doctorum, ἦ εἰς πάντα πλῶτον τῆς πληροφορίας τῆς συνέσεως, ubi εἰς propriam significationem retinet, nec necessum est, ut pro ἐν accipiatur. Nam agon precum inter alia respiciebat omnem illam abundantiam vel divitias πληροφορίας vel certitudinis intelligentiæ, Divitia cupiebat Apostolus.

Non plenitudinem sed certitudinem infert vox πληροφορίας, quod tum ex aliis locis, tum etiam ex illo Roman. XIV. vers. 5. manifestum. Unusquisque in mente sua (non impleatur, sed) certus esto. Nec scientiam, sed intelligentiam aut prudentiam σύνεσις notat: quæ in intelligentia ab ipsa scientia vel cognitione mysteriorum hic distinguitur, & ad eandem requiritur.

Ut enim exactiorem Dei & Patris & Christi cognitionem habeamus, & in ea firmiter persistamus, opus Ἵνα παρακληθῶσιν αἱ καρδίαι αὐτῶν) ut impleatur in illis vaticinium Es. XL. 1. 2. Συμβιβασθέντες ἐν ἀγάπῃ) Similitudo sumpta a cortinis templi.

Quod ibi est םוֹנֵיָהוּ vel σύνδεισος, id hic est συμβίβασον. Vide Exod. XXVI. multis locis. Vide Eph.

IV. 16. & hic infra 19. Καὶ εἰς πάντα πλῶτον τῆς πληροφορίας τῆς συνέσεως) Eis pro εἰς, & πλῶτον, ut fæpe diximus, abundantiam significat: Πληροφορία συνέσεως plenitudo scientiæ est scientia plena, id est, quanta esse in hoc seculo potest. Πληροφορία ἵνα πληρωθῶσιν ofendimus ad Rom.

XIV. 5. Hinc πληροφορία & πληροφορήμα plenitudo. Εἰς ἐπίγνωσιν τὸ μυστηρίου τὸ Θεοῦ κὶ Πατρὸς κὶ τοῦ χριστοῦ) Exaitiorem.

Myisterium dicit voluntatem illam DEI, quam Christus patefecit. Τὸ Θεοῦ κὶ Πατρὸς, id est, Dei qui idem Pater est noster, ut Eph. II. 3. IV. 6. Phil. IV. 20.

Mysterium Dei opus est divitiis certioris intelligentiæ vel certitudinis intellectu rerum divinarum sacrarum literarum. Mysterium Dei autem minus essentiam divinam, quemadmodum Anselmus de mysterio sacrosanctæ Trinitatis, Ambrosius de mysterio Deitatis Christi exponere, quam voluntatem Dei revelatam & Evangelium respicit. Nam Dei & Patris, ut & Christi mysterium indigitatur. Quid autem Patris nomen in mysterio importet, notum est: Et non male Crocius cum Calvino notat, cum Apostolus interposita copula Dei & Patris & Christi mysterium dixit, potentissimo argumento doceri, & Patrem & Christum esse eundem verum Deum. Si enim vox θεοῦ solam Patris personam spectaret, amittenda fuisset copula post θεοῦ & dicendum, in agnitione DEI Patris & Christi. Neque Christum a Deo magis alium esse indicat, quam Patrem, sed Patrem & Christum unum eundemque Deum esse prædicat. Conjungit autem cum Patre Christum, tum quia Pater per Filium revelavit mysterium, tum quia nec Pater absque Filio, nec Filius absque Patre cognosci potest. Pater enim est in Filio, & Filius in Patre, Solus Pater revelat Filium, & Christus Patrem. Vers.

3. 'Ἐν οἷς πάντες οἱ θησαυροὶ τῆς σοφίας καὶ τῆς γνώσεως ἀπόκρυφοι' in quo mysterio continentur omnes thesauri sapientiæ & scientiæ nempe salutaris.

Vide supra I. 9. Eph. 1. 8. 'Ἀπόκρυφος' cum dicit, similitudinem desumit ab arca, in qua pecuniæ servantur, indidem promendæ, ubi opus est Dan.

XI. 43. 'ἀπόκρυφοι τοῖς χρυσοῖς' & 1. Maccab. I. 24. 'ἔλαβε τοὺς θησαυροὺς τοὺς ἀποκρύφους' Sapientia thesauris comparari solet Prov.

VIII. 18. 19. Matth. XIII. 44. Pronomen & an Evangelium an v. Christi? Non de mysterio, sed de Christo hæc intelligenda. Nam id requirit 1. regula interpretationis, quod pronomen referendum sit ad immediate præcedens nomen.

Antecedit autem proxime nomen 'τῆς γνώσεως'. 2. Quia a Christo precatur ipsis omnes divitias certitudinis intelligentiæ spiritualis, ad exactiorem mysterii divini cognitionem, in Christo absconditos esse omnes thesauros sapientiæ & cognitionis docet. Is ergo abundanter omnem conferre potest certæ intelligentiæ, omnemque; cognitionem mysteriorum divinorum, qui fons & fundus est omnis sapientiæ & cognitionis.

Est itaque, inquit Apostolus, Theophylacto interprete, ab eo sapientia & scientia efflagitanda. 3. Non mysterium, sed Christus potius arca comparatur, in quo illi thesauri repositi sunt, & ex quo in omnes fideles istæ divitiæ redundant, de cujus plenitudine accipimus omnes gratiam pro gratia, Quicquid est sapientiæ & cognitionis in Evangelio, id non est absconditum, sed potius revelatum in Evangelio & per Evangelium nobis, quibus id proponitur.

5. Nuspiam in scripturis dicitur de Evangelio, quod in illo sint absconditi thesauri sapientiæ, sed Evangelium dicitur sapientia olim abscondita, jam revelata, Rom. XVI.

26. 6. Nec in mysterio continentur, aut absconditi sunt OMNES thesauri cognitionis, sed in Christo. Nam etsi thesaurus sapientiæ exhibeat Evangelium, non tamen omnes sapientiæ & cognitionis thesauri in eodem exhibentur.

Sunt infiniti præterea thesauri sapientiæ & cognitionis in Deo, utpote qui infinitæ sapientiæ est, qui non patent aut revelati sunt in Evangelio. Et conjunguntur σοφία & γνῶσις, adhibita insuper universalitatis nota, ut, quicquid ad thesauros sapientiæ & cognitionis pertinet, intelligi innuatur, uti Calvinus, Bullingerus, & Hyperius notant, duplicationem ad rem augendam pertinere. Neque vero restringi hoc a Grotio patimur ad sapientiam & cognitionem salutarem, quam sacræ literæ docent, Nam etsi nobis sapientia & cognitio, quæ in sacris literis continetur, sufficiat, neque a nobis exhauriri possit, non tamen OMNES in ea absolute THESAURI sapientiæ & cognitionis reconditi sunt in scriptura sacra.

Multa enim & innumera atque infinita habentur in arcanis divinæ sapientiæ & omniscientiæ penetralibus, quæ non revelata in sacris literis sunt. Multi thesauri omniscientiæ divina superant, quos nec electi, nec Angeli, cujuscunque ordinis & eminentiæ, penetrare possunt aut capere. 7. In illo sunt reconditi thesauri sapientiæ & cognitionis, in quo habitat tota plenitudo Deitatis, ut e collatione v. 3. & 9. constat. Ea vero non in mysterio, sed in Christo habitat. Ideo veteres hoc magno consensu de Christo explicant, idque agnoscit Crocius, imo Calviniani quoque plerique Marloratus, Aretius Gryneus, Perkinsus, Lubertus; non de mysterio, sed de Christo id interpretantur, unde Crocius Calvinum, & fere omnes Reformatos ita accipere fatetur, eosque omnino sequitur. Quæ proinde opponenda Hieronymo, Zanchio, Piscatori, & aliis diffidentibus in schola Reformatorum, qua ea nunc in dubium vocant οἱ ἐκ τῆς ἐναντίας, quam quod Christo secundum humanam naturam convenire omniscientiam negent.

Argumentum enim invictum est: Secundum Argumentum. quam naturam absconditi sunt in Christo omnes thesauri sapientiæ & cognitionis, secundum eam omniscientiam humanam naturam vere omnisciens est Christus omnisciens. At secundum humanam naturam vi unionis personalis absconditi sunt in CHRISTO omnes illi thesauri.

Ergo. Qui demonstrationi elidendæ etsi alias quoque exceptiones adhibeant, illis tamen abunde satisfactum examin. de person. Christi controv.

VII. membr. II. pag. 347. seqq. Nec est, quod obvertat Crocius, non esse hic sermonem de infinita sapientia & cognitione, qua Deus est sapiens & omnia cognoscit, sed qua fideles intelligunt & cognoscunt mysterium Dei & Christi. Confundantur enim ita diversa.

Nam de hac citra objectum precum sermo erat in verbis præcedentibus. Jam autem non de objecto agitur quidnam intendat & contendat Apostolus agone precum suarum, sed de causa & principio illius cognitionis & intelligentiæ, quam precibus suis exorare Colossensibus laborat: quam vero non ab Angelis sed unice a Christo ita obtinendam innuit. Fons ergo sapientiæ in Christo absconditus & inexhaustus cum rivulis inde in fideles omnes fine decremento ac defectu immensæ illius sapientiæ derivatis confundi non debet, sapientia creata nobis secundum mensuram donationis Christi concessa, cum immensa illa & infinita sapientia in Christo, qua eam obtinet ἐκ μέτρος, Ab Angelis ad Christum revocantur Colossenses, & quam in eodem secundum humanam naturam sapientiæ divinæ immensi thesauri reconditi sint, non dubitare vult, imo confidere jubet, facile exoratum iri eas divitias a Christo fratre nostro nobis ὁμοούσῳ, quæ unicuique sufficiant, utpote Spiritu S. uncto propter consortes suos non ad mensuram. Ne autem dicant, qui contradicunt, sapientiam intelligi finitam, quod Perkinsi, Parei, Bergii & Wendelini est commentum, notanda est propria verborum emphasis: Non dicit solum cognitionem in Christo absconditam, sed & sapientiam, nec solum cognitionem & sapientiam aliquam, sed thesauros cognitionis & sapientiae: nec hoc solum, sed ut exprimat divinam sapientiam, addit OMNES thesauros cognitionis & sapientiae esse in Christo absconditos. Qui vero omnes thesauros dicit sapientiae & scientiae, quid aliud exprimit, quam OMNISCIENTIAE & OMNISAPIENTIAE divinathesauros? In quo finitae saltem sapientiae thesauri absconditi sunt, in eo OMNES thesauri sapientiae absconditi vere dici nequeunt; quia praeter scientiae thesauros longe ditiores & eminentiores thesauri dantur divinae sapientiae. Quae totalitas omnimoda & absoluta thesaurorum omnium sapientiae, quae nihil relinquat residuum, emphatice exprimitur ab, Arabe Interprete voce גמץ omnes, toti, universi a גמץ congregare, colligere, copulare, designante omnimodam rei universalitatem, ut intelligatur ὅλως, ὅλον τι, totaliter totum, sine aliquo defectu, ut observat B.

Dn. D. Myslenta disp. prior. super hunc locum th.

18. unde Patres ὁμοθυμαδὸν locum praesentem de omniscientia divina & infinita accepere, Cyrillus Alexandr.

Chrysostomus, Graecus scholiastes, Theophylactus, Damascenus, Isidorus Pelusiota, Ambrosius item, Hieronymus, Fulgentius, Remigius, Dionysius Carthusanus, Lyranus, Thomas, aliaeque Pontificiis necnon Reformatis Bullinger, Sibrandus, Lubbertus, Maresius & alii, qui Deitatem Filii DEI ex hoc loco probant, ut loco citato ostendimus.

## 2:4
Ver. 4. Τῦτο δὲ λέγω, ἵνα μή τις ὑμᾶς παραλογίζηται (But this I say, lest any man should beguile you). Already then there were those in Phrygia who were casting the seeds of a heresy, which was called κατὰ φύγας (the Cataphrygians).

Some mixed Jewish, others Pythagorean dogmas and institutions with the Christian religion, and they despised others who did not follow the same as if they were unskilled and carnal. Παραλογίζηται (beguile) corresponds to the Hebrew רמה (deceive) and התל (mock), for which is also placed πλανᾶν (to lead astray), 1 Cor. VI. 9, XV. 33, Gal. VI. 7, 2 Cor. XI. 3, 2 Thess. II. 3. 'Εν πιθανολογίᾳ (with enticing words) in a specious speech.

That they might remain in the πληροφορίᾳ της συνέσεως (full assurance of understanding), it was necessary that they take heed, lest they be seduced by false teachers.

But whether that heresy, which was called κατὰ φύγας, had already obtained at that time, does not appear. The followers of Montanus were those in Phrygia, and Priscilla and Maximilla boasted of revelations, and they adhered to Montanus, who called himself the Father, as Epiphanius testifies, book

II. Tom. I. against Heresies XLVIII. But nothing of such a kind, as is here reproved in the seducers of the Colossians, is found in their heresy.

And therefore, neither by reason of the times nor by reason of the dogmas do they fit here. The opinion of others is more convenient, that the Pseudo-Apostles of that time are designated, who brought forward that the way to God lay open not through the Son, but through Angels, and who wished that most Jewish statutes and the customs of the nations be observed, as Theophylact testifies.

Yet the words are conceived generally, so as to exclude all impostors, who seduce the simpler ones with Logical Paralogisms and persuasions colored by Rhetorical artifice for the sake of deceiving, Rom.

XVI. 18. but especially those who lead away from Christ, the only head of the Church and Mediator, and his Evangelical doctrine.

Latin:

Vers. 4. Τῦτο δὲ λέγω, ἵνα μή τις ὑμᾶς παραλογίζηται Jam tum erant, qui in Phrygia femina jaciebant haereseos, quae dicta κατὰ φύγας.

Miscebant alii Judaica, alii Pythagorica tum dogmata tum instituta Christianae religioni, & caeteros non eadem sequentes quasi imperitos & carnales spernebant. Παραλογίζηται respondet Ebraeo רמה, & התל, pro quibus ponitur & πλανᾶν, 1 Cor. VI. 9. XV. 33. Gal. VI. 7. 2. cor. XI. 3. 2. Thess. II. 3. 'Εν πιθανολογίᾳ oratione speciosa.

Ut in πληροφορίᾳ της συνέσεως manerent, opus erat, ut caverent, ne seducerentur a falsis doctoribus.

An vero tum haeresis illa, quae dicta κατὰ φύγας, jam obtinuerit, non apparet. Montani sectatores erant illi in Phrygia, & Priscilla ac Maximilla jactabant revelationes, & Montano, qui seipsum Patrem dicebat, adhaerebant teste Epiphanio l.

II. Tom. I. contra Haeres. XLVIII. Nihil autem tale, quid in seductoribus Colossensium hic reprehenditur, in illorum haeresi reperitur.

Ideoque nec ratione temporum nec ratione dogmatum huc faciunt. Convenientior est aliorum sententia, quod Pseudo-Apostoli istius temporis designentur, qui non per Filium, sed per Angelos ad Deum viam patere adferebant, quique Judaica statuta pleraque & gentium mores servari volebant, teste Theophylacto.

Verba tamen generaliter concepta sunt, ut omnes impostores excludant, qui Paralogismis Logicis, & persuasionibus artificio Rhetorico ad decipiendum coloratis simpliciores seducunt, Rom.

XVI. 18. maxime autem illi, qui a Christo unico capite Ecclesiae ac Mediatore, ejusque Evangelica doctrina abducunt.

## 2:5
Ver. 5. Εἰ γὰρ τῇ σαρκὶ ἄπειμι, ἀλλὰ τῷ πνεύματι σὺν ὑμῖν εἰμι (For though I be absent in the flesh, yet am I with you in the spirit). The same sense as 1.

Cor. V. 3. God revealed to Paul what was happening at Colossae.

That cannot be gathered from these words. He says he is present in Spirit, not because he knew by the Spirit or by immediate revelation what was being done at Colossae; but because he is present with them in mind, affection, prayers, and desire. But what order, what firmness of faith is in them, although I would not deny that it was revealed to him by the Spirit: Inasmuch as He inspired his mind with these very words testifying about them; yet I do not think this is indicated by those words, in the manner that was believed by Ambrose, Anselm, and Lombard. The common interpretation, both of the Reformed and of most of the Papists, Justiniani, Cornelius a Lapide, and others, is that the Apostle, although absent in body by a great interval of places, is nevertheless present in mind, and cares for their salvation no less than if he were present himself.

Whence the Colossians ought to receive this epistle as if the Apostle were inspecting everything in person, and were speaking to them present in body. Concerning the συναφείᾳ (connection) of the words, Theophylact not unaptly: But in order to follow the context of the speech twice, it should have been said, even if I am absent in body: yet in spirit I behold these deceivers.

But he turns the discourse to praise. Χαίρων καὶ βλέπων ὑμῶν τὴν τάξιν (Joying and beholding your order). It is a hendiadys.

For this is what he means: I rejoice, seeing that all things among you are done rightly and in order. רצף order. Aquila: See 1 Cor. XIV. 40. The word of seeing generally denotes knowledge, as has been observed elsewhere, I rejoice knowing or understanding. He had understood this, however, from Epaphras. Καὶ τὸ στερέωμα τῆς εἰς χριστὸν πίστεως ὑμῶν (And the stedfastness of your faith in Christ). רסוס אמונתכם.

See 1 Pet. 5.9. Theophylact weighs the emphasis of the words thus: Τὸ στερέωμα τῆς πίστεως ὑμῶν (The stedfastness of your faith), that is, your confirmed and immovable faith, just as if some battle line were drawn up, which order and institution was preserved by them, with mutual charity confirming all things, nor were there any dissensions among them.

Nay, even faith itself is as it were a certain firmament, which prevents perverse thoughts from arising, which beget dissensions in those who are wavering and various. Where true faith is either entirely absent, or the mind wavers and alternates concerning it, there the external order, whether common or Ecclesiastical, although beautiful in itself, little gladdens the saints.

Latin:

Vers. 5. Εἰ γὰρ τῇ σαρκὶ ἄπειμι, ἀλλὰ τῷ πνεύματι σὺν ὑμῖν εἰμι Idem sensus, qui 1.

Cor. V. 3. Deus Paulo revelabat, quae Colossis fierent.

Id ex his verbis colligi non potest. Praesentem se Spiritu dicit, non quod in Spiritu vel immediate revelatione cognosceret, quae Colossis agerentur; sed quod ipsis animo, affectu, precibus, desiderio adsit. Qualis vero ordo, quae fidei firmitas illis fit, etsi a Spiritu eidem revelatum non negarim: Siquidem haec ipsa verba de illis testantia menti ejus inspirarit; non tamen illis verbis hoc indicari arbitror, quemadmodum ab Ambrosio, Anselmo, & Lombardo creditum fuit. Communis interpretatio & Reformatorum, & a Pontificiis plerorumque, Justiniani, Cornelii a Lapide, aliorum, Apostolum, etsi magno locorum intervallo corpore absit, animo tamen adesse, nec minus ipsorum salutem curare, ac si praesens ipse adesset.

Unde Colossenses hanc epistolam sic accipere debebant, ac si Apostolus coram omnia inspiceret, ac verba ad eos faceret praesens corpore. De verborum συναφείᾳ non inconcinne Theophylactus: Ut autem orationis contextum bis sectaretur, dicendum itaque fuisset, etsi care absum vel corpore: Spiritu tamen deceptores hosce conspicio.

Sed in laudem divertit sermonem. Χαίρων καὶ βλέπων ὑμῶν τὴν τάξιν Est ἡ διὰ δυοῖν.

Hoc enim vult: Gaudeo, videns cuncta apud vos recte agi ac ordine. רצף τάξις Aquila: Vide 1. Cor. XIV. 40. Verbum videndi generatim cognitionem notare, alias observatum, gaudeo cognoscens vel intelligens. Intellexerat autem id Epaphra. Καὶ τὸ στερέωμα τῆς εἰς χριστὸν πίστεως ὑμῶν Firmitatem fidei vestrae in Christum. רסוס אמונתכם.

Vide 1. Pet. 5.9. Vocum emphasin sic expendit Theophylactus: Τὸ στερέωμα τῆς πίστεως ὑμῶν, hoc est, obfirmatam vestram & immobilem fidem, tanquam instructa acies aliqua fit, qui ab his servaretur ordo & institutio, charitate mutua omnia obfirmante, nec ulle inter hos erant dissidia.

Quin etiam fides ipsa perfe velut firmamentum quoddam est, quae praevos prohibeat cogitatus subire, qui dissensiones pariant nutabundis & variis. Ubi fides vera vel prorsus exulat, vel animus circa eam nutat & alternatur, ibi ordo externus sive communis sive Ecclesiasticus, quamvis per se pulcher, parum exhilarat sanctos.

## 2:6
Ver. 6. ὡς οὖν παρελάβετε τὸν χριστὸν Ἰησοῦν (As ye have therefore received Christ Jesus). He again called the doctrine of Christ itself Christ Jesus.

And παραλαμβάνειν (to receive) is the proper word for learners, 1 Cor. XI. 23, XV. 1, 3, Gal. I. 9, Philipp. IV. 9. 'Εν αὐτῷ περιπατεῖτε (walk ye in him) express it in act.

For that is what it is to walk in him,

Rom. XI. 4, VIII. 1, 4, and elsewhere. Although it can be accepted concerning the doctrine with Theodoret, and the matter seems to return to the same thing, since Christ Jesus our Lord is the proper object and nucleus of the whole Gospel: Yet it is not necessary that we admit a Metonymical sense, when the proper one can have a place, and the reception of Jesus Christ made through faith can be understood.

For what else is faith than the λῆψις (taking) and παράληψις (receiving) of Christ Jesus our Lord, whom we embrace with true confidence of heart, along with his merit and the benefits obtained for us, and make our own? He is exhibited to us through the Gospel and the preaching of the same; but he is received and apprehended through faith: and thus we also walk in him, when we proceed in faith and in obedience to him.

Nothing, says Theophylact, interpreting after Chrysostom, do we introduce that is foreign: For whatever you had received, that we demand, namely Christ Jesus and Lord, not Angels, whom we have not preached: Walk in him: For he himself is the way, which leads to the Father, do not walk in the path accepted from the Angels: For this does not lead there.

Latin:

Vers. 6. ὡς οὖν παρελάβετε τὸν χριστὸν Ἰησοῦν Christum Jesum rursus dixit ipsam Christi doctrinam.

Et παραλαμβάνειν propria vox discentibus, 1. Cor. XI. 23. XV. 1. 3. Gal. I. 9. Philipp. IV. 9. 'Εν αὐτῷ περιπατεῖτε actu id exprimite.

Id enim ῇλε περιπατεῖν,

Rom. XI. 4. VIII. 1. 4. & alibi. Quanquam de doctrina accipi possit cum Theodoreto, & res eodem videatur redire, quum objectum proprium & nucleus totius Evangelii Christus Jesus Dominus noster fit: Non tamen necessum est, ut Metonymicum admittamus sensum, quum proprius locum habere queat, & susceptio Jesu Christi per fidem facta intelligi.

Quid enim aliud est fides, quam λῆψις & παράληψις Christi Jesu Domini nostri, quem cum suo merito & beneficiis nobis partis vera cordis fiducia amplectimur, nobisque propriamus? Exhibetur nobis per Evangelium & praeconium ejusdem; suscipitur vero & apprehenditur per fidem: atque ita in eo etiam ambulamus, cum in fide & obsequio ejus pergimus.

Nibil, inquit, Theophylacto post Chrysostomum interprete, alienum ingerimus: Quodcunque enim accepisses, illud exigimus, Christum scilicet Jesum & Dominum, non Angelos, quos non praedicavimus: In ipso ambulate: Ipsenamque est via, quae ducat ad Patrem, nolite Angelorum acceptum id iter incedere: Hoc enim non eo traducit.

## 2:7
Ver. 7. 'Εῤῥιζωμένοι (Rooted). See Eph. III. 18, Matth. XIII. 6. Be far other than those, of whom Esaias XL.

24. Καὶ ἐποικοδομούμενοι ἐν αὐτῷ (And built up in him). Acts

XX. 32, Eph. II. 20, founded in Christ, who is the foundation, 1 Cor. III. 11. Καὶ βεβαιούμενοι ἐν τῇ πίσει (And stablished in the faith). נכונים. Καθὼς ἐδιδάχθητε (As ye have been taught). Eph.

IV. 21. Περισσεύοντες ἐν αὐτῇ ἐν εὐχαριστίᾳ (Abounding therein with thanksgiving).

Growing in faith through thanksgiving, 1 Cor. 14:12, 2 Cor. 8:7, God accumulates the grateful with greater gifts. In the manuscript, en autō is missing. A double metaphor explains the firmness of faith: namely, from a tree properly rooted, and from a building resting on a solid foundation, so that they may strike firm roots in Christ as the only firmest [foundation], and draw vital sap and vigor from Him Himself, and, built upon Him as an immovable rock, stand against any storms whatsoever. Truly, says Chrysostom, faith is a building, by which one believes, or the Evangelical doctrine, and it is a work of a strong foundation and builder, and safe construction. Which he then explains in his own words, bebaioumenoi en tē pistei, confirmed in faith, that is, according to the interpreter Theophylact, firmly having embraced God through faith, not by captious arguments or any flowing speech. For if a building and structure are placed on foundations that are less firm for sustaining the weight, they indeed fail and collapse. He applies this to the goal thus: By a constant step, you have reached perfection. For one must not cling now to Christ, now to Angels. But when, (says Theophylact) AS YOU HAVE LEARNED, he says, he subjected the discipline as if for a foundation. But "abounding" [is] the limit of the motion for the foundations laid, the form of which you yourselves have received, but rather one must progress and boast in these. Furthermore, he shows that thanks are to be given abundantly by us faithful to GOD, because He has made us worthy of such great grace. And that it is not to be ascribed to our own progress that we have been rendered worthy of it.

Latin:

Vers. 7. 'Εῤῥιζωμένοι Vid. Eph. III. 18. Matth. XIII. 6. Longe alii este, quam illi, de quibus Esaias XL.

24. Καὶ ἐποικοδομούμενοι ἐν αὐτῷ AG.

XX. 32. Eph. II. 20. fundati in Christo, qui fundamentum est, 1. Cor. III. 11. Καὶ βεβαιούμενοι ἐν τῇ πίσει נכונים. Καθὼς ἐδιδάχθητε Eph.

IV. 21. Περισσεύοντες ἐν αὐτῇ ἐν εὐχαριστίᾳ

Per gratiarum actionem crescentes in fide, 1. Cor. XIV. 12. 2. Cor. VIII. 7. Deus gratos maioribus cumulat donis. In Manuscripto deest ἐν αὐτῷ. Gemina Metaphora explicatur firmitudo fidei: nempe ab arbore probe radicatam, & ab adificio solido fundamento innixo, ut in Christo ceu solo firmissimo firmas agant radices, & ab ipso succum vitalem ac vigorem hauriant, ipsi tanquam petræ immobili superstructi adversus turbines quosvis consistant. Revera, inquit Chrysostomus, adificium est fides, qua creditur, vel doctrina Evangelica, & opus est forti fundamento fab lique, & tuta adificatione. Quod propriis deinde verbis explicat, βεβαιούμενοι ἐν τῇ πίστει, confirmati fide, hoc est, interprete Theophylacto, firmiter Deum per fidem complexi, non captionibus vel fusibili ulla oratione. Edificium namque & structura si sint fundamentis imposita, quæ oneri sustinendo minus sint firma, fallunt quidem & collabuntur. Id ad scopum sic applicat: Constanti gradu perfetis. Neque enim nunc Christo, nunc Angelis inberendum. Cum autem, (inquit Theophylactus) SICUT ET DIDICISTIS, inquit, tanquam pro fundamento disciplinam subjecit. Abundantes vero pro injecta fundamentis motum limes, quorum ipsi acceperitis formam, sed proficiendum in bis potius erit & gloriandum. Affatim praterea & gratias esse fidelibus nobis DEO agendas effendit, quod tanta nos gratia dignos effecerit. Nec nostro id esse profectui adscribendum, quod ea simus digni redditi.

## 2:8
Vers. 8. Blepete mē tis hymas estai ho sylagōgōn dia tēs philosophias kai kenēs apatēs, estai ho sylagōgōn for sylagōgē, a manner of speaking also customary among the more elegant Greeks. Syla is that which is led away by force, as in battles. Sylagōgōn as if to lead away by force. Thus we say, the girl who has plundered me. For we are accustomed to take metaphors for those things which have a similar effect. Then there is dia dia. For dia tēs philosophias kai kenēs apatēs means the same as dia tēs kenēs apatēs tēs dia philosophias. He used the very Greek word philosophias, because it was accepted. But in truth, it deceived men. For it either did not promise eternal life, or it did not show the true and certain way that would lead to it. Therefore, I do not wonder at the decree made in the times of the Hasmoneans: Cursed be he who teaches his son Greek Philosophy: Not that it is evil to know it in itself, but because they saw much danger in it. And certainly it must be admitted that, after the Jews gave themselves to Greek books, that ancient doctrine was in many ways interpolated. Kata tēn paradosin tōn anthrōpōn.

Rightly. For what those Greeks taught was from human in to pason [sic] ingenuity. But what certain thing can be held concerning God and God's decrees, unless God teaches? Hence the perpetual and inexplicable quarrels among Philosophers: And much labor in those things which are neither certain in themselves, nor make men better. Kata ta stoicheia tou kosmou according to an institution not coming from heaven, but of this world, and therefore partly false, partly imperfect. Regarding the word stoicheia see Gal. 4:3, 9. Kai kata Christon) Not such as is Christ's, brought down from heaven, John 3:13, 31, 6:33, 37, 41.

See, he says, that they may diligently attend, look around on all sides, and therefore be vigilant, not be secure, nor sleep, Matt. 13:25, Acts 20:28, Phil. 4:2. Nor does he require this only from Bishops or Deacons, but from all to whom the epistle is inscribed: Which warning therefore concerns everyone, Matt. 7:14, Rom. 16:17, 1 John 4:1. The word sylagōgōn is properly to carry off booty or to plunder in the manner of enemies, therefore it is rendered by "depradari" [to plunder] by Ambrose, and by "spoliare" [to despoil] by Hilary in book XII of De Trinitate. Nor does the Syrian [version] say otherwise. For such people plunder and despoil us not only of true knowledge and true faith, but of grace, salvation, and even Christ Himself and God, and the enjoyment of Him. But interpreters inquire at whom he points his finger here, as the plunderers of that time (even though the warning extends to all because of the parity of the reason).

Grotius, as it appears, is not consistent with himself. For he previously said that the Montanists were being noted, now he judges that Greek philosophy is being rebuked, which either did not promise eternal life, or did not show the way to it; Clement of Alexandria in book I of the Stromata thinks the philosophy of Epicurus is condemned, which removed providence and counted pleasure among the number of the gods. But these do not fit the Apostle's present refutation.

Cornelius à Lapide wishes the Platonic philosophy concerning Angels, Intermediate Gods and Mediators, and Apollonius of Tyana, and other philosophers who were then going around the world to lead the Christian people to themselves and their dogmas, to be noted; and likewise Simon Magus with his followers, who would patch together their dogmas from the figments of Plato and other philosophers as if a patchwork quilt, and he accepts the elements of the world as nothing other than the rudiments of vain philosophy concerning the production and government of the world: e.g., the Platonists' [teachings] concerning Angels as creators of the world and mediators of men before God, etc. But let them consider those things concerning philosophy, and concerning the traditions of men and the elements of the world, which indeed seem to be different: not to mention that it is not certain that such things were taught either by Simon Magus or by Apollonius of Tyana, or that they were taught in Phrygia.

Guil. Estius thinks those are designated who existed in the time of the Apostles and in those places where the Apostles were, mixing secular philosophy with the religion of the Jews, teaching many things about God, about the Son of God, about Angels, the world and its creation, and about the purification of men, partly taught by the Platonists, partly invented from their own brain, false and vain: and that Simon Magus and the Gnostics were of that kind. But he notes the traditions of the scribes and Pharisees, about which [we read in] Matt. 15 and Mark 7. By the elements of the world [he understands] the elements or rudiments of secular philosophy, such as those taught by the Platonists and Simonians, or the carnal ceremonies of the Mosaic law, in this sense: beware lest anyone plunder you through philosophy and empty deceit: Likewise, lest anyone do that according to or through the traditions of men and the elements of the world, as the former was placed against the Simonians, the latter against the Judaizers. To us it seems most consistent that it is not true Philosophy that is condemned, which is a gift of God, which Cornelius rashly accuses Luther of understanding here (with Dan. Hofmann of Helmstedt and some others opposing philosophical truth and Theological [truth] to each other aphilosophōs and atheologōs, the depravation of which B. D. Grawerus also noted, and we also noted in [our] Natural and Revealed Theology by profession), but the philosophy which was then boasted of, namely vain and deceptive, as the Apostle explains himself, which we gather from this Apostolic refutation was received from the Platonists, and interpolated by Pseudo-Apostles, and also disseminated in Phrygia mixed with the Christian religion, Theophylact not denying it; but the Jewish traditions according to the elements of the world, that is, external ceremonies, which are so called in Gal. 4:3, 9, made the religion more confused, as being patched together by a worst Syncretism from the tenets and dogmas of Christians, Platonists, and Jews. But it is rash for all those things to be referred by Grotius to the Philosophy of the Greeks: since from the appended Apostolic refutation it is manifest that Judaizers are also noted, urging external circumcision and other ceremonies regarding days and foods, and concerning these the elements of the world ought to be understood in the parallel passage.

The elements of legal observance were indeed like the principles of the Jewish religion: they were elements for a rude people, by which they were to be led. is returned to Christ, who is shadowed forth by the same, which were considered as elements and rudiments of Christian distinction, Heb. V. 12. and because they were delivered to Christ, once exhibited, as necessary for salvation, they were a corruption of the Gospel.

That Greek philosophy did not deliver eternal life or the manner of attaining it! that is a matter of imperfection, but not of the empty deceit (κενῆς ἀπάτης), which the Apostle condemns here. By the words "and not according to Christ" is exhibited the general method of refuting all deceptions: inasmuch as by them that form of religion is introduced, which is neither delivered by Christ, nor delivers Christ alone, and his redemption or faith in Christ, but leads away from Christ to another, and joins other mediators to Christ, and requires other things besides the redemption of Christ for salvation.

PART II.

DOGMATIC, Explaining the doctrine concerning Christ, concerning baptism, and concerning faith.

Latin:

Vers. 8. Βλέπετε μή τις ὑμᾶς ἐσαι ὁ συλαγωγῶν διὰ τῆς φιλοσοφίας καὶ κενῆς ἀπάτης, ἴσαι ὁ συλαγωγῶν pro συλαγωγῇ, loquendi genus etiam elegantioribus Græcis usitatum. Σῦλα est id, quod per vim abducitur, ut in reppreliis. Συλαγωγῶν quasi per vim abducere. Sic dicimus, quæ me prædata puella est. Solemus enim translationes fumere ad ea, quæ parem habent effectum. Deinde est διὰ διὰ. Nam διὰ τῆς φιλοσοφίας καὶ κενῆς ἀπάτης idem valet, quod διὰ τῆς κενῆς ἀπάτης τῆς διὰ φιλοσοφίας. Ipsam vocem Græcam usurpavit φιλοσοφίας, quia erat recepta. Vere autem ea fallebat homines. Nam aut vitam æternam non promittebat, aut viam, quæ eo duceret, veram certamque non monstrabat. Itaque non miror Hasmonæorum temporibus factum decretum: Maledictus fit, qui docet filium suum Philosophiam Græcam: Non quod per se eam nosse malum fit, sed quod multum in ea viderent periculi. Et certe fatendum est, postquam Judæi Græcis libris se dedere, veterem illam doctrinam multis modis fuisse interpolatam. Κατὰ τὴν παράδοσιν τῶν ἀνθρώπων.

Recte. Nam quod Græci illi docebant, ex humano ἰν τὸ πᾶσον erat ingenio. De Deo autem Deique decretis quid certi haberi potest, nisi Deo docente? Ideo perpetuæ & inexplicabiles inter Philosophos rixæ: Et plurimus labor in iis, quæ nec per se certa sunt, nec homines reddunt meliores. Κατὰ τὰ στοιχεῖα τοῦ κόσμου secundum institutionem non à cœlo venientem, sed hujus mundi, ac proinde falsam partim, partim imperfectam. De voce στοιχεῖα vide Gal. IV. 3. 9. Καὶ κατὰ χρισὸν) Non qualis est Christi à cœlo delata Joh. III. 13. 31. VI. 33. 37. 41.

Videte, inquit, ut diligenter attendant, undique circumspiciant, ideoque vigilent, non securi sint, neque dormiant, Matth. XIII. 25. Actor. XX. 28. Phil. IV. 2. Nec tantum id ab Episcopis aut Diaconis requirit, sed ab omnibus, quibus inscripta est epistola: Quæ monitio proinde omnes etiam concernit, Matth. VII. 14. Rom. XVI. 17. 1. Johan. IV. 1. Verbum συλαγωγῶν proprie est hostium more prædam agere, aut spoliare, ideo per depradari ab Ambrosio, per spoliare ab Hilario libr. XII. de Trinit. redditur. Nec aliter Syrus. Tales enim deprædantur nos & spoliant non tantum vera cognitione ac vera fide, sed gratia, salute, adeoque Christo ipso & Deo, ejusque fruitione. Ad quosnam vero hic digitum intendat, ceu istius temporis prædones, (etsi ad omnes sese ob paritatem rationis admonitio porrigat) disquirunt Interpre tes.

Grotius, ut apparet, sibi ipsi non constat. Nam prius Montanistas notari dixit, jam Græcorum philosophiam reprehendi, quæ aut vitam æternam non promisit, aut viam ad eam non monstravit, cenfer, Clemens Alexandr. libr. I. Stromat: damnari putat Philosophiam Epicuri, quæ sustulit providentiam, & in Deorum numerum retulit voluptatem. Sed hæc præsenti Apostoli elencho non conveniunt.

Cornelius à Lapide Philosophiam Platonicam de Angelis, Diis Mediis & Mediatoribus, & Apollonium Thyaneum, aliosque Philosophos, qui tum orbem circumibant, ut populum Christianum ad se & sua dogmata traducerent; itemque Simonem Magum cum suis notari vult, qui dogmata sua ex figmentis Platonis & aliorum Philosophorum quasi centonem confarcinarent, nec aliter elementa mundi accipit, quam de rudimentis vanæ philosophiæ circa mundi productionem & gubernationem: v. g. Platonirum de Angelis mundi conditoribus & hominum mediatoribus apud Deum &c. Sed ita considerent illa de philosophia, & de traditionibus hominum ac elementis mundi, quæ vero diversa esse videntur: ut taceam, non constare, talia vel à Simone Mago, vel ab Apollonio Thyaneo tradita esse, aut tradita esse in Phrygia.

Guil. Estius eos designari putat, qui tempore Apostolorum & iis locis, in quibus Apostoli versabantur, extiterunt, secularem philosophiam cum religione Judæorum miscentes, multa de Deo, de Dei Filio, de Angelis, mundo & ejus creatione, deque purgatione hominum partim à Platonicis præcepta, partim ex proprio cerebro adinventa, falsa & vana tradentes: & ex eo genere fuisse Simonem Magum & Gnosticos. Traditiones autem notari scribarum & Pharisæorum, de quibus Matth. XV. & Marc. VII. Per elementa mundi elementa vel rudimenta secularis philosophiæ, qualia à Platonicis, & Simoniacis tradita, vel carnales ceremonias legis Mosaica, hoc sensu, cavete, ne quis vos deprædetur per philosophiam & inanem fallaciam: Item, ne quis id faciat secundum vel per traditiones hominum & elementa mundi, ut prius contra Sisimoniantes, posterius contra Judæizantes positum. Nobis id videtur maxime consentaneum, damnari non Philosophiam veram, quæ donum Dei est, quam à Luthero hic intelligi, temere criminatur Cornelius, (in Dan. Hofmanno Helmstad. aliisque nonnullis philosophicam veritatem & Theologicam ἀφιλοσόφως & ἀθεολόγως sibi invicem opponentibus, etiam depravationem B. D. Grawerus notavit, notavimus & nos in Theol. Naturali & Revel. ex professo) sed philosophiam, quæ tum jactabatur, vanam nempe ac deceptoriam, uti sese explicat Apostolus, quam à Platonicis acceptam, & à Pseudo-Apostolis interpolatam, nec non cum Christiana religione confusam in Phrygia disseminatam ex hoc Apostoli elencho colligimus, non abnuente Theophylactu; traditiones autem Judæicas secundum elementa mundi, hoc est, externas ceremonias, quæ ita vocantur Gal. IV. 3. 9. admixtas, magis confusam reddidisse religionem, utpote pessimo Syncretismo confarcinatam è Christianorum, Platonicorum & Judaicorum placitis & dogmatibus. Temere autem omnia illa à Grotio ad Philosophiam Græcorum referuntur: quum ex subjuncta confutatione Apostolica notari etiam Judaizantes, circumcisionem externam, & ceremonias alias in diebus ac cibis urgentes, manifestum sit, & de his elementa mundi in loco parallelo intelligi debeant.

Erant utique legalis observantiæ elementa veluti ac principia Judaicæ religionis: erant populo rudi elementa, quibus ducetur. retur ad Christum iisdem adumbratum, quæ ab elementis & rudimentis Christianæ distinctionis, Ebr. V. 12. & quia Christo exhibito ceu necessaria ad salutem tradebantur, corruptela erant Evangelii.

Quod philosophia Græca vitam æternam vel modum ejus consequendæ non tradiderit! id imperfectionis est, non autem κενῆς ἀπάτης, quam hic damnat Apostolus. Verbis & non secundum Christum exhibetur ratio generalis confutandi omnes deceptiones: utpote quibus introducatur ea religionis forma, quæ nec à Christo tradita, nec Christum solum, ejusque redemptionem aut fidem in Christum tradit, sed à Christo alio traducit, aliosque Christo adjungit mediatores, alia præter redemptionem Christi ad salutem requirit.

PARS II.

DOGMATICA, Explicans doctrinam de Christo, de baptismo, & de fide.

## 2:8
V. 8. Let no one disqualify you

Jerome says this word, like some others, is from the Cilician language.

But others have noted that it is found also among others.

It is , however, to disqualify (καταβραβεύειν) to exact a prize, which Pausanias called to receive a crown (κότιον παραλαμβάνω), as noted by Scaliger.

Prize , however, he understands in this place to be the liberty granted by Christ.

Grotius explains these things differently elsewhere, namely in the explanation of the decalogue, page 30 for me. Let no one disqualify you, let no one take away your honor, namely that which is proper to Christians, so that they have the right of invoking God through the Word (διὰ τὸ λόγῳ), as Origen often notes, most openly indeed in book V. those who are circumcised towards God and to serve another with Him, not allowing us to be called away, so that besides God we serve another, as the same book says.

VIII. This sense might seem more convenient.

For it is not situated in our liberty, that is, whether we wish to approach the Father through CHRIST, or indeed through angels, since Christ is the only way to the Father, John XIV. 6. the only Mediator of God and men, 1. Tim.
