II. 6. through whom alone access to the Father is open: nor can other Mediators be chosen without contempt for the office of Christ, without impiety and idolatry, which is committed even then, when another mode of worshipping GOD is used than that which is prescribed by GOD.

Nor , however, does that sense merit assent.

For that honor, that we have the right of invoking GOD through the Son, is not the prize of our struggle, which we might obtain from an umpire.

Theodoret explains to disqualify (καταβραβεύειν) as to judge unjustly (ἀδίκως βραβεύειν), or for an umpire to perform his office poorly.

But those who are struggling cannot prevent or avert that, as they have no power against those who distribute the prizes.

And therefore neither Photius, who rendered that word as to condemn (καταπείνειν), nor Beza’s earlier version, let no voluntary moderator decide about you, is suitable.

Whence he amended it thus in the later version: Let no one of his own accord take upon himself the role of judge against you, which Erasmus Schmid followed: let no one of his own accord take upon himself the role of judge against you.

Which Crocius explains thus: Beware in every way, lest any umpire rule you, domineer over you imperiously, so that as a president of the contest he might pronounce against you according to his own whim, and he prefers this to other interpretations.

But that OF HIS OWN ACCORD (ULTRO) does not fit well enough.

For it is not ours to prevent anyone from taking upon himself of his own accord the role of an umpire over us imperiously.

If , therefore, that "willing" (θέλων) refers to this word, and not to the following ones, it will have to be rendered not "of his own accord," but with Grotius, "even if you wish."

By which method we do not subtract the calculation from that interpretation, from which B. is not alien, as far as the matter is concerned.

Luther’s version: let no one move the goal from you, by which he seems to have looked to the struggle of those running in the stadium, where the umpires can change the finish line to the detriment of the runner, and like umpires rule the race poorly.

A little B. departs from that explanation.

Osiander: let no one intercept your palm, i. e. let no superstitious holiness lead you away from true piety, so that wandering from the true goal you might fall short of the prize of eternal life.

For those who lead men to elective cults, these avert them from the true and salutary course of piety, and running and fatiguing themselves in vain, they do not obtain eternal salvation.

With which B. agrees.

Our Hunnius: Let no impostor with superstitious perverse dogmas intercept from you the palm of eternal life prepared for you through the victorious and triumphant CHRIST.

Such a sense Cornelius also brought forward: Let no one oppose himself to your prize, let no one intercept your prize and reward. or avert, let no one render you unworthy of the crown prepared for you, says Vatablus, and as Chrysostom and his followers say, let no one defraud you of your reward, as if he were saying: You have been called to the prize of heavenly glory, you must run toward it, and you have begun to run toward it through the faith and religion of Christ.

See to it that the Innovators do not turn you away from this course and prize through the faith and superstition of Angels, which they introduce.

B. however seems simpler.

Luther's interpretation and that of Cornelius à Lapide, which he proposes as if it were his own, though taken from Beza: Just as he said concerning the Judaizers v. 16. Let no one judge you, that is, as if a Judge were presiding over you, judging and condemning you: Thus he says here concerning the heretical Angel-worshippers: Let no one disqualify you (καταβραβευέτω), that is, let no one as a judge of the games rule you, judge you, or dominate you with authority, so that to judge and to preside as a judge is almost the same as to disqualify (καταβραβεύειν). For the heretics, just as the Judaizers, wished to pass judgment on Christian matters, on Christ, and on the articles of faith, and to preside as if they were judges. As if he were saying: These Innovators are proud, puffed up, and as the French say, font le brave, and they want to teach by their own wisdom, and to prevail over and dominate everyone; in short, they want to be judges of the games, and as if judges of the games to preside over the contest of Christians, and to impose upon it new laws and religions.

Act therefore, O Colossians, explode their arrogance, do not suffer them to become insolent against you, do not let them dominate and command you; nay, do not let them dominate and command Christ himself and the Church.

Thus it is to be preferred entirely to the Vulgate version, "let no one seduce you"; to Castellio, "let no one supplant you"; to Valla, "let no one call you back from the contest by proposing a prize"; to August. ep. LIX, "let no one convince you"; to the Ambrosian, "let no one overcome you"; and also to the Hieronymian epist. CLI. ad Algas. quaest. 10, "let no one receive the prize against you." (θειλων) that is, even if he greatly desires it.

Thus he refers this to the preceding word. Others, however, prefer to refer it to what follows. Augustine joins it with humility, as if he were saying, wishing to seem humble, affecting humility, which in the popular African custom is said to be thelodibitem and theolapientem, for one who affects riches and wisdom; the Blessed Luther joins it with the participle ἐμβατεύων, der nach eigener Wahl einher gehet [who walks according to his own choice]; whence in the last verse the word ἐθελοθρησκείας; which Grotius does not disapprove.

It is well. For such people walked according to their own choice, not according to the will of God. However, he prefers the sense of Beza and Piscator, that no one should usurp power over you by his own impulse, will, and judgment, of which we have already spoken.

Latin:

V. 8. Μηδεὶς ὑμᾶς καταβραβευέτω

Hieronymus hanc vocem, ut alias nonnullas ait esse ex Cilicium lingua.

At notarunt alii reperiri & apud alios.

Est autem καταβραβεύειν premium exigere, quod κότιον παραλαμβάνω dixit Pausanias, ut Scaligero notatum.

Præmium autem intelligit hoc quidem loco libertatem a Christo indultam.

Aliter hæc explicat Grotius alibi, nempe in explanatione decalogi pag. mihi 30. Μηδεὶς ὑμᾶς καταβραβευέτω, nemo vobis honorem auferat, nempe eum, qui proprius est Christianorum, ut jus habeant Deum invocandi διὰ τὸ λόγῳ per verbum, ut sæpe notat Origenes, apertissime vero libro V. ἃ περιτάμενοι πρὸς τῷ θεῷ καὶ ἄλλῳ τινὶ δαλέυειν μετ’ αὐτῦ, non avocari nos sinentes, ut præter Deum & alteri serviamus, ut ait idem libr.

VIII. Convenientior hic sensus videri possit.

Non enim in libertate nostra hoc situm est, id est, an adire velimus Patrem per CHRISTUM, an vero per angelos, quum unica ad Patrem via Christus sit, Johan. XIV. 6. unicus Dei & hominum Mediator, 1. Tim. II. 6. per quem solum patet aditus ad Patrem: nec alii Mediatores fine contemptu officii Christi, fine impietate atque idololatria eligi possint, quæ committitur etiam tum, ubi alius DEUM colendi modus, quam præscriptus est a DEO, adhibetur.

Nec tamen sensus ille assensum meretur.

Nam bonor ille, quod jus habeamus DEUM per Filium invocandi, non est præmium nostri certaminis, quod a brabeuta consequamur.

Theodoretus καταβραβεύειν explicat per ἀδίκως βραβεύειν, vel brabeuta officio male fungi.

Sed id certantes præcavere, aut avertere non possunt, qui nihil valent contra eos, qui præmia distribuunt.

Ideoque nec Photii, qui per καταπείνειν illud verbum reddidit, nec Bizæ prior versio, nullæ voluntarius moderator de vobis statuat, convenit.

Unde ita emendavit posteriori versione: Nemo adversus vos rectoria partes ultro sibi fumat, quem sequutus est Erasmus Schmidius: nemo adversus vos judicia partes sibi fumat ultro.

Quod sic explicat Crocius: Cavete omnibus modis, ne quisquam brabeuta vos regat, vobis imperiose dominetur, ut tanquam agonis præfes contra vos pro arbitrio suo pronuntiet, aliisque interpretationibus præfert.

Sed illud ULTRO non satis congruit.

Nam nec id nostrum est prægavere, ne quis in nos ultro sibi imperiose brabeutæ partes fumat.

Si ergo illud θέλων ad hoc verbum, & non ad sequentia refertur, non ultro, sed cum Grotio reddendum erit, etiam si velis.

Quo pacto non subducimus calculum isti interpretationi, a qua non aliena, quantum ad rem B.

Lutheri versio: lasset euch niemand das Ziel verrucken, qua respexisse videtur ad certamen decurrentium in stadio, ubi arbitri metam possunt mutare in fraudem currentis, & brabeutarum instar cursum male regunt.

Paululum ab abit illa explanatione abit B.

Osiander: ne quis vobis palmam intervertat, i. e. ne qua vos superstitiosa sanctimonia a vera pietate abducat, ut a scopo vero aberrantes præmio vitæ æternæ excidatis.

Qui enim ad electitios cultus homines deducunt, hi eos a vero & salutari pietatis cursu avertunt, et frustra currentes & se fatigantes æternam salutem non consequantur.

Cui consonat B.

Hunnius noster: Ne quis impostor superstitiosis perversis dogmatibus intervertat vobis vitæ æternæ palmam per victorem & triumphantem CHRISTUM vobis paratam.

Qualem etiam sensum adduxit Cornelius: Nemo brabeo vestro sese opponat, nemo brabeum ac præmium vestrum intercipiat. vel avertat, nemo corona vobis praeparata indignos vos reddat, inquit Vatablus, & ut Chrysostomus cum suis, nemo praemio vestro vos defraudet, quasi dicat: Vocati estis ad brabeum caelestis gloriae, eo procurrendum est, & eo procurre capistis per fidem & religionem Christi.

Videte, ne ab hoc cursu & brabeo Novantes vos avertant per fidem & superstitionem Angelorum, quam inducunt.

Simplicior tamen videtur B.

Lutheri interpretatio & illa Cornelii à Lapide, quam à Beza acceptam velut abs se inventam proponit: Sicut de Judaizantibus dixit v. 16. Nemo vos judicet, id est, quasi Judex vobis praesideat, vos judicet & damnet: Ita de hereticis Angelicis hic dicit: Nemo vos καταβραβευέτω, id est, nemo quasi brabeuta vos regat, vos judicet, vobis imperio se dominetur, ut pene idem sit judicare, & quasi judicem praesidere, quod καταβραβεύειν. Tam enim heretici, quam Judaizantes de re Christiana, Christo & articulis fidei censere, & quasi judices praesidere volebant. Quasi dicat: Hi Novantes sunt superbi, tumidi, & ut dicunt Galli, font le brave, vo-luntque sua sapientia docere, omnibusque praevalere & dominari, denique volunt esse brabeuta, & quasi brabeuta agoni Christianorum praesidere, eius novas leges & religiones preficere.

Agite ergo, o Colossenses, fistum eorum explodite, nolite pati, ut contra vos insolescant, ne eos vobis; imo Christo ipsi & Ecclesiae βραβεύειν dominari & imperare finatis.

Sic praeferendum omnino tum Vulgate versioni, nemo vos seducat; tum Castellioni, nemo vos supplantet; tum Valle, nemo proposito praemio vos ad certamen revocet; tum August. ep. LIX. nemo vos convincat; tum Ambrosiane, nemo vos devincat; tum etiam Hieronymiane epist. CLI. ad Algas. quaest. 10. nemo adversum vos bravium accipiat. (θειλων) id est, etiam si maxime id velit.

Ita ad verbum praecedens hoc refert. Aliis tamen ad sequentia referre malunt. Augustinus id conjungit cum humilitate, quasi dicat, volens videri humilis, affectans humilitatem, quod consuetudine Africana populari dicatur, θελοδιβιτεμ & θελολαπιεντεμ dici, qui divitias & sapientiam affectet; Beat. Lutherus conjungit cum participio ἐμβατεύων, der nach eigener Wahl einher gehet; unde v. ultimo vox ἐθελοθρησκείας; Quod non improbant Grotius.

Res bene, habet. Tales enim secundum electionem propriam, non secundum Dei voluntatem incedebant. Praefert tamen sensum Beza, Piscatoris, ne quis sua sponte, voluntate ac arbitrio imperio se in vos potestatem usurpet, de quo jam diximus.

## 2:9
V. 9. "For in him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily" (ὅτι ἐν αὐτῷ κατοικεῖ πᾶν τὸ πλήρωμα τῆς θεότητος σωματικῶς). Not in vain, he says, did I say this. For the doctrine of Christ excels not only philosophy, but also the law of Moses by much. Augustine understood this passage very well, when he wrote: In him dwells the fulness of the divinity bodily, in the temple it had dwelt shadowily, so below in verse 17 are opposed shadow (σκιά) and body (σῶμα). In the Old Testament there is a shadow, in the Gospel the thing is called body (σῶμα) by a certain familiarity. Thus bodily (σωματικῶς) is often for the Greeks to make solid. This is a remarkable distortion of a most illustrious oracle, favoring not only the mystery of the union and hypostatic communication for certain Calvinists, but even for the Socinians themselves, who undermine the Deity of Christ; which also perverts the subject and the predicate of the passage.

The subject is Christ, and not truly the doctrine of Christ; for the fulness of the Deity is said to dwell in Christ; but Christ is one thing, and the doctrine of Christ is another. Nor is the doctrine concerning Christ, or of Christ, a dwelling-place, but Christ himself, who by reason of his human nature is compared to a temple, John II. 19, and to a tabernacle, Heb. IX. 15. Furthermore, the predicate, namely the indwelling of the whole fulness of the Deity, does not befit the doctrine of Christ. But it befits Christ according to his human nature. Now this distortion is such, that nothing else is expressed than that the doctrine of Christ excels not only Philosophy, but also the law of Moses by much. These differ as much as heaven from earth, to possess the indwelling whole fulness of the Deity, and to excel philosophy and the Mosaic law; nor is any comparison of the excellence of these instituted here, but philosophy being left behind as true, and the Mosaic law being left behind in its value, one is commanded to beware of deceptive philosophy, and the mixture of legal ceremonies with Evangelical doctrine.

But in order that the Evangelical doctrine might be established, he wished to repeat the same here, and to apply it elenctically against the antithesis and contrary dogmas. Therefore, first he repeats the doctrine concerning the hypostatic union and communication, as it is the foundation of the other dogmas. If this divine good pleasure (εὐδοκία) had not been, that the whole fulness of the Deity should dwell in Christ, we could neither accomplish the business of redemption, nor enjoy the benefits of the same through baptism into the death of Christ, nor aspire to salvation through faith in Christ, which was already established from chapter I. 19.

Others say that the first proof is exhibited here by the words of the major proposition, and "not according to Christ" tacitly premised. But they make this the major: What doctrine does not deliver Christ alone, his redemption and faith, that is to be avoided: Reason: Because in Christ dwells all the fulness of the divinity. Thus Crocius. But the consequence does not appear. He renders this: In whom is the whole fulness of the Deity, if you have him, you will not suffer anything necessary for salvation to be thrust upon you outside of him. But by that reasoning the same could be said of God the Father according to Crocius. If, however, nothing outside of God the Father is necessary to be believed, then neither is the hypostatic union of Christ. Nor is anything else indicated by the passage of Augustine alleged.

He says nothing about the excellence of Evangelical doctrine over Philosophy or the Mosaic law. In the Old Testament there was a shadow, but the body is in Christ. As therefore in the temple of Solomon the divine majesty dwelt shadowily: So in the body, which we have in Christ, in the temple of the humanity of Christ dwells the very fulness of the divinity, no longer shadowily, but bodily (σωματικῶς) in a most real and most perfect manner, not for a time and transiently (παρασατικῶς), but eternally and hypostatically (ὑποστατικῶς), just as the word bodily (σωματικῶς) is explained by some in a not evil sense: Which, however, we judge to be more rightly explained of the subject, than of the mode: Bodily (σωματικῶς), that is, in the body, or by reason of his body, so that the subject of the indwelling, or the temple of the indwelling divinity, may be expressed.

Which explanation is preferred by Augustine in epistle VII to Dardanus. Not therefore bodily, because God is corporeal, but he either used a transferred word, as if he had dwelt in a temple made by hands, not bodily, but shadowily, that is, by prefiguring signs; for the Apostle calls all those observances shadows of things to come, even by the transferred word itself: or certainly it is said bodily, because God dwells in the body of Christ, which he assumed from the virgin, as in a temple. It is also preferred by Theodoret, bodily, that is, as in his own proper body. It is proved by Oecumenius: bodily (σωματικῶς) is the same as in the flesh (ἐνάρκως) and made flesh (σεσαρκωμένος); and also by Damascene, that is, in his flesh (ἐν σαρκὶ αὐτῦ).

See also Athanasius, Orat. IV. against the Arians, and Orat. II. on human nature. Cyril, book later, on faith to the Queens. Crocius acknowledges both explanations as orthodox, even if neither seems genuine to him: Since he dwelt even in the Prophets in the saints, and truly not shadowily, and even now will so dwell in the saints, 2 Cor. VI. But did he dwell in any of the Prophets?

Does the whole fulness of the Deity dwell today in any of the saints, as in a temple or his own proper body? Crocius acknowledges that the subject is Christ: The Apostle, he says, begins the discourse concerning Christ, concerning that head of the Church, and continues to treat of the same.

Therefore he necessarily receives it concerning him. But he says "in him" (ἐν αὐτῷ) not "in them" (ἐν αὐτοῖς), so that he may teach that Christ is one, not many, and the unity of the person of one Christ. He acknowledges that the word "to dwell" (κατοικεῖν) signifies not a temporary but a perpetual indwelling, and therefore is distinguished from "to sojourn" (παροικεῖν) Heb. XI. 9, 1 Pet. I. 7. Nor is it said "he dwelt" (κατώκησε), but "he dwells" (κατοικεῖ), so that the continuous indwelling may be expressed so much the more clearly.

He acknowledges that it is said that Christ gives not only excellent gifts, not certain idioms of the Deity, but that the whole and full Deity dwells in him. He praises the interpretation of Theophylact and the Greek scholiasts, which is thus: Essentially (Οὐσιωδῶς), and not relatively (σχετικῶς). And as the soul dwells in the body, he says, so he dwelt in the assumed man. But how did the soul dwell in the body? Clearly without confusion, indivisibly. Can this therefore also be said of the indwelling in the saints? He praises Augustine, because he wrote thus in the cited place: Is there also, besides this, that the whole fulness of the Deity dwells in that body as in a temple, something else, which differs between that head, and the excellence of any member? There is clearly, that by a certain singular assumption of that man, one person was made with the Word.

He praises Theodoret saying thus: Christ does not receive any of the graces individually, as Moses: For he is God and man, and that which is seen, has the united divinity of the only-begotten. Is it permitted to affirm such things also concerning the indwelling in the saints? What then is solid for our argument will Crocius reply? To whom the whole fullness of the divinity has communicated itself, to him the essential idioms of the Deity are really communicated. But to the human nature of Christ. Therefore. 1.

He replies: That the Apostle does not name communication, but inhabitation. But what else does communication imply than possession? If the whole fullness of the Deity inhabits the human nature, it must possess it; if it possesses it, it must have received it communicated to it for possession, because inhabitation is noted as perpetual and continuous, and since it is granted to inhabit not in a shadowy, effective, and relative or separable way; but in a far more eminent, most perfect, inseparable, and personal way, it must be that the fullness of the Deity has been truly and really communicated to it.

We argue now thus: If the human nature possesses the whole fullness of the Deity, and is inhabited by the fullness of the Deity in a certain singular way, it must have been made a participant of the fullness of the Deity, and thus a divine, true, and real communication of the human nature intervenes. But the former is true. Therefore also the latter. 2.

He replies 2. Crocius: The essential idioms of the Deity are said to be really communicated to the flesh either in the person, or in itself, so that it becomes and is rightly called omnipotent, omniscient, and omnipresent. The former sense is admitted, the latter is by no means concluded from the Apostle, because he describes that by the λόγῳ (Word) and the union of the flesh in the unity of the person: but the union was made with the properties of each nature preserved, nor does the Apostle name three idioms, but the whole fullness of the divinity. Resp. It cannot be subsisted in the person. For the person is not a third thing distinct from the two natures: therefore if they are said to be communicated to the person, we ask according to which nature, whether according to the divine, or indeed according to the human nature? But nothing could be communicated to the divine nature, or to Christ according to the divine nature in time. It remains therefore that it be admitted that those things were communicated to Christ according to the human nature, which even the κατοίκησις (inhabitation) itself teaches. For every inhabitation presupposes a habitation. Since therefore the inhabitation here fully presupposes the τῷ λόγῳ (Word), there is no doubt that the Apostle also intended the temple of inhabitation to be expressly signified. Add that one can hardly without ἀδολεσχία (babbling) utter the Apostle's proposition: In the person of Christ dwells the whole fullness of the Deity σωματικῶς (bodily), unless the subject be the flesh, nor can the Deity of Christ be posited as the subject, in which, because of the highest simplicity, a distinction between the inhabitant and that which is inhabited has no place. Nor indeed do we deny, but rather we profess, that all the idioms of the Deity have been communicated to the human nature of Christ, and that all are possessed by it. From this, however, it is not to be inferred: that Christ according to his human nature is eternal, immense, independent, etc., because those idioms are indeed possessed by the human nature, but they are not usurped, and therefore they do not infer the denomination. The reason is at hand: For they are ἀνενέργητα (inoperative), nor do they contribute anything to the end of the union. 3. He replies 3. Just as the Deity is communicated, and the essential idioms of the Deity: But the Deity is communicated by hypostatic union, not however by transfusion, or in such a way that the humanity has become the humanity of God, neither God nor Deity. Therefore similarly the idioms are communicated to the humanity, so that it may be of an omnipotent, everywhere present humanity, not so that it may be omnipotent and everywhere present.

Resp. Hypostatic union and communication are distinguished as antecedent and consequent: and such as the union is, such also is the communication. Since therefore a true and real union takes place between the divine and the human nature, a true and real communication must intervene. No one of our own approves of transfusion; one must confess that only a true communication intervenes through hypostatic union between each nature, as we have taught ex professo, Exam. de perf. Christi Controv. III. Membr.

II. Nor indeed is the human nature said to be omnipotent: So also the human nature is not to be called God or Deity. For thus Paronymous and Synonymic predication is confused: Just as I do not say: Humanity is omnipotence: So neither is it to be said: Humanity is Deity: But the human nature has or possesses the divine nature, or is even θεοθεῖσα (deified), as the Ancients love to speak, just as the divine nature is not human, or flesh, but the divine nature is ἐνανθρωπήσασα (having become man) or inhumanated, if it be permitted to speak so, or incarnate. Whence Dionysius the Areopagite, as Damascene reports, says that God divinely and fully communicated himself to us in one substance of persons, and S. Basil on the incarnation of the Word: Ἡ ἀνθρωπίνη τῷ κυρίῳ σὰρξ αὐτὴ μέτοχε τῆς θεότητος (The human flesh of the Lord is itself a participant of the Deity): The human flesh of the Lord itself has been made a participant of the Deity. Theophylact uses a simile about the union of soul and body, in which the communication of both is clear: Because in him dwells all the fullness of the divinity bodily, that is, whatever God the Word is, he dwells in him. But lest perhaps, hearing that he has inhabited this, you might think that he has done so by dwelling and operating, just as the Prophets were accustomed to, in whom God inhabited, according to what is written: And I will inhabit in them and will walk, he added bodily, to wit: that is, not by any operation, but by substance and as if embodied, and existing as one substance with the assumed flesh.

Or it can be understood in this way. Namely, as in a body, when the soul inhabits, it lives in the body substantially and inseparably and without any admixture. Yet the soul itself exceeds the body, while the body dies. But God, the Word, has never been separated from the assumed flesh.

But these things have been treated most fully in the cited place. We now apply the present aphorism only to demonstrate the Deity of Christ: For here is ascribed to Christ not only θεότης (Deity), which is the form of God, so to speak, and thus the divine essence itself: But τὸ πλήρωμα τῆς θεότητος (the fullness of the Deity), that is, full, integral, and perfect Deity, lest anyone perhaps might think that Christ is God only metaphorically, or by analogical attribution, or in an imperfect way. And not only that, but for the sake of greater emphasis the universal particle is added, and thus πᾶν τὸ πλήρωμα τῆς θεότητος (all the fullness of the Deity) is vindicated for Christ, so that it may be hinted that the Deity belongs to Christ in the most absolute and most perfect way: But to whom belongs full, omnimodal, absolute, and perfect Deity, to him cannot be denied essential, eternal, immense Deity.

Who is God in the absolute sense, of the most perfect kind, is surely the highest and most exalted God. But let us pursue the arguments that can be drawn from this passage, (1) From the name θεότης: for it denotes the divine essence, by which God is what he is, just as ἀνθρωπότης denotes the essence of man, by which man is what he is. Nor does θεότης occur anywhere in the sacred writings where it designates qualities not divine but created. Among the Fathers also orthodox is only used for essential Deity. Athanas. serm. against the Arians. Gregor. Nazianz. on Theology. Damascen. b. 1. on the Orthodox faith. And therefore the Syrian expressed it with the word אלהותא, the Arab with אלהות, which precisely denotes the essence of God itself, and nowhere denotes quality or any finite gifts. See Acts XVII. 29. Rom. I. 20. But also the word θεότης, which Enjedinus contends has the same meaning as this word θεότης, signifies the divine essence, and imports a true, infinite, and essential Deity, Rom. I. 20. Wisd. XIII. 9. nor is it used otherwise anywhere in the sacred writings: and Enjedinus himself admits on p. 358 that θεότης is taken for the substance of God in Rom. I. (2) from the denomination of τὸ πληρώματος τῆς θεότητος. The Apostle does not say the fullness of the gifts of the Deity, or of grace, and of the knowledge of the divine will, but simply the fullness of the Deity. Furthermore, he calls it the fullness of the Deity by a customary Hebraism, the full and perfect Deity, just as it is said the fullness of a house, that is, a full and perfect house, Num. XXIV. 13. the fullness of stature, that is, the whole and perfect stature, 1. Sam. XXII. 20. And therefore he implies that nothing of the Deity can be thought or said which does not belong to Christ. πλήρωμα denotes an all-encompassing and consummate perfection, and implies the lack of every defect.

The Syriac interpreter uses the word כְּמָל, which denotes all-encompassing perfection, absolute fullness, and integrity, descending from כָּמַל to be completed, to be perfect or consummate. Thus indeed he renders אלהות כְּמָל in אלהי חל in which the most perfect fullness of the Deity dwells. (3) from the addition of the word ALL. For he claims for Christ the whole fullness of the Deity, that is, a Deity full, absolute, and perfect in all ways: and whatever of the Deity there is anywhere at all. But if at least some gifts, and those finite, belonged to Christ, πᾶν τὸ πλήρωμα, the whole fullness of the Deity, could not be ascribed to him. If anything pertaining to the full and perfect Deity of the Father did not belong to Christ, πᾶν τὸ πλήρωμα, the whole fullness of the Deity, would be falsely ascribed to Christ. For he who says the whole fullness of the Deity excludes nothing that makes for a full and absolute all-encompassing Deity (4) from the connection of the text. Because of which fullness Christ is the genuine principle of salvation, it is not finite or created, but infinite and uncreated, since a genuine principle of salvation presupposes not a finite, but an infinite virtue, which implies an infinite essence. But because of this fullness, of which the Apostle speaks, Christ is the genuine principle of salvation. Conf. Col. II. 6. Job XIV. 6. 1. Cor. III. 11. (5) from the collation with chap. I. 19. where the indwelling fullness likewise implies an infinite Deity, according to the interpretation of Cyril and Primasius, since it is not fitting for anyone but the true God by nature to be Creator, Preserver, Redeemer, and Conciliator, and our head. (6) from the description of fullness handed down in Job I. 14. 16. Christ is said to be πλήρης χάριτος καὶ ἀληθείας, full of grace and truth, and it is implied at the same time that he is full of the glory proper to the only-begotten Son, which is truly divine. That fullness is attributed to him which is absolutely infinite, since all receive from that fullness, nor does it ever fail in any way: just as here we are said to be made complete in him, so that an all-encompassing consummation redounds to us, since we indeed begin to be completed here, but in the other life we shall be fully completed. (7) from the attribution of divine omniscience v. 3. For since the whole fullness of the Deity includes divine and infinite omniscience, how can it be taken otherwise than of the infinite essence of GOD, from which it is inseparable? (8) from the interpretation of the Church.

Since the principal Doctors of the Church (and therefore the Catholic Church herself) have interpreted it not of most excellent, finite gifts, but of the essential Deity itself, and have concluded from thence that Christ is the true essential God, as can be seen everywhere in Athanasius, Basil, Cyril, Theodoret, Ambrose, Augustine, and others. B. D. Myslenta pursues these and other arguments at greater length in diss. 2 on this passage, ib. 16. seq.

But the adversaries raise various objections (1) that in Christ in this place is the same as in the doctrine of Christ, or in the faith and confession of Christ, since Christ is opposed not to persons, but to doctrine: Thus Enjedinus, Socinus, and almost all. (2) that divinity is nothing other than the will of God itself. in def. animadv. p. 194. Smalz. on the divinity of Christ p. 23. Volk. on true Religion b. 5. c. 10. p. 43. (3) that fullness denotes not essence, but quality, every fullness, that is, any perfection whatsoever: that by the fullness of divinity nothing else is to be understood than the most excellent gifts of God: thus Enjedinus (4) Eph. III. 19. he asserts that all the pious can attain the fullness of God, and that this is the same as the whole fullness of the Deity here. That all fullness is also attributed to them 1. Cor. I. 4. But God is said to be and to dwell wholly in Christ and in the pious, when he exerts his presence, power, authority, and kindness in them and through them. This again Enjedinus. (5) that God and the Deity are said to dwell in many things, which nevertheless are not for that reason the eternal God Ps. CXXXI. 13. Matt. XXIII. 22. Job XIV. 23. 1. John III. 14. Enjed. p. 356. (6) that our explanation concerning the eternal Deity of Christ does nothing for the purpose of the Apostle, who exhorts not to fall away from the doctrine of Christ. Enjed. 364.

We answer to (1) the little word ἐν αὐτῷ does not refer to the doctrine of Christ, but to Christ himself, as is plain from the text. (2) The name of Christ taken metonymically for the doctrine, or the Gospel of Christ, has nowhere yet been proven. (3) Nor is it proper to depart from the proper signification unless compelled by necessity, which here there is none. (4) What of it that that metonymical signification has no place: Because the indwelling, and that bodily, of the Deity by no means suits the doctrine or Gospel of Christ. For where in the Gospel is it said that the fullness of the Deity dwells bodily, or anything similar? Besides, Christ is understood by the name of Christ, whom the Colossians had received as their Lord, in whom they were rooted, in whom they believed v. 5. 6. 7. in whom all the treasures of knowledge were hidden v. 3. (6) He is here indicated by the name of Christ who is the head of every principality and Magistracy, in whom they were circumcised, with whom they were buried, in whom they had risen again, who was raised from the dead &c. as is most evident from vers. 10. seq. How ineptly therefore the doctrine of Christ is to be understood here, anyone sees, (7) in him is said to dwell the whole fullness who is the head of the Church, the firstborn from the dead, in whom all things consist, and in whom all things were created, who is the image of God invisible, and firstborn before all creatures, which stands clearer than the sun from chap. I. 15. 16. 17. 18. 19. But who will say that these things are to be understood of the doctrine of Christ, and not rather of Christ himself? To say nothing, that the adversaries themselves acknowledge these things are to be received of Christ himself, especially since Enjedin. explains the Deity dwelling in Christ, ut in più &c. Constract. our author on the divine essence p. 510. To (2) There is no need that we now add anything, since we have fully discussed that most vain gloss, and taught that Deity is here taken for the divine essence l. c. p. 519. seq. Enjedinus certainly he confesses and concedes p. 358 that the word θεός denotes substance, and therefore he cannot deny that θεότης denotes Deity, or the substance of God; but he is prone to the suspicion that it was written by the Apostle as θεότητος, which word some overly religious or negligent scribes might have transformed into θεότητα.

But if a place for such a suspicion is left, where no Codex at all, nor any reason provides a cause, what then will be certain in the Scriptures?

Ad (3) Enjedinus falsely denies that Paul asserts that the Deity dwells in Christ, since the Apostle makes mention of the Deity most explicitly, not merely of fullness: indeed, the fullness of the Deity becomes the full Deity.

Although, therefore, in chapter I. 19, mention is made of absolute fullness, here, however, the fullness of the Deity is commemorated, and from it the prior passage is illustrated. And to whom properly will πλήρωμα be attributed, except to the Deity itself? What shall we call absolute πλήρωμα, perfection without defect, if not the Deity itself, the perfection of perfections? It may also seem that the Apostle used the word πλήρωμα to oppose the true πλήρωμα to the fictitious pleroma of the Gnostics, and, as Origen speaks, to designate τὴν ἀρχὴν μετοχὴν τῆς θεότητος [the beginning of the participation of the Deity]. But that not only finite gifts, but the infinite Deity is designated here, has been shown in tract. de eff. div. unit.

Ad (4) I respond. Those things are most distinctly different: that all the fullness of the Deity dwells in Christ bodily, and that the faithful are filled with them πᾶν τὸ πλήρωμα τοῦ θεοῦ [all the fullness of God]. Those things are very distinct: that all the fullness of the Deity dwells in Christ bodily, and that the faithful are filled with them πᾶν τὸ πλήρωμα τοῦ θεοῦ [all the fullness of God].

There, τὸ πλήρωμα is taken truly, here passively. For it signifies both that which fills, as in John I. 16 and Colossians II. 9, and that which is filled, as in Romans XI. 25, XV. 29. In which latter sense it also occurs in Ephesians I. 23, V. 18, Colossians I. 14, II. 10.

Add that the faithful are said to be filled with the fullness of GOD: but Christ is said to be the one who fills all in all, πλήρωμα ὡς [fullness as] in Ephesians

I. 23. Furthermore, the diversity also shines forth from this, that the fullness of the Deity of the Ebionites is said to be full and perfect Deity: but here the fullness of GOD, with which the faithful are filled, but from various gifts, with which they are filled divinely, which is most evident from 1 Corinthians 1. 4. πλήρωμα τῆς θεοῦ [fullness of God] is said in a causal sense, because that fullness comes from GOD: but πλήρωμα τῆς θεότητος [fullness of the Deity] is said formally, if I may so speak, because the Deity itself, most perfect, dwells in Christ.

What of the fact that Enjedinus has contradicted himself and speaks against his own mouth: For when he had said on p. 357 that nothing is attributed here to Christ that is not also accustomed to be attributed to pious men: Yet soon after, on page 360, he says that God is said to dwell in Christ with all His fullness; because whatever He has determined to confer of goods and gifts upon His Church, He is accustomed to give to the pious through Christ, and in Christ, and therefore the Apostle added the word σωματικῶς [bodily], so that he might make a distinction between Christ and the pious, and signify that God dwells in Christ more abundantly than in others: that God formerly dwelt in others shadowily, spiritually, particularly, τυπικῶς [typically], but in Christ truly, perfectly, most abundantly, and totally.

In nothing is the whole fullness of the Deity said to dwell bodily, which is asserted here concerning Christ: Even if God is said to dwell or be in the temple, in the people, etc., yet such a κατοίκησις [dwelling] is far different, namely merely παραστατική [representative], and not κατὰ περιχώρησιν, καὶ συνδύασιν ὑποστατικήν [by indwelling and hypostatic union]. One must distinguish between the typical presence in the temple of Solomon, the spiritual in the faithful, and the personal or hypostatic in Christ. In those, God dwells in such a way that not one ὑφιστάμενον [subsistent] is constituted, nor are they therefore called GOD, but of GOD.

But in Christ, or the human nature of Christ, He dwells in such a way that it constitutes one ὑφιστάμενον, and that thence Christ is, and is called, God blessed forever.

And therefore all the fullness of the Deity is attributed to Christ, not only παρωνύμως [by name], but also συνωνύμως [synonymously], since it is certain from the scriptures that Christ is God. What kind of Deity, therefore, according to which Christ is God, we are taught by this very thing, that the absolute and perfect Deity in all ways dwells in Him, namely that He is God not in a certain respect, but absolutely, not imperfectly, but in the most perfect manner, not according to some participation or denomination of divinity, but according to a full and in all ways absolute and perfect possession of the Deity.

Enjedinus illustrates this inhabitation by the example of the soul, which is wholly in the whole body, and wholly in all its parts p. 359. Therefore, as the soul dwells in the body in such a way that it pertains to constituting the essence of man, so also Deity dwells in Christ, so that it pertains to constituting His essence. As that is predicated συνωνύμως of man, and essentially: so also Deity is predicated of Christ συνωνύμως and essentially.

Why would it not pertain to the Apostle's purpose to assert here the true and essential Deity for Christ? For is not that reason most pregnant, why one must adhere solely to the doctrine of Christ, leaving behind the traditions of men, because Christ, who delivered that doctrine, is not ψιλὸς ἄνθρωπος [a mere man], but true God by nature? Why should one not follow τὰ στοιχεῖα κόσμου [the elements of the world], and the rites, and the old sacred things, when there is no longer any need for such shadowy things, which once prefigured Christ: since in Christ all the fullness of the Deity dwells bodily.

Just as in the O.T. the Deity dwelt in the temple, as a type, so in the flesh of Christ dwells the whole fullness of the Deity σωματικῶς [bodily] as in its own body; the true temple, shadowed forth by that typical temple. Does not this αἰτιολογία [reasoning] cohere perfectly, that salvation is not to be sought in any other means whatsoever, whether Philosophy or Mosaic laws, but in Christ alone, because He is not a naked man, but true God, and thus is deservedly recognized as the highest and only principle of our salvation: outside of whom there is no cause of our salvation.

Conf. Job Conf. Job XIV. 6. Act. IV. 12. X. 43. XV. 11. But who would doubt that the Colossians had the gravest cause for adhering to Christ alone, to so great a Teacher, inasmuch as in Him dwelt all the fullness of the Deity bodily, who is God by the most absolute reason, in whom they themselves were filled uniquely with various gifts, and who is the head of every power and principality, and therefore beyond controversy before all others, even the angels themselves (whose θρησκεία [worship] the Apostle reproves in v. 18, recalling them to the θρησκεία and worship of Christ alone, or of the head of every power), He was to be heard.

Conf. Matt. XVII. 5. For that the Apostle added this part, that Christ is the head of all principality, Estius in his commentary on this passage not rashly observes, so that he might call them away from the worship of Angels, which Simon Magus was teaching. B. Theodoret in his commentary on this passage thus sets forth this τῆς συνεχείας [of the connection] reasoning: The divine Apostle, wishing to signify the difference between the law and grace, opposed Christ to the need of the elements, and by the mutual comparison of both, wishing to show how far He is superior, added that in Him dwells all the fullness of divinity bodily, that is, as in His own body. For He did not receive some singular grace, he says, as Moses did: for He is God and man, and that which is seen has the divinity of the only-begotten united to it.

Our Chemnitz, Tr. on the two natures in Christ, ch. 24, p. 335, explains it thus: That not only does Christ, for his own person, have in his assumed human nature the whole fullness of the Godhead personally: But that we also, who are his members, flesh of his flesh, and the firstborn brothers of this brother, have all things that are necessary for redemption, liberation, and defense against enemies, for grace, reconciliation, acceptance, being heard; for help before God, and whatever is necessary for our conversion, illumination, justification, sanctification, vivification, preservation, salvation; why not, I say, have all those most perfect goods, and in the most accumulated fullness, in Christ, incarnate, crucified, and resurrected for us: so that then, as if from the head into us, as if into the members, those goods are derived, flow, are conferred, and are supplied from his fullness.

And from this Paul concludes that we have no need of other elements of the world for salvation, since we have his whole fullness in Christ. And conversely, that he who scrapes together all other things lacks salvation if he does not have Christ.

If, therefore, Enjedinus’s gloss, by which he understands nothing other than the most excellent gifts of God by the fullness of the Godhead, is considered to cohere with the Apostolic exhortation that one must adhere to the doctrine of Christ, how much more will the interpretation of the Catholic Church, and the proper emphasis of the words shining forth, be congruent? If one must adhere to that doctrine to which the most excellent gifts are divinely conferred, how much more to that which is God in an absolute and most perfect reason, i.e., to the supreme God himself? And let these things suffice for the vindication of this oracle.

Latin:

V. 9. ὅτι ἐν αὐτῷ κατοικεῖ πᾶν τὸ πλήρωμα τῆς θεότητος σωματικῶς) Non frustra inquit hoc dixi. Nam Christi doctrina non modo philosophiæ, sed & legis Mosis plurimum præstat. Optime hunc locum intellexit Augustinus, cum scripsit: In ipso inhabitat plenitudo divinitatis corporaliter, in templo habitaberat umbratiliter, sic infra 17. opponuntur σκιά & σῶμα. In veteri testamento est umbra, in Evangelio res σῶμα per familitu tinem quandam dicitur. Ita σωματικῶς Græcis fæpe est folidare. Insignis hæc est detorsio illustrissimi oraculi, non tantum Calvinianis quibusdam unionis & communicationis hypostaticæ mysterium, sed etiam Socinianis ipsis Deitatem Christi labefactantibus, velificans; quæ & subjectum pervertitur & Detorsio il. inftre loci prædicatum.

Subjectum Christus est, non vero doctrina Christi; nam in Christo habitare dicitur plenitudo Deitatis; aliud vero est Christus, aliud doctrina Christi. Neque habitaculum est doctrina de Christo, aut Christi, sed Christus ipse, qui ratione humanæ naturæ templo, Joh. II. 19. & tabernaculo, Ebr. IX. 15. confertur. Porro non convenit doctrinæ Christi prædicatum, inhabitatio nempe totius plenitudinis Deitatis. Convenit autem Christo secundum humanam naturam. Detorsio autem meha hæc est, quod nihil aliud exprimatur, quam doctrinam Christi non modo Philosophiæ, sed & legis Mosis plurimum præstare. Toto cœlo hæc differunt, possidere inhabitantem totam Deitatis plenitudinem, & præstare philosophiæ ac legis Mosaicæ; nec comparatio ulla præstantiæ istorum hic instituitur, sed relicta philosophia vera, relicta Mosaica lege in suo valore, caveri jubetur deceptrix philosophia, & mixtura ceremoniarum legalium cum doctrina Evangelica.

Quo vero constet Evangelica doctrina, repetitam hic eandem voluit, & elenctice applicare adversus antithesin & dogmata contraria. Primum itaque repetit doctrinam de unione & communicatione hypostatica, utpote quæ fundamentum est cæterorum dogmatum. Nisi εὐδοκία divina hæc fuisset, ut in Christo habitaret tota Deitatis plenitudo, neque redemptionis negotium expediri, neque per baptismum in mortem Christi ejusdem beneficiis frui, aut per fidem in Christum ad salutem adspirare possemus, quod è cap. I. 19. jam constitit.

Alii majoris propositionis verbis, & non secundum Christum tacite præmissæ hic primam exhiberi probationem ajunt. Majorem autem hanc faciunt: Quæ doctrina non tradit unice Christum ejus redemptionem at fidem, ea est cavenda: Ratio: Quia in Christo habitat omnis plenitudo divinitatis. Ita Crocius. Sed non apparet consequentia. Reddit hanc: In quæ est tota plenitudo Deitatis, illum fihabeas, non quicquam ad salutem necessarium extra illum tibi obtrudi patieris. Sed ea ratione de Patre juxta Crocium idem dici poterit. Si autem nihil extra Deum Patrem creditu necessarium, ergo nec unio Christi hypostatica. Nec aliud ab Augustino loco allegato indicatum.

Nihil ille de præcellentiæ doctrinæ Evangelicæ pra Philosophia aut lege Mosaica. In Veteri Testamento umbra fuit, sed corpus in Christo est. Ut ergo in templo Salomonis habitabat majestas divina umbratiliter: Ita in corpore, quod habemus in Christo, in templo humanitatis Christi habitat ipsa divinitatis plenitudo, non umbratiliter amplius, sed σωματικῶς corporaliter realissima & perfectissima ratione, non ad tempus & παρασατικῶς, sed in æternum & ὑποστατικῶς, quemadmodum à nonnullis vox σωματικῶς sensu non malo exponitur: Quam tamen rectius exponi censemus de subjecto, quam de modo: Σωματικῶς, hoc est, in corpore, vel ratione corporis ejus, ut exprimatur subjectum κατοικήσεως, vel templum inhabitantis divinitatis.

Quæ explicatio præfertur ab Augustino epist. VII. ad Dardan. Non idco corporaliter, quia corporeus est Deus, sed aut verbo translato usus est, tanquam in templo manufacto non corporaliter, sed umbratiliter habitaverit, id est, præfigurantibus signis; nam illas omnes observationes umbras futurorum vocat Apostolus ipso etiam translato vocabulo: aut certe corporaliter dictum est, quia in Christi corpore, quod assumpsit ex virgine, tanquam in templo habitat Deus. Præfertur etiam à Theodoreto, corporaliter, id est, tanquam in proprio furo corpore. Probatur ab Oecumenio: τὸ σωματικῶς idem est ac ἐνάρκως & σεσαρκωμένος; nec non à Damasceno, τυτίσι ἐν σαρκὶ αὐτῦ.

Vid. & Athanas. Orat. IV. contr. Arian. & Orat. II. de natur. Human. Cyrillus libr. poster. de fide ad Reginas. Utramque explicationem agnoscit orthodoxam Crocius, etsi neutra ipsi genuina videatur: Siquidem etiam in Prophetis habitavit in sanctis, & vere non umbratiliter, atque etiamnum ita habitabit in sanctis, 2.

Cor. VI. Num autem in Prophetarum ullo habitavit? Num habitat hodie in sanctorum ullo tota plenitudo Deitatis, tanquam in templo vel corpore proprio? Agnoscit Crocius, subjectum esse Christum: Capemt, inquit, Apostolus sermonem de Christo, de illo Ecclesiæ capite, de eodem pergit agere.

Ideo de illo necessario accipit. Dicit autem ἐν αὐτῷ non ἐν αὐτοῖς, ut Christum unum, non multos esse, doceat, & unius Christi persona unitatem. Agnoscit vocem κατοικεῖν non temporalem sed perpetuam inhabitationem significare, atque ideo à τῷ παροικεῖν distingui Ebr. XI. 9. 1. Petr. I. 7. Nec dici κατώκησε, sed κατοικεῖ, ut continua inhabitatio exprimatur tanto clarius.

Agnoscit non tantum excellentia dona dici dare Christo, non quadam Deitatis idiomata, sed totam in eo ac plenam habitare Deitatem. Laudat Theophylacti & scholiorem Græcorum interpretationem, quæ sic habet: Οὐσιωδῶς, ὅ ϰετικῶς. Καὶ ὡς ἂν οἰκήσῃ, φησὶν, ἐν σώματι ψυχὴ οὕτως ἐνῴκησε τῷ προσληφθέντι ἀνθρώπῳ. πῶς δὲ ἐνῴκει ψυχὴ σώματι; δηλονότι ἀσυγχύτως, ἀδιαιρέτως. An ergo etiam hoc de inhabitatione in sanctis dici potest? Laudat Augustinum, quod loco citato ita scripserit: An etiam præter hoc, quod tanquam in templo in illo corpore habitat omnis plenitudo Deitatis, est aliud, quod intersit inter illud caput, & cujuslibet membri excellentiam? Est plane, quod singulari quadam susceptione illius hominis una facta est persona cum Verbo. Laudat Theodoretum ita dicentem: Christus non singularum aliquam gratiam accipit, quemadmodum Moses: Deus enim est & homo, & id, quod videtur, habet unitam unigeniti divinitatem. Num talia etiam de inhabitatione in sanctis affirmare licet?

Ecquid ergo solidi ad argumentum nostrum reponet Crocius? Cui sese communicavit tota divinitatis plenitudo, illi sunt realiter communicata idiomata Deitatis essentialia. At humanae Christi naturae. Ergo. 1.

Regerit. Apostolum non communicationem, sed inhabitationem nominare. Quid vero communicatio aliud infert, quam possessionem? Si inhabitat humanam naturam Deitatis tota plenitudo, oportet, ut eam possideat, si possidet, oportet, eidem communicatam acceperit ad possessionem, quia inhabitatio notatur perpetua ac continua, & quum non umbratiliter, effice, ac relative aut separabiliter; sed longe eminentiori modo perfectissime, inseparabiliter & personaliter inhabitare concedatur, oportet ei vere ac realiter communicatam esse plenitudinem Deitatis. Atque hinc S. Ignatius in epist. ad Trallian. corpus Christi dixit σῶμα ἔχον τὸν θεὸν ἔνοικον. Epiphanius in Ancor. carnem Christi δοχεῖον τῆς θεότητος, receptaculum Deitatis; Gregorius Nyssenus apud Theodoretum, carnem capientem totum λόγον per περιχώρησιν.

Argumentamur jam ita: Si humana natura possidet totam Deitatis plenitudinem, & inhabitatur à Deitatis plenitudine modo quodam singulari, oportet eam participem factam esse plenitudinis Deitatis, adeòque intercedere communicationem humanae naturae divinam, veram & realem. At verum prius. Ergo & posterius. 2.

Regerit 2. Crocius: Essentialia Deitatis idiomata carni realiter communicata dicuntur vel in persona, vel in seipsa, ita ut fit & recte dicatur omnipotens, omniscía, & omnipraesens. Prior sensus ad-mittitur, posterior ex Apostolo minime concluditur, quia describit ille τῷ λόγῳ & carnis unione in unitate personae: at unio facta est salvis utriusque naturae proprietatibus, nec Apostolus tria nominat idiomata, sed totam divinitatis plenitudinem. Resp. Non potest subsisti in persona. Nam persona non est tertium quid distinctum à duabus naturis: ideo si personae communicata dicuntur, quaerimus secundum quam naturam, anne secundum divinam, an vero secundum humanam naturam? Atqui divinae naturae nihil communicari potuit, aut Christo secundum divinam naturam in tempore. Re-stat ergo, ut admittatur, Christo secundum humanam naturam ea communicata esse, quod etiam ipsa κατοίκησις docet. Nam omnis inhabitatio praesupponit habitaculum. Quum ergo hic plene praesupponit inhabitatio τῷ λόγῳ, dubium non est, quin etiam diserte templum inhabitationis expressum voluerit Apostolus. Adde quod vix sine ἀδολεσχία efferre propositionem Apostoli liceat: In persona Christi habitat tota plenitudo Deitatis σωματικῶς, nisi subiectum sit caro, nec Deitas Christi subiectum statui queat, in qua ob summam simplicitatem distinctio inhabitantis & ejus, quod inhabitatur, locum non habet. Nec vero negamus, sed ultro profitemur, omnia idiomata Deitatis communicata esse humanae Christi naturae, omnia ab eadem possideri. Inde tamen haud inferendum: Christum secundum humanam naturam esse aeternum, immensum, independentem &c. quia illa idiomata possidentur quidem ab humana natura, non autem usurpantur, ideoque nec denominationem inferunt. Ratio in promptu est: Sunt enim ἀνενέργητα, nec ad finem unionis quicquam faciunt. 3. Regerit 3. Quemadmodum Deitas communicata, & Deitatis idiomata essentialia: At Deitas communicata unione hypostatica, non autem transfusione, vel sic, ut humanitas facta sit Dei humanitas, non Deus neque Deitas. Ergo similiter idiomata humanitati sunt communicata, ut sit humanitatis omnipotentis, ubique praesentis, non ut sit omnipotens, & ubique praesens.

Resp. Unio hypostatica & communicatio distinguuntur ut antecedens & consequens: Et qualis est unio, talis etiam est communicatio. Quum ergo vera & realis inter naturam divinam, & humanam fit unio, vera etiam atque realis intercedat communicatio oportet. Transfusionem nemo nostratium probat, veram tantum communicationem, per unionem hypostaticam inter naturam utramque intercedere fateri oportet, ut ex professo docuimus Exam. de perf. Christi Controv. III. Membr.

II. Neque vero ut humana natura dicitur omnipotens: Ita etiam humana natura Deus vel Deitas dicenda. Nam confunditur sic praedicatio Paronymica & Synonymica: Quemadmodum non dico: Humanitas est omnipotentia: Ita nec dicere licet: Humanitas est Deitas: Sed humana natura habet vel possidet divinam naturam, vel etiam est θεοθεῖσα seu Deificata, ut loqui amant Veteres, uti nec divina natura est humana, vel caro, sed divina natura est ἐνανθρωπήσασα vel inhumanata, si ita loqui liceat, vel incarnata. Unde Dionysius Areopagita, referente Damasceno, divinitus, inquit, plene in una substantia personarum nobis se communicavit, & S. Basilius de incarn. Verbi: Ἡ ἀνθρωπίνη τῷ κυρίῳ σὰρξ αὐτὴ μέτοχε τῆς θεότητος: Humana Domini caro ipsa particeps facta est Deitatis. Theophylactus adhibet simile de unione animae & corporis, in qua luculenta est communicatio utriusque: Quia in ipso inhabitat omnis plenitudo divinitatis corporaliter, hoc est, quodcunque Deus est Verbum, in ipso habitat. Sed ne forte inhabitasse hunc audiens, existimes habitando & operatum esse, quemadmodum & Prophetae solebant, in quibus Deus inhabitabat, secundum quod scriptum est: Et inhabitabo in eis & inambulabo, corporaliter scilicet adjunxit: hoc est, non operatione aliqua, sed substantia & tanquam corporatus, & substantia una existens cum carne assumpta.

Vel potest hoc modo intelligi. Videlicet tanquam in corpore, cum inhabitat anima, corpore quidem hac vivit substantialiter & inseparabiliter & fine ulla admixtione. Anima tamen ipsa corpore excedit, corpus dum moritur. Deus autem, Verbum nunquam à carne assumpta sejunctus est.

Sed de his loco citato fusissime actum. Adhibemus jam tantum praesentem aphorismum ad demonstrandam Deitatem Christi: Adscribitur enim hic Christo non tantum θεότης, Deitas, quae est forma Dei, ut ita loquar, adeoque ipsa essentia divina: Sed τὸ πλήρωμα τῆς θεότητος, plenitudo Deitatis, seu plena, integra & perfecta Deitas, ne quis forte cogitet, metaphorice tantum, vel per analogicam attributionem, aut imperfecta ratione Christum Deum esse. Nec id solum, sed majoris emphaseos gratia additur particula universalis, adeoque vindicatur Christo πᾶν τὸ πλήρωμα τῆς θεότητος omnis plenitudo Deitatis, ut innuatur Deitatem Christo convenire absolutissima, perfectissimae ratione: Cui autem competit plena, omnimoda, absoluta & perfecta Deitas, illi denegari nequit essentialis, aeterna, immensa Deitas.

Qui absoluta, perfectissimae ratione Deus est, utique summus & altissimus est Deus. Sed prosequamur argumenta, quae ex hoc loco desumi possunt, (1) A nomine θεότης: Id enim notat divinam essentiam, per quam Deus est id, quod est, non secus atque ἀνθρωπότης notat essentiam hominis, per quam homo est id, quod est. Nec uspiam θεότης in sacris occurrit, ubi qualitates non divinas ac creatas designet. Apud Patres etiam orthodoxos tantum adhibetur pro essentiali Deitate. Athanas. serm. contra Arian. Gregor. Nazianz. de Theol. Damascen. l. 1. de Orthod. fid. Ideoque Syrus expressit voce אלהותא, Arabs אלהות, quæ præcife ipsam Dei essentiam, nuspiam vero qualitatem, vel dona aliqua finita denotat. Vide Act. XVII. 29. Rom. I. 20. Sed & vox θεότης, quam eundem sensum habere cum hac voce θεότης contendit Enjedinus, essentiam divinam significat, veramque infinitam & essentialem Deitatem importat, Rom. I. 20. Sap. XIII. 9. nec uspiam aliter in sacris adhibetur: fateturque ipse Enjedinus p. 358. θεότητα de substantia Dei accipi Rom. I. (2) a denominatione τὸ πληρώματος τῆς θεότητος. Non ait Apostolus, plenitudo donorum Deitatis, vel gratiæ, & notitiæ voluntatis divinæ, sed simpliciter plenitudo Deitatis. Adhæc plenitudinem Deitatis vocat per usitatum Ebraismum, plenam & perfectam Deitatem, qualiter dicitur plenitudo domus, hoc est, plena & perfecta domus Num. XXIV. 13. plenitudo staturæ, hoc est, tota & perfecta statura, 1. Sam. XXII. 20. Ideoque innuit, nihil Deitatis cogitari vel dici posse, quod Christo non competat. πλήρωμα notat omnimodam & consummatam perfectionem, infertque omnis defectus carentiam.

Ambs interpres utitur voce כְּמָל, quæ denotat omnimodam perfectionem, plenitudinem absolutam, & integritatem, descendens à כָּמַל compleri, perfectum vel consummatum esse. Sic enim reddit אלהות כְּמָל in אלהי חל quo habitat perfectissima plenitudo Deitatis. (3) vocis OMNIS adjectione. Omnem enim plenitudinem Deitatis Christo vindicat, id est, omnibus modis plenam, absolutam & perfectam Deitatem: & quicquid omnino uspiam Deitatis est. At si aliqua saltim dona, eaque finita Christo competerent, non posset ipsi adscribi πᾶν τὸ πλήρωμα omnis plenitudo Deitatis. Si quicquam ad plenam & perfectam Deitatem Patris spectans Christo haud competeret, falso Christo adscriberetur πᾶν τὸ πλήρωμα omnis plenitudo Deitatis. Qui enim omnem plenitudinem Deitatis dicit, nihil, quod ad plenam & absolutam omnimodam Deitatem facit, excludit (4) a connexione textus. Ob quam plenitudinem Christus est principium salutis genuinum, illa non est finita vel creata, sed infinita & increata, quum principium salutis genuinum virtutem non finitam, sed infinitam præfupponat, quæ essentiam infert infinitam. At ob hanc plenitudinem, de qua Apostolus, Christus est genuinum salutis principium. Conf. Col. II. 6. Iob. XIV. 6. 1. Cor. III. 11. (5) a collatione cum cap. I. 19. ubi plenitudo inhabitans itidem Deitatem infinitam interprete Cyrillo & Primasio infert, quum Creatorem, Conservatorem, Redemptorem, & Conciliatorem, ac caput nostrum esse non conveniat nisi vero natura Deo. (6) a plenitudinis descriptione Iob. I. 14. 16. tradita. Dicitur Christus πλήρης χάριτος καὶ ἀληθείας, plenus gratia & veritate, innuiturque simul plenus gloria Filio unigenito propria, quæ vere divina. Tribuitur ipsi ea plenitudo, quæ prorsus infinita est, quum omnes accipiant de illa plenitudine, nec unquam ullatenus ea deficiat: uti etiam hic in ipso dicimur reddi completi, ita ut retundet in nos omnimoda consummatio, quum hic quidem incipiamus compleri, in altera vita autem plene compleamur. (7) a omniscientia divinæ attributione v. 3. Quum enim omnis plenitudo Deitatis omniscientiam divinam, & infinitam includat, qualiter, quam de infinita DEI essentia, à qua illa inseparabilis est, ea accipi poterit? (8) ex interpretatione Ecclesiæ.

Quandoquidem Doctores præcipui Ecclesiæ (adeoqe ipsa Ecclesia Catholica) non de donis excellentissimis, finitis, sed de ipsa essentiali Deitate interpretati sunt, Christumque verum essentiam Deum esse inde concluferunt, ut apud Athanasium, Basilium, Cyrillum, Theodoretum, Ambrosium, Augustinum, & alios passim videre est. Pluribus hæc & alia argumenta exequitur B. D. Myslenta diff. 2. fuper h. l. ib. 16. seq.

Varia autem excipiunt adversarii (1) in Christo idem esse hoc loco, quod in doctrina Christi, vel in fide & confessione Christi, quum opponatur Christus non perfonis, sed doctrinæ: Ita Enjedinus, Socinus, & plerique omnes. (2) divinitatem nihil aliud esse, quam ipsam Dei voluntatem. in defens. animadv. pag. 194. Smalz. de divinit. Christi p. 23. Volk. de ver. Relig. l. 5. c. 10. p. 43. (3) Plenitudinem non essentiam, sed qualitatem denotare, omnem plenitudinem, id est, quamvis perfectionem: per plenitudinem divinitatis nihil aliud, quam dona Dei excellentissima intelligenda esse: ita Enjedinus (4) Epb. III. 19. Omnes pios posse plenitudinem Dei consequi, asserit, idemque hic esse omnem plenitudinem Deitatis. Omnem etiam plenitudinem iis tribui 1. Cor. I. 4. Dici autem Deum totum in Christo & più esse, & inhabitare, quando suam præfentiam, vim, potestatem, & benignitatem in illis & per illos exerit. Hæc iterum Enjedinus. (5) Deum & Deitatem multis rebus inhabitare dici, quæ tamen ob id non sunt æternus Deus Psal. CXXXI. 13. Mattb. XXIII. 22. Iob. XIV. 23. 1. Iob. III. 14. Enjed. p. 356. (6) Explicationem nostram de æterna Deitate Christi nihil facere ad propositum Apostoli, qui hortatur, ne à doctrina Christi deficiant. Enjed. 364.

Respondemus ad (1) vocula ἐν αὐτῷ non respicit Christi doctrinam, sed ipsum Christum, ut textu patet. (2) Christi nomen metonymice pro doctrina, vel Evangelio Christis fumi alicubi nondum probatum est. (3) Nec integrum est discedere à propria significatione, nisi cogente necessitate, quæ hic nulla. (4) Quid quod locum nullum habet metonymica illa significatio: Quia inhabitatio, eaque corporalis Deitatis haud convenit doctrinæ vel Evangelio Christi. Ubi enim in Evangelio dicitur inhabitare plenitudo Deitatis corporaliter, aut simile quidpiam? Adhæc intelligitur nomine Christi, quem cum Dominum suum susceperant Colossenses, in quo radicati erant, in quem crediderant v. 5. 6. 7. in quo reconditi erant omnes thesauri cognitionis v. 3. (6) Is hic nomine Christi indigitatur, qui est caput omnis principatus & Magistratus, in quo circumcisi, cum quo sepulti erant, in quo resurrexerant, qui resuscitatus erat à mortuis &c. ut evidentissimum est è vers. 10. seq. Quam inepte ergo hic intelligatur doctrina Christi, quivis videt, (7) in eo dicitur plenitudo tota habitare, qui est Ecclesia, primogenitus mortuorum, in quo omnia consistunt, & in quo omnia condita sunt, qui imago Dei est inconspicui, & primogenitus ante omnes creaturas, id quod sole clarius constat è cap. I. 15. 16. 17. 18. 19. Quis autem hæc de Christi doctrina, non verò de Christo ipso intelligenda esse dicet? Ut taceam, quod ipsi adversarii agnoscant de Christo ipso hæc accipienda esse, utpote cum Enjedin. in Christo habitare Deitatem explicat, ut in più &c. Constract. noster de essent. divin. p. 510. Ad (2) Non opus est, ut nunc quidquam addamus, cum gloffam illam vanissimam plene discusserimus, & Deitatem hic pro essentia divina accipi docuerimus l. c. p. 519. seq. Enjedinus certe fatetur & concedit p. 358. vocem θεός denotare substantiam, ideoque negare non potest, θεότητα Deitatem, vel substantiam Dei designare, pronus autem est in suspicionem ab Apostolo θεότητος fuisse scriptum, quam vocem quidam nimium religiosi aut librarii negligentes in θεότητα transformarint.

Sed si ejusmodi suspicionis locus relinquatur, ubi nullus prorsus Codex, nec ratio ulla causam præbet, quid tandem certi erit in Scripturis?

Ad (3) Falsò negat Enjedinus, Paulum Deitatem in Christo habitare asserere, quum disertissime Apostolus Deitatis mentionem faciat, non solius plenitudinis: imo plenitudo Deitatis fit plena Deitas.

Licet ergo cap. I. 19. absolute plenitudinis mentio fiat, hic tamen plenitudo Deitatis commemoratur, indeque prior locus illustratur. Et cuinam proprie πλήρωμα tribuetur, præterquam ipsi Deitati? Quid absolute πλήρωμα perfectionem fine defectu dicemus, quam ipsammet Deitatem, perfectionum perfectionem? Videri etiam potest Apostolus πλήρωμα vocem adhibuisse, ut opponeret verum πλήρωμα Gnosticorum commentitiis pleromafi, &, ut Origenes loquitur, designaret τὴν ἀρχὴν μετοχὴν τῆς θεότητος. Non autem dona tantum finita, sed infinitam Deitatem hìc designari, tract. de eff. div. unit. §. 181. ostensum.

Ad (4) Respond. Longe distinctissima illa sunt, plenitudinem omnem Deitatis habitare in Christo corporaliter, & fideles impleri eis πᾶν τὸ πλήρωμα τοῦ θεοῦ.

Ibi accipitur τὸ πλήρωμα ἀληθῶς, hìc passive. Significat enim tàm id quod implet, ut Job. I. 16. & Coloss. II. 9. tum id, quod impletur, ut Roman. XI. 25. XV. 29. Quo sensu posteriori etiam Epb. I. 23. V. 18. Coloss. I. 14. II. 10. occurrit.

Adde quod fideles dicantur impleri plenitudine DEI: Christus autem dicatur esse is, qui omnia in omnibus adimplet, πλήρωμα ὡς Epb. I. 23.

Præterea diversitas etiam inde elucet, quod plenitudo Deitatis Ebionimum dicatur plena & perfecta Deitas: hic autem plenitudo DEI, qua implentur fideles, sed de donis variis, quibus implentur divinitus, quod è 1. Cor. 1. 4. luculentissimum. πλήρωμα τῆς θεοῦ dicitur sensu causali, quod illa plenitudo fit à DEO: at πλήρωμα τῆς θεότητος dicitur formaliter, ut ita loquar, quod ipsa Deitas perfectissima in Christo habitet.

Quid quod Enjedinus sibi ipsi exederit & in os contradicat: Quum enim p. 357. dixisset, nihil hic tributi Christo, quod non etiam hominibus piis tribui soleat: Mox tamen pag. 360. ait, habitare dici Deum in Christo cum omni sua plenitudine; quia quicquid in Ecclesiam suam conferre bonorum & donorum constituit, id per Christum, & in Christo piis dare solet, & ideo adjecisse Apostolum vocem σωματικῶς, ut inter Christum & pios discrimen faceret, atque significaret, abundantius in Christo Deum habitare, quam in aliis: Deum olim in aliis habitasse umbralice, spiritualiter, particulariter, τυπικῶς, in Christo autem vere, perfecte, abundantissime, & totaliter.

Ad (5) Respond. In nulla re habitare dicitur tota plenitudo Deitatis corporaliter, quod hìc de Christo asseritur: Etsi dicatur Deus habitare vel esse in templo, in populo &c. ejusmodi tamen xατοίκησις longe alia est, nempe mera παραστατική, non autem κατὰ περιχώρησιν, καὶ συνδύασιν ὑποστατικήν. Distinguendum inter præsentiam typicam in templo Salomonis, spiritualem in fidelibus, & personalem vel bypostaticam in Christo. In illis ita habitat Deus, ut nec unum constituatur ὑφιστάμενον, nec inde illa dicantur DEUS, sed DEI.

In Christo autem, vel humana Christi natura ita inhabitat, ut unum constituat ὑφιστάμενον, utque inde Christus sit, & dicatur Deus benedictus in secula.

Ideoque omnis plenitudo Deitatis tribuitur Christo, non tantum παρωνύμως, sed etiam συνωνύμως, quandoquidem certum fit è scripturis, Christum Deum esse. Qualis ergo sit Deitas, secundum quam Christus Deus est, hoc ipso docemur, quod omnibus modis absoluta & perfecta Deitas in eo habitet, nimirum quod non secundum quid, sed absolute, non imperfecta, sed perfectissima ratione Deus fit, non secundum aliquam divinitatis participationem, vel denominationem, sed fecundam plenam, atque omnibus modis absolutam & perfectam Deitatis possessionem.

Enjedinus declarat hanc inhabitationem exemplo animæ, quæ in corpore toto tota, & in omnibus ejus partibus tota est p. 359. ut ergò anima ita habitat in corpore, ut ad hominis essentiam constituendam spectet, ita & Deitas habitat in Christo, ut pertineat ad constituendam ejus essentiam. Ut illa συνωνύμως prædicatur de homine, & essentialiter: ita etiam Deitas de Christo prædicatur συνωνύμως & essentialiter.

Ad (6) Respond. Quidni ad propositum Apostoli faceret, Christo hic adserere veram & essentialem Deitatem? Annon enim ratio illa prægnantissima est, cur unice Christi adhærescendum sit doctrinæ, relictis traditionibus hominum, quia Christus, qui eam tradidit doctrinam, non est ψιλὸς ἄνθρωπος, sed verus natura Deus? Cur sequenda non sint τὰ στοιχεῖα κόσμου elementa mundi, ritusque, & sacra vetera, quùm jam non opus sit ejusmodi umbratilibus rebus, quæ Christum quondam præfigurarunt: quandoquidem in Christo omnis plenitudo Deitatis corporaliter habitet.

Quemadmodum in V. T. Deitas habitabat in templo, ceu typo, ita in carne Christi habitat tota plenitudo Deitatis σωματικῶς ceu in proprio corpore; vero templo, per typicum illud templum adumbrato. Annon optime cohæret hæc αἰτιολογία, non esse in aliis quibuscumque mediis sive Philosophia, sive Mosaicis legibus, sed in solo Christo quærendam salutem, quia ipse non nudus homo, sed verus Deus fit, adeoque summum & unicum salutis nostræ principium merito agnoscatur: extra quem nulla fit salutis nostræ causa.

Conf. Job. XIV. 6. Act. IV. 12. X. 43. XV. 11. Quis vero ambigeret causam habuisse gravissimam Colossenses, uni & soli Christo, tanto Doctori, adhærendi, utpote in quo tota plenitudo Deitatis habitabat corporaliter, qui absolutissima ratione Deus est, in quo ipsi unice impleti erant variis donis, quique caput est omnis potestatis, & principatus, adeoque citra controversiam præ omnibus aliis, ipsis etiam angelis, (quorum θρησκείαν reprobat Apostolus v. 18. revocans ad θρησκείαν & cultum unius Christi, seu capitis omnis potestatis) audiendus.

Conf. Matt. XVII. 5. Hanc enim partem, quod Christus caput sit omnis principatus, ideò studiose adjecisse, non temere observat Estius in comm. ad h. l. ut avocaret à cultu Angelorum, quem Simon Magus tradebat. B. Theodoretus in comm. ad h. l. ita proponit hanc τῆς συνεχείας rationem: Divi-nus Apostolus volens significare differentiam legis & gratiæ elementorum egestati Christum opposuit, & per amborum invicem collationem volens ostendere, quam fit longe superior, adjecit, quod in ipso inhabitat omnis plenitudo divinitatis corporaliter, hoc est, tanquam in proprio corpore. Non enim singulare, inquit, aliquam gratiam accepit, quemadmodum Moses: Deus enim est & homo, & id quod videtur, habet unitam unigeniti divinitatem.

Chemnit. noster Tr. de duabus nat. in Christ. c. 24. p. 335. ita explicat: Quod non tantum Christi plus pro sua persona in assumpta sua humana natura personaliter habeat totam plenitudinem Deitatis: Sed quod & nos, qui sumus membra ejus, caro de carne ejus, & primogeniti hujus fratres, omnia quae ad redemptionem, liberationem & defensionem contra hostes, ad gratiam, reconciliationem, acceptionem, exauditionem; auxilium apud Deum, quaeque ad nostram conversionem, illuminationem, justificationem, sanctificationem, vivificationem, conservationem, salvationem, necessaria sunt; quidni, inquam, omnia illa bona perfectissima, & cumulatisima plenitudine habeamus in Christo, pro nobis incarnato, crucifixo, & resuscitato: ita deinde tanquam ex capite in nos, tanquam in membra illa bona ex ejus plenitudine deriventur, influant, conferantur, & subministrentur.

Ac inde concludit Paulus, nullis aliis elementis mundi nobis opus esse ad salutem, cum totam ejus plenitudinem habeamus in Christo. Ac vicissim, qui omnia alia corradat, salute carere, si Christum non habeat.

Quod si ergo Enjedini glossa, qua per plenitudinem Deitatis nihil aliud intelligit, quam dona Dei excellentissima, cohaerere censetur cum adhortatione Apostolica, quod adhaerendum sit Christi doctrinae, quanto magis congruet Ecclesiae Catholicae interpretatio, & verborum propria emphasis elucefcens? si adhaerendum illius doctrinae, cui dona excellentissima divinitus collata, quanto magis illi, quae absoluta, perfectissimaque ratione Deus est, h. e. ipsi summo Deo? Atque haec sufficiant pro vindicando isto oraculo.

## 2:10
V. 10 And you are filled, be content with him.

It is here take it, as just now βλέπετε (beware) in the precative mood. And πεπληρωμένοι (filled) as content. Because what is full desires nothing else. The Apostle explains here the benefit of Christ, not our duty: therefore, the precative or imperative mood does not obtain: But the indicative, as the Interpreters accept more fully. Nor is πεπληρωμένοι properly "you are content," but "filled," although that becomes a consequence of it. For if we are filled in Christ, we can be entirely content with Christ, nor ought we to seek another in order to be filled. And as in the preceding verse τὸ πλήρωμα (the fullness) was properly accepted: So also here the present participle πεπληρωμένοι must be accepted. For therefore in Christ, according to the paternal εὐδοκίαν (good pleasure), πᾶν τὸ πλήρωμα (all the fullness) of the Godhead had to dwell, so that through him, our redemption and reconciliation having been most fully made, we might be uniquely in him πεπληρωμένοι, you filled, and full through faith, not by our justice and satisfaction, not by the mediation of Angels, but by the justice, satisfaction, redemption, and mediation of Christ alone through faith in him. Therefore, Theophylact indeed spoke truly concerning the communication of the divine nature, yet not fully, nor sufficiently conveniently for the present matter: What did the Pope say? You have nothing less than he himself: Truly you also have been filled with divinity; nevertheless, in him, that is, by assumption: for after our nature was coupled to God, we also became partakers of the divine nature. For the matter here concerns that end of the hypostatic union and communication which looks to eternal salvation, namely, that it pleased the divine kindness to have the whole divine fullness dwell in the body assumed by the Son of GOD, so that through it, our reconciliation and redemption having been made, just as the Apostle had taught in chapter I, we might be rendered full through faith in him, filled with all those things which are necessary for attaining eternal salvation: because the Word became flesh full of grace and truth, that we might receive from his fullness grace for grace. Since he himself, having been made for us by God, becomes justice and redemption, so that he who boasts, may boast uniquely in him, 1 Cor. I. Therefore, our incipient and inherent justice does not contribute here, as the Catholic [theologian] says, but the imputed justice of Christ, as Melanchthon teaches; because if our fullness were in any way to be sought in our own justice, or if that contributed anything to that blessed fullness or to our salvation, the justice and redemption of Christ would not suffice for us, by whose grace, however, it pleased God that the whole fullness of the Godhead should dwell in the assumed humanity, it pleased that through it reconciliation should be plainly made, a full redemption, so that uniquely through faith in it a blessed fullness and full beatitude might consist. Ἐν αὐτῷ (In him) you are completed. We are not in Christ except through faith: Nor are we completed except in Christ, or insofar as we are in him: And therefore nothing else is designated than that in Christ himself, through that faith, we have that fullness by which we are perfect and just before God, Phil. III. 9, by which faith we receive Christ, as he had said in v. 5, 6, h. l., and being grafted into him, as if rooted in him, we draw all life and sap from him, and are so founded in him that we stand stable and firm against any impulses, v. 7, the consequence of which is that we are also rendered partakers of the divine nature in him, 2 Pet. I. 4. ὅ ἐστι κεφαλὴ πάσης ἀρχῆς καὶ ἐξουσίας (who is the head of all principality and power). Should not he who also commands the angelic classes suffice for you?

For he refers to what he had said above 1. 6, κεφαλὴ ὤν (being the head), he who has authority, 1 Cor. XI. 3, Eph. V. 3. But he says this on account of those who were instituting the worship of Angels or αἰῶνας (aeons).

As in the preceding words of this verse, having established the justice of faith alone in Christ the Redeemer, he entirely excludes all other things which are outside of Christ: So in the preceding he establishes the dignity of Christ, that he alone is the head of their principalities and powers, so that he might abstract them from the mediation of Angels, he makes Christ the Head, but not consubstantial, of the kind that he is the head of the faithful, but as superior and causing, as Theophylact has it, as being the Creator and Lord of the Angels, of whose creation he had treated in chapter I. 16. He is also the Head of the Angels by reason of his human nature itself, in which the Apostle had just said the whole fullness of the Godhead dwells, because he is established above all powers, Eph.

I. 20, and all Angels are commanded to adore him, Ps. XCVII. 8, Heb. I. 6, all powers are subject to him, 1 Pet. III. 22. Why therefore (says Theodoret, in translation) do you flee to the Angels, this very thing having been omitted? As if to leaders to be approached to the Father?

It seems worth the effort here also for the Blessed Hunnius to consider how he repeats these two things alternately, as if in turns, and deduces one from the other, namely, the consideration of the Majesty of Christ and our perfection in him. For just as he previously expressed his divine majesty in the dwelling of the fullness of the Godhead, and soon assigned as a sort of consequence of this our perfection in Christ: So after this, having been rendered thus, he now returns to the former notation of his Majesty, when he names him the head of all Principality and power, and soon will again betake himself to commending our sufficiency in Christ, once he is rightly acknowledged: clearly as he also inferred above from the shown Majesty, the omnificence or the wisdom and knowledge of all treasures hidden in Christ, the other, as a sort of consequence of this Majesty, namely, that the hinge of all Theological wisdom turns upon the knowledge of him.

Latin:

V. 10 Καὶ ἐστέ πεπληρωμένοι, illo contenti estote.

Est hic sume, ut modo βλέπετε in modo precativo. Et πεπληρωμένοι contenti. Quia quod plenum est, nihil aliud desiderat. Beneficium Christi non nostrum officium hic explicat Apostolus: non ergo modus precativus vel imperativus: Sed indicativus obtinet, ut plenius accipiunt Interpretes. Neque πεπληρωμένοι proprie est contenti estis, sed repleti, quamvis eo istud consequens fit.
