Si enim repleti sumus in Christo, contenti omnino esse possumus Christo, nec alium quaerere debemus ut repleamur. Et ut proprie versu praecedenti τὸ πλήρωμα accipiebatur: Ita etiam hic verbum praesens πεπληρωμένοι accipiendum est. Nam ideo in Christo secundum εὐδοκίαν Paternam debuit habitare πᾶν τὸ πλήρωμα tota plenitudo Deitatis, ut per ipsum redemptionem, & reconciliationem nostra plenissime facta, nos unice in ipso essemus πεπληρωμένοι vos repleti, & pleni per fidem, non nostra justitia & satisfactione, non Angelorum mediatione, sed unius Christi justitia, satisfactione, redemptionem ac mediatione per fidem in ipsum. Ideo vere quidem Theophylactus de communicatione divinae naturae, non tamen plene, nec ad rem praesentem satis commode: Papae quid dixit? Nihil minus habetis, quam ipse: Verum & vos divinitate impleti estis; verumtamen in ipso hoc est per assumptionem: postquam enim nostra natura Deo copulata est, etiam divinae naturae participes facti sumus. Agitur enim hic de fine illo unionis & communicationis hypostaticae, qui respicit aeternam salutem, quod nempe placuerit divinae benignitati, in corpore a Filio DEI assumpto habitare totam plenitudinem divinam, ut per id nostri reconciliatione & redemptione facta, quemadmodum cap. I. docuerat Apostolus, nos pleni redderemur per fidem in ipsum omnibus illis repleti, quae ad salutem aeternam consequendam necessaria sunt: quia Verbum caro factum est plenum gratia & veritate, ut de plenitudine ejus accipiamus gratiam pro gratia . Siquidem ipse factus nobis fit a Deo justitia & redemptio, ut, qui gloriatur, in ipso unice glorietur, 1. Cor. I. Non ergo huc facit inchoata, & inherens nostra justitia, ut Catholicius, sed imputata justitia Christi, ut Melanchthon docet; quia si in nostra justitia quaerenda ullo modo nostra plenitudo, aut si illa quicquam ad plenitudinem illam beatam vel ad salutem nostram conferret, non sufficeret nobis Christi justitia & redemptio, cujus tamen gratia placuit Deo, ut in humanitate assumpta habitaret tota Deitatis plenitudo, placuit, ut per eam plane fieret reconciliatio, plena redemptio, ut unice per fidem in eam constaret beata plenitudo, & plena beatitudo. Ἐν αὐτῷ in ipso estis completi. Non sumus in Christo, nisi per fidem: Nec completi sumus nisi in Christo, vel quatenus in ipso sumus: Ideoque nihil aliud designatur, quam quod in ipsomet Christo per fidem illam plenitudinem habeamus, qua perfecti & justi coram Deo sumus, Phil. III. 9. qua fide Christum suscipimus, ut v. 5. 6. dixerat h. l. eique insiti, tanquam radicati in ipso vitam & succum omnem trahimus ab ipso, & in eo sic fundamur, ut stabiles & firmi aduersus quosvis impetus consistamus, v. 7. cujus consequens est, quod divinae naturae in ipso etiam participes reddamur, 2. Petr. I. 4. ὅ ἐστι κεφαλὴ πάσης ἀρχῆς καὶ ἐξουσίας Nonne sufficere vobis debet is, qui & Angelicis classibus imperat?

Respicit enim, quod supra dixerat 1. 6. κεφαλὴ ὤν is, qui imperium habet, 1. Cor. XI. 3. Eph. V. 3. Hoc autem dicit ob eos, qui Angelorum sive αἰῶνας cultum instituebant.

Ut praecedentibus hujus versus verbis, stabilita solius fidei in Christum Redemptorem justitia, tonte excludit alia omnia, quae extra Christum sunt: Ita praecedentibus stabilit Christi dignitatem, quod unus ille sit caput ipsorum etiam principatum & potestatem, ut ab Angelorum mediatione abstractat, Caput facit Christum, sed non consubstantiale, cujusmodi caput est fidelium, sed tanquam superiorem & causantem, ut habet Theophylactus, utpote Creatorem & Dominum Angelorum, de quorum creatione cap. I. 16. egerat. Caput etiam est Angelorum ratione ipsius humanae naturae, in qua habitare plenitudinem totam Deitatis modo dixerat Apostolus, quia supra omnes potestates constitutus est, Eph.

I. 20. & omnes Angeli eum adorare jubentur, Psal. XCVII. 8. Ebr. I. 6. omnes potestates ei subjectae sunt, 1. Pet. III. 22. Cur ergo, (inquit Theodoretus interprete) hoc ipso omisso ad Angelos confugitis? tanquam ad Patrem adeundum Duces?

Opere pretium etiam hic videtur B. Hunnio, considerare, quomodo hac duo alternie velut vicibus repetat, & unum ex altero deducat, nimirum considerationem Majestatis Christi & nostra in illo perfectionis. Sicut enim antea divinam ejus majestatem expressit in habitatione plenitudinis Deitatis, & mox velut hujus consequens quoddam assignavit nostrum in Christo notitia perfectionem: Icz post hanc sic redditam nunc ad priorem Majestatis ipsius notationem revertitur, quando illum nominat caput omnis Principatus & potestatis, & mox iterum se recipiet ad commendandam nostram in Christo rite agnito sufficientiam: plane ut & supra ex ostensa Majestate omnificentia seu omnium thesaurorum sapientia & scientia in Christo reconditorum, inferebat alterum, tanquam bujusce Majestatis consequens quoddam, quod videlicet in ipsius notitia omnis sapientiae Theologicae vertatur cardo.

## 2:11
V. 11. Ἐν ᾧ περιετμήθητε περιτομῇ ἀχειροποιήτῳ (In whom you were circumcised with a circumcision made without hands). This is against those who were urging circumcision.

What need is there for an external sign, when the thing signified by it is openly exhibited? χειροποίητος περιτομὴ (circumcision made with hands) is that which was done by human hand, Eph. II. 11, ἡ ἐν σαρκί (that in the flesh), to this is opposed ἀχειροποίητος (made without hands), that which is done divinely. You have a similar opposition in Mark XIV. 58. 2 Cor. V. 1. Heb. IX. 11. 24. Περιτομὴ ἀχειροποίητος is that of the heart through the Spirit. See Rom. II. 29. and what is said there. Ἐν τῇ ἀπεκδύσει τοῦ σώματος τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν τῆς σαρκὸς) In that old circumcision there is ἀπέκδυσις, stripping off, but of a small piece of skin, here however of all the vices which flatter the flesh. Ἁμαρτία, that is, the habit of sinning; the body is attributed to this, as in Rom. VI. 6. For everything that is composed of many things is accustomed to be called by this word. Thus also we have μέλη below III. 5. In the Manuscript it is shorter with the same meaning; ἀπεκδύσει τοῦ σώματος τῆς σαρκὸς. Nor does the Latin read otherwise. Ἐν τῇ περιτομῇ τοῦ χριστοῦ) Not that of Abraham, but of Christ, who is greater than Abraham.

Now he proceeds specifically to overthrow the necessity of circumcision, and in that manner he delivers the application and fruit of the redemption of Christ, but not through the work performed, as the scholastics barbarously speak, of external circumcision, which the Pseudo-Apostles required for salvation, but which the Apostle now denies to be necessary, but through baptism, in which indeed remission of sins and liberation from the power of Satan does not happen ex opere operato, but by the force of divine institution sacramentally, or as if through an ordinary medium of salvation on the part of God, the fruit of the redemption and reconciliation made through the death of Christ is applied to us: which by that covenant succeeded into the place of circumcision, which had once been the sacrament of initiation, Gen. XVII., and the seal of the righteousness of faith, Rom. IV. 11, in which we are circumcised, not indeed by external bodily, but by internal and spiritual circumcision, of which Deut. X. 26, ch. XXX. 6. Jer. IV. 4. Rom. II. 29. For as in Baptism the whole body of sins is stripped off, laid aside, or put off, not only habitual or original, but also actual or any others in general, not through amputation, abscission, or physical removal, but through the forgiveness of sins and their removal from the face of God or non-imputation in the circumcision of Christ or by the force of the bodily circumcision of Christ, which he undertook for our sake, Luke II., so that he might free us from the observation and condemnation of the law, or bind himself to free us, and that he might exhibit that merit which in the Old Testament made circumcision a saving circumcision for the circumcised, and which can save all men, and through which alone they are saved, whoever are saved: or rather through circumcision analogically so called, that is, the sacrament of baptism, which Christ willed to be substituted for circumcision. This twofold effect of baptism seems to be delivered: The one is renewal and sanctification designated by the Apostle through the circumcision ἀχειροποίητον, the other is regeneration and the forgiveness or non-imputation of sins, indicated through the stripping off or abdication or rather the putting off of the body of the sins of the flesh. That one, even if it is posterior τῇ φύσει, is placed first, because the Apostle labors so much to exclude the external work of circumcision, that whatever once belonged to the sacrament of circumcision, he claims for baptism as the circumcision (analogically called) of Christ, or instituted by Christ. Concerning the former, Theophylact has it thus: He introduces a truly admirable benefit, when he says, you are circumcised in Christ. For such a circumcision is not by a mortal hand, but by the Holy Spirit. And it circumcises not some part, but the whole man. Concerning the latter, he speaks thus in his paraphrase: There indeed (in external circumcision) that male pudendum is covered by circumcision, with that fleshy veil removed; here however our whole body is stripped and laid bare, because the sins which we commit through the flesh are removed. Therefore, the law itself does not claim such a circumcision, but Christ, when he strips and despoils us in baptism, who are subject to the old life and sin, and thoroughly given over to the flesh. But that it is not through the ejection of sins, but their remission, because sins are taken away in baptism, not so that they are not present, but so that they are not imputed, as the Vulgate of Augustine's rule has it. By body indeed he seems to properly understand our body, but it is more correctly accepted as the body of sin, with Calvin as interpreter, and Grotius also admitting it, which is called the body of the sins of the flesh, because it arises from corrupt carnal generation; or also because this collection of vices exerts itself in the flesh, or in the part of man not yet regenerated, as the version of B. Luther and the interpretation of Crocius have it, or certainly our body is not to be understood ἁπλῶς by reason of substance (for it is certain that this is not laid aside but retained in baptism) just as neither is man simply denoted in his substance by the old man to be suffocated in baptism, but as it is entirely vitiated and corrupted by sin, as B. Hunnius explains.

The Old Interpreter here has inserted an Adversative, which neither the Greek Codices have, nor the Syriac, and he omitted the word OF SINS, and he so clearly perverts the sense: In whom also you are circumcised with a circumcision not made by hand in the stripping of the body of the flesh, BUT in the circumcision of Christ, buried with him in baptism, as if the sense were, with Cornelius as interpreter: You, O Christian Colossians, are circumcised with a circumcision not Jewish, which is by hands, and which consists in the stripping of the fleshy body, by which indeed the foreskin is cut off from the fleshy body, but you are circumcised in the circumcision, that is, the circumcision (for the Hebrew Beth is contact) of Christ, by which he circumcises not the body, but the soul from sins. If you ask, where and when you were thus circumcised by Christ? I answer, in baptism, indeed in this very thing, by which you were buried with Christ in baptism: For in baptism they are not only circumcised, but buried, and overwhelmed by expiatory waters, and all sins are absorbed. Estius here ingenuously rejects the Roman edition: 'Some wrongly place the adversative particle SED before it, with all approved copies resisting.' He also rejects the sense of Cornelius: 'The Greek scripture does not admit this sense, both because for "not made by hand" there is one infinite noun in Greek, as we have already said, so that the negation included in it does not exert its force upon what follows, and because of the genitive (of sins) interposed between body and flesh, which forces one to understand a spiritual circumcision: And thirdly, because for "putting off" there is a word which signifies the act of stripping off; Theophylact's interpreter translates it as "stripping"; which word is too awkwardly referred to that external circumcision, by which the foreskin of the flesh was cut off.' Whence, according to the Greek reading and the interpretation of all the Greeks, it is necessary to render this sense: By whom, Christ, you have also been circumcised, not with that external and carnal, but with an internal and spiritual circumcision, which is done without hands, and by which not one little skin is removed, but the body of the sins of the flesh, that is, the whole old man is laid aside and stripped off, which is a circumcision proper to Christ, not to Moses. Therefore, the body of the sins of the flesh, which the Apostle says is stripped off by this circumcision of Christ, is the same as the old man, whom he also calls elsewhere the body of sin, Rom. VI. Add that by external circumcision the body was not stripped off, but the smallest skin of one member was cut off. Others explain this stripping off of the body of the sins of the flesh also as concerning renewal, because they are said to be circumcised when they have stripped off that old man with his depraved desires, as Crocius holds; but since the principal scope of the Apostle is to exclude from the business of salvation all other things outside of Christ, and his redemption and reconciliation, he touched upon because of the analogy of circumcision and baptism, the Apostle is to be believed to be pointing to that interior circumcision, but because our salvation does not consist in it, he is pointing to the primary end of baptism and the scope of his own discussion, namely the remission of sins, which we have only through faith in Christ.

For by reason of it, that whole collection or mass of sins is put off, namely as regards guilt: for we put off the body of sin, not just some part or members, as Crocius admits, and therefore it is called a body, and not by reason of our renovation, although baptism is also the washing of the same, Tit. III. v. 5. For they are commanded later in chap. III. to mortify the members which are on the earth; therefore the same things have not been fully put off in baptism as regards renovation, which only begins, but is not yet complete. Crotius acknowledges this, that the whole body of sins is not fully and perfectly laid aside in one moment in baptism, but that as regards guilt at least it is fully laid aside, whereas as regards corruption we only begin to put off the acts.

Finally, the forgiveness of sins is clearly hinted at by the Apostle as intended, when in v. 13 it is expressly named, and the meritorious cause of the same is brought forward, the cross of Christ, through which the handwriting of the law, which was against us, has been blotted out. Which things will be clearer in what follows.

Latin:

V. 11. Ἐν ᾧ περιετμήθητε περιτομῇ ἀχειροποιήτῳ Hoc aduersus eos, qui circumcisionem urgebant.

Quid signo externo opus, cum res per illud significata aperte exhibeatur, χειροποίητος περιτομὴ est illa, quae manu humana fiebat, Eph. II. 11. ἡ ἐν σαρκί, huic opponitur ἀχειροποίητος, ea, quae fit divinitus. Similem oppositionem habes Marc. XIV. 58. 2. Cor. V. 1. Ebr. IX. 11. 24. Περιτομὴ ἀχειροποίητος est illa cordis per Spiritum. Vide Rom. II. 29. & ibi dicta. Ἐν τῇ ἀπεκδύσει τοῦ σώματος τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν τῆς σαρκὸς) In circumcisione illa veteri est ἀπέκδυσις הפשׁט, sed exiguæ pelliculæ, hic vero omnium vitiorum, quæ carni blandiun- tur. Ἁμαρτία id est pectandi consuetudo, huic corpus tri- buitur, ut Rom. VI. 6. Omne enim,quòd ex multis com- ponitur, solet hoc vocabulo appellari. Sic & μέλη infra habemus III. 5. In Manuscripto brevius sensu eodem ; ἀπεκδύσει τοῦ σώματος τῆς σαρκὸς. Nec aliter legit Latinus. Ἐν τῇ περιτομῇ τοῦ χριστοῦ) Non illa Abrahami, sed Christi, qui major Abrahamo.

Jam in specie ad profligandam circumcisionis ne- cessitatem progreditur, eaque ratione applicationem & fructum tradit redemptionis Christi, sed non per opus operatum, ut barbare scholastici lo- quuntur, circumcisionis externæ, quam ad salutem requirebant Pseudo-Apostoli, nunc autem neces- sariam esse inficiatur Apostolus, sed per baptismũ, in quo non quidem ex opere operato remissio pec- catorum & liberatio è potestate Satanæ contingat, sed vi divinæ institutionis sacramentaliter, seu tan- quam per medium salutis ordinarium ex parte Dei applicetur nobis fructus redemptionis & reconci- liationis per mortem Christi factæ: qui eo pacto in locum circumcisionis, quæ olim fuerat sacramen- tum initiationis, Gen. XVII. & sigillum justitiæ fidei, Rom. IV. 11. successit, in quo circumcidimur, non quidem externa corporali, sed interna spiritualique circumcisione, de qua Deut. X. 26. cap. XXX. 6. Jer. IV. 4. Rom. II. 29. Nam ut in Baptismo expoliatur deponiturque vel exuitur universum corpus pecca- torum, non tantum habitualium aut originalis, sed actualium etiam vel quorumvis in genere, non per amputationem, abscissionem, aut remotionem physi- cam, sed per peccatorum condonationem & à fa- cie Dei remotionem vèl non imputationem in circumcisione Christi sive vi circumcisionis Christi corporalis, quam nostri causa suscepit, Luc. II. ut à legis observatione ac condemnatione nos libera- ret, vel ad liberandum nos semet adstringeret, ut- que meritum illud exhiberet, quod in Vet. Test. circumcisis circumcisionem salutarem effecit, quodque omnes homines salvare potest, & per quod unice salvantur, quicunque salvantur: seu potius per circumcisionem analogice ita dictam, hoc est sacramentum baptismi, quod Christus surroga- tum voluit circumcisioni. Effectus hic geminus ba- ptismi tradi videtur: Alter est renovatio & sanctifi- catio per circumcisionem ἀχειροποίητον designa- tus ab Apostolo, alter regeneratio & peccatorum con- donatio aut non imputatio, per exspoliationem vel abdicationem aut exuitionem potius corporis pecca- torum carnis indicatus. Ille etsi posterior τῇ φύσει præmittitur, quia de circumcisionis opere externo excludendo sic laborat Apostolus, ut quicquid olim sacramento circumcisionis conveniebat, ba- ptismo ceu circumcisioni (analogice dictæ) Chri- sti, vel à Christo institutæ vindicet. De priori Theophylactus ita habet: Beneficium sane admiran- dum inducit, cum estis, inquit, in Christo vos cir- cumcisi. Neque enim mortali manu, sed Spiritu sancto talis sit circumcisio. Nec partem aliquam, sed totum hominem circumcidit. De posteriori sic loquitur in sua paraphrasi: Ibi quidem (in circumcisione ex- terna) pudendum illud virile circumcisione tegitur, carneo illo velamine dempto; hic vero corpus omne nostrum expoliatur, nudaturque, quia peccata de- muntur, quæ per carnem committimus. Circumci- sionem itaque hujusmodi non lex ipsa prætendit, sed Christus, cum nos in baptismo veteri vitæ & pecca- to obnoxios, & carni penitus deditos denudet & spo- liet. Quod vero sit non per peccatorum ejectio- nem, sed remissionem, quia peccata tolluntur in baptismo, non ut non insint, sed ut non imputentur, ut habet Vulgata Augustini regula. Per corpus qui- dem corpus nostrum proprie intelligere videtur, sed rectius de corpore peccati, interprete Calvino, fatente etiam Grotio id accipitur, quod corpus peccatorum carnis dicitur, quia ex corrupta car- nali generatione oritur; vel etiam quia congeries ista vitiorum in carne sese exerit, vel parte hominis nondum regenita, ut habet versio B. Lutheri, & in- terpretatio Crocii, aut certe corpus nostrum non intelligendum erit ἁπλῶς ratione substantiæ (hoc enim in baptismo non deponi sed retineri, con- stat) quemadmodum nec per veterem hominem in baptismo suffocandum homo simpliciter in sua substantia denotatur, sed qua peccato vitiatum totum & corruptum est, ut B. Hunnius explicat.

Vetus Interpres hic ingessit Adversativam, quam nec Græci Codices habent, nec Syri, & omisit vo- cem PECCATORUM, & sensum plane ita per- vertit: In quo & circumcisi estis circumcisione non manufacta in exspoliatione corporis carnis, SED in circumcisione Christi, consepulti ei in baptismo, quasi sensus sit, interprete Cornelio: Vos ô Chri- stiani Colossenses circumcisi estis circumcisione non Judaica, quæ sit manibus, quæque consistit in expo- liatione corporis carnei, qua nimirum de corpore carneo præscinditur præputium, sed circumcisi estis in circumcisione, id est, circumcisione (est enim Ebræum Beth contactus) Christi, qua non corpus, sed animam à peccatis circumcidit. Si quæratis, ubi & quando ita à Christo circumcisi sitis? Respondeo in baptismo, nimirum hoc ipso, quo Christo in baptismo estis consepulti: In baptismo enim non tantum cir- cumciduntur, sed sepeliuntur, & aquis piaculari- bus obruuntur, & absorbentur peccata omnia. Re- probat hic ingenue Romanam editionem Estius: Male quidam præponunt adversativam particulam SED, repugnantibus omnibus probatis exemplari- bus. Reprobat & sensum Cornelii: Sensum hunc Græca scriptura non admittit, tum quia pro non manufacta Græcis unum est nomen infinitum, uti jam diximus, ut proinde negatio in ea inclusa vim suam ad sequentia non exerat tum propter Geniti- vum, (peccatorum) inter corporis & carnis interpo- situm, qui cogit intelligi spiritualem circumcisionem: Ac tertio quia pro exspoliatione vocabulum est, quod significat actum exuendi, Theophylacti interpres ex- utionem vertit; quæ vox incommode nimis refertur ad externam illam circumcisionem, qua præputium carnis amputabatur. Unde secundum Græcam le- ctionem, & omnium Græcorum interpretationem hunc reddere sensum oportet: Per quem Christum etiam circumcisi estis non illa externa & carnali, sed interna & spirituali circumcisione, quæ fit sine manibus, & qua non una pellicula demitur, sed corpus peccatorum carnis, id est, totus vetus homo deponitur atque exuitur, quæ est circumcisio Chri- sto propria, non Mosi. Igitur corpus peccatorum carnis, quod hac Christi circumcisione exui dicit Apostolus, idem est cum veteri homine, quem & ali- bi vocat corpus peccati Rom. VI. Adde quod per ex- ternam circumcisionem non exutum fuerit cor- pus, sed minima pellicula unius membri præcisa. Alii exponunt hanc exuitionem corporis peccati car- nis etiam de renovatione, quod circumcisi dican- tur, cum veterem illum hominem cum suis pravis cupiditatibus exuerunt, ut Crocius habet; sed quum præcipuus scopus Apostoli sit, excludere à salutis negotio alia omnia extra Christum, ejusque redemptionem & reconciliationem, attigit qui- ob analogiam circumcisionis & baptismi indicandam Apostolus illam interiorem circumcisionem, sed quia in ea salus nostra non consistit, ad primarium baptismi finem, & tractationis suæ scopum hanc ἀπεκδύσεως spectare credendum est, remissionem peccatorum, quam nonnisi per fidem in Christum habemus.

Nam ejus ratione tota illa congeries ℘ massa peccatorum exuitur, nempe quod ad reatum: Corpus enim peccati, non partem aut membra quædam tantum exuimus, ut fatetur Crocius, ideo corpus nominari, non item ratione renovationis nostræ, etsi ejusdem etiam lavacrum fit baptismus, Tit. III. vers. 5. Jubentur enim postea cap. III. mortificare membra, quæ in terra sunt; non ergo eadem plane exuta sunt in baptismo quoad renovationem, quæ incipit tantum, non vero completa est. Agnoscit id Crotius, quod non plene & perfecte uno momento totum peccatorum corpus deponatur in baptismo, sed quod quoad reatum saltem plene, quoad corruptionem autem incipiamus solum exuere actus.

Denique condonationem peccatorum intenti ab Apostolo clare innuitur, cum v. 13. ea expresse nominatur, & causa ejusdem meritoria adducitur crux Christi, per quam deletum est chirographum legis, quod contra nos erat. Quæ & sequentibus clariora erunt.

## 2:12
V. 12. Buried with him in baptism) He commemorates the fact among Christians, which baptism figures.

For in baptism, as it was once administered, there was an image both of burial and resurrection, both of the visible Christ and the internal one in Christians, Rom. VI. 4. In whom also you are risen) Through whom you have also risen from the vices, which are called death, Matth. VIII. 22. Through the faith of the operation of God who raised him from the dead) Here the genitive of operation signifies the object of faith. So also Eph. III. 12. Philipp. I. 27. III. 9. He who believes that God was so powerful that He raised Christ from the dead, at the same time believes that power is not lacking to God to raise others also: to which power the promise is added, and deservedly the matter is held as certain.

The same sense is in Eph. I. 19. 24. V. 13. And you being dead in your trespasses) Being here has a past sense: We who were immersed in sins, and as it were dead.

The same sense and almost the same words, Eph. II. 1. &c. true life is to live for God. Others explain dead as a debtor of death, as Gen. XX. 3. And in the uncircumcision of your flesh) Just as the cleansing from vices is called circumcision by metaphor: so the vicious state is uncircumcision, by which name the Hebrews call everything that is to be cut off.

Wherefore that which signifies uncircumcision in Lev. XIX. 23 is translated as uncleanness. He has quickened you together with him) Just as He conferred new life on Christ from the death of the body: so also to us new life from the death of our souls. Having forgiven us all trespasses) Eph. IV. 32. The Latins also use 'to give' for 'to forgive'. Cicero said 'to give' enmities, Lucan VII 'to give' a penalty, 'to give' crimes, book XI, 'to give' labors, 'to give' wickedness in the same book. But since 'having forgiven' is of the past tense, the remission here is to be understood as to a certain thing, that is, to be made manifest, which would lead to repentance. See Luke XXIII. 33 and what is said there.

The Apostle explains what he had said about the putting off of the body of the sins of the flesh, and that with words both figurative and proper.

Figurative is the burial in baptism and the resurrection and quickening. Therefore he now names baptism, so that we may understand that in the same and through the same the body of sin is put off, and he does not make baptism merely a figure of the burial and resurrection, whether of Christ or of Christians; but the medium by which, what is partly ours by the death and burial, and also the quickening and resuscitation of Christ, is applied through faith, so that we may be rendered partakers of the fruit of the same.

By which name we are said to be buried with Christ in baptism, and since burial presupposes death, it is also hinted that we die with Christ, just as later in v. 13 we are expressly said to be QUICKENED with Christ, and also to be raised with Christ in the same baptism v. 12, and that all through faith in Christ, as that through which alone we are rendered partakers of the fruit of the death and burial and resurrection of Christ, as the Apostle taught, Rom. IV. 25, namely by believing in him as having died for our sins, and having been raised for our righteousness, so that in him and through him we may obtain the remission of sins and righteousness.

Because we are rendered partakers of this in baptism, we are said here to be buried and raised with Christ. Namely, we die with Christ, insofar as we become partakers of the death of Christ, as it is satisfactory and pacificatory and reconciliatory, Col.

I. 14, 19: For since that one died for all, in the judgment of God it is the same as if we had all died, and had rendered satisfaction to God. Whence the Apostle says we are dead with Christ, Col. III. 3, since he willed to be buried, so that our wickednesses might be placed in his sepulchre, Ef. LIII. 9, and the sins for which he died, and Ef. LIII. 9 which he had carried in his body upon the tree, he might bring with him into the sepulchre, so that they might be hidden from the face of God, and we in baptism might obtain the communion of his burial, we are said to be buried together with him in baptism, which is the fruit of those buried and hidden sins of ours, figured by the immersion into water: Through the same immersion or washing we are rendered partakers through faith in Christ who died and was buried for us, so that they do not appear before the face of God, and condemn us.

And this is the prior application, namely concerning our sins, for which the solution or satisfaction by the death of Christ, whose abolition Ebr. IX. 15 and hiding from the face of God was the burial of Christ, as regards merit. But when we die with Christ through faith, and when we are buried with him through the same faith, this is the solution and that abolition of ours which we perform, and apply to ourselves, then in truth, as regards the act itself, or as regards the efficacy and effect, we are rendered partakers of the same, which the Apostle teaches happens in our baptism.

Furthermore, the other application concerns our righteousness, for which Christ is said to have been raised, Roman. IV. 25, because through the resuscitation and quickening he brought back to us eternal righteousness and salvation, of which we are likewise rendered partakers in baptism: Inasmuch as we have been raised with Christ, as regards the merit which we have in Christ delivered for our sins, and raised for our righteousness, and by that reason we are also said to be quickened with him, because life has been acquired for us, Epb.

II. 5. Of. VI. 2, so as regards efficacy, we obtain righteousness and life and salvation as the fruit of the death and resurrection of Christ through faith, and so we are said to be raised again and quickened with him, which happens in baptism, in which we put on Christ with his merits and righteousness, and are clothed by him with the garment of righteousness and salvation, conf. Gal. III. 27. Ef. LXI. 10, and are rendered righteous and heirs of eternal life, Tu. III. 7, whence baptism is said to save us, 1. Petr. III. 21. Therefore, it is not a resurrection from vices as death, which happens in renovation, that is indicated here, but a CO-RESUSCITATION with Christ, who certainly was not raised from vices.

And this co-burial, co-quickening, and co-resuscitation happens through faith, which is nothing other than the application of the benefits acquired for us by the death, burial, quickening, and resuscitation of Christ.

Concerning which the blessed Hunnius: He explains the manner of our quickening and regeneration in baptism, and testifies that it is effected through faith in Christ, by whose intervention, sins being remitted, man is raised to the light of that spiritual life.

This faith is called the faith of the operation of God, not because it is directed toward the operation of God as its object, or toward the power of God which raises from the dead: for these are not the object of salvific or justifying faith; nor was it necessary to speak here of the power of God to be believed, as Chrysostom and Theophylact indeed thought, but rather of the method of obtaining salvation. Grotius himself here intimates that faith looks not so much to the power of God as to the grace made manifest in the Evangelical promises, of which, however, there is no mention here.

But faith is called τῆς ἐνεργείας τοῦ Θεοῦ, τῇ ἐγείραντος αὐτὸν ἐκ νεκρῶν, by reason of the cause, because it is of the same operation and efficacy to work faith in us as it was to raise Christ from the dead, as the Apostle taught in Eph. 1:19, which is illustrated by what follows: For before our regeneration, and before divine grace works faith in us, we are dead in sins, both on account of guilt, because we are debtors to death, which is the wages of sin, Rom.

6:last, and also as regards dominion, because we are so given over and subjected to sins, or sold under sin, and dead to it. Whence we are nothing but the foreskin of the flesh in a spiritual sense within us, we are flesh, and uncircumcised in heart and in our members, because whatever is born of the flesh is flesh, John 3:5. For the foreskin signifies uncleanness, Deut. 10:16, Jer. 4:4, cf. Lev. 19:23. Therefore, he understands not only original sin with the interlinear gloss and Lyranus; not only actual, carnal sins with the ordinary gloss, but all sins: for it follows concerning the forgiveness of all sins.

Guil. Estius makes and defends the Vulgate exposition of this place: God, when you had previously been spiritually dead through your offenses or sins, in which you lived, and through the foreskin of your flesh, that is, through the concupiscence and works of the flesh signified by the foreskin (for all these are a kind of death of the soul), has now, together with Christ rising, recalled you to spiritual life. Through regeneration and the operation of faith in us, we are freed from that death and recalled to the life which is from God, so that, rendered participants of the spiritual circumcision, or renewed by the Spirit, we may walk in newness of life.

In order that he might more effectively impress upon the minds of the Colossians these moments of affairs, in which the sum of our salvation consists, says the Blessed Hunnius, he instituted an antithesis between their former misery under Heathenism and the supreme and admirable happiness that followed under the Gospel.

Intending to express their former lot, he says: that they were dead in sins, understanding death not as that which is defined by the separation of souls from their bodies, but as the most sorrowful separation of the whole man from eternal life. He establishes the offenses as the beginning and cause of this great unhappiness, both the original one in which they were born, and the actual ones which spring from the original as from a poisonous fountain. This evil of origin, with its effects, namely actual sins, he calls the foreskin of the flesh, not understanding a fleshy membrane, which, like the rest of the body of man, has God as its author, and therefore cannot be held as sin; but by the word foreskin, he metaphorically strikes at the impurity of a nature luxuriating and inclining toward all evils.

SIMUL VIVIFICAVIT, the other part of the antithesis, explains the ineffable blessedness into which the Colossians were placed through Christ, by no merit of their own. Where the benefit mentioned above is repeated, namely vivification, or our being raised to spiritual and eternal life through Christ.

Which the Apostle now expresses in his own words, χαρισάμενος ἡμῖν πάντα τὰ παραπτώματα. Which are clearer than light. If GOD forgives us our sins, this is mere grace: our holiness or renovation contributes nothing here, our works nothing. For thus the χάρις, the grace of God, is proclaimed. But if it is by grace, it is not by works, otherwise grace would not be grace, Rom. 11:6, Eph. 4:7, 12. If that πλήρωσις of ours is situated in the forgiveness of sins, then it is not to be sought in our holiness or renovation.

If he vivified us with Christ in baptism, our sins being forgiven, and all of them at that, then there is no need for circumcision, nor should it be required as necessary for salvation. Why should they be compelled to cut off a particle of one member, who had already been buried with Christ as to the old man, and raised as to the new in baptism through faith? This would be nothing else than to stubbornly deny both the burial and resurrection of Christ and the communion which the saints have obtained with Him in baptism through faith, as Crocius says here.

Nor does reformation to the divine image make for this; for the Apostle says nothing of that. Crocius indeed wishes it to be said that Christ has recalled us to spiritual life, both by reforming the divine image lost through sin, and by taking away the guilt contracted through sin. But the Apostle only commemorates the latter, our sins being forgiven, although we do not deny that the former is connected with it; yet here, where he explains the method of obtaining eternal life, it is neither commemorated by the Apostle, nor has it a place, as it consists in faith alone and is absolved by the gratuitous remission of sins, without any intuition of our holiness.

Latin:

V. 12. Συνταφέντες αὐτῷ ἐν τῷ βαπτίσματι) Commemorat factum in Christianis, quod baptisma figurat.

Erat enim in baptisate, sicut olim administrabatur, imago & sepulturæ & resurrectionis, tum conspicuæ Christi, tum internæ in Christianis, Rom. VI. 4. Ἐν ᾧ καὶ συνηγέρθητε) Per quem & resurrexistis ex vitiis, quæ mors nominantur, Matth. VIII. 22. Διὰ τῆς πίστεως τῆς ἐνεργείας τοῦ Θεοῦ τοῦ ἐγείραντος αὐτὸν ἐκ νεκρῶν) Hic Genitivus ἐνεργείας objectum fidei significat. Sic & Eph. III. 12. Philipp. I. 27. III. 9. Qui credit Deum tam potentem fuisse, ut Christum à mortuis excitaverit, is simul credit, Deo non deesse potentiam, ut & alios excitet: cui potentiæ accedat promissio, merito ea res pro certa habetur.

Idem sensus Eph. I. 19. 24. V. 13. Καὶ ὑμᾶς νεκροὺς ὄντας ἐν τοῖς παραπτώμασι) Ὄντας hic sensum habet præteritum: Nos qui peccatis eramus immersi, ac velut immortui.

Idem sensus & ferme eadem verba, Eph. II. 1. &c. vera vita est Deo vivere. Alii mortuum exponunt mortis debitorem, ut Gen. XX. 3. Καὶ τῇ ἀκροβυστίᾳ τῆς σαρκὸς ὑμῶν) Sicut purgatio à vitiis per Metaphoram vocatur circumcisio: Ita status vitiosus ἀκροβυστία, quo nomine Ebræi appellant omne id, quod amputandum est. Quare ℘ quod ἀκροβυστίας lignificat Lev.

XIX. 23. vertitur ἀκαθαρσία. Συνεζωοποίησεν ὑμᾶς σὺν αὐτῷ) Sicut Christo novam contulit vitam ex morte corporis: Ita & nobis novam ex morte animorum. Χαρισάμενος ἡμῖν πάντα τὰ παραπτώματα) Eph. IV. 32. Donare pro condonare etiam Latini usurpant. Donare inimicitias dixit Cicero, pœnam donare Lucanus VII. donare crimina, libr. XI. labores donare, donare nefas eodem libro. Cum autem χαρισάμενος fit præteriti temporis, intelligenda hic remissio ad certum quid, id est, ad patefaciendam, quæ ad pœnitentiam duceret.

Vid. Luc. XXIII. 33. & ibi dicta. Explicat Apostolus, quod dixerat de ἀπεκδύσεως τοῦ σώματος τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν τῆς σαρκός, idque cum verbis figuratis, tum propriis.

Figuratis sepultura in baptismo & resurrectionis ac vivificationis. Baptismum ergo jam nominat, ut intelligamus, in eodem & per eundem exui corpus peccati, nec vero baptismum figuram tantum facit sepulturæ & resurrectionis sive Christi, sive Christianorum; sed medium quo, quod morte & sepultura, nec non vivificatione ac resuscitatione Christi nobis partim est, applicatur per fidem, ut fructus ejusdem participes reddamur. Quo nomine dicimur cum Christo sepeliri in baptismo, & quum sepultura præsupponat mortem, mori etiam nos cum Christo innuitur, quemadmodum postea v. 13.

CONVIVIFICARI cum Christo expresse dicimur, nec non cum Christo resuscitari in eodem baptisate v.

12. idque o- mne dia τῆς πίστεως per fidem in Christum, utpote per quam unice fructus mortis Christi & sepulturæ ac resuscitationis participes reddimur, ut docuit Apostolus, Rom. IV. 25. nimirum credendo in ipsum ceu propter peccata nostra mortuum, & propter justitiam nostram resuscitatum, ut in ipso & per ipsum remissionem peccatorum & justitiam consequamur. Cujus quia in baptismo participes reddimur, cum Christo sepeliri & resuscitari hic dicimur. Nimirum morimur cum Christo, quatenus mortis Christi, prout ea est satisfactoria & pacificatoria ac reconciliatoria, Col.

I. 14. 19. consortes evadimus: Cum enim unus ille pro omnibus mortuus est, in judicio Dei idem est, ac si omnes mortui essemus, ac Deo satisfactionem præstitissemus. Unde nos mortuos cum Christo dicit Apostolus, Col. III. 3. cum is sepeliri voluerit, ut ponerentur in sepulchro ejus improbitates nostræ, Es. LIII. 9. & peccata propter quæ mortuus est, & Es. LIII. 9. quæ portaverat in corpore suo super lignum, inferret secum in sepulchrum, ut à facie Dei absconderentur, nosque in baptismo communionem sepulturæ ejus nanciscamur, consepulti dicimur cum ipso in baptismo, qui fructus illius sepultorum & absconditorum peccatorum nostrorum, immersionem in aquam figurati: Per eandem immersionem sive ablutionem participes per fidem in Christum pro nobis mortuum & sepultum reddimur, ne illa coram facie Dei compareant, nosq; condemnent. Atque hæc prior applicatio, nempe concernens peccata nostra, pro quibus solutio vel satisfactio morte Christi, quorum ἀθέτησις, Ebr.

IX. 15. & absconsio à facie Dei sepultura Christi facta est, quantum ad meritum. Cum autem morimur cum Christo per fidem, & cum sepelimur cum eo eodem per fidem, hoc est solutionem & ἀθέτησιν illam nostram facimus, nobisque applicamus, tum revera, quoad actum ipsum, vel quantum ad efficaciam & effectum, reddimur ejusdem participes, quod in baptismo nostro fieri docet Apostolus.

Altera porro applicatio concernit justitiam nostram, ob quam Christus dicitur resuscitatus, Roman. IV. 25. quia per resuscitationem & vivificationem reduxit nobis æternam justitiam ac salutem, cujus in baptismo itidem reddimur participes: Siquidem ut cum Christo resuscitati sumus, quantum ad meritum, quod in Christo propter peccata nostra tradito, & propter justitiam nostram resuscitato habemus, eaque ratione vivificati etiam cum ipso dicimur, quia vita nobis acquisita est, Epb.

II. 5. Of. VI. 2. ita quantum ad efficaciam, consequimur justitiam & vitam ac salutem ceu fructum mortis & resurrectionis Christi per fidem, adeoque ita conresuscitari & vivificari cum ipso dicimur, id quod contingit in baptismo, in quo Christum cum meritis & justitia ejus induimus, ac veste justitiæ & salutis ab ipso amicimur, conf. Gal. III. 27. Es. LXI. 10. ac justi & hæredes vitæ æternæ reddimur, Tu. III. 7. unde baptismus nos salvos facere dicitur, 1. Petr. III. 21. Non ergo hic resurrectio ex vitiis ceu morte, quæ fit in renovatione, indigitatur, sed CONRESUSCITATIO cum Christo, qui certe è vitiis resuscitatus non est.

Et fit hæc consepultura, convivificatio ac conresuscitatio διὰ τῆς πίστεως per fidem, quæ quid aliud est, quam applicatio beneficiorum morte, sepultura, vivificatione ac resuscitatione Christi nobis acquisitorum. De quo B.

Hunnius: Modum explicat nostræ in baptismo, vivificationis & regenerationis, eamque per fidem in Christum effici testatur, cujus interventu remissis peccatis, homo ad illius spiritualis vita lucem resuscitatur.

Quæ fides dicitur operationis Dei, non quod in operationem Dei ceu objectum feratur, aut in virtutem Dei, quæ resuscitat ex mortuis: Hæc enim non sunt objectum fidei salvificæ aut justificæ; nec de potentia Dei credenda dicendum hic erat, uti quidem putavit Chrysostomus & Theophylactus, sed de ratione consequendi salutem, neq; tam potentiam Dei, quam gratiam in promissionibus Evangelicis factam fidem respicere Grotius hic ipse subinnuit, quarum tamen hic nulla mentio.

Dicitur autem fides τῆς ἐνεργείας τοῦ Θεοῦ, τῇ ἐγείραντος αὐτὸν ἐκ νεκρῶν, ratione causæ, quod ejusdem operationis & efficaciæ fit fidem in nobis operari, cujus erat resuscitare Christum à mortuis, ut Eph. I. 19. docuit Apostolus, quod illustrant ea, quæ sequuntur: Nam ante nostri regenerationem, & antequam fidem in nobis operetur divina gratia, nos in peccatis mortui sumus, tum ob reatum, quod mortis debitores, quæ stipendium peccati est, Rom.

VI. ult. tum quoad dominium, quod tantum peccatis dediti & fubjecti fimus, vel venundati sub peccatum, eique immortui. Unde nihil nisi præputium carnis sensu spirituali in nobis, caro sumus, & incircumcisi corde & membris nostris, quia quicquid ex carne natum est, caro est, Joh. III. 5. Præputium enim significat immunditiem, Deut. X. 16. Jerem. IV. 4 conf. Lev. XIX. 23. Non ergo tantum originale peccatum cum interlineari gloffa & Lyrano; non tantum actualia, carnalia cum gloffa ordinaria, sed peccata omnia intelligit: Sequitur enim de peccatorum omnium condonatione, Vulgatam expositionem hujus loci hanc facit ac tuetur Guil. tstus: Deus vos cum antes fuissetis spiritualiter mortui per delicta, feu peccata vestra, in quibus vivebatis, & per præputium carnis vestre, id est per concupiscentiam & opera carnis præputio significata (hæc enim omnia sunt mors quædam animæ) nunc una cum Christo resurgente, revocavit ad vitam spiritualem.

Per regenerationem autem fideique operationem in nobis à morte illa liberamur, & in vitam, quæ ex Deo est, revocamur, ut circumcisionis spiritualis etiam participes redditi, vel renovati per Spiritum in novitate vitæ ambulemus.

Ut hæc momenta rerum, inquit B. Hunnius, in quibus salutis nostræ summa consistit, efficacius animis Colossensium imprimeret, antithesin instituit pristine illorum miferiæ sub Ethnicismo, & infecutæ sub Evangelio summæ & admirandæ felicitatis.

Sortem pristinam expressurus ait: illos fuisse mortuos in peccatis, mortem intelligens, non qua distractione definitur animarum à corporibus suis, sed tristissima separatione totius hominis à vita eterna. Hujus tanta infelicitatis principium & causam constituit delicta cum originale, in quo nati sunt, tum actualia, quæ ex originali, tanquam venenato fonte, scaturiunt. Quod originis malum cum suis effectibus, nempe peccatis actualibus, vocat præputium carnis, non pelliculam carneam intelligens, quæ ut & reliquum corpus hominis Deum habet auctorem, ideoque pro peccato haberi nequit; sed præputii voce μεταφορικῶς impuritatem perstringens natura luxuriantis & ad mala omnia propendentis.

SIMUL VIVIFICAVIT altera pars antitheseos explicat ineffabilem beatitudinem, in quam per Christum, nullo suo merito sint collocati Colossenses. Ubi repetitur beneficium supra dictum, vivificatio scilicet, feu nostri ad vitam spiritualem & eternam per Christum resuscitato.

Quod propriis verbis jam ita effert Apostolus, χαρισάμενος ἡμῖν πάντα τὰ παραπτώματα. Quæ luce clariora sunt. Si DEUS condonat nobis peccata, mera hic est gratia: nihil confert huc nostra sanctitas aut renovatio, nihil opera nostra. Sic enim χάρις gratia Dei deprædicatur. Si autem ex gratia, non ex operibus, alioquin gratia non esset gratia, Rom. XI. 6. Eph. IV. 7. 12. Si in peccatorum condonatione illa nostra πλήρωσις sita, non ergo in nostra sanctitate aut renovatione quærenda.

Si vivificavit nos cum Christo in baptismo, condonatis nobis peccatis, iusque omnibus, non ergo opus circumcisione, nec ea ceu necessaria requirenda ad salutem. Cur ad particulam unius membri præcidendam essent compellendi, qui quod veterem hominem totum jam erant cum Christo sepulti, & quoad novum resuscitati in baptismo per fidem? Hoc nihil esset aliud, quam & sepulturam & resurrectionem Christi & communionem, quam sancti per fidem cum eo in baptismo sunt consecuti, præfracte abnegare, ut hic Crocius.

Neque huc facit reformatio ad imaginem divinam; de ea enim nihil Apostolus. Crocius sane in vitam spiritualem Christum nos revocasse dici vult, cum reformando imaginem divinam per peccatum amissam, tum auferendo reatum per peccatum contractum. Sed Apostolus posterius hoc tantum commemorat, condonatis nobis omnibus peccatis, cum quom etiam si illud connexum non diffiteamur; hic tamen ubi explicat rationem consequendæ æternæ vitæ, nec commemoratur ab Apostolo, nec locum habet, utpote quæ sola fide constat, ac gratuita peccatorum remissione absolvitur, fine nostræ sanctitatis intuitu.

## 2:14
V. 14. Ἐξαλείψας τὸ καθ’ ἡμῶν χειρόγραφον τοῖς δόγμασι) A comparison of the passage Eph. 2:15 shows that τὸ χειρόγραφον is the positive law of Moses, the law of commandments. And there, καὶ κεχειρογραφας, which is wont to be said of the law, here ἐξαλείψας, which is said of a handwriting and other things which are written חוב.

A creditor erasing a bond is understood by that very act to remit the debt, just as one who returns a promissory note. Thus, he who cancels a legacy frees the heir. The law of Moses is called χειρόγραφον by a certain similarity, because the people had bound themselves to keep the law, Deut. 27, Neh. 10. When he says חוב, he understands the Jews: for that law did not hold the Gentiles. Χειρόγραφον is the שטר התחייבות of the Hebrews in the prayers of the Jews. Τοῖς δόγμασι) by his doctrine.

See what we have said on the twin passage to this one in the Epistle to the Ephesians. Ὁ ἦν ὑπεναντίον ἡμῖν) which pressed upon us. חוב to press, whence the noun חוב, which in many places is translated ὑπεναντίος. See on this Acts 15:10. Καὶ αὐτὸ ἦρεν ἐκ τοῦ μέσου) Ἐκ μέσου ἀνελεῖν, even for the more elegant Greeks, such as Demosthenes, is to take away so that it does not appear. Thus ἐξέρχεσθαι ἐκ μέσου, Acts 17:33, 2 Cor. 6:17. Ἀπάξων ἐκ μέσου, Acts 23:10, ἐξαίρων ἐκ μέσου, 1 Cor. 5:2, ἐκ μέσου γίνεσθαι, 2 Thess.

2:7. Προσλώσας αὐτὸ τῷ σταυρῷ) It is the custom in some places to transfix antiquated edicts with nails. This seems to have been the case in Asia at that time, and Paul alludes to it. The subject here is not the positive law of Moses, as Crocius opines with Grotius; nor is it a parallel passage to Eph. 2:15. The subject is the moral law, on account of which we are all debtors, Rom. 3:19, 22. Therefore, we are all as it were convicted by a handwriting, and when we fail in paying, we are ordered to sell everything, and ourselves as well, Matt.

18:25; but because God forgives us all debts out of grace on account of Christ and His reconciliation, the handwriting which was against us is said to be erased. Nor does this debt and handwriting, this forgiveness of debt and erasure of the handwriting, concern only the Jews, but also the Gentiles. Paul is speaking of the Colossians, among whom there were more converted to CHRIST from Heathenism than from Judaism. The Apostle had dealt with the application of salvation, now he deals with the acquisition.

As he constituted the former in the remission of sins: so he attributes the latter to Christ, insofar as He erased the handwriting contrary to us, from which it was evident that we were debtors to God, liable to sins, and thus guilty of condemnation. By this handwriting, Ambrose understands sin, as do Haymo and Arias Montanus; but the debt, which is sin, is one thing, and the handwriting, which testifies to our debt, is another. Others understand the Decalogue or that obligation, Exod.

Exod. XXIV. 7.

All things which the Lord hath said, we will do: But the Decalogue is not deleted, nor that obligation expunged. Chrysostom & Theophylact explaining the decree of Gen. II. 17, which brought an obligation to death. Others interpret more conveniently the force of the moral law obliging to damnation; to which sense Sarisburiensis agrees; or rather the sentences laid down in the Mosaic decrees, which were like a handwriting, because they convicted us of debts, and on account of them rendered us guilty of death.

Moses did not indeed do this by himself through his legal decrees, so as to render us guilty, but insofar as we violated the precepts divinely proposed, which were proposed so that they might be observed: Properly, therefore, this handwriting is born from the comparison of legal decrees with our transgression, and it is our very conscience's conviction, and the divine conclusion under sin, Gal. III. 22. Rom. XI. 32. Therefore Thomas interprets it concerning the memory of sins in the mind of God and of the sinner. For Christ acted so that God might not wish to remember our sins. The locution is metaphorical, as if by contracting debts of sins we hand over into the hand of divine justice the obligation of legal decrees, to exact those debts from us.

Which obligation, which is the handwriting, Christ deleted with his own blood, and took out of the midst, having been affixed to the cross, in which, as B. Hunnius speaks, dying for our sins, as if by one stroke, by the profusion of his blood, he struck out and deleted all that sum of debts, and professed it to be fully dissolved to God the Father, while he took away the curse intended and dictated to us through the decree of the moral law, having himself become a curse for us.

What B. Hunnius adds concerning the Levitical abrogation of the law, although they are most true, I doubt, however, whether that obligation concerning the ceremonial law, which handwriting was proper to the Jews, or its abrogation through the exhibition of his own body, sufficiently agrees with this treatment, where it is a matter of the manner of obtaining salvation, and that not only to the Jews, but also common to the Gentiles. For although the Apostle includes himself with Timothy by the word 'of us' (ἡμῶν), yet these things concern not only the Jews, but also the Gentiles, just as in the third person, 'you were buried,' 'you rose again together,' the Apostle speaks no less than in the second, so that he may make the application, which is made through faith, more clearly to them and to himself; that it is argued here against the Judaizers, which Efius also wishes, cannot be proven. For the Apostle differs concerning the forgiveness of sins and its meritorious cause, which pertain to all.

But against the Judaizers follows v. 16, the refutation of the Apostle. 'To the decrees' (Τοῖς δόγμασι) is not to be referred to the word 'having blotted out' (ἐξαλείψας), as Efius wishes, as also Grotius, through his doctrine, as if the handwriting were said to be deleted by Christ through Evangelical doctrine: But to 'that which was against us' (τὸ καθ' ἡμῶν); because that handwriting was against us by the decrees of the Mosaic law. For it is not a matter of the deletion which is made through the Word, but which was made on the cross of Christ: Since if he deleted it so, it is said, that he took it out of the midst and affixed it to the cross, by which is indicated that that deletion of the handwriting was made through the death of Christ exhausted on the cross, because through the same the payment was performed for us, therefore the handwriting is said to be affixed to the cross as if already expunged, so that it might be plain to all concerning the payment. By which very grand and magnificent speech he renders us certain of the forgiveness of all our offenses, just as the Apostle further pursues the liberation from our enemies with a similar kind of diction and magnificence.

And not only, he says, Theophylact saying, did he delete, but he took out of the midst, that is, he brought it about that that handwriting might nowhere appear. And he did not confer it upon you, but affixing it to the cross he tore it asunder: which is without doubt a sign of one forgiving with a willing mind. For we were all subject to the sin of bread, while he himself, who committed nothing, afflicted with torments and tortures for us, dissolved our sins and punishments on the cross, and in it he tore the handwriting.

The things which Crocius has here are foreign, although specious: Christ nailed the ceremonial laws with the same nails by which he was crucified, on the same cross, so that they might henceforth have no force, or convict the faithful of sin, no otherwise than as handwritings are wont to be cancelled, and torn or defunct to be suspended from nails, after the debt has been paid. For he did not affix the ceremonial laws to the cross as hostile and contrary to us, but he fulfilled them as figures and types, of which the Apostle is not now speaking, but afterwards v. 17. which are a shadow, but the body is Christ's: These things are most different: Christ fulfilled the figures as body, because with his succeeding the shadows ceased; and the ceremonial laws, as contrary to us, were dissolved by Christ and affixed to the cross. In the sacrifices there was rather the deletion of sins, both figured typically and applied ritely, when they were offered through faith, than a handwriting contrary to us, which ought to be deleted through Christ on his cross.

Crocius says: As if the ceremonial law seemed to promise the deletion of sins: There was in the rites a confession of sins rather than a true expiation. That is not altogether true. It was not so much a confession of sins as the expiation of the sacrifice of Christ that was to be exhibited there. For sins could be brought and were confessed in many other ways by prayers, fasts, public confessions, so that there would have been no need for sacrifices; which indeed were instituted to represent the unique propitiatory sacrifice of the New Testament, and were to be offered through faith in the Messiah adumbrated therein to obtain the expiation of sins. The confession of sins was more prior to the sacrifice than intrinsic to the same, or of the essence of the sacrifice. But the representation of the sacrifice of Christ was as it were the form for the expiatory sacrifices, without which they were not, which they ought to have been by divine institution. They saw indeed sins as it were punished in those sacrifices which they offered: But it was not figured that they were to be punished in themselves, but in Christ, by handing them over into sacrifice for our sins. Vicarious satisfaction was therefore exhibited in them more than the condemnation of men. Therefore one must not seek in them a handwriting, which was against men through the decrees of the law, but one must seek rather the death of Christ, the deletory of the handwriting, and the expiatory of sin, through which we were subject to condemnation.

One must observe here the altogether beautiful and most pious gloss of Camerarius: 'To the decrees' (Τοῖς δόγμασιν), the usual ellipsis of 'with' (σὺν), together with the decree. Some Greeks, however, 'through the decrees' (dià τῶν δογμάτων), have interpreted it more inconsiderately, that is, through the decrees of piety and faith in him. For dogmas are legitimate choices, as in the epistle written to the Ephesians. But the speech is copious and in this place 'in the covered perseverance' (ἐν τῇ καλυμμένη ἐπιμονῇ).

He deleted, he took out of the midst.

He tore asunder 'by the nailing' (τῇ προσηλώσει).

What then? the obligation of our hand. Why therefore is anything else done or sought? and rather are not all the powers of all men strained, and the whole effort expended in giving thanks to the Liberator for so great a benefit. Τὰς γὰρ ἁμαρτίας ἡμῶν ἀναλαβὼν ὁ κύριος, κ. οἰκειοποιησάμενος τὴν ἡμῶν ὀφειλομένην δίκην αὐτὸς ἔδωκεν ὑπὲρ αὐτῶν — For the Lord having taken up our sins, κ. having made his own the penalty owed by us, he himself gave for them, just as the Greeks have most excellently commented on this place.

O Son of God, Savior Christ, kindle by thy Holy Spirit this light of saving knowledge in my dark mind also, so that from the contemplation of thy love my love may burn, and in me all things may be restrained, and mine may vanish. But thy truth and faith may flourish and be exercised, which is your work, in the elaborating of which let the thought of my mind and the inclination of my will and the study of my diligence serve your will, Amen.

Latin:

V. 14. Ἐξαλείψας τὸ καθ’ ἡμῶν χειρόγραφον τοῖς δόγμασι) Collatio loci Eph. II. 15. ostendit τὸ χειρόγραφον esse τὸν νόμον τῶν ἐντολῶν legem Mosis positivam. Et ibi καὶ κεχειρογραφας quod de lege dici solet, hic ἐξαλείψας quod de chirographo & rebus aliis, quæ scribuntur חוב.

Creditor delens cautionem, eo ipso remittere debitum intelligitur, ut & qui chirographum reddit. Sic qui legatum inducit, bæredem liberat. Lex autem Mosis per similitudinem quandam χειρόγραφον dicitur, quia populus se ad legem servandam obitrinxerat, Deut. XXVII. Nah. x. Cum dicit חוב, Judæos intelligit: Gentes enim illa lex non tenebat. Χειρόγραφον Ebræis שטר התחייבות in precibus Judæorum. Τοῖς δόγμασι) per suam doctrinam.

Vide quæ diximus ad geminum huic locum illius ad Ephesios. Ὁ ἦν ὑπεναντίον ἡμῖν) quod nos premebat. חוב premere, unde nomen חוב, quod multis in locis vertitur ὑπεναντίος. Dere vide Act. XV. 10. Καὶ αὐτὸ ἦρεν ἐκ τοῦ μέσου) Ἐκ μέσου ἀνελεῖν etiam elegantioribus Græcis, ut Demostheni, est auferre, ne compareat. Sic ἐξέρχεσθαι ἐκ μέσου, Actor. XVII. 33. 2. Cor. VI. 17. Ἀπάξων ἐκ μέσου, Act. XXIII. 10. ἐξαίρων ἐκ μέσου, 1. Cor. V. 2. ἐκ μέσου γίνεσθαι, 2.

Thessal. II. 7. Προσλώσας αὐτὸ τῷ σταυρῷ) Mos est quibusdam in locis clavis transfigendi edicta antiquata. Is tunc etiam in Asia videtur fuisse, & ad eum alludere Paulus. Non agitur hic de lege positiva Mosis, uti cum Grotio opinatur Crocius; nec locus parallelus est Epb. II. 15. Agitur de lege morali, ob quam debitores omnes sumus, Rom. III. 19. 22. Ideo chirographo quasi convincimur omnes, & quum solvendo non deficimus, omnia vendere jubemur, & nosmet ipsos, Matth.

XIIX. v. 25. quia vero condonat nobis ex gratia propter Christum, ejusque reconciliationem, Deus omnia debita, deleri dicitur chirographum, quod adversus nos erat. Nec Judæos tantum concernit hoc debitum & chirographum, hæc debiti condonatio & chirographi deletio, sed etiam gentiles. De Colossensibus loquitur Paulus, inter quos plures erant è gentilismo, quam è Judaismo ad CHRISTUM conversi. Egerat Apostolus de applicatione salutis, jam de acquisitione agit.

Utillam in remissione peccatorum constituit: Ita hanc Christo tribuit, quatenus chirographum nobis contrarium, ex quo constabat, nos debitores esse Deo, peccatis obnoxios, adeoque condemnationis reos, delevit. Per hoc chirographum Ambrosius peccatum intelligit, ut & Haymo & Ariasmontanus; sed aliud est debitum, quod peccatum est, aliud autem chirographum, quod de debito nostro testatur. Alii decalogum intelligunt vel obligationem illam,

Exod. XXIV. 7.

Omnia quae dixerit Dominus, faciemus: Sed Decalogus non est deletus, nec obligatio illa expuncta. Chrysostomus & Theophylactus de decreto Gen. II. 17. explicans, quod obligationem ad mortem inferebat. Convenientius autem vim legis moralis obligantem ad damnationem alii interpretantur; cui sensui accedit Sarisburiensis; vel potius sententias in decretis Mosaicis latas, quae erant instar chirographi, quia debitorum nos convincebant, & ob ea nos reos peragebant mortis.

Non quidem per se id agebat Moses decretis suis legalibus, ut reos nos redderet, sed quatenus nos praecepta divinitus proposita violavimus, quae ut observarentur proposita erant: Proprie ergo hoc chirographum nascitur ex decretorum legalium cum nostra transgressione comparatione, estque ipsa conscientia nostra conviclio, & divina sub peccato conclusio, Gal. III. 22. Rom. XI. 32. Ideo Thomas de memoria peccatorum in mente Dei & peccatoris interpretatur. Christus n. fecit, ut Deus peccatorum nostrorum non velit meminisse. Loquutio est Metaphorica, ac si peccatorum debita contrahendo justitiae divinae obligationem vi legalium decretorum in manum tradamus, debita illa a nobis exigendi.

Quam obligationem, quod chirographum delevit Christus proprio suo sanguine, & e medio sustulit, affixum cruci fue, in qua pro peccatis, ut B. Hunnius loquitur, nostris moriens, una quasi litura, sanguinis sui profusione, omnem illam debitorum summam dispunxit ac delevit, & ad plenum Deo Patri dissolutam esse professus est, dum maledictionem per decretum legis moralis intentatam nobis ac dictatam sustulit, factus ipse pro nobis maledictio.

Quae addit B. Hunnius de Levitica legis abrogatione, etsi verissima sint, dubito tamen, an huic tractationi, ubi de ratione consequendi salutem agitur, eaq; non Judaeis tantum, sed & gentibus communi, satis conveniat illa vel de lege ceremoniabili obligatio, quod chirographum Judaeis proprium erat, vel ejusdem per corporis ipsius exhibitionem abrogatio. Nam quamvis se Apostolus cum Timotheo voce ἡμῶν simul comprehendat, non tamen Judaeos solum, sed etiam gentiles haec concernunt, quemadmodum in tertia persona, consepulti estis, simul resurrexistis, non minus quam in secunda loquitur Apostolus, ut applicationem, quae per fidem fit, tum ipsis, tum sibi eo luculentius faciat; contra Judaizantes hic quidem verbis agi, quod Efius etiam vult, probari non potest. Nam de condonatione peccatorum ejusque causa meritoria differit Apostolus, quae omnes attinent.

Adversus Judaizantes autem sequitur v. 16. elenchus Apostoli. Τοῖς δόγμασι non est referendum ad vocem ἐξαλείψας, ut Efius vult, ut & Grotius, per suam doctrinam, quasi per doctrinam Evangelicam dicatur deletum chirographum a Christo: Sed ad τὸ καθ' ἡμῶν; quod contra nos fuerit illud chirographum decretis legis Mosaicae. Nam non de deletione, quae per Verbum fit, sed quae facta est in cruce Christi, agitur: Siquidem ita delevit se illud dicatur, ut e medio sublatum affixerit cruci, quo indicatur per mortem Christi in cruce exantlatam illam chirographi deletionem factam, quia per eandem pro nobis praestita est solutio, ideo chirographum ceu jam expunctum cruci affixum dicitur, ut omnibus palam de solutione constaret. Qua oratione valde grandi & magnifica nos certos reddit de condonatione omnium delictorum nostrorum, quemadmodum liberationem ab hostibus nostris parili dictionis genere ac magnificentia porro persequitur Apostolus.

Nec solum, inquit Theophylacto dicente, delevit, sed e medio sustulit, hoc est, ne uspiam appareret chirographum illud effecit. Nec vobis contulit, sed illud cruci affigens dilaceravit: quod procul dubio est libenti animo dimittentis indicium. Omnes namque eramus peccato panis obnoxii, cum ipse, qui nihil commisisit, tormentis & cruciatibus pro nobis affellus, in cruce nostra peccata dissolvit & poenas, in eaque & chirographum scidit.

Aliena sunt, quae Crocius hic habet, etsi speciosa: Christus iisdem clavis, quibus crucifixus est, in eadem cruce fixit leges ceremoniales, ne deinceps vim ullam habeant, aut fideles convincant peccati, non aliter, quam chirographa cancellari, & lacerata aut defuncta ex clavis suspendi solent, postquam debitum est solutum. Leges enim ceremoniales non cruci affixit ceu nobis hostiles & contrarias, sed tanquam figuras & typus implevit, quo de jam non agit Apostolus, sed postmodum v. 17. quae sunt umbra, futurum autem corpus Christus est: Maxime haec diversa: Christus ut corpus implevit figuras, quia eo succedente cessarunt umbrae; & leges ceremoniales, ut nobis contrariae, a Christo sunt dissolutae, crucique affixae. In sacrificiis erat potius peccatorum deletio, & figurata typice & applicata rite, cum offerebantur per fidem, quam chirographum nobis contrarium, quod per Christum delendum fuerit in cruce ejus.

Dicit Crocius: Ut ut lex ceremonialis promittere videretur peccatorum deletionem: Erat in ritibus confessio magis peccatorum, quam expiatio vera. Id non usquequaque verum. Non tam peccatorum confessio, quam sacrificii Christi expiatio illic exhibenda erat. Poterant enim multis aliis modis peccata conferri & confitebantur precibus, jejuniis, confessionibus publicis, ut opus non fuisset sacrificiis; quae vero ad repraesentandum unicum sacrificium propitiatorium Nov. Test. instituta erant, & per fidem in Messiam ibi adumbratum offerenda ad peccatorum expiationem consequendam. Praevia magis erat peccatorum confessio sacrificio, quam intrinseca eidem, vel de essentia sacrificii. Sed repraesentatio sacrificii Christi erat velut forma sacrificiis expiatoriis, fine qua non erant, quod esse debebant ex instituto divino. Videbant quidem puniri quasi peccata in illis sacrificiis, quae offerebant: Sed non figurabatur punitum iri in sese, sed in Christo, propter peccata nostra in sacrificium tradendo. Satisfactio ergo vicaria magis in illis exhibita, quam condemnatio hominum. Ideo non quaerendum in illis chirographum, quod contra homines per decreta legis erat, sed quaerenda potius mors Christi deletoria chirographi, & expiatoria peccati, per quod damnationi obnoxii eramus.

Observanda hic omnino perpulchra & pientissima glossa Camerarii: Τοῖς δόγμασιν, usitata ἔλλειψις τῆς σὺν, una cum decretu. Quidam tamen Graeci, dià τῶν δογμάτων, inconsideratius illi quidem interpreti sunt, id est, per decreta pietatis & fide in ipsum. Sunt enim dogmata electiones legitimae, ut in epistola scrip ad ephesios. Eft autem copiosa & hoc loco oratio ἐν τῇ καλυμμένη ἐπιμονῇ.

Delevit, sustulit e medio.

Difidit τῇ προσηλώσει.

Quid? obligationem manus nostrae. Cur ergo aliud agitur aut quaeritur? ac non potius omnes omnium vires intenduntur, & universum studium impenditur ad gratias agendas Liberatori pro tanto beneficio. Τὰς γὰρ ἁμαρτίας ἡμῶν ἀναλαβὼν ὁ κύριος, κ. οἰκειοποιησάμενος τὴν ἡμῶν ὀφειλομένην δίκην αὐτὸς ἔδωκεν ὑπὲρ αὐτῶν, quemadmodum praeclare Graeci commentati sunt hoc loco.

O Fili Dei Σῶτερ Christe, accend...e S. Spiritu tuo lucem hanc cognitionis salutaris in mea etiam caliginosa mente, ut de tui amoris contemplatione amor meus exardescat, & in me omnia compescantur, & evanescant mea. Tua autem veritas & fides vigeat & exerceatur, quod tuum est opus, in quo elaborando fac inserviat voluntati tuae omni cogitatio animi mei & voluntatis inclinatio & diligentia studium, Amen.

## 2:15
V. 15. Ἀπεκδυσάμενος τὰς ἀρχὰς καὶ τὰς ἐξουσίας, ἐδειγμάτισεν ἐν παρρησίᾳ θριαμβεύσας αὐτὰς ἐν ...αὐτῷ. Another similitude from the Roman triumphers, who were accustomed to show the captured enemies to the citizens. Τὰς ἀρχὰς καὶ τὰς ἐξουσίας, understand those demons, who were worshipped in idols, and whose worship the Asiatic philosophers wished to restore with some sort of peddling.

See Rom. III. 38. 1 Cor. XV. 24. Ἀπεκδυσάμενος that is, disarmed, just as ἰνδυσάμενος is to be armed, Rom. XIII. 12. Ephes. VI. 11. 14. Δειγματίζειν is what we have already said, to show. Δῆγμα is a Greek word, but one which also passes to the Jews, and is written הַדְגָמָה, with the ד placed for the ג, and vice versa. Hence δογματίζειν is formed in a like manner, as παραδειγματίζειν, Matt. I. 19. Heb. VI. 6. Ἐν παρρησίᾳ, that is, openly, with the whole world looking on. For the Hebrews use בְּפַרְהֶסְיָא. But Christ is said to have done what he did through the Apostles, acting in his name and by his power. Θριαμβεύσας here is said metonymically for νικήσας, when he had conquered. And he changed the gender, when he brought in αὐτὰς, when he had before said ἀρχὰς καὶ ἐξουσίας, namely, making the construction πρὸς τὸ σημαινόμενον ἐν αὐτῷ, namely, σταυρῷ, He conquered the demons not by fighting, but by suffering, which is a truly divine kind of victory. This gloss about the worship of demons destroyed by the Apostles is foreign. For it concerns that which was done by Christ himself, and that on the cross: that it concerns the powers themselves and the infernal principalities, not indeed the filitium worship of demons. From that which, according to the handwriting, deleted by Christ, was pressing us all, Gentiles alike and Jews; for the Apostle teaches that we were all liberated through Christ, as one who not only had to rescue us from the guilt of sin, the handwriting having been destroyed, which was contrary to us, but also from the power of the Devil, and therefore on the cross he not only affixed the deleted handwriting, but also conquered the Diabolical principalities, and celebrated a triumph over them. Note also the Grotius ἑαυτοῦμαχα. For at one time he says that by the Apostles, when they destroyed the worship of demons, the principalities were despoiled, at another time he says that Christ conquered the demons not by fighting, but by suffering, in these words, which who does not see to be most diverse? Grotius understands Ἀπέκδυσιν as the stripping off of armor, others interpret it as the deprivation and snatching away of spoils, as soldiers after a victory are accustomed to despoil conquered enemies. For men were the prey of the Devil, which spoil Christ the Redeemer of the human race snatched from their power. But the translation by Thomas is wrongly understood as those whom he led from hell into heaven, of saints. For neither were any saints in hell, nor is a glorious translation understood, but an ignominious one, such as that of captives in a triumphal procession. Nor is it necessary to take θριαμβεύσας metonymically, when he had conquered. For it can properly be understood: celebrating a triumph (over enemies publicly led). Therefore Theophylactus renders: On the cross, returning with victory over the conquered enemies, he leads a procession publicly, showing those bound in chains whom he has conquered. And so, setting up a trophy on the cross, the Lord, by the concurrence of Romans, as well as Gentiles and Jews, triumphed over the demons. Furthermore, that he led them away confidently, Theophylactus expounded, he made them unseemly, rendered them ignominious, put them to shame. For never was the Devil so put to shame. For he himself, expecting to hold Christ, lost those whom he had held otherwise. But openly, i.e., publicly, with all seeing. Ἐν αὐτῷ is not inappropriately understood of σταυρῷ. But since most Codices read ἐν αὐτῷ, Calvin testifying, the Vulgate and B. Luther render in semetipso, that Christ accomplished this not through others, not through the Apostles, but through himself, or not by another's, but by his own power. Some exemplars had that reading in the time of Origen, who nevertheless preferred the other, ἐν αὐτῷ, namely, σταυρῷ, hom. IIX. on John, which was also approved by Theophylactus and Oecumenius in their scholia; by which the cross is established, as it were a triumphal chariot, in which the Lord triumphed magnificently. Therefore neither reading is inconvenient: neither favors the Grotian conceit of a victory obtained through the Apostles, because the one expressly teaches that Christ triumphed over the demons through himself, while the other establishes the triumph on the cross, not in the Apostolic ministry. Camararius notes also another explanation: It pleased others more: Αὐτὸς ἡμᾶς θριαμβεύσας, i.e., making us glorious in himself as victors and triumphers, and indeed the Apostle used the word thus above, in the letter written later to the Corinthians. But the received sense concerning the triumph of Christ himself is to be preferred. The inference directed toward ἔλεγχον Theophylactus presents thus: If therefore not Angels died for you, but Christ himself, how do you establish that you yourselves are led to the Father through Angels? But let us now consider how the Apostle himself from these things infers his elenctic parænesis.

PART III. List of errors concerning external ceremonies & the worship of Angels.

Latin:

V. 15. Ἀπεκδυσάμενος τὰς ἀρχὰς καὶ τὰς ἐξουσίας, ἐδειγμάτισεν ἐν παρρησίᾳ θριαμβεύσας αὐτὰς ἐν ...αὐτῷ. Alia similitudo a triumphantibus Romanis, qui solebant Captos ostendere civibus hostes. Τὰς ἀρχὰς καὶ τὰς ἐξουσίας, intellige Daemonas illos, qui in idolis colebantur, & quorum cultum cum mangonio aliquo restituere volebant Asiatici Philosophi.

Vid. Roman. III. 38. 1. Cor. XV. 24. Ἀπεκδυσάμενος id est exarmatos, sicut ἰνδυσάμενος est armari, Rom. XIII. 12. Ephes. VI. 11. 14. Δειγματίζειν est quod jam diximus ostendere. Δῆγμα vox est Graeca, sed quae & ad Judaeos transit, & scribitur הַדְגָמָה, posito ד pro ג, et vice versa. Hinc δογματίζειν efficitur pari forma, qua παραδειγματίζειν, Matth. I. 19. Ebr. VI. 6. Ἐν παρρησίᾳ, id est, palam, toto mundo inspectante. Nam בְּפַרְהֶסְיָא Ebri usurpant. Dicitur autem Christus fecisse, quod per Apostolos fecit ex ipsius nomine ac vi agentes. Θριαμβεύσας hic est dictum μετωνυμικῶς pro νικήσας cum devicisset. Et mutavit genus, cum intulit αὐτὰς, cum ante dixisset ἀρχὰς καὶ ἐξουσίας, nempe constructionem faciens πρὸς τὸ σημαινόμενον ἐν αὐτῷ, nempe σταυρῷ, Vicit Daemonas non pugnando, sed patiendo, quod vere divinum victoriae genus. Aliena est haec glossa de cultu Daemonum per Apostolos destructo. Nam de eo agitur, quod a Christo ipso factum, idque in cruce: quod potestates ipsas & principatus infernales, non vero filitium cultum Daemonum concernit. Ab eo quod juxta chirographum, à Christo deletum, nos omnes premebat, gentiles pariter ac Judaeos; nos omnes enim per Christum liberatos docet Apostolus, utpote qui non tantum à peccati reatu, destructo chirographo, quod nobis contrarium erat, sed etiam à potestate Diaboli nos eripere debuit, ideoque in cruce non tantum deletum chirographum affixerit, sed etiam Diabolicos principatus devicerit, ac triumphum de iisdem egerit. Notanda etiam ἑαυτοῦμαχα Grotiana. Nam modo per Apostolos, cum destruxere Daemonum cultum, exspoliatos principatus, modo Christum vicisse Daemonas non pugnando, sed patiendo his verbis doceri ait, quae maxime diversa esse quis non videt? Ἀπέκδυσιν Grotius de armorum exuitione intelligit, alii de spoliorum privatione & ereptione interpretantur, ut post victoriam bellatores exspoliare hostes devictos solent. Homines enim praeda Diaboli fuere, quod spolium eripuit ex ipsorum potestate Christus Redemptor humani generis. Traductio vero perperam à Thoma de sanctis, quos ex inferno in caelum traduxerit, intelligitur. Nam nec sancti ulli in inferno fuere, nec traductio gloriosa, sed ignominiosa intelligitur, qualis est captivorum in triumphali pompa. Nec θριαμβεύσας Metonymice accipere est necessellum, cum devicisset. Proprie enim intelligi potest: Triumphum (de hostibus publice traductis) agens. Ideo Theophylactus reddit: In cruce Daemones devictis hostibus cum victoria remeans pompam publice ducit, ostentans catenis constrictos, quos vicerit. In cruce itaque tropaeum statuens Dominus, tam Romanorum, tum gentilium & Judaeorum con- cursu, de Demonibus triumphavit. Porro illud traduxit confidenter, exposuit Theophylactus, indecoros eos fecit, ignominiosos reddidit, pudefecit. Nunquam enim adeo pudefactus est Diabolus. Expedans enim ipse Christum tenere, quos alios habuit, amisit. Palam autem, i.e. publice, omnibus cernentibus. Ἐν αὐτῷ non incommode de σταυρῷ intelligitur. Sed quum plerique Codices legant ἐν αὐτῷ, Calvino teste, Vulgatus & B. Lutherus reddunt in semetipso, quod Christus id egerit non per alios, non per Apostolos, sed per semetipsum, vel non aliena, sed propria virtute. Habuere eam lectionem Origenis tempore nonnulla exemplaria, qui tamen alteram ἐν αὐτῷ scil. σταυρῷ praetulit hom. IIX. in Johannem, quae etiam Theophylacto & Oecumenio probata fuit in scholiis; qua crux constituitur, quasi currus triumphalis, in quo magnifice Dominus triumphavit. Neutra igitur lectio incommoda: neutra favet commento Grotiano de victoria per Apostolos obtenta, quia altera diserte Christum per semetipsum triumphasse Daemonas docetur, altera autem in cruce triumphus statuitur, non in ministerio Apostolico. Notat Camararius & aliam explicationem: Aliis magis placuit: Αὐτὸς ἡμᾶς θριαμβεύσας, i.e. reddens nos gloriosos in seipso victores atque triumphatores, atque ita sane verbo supra usus est Apostolus, epistola scripta ad Corinthios posteriore. Sed praeferendus receptus sensus de ipsius Christi triumpho. Illationem ad ἔλεγχον intentam sic exhibet Theophylactus: Si igitur non Angeli pro vobis, sed Christus ipse mortuus est, quo pacto illud astruitis, per Angelos vos ipsos ad Patrem deduci? Sed dispiciamus jam, quomodo Apostolus ipse ex his inferat parænesin suam elencticam.

PARS III. Elenchus errorum de ceremoniis externis & cultu Angelorum.

## 2:16
Vers. 16. Μὴ οὖν τις ὑμᾶς κρινέτω ἐν βρώσει ἢ πόσει, ἢ ἐν μέρει ἑορτῆς, ἢ νεομηνίας, ἢ σαββάτων) One clause comprehends both the Judaizers and the Pythagorizers. To abstain from wine perpetually was not Judaic; the Jews abstained from certain foods, the Pythagorists from far more. Those things concerning days pertain to the Judaizers. Κρινέτω, that is, κατακρινέτω, as Rom. II. 1. Do not admit such teachers, who exclude from the hope of salvation those not observing such things. Ἐν μέρει ἑορτῆς on account of the feast day. So 1. Petr. IV. 16. ἡμέρᾳ τούτῳ for this cause. But this ἐν μέρει corresponds to the Rabbinic מִקְצָת, as has rightly been noted by learned men. The feasts here are unleavened bread, the day of ashes, the Feast of Tabernacles, the day of ἱλαρμός.

Latin:

Vers. 16. Μὴ οὖν τις ὑμᾶς κρινέτω ἐν βρώσει ἢ πόσει, ἢ ἐν μέρει ἑορτῆς, ἢ νεομηνίας, ἢ σαββάτων) Una clausula comprehendit & Judaizantes & Pythagorizantes. Vino abstinere perpetuo non erat Judaicum, cibis nonnullis Judaei abstinebant, multo pluribus Pythagorittz. Illa de diebus Judaizantes spectant. Κρινέτω, id est, κατακρινέτω, ut Rom. IL 1.
