Ne admittite tales magistros, qui talia non observantes à spe salutis excludunt. Ἐν μέρει ἑορτῆς ex causa diei festi. Sic 1. Petr. IV. 16. ἡμέρᾳ τούτῳ hac de causa. Respondet autem hoc ἐν μέρει Rabbinico מִקְצָת, ut recte à viris eruditis notatum est. Ἑορταὶ hic sunt azyma, dies cener, scenopegia, dies ἱλαρμοῦ.

## 2:17
Vers. 17. Ἃ ἐστι σκιὰ τῶν μελλόντων) Which are indeed Jewish, Heb. VIII. 9. X. 1. Τὸ δὲ σῶμα τοῦ χριστοῦ) The solidity of things once sketched in a rude manner is Christ's, pertains to Christ, is to be sought from him alone. A similar opposition in Josephus, Jewish War II. 4: ἥκει παρὰ τὸ δισποτυ σκιὰν αὐτοῦ σώματος τῆς βασιλείας, ἧς ἥκουσι ἑαυτῷ τὸ σῶμα. Jerome on this passage: There is therefore no judgment under this shadow, which ceases with the body coming, because there is no need of an image when the truth is present.

Photius: Τὸ σῶμα τὸ χριστοῦ ταύτης ἡ ἀλήθεια. But our Manuscript draws these words to the following period. Τὸ δὲ σῶμα τοῦ χριστοῦ σκάδας ὑμᾶς καταβραβευέτω ὑμᾶς τὸ σῶμα τὸ χριστὸ, you, I say, whom the body of Christ is, 1 Cor. XI. 27. The same Photius makes mention of this distinction. And ἰσχυς at Levit. XV, who nevertheless expounds the doctrinal word as the body of Christ.

The received reading is rashly rejected, whose sense is clear in itself, and which is confirmed from Heb. X. 1: while the other is intricate, and does not suit the opposition of τῆς σκιᾶς. But whether these things look to the Pythagoreans does not appear. Nay, that they concern the Jews, not the Pythagoreans, is established by that opposition of the shadow of the body. For among these latter there was no figuring in the abstinence from wine or foods of that which was exhibited in Christ, and what was said concerning Christ did not at all apply to them. Therefore this distinction of foods & drinks equally regards those Judaizing, such as that which Lev. XI. delivers concerning foods, as far as the abstinence of the Nazarites from wine, Num. VI., and the necessity of feasts. Moreover, that inference of the particle ἣ looks not to what immediately precedes, as Crocius supposes a fault, who expounded the handwriting as concerning legal ceremonies. But the whole doctrine concerning Christ & faith delivered by the Apostle. And just as he opposed it to the necessity of circumcision for salvation, so now the Apostle turns it into an elenctic argument against the necessity of the distinction of foods & feast days, lest consciences by these same believe they are bound, just as Justinianus also defends the same interpretation of them, nor were the Judaizing Pseudo-Apostles troubling them.

Which Cornelius a Lapide approves.

Crocius for his part therefore carries that they had only a shadow of future things.

Cor. III. 10. chap. IX. 3. and judges that to be the simplest sense, which, upon the arrival of the body, which is Chri- teaches that it is most simple.

Latin:

Vers. 17. Ἃ ἐστι σκιὰ τῶν μελλόντων) Quae nempe Judaica, Ebr. VIII. 9. X. 1. Τὸ δὲ σῶμα τοῦ χριστοῦ) Soliditas rerum olim rudi modo adumbrata, Christi est, ad Christum pertinet, ab eo solo petenda est. Similis opposit. apud Josephum belli Judaici II. 4. ἥκει παρὰ τὸ δισποτυ σκιὰν αὐτοῦ σώματος τῆς βασιλείας, ἧς ἥκουσι ἑαυτῷ τὸ σῶμα. Hieronymus in hunc locum: Nullum ergo sub hoc judicium est, quod est umbra & cessat corpore veniente, quia imagine opus non est veritate praesente.

Photius: Τὸ σῶμα τὸ χριστοῦ ταύτης ἡ ἀλήθεια. At Manuscriptus, quo utimur, haec verba trahit ad periodum sequentem. Τὸ δὲ σῶμα τοῦ χριστοῦ σκάδας ὑμᾶς καταβραβευέτω ὑμᾶς τὸ σῶμα τὸ χριστὸ, vos, inquam, quē Christi corpus est, 1. Cor. XI. 27. Meminit hujus distinctionis idem Photius. Et ἰσχυς ad Levit. XV. qui tamen corpus Christi doctrinale verbum exponit.

Temere fuispecta redditur recepta lectio, cujus sensus per se patet, quae; ex Ebr. X. 1. confirmatur: quum ex adverso altera intricata sit, nec oppositioni τῆς σκιᾶς conveniat. Num autem ad Pytaguo- ristas haec spectent, non apparet. Imo quod Judaeos, non Pythagoricos attineant, ex illa σκιᾶς σώματος oppositione constat. Nulla enim apud hosce erat in vini aut ciborum abstinentia figuratio ejus, quod in Christo exhibitum est, quibus de Christo dicta nihil prorsus conitabat. Ideoque discrimen istud ciborum & potus aeque Judaizantes respicit, quale quod cibos Lev. XI. quoad Nazaræorum abstinentiam à vino, Num. VI. traditum, ac feriarum necessitas. Illatio autem ista particulæ ἣ facta non immediate antecedentia spectat, ut Crocio vitium, qui chirographum de ceremoniis legalibus exposuites Sed totam doctrinam de Christo & fide ab Apostolo traditam. Quam uti circumcisionis ad salutem necessitati opposuit, sic nunc in ulum elencticum adversus necessitatem discriminis ciborum & festorum dierum vertit Apostolus, ne conscientias iisdem obligari credant, quemadmodum easdem talibus interpretationem tuetur etiam Justinianus, nec in Pseudo-Apostoli Judaizantes turbabant.

Quas probat Cornelius a Lapide.

Crocius ejus causa conproinde tantum umbram habuisse rerum futura- fert 2.

Cor. III. 10. cap. IX. 3. eumque sensum simrum docet, quæ adventante corpore, quod Chri-plicissimum judicat.

## 2:18
(in humility and worship of Angels) And this is a hen dia dyoin [one thing by two].

For he understands "humility" as that which is "in the worship of Angels." It has the appearance of modesty not to dare to approach God, but to defer prayers to Angels to be carried to God, under which color the Philosophers defended polytheism, which Celsus also did, as we know from Origen.

We learn from Josephus that the names of the Angels were diligently guarded by the Essenes. Otherwise, it was not the public custom of the Jews to call upon Angels, except those who appeared to them, surely for fear that they would gradually relapse into the polytheism from which they had been delivered with such great labor. And this is noted by Origen against Celsus I. II. "For how did the scriptures of Moses hand down the lawgiver to the Angels?" and book V. "But these Angels, you have learned from their work to make them the object of your sacred rites, because God was not God but he did not find the command that was through the diaconal service to bring to us the things of God, to worship or adore instead of God. For all prayers, and supplications, and thanksgivings are to be sent up to the God over all through the Angel who is the high priest of the living Word and God." Origen treats the same matter three times in book VIII, where he says it is permitted to "praise or bless them."

And because this evil had prevailed in Phrygia, therefore the synod of Laodicea forbids "naming Angels and making assemblies," which is called hidden idolatry there. See Zonaras there. Christians are worshippers of the highest King and Prince, with Christ as their master, Arnobius book I, whom see.

so that through them we might arrive at God, whom they adorned with the scheme and pretext of humility, as Grotius, the patron of the Papists, acknowledges here with Theodoret and Theophylact, and that is evident from that Laodicean canon: Christians ought not, having abandoned the Church, to make congregations for Angels (Carranza in his Summa of councils rashly substitutes 'angles', whereas Theodoret and many others read 'Angels', and the text of the councils themselves has this, as Cornelius admits) in an abominable idolatry.

Whoever, however, is found to be secretly devoted to this idolatry, let him be anathema, because, abandoning our Lord Jesus Christ the Son of GOD, he has approached idols. Where Bellarmine, lib. I. de sanct. beat. 20, and Franciscus Longus à Cariolano in his Summa Concil. in his annotations on this canon, are in vain; and Cornelius à Lapide on this passage, who says that not just any veneration of Angels is forbidden, but only that which is proper to God, not dulia, but latria. For every invocation of Angels, every religious worship of them is condemned; whether it be called dulia or latria, which little distinction we explode elsewhere.

But that one ought to show veneration and honor to Angels, who would deny? Which the council in the following canon XXXV. & LI. attributes only to true martyrs, but not religious worship: Just as Augustine also testifies in libr. XX. contra Faustum c. XXI. concerning Christians: We honor the martyrs with the worship of love and society, with which holy men are honored in this life also. But concerning religious worship, see tract. XXIII. in Johann. This is the Christian religion, that one God be worshipped, not many Gods, &c.

Cornelius à Lapide is in vain while he brings forward various opinions to render the present passage doubtful, such as that some 1. wish that only the idolatry of the gentiles is condemned here, who worshipped their own genii, which is the opinion of Baronius. For the Apostle is not dealing with the gentiles here. 2. that some think the Jews are condemned, who worshipped the sun, moon, and stars; for the word is not about the worship of stars in this place, and stars are wrongly understood as Angels here with Ambrosiaster, nor is this a list of the Jews, for they were not openly idolaters at that time, but of heretics, therefore Cornelius himself rejects that opinion. 3. that by the religion of Angels, Judaism or the Jewish law is understood, given through Angels on Mount Sinai, which opinion he likewise rejects: Since the Jewish religion is nowhere called the religion of Angels, nor is there any talk of it here. 4. That the semi-Jews and semi-Platonists, Simon, Menander, Saturninus, Cerinthus, etc., are argued against in this place, who posited certain intermediate Gods, in place of Christ, and with him excluded; which likewise does not entirely please Cornelius, because this deals with the heresy proper to the Colossians, and Cerinthus above others, preferring Angels to Christ, so that he did not worship the Angel of the Jews, whose law he himself followed, but rather, as Epiphanius testifies, said that he was evil and detested him.

Although Bellarmine n. 5 wishes that the Simonians be taxed here also, who, having followed the Platonists, said that Angels were to be worshipped as lesser Gods, who also fashioned the world, and spoke through the Prophets, and through whom God ought to be appeased, citing Irenaeus, Tertullian, and Epiphanius as witnesses to that opinion, yet Justinian acknowledges that they attributed nothing of the sort to Simon, and Baronius admits that Simon or his disciples did not teach such a thing, Tom. I. Annal. ad ann. 60, to which Cariolanus also agrees.

What then was it? He imagines that there was a peculiar heresy among the Colossians, that Angels were more worthy than Christ, and were to be worshipped in a more excellent way, as if they were the saviors and mediators of men, and not Christ. But the traces of this fiction are in vain to seek in this place and in the aforesaid canon, and in Theodoret himself, as ἀμβατεύων teaches, so that it is not worth the effort either to repeat or to refute the stony conjectures, which he who desires may approach Crocius here. That gloss of Cornelius, by which ἐμβατεύων is snatched away to false Angel-olatries . For in Greek it means to set foot, to set foot somewhere, as in Nazianzen in Caesar: Σὺ δὲ μὴ τοῖς ὀρανοῖς ἐμβατεύεις ὠθεῖα ἡ ἱερὰ κεφαλή: So that he may intrude rashly, that they may intrude themselves into things which they do not understand, as Lombard explained. Nor is ἐς κεφαλὴν τὴν κεφαλὴν excluding Christ, or substituting Angels for Christ, as Cornelius wishes, but not holding to Christ, as Grotius explains, or as others in the same sense, not holding Christ as the head of the Church through faith.

For he who joins another Mediator to Christ, or another head to the Church, does not hold to Christ, nor does he leave this axiom to Christ. For there is one head of the Church, not many, one Mediator of God and men, not many. Theophylact is not wrong: He says, he who decrees such things does not hold the head, that is, the Son.

For he himself is the head of the Angels, as one who created all things. He is besides the head of the whole Church, although for the same reason, then especially, because we are his body, and he has been made a partaker of our members: then also, because the whole body of the Church consists of him, and simply has both its being and its well-being from him. And if anyone should fall from him, he has perished immediately.

Add now what Crocius further delivered concerning this passage in his explanation of the Decalogue: Paul adds ἐν ταπεινοφροσύνῃ, in humility. For it seems to be a certain submission of mind, not daring to approach God except through so many degrees, but such a thing is truly not so, since, as Origen rightly says, in the honor of God the good of those ministering to him is rightly comprehended, nor does it serve for use, ἵνα περισπᾶσθαι, & to be drawn away from that which is most necessary. He continues: Καὶ θρησκεία Ἀγγέλων, & worship of Angels. Where ἣ, as often, is placed κατ' ἐπεξήγησιν for the explanation of the words preceding. Θρησκεία, worship, is a word of middle significance: for it is used in a good sense, as Act. XXVI. 5. Jac. I. 27. & in a bad sense, as Sap. XI. 16. & XIV. 16. & in that sense which lies between both, as Jac. I. 26. & in this place; He explains what the Apostle is about to say, from μὴ ἐψαχας ἐμβατεύων, penetrating into those things which he has not seen. For this is the sense of the word ἐμβατεύειν, as appears 1. Maccab. XII. 25. XIII. 20. XV. 31. 40. For they do not know the Angels, who are said to be sent not without cause, Ebr. I. 14. who are present with them, or whether they are present: they do not know what they can do, what power they have. Which he also explains more fully in what follows, εἰκῇ Φυσιώμενος ὑπὸ τῶ νοὸς τῆς σαρκὸς αὐτῶ vainly puffed up by the mind of his flesh, in which place the force is of cogitation, as Rom. I. 28. & XIV. 5. Eph. IV. 17. 1. Tim. VI. 5. 2. Tim. III. 8. Tit. I. 15. But that σαφῶς flesh is opposed to divine revelation, as Matth. XVI. 17. Those who use names of Angels never placed in the scriptures, of which sort there are many in the book of Enoch bearing a false name, which attribute offices to them, by which words also in what manner each ought to address anyone, what they ought to ask from anyone — these things they do not receive from God or from the Angels themselves, so that they may be certain, but from human inventions, whose discipline pleases themselves, and who prefer themselves above others, whence Γνωσικῶν the name of Gnostics. It follows καὶ ἡ κεφαλὴν τὴν κεφαλὴν, ἐξ ὅ παντὸ σῶμα διὰ τῶν ἀφῶν καὶ συνδεσμῶν ἐπιχορηγούμενον καὶ συμβιβαζόμενον αὔξει τὴν αὔξησιν τῶ Θεῦ, & not holding the head, from which the whole body per nexus and joints supplied and confirmed, grows into the increase of GOD.

They do not hold themselves to Christ, that is, they are not content with Him as their advocate before God and the author of our purification, since they do not think it sufficient, who nevertheless is the head and the bond of the whole Church; hence it happens that those men, by enslaving themselves as it were to other angels, gradually withdraw themselves from the Church under the guise of greater knowledge, and from there divide themselves, having devolved, to be sure, through certain degrees to that idolatry (εἰδωλολατρείαν), which for this reason the Synod of Laodicea calls forbidden. Regarding things that can be sought by those means which are of human power, there is no doubt: Nor is it illicit to honor them with a bent or prostrate body, where such a custom obtains.

Nathan did this before David, 1 Kings 1:23. The writer of the lives of illustrious men on Conon: It is necessary, in the sight of Venus, that you venerate the King, which they call προσκυνέειν to him. The Greeks often say προσπίπτειν for it. Livy on the Carthaginian envoys: They prostrated themselves in the manner of those praying (having received the rite, I believe, from that region from which they originated).

He understands by the Phoenicians the neighbors of the Hebrews, whose custom Euripides expressed thus in the Phoenissae: Γονυπετὲς ἔδοξας προσπίπτω Σ' ἄναξ, τὸν οἴκοθεν νόμον σέβεσαι. Suppliant, O King, venerating thee with my knees, I fall before thee according to my country's custom. Josephus on David venerating King Saul: Προσκυνεῖται αὐτὸν πεσὼν ἐπὶ πρόσωπον, ὡς ἔθος, he venerates him falling prone upon his face, as is the custom.

But if in any nation that gesture is used only in divine matters, then it will no longer be lawful to use it before a King. For this reason the Greeks, among whom it was not the custom to be prostrated except in sacred rites, refused to venerate the King of the Persians in that manner, as we learn everywhere from histories. And a Christian among Sozomen, having venerated the King of the Persians, ceased afterwards, when he saw that it was being drawn into a different interpretation.

Christians also did not consider it alien to their religion to prostrate themselves before the images of Emperors. But after Julian had ordered the images of false gods to be added to his own images, the more prudent thought it better to tolerate any evils whatsoever than to prostrate themselves there. Gregory Nazianzen relates this. Tertullian to Scapula: We therefore worship the Emperor in such a way as is permitted to us, and as is expedient for him, as a man second to GOD, and whatever he is, he is such by GOD's appointment, and inferior only to GOD.

The same against the nations: Tempering the Majesty of Caesar below God: I commend him more to God, to whom alone I subject myself, but I subject myself to whom I do not equate. And shortly after: I will plainly call the Emperor Lord; but when I am not forced to call him Lord in the place of God. These are the words of Grotius in the cited place.

Who also speaks of the Angelic [heretics] far differently than Cornelius a Lapide, namely, not because they excluded Christ, but because they constituted Angels as additional Mediators: The Angelici, he says, are numbered among the heretics by Epiphanius, but he says he does not know what their institution was. It is most credible that it was such as is that which is approved by some among the Jews of the Cabalists, and disapproved by Josephus in the third book of the Foundations, chapter 18. They agree with the Pythagoreans and Platonists, whose opinion Jamblichus expresses for us, that men ought to be commended to the highest [God] through inferior and superior angels, and thus through many degrees, and they give them their names, give them their offices, and the power of dispensing benefits.

They establish some as dream-guides (oneiropompos), others as dream-senders (oniropompos), as Irenaeus teaches. The Apostle seems to be dealing with those who would introduce such things from Judaism into Christianity, Col. 2:18. For he speaks more mildly of them than to understand them as those who equated Angels to God, either by signs of properly divine honor, or by the performance of purely divine affections.

Yet he does not approve of the custom, nowhere handed down in the law, nowhere commanded in the Gospel, and also having no examples there. He constitutes the signs of properly divine honor as sacrifice, libation, incense, vows and oaths, the petitioning for things purely divine, the remission of sins, the Holy Spirit, eternal life. But the Papists have been convicted of all those things in truth.

See the Apodixis Theol. of B. Schroder on the dead being to be honored, not adored, and B. Gerh. conf. Cathol. etc. But that divine honor is to be a Mediator between God and men, and to be the head of the Church, because no man or angel suffices for the propitiation of the infinite justice of God and the government of the Church, since infinite virtue is required for those things, and the effects truly divine are attributed to our Mediator, and to the head of the Church, to him also, whom Grotius makes such, the remission of sins, the donation of the Holy Spirit and eternal life.

Let it be weighed now, what the Apostle is about to say in the present place concerning the office of the head of the Church, and what judgment he has passed on that heresy, because by the same we are led away from Christ, the palm is snatched from us, or the goal is overturned, will-worship (ἐθελοθρησκεία) is committed, the axiom or dignity belonging to Christ is not left. And when a cult not prescribed by God in His word is introduced, is not idolatry committed by that very fact? Κὴ ὃ κρατῶν τὴν κεφαλὴν) Not holding himself to Christ, whom God therefore gave as head of the Church, that through Him we might carry our desires to Him.

Many such advocates easily give occasion for schism, the Church retains unity, God is one and one Mediator, 1 Tim. 2:5. Εξ ἧ) Again it is a construction according to the meaning.

For when he had said head (κεφαλὴν), he brought in the rest in such a way, as if he had said hand (χεῖρα), which he indicated by the word head (κεφαλὴν). V. 19. Πᾶν τὸ σῶμα διὰ τῶν ἀφῶν καὶ συνδέσμων ἐπιχορηγούμενον καὶ συμβιβαζόμενον, αὔξει τὴν αὔξησιν τοῦ θεοῦ) He means this, that the unity of the Church must be retained: which cannot be done, unless the ranks of those in charge are retained, and they are obeyed in those things which pertain to the peace of the Church. Thus in time it occurs to those fetters, which having been placed, to pluck out, called according to flights (κατὰ φύγας).

A passage twin to this is Eph. 4:15, 16. there it is of the joint of the supply (ἁφῆς τῆς ἐπιχορηγίας), here of joints and bonds (ἁφῶν καὶ συνδέσμων), through limbs, and veins, and arteries, which are the nexus and bonds of the body, חברות ווללאות, there it is being fitted together and compacted (συναρμολογούμενον καὶ συμβιβαζόμενον), for which here it is supplied and compacted (ἐπιχορηγούμενον καὶ συμβιβαζόμενον).

But it is supplied (ἐπιχορηγούμενον), whence supply (ἐπιχορηγία) in that place to the Ephesians to receive those things which are necessary for nourishing the body, see Sirach 25:28. In the Glossary, I supply, I provide (ἐπιχορηγὰ). He grows the increase of God (αὔξει τὴν αὔξησιν τοῦ θεοῦ), he speaks in Greek, which the Latins also follow, when they say, to die a death, to strike a striker.

But the genitive of God (τοῦ θεοῦ) here signifies the cause. It grows by that increase which is from God. From the same we are both nourished and grow. Theophylact: As the vital Spirit is diffused from the brain into the rest of the body through the nerves, and all sensibility and motion is derived from the head itself: So also the body of the Church is supplied by Christ, that is, it receives from Him both life and the increase of the Spirit.

Which indeed, all then without doubt this Church obtains, when the Spirit is the nexus and bond to it. For He supplies a certain nexus and joints of increase. To them indeed to agree (that is, to correspond) will avail, nor will the Spirit Himself be supplied, nor will any increase of God, that is, the best life, any progress, be added. Cornelius a Lapide: As if he were to say: Just as the vital Spirit, which is necessary for life, sense, and motion, is diffused from the head into the whole body through nerves, joints, and articulations, and thus imparts to individual members the faculty of sensing and moving; so the Spirit of grace is derived from Christ as the head into the members connected to Him, namely into the faithful Christians through the joints of mutual union and charity, and supplies to them spiritual life and motion, and thus the whole body of the Church grows into the increase of God, that is, as the Syrian says, it grows of the increase of God, that is, the increase of faith and the Spirit of God. The wrath is from Chrysostom and Theophylact. Are these not of infinite virtue and truly divine effects? Do they in any way pertain to any of the Angels, either with Christ excluded, or alongside Christ? B. Hunnius rightly handed down the Apostle's inference: Do not commit yourselves to those idle Doctors, who have this goal set before them, to lead you away from Christ, rather than that you should see the head of God through faith once apprehended, so that you may retain it. For being thus engrafted into Him through joints and bands by means of the ministry of the Word and Sacraments, and compacted among yourselves by the fellowship of the same Spirit, faith, and charity, with the increase of Christ growing, that is, with God bestowing increases, you will progress in faith and piety. v.

Latin:

(ἐν ταπεινοφροσύνῃ καὶ θρησκείᾳ τῶν Ἀγγέλων) Et hic est βὶ διὰ δυοῖν.

Nam intelligit ταπεινοφροσύνην τὴν ἐν θρησκείᾳ Ἀγγέλων. Habet speciem modestiae non audere Deum accedere, sed ad Angelos preces deferre ad Deum deferen-das, quo colore defendebant Philosophi τὴν πολυθείαν, quod & Celsus fecit, ut ex Origene cognoscimus.

Ab Essenis diligenter custodita Angelorum nomina ex Josepho discimus. Alioqui publicus Judaeorum nomina ex Josepho discimus. Alioqui publicus Judaeorum nomina non fuit Angelos compellare, nisi eos, qui ipsis apparebant, nimirum metu, ne paulatim ad πολυθείαν tanto labore exutam relaberentur. Et hoc notatum Origeni contra Celsum I. II. Πῶς γὰρ τὰ γράμματα τῷ Μωϋσέως εὐρετομοθέτην παραδέδωκε βίβλον Ἀγγέλους; & lib. V. Τύτους δὲ Ἀγγέλους, ἀπὸ τῷ ἔργῳ αὐτῶν μεμαθήκατε ποιεῖν ἱερόσκομον αὐτῶν διὰ τὸ θεὸς οὐκ ἦν θεὸς οὐ τῶν ἱερῶν ποιεῖ ὀνομαζομένης γραφαῖς, ἀλλ' οὐχ εὗρε προστάξεως ἦν τῆς διὰ διακονο-τακῆς φέροιλας ἡμῖν τὰ τῷ Θεῷ, σέβειν ἢ προσκυνεῖν αἰτὶ τὸ Θεῷ. πᾶται μὲν γὰρ δέσει, ὡς προσευχή, κὶ ὀντύει, κὶ ὐχμαρισίαι διαπεμπτέοι τῷ ἐπὶ πᾶσι Θεῷ διὰ τὸ ἐπιτάτταν Ἀγγέλων ἀρχιερέως ἐμψύχου λόγῳ κὶν Θεῷ. Agit Origenes ter de eadem re libro VIII. ubi dicit, licere eos ὐψη-μὲν ὴ μακαρίζειν.

Et quia hoc malum invaluerat in Phrygia, ideo synodus Laodicensis vetat ἀγγέλους ὀνομαζειν κὶν συνάξεις ποιεῖν, que occulta idololatria ibidem dicitur. Vide ibi Zonaram. Christiani Christo magistro summi Regis Principis veneratores, Arnobius libro I. quem vide.

ut per eos ad Deum perveniamus, quem schemate ac prætextu humilitatis ornarunt, ut cum Theodoreto & Theophylacto agnoscit hic Grotius, Papistarum Patronus, idque è canone illo Laodiceno luculentum est: Non oportet Christianos derelicta Ecclesia ad Angelos (temere Carranza in Summa conciliorum subfstituit angulos, quum Theodoretus & alii plures non angulos, sed Angelos legant, idque habeat ipse conciliorum textus, fatente Cornelio) abominanda idololatria congregationes facere.

Quicunque autem inventus fuerit, occulta huic idololatriæ vacans, anathema sit, quoniam relinquens Dominum nostrum Jesum Christum Filium DEI, accessit ad idola. Ubi frustra sunt Bellarm. libr. I. de sanct. beat. 20. Franciscus Longus à Cariolano in Summa Concil. annot. ad hunc can. Cornelius à Lapide ad hunc locum, non quamlibet Angelorum venerationem, sed eam tantum, quæ Deo propria est, prohiberi, non duliam, sed latriam. Nam omnis invocatio Angelorum, omnis cultus religiosus eorum damnatur; sive dulia vocetur, sive latria, quam distinctionculam alias explodimus.

Venerationem autem & honorem Angelis exhibere deberet, ecquis negaret? Quem veris martyribus solum tribuit concilium canone sequenti XXXV. & LI. non vero cultum religiosum: Sicut & Augustinus libr. XX. contra Faustum c. XXI. de Christianis testatur: Colimus martyres cultu dilectionis & societatis, quo & in hac vita coluntur fandi homines. De religioso autem cultu tract. XXIII. in Johann. Hæc est religio Christiana, ut colatur unus Deus, non multi Dii, &c.

Frustra est Cornelius à Lapide, dum varias sententias affert, ut locum præsentem dubium reddat, utpote quod nonnulli 1. velint, damnari hic solum gentilium idololatriam, qui suos genios coluere, quæ Baronii est opinio. Non enim cum gentilibus hic negotium est Apostolo. 2. quod quidam putent, damnari Judæos, qui solem, lunam & stellas adorabant; non enim verbum hoc loco de cultu stellarum, & perperam per Angelos hoc loco stellæ intelliguntur cum Ambrosiaftro, nec Judæorum hic elenchus est, quemquam nec illi palam idololatræ tum fuerint, sed hæreticorum, ideo eam sententiam reprobat ipse Cornelius. 3. quod per religionem Angelorum Judaismus, vel lex Judaica intelligatur data per Angelos in monte Sinai, quam sententiam itidem rejicit: Siquidem Judaica religio nusquam religio Angelorum dicatur, nec de illa hic sermo fit. 4. Quod arguantur hoc loco semi-Judæi & semi-Platonici, Simon, Menander, Saturninus, Cerinthus & c. qui Deus quosdam medios posuerint, loco Christi, eoque excluso; quæ itidem non omnino placet Cornelio, quod hic de hæresi propria apud Colossenses agatur, quoque Cerinthus præ aliis, Angelos Christo præferens, adeo Angelum Judæorum, quorum legem ipse colebat, non adorarit, ut potius, teste Epiphanio, eum malum esse diceret ac detestaretur.

Quanquam vero Bellarminus n. 5. Simonianos hic taxari etiam velit, qui, Platonicos sequuti, Angelos quasi minores Deos adorandos dixerint, qui & mundum fabricarint, & per Prophetas loquuti sint, & per quos Deum placari oporteat, in eam sententiam testes citans Irenæum, Tertullianum, Epiphanium, agnoscit tamen Justinianus, nil tale illos Simoni tribuere, fateturque Baronius, tale quid non docuisse Simonem aut discipulos ejus Tom. I. Annal. ad ann. 60. cui accedit etiam Cariolanus.

Quid ergo tandem fuerit? Fingit apud Colossenses peculiare fuisse hæresin, Angelos esse digniores Christo, & excellentiori modo colendos, qui servatores mediatores hominum sint, non Christus. Sed hujus commenti vestigia frustra in hoc loco & in canone prædicto, & apud Theodoretum, ipsum quærere, ἀμβατεύων docet, ut operæ pretium non sit, vel repetere conjecturas lapideas, vel refellere, quod qui desiderat, Crocium hic adeat. Glossæ illa Cornelii, quâ ἐμβατεύων abripitur ad falsas Angelo-latrias . Nam Græcis id est pedem ponere, pedem inferre aliquo, ut Nazianzeno in Cæsar: Σὺ δὲ μὴ τοῖς ὀρανοῖς ἐμβατεύεις ὠθεῖα ἡ ἱερὰ κεφαλή: Ut ingerat ur temere, se eos ingerere in ea, quæ non intelligant, ut Lombardus exposuit. Neque ἐς κεφαλὴν τὴν κεφαλὴν ἀνὴ est excludens Christum, vel pro Christo subfituens Angelos, ut Cornelius vult, sed non tenens se Christo, ut Grotius explicat, vel ut eodem sensu alii, non tenens Christum caput Ecclesiæ per fidem.

Qui enim aliam Christo adjungit Mediatorem, vel caput aliud Ecclesiæ, non tenet se Christo, nec Christo hoc axioma relinquit. Unum enim est Ecclesiæ caput, non plura, unus Mediator Dei & hominum, non plures. Non male Theophylactus: Nequaquam, inquit, qui decernit hujusmodi, continet caput, hoc est, filium.

Ipse namque Angelorum est caput, ut qui cuncta condiderit. Est præterea vel totius Ecclesiæ caput, etsi ratione eadem, tum præcipue, quia illius corpus sumus, & ille nostrorum membrorum factus est particeps: tum etiam, quia ex eo corpus universum Ecclesia constat, & simpliciter esse hoc habet, & bene esse. Et si ab eo exciderit quispiam, periit illico.

Adde jam, quæ in explanatione Decalogi ulterius de hoc loco tradidit Crocius: Addit Paulus ἐν ταπεινοφροσύνῃ, in humilitate. Videtur enim esse animi quadam submissio, non audere, nisi per tot gradus Deum accedere, at tale id revere non est, cum, ut recte ait Origenes, in Dei honore recte comprehendatur bonus ipsi ministrantium, neque ex usu fit, ἵνα περισπᾶσθαι, & ab eo, quod maxime necessarium est, avocari. Pergit: Καὶ θρησκεία Ἀγγέλων, & cultu Angelorum. Ubi ἣ, ut sæpe, positum est κατ' ἐπεξήγησιν ad explicationem verborum præcedentium. Θρησκεία cultus, vox media est significationis: nam in bonam partem usurpatur, ut Act. XXVI. 5. Jac. I. 27. & in malam, ut Sap. XI. 16. & XIV. 16. & eo sensu qui inter utrumque est, ut Jac. I. 26. & hoc loco; Explicat, quod capit dicere Apostolus, à μὴ ἐψαχας ἐμβατεύων, penetrans in ea, qua non vidit. Is enim sensus est vocis ἐμβατεύειν, ut apparet 1. Maccab. XII. 25. XIII. 20. XV. 31. 40. Nesciunt enim Angelorum, qui non fine causa missi dicuntur, Ebr. I. 14. qui ipsis adsint, sive non adsint: nesciunt quid possint, quid valeant. Quod latius etiam sequentibus explicat, εἰκῇ Φυσιώμενος ὑπὸ τῶ νοὸς τῆς σαρκὸς αὐτῶ frustra inflatus sensu carnis suæ, quo loco vis est cogitatio, ut Rom. I. 28. & XIV. 5. Eph. IV. 17. 1. Tim. VI. 5. 2. Tim. III. 8. Tit. I. 15. Illud autem σαφῶς carnis opponitur patefactioni divinæ, ut Matth. XVI. 17. Quæ usurpant nomina Angelorum in scripturis nunquam posita, qualia multa sunt in libro Enochi falsum nomen præferente, quæ munia ipsis attribuunt, quibus verbis quoque modo quemque alloqui, quid à quovis poscere debeant, hæc non accerpere à Deo aut ab ipsis Angelis, ut certi esse possint, sed ex humanis commentis, quorum disciplina sibi placent, seque cætera præferunt, unde Γνωσικῶν Gnosticorum nomen. Sequitur καὶ ἡ κεφαλὴν τὴν κεφαλὴν, ἐξ ὅ παντὸ σῶμα διὰ τῶν ἀφῶν καὶ συνδεσμῶν ἐπιχορηγούμενον καὶ συμβιβαζόμενον αὔξει τὴν αὔξησιν τῶ Θεῦ, & non tenent caput, ex quo toti corpo per nexus et conjunctiones subministratum et confirmatum crescit in augmentum DEI.

Non tenent se Christo, id est, eo non sunt contenti apud Deum commendatore et purgationis nostrae opifice, cum non putant sufficere, qui tamen est caput et coagulum totius Ecclesiae, inde fit, ut illi homines alii aliis Angelis se velut mancipando, paulatim et ab Ecclesia specie majoris scientiae se subducant, et inde se dividantur, nimirum per gradus quosdam devoluti ad illam εἰδωλολατρείαν, quam propter hoc κεχωλυσμένην vocat, Laodicena Synodus. Rebus, quae ea peti possunt, quae humanae sunt opis, dubitandum non est: Neque vero flexo aut proflato corpore eos honorare illicitum est, ubi mos talis obtinet.

Fecit id Nathan coram Davide, 1. Reg. I. 23. Scriptor vitarum illustrium in Conone: Necesse est, in conspectum veneris, te venerari Regem, quod προσκυνέειν illi vocant. Graeci saepe pro eo dicunt προσπίπτειν. Livius de Legatis Carthaginiensium: More adorantium (accepto credo ritu ex ea regione, ex qua oriundi erant) procubuerunt.

A Phœnicibus intelligit vicinis Hebraeorum, quorum more Phœnissis Euripides sic expressit: Γονυπετὲς ἔδοξας προσπίπτω Σ' ἄναξ, τὸν οἴκοθεν νόμον σέβεσαι. Supplex te Rex venerans genubus Patrio advolvor de more tuis. Josephus de Davide Saulem Regem venerante: Προσκυνεῖται αὐτὸν πεσὼν ἐπὶ πρόσωπον, ὡς ἔθος, veneratur eum pronus cadens, ut moris est.

At si qua in gente is gestus tantum in re divina usurpetur, jam eum coram Rege usurpari licitum non erit. Ob id Graeci, quibus prosterni, nisi in sacris, mos non erat, eo more venerari Persarum Regem noluere, ut passim ex historiis discimus. Et Christianus apud Sozomenum Persarum Regem veneratus, destitit postea, ubi id aliovorsum interpretando trahi videt.

Etiam coram Imperatorum imaginibus procumbere non alienum a sua religione arbitrati sunt Christiani. At postquam suis imaginibus falsorum Deorum imagines addi jussent Julianus, prudentiores mala quavis potius toleranda duxere, quam ut ibi procumberent. Narrat Gregorius Nazianzenus. Tertullianus ad Scapulam: Colimus ergo Imperatorem sic, quomodo et nobis licet, et ipsi expedit ut hominem a DEO secundum, et quicquid est, a DEO confiscutum, et solo DEO minorem.

Idem adversus gentes: Temperans Majestatem Caesaris infra Deum: Magis illum commendo Deo, cui soli subjicio, subjicio autem cui non adequo. Et mox: Dicam plane Imperatorem Dominum; sed quando non cogor, ut Dominum Dei vice dicam. Haec Grotius loco citato.

Qui etiam de Angelicis longe aliter, quam Cornelius a Lapide, nimirum non quod Christum excluserint, sed quod Angelos praeterea Mediatores constituerint: Angelici, inquit, Epiphanio inter haereticos numerantur, sed eorum quale fuerit institutum, se nescire. Maxime credibile est, tale fuisse, quale est Cabalistarum inter Judaeos probatum quibusdam, improbatum Josepho albo libr. III. fundamentorum capite 18. Consent illi cum Pythagoricis et Platonicis, quorum sententiam nobis Jamblichus exprimit, per Angelos inferiores superiores, atque ita per multos gradus summis illis homines commendari debere, et illis dant sua nomina, dant officia, et dispensandorum beneficiorum facultatem.

Alios statuunt oneiropompos, alios oniropompos, ut Irenaeus docet. De his, qui talia ex Judaismo in Christianismum inferrent, agere videtur Apostolus, Col. II. 18. mitius enim de iis loquitur, quam ut eos intelligat, qui Angelos, aut honoris proprie divini signis, aut affectuum mere divinorum expeditione Deo equabant.

Neque tamen probat morem, nusquam in lege traditum, nusquam in Evangelio praeceptum, nulla quoque ibi habentem exempla. Honoris proprie divini signa constituit sacrificium, libamen, suffitum, vota et juramenta, expetitionem rerum mere divinarum, remissionem peccatorum, Spiritum Sanctum, vitam aeternam. Sed de illis omnibus rei peracti sunt Papistae ex vero. Vid.

B. Schroderi Apodixis Theol. de defunctis honorandis non adorandis, et B. Gerh. conf. Cathol. et c. Est autem honor ille divinus, Mediatorem esse inter Deum et homines, et caput esse Ecclesiae, quia ad placationem infinitae Dei justitiae et gubernationem Ecclesiae non sufficit ullus hominum aut Angelerum, quum infinita requiratur ad ea virtus, et effectus vere divini Mediatori nostro, et capiti Ecclesiae tribuantur, illi etiam, quos tales facit Grotius, remissio peccatorum, donatio Spiritus Sancti et vitae aeternae.

Expendatur modo, quod in praesenti loco jamjam de Ecclesiae capitis munere Apostolus dicturus, et quale judicium is tulerit de ista haeresi, quod per eandem seducamur a Christo, palma nobis praeripiatur, vel meta intervertatur, ἐθελοθρησκεία committatur, Christo axioma vel dignitas conveniens non relinquatur. Et quum cultus a Deo in verbo suo non praescriptus introducitur, annon eo ipso idololatria committitur? Κὴ ὃ κρατῶν τὴν κεφαλὴν) Non tenens se Christo, quem Deus ideo caput Ecclesiae dedit, ut per eum desideria nostra ad ipsum perferremus.

Multi illi commendatores facile schismati dant occasionem, Ecclesia unitatem retinet, Deus unus et unus Mesites, 1. Tim. II. 5. Εξ ἧ) Rursus est constructio πρὸς τὸ σημαινόμενον.

Nam cum dixisset κεφαλὴν, ita cetera intulit, quasi dixisset χεῖρα, quem per vocem κεφαλὴν indicabat. V. 19. Πᾶν τὸ σῶμα διὰ τῶν ἀφῶν καὶ συνδέσμων ἐπιχορηγούμενον καὶ συμβιβαζόμενον, αὔξει τὴν αὔξησιν τοῦ θεοῦ) Hoc vult, retinendam Ecclesia unitatem: quod fieri non potest, nisi retineantur praepositorum gradus, et eis pareatur in iis, quae ad Ecclesiae pacem pertinent. Ita in tempore occurrit foetis illis, quae posita erpuere, κατὰ φύγας dicta.

Locus huic geminus est Eph. IV. 15. 16. ibi est ἁφῆς τῆς ἐπιχορηγίας, hic ἁφῶν καὶ συνδέσμων, per artus, et venas, et arterias, quae sunt nexus et vincula corporis, חברות ווללאות, ibi est συναρμολογούμενον καὶ συμβιβαζόμενον, pro quo hic ἐπιχορηγούμενον καὶ συμβιβαζόμενον.

Elt autem ἐπιχορηγούμενον, unde ἐπιχορηγία in illo ad Ephesios loco accipere ea, quae corpori alendo sunt necessaria, vid. Sirach. XXV. 28. In Glossario ἐπιχορηγὰ, subministro, supredo. Αὔξει τὴν αὔξησιν τοῦ θεοῦ, Graece loquitur, quam et Latini sequuntur, cum dicunt, mortem mori, ferire ferviturem.

Genitivus autem τοῦ θεοῦ hic causam significat. Crescit illo incremento, quod a Deo est. Ex iisdem et nutrimur et crescimus. Theophylactus: Ut vitalis Spiritus a cerebro in reliquum corpus per nervos diffunditur, et a capite ipso fenfibilitas omnis et motus derivatur: Sic et Ecclesiae corpus a Christo subministratur, hoc est, ab eo et vitam accipit, et Spiritus incrementum.

Quod utid, omne tunc haud dubie hac Ecclesia adipiscitur, cum Spiritus illi nexus et impactus. Is namque nexum quendam et juncturas incrementa suppeditat. Illi quidem congruere (hoc est, correspondere) valebit, nec Spiritus ipse suppeditabitur, nec Dei incrementum, hoc est optima vita profectus ullus accedent. Cornelius a Lapide: Quasi dicat: Sicut Spiritus vitalis, qui ad vitam, sensum et motum est necessarius, a capite in totum corpus per nervos, juncturas et articulos diffunditur, itaque singulis membris facultatem sentiendi et movendi impertit; sic Spiritus gratiae a Christo quasi capite in membra illi connexa, puta in fideles Christianos per juncturas mutua unionis et charitatis derivatur, illisque spiritualem vitam et motum suppeditat, itaque totum Ecclesia corpus crescit in augmentum Dei, id est, ut Syrus, crescit augmento Dei, puta incremento fidei & Spiritus Dei. Ira ex Chrysostomo Theophylactus. Quæ annon sunt infinitæ virtutis & effecta verè divina? An Angelorum ulli vel excluso Christo, vel juxta cum Christo ullatenus conveniunt? Recte B. Hunnius illationem Apostoli tradidit: Nolite vos committere maleferiatis illis Doctoribus, qui hunc sibi scopum prefixum habent, ut abducant potius à Christo, quam fide Dei caput per fidem semel apprehensum videre ut retineatis. Huic enim sic insiti per commissuras & compagines mediante nimirum Verbi & Sacramentorum ministerio, & inter vos compacti societate ejusdem Spiritus, fidei, & charitatis, augescente augmento Christi, hoc est, Deo incrementa largiente proficietis in fide & pietate. v.

## 2:20
20. If you have died with Christ from the elements of the world, Christ has delivered us from that human institution.

He who dies is delivered from the inconveniences of life. Therefore, to die is also taken in a good sense, as in Rom. VI. 2. Elements are called any institution whatsoever, Gal. IV. 3. 9. where you will see why these are called elements of the world, namely because they were common to the Jews with other nations: there was nothing in those rites peculiar to the Jews, and they came more from the nations to the Jews through a certain condescension of God, than from the Jews to the nations. Why, as though living in the world, are you subject to decrees? This is that you are being taught by finite things, some of you indeed, as if life were to be composed for us not according to the example of Christ, but of the world.

Dead with Christ to the elements of the world they are called, that is, to Mosaic rites. For the Apostle returns to them: as he had said that we were buried with Christ: So he now says we are dead with Christ, looking back again to baptism and the application of Christ's merits made therein. For those rites were certain rudiments of faith, but worldly and external, Gal. IV. 3. 9. Crocius has not unsuitably rendered the sense of the argument: If in baptism you are dead with Christ to ceremonial laws, which were certain rudiments of the old world, and are free, what just cause can there be why you should suffer yourselves to be entangled in a new yoke of superstitious decrees, as if you were not yet dead with Christ and living the life of the world, hoping for salvation from Him through external things?

Yet I would not think that the old world is designated here, but that the elements of the world are spoken of from things that pertain to the world. Nor can I approve of Grotius's gloss, that these were common to the Jews with the nations, and came more from the nations to the Jews than from the Jews to the nations. Those nations imitated them out of an evil emulation by the instigation of the Devil; they were not indeed transferred from the nations to the Jews by a divine condescension.

Latin:

20. Εἰ ἀπεθάνετε σὺν Χριστῷ ἀπὸ τῶν στοιχείων τοῦ κόσμου Christus nos liberavit ab illa institutione humana.

Qui moritur, liberatur à vitæ incommodis. Ideo mori etiam in bonam partem sumitur, ut Rom. VI. 2. Στοιχεῖα dicuntur institutio quævis, Gal. IV. 3. 9. ubi videbis, cur hæc στοιχεῖα τοῦ κόσμου dicuntur, nimirum quia Judæis erant communia cum gentibus aliis: nihil in ipsis ritibus erat proprium Judæis, & magis à gentibus ad Judæos per συγκατάβασιν quandam Dei, quam à Judæis ad gentes venerant. Τί ὡς ζῶντες ἐν κόσμῳ δογματίζεσθε; hic est doceri vos finitis, quidam nempe vestrum, tanquam non ad Christi, sed ad mundi exemplum vita nobis esset componenda.

Mortui cum Christo clementis mundi dicuntur, id est, ritibus Mosaicis. Ad eos enim redit Apostolus: ut consepultos dixerat Christo: Ita jam mortuos ait cum Christo, respiciens iterum baptismum & in eo factam meritorum Christi applicationem. Ritus enim illi rudimenta quædam fidei sed mundana & externa, Gal. IV. 3. 9. Sensum argumenti non incommode reddidit Crocius: Si in baptismo cum Christo mortui à legibus ceremonialibus, quæ mundi veteris rudimenta quædam fuerunt, liberi estis, quæ justa causa esse possit, cur vos novo superstitionum decretorum jugo implicari patiamini, ac si nondum cum Christo mortui vitam mundi ageretis, cum eo ex rebus externis salutem sperantes.

Mundum tamen veterem hic designari non putarim, sed mundi elementa dici à rebus, quæ ad mundum pertinent. Nec approbare possum Grotii glossam, quod Judæis ea fuerint cum gentibus communia, & magis à gentibus ad Judæos, quam à Judæis ad gentes venerint. Imitata illæ sunt gentes ex κακοζηλία autore Diabolo; non vero à gentibus traducta illa ad Judæos, συγκατάβασιν divina.

## 2:21
V. 21. Do not touch, do not taste, do not handle.

And here is a mimesis, the mark of which the Syrian has placed here. For thus those masters used to speak. Tertullian against Marcion V. denies that these pertain to the law of Moses. To me it seems that he used common words, which would encompass both Jews and Philosophers, especially the Pythagoreans. Clement of Alexandria, Strom. III. [Greek text omitted].

And those former ones, do not touch, do not taste, pertain to foods, that is, do not touch so as to taste, Gen. III. 3. 22. But the latter, do not handle, pertains to avoiding women, which the Jewish priests did at certain times, but the Pythagoreans always. θίγω and θιγγάνω is Greek frequent in good writers.

It is found also in Exod. XIX. 12. and Heb. XI. 28. XII. 20. The same ones, who are the Doctors here, are touched upon by Clement, or whoever is the writer of the Constitutions VI. 16. Such things as those, the ones of ill name, slandering creation, marriage, procreation, birth, prophets; writing certain firm names, as they themselves say, of an Angel. But the truth is not so, serving the same demons; whose teaching flee &c.

Interpreters vary both as to the mimesis and as to those false doctrines. Ambrosiaster establishes no mimesis here, but wishes it to be said by Paul in his own person, deterring Christians from all desire for worldly things. But most others agree that these were spoken mimetically from the person of the false Doctors: Nor do we think we should depart from them.

Not a few think that those doctrines regard ceremonial laws, which were again being obtruded under the opinion of worship and necessity by false Apostles, e.g., concerning not touching the unclean, not eating swine's flesh, and other forbidden foods. This does not please Crocius.

He assigned three corruptions, according to their own interpretation, the first of which relies on curious speculations, of which v. 8 it is said, that they appear by the voice of philosophies, which are designated by the words of empty deception: The second in manifestly superstitious rites fabricated by human ingenuity, which are noted by the words according to the tradition of men, v. 8. The third in a mixture of legal observations with the Gospel through the words, according to the elements of the world, v. 8. the same 8. of which a general refutation is had in v. 8.

9. 10; but the species indeed in the first place the third regarding the necessity of circumcision, v. 11. 12. 13. and legal worship in general, v. 14. 15. and also certain species of the same, the choice of foods and the observation of times, v. 16. 17. But in the second place he institutes a refutation of the first corruption concerning the worship of Angels, v. 18. 19. Thirdly, finally, the profligation of the second corruption is undertaken, v. 20. sqq. But to this dissolution it seems to intercede, that the last refutation concerns the elements of the world, that is, by Crocius's own interpretation, Mosaic rites, which he himself referred to the third kind of corruptions.

Since therefore in this last list both of the elements of the world, that is, of Mosaic rites, v. 20. and of the tradition of men, v. 22. mention is made, I would indeed think that three kinds of corruptions are established, but which have been reduced to a dichotomy, v. 8. but for the sake of refutation they are so treated that a triple refutation emerges. First of Mosaic ceremonies concerning circumcision and other Levitical constitutions obtruded by Judaizers: then indeed of Pseudo-Philosophical dogmas concerning Angels invented from the fable of the Platonists: thirdly, finally, of certain mixed decrees, which were partly composed from Jewish ceremonies, partly from Platonic and Pythagorean institutions, and carried with them a certain appearance of wisdom and utility.

And in this we easily accede to the Grotian opinion. For those, do not touch, do not taste, do not handle, although they may have been taken in great part from Mosaic rites, from which we have been liberated, who have died with Christ through faith in baptism, and therefore had a greater appearance, yet they seem to be interpolated from Gentile tenets: and thus are reckoned among the traditions and doctrines of men, especially because Levitical constitutions, having already reached their end, were being brought in by postliminy by nothing but human laws, and were being mixed with Philosophical tenets. Olandrina's paraphrase is as follows: If anyone says to you, that one must abstain from conjugal custom, and that a wife must not be touched, as if in that abstinence there were worship of God, do not believe. If anyone forbids certain foods, lest by tasting your conscience be contaminated, do not believe. If anyone wishes to forbid, that you should not touch this or that thing, namely, lest you be polluted, do not believe: because to the clean all things are clean.

And indeed foods are consumed and digested, while we use them: (For food for the belly, and the belly for foods, but God will destroy both this and that, 1. Cor. 6.) Therefore in the use of those corruptible things there is neither holiness, nor sin: provided we do not abuse the creatures of God, or offend the weak in faith. Therefore, those who superstitiously observe these things: and in the use of them sin, but in abstinence holiness constitute, it is not done according to the rule of the Word of God, but according to human doctrines and opinions. Clement of Alexandria, lib. III. Stromat., says: it is the care of those who are content to abstain from wine, feasts, and venery, for Angels and Demons. But that "touch not, taste not" is to be referred not only to foods and in a composite sense, which is not even found in Gen. III. 3, but first to those things which, as unclean, ought not to be touched, and later to foods in a divided sense. Nor do we think the word ἀποχρήσῃ should be changed. All those things are said to be corrupted by abuse, because although they had their use as things delivered by God, now, however, because they ought to have ceased, and are delivered under the opinion of worship and necessity, they perish by that abuse. Thus Chrysostom notes those things prescribed by the commands and doctrines of men, he says, ceremonial laws, which now are the doctrines of men, the prescription of their time having elapsed, or the dogmas of the Greeks are taxed. And it is not inconvenient that both are noted in the stated place.

Many indeed, with Jerome and Theophylact, explain it concerning excretion through the bowels, and compare Matt. XV. 2: Calvin, Piscator, the Belgians, the Deventerians, Crocius, and among the Papists, Sasbout. But the translation of B. Luther seems more convenient: welches sich doch alles unter Händen verzehrt [which all consumes itself under the hands], because all those things are vain and useless. Or as the Ernestine Bible has it: *Welches vergeblich also gehalten wird/ weil es in äusserlichen vergänglichen Dingen bestehet/ und weder rein noch unrein machet* [Which is thus held in vain, because it consists in external perishable things, and makes neither clean nor unclean]. B. Hunnius: These seem to have the force and momentum of a cause, for which this dogma is to be rejected, since foods and other goods are given to us here by God for an end, so that they may be corrupted by their abuse, that is, so that they may serve the use of men, and thus by serving us be consumed. Unless perhaps they are hinted to bring about total destruction, insofar as they are prescribed by the Pseudo-Apostles, as Ambrose has it, and also August. epist. 109. All these things are more conducive to corruption, when one abstains from them with superstition, so that a man abuses them, that is, does not use them according to the doctrines and precepts of men. Which sense Cornelius a Lapide prefers: Who says: Which observance of superstitious worship of Angels already mentioned brings about destruction, and eternal damnation to those who observe them, and in them and in their Angels, whom they thus worship, they hope, but not in Christ, so Ambrose and Augustine. Erasmus Schmidius: Τῇ ἀποχρήσῃ [abuse], he says. For the law commands to abstain from the touch and taste of certain things for a certain end; if, however, they are extended beyond that, they are drawn into abuse against the law.

Latin:

V. 21. Μὴ ἅψῃ, μη γεύσῃ, μη θίγῃς

Et hic μίμησις, cujus notam hic apposuit Syrus. Sic enim magistri illi loquebantur. Tertullianus adversus Marcionem V. negat, hæc ad legem Mosis pertinere. Mihi videtur verbis usus communibus, quæ & Judæos & Philosophos, præsertim Pythagoristas comprehenderent. Clemens Alexandr. Strom. III. ἀπείλει διὰ φροντίδος ἐςὶ τὸ τοῖς μάγοις, οὔτε μὴ ἅψῃ, οὔτε μὴ γεύσῃ καὶ ἀφροδισίων ἀπέχεσθαι, λατρεύουσι Ἀγγέλοις ἢ δαίμοσιν.

Ac priora illa, μὴ ἅψῃ, μὴ γεύσῃ, ad cibos pertinent, id est, ne tangas ut gustes, Gen. III. 3. 22. Posterius vero illud μὴ θίγῃς pertinet ad vitandas fæminas, quod Judæi sacerdotes certis temporibus faciebant, Pythagoristæ vero semper. θίγω & θιγγάνω Græcum est frequens bonis scriptoribus.

Invenitur & exod. XIX. 12. & ad Ebr. XI. 28. XII. 20. Iidem, qui hic Doctores, tanguntur à Clemente, aut quisquis est scriptor Constitutionum VI. 16. Τοιαῦτα ἃ ἰν τοῖσαι οἱ δυσώνυμοι, διαβάλλοντες δημιουργίαν, γάμον, τεκνογονίαν, τόμον, προφῆται· Βέβαια τινα ὀνόματα ἐγ. γράφοντες, ὡς αὐτοὶ φασιν Ἀγγέλου. Τὸ δ' ἀληθὲς οὐ πεῖ, δαιμόνων τοῖς αὐτοῖς ὑπηρετῶν· ὧν φεύγετε τὴν διδασκαλίαν &c.

Variant interpretes tum quod mimesin, tum quoad falsas illas doctrinas. Nullam mimesin hic statuit Ambrosiaster, sed à Paulo hæc in propria persona Christianos ab omni cupiditate rerum mundanarum deterrente dici vult. Sed alii plerique omnes μιμητικῶς ex persona falsorum Doctorum ea dicta esse consentiunt: Neque ab iis discedendum arbitramur.

Doctrinas autem illas non pauci leges ceremoniales respicere censent, quæ iterum obtrudebantur sub opinione cultus & necessitatis à falsis Apostolis, v. g. de non tangendo immundo, de non edenda carne suilla, aliisque cibis vetitis. Non placet id Crocio.

Tres autem affignavit corruptelas, secundum ἰδίαν ἐπίλυσιν, quarum prima nitatur curiosis speculationibus, de quibus v. 8. dicatur, quod appareant voce philosophias, quod designatæ sint vocibus inanis deceptionis: Secunda in manifeste superstitiosis ritibus ab humano ingenio confictis, que notentur verbis secundum traditionem hominum, v. 8. tertia in mixtura observationum legalium cum Evangelio per verba, secundum elementa mundi, v. 8. eodem 8. quarum confutatio generalis v. 8.

9. 10. habeatur; species vero primo quidem loco tertia quoad circumcisionis necessitatem, v. 11. 12. 13. & cultum legalem in genere, v. 14. 15. nec non species ejusdem certas, delectum ciborum & observationem temporum, v. 16. 17. Altero autem loco primæ corruptelæ de cultu Angelorum instituat confutatio, v. 18. 19. Tertio denique loco suscipiatur profligatio secundæ corruptelæ, v. 20. sqq. Sed huic διαλύσει intercedere videtur, quod ultima confutatio elementa mundi concernat, hoc est, interprete ipso Crocio, ritus Mosaicos, quos ad tertium genus corruptelarum ipse retulit.

Quum ergo in hoc ultima elencho & elementorum mundi, hoc est rituum Mosaicorum, v. 20. & traditionis hominum, v. 22. mentio fiat, triplicis generis corruptelas statui quidem censerem, sed quæ ad διχοτομίαν redactæ fuerint, v. 8. ob confutationem autem ita tractentur, ut triplex ἔλεγχος emergat. Primum Mosaicorum ceremoniarum de circumcisione aliisque Leviticis constitutionibus à Judaizantibus obtrusis: deinde vero Pseudo Philosophicorum dogmatum de Angelis è febola Platonicorum invetorum: tertio denique de mixtis quibusdam decretis, quæ partim è ceremoniis Judaicis, partim ex Platonicis & Pythagoricis institutis conflata fuerint, & specie quadam sapientiæ & utilitatis præ se tulerint. Et in hoc facile accedimus Grotiane sententiæ.

Nam illa μὴ ἅψῃ, μὴ γεύσῃ, μὴ θίγῃς etsi à ritibus Mosaicis, à quibus liberati sumus, qui per fidem cum Christo mortui sumus in baptismo, magnam partem petita fuerint, ideoque majorem speciem habuerint, interpolata tamen è gentilibus placitis videntur: atque ita traditionibus & doctrinis hominum accensentur, imprimis quia Levitice constitutiones jam finem consequutæ, non nisi humanis legibus postliminio invehebantur, & cum Philo-sophicis placitis commiscebantur. Olandrina paraphrasis sic habet: Si quis vobis dixerit, abflinendum esse à consuetudine conjugali, neque uxorem attingendam, quasi in ea abstinentia cultus Dei sit, nolite credere. Si quis certos cibos prohibuerit, ne gustando conscientia vestra contaminetur, nolite credere. Si quis velit prohibere, ne hanc vel illam rem attingatis, ne videlicet polluamini, nolite credere: quia mundis omnia sunt munda.

Et sane cibi absumuntur & digeruntur, dum illis utimur: (Esca enim ventri, & venter escis, Deus autem & hunc & hanc destruet, 1. Cor. 6.) Itaque in usu istarum rerum corruptibilium neque sanctitas est, neque peccatum: modo creaturis Dei non abutamur, aut infirmos in fide offendamus. Quod igitur istas res superstitiose observant: & in usu earum peccatum, in abstinentia vero sanctitatem constituunt, id non fit secundum regulam Verbi Dei, sed secundum doctrinas & opiniones humanas. Clemens Alexandrinus lib. III. Stromat. inquit: conlentibus Angelos & Daemonas cura est vino, epulis & venere abstinere. Illa autem μὴ ἁψῇ, μὴ γεύσῃ non ad cibos tantum & sensu composito, qui ne quidem Gen. III. 3. reperitur, sed prius ad ea, quae ceu immunda attingi non debebant, posterius ad cibos sensu diviso, referenda. Vocem etiam ἀποχρήσῃ non arbitramur immutandam. Omnia illa corrumpi dicuntur abusu, quia utut qua divinitus tradita erant, suum habuere usum, nunc tamen, quia cessare debuerunt, & sub opinione cultus & necessitatis traduntur, abusu illo pereunt. Ita Chrysostomus verbis praescripta mandatis & doctrinis hominum notat, ait, leges ceremoniales, quae nunc sint doctrinae hominum elapso temporis fui praescripto, aut Graecorum dogmata taxari. Utraque autem dicto loco notari non inconveniens.

Plerique sane cum Hieronymo & Theophylacto de egestione per secessum exponunt, & Matth. XV. 2. conferunt: Caluinus, Piscator, Belgae, Daventinus, Crocius, & e Pontificiis Sasbout. Sed convenientior videtur B. Lutheri translatio: welches sich doch alles unter Händen verzehrt/ quod frustranea sint & vana ista omnia. Vel ut Biblia habent Ernestina: Welches vergeblich also gehalten wird/ weil es in äusserlichen vergänglichen Dingen bestehet/ und weder rein noch unrein machet. B. Hunnius: Videntur haec vim atque momentum habere causae, ob quam rejiciendum sit hoc dogma, quandoquidem cibi aliaque bona hic nobis fine data & a Deo concessa, ut suo corrumpantur abusu, id est, ut usui hominum subserviant, atque sic inserviendo nobis absumantur. Nisi fortallis omnino interitum afferre illa innuantur, quatenus a Pseudo-Apostolis praescripta sunt, ut habet Ambrosius, nec non August. epist. 109. omnia haec magis ad corruptionem valent, cum superstitione ab iis abstinetur, ut eis homo abutatur, id est, non eis utatur secundum doctrinas & praecepta hominum. Quem sensum praefert Cornelius a Lapide: Quaidicat: Quae observantia superstitiosi cultus Angelorum jam dicta interitum afferunt, & damnationem aeternam iis, qui ea observant, in iisque & in suis Angelis, quos ita colunt, sperant, non autem in Christo, ita Ambrosius & Augustinus. Erasmus Schmidius: Τῇ ἀποχρήσῃ, inquit, abusu. Etenim certo fine lex jubet a quorundam tactu & gustu abstinere; si tamen ea ultra extendantur, in abusum contra legem trahuntur.

## 2:22
V. 22. Ἅτινά ἐστι πάντα εἰς φθορὰν τῇ ἀποχρήσει [Which are all to perish with the using]) Oecumenius and Theophylact read Τήπαο-χρείας. Thus the Greeks call that which the Latins call egetum or excretion. He means this: What is the great thing, to command many things about those which perish by excretion? A similar sense is in the words of Christ, Matt. XV. 17.

This pertains to those two former things, of which he had treated. Κατὰ τὰ ἐντάλματα καὶ διδασκαλίας ἀνθρώπων [After the commandments and doctrines of men]) This ought to be referred to what is more remote, namely to that dogmatizesthe.

These things were discovered by men, they did not come primarily from God. Entalmata are those things which are commanded by human laws, didaskaliai are those which are taught by Philosophers.

Latin:

V. 22. Ἅτινά ἐστι πάντα εἰς φθορὰν τῇ ἀποχρήσει) Τήπαο-χρείας legerunt Oecumenius & Theophylact. Sic Graeci vocant id, quod Latini egetum vel egestionem. Hoc vult: Quid magni est, multa praecipere de eis, quae egesta pereunt? Similis sensus in Christi verbis Matth. XV. 17.

Pertinet hoc ad illa duo priora, de quibus egerat. Κατὰ τὰ ἐντάλματα καὶ διδασκαλίας ἀνθρώπων)

Hoc debet referri ad remotius, nempe ad illud δογματίζεσθε. Ab hominibus ista reperta sunt, non primitus a Deo venerunt. Ἐντάλματα sunt, quae legibus humanis jubentur, διδασκαλίαι, quae a Philosophis praecipiuntur.

## 2:23
V. 23. Ἅτινά ἐστι λόγον μὲν ἔχοντα σοφίας ἐν ἐθελοθρησκείᾳ καὶ ταπεινοφροσύνῃ, καὶ ἀφειδίᾳ σώματος, οὐκ ἐν τιμῇ τινι πρὸς πλησμονὴν τῆς σαρκός [Which things have indeed a show of wisdom in will-worship and humility, and severity to the body, not in any honor to the satisfying of the flesh]) Here μὲν is placed with the following δὲ at its end, as also Acts III. 21. Rom. I. 8. III. 2. XI. 13. below II. 18., and that by ἀποσιώπησιν τε ἀντίθετα [aposiopesis with antithesis], which is easily supplied. These have a reason not foolish, if the cautions are present: will-worship, if these things are undertaken spontaneously, not abominating those things which God created. Ἐθελοθρησκεία is a middle term, signifying rites or ceremonies, as the Glossaries expound it. Its origin is from the Thracians, as Plutarch teaches Alexander. See above 18. Acts XXVI. 5. Jac. I. 26. 27. Ἐθελοθρησκεία rites or observances voluntarily undertaken, which רְעוּת is rendered by the Greek Interpreters ἐθελοθρησκεία. He adds καὶ ταπεινοφροσύνῃ, that is, with that modesty of mind which does not condemn others living differently, Rom. XIV. 3. 4. Eph. IV. 2. Καὶ ἀφειδίᾳ σώματος, ἐκ ἐν τιμῇ τινι πρὸς πλησμονὴν τῆς σαρκός [and severity to the body, not in any honor to the satisfying of the flesh].

Where these words are thus to be construed, οὐκ ἐν τιμῇ τινι πρὸς πλησμονὴν τῆς σαρκός [not in any honor to the filling of the flesh]. Thus far they are good, if they have this proposed to themselves, to treat the body harshly, and not to yield to the flesh unto satiety. Φειδὴ & ἀφειδίᾳ is to have gently. Contrary to this is ἀφειδίᾳ, as σωματία ἀφειδῶν in Lucian: whence here the name ἀφειδία. The Hebrews would say: אַכְזָרִיוּת. But τιμὴ σαρκὸς is the care which is bestowed upon the flesh, as 1. Cor. XII. 23. 1. Tim. IV. 17. Πλησμονὴ Gen. XLI. 30. Exod. XVI. 3. & elsewhere. These things understood, it is easy to supply that which is left unsaid, namely the ἀντίθετον, that these ἀποχραί of Pythagoras are more harmful than useful, if they are undertaken as necessary for salvation, that is, if they become things done not δι' ἄσκησιν, but διὰ βδελυρίαν, as the Apostolic Canon LI. speaks; if on that account others are despised, if no less delicately is the body kept with herbs, legumes, fruits cooked for delights.

Philo in his book: The worse lies in wait for the better: "If you are to behold foods or drinks, do not approach them in wickedness, or refuse and neglect them with contempt, or be neglected without preparations for the body, or use them for your own salvation, or receiving without that which is of its own error will show the true way of continence. For what are pursuits, unconquerable and unwearied labors, and also with their corruptions disturbing soul and body. Nor if anyone uses contempt or purification, because he indeed suffers well in his own soul, but the body in a base one. Nor should you look upon everything under an abundance of ships with most brilliant provisions and expenses, making them sufficiently pure, and putting an end to impiety, luxury adorning the temple as a votive offering, abundantly bringing in materials and arts of a wandering child and honors more precious than honor, reading aloud with a sword by command and year on the way toward piety, worship instead of a true ruler. And giving gifts to the unjust one, who cannot receive such things, and flattering the unflatterable. There will not arise a sight of service through exercise, but it is again genuine, offering matter of the soul and a single sacrifice of truth. But the spurious ones are to be dragged away — there then, whatever things you show off through external abundance.

Here are not brought forward cautions, under which those commandments and doctrines of men have a reason not foolish, but schemata, by which they are painted, so that they show forth some reason of wisdom, because it is a freely chosen religion, which is undertaken for the sake of humility, because it is directed to the neglecting of the body.

The former of which, ethelothreskeia, is to be referred to the first genus of corruptions of the false Apostles, who freely and at their own will chose which things they observed from the Levitical constitutions with Christian decrees: The second, humility, concerns the second genus of corruptions concerning the worship of Angels.

The last, neglecting of the body, because they did not spare the body, pertains to the third genus of corruptions, which was mixed from Judaism and Platonism, and to which it ought to reconcile a certain appearance.

Nor indeed are these approved by the Apostle, or praised as wise constitutions, which seems to Grotius: But according to the common consent of all Interpreters they are disapproved and reprehended.

Ostander therefore explains it thus: And these things indeed before the judgment of human reason have a show of heavenly wisdom, while men suddenly invent new divine worships of their own accord and at their own will, and with feigned and simulated humility they dazzle the eyes of men, while they do not spare their own body, but with vigils, fasts, and other laborious and troublesome exercises they afflict it, and neither have due honor for their body, nor do they care for it, by which it might be satisfied, nourished, and preserved with necessary things.

But the Lord utterly averts that fillam, superstition, and humanly invented holiness and religion.

With which B. Hunnius agrees, others agree, even the Pontifical Interpreters, as far as these things are concerned, that these have only a s how of wisdom, and by such figments they are fermented, and are false and mere superstition. Vatablus translates logon as speciem [show]; Chrysostom, sermonem [word]; the Vulgate, rationem [reason]; as if the Apostle were saying, as Cornelius interprets: This false religion seems to bring forward reasons and wise words, which they offer in the show of piety for their own superstition.

But the sense of Grotius, as far as I know, has come into no one's mind.

You might find a certain analogy in Estius of the Pontificians concerning those things beyond works of supererogation and holy affliction of the body of believers, but that as new and excessively violent, and alien to the scope of the Apostle, is deservedly disapproved by Estius. ἐθελοθρησκεία, although it may be explained concerning rites voluntarily undertaken, as Camerarius explained it by voluntary worship: and Erasmus Schmidius has labored at length to show that this word formally signifies voluntary and spontaneous worship, which is rendered without coerci…on, it is not to be denied, however, nor does Schmidius deny it, that Paul is here dealing with superstitions and cults introduced by one's own judgment; he denies at least that in this word by itself such a signification has force, and he confesses that the Apostle is enumerating in this place the colors with which false Doctors are accustomed to adorn their human traditions and their own αὐθαίρετον [self-chosen] worship, so that they may be thought to have λόγοv σοφίας [a show of wisdom]: The first of which is ἐθελοθρησκεία, a spontaneous and prompt performance.

For it happens that the followers of false doctrine are much more studious, prompt, and more spontaneous in their false religion than those who follow the true: Just as we see that the Papists are more diligent in their worship than we are in ours, and are much more liberal in preserving and propagating religion than our men are in ours, Luc. 16, 8. The second is ταπεινοφροσύνη [humility], a zeal for humility, even if feigned; which appears in false Doctors even today. The third is ἀφειδία σώματος [severity to the body], because they also do not spare their own body, with fasts, vigils, journeys, satisfactions, etc. By all these and similar things they strive that their own αὐθαίρετος [self-chosen] worship, which in ἐθελοθρησκεία may seem to have a show of holiness, and therefore may find more supporters. I do not see, however, why one should depart from the version of B. Luther, durch selb-erwählte Geistlichkeit [self-chosen spirituality], and why it should be rendered: Frenwillig-geleisteten Gottesdienst [voluntarily-performed divine service], as the most learned Interpreters of the Greek language have explained it as superstition, Theodoret, Chrysostom, Theophylact, Erasmus of Rotterdam, as also the Vulgate and Ambrosiaster. Jerome to Hedibia interprets it as false religion. Stephanus translates it as worship which each one chooses by his own judgment, such as is not approved by God, which is not true, but false, not consonant with divine law, but brought in outside and beyond the law, just as every superstition and elective worship is disapproved by God. William Estius notes that it cannot be taught that ἐθελοθρησκεία is ever taken in a good sense. But that ἐθελοθρησκεία is praised, if the τὰ ἐντάλματα & διδασκαλία ἀνθρώπων [commandments and doctrines of men] are voluntarily undertaken, or Levitical human constitutions are introduced again by authority after they have expired, provided we do not abominate those things which God created, for the sake of Papistical superstitions, Grotius seems to have invented; certainly such a gloss does not appear from the text, just as no one has explained ταπεινοφροσύνην [humility] as that modesty which does not condemn others living differently, but as feigned humility, as it is used in verse 18. The rest are inverted at will by Grotius, so that he excuses this sense, that they are good to that extent, if they propose this to themselves, to treat the body harshly, and not to indulge the flesh to satiety. No one finds that sense in those words, all find the contrary: That it is not praised here, but that this ἀφειδία σώματος [severity to the body] is blamed, by which the honor due to it is denied, the due nourishment is withheld, so that it is rendered unable to perform its duties, when yet God has created it to be filled and refreshed, lest by excessive abstinence it be rendered useless for performing its duties, as B. Hunnius holds. It seems, says Theophylact, that the decree of this [sect] carries before it a certain piety and moderation, and makes small account of the body, since it abstains from foods, although God has conferred honor both on the body, and granted foods and nourishments, so that by these the flesh, wearied out, might persist, and willingly command over its vices. But these men by no means honorably use the body itself, seeing that they deprive it of power, and take away its judgment, nor do they allow it to hold rule of itself spontaneously. This is open servitude, says Theodoret, and an abolition of the honor given. Nor do the Papist Interpreters differ: Cornelius à Lapide explains it as abstinence and austerity of life, by which they do not spare the body, but afflict it immoderately and superstitiously: Not in honor to satiety of the flesh, that is, with the honor or necessary aid denied to the body for satisfying hunger. For honor among the Hebrews is not only verbal or ceremonial, but also real, which is nothing other than the supply of necessary things or resources. The Apostle perceived, says Estius, that that wisdom or those precepts were such, whereby the due honor belonging to the body for filling, that is, the just refreshment of the flesh, is withdrawn, while namely by immoderate and foolishly devised abstentions the body is exhausted, against that saying, no one ever hated his own flesh, but nourishes and cherishes it, Eph. 5. Whence he also commands his disciple: Drink no longer water, but use a little wine for your stomach's sake and your frequent infirmities, 1. Tim. 5. Into the same understanding one falls back, if the negation be repeated in the other member after this manner: Not to satiety of the flesh. For then the sense will be: Those precepts of men do not conduce to satiety of the flesh, but rather, with a necessary satiety, of which the Psalmist: The poor shall eat and shall be satisfied, they defraud the flesh: as here the figure occurs, by which less is said than is understood: Such is that saying of the Prophet: They did what I did not command them, that is, they did all things contrary to my precepts. Therefore Grotius wished to sail only with the unwilling Papists here, nor is he truly or with their advantage sailed along. That ἀντιθέσιον [opposition], which he wishes is here subtly implied, teaches this, namely that these Pythagorean ἀποχαί [abstinences] are more harmful, even if undertaken as if necessary to salvation, if on that account others are despised, if the body is no less delicately kept from herbs, legumes, fruits cooked for delights. All which things occur rather in Papal religions or superstitions, the matter itself teaches. For those are established, if not necessary, yet most useful to salvation: Those who observe them wish to be held religious above others: Their abstinence is often greater luxury than the common manner of living of others who do not observe distinctions of foods.

PARS III. EPISTOLAE NOTHETIKH Admonishing to a life worthy of Christians.

Latin:

V. 23. Ἅτινά ἐστι λόγον μὲν ἔχοντα σοφίας ἐν ἐθελοθρησκείᾳ καὶ ταπεινοφροσύνῃ, καὶ ἀφειδίᾳ σώματος, οὐκ ἐν τιμῇ τινι πρὸς πλησμονὴν τῆς σαρκός) Est hic μὲν positum fine sequenti δὲ, ut & Act. III. 21. Rom. I. 8. III. 2. XI. 13. infra II. 18. idque per ἀποσιώπησιν τε ἀντίθετα, quod facile suppletur. Habent ista rationem non stultam, si adsint cautiones, ὃν ἐθελοθρησκεία, si sponte ista suscipiantur, non abominando ea, quae Deus creavit. Ἐθελοθρησκεία est vox media, significans ritus aut ceremonias, ut Glossaria exponunt. Origo a Thracibus, ut docet Plutarchus Alexandro. Vide fupra 18. Act. XXVI. 5. Jac. I. 26. 27. Ἐθελοθρησκεία ritus sive observationes sponte susceptae, quae רְעוּת Graecis Interpretibus ἐθελοθρησκεία. Addit καὶ ταπεινοφροσύνῃ, id est, cum ea modestia animi, quae alios aliter viventes non damnet, Rom. XIV. 3. 4. Eph. IV. 2. Καὶ ἀφειδίᾳ σώματος, ἐκ ἐν τιμῇ τινι πρὸς πλησμονὴν τῆς σαρκός.

Ubi sic contruenda haec, οὐκ ἐν τιμῇ τινι πρὸς πλησμονὴν τῆς σαρκός. Eatenus bona sunt, si hoc sibi propositum habeant, dure tractare corpus, neque carni obsequi ad saturitatem. Φειδὴ & ἀφειδίᾳ est molliter habere. Huic contrarium ἀφειδίᾳ, sicut σωματία ἀφειδῶν apud Lucianum: unde hic nomen ἀφειδία. Ebraei dicerent: אַכְזָרִיוּת. Timi vero σαρκὸς est cura, quae carni praestatur, ut 1. Cor. XII. 23. 1. Tim. IV. 17. Πλησμονὴ Gen. XLI. 30. Exod. XVI. 3. & alibi. His intellectis facile est supplere id, quod reticetur ἀντίθετον, nempe istas ἀποχρὰς Pythagoras magis noxias esse quam utiles, si velut ad salutem necessariae suscipiantur, id est, si fiant ἃ δι ἀσκη-σιν, ἀλλὰ διὰ βδελυρίαν, ut loquitur canon Apostolicus LI. si ob id contemnantur alii, si non minus laute habeatur corpus ex herbis, leguminibus, pomis ad delitias coctis.

Philo libro: Pejorem insidiari meliori: Ἐὰν εἶναι θεάση σιτὰ ἢ ποτὰ μὴ ἐν κακῷ προσείμενος, ἢ λυτὰ κἀμελήσας παραιτεῖσθαι, ἢ ἄνευ περὶ τὸ σῶμα σκευασμάτων ἀμελεῖσθαι, ἢ χάριν ἰδίου σωτηρίας χρεώμενος, ἢ ἄνευ ὅτου λάβων ὅπερ αὐτοῦ πλάνης τὴν ἀληθῆ δ᾽ ἐγκρατείας ὁδὸν δείξει. ἃ γὰρ ἐστι ἐπιτήδευσις, ἀνίκετοι καὶ ἀτρύτοι πόνοι, λυτὰ κἀὶ ταῖς κακώσεσι ψυχὴν κὶ σῶμα ἐκταραχθίζοντες. Μηδ᾽ εἴτις πε-ριφρονήσεως ἢ καθαρεύσεως χρώμενος, διότι κει μὲν ἐυπαθεῖ τῇ ἰδίᾳ, τὸ δὲ σῶμα φαύλῃ. Μηδ᾽ ἐπὶ πᾶν ὑπὸ περιουσίας νεῶν ἰδεύῃ λαμπρόταται χορηγίαις δαπάναις, ἐκ ἱκα-τοῦντας ἁγνὸν, κἀὶ δυσθίαν ἐπαύσει, ἡ πολυτέλεια ἀναθήματι κοσμῶν τὸ ἱερὸν, ἀφθόνως μὲν ὕλας, τέχνας δὲ παιδὸς ἀγύρτου κἀὶ τιμῆς τιμιωτέρας ἐσάγων μετ᾽ ἐνσίου ἀναγιγνώσκειν ἐπι-νιταγμε κἀὶ ἐτος τῆς πρὸς ἐυσεβείαν ὁδῷ, θρησκεία ἀντὶ ἰσ-τῇ ἡγέμονι. Καὶ δῶρα τῇ ἀδικαστῇ διδὸς, ἀδύποτε ληψο-μένῃ τὰ τοιαῦτα, κὴμ κολακεύων τὸ ἀκόλακεντον. Οὐ γενήσει ἰδὶν θεραπείας ἀσκήσεως, γνήσιον δ᾽ ἐστὶν αὖ ψυχῆς ὕλην κἀὶ μίην θυσίαν Φερήσης ἀληθείας. Τὰς δὲ νόθας ἀποσύρεσθαι τό-θι δ᾽ ὅσα δια τὸν ἐκτὸς ἀφθονίαν ἐπιδείξης.

Non hic cautiones adducuntur, sub quibus illa ἐντάλματα & διδασκαλίαι ἀνθρώπων rationem non stultam habent, sed fihemat, quibus pingantur, ut prae se ferant rationem aliquam sapientiae, quod libere electa sit religio, quae humilitatis causa suscepta, quod ad ἀφειδίαν τῷ σώματι directa sit.

Quorum prius ἐθελοθρησκεία ad primum genus corruptelarum fallorum Apostolorum referendum, qui libere & pro arbitrio eligebant, quas e Leviticis constitutionibus cum Christianis decretis observabant: Alterum ταπεινοφροσύνῃ concernit secundum genus corruptelarum de Angelorum θρησκεία.

Postremum ἀφειδίᾳ τῷ σώματι, quod non parcerent corpori, pertinet ad tertium corruptelarum genus, quod mixtum erat e Judaismo & Platonismo, eique speciem quandam conciliare debebat.

Nec vero haec probantur ab Apostolo, aut laudantur ceu sapientes constitutiones, quod videtur Grotio: Sed juxta communem omnium Interpretum consensum improbantur, & reprehenduntur.

Ostander itaque sic explicat: Et hae quidem coram judicio rationis humanae habent speciem sapientiae caelestis, dum homines novos subinde cultus divinos sponte & pro arbitrio suo excogitant, & humilitate ficta & simulata hominum oculos perstringunt, dum corpori suo non parcunt, sed vigiliis, jejuniis, & aliis laboriosis & molestis exercitiis illud affligunt, neque corpori suo debitum honorem habent, neque illud curant, quo necessariis rebus saturetur, alatur & conservetur.

Sed Dominus istam fillam, superstitionem & humanitus excogitatam sanctimoniam & religionem prorsus aversatur.

Quibus consonat B. Hunnius, consonant alii, etiam Pontificii Interpretes, quantum ad haec quod haec specie solum habeant sapientiae, talibusque figmentis se-fernent, sint aut falsa & mera superstitio. Λόγον Vatablus vertit speciem; Chrysostomus, sermonem; Vulgatus rationem; quasi dicat Apostolus, interprete Cornelio: Falsa hac religio videtur afferre rationes & sermones sapientes, quos in speciem pietatis obtendunt fue superstitioni.
