Sensus vero Grotii nemini, quod sciam, in mentem venit.

Analogum quendam invenias apud Estium Pontificiorum quorundam trans ea supererogationis & sanctam corporis afflictionem credentium, sed ille ut novus & nimium violentus, & à scopo Apostoli alienus merito improbatur ab Estio. ἐθελοθρησκεία etsi exponatur de ritibus sponte susceptis, ut Camerarius exposuit per cultum voluntarium: & Erasmus Schmidius prolixe ostendere conatus est, vocem illam formaliter voluntarium & spontaneum cultum, qui sine coactione praestatur, significare, non negandum tamen, neque id negat Schmidius, Paulum hic agere de superstitionibus, & proprio arbitratu introductis cultibus, negat saltem in hoc verbo per se eam significationem vim inesse, ac fatetur, enumerare hoc loco Apostolum colores, quibus falsi Doctores suas traditiones humanas, & suum αὐθαίρετον cultum exornare solent, ut λόγοv σοφίας habere putentur: Quorum primus est ἐθελοθρησκεία spontanea & prompta praestatio.

Fit enim ut falsae doctrinae asseclae multo sint in sua falsa religione studiosiores, promptiores & magis spontanei, quam qui veram sectantur: Sicut videmus Pontificios in cultu suo magis sedulos esse, quam nos in nostro sumus, & ad conservandam ac propagandam religionem multo liberaliores esse, quam nostri homines ad nostram, Luc. 16, 8. Secundus est ταπεινοφροσύνη humilitatis studium, licet simulate; quod in falsis Doctoribus hodieque apparet. Tertius ἀφειδία σώματος, quod etiam corpori suo non parcant, jejuniis, vigiliis, itineribus, satisfactionibus, &c. Quibus omnibus & similibus id agunt, ut suus αὐθαίρετος cultum, quem ἐν ἐθελοθρησκεία speciem sanctitatis habere videatur, & ideoque plures adstipulatores inveniat. Non video tamen, cur à B. Lutheri versione, durch selb-erwählte Geistlichkeit, discedendum, & reddendum sit: Frenwillig-geleisteten Gottesdienst, quemadmodum Graecae linguae peritissimi Interpretes exposuere per superstitionem, Theodoretus, Chrysostomus, Theophylactus, Erasmus Roterodamus, ut & Vulgatus & Ambrosiaster. Hieronymus ad Hedibiam falsam religionem interpretatur. Stephanus vertit cultus, quem quisque arbitratu suo delegit, qualis Deo non probatur, qui non verus, sed falsus, non consentaneus legi divinae, sed extra & praeter legem invectus, uti omnis superstitio & cultus electitius improbatur à Deo. Guilielmus Estius notat doceri non posse, ἐθελοθρησκείαν ulquam accipi in bono. Laudari autem ἐθελοθρησκείαν, si sponte suscipiantur τὰ ἐντάλματα & διδασκαλία ἀνθρώπων aut Levitica constitutiones humana iterum autoritate, postquam expirarunt, introducantur, modo non abominemur ea, quae Deus creavit, in gratiam Papisticarum superstitionum videtur commentus esse Grotius, è textu certe talis glossa non comparet, quemadmodum nec ταπεινοφροσύνην de ea modestia, quae alios aliter viventes non damnet, quisquam exposuit, sed de ficta humilitate, uti vers. 18. adhibetur. Caetera pro arbitrio invertuntur à Grotio, ut hunc exculpat sensum, eatenus bona sunt, si hoc sibi propositum habeant, dure tractare corpus, neque carni obsequi ad saturitatem. Nullus istum in verbis illis invenit sensum, omnes contrarium: Non laudari hic, sed culpari eam ἀφειδίαν σώματος, qua debitus ei negetur honos, debitum substrahatur alimentum, ut inhabile reddatur ad officia sua obeunda, cum tamen Deus condiderit ad explendum & reficiendum corpus, ne nimia abstinentia reddatur inutile ad sua praestanda officia, ut B. Hunnius habet. Videtur, inquit Theophylactus, decreti hujus indulor pietatem quandam prae se, & moderantiam ferre, & corpus, cum ab escis abstineat, parvifacere, tametsi Deus honorem & corpori detulit, & cibos concessit, & alimenta, ut his caro exfatiata perstaret, & volens vitiis imperaret. Hi vero haudquaquam honorifice corpore ipso utuntur, quippe quod potestate privant, & arbitrium demunt, nec sinunt, ut sponte suis ipsius imperium teneat. Hoc est aperta servitus, inquit Theodoretus, & dati honoris ablatio. Nec aliter Pontificii Interpretes: Cornelius à Lapide de abstinentia atque vita austeritate exponit, qua corpori non parcunt, sed illud immoderate & superstitiose affligunt: Non in honore ad saturitatem carnio, id est negato corpori honore vel subsidio necessario ad famem exfaturandam. Honor enim Ebrais non tantum verbalis aut ceremonialis, sed & realis est, qui non est aliud quam necessariarum rerum vel opum subministratio. Sensit Apostolus, inquit Estius, sapientiam illam aut praecepta talia esse, per qua corpori debitus honor pertinens ad expletionem, id est, justam refectionem carnis, subtrahatur, dum videlicet immoderate & stulte excogitatis abstinentiis corpus exhauritur, contra illud, nemo unquam carnem suam odio habuit, sed nutrit & fovet eam, Eph. 5. Unde & discipulo suo praecipit: Noli adhuc aquam bibere, sed utere modico vino propter stomachum tuum & frequentes tuas infirmitates, 1. Tim. 5. Eodem recidet intelligentia, sinegatio repetatur in altero membro ad hunc modum: Non ad saturitatem carnis. Tum enim sensus erit: Illa hominum praecepta non facere ad saturitatem carnis, quin potius necessaria saturitate, qua Psalmographus: Edent pauperes & saturabuntur, carnem defmudare: ut hic fit figum, qua minus dicitur, quam intelligatur: Quale est illud apud Prophetam: Fecerunt, qua non praecepti eis, id est, fecerunt omnia, praeceptis meis contraria. Papistis ergo non nisi invitis hic velificari voluit Grotius, nec vere aut cum commodo ipsorum velificatur. Docet id ἀντιθέσιον, quod hic subinnuit vult, nempe istas ἀποχάς Pythagoricas magis noxias esse, sivelut ad salutem necessariae suscipiantur, si ob id contemnantur alii, si non minus laute habeatur corpus ex herba, leguminibus, pomis ad delitias cocta. Quae omnia in religionibus vel superstitionibus potius Papalibus occurrere res ipsa docet. Illae enim si non necessariae, maxime tamen utiles ad salutem statuuntur: Illas qui observant, prae caeteris religiosi haberi volunt: Illorum abstinentia saepe major est luxus, quam aliorum, discrimen ciborum non observantium, communis vivendi ratio.

PARS III. EPISTOLAE NOTHETIKH Ad vitam Christianis dignam commonefaciens.

## 3:1 Argument
CHAPTER III. ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

From the communion of the resurrection of Christ, the Apostle deduces an exhortation to seek those things which are above, since we have died spiritually in baptism, and therefore the members which are on earth should be mortified, and to put off the old man, and to put on the new, and for that cause the Word of God should dwell in us richly, with due Eucharist.

There are therefore two parts: I. General, concerning the common duties of believers, to v. 17. II. Special, concerning their proper duties, to v. 26.

PART I. Exhibiting common precepts.

This inference is from our resuscitation with Christ, by which we have been made partakers of the fruits of the death and exaltation of Christ. For resuscitation presupposes death, and at the same time embraces the glory of Christ. For He rose again unto glory, not that He might remain on earth, but that He might show Himself alive, and thus, being lifted up from the earth into heaven, might be exalted to the right hand of GOD.

For since in baptism we are made partakers of the fruits of the death, resurrection, ascension, and sitting at the right hand of GOD—namely, of redemption, reconciliation with God, remission of sins, justice, and heavenly gifts, especially the Holy Spirit, who is poured into us in baptism, and of the inheritance of eternal life—and since we wish not to fall from that grace, it is necessary that we lead a life worthy of Christ, and seek those things which are above, where Christ sits at the right hand of GOD, not those things which are on earth, which we ought not even to relish, much less seek.

Others deduce these things from a spiritual resurrection: You have risen spiritually (so the Osiandrine paraphrase has it) with Christ, for you have been awakened from the death of sin into a spiritual life, so that you now live unto GOD. Think, therefore, that you also have spiritually ascended with Christ to the heavens. Therefore seek heavenly things, not carnal ones.

But here is properly understood the communion of benefits procured by the departure of Christ to the Father, or by His death and resurrection, or the communion of the death and resurrection of Christ, as far as concerns His merits, to which we are admitted in baptism. For the Apostle proceeds from the benefits received from Christ to the duties owed to Christ. And it is certain that regeneration and renewal pertain to these, and to this, the mortification of earthly members, no less than vivification and the excitation to a new life.

As far, however, as concerns the formal notion, they properly infer communion with the resuscitation of Christ, which we obtain through faith in baptism, as if we were resurrected with Him unto heavenly glory, being made partakers of justice, not of glory, procured for us by Christ through His death and resurrection. For we put on there the justice of Christ, and become heirs of eternal life through regeneration. Connected or consequent to this benefit is that resurrection of renewal, so that we may walk in newness of life.

Therefore, the explanation of Crocius does not exhaust the meaning of the Apostle: In baptism they rose again with Christ in the mystery signifying the thing, and in the truth of the thing as regards its inception.

For that which is the chief thing is omitted: namely, the application of the justice of Christ, for which Christ rose again, Rom. 4:23.

Theophylactus applies these things by the force of the connection of the preceding ones in this way: If you have risen with Christ, it is necessary that you be occupied in heaven, where He sits at the right hand of the Father, in which heaven there is an observance of either days or times. Furthermore, you must also relish heavenly things, not earthly ones. For these cautions about foods and times consist of earthly precepts.

Nor did Paul have enough in saying what things are in heaven, and where Christ might consist, but he added that He sits at the right hand of GOD, so that he might more and more detach our mind from these earthly things.

Which, however much I would not deny that they are connoted here in a certain way, insofar as they could lead us away from the life which they had in Christ: yet this exhortation is without doubt more general: He wants heavenly things to be sought, to be sought with mind, will, zeal, and all strength. Tà ἄνω (The things above), not τὰ ἐπί (the things upon [the earth]), says Crocius, which are in the air, which are in the starry heaven. What then are they? Without doubt, those which, from His mind, are above the air and above the starry heaven in the city built above the firmament.

He wants heavenly glory, which is to be obtained there, to be sought as the end, according to the interpretation of Crocius. But how could GOD seriously will that, as regards all the Colossians according to the mind of Crocius, since He did not choose some of them by absolute decree unto life or glory?

Nor do these things require only the end, or heavenly glory: Seek the things above: but they also demand that we have our minds and hearts upward, and that we do not allow ourselves to be distracted by earthly things from those things which are required for attaining the things above.

We ought also to seek the kingdom of grace, to be begun in us through the Word of the Gospel. Seek the kingdom of God and His justice, Christ warns, Matt.

6:33. Where then is that kingdom of grace, asks B. Hunnius?

Certainly, he answers, above. But is it truly in some supreme place far removed from us?

Hear Christ answering in Luke 17: The kingdom of God is within you.

And yet it is said to be above, because it is not of this world, John 18. So also Christ bids us seek His justice, that is, justice availing before God, which, although it is not from earthly things, but from heavenly goods, is not, however, so arranged that we are tempted to seek it outside the orbs of all the heavens.

Since Paul says that this justice of faith is near you, and thus in your heart, Rom. 10, so also we seek Him with Christ, according to that: Do you not know yourselves, that Christ Jesus is in you, 2 Cor. 13.

I Cor. XIII.

We certainly do not seek something earthly, but something heavenly, however much there is no need for us to fly above the firmament with our thoughts for this matter, but only to examine ourselves, whether we are in the faith, as he adds in the same place.

For through faith Christ dwells in our hearts, Eph. 3, and is in us, 2 Cor. 3.

And that I may proceed to examples: when we seek peace of conscience, consolation, and other sanctifying gifts of the Holy Spirit, we seek certainly not earthly things, but those which are above.

Not that they are sent down to us in a local way through the firmament and the spheres of the Planets, but that they are conferred by the Holy Spirit alone, than whom there is nothing more eminent.

In which sense Christ also refers regeneration among heavenly goods, while He confirms that we are born again from above. Is that regeneration, therefore, derived from the supra-mundane heaven of the Sacramentarians? By no means. But it is so named because it is perfected only by the virtue of God, than which when there is nothing more exalted (in exaltation, namely, not in place, but in defined Majesty), that regeneration is deservedly said to come to us from above, since it proceeds from God, however much it may be perfected in these lands by means of baptism, and thus in our hearts.

This is B. Hunnius: to whom Crocius is more mute than the frog of Serapia.

He warns at least that Hunnius tries in vain to prove that by "things above" are understood those things which pertain to God, to the kingdom of God, to justice, to newness of life, to the peace and joy of the Holy Spirit: since the Reformed do not deny this.

Let Bullinger say: The things above are grace, faith, and Christian purity: let Aretinus explain them concerning the means to salvation. Let Crocius himself understand the increase of the knowledge of God and of Christ, of faith, of charity, of hope, of all virtues, by which the heavenly life is carried on.

But who does not see that Hunnius is not proving that which is beyond controversy, but the very thing in question (τὸ κρινόμενον), that those things are not in some supreme place far removed from us, which are not outside the spheres of all the heavens are to be sought, etc. But why did he reply nothing to those Hunnius-like proofs, if he could?

They therefore stand unshaken by him. Οὐ ὁ χρισὸς ἐν δεξιᾷ τῷ Θεῷ κάθηται (Is not Christ sitting at the right hand of God) next to the Father in majesty, Matt. 22:24, 26:64, Mark 12:36, 13:19, Luke 20:42, Acts 2:34, Rom. 8:34, Eph. 1:20. What does sitting at the right hand of God imply?

Not only next in majesty, but ἰσότιμος (equal in honor) of the same majesty and glory with the Father. For the Father has given all judgment to the Son, that all may honor the Son, καθὼς (just as) they honor the Father, John 5:22-23. Therefore he is said to sit at the very right hand of God, that is, to be a partaker of his glorious power and of the right hand of God's majesty, and by the same power and Majesty to rule all things with the Father. For that sitting implies ruling or dominating, and the right hand of God implies infinite divine power. See Exam. Doctr. Reform. on the perfection of Christ, p. 511 ff. Therefore the Calvinists are again inept, when they make a certain place of heaven either from the right hand of God with the Helvetic confession, or gather a heavenly place from the word ἄνω (above): since those heavenly things are not by place, but by sublimity.

He had severely chastised all that, and solidly refuted it, B. Hunnius, so that Crocius found nothing in the place and fane of his own men, with which I will not say he satisfied the same, but only plastered over his fiction with some reason. Chrysostom at least, Vol. III, on the passion and cross, explained these phrases clearly: When I shall say that God is sitting in the heights, believe HIM to be E V E R Y W H E R E P R E S E N T. Therefore he holds that sitting in the heights and being everywhere present are equivalent. But here the Apostle opposes heavenly things to earthly. And what the earthly things are, he himself explains: Mortify your earthly members. Hence, conversely, it is gathered that under the name of heavenly things, which the Apostle bids us seek, the contraries come here; what sort these are, is evident from the words of Christ, Matt. 6: Seek the kingdom of God and his righteousness. Although it is not denied that the kingdom of glory is expected only in the other age, yet even in this life he bids us seek the kingdom of grace to be begun in us through the word of the Gospel. But where that kingdom of grace happens, we explained a little before in the words of B. Hunnius. Nor do the words of Augustine, Epist. 57 to Dardanus, help Crocius at all: Do not doubt that Christ our Lord, the only-begotten Son of God, equal to the Father, and the same Son of man, than whom the Father is greater, is everywhere WHOLLY present as God, and in some place of heaven on account of the mode of a true body. For he speaks of the property of each nature, and indeed makes the property of the divine nature to be everywhere, but the human nature, according to the property of nature or the mode of a true body, to be in some place, which who has ever denied?

Nor yet does he say that Jesus Christ is above the starry heaven, nor does he deny that Christ according to his Human nature by the power of personal union and exaltation to the right hand of GOD governs all things, and is present to all things which he governs; nay, he says that Christ is everywhere WHOLLY present as God, or according to the property of the divine nature, which cannot be denied to the Human nature in the subsisting hypostasis λόγῳ (by the Word). And just as it is necessary for a nature to be present where the hypostasis is at hand, in which that nature subsists: So the whole Christ could not be said to be everywhere present, if only the divine nature were present, not the human. For without the human nature Christ is not whole. Crocius praises Calvin for observing that the Apostle makes mention of this Majesty, that Christ sits at the right hand of God, to signify that Christ embraces us by his power, nor should we think that distance of place is the cause of separation between us and him.

That Christ sits at the right hand of God according to his Human nature is a matter of confession. Therefore this will have to be attributed to Christ according to his Human nature entirely. In refuting the cavils of the atheists, the Socinians are likewise not at all unrelated, as we showed in refuted Socinianism; therefore the Father sitting at the left, and being in the kingdom inferior to the Son, observes Crocius, is a manner of speaking condescending to our capacity, thus designating the supreme glory of Christ, which he received from the Father: therefore Paul raises the minds of the Colossians to the highest degree of glory, to which Christ has been exalted as King and head of the Church, with SUPREME power in heaven and in earth, fully reigning over the Church and all created things. Since, then, τὸ sedere in dextra DEI (sitting at the right hand of GOD) belongs to Christ according to his Human nature, how can supreme power in heaven and in earth be denied to him? And what other power is supreme in heaven and in earth, except infinite and divine power? For to establish a twofold supreme power in heaven and in earth, one infinite, the other indeed not infinite, is ἀθεόλογον (contrary to theology) equally and ἀφιλόσοφον (contrary to philosophy). The Pope! Chrysostom here exclaims, to what has he raised our mind?

How did he fill them with the great Spirit? It was not enough for him to have said, the things that are above, nor where Christ is: but he adds, sitting at the right hand of God: which Theophylactus, repeating in his usual manner, adds: That he may draw our mind more away from the earth. Τὰ ἄνω φρονεῖτε, μὴ τὰ ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς (Set your minds on things above, not on things on the earth) — send your affections to heaven, and let your souls take no care for earthly things, like those of whom Phil. 3:19. He had said before, Seek; now φρονεῖτε (set your minds); for he requires not only zeal in seeking heavenly things, but wills that every thought be directed to things above, none to earthly things.

Therefore, by those things which pertain to the kingdom of God, but by these, not just any earthly things, but those which are adverse to the kingdom of God. Most understand this of vicious desires, and prove that sense from v. 5. Here τὰ ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς (things upon the earth) seem to be taken more broadly by Crocius, so as to include riches, pleasures, honors, conveniences. He forbids, therefore, he says, the care of earthly and perishable things, by which they slip away in a point of time, not that it is in no way permitted to care for things that pertain to the present life, but first, that they do not make anything on this earth the goal of their religion; second, that they do not place hope and trust in it; third, that they do not establish the worship of God and righteousness in external things, in which the Pseudo-Apostles established piety; fourth, that they do not fix their mind on any thing which, by the institution of Christ, does not lead to the goal proposed above in the heavens. Finally, that they do not give themselves to those things which lead or draw them away from the heavenly goal and path. Which, however they may be right in other respects, whether they nevertheless fit this place, may seem doubtful. For simply, as it appears, the setting of affection on heavenly and infernal, celestial and terrestrial things is forbidden, which he declares a little later in these words, when he says: Mortify therefore your members which are upon the earth, fornication, uncleanness, etc. Therefore, the Christian man who leads a holy and blameless life and is held by the desire of celestial and eternal life dwells in the heavens with Christ (though still mortal): but he who is immersed in carnal and forbidden pleasures and lusts thinks of and desires earthly things dwells on the earth. Nor indeed can that be taken away from the members of the old Adam, when one so adheres to earthly things that he establishes the goal of his religion in them, places his hope and trust, fixes his mind on them, and through them is torn away from heavenly things. to be torn away.

Therefore that explanation of the Apostle is adequate, through the members of the old Adam, and they are comprehended either under evil desire, or that avarice which I have mentioned. v. 3. For you have died) You have professed to put off your former life in baptism, above 11, 12.

Latin:

CAPUT III. ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

E communione resuscitationis Christi deducit Apostolus adhortationem ad ea quaerenda, quae sursum sunt, siquidem spiritualiter mortui simus in baptismo, ideoque mortificata membra sint, qua in terra sunt, & veterem hominem exuere, novum vero induere, atque ea de causa Verbum Dei opulenter in nobis habitare debeat, cum debita Eucharistia. In specie autem monet uxores & viros, liberos & parentes, servos & dominos de debitis officiis.

Partes ergo duae sunt: I. Generalis de officiis fidelium communibus ad v. 17. II. Specialis, de officiis propriis ad v. 26.

PARS I. Praecepta communia exhibens.

Illatio haec est à nostra cum Christo resuscitatione, qua participes facti sumus fructus mortis & exaltationis Christi. Nam resuscitatio praesupponit mortem, complectitur simul gloriam Christi. Resurrexit enim ad gloriam, non ut in terris maneret, sed vivum se demonstraret, atque ita è terris in coelum evectus ad dextram DEI exaltaretur.

Quum enim in baptismo fructus mortis, resurrectionis, ascensionis & consessus ad dextram DEI, redemptionis nempe, reconciliationis cum Deo, remissionis peccatorum, justitiae & donorum coelestium, imprimis Spiritus Sancti, qui in nos effunditur in baptismo, ac haereditatis vitae aeternae participes reddamur, ac gratia illa excidere velimus, oportet, ut vitam Christo dignam geramus, & ea quaeramus, quae sursum sunt, ubi Christus ad dextram DEI sedet, non ea, quae in terra sunt, quae ne sapere quidem debemus, nedum quaerere.

Alii spirituali resurrectione haec deducunt: Vos spiritualiter, (ita habet Osiandrina paraphrasis) cum Christo surrexistis, nam à morte peccati excitati estis in vitam spiritualem, ut jam vivatis DEO. Cogitate igitur, vos etiam spiritualiter cum Christo ad caelos adscendisse. Itaque coelestia quaerite, non carnalia.

Sed hic proprie communio beneficiorum abitu Christi ad Patrem, vel morte ac resurrectione ejus comparatorum, vel communio mortis & resurrectionis Christi, quantum ad ejusdem merita, ad quam in baptismo admittimur, intelligitur. A beneficiis enim à Christo acceptis ad officia Christi debita procedit Apostolus. Ad illa autem pertinere regenerationem ac renovationem, & ad hanc mortificationem membrorum terrenorum, non minus quam vivificationem & ad novam vitam excitationem, certum est.

Quoad tamen formalem significationem illa communionem cum resuscitatione Christi proprie inferunt, quam per fidem in baptismo consequimur, quasi cum ipso resuscitati ad coelestem gloriam, utpote justitiae, non gloriae, à Christo per mortem & resurrectionem ejusdem nobis comparatae participes redditi. Induimus enim ibi justitiam Christi, & haeredes evadimus per regenerationem vitae aeternae. Cui beneficio connexum vel consequens est illa resurrectio renovationis, ut in vita novitate ambulemus.

Non ergo sensum Apostoli exhaurit Crocii explicatio: In baptismo resurrexerunt cum Christo in re significante mysterio, tum in rei veritate quoad inchoationem.

Praetermittitur enim id, quod praecipuum: Justitiae nempe Christi applicatio, ob quam Christus resurrexit, Rom. IV. 23.

Applicat haec vi connexionis superiorum specialiter Theophylactus hoc modo: Si consurrexius cum Christo, necesse est, ut in caelo vos, ubi ille assidet Patri ad dexteram diverfemini, quo in caelo est vel dierum vel temporum observatione. Sunt praeterea vobis & caelestia sapienda, non terretria. He escarum namque & temporum cautiones terrenis constant praeceptis.

Nec satis habuit Paulus, que in caelo sunt dicere, & ubi Christus consisteret, sed in dextra DEI sedet, adjetit, ut magis ac magis animum nobis ab his terrenis disjungat.

Quae utut hic certo modo, quatenus à vita, quam in Christo habebant, abducere poterat, connotari non negarim: generalior tamen fine dubio haec est paraenesis: Quaeri vult superna, quaeri mente, voluntate, studio, omnibus viribus. Tà ἄνω non τὰ ἐπί, inquit Crocius, quae in aere, quae in caelo sidereo. Quid ergo sunt? Sine dubio, quae ex mente ejus, supra aerem, & supra caelum sidereum in civitate super firmamentum extructa.

Gloriam coelestem, quae illic obtinenda, vult quaeri, tanquam finem, interprete Crocio. Sed quomodo id ferio DEUS potuit velle, quoad omnes Colossenses ex mente Crocii, siquidem nonnullos eorum absoluto decreto non elegit ad vitam vel gloriam.

Neque finem tantum haec requirunt, vel coelestem gloriam: Superna quaerite: sed etiam postulant, ut sursum mentes & corda nostra habeamus, nec per terrena nos ab iis, quae ad superna consequenda requiruntur, abstrahi patiamur.

Quaerere etiam debemus etiam regnum gratiae, per Verbum Evangelii in nobis inchoandum. Quaerite regnum Dei & justitiam ejus, monet Christus, Matth. 6. 33.

Ubi ergo illud gratia regnum, quaerit B. Hunnius? Utique, respondet, supra.

Num vero in supremo quopiam loco à nobis diffito longe?

Audi respondentem Christum Luc. XVII. Regnum Dei est intra vos.

Atque nihilominus dicitur esse supra, quia non est de hoc mundo, Job. XVIII. Sic quoque Christus quaerere jubet justitiam ejus, hoc est, justitiam coram Deo valentem, quae licet non sit ex terrenis, sed supernis bonis, non tamen ita comparata est, ut eam extra calorium omnium orbes quaerere tentamur.

Quandoquidem hanc fidei justitiam Paulus esse ait prope te, adeoque in corde tuo, Rom. X. ita quoque cum Christo ipsum quaerimus, secundum illud: Annon cognoscitis vosmetipsos, quod Christus Jesus in vobis sit, 2.

Cor. XIII.

Quaerimus certe non terrestre quippiam, sed supernum, quantumvis ad hanc rem opus non sit nobis cogitationibus evolare supra firmamentum, sed tantum nos explorare, num simus in fide, sicut ibidem addit.

Per fidem enim habitat Christus in cordibus nostris, Eph. III. & in nobis est, 2. Cor. III.

Et at in exemplis pergam, quando quaerimus pacem conscientiae, consolationem, aliae Spir. S. sanctificantia dona, quaerimus utique non terrena, sed ea, quae supra sunt.

Ideo namque dona haec defuper à Patre luminis descendere praedicantur, Jac. I. Non quod ea per firmamentum & Planetarum sphaeras localo modo ad nos demittantur, sed quod à solo Spiritu S. quo non quicquam eminentius est, illa conferantur.

Quo sensu & regenerationem Christus refert inter superna bona, dum nos renasci confirmat è supernis. Ergone proficitur illa ex caelo supramundano Sacramentariorum? Nequaquam. Sed ideo sic nominatur, quod non nisi virtute Dei perficitur, quo cum nihil excelsius sit, (celsitudine scil. non loco, sed Majestate definita) merito è supernis illa regeneratio nobis dicitur provenire, cum à Deo proficiscitur, quantumvis ea in his terris mediante baptismo, adeoque in cordibus nostris perficiatur.

Haec B. Hunnius: ad quae magis mutus est Crocius, quam rana Serapia.

Monet saltem, frustra Hunnium probare, per superna in-telligi, quae ad Deum, ad regnum Dei, ad justitiam, ad novitatem vitae, ad pacem & gaudium Spiritus Sancti pertinent: Siquidem Reformati hoc non negent.

Bullingerus dicat: Superna sunt gratia, fides, & puritas Christiana: Aretinus de mediis ad salutem explicet. Crocius ipse incrementum cognitionis Dei & Christi, fidei, charitatis, spei, omnium virtutum, quibus vita coelestis traducitur, intelligat.

Sed quis non videt, Hunnium non illud probare, quod extra controversiam, sed ipsum τὸ κρινόμενον, quod illa non sint in supremo quodam loco à nobis diffito, quod non extra omnium calorum orbes quaerenda sint, &c. Cur vero ad illas probationes Hunnianas, si potuit, nihil reposuit?

Stant ergo per ipsum inconcussae. Οὐ ὁ χρισὸς ἐν δεξιᾷ τῷ Θεῷ κάθηται Patri majestate proximus, Matth. XXII. 24. XXVI. 64. Marc. XII. 36. XIII. 19. Luc. XX. 42. Act. II. 34. Rom. VIII. 34. Eph. I. 20. In dextra Dei sedere quid inferat?

Non tantum proximus majestate, sed ἰσότιμος ejusdem majestatis & gloriae cum Patre. Nam Filio dedet Pater omne judicium, ut omnes honorent Filium, καθὼς sicut honorant Patrem, Joh. V. vers. 22. 23. Ideo sedere dicitur in ipsa dextra Dei, hoc est, potentiae ejus gloriosae, & dextra Dei majestatis particeps esse, eademque potentia & Majestate cum Patre regere omnia. Nam sedere illud regere vel dominari, & dextra Dei infinitam Deivirtutem infert. Vid. Exam. Doctr. Reform. de perf. Christi pag. 511. seqq. Inepti itaque rursus sunt Calviniani, cum certum caeli locum vel e dextra Dei faciunt cum Helvetica confessione, vel e voce ἄνω locum supernum colligunt: Cum superna illa sint non loco, sed sublimitate.

Castigarat omne illud graviter, & solide refutarat B. Hunnius, ut Crocius nihil in loco & fano virum suarum invenerit, quo non dicam satisfaceret eidem, sed solum incrustaret aliqua ratione commentum suum. Chrysostomus utique Tom. III. de pass. & cruce has phrases luculenter exposuit: Quando dixero Deum sedentem in excelsis, U B I Q U E E U M credite esse P R A E S E N T E M. Pro aequipollentibus ergo illa habet in excelsis sedere, & ubique praesentem esse. Tum vero hic opponit superna terrenis Apostolus. Quae vero terrena sint, ipse explicat: Mortificate membra vestra terrena. Hinc a converso colligitur supernorum nomine, quae quaerere nos jubet Apostolus, venire hic contraria; quae qualia sint, è verbis Christi, Matth. VI. Quaerite regnum Dei & justitiam ejus, patet. Quanquam vero non negetur, regnum gloriae in altero demum expectari seculo, tamen & in hac vita nos jubet quaerere regnum gratiae per verbum Evangelii in nobis inchoandum. Ubi autem illud regnum gratiae fit, paulo ante verbis B. Hunnii exposuimus. Nec quicquam juvant Crocium verba Augustini epist. LVII. ad Dardanum: Christum Dominum nostrum unigenitum Dei Filium, aqualem Patri, eundemque hominis Filium, quo major est Pater, & ubique totum praesentem non dubites tanquam Deum, & in loco aliquo caeli propter veri corporis modum. Loquitur enim de proprietate naturae cujusque, & divine quidem naturae proprietatem facit ubique esse, humane autem quoad proprietatem naturae, vel veri corporis modum in aliquo loco esse, quod quis negavit unquam?

Nec tamen dicit, Jesum Christum esse supra sidereum caelum, nec negat, Christum secundum Humanam naturam vi unionis personalis & exaltationis ad dextram DEI omnia gubernare, rebusque omnibus, quas gubernat, adesse; imd Christum ubique TOTUM praesentem tanquam Deum dicit, vel secundum proprietatem naturae divinae, quae Humanae naturae in hypostasi λόγῳ subsistenti denegari nequit. Ac veluti naturam adesse oportet, ubi hypostasis praesto est, in qua natura illa subsistit: Ita totus Christus ubique praesens dici non posset, si divina tantum natura praesens esset, non humana. Sine enim humana natura Christus non est totus. Laudat Crocius Calvinum observantem, hujus Majestatis, quod Christus sedeat ad dextram Dei, mentionem inferre Apostolum, ut significaret, Christi sua virtute nos complecti, nec loci distantiam causam divortii inter nos & ipsum esse putemus.

At Christum secundum Humanam naturam ad dexteram Dei sedere in confesso est. Id ergo Christo secundum Humanam naturam omnino tribuendum erit. Refellens cavillum atheorum, aeque non alieni omnino sunt Sociniani, ut in Socinismo profligato ostendimus; Patrem igitur sedere ad sinistram, & in regno esse inferiorem Filio, observat Crocius scripturam, ad nostrum captum condescendentem, sic summam Christi gloriam designare, quam à Patre accepit: Animos igitur Colossensium Paulum ad summum gloriae gradum attollere, in quem Christus evectus tanquam Rex caputque Ecclesiae SUMMA potestate in caelo & in terra super Ecclesiam & omnia creata plene regnat. Quum ergo Christo secundum Humanam naturam competat τὸ sedere in dextra DEI, quo modo denegari ei potest summa potestas in caelo & in terra? Quae autem alia est summa in caelo & in terra, nisi potestas infinita ac divina? Nam potestatem summam in caelo & in terra geminam, aliam infinitam, aliam vero non infinitam statuere, ἀθεόλογον pariter & ἀφιλόσοφον. Papa! exclamat hic Chrysostomus, quo mentem nostram evexit?

Quomodo eos magno implevit Spiritu? Non satis habuit, dixisse, quae sursum sunt, neque ubi est Christus: Sed addit, in dextra Dei sedens: Quae repetens pro more suo Theophylactus addit: Ut magis à terra nostrum animum abducat. Τὰ ἄνω φρονεῖτε, μὴ τὰ ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς Affectus vestros in celum mittite, ne estote curae in terras animae, ut illi de quibus Phil. III. 19. Quarite, dixerat antea, jam φρονεῖτε; non enim tantum studium quaerendi superna requirit, sed etiam omnem cogitationem ad superna directam esse vult, nullam ad terrena.

Per illa ergo, quae ad regnum Dei pertinent, per haec vero non qualibet terrestria, sed quae regno Dei adversa sunt. Plerique de vitiosis cupiditatibus intelligunt, eumque sensum è v. 5. probant. Latius hic accipi videntur τὰ ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς Crocio, ut includant opes, voluptates, honores, commoda. Prohibet igitur, inquit, curam terrestrium & caducorum, qua puncto temporis labuntur, non quod nullo modo liceat curare, ad vitam praesentem pertinent, sed primo ne metam constituant suae religionis quicquam in hac terra; secundo ne spem & fiduciam in eo collocent; tertione in rebus externis, in quibus Pseudo-Apostoli pietatem constituebant, cultum Dei & justitiam statuant; quarto ne animum ulli rei affigant, quae ex Christi institutione non ducat ad metam supra caelis propositam. Denique ne iis se dedant, quae à superna meta & via aliorum ducunt trahuntve. Quae utut alias sese recte habeant, an tamen huic loco conveniant, dubium videri queat. Nam simpliciter, ut apparet, prohibetur τὸ φρονεῖν τὰ superna & inferna, caelestia & terrestria, paulo post his verbis declarat, cum inquit: Mortificate ergo membra vestra, quae sunt super terram, fornicationem, immunditiam &c. In caelis ergo cum Christo versatur homo Christianus, (adhuc mortalis) qui sanctam & inculpatam vitam ducit, & caelestia atque aeterna vita desiderio tenetur: in terris autem degit, qui carnalibus & prohibitis voluptatibus & concupiscentiis immersus terrena cogitat & desiderat. Neque vero illud à membris veteris Adami eximi potest, cum quis ita terrenis adharet, ut in illis metam religionis sue constituat, spem & fiduciam collocet, animum iis affigat, & per ea à supernis se divelli. patiatur.

Adaequata ergo est illa Apostoli ἐξήγησις per membra veteris Adami, & vel sub cupiditate mala, & avaritia illa, quae dixi, comprehenduntur. v. 3. Ἀποθάνετε γὰρ) Vitam priorem vos exuere professi estis in baptismo supra il.

## 3:3
And your life is hidden with Christ in God) He calls the right to the thing by the name of the thing.

That heavenly life is indeed unknown to the world, yet it is reserved for you by God, in the same place where Christ is.

See above I §.

2. Tim.

8. This pertains not only to the profession made in baptism, but to the power and effect of baptism.

We are dead to sins or to sins and the filth of desires in baptism in two ways: 1. in that the putting away of sin happens through forgiveness, and having been made participants, through baptism, of the fruits of the death of Christ, concerning which the Apostle had discoursed in chapters I and II, we obtain the remission of sins through his blood and reconciliation through his cross, and we are received into the grace of GOD:

For thus we are dead to sin with Christ, as was said before, WE HAVE RISEN WITH CHRIST, because Christ died for us to sin, Rom. VI. ver.

10, and the old Adam was crucified with CHRIST, that the body of sin might cease, that we might no longer serve sin, v. 6. 2.

By the mortification of sin in renewal.

For we are not only regenerated and obtain the remission of sin, but we are also renewed and sanctified through baptism, and thus sin is mortified in us, and we, having died to sins, as the Vulgate renders it (which Schmidius however explained as 'freed from sins'), live to righteousness, 1. Petr.

24. In which latter sense many explain it;

Crocius says, Resurrection presupposes death.

They have risen with Christ. Therefore, they were previously dead with him through baptism and the conversion of morals to sin, to the flesh, to the world, to carnal conversation, to the elements of the world, and to themselves.

If they are dead, therefore they ought not to care for earthly things.

Therefore they ought not to be moved by external appearance, nor seek life in external things: For the dead do not care for these.

Therefore they ought not to follow those laws and observances of the Pseudo-Apostles regarding food, drink, and other external things.

But here there is a doubt: in what way are they said to be dead with Christ in that sense?

Has Christ also died to sin, to the flesh, to the world, to the elements of the world, and to himself through the conversion of morals?

How also does that reasoning of the Apostle fit: You are dead to sin through conversion, and the mortification of the flesh and the world: Mortify therefore the members which are on the earth?

For thus the conclusion and the reason of the proof seem to coincide?

And why would the Apostle have passed over the chief fruit of the death of Christ and of baptism?

Finally, how will the Apostolic opposition be consistent with itself?

You are dead (with Christ) and your life is hidden with Christ in God? For our life is not there as a newness of life, which might follow that death by which the old man in us is submerged or mortified: but it is that life which, having obtained the remission of sins through faith in Christ, we live as participants of the righteousness of Christ and of salvation through communion with the life of Christ, having been raised from death and vivified for the sake of our righteousness and salvation.

Which life is also Christ, because we live in Christ, Gal. II. 20, and it is called life with Christ, as with whom we have been vivified, since for our own sakes he was put to death in the flesh, but vivified in the Spirit, having suffered and died for sins, the just for the unjust, 1.

Petr.

18. Add Joh.

2. And it is called life hidden in God, either because we do not yet fully grasp this mystery here, which because Christ was vivified for us, Christ becomes our life through faith, or because the essence, dignity, and blessedness of this life, which is its full complement, is for the most part still hidden, which is laid up for us in God, 1.

Cor.

II. 9. 2.

Petr.

4. Crocius says it is the hidden life of nature, of grace, of glory.

But that is foreign to the life of the body in this place.

For what does it matter here that that life was buried under the ignominy of the cross and various miseries?

And therefore Crocius himself acknowledges: Primarily (though he would have more correctly said 'solely') this pertains to the life of grace and glory.

Concerning the life of grace, they had, he says, the Spirit of Christ, who is the Spirit of life, of righteousness, and of holiness: The world was ignorant of him, he had infused vital power, he produced vital actions in them, but a great part lay hidden within.

But it is called hidden, not that the Holy Spirit is hidden, who is the author of the life of the reborn spiritually.

But as the Apostle says that we are dead with Christ, as vivified and enjoying life with Christ, even if it is still hidden and lying latent in God; so also he says we are to be manifested in glory with Christ: When Christ your life shall appear, which will happen in the appearing of his glory, Tit. II.

13, who is now our life both by the merits of life acquired, Job. VI. 51, through him, and in him we live through faith, when our life is in him, and he lives in us, and we in him, righteous by his righteousness, saved by his salvation, of which Zach. IX.

9, we are saved, we are alive by his life, and we enjoy the life of grace solely through faith, apprehending him as true life, and in him we are preserved unto eternal life through faith.

Who therefore as our life will be fully manifested in the other age, when we shall have eternal life in him, both in body and in soul, and then we shall be manifested also in glory with him.

Therefore one must strive for this glory: and for its sake leave earthly things, lest we be torn away from it by Christ shared with us, communicated to us in Christ, appropriated to us in baptism and with the righteousness and life of Christ, and truly now ours through faith, even if still hidden in God until the full manifestation.

In the second coming, says Theophylact, Christ is to appear, and will offer himself to all as God, coming with glory and the company of Angels, then at last you also will appear: and not indeed simply, but in the same glory.

Seek him therefore, not this present day.

In him, I say, strive with all zeal to attain life; for then your life, which is true, will be manifest.

For the present is death, because it consists of the ebb and flow of corruption.

Do not seek either glory or honors in this age, since all our glory is to be in heaven.

For the pearl lies hidden, as long as the shell is concealed.

It, when opened, emits its own brightness of virtue.

And we likewise, as long as we must dwell in this corruptible body, ought to seek no glory while we lie hidden.

But when this corruptible shall be dissolved, then the glory itself, if we have been worthy of it for the deeds done, follows.

That, if we have been worthy of it for the deeds done, is to be understood rightly according to the analogy of faith.

For we are worthy only in Christ.

But we must act so that we are not rendered unworthy of it through sins.

Therefore let us preserve it, if we have not been unworthy of it for the deeds done.

For even if we have done all things, we ought to profess that we are unprofitable servants, Luc. XVII. 10. He is buried, says Chrysostom, our man, he is buried not in the earth, but in the water, not by death dissolving him, but by him who dissolves him in death, not by the law of nature, but by a command stronger than nature and dominion.

For what has been made by nature, someone may also dissolve.

But those things which are from his command, by no means. There is nothing more blessed than this burial, by which all are gladdened, both Angels and men, and the Lord of Angels. Confer on this Apostolic saying our meditations in the funeral sermon, which is titled: THE ART OF LIVING.

Latin:

11. 12. Καὶ ἡ ζωὴ ὑμῶν κέκρυπται σὺν τῷ χριστῷ ἐν τῷ θεῷ) Jus ad rem rei nomine appellat.

Vita illa caelestis ignota quidem est mundo, attamen a Deo vobis reservatur, ibidem, ubi Christus est.

Vide supra I §.

2. Tim.

8. Non ad solam professionem in baptismo factam, sed ad vim & effectum baptismi hoc pertinet.

Mortui autem ταῖς ἁμαρτίαις vel peccatis & ῥυπαῖς desideriis in baptismo bifariam sumus, 1. qua peccati ἀβέτησις per condonationem contigit, & participes facti, per baptismum, fructus mortis Christi, de quo c.

I. & II. differuerat Apostolus, redemptionis per sanguinem, & reconciliationis per crucem ejus, remissionem peccatorum consequimur, & in gratiam DEI recipimur: Ita enim mortui peccato sumus cum Christo, uti antea dicebatur, NOS CONSURREXISSE CUM CHRISTO, quia Christus peccato mortuus est pro nobis, Rom.

VI. vers. 10. & vetus Adam cum CHRISTO crucifixus est, ut cesset corpus peccati, ne deinceps serviamus peccato, v. 6. 2.

Qua peccati mortificationem in renovatione.

Nam non tantum regeneramur & remissione peccati consequimur, sed renovamur etiam & sanctificamur per baptismum, & ita mortificatur peccatum in nobis, nosque ταῖς ἁμαρτίαις ἀπογενόμενοι, peccatis mortui, ut Vulgatus reddit (quod tame Schmidius exposuit, a peccatis liberati) justitiae vivimus, 1. Petr.

24.

Quo posteriori sensu exponunt plerique, Crocius, Resurrectio, inquit, mortem praesupponit.

Resurrexerunt cum Christo. Cum codem igitur prius mortui sunt per baptismum & morum conversionem peccato, carni, mundo, carnali conversationi, elementis mundi & sibi ipsis.

Si mortui, non igitur curare debent terrifiria.

Non igitur externa moveri specie, non in externis vitam quaerere: Ea enim mortui non curant.

Non igitur leges illas & observantias Pseudo-Apostolorum in cibo, potu, & aliis externis rebus sectari debent.

Sed hic dubium est, quomodo eo sensu cum Christo mortui dicuntur?

Num & Christus per morum conversionem peccato, carni, mundo, elementis mundi, & sibi ipsi mortuus est?

Quomodo etiam ratio illa Apostoli quadrat: Mortui estis peccato per conversionem, & carnis ac mundi mortificationem: Mortificate igitur membra, quae in terra sunt?

Sic enim videtur conclusio & ratio probationis coincidere?

Et cur praeteriisset Apostolus praecipuum mortis Christi ac baptismi fructum?

Quomodo denique constabit sibi Apostolica oppositio?

Mortui estis (cum Christo) & vita vestra abscondita est cum Christo in Deo? Nen enim ibi vita nostra est novitas vita, quae ad illam mortem, qua vetus homo in nobis submergitur aut mortificatur, sequatur: sed est vita illa, quam remissionem peccatorum consecuti per fidem in Christo vivimus justitiae Christi ac salutis participes per communionem vitae Christi a morte resuscitati ac vivificati propter justitiam & salutem nostram.

Quae vita & Christus est, quia in Christo vivimus, Gal. 20. & vita cum Christo dicitur, utpote cum quo vivificati sumus, cum propter nos ipsos θανατωθεὶς μὲν σαρκὶ, ζωοποιηθεὶς δὲ τῷ Πνεύματι, mortificatus quidem est carne, vivificatus autem est Spiritu, utpote passus & mortuus pro peccatis, justus pro injustis, 1.

Petr.

18. adde Joh.

2. & vita in Deo abscondita nuncupatur, sive quod mysterium istud nondum plene hic capiamus, quod ob Christum pro nobis vivificatum Christus vita nostra fit per fidem, sive quod vitae hujus quidditas, dignitas ac beatitudo quod plenum complementum maximam partem adhuc abscondita, quae reposita nobis in Deo, 1.

Cor.

9. 2.

Petr.

4. Crocius absconditam dicit vitam naturae, gratiae, gloriae.

Sed illud de vita corporis alienum hoc loco est.

Quid enim huc facit, quod vita illa sub crucis ignominia & variis aerumnis sepulta fuerit?

Ideoque agnoscit ipse Crocius: Imprimis (rectius autem dixisset unice) ad vitam gratiae & gloriae haec pertinere.

De vita gratiae, habebant, inquit, Spiritum Christi, qui est Spiritus vitae, justitiae, & sanctitatis: Illum mundus ignorabat, ille vim vitalem infuderat, ille actiones vitales in illis edebat, sed magna pars latebat interius.

Sed abscondita dicitur, non absconditus Spiritus Sanctus, qui autor vitae renatorum spiritualis est.

Ut autem mortuos cum Christo, ut vivificatos & vita gaudentes eum Christo, etsi abscondita adhuc, & latente in Deo; ita etiam manifestandos in gloria cum Christo dicit Apostolus: Cum apparuerit Cum apparuerit Christus vita vestra, quod fiet ἐν ἐπιφανείᾳ τῆς δόξης, Tit. II.

13. qui nunc vita nostra est tum merito- bus vita acquisita, Job. 51. per ipsum, & in ipso vivimus per fidem, cum vita nostra fit in ipso, & ipse vivat in nobis, & nos in ipso, justitia ejus justi, salvatione ejus, de qua Zach.

9. salvi, vita ejus vivi simus, & vita gratiae unice per fidem, ipsum ceu veram vitam apprehendentem, fruamur, in eoque ad vitam aeternam per fidem futentem, ac conservemur.

Qui proinde ceu vita nostra in altero seculo plene manifestabitur, cum in ipso vitam aeternam habituri sumus, tum corpore, tum anima, & tunc manifestabimur nos etiam in gloria cum ipso.

Ad hanc ergo gloriam contendere oportet: ejusque causa terrena relinquere, ne ab eadem avellamur per Christum nobisparta, in Christo nobis communicata, in baptismo & cum Christi justitia & vita nobis appropriata, vereque jam nostra per fidem, etsi in Deo adhuc abscondita usque ad plenam manifestationem.

In secundo adventu, inquit Theophylactus, appariturus est Christus, & universis offeret se Deus, cum gloria & Angelorum comitatu adventans, tunc demum & ipsi patebitis: nec quidem simpliciter, sed eadem in gloria.

Illum igitur quaerite, non praesentem hunc diem.

In eo inquam assequi vitam omni studio adnitamini; tunc enim vestra, quae vera est, vita patet.

Praesens namque mors est, quia effluxus refluxusque constat corruptione.

Nolite hoc in seculo vel gloriam vel honores efflagitare, cum in caelo nostra omnis futura sit gloria.

Latet enim & margarita, quamdiu cochlea occultatur.

Illa reficta proprium emittit virtutis fulgorem.

Et nos item, quamdiu corruptibili hoc corpore est immorandum, debemus ut latitantes nihil gloriae quaerere.

At ut corruptibile hoc diffolvetur, tunc & gloria ipsa, si pro rebus gestis digni hac accipiendum, consequitur.

Illud si pro rebus gestis digni ea fuerimus, dextre secundum analogiam fidei accipiendum.

Digni sumus enim solum in Christo.

Sed id agendum, ut ne per peccata indigni reddamur eadem.

Ideo conservemur eam, si pro rebus gestis non indigni eadem fuerimus.

Nam etiam si omnia fecerimus, profiteri nos oportet, servos nos esse inutiles, Luc. 10. Sepultus est, inquit Chrysostomus, noster homo, sepultus est non in terra, sed in aqua, non morte ipsum dissolvente, sed eo qui in morte ipsum dissolvit, sepciente, non lege naturae, sed jussu fortiore, quam fit & natura, & dominium.

Nam quae facta sunt a natura, dissolverit etiam quispiam.

Quae autem ab ejus jussu, nequaquam. Hac sepultura nihil est beatius, qua omnes letantur & Angeli, & homines, & Dominus Angelorum. Confer de hoc dicto Apostolico meletemata nostra in exequiali concione, qui titulus: ARS VIVENDI.

## 3:3
V. 9. Eph. V. 3. Πάθος) By this word here are to be understood irrational vicious motions, such as ἔχθραι, ἔρεις, ζῆλοι, θυμοὶ, ἐριθεῖαι, Gal. V. 20. where also in verse 24 παθήματα and ἐπιθυμίαι are distinguished. Elsewhere it is taken more generally, as 1. Thess. IV. v. 5. The Syrian understood that vice, whence they are called Pathici, not rightly, as I think. Without cause Grotius is singular here.

On lust Chrysostom and Theophylact explain, who, he says, omits to explain properly, which could not be said honestly, but by uncleanness indeed and lust he sets forth every kind of foul intercourse: For foul lust is a certain rage of the body. Nor does it stand otherwise than a wound in the body, or a fever, or any other disease of that sort. Nor does the series or order of these vices admit anything else, and concerning anger follows v. 8. Therefore the opinion of Syrus and Sasbouthus is to be preferred, who understands lust against nature, whence παθητικός, one who suffers himself to be affected with foul lust, as a pathic boy, a pathic girl, and Cornelius à Lapide, who explains it of succubic lust, Rom. I. 27. nor also our blessed Luther: Schändliche Brunst. Ἐπιθυμίαν κακήν)

irrational motions of desire in which are drunkenness, revellings, and the like, Gal.

Latin:

V. 3. Πάθος) Hac voce hic intelligendi motus vitiosi ἄλογοι, quales sunt ἔχθραι, ἔρεις, ζῆλοι, θυμοὶ, ἐριθεῖαι, Gal. V. 20. ubi & commate 24. distinguuntur παθήματα & ἐπιθυμίαι. Alibi generalius sumitur, ut 1. Thess. IV. v. 5. Syrus id vitium intellexit, unde dicuntur Pathici, non recte, ut arbitror. Sine causa Grotius hic singularis est.

De libidine explicant Chrysostomus & Theophylactus, qui, omittit, inquit, proprie explicare, qua dici honeste non poterant, sed per immunditiam quidem & libidinem omnem faedi concubitus speciem prafert: Est enim turpis libido rabies corporis quaedam. Nec secus se habet, cum vulnus in corpore, aut febris, vel alius quivis istiusmodi morbus. Nec aliud admittit series vel ordo istorum vitiorum, & de ira sequitur v. 8. Praeferenda ergo Syri & Sasbouthi sententia, qui libidinem contra naturam intelligit, unde παθητικός, qui se affici turpi libidine patitur, ut puer pathicus, puella pathica, & Cornelii à Lapide, qui de libidine succuba explicat, Rom. I. 27. nec non B. Lutheri nostri: Schändliche Brunst. Ἐπιθυμίαν κακήν)

motus ἀλόγους τῆς ἐπιθυμίας in quibus μέθαι, κῶμοι & similia, Gal.

## 3:4
v. 4. Ὅταν ἡ ζωὴ φανερωθῇ) When He shall have appeared, about to judge the human race. See Matth. XXIV. 30. Ἡ ζωὴ ἡμῶν) who is the cause of life for us. Metonymy, John XI. 25. Τότε καὶ ὑμεῖς σὺν αὐτῷ φανερωθήσεσθε ἐν δόξῃ) you shall appear with honor and splendor, 1. John III. 2. where you have the same word φανερωθῇ. Νεκρώσατε οὖν τὰ μέλη ὑμῶν τὰ ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς) Take away power more and more from all parts of the vices. Just as the whole habit of sinning is called a body, Rom. VI. 6. above II. 11. So the individual parts are called members. But lest they be understood as members of the human body, he added τὰ ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς, where there ought to be understood from the preceding τὰ φθαρτὰ, those affections which are carried toward earthly things. Νεκρὸς is taken here, just as ἀποθνήσκειν, Rom. V. 2. it is the same as σάρκα φανεῖν, Gal. V. verse 24. There is in this a mystical fulfillment of the legal sacrifices. Origen in the Philocalia: The word is more strengthened and nourished by meditation, and confirmed by doctrines toward the good, and prayer having been confirmed, having become a trial of the irritation and the burning of desire.

This inference is from the benefit received in baptism to the duty to be performed throughout our whole life. Concerning which, after Chrysostom, Theophylact says: But in what way, since he said above, you have been buried with Christ, you have put off the body of sins and of the flesh, now again (he says) mortify the members? Because that former mortification was a benefit of baptism, which had been admitted to us before: But this mortification, which is suggested to us in the present, is done by our own will, which also deletes sins after baptism. Nay rather, it does not even allow them to germinate or revive, because it kills the wisdom of the flesh. Nor does it act otherwise than someone would, who, having obtained a statue from someone that is rusty and covered with filth, in taking it back, cleans and polishes it, and renders it shining and conspicuous, and then hands it over to the one who has it to be cared for, and enjoins him, that he should not only let the rust not be entirely wiped away, but that he should scrape off even the ingrained rust hereafter. Thus also Cornelius à Lapide from Chrysostom and Theophylact notes a twofold death and mortification, the former, by which past sins are deleted and mortified. This was done in baptism. Of this the Apostle says: You are dead. The latter, by which the motions of concupiscence are mortified. For these motions, daily reborn after baptism, must be assiduously mortified by the justified. Whence the Apostle says: Mortify: as if he were to say: You are dead to sins, you have renounced them, you have professed that you die to them in baptism. It remains, therefore, that you mortify the motions of concupiscence daily springing up again, lest they drag you back into former sins through consent. From which, if they are rightly understood, our explanation previously handed down is confirmed.

Crocius says, it is a mistake (in baptism), all guilt having been taken away by gratuitous remission, so that sin could not condemn them, which is the life of sin. There remained, however, as I said, corrupt concupiscence, which, though wounded, was not thus given to death, but that it would spring up again, and like an evil root would scatter evil branches from itself, and in them would bear evil fruits. But he said members with respect to the old man, corrupt desires, or corrupt habits, not so much those which exert themselves through the members of the human body, as corrupt concupiscence occupies the whole man with his faculties, of which as it were parts and members are the various kinds of sins, so that Grotius is not wrong, with Ambrose going before him, while this alone is referred not so much to the habit of sinning, which does not obtain in all, as to habitual corrupt concupiscence, which is called original sin. All sins, says Crocius, make a certain body or old man, whose members are each corrupt affection and individual sins, which exert themselves and inhere in all the members of the natural body, and just as the members of the natural body serve us for performing the works of nature; so corrupt affections serve the old man like instruments for performing the works of sin. The word members does not denote substance, but both intimate conjunction and origin, namely that the old man did not dwell outside them, but had fixed his seat in their inmost marrow, and therefore he was to be slain not without, but within them. Then, that such as they are, sins become from them, not from God, who gave the members of the body, he had not given the members of the old man. Therefore they are said to be mortified by the same metaphorically and figuratively, as rightly B.

Hunnius rightly warns, because indeed their force and impetus is weakened and broken by the virtue of the indwelling Spirit, and with it they are declined, as being diametrically contrary to the profession, study, and care of Christians (which is to seek heavenly things). Πορνείαν)

Here that word is to be taken so generally that it also comprehends adultery, just as Matth.

V. 32. Now the members which are on the earth are explained: but these are not to be understood only as acts, but also as corrupt affections, because the flesh is to be crucified σὺν τοῖς παθήμασι, καὶ ταῖς ἐπιθυμίαις, Gal. V. 24. Behold, he interprets what those members are, and he mentions fornication first because that vice is everywhere and dominates most, says Theophylact. Conf.

1. Cor. VI. 9. Ἀκαθαρσίαν) On this word see Rom. I. 24. 2. Cor. XII. v. 12. Gal. V. 9. Eph.

Latin:

v. 4. Ὅταν ἡ ζωὴ φανερωθῇ) Ubi apparuit judicaturus humanum genus. Vid. Matth. XXIV. 30. Ἡ ζωὴ ἡμῶν) qui causa nobis est vitae. Μετωνυμία Joh. XI. 25. Τότε καὶ ὑμεῖς σὺν αὐτῷ φανερωθήσεσθε ἐν δόξῃ) apparebitis cum honore ac splendore, 1. Joh. III. 2. ubi habes idem verbum φανερωθῇ. Νεκρώσατε οὖν τὰ μέλη ὑμῶν τὰ ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς) Vim magis ac magis adimite omnibus vitiorum partibus. Sicut tota peccandi consuetudo corpus dicitur, Rom. VI. 6. supra II. 11. Ita partes singulae dicuntur membra. Ne autem intelligere rentur corporis humani membra, addidit τὰ ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς, ubi subintelligi debet ex praecedentibus τὰ φθαρτὰ, eos affectus, qui ad terrena feruntur. Νεκρὸς hic sumitur, quomodo ἀποθνήσκειν, Rom. V. 2. idem est σάρκα φανεῖν, Gal. V. vers. 24. Eit in hoc implementum μυσικὸν sacrificiorum legalium. Origenes in Philocalia: Ὁ λόγος ἐστὶ ἐπὶ πλέον ἰσχυροποιηθεὶς καὶ τραφεὶς τῇ μελέτῃ, καὶ βεβαιωθεὶς τοῖς δόγμασι πρὸς τὸ καλὸν, ἡ εὐχὴ γε τε βεβαιωθεῖσα γεγενημένος ἀνακρίσει τῆς ἐρεθισμὸς καὶ ὑπεκκαῦ τῆς ἐπιθυμίαν.

Illatio haec è beneficio in baptismo accepto ad officium per totam vitam nostram praestandum. De quo post Chrysostomum Theophylactus: Verum quo pacto cum superius diceret, consepulti cum Christo estis, exuistis peccatorum & carnis corpus, nunc rursum membra (inquit) mortificate? Quia prior illa mortificatio baptismi beneficium erat, quod nobis antea esset admissum: Hac autem, quae in praesenti nobis suggeritur mortificatio, nostra fit voluntate, que & post baptisinum delet peccata. Quin potius nec germinare hac finit vel reviviscere, quia carnis enecet sapientiam. Nec secus agit, quam faceret quispiam, qui statuam apud quempiam nactus rubiginosam & situ obsitam retractans tergit expolitque, coruscamque & conspicuam reddit, deinceps cam habenti demandet curandam, injungatque, ut rubiginem nec prorsus absterfam non solum defat, sed vel inhefuram abradat imposterum. Ita & Cornelius à Lapide è Chrysostomo & Theophylacto duplicem notat mortem & mortificationem, priorem, qua praeterita peccata delentur & mortificantur. Hec facta est in baptismo. De hac dicit Apostolus: Mortui estis. Posteriorem, qua motus concupiscentiae mortificantur. Hi enim motus quotidie post baptisinum renascentes assidue justificato sunt mortificandi. Unde dicit Apostolus: Mortificate: quasi dicat: Mortui estis peccatis, iis renunciastis, iis vos mori professi estis in baptismo. Restat ergo, ut concupiscentiae motus indies repullulantes mortificetis, ne illi in pristina peccata per consensum vos pertrahant. Ex quibus, si recte accipiantur, nostra explicatio antea tradita, confirmatur.

Errat (in baptismo) inquit Crocius, ablatus omnis reatus per gratuitam remissionem, ut peccatum eos damnare non posset, quae est peccati vita. Remanserat tamen, ut dixi, concupiscentia prava, quae vulnerata quidem, at non sic morti data erat, quin repullularet, & instar male radicis malos ramos de se spargeret, & in illis malos fructus ferret. Membra autem dixit respectu veteris hominis prava desideria, vel habitus pravos, non tam quae per membra corporis humani se exerunt, quum concupiscentia prava hominem totum cum suis facultatibus occupant, cujus quasi partes & membra sunt diversa peccatorum genera, ut non male Grotius, praeunte Ambrosio, dum solum id non tam ad consuetudinem peccandi, quae in omnibus non obtinet, quam ad habitualem concupiscentiam pravam, quae peccatum originale dicitur, referatur. Omnia peccata, inquit Crocius, faciunt quoddam corpus seu veterem hominem, cujus membra sunt singuli pravi affectus & peccata singula, quae exerunt & inhaerent in omnibus corporis naturalis membris, & quemadmodum membra corporis naturalis nobis inserviunt ad opera naturae perficienda; sic vitiosi affectus homini veteri inserviunt velut instrumenta ad perficienda opera peccati. Vox vestra non arguit substantiam, sed tum intimam conjunctionem, tum originem, quod nempe vetus homo non extra ipsos bofbitaretur, sed in intimis medullis sedem fixisset, proinde non foris, sed in ipsis trucidandus esset. Deinde quod qualia qualia peccata fiant, ab ipsis essent, non à Deo, qui corporis membra dederat, veteris hominis membra non dederat. Mortificari ergo eadem itidem Metaphorice dicuntur & figurate, ut recte B.

Hunnius monet, quod nimirum illorum vis atque impetus debilitatur & infringitur virtute inhabitantis Spiritus, & cum illa declinantur, tanquam professioni, studio atque cura Christianorum (que est quaerere caelestia) a diametro contraria. Πορνείαν)

Hic ea vox ita generaliter sumenda est, ut & adulterium comprehendat, quemadmodum Matth.

V. 32. Explicantur jam membra, quae in terra sunt: non autem intelligendi hec tantum actus, sed etiam affectus pravi, quia caro crucifigenda est σὺν τοῖς παθήμασι, καὶ ταῖς ἐπιθυμίαις, Gal. V. 24. Ecce, interpretatur, qua illa sint membra, & fornicationem eo prius meminit, quia passim id vitium & maximè dominetur, ait Theophylactus. Conf.

1. Cor. VI. 9. Ἀκαθαρσίαν) De hac voce vide Rom. I. 24. 2. Cor. XII. v. 12. Gal. V. 9. Eph.

## 3:6
V. 6. Δι ἃ ἔρχεται ἡ ὀργὴ τοῦ θεοῦ ἐπὶ τοὺς υἱοὺς τῆς ἀπειθείας ἔρχεται is present for future, which is frequent in this verb.

Let punishments come Eph. V. 6. See also Gen. XXXII. 20. Theophylactus applies this specially to Avarice: and the wrath of future judgment, and the indignation of the present age, have seized such men, who have addicted themselves to silver and gold.

But this judgment remains for all those, and similar sins, which are recounted here. Conf. 1. Cor. VI. 9. Gal. V. 17. Yea, all the children of incredulity, by which name are understood not only those who, as Theophylactus wills, are immersed in vices through ignorance, but by a certain stubbornness and perfidy, which they have so exercised, that they have merited to be adopted from incredulity itself into children, and from it have received both the form and the sign, so that they can be easily distinguished.

But since the wages of every sin is death, Rom. VI. v. ult. and we do not obtain the remission of sins except through faith, all incredulous persons, who in the Hebrew phrase are called children of incredulity, are subjected to the wrath of God; ὁ ἀπειθῶν, he who does not believe in the Son, shall not see life, but the wrath of God remains upon him, Joh. XIII. 36. But whoever believes in the Son, even if he has been addicted to those vices, provided that true repentance having been performed, he apprehends the merit of Christ by true faith, he shall obtain the remission of sins, Eph.

X. 43. and so he does not perish, but has eternal life, Johan. III. 16. V. 7. Ἐν οἷς ὑμεῖς περιεπατήσατέ ποτε You directed your actions according to those motions.

For that is הלך. Thus κατὰ σάρκα περιπατεῖν, Rom. VIII. 1. 4. 2. Cor. X. 3. See also Eph. II. 2. IV. 17. Ὅτε ἐζῆτε ἐν αὐτοῖς When you were perpetually moved by such affections.

For to be moved is to live, See Rom. VI. 3. V. 8. Νυνὶ δὲ ἀπόθεσθε καὶ ὑμεῖς τὰ πάντα See that no poison remains, Eph.

IV. 22. 23. According to Aretius, by the verb περιπατεῖν are noted equal sins, by the verb ἐν the original. Crocinus proves: Not inelegantly, It is certain that they differ, just as the fecund and primary act: as Calvin speaks, power and act, or ἐνέργεια and habit. Thus Beza.

Since they lived in them dead to justice, it was not a wonder that they were occupied by them. They were carried off tyrannically by the power of sin reigning in them. But that those dead with Christ should henceforth wish to be involved in them is too monstrous. Theophylactus raises a doubt here, how they are commanded to put them away, who no longer lived in them, because he had said, when you lived in them? He answers, that the Apostle wills this: Sin formerly dominated you, and had constrained your life not yet washed by baptism, and held it more violently, whence the abdication from vices was difficult. But now the sin which had settled in you has been finished by death through baptism. Whence it happens that the vices themselves can easily be put away as garments. And you will not execute it further, that you lead your life under the tyranny of vices, for you are also yourselves dead to these.

The particle he says also that those things which follow are to be put away. Ὀργή, θυμός You have these thus distinguished also in Eph.

IV. 31. By wrath he does not understand that which is of duty, and is borne against the vices of persons rather than the persons themselves: But that which is borne not against the life, but against the persons themselves, having arisen from private causes, and burning with the desire of vengeance.

By θυμὸν is signified incandescence, when through the commotion of the mind the blood boils around the heart, and the ardor of indignation breaks out through the eyes and face, and betrays itself openly by hostile gesture. Κακίαν See Rom.

I. 29. 1. Cor. V. 8. XIV. 20. Eph. IV. 31. Tit. III. 3. 1. Petr. II. 1. Those places do not agree. For here κακία is not accepted so generally, as to embrace everything which is contrary to God, to piety, to virtue, but it notes the malignity and malevolence of the mind, which envies the commodities of the neighbor even to envy, and strives intensely to oppose and harm them in all ways, as the Blessed Hunnius rightly says in this place.

The order and connection of the vices teaches this: The opposition of the virtues confirms it, v. 12. seqq. Βλασφημία Matth. XV. v. 19. Marci VIII. vers. 22. Eph. IV. 31. Not generally blasphemy either against God, or against men, nor blasphemy against God, but evil-speaking, which lacerates the reputation of the neighbor with reproaches and execrations, and devotes him to curses, is insinuated.

Which the context sufficiently indicates. Αἰσχρολογίαν ἐν τῷ στόματι ὑμῶν this is construed with ἀπόθεσθε, as if that word had been repeated here, it is called πείσυναμα.

What is αἰσχρολογία here, that is called αἰσχρότης, Eph. V. vers. 4. By αἰσχρολογία is noted filthy, unwashed, and obscene speech about things base and abhorrent to the minds and ears of the pious.

Regarding that ἐν τῷ στόματι ὑμῶν Theophylactus in this place has it thus: He said truly, from the mouth, that is, what has been sanctified by the communication of the Lord's body. It is absurd, therefore, that that mouth should be defiled by the filthiness of speech, which receives Christ. Theophylactus believes, therefore, that the body of the Lord is received by the mouth, which Crocinus perverts in vain: The mouth receives the Lord's body by a signifying mystery, not in the truth of the thing. For it is not food of the belly, but of the mind.

For Theophylactus speaks clearly about the communication of the body of the Lord itself: In which is the power of restoration, which because the mouth is defiled by the filth of speech, which has been sanctified by the communication and reception of the very body of the Lord.

Latin:

V. 6. Δι ἃ ἔρχεται ἡ ὀργὴ τοῦ θεοῦ ἐπὶ τοὺς υἱοὺς τῆς ἀπειθείας ἔρχεται praesens pro futuro, quod in hoc verbo frequens.

Veniant poenae Eph. V. 6. Vide & Gen. XXXII. 20. Applicat specialiter Auaritiae Theophylactus: & futuri judicii ira, & praesentis seculi indignatio istiusmodi homines prehensae, qui se argento & auro addixerunt.

Sed hoc judicium manet omnia illa, iisque similia peccata, quae hic recensita. Conf. 1. Cor. VI. 9. Gal. V. 17. Imo omnes filios incredulitatis, quo nomine non tantum intelliguntur illi, qui ut Theophylactus vult, per ignorantiam, vitiis immersi sunt, sed pervicacia quadam atque perfidia, quam ita exercuere, ut ab incredulitate ipsa adoptari in filios promeruerint, ex eaque & formam acceperint & signum, ita ut dignosci facile possint.

Sed quum cujusvis peccati stipendium mors sit, Rom. VI. v. ult. nec nisi per fidem remissionem peccatorum consequamur, omnes increduli, qui phrasi Ebraea, filii incredulitatis dicuntur, irae Dei subjiciuntur; ὁ ἀπειθῶν, qui non credit Filio, non videbit vitam, sed ira Dei manet super ipsum, Joh. XIII. 36. Quisquis vero credit in Filium, etsi vitiis illis deditus fuerit, dummodo vera poenitentia acta, vera fide Christi meritum apprehendat, remissionem peccatorum adipiscietur, Eph.

X. 43. adeoque non perit, sed vitam aeternam habet, Johan. III. 16. V. 7. Ἐν οἷς ὑμεῖς περιεπατήσατέ ποτε Actiones vestras secundum illos motus dirigebatis.

Id enim est הלך. Sic κατὰ σάρκα περιπατεῖν, Rom. VIII. 1. 4. 2. Cor. X. 3. Vide & Eph. II. 2. IV. 17. Ὅτε ἐζῆτε ἐν αὐτοῖς Cum talibus affectibus perpetuo moveremini.

Nam moueri est vivere, Vide Rom. VI. 3. V. 8. Νυνὶ δὲ ἀπόθεσθε καὶ ὑμεῖς τὰ πάντα Videte, ne quid veneni resideat, Eph.

IV. 22. 23. Secundum Aretium verbo περιπατεῖν notantur peccata aequalia, verbo ἐν originale. Probat Crocinus: Non ineleganter, Certum est differre, sicut actus fecundus & primus: velut Caluinus loquitur, potentia & actus, seu ἐνέργεια & habitus. Sic Beza.

Cum in iis viverent mortui justitiae, mirum non erat, iis occupari. Raptabantur tyrannice vi peccati in ipsis regnantis. Sed mortuos cum Christo in iis versari deinceps uelle, nimis monstrosum. Dubium hic mouet Theophylactus, quomodo deponere ea jubeantur, qui jam non, amplius in illis vivebant, quia dixerat, cum viveretis in illis? Respondet, id velle Apostolum: Vobis olim peccatum dominabatur, vitamque vestram nondum baptismo ablutam constrinxerat, & violentius detinebat, unde difficilia erat à vitiis abdicatio. Nunc vero quod infederat vobis peccatum per baptismum morte confectum est. Quo fit ut facile possint vesti in modum vitia ipsa deponi. Nec ultra id exsecutabitis, sub vitiorum tyrannide vitam vos ducere, estis namque & his ipsi demortui.

Particula inquit etiam ea, quae sequuntur, deponenda esse. Ὀργή, θυμός Haec ita distincta habes & Eph.

IV. 31. Per iram non eam, quae officii est, & aduersus vitia personarum magis, quam personas ipsas fertur, intelligit: Sed eam, quae fertur non in vita, fed in personas ipsas, ex privatis orta causis, & vindictae cupiditate flagrans.

Per θυμὸν excandescentia significatur, cum prae commotione animi sanguis ebullit circa cor, & ardor indignationis per oculos atque vultum erumpit, & inimico gestu se palam prodit. Κακίαν Vide Rom.

I. 29. 1. Cor. V. 8. XIV. 20. Eph. IV. 31. Tit. III. 3. 1. Petr. II. 1. Non conveniunt ea loca. Nam hic κακία non ita generaliter accipitur, ut omne id, quod Deo, quod pietati, quod virtuti contrarium est, complectatur, sed animi malignitatem & malevolentiam notat, quae proximi commoditatibus ad liuorem usque invidet, eisque modis omnibus obstare & obesse impense studet, ut recte hoc loco Beat.

Hunnius. Docet id ordo & συνέχεα vitiorum: Confirmat oppositio virtutum, v. 12. seqq. Βλασφημία Matth. XV. v. 19. Marci VIII. vers. 22. Eph. IV. 31. Non generaliter blasphemia sive in Deum, sive in homines, neque blasphemia in Deum, sed maledicentia, quae convitiis, & execrationibus proximi famam lacerat, eumque diris devovet, insinuatur.

Quod contextus satis indicat. Αἰσχρολογίαν ἐν τῷ στόματι ὑμῶν hoc construitur cum ἀπόθεσθε, quasi ea vox hic repetita esset, id dicitur πείσυναμα.

Quod hic est αἰσχρολογία, id dicitur αἰσχρότης, Eph. V. vers. 4. Per αἰσχρολογίαν notatur sermo spurcus, illotus, atque obscoenus de rebus turpibus & abhorrentibus à piorum animis atque auribus.

Ad illud ἐν τῷ στόματι ὑμῶν Theophylactus in hunc locum ita habet: Aperte, vero ex ore dixit, id est, quod ex Dominici corporis communicatione sanctificatum est. Abfurdum itaque, ut os illud sermone foeditate coinquinetur, quod Christum suscipit. Ore ergo corpus Domini suscipi credit Theophylactus, quod frustra fic pervertit Crocinus: Os corpus Dominicum suscipit significante mysterio, non rei veritate. Non enim est cibus ventris, sed mentis.

Nam diserte loquitur Theophyl. de communicatione ipsius corporis Dominici: Inq; eo vis est ἐπανορθώσεως, quod fœdetur os spurcitie sermonis, quod sanctificatum est communicatione ac receptione ipsius corporis Dominici. Quod manet cibus mentis, non corporis, quantum ad finem, quia non alendi corporis, sed nutriendæ animæ destinatus hic cibus. v.

## 3:9
Which remains the food of the mind, not of the body, as to its end, because this food is destined not for the nourishing of the body, but for the nourishing of the soul. v. 9. Do not lie to one another Eph. IV. 25. That anger and indignation and malice [κακίαν], which come from the heart; so also evil-speaking, foul language, and lying, which overflows from the mouth, lest the speech of those, which ought to be seasoned with the salt of Christian prudence, be rendered insipid, that is, loathsome to pious and honest ears, but to God inaccessible and abominable, he notes with a just correction [ἐπανορθώσει]. But he points here to the lying by which the will delights to deceive its neighbor successfully, or to inflict damage upon him, while either his reputation is blackened or quarrels are stirred up among those who were previously joined in spirit and purpose. The Apostle, says Chrysostom here, has reviewed all the members: the heart for indignation, the mouth for evil-speaking, the eyes for fornication, the hands and feet for avarice, and lying for the soul itself, and for the old mind that it refashions. v. 10. Having put off the old man Thus he calls the former manner of living, as also Rom. VI. 6. and Eph. IV. 22. where it is 'to put off' [ἀπόθεσθαι], which is here 'to put off' [ἀπεκδύσασθαι].

Morals are like the garments of the soul. See above II. 11. Rom. XIII. 14. Gal. III. 27. Eph. IV. 24. VI. 11. He understands not so much the former manner of living—for the faithful had already put this off through conversion—as the depraved, congenital concupiscence, which, although they cannot here put off entirely as regards all members, they must nevertheless strive toward it with every effort, and so mortify the members of the old man that they contend to put him off entirely in act as well. Beza and the Belgians interpret the word 'having put off' [ἀπεκδυσάμενοι] as 'when you have put off,' namely in baptism, so that a reason may be given why the earthly members are to be mortified and these enumerated sins are to be put off, because, namely, they had already begun to put off the corrupt nature in baptism; but the interpretation of the Blessed Luther, which Piscator also followed, is better, because this becomes a word of command here, namely that they ought to strive with all the zeal they can to put off not only certain more notable members of the old man, not only to put off some other sins, but to put off the whole old man, propagated even from Adam to them, along with all his deeds or works.

The old man clings to us from the old generation, the new is from regeneration. The former comes by the name of the flesh, the latter by the name of the Spirit: which two always oppose each other in the regenerate man, Rom. VII. Gal. V. 17. and therefore one must always be occupied in putting off the old man more and more, and in putting on the new, so that the flesh may be subdued and the Spirit may be renewed upright in our inward parts. And having put on the new See in the place cited

Eph. IV. 24. The one being renewed [τὸν ἀνακαινούμενον] Thus 'renewal' [ἀνακαίνωσις] is said in Rom. XII. 2. Tit. III. 5. He adds this because one must progress daily more and more in the way of piety.

Thus 1 Tim. II. 4. Heb. X. 26. Tit. I. v. 1. And the image of Him who created him [Καὶ εἰκόνα τοῦ κτίσαντος αὐτὸν] To the image of God, who made us a new creature through Christ, Eph. II. 10, 15. III. 9. IV. 24. Adam was created to a certain image of God, in intellect, free will, and dominion.
