But we are created to a far more perfect one, such as Christ exhibited in justice, holiness, truth, and goodness. See above I. 15. v. 11. in which creation.

Rather, in which 'renewal' [ἀνακαίνωσεί], or renovation: for it is rightly said that in it there is no difference between Greek and Jew. But what does this have to do with the ancient creation, in which we were created to the image of the creator God? Compare Gal. III. 28. They are commanded to put on the new man.

As the old man consisted in his members, which constituted a certain body of sin: so also the new man has his members, a new mind, a new heart, new affections, new motions, a new life: which novelty, however, is not essential or substantial, such as the μεταμόρφωσιν of the old man into a new one which fanatics, Weigelians, and others dream of: But Accidental, as regards the new qualities, dispositions, and habits of virtue of mind and will, and the new actions proceeding from them. Hiero-Psaltes called it a new Spirit, Ps. LI. 12. a new heart, Ezec. 36. v. 26.

But the new man is said to be renewed, because he was once new in the first creation, but that one is judged to have been stripped off through the fall, whence renewal is needed through the Holy Spirit, which is begun in baptism, Tit. III. 5. but continuation is needed, so that we may be renewed from day to day, and be transformed from glory into glory, 2 Cor. IV. 15. III. 18. For what was not previously something new cannot be said to be RENEWED. But by ἐπίγνωσιν, unto which we are renewed, not knowledge in general of divine things is understood, whereby we are deprived through the corruption of our nature, 1 Cor. II. verse 14., but through experience of the divine goodness. By the image of Him who created him, the image of God, which was granted or co-created to us in the first creation, is understood, unto which we are renewed, and which is repaired in us through the Holy Spirit, which consists with respect to the intellect in the knowledge of God, as with respect to the will in justice & holiness, Eph. IV. 24. Therefore by the word κτίσαν not a new creation, but that old and first one is understood, because we were all founded in Adam to the image of GOD in the knowledge of GOD.

For 1. the word κτίζειν denotes creation in its proper sense, from which one must not depart unless compelled by necessity. 2. When placed absolutely, it is understood of that primordial creation. 3. This man is said to be both new and renewed to the image of GOD: He is renewed as to that 'renewal' [ἀνακαίνωσιν] which we now attain in Christ: He is new in relation to the old, corrupt Adam, which corruption was indeed contracted through sin, when in the first creation Adam had been created to the image of his creator GOD.

To the old man, says the Blessed Hunnius, clings the ignorance of God: and the old man is that deformed image of Satan, which, in place of the image of God concreated to the first men in the beginning, but abolished through the fall, succeeded by a most unhappy exchange. Therefore, the new man is put on when man is repaired to that pristine image of God, in which the true knowledge of the creator shines.

Nor indeed was he created only to a certain image of God in intellect, free will, and dominion, as if the image of GOD which we now attain in renewal were far more perfect.

For this renewal in the present life is far more imperfect than the primeval image, both as regards knowledge of divine things and as regards holiness and justice, since that is still obscured by many shadows on account of native and hereditary ignorance: but this one is joined with a perpetual struggle of flesh and Spirit, which had no place in the state of integrity. The passage Col. I. 15. does not help Grotius, but stands against him. For if the word κτίζειν must be taken here in that sense in which, wherever κτίσεως is used, when the Son of God is called πρωτότοκος πάσης κτίσεως, it designates not a new creation but the primeval creation, then it must designate the primeval creation in this place.

For we have shown that it is designated there for that place. Compare what has been said on Eph. IV. 24.

Latin:

9. Μὴ ψεύδεσθε εἰς ἀλλήλους Eph. IV. 25. Ut iram & indignationem & κακίαν, quæ ex corde; Ita maledicentiam, turpiloquium, & mendacium, quæ ex ore redundat, ne his sermo illorum, quem sale prudentiæ Christianæ conditum esse oportet, reddatur insipidus, hoc est, piis atque honestis auribus exotus, deo autem invius & abominabilis, justâ ἐπανορθώσει notat. Mendacium autem hic indigitat, quo gaudet vis feliciter fallere proximum, vel eidem insuper inferre damnum, dum vel fama ejus denigratur, vel lites feruntur inter eos, qui prius animis atque studiis conjuncti erant. Cuncta membra, inquit hic Chrysostomus, recensuit Apostolus, cor indignationem, os maledicentiam, oculos fornicationem, avaritiam manus & pedes, mendacium animum ipsum, & mentem veterem reficientia. v.

10. Ἀπεκδυσάμενοι τὸν παλαιὸν ἄνθρωπον Sic vocat pristinam vivendi rationem, ut & Rom. VI. 6. & Eph. IV. 22. ibi est ἀπόθεσθαι, quod hic ἀπεκδύσασθαι. Mores sunt velut vestes animi. Vide supra II. 11. Rom. XIII. 14. Gal. III. 27. Eph. IV. 24. VI. 11. Non tam pristinam vivendi rationem, hanc enim fideles jam exuerant per conversionem, quàm concupiscentiam pravam congenitam intelligit, quam etsi exuere penitus hic nequeant, quantum ad omnia membra, in id tamen inniti debent omni opere, adeoque ita mortificare membra veteris hominis, ut eundem prorsus deponere actu etiam exuere contendant. Beza & Belgæ vocem ἀπεκδυσάμενοι interpretantur cum exueritis, scilicet in baptismo, ut ratio reddatur, cur mortificanda sint membra terrena, & deponenda ista peccata recensita, qua scilicet jam in baptismo naturam corruptam exuere cœperint; sed præstat Beat. Lutheri, quam etiam sequutus Piscator interpretatio, quod hic fit verbum mandati, quod scilicet non tantum mortificare membra quædam insigniora veteris hominis, non tantum deponere alia nonnulla peccata, sed totum veterem hominem exuere, adeo ab Adamo ad ipsos propagatum, exuere, quanto possint studio, debeant cum factis vel operibus ejus omnibus.

Vetus homo ex veteri generatione inhæret, novus est à regeneratione. Ille carnis, hic Spiritus nomine venit: Quæ duo in homine renato sibi semper adversantur, Rom. VII. Gal. V. 17. ideoque semper occupari debet in veteri homine magis magisque exuendo, novo autem induendo, ut caro subigatur, Spiritus autem rectus in visceribus nostris innovetur. Καὶ ἐνδυσάμενοι τὸν νέον Vide dicto loco Eph.

IV. 24. Τὸν ἀνακαινούμενον Sic ἀνακαίνωσις dicitur Rom. XII. 2. Tit. III. 5. Hoc addit, quia quotidie magis magisque proficiendum est in via pietatis. Εἰς ἐπίγνωσιν Cognitionem intelligit ipsam experientiam bonitatis in nos divinæ.

Sic 1. Tim. II. 4. Ebr. X. 26. Tit. I. v. 1. Καὶ εἰκόνα τοῦ κτίσαντος αὐτὸν Ad imaginem Dei, qui nos per Christum fecit novam creaturam, Eph. II. 10. 15. III. 9. IV. 24. Adamus ad quandam Dei imaginem conditus, intellectu, libera voluntate, dominatu. At nos ad longe perfectiorem, qualem Christus exhibuit justitia, sanctitate, veritate, bonitate. Vide supra I. 15. v. 11. ὅτῳ in qua creatione.

Imo in qua, ἀνακαίνωσεί, vel renovatione: Nam in ea nullam esse differentiam Græci & Judæi recte dicitur. Quid vero hoc ad creationem antiquam, in qua ad imaginem Dei conditoris sumus conditi? Conf. Gal. III. 28. Induere jubentur novum hominem.

Ut vetus hominis membris suis constabat, quæ corpus quoddam peccati constituebant: Ita & novus homo membra sua habet, novum animum, novum cor, novos affectus, novos motus, novam vitam: Quæ vero novitas non essentialis aut substantialis est, qualem μεταμόρφωσιν hominis veteris in novum somniant fanatici, Weigeliani aliique: Sed Accidentalis, quoad novas virtutum mentis & voluntatis qualitates, dispositiones & habitus, novasque actiones inde prodeuntes. Novum Spiritum dixit Hiero-Psaltes, Ps. LI. 12. novum cor, Ezec. 36. v. 26.

Renovatus autem dicitur novus ille homo, quia novus quondam fuit in prima creatione, sed vidicatur ille exutus est per lapsum, unde renovatione opus est per Spiritum Sanctum, quæ in baptismo inchoatur, Tit. III. 5. sed continuatione opus, ut de die in diem renovemur, de claritate in claritatem transformemur, 2. Cor. IV. 15. III. 18. Nam RENOVARI dici non potest, quod antea novum aliquid non fuit. Per ἐπίγνωσιν vero, ad quam renovamur , per experientia bonitatis divinæ, sed notitia intelligitur rerum divinarum in genere, qua per naturæ nostræ corruptionem destituimur, 1. Cor. II. vers. 14. Per imaginem ejus, qui creavit ipsum , imago Dei, quæ in prima creatione nobis concessa vel concreata est, intelligitur, ad quam nos renovamur, quæque in nobis reparatur per Spiritum Sanctum, quæ ratione intellectus consistat in cognitione Dei, ut ratione voluntatis in justitia & sanctitate, Eph. IV. 24. Per verbum itaque κτίσαν non nova creatio, sed vetus illa & prima intelligitur, quia in Adamo conditi omnes sumus ad imaginem DEI in cognitione DEI. Nam 1. verbum κτίζειν sensu proprio notat creationem, à quo recedendum non est, nisi cogente necessitate.

2. absolute positum de creatione illa primæva intelligitur. 3. Homo hic & novus & renovatus ad imaginem DEI dicitur: Renovatur quod illam ἀνακαίνωσιν, quæ nunc consequimur in Christo: Novus in relatione ad veterem corruptum Adamum, quæ vero corruptio per peccatum contracta, quum in prima creatione Adam fuerit ad imaginem fui conditoris DEI creatus.

Veteri homini, inquit Beat. Hunnius, adhæret ignorantia Dei: estque homo vetus Satane illa imago deformis, quæ in locum imaginis Dei primis hominibus initio concreata, per lapsum autem abolita, infelici admodum commutatione successit. Tunc ergo novus homo induitur, quando ad pristinam illam Dei imaginem, in qua lucet agniti vera creatoris, homo reparatur.

Nec vero tantum ad aliqualem Dei imaginem conditus fuit intellectu, libera voluntate, dominatu, ac si perfectior longe fit imago DEI, quam nunc consequimur in renovatione.

Nam hæc renovatio in præsenti vita ex adverso longe imperfectior est præmæva imagine, tum quoad cognitionem rerum divinarum, tum quoad sanctitatem & justitiam, siquidem illa multis tenebris adhuc obfuscetur ob ignorantiam nativam & hæreditariam: Hæc vero cum perpetua lucta carnis & Spiritus conjuncta fit, quæ in statu integritatis locum nullum habuit. Locus Col. I. 15. nihil juvat Grotium, sed eidem adversatur. Nam si vox κτίζειν eo sensu hic accipienda, quæ ubi κτίσεως usurpatur, cum Filius Dei πρωτότοκος πάσης κτίσεως dicitur, non novam creationem, sed creationem primævam designet hoc loco oportet.

Illic enim eam designari ad istum locum ostendimus. Conf. quæ ad Eph. IV. 24. dicta sunt.

## 3:11
Οὐκ ἔνι Ἕλλην καὶ Ἰουδαῖος (There is neither Greek nor Jew). Such things are often contrasted, as in Rom. 1:14, 16; ch. 2:9, 10; ch. 3:9; ch. 10:12; 1 Cor. 1:24; ch. 10:32; ch. 12:13; Gal. 3:8. Moreover, elsewhere the word "Greeks" encompasses the whole human race outside of the Jews; but here, as the following words indicate, it is taken more strictly for those who were of the Greek language. Περιτομὴ καὶ ἀκροβυστία (Circumcision and uncircumcision), that is, circumcised or uncircumcised.

Thus Rom. 4:9; Gal. 2:7, 8, 9; Eph. 2:11; Phil. 3:5. The sense here is the same as in Gal. 5:6; ch. 6:15. Βάρβαρος (Barbarian). That name was given by the Greeks to all who were not acquainted with the Greek language.

It was used especially of the Phrygians. In Euripides, Peleus says to Menelaus: Βεβαξάμενος χρόνος ὧν ἐν βαξάροις. Horace: Græcia Barbaria lento collisa duello. Σκύθης (Scythian). The discourse grows. For among the barbarians, the Scythians were the most barbaric, half-wild men.

Therefore, Aeschines uses this name as a term of reproach against Demosthenes. Seneca in the Troades: Quis Colchus hoc, quis sedis incertæ Scytha commisit? It is certain that nations differ greatly in character: Sed Nemo adeo ferus est, qui non mitescere possit, Si modo culturæ patientem præbeat aurem.

Anacharsis the Scythian is a witness to this. That passage from Valerius Maximus, ch. 3.3, does not depart from this: "Virtue, therefore, does not allow itself to be reached by fastidious approaches, nor does it offer its bounty with any discrimination of persons, but being equally exposed to all, it estimates what you have brought of desire rather than what you have brought of dignity." Δοῦλος, ἐλεύθερος (Bond, free). Not even the fortune of one's birth stands in the way.

1 Cor. 7:21, 22; ch. 12: 13. See what we have brought to that former passage to the Corinthians.

Add Gal. 3: 28. Ἀλλὰ τὰ πάντα ἐν πᾶσι Χριστός (But Christ is all and in all). This is the only distinction that now holds value, how much one has drawn from Christ: Πάντα ἐν πᾶσι (All in all). All things in all, namely, those things which pertain to salvation. For Christ has been made unto us wisdom, righteousness, sanctification, and redemption, 1 Cor. 1:

29. V. 12. Ἐνδύσασθε οὖν ὡς ἐκλεκτοὶ τοῦ Θεοῦ ἅγιοι καὶ ἠγαπημένοι, σπλάγχνα οἰκτιρμοῦ (Put on therefore, as the elect of God, holy and beloved, bowels of mercies). This discourse is very apt for moving the soul, as are many in Paul. Being affected by great benefits from God, gifted with the Spirit, and loved by Him in the highest degree, see what you ought to do in return. Σπλάγχνα οἰκτιρμοῦ, just as in Phil. 2:1, σπλάγχνα, οἰκτιρμοῦ. Those words of the same or similar meaning, bound together, have great efficacy.

Concerning the verb ἐνδύσασθε, see above at verse 10. Put on, namely, as a decent garment, pleasing to God and the angels, and necessary for yourselves; not one which you might cast off again, but one you should wear perpetually in the eyes of God and the saints, without which you will be deformed and unseemly.

They were born with the impure rags of the old man, therefore they were ordered to put them off: the adornment of virtues did not inhere in nature, therefore He commands them to put it on, as Crocius not inappropriately notes here. That election from eternity to glory is understood in this place, the same author teaches.

Not incorrectly. But that true holiness comes from it, that we do not approve. For election is not the cause of holiness, such that the latter depends on the former, even if we are elected so that we may be holy, Eph. 1:4; the end of election is holiness, not its effect. He did not say "put on mercy," as Theophylact warns, but "bowels of mercy": both so that he may not seem to despise those who are worthy of mercy, and so that he may show that it is to be granted from the affection of the mind: and not in the manner of brothers, but as parents are accustomed to be more inclined toward their children.

Nor would you say that this one or that one has committed crimes, and therefore one should not spare the delinquent, since the bowels of mercy demand the very same thing. Χρηστότητα (Kindness), 1 Cor. 6:6;

Gal. 5:12; Tit. 3:4. Ταπεινοφροσύνη (Humility), Acts 20:19; Col. 2:18, 23; ch. 3:2; 1 Pet.

5:5. Πραΰτητα (Meekness), 1 Cor. 4:21; 2 Cor. 10:1; Gal. 5:22; ch. 6:1; Eph. 4:2. Μακροθυμία (Longsuffering), 2 Cor. 6:6; Gal. 5:22; Eph. 4:2; above ch. 1:11; 2 Tim. 3:10; ch. 4:2; Heb. 6:12; 1 Cor. 13:4; 1 Thess. 5:14; James 5:8. We add only the phrasing of Theophylact:

"Whoever," he says, "has carried bowels of mercy with him, these things necessarily follow. For what father does not show himself more benign to his children, not humble, not indulgent? By not resisting anything, does he not permit and indulge all things? What parent, I ask, does not bear these things more tolerantly?" See how he has placed these in order.

For benignity begets humility. Furthermore, that one should be more benign and instructed in good morals, and that he should be humble, follows necessarily. From humility, modesty also has its origin. For, on the contrary, whoever is proud and insolent will also necessarily be irascible.

From modesty arises patience, i.e., greatness of soul. B. Hunnius succinctly explained these things thus: In the first place, he places bowels of mercies, by which he expresses that pious, sincere, and ardent affection of commiseration toward miserable and afflicted persons, by which sense the bowels themselves are moved to mercy.

Secondly, he recounts benignity, so that you are not only well-affected in your heart toward your neighbor, but that you bring forth and express that χρηστότητα of yours into the work itself by doing good.

Thirdly, he counts humility among the former. This virtue is also a singular, decent, and illustrious gem in that spiritual adornment of the Christian man, namely, that humility of mind which does not think arrogantly of itself, but with a humility that is not feigned, humbles itself before God and men.

Fourthly, he places πραΰτητα, meekness, which consists in the placid and quiet spirit of a man, in the sweetness of manners and the convenience of conversation. In the fifth place, longsuffering (μακροθυμία) is mentioned, which itself also wonderfully adorns the habit of a Christian man.

Longsuffering is when one knows how to bear the manners of others, even if they are less convenient, placidly, and indeed to tolerate injuries with an equal mind, just as the Apostle himself adds the description: "forbearing one another," as if he were saying: it is not fitting to be exacerbated by every word or even inconvenient deed, but it is right that you should tolerate one another.

1. Cor. 7. 21. 22. c. 12. 13. Vide quid ad priorem illud ad Corinthios locum attulimus.

Cor. 1. 29. V. 12. Ἐνδύσασθε οὖν ὡς ἐκλεκτοὶ τοῦ Θεοῦ ἅγιοι κὶ ἠγαπ-μένοι, σπλάγχνα οἰκτιρμοῦ) Valde apta ad commovendos animos hæc oratio, ut multæ in Paulo. Magnis a Deo affecti beneficiis, Spiritu donati, summe ab ipso dilecti, videte, quid vicissim facere debeatis. Σπλάγχνα οἰκτιρ-μοῦ, sicut Phil. 2. 1. σπλάγχνα, οἰκτιρμοῦ. Voces istæ ejusdem aut propinqui significatus inter se vinctæ magnam habent efficaciam.

De verbo ἐνδύσασθε vide supra 10. Induimini scilicet tanquam veste descente, Deo & Angelis gratæ, vobis autem necessaria, non quam iterum exuatis, sed gestetis perpetuo in Dei & sanctorum oculis, fine qua futuri estis deformes & indecori.

Cum impuris veteris hominis laciniis erant nati, ideo exuere jussi: Virtutum ornatus non inhærebat natura, ideo jubet induere, ut hic non incommode Cro-cius. Electionem ab æterno ad gloriam factam hoc loco intelligi, idem docet. Non inrecte.

Sed quod ab ea veram sanctitatem esse, illud non probamus.
