Cor. 4. 21. 2. Cor. 10. 1. Gal. 5. 22. cap. 6. 1. Eph. 4. 2. Μακροθυμία) 2. Cor. 6. 6. Gal. 5. 22. Eph. 4. 2. supra c. 1. 11. 2. Tim. 3. 10. c. 4. 2. Ebr. 6. 12. 1. Cor. 13. 4. 1. Thess. 5. 14. Jacob. 5. 8. Adjicimus tantum Theophylacti phrasin: Qui secum, inquit, misericordia viscera tuleris, necessario & hæc consequuntur.

Quis n, Pater non se ad liberos præstat benigniorem, non humilem, non indulgentem? Nihil iie obsistendo non cuncla permittat,indulgeatq;? Quis inquam parens non ferat hos tolerantius? Vide quam hæc ex ordine posuit.

Benignitas namq; humi-litatem parit. Quin, benignior fuerit & opimiis moribus instructus, & bumilis sit necessario sequitur. ab humilitate habet & modestia ortum. Nam contra qui superbus & insolens fuerit, & iracundus sit, erit necesse.

A modestia oritur patientia, b. e. animi magnitudo. B. Hunnius succincte hæc ita exposuit: Pri-mo loco viscera miserationum ponit, quibus exprimit pium illum fincerum & ardentem commiserationis affectum erga personas miseras & afflictas, præ quo sensu misericordia ipsa commoveantur viscera.

Secundo recenset benignitatem, quæ non tantum in corde sis bene affectus erga provimum, sed in opus ipsum tuam illam χρηστότητα benefaciendo proferas & expromas. Ter-tio humilitatem prioribus annumerat.

Est & hæc virtus fingulare decq ac prælustris gemma in spirituali illo ornatu hominis Christiani, videlicet animi humilitas illa, quæ non arroganter de se sentit, sed demissione minime simulata coram Deo & hominibus se humiliat.

Quarto πραΰτητα ponit manfuetudinem, quæ consistit in Spiritu hominis placido & quieto, in suavitate morum & commoditate conversationis. Quinto loco memoratur longanimitas μακροθυμία, quæ ipsa quoque Christiani hominis habitum mirifice exornat.

Est 4. longanimitas, cum quis aliorum mores etiam minus commodos placide ferre, quin & injurias æquo animo tolerare novit, sicut Apostolus ipse descriptionem adjicit: sufferentes vosmetipsos, ac si dicat: non decet ad quodvis verbum, vel etiam factum incommodus exacerbari, sed par est, ut vos invicem toleretis.

## 3:13
V. 13. Ἀνεχόμενοι ἀλλήλων (Forbearing one another), Eph. 4:2. Καὶ χαριζόμενοι ἑαυτοῖς (And forgiving one another). Here ἑαυτοῖς is placed for ἀλλήλοις, as in Matt. 12:26; Mark 10:26; Luke 21:1, 13. The same words in Eph. 4:32. Ἐάν τις πρὸς τινα μομφὴν (If any man have a quarrel against any). This is what is said in Matt. 5:23: "that thy brother hath ought against thee." Μομφὴν ἔχειν is a very good Greek idiom, found also in Euripides and Aristophanes. He does not say "tolerating others," but "one another," so that he may intimate that there is no one among all who does not stumble, and thus is in need of fraternal tolerance as well.

"Mutual patience," says Theophylact, "tolerate one another; you will bear him, he will bear you, on the condition that your mutual faults are not investigated too bitterly. Indeed, consider these things as small, and do not esteem those things which are admitted against you as great."

Note how Paul himself would make little of these things, inasmuch as he has expressed them under the name of a "complaint." Καθὼς καὶ ὁ Χρισὸς ἐχαρίσατο ὑμῖν (Even as Christ forgave you). And this we have in Eph. 4:32. Οὕτω καὶ ὑμεῖς (So also do ye), supply "do."

Which word is also understood elsewhere. Let us hear Theophylact again: "What he always does, he exhorts them by the example of Christ, bringing the same into the argument. Yet above, he made those things which they committed against one another seem wicked, when he had expressed them under the name of a complaint.

But when he brings forth Christ, he persuades that, even if the things admitted against us are grave, we should be beneficent even to those who offend us. If, finally, we ourselves excel and are of a more excellent fortune, while they are meager and perhaps inferior, these are nevertheless to be borne, and all things are to be dismissed.

Nor is only that to be done, but death itself is to be undergone for them. Indeed, even after death it will be (if it be permitted) to deserve well of these very ones, just as the Lord has deserved well of you after His death." V.

Latin:

V. 13. Ἀνεχόμενοι ἀλλήλων) Ephes. 4, 2. Καὶ χαριζόμενοι ἑαυτοῖς) Hic ἑαυτοῖς positum pro ἀλλή-λοις, ut Matth. 12, 26. Marc. 10, 26. Luc. 21, 1. 13. Eadem verba Eph. 4. 32. Ἐάν τις πρὸς τινα μομφὴν) Hoc est, quod dicitur Matth. 5, 23. ὅτι ὁ ἀδελφός σου ἔχει τι κατά σου. Μομφὴν ἔχειν loqutio bene Græca est & apud Eurip. & Aristophanem. Non ait tolerantes alios, sed alii alios, ut innuat, neminem esse inter omnes, qui non impingat, adeoq; fraterna etiam tolerantia indigeat.

Mutua,inquit Theophylactus, patientia vos tolerate, tu illum tuleris, ille te semt, ea lege, ut non acerbius vestra invicem inquirantur commissa. Quin pro parvis hæc ducite, nec magna illa, quæ in vos admittuntur, existimetis.

Adverte, quemadmodum hæc ipsa & Paulus parvi faceret, utpote quæ sub querelæ nomine ita expresserit. Καθὼς καὶ ὁ Χρισὸς ἐχαρίσατο ὑμῖν) Et hoc habemus Eph. 4. 32. Οὕτω καὶ ὑμεῖς) supple facite.

Quod verbum & alibi subauditur. Audiamus iterum Theophylactum: Quod semper agit, illos exemplo Christi hortatur, idem in argumen-tum inducens. Superius tamen, quæ in se invicem iidem delinquerent, ut prava viderentur, effecit, cum hæc sub quæstionis nomine expressisset.

Cum vero Chri-stum producit, suadet, etsi gravia fint, quæ in nos ad-mittuntur, vel in eos ipsi beneficii simus, qui nobis officiant. Si demum vero ipsi excellimus, & præstantiori fortuna sumus, tenues vero fint illi & forte inferiores, ferendos tamen hos esse, & missa omnia facienda.

Ne-que id modo agendum, sed mors etiam pro bis obeunda. Quin vel post mortem erit (si liceat) de bis ipsis bene merendum, quemadmodum & post obitum de vobis est bene meritus Dominus.

## 3:14
14. Ἐπὶ πᾶσι δὲ τούτοις τὴν ἀγάπην (And above all these things [put on] charity), namely, ἐνδύσασθε, which must be repeated here from afar. Such are many things in Paul. Ἥ τις ἐστὶ σύνδεσμος τῆς τελειότητος (Which is the bond of perfectness), which is the most perfect bond, namely, joining souls together.

The same sense in Eph. 4:3. In the Manuscript, ἥ ἐστι σύνδεσμος with the construction made according to the thing. Therefore, this has nothing to do with perfection standing before God, by which we might be justified: which some Papists conclude from this. For charity is not said to render us perfect before God or to justify us, but it is the bond of perfection, because we are joined by no bond of mutual perfection more than by charity.

Charity is called σύνδεσμος τῆς τελειότητος, not because it renders us perfect for standing before the judgment of God, but because individual believers, as members of one mystical body, are so perfected through charity that nothing is lacking to any, but necessary things are supplied to individuals from mutual fellowship with the other members.

Regarding those things, above all, Theophylact: Since it can happen that someone bestows gifts, yet does not do so from a true sense of duty, but under a certain pretext of benevolence and simulation bestows something, Paul opens the way by which we can truly bestow gifts. Regarding the bond of perfection: Charity, he says, when it is present, will contain all these things: but if it is absent, they will be dissolved, and will be shown to have been feigned and of no moment, whatever we have brought to our neighbor. Just as in a constructed house, if the joints are missing, and the connections that hold it together, it will collapse all the sooner. And likewise in the body, if the joints and nerves are absent, it must necessarily perish and be dissolved.

Latin:

V. 14. Ἐπὶ πᾶσι δὲ τούτοις τὴν ἀγάπην) nempe ἐνδύσα-θε, quod ex longinquo repeti hic deber. Qualia multa apud Paulum. Ἥ τις ἐσὶ σύνδεσμος τῆς τελειότητος) quod vinculum est perfectissimum, animos scilicet conjungens.

Idem sensus Eph. 4, 3. In Manuscripto ἥ ἐσι σύνδεσμος constru-ctione ad rem facta. Nihil ergo hoc ad perfectione coram Deo consi-stentem, qua justificemur: quam Papiculæ nonnulli hinc concludunt. Non n, charitas nos vel perfectos coram Deo reddere vel justificare dicitur, sed vinculu est perfectionis, quod nullo vinculo perfecti9 mutui conjungamur, quam charitate.

Dicitur charitas σύνδεσμος τῆς τελειότητος, non quod nos perfectos reddat ad consistendum coram Dei judicio, sed quia singuli fideles, tanquam unius corporis mystici membra per charitatem ita perficiuntur, ut nulli quidquam desit, sed singulis necessaria suppetant ex mutuo cum cæteris membris consortio.

Ad illa super omnia Theophylactus: Cum fieri possit, ut munera quis largiatur, nec tamen id ex vero officio agat, sed prætextu quadam benevolentiæ & simulatione quid tribuat, Paulus viam patefacit, qua vera possimus munera elargiri. De συνδέσμῳ vero τῆς τελειότητος: Charitas, inquit, cum aderit, hac omnia continebit: Si vero deerit, dissolventur, arguenturque & commentitia exstitisse, & nullius momenti, quæcunque in proximum intulerimus. Quemadmodum & in domo constructa, si compages desint, & nexus, qui eam contineant, ocyus collabetur. Itemque & in corpore, si juncturæ aberunt & nervi, pereat necesse est, & dissolvatur.

## 3:15
15. And let the peace of Christ rule in your hearts: let peace judge in your hearts, namely, if there is any controversy among you.

The pursuit of peace acts in place of a judge: to rule is properly said of the judges of the games. But it is transferred to any judges, as in Plutarch several times. Hesychius does not depart from the sense when he says to rule, to mediate; a good man is a judge to himself.

In the Manuscript: the peace of Christ. To which you were called) 1 Cor. 7, 15. In one body) that is, into one body, that you might be one body, which cannot happen except through peace, 1 Cor. 10, 16.

These things are from Theophylact, whom it is a pleasure to hear: We indeed, for the most part, when affected by insults through some one person, are soon overcome by various struggles of thought, some of which incite us to vengeance, others to tolerance. If the peace of God is then present with us, just as some fair judge and president of the contest, we will judge that the palm of victory should be deferred to those who have persuaded us to tolerate injuries with an even mind, and these same thoughts and movements of the soul that were previously brought forward will have been conceded, and they will together tolerate the injuries inflicted. Therefore, let the peace of such a judge perform its office in us, not anger or altercation, or some human peace, which is perfected by opposing and avenging, since that of God and Christ is firmer and indissoluble, which no mortal good can effect: Just as the reconciliation of God with us would have been initiated by no other means, except that He alone by His clemency and charity dissolved the enmities which He had once exercised against us.

It is called the peace of God, because it is not given by men, but by God, the Author of every good. It is not reconciled through men, but through God, since God acquired it with His own blood. Yet that peace with God is not what is called the peace of God, Phil. 4, 7. but peace among men, because we have been called to this peace into one body, concerning which Theophylact says: For what? for what other reason are we one body, than that we might fervently love one another's peace, as members, and not be distrustful.

Which is also of God, because it pleases God, and is conformable to the Divine will. To which is opposed the peace of Satan and the world. And be thankful) mindful of the benefits which you have received from God.

In the glossary, thankful means gratified, grateful. Others also understand this regarding gratitude toward God: But it follows next regarding this in v. 17. Here the Apostle is occupied in explaining the mutual duties of benevolence and charity.

Therefore Crocius more correctly explains the study of mutual gratitude. V.

16. Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly) let the Evangelical doctrine never depart from your minds. For that is to dwell, as 2

Tim. 1, 5. In Hebrew, richly, that is, abundantly, as 1

Tim. 6, 17. Tit.

3, 6. 2 Pet.

1, 11. In the Manuscript, the word of God. The medium through which it is effected that we die and live with Christ, that we seek and sigh for heavenly things, that we mortify the members which are on earth, that we put off the old man and put on the new, and be adorned with those spiritual ornaments as with a garment, and the word of Christ.

Previously he had introduced baptism as a medium for them, ch. 2. Now he teaches that the Word of Christ also pertains to these things. He had spoken immediately before of the affections of mercy and charity, and things pertaining thereto, and had opposed them to the affections of wicked anger and indignation: Now he admonishes regarding the use of the tongue for information and exhortation, and also the celebration of the Lord, which he opposes to the abuse of the tongue and the sins of the mouth, and he wishes the Word of the Lord to dwell cautiously in you in all wisdom.

Grotius explains that word 'dwell' too thinly. Theophylact unfolds its emphasis more: For the Word of God does not simply exist in you, but he said 'dwell', and abundantly.

For if we abound in the knowledge of the sacred scriptures, we will easily bear both hardships and calamities, and any kind of evil. Nor would he suffer any slight loss, just as some wealthy man, and would count it as nothing. He does not say 'sojourn', but 'dwell'.

Strangers are accustomed to stay for a time; but 'to dwell' signifies a constant mansion, yet not absolutely immovable. A guest received into a house becomes familiar to us, we enjoy his sight, conversation, and company, and if he is agreeable, we assign him a comfortable habitation, we perform duties, we are reluctant to let him go from us: All these things can be applied to the force of this metaphor. But the Word of Christ ought to dwell in us, not in some part of itself, but the whole, not sparingly, but copiously, richly, so that we may diligently read and hear it, speak of it everywhere, always meditate upon it, and delight in it alone.

Moreover, the Apostle addresses not only the clergy, whom the Papists call so, but also the Laity, barring no one from the reading of scripture, which the Pope does, but exhorting all to the same. Whence Chrysostom: Hear, as many of you as are worldly, and preside over wives, how he commands you above all to read the scriptures, and that not simply, nor incidentally, but with great diligence.

This is that, says Chrysostom in homily II on Matthew, which corrupts everything, that you think the reading of the scriptures pertains to monks alone. Which I would like the Papists to note.

In all wisdom) And here, as elsewhere, it stands for 'with', true wisdom accompanies the Gospel 1 Cor. 1, 30. ch.

2, 6. Eph. 1, 8. Teaching and admonishing one another) 'Be' must be repeated here, so that 'the word of Christ dwell in you' may be as a parenthesis, and again 'one another' for 'each other'.

It is also to some extent the duty of private individuals both to teach and to admonish. Why the customary sense of the preposition 'in' is not retained, so that the manner is insinuated in which the word of God ought to dwell in us, not in carnal prudence, nor that we should abuse it for jest, for errors or heresy, for the pleasures of the world, but that 'in wisdom', in spiritual wisdom, it may exist in us, and remain, and be treated with prudence, its genuine sense be investigated and applied to use, and be rendered familiar and closer to us, so that we may mutually edify one another by teaching, that is, by instructing from the same in the Christian faith, and by admonishing to perform the duties of piety. The public office of teaching belongs to Pastors, the familiar one to all.

In psalms, hymns, spiritual songs) How these differ, see Eph. 1, 19. Such recitations have the power of teaching and admonishing. Singing in grace in your hearts to the Lord) In grace, that is, graciously, amiably.

Thus 'in grace to those who hear' Eph. 4, 29. 'In the heart' or, as it is in the Manuscript, 'in the hearts', that is, not with the voice alone, but with the affection of the soul, as in the passage to the Ephesians. Although psalms, hymns, and odes have the power of teaching and admonishing, yet here it is treated particularly of them; for after he had admonished that the word of God should dwell in us or among us in all wisdom, by which we might be teaching and exhorting one another: Now he wishes that we should sing sweetly and from the heart with psalms and hymns and odes to the glory of God, for our own and others' edification.

For a psalm, as St. Basil says in the prologue to the Psalms, is the tranquility of souls, the arbiter of peace to be entered into, a charm- an amulet for driving away demons, an angelic guardian and conciliator, a shield of security amidst nocturnal fears, a rest from daily labors, a tutelary protection for infants, an ornament for those in the flower of their age, a comfort for the elderly, and finally, it is most suitable for adorning women. ἐν χάριτι (in grace) Theophylactus explains as with grace, and a certain spiritual joy of the soul.

He adds, or because they were to be sung by grace, having attained that gift. But the former explanation is more suitable here. ἐν ταῖς καρδίαις (in the hearts), he says, the same interpreter, it is not to be sung only with the mouth, but also with the hearts, that is, with attention and diligence.

For that is proper to singing to God. Otherwise, to pour out the voices of men merely into the air. He adds also in the hearts, that is, not for boasting and ostentation. For even if you are in the marketplace, you can sing to the Lord silently by yourself, with no one hearing.

Which in sense can well be comprehended under the former. For we are commanded to sing psalms to God from the heart with an expressed and sonorous voice, and then also with the mind alone, though the former is especially looked to in the present.

Concerning psalms, hymns, and odes, we have spoken in Eph. 5, 19. V. 17. καὶ πᾶν ὅ, τι ἂν ποιῆτε ἐν λόγῳ ἢ ἔργῳ, πάντα ἐν ὀνόματι Κυρίου Ἰησοῦ (and whatsoever you do in word or in work, all in the name of the Lord Jesus) Namely ποιῆτε (you do), which is understood from the preceding. ποίη מַעֲשֵׂיכֶם לְשֵׁם שָׁמַיִם (your works for the sake of heaven) is sometimes opposed to words, but here it is taken so loosely that it also comprehends words.

For even he who speaks, does something. It is a saying of the Hebrews: יְהִיוּ כָל מַעֲשֵׂיכֶם לְשֵׁם שָׁמַיִם (let all your works be for the sake of heaven). This can also be done then by the mind alone, as when we meditate on something in the mind, which ought to be done entirely in the name of Jesus, and then at the same time with the mouth, when sonorous prayers are added, in every work or word.

Which Theophylactus illustrates thus: If you take food (he says) or drink, if you travel anywhere, do all things in the name of God, that is, that He may be present, invoke Him, that He may bring help, that having first prayed to Him, you may immediately undertake whatever it is: For the name of God drives away demons, and makes all things succeed easily for you and according to your wish.

He adds that the Apostle particularly reminds them in this place, that leaving aside the Angels, whom they believed to be leaders to the Father, they should invoke Jesus.

Which is also the observation of Theodoret. Cornelius à Lapide does not admit that this is simply a precept, except that all works ought to be such as can result in the glory of Christ, so that Christ may be the end of life and of all actions.

But if individual works are to be referred to the glory of Christ by act or by virtue, that is only a counsel, not a precept: Since we can perform morally good acts without an actual or even virtual relation to Christ. But it is false that the Apostolic writings hand down only counsels, not precepts.

For He binds the Colossians to those things which He prescribes. Nor does He only want all things to be done in such a way that they can be referred to the glory of Christ: But He commands all things, whether in word or in work, to be done in the name of the Lord Jesus. For whatever is not of faith, is sin, Rom. 14, 23. Although, such is our imperfection, we do not do all things in the name of Jesus, or by invoking His name, or to the glory of His name, yet it is not for that reason not a precept.

For many things are commanded, which indeed are not always performed because of our imperfection. Even if we do not actually think of the glory of Christ in any business, it is nevertheless necessary that it be fixed and firm in our hearts as a habit, the purpose of relying on Christ and referring the actions of our whole life to His glory. εὐχαριστοῦντες τῷ Θεῷ καὶ Πατρὶ δι᾽ αὐτοῦ (giving thanks to God and the Father through Him) He explains what it is to do and say all things in the name of Christ, namely, to give thanks to God the Father for deeds and words through Christ. δι᾽ οὗ καὶ πατρὶ (through whom also to the Father), as above c. 1, 3. where you have an example of this thanksgiving, as also Rom. 1, 8. c. 7, 25. This is not an explanation of the former, but a peculiar exhortation; for He wants us both to begin all things with prayers, and to proceed, and He commands us to give thanks to God for all benefits.

God blesses all things which we undertake in the name of Jesus, therefore for His grace it is most necessary that we give thanks for the sake of gratitude. Thanks are to be given through Jesus Christ, not through Angels, as the Pseudo-Apostles wanted.

As Theophylactus says, the Son has brought us ourselves to the Father: so also the thanks which we ourselves give, He offers to the Father, since by His intercession all good things happen to us. He says, however, to God and the Father, because to our God, who is the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, thanks are to be given, in whom He pursues us with Fatherly favor, and because thus thanks are at the same time referred to the Son, through whom and by whom the blessing is both acquired for us and conferred.

PARS II.

CAPITIS III.

Delivering special precepts for various states.

Latin:

15. Καὶ ἡ εἰρήνη τοῦ Χριστοῦ βραβευέτω ἐν ταῖς καρδίαις ὑμῶν: Pax in cordibus vestris dijudicet, nempe si quid est inter vos controversum.

Pacis studium fit vice judicis: βραβεύειν proprie dicitur de judicibus ἀγώνων. Sed transfertur ad judices quosvis, ut apud Plutarchum aliquoties. Non abit à sensu Hesychius, cum dicit βραβεύειν, μεσιτεύειν, Vir bonus sibi judex est.

In Manuscripto: ἡ εἰρήνη τοῦ Χριστοῦ. Εἰς ἣν ἐκλήθητε) 1 Cor. 7, 15. Ἐν ἑνὶ σώματι) id est, εἰς ἓν σῶμα, ut unum essetis corpus, quod nisi per pacem fieri non potest, 1 Cor. 10, 16.

Hæc à Theophylacto, quem ipsum audire juvat: Nos quidem plerumque, contumeliis per aliquem unum affectos vario certamine mox subeunt cogitatus, quorum alii ad vindictam nos concitant, ad tolerantiam alii. Si Dei pax tunc nobis aderit, perinde ac acquiffimus judex aliquis & certaminis præses, victoriæ palmam his deferendam censebimus, qui istis suaserint æquo ut animo injurias toleremus, bis ipsis & concessere sunt postmodum, quæ antea adferebantur cogitationes & animi motus, & illatas injurias una tolerabunt. Pax itaque istiusmodi judicis in nobis fungatur officio, non iræ vel altercatio, vel humana pax aliqua, quæ obstando & vindicando perficitur, cum Dei & Christi firmior fit & insolubilis, quam nullum mortale bonum efficiat: Sicut & Dei nobiscum conciliatio ne alia nulla fuerit inita, nisi quia ille sola ejus clementia & charitate inimicitias solvit, quas olim in nos exercuerat.

Dicitur Dei pax, quia non ab hominibus datur, sed à Deo, omnis boni Autore. Non per homines conciliatur, sed per Deum, quum eam Deus sanguine suo acquisiverit. Non tamen est pax illa cum Deo, quæ pax Dei dicitur, Phil. 4, 7. sed pax inter homines, quia ad hanc pacem vocati sumus in unum corpus, quo de Theophylacto: Quod enim? quam aliam ob causam fums unum corpus, quam ut veluti membra alter alterius pacem servemus, & non diffideamus.

Quæ Dei etiam est, quod Deo placeat, & voluntati Divinæ conformis fit. Cui opponitur pax Satanæ & mundi. Καὶ εὐχάριστοι γίνεσθε) memores beneficiorum, quæ à Deo accepistis.

In glossario εὐχάριστος gratificatus, gratus. De gratitudine erga Deum etiam alii nonnulli intelligunt: Sed de ea deinceps sequitur v. 17. Hic in explicandis mutuis benevolentiæ & charitatis officiis occupatur Apostolus.

Ideo rectius Crocius de mutua gratitudine studium explicat. V. 16. Ὁ λόγος τοῦ Χριστοῦ ἐνοικείτω ἐν ὑμῖν πλουσίως) Evangelica doctrina nunquam ex animis vestris abeat.

Id enim est ἐνοικεῖν, ut 2 Tim. 1, 5.

Ebræis שכן πλουσίως, id est, abundanter, ut 1 Tim. 6, 17.

Tit. 3, 6.

2 Petr. 1, 11.

In Manuscripto ὁ λόγος τοῦ Θεοῦ. Medium per quod efficitur, ut cum Christo moriamur & vivamus, ut superna quæramus & suspiremus, membra, quæ in terris sunt, mortificemus, veterem hominem exuamus, novum induamus, & ornamentis illis spiritualibus ceu veste exornemur, et verbum Christi.

Antea baptismum ceu medium eorum introduxerat, cap. 2. Jam Verbum etiam Christi ad ea facere docet. Proxime de affectibus misericordiæ & charitatis, eoque pertinentibus dixerat, eosque affectibus pravæ iræ & indignationis opposuerat: Jam de linguæ usu monet ad informationem & exhortationem, necnon celebrationem Domini, quem opponit abusui linguæ & peccatis oris, illiusque cauta habitare vult in vobis Verbum Domini in omni sapientia.

Nimis aute tenuiter illud ἐνοικείτω explicat Grotius. Magis emphatin ejus evolvit Theophylactus: Neque n. simpliciter in vobis fit Dei Verbum, sed inhabitet dixit, & effluenter.

Nam si sacrarum literarum abundabimus cognitione, facile & ærumnas & calamitates, & quodvis malum genus tulerimus. Nec se cus quam vir quispiam opulentus jacturam aliquam tenuem pateretur, & nihili duceret.

Non ait παροικείτω, sed ἐνοικείτω. Peregrini solent commorari ad tempus; at ἐνοικεῖν constantem mansionem significat, non tamen absolute immobilem. Hoipes domo exceptus fit nobis familiaris, illius conspectu, colloquio, conversatione fruimur, & si commodus sit, commodam ei habitationem assignamus, præstamus officia, ægre à nobis dimittimus: Hæc omnia vim metaphoræ hujus applicari possunt.

Inhabitare a. debet in nobis Verbum Christi, non aliqua sui parte, sed totum, non parce, sed copiose, πλουσίως opulenter, ut id diligenter legamus & audiamus, de illo ubique loquamur, id semper meditemur, eo unice delectemur. Cæterum alloquitur Apostolus non clericos tantum, quos Papistæ vocant, sed etiam Laicos, nemine arcens à lectione scripturæ, quod Papa facit, sed omnes ad eandem exhortans. Unde Chrysostomus: Audite, quotquot estis mundani, & uxoribus præestis aliter, quomodo & vobis potissimum præcipiat scripturas legere, idq; non simpliciter, neg; obiter, sed magna diligentia.

Hoc illud est, inquit Chrysostomus homil. II. in Matth. quod omnia una quæque peste corrumpit, quod lectionem scripturarum putatis ad solos monachos pertinere.

Quod notent velim Papistæ. Ἐν πάσῃ σοφίᾳ) Et hic ut alibi valet σὺν, vera sapientia Evangelium comitatur 1 Cor. 1, 30. c.

2, 6. Eph. 1, 8. Διδάσκοντες ἐν νουθετοῦντες ἑαυτούς) Repetendum hic γίνεσθε, ut illud, ὁ λόγος τοῦ Χριστοῦ ἐνοικείτω ἐν ὑμῖν, sit quasi parenthesis, & rursum ἑαυτούς pro ἀλλήλους.

Est etiam privatorum aliquatenus & docere & monere. Cur non retineatur usitatus præpositionis ἐν sensus, ut modus insinuatur, quo verbum Dei in nobis habitare debeat, non in prudentia carnali, no ut eo abutamur ad jocum, ad errores vel hæresin, ad voluptates mundi, sed ut ἐν σοφίᾳ in sapientia spirituali in nobis fit, maneatque, tractetur cum prudentia, genuinus sensus ejusdem indagetur & ad usum applicetur, nobisque familiaris & propius reddatur, ut mutuo nos ædificemus docendo, ed est, instituendo ex eodem in fide Christiana, & commonefaciendo ad præstanda pietatis officia.

Publicum docendi munus est Pastorum, familiare omnium. Ψαλμοῖς ὕμνοις ᾠδαῖς πνευματικαῖς) Hæc quid differant, vide Eph. 1, 19. Recitationes tales vim habent docendi & monendi. Ἐν χάριτι ᾄδοντες ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ ὑμῶν τῷ Κυρίῳ) Ἐν χάριτι, id est, χαρίεντως amabiliter.

Sic iva ἐν χάριτι τοῖς ἀκούουσι Eph. 4, 29. Ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ aut, ut est in Manuscripto, ἐν ταῖς καρδίαις, id est, non sola voce, sed cum affectu animi, ut dicto ad Ephesios loca. Quanquam psalmi, hymni, & ode vim habeant docendi & monendi, hic tamen peculiariter de illis agitur; Postquam enim monuerat, ut verbum Dei habitet in nobis vel inter nos in omni sapientia, quo docentes & exhortantes invicem simus: Jam vult, ut psalmis & hymnis & odis suaviter & ex animo canamus ad Dei gloriam, nostri & aliorum ædificationem.

Est enim psalmus, dicente S. Basilio proœm. in Psalm. animarum tranquillitas, arbiter ineundæ pacis, amuletum profligandis daemonibus, Angelica tutela conciliator, scutum securitatis inter timores nocturnos, diurnorum requies laborum, infantium tutelaris protectio, consistentium in ætate flore decus, fenum solamen, denique mundus est mulieribus exornandis aptissimus. ἐν χάριτι Theophylactus exponit cum gratia, & spirituali quadam animi jucunditate.

Addit vel quia ex gratia erant decantandi id muneris assequuti. Sed prior explicatio hic magis convenit. ἐν ταῖς καρδίαις, non inquit, eodem interprete, solum ore est decantandum, sed & cordibus, hoc est, cum attentione & diligentia.

Id enim proprium est Deo canere. Alias vero hominum voces duntaxat in aerem fundere. Addit etiam in cordibus, id est, non ad jactantiam & ostentationem. Nam si vel in foro versaberis, poteris tecum ipse tacitus, audiente nemine, Domino decantare.

Qui sensu bene sub priori comprehendi potest. Nam jubemur animitus expressa & sonora voce, tum etiam sola mente psalmos Deo decantare, maxime tamen prius in præsenti respicitur.

De psalmis, hymnis & odis diximus Eph. 5, 19. V. 17. καὶ πᾶν ὅ, τι ἂν ποιῆτε ἐν λόγῳ ἢ ἔργῳ, πάντα ἐν ὀνόματι Κυρίου Ἰησοῦ Nempe ποιῆτε, quod ex præcedente subintelligitur. ποίη מַעֲשֵׂיכֶם לְשֵׁם שָׁמַיִם interdum opponitur dictis, hic vero ita laxe sumitur, ut & dicta comprehendat.

Nam & qui dicit, agit aliquid. Ebræorum dictum est: יְהִיוּ כָל מַעֲשֵׂיכֶם לְשֵׁם שָׁמַיִם Hoc etiam tum animo solum fieri potest, utpote cum meditamur aliquid mente, quod omnino in nomine Jesu fieri debet, tum simul ore, cum preces sonoræ accedunt, in omni opere vel verbo.

Quod ita illustrat Theophylactus: Si cibum (inquit) vel potum defumis, si peregre aliquo proficisceris, cuncta in Dei nomine facito, hoc est, ut adsit, illum invoca, ut opem ferat, ut prius illum precatus mox ego quodcunque aggredere: Nam Deinomen Damones abigit, facitque, ut facile tibi cuncta & ad votum succedant.

Addit, Apostolum id peculiariter hoc loco commonefacere, ut Angelis omissis, quos esse ad Patrem crederent Duces, Jesum invocent.

Quæ etiam est Theodoreti observatio. Cornelius à Lapide non admittit simpliciter hoc esse præceptum, nisi quod omnia opera talia esse debeant, quæ cedere possint in gloria Christi, ut Christus vitæ actionumque; omnium finis sit.

Si vero singula opera actu aut virtute ad Christi gloriam referenda, consilium id tantum esse, non præceptum: Siquidem actus moraliter bonos facere possumus fine actuali imo virtuali relatione ad Christum. Sed falsum est, Apostolicum consilia tantum tradere, non præcepta.

Obligat enim Colossenses ad ea, quæ præscribit. Neque tantum ita omnia fieri vult, ut possint ad gloriam Christi referri: Sed omnia, sive verbo, sive opere fieri jubet in nomine Domini Jesu. Quicquid n. non est ex fide, peccatum est, Rom. 14, 23. Quanquam vero, quæ nostra est imperfectio, non faciamus omnia in nomine Jesu, vel invocato ejus nomine, vel ad nominis ejus gloriam, non tamen ideo id præceptum non est.

Nam multa præcipiuntur, quæ vero semper ob imperfectionem nostram non præstantur. Etsi actu non cogitemus in negotio quovis de Christi gloria, est tamen necessarium, ut in habitu sit fixum firmumque; in cordibus nostris propositum innitendi Christo & vitæ nostræ totius actiones ad ejus gloriam referendi. εὐχαριστοῦντες τῷ Θεῷ καὶ Πατρὶ δι᾽ αὐτοῦ Explicat, quid fit in nomine Christi omnia facere ac loqui, nimirum de factis dictisque Deo Patri gratias agere per Christum. δι᾽ οὗ καὶ πατρὶ, ut supra c. 1, 3. ubi exemplum habes hujus gratiarum actionis, quemadmodum & Rom. 1, 8. c. 7. 25. Non hæc est ἐπεξήγησις priorum, sed peculiaris παραίνεσις; nam & omnia vult, cum precibus auspicemur, ac pergamus, & pro omnibus beneficiis gratias agere Deo jubet.

Deus benedicit omnibus, quæ in nomine Jesu suscipimus, Pro ejus ergo gratia æquissimo necessarium est, ut gratias agamus gratitudinis causa. Per Jesum Christum agendæ gratiæ, non per Angelos, ut Pseudo Apostoli volebant.

Quemadmodum inquit Theophylactus, nos ipsos filius ad Patrem traduxit: sic & quas ipsi agimus gratias, Patri is offert, quippe cujus intercessione bona nobis universa contingant. Dicit autem Deo & Patri, quod Deo nostro, qui est Pater Domini nostri Jesu Christi, gratiæ agendæ sint, in quo nos Paterno persequitur favore, quodque ita simul Filio referantur gratiæ, propter quem & per quem nobis benedictio & acquisita est, & confertur.

PARS II.

CAPITIS III.

Præcepta specialia pro diversis statibus tradens.

## 3:18
V. 18. Αἱ γυναῖκες ὑποτάσσεσθε τοῖς ἀνδράσι (Wives, be subject to your husbands) Namely ἰδίοις (your own), which is added in Eph. 5, 22. 24. Be subject, each of you, to your own man.

For it is the passive for the reciprocal. With a subjection not servile, but connubial, which embraces faith, love, honor, and obedience, such as becomes wives. But He preferred to name subjection, because they are generally not willingly subject, they love to live by their own will, or even to rule. δι᾽ ἀνῆκεν ἐν Κυρίῳ (as it is fitting in the Lord) is to be distinguished from ἀνῆκεν (it is fitting), so that ἐν Κυρίῳ (in the Lord) may be a restriction of that subjection, such as in Ephes. 6, 1. ὡς ἀνῆκεν (as it is fitting), as it is right. Τῦτο γάρ ἐσι δίκαιον (for this is just), in the same place to the Ephesians. In the Lord is not so much to be taken as a restriction, for that is already contained in the word ἀνῆκεν (it is fitting), as it is to be taken as a cause: That is, because of the Lord, as Chrysostom and Theophylactus interpret; which is evident from v. 20, 22. 23. In the Lord, however, that is, says Theophylactus, because of the Lord, subject yourselves.

For I would not have demanded that subjection merely as natural, for that is what it pretends, when he says as it is fitting, but especially by the grace of God, that you may rightly show yourselves more obedient. V. 19. οἱ ἄνδρες ἀγαπᾶτε τὰς γυναῖκας (Husbands, love your wives) Eph. 5, 25. Καὶ μὴ πικραίνεσθε πρὸς αὐτάς (And be not bitter toward them) Here the active is for the reciprocal, after the manner of the Hebrew מָרַר, which signifies to behave bitterly.

And it is sometimes translated by πικραίνεσθε (be bitter) or πικραίνεσθαι (to be bitter), sometimes by παροργίζειν (to provoke to anger), which we have in Eph. 6, 4. Nor by blows, nor by curses is a wife to be exasperated, the Hebrews teach in Musar.

See how He consults what is fitting for each of these.

For women, subjection; for men, benevolence toward their wives. For the love of subjects toward Princes is not so much required as the charity of Princes toward subjects is demanded. For when a woman is loved, she also returns a reciprocal vicissitude of love, she softens to obey her husband, and shows herself kind.

And because it generally happens that he who is affected by love is exasperated, since it is known that wars and dissensions arise more bitterly even among those joined by the highest charity, therefore He says: Do not be bitter.

For it happens with a certain great bitterness of soul, that one should be at variance with his own member, as Theophylactus has it here. Rigor, says Ambrose, softens the manly law, lest he prevail by power, less that which is in the dominion of the wife, but to look back at the affection, because the woman is his flesh, lest by humiliating her more he exasperate her, and force contrary things.

Latin:

V. 18. Αἱ γυναῖκες ὑποτάσσεσθε τοῖς ἀνδράσι Nempe ἰδίοις, quod additur Eph. 5, 22. 24. Suo-quæque viro vos subjicite.

Est enim passivum pro reciproco. Subjectione non servili, sed connubiali, quæ fidem, amorem, honorem, obsequium, quale decet uxores, complectitur. Maluit autem subjectio-nem nominare, quia fere non libenter subjiciuntur, amant suo arbitrio vivere, aut etiam imperare. δι᾽ ἀνῆκεν ἐν Κυρίῳ distinguendum de ἀνῆκεν, ut ἐν Κυρίῳ sit restrictio illius ὑποτάσσεως, qualis Ephes. 6, 1. ὡς ἀνῆκεν, ut æquum est. Τῦτο γάρ ἐσι δίκαιον, ibidem ad Ephelios. In Domino non tam ut restrictio accipienda, ea enim jam in voce ἀνῆκεν habetur, quam ut causa: Id est propter Dominum, ut Chrysostomus & Theophylactus interpretantur; quod è v. 20, 22. 23. patet. In Domino autem, hoc est, inquit Theophylactus, propter Dominum vos ipsas subjicite.

Non enim naturalem modo subjectionem illam exegerim, Id namque prætendit, cum ut oportet inquit, sed Dei maxime gratia, ut vos jure obsequentiores præstetis. V. 19. οἱ ἄνδρες ἀγαπᾶτε τὰς γυναῖκας Eph. 5, 25. Καὶ μὴ πικραίνεσθε πρὸς αὐτάς Hic adtivum pro reciproco, ad instar Ebræi מָרַר, quod significat amare se gerere.

Et modo vertitur per πικραίνεσθε aut πικραίνεσθαι, modo per παροργίζειν, quod habemus Eph. 6, 4. Neque verberibus, neque maledictis exasperandam uxorem docent Ebræi in Musar.

Vide quemadmodum, quæ horum cuique competunt, consulat.

Fæminis quidem subjectionem, viru in uxores benevolentiam. Neque enim subditorum adeo requiritur in Principes amor, ut Principum in subditos charitas poscitur. Mulier namque cum adamatur, & ipsa reciprocam refert amoris vicissitudinem, obsequi vir mansuescit, & benignum se præbet.

Et quia plerumque evenit, ut exasperetur, qui fit vel amore affectus, cum constet vel inter summa charitate conjunctos bella & dissidia oboriri acerbius, propterea inquit: Nolite amari esse.

Fit enim cum ingenti quadam animi amaritudine, ut cum suo membro quisquam dissideat, ut hic habet Theophylactus. Rigorem, inquit Ambrosius, virilis legis emollit, ne potestate prævaleat, minus quæ sii in dominatu uxoris, sed debitre-picere affectum, quia mulier caro ejus est, ne plus illam humilians exacerbet, & contraria cogiset.

## 3:20
V. 20. Τὰ τέκνα ὑπακούετε τοῖς γονεῦσι κατὰ πάντα (Children, obey your parents in all things) This generality also is to be restricted, with that understood which is expressed to the Ephesians, ἐν Κυρίῳ (in the Lord).

So also below κατὰ πάντα (in all things), v. 22. and ἐν παντὶ (in everything) Eph. 5, 29. Τῦτο γάρ ἐσι εὐάρεστον ἐν Κυρίῳ (For this is well-pleasing in the Lord), better other codices in the Lord, as Eph. 5, 10. ישר לפני אלהים (upright before God). Nothing else can please God, says Ambrose, except what is just and pious. Then children can have God propitious, if they pay the due honor to their parents.

But He said obedience, not honor, because obedience is most desired by many, who show honor, but obey with difficulty, as if honor could consist without obedience. In all things, namely both in goods that are good in themselves, and in those that are indifferent, however heavy and troublesome they may be.

For parents do not have the power to command evil things, nor is obedience owed to them in such matters.

For of pious parents, addressing the children, as Theophylact warns, he said "in all things." Bellarmine, lib. II. de Monach. cap. 21, restricts this to children while they are small. But the Apostle makes no distinction between small children and adults, and Scripture commands all children whatsoever to show honor to their parents, by virtue of the fourth commandment, which obligates everyone.

Basil the Great, without distinction of those who have reached puberty and those who have not, teaches that children are not to be received into monasteries unless they are offered by their parents, which he explains at length in question 15, and the Council of Gangra defines it thus in c. 16: Whoever children depart from their parents under the pretext of divine worship, and do not render due reverence to them, let them be anathema.

Latin:

V. 20. Τὰ τέκνα ὑπακούετε τοῖς γονεῦσι κατὰ πάντα Hæc quoque generalitas restringenda, subaudito illo quod ad Ephelios exprimitur, ἐν Κυρίῳ.

Sic & infra κατὰ πάντα, v. 22. & ἐν παντὶ Eph. 5, 29. Τῦτο γάρ ἐσι εὐάρεστον ἐν Κυρίῳ , Melius alii codices Κυρίῳ, quoniodo Eph. 5, 10. ישר לפני אלהים Non potest aliud placere Deo, inquit Ambrosius, nisi quod justum & pium est. Tunc possunt filii Deum habere propitium, si debitam honorificentiam rependant parentibus.

Obedientiam autem dixit, non honorem, quia maxime obedietia desideratur à multis, qui honorem exhibent, at ægrè obediunt, quasi honor constet sine obedientia. In omnibus scilicet tum per se bonis, tum mediis, quamvis gravibus & molestis.

Mala enim imperandi potestatem non habent parentes, nec in illis debetur ipsis obedientia.

Piorum enim parentum liberis verba faciens, monente Theophylacto, dixit per omnia. Bellarminus lib. II. de Monach. cap. 21. restringit ad liberos, dum parvuli sunt. Sed nullam distinctionem facit Apostolus inter liberos parvulos, & adultos, & quosvis omnino liberos jubet scriptura honorem parentibus exhibere, vi quarti praecepti, quod omnes obligat.

Basilius m. citra distinctionem puberum & impuberum docet liberos non esse in monasteria recipiendos, nisi à suis parentibus offerantur, in quaestion. fuse explicat. q. 15. & concilium Gangrense ita definit c. 16. Quicunque filii à parentibus praetextu Divini cultus abscedunt, nec debitam reverentiam illis dependunt, anathema sit.

## 3:21
V. 21. Theophylact and Crotius understand corrupt concupiscence in general, but because special sins are recounted here, Grotius has a more correct explanation here.

Namely, the Apostle recalled the members, both external, to the affections and acts of the concupiscible faculty, which he then recounts specifically as fornication, uncleanness, passion, and then generally embraces under the word of evil desire. Καὶ τὴν πλεονεξίαν)

After the genus he named the species, the excessive desire of having. Ἥτις ἐστὶ ἡ εἰδωλολατρεία) See Eph. V. 5. and what is said there. Beautifully here Chrysostom: Therefore he also μετέβρασε, as if introducing some strong man, and leading to a greater emphasis. And he rightly said: Which are upon the earth: Here indeed they remain, and here much more are they corrupted and perish than those members. sin is earthly. For the body is sometimes indeed seen as beautiful, but the former never, and all things which are above the earth, these members covet.

If the eye be such, it does not see what is in the heavens, if the ear, if the hand, if you name any member. The eye sees bodies and beauties and these figures, which are from the earth. It is delighted by these. The ear by soft ways, the cithara, and the pipe, and by base speech. But these things are about the earth. After, therefore, he has placed them above near the throne, then he says, mortify your members upon the earth.

For it is not there, in which it behooves them to work: and this clay is worse than that. For that clay indeed becomes gold. For it behooves, he says, this corruptible to put on incorruption. But this clay cannot again be melted and fused. Wherefore these are more upon the earth than those. Therefore he did not say, which are from the earth, but which are upon the earth: For it is possible that these are not from the earth.

For this indeed it is necessary to be upon the earth. But that is by no means necessary. For the ear indeed when it hears nothing from those things which are spoken here, but from those which are in heaven, it is not upon the earth: When the eye sees nothing from those things which are here, but what is above, it is not upon the earth. When the mouth speaks nothing from those things which are here, it is not upon the earth. When the hand has done nothing from those things which are evil, it is not from those things which are upon the earth, but from those which are in the heavens. Christ also says this: If thy right eye scandalize thee, this is, if thou lookest immodestly, pluck it out, this is, the evil thought.

Ambrose says this is added, so that it may demonstrate that avarice is nothing more wicked, and that it is called idolatry, because it serves gold and silver as its God, and places its trust in it, just as the idolater in a golden and silver idol, conf. Matth. VI. 22. The firstborn, says Theophylactus, is evil concupiscence, the son of the desire of having, which he called avarice, which worships gold and silver, since it covets only these.

Latin:

V. 21. Concupiscentiam pravam in genere intelligit Theophylactus & Crocius, sed quia hic recensentur specialia peccata, rectius hic habet Grotius explicatio.

Nimirum revocavit Apostolus membra tertum externos, ad affectus & actus τῆς ἐπιθυμικῆς, quas tum speciatim recenset πορνείαν, ἀκαθαρσίαν, πάθος, tum generatim complectitur voce ἐπιθυμίας κακῆς. Καὶ τὴν πλεονεξίαν)

Post genus nominavit speciem, nimiam habendi cupiditatem. Ἥτις ἐστὶ ἡ εἰδωλολατρεία) Vid. Eph. V. 5. & ibi dicta. Pulchre hic Chrysostomus: Propterea etiam μετέβραvoc, tanquam aliquem virum fortem introducens, & ad majore deducens emphasim. Et recte dixit: Quae sunt super terram: Hic n. manent, & hic multo magis corrumpuntur & intereunt qua bac membra. peccatum est terrestre. Nam corpus aliquando quidem pulchrum cernitur, illa autem nunquam, & omnia, quae sunt supra terram, concupiscunt haec membra.

Si talis sit oculus, non videt, quae sunt in caelis, si auris, si manus, si quouis membrum dixeris. Oculus videt corpora & pulchritudines & figuras has, quae sunt ex terra. His delectatur. Auris mollimodo, cithara, & fistula, & turpi sermone. Hac autem sunt circa terram. Postquam ergo superius eos collocarit juxta thronum, tunc dicit, mortificate membra vestra super terram.

Non enim illic, in quo ea operari oportet: & hoc lutum est ille pejus. Nam illud quidem lutum fit aurum. Nam oportet, inquit, corruptibile hoc induere incorruptionem. Hoc autem lutum non potest rursus fundi & conflari. Quamobrem haec magis sunt supra terram, quam illa. Propterea non dixit, quae sunt è terra, sed quae supra terram: Fieri enim potest, ut haec non sint è terra.

Nam hac quidem necesse est, esse supra terram. Illa autem nequaquam est necesse. Nam auris quidem quum ex iis, qua hic dicuntur, nihil audit, sed ex iis, quae sunt in caelia, non est super terram: Quando oculus nihil videt ex iis, quae sunt hic, sed quae supra, non est super terram. Quando os nihil loquitur ex iis, quae hic sunt, non est super terram. Quando manus nihil fecerit ex iis, quae mala sunt, non est ex iis, quae sunt supra terram, sed ex iis, quae sunt in caelis. Hoc etiam dicit Christus: Si oculus tuus dexter te scandalizet, hoc est, si aspiciis impudice, exscinde eum, hoc est, malam cogitationem.

Addi hoc ait Ambrosius, ut auaritia nihil scelestius esse demonstret, idololatriam autem vocari, quia servit auro & argento tanquam Deo suo, & in illo fiduciam suam collocat, sicut idololatra in idolo aureo & argenteo, conf. Matth. VI. 22. Primogenitus, inquit Theophylactus, prava concupiscentia filius habendi cupiditas est, quam auaritian nuncupavit, quae aurum argentumque colat, cum sola haec concupiscit.

## 3:21
V. 21. Οἱ πατέρες μὴ ἐρεθίζετε τὰ τέκνα ὑμῶν) This is ἐρεθίζετε, which is παροργίζετε in Ephesians, which very word the Manuscript also has here. It is translated ἐρεθίζεν, Prov. 19, 8. see also 2 Cor. 9, 2. Ἵνα μὴ ἀθυμῶσι) That they may not lose heart. It is translated ἀθυμῶσι, 1 Kings 5, 8. 1 Chron. 13, 11. He inculcates this especially to fathers, because mothers are wont to be more indulgent.

Fathers, however, are sometimes too severe, as being more irascible, who, if children commit a fault, carried away by that emotion, do not keep a just measure in punishment. He therefore commands that prudence and moderation be applied. Let education indeed not be lax, but where there is need, severe, lest children become worse through the indulgence of their parents. Meanwhile, let that severity be tempered by paternal gentleness of affection, which so tempers punishment and correction that it may be liberal and fruitful, not too harsh or tyrannical. For fathers, as Ambrose teaches, ought to remember that they themselves were once children, and children should consider that they themselves will be fathers, so that by the balanced counsel of both parties, both children may be submissive and fathers modest.

Whence he uses the name of Father, which alone can bend minds toward clemency, kindness, and gentleness. Note, as Theophylact warns, how prudently he has here broken the anger of parents toward their children. For he has moved their bowels when he said: That they may not become small-minded, that is, that they may not despair.

For parents strive especially that children may not lose heart. Vers. 22. Οἱ δοῦλοι ὑπακούετε κατὰ πάντα τοῖς κατὰ σάρκα Κυρίοις) Eph. 6, 3. Μὴ ἐν ὀφθαλμοδουλείαις ὡς ἀνθρωπάρεσκοι) μὴ κατ᾽ ὀφθαλμοδουλείαν, Eph. 6, 6. Ἀλλ᾽ ἐν ἁπλότητι καρδίας) And this is in the said place in Ephesians. Φοβούμενοι τὸν Θεὸν) ποιοῦντες τὸ θέλημα τὸ Θεῦ in Ephesians. God willed that there be various stations of men, and that each live content with his own.

In the Manuscript: φοβούμενοι τὸν Κύριον. Vers. 23. Καὶ πᾶν ὅ, τι ἂν ποιῆτε) in your ministry. Ἐκ ψυχῆς ἐργάζετε) with an equal mind, without murmuring. Ὡς τῷ Κυρίῳ, κὴ ἐκ ἀνθρώποις) namely, doing this, namely, Christ is served, when his laws are obeyed, one of which is this, that faith and obedience be shown to those set over us by human law. See the said place in Eph.

Latin:

V. 21. Οἱ πατέρες μὴ ἐρεθίζετε τὰ τέκνα ὑμῶν) Hic est ἐρεθίζετε quod παροργίζετε ad Ephesios, quam ipsam vocem & hic habet Manuscriptus. vertitur ἐρεθίζεν, Prov. 19, 8. vide & 2. Cor. 9, 2. Ἵνα μὴ ἀθυμῶσι) Ne animo concidant. vertitur ἀθυμῶσι, 1. Reg. 5, 8. 1. Paral. 13, 11. Inculcat hoc praecipue patribus, quia matres indulgentiores esse solent.

Patres autem quandoque nimium severi, utpote magis iracundi, qui, si delinquant liberi, affectu illo abrepti, justum in castigatione modum non servant. Jubet ergo prudentiam & moderationem adhiberi. Sit quidem educatio non laxa, sed ubi opus est, severa, ne parentum indulgentia deteriores evadant liberi. Interim illa severitas tincta sit paterna mansuetudine affectu, cui castigationem & correptionem ita temperet, ut liberalis sit & fructuosa, non aspera nimis aut tyrannica. Debent enim, docente Ambrosio, recordari patres, quia fuerunt & ipsi filii, considerare autem filii, quia & ipsi futuri sunt patres, ut aequo librato consilio utriusque partis & filii subjecti sint, & patres modesti.

Unde Patris nomen adhibet, quod vel solum ad clementiam, benignitatem, mansuetudinem animos potest flectere. Adverte, monente Theophylacto, quam prudenter parentum in liberos iram hic fregerit. Flexit namque illorum viscera, cum dixit: Ne animo fiant pusillo, hoc est, ne desperent.

Nituntur enim praecipue genitores, ne animo concidant liberi. Vers. 22. Οἱ δοῦλοι ὑπακούετε κατὰ πάντα τοῖς κατὰ σάρκα Κυρίοις) Eph. 6, 3. Μὴ ἐν ὀφθαλμοδουλείαις ὡς ἀνθρωπάρεσκοι) μὴ κατ᾽ ὀφθαλμοδουλείαν, Eph. 6, 6. Ἀλλ᾽ ἐν ἁπλότητι καρδίας) Et hoc est dicto loco ad Ephesios. Φοβούμενοι τὸν Θεὸν) ποιοῦντες τὸ θέλημα τὸ Θεῦ ad Ephesios. Deus varias esse voluit hominum fortes, & quemque sua contentum vivere.

In Manuscripto: φοβούμενοι τὸν Κύριον. Vers. 23. Καὶ πᾶν ὅ, τι ἂν ποιῆτε) in ministerio vestro. Ἐκ ψυχῆς ἐργάζετε) aequo animo, ἄνευ μιμψιμοιρίας. Ὡς τῷ Κυρίῳ, κὴ ἐκ ἀνθρώποις) nempe ποιῦντες τοῦτο, nempe Christo servitur, cum ipsius paretur legibus, quarum haec una est, ut supra nos jure humano constitutis exhibeatur fides & obedientia. Vide dictum locum Eph.

## 3:24
6, 6. 7. Εἰδότες ὅτι ἀπὸ Κυρίου ἀπολήψεσθε τὴν ἀνταπόδοσιν τῆς κληρονομίας) This genitive is explanatory. For the reward is the heavenly inheritance, that is, the perpetual possession, Eph. 1, 1. 4. 8. Heb. 4, 15. 1 Pet. 1, 4. Reward.

He instructs the servants more lengthily than the others, lest the name of the Lord be blasphemed through the perversity and disobedience of servants, 1 Tim. 6, 1, since there were not lacking those who, abusing Christian liberty, [claimed] that no one of the faithful ought to serve, a heresy which had already arisen among the Jews, as Estius notes here. For the Gospel does not abolish the state, therefore they are commanded to serve masters according to the flesh indiscriminately, whether they be Christians or not, and that faithfully, and it is promised to them by the Lord, whom they serve, when they perform due service to their masters, a reward, not out of merit, as the Papists, Estius, Cornelius à Lapide, and others prattle; but out of grace.

For what proportion is there between services rendered to masters, and that inestimable and eternal reward in the heavens? And therefore this reward is not owed, but unowed, not obtained by merit, but purely gratuitous, Rom. 6. v. last. c. 8, 16. what kind of reward, which are said to be at once a gift of God, children, Ps. 127, 4. Cf. Ps. 103, 2. Ps. 116, 12. Which the word inheritance also indicates; that we are to obtain the inheritance, not by merit, as mercenaries, but by the right of adoption, as sons.

For to sons the inheritance is not conferred by the merit of obedience, but by the right of sonship; Cf. Rom. 8, 17. Gal. 4, 7. Τῷ γὰρ Κυρίῳ δουλεύετε) In the Manuscript: τῷ Κυρίῳ. It is corrected to Christ.

You are servants of Christ , look to Him as the Lord of all, Eph. 6, 6. The Vulgate has: Serve the Lord Christ. That does not fit, since in the Greek it is τῷ γὰρ Κυρίῳ δουλεύετε, for you serve the Lord Christ.

The reason is therefore given why they ought not to doubt about the reward to be received from the Lord, if indeed they serve Him, who, as Theophylact has it, disposed the order of things and servitude. Estius admits that the Greek and Syriac text, as well as the Ambrosian, agree with this explanation; and that the Greek reading presents a clearer sense. Ὁ δὲ ἀδικῶν κομιεῖται, ὃ ἠδίκησε) he who does wrong, that is, the servant, unfaithful to his master, or the master harsh toward his servant.

And it is a metonymy, what he did wrong, that is, the punishment of his injustice. A similar expression 2 Cor. 5, 10. Eph. 6, 8: Peter explains the same more fully. Καὶ οὐκ ἔστι προσωποληψία) namely, with Christ, Eph. 6, 9. He will no more spare unjust masters than unjust servants.

Thus he anticipates the wicked presumptions of masters. Who will plead the cause of our servants? Who will summon us to justice? Thus he meets perfidious servants, who dream that their frauds are not perceived by their masters, nor will be avenged by God upon them, as being miserable persons. For with God there is no respect of persons, who will repay as well the injuries of masters as the perfidy of servants, both here and in the future age.

Some Christian, says Theophylact, who is subject to servitude, if he has done an injury to a Gentile master, under whose dominion he is, let him by no means think that he will escape judgment and condemnation. For Christ has no respect of persons, so that He would spare him who has been a wrongdoer to Him, because he has offended against a Gentile master. Which is also to be understood of masters, he warns.

Latin:

6, 6. 7. Εἰδότες ὅτι ἀπὸ Κυρίου ἀπολήψεσθε τὴν ἀνταπόδοσιν τῆς κληρονομίας) Hic Genitivus est ἐξηγητικός. Nam merces est coelestis haereditas, id est, perpetua possessio, Eph. 1, 1. 4. 8. Ebr. 4, 15. 1. Petr. 1, 4. Ἀνταπόδοσιν .

Prolixius instituit servos, quam caeteros, ne nomen Domini blasphemetur per proterviam & inobedientiam servorum, 1. Tim. 6, 1. quum non defuerint, qui male utentes libertatem Christianam, neminem fidelium servire debere, qualis haeresis jam ante apud Judaeos orta fuerat, notante hic Estio. Evangelium enim non abolet politiam, ideo Dominis secundum carnem promiscue, sive Christiani sint, sive non sint, servire jubentur, idque fideliter, ac promittitur ipsis à Domino, cui serviunt, cum heris suis debita praestant fervitia, ἀνταπόδοσιν, non ex merito, ut nugantur Papistae, Estius, Cornelius à Lapide, alii; sed ex gratia.

Quae enim proportio inter servitia heris praestita, & inter mercedem illam inaestimabilem & aeternam in coelis? Ideoque non est merces haec debita, sed indebita, non ex merito obtingens, sed mere gratuita, Rom. 6. v. ult. c. 8, 16. qualis merces, quae donum simul Dei dicuntur, liberi, Psal. 127, 4. Conf. Psal. 103, 2. Psal. 116, 12. Quod etiam vox κληρονομίας indicat; nos haereditatem consecuturos esse, non ex merito, veluti mercenarios, sed jure adoptionis, tanquam filios.

Nam filiis haereditas non confertur ex obedientiae merito, sed jure filiationis; Conf. Rom. 8, 17. Galat. 4, 7. Τῷ γὰρ Κυρίῳ δουλεύετε) In Manuscripto: τῷ Κυρίῳ Corrigitur Χριστῷ.

Christi eltis servi, illum respicite omnium Dominum, Eph. 6, 6. Vulgatus habet: Domino Christo servite. Non id convenit, quum in Graeco fit τῷ γὰρ Κυρίῳ δουλεύετε, nam Domino Christo servitu.

Ratio ergo redditur, cur non dubitare debeant de ἀνταποδοσέᾳ Domino recipienda, siquidem ipsi serviant, quifcilicet rerum seriem & servitutem disposuit, ut habet Theophylactus. Huic explicationi Graecum & Syriacum textum, ut & Ambrosianum annuere fatetur Estius; Grecamque lectionem sensum exhibere planiorem. Ὁ δὲ ἀδικῶν κομιεῖται, ὃ ἠδίκησε) ὁ ἀδικῶν, id est, servus, infidelis Domino, aut Dominus in servum durus.

Et est μετωνυμία, ὃ ἠδίκησε, id est, poenam injustitiae suae. Par locutio 2. Cor. 5, 10. Eph. 6, 8: Petrus idem explicatius. Καὶ οὐκ ἔστι προσωποληψία) nempe apud Christum, Eph. 6, 9. Non magis Dominis iniquis quam servis iniquis parcet.

Sic pravas herorum praesumptiones praeoccupat. Quis fervorum nostrorum causam aget? Quis in jus nos vocabit? Sic servis perfidis occurrit, qui fraudes suas ab heris non perspici, nec à Deo in se, utpote personis miseris vindicatum iri somniant. Apud Deum enim non est personarum respectus, qui tam injurias herorum, quam perfidiam servorum rependet tum hic, tum in futuro seculo.

Christianus aliquis, inquit Theophylactus, qui fit servituti obnoxius, si gentili Domino, cujus sub ditione fit, injuriam fecerit, nequaquam existimet judicium & damnationem se evasurum. Neque enim ullus habet persona respectum Christus, ut ei qui fui scelator fit parcat, quod in gentilem herum deliquerit. Quod etiam de heris intelligendum monet.

## 4:1 Argument
CHAPTER IV. ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

After the instruction of masters, he exhorts to prayers, also for himself, and to Christian prudence, explains the reasons for sending Tychicus and Onesimus, in the name of certain colleagues and Epaphras, whom he commends for his faith toward them, and greets others, and having greeted some, he commands the epistle to be read among the Laodiceans, and also that Archippus be reminded to perform his duty rightly, he adds a greeting with his own hand, and warns that they be mindful of his bonds, concluding the epistle with a vow.

There are two parts: The former, parænetica (exhortatory), up to v. 6. The latter, epilogica (concluding), up to v. 18 and the end. PART I. PARÆNETICA.

Verf. 1. Masters, give unto your servants that which is just and equal (Ὁ Κύριοι τὸ δίκαιον καὶ τὴν ἰσότητα τοῖς δούλοις παρέχετε). These cohere with the preceding, nor should they have been severed. There is, indeed, even among unequals, such as between Master and servant, some right. But among the Hebrews, קָשָׁה [sic] and among the Hellenists, diakonian often signifies kindness. Isotēta (equality) here is truly that which to the Hebrews is קָשָׁה [sic], that which is fitting for each. Concerning this meaning, we have spoken at Mark c. 14, 56; that is, exact labor moderately, provide food and clothing, and in the seventh year, if they wish, manumit them. See the law in Deut. 15, 12 and following, and our [work] III. De jure belli ac pacis XIV. Others refer to dikaion (that which is just) not to kindness, but to justice, so that nothing inequitable is established regarding servants, as masters, because they almost always possessed servants as chattels by right of purchase, were not rarely accustomed to do. They understand tēn isotēta (equality) as the epieikeia (forbearance) to be employed toward servants in the imposing of punishments, by which they show themselves to be not heathens, but Christian masters. Crocius interprets the former as the rendering of due wages; the latter as the gentleness to be shown to servants. Chrysostom and Theophylact explain both as the retribution for labors. For you also have a Master in heaven (Ὅτι καὶ ὑμεῖς ἔχετε Κύριον ἐν οὐρανοῖς). Eph. 6, 9. In the Law of Moses, this reason is rendered because God redeemed them no less than you from Egypt; Deut. 10, 15. 42. 55. In the New Covenant, because Christ, who looks down upon all things from heaven, has redeemed you all. Concerning this, Theophylact says: Just as you have them as masters on earth, so also you have God, whose command must be obeyed. Whence it comes to pass that with the same measure with which you have measured to your servants, it shall be measured back to you by the Lord. The lordship of masters, therefore, is not absolute, but limited, because they themselves also have a Master in heaven, to whom they are bound to render an account, with whom there is no respect of persons.

Latin:

CAPUT IV. ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

Post informationem herorum, ad preces, etiam pro sese, & prudentiam Christianam hortatur, causas missi Tychici & Onesimi exponit, nomine quorundam collegarum & Epaprae, quem à fide erga ipsos commendat, aliorumque salutat, ac salutatis nonnullis epistolam apud Laodicenses prelegi, nec non Archippum de munere rite obeundo commonefieri jubet, manu sua salutationem addit, & vinculorum suorum memores sint, monet, voto concludens epistolam.

Partes duæ sunt: Prior παρανετικὴ ad v. 6. Poberior ἐπιλογικὴ ad v. 18. & ultimum. PARSI. PARÆNETICA., Verf.

1. Ὁ Κύριοι τὸ δίκαιον καὶ τὴν ἰσότητα τοῖς δούλοις παρέ-χετε) Hæc cohærent cum fuperioribus, neque scindenda fuere. Est quidem etiam inter inæquales, ut inter Dominum & fervum, jus aliquod. Sed Ebræis קָשָׁה & Hellenistis διακονίαν sæpe bonitatem fignificat. ἰσότητα vero hic est id quod Ebræis קָשָׁה quod cuique convenit. De quo significatu diximus ad Marcum c. 14, 56. hoc est, exigite operas moderate, victum & vestitum suppeditate, feptimo anno, fi velint, eos manumittite. Vide legem Deut. 15, 12, & fequentibus, & nostra III. de jure belli ac pacis XIV. Τὸ δίκαιον non ad bonitatem, sed ad justitiam referunt alii, ut nihil in fervis iniqui statuatur, ut heri, quia fervos fere ceu mancipia jure emptionis possidebant, haud raro folebant. τὴν ἰσότητα vero de ἐπιεικείᾳ in fervis adhibenda in pœnis irrogandis intelligunt, qua ostendunt, fe esse non Ethnicos sed Christianos heros. Illam de reddenda debitæ mercede interpretatur Crocius: Hanc de manfuetudine fervis exhibenda. Utramque Chryfostomus & Theophylactus de retributione laborum explicant. Ὅτι καὶ ὑμεῖς ἔχετε Κύριον ἐν οὐρανοῖς) Eph. 6, 9. In lege Motis ratio hæc redditur, quia Deus illos non minus quam vos ex Ægypto redemit; Deut. 10, 15. 42. 55. In novo fœdere, quia redemit vos omnes Christus, qui ex cœlo omnia despectat. De hoc ita Theophylactus: Quemadmodum vos illi in terris in dominos habent: Ita & vos Deum habetis, cujus est imperio obsequendum. Quo fit, ut eadem menfura, qua fueritis fervis emensi, à Domino fit vobis remetiendum. Herorum igitur dominium non est abfolutum, sed limitatum, quia & ipsi habent Dominum in cœlis, cui rationem reddere tenentur, apud quem non est perfonarum respectus.

## 4:2
Verf. 2. Continue in prayer (Τῇ προσευχῇ προσκαρτερεῖτε).

Rom. 12, 12. Watching in the same (Γρηγοροῦντες ἐν αὐτῇ). So that you may be attentive in prayers. Thus the Hebrews use קָשָׁה [sic]. He does not say "all," but "persevere in prayers," because one must insist upon prayers incessantly, 1 Thess. 5, 16. Nor only that, but he also commands to watch in them, both so that we may, by prayers, heed the snares of spiritual enemies diligently circling about, and so that we may pour forth prayers with an ever-vigilant attention, 1 Pet. 5, 8. Some think this refers to public, fixed, and solemn night vigils; others to private prayers, when sleepless nights are passed. But we ought to watch in prayers no less by day than by night. The Devil, as Theophylact says, certainly knows how much good prayers have in themselves, and therefore suggests desisting from them, of which thing Paul, not being ignorant, says, "insist upon prayer."

And since he who has shown perseverance in praying often dissolves into negligence and grows languid, he said "watching," that is, being awake and aroused, always offer yourselves to this work of adoration. With thanksgiving (Ἐν εὐχαρισίᾳ), that is, together with the giving of thanks. For the grateful memory of time past must be joined with the petition for the future, for oun (therefore), as above c. 4, 4. 16. and 2 Tim. 1, 13. and elsewhere. Theophylact says excellently: But in thanksgiving, that is, pray to God by giving thanks.

For true indeed are those prayers which are followed by grace, said to God for all things, of which we are either conscious or unconscious. And for the benefits received by us or even for the evils endured, and finally for the good things bestowed upon the whole race of men. Praying at the same time also for us, that God may open to us a door for the word) that is, an occasion, as 1 Cor. 16, 9. 1 Cor. 2, 12. Great is the honor of those whose prayers Paul wishes to be helped by, Rom. 15, 30. Philem. 22. To speak the mystery of Christ) In the Manuscript: with what boldness I shall speak, as in Eph. 6, 19. He calls it a mystery with respect to former times. See above c. 2, 2.

Latin:

Verf. 2. Τῇ προσευχῇ προσκαρτερεῖτε)

Rom. 12, 12. Γρηγοροῦντες ἐν αὐτῇ) Ita ut attenti fitis in precibus. Ita קָשָׁה ufurpant Ebræi. Non ait omne, sed in precibus perfevemte, quia instandum est precibus indefinenter, 1. Theff. 5, 16. Nec id tantum, sed vigilare etiam in iisdem jubet, tum ut hostes spirituales fedulo circumficientes eorum infidias precibus advertamus, tum ut semper vigilanti attentione preces fundamus, 1. Petr. 5, 8. Ad publicas statas & folemnes noctis vigilias respici nonnulli cenfent, alii ad privatas preces, cum noctes infomnes traducuntur. Sed non minus vigilare in precibus debemus interdiu, quam noctu. Callet utiq, dicente Theophylacto, Damon, quantum in fe boni habeant orationes, eog, & ab iis desistere fuggerit, cujus rei Paulus non ignarus, orationi, inquit, instate. Cumque & qui perfeverantiam orando prastiterit, in negligentiam sæpe refolvitur & languescit, vigilantes dixit, boe est, experrecti & exciti, recentiores vos semper adorationis id opus præbete. Ἐν εὐχαρισίᾳ) id est, simul cum gratiarum actione.

Conjungi enim debet grata exacti temporis memoria cum futuri postulatione, pro οὖν, ut supra c. 4, 4. 16. & 2. Tim. 1, 13. & alibi. Præclare Theophylactus: Sed in gratiarum actione, hoc est, gratias agendo Deum precemini.

He namque vera sunt preces, quas gratia subsequuntur, Deo pro omnibus dictæ, quorum nobis vel conscii fumus vel nescii. Proque acceptis per nos beneficiis vel malis etiam toleratis, ac pro bis demum, quæ in universum hominum genus collata sunt, bonis. Προσευχόμενοι ἅμα καὶ περὶ ἡμῶν, ἵνα ὁ Θεὸς ἀνοίξῃ ἡμῖν θύραν τῷ λόγῳ) id est, occafionem, ut 1. Cor. 16, 9. 1. Cor. 2, 12. Magnus eorum honos, quorum precibus Paulus velit juvari, Rom. 15, 30. ## 4:3
3. For which I am also in bonds (Δι ὃ καὶ δέδεμαι), I am bound for no fault, but because I am performing my office. Verf.

Verf. 3. Δι ὃ καὶ δέδεμαι) nullam ob culpam vinctus fum, sed quia officio meo fungor. Verf.

## 4:4
4. That I may make it manifest, as I ought to speak (Ἵνα φανερώσω αὐτῷ, ὡς δεῖ με λαλῆσαι). Not only that God may give me a great audience, but also fortitude of mind and abundance of expression. See 1 Cor. 9, 16. Great condescension, says Ambrose, that he judges the Apostles worthy, who are able to help him with prayers.

Note the humility, says Theophylact. Did Paul need the prayers of these? He adds later: He was indeed praying for this not only for the sake of humility, but to reveal the power of prayer, which, when poured forth by the brethren with charity and attention, is effective. For he had need of heavenly aid, which he knew the prayer of the brethren had abundantly procured for him, and at the same time, to induce them to pray. For if they were to pray for Paul, how much more ought they to insist upon prayers and vows for themselves?

He does not, however, say only "for me," but "for us," including Timothy as well. By the "door of the Word," Salmero and Cornelius à Lapide, with Anselm, understand the mouth, through which, as a door, speech goes forth, as if he were saying, that God may give us an open and free mouth, so that the following words may be exēgētikai (explanatory). Not inappropriately. Cf. Eph. 6, 19. The mystery of Christ is called so not only with respect to former times, but haplōs (simply). For it is an incomprehensible mystery at all times, that which is handed down concerning Christ in the Gospel, which, although we know it in part, as it has been revealed, especially in the New Testament, yet no one is able to attain it by reason, nor can we penetrate the abyss of Divine wisdom in this life; nay, it is a "great mystery of godliness," which the Apostle calls it, 1 Tim. 3, 15, so constituted that it is altogether hyper logon, hyper noun, hyper pasan katalēpsin tēs ktistēs physeōs (beyond reason, beyond mind, beyond all comprehension of created nature), as Justin is the author in ekthesei tēs pisteōs. That addition en parrēsia (with boldness) is not needed in this place. For he includes that in the words "as I ought to speak," to which Theophylact says: This is, that he may make me more confident. Not that I may be freed from bonds, but that I may so speak the mystery of Christ as I ought to speak, not remissly and timidly, but with the greatest boldness and faith. And he seeks to obtain by the prayers of the Church not only that he may preach the Word confidently and faithfully, but also prudently and dexterously with his co-workers, although he is indubious regarding the infallible assistance of the Holy Spirit as far as he himself is concerned; Haymo [says], so that I may know to whom, and what, and when, or how much I ought to speak. For the promise of the Holy Spirit does not exclude prayers, but includes them, Luke 11, 13.

Latin:

4. Ἵνα φανερώσω αὐτῷ, ὡς δεῖ με λαλῆσαι) Non tantum ut magnum mihi det Deus auditorium, sed & fortitudinem animi, & eloquendi copiam. Vide 1. Cor. 9, 16. Magna dignatio, inquit Ambrofius, quod dignos judicat Apostolos, qui ipsum adjuvare poffint precibus.

Attende humilitatem, inquit Theophylactus. Num Paulg horum indigebat precibus? Addit postea: Id sane non modo humilitatis gratia deprecabatur, sed ut & vim patefaceret orationis, quæ cum charitate & attentione à fratribus funderetur. Opus enim habebat cœlesti ope, quam sibi ubertim fratrum oratio enet comparatum, simul etiam, ut eos ad grandum induceret. Nam fi essent pro Paulo precaturi, quanto magis pro feipfis deberent precibus & votis insistere?

Non autem ait tantum pro me, sed pro nobis, Timotheum simul complectens. Per ostium Verbi Salmero & Cornelius à Lapide cum Anselmo os intelligunt, per quod quasi ostium fermo egreditur, quasi dicat, ut det Deus nobis os apertum & liberū, ut verba fequentia sint ἐξηγητικά. Non incommode. Conf. Eph. 6, 19. Mysterium Christi non tantum respectu priorum temporum, sed ἁπλῶς vocatur. Omnibus enim temporibus mysterium est incomprehensibile, quod de Christo in Evangelio traditur, quod etfi ex parte cognoscamus, qua revelatum est, imprimis in Novo Testamento, ratione tamen affequi nemo valet, nec sapientiæ Divinæ abyslum impetrare in hac vita possumus, imo μέγα λίαν τῆς εὐσεβείας μυςήριον, quod vocat Apostolus, 1. Tim. 3, 15. ita comparatum est, ut prorsus fit ὑπὲρ λόγον, ὑπὲρ νῦν, ὑπὲρ πᾶσαν κατάληψιν τῆς κτιῆς Φύσεως, autore Justino in ἐκθέσει τῆς πίσεως. Additamento illo ἐν παῤῥησίᾳ hic loci opus non est. Id enim comprehendit verbis, ὡς δεῖ με λαλῆσαι, ad quæ ita Theophylactus: Hoc est, ut fidenfiorem me faciat. Non ut vinculis eximar, sed ut Christi sic mysterium eloquar, ut me loqui oportet, non remisse & timide, sed summa cum audentia & fide. Nec tantum ut confidenter & fideliter, sed etiam ut prudenter & dextre Verbum prædicet cum cooperariis suis, precibus Ecclesiæ impetrari expetit, etfi de infalljbili assistentia Spiritus sancti quoad fe indubius, Haymo, ut sciam, cui, & quid, & quando vel quantum debeam loqui. Nam promissio Spiritus fandi non excludit preces, sed includit, Luc. 11, 13.

## 4:5
V. 5. Walk in wisdom toward them that are without (Ἐν σοφίᾳ περιπατῆτε πρὸς τοὺς ἔξω). Hōs exō (those who are without) are all non-Christians. 1 Cor. 5, 12. 13. With these he wishes one to live prudently, and to avoid all unnecessary things which could offend their minds. Therefore it follows. Strangers, according to Theophylact, are either those less familiar to us, or those who wander outside the court of our faith and are infidels. For these, although they dwell in this same world, because they are far from the Church and the heavenly kingdom, are said to be "without." Which the latter [interpretation] he himself also prefers, and it is deservedly to be preferred.

For one must converse with them altogether wisely, that is, with prudence—not indeed that of this world, but that which is of the children of light, Luke 16, 8. Cf. Matt. 10, 16. Before the Heathens, therefore, the Apostle wishes, as B. Hunnius interprets, that they walk wisely, lest, if they conduct themselves less providently toward the Heathens, they be implicated in their sins and crimes, or lest they themselves provide them any occasion for blaspheming the doctrine, or lest they deter those whom they could have won over by pious conversation through the grace of God from receiving the doctrine of the Gospel by the impiety of their life and morals. Redeeming the time) escaping dangers. We have spoken of this phrase at Eph. 5. 16. From the parallel passage it is clear that it does not sound so much of escaping dangers, as of seizing, and even redeeming at a price, the occasion and opportunity of doing good. He wishes, therefore, that they should rather redeem the opportunity, and be intent on all occasions of winning those who are outside, both by information and by example. Osiander's paraphrase agrees: When you have business with infidels, who are outside the Church of Christ, act very circumspectly, lest you fall into any danger (which could have been avoided): or say or do anything which could alienate their minds from religion. But also seize the occasion by which you may win them for Christ.

Latin:

V. 5. Ἐν σοφίᾳ περιπατῆτε πρὸς τοὺς ἔξω) ὡς ἔξω sunt omnes non Christiani. 1. Cor. 5, 12. 13. cum his vult prudenter vivi, & vitari omnia non necessaria, quæ eorum animos non possent offendere. Ideo fequitur. Extranei fecundum Theophylactum sunt, vel nobis minus familiares, vel qui extra fidei nostræ aulam divagantur, & infideles sunt. Hi enim etfi in eodem hoc mundo verfantur, quia ab Ecclesia & cœlesti regno longe abfunt, foris esse dicuntur. Quod posterius & ipse præfert & merito præferendum est.

Cum his enim omnino sapienter, id est, cum prudentia, non quidem quæ hujus fæculi, sed quæ filiorum lucis est, Luc. 16, 8. conversandum est. Conf. Matth. 10, 16. Coram Ethnicis ergo vult Apostolus, B. Hunnio interprete, ut sapienter ambulent, ne fi minus provide conferfentur Ethnicis, implicentur simul illorum peccatis & flagitiis, vel ne quam ipsi præbeant eis occafionem blasphemandi doctrinam, neve quos pia conversatione per Dei gratiam lucrari quiverant, eos impietate vitæ ac morum à suscipienda Evangelii doctrina absterreant. Τὸν καιρὸν ἐξαγοραζόμενοι) effugientes pericula. De hac loquutione diximus ad Ephes. 5. 16. E loco parallelo patet, non tam de effugendis periculis, quam de apprehendenda, & vel pretio redimenda occasione & opportunitate bene operandi haec sonare. Vult ergo, ut redimant potius opportunitatem, & ad omnes intenti sint occasiones lucrifaciendi eos, qui foris sunt, tum informatione, tum exemplo. Consonat paraphrasis Osiandri: Quando vobis negotium erit cum infidelibus, qui sunt extra Ecclesiam Christi, admodum circumspecte agite, ne vel in aliquod periculum, (quod caveri poterat) incidatis: vel aliquid dicatis aut agatis, quod ipsorum animos a religione abalienare possit. Sed & captate occasionem, qua illos Christo lucrifaciatis.

## 4:6
Ver. 6. Let your speech always be with grace) that is, let it be. Let your speech be pleasant. See above c. 4, 16. Here again for with. Crocius explains that 'with grace' as the grace of edification: But it is understood more correctly as the manner, so that it may be broader and more pleasant, as Theophylactus interprets, although the end of that pleasantness is that it may delight and confer much upon the hearers. Seasoned with salt) that is, savory. For things that are not salted are insipid.

Mystical explanation of the law, Levit. 2, 13. and elsewhere. Salt makes food savory, extracts harmful and superfluous humors, preserves from putrefaction, makes it fit for digestion, and wholesome for nourishment: Thus he wishes speech to be not insipid, nor over-salted, but salted, so that it may have that which pricks, and which is pleasant. He wishes that such prudence given from heaven should repress in all conversations idle and useless speech, remove the wicked, obscene, useless, and other duties, so that it becomes apt and useful for edification, as Crocius not unaptly says. Anselm had preceded him, who had explained these things a little more fully thus: Just as food, to which salt is mixed, becomes savory, and well-salted meat would not even putrefy; So also let your speech be, so that it may be received as savory food by the mouth of the heart of the hearers, it is not made insipid by foolishness, nor putrid by the admonition of carnal delight, nor corrupted by the admixture of falsehood, but always seasoned with the salt of spiritual wisdom, and uncorrupted by the integrity of truth, and breathing the odor of heavenly and incorruptible delight. And thus let your speech have the seasoning of Divine salt.

Theophylactus: Let it be seasoned with salt, that is, let it not be excessively effusive in joy and jest, nor entirely severe and harsh. Just as food, if it lacks salt, will be less pleasant: if too salted, it is rejected by the taste; so it happens that men cannot use both. Chrysostomus: Let not the grace and wit of speech reach the point where it is used out of place. For it is permitted, it is permitted to speak urbanely and wittily, but with such honesty and decorum as is fitting.

Worldly jests, especially virulent and filthy ones, are to be avoided. These corrupt the will and affections of men. Those who love these do not have salt in themselves, but decay and putrefaction, cf.

Mark 9, 50. Knowing how you ought to answer everyone) Here the infinitive is in place of the Gerund: Knowing how you ought to answer each one, namely, when questioned about the faith, 1. Pet. 3, 15. One must answer prudently not only about the faith, but also about those things which are either to be done or to be avoided, so that they may be proposed as wholesome and worthy of a Christian man.
