Nor, however, is this to be restricted to the business of religion.

For the Apostle speaks in general, whether they are questioned about religion, or about domestic affairs, whether by pagans, or by Jews, or by Christians. Therefore, the sense of Chrysostomus is too restricted. It is not fitting to speak in the same way with everyone, with [column break] Greeks, I say, and brothers.

By no means. For this is the height of madness. Similarly also Theophylactus: For one must answer the wealthy differently, and the needy differently. But if no necessity compels you, you should by no means call a Gentile foul and polluted, nor should you be contentious with him. But rather, if you yourself approach a Prince, pay him the fitting honors. If you are asked about foreign customs, you should call this impious inquiry: inasmuch as they are far removed from the truth.

For it is not to be tolerated that one should introduce an impious dogma, and Paul even argued with praise before the Athenians. But he rebuked Elymas, for he was worthy of rebuke. There are infidels, there are believers. There are heretics, there are orthodox. There are among the orthodox the firm, there are the weak, the unlearned and the skilled, there are the afflicted, groaning under the wound of conscience, there are the secure. The Apostle indicates that one must not speak in the same way with everyone. Therefore he demands prudence. Just as one medicine does not suit all bodies: So there is not one manner of answering for everyone, to this one soft and bland, to that one hard and severe; to this one shorter, to that one more diffuse; to this one enigmatic; to that one more explanatory.

PARS II. ΕΠΙΛΟΓΙΚΗ.

Latin:

Vers. 6. Ὁ λόγος ὑμῶν πάντοτε ἐν χάριτι) nempe esto. Sermo vester suavis esto. Vide supra c. 4, 16. Hic rursus pro σὺν. Crocius illud μετὰ χάριτος explicat de gratia aedificationis: Sed rectius de modo, intelligitur, ut latior sit, & jucundior, ut Theophylactus interpretatur, etsi finis suavitatis illius fit, ut oblectet, & audientibus conferat plurimum. Ἅλατι ἠρτυμένος) id est sapidus. Nam quae salita non sunt, ea sunt insipida.

Mystica explicatio legis Levit. 2, 13. & alibi. Sal sapidum reddit cibum, extrahit humores noxios & superfluos, conservat a putredine, reddit aptos ad digerendum, ac ad nutriendum salubres: Sic sermonem vult esse non insulsum, nec praefalsum, sed salsum, ut habeat, quod stringat, & quod jucundum sit. Vult ut talis prudentia caelitus data reprimat in omnibus colloquiis sermonem otiosum & inutilem, tollat improbum, obscaenum, inutilem, cetera officia, ut fit aptus & utilis ad aedificationem, ut non inconcinne Crocius. Praeverat Anselmus, qui paulo fusius haec ita exposuerat: Sicut cibus, cui sal immiscetur, fit sapidus, & caro bene salita non faceret nec purescit; Ita fit & sermo vester, ut quasi cibus sapidus recipiatur ab ore cordis audientium, non fit insipidus per insipientiam, nec putridus per admonitionem carnalis delectationis, nec corruptus per admixtionem falsitatis, sed semper sale spiritualis sapientiae conditus, & integritate veritatis incorruptus, atque odorem caelestis & incorruptibilis delectationis spirans. Et ita condimentum Divini salis habeat sermo vester.

Theophylactus: Sit sale conditus, id est, non sit supra modum in laetitiam & jocum effusior, non prorsus severus & asper. Quemadmodum esca, si sale careat, insuavior erit: Nimis salita à gustu repudiatur; ita fit, ut bis utrisque vesti nequeant homines. Chrysostomus: Ne sermonis gratia & lepor eo deveniat, ut eo utantur extra discrimen. Licet enim, licet urbane & lepide loqui, sed cum ea, quae par est, honestate & decore.

Sales mundani fugiendi imprimis virulenti ac spurci. Hi corrumpunt voluntatem & affectus hominum. Hos qui amant, non salem in se habent, sed tabem & putredinem, conf.

Marc. 9, 50. Εἰδέναι πῶς δεῖ ὑμᾶς ἐν ἑκάστῳ ἀποκρίνεσθαι) Hic infinitivus est vice Gerundii: Sciendo, quomodo respondere cuique debeatis, nempe de fide interrogati, 1. Petr. 3, 15. Non tantum de fide respondendum prudenter, sed etiam de iis, quae vel facienda vel fugienda, ut salutaria & homine Christiano digna proponantur. Neque tamen ad religionis negotium haec restringenda.

Nam in genere loquitur Apostolus sive de religione, sive de rebus familiaribus, sive à paganis, sive à Judaeis, sive à Christianis interrogentur. Ideo Chrysostomi sensus nimis restrictus est. Non oportet similiter loqui cum omnibus, cum [column break] Gracis inquam & fratribus.

Nequaquam. Hoc enim est extrema amentiae. Similiter & Theophylacti: Aliter namque opulento est respondendum, aliter inopi. Quod si nulla cogas necessitas, nequaquam gentilem foetidum dixeris & inquinatum, nec illi contiaberiis. Quin potius, si Principem ipse adieris, decentes illi honores deserto. Si fueris de alienis institutis rogatus, inquisitionara hac impia dixeris: quippe qua à vero longius absunt.

Neque enim est tolerandum, ut impium quis dogma inducat, apud Athenienses & Paulus vel coram cum laude multa disseruit. Elyman vero conviciatus est, erat namque convicio dignus. Sunt infideles, sunt fideles. Sunt haeretici, sunt orthodoxi. Sunt inter orthodoxos firmi, sunt infirmi, rudes & periti, sunt afflicti, sub vulnere conscientiae gementes, sunt securi. Non cum omnibus eodem modo loquendum esse, indicat Apostolus. Ideo prudentiam exigit. Sicut non unum pharmacum omnibus corporibus convenit: Sic non omnibus unus est respondendi modus, huic mollis & blandus, illi durus & severus; huic brevior, illi fusior; huic aenigmaticus; illa explicatior.

PARS II. ΕΠΙΛΟΓΙΚΗ.

## 4:7
Ver. 7. Tychicus, the beloved brother and faithful minister and fellow servant in the Lord, will make known to you all things concerning me) here added. You have the rest in Eph. 6, 21. And so Tychicus was to take his journey through Ephesus into Phrygia.

Latin:

Vers. 7. Τὰ κατ' ἐμὲ πάντα γνωρίσει ὑμῖν Τυχικὸς ὁ ἀγαπητὸς ἀδελφὸς καὶ πιστὸς διάκονος, καὶ σύνδουλος ἐν Κυρίῳ) hic additum. Cetera habes Eph. 6, 21. Itaque iter Tychicus per Ephesum erat sumpturus in Phrygiam.

## 4:8
Ver. 8. Whom I have sent to you for this very purpose, that he may know your circumstances) it should be read from the Manuscript: that you may know, as it is in Eph. 6, 22. And may comfort your hearts) Ibidem to the Ephesians. Dorotheus in his synopsis writes that Tychicus was the first Bishop at Chalcedon in Bithynia. Why Paul did not write these things, but entrusted them to Tychicus to be reported, Theophylactus holds thus: Or it is to be ascribed to prudence, since not all things are demanded by a letter, except certain necessary things, and those which seem to press more. Which is done so that, if the letters are not longer, they do not cause weariness by embracing many things, and so that there may be something left for the one departing, which he can report in person and gain authority by his presence. Or Paul twice declares his benevolence toward Tychicus, since he trusted him with things which he deemed least to be trusted by letter.

And there were some things which could not be explained by letters. With Onesimus, the faithful and beloved brother, who is one of you) Many servants from Phrygia, Mysia, and neighboring places. Their ancestors, having been sold in wars, had arrived, some in Macedonia, like Epaphroditus, others in Ephesus, like Onesimus. But Epaphroditus seems to have been made free himself, or his parents. Onesimus, therefore, was to approach the Churches of Phrygia before he went into Macedonia. Theodoret also said that Onesimus was a Phrygian in that [letter] to Philemon. Theophylactus, with Chrysostomus, also understands the same Onesimus to be the servant of Philemon, as does Oecumenius, the author of the Greek scholia.

But Calvin is singular without reason. He says it is uncertain who he was, and it is hardly credible that this was the servant of Philemon. I do not see what stands in the way, if it is established that he was the servant of Philemon, says Crocius. They will make known to you all things here) that is, what is being done here. In the report he joins Onesimus with Tychicus, not in the information, perhaps because he was a servant before, and that could be considered unworthy by the Colossians, that they should be informed by him, which reason Theodoret gives.

Latin:

Vers. 8. Ὃν ἔπεμψα πρὸς ὑμᾶς εἰς αὐτὸ τοῦτο, ἵνα γνῶ τὰ περὶ ὑμῶν) legendum est ex Manuscripto: ἵνα γνῶτε, quomodo est Eph. 6, 22. Καὶ παρακαλέσῃ τὰς καρδίας ὑμῶν) Ibidem ad Ephesios. Dorotheus in synopsi Tychicum scribit primum fuisse Episcopum Chalcedone in Bithynia. Cur ea non scripserit, sed Tychico referenda commiserit Paulus, ita habet Theophylactus: Vel id est prudentia adscribendum, cum non omnia epistola demandantur, nisi necessaria quaedam, & qua urgere magis videntur. Quod eo fit, ne si longiores fuerint epistolae, plurima complectendo fastidium pariant, & ut abeunti aliquid reliquum sit, quod possit praesens referre & vi auctoritatem paret. Vel bis dictu Paulus suam in Tychicum benevolentiam patefacit, cum plemque illi crederit, qua epistola minime credenda duxerit.

Et erant nonnulla, quae literis explicari non poterant. Σὺν Ὀνησίμῳ τῷ πιστῷ καὶ ἀγαπητῷ ἀδελφῷ, ὅς ἐστιν ἐξ ὑμῶν) Servi multi ex Phrygia, Mysia & vicinis locis. Horum majores bellis scilicet venditi alii in Macedoniam, ut Epaphroditi, alii Ephesum, ut Onesimi, pervenerant. Sed Epaphroditus liber factus videtur ipse, aut parentes ejus. Onesimus ergo prius aditurus erat Phrygiae Ecclesias, quam iret in Macedoniam. Phrygae fuisse Onesimum dixit & Theodoretus in illa ad Philemonem. Eundem Onesimum Philemonis servum etiam Theophylactus cum Chrysostomo intelligit, ut autor scholiorum Graecorum Oecumenius.

Calvinus vero praeter rationem singularis est. Incertum dicit, quis fuerit, & vix credibile, hunc fuisse servum Philemonis. Non video, quod obflet, si fhatuatur, Philemonis fuisse servum, ait Crocius. Πάντα ὑμῖν γνωρίσουσι τὰ ὧδε) id est, quae hic aguntur. In relatione adjungit Onesimum Tychico, non in informatione, forte, quod ille servus antea fuerit, idque indignum haberi possit Colossensibus, ut ab eo informentur, quam rationem reddit Theodoretus.

## 4:10
Verf. 10. Aristarchus my fellow-prisoner greets you, known in Macedonia, Acts 19:29, ch. 20:4, ch. 27:2, and long since converted to Christ, as appears here, and in the Acts, and Philem. v. 24.

A name common with many learned men in Greece. And Marcus the nephew of Barnabas , having become stronger now after that which is narrated in Acts 15:39, and therefore now dear to Paul, 2 Tim. 4:11. Phrynichus notes that Ἀνεψιὸς is used by the Attics, who are otherwise called ἐξάδελφοι, that is, either cousins-german on the father's side, or on the mother's side, or cousins. For the Greek word is translated by these three words in the glosses.

The Syrian is believed to be a cousin. Concerning whom you received commandments from Barnabas, letters of recommendation. If he comes to you, receive him . He adds to Barnabas's recommendation his own also: lest anything should be believed to remain of that old coldness. And Jesus who is called Justus . Namely, Jesus was the name among the Jews; among the Romans, Justus, not departing much from the name.

See what is said in Acts 13:9. Who are of the circumcision . Namely that Marcus, that is, Mordecai, and that Jesus. These only suppliant in the circumcision. Fellow-workers for the kingdom of God , that is, in the preaching of the Gospel: through which Gospel God reigns in men more perfectly than through the law, מַלְכוּת הָאֱלֹהִים in Hebrew.

See Matt. 4:17. Scripture knows nothing of that distinction between the law and the Gospel, that God reigns in men through the law, but more imperfectly, and through the Gospel more perfectly.

It joins the law and the Gospel in the kingdom of God; which in practice are most closely bound, but in their formal nature are most distinct. Not according to degree but species, nay, in their whole genus they are diverse.

Latin:

10. Ἀσπάζεται ὑμᾶς Ἀρίσταρχος ὁ συναιχμάλωτός μου in Macedonia notus, Act. 19, 29. c. 20, 4. c. 27, 2. & pridem ad Christum conversus, ut & hic, & in actis, & Philem. v. 24. apparet.

Nomen communem cum multis eruditis, in Græcia viris. Καὶ Μάρκος ὁ ἀνεψιὸς Βαρνάβα fortior jam factus post id, quod narratur Act. 15, 39. eoque charus jam Paulo, 2. Tim. 4, 11. Ἀνεψιὸς notat Phrynichus Atticis dici, qui alias ἐξάδελφοι, id est, aut patrueles, aut amitini, aut consobrini. Nam his tribus vocibus Græca illa vox in glossis vertitur.

Amitinum creditus Syrus. Περὶ οὗ ἐλάβετε ἐντολάς A Barnaba commendatitias. Ἐὰν ἔλθῃ πρὸς ὑμᾶς δέξασθε αὐτόν Adjungit ad Barnabæ commendationem etiam suam: ne quid crederetur reliquum-esse de vetere illo frigusculo. Καὶ Ἰησοῦς ὁ λεγόμενος Ἰῦστος Nempe Jesus dicebatur inter Judæos; inter Romanos nomine non multum ab-scedente Justus.

Vide quæ dicta Act. 13, 9. Οἵ ὄντες ἐκ περιτομῆς Nempe Marcus ille, id est, Mardochæus, & Jesus ille. Οὗτοι μόνοι supplexἐν τῇ περιτομῇ. Συνεργοὶ εἰς τὴν βασιλείαν τοῦ Θεοῦ id est in Evangelii prædicatione: Per quod Evangelium Deus in hominibus regnat perfectius, quam per legem, מַלְכוּת הָאֱלֹהִים Ebræis.

Vide Matth. 4, 17. De illo legis & Evangelii discrimine, quod per legem Deus in hominibus regnet, sed imperfectius, per Evangelium vero perfectius, nihil novit Scriptura.

Conjungit legem & Evangelium in regno Dei; quæ in praxi devinctissima, quod naturam autem distinctissima sunt. Non secundum gradum sed speciem, imo toto genere diversa.

## 4:12
Verf. 12. Who have been a comfort to me . Great solace, companions in labor. Παρηγορία מַבַּל יְגִיעָה. Epaphras greets you . The same who is Epaphroditus in the epistle to the Philippians. Who is one of you by origin, as above 9. A servant of Christ . A prince born of the Philippians. Always struggling for you in prayers , above ch. 1:1. That you may be perfect and filled in all the will of God . Concerning the word τελείων see 1 Cor. 2:6, 2 Cor. 14:20, Phil. 3:2, Eph. 4:13, above here ch. 1:28.

2 Cor.

14, 20. Philipp.

Full, namely, with the Spirit, as Eph.

1:8. Ἐν παντὶ θελήματι, that is, εἰς πᾶν θέλημα, to fulfill all the good pleasures of God. In the Manuscript it is πληροφορημένοι in the same sense. See what is above ch. 2:2 and here below 17. For ἦτε the Latin reads ἦτε. For I bear him witness . A huge testimony. That he has great zeal for you , an ardent study for you.

See John 2:17, Rom. 10:2. But in the Manuscript πολὺν πόνον for you, which the Latin also reads. And those in Laodicea, and those in Hierapolis . Both of which cities are in the same Phrygia.

See Strabo and Stephanus. There were also other cities called Hierapolis, as in Syria, in Caria. Luke the beloved physician greets you . Concerning whom see what we said regarding the Gospel written by him, 2 Tim. 4:11, Philem. 24.

And Demas . Who is also Demetrius, by a shortening of the name Demas, Dama in Latin, 2 Tim. 4:10, Philem. 24.

Others distinguish Epaphras from Epaphroditus, of whom we spoke before.

Ambrose in this place thinks that Epaphras was the Bishop of the Colossians; to others this is ambiguous, although it is certain that he taught at Colossae. But because in these salutations he made no mention of Peter, nay, of those of the circumcision listed here, in whose name he greets, he says of Aristarchus, Marcus, and Justus, that they alone were his fellow-workers, and for solace, Beza rightly gathers that Peter was not then at Rome, whence this epistle was written; nor had Cornelius anything to reply, except his own inventions, that they alone were with Paul, as if they were associates and domestics, or that Peter or the Pastor of the Church often traveled through other regions, there to found Churches, as the other Apostles did.

But it yields to no honor to Peter before, that he was not a fellow-worker with Paul for the kingdom of God, that he was not a solace to him in his bonds. But the latter does not suit the Roman Papacy of Peter for 25 years. If he was traveling through the whole world after the manner of the other Apostles, how did he sit as Bishop and Pope of Rome?

He had made a pact with Paul, that while he performed this duty among the Gentiles, he himself would preach the Gospel in the circumcision. How does that agree with that Roman Episcopacy of Peter?

Latin:

Vers. 12. Οἵτινες ἐγενήθησαν μοι παρηγορία Magnum solatium di laboris socii. Παρηγορία מַבַּל יְגִיעָה. Ἀσπάζεται ὑμᾶς Ἐπαφρᾶς Idem qui Epaphroditus in epistola ad Philippenses. Ὁ ἐξ ὑμῶν origine, ut supra 9. Δοῦλος Χριστοῦ Princeps cretus Philippensium. Πάντοτε ἀγωνιζόμενος ὑπὲρ ὑμῶν ἐν ταῖς προσευχαῖς supra c. 1, 1. Ἵνα ἦτε τέλειοι καὶ πεπληρωμένοι ἐν παντὶ θελήματι τοῦ Θεοῦ De voce τελείων vide 1. Cor. 2, 6.

2. Cor.

14, 20. Philipp.

3, 2. Eph. 4, 13. supra hic c. 1, 28. Pleni nempe Spiritu, ut Eph.

1, 8. Ἐν παντὶ θελήματι, id est, εἰς πᾶν θέλημα, ad omnia placita Dei implenda. In Manuscripto est πληροφορημένοι eodem sensu, Vide quæ supra c. 2, 2. & hic infra 17. pro ἦτε Latinus legitἦτε. Μαρτυρῶ γὰρ αὐτῷ Ingens testimonium. Ὅτι ἔχει ζῆλον πολὺν ὑπὲρ ὑμῶν ardens pro vobis studium.

Vide Joh. 2, 17. Rom. 10, 2. At in Manuscripto πολὺν πόνον ὑπὲρ ὑμῶν, quæmodo & Latinus legit. Καὶ τῶν ἐν Λαοδικείᾳ, καὶ τῶν ἐν ἱεραπόλει Quæ utraque urbs in eadem Phrygia.

Vide Strabonem & Stephanum. Fuere & aliæ urbes dictæ Hierapoles, ut in Syria, in Caria. Ἀσπάζεται ὑμᾶς ὁ Λυκᾶς ὁ ἰατρὸς ὁ ἀγαπητός De quo vide ad Evangelium ab ipso scriptum diximus, 2.

Tim. 4, 11. Philem. 24. Καὶ Δημᾶς Qui & Demetrius, compendio vocis Demas, Dama Latine, 2.

Tim. 4, 10. Philem. 24. Epaphram ab Epaphrodito alii omnes distinguunt, quo de antea diximus.

Colossensium Episcopum fuisse Epaphram Ambrosius in hunc locum putat; aliis id ambiguum est, etsi certum, quod Colossis docuerit. Quia vero in hisce salutationibus nullam Petri mentionem fecit, imo de τοῖς ἐκ περιτομῆς hic recensitis, quorum nomine salutat, Aristarcho, Marco & Justo ait, quod illi soli sibi συνεργοὶ fuerint, & solatio, Bezæ recte colligit, Romæ tunc non fuisse Petrum, unde hæc scripta epistola; nec habuit, quod reponeret Cornelius, nisi sua commenta, quod illi soli fuerint cum Paulo, quasi socii & domestici, vel quod Petrus seu Pastor Ecclesiæ sape discurreret per alias regiones, ibi, fundaret Ecclesias, ut alii Apostoli.

Sed prius nulli honori cedere Petro, quod Paulo non fuerit συνεργὸς εἰς βασιλείαν τοῦ Θεοῦ, quod eidem in vinculis solatio non fuerit. Posterius vero non convenit Papatui Petri Romano per 25. annos. Si aliorum Apostolorum more per totum orbem diffurrebat, quomodo seu Episcopus & Papa Romæ sedebat?

Pactus erat cum Paulo, ut hoc inter gentes munere fungente ipse in circumcisione Evangelium prædicaret. Quomodo id cum illo Petræ Romano Episcopatu convenit?

## 4:15
Verf. 15. Greet the brethren who are in Laodicea by epistle or messenger. And Nymphas, and the church in his house . Nymphas is a masculine name, as appears from the article. It is also a contraction from the name Nymphodorus, by which a famous physician was called in Pliny. This Nymphas seems to have lived somewhere in the country.

Mention of a domestic church is also in Rom. 16:5, 1 Cor. 17:20. Ambrosiaster wrongly understood it of a woman, whom he says was so devout that her whole house was signed with the sign of the cross, although he received support from Lombard.

For it follows concerning him in the masculine gender: Τὴν κατ' οἶκον αὐτοῦ. While he greets him separately, he declares him to be a great man, and provokes others to the same study.

For it is no small thing not to be numbered among others, says Chrysostom. Truly excellent, says Theophylact, was this man, who also had all his domestics as believers, and so, that his house was called a church. And therefore Paul imparts a greeting especially to him, and shows favor, when you call his family a church.

Which he does for this reason, that he may also induce others to imitate this, just as if they themselves were desirous of honor, they might imitate this Nymphas. Some, however, think that the church is noted in his house, because he received the saints into his hospitality. But that church were the saints in Colossae, and the faithful brethren in Christ, ch. 1 v. 2. But this domestic church is another, specially greeted by Paul, although also included in the inscription under the general name of saints and faithful.

Latin:

Vers. 15. Ἀσπάσατε τοὺς ἐν Λαοδικείᾳ ἀδελφοὺς per epistolam aut nuntium. Καὶ Νυμφᾶν, καὶ τὴν κατ' οἶκον αὐτοῦ Ἐκκλησίαν Nymphas Masculinum nomen est, ut ex articulo apparet. Id quoque contractum ex Nymphodori nomine, quo appellatus insignis medicus apud Plinium. Videtur hic Nymphas alicubi in agro habitasse.

Ecclesiæ domesticæ mentio etiam Rom. 16, 5. 1. Cor. 17, 20. Perperam de fœmina intellexit Ambrosiaster, quam tam devotam fuisse dicit, ut omnis domus ejus signo titulata esset crucis, etsi a Lombardo suffragium accepit.

Sequitur enim de eo in Masculino genere: Τὴν κατ' οἶκον αὐτοῦ. Dum seorsum salutat, virum magnum esse declarat, & alios ad idem studium provocat.

Non enim parum est aliis non annumerari ait Chrysostomus. Egregius sane, inquit Theophylactus, vir iste erat, qui & domesticos omnes fideles haberet, & ita, ut Ecclesia ejus domus appellaretur. Et ideo Paulus huic præcipue salutem impertit, gratificaturque, cum ejus familiam Ecclesiam nuncupas.

Quod eo facit, ut & alios ad hunc imitandum inducat, perinde etsi ipsi honoris sint cupidi, Nympham hunc imitentur. Ecclesiam tamen aliqui putant in domo illius notari, quod hospitio exceperit sanctos. Sed Ecclesia illa erant ἐν Κολοσσαῖς ἅγιοι, καὶ πισοὶ ἀδελφοὶ ἐν χρισῷ, cap. 1. v. 2. Alia autem est hæc domestica Ecclesia, specialiter à Paulo salutata, etsi etiam in inscriptione sub generali sanctorum & fidelium nomine comprehensa.

## 4:16
Verf. 16. And when the epistle is read among you , this one before. Thus τὰ χαρίσματα for χαρίσματα ταῦτα, Rom. 11:29. Cause that it also be read in the church of the Laodiceans , by that example sent, as was the custom among Christians.

He commanded it both because the information of one Church pertains to all, and could easily be communicated with neighbors, and because perhaps similar errors had been scattered in the Laodicean Church. And that from Laodicea , which you also read. This is the true reading: not from Laodicea. But it is rightly said of Laodicea, that which was to be in the power and dominion of the Laodiceans, as we showed also from civil law at the beginning to the Ephesians.

But that epistle of Paul was written to the Laodiceans in the same tenor as that to the Ephesians, but because Laodicea was nearer to the Colossians, he preferred that a copy be sought from there. Why that truer reading should be held, Grotius does not indicate.

Nor without cause should the received text be moved . It is certainly a sin that Grotius by his own daring substituted another reading without the support of any codex.

For all consistently read: That from Laodicea: which cannot be understood of an epistle written to the Laodiceans. Nor do the words of the Vulgate version bring in that sense: and that which is of the LAODICEANS. For these do not indicate any epistle to the Laodiceans, but rather one written by the Laodiceans.

Therefore the assertion of Bellarmine is vain, lib. IV. de verbo Dei cap. 4. IT IS CERTAIN that the epistle of Paul to the Laodiceans, of which he himself makes mention in Coloss. last chapter, has perished, which he therefore corrected in the recognition of his books to this place.

The Latin words are ambiguous: For what we read, and that which is of Laodi- censium est, can signify an epistle written to the Laodiceans, and written by the Laodiceans.

Theodoretus noted even in his own time that confused explanation: Some have thought that he himself wrote to the Laodiceans: Therefore, the faithful one which is in Laodicea. For they had written to him about some matters. But it is likely that they had either accepted those things which were being done at Colossae, or had labored under the same disease as they. And therefore he said that this epistle also was to be read by them.

So also Chrysostomus: For he did not say the one which is to the Laodiceans, but the one written from Laodicea. Oecumenius followed Chrysostomus: He did not say the one which was written from Laodicea: Not by Paul to the Laodiceans, but by the Laodiceans to Paul. For there was altogether something in it which would be of benefit to the Colossians.

Hieronymus in his catalogue of Ecclesiastical writers: Some read also to the Laodiceans; but it is exploded by all.

Philastrius on heresies: They say an epistle was also written to the Laodiceans. And because they added some things in it not thinking rightly, therefore it is not read in the Church, and if it is read by some, yet it is not read to the people in the Church. To whom add their own vote from our own people B.

Balduinus, B. D. Job. Behmius, from the Reformed Tottanus, Polanus, Witakerus, Drusius, Job. Crocius and others, from the Pontifical side Catharinus, Baronius in the year of Christ 60, no. 13. We therefore adhere more willingly to Chrysostomus and Theodoretus than to the others, so that no epistle was written by Paul to the Laodiceans.

Cornelius a Lapide: I answer, he says, and I say, that the Apostle here calls it the epistle of the Laodiceans, not his own, which he might have written to the Laodiceans, but that which the Laodiceans wrote to Paul, or certainly to the Colossians themselves, as Theodoretus wishes: In which there were some things which pertained to the matter of the Colossians, and accordingly the Apostle wished it to be read by them. That is evident from the Greek text, which has it thus: τὴν ἐκ Λαοδικείας, that is, the one which is from Laodicea, namely, written to me, read ye.

Thus Chrysostomus, Syrus, and Theodoretus. Where the Jesuit adds of his own, as if from the mind of Theodoretus, or certainly to the Colossians themselves: For that is neither found in Theodoretus, nor does it fit in any way.

Thus by the judgment of the chief Pontifical writers themselves, it is established that an epistle of Paul to the Laodiceans is not founded here. Nor therefore did they dare to insert it into their Vulgate. For it could not be called the epistle of the Laodiceans, because it was kept by them, since the received manner of speaking does not admit that, for example, an epistle written by anyone else should be called Grotius's epistle, which had been kept by Grotius.

How could they understand from that phrase that a certain Pauline epistle was being noted, perhaps long ago written to the Laodiceans, and kept by them, but now to be communicated to the Colossians to be read, especially because in the original text they read: τὴν ἐκ Λαοδικείας. But what Grotius thinks, that by the epistle to the Laodiceans is understood that which was written to the Ephesians, because he had sent the same epistle or one of the same tenor to both, that the Colossians could neither divine from these words, nor does it appear from elsewhere.

For where is any trace of that matter, that a certain epistle was given to the Laodiceans, and that it was the same, or of the same tenor with the epistle to the Ephesians? Tertullianus indeed says that the heretics boasted of something in jest, and he transfers that blame to Marcion.

For thus he says in book V against Marcion, chapter 11. I pass over here also concerning another epistle, which we have inscribed to the Ephesians: but the heretics to the Laodiceans.

And chapter 17. We have this epistle sent to the Ephesians indeed by the truth of the Church, not to the Laodiceans, but Marcion sometimes interpolated the title for it, as if he were a most diligent examiner even in that.

Therefore this Grotius agrees with Marcion, and the heretics, not, according to Tertullianus, with the Catholics. Although if Epiphanius is to be believed, from the epistle to the Ephesians, which he made the seventh of Paul, and wrote it to the Laodiceans according to him, distinct from what Marcion wanted, and made it the eleventh in order. Which however Epiphanius rejected as superfluous, extraneous, and alien from the Apostle, book I, Tom. III, against heresies 42, against Marcion.

Even if this last one is produced from another SUPERFLUOUS epistle placed outside the Gospel and the epistle.

For it did not seem good to the most miserable Marcion to cite this testimony from the epistle to the Ephesians, but from the epistle to the Laodiceans, which is not IN THE APOSTLE. But here we can compare Grotius with the Papists, Faber, Sixtus Senensis and others, who published or approved an epistle to the Laodiceans, which is not the same tenor as the epistle to the Ephesians, but rather could seem to be a certain epitome of the epistle to the Philippians.

But because others acknowledge it as supposititious and merely fabricated, Baronius calls it spurious, Sixtus Senensis himself in book II of his Bibliotheca, p. 113, offers reasons for doubting, there is no reason why we should make words about it. There are those who by the epistle written from Laodicea understand a Pauline one, some indeed the first to Timothy, others the epistle to Philemon. That opinion however has Theophylact, whom Bullinger and Hyperius followed: I seem to see, that there were some things written by Paul to the Colossians, as it was necessary that they should be known to the Laodiceans, and on the other hand that they should be open to the Colossians themselves, which had been signified to the citizens of Laodicea by letters.

For both were being corrected by the writings of the Apostle, in which there was much utility, because each of them was to recognize their own proper vices. Someone will ask, what was that epistle to the Laodiceans?

Namely, that which was written first to Timothy. For the Apostle sent this from Laodicea, although some say that the former wrote an epistle to Paul. But whether the matter is so, or otherwise, it is not certain to me.

For how could it happen that the Laodiceans could profit by their own letters? In which judgment of Theophylact these things are to be observed, 1. that he speaks only conjecturally: I seem to see, 2. that he brings forward only his own opinion, he does not provoke anyone else.

3. That he does not even have Chrysostomus, whom he almost reduced to a compendium, as agreeing or preceding. 4. This opinion does not fit in any way. For how could it be established either to the Colossians or the Laodiceans, which epistle Paul wrote from Laodicea; indeed whence was it established that a certain Pauline epistle was indicated here!

For he did not indicate by any point that it was his own epistle, which was also to be read by the Colossians, nor could they attain that by divining. Furthermore, how could he refer himself to an epistle which the Apostle wrote from Laodicea, when he had never seen Laodicea, that neighbor to Colossae, while he was writing this epistle to the Colossians, concerning which his words, Colossians 2:1, clearly teach us:

For I want you to know what a struggle I have for you and those who are in Laodicea, and as many as have not seen my face in the flesh. To these things Hieronymus Zanchius from the Reformed notes in his commentary on this place, that the first epistle to Timothy was written from another Laodicea, than that which was near Colossae.

But that Laodicea is noted in the vicinity, and in verse 14, it is evident. To say nothing of the fact that the subscription of the first epistle to Timothy seems suspicious to some, since the Claromontanus codex expresses no place, and Beza has it in manuscript as written from Macedonia.

Baronius rails against that opinion thus: What reason, he says, is there that he would have wanted an epistle written many years earlier to be read in the Church of the Colossians?

Latin:

Vers. 16. Καὶ ὅταν ἀναγνωσθῇ παρ' ὑμῖν ἡ ἐπιστολὴ ἡ πρὸ αὕτη. Sic τὰ χαρίσματα pro χαρίσματα ταῦτα, Rom. 11, 29. Ποιήσατε ἵνα καὶ ἐν τῇ Λαοδικέων ἐκκλησίᾳ ἀναγνωσθῇ exemplo eo misso, ut mos erat inter Christianos.

Jussit id tum quod informatio unius Ecclesiæ ad omnes pertineat, & facile cum vicinis communicari potuerit, tum quod fortassis similes errores in Laodicena Ecclesia sparsi fuerint. Καὶ τὴν Λαοδικείας ἥν καὶ ὑμεῖς ἀναγνῶτε. Hæc vera lectio: non ἐκ Λαοδικείας. Recte autem dicitur ἡ Λαοδικείας ea, quæ futura erat in potestate & dominio Laodicensium, ut ostendimus etiam ex jure civili initio ad Ephesios.

Erat autem illa Pauli epistola ad Laodicenses scripta eodem tenore, quo illa ad Ephesios, sed quia propior Colossensibus erat Laodicea, inde maluit exemplum peti. Cur illa verior lectio habenda sit, non indicat Grotius.

Nec sine causa loco movendus receptus textus. Piaculum certe est, quod Grotius proprius ausu aliam lectionem subfuktit sine ullius codicis suffragio.

Omnes enim constanter legunt: Τὴν ἐκ Λαοδικείας: Quæ de epistola ad Laodicenses scripta intelligi non possunt. Nec inferunt eum sensum verba Vulgatæ versionis: & ea, quæ LAODICENSIUM est. Hæc enim non indicant aliquam epistolam ad Laodicenses, sed potius à Laodicensis scriptam.

Ideo vanum est affertum Bellarmini libr. IV. de verbo Dei cap. 4. CERTUM est, perisse epistolam Pauli ad Laodicenses, cujus ipse meminit Coloss. cap. ultimo, quod proinde emendavit in recognit. libr. suorum ad hunc locum.

Verba Latinæ sunt ambiguæ: Quod enim nos legimus, & ea, quæ Laodicensium est, potest significare epistolam scriptam ad Laodicenses, & scriptam a Laodicensibus.

Notavit jam suo tempore illam incontitam explicationem Theodoretus: Quidam existimarunt, ipsum eum scripsisse ad Laodicenses: Itaque fidam quae est ea Laodicea. Illi enim de aliquibus rebus ad illum scripserant. Verisimile est autem, eos vel ea acceptasse, qua fiebant Colossis, vel eodem morbo cum eis laborasse. Et ideo dixit, hanc quoque epistolam eis esse legendam.

Sic etiam Chrysostomus: Non enim dixit eam, quae est ad Laodicenses, sed ex Laodicea scriptam. Chrysostomum sequutus est Oecumenius: Non dixit eam, quae ex Laodicea scripta est: Non a Paulo ad Laodicenses, sed a Laodicenis ad Paulum. Erat enim omnino in ea aliquid, quod prodesset Colossensibus.

Hieronymus in catal. Eccles. scriptor. Legunt quidam & ad Laodicenses; Sed ab omnibus exploditur.

Philastrius de haeresibus: Ajunt epistolam etiam ad Laodicenses scriptam. Et quia in ea addiderunt quaedam non bene sentientes, inde non legitur in Ecclesia, & si legitur a quibusdam, non tamen in Ecclesia legitur populo. Quibus calculum addunt suum e nostratibus B.

Balduinus, B. D. Job. Behmius, e Reformatis Tottanus, Polanus, Witakerus, Drusius, Job. Crocius alii, e Pontificiis Catharinus, Baronius ad ann. Christi LX. num. 13. Libentius igitur Chrysostomo ac Theodoreto inharemus, quam cateris, ut nulla a Paulo scripta fuerit epistola ad Laodicenses.

Cornelius a Lapide: Respondeo, inquit, & dico, Apostolum hic vocare epistolam Laodicensium, non suam, quam ad Laodicenses scripserit, sed eam, quam Laodicenses ad Paulum, vel certe ad ipsos Colossenses, ut vult Theodoretus, scripserint: In qua quaedam inerant, quae ad rem Colossensium pertinerent, ac proinde ab eis legi voluit Apostolus. Patet id ex Graeco textu, qui sic habet: τὴν ἐκ Λαοδικείας, id est, eam, quae ex Laodicea, scilicet ad me scripta est, vos legite.

Ita Chrysostomus, Syrus & Theodoretus. Ubi de suo addit Jesuita, quasi ex mente Theodoreti, vel certe ad ipsos Colossenses: Id enim nec in Theodoretu reperitur, nec congruit ullatenus.

Ita judicio ipsorummet Pontificiorum praecipuorum constat, hic non fundatam esse epistolam Pauli ad Laodicenses. Neque ergo in Vulgatam suam inferre eamdem ausi sunt. Non enim Laodicensium dici potuit epistola, quia ab illis servata, quum id recepta loquendi ratio non admittat, verbi gratia, Grotii epistolam dici, quae ab alio quocunque scripta a Grotio asservata sit.

Quomodo ex ea phrasi Colossenses intelligere poterant, Paulinam quandam epistolam notari, jam pridem forte ad Laodicenses scriptam, atque ab ipsis asservatam, nunc autem Colossensibus legendam communicandam, imprimis, quia in originali textu legebant: τὴν ἐκ Λαοδικείας. Quod autem putat Grotius, intelligi per epistolam ad Laodicenses eam, quae ad Ephesios scripta, quod eandem vel ejusdem tenoris epistolam utrisque transmiserit, id nec ex hisce verbis divinare poterant Colossenses, nec aliunde apparet.

Nam ubi ejus rei ullum vestigium, quod epistola ad Laodicenses quaedam data, & quod illa eadem fuerit, vel ejusdem tenoris cum epistola ad Ephesios? Tertullianus sane haereticos sale quid jactasse ait, eamque culpam in Marcionem transfert.

Ita enim ille libr. V. contr. Marc. cap. 11. Praetereo & hic de alia epistola, quam nos ad Ephesios praescriptam habemus: Haeretici vero ad Laodicenos.

Et cap. 17. Ecclesia quidem veritate epistolam istam ad Ephesios habemus emissam, non ad Laodicenos, sed Marcion ei titulum aliquando interpolare gessit, quasi & in isto diligentissimum explomtor.

Consentit ergo hic Grotius cum Marcione, & haereticis, non, secundum Tertullianum, cum Catholicis. Quamvis si Epiphanius fides habenda, ab epistola ad Ephesios, quam Pauli septimam fecit, eamque ad Laodicenos juxta ipsum scripta, distinctam quam voluerit Marcion, ac ordine undecimam illam fecerit. Quam tamen Epiphanius ceu superfluam, extraneam & ab Apostolo alienam rejecit l. I.

Tom. III. contra haeres. 42. contr. Marcion. Etiam si hos postremum ex alia SUPERFLUA extra Evangelium & epistolam posita epistola producatur.

Non enim visum est miserrimo Marcioni hoc testimonium ex epistola ad Ephesios citare, sed ex epistola ad Laodicenses, qua non est IN APOSTOLO. Committere autem hic possumus Grotium cum Papistis, Fabro, Sixto Senensi & aliis, qui epistolam ad Laodicenses ediderunt aut approbarunt, quae non eum epistola ad Ephesios ejusdem tenoris est, sed potius epitome quaedam epistolae ad Philippenses videri queat.

Verum quia eam supposititiam mereque confictam alii agnoscunt, Baronius spuriam dicit, Sixtus Senensis ipse l. II. Bibl. p. 113. rationes dubitandi profert, non est, quod de illa verba faciamus. Sunt qui per epistolam ex Laodicea scriptam Paulinam quandam intelligant, aliqui quidem priorem ad Timotheum, alii epistolam ad Philemonem. Illa sententia autem habet Theophylactum, quem sequuti sunt Bullingerus & Hyperius: Videre videor, fuisse nonnulla Colossensibus a Paulo scripta, ut Laodicensibus innotescerent, necessarium erat, & contra Colossensibus ipsis paterent, que Laodicea civibus fuissent per literas significata.

Utrique namque Apostoli scriptis castigabantur, in quibus eo plurimum inerat utilitatis, quia horum singuli propria vitia emns recognituri. Quaret aliquis, quenam illa fuit ad Laodicenses epistola?

Ea nimirum, qua ad Timotheum prior conscripta est. Hanc namque ex Laodicea transmisit Apostolus, tametsi dicant nonnulli, ad Paulum priores scripsisse epistolam. Utrum vero res ita se habeat, aut secus, mihi nihil constat.

Qui enim poterat fieri, ut propriis literis Laodicenses proficerent? In quo Theophylacti judicio haec observanda, 1. quod σοχαστικῶς tantum loquatur: Videre mihi videor, 2. quod suam solum sententiam proferat, non ad alium quenquam provocet. 3.

Ne Chrysostomum quidem, quem fere in compendium redegit, consentientem aut praevium habeat. 4. Non convenit ullatenus haec sententia. Nam quomodo constare poterat sive Colossensibus sive Laodicenis, quam epistolam a Laodicea Paulus scripserit; imo unde constitit, quod epistola quaedam Paulina inditigata hic fuerit!

Non enim suam esse illam epistolam, quae legenda etiam a Colossensibus, ullo apice indicavit, nec id divinando assequi ipsi poterant. Porro quomodo potuit sese referre ad epistolam, quam ex Laodicea scripserit Apostolus, quum Laodiceam illam vicinam Colossis nunquam viderit, dum hanc ad Colossenses exararet epistolam, quo de verba ejus, Coloss.

2, 1. luculenter nos edocent: Nam volo vos scire, quantum certamen habeam de vobis & iis, qui sunt Laodicea, & quotquot non viderunt faciem meam in carne. Ad haec notat e Reformatis Hieronymus Zanchius in comment.

Ad hunc locum, epistolam priorem ad Timotheum ex alia Laodicea scriptam fuisse, quam quae vicina Colossis fuit. Hic autem Laodiceam in vicinia notari, & versu 14. patet. Ut taceam, quod subscriptio prioris ad Timotheum nonnullis suspecta videatur, quam Claromontanus codex nullum locum exprimat, & Beza M. s. habeat, eam scriptam esse ex Macedonia.

Baronius ita illi sententiae influtat: Quae, inquit, subsit ratio, ut epistolam ante plures annos scriptam legi voluisset in Ecclesia Colossensium?

## 4:17
Vers. 17. Βλέπε τὴν διακονίαν ἣν παρέλαβες ἐν Κυρίῳ, ἵνα αὐτὴν πληροῖς) A Hebraism for βλέπε ἵνα πληροῖς ἐν Κυρίῳ τὴν διακονίαν, ἣν παρέλαβες.

Moreover, מִלּא is to perform well, as above 1, 25.

The same is πληροφόρησις, 2.

Tim. 4, 5. ἐν Κυρίῳ according to the precepts of the Lord, which are in Matthew 10 and elsewhere. He seems to have found something lacking in Archippus, or at least he had need of this admonition.

Theophylact with Chrysostom: Why, he says, had he given no letters to this man, but signified his commands through messengers?

Perhaps because this man had less need of letters, who was in need of few and slight admonitions.

But, Theophylact adds a little later, he attempts certain things in this place when he says in the Lord.

For he makes Archippus more diligent to execute the work of the Lord, and renders the Colossians obedient to Archippus, as those who have already been handed over to his care by the Lord.

Moreover, for this reason he enjoins them to notify the Preceptor Archippus, so that when they have been rebuked by Archippus, they may not be able to burden him with the bitterness of this, since they are not unaware that they are being chastised by Paul's command, and that they themselves have delivered Paul's mandates. Ὁ ἀσπασμὸς τῇ ἐμῇ χειρὶ Παύλου) What has been written up to this point was written by the hand of a scribe.

But this, up to the end, Paul wrote with his own hand, 1. Corinth.

16, 21. 2. Thess. 3, 17. Crocius restricts the things written by the Apostolic hand to the salutation of the whole Colossian Church, which he seems to decide had fallen out here, when he had subscribed ἀσπάζομαι ὑμᾶς or ἐνέρρωσο, or something similar, with Oecumenius as author, Grotius seems to think, just as Cajetan also conjectures, that the end is mutilated, since it lacks the integrity of this sign, (2. Thess. 3, 17.) Sam. Maresius not denying it in Concord. discordi cap. IX. p. 154. That the epistle to Philemon is referred to here, not only Raphael Eglinus among the Reformed maintains, which ought to have been sent by Onesimus and read at Colossae, or for the sake of Onesimus himself, who was a Colossian by birth, as Jo.

Crocius reports his opinion, but also among our own, B. Johannes Affelmannus in his illustrious Theological questions, heptad 1, quest. 10, thesis 10, judged: I, he says, when I see that considerations not to be despised can be opposed to each of these opinions, I will say, saving the judgment of others, what seems so to me.

I think that by the epistle from Laodicea (interpreters add of their own, which was written), which Paul wishes to be read at Colossae, is understood the epistle written about Onesimus to Philemon, which is read to this day in the biblical text. Concerning which opinion I will not doubt that those who have diligently weighed the circumstances of the place, persons, and time will judge candidly. Although I admit that the circumstances of persons or time do not conflict, but rather agree perfectly; yet as far as the place or term is concerned, it seems to be assumed without foundation that Onesimus was sent to Laodicea, and that Philemon lived at Laodicea.

That Onesimus was indeed sent to the Colossians, and that he is a Colossian, is evident from chapter 4, 9, but not so to the Laodiceans. It also seems to be supposed that the text should perhaps be supplemented, as Stapleton wanted, not that the epistle from Laodicea was written, but that it was TO BE SOUGHT or TO BE SENT: which supplement is too arbitrary, if not violent.

But as for the term from which, it is clear from the subscription, which I think cannot be called into doubt, that Paul's epistle to Philemon was sent from Rome by Onesimus. Therefore it was not sent from Laodicea. Yet the words as they lie demand this meaning.

Whence these things cannot be understood concerning the Pauline epistle, inasmuch as it was not sent from Laodicea.

And since it is not established by any solid evidence that this is the epistle of Paul which is being discussed, I do not see why I should depart from those who understand here the epistle of the Laodiceans, or of someone from the Laodiceans, written to Paul; which he communicated to the Colossian Church, so that it might be read by it. Although Stapleton (T. I. Auth.

Eccl. defens. l. 2. c. 2. p. 941) calls this into doubt from the fact that it was fitting that only those things which made for faith and piety should be read in the churches and assemblies of the faithful, and therefore that the Apostle spoke only of some epistle of his own, which was worthy to be read publicly for the edification of the faithful: yet that reason does not move us. For why could there not be contained in private letters of the Laodiceans given to the Apostle such things from which the Colossians could be edified, or at least from which the things which he was then writing, or which he desired to be carried to the Colossians by Tychicus and Onesimus, could be more fully understood, and from which the state of the churches could be more rightly amended through the mutual communication of the churches?

For they, says Theodoret of the Laodiceans, had written to him (Paul) about some matters. It is likely, however, that they either accused those things which had been done at Colossae, or suffered from the same disease as they.

And therefore he said that this epistle also was to be read by them. Similarly Oecumenius: For there was ALTOGETHER in that epistle (which had been written by the Laodiceans to Paul) something which would profit the Colossians. Ἦν γάρ τι παύλως ὠφελέν ἐν αὐτῇ Κολοσσᾶις.

Whether you say it was to be sought from the Laodiceans, as it was to be communicated to them as if inscribed to them by the Colossians, which Cornelius à Lapide hints; or you decide that a copy of the same, as they call it, was already communicated to the Colossians by Paul together with the epistle inscribed to them, which could seem to be seen from the words of the Apostle, τὴν ἐκ ΛΑΝΔ (demonstratively) from Laodicea, (written to me), so that you also may read, it does not matter much, provided the words of Paul are at least not twisted; which is done altogether by Stapleton and Grotius concerning the Pauline one to the Laodiceans; therefore, says Stapleton, he now calls it from Laodicea, because it was to be sought from there, and was now not so much Paul's as the Laodiceans', to whom and for whose sake Paul had sent it, and in whose possession it now remains as their own. But was there not a sign and testimony of the genuineness of the Apostolic epistle, which is still read by the Greeks in all the codices, and has escaped no one, "the salutation with my own hand, Paul"? What then was the need of another sign? Indeed, this very thing is what he had established as the sign of his epistles, 2 Thess. 3:17.

For this reason, the opinion of Grotius seems more convenient. That he wished to write these things with his own hand, Theodoret thinks was done to testify that he taught freely, and to command that they not be fervent regarding the law (ceremonial or necessary). But Theophylact says, that he might make the imparted salvation more firm, and that he might corroborate the mandates of the epistle.

All these causes can be accepted together. But primarily it was done to procure authority for the letters. "Remember my bonds" (Col. 4:18). An excellent admonition.

See what I bear: Be ye also prepared to bear evils, and whatever troublesome things may happen, bear them bravely. Theodoret explains the sense thus: Imitate me, and whatever troublesome things may happen, bear them bravely. O, what great consolation, exclaims Chrysostom!

For this suffices to exhort them to all things, and to render them stronger for the contests. But it also rendered them more familiar. Add that it so moved them to sympathy in bonds, and to the beneficence of succoring him. "The grace be with you." Namely, of Christ: What is added elsewhere is here understood: although the Latin also added, of our Lord. But he added, beyond the faith of the Greek Codices.

Theophylact applies the wish to the present matter thus: If this grace be present with you, whether pressure afflicts you, or shackles hinder you, and prison restrains you, they could in no way harm you by this. But the wish is undoubtedly general, which was solemn in the letters of the Apostle. We conclude this epistle with Theodoret: We ought also to remember those bonds always, and to perceive the utility that comes from the memory, and to pray that we do not enter into temptation.

But if this should happen, to love the Divine economy, and to show one's own greatness of soul, and to invoke the help of Divine grace. For thus it will be possible that we both contend, and conquer, and attain those things which have been promised and announced by Christ. With whom, to the Father, with the most holy Spirit, belongs glory and magnificence, now and always and for ever and ever. AMEN.

Latin:

Vers. 17. Βλέπε τὴν διακονίαν ἣν παρέλαβες ἐν Κυρίῳ, ἵνα αὐτὴν πληροῖς) Ebraismus pro βλέπε ἵνα πληροῖς ἐν Κυρίῳ τὴν διακονίαν, ἣν παρέλαβες.

Est autem מִלּא bene perfungi ut supra 1, 25.

Idem est πληροφόρησις, 2.

Tim. 4, 5. ἐν Κυρίῳ secundum Domini praecepta, quae sunt Matth. 10. & alibi. Videtur aliquid desiderasse in Archippo, vel certe monitione hac opus habuit.

Theophylactus cum Chrysostomo: Cur, inquit, huic nullas dederat literas, sed per nuncios mandata significabat?

Forte quod minus erat huic literis opus, qui paucis & exilibus monitis indigebat.

Duo autem, subjicit paulo post Theophylactus, quaedam hoc loco molitur, cum dicit in Domino.

Nam & Archippum facit folertiorem ad opus Domini exequendum, & Colossenses reddit Archippo morigeros, ut qui illi a Domino in curam jam sint traditi.

Ceterum idcirco illis injungit, ut Praeceptori Archippo denuncient, ut cum ab Archippo fuerint acrepati, ne illum queant acrimonia hujus imumulare, cum minus ignorent, Pauli jussu se castigari, & ipsimet Pauli mandata detulerint. Ὁ ἀσπασμὸς τῇ ἐμῇ χειρὶ Παύλου) Quae hucusque scripta sunt, ea scripta erant scribae manu.

Haec vero ad finem usque sua manu scripsit Paulus, 1. Corinth. 16, 21. 2. Thess. 3, 17.

Restringit manu Apostolica scripta ad salutationem totius Ecclesiae Colossensis Crocius, quam hic excidisse, quum subscripserit ἀσπάζομαι ὑμᾶς vel ἐνέρρωσο, aut simile quid, Oecumenio autore, statuere videtur Grotius, quemadmodum & Cajetanus conjectat, calcem esse mutilam, quoniam careat integritate hujus signi, (2. Thess. 3, 17.) non abnuente Sam. Maresio in Concord. discordi cap. IX. p. 154. Epistolam ad Philemonem hic respici, non tantum a Reformatis Raphael Eglinus statuit, quae per Onesimum missa & legi debuerit Colossis, vel ipius Onesimi causa, qui erat patria Colossaeus, ut refert eius sententiam Jo.

Crocius, sed etiam a nostris B. Johannes Affelmannus in illustr. quaestion. Theologic, heptade quaest. 1. thes. 10. censuit: Ego, inquit, cum videam, singulis histe sententiis opponi posse considerationes non contemnendas, dicam salvo aliorum judicio, quo mihi videatur.

Existimo per epistolam ex Laodicea, (interpretes de suo addunt, quae scripta est) quam vult Paulus legi Colossis, intelligi epistolam scriptam de Onesimo ad Philemonem, quae hodieque legitur in textu biblico. de qua sententia non dubitabo candide judicaturos, qui e textu loci, personarum & temporis circumstantias diligenter expenderint. Quanquam vero fatear, non repugnare circumstantias personarum aut temporis, sed apprime congruere; quod tamen ad locum vel terminum attinet, fine fundamento assumi videtur, Laodiceam missum fuisse Onesimum, ac Philemonem Laodiceae habitasse.

Ad Colossenses sane Onesimum missum, eumque Colossensem esse, e cap. 4, 9. constat, non item ad Laodicenses. Supponi etiam id videtur, textum sic forte supplendum esse, ut Stapletonus voluit, epistolam ex Laodicea non scriptam, sed PETENDAM vel MITTENDAM: quod supplementum nimis arbitrarium est, si non violentum.

Quod vero ad terminum a quo, Roma missam esse epistolam Pauli ad Philemonem per Onesimum à subscriptione, quam non in dubium vocari posse arbitror, patet. non ergo ex Laodicea missa. Quem sensum tamen postulant verba ut jacent.

Unde de Paulina epistola, utpote quae e Laodicea missa non est, intelligi haec non possunt.

Et quum nullo solido indicio constet, Pauli hanc epistolam esse, de qua disquiritur, non video cur ab iis discedere debeam, qui epistolam Laodicensium, vel alicujus e Laodicensibus ad Paulum scriptam hic intelligunt; quae Ecclesiae Colossensi communicavit, ut ab eadem legeretur. Quod etsi Stapletonus T. I. Auth. Eccl. defens. l. 2. c. 2. p.

941. ex eo in dubium vocet, quod in Ecclesiis & conventibus fidelium non nisi ea legi par fuerit, quae ad fidem & pietatem facerent, adeoq; non nisi de sua aliqua epistola, quae propter aedificationem fidelium digna esset, quae publice legeretur, Apostolum loqui: ratio tamen ea nos non movet. Nam quidni in privatis Laodicensium literis ad Apostolum datis contineri poterant talia, ex quibus Colossenses aedificari, vel certe ad ea, quae tum scribebat, aut per Tychicum & Onesimum perferri ad Colossenses cupiebat, plenius intelligenda, & ex iis statum Ecclesiarum rectius emendandum e mutua Ecclesiarum communicatione conducere potuerit.

Illi enim, inquit Theodoretus de Laodicensibus, de aliquibus rebus ad eum (Paulum) scripserant. Verisimile est autem, eos vel ea accusasse, que Colossis facta fuerant, vel eodem cum bis morbo laborasse.

Et ideo dixit, hanc quoque epistolam iis legendam esse. Similiter Oecumenius: Erat enim OMNINO in ea epistola, (quae à Laodicenis ad Paulum perscripta erat) aliquid, quod prodesset Colossensibus. Ἦν γάρ τι παύλως ὠφελέν ἐν αὐτῇ Κολοσσᾶις.

Sive autem eam dicas petendam fuisse e Laodicensibus, uti a Colossensibus sibi inscripta communicanda iisdem erat, quod Cornelius à Lapide innuit; sive a Paulo copiam ejusdem quem vocant, Colossensibus jam simul cum epistola iis inscripta communicatam statuas, quod videri posset e verbis Apostoli, τὴν ἐκ ΛΑΝΔ (δεικτικῶς) ex Laodicea, (ad me icritam), ut & vos legatis, non multum refert, dum verba Pauli saltem non torqueantur; quod omnino a Stapletono & Grotio de Paulina ad Laodicenses fit; ideo ex Laodicea, inquit Stapletono, nunc vocat, quia inde petenda erat, jamque non tam Pauli, quam Laodicensium erat, ad quos & propter quos illam Paulus miserat, & penes quos tanquam eorum propria jam remanent. Sed annon signum ac testimonium γνήσιότητος Apostolicae epistolae fuerat, quod adhuc legitur Graecis in omnibus codicibus, nulli excidit ὁ ἀσπασμὸς τῇ ἐμῇ χειρὶ Παύλου? Quid ergo attinebat aliud signum? Imo hoc ipsum est, quod σημεῖον fuarum epistolarum constituerat 2. Thess. 3, 17.

Id eo convenientior videtur Grotii sententia. Quod manu sua haec scribere voluerit, Theodoretus factum esse censet, ut testaretur, libere se docere, & jubere, ne legem (ceremonialem seu necessariam) fervent. Theophylactus vero, Ut impartitam salutem faceret firmiorem, & ut mandata epistola corroboraret.

Quae omnes causae conjunctim accipi possunt. Sed imprimis id factum, ut αὐθεντίαν literis conciliaret. Μνημονεύετε με τῶν δεσμῶν) Egregia monitio. Videte quae feram: Vos quoque ad mala ferenda parati este, & quae molesta evenerint, ferte fortiter.

Theodoretus sensum ita exponit: Me imitemini, & quae molesta evenerint, ferte fortiter. Pape, quanta consolatio, exclamat Chrysostomus! Hoc enim sufficit ad eos ad omnia adhortandos, & ad reddendos eos fortiores ad certamina.

Sed & eos reddebat magis familiares. Adde quod ita commoverit eos ad συμπάθειαν in vinculis, & ad beneficentiam succurrendi ipsi. Ἡ χάρις μεθ' ὑμῶν) Nempe Christi: Quod alibi additur, hic subauditur: quanquam Latinus etiam addidit, Domini nostri. Addidit autem praeter Graecorum Codicum fidem. Ad rem praesentem votum ita applicat Theophylactus: Si vobis praesto hac gratia fuerit, sive pressura affligant, sive praepediant compedes, & carcer coerceat, nil potuerunt hac vobis obesse.

Generale autem fine dubio est votum, quod solenne erat in literis Apostolo. Concludimus hanc epistolam cum Theodoreto: Eorum quoque vinculorum meminisse nos oportet semper, & quae ex memoria provenit, utilitatem percipere, & orare, ut non intremus in tentationem. Sin autem hoc acciderit, amare Divinam oeconomiam, & propriam animi magnitudinem ostendere, & Divinae gratiae auxilium invocare.

Ita enim fieri poterit, ut & concertemus, & vincamus, & quae a Christo promissa & renunciata sunt, assequamur. Cum quo Patri, cum sanctissimo Spiritu convenit gloria & magnificentia, nunc & semper & in secula seculorum. AMEN.

# 1 Thessalonians

## 1:1 Introduction
[Abraham Calov, Biblia Novi Testamenti Illustrata (Vol. 2, Part 1). English: machine translation, The Faith Received (Mere Orthodoxy); the original follows each comment.]
ANNOTATIONS ON THE FIRST TO THE THESSALONIANS.

Latin:

ANNOTATA AD PRIOREM AD THESSALONICENSES.

## 1:1 Introduction: Preface of Grotius
PREFACE OF GROTIUS.

This is indeed called the prior one, but as we have said in our commentary published heretofore, the order has been inverted by those who collected and arranged the epistles.

And the same thing happened here as in the Maccabees, where the first book is placed in the third position, and for that reason, because that book became known to the Greek Christians later (for the Latins have not yet received that book). In like manner, among the books of the New Testament, the epistle to the Hebrews as Pauline, and the Apocalypse as John's, received the last place, because the authority of those books was for a long time in obscurity or controversy.

What is called the posterior to the Thessalonians was written to Jason the Jew, a kinsman of Silas and Timothy, and to other Judaizing Christians, who, after the persecution that arose after the death of Stephen, had withdrawn from Judea into Syria and thence further away. But that epistle, because it contained the crimes of Gaius the Prince in very express words, but, as the matter required, harsh ones, could not be published without harm to the Church, while Claudius was reigning at Rome, that is, before Galba.

And so, when it began to be published, it began to be added to the Pauline epistles written to the Churches (for those written to individuals have the last place). But this epistle, which is therefore called the prior because it had already occupied its place before the other in the volume of Pauline epistles, was written not long after Paul had been at Thessalonica, certainly not at Athens, as some have inscribed at the end of the epistle, but at Corinth, as we shall say below.

Ionicenses ch. 3.

Paul testifies that he had sent Timothy to the Thessalonians, whose Church's faith had already been celebrated throughout the world: but Timothy, finally, after the Council of Jerusalem, he joined to himself, having been circumcised, Acts 16:3. And furthermore, many having been converted to the faith at Thessalonica, he arrived the following year at Athens, and thence at Corinth, Acts 17:11, whither Silas and Timothy migrated to him from Macedonia, Acts 18:5.

What is more clear than that the prior epistle to the Thessalonians was written long after the departure of Gaius? For the fourth and last year of the Principate of Gaius falls in the year 43 from the birth of CHRIST, whereas the Council of Jerusalem was finally celebrated in the year 51 of Christ.

Seeing that this chronology utterly overturns his own fabrication about the impiety of Gaius, predicted by the S. Apostle in the posterior to the Thessalonians, (Grotius) did not fear to commute the last to the first, and the sum to the bottom: Truly, from the prior to the Thessalonians he makes the posterior; from the Church of Thessalonica, to which the posterior is inscribed just as the prior, he deprives certain ones, Jason the Jew, and some other Judaizing Christians, who had withdrawn from Judea into Syria, and thence further away on account of the persecution that arose after the death of Stephen. But that it is posterior in time of writing, but not written prior to the Thessalonians, which is called the second to the Thessalonians, is testified both by the constant and unanimous opinion of Interpreters and of any Doctors whatsoever, and is convinced by the order received in all Greek, Syriac, Latin, and other language codices, which to have been inverted by those who collected and arranged the epistles is a vain and rash accusation against the judgment and approbation of the whole Church, for so many centuries, contrary to the age of the Apostle.

OBSERVATIONS.

Nothing else does Grotius here, than to procure faith, which it has none, for his own very recent fabrication, devised in favor of the Roman Anti-Christ , or rather to decline the absurdity of the same.

It is indeed thus: In the posterior epistle to the Thessalonians, the Apostle prophesies of no one other than Gaius, which place hitherto both the Ancients and recent Doctors have interpreted with great consensus concerning the Anti-Christ. But because in the prior to the Thessalonians

the third book of the Maccabees is irrelevant, for it was never received by the Church, but is rejected even by the Papists themselves as apocryphal.

Let the Epistle to the Hebrews also be placed in the last position, because some have doubted whether it is Pauline; but who has doubted that the latter to the Thessalonians is Pauline?

Yet Athanasius in his Synopsis and Theodoret in his Commentary placed it before the epistles written to individual persons, Timothy, Titus, and Philemon. Not to mention that Baronius, by reason of the time, made it the latest of all in the year 60, no. 18. But those who interpret the passage 2 Thess. 3:15 concerning the same do not admit that it became known later than the others. Finally, the Apocalypse of John attained the last place not so much because of its disputed authority as because of the reason of time and subject matter, since it is a Prophetic book.

After all the other books of the New Testament it was written, Athanasius, or Dorotheus in his Synopsis, did not doubt, nor Theophylact in his preface to the Gospel of John, nor Nicephorus in book II, ch. 42, book III, ch. 9, and others. But what need is there for conjectures, when in 2 Thess. 2:2 it is sufficiently insinuated that the epistle to the Thessalonians had already been given before, μήτε διὰ λόγου, μήτε δι' ἐπιστολῆς ὡς δι' ἡμῶν, neither by word, nor by epistle as if from us. For those who wished to persuade the Thessalonians of the imminent destruction of the world pretended that the Apostle had intended this in the former epistle, ch. 4:15-18, indicating that the last day would overtake him and others then living, surviving, and in the land of the living. When Samuel Maresius had proposed this against the Grotian interpretation in his dissertation on the Antichrist, Grotius did not attempt to refute anything in his appendix to the interpretation of the New Testament passages concerning the Antichrist: which is sufficiently clear, that Paul is not speaking of any true epistle, but of supposititious epistles.

Maresius responds in his Concordia discors, or Antichristo revelato, ch. IX, p. 148. If this were either the first, or at least among the first of Paul's epistles, at which time his name was not yet so famous, how can it be imagined that there was a danger then that supposititious letters would be passed off as his true ones, or rather that they were already supposititious?

Where it must be observed that the first of all Pauline epistles must be established as that which has hitherto been believed to be the second and later one to the Thessalonians. For the two epistles to the Thessalonians are the first of all. It is therefore not likely that deceivers would have wished to attribute to Paul an epistle that was not yet known, or that he was accustomed to give letters to the Churches. Add that in 2 Thess. 3:17 the Apostle writes: The salutation by my hand, Paul, this is the sign in the epistle, so I write. Which words would not fit well, unless he had already written at least one epistle. But he would not have written any, if this were the first to the Thessalonians. For it should have been said, not, so I write, but so I am about to write in every epistle.

Thess. 2:2 can be taken thus, that no one may move you from your mind or terrify you neither by Spirit, nor by word, nor by epistle, as if from us, namely, tradition or revelation, for instance, by the false interpretation of our epistle, its ψευδεπιγραφείαν (pseudepigraphy). For these three are the chief tricks of deceivers: to boast of the Spirit or revelation, to sell tradition as the unwritten Word, and to pervert the written Word of God by false interpretation, which sense is handed down by Lyranus: in another way thus, neither by epistle, etc., the preceding note: and by Thomas: Neither by epistle as if sent by us, which in the first epistle, unless it is well understood, seems to say, to inflate the coming of the Lord, as there, then we who live, although Tuelmannus alternatively [interprets it] as an epistle written in our name, or otherwise than we intended it to be understood. Erasmus has it thus: Paul does not want them to be moved neither by the Spirit as if proceeding from Paul, nor by word, brought in Paul's name, nor by epistle; he prefers to understand these things concerning the epistle supposed to be Paul's, with Chrysostom, Theophylact, and Ambrose; the passage is clearer in 2 Thess. 2:15: Hold the traditions, εἴτε διὰ λόγου, εἴτε δι' ἐπιστολῆς ἡμῶν, whether by word or by our epistle you have learned. For what could he have hinted more clearly, that this epistle is not the first, but that they had already received another prior one from the Apostle?

That which Grotius invents in his appendix, that this can be understood of another which has perished, is supported by no argument and no testimony. For all explain it unanimously concerning the former, and it testifies only to the self-contradiction of Grotius, as he affirms that this (the later one) is the former one, because then for the first time Paul's hand was seen in Thessalonica, 2 Thess. 3:17. How then before the first seen hand of Paul did they receive another still earlier one from the hand of Paul, which is now missing? But what will Grotius finally achieve with his fervent order of epistles?

For both epistles to the Thessalonians have the inscription in the name of Paul, and Silvanus, and Timothy, whom Paul joined to himself only after the council of Jerusalem, Acts 15:40, ch. 16:3, which was celebrated much after the exile of Caius. Who, therefore, after the death of Caius prophesied concerning the impiety of the same man as the Apostle in the epistle to the Thessalonians? Both are inscribed to the Church of Thessalonica, after it was founded by Paul; but Paul came to Thessalonica only then, and there sowed the seed of the Gospel, after he had been called into Macedonia by a Divine vision, Acts 16:9, ch. 17:1 seqq., that this happened after the principate of Caius cannot be denied; Grotius not attending to the former difficulty about Silvanus and Timothy, by which he could by no means have extricated himself: so that he may escape this one concerning the Church of Thessalonica being founded, he makes use of a new falsehood, namely, that the second epistle is not inscribed to the Church of Thessalonica gathered from the Greek Macedonians, but to certain Jews exiled there; but it is an absurd falsehood, an empty evasion. For the inscription of both epistles has exactly the same relation to the Church. But how will he feign certain exiled Jews out of the Church of Thessalonica converted by Paul to the faith of CHRIST: whom he calls Christianizing, when those who were scattered into Samaria after the death of Stephen through the persecution of Saul and others should rather be called converted and Christians? Grotius affirms that they withdrew from Judea not only into Syria, but also into Macedonia and even Thessalonica, and that under the very principate of Caius: But whence, I ask, will he give credibility to this assertion? The history of the Acts of the Apostles teaches the contrary.

For when Paul came to Thessalonica, he found no Christian Church there, and he preached the Gospel there for the first time. A synagogue of the Jews, not a Church of Christians, had been there, Acts 17:7, they came (Paul and Silas) to Thessalonica, where there was a synagogue of the Jews. But according to his custom Paul entered unto them, and for three sabbaths he reasoned, opening to them from the scriptures, and insinuating, that Christ must needs have suffered, and risen again from the dead, and that this is Jesus Christ, whom I ANNOUNCE to you. The

Jesus was therefore first announced to them, nor was anyone found there before this proclamation of the Gospel who believed in Jesus, let alone a certain Church, or exiles from the Jews converted to the faith of Jesus. Therefore Luke adds, "and some of them believed, and were joined to Paul and Silas, and of the devout Gentiles a great multitude" [Acts 17:4] (τῶν σεβομένων ἑλλήνων πολὺ πλῆθος). St. Luke indeed teaches that those who had been dispersed from the affliction that arose because of Stephen had traveled as far as Phoenicia, and Cyprus, and Antioch, Acts 11:19. But that they had reached Macedonia and the Thessalonians, and that Jason was also of their number, cannot be proven by any document. This, therefore, must likewise be relegated to the Grotian inventions.

Now if we look to the reign of Gaius, the fiction that the Pauline epistle to the Thessalonians was written in the second year of his principate cannot by any means be reconciled with chronology. Let us assume the calculation of Dionysius Petavius, whom Grotius extols above others. He has this to say regarding the death of Tiberius in Book V, Part II of his *Rationarium Temporum*, ch. 1, p. 265: "Amidst these honors, he dies, having cursed himself no less than all others, on the Kalends of April, in the 23rd year of his reign, in the 77th year of his life, in the year of Christ 37." Regarding his successor, Gaius Caesar Caligula, he writes thus in ch. II, p. 267: "Finally, on the 9th day before the Kalends of February, he was killed by Chaerea, Cassius, Tribune of the Praetorian cohort, and other conspirators in the year of Christ 41, having reigned for 3 years, 10 months, and 8 days, as Suetonius writes, ch. 59." Again, in Part II, Book IV, ch. V, p. 229: "The death of Tiberius," he says, "is attributed by Suetonius, Tacitus, Dio, and others to the year of the city 790, in the consulship of Acerronius and Pontius: 82 of Christ 37." But it is acknowledged by all interpreters and chronologists that the Council of Jerusalem was held not before the year 41, but in the year 51 of Christ, or certainly not under Gaius, but under the principate of Claudius. After which, finally, both Silvanus and Timothy were mentioned as Paul's companions and colleagues, 2 Thess. 1:1, as Luke testifies, and were taken on. Grotius must therefore have been bleary-eyed here when he appeals to Dionysius Petavius in his preface to 2 Thess. "According to the most accurate chronologists," he says, "among whom I hold in the first place the man of true learning and piety, Dionysius Petavius, Saul, who is also Paul, was converted to Christ in the thirty-sixth year of Tiberius." After that, Tiberius presided over Roman affairs for three years. But according to Petavius, Tiberius did not preside for 39 years, but 23. Paul, however, according to the same, was converted in the year of Christ 37, or the third year after the death of Christ and Stephen, as he has in Part I, Book 5, ch. I, p. 265, which year Petavius had made the year of Tiberius's death. This so palpable a parachronism, by which Grotius wished to assist his cause most poorly, this perversion of Petavius's opinion, is a clear indication of how the Great Man did not hesitate to mix and confuse everything, so that by any means he might defend the absurdity of his hypothesis. Although that calculation falsely attributed to Petavius cannot help him at all. For imagine that Tiberius presided for 39 years, in whose 15th year Christ was baptized, Luke 3, and in the 19th was crucified; if Paul was converted in the 36th year of Tiberius, that is, 17 years after the death of Christ, and Tiberius died two years later and Gaius succeeded him, it is necessary that Tiberius died in the 20th year after the death of Christ, that is, in the 54th year from the birth of Christ, which is the twelfth or thirteenth year of Claudius. For he succeeded, according to Petavius p. 270, after Gaius was removed from the living in the year of Christ 41. How, therefore, was the later epistle to the Thessalonians written in the second year of Gaius, that is, according to Petavius, in the year of Christ 39? For Gaius presided over the empire for four years, and Paul could predict in the same the impiety of Gaius in the aforementioned year of Christ 39, which

had already died 13 years before? But the Great Man takes another calculation from the same Jesuit's reckoning, and one that is completely different (so consistent is he with himself!) in the appendix: "He," he says, "who added much to the diligence of all others, even Cardinal Baronius, Dionysius Petavius, proves that Stephen was stoned in the year 31 after the birth of Christ, and that Saul, who is also Paul, was converted in the year 33, and went to Caesarea in the year 36, after which time Tiberius reigned over the Romans for three years." Here the Grotian *parorama* (oversight) seems to betray itself, because he confused the years of Tiberius with the years of Christ, or perhaps he wished to say that Paul was converted in the year 36, not of Tiberius, but of Christ. But in truth, not even in this way can the calculation of Petavius, whom he praises so highly, be consistent with itself. For a little earlier, the Jesuit taught from the *Rationarium Temporum* that Paul was converted not in the year 33 after the birth of Christ, but in the year 37, not six years before the death of Tiberius, but in the very year of his death, the 23rd of his reign, as Grotius says he asserts. These things I cannot reconcile.

How great a parachronism Grotius also committed when he wrote in the appendix that that dispersion was eight years prior to the Gaius principate, Marets shows clearly in *Antichristus Revelatus*, Book I, ch. 14, p. 233. Tiberius reigned for 22 years and about 7 months. That same Petavius, whom he thinks he is following, explicitly states this in the *Chronology of the Roman Emperors* appended to the book of Epiphanius *On Weights and Measures*, and criticizes Eusebius and Epiphanius, who had ascribed 23 full years to him. According to Luke, it was already the fifteenth year of Tiberius when John the Baptist began to perform his public duty, XVI according to the same Petavius, when Christ was baptized. To these add the four Passovers of Christ's course, which we have demonstrated from the Gospel and from Grotius himself, who furthermore acknowledges at Luke 12:7 that Christ taught for three years, even if he denies that Luke pertains to that. Thus the death of the Lord will fall in the 19th year of Tiberius. If, therefore, the dispersion which followed the death of Stephen was a full EIGHT years prior to the Gaius principate and the death of Tiberius, it is necessary either that Tiberius reigned for more than 27 years, contrary to the testimony of all historians, or that Stephen was stoned a full four years before the death of Christ, and before he was baptized. Nor is it probable that the persecution of the Jerusalem Church began while Tiberius was still alive, since he himself, as Tertullian testifies in *Apologeticus* ch. 5, having learned from Pilate's letters what had happened to Christ, proposed to the Senate that he be numbered among the gods, and threatened the accusers of the Christians with the penalty of death. Whence it does not seem consistent that the Jews would have dared anything publicly against the Christians while Tiberius was alive. If, therefore, the martyrdom of Stephen happened under Gaius, and therefore Paul was not converted before his second year, whom Petavius says was converted in the third year after the death of Stephen, how could he have prophesied in the second year of Gaius about the impiety of Gaius that was soon to be revealed, when he himself had not even become a Christian before the second year of Gaius?

Furthermore, that Timothy was joined to Paul already in the second year of Gaius, in which Grotius wishes the epistle which is inscribed as the second to the Thessalonians to have been written, just as he is joined in its title, is by no reason consistent with the truth. Grotius indeed invents in the appendix, concerning the mother of Timothy and Timothy himself, that they were from that dispersion which took place after the death of Stephen. But Timothy was a Lycaonian, not a Jew: And at the time of that *diaspora* it was not yet established among the faithful that Gentiles were to be taken in, at which time Timothy must also have still been a boy; or at least he was not of an age at which he could be joined to Paul in writing to the fugitive Thessalonians.

Thessalonian epistle. Grotius also imagines that he brought that dispersion, Silas or Silvanus. But since all who had been dispersed at that time are said to have gone on the way, Acts 8:4, ch. 11:19, 20, and it is read of no one that he returned, what fact is it that Silas returned to Jerusalem? And how could he have been joined to Paul in the letters to the Thessalonians according to the year of Gaius, who was not added as a companion to Paul until long after the passing of Gaius except in the Council of Jerusalem.

It is added that it was necessary for Paul the Apostle, as well as his colleagues Silvanus and Timothy, to have been present with the Thessalonians before they wrote this epistle to them, who indeed arrived in Thessalonica only after the Council of Jerusalem, and after Paul was called by God into Macedonia, as is evident from Acts 16 and 17. The very words of the epistle testify to this. For the Thessalonians were also called by their preaching, and are commanded to hold to what they had received from them by word of mouth, 2 Thess. 2:13. To which he also called you THROUGH OUR GOSPEL, and v. 14, therefore brothers stand firm, and hold to the traditions which you have learned whether by WORD, or by our epistle: To which words Theodoret: You have the doctrine as a rule, the words which we delivered to you, which we also preached to you PRESENT, and wrote to you ABSENT. But when did Paul, Silvanus, and Timothy preach PRESENT to the Thessalonians, unless when, having traveled through Amphipolis and Apollonia, they came to Thessalonica, and some of the Jews, and a great multitude of Greeks, joined themselves to Paul and Silas, Acts 17:1, 4. To the rule of the same presence and conversation in the Church of Thessalonica, Paul, Silvanus, and Timothy recall the Thessalonians, ch. 3, v. 7 seqq.
