For you yourselves know how you ought to imitate US; because we were not idle AMONG YOU, nor did we eat bread from anyone without payment, but in labor and toil, working night and day, so that we might not burden any of you. Not as though we did not have the authority, but that we might give ourselves as a pattern to you to imitate us. For even when WE WERE AMONG YOU, we DECLARED THIS TO YOU, that if anyone does not want to work, neither let him eat. With what face, therefore, can it be denied in the Church of Thessalonica, as to which this epistle is directed, and in which it is evident from the epistle 1 to the Thess. ch. 2:9 and ch. 4:6, 11 that those things happened, where those things are read in almost the same words, that Paul with these colleagues had been present before he wrote it? But no sane person would say that they were present with them in the second year of Gaius. Nor can it be reconciled with the history of the Acts of the Apostles that the Church was gathered at Thessalonica, or that Paul was at Thessalonica with Silvanus and Timothy, before the Council of Jerusalem held in the ninth year of Claudius, the successor of Gaius.

Since, therefore, the inventions of Grotius are refuted—that the second epistle to the Thessalonians preceded the first in order of time, that it was written in the second year of Gaius Caligula, and before Paul had come to Thessalonica, that it was written to a few exiles from the dispersion after the death of Stephen, who had not yet formed a congregation, in which, both in the refutation of the Annotators on chapter 2 of the second epistle to the Thessalonians, and in the Antichrist revealed, he whom he traduces by the name of Borborite in the appendix stopped the mouth of Grotius—it is sufficiently evident already that the second is indeed the second, and was inscribed to a Church already established, and was written only after Paul had come to Thessalonica with Silvanus and Timothy, which arrival, by Grotius's own admission, happened long after the times of Gaius, indeed after the ninth year of Claudius, what is more certain than that the former words of this prophecy in 2 Thess. 2 cannot be understood of Gaius in any way, just as the latter cannot be understood of Simon Magus, whom Grotius relegates to the second year of Claudius: unless he maintains that Paul here only predicted past events, which would be the mark of a seducer, not a Doctor of the Gentiles, a charlatan, not an Apostle, as Marefius rightly says. There is, therefore, no reason why he should reject the cause of the changed order of both epistles to the Thessalonians in the biblical code to the fear of Christians in the primitive Church; which is in truth also futile.

For what danger threatened Christians during the reign of Claudius, such that this epistle, if written under Gaius, could not be published? Did not the Senate, after Gaius was dead, turn its mind to liberty, and did not Claudius rescind the acts of Gaius, remove the images, and melt down all the coins stamped with his likeness, of which Suetonius and Dio bear witness? What danger would have been feared on account of this epistle, since all the things which Grotius now snatches at for Gaius are so arranged that they neither refer to Gaius, nor has it ever occurred to anyone for sixteen centuries, through a fever, to refer them to him? What danger would there have been in the prophecy being spread after the death of Gaius among Christians, which had preceded concerning him, when Philo the Jew published his Philippic, which he inscribed on the embassy to Gaius, written in such open words against the same, with impunity? It would also be like a prodigy that under Claudius and Nero the matter was so public that no one, even among the Gentiles who might have happened upon the Pauline epistle, would not have immediately recognized Gaius in it, from which danger would have been feared by the Christians. But with the Caesars extinct and Nero, the last of them, confessed, such a forgetfulness of things done thirty years before had seized everyone that from that time to our own age no Christian has existed who could perceive the genuine meaning of the prophecy, which had been entirely dealt with without the spectacles and work of Grotius. Finally, it is unheard of that any epistle or book in the Canonical scriptures should be called prior, at least for the reason that it had already occupied its place before another epistle or book in the volume of Apostolic epistles and in the Biblical code.

But let us dismiss the paradoxes and the most inept inventions of Grotius, which he devised to substitute Gaius into the place of the Roman Anti-Christ in the later epistle to the Thessalonians.

But concerning the time of the writing of the first epistle, we do not disagree with him, namely that it was written not long after Paul had been at Thessalonica. But he arrived at Thessalonica in the year of Christ LI, which was the Xth of Claudius. For Petavius is the author in P. II. L. IV. of the rationarium of times, page 230, that Claudius began to reign in the year of Christ XLI. According to Baronius, the first year of Claudius falls in the year of Christ LXIII, and in the year of Christ LI, the IXth of Claudius, the Council of Jerusalem was celebrated…, in which year Baronius asserts in the year of Christ II, n. LXXIII, that Paul and Silas also left Philippi and came to Thessalonica for the first time: concerning which Luke Acts 17:1. But in the following year, LI, he taught at Athens, where he awaited Silas and Timothy, Acts 18.

As for the place of writing, not only those who added the final clauses, but also Athanasius, Theodoret, and Oecumenius and others, judged that it was written at Athens, namely that Paul, just as he sent Timothy to Thessalonica from Athens , so also, while he was staying there, wrote to the same Thessalo nicenses the first epistle, 1 Thess. 3, v. 1. But Grotius preferred to follow Baronius to the year of Christ 52, n. 14, just as he did Beza: that it was given at Corinth by Paul, rather than at Athens.

With whom also agree Benedictus Pererius, and Justinianus, as we have warned in the prolegomena to the epistle to the Romans, as well as Cornelius à Lapide, and others. And Beza observes at the end of the epistle, in the Clarmontano …nt codex, as it is in most Greek codices, which the Latin and German ones follow: πρὸς θεσσαλονικεῖς πρώτην ἐγράφη ἀπὸ Ἀθηνῶν, but without mention of the place in this way: Ἐπλερώθη πρὸς θεσσαλονικεῖς πρώτη.

Beza urges this argument primarily, because Paul in the second chapter makes mention of Timothy, from whom he endured being left alone at Athens, when he sent him to the Thessalonians. Therefore Silas had not then returned to Paul. He adds then, that Timothy had returned to him again, from which he had understood what the constancy of the Thessalonians was.

But it is clear from the Acts of the Apostles, when Paul having departed from Athens, where he had substituted Silas and Timothy while waiting, had come to Corinth, and had been occupied there for some time, then at last they returned to him, by whose arrival he was also greatly confirmed, Acts 17, v. 14 and 16. Therefore Sylvanus is that same person whom Luke calls Silas, and when they had come to Corinth, and Timothy, who had been sent from Athens again (which Luke passed over) to Thessalonica by Paul, had reported the state of the Church of the Thessalonians, this epistle was sent to them in the common name of the three of them from Corinth.

But Silas, who is also Sylvanus, it appears from the Acts of the Apostles, was left at Berrhoea with Timothy, and having returned again from Athens to Thessalonica, he finally assumed him on his return, so that they might come to Corinth together.

But in that argument many things are assumed precariously; it is also false that Paul was left alone at Athens, with Timothy having been sent away.

That is not held in 1 Thess. 3, 1, but those two, Paul and Sylvanus, were left alone.

However, that argument pleased Justinianus, as having proceeded from a heretic; indeed also Baronius; but not Alphonso Salmeron, who in Tome XV, disp. I, on the Epistle to the Thessalonians, denies that it is solid, since Paul could have gone again from Corinth to Athens, and written it there.

Crocius replies for Beza; that that journey cannot be proven.

For it is certain that Paul had left Timothy with Silas in Macedonia; when he was setting out for Athens, and from there had given a command to those who were escorting him to Silas and Timothy, that they should come to him as quickly as possible, and had waited for them there, Acts 17, v. 14, 15, 16. It is also certain that Silas and Timothy, returning from Macedonia at the command of Paul, did not find Paul at Athens, but because he had already departed from there, at Corinth, Acts 18, 1, 5. Furthermore, it is certain that Paul and Silas had sent Timothy from Athens to Thessalonica.

For this is testified by λευκάδι φωνῇ, 1 Thess. 3, v. 1, 2. Wherefore no longer bearing this (your) longing, we thought it best to be left alone at Athens: And we sent Timothy our brother, etc.

Who are those who thought it best that they be left alone at Athens? Who sent Timothy from Athens into Macedonia, or to the Thessalonians? Certainly not Paul alone, but Sylvanus, who is joined to him in the title of the epistle with him.

Although the primary roles were Paul's, just as the Apostle speaks of himself individually later in v. 5: Wherefore I also no longer bearing your longing, I sent, etc.

But from where did Paul and Sylvanus send Timothy?

Not from Corinth, to which Silas and Timothy had first come to Paul from Macedonia, Acts 18, 1, 5, and from where after a year and a half stay in that city he set out for Ephesus, and further to Caesarea and Antioch, and into Galatia and Phrygia, Acts 18, 18, 19, 22. Now the Apostle had indeed returned to Ephesus, Acts 19, 1, in which place he stayed for two years and three months, v. 8 and 10, and there in the Spirit he proposed to himself to travel through Macedonia and Achaia, and to head to Jerusalem, and sent Timothy and Erastus from there into Macedonia: since he had still stayed for a time in Asia, v. 22. But this is clearly another, much later, and from a different place, sending away of Timothy with Erastus.

We have already noted that Timothy alone was sent by Paul and Sylvanus to Thessalonica. It would be necessary, therefore, for those three, when this mission was taking place, to have stayed at Athens: and therefore it is necessary that Paul, after he had arrived at Corinth to Silas and Timothy, set out for Athens together with them.

Which we now judge to be entirely evident.

That stay of a year and a half among the Corinthians can well consist with a short excursion to the Athenians.

For Athens was distant from Corinth only eighteen miles. Whether Timothy, returning from Macedonia to Paul and Sylvanus, found them at Athens, or indeed at Corinth, and whether from there, or from here after the return of Timothy, Paul, Sylvanus, and Timothy wrote this epistle, it is not so clear to see in the scriptures.

But that the epistle could have been sent from there or from here, there should be no doubt. That Beza's argument is not entirely solid, so that for its sake Justinianus with Pererius and Cornelius à Lapide had to depart from the common opinion, is now placed on the table.

But that this epistle was written at Athens rather than at Corinth, is confirmed not only by the customary final προσθήκη, which the variation of one codex cannot move, and the authority of the ancients, and the consensus of most recent writers, but primarily by the longing of Paul and Sylvanus, which they could scarcely endure, to experience the state of the Church of the Thessalonians from Timothy, whom they had sent away to Athens, soon to return, for which reason they stayed at Athens as a closer place; for they could not have had an inconvenience in lodging with Dionysius, or Damaris, and others converted there: and also the words of the Apostle εὐδοκήσαμεν καταλειφθῆναι ἐν Ἀθήναις μόνοι: ὅ ἐ from which it appears that they wished to remain alone, and to stay at Athens, until the return of Timothy.

Athens was distant from Berrhoea by sea 66 miles by journey, from there 15 miles still remained to Thessalonica. Thus, therefore, going and returning from Athens to Thessalonica, and from Thessalonica in turn to Athens, about 160 miles had to be covered by Timothy partly by ship, partly by foot journey, for which at least two weeks were required.

If he also stayed at Thessalonica for two weeks, within the space of one month he could return to Athens to Paul and Sylvanus, and from there with them dispatch this epistle to the Thessalonian Church.

And so much for the place of writing.

Although the time cannot be defined so precisely, it appears, however, that the epistle was not written in the first three years from the conversion of the Apostle, Gal. 1, 17, 18, nor in the following 14 years, Gal. 2, 1, when at that time he had not yet come to Thessalonica, Acts 17, whence Baronius refers the writing to the tenth year of the Apostleship of Paul, 52 of Christ, 10 of Claudius.

That this is the first of all the Apostolic epistles, both ancient and modern Doctors generally agree, Theodoret, Chrysostom, & Ussher, Crocius, & most of our own, as well as the Pontifical Cornelius a Lapide and others. The occasion of the writing was the highest [concern] for the faith of the Church of Thessalonica, recently planted by Paul, Acts 17, which had spread everywhere, 1 Thess. 1:8. In which, therefore, he wished to confirm them, not only by the mission of Timothy first, 1 Thess. 3:2, when he himself was hindered from visiting them, as he had twice proposed to himself, 1 Thess. 2:18, but also subsequently by the dispatch of this letter, lest any among them should waver in the faith because of tribulations, and that he might testify his joy concerning their constancy, after he had been made certain of the same by Timothy upon his return, 1 Thess. 3:3, 8. Then [there was] the doubt which had arisen among the Thessalonians concerning the coming of the Lord, regarding those who are found surviving in the same, about which the Apostle informs his Thessalonians, ch. 4:13, and at the same time exhorts them to vigilance, since the day of the Lord is to come unexpectedly.

The occasion, therefore, of the epistle and its argument Theodoret has assigned thus: The Thessalonians indeed hold the first place in Macedonia: they received the salutary preaching willingly and eagerly. But the divine Apostle here also laid the foundations of piety. While the Jews indeed contradicted and openly resisted, but labored in vain, for the Gospel overcame the waves and tempests. When blessed Paul had avoided their snares, and came from Thessalonica to Beroea, and from Beroea sailed to Athens. But since he was perpetually concerned for those who had believed, he sent the most blessed Timothy from Athens to Thessalonica, that he might support and confirm them, and make them more powerful against all the machinations of their adversaries. He, having returned, praised indeed their impregnable faith: but said that they had need of some doctrine of exhortation concerning certain questions which were being moved among them. He wrote therefore the epistle, first indeed praising the firmness of their faith: then exhorting them to expect the resurrection of the dead: but not to inquire too curiously concerning the coming of the Lord.

Furthermore, he also exhibited to them an exhortation of moral doctrine. The whole epistle is exhortatory, first to constancy and progress in the Christian religion, then also to holiness of life, yet intermixed with information concerning the resurrection of the dead, which is indeed directed to the παράκλησιν (consolation) of those grieving over the dead.

According to Camerarius, the type of the epistle is friendly and laudatory and self-commendatory, but if you look at the scope, it is properly hortatory, both to constancy in the faith, which is spent on the first three chapters, and to holiness in life in the remaining two chapters. As for the former exhortation, it is indirect, because by thanksgiving, commendation, the sending away of Timothy, and the consolation received thence, the desire for more abundant present information, and the vow of fuller confirmation, they are easily excited to perseverance in the acknowledged faith. But the latter exhortation is direct.

In the former, the first chapter is laudatory concerning their faith, which has spread through the world. The second is connective, both of the Apostolic proclamation and of maternal and paternal affection toward them, and of their obedience and patience in tribulations. The third is friendly, both because of the mission of Timothy out of love and solicitude toward them, and because of the exultation and thanksgiving for the joyful news of their faith; and because of the prayer that God may direct his way to them, and comfort their hearts.

The remaining two chapters exhort partly to the observation of the precepts delivered, especially with regard to impurity, and the visitation of injustice, brotherly love, and the tranquil dispatch of their labors: partly to the flight from excessive mourning over the dead, together with information concerning the rapture of the dead and the living to meet the Lord, ch. 4: partly to vigilance, sobriety, and preparation for the coming of the Lord: To which are subjoined various admonitions, and vows, and salutations,

PARS I. EPISTOLAE Exhortation to constancy in the faith.

Latin:

PRÆFATIO GROTII.

Prior quidem haec dicitur, sed ut nos in nostra edita antehac commentatione diximus, inversus est ordo ab iis, qui epistolas collegerunt & digesserunt.

Idemque hic evenit, quod in Macabaicis, ubi liber primus tertio loco est positus, & ideo, quod serius Christianis Graecis, (nam Latini eum librum nondum recepere) is liber innotuit. Pari modo inter Novi Testamenti libros epistola ad Ebraeos quasi Paulina, & Apocalypsis quasi Johannis ultimum acceperunt locum, quia eorum librorum auctoritas diu in obscuro aut controverso fuit.

Quae dicitur posterior ad Thessalonicenses, scripta est ad Jasonem Judaeum, Silae & Timotheae cognatum, & alios Judaeos Christianizantes, qui orta post Stephani mortem persecutione ex Judaea in Syriam inde longius concesserant. Ea vero epistola quia continebat facinora Caji Principis, verbis valde expressis, sed, quantum res exigebat, asperis, publicari fine malo Ecclesiae non potuit, regnante Romae Claudio domo, id est, ante Galbam.

Itaque cum primum publicari coepit, tunc epistolis Paulis ad Ecclesias scriptis (nam ad singulos scriptae postremum habent locum) coepit addi. Haec vero epistola, quae ideo prior dicitur, quod ante alteram jam locum suum occupasset in epistolarum Paulinarum volumine, scripta est non multo, postquam Thessalonicae Paulus fuerat, non sane Athenis, ut quidam epistolae fini adscripsere, sed Corinthi, ut dicemus infra.

Ionicenses cap. 3.

Paulus Timotheum ad Thessalonicenses, cujus Ecclesiae fides per orbem jam celebrata fuit, se ablegasse testatur: Timotheum autem demum post concilium Hierosolymit. circumcisum sibi adjunxit, Act. 16, 3. & porro multis Thessalonicae ad fidem conversis, anno sequenti Athenas pervenit, ac dehinc Corinthum, Act. 17, 11. quo ad eundem e Macedonia Silas & Timotheus migrarunt, Act. 18, 5. quid luculentius est, quam longe post Caji excessum priorem epistolam ad Thessalonicenses exaratam esse?

Incidit enim annus quartus & ultimus Cajani Principatus in annum XLIII. a nativitate CHRISTI, quum concilium Hierosolymitanum demum LI. Christi anno celebratum sit.

Hanc chronologiam quum penitus evertere suum commentum de Caji impietate, à S. Apostolo posteriori ad Thessalonicenses praedicta, videt (Grotius), ultima primis, summa imis commutare veritus non est: Nimirum e priori ad Thessalonicenses facit posteriorem; ex Ecclesia Thessalonicensi, cui posterior aeque ut prior inscripta est, privat os quosdam, Jasonem Judaeum, & alios nonnullos Judaeos Christianizantes, qui ex Judaea in Syriam, & inde longius ob persecutionem post mortem Stephani ortam concesserint. Sed posteriorem esse scriptionis tempore, non vero prius scriptam eam, quae altera dicitur ad Thessalonicenses, tum constans & unanimis Interpretum & quorumvis Doctorum sententia testatur, tum ordo in omnibus codicibus Graecis, Syriacis, Latinis, aliarumque linguarum receptus convincit, quem inversum esse ab iis, qui epistolas collegerunt & digesserunt, vana ac temeraria est accusatio totius Ecclesiae judicio & approbationi, per tot secula, inde ab Apostoli aetate contraria.

OBSERVATIONES.

Nihil aliud hic agit Grotius, quam ut commento suo nuperrimo, in gratiam Anti-Christi Romani excogitato fidem, quam nullam habet, conciliet, aut absurditatem ejusdem potius declinet.

Id vero ita habet: In posteriori ad Thessalonicenses epistola non de alio, quam Cajo vaticinari Apostolum, quem locum hactenus & Veteres & recentiores Doctores magno consensu de Anti-Christo interpretati sunt. Quia vero priori ad Thessalonicenses

Liber tertius e Maccabaicis nihil ad rem facit, hic enim nunquam receptus est ab Ecclesia, sed ceu apocryphus ab ipsis etiam Pontificiis reprobatur.

Sit etiam epistola ad Ebraeos ideo, quod nonnulli, an Paulina sit, dubitarint, postremo loco collocata; sed quis dubitavit de posteriori ad Thessalonicenses, eam Paulinam esse?

Istam tamen Athanasius in Synopsi & Theodoretus in Comment. præmisere Paulinis ad singulares personas scriptis, Timotheum, Titum, Philemonem. Ne dicam, quod Baronius eam temporis ratione novissimam omnium fecerit ad ann. LX. n. 18. Serius autem aliis innotuisse eandem non admittunt, qui locum 2. Thess. 3, 15. de eadem interpretantur. Apocalypsis denique Johannis non tam propter autoritatem ejus controversam, quam ob temporis & materie rationem, quia Propheticus liber est, ultimam consecuta est locum.

Post omnes alios libros Novi Testamenti scriptam non dubitarunt Athanasius, aut Dorotheus in Synopsi, nec Theophylactus in præfat. in Evangel. Johan. nec Nicephorus libr. II. cap. 42. libr. III. cap. 9. aliique. Quid vero conjecturis opus, quum 2. Thess. 2, 2. id satis insinuatur, prius jam epistolam ad Thessalonicenses datam, μήτε διὰ λόγου, μήτε δι' ἐπιστολῆς ὡς δι' ἡμῶν, neque per sermonem, neque per epistolam tanquam a nobis. Id enim prætendebant, qui imminentem mundi interitum Thessalonicenses persuadere cupiebant, epistola priori hoc voluisse Apostolum, cap. 4, 15. 16. 17. 18. indicatum, novissimam diem ipsum aliosque tum viventes, superstites, & in vivis deprehensuram esse. Quod quum adversus interpretationem Grotianam Samuel Maresius in dissertatione de Antichristo proposuisset, ne quicquam Grotius in appendice ad interpretationem locorum Novi Testamenti de Anti-Christo diluere conatus est: quod satis apertum sit, non de vera aliqua epistola, sed de supposititiis epistolis Paulum loqui.

Respondet Maresius in concordia discordie, vel Antichristo revelato cap. IX. pag. 148. Si hæc vel prima, vel saltem inter primas Pauli epistolas erat, quo tempore nondum ita celebre illi nomen, qui potest fingi, periculum tum fuisse, ne supposititia literæ pro veris illius obtruderentur, imo revera supposititias jam fuisse.

Ubi observandum, primam omnino sic statuendam esse omnium epistolarum Paulinarum, quæ altera & posterior hactenus credita est ad Thessalonicenses. Nam epistolæ duæ ad Thessalonicenses sunt omnium primæ. Non ergo verisimile fuisse, aut supponere voluisse seductores Paulo epistolam, quæ nondum constabat, literas ad Ecclesias dare consuevisse. Adde quod 2. Thess. 3, 17. scribat Apostolus: Salutatio manu mea Pauli, hoc signum est in epistola, ita scribo. Quæ verba non satis convenirent, nisi jam aliquam ad minimum epistolam scripsisset. Sed nullam scripsisset, si hæc prima foret ad Thessalonicenses. Dicendum enim fuisset, non, ita scribo, sed ita scripturus sum in omni epistola .

Verba ergo 2. Thess. 2, 2. ita possunt accipi, ne quis vos dimoveat a vestro sensu aut terreat neque per Spiritum, neque per sermonem, neg; per epistolam, tanquam a nobis, scilicet traditium aut revelatum, puta per epistolæ nostrae ψευδεπιγραφείαν fallam interpretationem. Hæc enim tria præcipua sunt seductorum τεχνήδεια, jactare Spiritum seu revelationem, venditare traditionem ceu Verbum non scriptum, & depravare falsa interpretatione scriptum vel verbum Dei scriptum, qui sensus traditur a Lyrano: alio modo sic, neque per epistolam & c. notam praecedentem: & a Thoma: Neque per epistolam tanquam per nos missam, quod in prima epistola, nisi bene intelligatur, videtur dicere, inflare Domini adventum, ut ibi, deinde nos, qui vivimus, etsi Tuelmannus alternative per epistolam nostro nomine scriptam, vel aliter, quam volebamus intellectam. Erasmus sic habet: Paulus non vult eos commoveri neq; per Spiritum tanquam a Paulo profectum, neque per sermonem, Pauli nomine allatum, neg; p;r epistolam malit haec de epistola, Paulo supposita, cum Chrysostomo, Theophylacto, & Ambrosio astro intelligere, luculentior est locus, 2. Thess. 2, 15. Retinete traditiones, εἴτε διὰ λόγου, εἴτε δι' ἐπιστολῆς ἡμῶν, sive per sermonem, sive per epistolam nostram didicistis. Quid enim clarius innuere poterat, epistolam hanc non esse primam, sed eos jam aliam priorem ab Apostolo accepisse?

Quod comminiscitur Grotius in appendice, hoc de alia, qua perierit, intelligi posse, neque argumento ullo, neque ullo testimonio constat. Omnes enim ὁμοθυμαδὸν de priori explicant, & ἑαυτομαχίαν tantum Grotii testatur, utpote qui hanc (posteriorem) priorem ideo esse affirment, quia tum primum Thessalonicæ visa Pauli manus, 2. Thess. 1, 3, 17. Quomodo ergo ante primum visam Pauli manum aliam adhuc priorem a manu Pauli acceperunt, quæ nunc desideretur? Sed quod proficiet tandem Grotius cum infervo suo epistolarum ordine?

Nam utraque ad Thessalonicenses habet ἐπιγραφὴν nomine Pauli, & Silvani, & Timothei, quem utrumque sibi junxit Paulus demum post concilium Hierosolymitanum, Act. 15, 40. cap. 16, 3. quod multum post Caji exilium celebratum est. Qui ergo post excessum Caji de impietate ejusdem vaticinatus est Apostolus in epistola ad Thessalonicenses? Utraque inscripta est Thessalonicensi Ecclesiae, postquam ea fundata est a Paulo; qui vero demum Thessalonicam venit, ibique femina iparsit Evangelii, postquam vocatus est in Macedonia visione Divina, Act. 16, 9. cap. 17, 1. seqq. quam contigisse post Caji principatum negari non potest; Grotius non advertens priorem de Silvano & Timotheo difficultatem, qua se minime expedire potuisset: hanc de Ecclesia Thessalonicensi fieri fundata ut effugiat, novo ἐψεύματι utitur, nimirum epistolam alteram non inscriptam esse Ecclesiae Thessalonicensi e Graecis Macedonibus collectae, sed Judais quibusdam illic exulantibus, sed ineptum est ἐψεύμα, vanum χενοφύγετον. Nam eadem prorsus ratione ad Ecclesiam habet utriusque epistolae inscriptio. Quomodo autem ex Ecclesia Thessalonicensi a Paulo ad fidem CHRISTI conversa effinget exules quosdam Judaeos: quos Christianizantes vocat, quum conversi & Christiani potius dicendi sint, qui post Stephani obitum per Sauli & aliorum persecutionem dispersi erant in Samariam? Ex Judaeon non in Syriam tantum, sed in Macedoniam etiam ac Thessalonicam eos concessisse, idque sub ipsius Caji principatu affirmat Grotius: Sed unde, obsecro, fidem assertioni faciet? Contrarium docet historia actuum Apostolicorum.

Cum enim Paulus Thessalonicam venit, nullam ibi Ecclesiam Christianos invenit, ac primum illic Evangelium praedicavit. Synagoga Judaeorum non Ecclesia Christianorum illic fuerat, Act. 17, 7. venerunt (Paulus & Silas) Thessalonicam, ubi erat synagoga Judaeorum. Secundum consuetudinem autem Paulus introivit ad eos, & per sabbata tria disseruit, eis ex scripturis adaperiens, & insinuans, quia Christum oportuit pati, & surgere a mortuis, & quia hic est Jesus Christus, quem ego ANNUNCIO vobis.

Primum ergo illis annunciatus est Iesus, nec repertus ibi quisquam ante hoc Evangelii præconium, qui crederet in Iesum, nedum Ecclesia quædam, aut exules è Iudæis ad fidem Iesu conversis. Ideo addit Lucas, & quidam ex iis crediderunt, & adiuncti sunt Paulo & Sile, & de colentibus gentilibusque Ecclesia magna τῶν σεβομένων ἑλλήνων πολὺ πλῆθος. Docet utique S. Lucas, eos, qui dispersi fuerant ex afflictione orta ob Stephanum, transiisse usque in Phœniciam, & Cyprum, & Antiochiam, Act. 11. 19. Sed in Macedoniam & ad Thessalonicenses eos pervenisse, Iasonem quoque ex illorum numero fuisse, nullo documento probari potest. Hoc ergo itidem inter commenta Grotiana reponendum.

Iam fi ad imperium Caji respicimus, nullo pacto cum chronologia in gratiam redigi poterit figmentum de Paulina ad Thessalonicenses epistola scriptum secundo Principatus eius anno. Assumamus Dionysii Petavii computum, quem præ aliis extollit Grotius. Is de morte Tiberii L. V. partis II. rationarii temporum cap. 1. p. 265. ita habet: Inter hæc decora non magis omnibus aliis, quam sibi execratus ipse moritur Calendis Apr. imperii anno 23. Chriſti 37. vitæ agens octavum & septuagesimum. De successore vero Cajo Cæsare Caligula cap. II. p. 267. sic scribit: Ad extremum 9. Kal. Febr. à Chærea, Cassio, Tribuno cohortis Prætoriæ & aliis coniuratis interfectus est anno Christi 41. cum imperasset annis 3. mensibus 10. ac diebus 8. ut scribit Suetonius c. 59. Div. 59. Rursus parte II. libr. IV. cap. V. p. 229. Mors Tyberii, inquit, à Suetonio, Tacito, Dione, aliisque tribuitur anno u.c. 790. Acerronio & Pontio coss: Iuliano 82. Christi 37. At Concilium Hierosolymitanum non ante annum 41. sed anno 51. Christi, aut certe non sub Cajo, sed sub Claudii Principatu habitum esse in confesso est penes omnes Interpretes & Chronologos. Post quòd demum & Silvanus & Timotheus commemorati ceu Pauli socii & collegæ, 2. Theff. 1. 1. Luca teste, assumpti sunt. Cucurbitas ergo hic lippiisse Grotium oportet, cum ad Dionysium Petavium provocat in procem. 2. ad Theffal. Secundum accuratissimos, inquiens, chronologos, in quibus præcipuo loco habeo Virum vere eruditionis & pietatis Dionysium Petavium, conversus est ad Christum Saulus, qui & Paulus, anno Tiberii trigesimo sexto. Post id tres annos rebus Romanis præfuit Tiberius. Atqui secundum Petavium Tiberius non 39. annis præfuit, sed 23. Paulus vero conversus secundum eundem est anno Christi 37. vel tertio à morte Christi Stephanique, ut habet part. I. l. 5. c. I. p. 265. quem annum emortualem Tiberii fecerat Petavius. Hic tam palpabilis parachronismus, quo causæ pessime succurrere voluit Grotius, hæc sententiæ Petavii perversio luculento est indicio, quomodo miscere ac confundere Vir Magnus omnia non dubitarit, ut quacunque ratione absurditatem suæ hypotheseos tueretur. Quanqua ille Petavio falfo tributus calculus nihil eū juvare possit, Nam finge, 39. annis præfuisse Tiberium, cujus anno 15. Christus baptizatus est, Luc. 3. anno 19. crucifixus, si Paulus conversus anno 36. Tiberii, id est, 17. à morte Christi, ac biennio post defuncto Tiberio successit Cajus, neceffum est 20. anno à morte Christi defunctum esse Tyberium, hoc est, nativitate Christi anno 54. qui duodecimus, vel tertius & decimus est Claudii annus. Succeffit enim secundum Petavium p. 270. Cajo vivis exempto anno Christi 41. Quomodo ergo fecundo Caji anno exarata est pofterior epistola ad Thessalonicenses, hoc est, secundum Petavium anno Christi 39? Nam Cajus per quatuor annos imperio præfuit, ac prædicere in eadem Paulus potuit impietatem Caji antedicto Christi 39. qui

iam ante 13. annos defunctus erat? Sed alium init ex ejusdem Iesuitæ calculo computum Vir Magnus, eumque prorsus diversum (ita sibi constat!) in appendice: Is, inquit, qui ad omnium aliorum etiam Cardinalis Baronii diligentiam plurimum adjecit, Dionysius Petavius probat, Stephanum lapidatum anno post Christum natum 31. Saulum, qui & Paulus, conversum anno 33. ivisse Cæsaream anno 36 post quod tempus imperasse Romanis Tyberium per annos tres. Hic prodere se videtur Grotianū παρόραμα, quod confuderit annos Tyberii cum annis Christi, aut fortassis dicere voluerit, Paulum anno non Tiberii sed Christi 36. conversum esse. Verum enimvero ne fic quidem costare sibi potest Petavii, quem tantopere laudat, computus. Nam loco paulo ante è Rationario temporum docuit Iesuita, Paulum non anno 33. post Christum natum, sed anno 37. conversum esse, non sex annis ante mortem Tiberii, sed ipso mortis ejus anno, imperii 23. ut eundem af-ferere ait Grotius. Quæ ego conciliare non possum.

Quantus etiam parachronismus Grotii commiffus fit, cum in appendice fcripfit, disperſionem illam, poft Stephani mortem octennio fuiſſe priorem Cajano Principatu, Marefius luculenter oftendit in Antichrifto revelato l. I. cap. 14. p. 233. Tiberius imperavit annos 22. & 7. menfes, aut circiter. Ille ipfe Petavius, quem putat fe fequi, diferte hoc habet in Romanorum Imperatorum Chronologia ad librum Epiphanii de ponderibus & menfuris, carpique Eufebium & Epiphanium, qui 23. annos integros illi adfcripferant. Juxta Lucam jam erat annus decimus quintus Tiberii, cum Johannes Baptista munere fuo publico fungi capit. XVI. fecundum eundem Petavium, cum Chriſtus eft baptizatus. His adde quatuor paſchata curriculi Chriſti, quæ demonſtravimus ex Evangelio & ipfo Grotio, qui infuper ad Lut. 12. 7. agnofcit, tres annos Chriſtum docuiffe, etſi neget, illum Luca eo pertinere. Sic incidet mors Domini in Tiberii 19. Si ergo disperſio, quæ Stephani mortem fequuta eſt, OCTENNIO toto fuit prior Cajano principatu & Tiberii morte, oportet vel Tiberium imperaſſe plus quam 27. annos contra omnium Hiſtoricorum fidem, vel Stephanum lapidatum fuiſſe toto quadriennio ante mortem Chriſti, & priusquam eſſet baptizatus. Neq; vero probabile eſt, vivente adhuc Tiberio cœpiſſe perſecutionem Hierofolymitanæ Eccleſiæ, quum ipſe, Tertulliano Apolog. cap. 5. teſte, cognitis è Pilati literis, quæ Chriſto contigerant, de illo inter Deos referendo Senatui propofuerit, & Chriſtianorum accuſatoribus capitis periculum commi-natus fit. Unde haud conſentaneum videtur, Judæos quicquam publice aufuros fuiſſe adverſus Chriſtianos, Tiberio ſuperſtite. Si ergo Stephani martyrium ſub Cajo contigit, ideoq; ante fecundum ejus annum Paulus converſus non fit, quem tertio à Stephani nece anno converſum dicit Petavius, quomodo altero Caji anno de Caji mox retegenda impietate vaticinari potuerit, qui ne quidem ipſe ante fecundum Caji annum Chriſtianus factus fuerit.

Porro Timotheum Paulo jam anno fecundo Caji, quo exaratam vult Grotius epiſtolam, quæ fecunda ad Theſſalonicenſes inſcribitur, adjunctum fuiſſe, quemadmodum in ejusdem titulo adjungitur, nulla ratione conſentaneum vero eſt. Fingit fane Grotius in appendice, de matre Timothei, deque ipfo Timotheo, quod ex disperſione illa, quæ poſt Stephani necem facta eſt, fuerint. Sed Timotheus Lycaonius fuit, non Judæus: Et tempore illius διασπορᾶς nondum conſtitit fidelibus, gentiles aſſumendos eſſe, quo etiam tempore Timotheum adhuc puerum fuiſſe oportet; aut certe non ea fuit ætate, qua jungi potuerit Paulo in exaranda ad profugos Thef.

Thessalonicenses epistola. Fingit etiam Grotius, disperſionem illam Silam vel Sylvanum adduxisse. Sed quum omnes, qui dispersi tum fuerant, in via abuisse dicantur, Act. 8, 4. cap. 11, 19, 20. de nemine vero legatur, quod redierit, qui factum, quod Sila redierit Hierosolymam? Et quomodo adjungi poterat Paulo in literis ad Thessalonicenses secundum de Caji anno, qui non nisi in concilio Hierosolymitano Paulo comes additus longe post excessum Caji .

Accedit, quod Thessalonicensibus jam præsto fuisse oporteat tum Paulum Apostolum, tum etiam collegas ejusdem Sylvanum & Timotheum, antequam ad eosdem hanc exararent epistolam, qui vero Thessalonicam demum post concilium Hierosolymitanum, & post vocatum Divinitus in Macedoniam Paulum venere, ut ex Act. 16. & 17. constat. Illud verba ipsa epistolæ testantur. Nam & vocati sunt Thessalonicenses per præconium ipsorum, & jubentur tenere, quæ acceperant ab ipsis per sermonem, 2. Thessal. 2, 13. Ad quod & vocavit vos PER EVANGELIUM NOSTRUM, & vers. 14. itaque fratres state, & tenete traditiones, quas didicistis sive per SERMONEM, sive per epistolam nostram: Ad quæ verba Theodoretus: Habetis doctrinam regulam sermones, quos vobis tradidimus, quos & PRÆSENTES vobis predicavimus, & absentes scripsimus. Quando vero Paulus, Sylvanus, & Timotheus PRÆSENTES prædicarunt Thessalonicensibus, nisi cum peragrata Amphipoli & Apollonia Thessalonicam venere, & Paulo ac Silæ se adjunxere nonnulli ex Judæis, & magna multitudo Græcorum, Act. 17, 1. 4. Ad ejusdem præsentiæ & conversationis in Ecclesia Thessalonicensi regulam revocant Paulus, Sylvanus & Timotheus Thessalonicenses cap. 3. v. 7. seqq. Ipsi enim scitis, quemadmodum oporteat imitari NOS; quoniam non inquieti fuimus INTER VOS, neque gratis manducavimus panem ab aliquo, sed in labore, & in fatigatione nocte & die operantes, ne quem vestrum gravaremus. Non quasi non habuerimus potestatem, sed ut nosmetipsos daremus formam vobis ad imitandum nos. Nam & cum ESSEMUS APUD VOS, hoc DENUNTIABAMUS VOBIS, quoniam si quis non vult operari, nec manducet. Quæ fronte ita que negari poterit in Ecclesia Thessalonicensi, utpote ad quam hæc epistola directa est, & in qua illa contigisse ex epistola 1. ad Thessal. cap. 2, 9. & cap. 4, 6. 11. constat, ubi illa totidem fere verbis leguntur, Paulum cum hisce collegis fuisse præsto fuisse, antequam eam exararet? Cui vero affuisse illos secundo Caji anno nemo sanus dixerit. Nec ante concilium Hierosolymitanum nono Claudii Successoris Caji habitum, vel Ecclesiam Thessalonicæ collectam, vel Thessalonicæ Paulum cum Sylvano & Timotheo fuisse, cum bistoria actuum Apostolicorum conciliari potest.

Quum ergo profligatis Grotii commentis, quod secunda ad Thessalonicenses ordine temporis primam præcefferit, quod altero Caji Caligulæ anno scripta sit, & priusquam Thessalonicam Paulus venisset, quod scripta sit ad paucos e disperſione post mortem Stephani exules, qui cœtum nondum fecerant, in quibus cum in refutatione Annotatorum ad caput 2 secundæ ad Thessalonicenses, tum in Antichristo revelato, ille quem Borboritæ nomine in appendice traducit, os oppilavit Grotio, id satis jam constet, & secundam revera esse, & Ecclesiæ jam constitutæ inscriptam, & non nisi postquam Paulus Thessalonicam cum Sylvano & Timotheo venisset, exaratam, qui adventus; fatente Grotio, longe post Caji tempora, imo post annum nonum Claudii contingit, quid certius est, quam de Cajo neutiquam intelligi posse verba priora hujus vaticinii 2. Thessal. 2. quemadmodum nec posteriora de Simone Mago, quem in Claudii secundum rejicit Grotius: nisi statuat, Paulum hic tantum prædixisse præterita, quod seductoris esset, non gentium Doctoris, agyrta, non Apostoli, ut recte Maresius. Non ergo est, quod causam immutati in Ecclesia & codice biblico ordinis utriusque ad Thessalonicenses rejiciat in metum Christianorum in primitiva Ecclesia; quæ revera etiam futilis est.

Quodnam enim periculum Christianis regnante Claudio imminuit, ut publicari hæc epistola, si sub Cajo scripta, non potuerit? Annon, Cajo defuncto, Senatus animum adjecit ad libertatem, Claudius vero acta Caji rescidit, simulachra sustulit, conflatis omnibus numismatis ejus effigie consignatis, de quibus Suetonius & Dio testimonium perhibent. Qui etiam periculum ob hanc epistolam metuendum fuisset, siquidem omnia, quæ ad Cajum jam abripit Grotius, ita comparata, ut nec Cajum referant, nec referre illum unquam ulli per sedecim secula per febrim in mentem venerit? Quid periculi fuisset, vulgari post obitum Caji inter Christianos vaticinium, quod de illo præcessisset, cum Philo Judæus Philippicam suam, quam inscripsit de legatione ad Cajum, in eundem tam apertis verbis conscriptam impune vulgaverit? Portento etiam simile foret, sub Claudio & Nerone rem ita palam fuisse, ut nemo, etiam Ethnicos, qui forte in Paulinam epistolam incidisset, statim Cajum in ea non agnovisset, unde periculum metuendum Christianis fuerit. Cæsaribus autem extinctis & confosso Nerone eorum ultimo, tantam oblivionem rerum triginta ante annos gestarum cœpisse omnes, ut nemo ab illo tempore ad hanc nostram ætatem Christianus extiterit, qui vaticinii genuinum percipere potuerit sensum, de quo actum omnino erat absque Grotii conspicillis & opera. Denique inauditum est, epistolam aliquam, vel librum in Canonicis scripturis priorem dici, eo saltem nomine, quod ante alteram epistolam vel librum alterum jam locum suum occupasset in epistolarum Apostolicarum volumine, & in codice Biblico.

Sed mittamus paradoxa, & εὐρήματα ineptissima Grotii, quæ ad Cajum in locum Anti-Christi Romani, in posteriori ad Thessalonicenses epistola furrogandum excogitavit.

De tempore autem scriptæ prioris epistolæ haud ægre annuimus eidem, scriptam nempe eam esse non multo postquam Thessalonicæ Paulus fuerat. Thessalonicam autem pervenit anno Christi LI. qui Claudii X. fuit. Nam Claudium anno Christi XLI. imperare cœpisse Petavius auctor est P. II. L. IV. rationarii temporum pag. 230. Secundum Baronium annus primus Claudii incidit in annum Christi LXIII. & anno Christi LI. Claudii IX. cele bratum est concilium Hierosolymitanum, quo anno etiam Paulum & Silam Philippis egressos Thessalonicam primum venisse, Baronius ad ann. Christi II. n. LXXIII. asserit: Quo de Lucas Act. 17. 1. Sequenti autem LI. anno docuit Athenis, ubi expectavit Silam atque Timotheum Act. 18.

Quod ad locum scriptionis, Athenis eam exaratam esse censuere non modo, qui finalas clausulas adjecerunt, sed etiam Athanasius, Theodoretus & Oecumenius aliæque, Paulum nempe, sicut Athenis misit Timotheum Thessalonicam: Ita etiam, dum ibidem moraretur, scripsisse ad eosdem Thessalo- nicenses primam epistolam, 1. Thessal. 3. vers. 1. Grotius autem maluit sequi Baronium ad ann. Christi LII. n. XIV. quemadmodum ille Bezam: Corinthi potius eam datam fuisse a Paulo, quam Athenis.

Quibus consentiunt etiam Benedictus Pererius, & Justinianus, ut in prolegom. in epist. ad Romanos monuimus, nec non Cornelius à Lapide, aliique. Et observat Beza sub calcem epistolæ, in Clarmontano codice non haberi, ut in Græcis codicibus plerisque, quos Latini & Germanici sequuntur: πρὸς θεσσαλονικεῖς πρώτην ἐγράφη ἀπὸ Ἀθηνῶν, sed fine loco mentione hoc modo: Ἐπλερώθη πρὸς θεσσαλονικεῖς πρώτη.

Argumentum hoc imprimis urget Beza, quod Paulus in secundo capite meminerit Timothei, a quo sustinuerit solus relinqui Athenis, quum eum ad Thessalonicenses mitteret. Itaque Silas tum non redierat ad Paulum. Subjicit deinde, Timotheum ad se iterum rediisse, ex quo intellexisset, que Thessalonicensium esset constantia.

Liquet autem ex actis Apostolorum, quum Paulus digressus Athenis, ubi substituerat Silam & Timotheum expectans, Corinthum venisset, & aliquandiu illic esset versatus, tum demum illos ad eum rediisse, quorum etiam adventu sit magnopere confirmatus Actor. 17. vers. 14. & 16. Itaque Sylvanus ille ipse est, quem Lucas Silan vocat, quumque illi Corinthum venissent, & Timotheus Paulo, a quo Athenis rursum (quod Lucas præterierit) Thessalonicam missus fuerat, Ecclesiæ Thessalonicensium statum renuntiaffet, hæc epistola ad illos communi ipsorum trium nomine Corintho fuit missa.

Silan autem, qui & Sylvanus, apparet ex Apostolorum actis, Berrhææ relictum cum Timotheo, & rursus Athenis Thessalonicam regressus, ipsum tandem in reditu assumeret, ut una Corinthum venirent.

Sed in eo argumento multa assumuntur precario; id etiam falsum, quod Paulus solus relictus Athenis fuerit, ablegato Timotheo.

Non id habetur 1. Thessal. 3. 1. sed duo illi Paulus & Sylvanus soli remanserunt.

Placuit tamen argumentum illud Justiniano, ut ab hæretico profectum; imo & Baronio; Non item Alphonso Salmeroni, qui Tomo XV. disp. I. in Epist. ad Thessalon. id solidum esse negat, quum Paulus iterum Corintho Athenas ivisse, ibidemque scripsisse potuerit.

Reponit pro Beza Crocius; Non probari posse illam profectionem.

Nam certum est, Paulum reliquisse Timotheum cum Sila in Macedonia; Cum Athenas proficisceretur, & inde illis, qui ipsum deducebant mandatum dedisse ad Silam & Timotheum, ut quam citissime ad se venirent, ibique eos expectasse, Actor. 17. v. 14. 15. 16. Certum & illud, Silam & Timotheum e Macedonia ad mandatum Pauli reduces Paulum non offendisse Athenis, sed quia inde profectus jam erat, Corinthi, Actor. 18. 1. 5. Certum porro, Paulum & Silam Timotheum Athenis misisse Thessalonicam.

Id enim testantur λευκάδι φωνῇ, 1. Thessal. 3. vers. 1. 2. Quamobrem hoc (vestri) desiderium non amplius ferentes optimum duximus soli Athenis relinqui: Mimusque Timotheum fratrem nostrum &c.

Quinam illi sunt, qui duxere optimum, ut soli Athenis relinquerentur? Quinam misere Timotheum Athenis in Macedoniam, vel ad Thessalonicenses? Non certe solus Paulus, sed qui ei adjunctus est in titulo epistolæ cum ipso Sylvanus.

Quamvis enim partes primariæ Pauli fuerint, quemadmodum ideo postea de se sigillatim ita loquitur Apostolus vers. 5. Quamobrem ego etiam non amplius ferens vestri desiderium misi &c.

Unde autem miserunt Paulus & Sylvanus Timotheum?

Non Corintho, quo ad Paulum e Macedonia primum Sila & Timotheus venerant, Actor. 18. 1. 5. & unde post sesquiennalem commorationem in illa civitate Ephesum, ac porro Cæsariam & Antiochiam, & in Galatiam & Phrygiam profectus est Actor. 18. 18. 19. 22. Jam Ephesum quidem reversus est Apostolus, Actor. 19. 1. quo loco per biennium & tres menses substitit, vers. 8. & 10. ibique in Spiritu sibi proposuit per Macedoniam & Achaiam proficisci, & Hierosolymam tendere, & misit inde Timotheum & Erastum in Macedoniam: Siquidem adhuc ad tempus substiterit in Asia, v. 22. Sed hæc plane alia est, multum posterior, & e diverso loco cum Erasto Timothei ablegatio.

Timotheum solum a Paulo & Sylvano Thessalonicam missum esse jam notavimus. Oporteret ergo illos tres, quum hæc missio fieret, Athenis hæsisse: ideoque necessum est, ut Corintho Paulus, postquam eo devenerat ad ipsum Sila & Timotheus, Athenas una cum illis profectus sit.

Quæ jam patere omnino censemus.

Illa vero per sesquiennalem commoratio penes Corinthios bene consistere potest cum excursu ad exiguum tempus ad Athenienses.

Distabant enim Athenæ Corintho tantum octodecim miliaribus. Utrum autem Timotheus e Macedonia ad Paulum & Sylvanum redux ipsos Athenis invenerit, an vero Corinthi, & num inde, vel hinc post reversionem Timothei Paulus, Sylvanus, & Timotheus hanc epistolam exararint forte, non adeo luculentum videre in scripturis est.

Potuisse autem sive illinc, sive hinc epistolam mitti, dubium esse non debet. Argumentum certe Beze omnino solidum non esse, ut ejus causa Justinianus cum Pererio & Cornelio à Lapide à communi sententia recedere necessum habuerit, nunc in solis disco positum est.

Quod autem Athenis potius, quam Corinthi exarata hæc epistola sit, non tantum consueta finalis προσθήκη, quam unius codicis variatio non potest locomovere, & auctoritas veterum, & consensus recentiorum plerorumque, confirmat, sed imprimis desiderium Pauli & Sylvani, quod vix sustinere poterant, ex Timotheo, quem Athenis ablegarunt, mox reverfuro, statum Ecclesiæ Thessalonicensis experiendi, ejus causa Athenis loco viciniore, subsistere; non enim incommodum habere poterant hospitium penes Dionysium, aut Damarim, aliosque illic conversos: nec non verba Apostoli εὐδοκήσαμεν καταλειφθῆναι ἐν Ἀθήναις μόνοι: ὅ ἐ quibus id apparet, voluisse eos solos manere, ac subsistere Athenis, usque ad reditum Timothei.

Distabant Athene Berrhæa mari 66. miliarium itinere, inde adhuc restabant usque ad Thessalonicam 15. miliaria. Ita ergo Athenis Thessalonicam, & Thessalonicam vicissim Athenas eundo & redeundo, 160. miliaria circiter conficienda erant Timotheo partim navigio, partim pedestri itinere, ad quæ adminimum duæ septimanæ requirebantur.

Si per duas etiam septimanas Thessalonicæ substiterit, intra mensis unius spatium Athenas ad Paulum & Sylvanum reverti potuit, & inde cum illis hanc epistolam ad Thessalonicensem Ecclesiam expedire.

Atque hæc de scriptionis loco.

Quanquam vero tempus adeo præcise definiri non possit, id tamen apparet, epistolam non scriptam prioribus tribus annis a conversione Apostoli, Galat. 1. 17. 18. neque sequentibus annis 14. Gal. 2. 1. quum isto tempore nondum venerit Thessalonicam, AB. 17. unde ad annum Apostolatus Pauli decimum obavū, Christi LII. Claudii X. scriptionem refert Baronius.

Omnium utique primam inter Apostolicas epistolas hanc esse Doctores cum veteres tum recentiores fere consentiunt, Theodoretus, Chrysostomus, & Usserius, Crocius, & nostris plerique, nec non Pontificiis Cornelius a Lapide aliique. Occasio scriptionis fuit summa de fide Ecclesiae Thessalonicensis recens a Paulo plantatae, Act. 17. quae ubique percrebuerat, 1. Thessal. 1, 8. in qua proinde illos non modo missione Timothei primum, 1. Thessal. 3, 2. quum ipse impeditus fuerit, eos invisere, prout bis sibi proposuerat, 1. Thessal. 2, 18. sed etiam deinceps harum literarum expeditione confirmare voluit, ne quisquam inter ipsos propter tribulationes in fide vacillaret, & ut gaudium suum de ipsorum constantia testaretur, postquam de eadem a Timotheo reduce factus erat certior, 1. Thessal. 3, 3. 8. tum dubium, quod inter Thessalonicenses fubortum erat de adventu Domini, quod ad illos, qui superstites in eodem offenduntur, de quo Thessalonicenses suos informat Apostolus cap. 4, 13. simulque ad vigilantiam, quum inopinato dies Domini adventurus est, eosdem exhortatur.

Occasionem itaque epistolae & argumentum sic assignavit Theodoretus: Thessalonicenses quidem in Macedonia primas obtinet: Salutarem autem praedicationem lubenter & alacriter suscepit. Divinus autem Apostolus hic quoque fecit fundamenta pietatis. Judaeis quidem contradicentibus & aperte repugnantibus, sed frustra laborantibus, fluctus enim ac tempestates superabat Evangelium. Cum eorum insidias declinaffet B. Paulus, & Thessalonicam venit Berraeam, & Berraeam navigavit Athenas. Cum autem eorum, qui crediderant, perpetuo curam gereret, beatissimum Timotheum Athenis misit Thessalonicam, ut eos fulciret & confirmaret, & omnibus adversariorum machinationibus potentiores efficeres. Is reversus laudavit quidem eorum fidem inexpugnabilem: dixit autem, eos opus habere aliqua exhortationis doctrina de quibusdam quaestionibus, que apud eos movebantur. Scripsit ergo epistolam, primum quidem laudans eorum fidei firmitatem: deinde adhortans, ut mortuorum resurrectionem expectarent: de Domini autem adventu ne nimis curiose inquirerent.

Porro autem eis quoque exhibuit moralis doctrinae adhortationem.

Tota epistola exhortatoria est primum ad constantiam & profectum in religione Christiana, deinde etiam ad vita sanctitatem, intermixta tamen informatione de resurrectione mortuorum, quae vero ad παράκλησιν dolentium super mortuos directa est. Juxta Camerarium epistolae τύπος Φιλικός est & ἐπαινετικός & ἑαυτοσυστατικός, sed si scopum respicias, proprie est παρααινετικός tum ad constantiam in fide, qui impenduntur tria priora capita, tum ad sanctimoniam in vita in reliquis duobus capitibus. Quod ergo ad priorem paranefin, indirecta ea est, quia gratiarum actione, commendatione, Timothei ablegatione, ac inde accepta consolatione, desiderio uberioris praesentis informationis ac voto confirmationis plenioris facile ad perseverantiam in agnita fide excitantur. Posterior autem paranefis directa est.

In priori caput primum ἐγκωμιαστικόν est de fide ipsorum, quae per orbem percrebuit. Alterum συναπτικόν tum praeconii Apostolici & affectus materni & paterni erga ipsos, tum obsequii & patientiae ipsorum in tribulationibus. Tertium Φιλικόν est, tum ob missionem Timothei ex amore & sollicitudine erga ipsos, tum ob exultationem & gratiarum actionem ob laetum de ipsorum fide nuntium; tum ob precationem, ut Deus viam suam ad ipsos dirigat, eorumque corda confortet.

Reliqua duo capita hortantur partim ad praeceptorum traditorum observationem, cumprimis quoad impudicitia, & injustitia visitationem, fraternam dilectionem, & tranquillam laborum suorum expeditionem: partim ad nimie mastitia de mortuis fugam, cum informatione de mortuorum & viventium raptu in occursum Domini, cap. 4. partim ad vigilantiam, sobrietatem, ac praeparationem ad adventum Domini: Quibus subjunguntur varia monita, ac vota, & salutationes,

cap. 5. PARS I. EPISTOLAE Paranefis ad constantiam in fide.

## 1:1 Argument
CHAPTER I. ΕΓΚΩΜΙΑΣΤΙΚΟΝ (Laudatory).

ARGUMENT & PARTITION.

Having premised a votive salutation, the Apostle, together with his colleagues, gives thanks to God for the faith, charity, and hope of the Thessalonians, and preaches that the Gospel was efficacious among them, and that amid many tribulations they received the word, and were made a type of the faithful in Macedonia and Achaia, since their faith is celebrated everywhere, as well as their conversion to God, and to the expectation of His Son, our Redeemer, raised from the dead.

Its parts are two; yet with the customary inscription and salutation premised: The former is thanksgiving to God for their faith, and its encomium, to v. 7. The latter is the confirmation of the encomium of the Thessalonians from the spreading of the Gospel and the fame scattered through the world concerning their conversion, to v. 10.

PART I. CAPITIS I.

Thanksgiving to God for the faith of the Thessalonians, and his eulogy of them.

Verf. 1. Παυλὸς καὶ Σιλουανὸς Silvanus and Silas are the same name, but pronounced differently, as Jerome and others have noted. Silas is called here Acts 15:22, 27, 33, 34, 40; ch. 16:19, 25, 29; ch. 17:4, 10, 14, 15; ch. 18:5. Silvanus in this place and 2 Cor. 1:19, 2 Thess. 1:1, 1 Pet. 5:12. From the places in Acts it appears that he was among the first Christians.

Dorotheus, De Sila, holds Silam and Silvanus to be different, constituting the latter as the epistle to the Thessalonians, the former to the Corinthians, to whom Alfonfus Salmero writes, but the ancients and most moderns deny this, and Dorotheus is of little faith in such matters, in the judgment of great men. But among the first Christians, that is, those who were of the first dispersion, which happened after the death of Stephen, which Grotius was persuaded of, that he was from the Acts of the Apostles, does not appear. But he is introduced, that is, Grotius, τῇ ὑποθέσει δαλέων (speaking on the hypothesis) concerning the second epistle to the Thessalonians written in the second year of Gaius, in which ch. 1:1 he is also joined to Paul. Moreover, he himself, and Judas with Barnabas are called leaders in the cited place of Acts, and also prophets of the same chapter v. 32. They are also called Apostles, 1 Thess. 2:7, with Paul, Silvanus and Timothy. And therefore, without doubt, they were distinguished Doctors, although not properly, the Holy Spirit calls them Apostles, of which kind Paul was immediately called, and θεόπνευστος (divinely inspired), yet to others yet he prefers them to the Doctors by this name, as we have observed before.

And this is perhaps the reason why Paul did not profess himself an Apostle at the threshold, which was done by him elsewhere, Rom. 1, 1. 1 Cor. 1, 1. Gal. 1, 1. Eph. 1, 1. even when he joined Timothy to himself, 2 Cor. 1, 1. Phil. 1, 1. Eph. 1, 1. Col. 1, 1. namely, because below in c. 2, 2. he wished to designate himself and his associates by the name of Apostles of Christ.

Now Silvanus was a companion of Paul's travels, Acts 15, 40. cast into prison with him at Philippi, and miraculously liberated, c. 16, 22. seqq. he went with Paul to Beroea, when the Jews were stirring up a tumult against them in Thessalonica, c. 17, 5. 6. 11. In a similar storm stirred up by the same people at Beroea, while Paul was crossing by sea to Athens, Silas remained in Macedonia with Timothy, until they were called away by Paul's command, Acts 17, 14. 15. to whom they came at Corinth, Acts 18, 5. De Timotheo Καὶ Τιμόθεον And this man and Silas Paul had taken to himself into Macedonia, because they had kinsmen there.

Concerning Timotheus

And therefore he added their names here, because they were already known even to those of the Thessalonians who had been converted from the Gentiles by the work of Paul. That Timothy and Silas had kinsmen at Thessalonica, he asserts rashly, without any testimony of antiquity: and no less boldly he feigns against historical truth that, besides those who were converted there by the work of Paul, others converted earlier from the Jews dwelt there. For Paul found none when he arrived there, Acts 17. and by the testimony of all antiquity the Thessalonians were first converted by Paul. If Silvanus and Timothy had found Christians there with Paul and had known them as kinsmen, why would they not have betaken themselves to them, or taught in the synagogue of the Jews?

Would the Thessalonian Jews have tolerated such Christians from the circumcision in their synagogue before Paul's arrival? Would those Christians, who had confederated at Thessalonica, if one gives credence to Grotius in his commentary on 2 Thess. 2, have hidden the mysteries of the Gospel from their own countrymen in the same city long before Paul came there, or if they had concealed the Christians, so that the Jews there heard Paul preaching about it for the first time? What? That the Church of the Thessalonians consisted chiefly of Gentiles, not of Jews who had fled there, is evident from 1 Thess. 2, 14. c. 1, 9. for there the Thessalonian believers are said to have suffered the same things from their own countrymen as the Churches of Judea suffered from the Jews, but here they were converted from idols to the true and living God.

Paul adds Silvanus and Timothy to himself here, as companions of his Macedonian journey, approvers and witnesses of the labors and dangers of those about whom he writes, even if this whole epistle is Divinely inspired to the Apostle alone, and dictated to him even with this inscription. Τῇ Ἐκκλησίᾳ Θεσσαλονικέων To that Church, which once consisted of Jews. Where it now also consisted of many Greeks. He does not name Presbyters and Deacons here, because the Church was recent, and had not yet received its full form. The same fiction recurs, that the Church of the Thessalonians once consisted of Jews. Where did Luke teach this? Where is the Ecclesiastical antiquity? And who, I pray, were they?

That there was no Church there before Paul gathered it, is clear even from the calling of the Apostle, Acts 9, 9. For if Christians already known to Paul and Silvanus and Timothy had been there, he would undoubtedly have visited them, and there would have been no need for the Angel's warning to betake himself to Macedonia. And it is confirmed, because the Beroeans, being more noble than the Thessalonian Jews, received the Word of God with all readiness upon the arrival of Paul. That Christians driven by persecution from Judea, stirred up on account of Stephen's death, first came to Syria, and then, the same storm pressing, crossed the sea and came to Macedonia, is a Grotian fable, not true historical reality.

And how could a Church be considered recent, which had already sat there for 12 years, and before that twelfth year had already been honored by the Apostle with the name of the Church, 2 Thess. 1, 1. as Grotius trifles? Had it not within such a space of time obtained any Presbyter, any Deacon? But because not even then did they constitute any certain person fully ordained, after the ministry of Paul was added, and not even with Silas and Timothy having set out, how could there have been a Church there twelve years before?

Theophylact has this to say concerning this Church, to which this former epistle was inscribed: Although they were very few of those who had received the faith, not yet very firmly established in it: Yet he calls even these a Church, so that he might at least console them with this name. Ἐν θεῷ Πατρὶ καὶ Κυρίῳ Ἰησοῦ Χριστῷ that is, which existed, with God the Father and Christ acting. Thus the Syrian rightly accepts it. Not so much the origin of the Church, as its internal constitution is expressed by that phrase. For the particle ἐξ (from) is not used, but ἐν (in), which is noted to be in God the Father and Jesus Christ, because they constitute the Church, who through faith adhere to God the Father, and are in Jesus Christ, Rom. 8, 1. as being grafted into the same as the true vine, John 15, 1. and living in the same through faith, Gal. 2, 20. as living members of his mystical body, 1 Cor. 12, 13. Eph. 4, 15. 16. A great dignity, says Chrysostom, to which nothing can be equal.

If the Church is in God, the Gentiles will not be in the true and living God, but in false Gods and idols. The Jews indeed professed God as the creator of heaven and earth, but not God the Father, and the Lord Jesus Christ. From which conjunction of the Father, and the Lord Jesus Christ with the words in God, Chrysostom concludes that both the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ are called God equally, in whom the Thessalonian Church had been. For I and the Father are one, says Christ John 10, 30. Χάρις ὑμῖν καὶ εἰρήνη ἀπὸ Θεοῦ Πατρὸς ἡμῶν καὶ Κυρίου Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ 1 Cor. 1, 3. 2 Cor. 1, 2. Gal. 1, 3. Eph. 1, 2. Phil. 1, 2. Col. 1, 2. That 'from God' and the following are absent in some Codices, nor does the Syrian read them.

Theophylact: He prays for grace and peace for them, he says, that they may progress more and more in Divine gifts, and attain peace, not being proud toward one another. Without the grace of God we cannot arrive at the peace of reconciliation: Indeed, we have nothing peaceful, except through his grace. For grace is given freely without preceding merits, and through this, while he remits sins, we approach the peace of reconciliation. Verf.

Latin:

CAPUT I. ΕΓΚΩΜΙΑΣΤΙΚΟΝ.

ARGUMENTUM & PARTITIO.

Pramissa votiva salutatione Apostolus cum collegis gratias Deo agere pro fide, charitate, ac spe Thessalonicensium testatur, ac praedicat, quod Evangelium efficax inter eos fuerit, quodque inter multas tribulationes verbum susceperint, ac typus fidelium in Macedonia & Achaia facti sint, quum fides ipsorum undique celebretur, ac conversio ad Deum, & expectationem Filii ejus, Redemptoris nostri, a morte resuscitati.

Partes ejus duae sunt; praemissa tamen inscriptione ac voto consueto: Prior gratiarum actio ad Deum pro fide ipsorum, ejusque elogium, ad v. 7. Posterior confirmatio elogii Thessalonicensium a divulgatione Evangelii ac fama per orbem sparsa de conversione ipsorum, ad v. 10.

PARS I. CAPITIS I.

Gratiarum actio ad Deum pro fide Thessalonicensium, ejusque elogium.

Vers. 1. Παυλὸς καὶ Σιλουανὸς Idem nomen est Silvanus & Silas, sed aliter atque aliter elatum, ut Hieronymus & alii notarunt. Silas hic dicitur Actor. 15, 22. 27. 33. 34. 40. cap. 16, 19. 25. 29. cap. 17, 4. 10. 14. 15. cap. 18, 5. Sylvanus hoc loco & 2. Corinth. 1, 19. 2. Thessal. 1, 1. 1. Petr. 5, 12. Ex locis actorum apparet, eum fuisse inter primos Christianos.

Silam & Silvanum pro diversis habet Dorotheus, De Sila. hunc Thessalonicensium, illum Corinthiorum epistolum constituens, cui scribit Alfonsus Salmero, sed antiqui & recentiores plerique abnuunt, & exiguae fidei est in talibus Dorotheus, magnorum virorum judicio. Inter primos autem Christianos, hoc est, eos, qui e prima διασπορᾷ, quae post mortem Stephani contigit, fuere, quod persuasum Grotio, eum fuisse ex Actis Apostolici, non apparet. Introducitur autem id est Grotius τῇ ὑποθέσει δαλέων de epistola secunda ad Thessalonicenses secundo Caji anno scripta, in qua cap. 1. v. 1. Paulo etiam adjunctus est. Ceterum ipse, & Judas cum Barnaba dicuntur ἡγούμενοι loco citato Actorum, nec non προφῆται capitis ejusdem v. 32. vocantur etiam Ἀπόστολοι, 1. Thessal. 2, 7. cum Paulo Silvanus & Timotheus. Ideoque, fine dubio, infignes fuere Doctores, etsi non κυρίως, Apostolos vocat Spiritus sanctus, cujusmodi Paulus erat immediate vocatus, & θεόπνευστος, Divinitus inspiratus, aliis tamen Doctoribus isto nomine præfert, ut antehac observavimus.

Atque hæc forte causa est, cur Paulus non in limine se professus sit Apostolum, quod alias ab ipso factum, Rom. 1, 1. Cor. 1, 1. Gal. 1, 1. Epb. 1, 1. etiam cum Timotheum sibi adjunxit, 2. Cor. 1, 1. Philipp. 1, 1. Epb. 1, 1. Col. 1, 1. quod nempe infra c. 2, 2. se & socios nomine ἀποστόλων Χριστοῦ indigitare voluerit.

Fuit autem Silvanus socius peregrinationis Pauli, Act. 15, 40. cum eo Philippis in carcerem conjectus, & miraculose liberatus, c. 16, 22. seqq. cum Paulo profectus est Berhæam, cum Thessalonica tumultum adversus ipsos excitarent Judæi, c. 17, 5. 6. 11. Simili tempestate ab iisdem Berhœæ excitata, Paulo per mare Athenas trajiciente, substitit in Macedonia Sila cum Timotheo, donec mandato Pauli avocarentur, Act. 17, 14. 15. ad quem Corinthi venerunt, Act. 18, 5.

De Timotheo

Καὶ Τιμόθεον Et hunc & Silam Paulus sibi in Macedoniam adsumpserat, quod ibi cognatos haberent. Et ideo hic eorum addidit nomen, quod jam noti essent etiam illis Thessalonicensium, qui ex gentibus erant conversi, Pauli opera. Timotheum & Silam cognatos habuisse Thessalonicæ temere, sine ullo antiquitatis testimonio, adfererit: nec minus audacter fingit contra historicam veritatem, præter eos, qui Pauli opera illic conversi fuere, alios prius conversos è Judæis ibi habitasse. Nullos enim invenit Paulus, quum eo perveniret, Act. 17. & totius antiquitatis testimonio Thessalonicenses primum conversi sunt à Paulo. Si Christianos ibi Silvanus & Timotheus invenissent cum Paulo eosque cognatos, cur ad illos sese non recepissent, aut in Judæorum synagoga docuissent?

An Thessalonicenses Judæi tales ex circumcisione Christianos in sua synagoga ante Pauli adventum tolerassent? Num isti Christiani, qui Thessalonicæ confederant, si Grotio in commentatione ad 2. Thess. 2, fides, multo prius, quam eo Paulus veniret, suos saltem populares in eadem urbe mysteriis um celassent Evangelii, aut si dissimulassent Christianos, ut Judæi ithic primum concionantem Paulum de eo audiverint? Quid? quod Ecclesiam Thessalonicensium ex gentibus potissimum coaluisse, non ex Judæis eo profugis constat ex 1. Thess. 2, 14. c. 1, 9. illic enim dicuntur Thessalonicenses fideles eadem passi à popularibus suis, quæ Ecclesiæ Judææ à Judæis, hic vero conversi ab idolis ad verum & vivum Deum.

Adjungit autem hic sibi Silvanum & Timotheum Paulus, velut socios peregrinationis Macedonicæ, laborum & periculorum approbatores & testes eorum, de quibus scribit, etsi epistola hæc tota soli Apostolo Divinitus inspirata, etiam hac ἐπιγραφῇ eidem dictata. Τῇ Ἐκκλησίᾳ Θεσσαλονικέων Ei Ecclesiæ, quæ olim ex foliis Judæis constitit. Ubinam nunc etiam ex multis Græcis constabat. Non nominat hic Presbyteros & Diaconos, quia recens erat Ecclesia, nec dum formam plenam acceperat. Recurrit idem commentum, Ecclesiam Thessalonicensium olim ex foliis Judæis constitisse. Ubinam hoc docuit Lucas? Ubi antiquitas Ecclesiastica? Et quinam fuere illi obsecro?

Nullam Ecclesiam ibi fuisse, antequam Paulus eam collegerit, vel ex vocatione Apostoli liquet, Act. 9, 9. Nam si jam ibi fuissent Paulo & Silvano ac Timotheo noti Christiani, ultra fine dubio illos invisisset, nec opus fuisset Angeli monitione, ut se in Macedoniam conferret. Et confirmatur, quod Berrhoënses cum Judais Thessalonicensibus seu generosiores sub adventum Pauli cum omni alacritate Verbum Dei susceperint. Christianos persecutione pulsos è Judæa, ob Stephani mortem excitata, in Syriam primum venisse, inde vero, eadem urgente procella, superato mari in Macedoniam venisse, fabula est Grotiana, non vera veritas historica.

Et quomodo recens foret habenda Ecclesia, quæ jam per 12. annos illic consederit, & ante illud duodecimum jam τῆς Ἐκκλησίας nomine honorata fuerit ab Apostolo, 2. Thess. 1, 1. ut nugatur Grotius. Anne intra tantum temporis spatium nullum nacta erat Presbyterum, nullum Diaconum? Quia vero ne tum quidem certum aliquem plene ordinatum constituebant, postquam accessit ministerium Pauli, nec non eo profecto Sila & Timotheo, quomodo jam ante annos duodecim ibi fuerit Ecclesia?

Theophylactus de hac Ecclesia, cui prior hæc epistola inscripta fuerit, ita habet: Etsi perpauci erant ex his, qui fidem exceperant, in ea nondum admodum obfirmati: Tamen & hos Ecclesiam dicit, ut saltem hoc nomine consoletur. Ἐν θεῷ Πατρὶ καὶ Κυρίῳ Ἰησοῦ Χριστῷ id est, quæ extitit, id agente Deo Patre & Christo. Ita recte accipit Syrus. Non tam origo Ecclesiæ, quam interna constitutio ea phrasi exprimitur. Non enim adhibita particula ἐξ, sed ἐν, quæ notatur in Deo Patre & Jesu Christo esse, quia constituunt Ecclesiam, qui per fidem adhærent Deo Patri, & in Jesu Christo sunt, Rom. 8, 1. utpote insiti eidem ceu viti veræ, Job. 15, 1. & viventes in eodem per fidem, Gal. 2, 20. ceu membra viva corporis ejus mystici, 1. Cor. 12, 13. Eph. 4, 15. 16. Magna dignitas, inquit Chrysostomus, cui nihil par esse queat.

Si in Deo est Ecclesia, gentiles in Deo non erunt vero & vivo, sed in falsis Diis & idolis. Judæi profitebantur quidem Deum conditorem cœli & terræ, non autem Deum Patrem, & Dominum Jesum Christum. E qua conjunctione Patris, & Domini Jesu Christi cum vocibus ἐν θεῷ Chrysostomus concludit, & Patrem & Dominum Jesum Christum ex æquo Deum dici, in quo fuerat Ecclesia Thessalonicensis. Ego enim & Pater unum sumus, inquit Christus Joh. 10, 30. Χάρις ὑμῖν καὶ εἰρήνη ἀπὸ Θεοῦ Πατρὸς ἡμῶν καὶ Κυρίου Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ 1. Cor. 1, 3. 2. Cor. 1, 2. Gal. 1, 3. Eph. 1, 2. Phil. 1, 2. Col. 1, 2. Illa ἀπὸ Θεοῦ & sequentia absunt in Codicibus nonnullis, neque ea legit Syrus.

Theophylactus: Gratiam his, inquit, comprecatur & pacem, ut Divinis in donis magis ac magis proficiant, pacemque assequantur, nihil invicem superbientes. Sine gratia Dei ad pacem reconciliationis pervenire non possumus: Imo nihil pacificum, nisi per gratiam ejus habere valemus. Gratia enim gratis datur fine præcedentibus meritis, & per hanc, dum culpas remittit, accedimus ad pacem reconciliationis. Vers.

## 1:2
2. Εὐχαριστοῦμεν τῷ Θεῷ πάντοτε περὶ πάντων ὑμῶν Rom. 1, 8. 1 Cor. 1, 4. Eph. 1, 16. c. 5, 20. Phil. 1, 3. Col. 1, 3. 12. Μνείαν ὑμῶν ποιούμενοι ἐπὶ τῶν προσευχῶν ὑμῶν Rom. 1, 9. Eph. 1, 6. Philem. v. 4. These celebrate not only God by thanksgiving for the grace shown to the Thessalonians, but also commend their faith, and add a prayer as a proof of love, because they are frequently mindful of them in their prayers, without intermission holding in their mind their faith, love, and hope.

Theophylact, with Chrysostom leading: He begins, he says, from their praise immediately. For when he gives thanks to God for these things, he shows that those things have alr eady been accomplished, for which thanks can be given to God, and the same can be extolled with praises, by whose gift they have performed things more rightly. At the same time he instructs them in humility, when he argues that all things are to be ascribed to God, not to us mortals. And further: Thanks are referred to God for good works, for to remember anyone while praying is an argument of charity. Nor only, he says, when we pour out prayers to God, do we repeat the memory of you, but also always at other times.

Which indeed I demonstrate as the sum of the Apostle's benevolence toward them, Adia-

ANNOTATIONS ON I. A

Ἀδιαλείπτως μνημονεύοντες ὑμῶν τῶ ἔργο τῆς πίστεως) That you received me so kindly, and sent me away with such care, Acts 17:7, 10. He calls that the work of faith, which proceeds from faith and perfects faith. Not every work shows faith, but that which has as its companion the alacrity of the soul, and constancy, even in evils. Thus Chrysostom here.

Although the work of faith can not inappropriately be called that which proceeds from faith, yet a work of such a kind does not perfect faith. That smacks of Popery regarding formed faith. It is a fruit, not the form or essential perfection of faith. But faith here is clearly distinguished from charity and hope: therefore it ought not to be confused with them. Chrysostom more correctly understands the constancy of faith: What is the work of faith? That no one has broken your constancy. If you believe, you suffer all things: If you do not suffer, you do not believe: And Jerome, saying that that faith is retained in memory, which both the labor of justice, and the affection of charity, and the tolerance of passions proved. Nor perhaps is it less appropriately the work of faith itself, which the Holy Spirit works in us, because faith is the work of God, John 6:29. or more conveniently πίσις ἐνεργῆς by Hebraism, since other things are also expressed in this way, κόπος ἀγάπης, laborious charity, and ὑπομονὴ ἐλπίδος, ἐλπὶς ὑπομονητικὴ, patient hope, as Camerarius notes, that this figure of Hebrew speech is singular and frequent, just as the herb of poison, and the offspring of the Gods, is called a poisonous herb, and a Divine offspring. But why should we not say properly the work of faith, because the constancy of faith is truly a Divine work, and it is not a naked recognition, but trust is required for it, which is a huge ἔργον, since it must persist constantly against various temptations? Not indeed such a work, as are those which flow from faith, but that by which with desire, contention, agony, captivity of the intellect, and τῶ φρονήματος τῆς σαρκὸς, we rest with full acquiescence of the will in God the Father and our Lord Jesus Christ, nor do we allow ourselves to be moved from that trust; Conf. 2 Thess. 1:3, 11. Nor can this explanation brought by Jerome and Chrysostom be reduced with difficulty, which Theophylact followed as the latter: Of the work of your faith, that is, of your constancy in the faith undertaken. For that is more truly the work of faith, when we remain stable in the faith, not merely boasting of faith in words or leading by glory.

Καὶ τῶ κόπω τῆς ἀγάπης) Thus also Heb. 6:10. Love is much by itself, but much greater, if troublesome labors are added. For that is κόπος.

Love is to help one's neighbor with prayers: but not labor in that love; unless you succor your neighbor by the effect itself, 1 John 3:18, James 2:16. What is the labor, says Chrysostom, and with him Theophylact, to love simply? No labor. But to love genuinely and sincerely, is much labor. For when, tell me, I pray, countless things are moved, which try to lead us away from love, and we resist against all things: is it not labor? It is understood, however, not only as laborious charity according to the first, but also according to the second table of the law; concerning the love of both neighbor and God, without whom no love of neighbor is sincere, these things are to be accepted.

Καὶ τῆς ὑπομονῆς τῆς ἐλπίδος τῶ Κυρίω ἡμῶν Ἰησῶ Χριστῶ) Here this Genitive twice denotes the cause. For both the hope of eternal life is the cause of patience, Romans 5:3, and Christ is the cause of that hope.

Rather, the adjunct of hope is noted, which ought to be persevering and bound with patience, lest we be cast down from the hope of life by the waves of tempests, or through impatience in tribulations we cast away hope, therefore it is called the anchor of the soul from its firmness, Heb. 6:19, then the object, which is our Lord Jesus Christ, in whom our hope ought to be fixed, if it is to be firm and constant, Jerem. 17:7, Ps. 2:12: and who is the sole foundation as of faith, so also of our hope, 1 Cor. 3:11, Heb. 6:20. In Him alone the Thessalonians founded their hope, thence they sustained all things with a firm mind.

Latin:

2. Εὐχαριστοῦμεν τῷ Θεῷ πάντοτε περὶ πάντων ὑμῶν Roman. 1, 8. 1. Cor. 1, 4. Eph. 1, 16. c. 5, 20. Phil. 1, 3. Col. 1, 3. 12. Μνείαν ὑμῶν ποιούμενοι ἐπὶ τῶν προσευχῶν ὑμῶν Rom. 1, 9. Eph. 1, 6. Philem. v. 4. Hæc gratiarum actione non tantum Deum pro gratia Thessalonicensibus exhibita celebrant, sed ipsorum etiam fidem commendant, adduntque precationem amoris documentum, quod frequenter ipsorum memores sint in orationibus suis, fine intermissione animo suo tenentes fidem, dilectionem, ac spem ipsorum.

Theophylactus præeunte Chrysostomo: Ab eorum, inquit, mox laude principium sumit. Cum enim Deo pro his gratias agit, ostendit, & se ea jam esse peracta, quibus & Deo possint gratiæ agi, & laudibus idem ile efferri, cujus munere bi rectiora peregerint. Simul & ad humilitatem hos infruit, cum arguat cuncta Deo esse non nobis mortalibus adscribenda. Et porro: Gratia Deo ex bonis operibus referuntur, inter precandum namq, cujuspiam reminisci, charitatis est argumentum. Nec modo, inquit, cum preces ad Deum fundimus, repetimus nos vestri memoriam, sed & alias semper.

Quod utique demonstrem summam in hos Apostoli benevolentiam, Adia-

ANNOTATA AD I. A

Ἀδιαλείπτως μνημονεύοντες ὑμῶν τῶ ἔργο τῆς πίστεως) Quod me tam benigne excepiftis, tanta cum cura di- miliftis, Actor. 17, 7. 10. Opus fidei vocat id, quod ex fide proficiscitur & fidem perficit. Non quodvis opus oftendit fidem, sed quod comitem habet alacritatem animi, & conftantiam, etiam in malis. Ita hic Chryso- stomus.

Opus fidei etsi non incommode dici possit, quod ex fide proficiscitur, non tamen opus ejusmo- di fidem perficit. Sapit id Papismum de fide for- mata. Fructus est, non forma vel perfectio fidei essentialis. Fides autem hic diferte distinguitur a charitate ac spe: ideo cum illa confundi non de- bet. Rectius constantiam fidei intelligit Chrysosto- mus: Quid est opus fidei? quod nemo constantiam vestram infregit. Si credis, omnia patere: Si non pateris, non credis: Et Hieronymus illam fidem memoria retineri, inquiens, quam & justitiae labor, & charitatis affectus, & passionum tolerantia com- probabant. Nec incommodius forte opus fidei est fides ipsa, quam operatur in nobis Spiritus sanctus, quia fides est opus Dei, Johan. 6, 29. vel commo- dius πίσις ἐνεργῆς per Ebraismum, quum alia ita etiam efferantur, κόπος ἀγάπης, charitas laboriosa, & ὑπομονὴ ἐλπίδος, ἐλπὶς ὑπομονητικὴ, spes patiens, ut Camerarius notat, Ebraici sermonis hanc figu- ram singularem & frequentem esse, quemadmodum herba veneni, & Deorum soboles, venenata herba dicitur, & soboles Divina. Quidni vero dicamus proprie opus fidei, quia vere Divi- num opus est fidei constantia, & non est nuda agni- tio, sed ad eam requiritur fiducia, quae ingens ἔργον est, cum constans adversus tentationes va- rias persistere debet? Non quidem tale opus, qua- lia sunt, quae ex fide fluunt, sed quo cum desiderio, contentione, agone, captivatione intellectus, & τῶ φρονήματος τῆς σαρκὸς, plena voluntatis ac- quiescentia in Deo Patre & Domino nostro Jesu Christo recumbimus, nec ab ea fiducia nos dimo- veri patimur; Conf. 2. Thess. 1, 3. 11. Nec difficulter reduci haec potest adducta Hieronymi & Chrysosto- mi explicatio, quem posteriorem ita sequutus est Theophylactus: Operis fidei vestrae, hoc est, constantiae vestrae in fide susceptae. Illud namque verius est fidei opus, cum stabiles in fide perstamus, non verbis fidem duntaxat jactare vel gloria ducere.

Καὶ τῶ κόπω τῆς ἀγάπης) Sic & Ebr. 6, 10. Multum est per se dilectio, sed multo majus, si accedant molesti la- bores. Id enim κόπος.

Amor est precibus juvare proximum: sed non labor in illo amore; nisi effectu ipso proximo succurras, 1. Joh. 3, 18. Jac. 2, 16. Quisnam est la- bor, inquit Chrysostomus, & cum eo Theophyla- ctus, simpliciter diligere? Nullus labor. Germane autem & sincere diligere, multus est labor. Quando enim, dic quaeso, innumera moventur, quae à dile- ctione abducere nos conantur, nosque adversus omnia resistimus: annon labor est? Intelligitur autem non tantum charitas laboriosa secundum primam, sed & secundum alteram legis tabulam; de amore tum proximi tum Dei, sine quo nullus amor proximi, sincerus est, haec accipienda.
