Καὶ τῆς ὑπομονῆς τῆς ἐλπίδος τῶ Κυρίω ἡμῶν Ἰησῶ Χριστῶ) bis hic Genitivus causam denotat. Nam & spes vitae aeternae causa est patientiae, Roman. 5, 3. & Christus causa illius spei.

Notatur potius tum adjunctum spei, quod esse debeat perseverans & cum patientia devincta, ne fluctibus tempestatum nos à spe vitae dejiciamur, aut per impatientiam in tribulationibus spem ab- jiciamus, ideo dicitur anchora animae à firmitudi- ne, Ebr. 6, 19. tum objectum, quod est Dominus no- ster Jesus Christus, in quem spes nostra defixa esse debet, si firma & constans sit, Jerem. 17, 7. Ps. 2, 12.: quique fundamentum unicum est ut fidei, sic et- iam spei nostræ, 1. Cor. 3, 11. Ebr. 6, 20. In illo so- lo fundabant spem Thessalonicenses, inde sustine- bant omnia animo firmo.

## 1:3
Ἔμπροσθεν τοῦ Θεοῦ καὶ Πατρὸς ἡμῶν) Neither the Syrian reads this, nor the Arab. Versions do not prejudice the authentic text, in which those things are constantly read, and have been expounded by Greek Interpreters, and they contribute to the sincerity of faith, charity, and hope, whence Theodoret says they were added, so that God may be acknowledged as the inspector of all those things, I add, so that they may be approved by this our Epoptes.

Latin:

Ἔμπροσθεν τοῦ Θεοῦ καὶ Πατρὸς ἡμῶν) Hoc neque Syrus le- git, neque Arabs. Versiones non præjudicant textui authentico, in quo constanter illa leguntur, & à Græcis Inter- pretibus exposita sunt, ac faciunt ea ad sinceritatem fidei, charitatis, & spei, unde Theodoreto ea adje- cta dicit, ut Deus illorum omnium inspector agno- scatur, addo, ut ea huic nostro Epoptæ probe- tur.

## 1:4
Vers. 4.

Εἰδότες) Here a new sense begins; and this participle is constructed with that which follows immediately, ἐγενήθητε. Thus Grotius refers this to the Thessalonians, which was also done by Theodoret: But it is more correctly referred by Chrysostom and Theophylact and most other Interpreters to Paul and his associates. For they appeal to the Thessalonians' knowledge of what they themselves were like, in the following verse 5, and testify that they have become their imitators, to whom therefore that ἐγενήθητε v. 6 pertains, which cannot be denied. The reason is therefore given, why they always retain the memory of them, and make mention of them in their prayers, because, namely, they know that they are elect.

Brethren beloved by God) Coloss. 3, 12. Beloved by God ידידי יהוה. A similar expression 2. Thess. 2, 13. If you regard the common punctuation of the Greek codices, that ὑπὸ Θεοῦ is not to be connected with the preceding word ἠγαπημένοι, but with the following τὴν ἐκλογὴν ὑμῶν, as Theophylact has it with Chrysostom, because we know for certain that you have been chosen by God.

Your election) How GOD has separated you from the world. See what has been said at Ephes. 1, 4. and add 2. Petr. 1. v. 10. Grotius seems to understand election to faith, which he distinguishes from election to eternal life. Although indeed one should not agree with the Reformed, who wish that all who are elected to faith are also elected to eternal life, and that all true believers persevere in faith and are saved, and thus were predestined to salvation from eternity, when on the contrary it is undoubted from the scriptures that some believe only for a time, and that dogma, that believers cannot fall away from faith, has been expressly condemned in the Augsburg Confession, of which the Reformed boast themselves to be associates, in article XII, yet there is not a twofold election handed down in the scriptures, one to faith, the other to salvation: But when the eternal election of believers is discussed, predestination to life is understood. Nor indeed did God choose only some by a certain absolute decree, to whom he might wish to give faith, but having provided faith to all, he wishes all to come to the faith or acknowledgment of the truth, and to be saved, Acts 17, 31. 1. Tim. 2, 4. and for that purpose he ordered the Gospel to be preached to all, through which he wishes to excite faith in the hearts of those who hear it, which is therefore called the Word of faith, Rom. 10, 8. 17. and he wishes that they be saved through it, John 5, 34. These things I say to you, that you may be saved, just as the Gospel itself is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes, as the Apostle testifies, Rom. 1, 16. To Justinianus it does not seem probable that Paul knew the predestination of the Thessalonians by divine revelation, or that he would declare it to them, because that could have harmed rather than helped. But Paul does not say that all are elected, even though he writes to the whole assembly of the Church. For there were, without doubt, even in that assembly some not elect, some temporary.

Nor is it necessary that we say that Paul knew this of others by the certainty of faith, that they are of the number of the elect: It is enough if he judged so from the signs according to the canon of charity.

Concerning election to salvation, B.

Hunnius, B. Osiander, B. Balduinus, Flacius, and others of ours explain it: as also the Reformed, and even from the Papists Thomas, whose paraphrase is this: I know with certainty that you are elect, and that you have obtained this election not by your merit, but freely from God.

Latin:

Vers. 4.

Εἰδότες) Hic novus sensus incipit; & construitur hoc participium cum illo, quod mox sequitur ἐγενήθητε. Sic refert hoc Grotius ad Thessalonicenses, quod & à Theodoreto factum: Sed rectius à Chry- sostomo & Theophylacto ac plerisque aliis Interpre- tibus ad Paulum & socios refertur. Nam ad Thes- salonicensium scientiam quales fuerint ipsi, versu se- quenti 5. provocant, eosque sui imitatores factos esse testantur, ad quos proinde illud ἐγενήθητε v. 6. pertinet, quod negari non potest. Ratio ergo redditur, cur semper ipsorum memoriam retine- ant, & in orationibus suis pro iisdem mentionem faciant, quia nempe sciant, illos esse electos.

Ἀδελφοὶ ἠγαπημένοι ὑπὸ Θεοῦ) Coloss. 3, 12. Ἠγαπημένοι ὑπὸ τοῦ Θεοῦ ידידי יהוה. Similis loquutio 2. Thess. 2, 13. Si vulgatam distinctionem codicum Græcorum respicias, illud ὑπὸ Θεοῦ non connectendum cum præcedenti voce ἠγαπημένοι, sed cum sequenti τὴν ἐκλογὴν ὑμῶν, ut Theophylactus habet cum Chryso- stomo, quia certo scimus, à Deo vos esse electos.

Τὴν ἐκλογὴν ὑμῶν) Quomodo DEUS vos è mundo secreverit. Vide quæ dicta Ephes. 1, 4. & adde 2. Petr. 1. v. 10. Videtur Grotius electionem ad fidem, quam di- stinguit ab electione ad vitam æternam intelligere. Quanquam vero non assentiendum sit Reforma- tis, qui omnes ad fidem electos ad vitam æternam etiam electos esse volunt, omnesque vere fideles perseverare in fide, atque salvari, adeoque ab æter- no ad salutem prædestinatos esse, quum contrà è scripturis indubium sit, nonnullos ad tempus tan- tum credere, ac dogma illud, quod fideles à fide deficere non possint in Augustana Confessione, cujus se socios jactitant Reformati, diserte damnatum sit artic. XII. non tamen gemina, in scripturis tradita est, electio, altera ad fidem, altera ad salutem: Sed cum de electione æterna fidelium agitur, prædestinatio ad vitam intelligitur. Neque vero Deus quos- dam tantum elegit decreto quodam absoluto, qui- bus fidem dare velit, sed omnibus fidem παρασχὼν, omnes vult ad fidem vel agnitionem veritatis per- venire, ac salvari, Actor. 17, 31. 1. Tim. 2, 4. eoque fine omnibus Evangelium prædicari jussit, per quod fidem excitare vult in cordibus eorum, qui id audiunt, quod ideo Verbum fidei dicitur, Rom. 10, 8. 17. ac vult, ut per illud salventur, Joh. 5, 4. Hæc dico vobis, ut salvemini, quemadmodum Evange- lium ipsum potentia Dei est ad salutem omni creden- ti, teste Apostolo, Rom. 1, 16. Justiniano non vide- tur probabile Paulum Thessalonicensium prædestina- tionem divinitus cognovisse, aut eam ipsis declaratu- rum esse, quod obesse non prodesse id potuerit. Sed non dicit Paulus, omnes esse electos, etsi ad totum cœtum Ecclesiæ scribat. Fuere enim, sine dubio, etiam in illo cœtu nonnulli non electi, nonnulli πρόσκαιροι.

Neque necessum est, ut dicamus, certitudine fidei hoc cognovisse de aliis Paulum, quod e numero electorum sint: Satis est, si ita judicarit ex signis juxta charitatis canonem.

De electione ad salutem explicant B.

Hunnius, B. Osiander, B. Balduinus, Flacius, aliique e nostris: necnon Reformati, etiam è Pontificiis Thomas, cujus hæc est paraphrasis: Cognosco certitudinaliter, vos esse electos, & hanc electionem non meritu vestru, sed à Deo effis gratuite adepti.

## 1:5
Vers. 5. Ὅτι τὸ Εὐαγγέλιον our doctrine.

See what we have said in the Prolegomena to the Gospels.

Thus Romans 16, 25. 2 Thess. 2, 14. 2 Tim. 2, 8. Οὐκ ἐγενήθη εἰς ὑμᾶς ἐν λόγῳ μόνον eis ὑμᾶς, that is, among you.

In the Manuscript, πρὸς ὑμᾶς in the same sense. It did not stand, he says, within words. Ἀλλὰ καὶ ἐν δυνάμει with healing, with the expulsion of demons, 1 Cor. 2, 4. Καὶ ἐν Πνεύματι ἁγίῳ καὶ ἐν πληροφορίᾳ πολλῇ that is, in πληροφορίᾳ πολλῇ Πνεύματι ἁγίῳ, concerning which kind of speaking we have spoken at John 3, 5. And that truly is, with great arguments of the Holy Spirit dwelling in you.

Understand, however, not only those miraculous gifts, but also the works of love and patience.

See Luke 1, 1. and what is said there. By arguments he proves the election of the Thessalonians partly from the efficacy of the Gospel in this verse, partly from living experience v. 6, 7. The words εἰς ὑμᾶς have emphasis, because it does not sound only of the Gospel externally, but of the Ministers, as those whom God works through the Gospel to the hearers, and as it were enter into their hearts.

For as God is to be regarded here κυρίως, who wills to enter into us through the word, and dwells in our hearts through faith, Job 14, 23. Eph. 3, 15. Thus the Doctors of the Word intervene διακονικῶς, as those whose ministry and work God uses, through whom He enters into us, through whom He converts and regenerates us, etc.

By δύναμιν the Apostle does not understand the miracles of healings, the expulsion of demons, etc., whether here or in the parallel passage 1 Cor. 2, 8, but the power and efficacy of the Gospel, which is δύναμις θεοῦ, Rom. 1, 16, or by hendiadys, ἐν δυνάμει καὶ ἐν Πνεύματι ἁγίῳ in the spiritual power of the Holy Spirit, which exerts itself ἐν πληροφορίᾳ πολλῇ, in much assurance, as an effect and operation. For this the Holy Spirit works in us through the Gospel. πληροφορία does not denote arguments, but trust, certainty, firm persuasion, confidence: nor is it that the words are to be transposed, that ἐν Πνεύματι ἁγίῳ καὶ πληροφορίᾳ πολλῇ is done through many arguments of the Holy Spirit.

We have refuted the corruption of the passage John 3, 5 in this place. Extraordinary gifts or miracles of healings and the expulsion of demons are neither common to the Thessalonians nor were they published there, Acts 17, nor if they had exerted themselves, could they be held as common to the faithful, but are the property of a few; hence they could not be brought forward as causes of the election of the Thessalonians.

More rightly therefore B. Hunnius: From this mark we establish concerning your election to salvation, because the preaching of the Gospel bore fruit in you, and was fixed not in speech alone or empty preaching, but in the power of the Holy Spirit, who powerfully exerted His own efficacious force in you, illuminating you, converting, regenerating, renewing, and consolidating you in faith. Which is also the interpretation of Osiander and others of ours, and is preferred by Crocius:

Calvin, he says, interprets it as the spiritual energy of the doctrine, as 1 Cor. 2, 4. Bullinger, whom I follow, as the efficacy and working power in the hearts of the faithful.

In the same way Zanchius. And further on the words and in the Holy Spirit: The Greek Scholia advise that they refer either to Paul, who preached by the power of the Holy Spirit, or to the Thessalonians, who received the Holy Spirit.

Theophylact is not much different. Theodoret holds the latter, naming grace. You say that the author of the power is indicated: no otherwise Bullinger and Aretius.

Not badly.

Zanchius refers it to the gifts of the Holy Spirit, which were given to believers, as Gal. 3, 5, which, especially, pleases me. Concerning πληροφορίᾳ it holds thus: The ancient interpreter translates φόρᾳ πολλῇ as in much fullness, which Lombard interprets as said of the fullness of gifts, lest they should think themselves inferior to the Jews, and to have received less than they.

Thomas repeats and adds, in the fullness of much instruction, because the Apostle had influenced them in all things necessary for faith. But πληροφορία denotes a certain and full persuasion: hence the Apostle shows that they were not wavering, but consolidated in faith, so that they might have faith in the proclamation without any doubt.

Which πληροφορίαν we judge is to be understood not only of certain persuasion, but especially also of the trust which we place in the grace of God and the redemption of Christ preached in the Gospel, which is the soul of faith and of the faithful, and exerts itself in πληροφορίᾳ not only in the intrepid confession of faith, but also especially in the firm adhesion of the heart, and full acquiescence in God, even in the very heat of temptations and persecutions, 1

Pet. 1, 7. Rom. 4, 21. 2 seqq. Ephes. 2, 12. Heb. 5, 16. Conf. Roman. 4, 21. Col. 2, 2. Heb. 6, 11. cap. 10, 22. Vers. 6. Καθὼς οἴδατε, καθὼς ἐγενήθημεν ἐν ὑμῖν δι ὑμᾶς You remember what manner of men we were among you, and that for your sake, that we might convert you, that we might retain you in faith. Καὶ ὑμεῖς μιμηταὶ ἡμῶν ἐγενήθητε Kaj here is valid as 'so' in the Hebrew manner.

Concerning the sense see 1 Cor. 4, 16. C. 11, 1. Καὶ τοῦ Κυρίου The Syriac has 'of the Lord'.

The Manuscript has 'and of God', as Eph. 5, 1. Δεξάμενοι τὸν λόγον ἐν θλίψει πολλῇ A sign of a great spirit to embrace such a word in the presence of danger.

He touches upon the history, which is Acts 17, 5. 6. 7. 8. 9. 10. Μετὰ χαρᾶς Πνεύματι ἁγίῳ With joy proceeding from the Holy Spirit, which follows faith.

See Acts 5, 41. The same thing χαρᾷ ἐν Πνεύματι ἁγίῳ, Rom. 14, 17. Vers. 7. Ὥστε γενέσθαι ὑμᾶς τύπους πᾶσι τοῖς πιστεύουσιν, ἐν μόνον ἐν τῇ Μακεδονίᾳ καὶ τῇ Ἀχαΐα Τύπους to the Rabbis שׁוֹרֶשׁ, or טוֹפֶס or טוֹפְסָא, is an exemplar.

See Phil. 3, 17. Great was the virtue of the Thessalonians, which shone forth not only to their own countrymen, but also to the Achaeans.

But there is more, which follows. He confirms this fruit of the Gospel proclamation from experience, namely, that to the proper knowledge of the Thessalonians, what manner of men they were among them, for their sake, the Apostle and his colleagues not only in doctrine, but also in life, not only by acting and working, but also by suffering and tolerating, so that they might set themselves forth as a type in both proclamation and example, which the Thessalonians might observe, and also regarding the public documents and specimens of the faithful of this Church: since they showed themselves not only imitators of Paul and of the Lord Himself, as an example of all examples, regarding the zeal of faith and piety, and constancy, but also as a type of other Churches in Macedonia, Philippi, Berrhoea, etc., and Achaia, where the Corinthian Church was eminent, not only by receiving the Word of the Gospel in much θλίψει and affliction, but also by deriving joy therefrom in the Holy Spirit, even in the most grievous persecutions and temptations, such as are noted in part, Acts 17, in Jason and his house. They were therefore a type of the promptness of faith, of alacrity, trust, patience, constancy.

Although therefore the Word of the Gospel could not be received by you without affliction and pressure, yet from the midst of the darkness of tribulations shone forth the pleasant light of spiritual joy and gladness excited by the Holy Spirit in your hearts, by which it might then without any difficulty disperse that dense cloud of adversity, lest succumbing to them you should retreat from the heavenly truth.

By this laudable perseverance

You have shone before, and like a torch have held a light before all the Churches throughout Achaia and Macedonia with a salutary example, as this blessed Hunnius says. Similarly Theophylact: He strengthens them indeed both by praising and by admonishing, saying that they are by no means inferior in undergoing dangers. Alas, what and how great is that praise, to have been made imitators of the Preceptor immediately, and not only of him, but also of the Lord Jesus. But in what way have these now been rendered followers of God? Because He also, while enduring many evils, was rejoicing, and was offering Himself to these willingly, and so vehemently, that He would address the Father thus: Glorify me, Father, John 17. Concerning the joy of the Holy Spirit in tribulations, Theophylact says thus: For the Spirit does not allow you to grieve, for even if pain were to torment the bodies, yet through the Spirit joy and sweetness were imparted to the mind. For just as it is evident that through the Spirit those three children were breathed upon by dew in the midst of the flames, and remained untouched by the fire, so the same Spirit in the crisis of life, when the flesh is tormented, renders us more joyful, and fills us with joy, when He proposes to us those good things that are to be our reward to be looked upon. Note, however, that someone becomes a follower of the Lord then, when he endures crises and evils with the cheerfulness of the Spirit and of the mind. We add also what he has concerning the type of other Churches in Macedonia and Achaia: But finally, he says, Paul came to these. He says, therefore, you have shone so much from virtue, that you have instructed those who preceded me. But they have imitated Paul in this, because although he was later than the other Apostles, he nevertheless surpassed them by a long interval. See how he said not that these were made a form for those about to believe, but that they had exhibited a form to those already believing, namely, how one ought to believe. And because with a certain ardor of mind, and with the greatest promptness in undergoing danger. But by Achaia, Theophylact understands all of Greece: In which he followed Chrysostom, who also with Oecumenius in the Greek scholia understood all of Greece, and how they were made types or patterns for all believers, he explains thus: Yet you have shone forth, so that you have become teachers of those who preceded us. For he does not say, so that you might be made a form for believing, but to those who were already believing, you have been made a form.

PART II. OF CHAPTER I.

Confirmation of the eulogy of the Thessalonians.

Latin:

Vers. 5. Ὅτι τὸ Εὐαγγέλιον nostra doctrina.

Vide quæ in Prolegomenis ad Evangelia diximus.

Sic Romanor. 16, 25. 2. Thess. 2, 14. 2. Tim. 2, 8. Οὐκ ἐγενήθη εἰς ὑμᾶς ἐν λόγῳ μόνον eis ὑμᾶς, id est, apud vos.

In Manuscripto, πρὸς ὑμᾶς sensu eodem. Non stetit, inquit, intra verba. Ἀλλὰ καὶ ἐν δυνάμει cum sanatione, cum expulsione Dæmonum, 1. Cor. 2, 4. Καὶ ἐν Πνεύματι ἁγίῳ καὶ ἐν πληροφορίᾳ πολλῇ id est, in πληροφορίᾳ πολλῇ Πνεύματι ἁγίῳ, de quo loquendi genere diximus ad Joh. 3, 5. Id vero est, cum magnis argumentis habitantis in vobis Spiritus sancti.

Intellige autem non mirifica tantum illa dona, sed & dilectionis & patientiæ opera.

Vide Luc. 1, 1. & ibi dicta. Argumentis probat electionem Thessalonicensium partim ab Evangelii efficacia hoc verlu, partim à viva experientia v. 6. 7. Voces εἰς ὑμᾶς emphasin habent, quod non sonet solum Evangelium extrinsecus, sed Ministri, utpote quos operatur Deus per Evangelium ad auditores, & in corda ipsorum veluti ingrediantur.

Ut enim Deus κυρίως hic spectandus, qui vult per verbum ad nos ingredi, & per fidem habitat in cordibus nostris, Job. 14, 23. Eph. 3, 15. Sic interveniunt Doctores Verbi διακονικῶς, utpote quorum ministerio & opera Deus utitur, per quos ingreditur ad nos, per quos convertit & regenerat nos &c.

Per δύναμιν non intelligit Apostolus miracula sanationum, expulsionem Dæmonum &c. sive hic, sive in loco parallelo 1. Cor. 2, 8. sed virtutem & efficaciam Evangelii, quod est δύναμις θεοῦ, Rom. 1, 16. sive per hendyaden, ἐν δυνάμει καὶ ἐν Πνεύματι ἁγίῳ in virtute spirituali Spiritus sancti, quæ se exerit ἐν πληροφορίᾳ πολλῇ, in multa fiducia, ceu effectu & operatione. Hanc enim Spiritus sanctus per Evangelium operatur ia nobis. πληροφορία non notat argumenta, sed fiduciam, certitudinem, firmam persuasionem, confidentiam: nec est, ut verba trajiciantur, quod ἐν Πνεύματι ἁγίῳ καὶ πληροφορίᾳ πολλῇ fit per argumenta multa Spiritus sancti.

Loci Joh. 3, 5. corruptelam istic loci profligavimus. Dona extraordinaria vel miracula sanationum & expulsionis Dæmonum neque Thessalonicensibus communia vel edita ibi sunt, 18. 17. neque si exeruissent sese, fidelibus communia haberi possunt, sed paucorum propria sunt; proinde seu causæ electionis Thessalonicensium adduci non potuere. Rectius proinde B.

Hunnius: Ex hac nota statuimus de electione vestri ad salutem, quia prædicatio Evangelii fructificavit in vobis, fuitque fixa non in sermone solum seu inani prædicatione, sed in virtute Spiritus Sancti, qui suam in vobis falsificam vim potenter exseruit, illuminans vos, convertens, regenens, renovans & in fide consolidans. Quæ etiam ἐξήγησις est Osiandri & aliorum e nostris, & præfertur à Crocio: Calvinus, inquit, spiritualem doctrinam energiam interpretatur, sicut 1.

Cor. 2, 4. Bullingerus, quem sequor, efficaciam & vim agentem in cordibus fidelium.

Eodem modo Zanchius. Et porro ad verba & in Spiritu sancto: Scholia Græca vel ad Paulum, qui virtute Spiritus sancti prædicaverit, vel ad Thessalonicenses referri monent, qui Spiritum sanctum acceperint.

Non multo aliter Theophylactus. Posterius tenet Theodoretus gratiam nominans. Calpinus virtutis autorem indicari dicis: non aliter Bullingerus & Aretius.

Non male.

Zanchius ad dona Spiritus sancti refert, quæ credentibus dabantur, sicut Gal. 3, 5. quod, imprimis mihi placet. De πληροφορίᾳ sic habet: Vetus interpres vertit φόρᾳ πολλῇ in plenitudine multa, quod Lombardus de plenitudine donorum dictum interpretatur, ne putarent, se judeis esse inferiores, & minus accepisse, quam illi.

Thomas repetit & addit, in plenitudine multa instructionis, quia Apostolus eos influxerit in omnibus ad fidem necessariis. At πληροφορία certam plenamque persuasionem notat: proinde ostendit Apostolus, non befasfe dubios, sed in fide consolidatos esse, ut citra omnem dubitationem præconio fidem haberent.

Quam πληροφορίαν non tantum de certa persuasione, sed inprimis etiam de fiducia, quam in gratiam Dei & redemptionem Christi in Evangelio prædicatam collocamus, intelligendam censemus, quæ anima est fidei & fidelium, & exerit sese πληροφορίᾳ non tantum in intrepida fidei confessione, sed etiam maxime in firma adhæsione cordis, & acquiescentia plena in Deo, in ipso etiam tentationum & persequutionum æstu, 1.

Petr. 1, 7. Rom. 4, 21. 2. seqq. Ephes. 2, 12. Ebr. 5, 16. Conf. Roman. 4, 21. Col. 2, 2. Ebr. 6, 11. cap. 10, 22. Vers. 6. Καθὼς οἴδατε, καθὼς ἐγενήθημεν ἐν ὑμῖν δι ὑμᾶς Meministis quales fuerimus inter vos, idque vestri causa, ut nimirum vos converteremus, ut in fide retineremus. Καὶ ὑμεῖς μιμηταὶ ἡμῶν ἐγενήθητε Kaj hic valet sic more Ebræo.

De sensu vide 1. Cor. 4, 16. C. 11, 1. Καὶ τοῦ Κυρίου Syrue ὁ τοῦ Κυρίου.

Manuscriptus καὶ Θεοῦ, ut Eph. 5, 1. Δεξάμενοι τὸν λόγον ἐν θλίψει πολλῇ Magni animi signum sermonem talem amplecti præsente periculo.

Tangit historiam, quæ est Act. 17, 5. 6. 7. 8. 9. 10. Μετὰ χαρᾶς Πνεύματι ἁγίῳ Cum gaudio proficiscente ex Spiritu sancto, qui fidem sequitur.

Vide Act. 5, 41. Id ipsum χαρᾷ ἐν Πνεύματι ἁγίῳ, Rom. 14, 17. Vers. 7. Ὥστε γενέσθαι ὑμᾶς τύπους πᾶσι τοῖς πιστεύουσιν, ἐν μόνον ἐν τῇ Μακεδονίᾳ καὶ τῇ Ἀχαΐα Τύπους Rabbinis שׁוֹרֶשׁ, vel טוֹפֶס vel טוֹפְסָא, est exemplar.

Vide Phil. 3, 17. Magna fuit virtus Thessalonicensium, quæ non tantum popularibus suis, sed & Achæis præluxerit.

Sed plus est, quod sequitur. Hunc fructum præconii Evangelici confirmat ab experientia, puta, quod ad notitiam propriam Thessalonicentium, quales inter ipsos fuerint, propter ipsos, Apostolus & collegæ ejus non solum in doctrina, sed etiam in vita, non solum agendo & operando, sed etiam patiendo & tolerando, ut sese sisterent & præconio & exemplo typum, quem observerent Thessalonicenses, nec non quoad publica fidelium istius Ecclesiæ documenta & specimina: quum sese non tantum imitatores Pauli & Demini ipsius, tanquam exempli exemplorum omnium, quoad zelum fidei & pietatis, ac constantiam, sed etiam typum aliarum Ecclesiarum in Macedonia, Philippis, Berrhææ &c. & Achaia, ubi Corinthiaca Ecclesia eminebat, exhibuerint, non tantum suscipiendo in multa θλίψει & afflictione Verbum Evangelii, sed etiam gaudium inde percipiendo in Spiritu sancto, etiam in gravissimis persecutionibus & tentationibus, quales ex parte notatæ sunt, Act. 17. in Jasone, ejusque domo. Typus itaque erant fidei promptitudinis, alacritatis fiducia, patientiæ, constantiæ.

Quamvis igitur non fine afflictione & pressura potuit à vobis recipi Verbum Evangelii, tamen è media caligine tribulationum emicuit grata lux spiritualis gaudii & lætitiæ per Spiritum sanctum in cordibus vestris excitata, qua densam illam nebulam adversitatis tum nullo negotio discuteret, ne succumbentes iis resliretis à verime cœlesti.

Hac laudabili perseverentia

praluxistis, & ceu facem quandam pretulistis saluta- ri exemplo cunctis per Achaiam & Macedoniam Ecclesiis, ut hic B. Hunnius. Similiter Theophyla- żtus : Hos quidem & laudando & monendo corrobo- rat, inquiens, eos nequaquam se esse pericula subeundo inferiores. Vah qualis illa & quanta est laus, confe- stim imitatores Præceptoris esse effectos, nec hujus mo- do, quin & Domini Jesu. At quonam pacto hi sunt Dei jam redditi sectatores? Quia & ille mala pluri- ma tolerans gaudebat, & his se ultro offerebat, & eni- xe adeo, ut sic Patrem alloqueretur : Glorifica me Pa- ter Joh. 17. De gaudio Spiritus sancti in tribula- tionibus ita Theophylactus : Neque enim Spiritus do- lere vos sinit, Nam etsi corpora dolor excruciaret, per Spiritum tamen animo gaudium & suavitas indeba- tur. Nam quemadmodum constat, per Spiritum in mediis flammis tres pueros illos rore fuisse afflatos, & intactos ab igne mansisse, sic Spiritus idem in vitæ dis- crimine, cum caro excruciatur lætiores nos reddit, & gaudio explet, cum bona illa nobis in mercedem futu- ra visenda proponit. Adverte autem tunc fieri quem- piam Domini sectatorem, cum discrimina & mala tolerat cum Spiritus & animi hilaritate. Addimus etiam quæ de typo aliarum Ecclesiarum in Mace- donia & Achaia habet : Atqui postremo, inquit, ad hos Paulus venit. Inquit itaque, adeo vos claruistis ex virtute, at eos, qui me prævenerunt, vos instruxeri- tis. Paulum vero in hoc illi sunt imitati, quia cum cæ- teris posterior fuisset Apostolis, hos tamen longo inter- vallo excessit. Vide ut non formam dixerit credituris hos fieri, sed credentibus jam formam exhibuisse, quemadmodum scilicet credendum sit. Et quia cum animi quodam ardore, & periculo adeundo summa cum promptitudine. Per Achaiam autem totam Græciam intelligit Theophylactus : In quibus se- quutus est Chrysostomum, qui etiam cum Oecume- nio in scholiis Græcis totam Græciam intellexit, & quomodo typi vel exemplaria omnibus creden- tibus facti sunt, sic exponit: Tamen resplenduistis, ut eorum, qui nos præcesserant, Doctores facti sitis. Non enim dicit, ut facti sitis forma ad credendum, sed iis, qui jam credebant, facti estis forma.

PARS II. CAPITIS I.

Confirmatio elogii Thessalonicensium.

## 1:8
Vers. 8. For from you the word of the Lord has sounded forth, not only in Macedonia and Achaia, but also in every place your faith toward God has gone forth) There is a transposition. The direct construction would have been: Not only has the word of the Lord sounded forth from you in Macedonia and Achaia. That word ἐξήχηται (has sounded forth) is the Hebrew הָמָה, Joel 3:14. It is found also in Sirach 40:15. The same as נִשְׁמַע. Many merchants from Thessalonica were trading throughout all of Greece. Then the fame spreads itself more widely, as can be seen in Rom. 1:8.

So that you have no need to say anything) There is no need for me to preach what I did among you, or what kind of people you were toward me and the Gospel. The matter is already known to all.

He confirms what he said, that they were made a type of the Churches in Macedonia and Achaia, and also concerning the alacrity of the Thessalonians in the reception of the Word, both from the propagation of the Word to the Churches, and from the public fame and the struggle of the faith of the Thessalonians throughout the whole world. For that is what he says, with blessed Hunnius as interpreter, from you, as the firstfruits of those provinces in the Gospel, the word of the Lord has sounded forth, so that like a most powerful thunder it might resound far and wide from your city to the foreign shores of Greece. He writes that the fame of the faith of the Thessalonians, which is in God, has flowed not only to the neighboring regions of Greece, but also to foreign peoples and nations: where by the word faith he designates not only knowledge of the Evangelical doctrine, but at the same time trust, which the paraphrase (in God) declares not obscurely. He records that this faith of theirs has shone forth in such a way that there is no need to say anything, or to institute a further eulogy of it. Concerning the propagation of the Word through fame, Theodoret explains these things thus: But that word, from you the word of God has resounded, he said, not that the preaching began from there, but that their alacrity toward Divine things, which was commonly boasted of, moved many to follow piety with great zeal. To which also the commentary of Theophylact tends: For from you the word of the Lord has been divulged, that is, concerning your virtue. And further: Macedonia indeed and Achaia have been filled with the word through you, and with your doctrine by example. And what is to be held in the place of a miracle, in so short a time you have disseminated so much faith through all places. Although indeed the proclamation of the Word did not begin among the Thessalonians, yet it was divulged more abundantly and propagated even in those places in which the Gospel had already been disseminated before, and the blast of the trumpet of the word of the Lord resounded from there among other cities also in those regions. Concerning the word ἐξήχηται, Theophylact says: He spoke according to the metaphor of a trumpet, which excited the hearing by the blast of sounds. Furthermore, concerning the fame of the faith ἐν παντὶ τόπῳ, that is, throughout the whole world, where there is knowledge of the faith and of the faithful, with Chrysostom as interpreter, the word ἐξελήλυθεν is used, concerning which Theophylact says: He discussed faith no differently than about some animate thing, when he said that it had both gone forth, and had traveled through, and was now spread abroad. Who, regarding the following words, so that it is not necessary for us to say anything, has it thus: So, he says, is the fame of your faith now both vehement and so very celebrated, that the faithful do not wait for me to proclaim your praises. But as often as I have begun to say something about you, so that I might also lead them to an ardor of faith by praising you, they themselves anticipate me, and recount your former virtues.

Latin:

Vers. 8. Ἀφ’ ὑμῶν γὰρ ἐξήχηται ὁ λόγος τῦ Κυρίε, ὐ μόνον ἐν τῇ Μακεδονίᾳ κὰι τῇ Ἀχαΐᾳ, ἀλλὰ κὰι ἐν παντὶ τόπῳ ἡ πίστις ὑμῶν ἡ πρὸς τὸν Θεὸν ἐξελήλυθεν) Est transpositio. Recta con- structio fuerat: Ὀυ μόνον ὁ λόγος τῦ Κυρίυ ἀφ’ ὑμῶν ἐξήχη- ται ἐν τῇ Μακεδονίᾳ κὰι τῇ Ἀχαΐᾳ. Illud ἐξήχηται personuit est המן, Joel. 3, 14. Reperitur & Sirach. 40, 15. Idem quod נשמע. Multi ex Thessalonica mercatores per Græ- ciam omnem negotiabantur. Deinde fama latius se spar- git, ut videre est Rom. 1, 8.

Ὡστε μὴ χρείαν ὑμᾶς ἔχειν λαλεῖν τι) Nihil opus est, me prædicare, quæ apud vos feci, aut quales vos erga me & Ev- angelium fueritis. Res nota jam est omnibus.

Confirmat, quæ dixit, quod typus facti sint Ec- clesiarum in Macedonia, & Achaia, nec non de alacritate Thessalonicensium in receptione Verbi,tum è propagatione Verbi ad Ecclesias,tum è fama pu- blica & colluctatione fidei Thessalonicensium per totum orbem. Id enim est, quod dicit, interprete B. Hunnio, à vobis, tanquam primitiis illarum pro- vinciarum in Evangelio, pertonuit sermo Domini, ut tanquam validissimum tonitru ex vestra urbe ad exteras Græciæ oras longe lateque percrebresceret. Non advicinas duntaxat Græciæ regiones, sed ad ex- teras quoque gentes & nationes dimanasse scribit fa- mam fidei Thessalonicensium, quæ sit in Deum: ubi fidei voce non notitiam duntaxat doctrinæ Evangeli- cæ, sed simul fiduciam designat, quod paraphrasis (in Deum) non obscure declarat. Hanc illorum fidem sic inclaruisse memorat, ut opus non sit loqui quic- quam, aut ulteriorem ejus laudationem instituere. De propagatione Verbi per famam hæc ita expli- cat Theodoretius: Illud autem, à vobis resonuit sermo Dei, dixit, non quod prædicatio illinc cœperit, sed quod eorum ad res Divinas, quæ vulgo jactabatur, alacritas, multos ad pietatem magno studio sequen- dam commoverit. Quo etiam abit Theophylacti commentarius: A vobis enim divulgatus est sermo Domini, hoc est, de vestra virtute. Et porro: Ma- cedonia quidem & gratia sermone per vos, & doctri- na vestra exemplo repleta est. Et quod miraculi est lo- co habendum, tam brevi per omnia loca tantum fidei disseminastis. Quanquam vero apud Thessaloni- censes non cœperit præconium Verbi,divulgatum tamen uberius est ac propagatum etiam in illis lo- cis, in quibus jam ante disseminatum erat Evange- lium, ac clangor tubæ sermonis Domini personuit inde apud alias quoque civitates in istis regioni- bus. De verbo ἐξήχηται Theophylactus: Disso- nuit ad tubæ metaphoram dixit, quæ sonorum clango- re auditum excitavit. Porro de fama fidei ἐν παν- τὶ τόπῳ, hoc est per totum orbem, ubi est fidei & fidelium notitia, interprete Chrysostomo, adhi- betur verbum ἐξελήλυθεν, de quo Theophylactus: Non secus de fide disseruit, ac de re quadam animata, cum eam dixit & prosectam fuisse, peragrasseque, & esse jam divagatam. Qui ad verba sequentia, ita ut non sit necesse nobis quicquam loqui, sic habet: Adeo, inquit, & vehemens est, & tam celeberrima fi- dei vestræ jam fama, ut nec me laudes vestras prædi- caturum fideles expectent. Quin quotiescunque de vobis dicere aliquid cœperim, ut & illos vos laudando ad fidei ardorem traducam, me ipsi præveniant, & ve- stras virtutes priores enarrent.

## 1:9
Vers. 9.

For they themselves report concerning us what manner of entry we have unto you) Αὐτοὶ, that is, who are in all places. That noun did not precede, but it is sufficiently understood from that ἐν παντὶ τόπῳ. It is a construction κατὰ τὸ σημαινόμενον. They relate how, from the few Jews who had received us, the Church suddenly grew into a great number.

The reason is given why there is no need for further recommendation: Inasmuch as other peoples, having been informed everywhere by public report, announce, proclaim, and celebrate what manner of entry Paul and his colleagues had to the Thessalonians, and with what readiness and what fruit they received them.

And how you turned) you who are from the Gentiles. Ἐπιστρέψατε here has the force of a reciprocal, as in Luke 17:4, Acts 3:9 and 9:35, ch. 11:21, ch. 14:15, and elsewhere.

Not that they converted themselves by their own powers, but that they were not like tree trunks, but having been converted by God, they converted themselves according to that passage in Jeremiah 31:18: Turn me, that I may be turned.

To God from idols) Acts 14:14. There ἀπὸ τῶν ματαίων is the same as here ἀπὸ τῶν εἰδώλων = אלילים.

To serve) that is, εἰς τὸ δουλεύειν. See Ephesians 1, verse 4.

To the living God) אל חי, Matthew chapter 16, verse 16. John 6, verse 69.

And true) not those fictitious ones, such as Jupiter, Neptune, Alexander. Thus John 17:3.

These things are said antithetically. He named him living, says Theodoret, inasmuch as idols do not live: But true, inasmuch as those are falsely called Gods. He is called living, because he lives in himself, from himself, and by himself, and gives life to all, so that he may be distinguished from inanimate idols, which neither have life in themselves, nor can confer it upon others. True, not because he is truthful, but because he alone is by nature the true God, John 17:3, so that he may be distinguished from those who are not by nature Gods, and are therefore falsely held to be Gods, Gal. 4:8. Although indeed God the Father is understood, because his Son is commemorated in v. 10, yet the Son or the Holy Spirit is not excluded, because they were serving the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit, inasmuch as they were baptized in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. But the Father is proclaimed as the origin of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, since the Son is from the Father by generation, and the Holy Spirit by eternal procession, and these three are one, 1 John 5:7.

Latin:

Vers. 9.

Αὐτοὶ γὰρ περὶ ἡμῶν ἀπαγγέλλουσιν ὁποίαν εἴσοδον ἔχομεν πρὸς ὑμᾶς) Αὐτοὶ, id est, qui in omnibus sunt locis. Non præcessit id nomen, sed ex illo ἐν παντὶ τόπῳ satis intelligi- tur. Est constructio κατὰ τὸ σημαινόμενον. Narrant illi, quomodo ex paucis, qui nos exceperant Judæis, in magnum numerum Ecclesia subito excreverit.

Causa redditur, cur ulteriori commendatione opus non sit: Siquidem alii populi passim per fa- mam publicam edocti annuntient, prædicent, ac celebrent, qualem ingressum habuerint Paulus & collegæ ad Thessalonicenses, quanta promptitudi- ne & quanto fructu susceperint ipsos.

Καὶ πῶς ἐπεστρέψατε) vos qui ex gentibus estis. Ἐπιστρέ- ψατε hic vim habet reciproci, ut Luc. 17, 4. Actor. 3, 9. & 9, 35. c. 11, 21. c. 14, 15. & alibi.

Non quod ipsi se viribus suis converterint, sed quod non instar truncorum fuerint, sed conversi Divinitus se converterint juxta illud Jerem. 3, 10. Converte me, ut convertar.

Πρὸς τὸν Θεὸν ἀπὸ τῶν εἰδώλων) Actor. 14, 14. Ibi ἀπὸ τῶν ματαίων idem quod hic ἀπὸ τῶν εἰδώλων = אלילים.

Δουλεύειν) id est, εἰς τὸ δουλεύειν. Vide Ephes. 1, vers. 4.

Θεῷ ζῶντι) אל חי, Matth. cap. 16. vers. 16. Johan. 6. vers. 69.

Καὶ ἀληθινῷ) non fictis illis, quales Jupiter, Neptunus, Alexander. Sic Joh. 17, 3.

Ἀντιθετικῶς hæc dicuntur. Viventem nomina- vit, inquit Theodoretus, utpote quod idola non vivant: Verum autem, utpote, quod illa Dii falso vocentur. Vivens dicitur, quia in se, ex se, & per se vivit, & vi- tam dat omnibus, ut discernatur ab idolis inanima- tis, quæ nec in se habent vitam, nec aliis conferre possunt. Verus, non quod verax sit, sed quod unus ille solus verus natura Deus sit Joh. 17, 3 ut ab illis, qui natura Dii non sunt, adeoque falso pro Diis habentur, Gal. 4, 8. discernatur. Quanquam verò intelligatur Deus Pater, quia Filius ejus v. 10. com- memoratur, non tamen excluditur Filius, aut Spiri- tus sanctus, quia serviebant Patri, & Filio, & Spiri- tui sancto, utpote in nomine Patris & Filii & Spiri- tus sancti baptizati. Sed Pater prædicatur ceu origo Filii & Spiritus sancti, quum à Patre sit Filius per generationem, & Spiritus sanctus per processio- nem æternam, & hi tres unum sint, 1. Joh. 5, 7.

## 1:10
V. 10. And to wait for his Son from the heavens) Philipp. 3:20.

Whom he raised from the dead Jesus) And here there is a transposition for Jesus, whom he raised from the dead, as in Acts 4:10.

Him who delivers us from the wrath to come) There is here a present for a future twice: delivering for about to deliver: then coming, that is, future, in which word there is frequent use of the present for the future. And wrath signifies punishment, namely that which will be inflicted at the final judgment, as Rom. 5:9, Eph. 5:6, Col. 3:6. In Hebrew you would say: גאלנו מחרון הבא.

A twofold end of conversion is assigned: 1. the worship of the true God, 2. the expectation of the coming of the Son of God: Cf. Tit. 2:12, 13. By this reasoning the chief heads of the Christian faith are exhibited together, comprised in the confession of the Thessalonians: Concerning the living and true God, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Concerning the Son of God's being delivered for us unto death and his raising from the dead, concerning the redemption of Jesus, as also concerning the final judgment. Furthermore, the significance of the present is to be retained in the word delivering on account of continuous liberation; because he not only delivered us, as far as merit and acquisition are concerned, but he delivers us perpetually, as far as act and application are concerned: he not only reconciled us by his death, but he also makes us participants of that reconciliation, so that we may enjoy the same, and be delivered from the wrath to come or rather coming. For this also can be taken in the present. For wrath or punishment is called coming, because it always threatens, and approaches daily with, as it were, silent steps.

Latin:

V. 10. Καὶ ἀναμένειν τὸν υἱὸν αὐτῶ ἐκ τῶν ὀυρανῶν) Phi- lipp. 3, 20.

Ὃν ἤγειρεν ἐκ νεκρῶν Ἰησοῦν) Et hic transpositio est pro Ἰησοῦν, ὃν ἤγειρεν ἐκ νεκρῶν ut Act. 4, 10.

Τὸν ῥυόμενον ἡμᾶς ἀπὸ τῆς ὀργῆς τῆς ἐρχομένης) Est hic præsens pro futuro bis: ῥυόμενον pro ῥυσόμενον: deinde ἐρ- χομένης, id est, venturæ, in quo verbo frequens usus Præ- sentis pro futuro. Et ὀργὴ pœnam significat, scilicet il- lam, quæ judicio ultimo inferetur, ut Rom. 5, 9. Eph. 5, 6. Col. 3, 6. Ebraice diceres: גאלנו מחרון הבא.

Conversionis finis geminus assignatur, 1. cultus ve- ri Dei, 2. expectatio adventus Filii Dei: Conf. Tit. 2, 12. 13. Qua ratione Christianæ fidei capita præci- pua simul exhibentur in confessione Thessaloni- censium comprehensæ: De Deo vivo, & vero Pa- tre, Filio, & Spiritu sancto. De Filii Dei pro nobis traditione in mortem & excitatione è mortuis, de re- demptione Jesu, ut & de extremo judicio. Cæterum retinenda est præsentis significatio in verbo ῥυόμε- νος propter continuam liberationem; quia non tan- tum liberavit nos, quantum ad meritum & acquisi- tionem, sed liberat nos perpetuo, quantum ad actum & applicationem: non tantum reconciliavit morte sua, sed etiam participes nos facit illius reconcilia- tionis, ut eadem fruamur, & ab ira ventura vel po- tius veniente liberemur. Nam & hoc in præsenti accipi potest. Ira enim vel pœna dicitur ἐρχομένη, quia semper imminet, & tacitis quasi gressibus quotidie propius accedit.

## 2:1 Argument
CHAPTER II. WHICH IS COMMENDATORY.

ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

The Apostle appeals to the testimony of the Thessalonians, concerning his entry to them and his alacrity and faithfulness in preaching the Gospel, and his maternal affection toward them, and his blameless conduct, and his paternal admonitions to a life worthy of their calling; and he proclaims the grace of God, because they received the Word, and became imitators of the Churches in Judea in enduring persecutions; finally, he testifies to his desire to see them, as the crown of his glory.

There are two parts: The former deals with the administration of the Apostolic office among the Thessalonians, up to v. 12. The latter with the fruit of the same, the constancy of the Thessalonians in the faith, up to v. 20.

PART I. Concerning the administration of the Apostolic office among the Thessalonians.

V. 1. For you yourselves know, brethren, that you deservedly retain that hope of eternal life. For those things which we announced to you are true, nor did we give you even the slightest reason why you should suspect otherwise. Ὄιδατε means you remember.

These things do not tend toward retaining the hope of eternal life, but toward explaining and further confirming those things which he had briefly touched upon, ch. 1, 5, as to what kind of persons Paul and his colleagues were among the Thessalonians, and on their account, in which part he again appeals to their own knowledge, which seems to have been done on account of false teachers, lest they should insinuate themselves into the same position. He had appealed before, v. 9, to the testimony of other churches, ch. 1; now he appeals to the judgment of the Thessalonians themselves concerning his entry to them.

Τὴν εἴσοδον ἡμῶν τὴν πρὸς ὑμᾶς, ὅτι ὀυκενὴ γέγονε) Κενὴ, that is, lying, deceitful. שָׁוְא which is often translated as κενὸν. We did not come to you to deceive, namely I, Silas, and Timothy, whom he also joins to himself in the office of teaching, as in 2 Cor. 1, 19. Whence is it evident that the arrival was not vain? From that which follows.

The Apostle does not remove from himself by these words a lie or falsehood, but an ineffective result. For he protests about error later in v. 3; here, however, he confirms the fruit of his preaching, just as all interpreters agree on this, that εἴσοδον ὀυκενὴν is an entry not vain, which the word properly signifies, namely that the arrival was not empty, but fruitful and pregnant with fruits worthy of the Evangelical profession, as B. Hunnius and Osiander say, or rather, as Flacius says, that he did not undertake that preaching rashly or out of some carnal affection, nor did he mix in false doctrine or any deceit at all, nor did he add a shameful life, nor finally an unfruitful preaching: he who does not badly fix the proposition here, and determines that this predicate is to be explained in the following eleven verses, namely how the entry was not vain. All of which pertains to their confirmation and inflammation in the received religion and its progress.

Latin:

CAPUT II. QUOD ΣΥΣΤΑΤΙΚΟΝ.

ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

Apostolus provocat ad testimonium Thessaloni- censium, de ingressu ad ipsos & alacritate, ac fidelitate in prædicando Evangelio, & affectu materno erga ipsos, ac conversatione incul- pabili, & paternis commonitionibus ad di- gnam vocatione vitam; prædicatque Dei gra- tiam, quod Verbum susceperint, & imitatores facti sint Ecclesiarum in Judæa in tolerandis persecutionibus, testatur denique de deside- rio suo ipsos videndi, ceu coronam gloriæ suæ.

Partes duæ sunt: Prior agit de officii Apostoli- ci penes Thessalonicenses administratione, ad v. 12. Posterior de fructu ejusdem, constantia Thessaloni- censium in fide ad v. 20.

PARS I. De officii Apostolici penes Thessalonicenses administratione.

V. 1. Αὐτοὶ γὰρ ὄιδατε ἀδελφοὶ) merito illam spem vi- tæ æternæ retinetis. Vera enim sunt, quæ vobis annun- tiavimus, neque vel minimam vobis causam dedimus, cur aliter suspicaremini. Ὄιδατε meministis.

Non hæc tendunt ad spem vitæ æternæ retinen- dam, sed ad explicanda & confirmanda ulterius ea, quæ breviter attigerat, cap. 1, 5. quales fuerint inter Thessalonicenses, & propter ipsos, Paulus, & col- legæ, qua in parte denuo ad ipsorummet propriam notitiam provocat, quod videtur ob falsos Docto- res, ne qua illi se iisdem ingerent factum. Provoca- rat antea v. 9. ad testimonium Ecclesiarum aliarum, cap. 1. jam ad ipsorum Thessalonicensium judicium provocat de ingressu suo ad ipsos.

Τὴν εἴσοδον ἡμῶν τὴν πρὸς ὑμᾶς, ὅτι ὀυκενὴ γέγονε) Κενὴ, id est, mendax, fallax. שָׁוְא quod sæpe κενὸν vertitur. Non decepturi ad vos venimus, nempe ego, Silas & Timo- theus, quos sibi etiam in docendi munere adjungit, ut 2. Cor. 1, 19. Unde constat, adventum non fuisse vanum? Ex eo quod sequitur.

Non mendacium hisce a se removet, aut falsita- tem Apostolus, sed irritum successum. Nam de er- rore protestatur postea v. 3. hic vero confirmat fructum præconii sui, quemadmodum Interpretes omnes in eo consentiunt, εἴσοδον ὀυκενὴν esse ingres- sum non vanum, quod proprie vox sonat, quod nempe non inanis fuerit adventus, sed fructibus Ev- angelicæ professione dignis fœcundus, & gravidus, ut B. Hunnius & Osiander, vel potius, ut Flacius, quod non temere, aut carnali quodam affectu eam præ- dicationem susceperit, nec falsam doctrinam, aut ullum omnino dolum admiscuerit, nec vitam tur- pem, nec denique prædicationem infrugiferam adjunxerit: qui non male hic propositionem figit, ac prædicatum illud sequentibus undecim versibus ex- poni statuit, quomodo nempe introitus non fuerit vanus. Quæ omnia pertinent ad confirmationem, inflammationemque ipsorum in receptæ religione ejus- que profectu.

## 2:2
V. 2. Ἀλλὰ προπαθόντες καὶ ὑβρισθέντες, καθὼς ὄιδατε, ἐν Φιλίπποις) You note that I had already suffered many things for the sake of that matter for which I was coming to you. The history is touched upon, which is in Acts 16, 12.

Ἐπαῤῥησιασάμεθα ἐν τῷ Θεῷ ἡμῶν λαλῆσαι ὑμῖν τὸ ἐυαγ- γέλιον τῦ Θεῦ) We had confidence in God to speak to you. The same manner of speaking is in Eph 6, 20.

Ἐν πολλῷ ἀγῶνι) In great dangers. See above Coloss. 1, 29. It is a metonymy. Thus also the Greeks say: Ἀγὼν πρόφασιν ὀυκ ἀναμένει. In danger one must not hesitate.

He removes from himself here, as the adversative ἀλλὰ teaches, something that could have contributed to a κενὴν εἴσοδον, namely that vanity, as if he had rushed to them to preach rashly, and he teaches the contrary, namely that he preached the Gospel to them with great παῤῥησίᾳ in God, in much struggle, because through great affliction and insult, which, as was not unknown to them, he had sustained at Philippi (which certainly is accustomed to restrain human rashness), he proceeded to them, and undertook to teach them, and that with great confidence in the Lord, nor did he allow himself to be deterred from it by afflictions and persecutions. All of which he refers back to the strengthening of the Lord as received at the same time. For it is in the Lord, and in the name of the Lord, and in the power of the Lord. Although we escaped dangers, he says, interpreting Theophylact, in Philippi, we again exposed ourselves to others. You see how he always ascribes the sum of all his deeds to God. For having confidence, he says, in God, that is, we received both strength and vigor from him.

Latin:

V. 2. Ἀλλὰ προπαθόντες καὶ ὑβρισθέντες, καθὼς ὄιδατε, ἐν Φιλίπποις) Notatis me multa jam perpessum ejus rei causa, ob quam ad vos veniebam. Tangitur historia, quæ est Act. 16, 12.

Ἐπαῤῥησιασάμεθα ἐν τῷ Θεῷ ἡμῶν λαλῆσαι ὑμῖν τὸ ἐυαγ- γέλιον τῦ Θεῦ) In Deo fiduciam habuimus, ut loquere- mur. Idem loquendi genus Eph 6, 20.

Ἐν πολλῷ ἀγῶνι) In magnis periculis. Vide supra Coloss. 1, 29. Est Μετωνυμία. Sic & Græci dicunt: Ἀγὼν πρόφασιν ὀυκ ἀναμένει. In periculo non est cunctan- dum.

Removet hic a se, quod adversativa ἀλλὰ docet, aliquid, quod ad κενὴν εἴσοδον facere poterat, eam nempe vanitatem, quasi temere ad prædicandum iis accurrisset, ac contrarium docet, quod scilicet cum magna παῤῥησίᾳ in Deum, in multo certami- ne Evangelium ipsis prædicarit, quia per magnam afflictionem & contumeliam, quam, quod iis non i- gnotum esset, Philippis sustinuerat (quæ utique hu- manam temeritatem coërcere solet), ad ipsos per- rexerit, eos docere, idque magna cum fiducia, susceperit in Domino, nec per afflictiones & persecutiones ab eo sese absterreri passus sit. Quod omne confortationi Domini ita simul acce- ptum refert. Nam in Domino est & in nomine Domini & in virtute Domini. Etsi pericula, inquit interprete Theophylacto, in Philippis evasimus, aliis rursum nos ipsos objecimus. Vides ut semper gestorum omnium Deo summam adscribat. Fiduciam enim inquit habentes in Deo, hoc est ab eo & vires & ro- bur accepimus.

## 2:3
V. 3. Ἡ γὰρ παράκλησις ἡμῶν) Our exhortations to you, Acts 15, 31. Rom. 12, 8. It is spoken excellently of prophecy in Acts 4, 36. c. 13, 15.

Ουκ ἐκ πλάνης, ὀυδὲ ἐξ ἀκαθαρσίας, ὀυδὲ ἐν δόλῳ) That those exhortations had their origin neither from a desire to seduce, nor from any impure affection, nor indeed was there any deceit mixed in with them, it appeared sufficiently to you. πλάνη is מִרְמָה, Prov. 14, 8. Ἀκαθαρσία elsewhere signifies lusts: here it corresponds to the Hebrew נְבָלָה, as in Hosea 2, 10. Nahum 3, 6. Moreover, נְבָלָה is τὸ ἄσχημον, and it is so translated elsewhere: and it comprehends all the vices which were figured in the law by unclean animals.

Why παράκλησις is accepted there as Prophecy, but not as consolation or exhortation, no reason appears. Furthermore, the Apostle here removes from himself and his colleagues all causes corrupting the doctrine, namely every seduction, every impurity, every deceit. Πλάνη pertains to the error of the dogma itself or the kind of false doctrine. Impurity is rightly referred to the affection or desire to deceive. Others refer it to impure doctrine and life; which pleases Crocius. But impure doctrine pertains to πλάνην, whereas life is not being discussed here, but rather παρακλήσει. Deceit denotes the very method of deceiving. However, the Pseudo-Apostles seem to be tacitly noted here.

Latin:

V. 3. Ἡ γὰρ παράκλησις ἡμῶν) Nostra ad vos monita, Act. 15, 31. Rom. 12, 8. Eximie dicitur de prophetia Act. 4, 36. c. 13, 15.

Ουκ ἐκ πλάνης, ὀυδὲ ἐξ ἀκαθαρσίας, ὀυδὲ ἐν δόλῳ) Monita illa neque ex seducendi studio, neque ex ullo affectu impuro ortum habuisse, neque vero dolum eis admix- tum satis vobis apparuit. πλάνη est מִרְמָה, Prov. 14, 8. Ἀκαθαρσία alibi libidines significat: Hic respondet E- bræo נְבָלָה, ut Oseæ 2, 10. Nahum. 3, 6. Est autem נְבָלָה τὸ ἄσχημον, & sic vertitur alibi: comprehenditque omnia vitia, quæ in lege per immunda animalia figurabantur.

Quare de Prophetia illic accipiatur παράκλησις non vero consolationem vel exhortationem no- cet, nulla apparet ratio. Removet autem hic por- ro Apostolus à se & collegis suis omnes causas do- ctrinam corrumpentes, omnem nempe seductio nem, omnem impuritatem, omnem dolum. Πλάνη pertinet ad errorem ipsum dogmatis aut genus doctrinæ falsæ. Impuritas ad affectum aut studium decipiendi recte refertur. Alii ad impuram doctri- nam & vitam referunt; Quod placet Crocio. Sed doctrina impura ad πλάνην pertinet, de vita autem hic non agitur, sed de παρακλήσει. Dolus notat ipsum modum fallendi. Videntur autem tacite hic notari Pseudo-Apostoli.

## 2:4
Ver. 4.

Ἀλλὰ καθὼς δεδοκιμάσμεθα ὑπὸ τῦ Θεῦ πισευθῆναι τὸ Εὐαγγέλιον) Twice a Greek expression using passives, which would be more clearly stated by actives thus: Καθὼς ὁ Θεὸς ἐδοκίμασε πισέυσαι ἐμοὶ τὸ ἐυαγγέλιον. For δοκιμάζειν with an infinitive signifies the will to bring a thing about, Rom. 1, 28. We have Ἐκ πίσευθην indeed Εὐαγγέλιον in a similar manner of speaking, 1 Tim. 1, 11.

Οὕτω λαλῦμεν) that is, we are accustomed to speak. Thus we utter that, just as it has been entrusted to us. We adulterate nothing.

Οὐχ ὡς ἀνθρώποις ἀρέσκοντες) The same sense in Galat. 1, 10. not men-pleasers.

Ἀλλὰ τῷ Θεῷ τῷ δοκιμάσαντι τὰς καρδίας ἡμῶν) Principally, of course, how this is to be understood appears in 1 Cor. 10, 33. Δοκιμάζειν, here is to explore, as 1 Petr. 1, 7. It is the work of God to explore and search the minds, Roman. 8, 27. 1 Sam. 16, 7. 1 Reg. 8, 39. 1 Paral. 28, 9. 2 Paral. 6. v. 30. Psal. 7, 10. Ps. 44, 22. Jerem. 17, 10. c. 20, 12. Luc. 16, 15. Actor. 1, 24. c. 15, 8. 1 Joh. 3, 20.

Now, against the sincerity of his doctrine, he brings forward first that it was entrusted to him by God himself, then that it was delivered not according to the pleasure of men, but as it is approved by God, who also tests the hearts, with what zeal and affection all things are done.

Latin:

Vers. 4.

Ἀλλὰ καθὼς δεδοκιμάσμεθα ὑπὸ τῦ Θεῦ πισευθῆναι τὸ Εὐαγγέλιον) Bis Græca loquutio per passiva, quæ a- pertius per activa sic enuntiarentur: Καθὼς ὁ Θεὸς ἐδο- κίμασε πισέυσαι ἐμοὶ τὸ ἐυαγγέλιον. Nam δοκιμάζειν cum Infinitivo voluntatem rei efficiendæ significat Rom. 1, 28. Ἐκ πίσευθην vero Εὐαγγέλιον pari loquendi genere habemus 1. Tim. 1, 11.

Οὕτω λαλῦμεν) id est, solemus loqui. Sic illud eloqui- mur, sicut nobis commissum est. Nihil adulteramus.

Οὐχ ὡς ἀνθρώποις ἀρέσκοντες) Idem sensus Galat. 1, 10. non famas ἀρέσκοι.

Ἀλλὰ τῷ Θεῷ τῷ δοκιμάσαντι τὰς καρδίας ἡμῶν) Præci- pue scilicet, quomodo hoc intelligendum apparet 1. Cor. 10, 33. Δοκιμάζειν, hic est explorare, ut 1. Petr. 1, 7. בחן Dei est explorare & scrutari animos Roman. 8, 27. 1. Sam. 16, 7. 1. Reg. 8, 39. 1. Paral. 28, 9. 2. Paral. 6. v. 30. Psal. 7, 10. Ps. 44, 22. Jerem. 17, 10. c. 20, 12. Luc. 16, 15. Actor. 1, 24. c. 15, 8. 1. Joh. 3, 20.

Jam contra sinceritatem doctrinæ suæ adferit primo, quod à Deo ipso sibi commissa, deinde quod non secundum hominum placitum, sed prout Deo probatur, ea tradita sic, qui etiam corda probat, quo studio, & affectu omnia fiant.

## 2:5
Ver. 5.

Οὔτε γάρ ποτε ἐν λόγῳ κολακείας ἐγενήθημεν) It is a Hebraism, such as also below 7 and 10, where 'to be' is used for 'to conduct oneself'. We have never been accustomed to flattering speech.

Καθὼς εἴδατε) You yourselves are witnesses. By contrast, he notes the new Teachers, as to the Philippians.

Οὔτε ἐν προφάσει πλεονεξίας) Nor have we used pretexts to veil avarice. Concerning the word προφάσεως see what is at Mark 12, 40; concerning the sense see 2 Cor. 2, 17.

Θεὸς μάρτυς) He took men as witnesses of his words: God himself as witness of his mind. And here Paul swore, as also often elsewhere.

Latin:

Vers. 5.

Οὔτε γάρ ποτε ἐν λόγῳ κολακείας ἐγενήθημεν) Est Ebræi- smus, qualis & infra 7. & 10. ubi esse ponitur pro versari. Nunquam affuevimus sermoni adulatorio.

Καθὼς εἴδατε) Vos ipsi testes estis. Ex contrario no- tat novos Doctores, ut ad Philippenses.

Οὔτε ἐν προφάσει πλεονεξίας) Neque usi sumus prætex- tibus ad velandam avaritiam. De voce προφάσεως vide quæ ad Marcum 12, 40. de sensu vide 2. Cor. 2, 17.

Θεὸς μάρτυς) Verborum homines sumpsit testes: mentis ipsum Deum. Et hic juravit Paulus, ut & sæpe alibi.

## 2:6
Verse 6.

Nor seeking glory from men, nor from you, nor from others) There are many who teach new things not for the sake of gain, but for the sake of vainglory. Not even this applied to Paul and his companions. They were not like the philosophers, bags full of empty conceit, see John 5:44.

Furthermore, the Apostle removes from himself the vices unbecoming to upright Doctors, as regards speech, flattery, and as regards the mind, avarice and ambition. They derive kolakeian from kolon, because flatterers serve the belly. Since he had anticipated their praises, says Theophylact, lest he render them more suspicious, just as if he had brought them in for the sake of fawning, he says: I have not used the language of flattery before, which is the mark of those who are deceived and those who deceive, nor do I use it now. Theodoret: He called them to witness, he says, concerning flattery. For the words of flatterers are open to those who hear; but avarice, not to them indeed, but to Him who is the inspector of all things. For the scope and purpose of what is done often remains hidden from men. He called avarice preaching for the sake of acquiring money or doing business. How he removes avarice, Theophylact says thus: Nor have we finished this duty of preaching among you out of a desire for money. But that we have not preferred anything by fawning, your testimony is enough: but that I have no lust for possessing, God is witness, but to you it is uncertain. As for glory, the Apostle does not say, we did not receive honor, or we refused what was shown to us and our ministry; but he denies that he hunted for glory from anyone, which is ambitious, Matt. 23:15 seqq. Verse 7. Being able to be a burden) Since we had the right of living at your expense, which is epibaresai below 11. On the contrary, he who does not do this is said to keep himself abare, 2 Cor. 11:9. As Apostles of Christ) As other Apostles do, 1 Cor. 9:6, and indeed by right, as is shown in the same place. But we were gentle in the midst of you) But here parelkei in the Hebrew manner. Thus Homer: He was a gentle father; we were very benign, we yielded from our right, so that we might spare you. The Latin reads infants. But the Greek codices and interpreters read gentle. As a nurse warms her own children) A nurse is called a mother, who gave the breast to Plautus, thus her foster children are called her children. Thalpei warms, as 1 Kings 1:24. Galen: Warmed by the fire. This Greek word is also used of birds that incubate an egg, Job 39:14, or their brood, Deut. 22:6. Procopius on Isaiah 49:22 refers to the office of a nurse, and brings this passage for the mystical fulfillment. A similar comparison from a nurse carrying a child in her bosom, Num. 11:12. Thus yearning for you) It is a poetic word, as is also himeros. It exists also in Job 3:21 for hakah. They are placed not only for desire, but also for love, as: I desire you with my eyes and sweet desire takes me. Not less loving you, he says, than a nurse or her foster children. We were ready) We are prompt. You have eudokeo with the infinitive in Luke 12:32, Rom. 15:26, 1 Cor. 1:21, 2 Cor. 5:8, Gal. 1:15. In that construction it is proper to the LXX interpreters. And Jerome intends this. The word itself otherwise exists in Polybius and others. To impart to you not only the Gospel of God) As we have already done. But also our own souls) that is, even to spend our life for you. For it is a syllepsis. For metadounai is properly said of the Gospel: of life by a certain metonymy. Thus metadidomi is generally taken, and Rom. 1:11. Heauton among the Greeks is of every person. Because you have become beloved) Past for present in the Hebrew manner. For you are most dear to us. The Apostle removes the vice of avarice especially from himself by clear indications by their own testimony or notorious experience. Concerning which Theodoret: We had been commanded, he says, to live from the Gospel, but we did not use the power. But he said that to be a burden, referring to those who do not willingly provide. Others wrongly refer these things to declining ambition, as Ambrosiaster: When we could have been in honor among you. Calvin and Piscator and others in authority. Theophylact proposes both. But the text and the opposition teach that it is a matter of the right of being burdensome with the expenses of food being provided, and thus every suspicion of avarice is removed. The words, as Apostles of Christ, others do not take comparatively, but positively, or argumentatively, as those who perform the Apostleship of Christ, although Silvanus and Timothy were not Apostles of the same order as Paul. For he was the highest Apostle, but they were instructed with Apostolic gifts, and were Doctors of the universal Church applied to the Apostolic duty, yet not called immediately by Christ, nor divinely inspired. If it were a comparison, it would rather be said, as the Apostles of Christ. In the midst of you seems to refer to equality, in the midst of you, that is, equally toward all. Not flattering toward these, morose toward those. Chrysostom understands the nurse as distinct from the mother, but the Apostle rather compares himself to a mother nursing her own children, whose affection is more tender. Nothing is milder, nothing more placid, nothing more benign than a mother. She lowers herself to all duties, there is none so sordid that she does not take upon herself, she flees no labor, no trouble, she cherishes in her bosom, she offers her own blood to be sucked, she carries, she cares for the sick, she wipes away the soiled, she calms the weeping, she spends sleepless nights while they sleep, she desires to see and embrace the absent, she babbles with the babbling, she plays with those playing, and if she could, she would spend her soul for them.

Does he flatter, so that he may obtain glory from it? Does he demand money from the children? As Crocius does here. Theophylact does not read ἱμειρόμενοι, but ὁμειρόμενος from ὁμᾶ & εἴρω, to bind, that is, bound to you. But that reading is more customary, which Chrysostom also retained. Theophylact explains the rest thus: Therefore we not only received nothing from you, but if it were possible, εὐδοκῶμεν, that is, we greatly desire even to empty out our souls in you, and to pour them forth. To hand over the Gospel, this is a sign of goodness: But to bestow one's soul, this is more difficult, and a sign of fervent love. Although indeed these things, and those which follow, look toward the removal of avarice: the words are nevertheless so arranged that, just as he has described his ministry negatively up to this point: so now he describes it affirmatively, and in the same he sets forth his 1. desire and maternal affection, 2. zeal for communicating the Gospel even with the expense of his life, 3. love more than maternal, in that he is willing even to lay down his soul for them, 4. assiduity in laboring, 5. innocence of life, 6. solicitous and paternal exhortations, consolations, and doctrines, by which he perpetually instructed and excited them to every holy duty pleasing to God.

Latin:

Vers. 6.

Οὔτε ζητῦντες ἀπ’ ἀνθρώπων δόξαν, ὔτε ἀφ’ ὑμῶν, ὔτε ἀπ’ ἄλλων) Multi sunt, qui nova doceant non lucri, sed glo- riolæ causa. Ne hoc quidem in Paulum, ejusque comites cadebat. Non erant quales Philosophi κενῆς οἰήσεως ἔμ- πλεοι ἀσκοὶ, vid. Joh. 5, 44.

Removet præterea Apostolus à se vitia, probos Doctores dedecentia,qua sermonem, adulationem, qua animum, avaritiam & ambitionem. Κολακείαν à κόλον deducunt,quod adulatores ventri serviant. Cum horum & laudes, inquit Theophylactus, antici- passet, ne illas reddat suspectiores, perinde ac assentan- di gratia has ingessisset, neque antehac alias (inquit) adulationis sum usus sermone, quod deceptorum est, & fallentium,neque nunc utor. Theodorelus: De adu- latione, inquit, quidem vocavit ipsos in testimonium. Verba enim adulatorum aperta sunt iis, qui audiunt; avaritia autem,non ipsos utique.sed eum,qui est inspe- ctor universorum. Sæpe enim latet homines ejus,quod fit, scopus & institutum. Avaritiam autem vocavit prædicare pro pecuniis parandis aut re facienda. Quo- modo avaritiam removeat,ita Theophylactus: Neq; pecuniarum cupiditate apud vos prædicandi hoc mu- nere sumus defuncti. Quod autem nihil nos prætuleri- mus assentando,vestrum sat est testimonium: quod ve- ro nulla mihi insu habendi libido, Deus est testis,sed vo- bis incertum. Quod ad gloriam, non ait Apostolus, non accepimus honorem, seu recusavimus exhibi- tum nobis & nostro ministerio; sed negat, se aucu- patum esse à quoquam gloriam, quod ambitiosum est, Matth. 23, 15. seqq. Vers. 7. Δυνάμενοι ἐν βάρει εἶναι) Cum jus haberemus vivendi vestro sumptu, quod ἐπιβαρῆσαι infra 11. Ex contrario, qui id non facit, dicitur se servare ἄβαρῆ, 2. Cor. 11, 9. Ὡς χριστῦ Ἀπόστολοι) Sicut Apostoli alii faciunt, 1. Cor. 9, 6. & quidem jure, ut ibidem ostenditur. Ἀλλ’ ἐγενήθημεν ἤπιοι ἐν μέσῳ ὑμῶν) Ἀλλὰ hic παρέλκει more Ebræo. Sic Homerus: Πατὴρ ὡς ἤπιος ἦεν; beni- gni admodum fuimus, cessimus de jure nostro, ut vo- bis parceremus. Latinus legit νήπιοι. At Græci codices & Interpretes ἤπιοι. Ὡς ἂν τροφὸς θάλπῃ τὰ ἑαυτῆς τέκνα) Sicut nutrix ma- ter dicitur, quæ mammam dedit Plauto, sic alumni li- beri ejus vocantur. Θάλπει calefacit, ut 1. Reg. 1, 24. Galenus: Παρὰ τῷ πυρὶ θαλφθείς. Usurpatur & hæc vox Græca de avibus, quæ incubant ovo, Job. 39, 14. aut pul- litiei, Deut. 22, 6. Procopius ad Esaiam 49, 22. humeris portabuntur refert ad nutricis officium, & ad mysticum im- plementum affert hunc locum. Par similitudo à nutrice sinu portante puerum Num. 11, 12. Οὕτως ἱμειρόμενοι ὑμῶν) Vox est Poëtica, ut & ἵμερος. Extat & Job. 3, 21. pro חכה. Ponuntur autem non de desiderio tantum, sed & de amore, ut: ἱὲς σέο σὺν ὄφραισι καί με γλυκὺς ἵμερος αἱρεῖ. Non minus amantes vestri inquit, quam nutrix aut alumno- rum. Εὐδοκῆμεν) Prompti sumus. Εὐδοκέω cum infinitivo habes Luc. 12, 32. Rom. 15, 26. 1. Cor. 1, 21. 2. Cor. 5, 8. Gal. 1, 15. In ea constructione est propria LXX. interpretum. Et hoc vult Hieronymus. Vox ipsa alioqui extat apud Po- lybium & alios. Μεταδῦναι ὑμῖν οὐ μόνον τὸ Εὐαγγέλιον τῦ Θεῦ) Sicut jam fecimus. Ἀλλὰ καὶ τὰς ἑαυτῶν ψυχὰς) id est, etiam vitam vobis impendere. Est enim σύλληψις. Nam μεταδίναι de Evan- gelio proprie dicitur: De vita per Metonymiam quan- dam. Sic ferme sumitur μεταδιδόναι, & Rom. 1, 11. Ἑαυ- τῶν apud Græcos omnis est personæ. Διότι ἀγαπητοὶ ὑμῶν γεγένησθε) Præteritum pro præ- senti more Ebræo. Charissimi enim nobis estis. Avaritiæ imprimis vitium luculentis indiciis à se removet Apostolus proprio ipsorummet testi- monio vel notoria experientia. Quo de Theodore- tus: Præceptum quidem, inquit, nobis fuerat, ut de Evangelio viveremus, sed potestate usi non sumus. Illud autem oneri esse dixit, referens ad eos, qui non lu- benter præbent. Perperam alii hæc referunt ad ambi- tionem declinandam, ut Ambrosœster: Cum apud vos possemus in honore esse. Calvinus & Piscator aliiqve in autoritate. Theophylactus utrumque proponit. Sed textus & oppositio docet, de jure eos ἐπιβαρῆ-ἐπιβαρέον- τας sumptibus alimentorum præbendorum agi, adeo- que omnem suspicionem avaritiæ removeri. Verba, ut Apostoli Christi, alii non comparative accipiunt, sed posiţve, vel ratiocinative, utpote qui Apostolatu Christi fungimur, quamvis non ejusdem ordinis Apostoli fuerint Silvanus & Timotheus cum Paulo. Hic enim summus Apostolus erat, illi vero Aposto- licis donis instructi, & ad Apostolicum munus adhi- biti Doctores universalis Ecclesiæ, non tamen vel immediate à Christo vocati, vel divinitus inspirati. Si comparatio esset, diceretur potius, ὡς οἱ Ἀπόστολοι Χριστῦ. Ἐν μέσῳ ὑμῶν æqualitatem referre videtur, in medio vestrum, id est, erga omnes pariter. Non erga hos blandi, erga illos morosi. Nutricem Chryso- stomus à matre distinctam intelligit, sed Apostolus potius matri proprios liberos nutrienti sese com- parat, cujus affectus est tenerior. Matre nihil mitius, nihil placidius, nihil benignius. Ad omnia officia se de- mittit, nullum tam sordidum est, quod in se non reci- piat, nullum fugit laborem, nullam molestiam, fovet in sinu, sanguinem suum præbet sugendum, portat, curat ægros, extergit sordidatos, placat plorantes, illis dormi- entibus ipsa noctes ducit pervigiles, absentes desiderat videre ac complecti, cum balbutientibus balbutit, collu- dit ludentibus, ac si posset animam ipsis impenderet.

Num adulatur, ut gloriam inde consequatur? Num pecuniam exigit à liberis? ut hic Crocius. Theo- phylactus non legit ἱμειρόμενοι, sed ὁμειρόμενος ex ὁμᾶ & εἴρω necto, id est, devincti vobis. Sed usi- tatior est illa lectio, quam etiam retinuit Chrysosto- mus. Cætera ita exponit Theophylactus: Non so- lum igitur nihil à vobis accepimus, sed si fieri posset, εὐδοκῶμεν, hoc est, valde volumus vel animas nostras in vobis evacuare, effundereque. Tradere autem Ev- angelium, hoc bonoritatis: Animam vero largiri, dif- ficilius, & ferventis amoris est indicium. Quan- quam vero hæc, & quæ sequuntur, ad removendam avaritiam spectent: Verba tamen ita comparata sunt, ut quemadmodum negative hactenus mini- sterium suum descripsit: ita jam affirmative id de- scribat, & in eodem suam exponat 1. cupiditatem & affectum maternum, 2. studium communicandi Ev- angelium vel cum dispendio vitæ, 3. amorem plus quam maternum, eo quod vel animam ponere pro ipsis velit, 4. assiduitatem in laborando, 5. innocen- tiam vitæ, 6. folicitas & paternas adhortationes, con- solationes, doctrinas, quibus eos perpetuo ad quod- vis Deo gratum sanctumque officium instruxit at- que excitavit.

## 2:9
Vers. 9.

For you remember, brothers, our labor, and our toil) Κόπος in bearing טֹרַח, μόχθος in doing עָמָל. For night and day working) Truly wonderful goodness. See Acts 18, 3. 1 Cor. 4, 12. In order not to burden any of you) That I might not be a burden to anyone. See above 7. We preached to you the Gospel of God) εἰς ὑμᾶς for ὑμῖν: לָכֶם. Theophylact on this passage: Do not remember, he said, the benefits which I have conferred upon you, but you have become mindful of the labors. Nor only of these, but you also remember the fatigues and weariness, with which I was affected by working not only during the day, but also at night. Oh, what great solicitude was in Paul, that he might not offend anyone! He argues furthermore that the Thessalonians did not abound much in these external goods, when he says, that we might not burden any of you. That nocturnal and diurnal labor can be extended both to the administration of his office and to manual labor, by which he provided a living for himself and his own, Acts 20, 34. In both of which he appeals to their own knowledge.

Latin:

Vers. 9.

Μνημονεύετε γὰρ, ἀδελφοὶ, τὸν κόπον ἡμῶν, καὶ τὸν μόχθον) Κόπος in ferendo טֹרַח, μόχθος in agendo עָמָל. Νυκτὸς γὰρ καὶ ἡμέρας ἐργαζόμενοι) Mira sane bonitas. Vide Act. 18, 3. 1. Cor. 4, 12. Πρὸς τὸ μὴ ἐπιβαρῆσαί τινα ὑμῶν) Ne cuiquam gravis es- sem. Vide supra 7. Ἐκηρύξαμεν εἰς ὑμᾶς τὸ Εὐαγγέλιον τοῦ Θεοῦ) εἰς ὑμᾶς pro ὑμῖν: לָכֶם. Theophylactus in hunc locum: Non reminisca- mini, dixit, beneficiorum, quæ vobis contulerim, sed laborum memores estis effecti. Neque horum dunta- xat, quin & defatigationes & lassitudines recordemi- ni, quibus non interdiu solum, sed & noctu infudan- do affectus sum. O quanta inerat Paulo, ne quem offenderet, solicitudo! Arguit præterea Thessaloni- censes, non multum bonis externis his abundasse, cum inquit, ne quem vestrum gravaremus. Labor ille nocturnus, & diurnus extendi potest tum ad officii administrationem, tum ad manuariam operatio- nem, qua victum sibi parabat suisque Actor. 20, 34. In quo utroque ad propriam ipsorum notitiam provocat.

## 2:10
V. 10. You are witnesses, and God) See above 5. Now he deals with his life and conversation among the Thessalonians, calling them themselves and God as witnesses. For they could testify concerning his external conversation, as irreprehensible, God concerning the internal piety of the soul. Although faith, says Theophylact, is to be placed in God, yet since it is by no means open to men whether these things are confirmed by the testimony of God, he calls those also to whom the discourse is held as witnesses. We add the gloss of Flacius: He makes three parts of the Christian life, that it be holy, which faith and the fear of God provide; that it be just, which is done while we not only harm no one, but also benefit all, as far as it is possible; that it be finally blameless, which pertains to the remaining morals, chastity, sobriety, and moderation in all things. He cites two witnesses, not only them, but also God, because He alone can see and judge the movements of the heart. But what he says: We lived for you, the sense is, for that reason I showed myself such to you all the more studiously, so that I might the more edify you, and offer scandal to no one. It is known that such locutions signify that something is done for the advantage or disadvantage of another. As holily, and justly, and blamelessly we behaved toward you who believe) We behaved, as above 5 and 7. Ὁσίως is referred to God, as εὐσεβῶς, Tit. 2, 12. Δικαίως to actions, which pertain to society: Ἀμέμπτως as σωφρόνως to Titus, to those things which look to each person separately.

He does not appeal to the infidels, but to the faithful. For those were slandering the Apostles, by whom the Apostle was proclaimed, according to Theophylact, as a certain irreligious and impious and idle sower of ravings, and as one who professed nothing sound.

Latin:

V. 10. ὑμεῖς μάρτυρες, καὶ ὁ Θεός) Vide supra 5. Nunc de vita & conversatione inter Thessaloni- censes agit, ipsosmet & Deum testem appellans. Ipsi enim de externa conversatione, ceu irrepre- hensibili, testari poterant, Deus de interna animi pietate. Etsi fides, inquit Theophylactus, Deo est ad- hibenda, tamen cum nequaquam hominibus pateat, utrum hæc Dei testimonio comprobentur, & ipsos, ad quos sermo habetur, testes vocat. Addimus glossam Flacii: Tres partes vita Christiana facit, ut sit sancta, quod fides ac timor Dei præstat, ut sit justa, quod fit, dum non solum nemini obsumus, sed etiam omnibus, quoad fieri potest, prosumus, ut sit denique inculpata, quod ad reliquos mores pertinet, castitatem, sobrieta- tem, & moderationem in omnibus. Duos vero testes citat, non ipsos tantum, sed & Deum, quia ille solus potest cordis motus aspicere ac judicare. Quod au- tem dicit: Vobis vixerimus, sensus est, ideo me vobis talem tanto studiosius præstiti, ut eo magis vos ædifica- rem, neminique scandalum præberem. Notum est tales locutiones significare aliquid fieri in commodum aut damnum alterius. Ὡς ὁσίως, καὶ δικαίως, καὶ ἀμέμπτως ὑμῖν τοῖς πιστεύουσιν ἐγενήθημεν) Versati sumus, ut supra 5. & 7. Ὁσίως ad Deum refertur, ut εὐσεβῶς, Tit. 2, 12. Δικαίως ad actiones, qui ad societatem pertinent: Ἀμέμπτως ut σωφρόνως ad Ti- tum, ad ea, quæ seorsim quemque spectant.

Ad infideles non provocat, sed ad fideles. Illi enim calumniabantur Apostolos, a quibus & irre- ligiosus & impius & iners quidam deliramento- rum proseminator, & tanquam qui nihil sani pro- fiteretur Apostolus, teste Theophylacto proclama- batur.

## 2:11
V. 11. As you know how we, as a father his own children, exhorting you and comforting and testifying) Supply we were, which is understood in the Hebrew manner. We warned, he says, the idle, we comforted the sorrowful, we bore witness to the ignorant, but and testifying is absent in the Manuscript.

Again he calls these as witnesses, which is truly a sign of humility, that they might observe that he did nothing through insolence. Theophylact: But it is especially a sign of the confidence of the cause. To the words each one of you, Chrysostom exclaims: Papa! In such a multitude he omits no one: not the small, not the great, not the poor, not the rich. Cf. Acts 20, 31. He compares himself to a father, because he cared for them not as a Master for disciples, as a tutor for wards, but as a Father for his own children, who loves his children tenderly as if they were a part of his own substance, and desires them to be most happy. The pronoun you is redundant by the idiom of the Hebrews. From these things, however, it appears that Paul taught there for a sufficiently long time, just as from the fact that he testifies in Phil. 4, that the Philippians sent expenses once and again to him while he was staying in Thessalonica.

Latin:

V. 11. Καθάπερ οἴδατε ὡς ἕνα ἕκαστον ὑμῶν, ὡς πατὴρ τέκνα ἑαυτοῦ παρακαλοῦντες ὑμᾶς καὶ παραμυθούμενοι καὶ μαρ- τυρόμενοι) Supple fuimus, quod subauditur more Ebræo. Monuimus, inquit, desides, consolati sumus mœstos, te- stimonium diximus ignaris, sed καὶ μαρτυρόμενοι abest in Manuscripto.

Rursum hos in testes vocat, quod sane est humi- litatis indicium, quod nihil se per insolentiam age- re, observent. Theophylactus: Maxime vero in- dicium est confidentiæ causæ. Ad verba ἕνα ἕκαστον ὑμῶν, exclamat Chrysostomus: Papa! in tanta mul- titudine neminem omittit: non parvum, non magnum, non pauperem, non divitem. Conf. Act. 20, 31. Patri se comparat, quod ipsorum, non ut Magister disci- pulorum, ut tutor pupillorum, sed ut Pater libero- rum suorum curam gesserit, qui liberos ceu sub- stantiæ suæ partem tenerrime amat, & felicissimos esse cupit. Pronomen ὑμᾶς παρέλκει Ebræorum idiotismo. Ex hisce autem apparet, Paulum satis diu illic docuisse, sicut ex eo, quod Phil. 4. testatur, Philippenses semel atque iterum Thessalonicæ a- genti sumptus misisse.

## 2:12
V. 12. In order that you might walk worthily of God. See Col. 1, 10, where the locution is the same. Of Him who calls you into His own kingdom and glory) See 1 Pet. 5, 10. In the Manuscript having called, as Gal. 1, 6.
