As he had already testified to their faithfulness in duty: so he now indicates the end, toward which all things had been directed, namely that they might walk in the way of both truth and justice, before God and men, not only as is worthy of them, as those who have been converted, but as is worthy of God, who had called them out of mere grace, nay, was continuing to call them—which the word of the present tense implies—them who were truly given over to wretched idols, and slaves of sin, and thus guilty of eternal damnation, from darkness to light, from sin to justice, from the servitude and power of Satan to His kingdom and to glory. Is it not necessary to walk worthily of God when one is affected by such great grace from God? Is it not necessary to persevere in faith? Is it not necessary to proceed in the course of piety, for whom such a goal, the kingdom of God itself, and the enjoyment of Divine glory is designated by God?

PART II. Concerning the fruit of the Apostolic ministry, the constancy of the Thessalonians in the faith.

Latin:

V. 12. Εἰς τὸ περιπατῆσαι ὑμᾶς ἀξίως τοῦ Θεοῦ. Vide Col. 1, 10. ubi locutio eadem. Τοῦ καλοῦντος ὑμᾶς εἰς τὴν ἑαυτοῦ βασιλείαν καὶ δόξαν) Vide 1. Petr. 5, 10. In Manuscripto καλέσαντος, ut Gal. 1, 6.

Ut fidelitatem in officio jam testatus erat: ita finem nunc indicat, quorsum omnia directa fue- rint, ut nempe ambularent in via tum veritatis, tum justitiæ, coram Deo & hominibus, non tantum sicut dignum idipsis, ceu conversis, sed sicut dignum est Deo, qui vocaverat ex mera gratia, imo vocare pergebat, quod verbum Præsentis temporis innuit, ipsos miseris profecto idolis deditos, & peccati ser- vos, adeoque damnationis æternæ reos, a tenebris ad lucem, a peccato ad justitiam, a servitute ac po- testate Satanæ ad regnum suum & ad gloriam. An- non digne Deo ambulandum tanta hac gratia a Deo affectatis? Annon in fide perseverandum? Annon in pietatis cursu pergendum, quibus sco- pus talis, ipsum Dei regnum, Divinæque gloriæ fruitio a Deo designatur?

PARS II. De fructu Apostolici ministerii, constantia Thessalonicensium in fide.

## 2:13
Vers. 13. For this cause also we thank God without ceasing, see above 1. 2. 3.

Because when you received the word of hearing from us of God) This is a transposition for the word of hearing of God, a message about God. The Hebrews cannot express this sufficiently with one word; they say the word of hearing, as in Heb. 4, 2. דבר שמע of God, that is, about God. Concerning the word παραλαμβάνειν see 1 Cor. 11, 23. c. 15, 1. 3. Gal. 1, 9. 12. Phil. 4, 9. Coloss. 2, 6.

You received the word of men,) that is, as the word of men, which must be supplied from what follows, as the Greeks note here.

But, as it is truly, the word of God) And here 'as' is missing, which is understood from that 'as' (καθώς). The word of God is called the Evangelical sermon by way of eminence.

Which also works in you who believe) That word received through faith produces excellent works. It works (ἐνεργεῖται) is passive in sound, active in sense, as in Rom. 7, 5. Gal. 5, 6. Eph. 3, 20. See 1 John 3, 9. it works patience.

Up to this point, by the narration of his own actions, preaching, and life in their conversion, he has endeavored to confirm and excite them to constancy and progress; now he also does the same thing from the commemoration of their conversion and progress through four verses, as Flacius notes. Finally, to the very end of the chapter, he performs this by the commemoration of his affection toward them, and of his confidence concerning them, and of his future boasting in the coming of the Lord; with which gentle and sweet testimony he soothes their minds to fulfill his joy in the four final verses. Now, therefore, he proclaims the most illustrious fruits of his preaching: the serious embrace of the true religion, and the pious imitation of the principal Churches, even regarding constancy in persecution. He figures and adorns this exposition, however, with thanksgiving toward God, in order to show that it is an excellent matter and a signal benefit of God, and that God is both to be celebrated and prayed to for it. Which he establishes here in three moments: namely, that they acknowledged his doctrine to be the Word of God, that they received the same with due reverence and use or practice of it, and that they experienced its living efficacy, regeneration, tranquility of heart, and the testimony of the Spirit. He convinces them, therefore, by their own confession and experience in themselves, that this religion is the true and salutary religion of God, and that God himself acts with them through it. Whence it follows that they ought in all ways to persevere and progress in that very doctrine and all other doctrines, or even to abhor the corruptions of this one, which is also the primary scope of this part, which was rightly observed by Flacius, who urges this sentiment of the Apostle here against Schwenkfeldian fanaticism and the remaining calumniators of Holy Scripture, especially against the Papists.

Λόγον ἀκοῆς, which for Theophylact is preaching, or the word which is believed by hearing, is properly the Word, accepted through hearing, which the Apostles had heard from God, as in Isaiah 53:1. The preaching of the Prophets is called their report, and therefore τῷ Θεῷ is added, as if he were saying, this is the Word of God. Therefore, the Word of God is not called objective, because it treats of God, but in respect of its principle, because it is from God. Others, with Lombard, refer the pronoun ὃς to God, others to λόγον τῷ Θεῷ. The latter is more suitable. For it is occupied in preaching not the virtue and efficacy of God, but of the Gospel and of the Evangelical proclamation. Oecumenius observes that the word ἐνηργεῖται can be explained both actively and passively. Theophylact accepted it passively, it is demonstrated by the works themselves. Others prefer to understand it actively, that Paul gives thanks to God for the efficacy of the Gospel, which was working among the Thessalonians, not looking at external extraordinary signs, which seemed so to Theodoret, but primarily internal operations, because it begets true confidence of heart, unshaken hope, unbroken constancy, singular patience, and wonderful joy in adversities along with other virtues and spiritual motions. The discourse had already acted, yet he does not say, it acted, but it acts: because the Word of the Lord continues to act, it does not cease. He does not say, with you, as if both the Word of God and they themselves were working, but in you, so that all efficacy may be of God, and the praise of Divine grace may be attributed. But the fact that he makes mention of believers is not to be understood exclusively, but appropriatively or specificatively, that he holds those to whom he writes as believers by the judgment of charity, and wishes them to be such, and appropriates this grace to them: which God wishes to be denied to no one, caring for the Word to be preached to that end, which is living and efficacious for converting souls, so that all may be converted through it. Therefore, let the absolute decree be banished from here, which those Crocian things savor of.

He speaks of salutary operation: for he restricts it to believers, when in others the discourse also has its own efficacy. From the intention of God and the virtue implanted, it has salutary efficacy among all, unless they impede it and place an obstacle. For it does not act in an irresistible manner.

Latin:

Vers. 13. Διὰ τοῦτο καὶ ἡμεῖς εὐχαριστοῦμεν τῷ Θεῷ ἀδια- λείπτως, supra 1. 2. 3.

Ὅτι παραλαβόντες λόγον ἀκοῆς παρ᾽ ἡμῶν τοῦ Θεοῦ) Est trajectio pro λόγον ἀκοῆς τοῦ Θεοῦ, nuntium de Deo. Id Ebræi cum una voce satis eloqui non possunt, dicunt λόγον ἀκοῆς, ut Ebr. 4, 2. דבר שמע τοῦ Θεοῦ, id est, de Deo. De voce παραλαμβάνειν vide 1. Cor. 11, 23. c. 15, 1. 3. Gal. 1, 9. 12. Phil. 4, 9. Coloss. 2, 6.

Ἐδέξασθε ὀ λόγον ἀνθρώπων,) id est, ὡς λόγον ἀνθρώπων quod ex sequenti supplendum est, ut notant hic Græ- ci.

Ἀλλὰ, καθώς ἐστιν ἀληθῶς, λόγον Θεοῦ) Et hic deest ὡς, quod ex illo καθώς subintelligitur. Λόγον Θεοῦ per emi- nentiam dicitur sermo Evangelicus.

Ὃς καὶ ἐνεργεῖται ἐν ὑμῖν τοῖς πιστεύουσιν) Sermo ille per fidem receptus egregia producit opera. Ἐνεργεῖται sono passivum, sensu activum, ut Rom. 7, 5. Gal. 5, 6. Eph. 3, 20. Vide 1. Joh. 3, 9. operatur patientiam.

Hactenus narratione suarum actionum, prædica- tionis & vitæ in ipsorum conversione confirmare & excitare eos conatus est ad constantiam profectumque, nunc etiam à commemoratione ipsorum conversionis & profectus idipsum agit per quatuor versus, notante Flacio. Denique ad finem usque capitis id præstat commemoratione affectus sui erga ipsos, & confiden- tiæ de ipsis, ac gloriationis suæ futuræ in adventu Do- mini; qua blanda & suavi testificatione demulcet animos eorum ad implendum gaudium suum qua- tuor postremis versibus. Jam igitur prædicat fru- ctus præconii sui præclarissimos, seriam ample- xionem veræ religionis, & piam imitationem præ- cipuarum Ecclesiarum, etiam qua constantiam in persecutione. Figurat autem & ornat istam ex- positionem gratiarum actione erga Deum, ut os- tendat, esse rem eximiam, & insigne Dei benefi- cium, Deumque pro eo & celebrandum & oran- dum esse. Quod hic in tribus momentis consti- tuit, quod nempe agnoverint suam doctrinam Verbum Dei esse, quod eandem debita cum reve- rentia & usu ejus aut praxi exceperint, & quod vi- vam ejus efficaciam, regenerationem, tranquillita- tem cordis & testificationem Spiritus experti sint. Convincit ergo eos propria ipsorum confessione ac ex- perientia in seipsis, quod hæc religio sit vera ac saluta- ris Dei religio, quodque ipse Deus per eam cum illis agat. Unde sequitur, eos omnibus modis debere & perseverare & proficere in ista ipsa doctrina & omni- bus aliis doctrinis, vel etiam hujus corruptelis ab- horrere, qui etiam est primarius hujus partis scopus, quod recte observatum à Flacio, qui hanc senten- tiam Apostoli hic urget contra fanatismum Schvenckfeldianum, & reliquos scripturæ sacræ calumniatores, præsertim contra Papistas.

Λόγον ἀκοῆς, qui Theophylacto est prædicatio, vel verbum quod audiendo creditur, proprie est Verbum, per auditum acceptum, quod scilicet à Deo audierant Apostoli, ut Esa. 53, 1. Prophetarum præconium dicitur auditus ipsorum, ideoque additur τꭣ Θεꭣ, quasi dicat, hoc est Verbum Dei. Verbum ergo Dei non objective dicitur, quod de Deo agit, sed principii respectu, quod à Deo est. Pronomen ὃς alii cum Lombardo referunt ad Deum, alii ad λόγον τꭣ Θεꭣ. Posterius magis convenit. Ver- satur enim in prædicanda non Dei, sed Evangelii, & præconii Evangelici virtute & efficacia. Ver- bum ἐνηργεῖται & active & passive explicari posse, observat Oecumenius. Theophylactus passive ac- cepit, ex ipsis operibus demonstratur. Alii ma- lunt active intelligere, quod Paulus gratias agat Deo pro Evangelii efficacia, quod operabatur in- ter Thessalonicenses, non respiciens externa signa extraordinaria, quod Theodoreto visum, sed opera- tiones imprimis internas, quod gignat veram cor- dis fiduciam, spem inconcussam, infractam constan- tiam, singularem patientiam, & mirabilem in ad- versis lætitiam cum aliis virtutibus & motibus spi- ritualibus. Jam egerat sermo, non tamen inquit, egit, sed agit: quia pergit agere, non cessat Verbum Domini. Non dicit, vobiscum, quasi & Verbum Dei & ipsi operentur, sed in vobis, ut omnis effica- cia sit Dei, ac Divinæ gratiæ laus tribuatur. Quod autem credentium mentionem facit, non exclusive intelligendum, sed appropriative vel specificative, quod illos, ad quos scribit, judicio charitatis pro credentibus habeat, ac tales esse velit, illisque hanc gratiam appropriet: quam nemini denegatam vult Deus, ea fini Verbum prædicari curans, quod vi- vum est & efficax ad convertendas animas, ut o- mnes per illud convertantur. Absolutum ergo decretum hic exulet, quod sapiunt illa Crociana.

Loquitur de operatione salutari: Restringit enim ad credentes, cum in aliis suam quoque habeat ser- mo efficaciam. Ex intentione Dei & virtute in- sita penes omnes habet efficaciam salutarem, nisi impediant, & obicem ponant. Non enim agit modo irresistibili.

## 2:14
V. 14. For you, brothers, became imitators of the Churches of God which are in Judea in Christ Jesus) Τῶν οὐσῶν, the present for the past, as the Hebrews often use participles, because they do not properly have participles for the past. Many and great Churches of God through Christ had been made in Judea, both directly and by the ministry of the Apostles. But most were dispersed, with a few left for seed, as appears in Acts 8:4, ch. 11:19. And some had gone to Thessalonica, to whom these things especially pertain.

He proves the efficacy of the Word of God preached by him in them from their illustrious constancy in the cross, and at the same time he does this so that the virtue praised in them may grow. He says, therefore, that they performed the very same constancy in the persecution from their own countrymen that the Jewish Churches performed in the persecution of the Jews. There is, therefore, a certain amplification of praise, that he compares them with the primary Churches, from which the rest had been born and propagated as if they were daughters, because the law of the Lord had gone out from Zion, and his word from Jerusalem according to the prophecies, as Flacius rightly says here. There is no doubt that these things pertain to the primitive Christian Churches, gathered from the Jews. But that some from those dispersed on account of persecution had gone to Thessalonica is a Grotian invention. For Paul found no one there who first scattered the seeds of Evangelical doctrine to those to whom this epistle was written, and therefore as a nurse and mother he warmed, cherished, nourished, and carried them; as a Father he admonished, comforted, and informed them, as those whom he begot in the Lord through the Gospel. It is also false that these things pertain especially to the Jews exiling in Thessalonica. They pertain to the Church planted by the Apostle from the Jews and primarily from the Gentiles, which he compares with the primitive Churches from the Jews for the sake of honor.

That you also suffered the same things by your own countrymen, just as they also by the Jews) You lost your own things, you were cast out as a part, συμφυλεταὶ, ὁμόεθνοι, as Hesychius interprets, בני שבטכחן בני עמכם for the Hebrews, here the Syrian בני שרבחתן—the Greeks say φῦλα for שׁבט. That αὐτοὶ makes the construction κατὰ τὸ σημαινόμενον.

As for persecution in general, and its tolerance, not in particular, as for the loss of things and property and expulsion, the Thessalonians are compared to the Hebrews or Jews. By the name Συμφυλετῶν, Cornelius à Lapide also understands the Jews, as does Grotius. Ambrose, however, and others interpret it as fellow citizens. Crocius as fellow citizens, who belonged to the same tribes, understood not in the Jewish manner, but in the Roman and Greek: which is more appropriate. For the word ὑμεῖς embraces not only converted Jews, but also Gentiles, since more are read to have been converted from the Gentiles than from the Jews, Acts 17, who had their persecutions from their fellow citizens, especially the Jews, just as the Jews had already rioted against Paul and his companions and their host Jason, and his house, whom, although they dismissed them then having received satisfaction, it appears from this passage, however, that they did not rest, but subsequently stirred up new persecutions out of envy, as the Church of the Thessalonians grew.

Latin:

V. 14. Ὑμεῖς γὰρ μιμηταὶ ἐγενήθητε, ἀδελφοὶ τῶν Ἐκκλη- σιῶν τοῦ Θεοῦ τῶν οὐσῶν ἐν τῇ Ἰουδαίᾳ ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ) Τῶν οὐσῶν Præsens pro Præterito, quomodo participia sæpe usur- pant Ebræi, quia participia apud ipsos præteritum pro- prie non habent. Multæ & magnæ Ecclesiæ Dei per Christum, tum directe, tum Apostolorum ministerio, factæ fuerant in Judæa. Sed dispersi erant plerique, paucis ad sementem relictis, ut apparet Act. 8, 4. c. 11, 19. Et quidam Thessalonicam concesserant, ad quos præ- cipue hæc spectant.

Probat Verbi Dei à se prædicati in eis efficaciam à constantia præclara ipsorum in cruce, simulque id agit, ut laudata virtus in eis crescat. Dicit igitur ipsos eandem prorsus constantiam præstitisse in persecutio- ne à suis popularibus, quam Ecclesiæ Judaicæ præsti- terunt in persecutione Judæorum. Est ergo quædam amplificatio laudis, quod eos confert cum primariis Ecclesiis, unde reliquæ tanquam filiæ quædam natæ ac propagatæ fuerant, quia lex Domini de Sion, & ver- bum ejus de Hierusalem secundum prophetias exie- rat, ut recte hic Flacius. Pertinere hæc ad primi- tivas Ecclesias Christianas, è Judæis collectas, du- bium nullum est. Sed ex iis dispersis ob persecu- tionem quosdam Thessalonicam concessisse, com- mentum Grotianum est. Nullos enim ibi invenit Paulus, qui primus semina doctrinæ Evangelicæ sparsit illis, ad quos exarata est hæc epistola, ideoque ceu nutrix & mater eos calefecit, fovit, enutrivit, portavit; ceu Pater monuit, solatus est, atque in- formavit, utpote quos per Evangelium genuit in Domino. Falsum etiam est præcipue ad Judæos Thessalonicæ exulantes hæc spectare. Pertinent ad Ecclesiam ab Apostolo plantatam è Judæis & im- primis è gentibus, quam honoris causa confert cum Ecclesiis è Judæis primitivis,

Ὅτι τὰ αὐτὰ ἐπάθετε καὶ ὑμεῖς ὑπὸ τῶν συμφυλετῶν, κα- θὼς καὶ αὐτοὶ ὑπὸ τῶν Ἰουδαίων) Res vestras amisistis, pars fuistis ejecti, συμφυλεταὶ, ὁμόεθνοι interpretante Hesychio בני שבטכחן בני עמכם Ebræis, Syro hic בני שרבחתן-Græ- ci φῦλα dicunt pro שׁבט. Illud αὐτοὶ constructionem facit κατὰ τὸ σημαινόμενον.

Quantum ad persecutionem in genere, ejusque to- lerantiam, non in specie, quantum ad rerum & fa- cultatum amissionem & ejectionem comparantur Thessalonicenses Ebræis vel Judæis. Συμφυλετῶν nomine Cornelius à Lapide etiam Judæos intelligit, ut Grotius. Ambrosius vero, aliique concives id in- terpretantur. Crocius concives, qui ad easdem tri- bus, more non Judæo, sed Romano & Græco intelle- ctas, pertinebant: Quod convenientius est. Nam vox ὑμεῖς non tantum Judæos conversos, sed etiam gentes complectitur, siquidem plures è gentibus conversi legantur, quam è Judæis, Actor. 17. qui à concivibus suis, Judæis maxime, suas habuere per- secutiones, quemadmodum Judæi tumultuati jam sunt adversus Paulum, & socios, & hospitem eo- rum Jasonem, ac domum ejusdem, quos utut tum accepta satisfactione dimiserint, ex hoc loco tamen apparet, non quievisse, sed novas persecutiones deinceps, ex invidia, cum accresceret Ecclesia Thessalonicenses, excitasse.

## 2:15
V. 15. Τῶν καὶ τὸν Κύριον ἀποκτεινάντων Ἰησοῦν) What wonder is it if they rage against us, who killed our Lord, namely when they extorted his punishment from Pilate in every way, Acts 2:23, ch. 3:15. Disciples ought not to expect a better lot than the master's was, Matthew 10:24, Luke 6:40, John 15:20.

Καὶ τοὺς ἰδίους Προφήτας) They have been such for a long time now. Matthew 2:12, ch. 23:31, 37, Luke 6:23, ch. 12:34. In those places Matt. 2, 12. Luke 12, 34. nothing is held concerning these. See rather Matt. 21, 34. Acts 7, 34. But since not the same persons who killed the old Prophets killed Christ, the whole body is regarded here. Theophylact has it thus in this place: Some perhaps might say that they killed Christ the Lord because they were ignorant of him as well. Did they not also know their own Prophets, whose writings they themselves even produce, why therefore did they kill these too? It is therefore clearly evident that they do nothing out of a zeal for truth, but are carried headlong into this savagery as if rabid.

Καὶ ἡμᾶς ἐκδιωξάντων) See the stated places Acts 8, 4. chap. 11, 19.

The passage Acts 8, 4. is irrelevant. For Paul was then among those persecuting the primitive Church, not among those who were suffering persecution. Nor can Sylvanus and Timothy be counted among these; nor does any such thing appear from Acts 11, 19. But the Jews drove Paul out of Antioch, Acts 13, 57. Iconium, Acts 14, 5. 6. Lystra, v. 19. They persecuted Paul and Silas at Philippi with insults and scourging, Acts 16, 23. and drove them out of the city, v. 39. What Paul had suffered from the Jews, he himself recounts in 2 Cor. 11, 24. seqq. But it brings immense consolation that such great men, and the Son of God himself, have the cross as companions and leaders. For no one will easily have perished with such companions.

Καὶ Θεῷ μὴ ἀρεσκόντων) They were truly θεοστυγεῖς, as Josephus calls them in the history of these times.

It is a meiosis, they do not please God, that is, they displease him greatly. For they were rejected by God because of unbelief and stubbornness. They seemed indeed to fight for the law, but because they did not look to Christ, the end of the law, they could not please God.

Καὶ πᾶσιν ἀνθρώποις ἐναντίων) with no love for outsiders, they were seditious against the Romans, against the Parthians, at home, and abroad.

Something more is said, which Crocius expresses from Chrysostom, although not sufficiently in accordance with Calvinistic Theology. It pleases God that the Gospel be preached to the whole world to Jews and Gentiles for salvation. Since therefore the Jews were hindering this with all their might, they certainly show that they are common enemies of the whole world, whose salvation they hinder and oppose. If, says Theophylact, all things salutary are to be announced to the world, and these men hinder that these things be done, they are therefore convicted of opposing all men, and being the common enemies of all. For it is a certain supreme perversity to interfere with common salvation.

Latin:

V. 15. Τῶν καὶ τὸν Κύριον ἀποκτεινάντων Ἰησοῦν) Quid mi- rum est, si in nos sæviunt, qui Dominum nostrum interfece- runt, nempe cum à Pilato pœnam ejus omni modo extor- serunt, Act. 2, 23. c. 3, 15. Non debent discipuli meliorem sortem expectare, quam magistri fuit, Matth. 10, 24. Luc. 6, 40. Joh. 15, 20.

Καὶ τοὺς ἰδίους Προφήτας) Jam olim tales sunt. Matth. 2, 12. c. 23, 31, 37. Luc. 6, 23. c. 12, 34. In illis locis Matth. 2, 12. Luc. 12, 34. nihil de his habetur. Vid. potius Matth. 21, 34. Actor. 7, 34. Quum autem non eædem personæ Prophetas ve- teres, quæ Christum occiderent, totum corpus hic respicitur. Theophylactus hoc loco ita habet: Dixerint forte nonnulli, ideo illos Christum Domi- num occidisse, quia & hunc ignorassent. Nonne & suos norant Prophetas, quorum ipsi vel scripta produ- cunt, cur ergo & hos necavere? Est itaque plane per- spicuum, nihil hos facere veritatis ardore, sed tan- quam rabidos in hanc feritatem deferri præcipites.

Καὶ ἡμᾶς ἐκδιωξάντων) Vide dicta loca Actor. 8, 4. cap. 11, 19.

Locus Actor. 8, 4. alienus est. Paulus enim tum erat inter persequentes Ecclesiam primiti- vam, non inter eos, qui persecutionem patieban- tur. Nec his accenseri possunt Sylvanus & Timo- theus; neque tale quid ex Actor. 11, 19. apparet. Exegerunt autem Judæi Paulum Antiochia, Act. 13, 57. Iconio, Actor. 14, 5. 6. Lystra, v. 19. Per- sequuti sunt Paulum & Silam Philippis contume- liis & fustigatione, Actor. 16, 23. eosque civitate exegerunt, v. 39. Quæ passus à Judæis Paulus fue- rat, recenset ipse 2. Cor. 11, 24. seqq. Ingentem au- tem consolationem affert, tantos viros, & Filium Dei ipsum habere crucis socios & antesignanos. Nemo enim cum talibus sociis facile perierit.

Καὶ Θεῷ μὴ ἀρεσκόντων) Erant vere θεοστυγεῖς, quo- modo eos Josephus in horum temporum historia appel- lat.

Μείωσις est, non placent Deo, id est, maxime dis- plicent. Nam reprobati à Deo erant ob incredu- litatem & contumaciam. Videbantur quidem pro lege pugnare, sed quia finem legis Christum non respiciebant, Deo placere non poterant.

Καὶ πᾶσιν ἀνθρώποις ἐναντίων) nulla in extraneos dile- ctione seditiosi erant contra Romanos, contra Parthos, do- mi, forisque.

Amplius quid dicitur, quod exprimit è Chryso- stomo Crocius, licet non satis convenienter Theo- logiæ Calvinisticæ. Deo placet, toto orbe Ju- dæis & gentibus prædicari Evangelium ad salutem. Cum igitur Judæi id impedirent pro virili, utique ostendunt, se esse communes hostes totius orbis, cujus salutem impediunt impugnantque. Si ter- rarum orbi, inquit Theophylactus, sunt salutaria quæque nuntianda, & hi, quo minus hæc fiant, impe- diunt, cunctis ergo hominibus obsistere, & communes omnium hostes coarguuntur. Est namque summa quæ- dam perversitas communem interpellare salutem.

## 2:16
Verse 16.

Κωλυόντων ἡμᾶς τοῖς ἔθνεσι λαλῆσαι, ἵνα σωθῶσι) They are truly dogs in the manger Luke 11, 52.

He continues to describe the fury of the persecuting Jews, who are so insane that they neither want to accept the true religion themselves, nor allow it to be preached to the Gentiles. They did not simply forbid speaking to the Gentiles, for they themselves spoke to the Gentiles, and tried to draw them into their own society. What then were they saying to the Gentiles, that they ought to be circumcised and kept by Moses, they not only did not forbid, but even helped, and praised: But they opposed the doctrine concerning salvation to be obtained through faith in Christ alone without the works of the law. They forbade this to be spoken of everywhere by stirring up riots. Furthermore, they contended that the Gospel was being profaned by Paul, while he spread it to the uncircumcised. Thus they truly stood in the way of the salvation of the Gentiles, which depends on faith in the Gospel, as Crocius rightly says here.

Εἰς τὸ ἀναπληρῶσαι αὐτῶν τὰς ἁμαρτίας πάντοτε) Here εἰς τό, as often ἵνα, is ἐκβατικόν. This remained, that they should fill up the measure of their crimes. The expression is taken from Gen. 15, 16. See also Matt. 23, 32.

Theophylact: He now speaks of those sins which they committed formerly against the Prophets, and subsequently against Christ, and finally against us, as if he were saying: That they show themselves to have sinned in the greatest possible way, and to have reached a measure now full of wickedness and the pinnacle of crimes.

Ἔφθασε δὲ ἐπ᾿ αὐτὸς ἡ ὀργὴ εἰς τέλος.) At last the punishment is near: Namely, the destruction of the nation, an image of the future judgment. Ἔφθασε in the past tense has the sense of the present, as in Matt. 12:48, Rom. 9:31, 2 Cor. 10:14. Εἰς τέλος. עַד כָּלָה, Dan. 9:27, ἕως τῆς συντελείας. See what is said on Matt. 24:15.

The word ἔφθασε seems to Beza to declare something sudden and unexpected. Aretius notes that it signifies that they fell into these miseries by their own fault, not by any decree of God. Regarding this, Crocius adds this critique: If you understand it concerning an absolute decree, it is well. For God neither decrees nor inflicts punishment except on account of sin. Otherwise, Cornelius à Lapide rightly notes that they were destined for punishment by the decree of God. Wrath signifies the vengeance of God. Thus, when placed absolutely, it is understood in Rom. 4:15, ch. 12:19. Crocius says these things as if he were a stranger to the absolute decree of reprobation, which he knew that great lights among the Reformed had defended tooth and nail. However, he does not explain sufficiently. He says that vengeance is various. 1. They are, he says, blinded in mind and hardened in heart by the just judgment of GOD, Rom. 11. 2. Devoted to the destruction of the body. For Titus was about to overthrow them. 3. Finally, eternal hell awaited them. If none of these punishments are to be attributed to an absolute decree, the matter is correctly stated. But since the punishment of eternal hell is referred to the destination of the Divine decree, and it is denied that this is absolute, that Divine destination and reprobation ought to have been unfolded. For the Reformed make a twofold act of it: one negative, exclusion from glory; the other positive, pre-damnation to eternal ignominy. And they make the latter absolute, even though they protest that they do not wish to make the former absolute. But if the Jews were rejected from eternal life by an absolute decree, how can they do otherwise than perish by eternal death by an absolute decree? For he who is not saved, perishes and is damned. However, what is said here about the Jews must be understood with an exception. For it is evident from Rom. ch. 11 that wrath did not overtake all εἰς τέλος, that is, finally. Regarding the phrase εἰς τέλος, Theophylact says: It is not given, he says, as formerly a return from captivity and an arrival at the promised land, but the wrath of God has reached these people unto the end, that is, the wrath of God is always to remain upon them. He shows furthermore, when he says 'unto the end,' that this Divine wrath had been due to them from the beginning and had been intended by the prophecy and threats of the Prophets.

Latin:

Vers. 16.

Κωλυόντων ἡμᾶς τοῖς ἔθνεσι λαλῆσαι, ἵνα σωθῶσι) Sunt vere canes in præsepi Luc. 11, 52.

Pergit describere furorem persecutorum Judæo- rum, qui adeo insaniant, ut nec ipsi veram religio- nem suscipere velint, nec pati, ut gentilibus præ- dicetur. Non simpliciter prohibebant loqui genti- bus, nam ipsi loquebantur gentibus, & conabantur eas in societatem suam pertrahere. Quid igitur loque- bantur gentibus, quod circumcidi & per Mosen serva- ri deberent, eos non tantum prohibebant, sed & juva- bant, tollebantque laudibus: At opponebant se do- ctrinæ de salute per solam fidem in Christum absque operibus legis consequenda. Hanc loqui prohibebant ubique tumultibus excitatis. Præterea contendebant, Evangelium profanari à Paulo, dum incircumcisis vulgaret. Ita revera obstabant gentium saluti, quæ pendet ab Evangelii fide, ut recte hic Crocius.

Εἰς τὸ ἀναπληρῶσαι αὐτῶν τὰς ἁμαρτίας πάντοτε) Hic εἰς τό ut sæpe ἵνα, est ἐκβατικόν. Hoc restabat, ut men- suram facinorum suorum implerent. Loquutio desum- pta ex Gen. 15, 16. Vide & Matth. 23, 32.

Theophylactus: Ea nunc dicit peccata, quæ olim in Prophetas & in Christum deinceps, & in nos de- mum hi commisere, tanquam id inquiat: Ut osten- dant sese maximum in modum deliquisse, attigisseque jam refertam nequitiæ mensuram & scelerum api- cem.

Ἔφθασε δὲ ἐπ᾿ αὐτὸς ἡ ὀργὴ εἰς τέλος.) Tandem pro- pe est pœna: Excidium nempe gentis, futuri judicii imago. Ἔφθασε in Præterito elatum sensum habet præ- sentis, ut Matth. 12, 48. Roman. 9, 31. 2. Corinth. 10. 14. Εἰς τέλος. עַד כָּלָה, Dan. 9, 27. ἕως τῆς συντελείας. Vide quæ ad Matth. 24, 15.

Verbum ἔφθασε Bezæ videtur aliquid subitum & inexpectatum declarare. Aretius notat, signi- ficare, quod propria sua culpa inciderint in has mi- serias, non Dei aliquo decreto. Quo de hanc Crocius addit ἐπίκρισιν: Si de absoluto decreto in- telligas, bene habet. Deus enim nec decernit, nec infli- git pœnam, nisi ob peccatum. Alioqui bene adver- tit Cornelius à Lapide, decreto Dei destinatos esse pœ- næ. Ira significat ultionem Dei. Sic absolute posi- ta accipitur Roman. 4, 15. cap. 12, 19. Hæc Crocius quasi alienus à decreto reprobationis absoluto, quod non ignoravit magna inter Reformatos lu- mina πὺξ καὶ λὰξ defendisse. Non explicat au- tem satis. Ultionem illam variam dicit. 1. Mente, inquit, sunt excæcati, & corde indurati justo DEI judicio, Rom. 11. 2. Exitio corporis devoti. Ti- tus enim eos erat eversurus. 3. Denique æterna eos manebat gehenna. Si nulla harum pœnarum absoluto decreto tribuenda, recte se res habet. Sed cum æternæ gehennæ pœna ad destinationem de- creti Divini refertur, idque absolutum esse nega- tur, evolvenda erat destinatio & reprobatio illa Divina. Geminum enim ejus actum faciunt Re- formati, alium negativum, exclusionem à gloria, alium positivum, prædamnationem ad æternam ignominiam. Et illam absolutam faciunt, utut hanc protestentur, se nolle facere absolutam. At si rejecti sunt à vita æterna ex absoluto decreto Ju- dæi, quomodo aliter possunt, quam morte æterna perire decreto absoluto? Qui enim non salvatur, perit, & damnatur. Quæ autem de Judæis hic di- cuntur, intelligenda sunt cum exceptione. Nam non omnes occupare iram εἰς τέλος, id est, finali- ter, è Rom. cap. 11. constat. De voce εἰς τέλος Theophylactus: Non datur, inquit, ut quondam ex captivitate reditus, & ad terram promissionis per- ventus, sed in finem usque in hos ira Dei pervenit, id est, semper in hos permansura est Dei ira. Ostendit præterea, cum usque in finem inquit Divinam hanc iram à principio fuisse his debitam & Prophetarum vaticinio comminationibus intentatam.

## 2:17
Vers. 17.

Ἡμεῖς δὲ ἀδελφοὶ ἀπορφανισθέντες ἀφ᾽ ὑμῶν) Thus Gorgias: Τῶν φίλων ὀρφανισθεῖσα.

Πρὸς καιρὸν ὥρας) the same as πρὸς ὥραν, 2 Cor. 8:8, Gal. 2:5, Philem. v. 15, πρὸς καιρὸν Luke 8:13, 1 Cor. 7:5, which we read in Gen. 17:10 as כְּעֵת חַיָּה, which the LXX translated as κατὰ καιρὸν ἐκ ὥρας. The Latins also say 'at the moment of an hour,' as has been noted by others.

Προσώπῳ ὀ καρδίᾳ) He graphically depicts the disposition of those who love.

Though absent, he hears and sees him, though he is absent.

Περισσοτέρως ἐσπουδάσαμεν) יִחֵד בְּהֶלֶט, or with the Rabbis הִשְׁתַּדְּלָנוּ. Paul loves to augment further words that are already augmentative by themselves. Thus περισσοτέρως 2 Cor. 1:12, ch. 2:4, ch. 7:13, 15, ch. 11:23, ch. 12:15, Gal. 1:14, Phil. 1:34. Thus he says ὑπερνικᾷν, ὑπερπερισσεύειν, ὑπερπλεονάζειν.

Τὸ πρόσωπον ὑμῶν ἰδεῖν ἐν πολλῇ ἐπιθυμίᾳ) A similar wish 1 Cor. 16:7, 2 Cor. 12:14, 2 John v. 13, 3 John v. 14. That the Apostle may comfort them in their calamities, and render their spirit constant, he sets forth both his own longing, as a sure sign of love, and the confidence he has conceived concerning them, and testifies how great a joy he promises himself from them even at the day of the coming of the Lord. Furthermore, because he compares himself to a mother and a father, who are accustomed to long for their children exceedingly, and desire to be present with them with the most ready counsel and aid, he declares in this also a similar affection toward them. Earlier, says Theophylact, he called them children in the manner of a father and some nurse. But now he affirms they are desolate and orphaned, which is truly the way of children who are missing their parent. From which one may learn with what longing the Apostle pursued them, and he pretends the sorrow in which he was, which he had begun to feel from their separation. Nor did he consider it enough to say that he was desolate of them, but he added for the time of an hour, that is, for a very short time, and which can be computed in the space of one hour, or rather of a moment. Conf. Tob. X. v. 1. 3. 4. 7. He does not say, however, that he was entirely orphaned, but only in the sight of the body. It is a beautiful addition, says Theodoret, in face, not in heart: For that which is, I am deprived of sensible sight, but I enjoy continually that which falls into the understanding.

Latin:

Vers. 17.

Ἡμεῖς δὲ ἀδελφοὶ ἀπορφανισθέντες ἀφ᾽ ὑμῶν) Sic Gor- gias: Τῶν φίλων ὀρφανισθεῖσα.

Πρὸς καιρὸν ὥρας) idem quod πρὸς ὥραν, 2. Cor. 8, 8. Ga- lat. 2, 5. Philem. v. 15. πρὸς καιρὸν Luc. 8, 13. 1. Cor. 7, 5. quod Gen. 17, 10. legimus כְּעֵת חַיָּה, id LXX. verterunt κατὰ καιρὸν ἐκ ὥρας. Etiam Latini dicunt horæ momento, ut ab aliis notatum est.

Προσώπῳ ὀ καρδίᾳ) Graphice depingit ingenium a- mantium.

Illum absens absentem auditque videtque.

Περισσοτέρως ἐσπουδάσαμεν) יִחֵד בְּהֶלֶט, aut cum Rab- binis הִשְׁתַּדְּלָנוּ. Amat Paulus vocabula per se augen- tia amplius augere. Sic περισσοτέρως 2. Cor. 1, 12. c. 2, 4. c. 7, 13. 15. c. 11, 23. c. 12, 15. Gal. 1, 14. Philipp. 1, 34. Sic dicit ὑπερνικᾷν, ὑπερπερισσεύειν, ὑπερπλεονάζειν.

Τὸ πρόσωπον ὑμῶν ἰδεῖν ἐν πολλῇ ἐπιθυμίᾳ) Simile votum 1. Cor. 16, 7. 2. Cor. 12, 14. 2. Joh. v. 13. 3. Joh. v. 14. Ut soletur eos Apostolus in calamitatibus, & animum reddat constantem, tum desiderium suum, ceu amoris certum indicium, tum confiden- tiam de ipsis conceptam exponit, ac quantum gau- dium etiam ad diem adventus Domini ex illis sibi promittat, testatur. Porro quia comparat se Matri & Patri, qui oppido desiderare solent li- beros, iisque præsentissimo consilio & auxilio ad- esse optant, in eo etiam affectum similem erga ipsos declarat. Superius, inquit Theophylactus, Patris more & nutricis cujuspiam filios appellavit. Nunc vero desolatos affirmat & orbos, quod sane libe- rorum est, conquirentium Genitorem. Unde per- discere licet, quanto illos desiderio prosequeretur Apo- stolus, & mœrorem, in quo esset, prætendit, quem ex il- lorum sejunctione cœpisset. Neque sat illud habebat, ut diceret sese ab his desolatos, sed ad horæ tempus sub- jecerit, hoc est, brevi admodum tempore, & quod unius possit horæ, vel momenti potius spatio compu- tari. Conf. Tob. X. v. 1. 3. 4. 7. Non autem totum se orbatum dicit, sed tantum corporis adspectu. Pul- chra est adjectio, ait Theodoreius, facie, non corde: Pro eo, quod est, sum sensili privatus adspectu, sed eo, qui cadit in intelligentiam, fruor assidue.

## 2:18
Διὸ ἠθελήσαμεν ἐλθεῖν πρὸς ὑμᾶς ἐγὼ μὲν Παῦλος καὶ ἅπαξ καὶ δίς) And here something is implied, which may correspond to the little word μὲν: namely, Timothy and Silas once. Ἅπαξ καὶ δὶς, that is, more often. Thus Nehem. c. XIII, v. 20. Phil. IV. v. 16.

That I INDEED Paul seems to Chrysostom to be inserted, so that he may declare that he loves them more than others: Others prefer that this was done because Timothy had already been sent to them, 1. Thess. III. v. 12. The plural therefore is to be referred to Paul and Silas.

Καὶ ἐνέκοψεν ἡμᾶς Σατανᾶς) καὶ for but, in the Hebrew manner. Concerning the word ἐγκόπτω see Rom. XV. 22. Gal. V. 7. The Rabbis would say מחא. But Satan hindered this, by injecting into him the necessity of disputing more often with the Stoics and Epicureans, who were at Athens.

Those impediments lie hidden. Theophylact understands it of temptations. Which was also the opinion of Theodoret, who is very ancient: Mutual temptations retarded our readiness of mind, and the common enemy is accustomed to stir those up. For which reason he said that he had forbidden him, so that he might not come to them. Here τὸ ἀπέχειν is better.

Latin:

Διὸ ἠθελήσαμεν ἐλθεῖν πρὸς ὑμᾶς ἐγὼ μὲν Παῦλος καὶ ἅπαξ καὶ δίς) Et hic aliquid subricetur, quod voculæ μὲν respondeat: nempe Timotheus & Silas semel. Ἅπαξ καὶ δὶς, id est, sæpius. Sic Nehem. c. XIII, v. 20. Phil. IV. v. 16.

Illud ego QUIDEM Paulus Chrysostomo interseri videtur, ut declaret, se magis illos dili- gere, quam alios: Alii malunt id factum, quia Ti- motheus ad eos jam missus erat, 1. Thess. III. v. 12. Pluralis ergo referendus erit ad Paulum & Silam.

Καὶ ἐνέκοψεν ἡμᾶς Σατανᾶς) καὶ pro sed, more Ebræo. De voce ἐγκόπτω vide Rom. XV. 22. Gal. V. 7. Rabbini dicerent מחא. Impedivit autem hoc Satanas, injecta ei necessitate disputandi sæpius cum Stoicis & Epicureis, qui Athenis erant.

Impedimenta illa latent. De tentationibus intelligit Theophylactus. Quæ etiam Theodoreti longe vetustissimi fuit sententia: Nostram animi promptitudinem retardarunt mutuæ tentationes, eas autem solet movere communis hostis. Qua de causa dixit eum prohibuisse, ne veniret ad eos. Præstat hic τὸ ἀπέχειν.

## 2:19
Vers. 19. Τίς γὰρ ἡμῶν ἐλπὶς, ἢ χαρὰ, ἢ στέφανος καυ- χήσεως, ἢ οὐχὶ καὶ ὑμεῖς ἔμπροσθεν τῦ Κυρίε ἡμῶν Ἰησῦ Χρισῦ ἐν τῇ αὐτῦ παρουσίᾳ) These ought to be construed thus: Τίς γὰρ ἡμῶν ἐλπὶς, ἢ χαρὰ, ἢ σέφανος καυχήσεως ἔμπροσθεν τῦ Κυ- ρίε ἡμῶν Ἰησῦ Χρισῦ ἐν τῇ αὐτῦ παρουσίᾳ, ἢ οὐχὶ κὶ ὑμεῖς; What is it, from whence shall I hope for a reward, truly rejoice, with what shall I be adorned, standing before Christ at his coming? Are not you also among others that? Στέφανος καυχήσεως עטרת תפאות, Prov. VI. 31. Ezech. XVI. 12. XXIII. 42. It is called a crown not for daily use, but which is taken for exceptional adornment on days of supreme joy. Thus such illustrious churches built by him throughout Macedonia adorned Paul. See 2. Cor. c. VII. v. 4. In the Manuscript it is σέφανος ἀγαλ- λιάσεως.

Latin:

Vers. 19. Τίς γὰρ ἡμῶν ἐλπὶς, ἢ χαρὰ, ἢ στέφανος καυ- χήσεως, ἢ οὐχὶ καὶ ὑμεῖς ἔμπροσθεν τῦ Κυρίε ἡμῶν Ἰησῦ Χρισῦ ἐν τῇ αὐτῦ παρουσίᾳ) Construi hæc sic debent: Τίς γὰρ ἡμῶν ἐλπὶς, ἢ χαρὰ, ἢ σέφανος καυχήσεως ἔμπροσθεν τῦ Κυ- ρίε ἡμῶν Ἰησῦ Χρισῦ ἐν τῇ αὐτῦ παρουσίᾳ, ἢ οὐχὶ κὶ ὑμεῖς; Quid est, unde præmium sperabo, vere gaudebo, quo ornabor, stans coram Christo in ejus adventu ? Nonne inter alios & vos id estis? Στέφανος καυχήσεως עטרת תפאות, Prov. VI. 31. Ezech. XVI. 12. XXIII. 42. Vocatur corona non quotidiana, sed quæ diebus summæ lætitiæ ad eximium ornatum sumitur. Sic Paulum ornabant tam præclaræ per Macedoniam structæ ab ipso Ecclesiæ. Vide 2. Cor. c. VII. v. 4. In Manuscripto est σέφανος ἀγαλ- λιάσεως.

## 2:20
Ὑμεῖς γάρ ἐστε ἡ δόξα ἡμῶν καὶ χαρά) You are especially worthy of such titles.

They are not called the hope of the Apostle because he hoped for a reward from them: But because he had conceived an excellent hope concerning their perseverance, as they were a joy to him, because he rejoiced in their faith. Concerning which Theophylact: In you, he says, all my hope is placed. For I am about to have great confidence before God, thanks to you, and for that reason I am carried away with joy, because you are to be a crown and glory to me, that is, excellent and bright. Although in the present you have produced this glory for me, and in the future you are soon to produce it. Which he further explains thus: Someone will say: Does all your hope, O Paul, rest upon the progress of the Thessalonians? By no means, he says. For one must not trust in these alone, which he clearly shows when he says: And you, but that there are many others, concerning whom he ought to hope as well as possible. For how great is that glory, to have offered to God so ample a Church, and one so approved and pleasing? Theodoret wishes there to be an allusion to the manner of mothers coaxing their children: Since he likened himself to a mother, who nourishes her own children, he imitates her words also. For they are accustomed to call infants both hope and joy, and things of that sort. Which pleases Theophylact, although he does not rest in it, but unfolds the force of the words in the sense we have mentioned: Are not such words therefore those of mothers, calling their smaller children charmingly with a certain immense ardor of the bowels and burning of love? Would it not have been enough, to express his most ardent desire, to have said crown, unless he had added glory also?

Latin:

Ὑμεῖς γάρ ἐστε ἡ δόξα ἡμῶν καὶ χαρά) Vos præcipue digni talibus titulis.

Non dicuntur spes Apostoli, quod inde præmium sperarit: Sed quia spem optimam de ipsorum perseverantia conceperat, ut gaudium ipsi erant, quia lætabatur ipsorum fide. Quo de Theophy- lactus: In vobis, inquit, spes mea sita est omnis. Plurimum enim apud Deum confidentia, vestri gratia habiturus, eoque & lætitia efferor, quia corona mihi futuri estis & gloria, hoc est, excel- lenti & clara. Tametsi in præsenti hanc mihi gloriam peperistis, & in futurum sitis mox pari- turi. Quod porro sic explicat: Dicet aliquis: Num spes tua omnis, o Paule, ex profectu Thes- salonicensium nititur? Nequaquam inquit. Neque enim his solum fidendum, quod plane ostendit, cum dicit: Et vos, sed alios esse quam multos, de qui- bus sit ipsi quam optime sperandum. Quanta enim illud est gloriæ, tam amplam Deo obtulisse Ecclesiam, & tam probatam & placitam? Theo- doretus alludi vult ad matrum blandientium li- beris morem: Quoniam seipsum matri assimila- vit, quæ nutrit suos filios, ejus quoque verba imi- tatur. Ea enim infantulos & spem & gaudium, & quæ sunt ejusmodi, appellare consueverunt. Quod placet Theophylacto, etsi eo non acquie- scat, sed vim vocum eo, quo diximus, sensu evolvat: Nonne igitur ejusmodi verba matrum sunt, viscerum immenso quodam ardore & amo- ris flagrantia, pueros minores lepide appellantium? Nonne satis fuisset, ut ejus ardentissimam cupidi- tatem exprimeret, coronam dixisse, nisi & gloriam adjecisset?

## 3:1 Argument
CHAPTER III. WHICH IS FRIENDLY.

ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

The Apostle declares his singular love, in that he sent Timothy to the Thessalonians to comfort them, and upon the report of their faith brought back by the same, he was affected with great consolation and joy, and prays night and day that it may be permitted him to see them, desiring meanwhile that they may grow in charity, be confirmed in faith, and be blameless in holiness at the coming of Christ.

There are two parts: I. The cause of the sending away of Timothy, to verse 5. II. The joys of his return, the desires of seeing them, and the prayers to verse 13.

PART I. The cause of the sending away of Timothy.

Ver. 1. Διὸ μηκέτι ςέγοντες) No longer bearing, namely, that we are separated by such great intervals. The Greeks use the word ςέγειν in this sense, and Paul himself does so in 1 Cor. 9:12, 13:7, and below in ch. 3:5. In Hebrew it is התאפק.

Εὐδοκήσαμεν καταλειφθῆναι ἐν Ἀθήναις μόνοι) We have spoken above at 2:8 concerning this construction of εὐδοκεῖν. This is sad, but yet we had gladly done this, both I and Silas, for your sake. He treats, however, of a matter already completed for some time, as appears below in verse 6. Whence both this and the following will be rightly translated by the pluperfect.

Latin:

CAPUT III. QUOD ΦΙΛΙΚΟΝ.

ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

Amorem suum singularem declarat Apostolus, quod Timotheum ad Thessalonicenses mi- serit, ad eosdem confortandos, fideque ipsorum ab eodem reduce nunciata, magno solatio, gaudioque affectus sit, ac noctes & dies precetur, ut liceat ipsos videre, vo- lens interea, ut crescant in charitate, confirmentur in fide, & inculpabiles sint in sanctitate ad adventum Christi.

Partes duæ sunt: I. Ablegationis Timothei causa, ad v. 5. II. Reditus gaudia, videndi eos de- sideria, ac vota ad v. 13.

PARS I. Ablegationis Timothei causa.

Vers. 1. Διὸ μηκέτι ςέγοντες) Non ultra ferentes, nempe tantis intervallis nos disjungi. Vocem ςέγειν hoc sensu & Græci usurpant, & ipse Paulus 1. Cor. IX, 12. XIII. 7. infra c. III, 5. Ebræis id התאפק.

Εὐδοκήσαμεν καταλειφθῆναι ἐν Ἀθήναις μόνοι) De hac constructione εὐδοκεῖν diximus supra II. 8. Triste hoc, sed ta- men hoc libenter feceramus & ego & Silas vestri causa. Agit autem de re jam aliquandiu exacta, ut apparet infra 6. Unde recte per plusquamperfectum vertetur & hoc & se- quentia.

## 3:2
Ver. 2. Καὶ ἐπέμψαμεν Τιμόθεον τὸν ἀδελφὸν ἡμῶν κỳ διά- κονον τῶ Θεῶ κỳ συνεργὸν ἡμῶν ἐν τῷ Εὐαγγελίῳ τῶ Χριςῶ) In some Codices διάκονον τῶ Θεῶ, in others συνεργὸν ἡμῶν is missing. We have had similar titles given to Tychicus in Colossians ch. 4:7 and Ephesians ch. 6:21. See also concerning Titus in 2 Cor. 8:23. We see equal titles given to this same Timothy in Rom. 16:21, 1 Cor. 4:17, 16:21. Ἐπέμψαμεν we had sent, namely, from Athens. For both Timothy and Silas had come to Paul at Athens, Acts 17:15.

Εἰς τὸ ςηρίξαι ὑμᾶς, κỳ παρακαλέσαι ὑμᾶς περὶ τ' πίςεως ὑμῶν) That we might both strengthen and console you through Timothy in those things which pertain to faith. For they who suffer adversity for the sake of faith have need of both. In the Manuscript: Παρακαλέσαι ὑπὲρ t.

They explain here first the desire, which they could not long endure, of knowing something certain about the Thessalonians, after they had been for some space of time at Corinth, where Silas and Timothy had come to Paul, Acts 18:5. For because of the distance of the place, since Corinth was distant from Thessalonica by almost a hundred miles, they seem not to have had the opportunity of certainly exploring the state of the Church, which had been founded not long before and was exposed to various temptations. Then the counsel or resolution, that those two, Paul and Silvanus, wished to be left alone at Athens, and to send away Timothy, a faithful and dear companion, to the Thessalonians. Although they were in need of him in so ample a harvest, which by divine instructed by an oracle to hope there, the Apostle had [reason to hope], Acts 18:10. Not only as a beloved brother, but also as a faithful minister of God and fellow-worker in the Gospel, yet for the sake of the Thessalonians he wished to be deprived for a time of his presence. He adds, therefore, those praises of Timothy, as Theophylact advises, not so much to commend him, but rather to honor them, since he had interrupted a man so very necessary to himself, and one devoting effort to the preaching of the Gospel, for the sake of the ministry of the work undertaken by them. Although indeed the Vulgate, along with Theodoret, does not have 'helper,' nor does Ambrosiaster, nor Beza's Clermont codex: yet other codices have it with great consensus. Chrysostom, Theophylact, and Oecumenius also read it. The place of the mission is Athens. Therefore, Paul must have departed there with Silvanus and Timothy. For these did not come to Paul at Athens, as seems to Grotius, even though he had hoped for their arrival there from Macedonia and had waited for them there for a time, which is the only thing contained in Acts 17:15, but they had finally come to Paul at Corinth from Macedonia, Acts 18:5. Nor indeed should one imagine, with Beza at the end of this epistle, that Timothy had come to Paul at Athens from Macedonia before he himself betook himself to Corinth, and that he was sent back from Athens to Thessalonica by Paul, who alone endured being left at Athens, provided that Silas had not yet returned to Paul: for this contradicts the present passage, where not Paul alone, but also Silas or Silvanus are said to have sent away Timothy, and those two alone remained there. Wherefore it is necessary that both Silas and Timothy had already returned to Paul from Macedonia, which we know from Luke happened at Corinth, Acts chapter 18, verse 5. And therefore Beza is mistaken in his conjecture, as if Silas or Silvanus had remained at Beroea while Timothy returned to Athens and again from Athens to Thessalonica. For how could Silas have sent away Timothy together with Paul from Athens if he had remained at Beroea? That, therefore, remains for us to say: that Silas returned with Timothy to Paul, which Luke reports happened at Corinth, and that with the Apostle he sent Timothy to the Thessalonians: since this was done at Athens, nothing is more certain than that these three, Paul, Silvanus, and Timothy, traveled from Corinth to Athens, which were only eighteen miles apart, so that from there this sending away of Timothy by the other two could take place. Concerning which we spoke in the preface.

Crocius is also mistaken, asserting that Silas and Timothy indeed remained at Beroea, but came to Athens when called by Paul. What he acknowledges Luke does not report, he thinks is openly gathered from this passage. Luke reports entirely that they were summoned by Paul and found him at Corinth. Although, therefore, it is openly evident from this passage that they were at Athens, it must be established that they traveled there with Paul, perhaps because they wanted to visit Dionysius or others, or also because Paul and Silas wanted to send Timothy away from there. Crocius asks in vain how Paul says he was left alone at Athens if he alone sent Timothy, and he answers that perhaps for a similar reason he sent Silas elsewhere. Paul does not say that he was left alone, but Paul and Silvanus speak in the plural: 'we thought it best to be left alone at Athens.' Which do not refer to one person, namely Paul alone, but to two, Paul and Silvanus, who were left alone, Timothy having been sent away. Paul does not like to speak of himself alone in the plural.

Thirdly, the cause of the plan is explained, both the stabilization or confirmation, and the exhortation or admonition regarding the faith. How Luther, Beza, and others translate 'to exhort,' Erasmus, Bullinger, Hyperius, and Aretius explain, but that is already included in the word 'to strengthen'; then a certain investigation of the same because of the fear of temptation, which cause the Apostle makes his own, as founder, curator, and inspector of the Thessalonian Church, indeed as a father solicitous for his children, and a most loving mother for her offspring. 'But we sent him,' says Theodoret, 'not that he might bring you another doctrine, but that he might confirm you in the former, and exhort you to bear the snares of adversaries with a brave spirit, and that you might not be shaken and moved away from your former conviction.'

Latin:

Vers. 2. Καὶ ἐπέμψαμεν Τιμόθεον τὸν ἀδελφὸν ἡμῶν κỳ διά- κονον τῶ Θεῶ κỳ συνεργὸν ἡμῶν ἐν τῷ Εὐαγγελίῳ τῶ Χριςῶ) In quibusdam Codicibus διάκονον τῶ Θεῶ, in quibusdam συνεργὸν ἡμῶν deest. Similes titulos Tychico datos ha- buimus Coloss. c. IV. v. 7. & Eph. c. VI. v. 21. Vide & de Tito 2. Cor. VIII. 23. Huic ipsi Timotheo pares dari titulos vi- demus Rom. XVI. 21. 1. Cor. IV. 17. XVI. 21. Ἐπέμψαμεν miseramus, nempe Athenis. Athenas enim ad Paulum ve- nerant & Timotheus & Silas Act. XVII. 15.

Εἰς τὸ ςηρίξαι ὑμᾶς, κỳ παρακαλέσαι ὑμᾶς περὶ τ' πίςεως ὑμῶν) Ut vos per Timotheum & roboraremus & consola- remur in iis, quæ ad fidem pertinent. Utroque enim opus habent, qui ob fidem adversa patiuntur. In Manuscripto: Παρακαλέσαι ὑπὲρ t.

Explicant hic primo desiderium, quod diu susti- nere non potuerint, cognoscendi aliquid certi de Thessalonicensibus, postquam nempe per ali- quod temporis spatium Corinthi, quo ad Paulum venerant Silas & Timotheus, Act. XIIX. 5. fuerant. Ob longinquitatem enim loci, cum Corinthus Thessalonica centum fere milliari bus distaret, vi- dentur non habuisse occasionem certo explorandi statum Ecclesiæ non ita pridem fundatæ, variisque tentationibus expositæ. Deinde consilium vel pla- citum, quod duo illi Paulus & Silvanus soli relinqui voluerint Athenis, & Timotheum fidum & cha- rum socium Thessalonicum ablegare. Quo etsi ægre carebant in tam ampla messe, quam divino oraculo edoctus ibi sperare habebat Apostolus, Act. XIIX. 10. non tantum ceu fratre dilecto, sed etiam ceu fideli ministro Dei & σύνεργω̃ in Evan- gelio, Thessalonicensium tamen causa ad tempus orbari voluere ipsius παραςάσει. Addit ergo elogia illa Timothei, Theophylacto monente, non adeo, ut eum collaudet, sed ut illos potius honoribus prosequa- tur, cum hominem sibi tam maxime necessarium, & operam in prædicando Evangelio navantem, isto- rum gratia suscepti operis ministerio interpellaue- rit. Quanquam vero Vulgata cum Theodoreto non habeat adjutorem, nec Ambrosiafter, nec Cla- remontanus Bezæ codex: Habent tamen alii codi- ces magno consensu. Legunt etiam Chrysostomus, Theophylactus, Oecumenius. Locus missionis Athenæ sunt. Eo ergo digressum oportet esse Paulum cum Silvano & Timotheo. Hi enim non Athenis, quod Grotio videtur, etsi illic spe- rarat adventum ipsorum è Macedonia, eosque ibi- dem ad tempus expectarat, quod solum Act. XVII. v. 15. habetur, sed Corinthi demum ad Paulum ve- nerant è Macedonia, Act. XIIX, 5. Neque vero fingendum cum Bezæ ad calcem hujus epistolæ, Timotheum Athenis ad Paulum venisse è Mace- donia, antequam ipse Corinthum se conferret, & Athenis remissum Thessalonicam à Paulo, qui so- lus sustinuerit relinqui Athenis, siquidem Silas tum nondum redierit ad Paulum: Nam hoc con- trariatur loco præsenti, ubi non Paulus solus, sed & Sila vel Silvanus dicuntur ablegasse Timotheum, & illi duo soli ibidem remansisse. Quapropter necessum est, redierit jam tum ad Paulum & Sila & Timotheus è Macedonia, quod Corinthi factum Luca auctore, Actor. cap. XIIX. vers. 5. novimus. Ideoque fallitur Bezæ in conjectura sua, quasi Sila vel Silvanus Berrhœæ manserit, dum Timotheus Athenas, & rursus Athenis Thessalonicam regrede- retur. Quomodo enim potuisset Timotheum una cum Paulo ablegare Athenis Sila, si Berrhœæ re- mansisset? Id ergo restat dicamus, rediisse Silam cum Timotheo ad Paulum, quod Corinthi factum refert Lucas, & cum Apostolo misisse Timotheum ad Thessalonicenses: Quod quum factum sit Athe- nis, nihil certius est, quam tres hosce Paulum, Sil- vanum & Timotheum Corintho Athenas, quæ octodecim tantum distabant milliaribus, profe- ctos esse, ut inde hæc Timothei ablegatio fieri à re- liquis duobus potuerit. Quo de in præfatione di- ximus.

Fallitur & Crocius, Silam & Timotheum qui- dem Berrhœæ remansisse, sed vocatos ad Paulum venisse Athenas affirmans. Quod agnoscit, Lucam non referre, putat autem ex hoc loco aperte colligi. Refert omnino Lucas, eos accersitos à Paulo, Co- rinthi eum invenisse. Licet ergo ex hoc loco aperte constet, quod Athenis fuerint, eo tamen profectos esse cum Paulo statuendum, forte quod Dionysium aut alios invisere, aut etiam quod Pau- lus & Sila inde Timotheum ablegare voluerint. Frustra quærit Crocius, quomodo Paulus se solum relictum dicat Athenis, si solum misit Timo- theum, & respondet, fortasse similem ob causam Si- lam alio misisse. Non id dicit Paulus, se solum reli- ctum, sed in plurali Paulus & Silvanus loquuntur εὐδοκήσαμεν καταλειφθῆναι ἐν Ἀθήναις μόνοι, optimum duximus, soli Athenis relinqui. Quæ non unam referunt personam, Paulum nempe so- lum, sed duos Paulum & Sylvanum, qui μόνοι SO- LI misso Timotheo relinquebantur. Paulus de se solo non amat in plurali loqui.

Tertio consilii causa exponitur tum stabilitio vel confirmatio, tum exhortatio vel commonitio s, de fide. Quomodo παρακαλέσαι B. Lutherus, Beza & alii reddunt, Erasmus, Bullinger, Hype- rius, Aretius exponunt, sed id in voce στηρίξαι jam comprehensum; tum certa exploratio ejusdem propter tentationis metum, quam causam sibi propriam facit Apostolus, ceu fundator, curator & inspector Thessalonicensis Ecclesiae, imo ceu Pater solicitus de filiis, & mater amantissima libe- rorum. Misimus autem ipsum, inquit Theodo- retus, non ut aliam vobis afferret doctrinam, sed ut vos in priori confirmaret, & hortaretur ad forti animo ferendas adversariorum insidias, & ne labe- factaremini, & à priori sententia dimoveremini.

## 3:3
Τῷ here has the same value as elsewhere εἰς τὸ. For in both ways the Hebrew is translated, which is in לכן. See above 2:19. Chrysostom and other Greek interpreters explain σαίνεσθαι by ϑορυβεῖσθαι; Hesychius, ταράττεσθαι. The use of that word is indeed frequent in the movement of a tail, but in antiquity it had the same value as σείειν. And I think the Cilicians used it so. In Hebrew it would be עשש.

Theophylact refers this to the afflictions of Paul: for when they sometimes suffer because of the vexations of their Teacher, they still had to be confirmed and exhorted, lest they fall from the faith. For disciples are not a little disturbed, and as it were distrustful, when their Teacher is so greatly afflicted by hardships and evils, just as soldiers are accustomed to be when they see their Commander affected by wounds. It should rather be referred, with Theodoret, to the afflictions of the Thessalonians, or certainly to the afflictions of both Paul and themselves; compare verse 4.

Beza advises that the word σαίνεσθαι can be taken in the middle voice, for 'to fawn,' lest the faithful, in a time of persecution, by pretending and dissembling, fawn upon the world. But the passive sense is more appropriate, since it concerns the passions of the soul, so that no one may be moved by afflictions.

For you yourselves know that we are appointed for this, called for this. Concerning the use of the word κεῖσθαι, see what we said on Luke 2:34. Concerning the sense, see Romans 8:17, 30; 1 Corinthians 1:9. Εἰς τῦτο לזאת.

This must be referred entirely to the afflictions, and not indeed to the consolation of the Apostles. For although Ministers of the Word are appointed to this office, that they may establish and exhort their hearers or their Church: yet that is not what is being treated here. Rather, the faithful are raised up by divine ordination, by which He has placed us for this, that we might be tested by afflictions, Job ch. XIII. v. 13. Lam. ch. III. 12. Rom. ch. VIII. v. 29. Let us hear, therefore, as Theophylact warns, how it is necessary for those who have received the faith of Christ to be exposed to temptations and pressures. For these things are not said only concerning the Apostles. If, therefore, we are instituted for this, what wonder is it if we are pressed? From which it happens that it is not fitting for us to be disturbed not only by past evils, but not even by future ones that are imminent. For that is most appropriate for us.

Latin:

Τῷ μηδένα σαίνεσθαι ἐν ταῖς θλίψεσι ταύταις) Τῷ hic va- let idem quod alibi εἰς τὸ. Utroque enim modo vertitur Ebræum, quod est in לכן. Vide supra II. 19. Σαίνεσθαι per ϑορυβεῖσθαι exponunt Chrysostomus & alii Interpretes Græci; Hesychius, ταράττεσθαι. Usus quidem frequen- ter ejus vocis est in motu caudæ, sed antiquitus idem valuit, quod σείειν. Et puto sic usos Cilicas. Ebræis es- set עשש.

Id ad afflictiones Pauli refert Theophylactus: Cum enim ob Præceptoris divexationes laborent nonnunquam, tamen & confirmandi erant & ex- hortandi, ne à fide exciderent. Non enim parum obturbantur discipuli, & quasi diffidunt, Præce- ptore ærumnis & malis tantopere afflicto, ut mi- lites solent, cum Ducem spectant affectum vulne- ribus. Referendum potius cum Theodoreto ad Thessalonicensium afflictiones, vel certe ad utras- que & Pauli & ipsorum afflictiones, conf. v. 4.

Vocem σαίνεσθαι in media voce accipi posse mo- net Beza, pro abblandiri, ne fideles tempore per- secutionis simulando, dissimulandoque blandi- antur mundo. Sed magis congruit passivus sensus, quum de animi passionibus agatur, ut nemo afflictionibus commoveatur.

Αὐτοὶ γὰρ οἴδατε, ὄτι εἰς τῦτο κείμεθα) A Deo in id positi, in id vocati sumus. De usu vocis κεῖσθαι vide quæ diximus ad Luc. II. 34. De sensu vide Rom. VIII. 17. 30. 1. Cor. I. 9. Εἰς τῦτο לזאת.

Referendum id omnino ad afflictiones, non vero ad consolationem Apostolorum. Nam etsi ad hoc munus constituti sint Ministri Verbi, ut stabiliant & exhortentur auditores vel Eccle- siam suam: Id tamen hic non agitur. Eriguntur potius fideles divina ordinatione, qua ad id po- suit nos, ut afflictionibus probaremur, Job. c. XIII. v. 13. Thren. c. III. 12. Rom. c. IIX. v. 29. Audiamus ergo, monente Theophylacto, quemad- modum qui Christi fidem exceperint, tentationi- bus oporteat esse & pressuris expositos. Neque enim de Apostolis hæc solum sunt dicta. Si itaque ad id nos sumus instituti, quid mirum, si premi- mur? Quo fit, ut non modo præteritis malis, sed ne futuris quidem imminentibus obturbari nos de- ceat. Id enim nobis maxime congruit.

## 3:4
Vers. 4. For even when we were with you, we told you beforehand that we were to suffer affliction, just as it also came to pass, and you know) Πρὸς here is 'with', as in John ch. I. v. 1. When he says μέλλομεν, he shows the evils predicted by him, both those that were to happen to himself and those that were to happen to the Thessalonians: both so that they, by the testimony of divine pre-signification, with the event following, might become firmer in the faith, and so that they might be less moved by the matter being premeditated, John XIII. 19. Add also Acts XIV. 22.

Greatly, says Theophylact, he consoles the disciples, when future evils are announced from afar by the Teacher. It is by no means right, therefore, for them to be disturbed, as if by things occurring unexpectedly, and for that reason Christ addresses the disciples thus: I have told you before it happens, that, when it has happened, you may believe. And not only did Paul predict those things to them, but many other things, as he had announced beforehand, also reached their end.

Latin:

Vers. 4. Καὶ γὰρ ὅτε πρὸς ὑμᾶς ἦμεν, προελέγομεν ὑμῖν, ὄτι μέλλομεν θλίβεσθαι, καθὼς κὶ ἐγένετο κὶ οἴδατε) Πρὸς hic est apud, ut Joh. c. I. v. 1. Cum dicit μέλλομεν, osten- dit prædicta à se mala, tum quæ sibi, tum quæ Thessa- lonicensibus erant eventura: tum ut hi divinæ præsigni- ficationis testimonio, subsequente eventu, in fide firmio- res evaderent, tum ut minus commoverentur re præme- ditata, Joh. XIII. 19. Adde & Act. XIV. 22.

Magnopere, inquit Theophylactus, discipulos con- solatur, cum à Præceptore longe mala futura de- nuntiantur. Nequaquam igitur hos obturbari par est, tanquam ex rebus ex insperato occurrsan- tibus, eoque Christus discipulos ita alloquitur: Dixi vobis, antequam fiant, ut, cum facta fuerint, credatis. Nec solum Paulus illis prædixit, sed alia pleraque, uti prænunciaverat, & finem sunt nacta.

## 3:5
Vers. 5. For this reason I also, no longer bearing it) Not bearing any longer to be ignorant of your affairs. See above 1. I sent to know your faith) That I might know in what state your faith is. And here I sent must be translated, I had sent. Lest the tempter should have tempted you) A participle for a verbal; Tempting, that is, the tempter המנסה, Matth. IV. v. 3. namely the Satan, as it is explained 1. Cor. VII. 5. in which place the verb to tempt is taken no less than here, so that it includes the effect intended by the tempter: as to give, Deut. XXIX. v. 4. John VI. 39. 2. Tim. II. 25. of which kind I have noted others elsewhere. But before lest, fearing is understood, as taking heed in Rom. XI. 21. usually to fall away before the words if and lest and similar, both in Greek and Latin.

And our labor should be in vain) So that our labor in instructing you should have fallen into vanity. Thus to receive in vain 2. Cor. VI. 1. to run in vain, Gal. II. 2. Our labor is not in vain, 1. Cor. XV. 58. The grace was not made empty, 1. Cor. XVI. 10.

Erasmus Schmidius here and in chapter V. 1. wishes it to be understood that your desire is implied. But Camerarius speaks rather of his own desire at v. 1. No longer bearing it elliptically, so that your desire or anxiety or zeal, or something of that sort is missing, not bearing any longer. Therefore Paul now explains his own proper solicitude, just as he had previously testified to the care common with his colleagues: and he appropriates the mission of Timothy to himself, so that they might know it was done primarily by his own authority and commission, and understand with how much love and desire he is carried toward them. He is solicitous both about their faith, whether they persevere constantly in the same, and lest a place be left for the tempter by some, or if it has perhaps been left by some, that it might be restored by the sacred ministry of Timothy, lest the labor of the Apostle and his colleagues be rendered void regarding them. For that reason, since I could no longer bear the greatest solicitude, I sent, desiring to know whether any harm had come to you from the temptations, and whether we have been frustrated in the labor which we undertook for you, as Theodoret has it. And these things concerning the first part. Compare now if you like the Thessalonian Apostolic curriculum, or the farewell Sermon held at Danzig in the year 1650, the subject of which was the former part of this chapter.

PART II. Paul's joy from the report of the returning Timothy.

Latin:

Vers. 5. Διὰ τοῦτο κἀγὼ μηκέτι στέγων) Non ultra ferens ignarus esse rerum vestrarum. Vide supra 1. Ἔπεμψα εἰς τὸ γνῶναι τὴν πίστιν ὑμῶν) Ut scirem, quo se loco habeat fides vestra. Et hic ἔπεμψα vertendum, miseram. Μήπως ἐπείρασεν ὑμᾶς ὁ πειράζων) Participium pro ver- bali; Tentans, id est, tentator המנסה, Matth. IV. v. 3. nimirum ὁ Σατανᾶς, ut exponitur 1. Cor. VII. 5. quo loco non minus, quam hic verbum πειράζειν ita sumitur, ut effe- ctum destinatum tentatori includat: ut dare, Deut. XXIX. v. 4. Joh. VI. 39. 2. Tim. II. 25. cujusmodi & alia alibi an- notavimus. Subintelligitur autem ante μήπως metuens, ut cavens Rom. XI. 21. usitate ἐκπίπτει ante voces si & ne & similes & Graecis & Latinis.

Καὶ εἰς κενὸν γένηται ὁ κόπος ἡμῶν) Ita ut labor noster in vobis instituendis in vanum ceciderit. Sic εἰς κενὸν δέ- ξασθαι 2. Cor. VI. 1. εἰς κενὸν τρέχειν, Gal. II. 2. Ὁ κόπος ἡμῶν οὐκ ἔστι κενὸς, 1. Cor. XV. 58. Ἡ χάρις οὐ κενὴ ἐγενή- θη, 1. Cor. XVI. 10.

Erasmus Schmidius hic & cap. V. 1. vult, subin- telligendum esse τὸν πόθον ὑμῶν desiderium vestrum. Sed de suo potius desiderio loquitur Camerarius ad v. 1. Μηκέτι στέγοντες ἐλλειπτικῶς, ut desit τὸν πό- θον seu μέριμναν seu σπουδὴν, ἢ τοιοῦτό τι, non magis continentes. Propriam ergo suam solici- tudinem jam exponit Paulus, quemadmodum antea communem cum collegis curam testatus erat: sibique missionem Timothei appropriat, ut sua imprimis autoritate ac commissione fa- ctam norint, ac quanto amore & desiderio in ipsos feratur, intelligant. Solicitus autem est tum de fide ipsorum, anne constanter in eadem perseverent, tum ne tentatori locus a quibus- dam relinquatur, aut si relictus forte a nonnullis sit, ut sacro Timothei ministerio restauraretur, ne quoad illos labor Apostoli & collegarum irritus reddatur. Ea de causa, cum maximam solicitu- dinem amplius ferre non possem, misi, scire deside- rans, num ex tentationibus aliquid damni vobis ac- cesserit, & frustrati simus labore, quem pro vobis suscepimus, ut habet Theodoretus. Atque haec de prima parte. Confer jam si lubet curriculum Thessalonicense Apostolicum, seu Concionem valedictoriam Dantisci Anno 1650. habitam, cujus materia fuit prior hujus capitis pars.

PARS II. Pauli e Timothei reducis relatione laetitia.

## 3:6
Vers. 6. But when Timothy had just come to us from you) When indeed Timothy has now returned to us from you. Concerning the word just, see Matth. IX. 18. Hence it appears that this epistle was written at Corinth, not at Athens. See Acts XVIII. v. 5.

But why could he not have returned to Paul and Silvanus at Athens, when he was returning from the Thessalonians? That arrival to Paul, of which Acts XVIII. 5 speaks, is far different in terms of time and place and persons: Of time indeed, because then for the first time he is said to have come to him from Macedonia, where the Apostle had left Timothy: Of place or the terminus from which and to which: That was Beroea, not Thessalonica, Acts XVII. 13, 14, this is Corinth: Of persons, because there not only Timothy came to Paul, but Silas with him. But in this place Paul and Silvanus say to us, Timothy returning to US from you Thessalonians.

And having brought us good news) Here to bring good news is taken not in that sense proper to these books, but in the more common meaning, which corresponds to the Hebrew בשר, as can be seen 1. Sam. ch. XXXI. v. 9. 2. Sam. I. v. 20. ch. XVIII. vers. 19, 31, and elsewhere. Timothy announced to me an exoptable message.

See how much joy Paul shows, as Theophylact warns with Chrysostom. For he did not say announcing, but evangelizing, so that he might express the greatness of their faith and charity, in which they had already been strengthened and established.

Your faith and love) An excellent and life-giving pair.

And that you have good remembrance of us) It is a remembrance. For by memory he understands mention, and he understands good, in a good sense, that is, honorable.

Longing to see us, just as we also you) For the desires of those who love are mutual.

Latin:

Vers. 6. Ἄρτι δὲ ἐλθόντος Τιμοθέου πρὸς ἡμᾶς ἀφʼ ὑμῶν) Cum vero jam a vobis ad nos redierit Timotheus. De voce ἄρτι vide Matth. IX. 18. Hinc apparet Corinthi scri- ptam hanc epistolam, non Athenis. Vide Actor. XVIII. v. 5.

Cur vero non redire ad Paulum & Silva- num potuerit Athenis, cum a Thessalonicensi- bus reverteretur? Ille ad Paulum adventus, quo de Act. XVIII. 5. longe alius est & temporis & loci & personarum ratione: Temporis quidem, quia tum primum e Macedonia, ubi reliquerat Timotheum Apostolus, venisse dicitur ad ipsum: Loci vel ter- mini a quo & ad quem: Ille erat Berrhoea, non Thessalonica, Act. XVII. 13. 14. hic Corinthus: Personarum, quia ibi ad Paulum non solus Ti- motheus venit, sed cum ipso Sila. At hoc loco πρὸς ἡμᾶς inquiunt Paulus & Silvanus, ad NOS redeunte a vobis Thessalonicensibus Timo- theo.

Καὶ εὐαγγελισαμένου ἡμῖν) Hic εὐαγγελίζεσθαι sumitur non in illo his libris proprio, sed in communiore signi- ficatu, qui respondet Ebræo בשר, ut videre est 1. Sam. c. XXXI. v. 9. 2. Sam. I. v. 20. cap. XVIII. vers. 19. 31. & alibi. Nuntium exoptabilem mihi nuntiavit Timo- theus.

Vide quantum prae se ferat laetitiae Paulus, monente cum Chrysostomo Theophylacto. Non enim annunciante dixit, sed evangelizante, ut & illorum fidei & charitatis exprimat magnitu- dinem, in qua obfirmati jam essent & stabili- ti.

Τὴν πίστιν καὶ τὴν ἀγάπην ὑμῶν) Egregiam &' salutife- ram ξυνωρίδα.

Καὶ ὅτι ἔχετε μνείαν ἡμῶν ἀγαθὴν πάντοτε) Est Mνη- νομία. Nam per memoriam intelligit mentionem, & bonam intelligit, in bonam partem, id est, honorifi- cam.

Ἐπιποθοῦντες ἡμᾶς ἰδεῖν, καθάπερ καὶ ἡμεῖς ὑμᾶς) Mutua enim sunt amantium desideria.

## 3:7
Vers. 7. For this cause we were comforted, brethren, over you) παρέκλήθημεν נחמנו, in Niphal, as 2 Sam. XIII. 39. Ἐφʼ ὑμῖν on your account.

In all our affliction and distress by your faith) And here there is a transposition; for the direct construction would have been, by your faith in all our affliction and distress. Concerning the meaning of the word ἀνάγκης, which the Hebrews of those times also used, see what is said at Luke XXI. 23.

As if giving thanks, says Theophylact, he was acting toward them, because they had not departed at all from the faith. For he says, we do not seem to feel sad things in any way, and the evils in which we are involved, but we have been comforted, and have breathed again, not from one of the evils, but from every pressure. For so great is that joy, which I have received from your faith and love, that it outweighs all my necessities and evils. Theophylact seems to take these things not only concerning the comfort received from there, but also concerning the faith of Paul being strengthened in his afflictions from this news, because of the words by your faith: You, he says, have confirmed me, when the matter was far otherwise. For although he himself was yielding to no temptations, he was rather strengthening them. Meanwhile, he bestows his praise upon them, just as if he were saying: Through this faith of yours, you have by no means allowed me to feel the temptations. Thus he fixes a sting in their minds, by which they may be impelled to constancy. Three things, says Theodoret, which are to be pursued with love and held in high esteem he has set forth: faith, and love, and the memory of the Teacher. Faith signifies the constancy of piety and religion. Love, however, which consists in action, signifies virtue. But the remembrance of the Teacher and the desire for him bears witness to the love of the doctrine. These things, he says, have caused us to be of good courage: and to have forgotten the afflictions which are brought upon us, which indeed we have sustained on account of your faith.

Latin:

Vers. 7. Διὰ τοῦτο παρεκλήθημεν ἀδελφοὶ ἐφʼ ὑμῖν) παρέ- κλήθημεν נחמנו, in Niphal, ut 2. Sam. XIII. 39. Ἐφʼ ὑμῖν vestri causa.

Ἐπὶ πάσῃ τῇ θλίψει κᾲ ἀνάγκῃ ὑμῶν διὰ τῆς ὑμῶν πίστεως) Et hic trajectio est; Recta enim constructio fuerat, διὰ τῆς ὑμῶν πίστεως ἐπὶ πάσῃ τῇ θλίψει κᾲ ἀνάγκῃ ὑμῶν. De significatu vocis ἀνάγκης, qua & Ebræi istorum tempo- rum utebantur, vide dicta ad Luc. XXI. 23.

Tanquam gratias, inquit Theophylactus, istis agebat, quod a fide nihil secesserant. Neque enim inquit videmur tristia quoquam modo sentire, & mala, in quibus versamur, sed consolati nos su- mus, & respiravimus non unis ex malis, sed ex omni pressura. Nam tantum est id gaudium, quod vestra ex fide accepi & charitate, ut cunctis prae- ponderet necessitatibus meis & malis. Non de solatio tantum inde accepto, sed etiam de fide Pauli ex hoc nuntio in afflictionibus roborata Theophylactus haec accipere videtur ob verba διὰ τῆς ὑμῶν πίστεως: Vos, inquit, me confirmastis, cum longe aliter se res haberet. Nam ipse cum tentationibus nihil succumberet, illos potius corro- borabat. Interim suam in hos laudem confert, perinde ac si inquiat: Per fidem hanc vestram haudquaquam sivistis, ut tentationes sentirem. Sic aculeum infigit animis, quo impellantur ad constantiam. Tria, inquit Theodoretus, quae sunt amore prosequenda & magni facienda posuit, fidem, & charitatem, & Doctoris memoriam. Si- gnificat autem fides quidem pietatis & religionis constantiam. Charitas vero, quae in actione con- sistit, virtutem. Doctoris autem recordatio & ejus desiderium fert testimonium de amore doctrinae. Haec, inquit, effecerunt, ut bono animo essemus: & quae nobis afferuntur afflictionum obliti simus, quas quidem propter fidem vestram sustinuimus.

## 3:8
Vers. 8. For now we live) That is, we lead a joyful life. For the Hebrews, as in Ps. XXII. 27, and the Greeks and Latins use this word in this way.

If you stand fast in the Lord) Thus you persist both now and in the future. Concerning this use of the word στήκειν, see Rom. XIV. 4, 1 Cor. XVI. 13, Philipp. IV. 1.

This expression seems to import something more. For as the falling away of the faithful was like death to Paul, so it was to him a kind of quickening, when he understood that his own, about whom he had been anxious, were persisting constantly in the faith. For, says Theophylact, he did not say these things to us for comfort, but as life, arguing that he considers their offense as death, and their progress as life, and that he considers those to be standing fast who are strengthened in Christ. We consider your confirmation to be our life, says Theodoret. It is death to a father if his children behave badly; but the piety and obedience of children is the life of the father. The Apostle compares himself to a father with respect to the Thessalonians, whom he had begotten in Christ, chap. II. 11.

Latin:

Vers. 8. Ὅτι νῦν ζῶμεν) Id est, laetam vitam agimus. Ita enim hanc vocem & Ebræi, ut Ps. XXII. 27. & Graeci & La- tini usurpant.

Ἐὰν ὑμεῖς στήκετε ἐν Κυρίῳ) Sic & nunc & in poste- rum perstatis. De hoc usu vocis στήκειν vide Rom. XIV. 4. 1. Cor. XVI. 13. Philipp. IV. 1.

Amplius quid haec loquutio importare vide- tur. Nam uti mortis instar Paulo erat defectio fidelium, ita ipsi veluti quaedam ζωοποίησις erat, cum suos in fide constanter persistere, de qui- bus solicitus fuerat, intelligebat. Neque enim, inquit Theophylactus, nobis consolationi fuere haec dixit, sed vita, arguens illorum offensionem pro morte se ducere, & profectum pro vita, & confi- stere eos existimare, qui in Christo sint roborati. Vestram confirmationem vitam nostram duci- mus, inquit Theodoretus. Patri mors est, si liberi male se gerant; at vita liberorum pietas, & obe- dientia. Patri se comparat Apostolus respectu Thessalonicensium, quos in Christo genuerat cap. II. 11.

## 3:9
Vers. 9. For what thanksgiving can we render to God περὶ ὑμῶν) What thanks, that is to say worthy, can we return. Paul looked to the words of Psalm 116:11.

Ἐπὶ πάσῃ τῇ χαρᾷ, ᾗ χαίρομεν δι᾿ ὑμᾶς ἔμπροσθεν Θεῦ) That is, with a sincere mind. See Luke ch. 1 v. 6 and what is said there.

The magnitude of the joy surpasses the praise that is sung by the tongue. For we cannot offer praise that corresponds to the joy brought to us by you, as Theodoret's paraphrase has it.

Latin:

Vers. 9. Τίνα γὰρ εὐχαριστίαν δυνάμεθα τῷ Θεῷ ἀνταποδοῦναι περὶ ὑμῶν) Quam gratiam, dignam scilicet, reddere possuimus. Respexit Paulus ad verba Psal. CXVI. 11.

Ἐπὶ πάσῃ τῇ χαρᾷ, ᾗ χαίρομεν δι᾿ ὑμᾶς ἔμπροσθεν Θεῦ) Id est, animo sincero. Vide Luc. cap. I. v. 6. & ibi dicta.

Vincit laudem, quæ à lingua decantatur, lætitiæ magnitudo. Non possumus enim laudem afferre, quæ lætitiæ nobis à vobis allatæ respondeat, ut habet Theodoreti paraphrasis.

## 3:10
Vers. 10. Νυκτὸς καὶ ἡμέρας) Always. Above ch. 2 v. 9.

Ὑπερεκπερισσῦ) An intensifying word, as in Eph. ch. 3 v. 20, below ch. 5:15.

Δεόμενοι) Asking, namely God, which is understood here, as in Rom. 1:10.

Εἰς τὸ ἰδεῖν ὑμῶν τὸ πρόσωπον) As above ch. 2, verse 18.

-— to hear and return familiar faces.
