Καὶ καταρτίσαι τὰ ὑστερήματα τῆς πίστεως ὑμῶν) To supply, if anything is required to perfect your faith. Concerning the word καταρτίσαι see 2 Corinthians ch. 13, verse 11, Galatians 6:1. Concerning the word ὑστερημάτων 1 Corinthians ch. 16 v. 17, Colossians ch. 1, verse 24. The sense is the same as in Romans ch. 1 v. 11.

Theophylact raises a doubt: Since he previously vindicated both the state and the strength of their faith, why does he now say that he will complete what is lacking in their faith? He answers: Either because they had not yet received all the doctrine, because the tradition concerning the resurrection of the dead, or other things of that kind, was still lacking to them: or because things pertaining to doctrine were lacking, rather than things pertaining to faith. The former answer does not fit: because without faith in the resurrection of Christ they could not have faith in Christ, nor hope of another life without the hope of resurrection, and it contradicts the explicit letter, Acts 17:3, he set before them that Christ had to suffer and rise from the dead. The latter is admitted. For faith can be complete regarding those things which are necessary to be believed for salvation, even if things can still be added to doctrine, so that τὰ ὑστερήματα, which are lacking, may be completed, and the faithful may be more abundantly informed and perfected in heavenly doctrine, Heb. 6:1.

Latin:

Vers. 10. Νυκτὸς καὶ ἡμέρας) Semper. Supra cap. II. v. 9.

Ὑπερεκπερισσῦ) Vox αὐξητικὴ, ut Eph. c. III. v. 20. infra c. V. 15.

Δεόμενοι) Rogantes, Deum scilicet, quod hic subauditur, ut Rom. I. 10.

Εἰς τὸ ἰδεῖν ὑμῶν τὸ πρόσωπον) Ut supra cap. II. vers. 18.

-— notos audire & reddere vultus.

Καὶ καταρτίσαι τὰ ὑστερήματα τῆς πίστεως ὑμῶν) Supplere, si quid ad fidem vestram perficiendam requiritur. De voce καταρτίσαι vide 2. Corinth. cap. XIII. vers. 11. Gal. VI. 1. De voce ὑστερημάτων 1. Corinth. cap. XVI. v. 17. Coloss. cap. I. vers. 24. Sensus idem, qui Rom. cap. I. v. 11.

Dubium movet Theophylactus: Cum superius & statum & fidei robur penes ipsos vindicarit, cur inquiat jam, se completurum, quæ fides desunt? Respondet: Vel quia nondum omnem acceperant doctrinam, quod defuerit adhuc illis traditio de resurrectione mortuorum, aut ejusmodi alia: vel quod defuerint potius, quæ ad doctrinam attinent, quam quæ ad fidem. Prior responsio non convenit: quia sine fide resurrectionis Christi fidem in Christum habere non poterant, neque spem vitæ alterius sine spe resurrectionis, & repugnat disertæ literæ, Act. XVII. 3. proposuit ipsis, quod Christus debuerit pati & resurgere à mortuis. Posterior admittitur. Nam fides integra esse potest quoad ea, quæ creditu necessaria sunt ad salutem, etiamsi doctrinæ adhuc addi possint, ut τὰ ὑστερήματα, quα deficiunt, compleantur, & fideles uberius in doctrina cœlesti informentur ac perficiantur, Ebr. VI. 1.

## 3:11
Vers. 11. Κατευθῦναι) הושׁר, Psalm 5 v. 9. See Luke ch. 1 v. 79. He prospered, the same as εὐοδῷ, Romans ch. 1 v. 10.

Latin:

Vers. 11. Κατευθῦναι) הושׁר, Psal. V. v. 9. Vide Luc. cap. I. v. 79. Prosperavit idem quod εὐοδῷ, Roman. cap. I. v. 10.

## 3:12
Ὑμᾶς δὲ ὁ Κύριος πλεονάσαι κὶ περισσεύσαι) These words have a Kal meaning elsewhere: but here a Hiphil, just as βασιλεύειν and many others. The Hebrews would say העשׁיר, may he enrich and make you wealthy.

Τῇ ἀγάπῃ εἰς ἀλλήλυς καὶ εἰς πάντας) Love also comes from God the Father: but it also requires our own effort, 1 Cor. ch. XIV, v. 1.

Thus he prays for divine friendship. That which is restricted to these, those, or the others, is human, says Chrysostom.

Καθάπερ κὶ ἡμεῖς εἰς ὑμᾶς) This must be taken as a parenthesis, and we must understand 'we are', in the Hebrew manner. We wish for you, he says, what we feel in ourselves.

What was ours, he says, with Theophylact as interpreter, we have already performed ourselves: what is yours, we pray that it may be done. But you have us as a measure and example of charity.

Latin:

Ὑμᾶς δὲ ὁ Κύριος πλεονάσαι κὶ περισσεύσαι) Hæc verba alibi habent significationem Kal: Hic vero Hiphil, quomodo βασιλεύειν & alia multa. Ebræi dicerent העשׁיר ditet vos ac locupletet.

Τῇ ἀγάπῃ εἰς ἀλλήλυς καὶ εἰς πάντας) Etiam dilectio à Deo Patre: Sed & studio nostro indiget, 1. Cor. cap. XIV. v. 1.

Sic divinam amicitiam precatur. Quæ adstringitur ad hos, illos, istos, humana est, inquit Chrysostomus.

Καθάπερ κὶ ἡμεῖς εἰς ὑμᾶς) Hoc sumendum ut παρένθεσις, & subaudiendum sumus, more Ebræo. Vobis, inquit, optamus, quod in nobis sentimus.

Quod nostra, inquit, Theophylacto interprete, interfuit, jam ipsi peregimus: quod vestra, ut fiat, oramus. Nos autem in charitatis mensuram habetis & exemplum.

## 3:13
Vers. 13. Εἰς τὸ στηρίξαι ὑμῶν τὰς καρδίας ἀμέμπτυς ἐν ἁγιωσύνῃ) Rom. 1. 11. XVI. 29. above 2. By loving one's neighbor, greater gifts are acquired from God, and especially constancy. That phrase ἀμέμπτυς ἐν ἁγιωσύνῃ is put for ἵνα ἧτε ἄμεμπτοι ἐν ἁγιωσύνῃ, as the following shows, when compared with Eph. V. 27. and 2 Cor. XI. 2. In the manuscript it is ἐν δικαιοσύνῃ.

Ἔμπροσθεν τῦ Θεῦ κὶ Πατρὸς ἡμῶν) For Christ presents us to God his Father as his own, Coloss. I. 22.

Ἐν τῇ παρουσίᾳ τῦ Κυρίε ἡμῶν Ἰησῦ Χριστῦ μετὰ πάντων τῶ ἁγίων αὐτῦ) A description of time, as above II. 19. The best books have ἁγίων. What those who have Ἀγγέλων have is an interpretation, from 2 Thess. I. 1. Matth. XVI. 27. XXV. 31.

Deut. XXXIII. 2. קדש מרבות the host of the holy ones, that is, of the Angels, which Jude v. 14 calls ἐν ἁγίαις μυριάσιν ἀυτῦ. So also Dan. IV. 10. 14. 20. VIII. 13. Mark joined both, μετὰ τῶν Ἀγγέλων τῶν ἁγίων, VIII. 34.

Our charity does not ensure that we are constant in faith. That is the work of divine grace alone. Therefore the Apostle prays to God night and day that He himself may establish our hearts. For it is grace that establishes hearts, Heb. XIII. 9. Our charity is too weak and imperfect to be able to establish and preserve hearts against the temptations of Satan. This is therefore a new object of the Apostolic prayer: the establishment of the heart, namely in the faith, by which hearts are purified, Acts XV. 9, in which they must be confirmed and established so that they may be guarded for salvation, which is the end of faith, 1 Pet. I. 5. 9. For he wishes to implore these three things in his prayers for them: charity, constant faith, and irreprehensible holiness; therefore he also wishes that they may abound or excel in mutual charity, and he desires that their hearts be established, and that they be ἄμεμπτα ἐν ἁγιωσύνῃ, irreprehensible in holiness. B. Hunnius correctly noted this: the third member of the vow, in which he wishes for them that they be confirmed from heaven in the faith, by which, having been purified in their hearts, they may be found irreprehensible in holiness: not, of course, that sanctification in this age can be perfect in every way and in every respect: but the pious are irreprehensible when they offer their obedience to God without hypocrisy, which, although it may be lacking, its imperfection is not imputed to the faithful, but is covered by the blood of Christ, and what is missing is supplied and compensated for by the obedience of the Savior Christ, performed for us according to the law and will of God the Father. For the Apostle is not to be believed to have neglected faith in his prayers, which was his primary concern: unless faith is primarily included under ἁγιωσύνῃ, without which there is no holiness, let alone anyone being ἄμεμπτος in holiness. Theophylact here notes a testimony of the most holy Trinity from Basil: he says that the Lord, who makes charity abound and hearts to be established in holiness, is the Holy Spirit, who is joined to God and our Lord Jesus Christ: understand the Lord to be the Holy Spirit, just as the Great Basil also thinks. For who else could it be besides this very Spirit, who is to confirm them in the sight of God and at the coming of Christ without complaint, that is, immaculate and pure? The passage of Basil is found in the book On the Holy Spirit, ch. 21, Tom. II of his works, p. 339. Which Lord does he pray may establish the irreprehensible hearts of the faithful Thessalonians before God and our Father at the coming of our Lord? Let those answer us who place the Holy Spirit with the ministering spirits who are sent for ministry. But they have nothing to answer. At the coming, he says, of the Lord. For there it will appear which is true holiness, and which is feigned, Mal. III. 17. 18.

THE SECOND PART OF THE EPISTLE: AN EXHORTATION TO HOLINESS IN LIFE.

Latin:

Vers. 13. Εἰς τὸ στηρίξαι ὑμῶν τὰς καρδίας ἀμέμπτυς ἐν ἁγιωσύνῃ) Rom. 1. 11. XVI. 29. supra 2. Diligendo proximum majora à Deo acquiruntur dona & præcipue constantia. Illud vero ἀμέμπτυς ἐν ἁγιωσύνῃ positum est pro ἵνα ἧτε ἄμεμπτοι ἐν ἁγιωσύνῃ, ut sequentia ostendunt, collata cum Eph. V. 27. & 2. Cor. XI. 2. In Manuscripto est ἐν δικαιοσύνῃ.

Ἔμπροσθεν τῦ Θεῦ κὶ Πατρὸς ἡμῶν) Nam Christus nos Deo Patri suo exhibet, ut suos Coloss. I. 22.

Ἐν τῇ παρουσίᾳ τῦ Κυρίε ἡμῶν Ἰησῦ Χριστῦ μετὰ πάντων τῶ ἁγίων αὐτῦ) Descriptio temporis, ut supra II. 19. Libri optimi habent ἁγίων. Quod quidem habent Ἀγγέλων est interpretamentum, ex 2. Thess. I. 1. Matth. XVI. 27. XXV. 31.

Deut. XXXIII. 2. קדש מרבות sanctorum militia, id est, Angelorum, quod Judas v. 14. ἐν ἁγίαις μυριάσιν ἀυτῦ. Sic & Dan. IV. 10. 14. 20. VIII. 13. Marcus utrumque conjunxit, μετὰ τῶν Ἀγγέλων τῶν ἁγίων, VIII. 34.

Charitas nostra non praestat, ut constantes simus in fide. Id solius gratiae divinae opus est. Ideo precatur Deum noctes & dies Apostolus, ut ipse stabiliat corda. Gratia enim est, quae corda stabilit, Ebr. XIII. 9. Nimis infirma & imperfecta est charitas nostra, quam ut adversus tentationes Satanae stabilire & conservare valeat corda. Est ergo hoc novum orationis Apostolicae objectum: Stabilitio cordis, in fide nempe, qua purificantur corda, Act. XV. 9. in qua confirmari ac stabiliri ea oportet, ut custodiantur ad salutem, quae finis est fidei, 1. Petr. I. 5. 9. Tria enim haec precibus suis exorare ipsis vult, charitatem, fidem constantem & sanctitatem irreprehensibilem, ideo & abundare vel exuperare eosdem vovet mutua charitate, & stabiliri corda, eademque ἄμεμπτα ἐν ἁγιωσύνῃ, irreprehensibilia in sanctitate desiderat. Notavit id recte B. Hunnius: Tertium membrum voti, quo optat illis, ut caelitus confirmentur in fide, qua purificati suis cordibus inveniantur irreprehensibiles in sanctimonia: non sane, quod sanctificatio in hoc seculo possit omnibus plane modis atque numeris esse perfecta: Sed irreprehensibiles sunt pii, quando sine hypocrisi Deo obsequia sua praestant, quae licet manca sint, illorum tamen imperfectio non imputatur fidelibus, sed Christi sanguine tegitur, &, quod deest, suppletur, & pensatur obedientia Servatoris Christi, pro nobis legi voluntatique Dei Patris exoluta. Non enim in precibus suis credendus est neglexisse fidem Apostolus, quae ipsi praecipue curae erat: nisi sub ἁγιωσύνῃ imprimis fides comprehendatur, sine qua nulla est sanctitas, nedum quisquam ἄμεμπτος in sanctimonia. Notat hic Theophylactus e Basilio testimonium sacrosanctae Trinitatis: Dominum, qui facit ut abundet charitas, & stabiliantur corda in sanctimonia, esse Spiritum Sanctum ait, qui conjungitur Deo, & Domino nostro Jesu Christo: Dominum, inquit, Spiritum Sanctum intellige, sicuti & Magnus Basilius sentit. Quis enim alius fuerit praeter hunc ipsum Spiritum, in Dei conspectu & Christi adventu sine querela, hoc est immaculatos & puros confirmaturus? Basilii locus habetur libr. de Spiritu Sancto cap. 21. Tom. II. oper. p. m. 339. Quem Dominum optat coram Deo & Patre nostro in adventu Domini nostri irreprehensibilia fidelium Thessaloncensium corda confirmata in sanctitate constabilire? Respondeant nobis, qui cum ministratoriis spiritibus, qui mittuntur ad ministerium, collocant Spiritum Sanctum. At non habent quod respondeant. In adventum inquit Domini. Ibi enim apparebit, quaenam sit vera, quae ficta sanctimonia, Mal. III. 17. 18.

PARS ALTERA EPISTOLAE PARAENESIS AD SANCTIMONIAM IN VITA.

## 4:1 Argument
CHAPTER IV. ARGUMENT AND DIVISION.

The Apostle exhorts them to walk as they had been instructed, to strive for sanctification, and specifically for chastity and justice, and not to despise the Apostolic warnings, which are those of God Himself, and to become ever more abundant in charity, to be tranquil, to work, and not to be given to idleness. He also warns them not to indulge too much in grief for the dead, while delivering on the occasion the mystery concerning the bringing of the dead and the living to Christ who is to come in the clouds.

There are therefore two parts: The former is hortatory regarding holy conduct, up to verse 12. The latter is hortatory regarding Christian moderation in mourning for the dead, up to verse 18.

PART I.

Hortatory regarding holy conduct.

Ver. 1. Τὸ λοιπὸν ὖν) A form of speech of one hastening to the end, as 2 Cor. XIII. 11. Gal. VI. v. 17. Eph. VI. v. 10. Phil. IV. v. 8.

Why of one hastening to the end? For the other part remains, and nearly half of the epistle, whether you consider the count of the verses or the subject matter and contents. He implies that this remains for Christianity, that holiness of life be joined with constancy in faith. According to Theophylact, 'as for the rest' is the same as 'assiduously and perpetually' and 'for the remaining time.' But just as he had prayed for holiness of life for them toward the end of the preceding chapter, so now he exhorts them to the same.

Ἐρωτῶμεν ὑμᾶς) Concerning this word see Acts III. 3. Philipp. ch. IV. 3.

Καὶ παρακαλῦμεν ἐν Κυρίῳ Ἰησοῦ) We beseech you by the Lord Jesus. For the discourse grows in intensity. Similar to Rom. ch. XII. v. 1.

By the Lord he asks servants, acquired by the death of the Lord: By Jesus, he asks those liberated from sins by the Savior. What greater adjuration could there be? Theophylact says: Attend, he says, to the humility: For he does not say that he himself is worthy, by exhorting or praying, to be trusted, but he takes Christ as his intercessor, as if he were saying this: Christ himself beseeches you through our intervention.

Καθὼς παρελάβετε παρ’ ἡμῶν) Above II. 13.

He does not refer to those things which he handed down above, but which were handed down by him when he was present with them. Theophylact: He wishes to refer not only to doctrine, but also to example. For what you have received, he says, consists not in words, but also in deeds. For by working and by acting the Apostle was teaching others. What then do we ourselves pray for? Certainly that you may abound more, that is, that you may strive to surpass even my precepts with good actions, and to endeavor beyond what I have enjoined upon you. For just as the earth produces not only what is demanded of it, so also the soul itself ought by no means to be content with having already done enough for the precepts, unless it has also exceeded them with deeds. But those things which do not sufficiently agree with the perfection of the Word of God and the divine law, and with the prohibitions of τῆς ἐθελοθρησκείας.

Τὸ πῶς δεῖ ὑμᾶς περιπατεῖν) The τὸ is redundant, as it often is. Concerning the sense see above II. 12.

The Τὸ is not redundant, but demonstrative: Namely that, how you ought to walk.

And to please God) In the Manuscript is added: As also you walk, which the Latin also reads.

The sense is: How you ought to walk, that you may please God. It is not necessary that we establish these as distinct. Lombard, Thomas, and Hugo Cardinalis refer the former to precepts, the latter to what they call Evangelical counsels of perfection. But Scripture knows no perfection beyond the precepts of God, because his precepts are of such perfection that they admit neither addition nor subtraction: nor does it have any apex of those Evangelical counsels. Nor does it distinguish them, but holds them for the same in this place Theodoret: We have shown you what manner of life is pleasing to God for all, apply zeal that you may keep what has been decreed for you. Nor does the Apostle call us back to counsels, but to παραγγελίας, that is, mandates, as interpreted by Grotius; he did not leave them free, but makes them necessary, which the word δεῖ OPORTET implies. These things therefore cannot be neglected without sin. The comparison also of Heb. XI. v. 5 with Gen. V. 22 teaches that the Holy Spirit interchanges that Enoch walked according to God, and that he pleased God, and does not truly hold these as so distinct that the one is the observation of God's precepts, the other of counsels. Which counsels of Evangelical perfection, if they were handed down only by Christ, how were they observed by Enoch? But that is clear from Heb. ch. XI. 6, that walking according to God and pleasing to God cannot have a place without faith, without which it is impossible to please God. The subject of the exhortation, however, is ἵνα περισσεύητε μᾶλλον, which Grotius did not touch: The form and norm is the Apostolic tradition or information. The end is τὸ ἀρέσκειν τῷ θεῷ to please God, that you may subsequently abound more and more, just as he had prayed for that in ch. III. 12, or that they may strive to excel or surpass not so much others as themselves daily, by progressing in the course of truth and piety, and by profiting in Christianity. Wrongly therefore do Hugo and Thomas snatch at abundance for supererogation, of which there is nothing in this text or elsewhere in the sacred code. τὸ περισσεύειν was referred to charity, ch. III. 12; it is referred to faith in Col. II. 7; to hope in Rom. XV. 13; to works of supererogation nowhere. Rightly Haymo: That you may abound, that you may grow more and more in faith and good works. For he pleases God who adorns the right faith, which he has, with the execution of virtues: And he abounds well, who, with the age of faith growing in himself, strives also to abound in holy works and in the study of virtues.

Latin:

CAPUT IV. ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

Adhortatur Apostolus, ut ambulent, prout informati erant, ut studeant sanctificationi, ac speciatim castimoniae & justitiae, non vero contemnant monita Apostolica, quae ipsius Dei, ac pleniores subinde fiant in charitate, tranquilli sint, laborent, non otio dediti sint. Monet etiam, ne maerori nimium indulgeant ob mortuos, ex occasione tradens mysterium de mor- tuorum & vivorum ad Christum in nubi- bus venturum adductione.

Partes igitur duæ sunt: Prior est monitoria ad sanctam conversationem, ad v. 12. Posterior mo- nitoria est, ad luctus de mortuis Christianam mode- rationem, ad v. 18.

PARS I.

Monitoria ad sanctam conversationem.

Vers. 1. Τὸ λοιπὸν ὖν) Loquutio properantis ad finem, ut 2. Cor. XIII. 11. Gal. VI. v. 17. Eph. VI. v. 10. Phil. IV. v. 8.

Cur ad finem properantis? Superest enim pars altera, & dimidium fere epistolæ, sive versuum computum, sive materiam & contenta respicias. Id restare ad Christianismum innuit, ut cum con- stantia in fide jungatur vitæ sanctimonia. Se- cundum Theophylactum de cætero idem est, quod assidue & perpetuo, & in reliquum tempus. Ut autem sanctimoniam vitæ precatus erat ipsis sub finem capitis præcedentis: Ita nunc ad ean- dem eos hortatur.

Ἐρωτῶμεν ὑμᾶς) De hac voce vide Act. III. 3. Philipp. c. IV. 3.

Καὶ παρακαλῦμεν ἐν Κυρίῳ Ἰησοῦ) Per Dominum Jesum obtestamur. Crescit enim oratio. Simile Rom. c. XII. v. 1.

Per Dominum rogat servos, morte Domini acquisitos: Per Jesum Salvatorem à peccatis libe- ratos. Qui poterat major esse obtestatio? Theo- phylactus: Attende, inquit, humilitatem: Non enim neque hortando aut precando dignum se dicit, cui fides possit præstari, sed Christum sibi pro depre- catore assumit, tanquam id inquiat: Christus ipse nostro vos interventu precatur.

Καθὼς παρελάβετε παρ’ ἡμῶν) Supra II. 13.

Non respicit ea, quæ supra tradidit, sed quæ ab eo tradita, cum præsens ipsis esset. Theophylactus: Non doctrinam tantum, sed exemplum etiam re- spici vult. Quod autem accepistis, inquit, non verbis, sed etiam rebus constat. Operando namque Apostolus, agendoque alios edocebat. Quid igitur nos ipsi precamur? Certe ut abundetis magis, hoc est, ut superare etiam mea præcepta bonis actionibus stu- deatis, ultraque, quam vobis injunxerim, eniti. Nam quemadmodum terra non modo quæ huic de- mandantur, producit. Sic & anima ipsa nequaquam esse debet præceptis fecisse jam satis contenta, nisi & factis illa excesserit. Quæ vero non satis conve- niunt Verbi Dei & legis divinæ perfectioni, & in- terdictis τῆς ἐθελοθρησκείας.

Τὸ πῶς δεῖ ὑμᾶς περιπατεῖν) τὸ abundat, ut sæpe. De sensu vide supra II. 12.

Τὸ non abundat, sed demonstrativum est: Illud nempe, quomodo debeatis ambulare.

Καὶ ἀρέσκειν Θεῷ) In Manuscripto additur; Καθὼς κὶ περιπατεῖτε, quod & Latinus legit.

Sensus est: Quomodo ambulare debeatis, ut Deo placeatis. Non necessum est, ut hæc distincta statuamus. Lombardus, Thomas & Hugo Cardinalis prius ad præcepta, posterius ad consilia Evangelica, quam vocant, perfectionis referunt. Sed Scriptura ultra Dei præcepta nullam perfectionem novit, quia præcepta ejus perfectionis sunt, ut nec addi- tionem, nec detractionem admittant: neque de consiliis illis Evangelicis apicem ullum habet. Nec ea distinguit, sed pro iisdem habet hoc loco Theodoretus: Ostendimus vobis, quænam vita universorum Deo grata sit, studium adhibete, ut quæ sunt vobis decreta, custodiatis. Nec ad con- silia nos revocat Apostolus, sed ad παραγγελίας, hoc est, mandata, interprete Grotio; non libera reliquit, sed necessaria facit, quod verbum δεῖ OPORTET innuit. Negligi ergo citra peccatum hæc non possunt. Collatio etiam Ebr. XI. v. 5. cum Gen. V. 22. docet, quod permutet Spiritus Sanctus, quod Enoch ambulavit secundum Deum, & quod Deo placuerit, non vero hæc ita distincta habeat, ut alterum sit præceptorum Dei observatio, alterum consiliorum. Quæ Evangelicæ perfectionis consilia, si à Christo demum tradita, quomodo ab Enocho observata? Id autem ex Ebr. c. XI. 6. liquet, ambulationem secundum Deum & Deo placentem non posse locum habere sine fide, sine qua impossibile est Deo placere. Adhortationis autem materia est, ἵνα περισσεύητε μᾶλλον, quam non tetigit Grotius: Forma & norma est traditio vel informatio Apostolica. Finis est τὸ ἀρέσκειν τῷ θεῷ placere Deo, ut subinde magis magisque abundetis, quemadmodum id precatus erat cap. III. 12. vel ut excellere aut superare non tam alios quam seipsos quotidie annitantur, progrediendo in cursu veritatis & pietatis, & proficiendo in Christianismo. Perperam ergo Hugo & Thomas abundantiam ad supererogationem abripiunt, de qua nihil in hoc textu aut alibi in sacro codice. Ad charitatem referebatur τὸ περισσεύειν, cap. III. 12. ad fidem refertur Col. II. 7. ad spem Rom. XV. 13. ad opera supererogationis nuspiam. Recte Haymo: Ut abundetis, ut magis ac magis crescatis in fide & bonis operibus. Ille enim placet Deo, qui fidem rectam, quam habet, executione virtutum decorat: Et ille bene abundat, qui, crescente ætate fidei in se, studet etiam abundare in sanctis operibus & in studio virtutum.

## 4:2
Vers. 2. For you know what mandates we gave to you) take παραγγελίας here as precepts, as in Acts ch. XVI v. 24. מצוות.

Through the Lord Jesus) Supply, having received. These precepts the Apostles had received from God through Christ.

For you know, he says, lest anyone should pretend ignorance. They handed them down therefore clearly, so that all could understand. Otherwise that οἴδατε would not be appropriate. Moreover, Crocius here corrects his Beza, when he noted: that the word παραγγελία properly signifies that kind of mandates which are promulgated having been received from another, so that he who commands in his own name is said to διαγγέλλειν, he who in another's is said to παραγγέλλειν: That this distinction does not have a place everywhere: For it is attributed to God in Acts XVII. 30, and likewise to Christ commanding in his own name, Matt. X. 5, Mark VI. v. 6, VIII. v. 6, 1 Cor. VII. 10. Conversely, διαγγέλλειν is attributed to a man appointed as a herald, Luke IX. 60.

Latin:

Vers. 2. Οἴδατε γὰρ, τίνας παραγγελίας ἐδώκαμεν ὑμῖν) παραγγελίας hic accipe præcepta, ut Actor. cap. XVI v. 24. מצוות.

Διὰ τοῦ Κυρίου Ἰησοῦ) Supple, accepta. Præcepta ista Apostoli à Deo per Christum acceperant.

Nostis enim, inquit, ne quis ignorantiam prætexat. Tradidere ergo luculenter, ut omnes intelligere potuerint. Alias non conveniret illud οἴδατε. Cæterum corrigit hic Bezam suum Crocius, cum annotaret: quod vox παραγγελία proprie illud mandatorum genus significet, quæ ab alio accepta promulgantur, ut qui suo nomine imperat διαγγέλλειν, qui alieno παραγγέλλειν dicatur: Quod distinctio illa non ubique locum habeat: Nam Deo tribuitur Act. XVII. 30. itemque Christo suo nomine mandanti, Matth. X. 5. Marci VI. v. 6. VIII. v. 6. 1. Cor. VII. 10. Contra διαγγέλλειν tribuitur homini præconi constituto Luc. IX. 60.

## 4:3
Vers. 3. For this is the will of God) In the Manuscript τὸ θέλημα. He does not treat here of some absolute decree, such as that concerning judging the world, or raising the dead: But of that which God wills προηγουμένως, which he wishes, which he desires. The same is βουλὴ Θεοῦ in Luke VII. 30. See Matt. ch. XXIII. v. 37.

Your sanctification) Rom. VI. 19, 22, 1 Corinth. ch. I. v. 30.

Indeed, what he mandates and commands, and that with a most grave threat added against violators of the divine will. Crocius explains it concerning the revealed will and the precepts explained, by which it is declared what he approves, what he disapproves, what he commands, what he forbids. But one must beware, lest another hidden will be feigned, which the Calvinists are accustomed to oppose to the revealed one. Beza and Cornelius indeed restrict sanctification, as it seems Chrysostom and Theophylact also do, to chastity, but it is more rightly understood generally with Blessed Luther, Calvin, and others as the complex of all virtues, or even with faith included at the same time: without which there is no heart purification, no sanctification. Thus the will of God is completely accepted, the cause adequately responds to the preceding warning, and the opposite, which follows, that you abstain from fornication, is subjoined as a necessary consequence. For fornication is most opposed to sanctification, and likewise to faith and holiness, by which faith is shaken off, and holiness is eliminated both of mind and of time, 1 Cor. VI. Which must also be held concerning injustice. Yet there is no reason why we should disagree with those who restrict ἁγιασμὸν to the virtues following faith, provided that the constancy of faith has been dealt with in the former part: provided it is not narrowed too much, which was done in Beza's version, this is the will of God, namely your sanctification, THAT IS, that you abstain from fornication.

Latin:

Vers. 3. Τοῦτο γάρ ἐστι θέλημα τοῦ Θεοῦ) In Manuscripto τὸ θέλημα. Non agit hic de absoluto aliquo decreto, quale est de judicando mundo, de resuscitandis mortuis: Sed de eo, quod Deus vult προηγουμένως, quod optat, quod desiderat. Idem βουλὴ Θεοῦ Luc. VII. 30. Vide Matth. c. XXIII. v. 37.

Ὁ ἁγιασμὸς ὑμῶν) Rom. VI. 19. 22. 1. Corinth. cap. I. v. 30.

Imo quod mandat & imperat, idque addita comminatione gravissima in violatores voluntatis divinæ. Crocius explicat de voluntate revelata & præceptis explicata, quibus declaratur, quid probet, quid improbet, quid præcipiat, quid prohibeat. Sed cavendum, ne fingatur alia voluntas abscondita, quam revelatæ opponere solent Calviniani. Sanctificationem restringunt quidem Beza, & Cornelius, ut videtur etiam Chrysostomus ac Theophylactus, ad castitatem, sed rectius generaliter intelligitur cum B. Luthero, Calvino, & aliis de virtutum omnium complexu, vel etiam simul inclusa fide: sine qua nulla est cordis purificatio, nulla sanctificatio. Sic voluntas Dei complete accipitur, causa adaequate praecedenti monito respondet, & oppositum, quod sequitur, ut abstineatis a scortatione, ceu necessarium consequens subjungitur. Maxime enim adversatur ut sanctificationi, sic & fidei ac sanctitati scortatio, qua fides excutitur, & sanctitas eliminatur tum animi, tum temporis, 1. Cor. VI. Quod etiam de injustitia habendum. Non tamen est, quod refragemur illis, qui ἁγιασμὸν ad virtutes fidem consequentes restringunt, siquidem de fidei constantia priori parte actum sit: modo ne arctetur nimis, quod in versione Bezae factum, haec est voluntas Dei, nempe sanctificatio vestra, ID EST, ut abstineatis a scortatione.

## 4:4
Vers. 4. That you abstain from fornication) He touches specifically on those sins which were considered of little account by the Greeks. See what was said in Acts XV. 20.

That each of you know how to possess his own vessel in sanctification and honor) Some explain this from 1 Sam. chap. XXI. vers. 5. But it is more true that those things are understood there which were prepared for a journey. Therefore I take σκεῦος here to be the body itself, which he honors who keeps it chastely: he who does otherwise, dishonors it, 1 Cor. chap. VI. v. 18. Rom. chap. I. v. 24. Also Rabbi Akiba in the book above the letters calls the body כלי. Indeed the body is the instrument of the mind. Barnabas calls Christ's body the vessel of the Spirit.

Latin:

Vers. 4. Ἀπέχεσθαι ὑμᾶς ἀπὸ τῆς πορνείας) Specialiter tangit ea peccata, quae a Graecis minimi fiebant. Vide quae dicta Act. XV. 20.

Εἰδέναι ἕκαστον ὑμῶν τὸ ἑαυτοῦ σκεῦος κτᾶσθαι ἐν ἁγιασμῷ καὶ τιμῇ) Quidam explicant ex 1. Sam. cap. XXI. vers. 5. Sed verius ibi ea intelligi, quae ad iter erant comparata. Itaque σκεῦος hic accipio ipsum corpus, quod honorat, qui caste id habet: qui aliter, id dehonestat, 1. Cor. c. VI. v. 18. Rom. cap. I. v. 24. Etiam Rabbi Akiba in libro supra literas corpus vocat כלי. Nimirum corpus instrumentum est animi. Barnabas Christi corpus vocat σκεῦος τοῦ Πνεύματος.

## 4:5
Vers. 5. Not in the passion of desire) ἐπιθυμία is a movement of the mind: πάθος is a vice, an evil habit. Cicero, Tusculan Disputations III, fears, lusts, irascibility, which the Greeks call πάθη. Cicero, Quintilian, and Gellius have translated these as affects and affections elsewhere. In the Glossary: πάθος is a vice. Thus Rom. chap. I. v. 26. shameful passions. Here it is taken for the vices of the concupiscible part, and for the vices of the irascible part, Coloss. III. 5. as we said there.

Just as also the nations that do not know God) And here the καὶ is redundant, as also below in 13. Concerning the sense, see Eph. chap. IV. v. 17. They are ignorant of GOD, who are ignorant of His will.

Under fornication is included adultery, as in Matt. chap. V. 32. chap. XIX. v. 9. Rom. I. v. 29. 1 Corinth. chap. VII. v. 3. Eph. V. 3. although they are sometimes distinguished, Matt. chap. XV. v. 19. Mark chap. VII. v. 21. Gal. chap. V. v. 19. yet it does not at the same time include idolatry here, which is spiritual fornication, and the love of earthly things before God, all of which Haymo wishes the word to include in this place. Augustine interprets σκεῦος inconveniently in book I de nuptiis & concupisc. chap. 8, and book IV contr. Jul. chap. 10, as a wife, to which Lombard, Thomas, Hugo, and Hyperius do not entirely disagree. For this exhortation pertains as much to wives as to husbands. More correctly, therefore, with Tertullian, Theodoret, Chrysostom, and Theophylact, it is explained as each person's own body, which is called the vessel of the soul by Plato. The Apostle wishes it to be kept holy, and to be held in honor, lest we contaminate it through uncleanness and affect it with ignominy. Since the bodies of Christians are also vessels and temples of the Holy Spirit, 1 Cor.

c. VI. v. 19. But he does not command abstinence from the marriage embrace, which Haymo wishes to be required here as the honor of the body, but on the contrary the Apostle in 1 Cor. chap. VII. v. 5. This is not to be taken in such a way, says Augustine in book I de nupt. & concupisc. chap. 8, as if the Apostle had prohibited the conjugal, that is, the lawful and honorable intercourse, which was certainly called chastity by Paphnutius in the Nicene Council, book I of the Ecclesiastical History of Socrates, chap. 8. By fornication, however, he teaches 1. that the sanctification of the body is lost, 2. that the honor due to it is violated, 3. that we are rendered liable to gentile desire, that is, to turn from Christians into gentiles, 1 Petr. chap. IV: 3. Eph. IV. 3.

4. to slip into atheism. Because they are compared to the nations which have not known God, and deny God, who is chastity itself, and whose will is our sanctification. Those who, says Theophylact, have no knowledge of God, nor hope for the retribution of good and evil deeds, it is necessary that they give themselves entirely to pleasure, and ascribe everything to it. Which he attributes to the internal passions themselves of desire, and therefore he wishes one to be preserved not only from external acts of luxury, but also from the internal flames of lust, which are called passions, because this passion is so vehement that a man corrupted by it seems to suffer rather than to act.

Latin:

Vers. 5. Μὴ ἐν πάθει ἐπιθυμίας) ἐπιθυμία est motus animi: πάθος vitium, malus mos. Cicero Tusculanarum III. formidines, libidines, iracundia, quae Graeci πάθη appellant. Affectus & affectiones alibi transtulere Cicero, Quintilianus, Gellius. In Glossario: πάθος vitium. Sic Rom. cap. I. v. 26. πάθη ἀτιμίας. Hic accipitur pro vitiis partis concupiscentis, & pro vitiis θυμοειδοῦς Coloss. III. 5. ut ibi diximus.

Καθάπερ καὶ τὰ ἔθνη τὰ μὴ εἰδότα τὸν Θεόν) Et hic καὶ abundat, ut & infra 13. De sensu vide Ephes. cap. IV. v. 17. Ignorant DEUM, qui voluntatem ejus ignorant.

Sub πορνείᾳ comprehenditur μοιχεία vel adulterium, ut Matth. c. V. 32. cap. XIX. v. 9. Rom. I. v. 29. 1. Corinth. cap. VII. v. 3. Eph. V. 3. etsi quandoque distinguantur, Matth. cap. XV. v. 19. Marc. cap. VII. v. 21. Gal. cap. V. v. 19. non tamen simul hic complectitur idololatriam, quae spiritualis est fornicatio, & rerum terrenarum amorem prae Deo, quae omnia vocem hoc loco complecti vult Haymo. Incommode σκεῦος interpretatur Augustinus libr. I. de nuptiis & concupisc. cap. 8. libr. IV. contr. Jul. cap. 10. de uxore, cui non omnino abnuunt Lombardus, Thomas, Hugo, Hyperius. Pertinet enim haec paraenesis tam ad uxores, quam ad viros. Rectius proinde cum Tertulliano, Theodoreto, Chrysostomo, Theophylacto de proprio cujusque corpore explicatur, quod vas animae Platoni dicitur. Sanctum id servari vult Apostolus, & in honore haberi, ne per immunditiem id contaminemus & ignominia afficiamus. Siquidem Christianorum corpora vasa etiam sint ac templa Spiritus Sancti, 1. Cor.

c. VI. v. 19. Non autem abstinere a connubiali complexu jubet, quem honorem corporis hic requiri vult Haymo, sed contra Apostolum 1. Cor. c. VII. v, 5. Hoc non sic accipiendum est, inquit Augustinus l. I. de nupt. & concupisc. c. 8. tanquam prohibuerit Apostolus conjugialem, hoc est licitum honestumque concubitum, qui castimonia certe appellatus est a Paphnutio in Niceno Concilio libr. I. Hist. Eccles. Socrat. cap. 8. Scortatione vero docet 1. sanctificationem corporis deperdi, 2. honorem ei debitum violari, 3. gentilis cupiditatis nos obnoxios reddi, hoc est, e Christianis gentiles evadere, 1. Petr. cap. IV: 3. Eph. IV. 3.

4. in atheismum prolabi. Quia gentibus tales comparantur, quæ non noverunt Deum, ab- negantque Deum, qui est ipsa castitas, & cujus voluntas est sanctificatio nostra. Qui nullam, inquit Theophylactus, habent Dei cognitionem, neque retributionem bonorum pravorumque faci- norum sperent, necesse est, unde voluptati se totos addicunt, & illi universa adscribunt. Quæ ipsis etiam passionibus internis tribuit τῆς ἐπιθυμίας, ideoque non servari tantum vult ab externis, luxu- riæ actibus, sed etiam à flammis libidinis interio- ribus, quæ πάθη dicuntur, quia hæc passio tam vehemens est, ut homo illa corruptus pati potius, quam agere videatur.

## 4:6
Vers. 6. That no man go beyond and defraud his brother in the matter) Since the Thessalonians were great merchants, as we said above I. 8, the Apostle deservedly inculcates upon them those precepts which he also inculcated upon the Ephesians, Eph. IV. v. 11. ὑπερβαίνειν is עבר, to violate covenants, Deut. XVII. 2. and elsewhere; πλεονεκτεῖν indeed is עשק, in contracts to take more for oneself than the equality of thing with thing, or of price with thing, allows. Ἐν τῷ πράγματι, perhaps better ἔν τινι πράγματι, in some business. The word business is general enough, but it is properly said of trade, whence πραγματεύομαι, I trade: πραγματεία, trade, in the Glossary; See Levit. XXV. v. 14, 17, and what we have said on that passage. There is there אחיך, which is ἀδελφόν here.

While rejecting that not sufficiently religious correction of the phrasing of the Holy Spirit (perhaps better ἔν τινι πράγματι: for why should you not explain ἐν τῷ πράγματι as in any business whatsoever, for example, in buying, selling, letting, hiring, and exchange), we do not disapprove of the annotation of Grotius. For these things are not to be understood as concerning adultery, which Cajetan, Erasmus, Salmero, Cornelius à Lapide, Ludovicus de Dieu, along with Jerome, Chrysostom, and Theodoret, think; from whom Chrysostom explains τὸ ὑπερβαίνειν thus: God gave to each man his own wife, He set the bounds of nature, that custom with one. Therefore, that which is done with another is a transgression, robbery, and fraud, nay, worse and more grievous than any robbery. Theodoret, however, noted that πλεονεξία, the desire for having more, is here likewise called adultery. For he who touches what does not pertain to him, who violates another's marriage, and the bed that belongs to another, offers violence. For πλεονεκτεῖν is properly to defraud and to plunder by fraud, 2 Cor. ch. VIII, v. 2, ch. XII, v. 18 (as Chrysostom and Theophylact explain it there), whence πλεονεξία is avarice. And he is said to ὑπερβαίνειν who transcends the rules of justice, who as it were tramples his brother underfoot, in which way Ambrosiaster, Anselm, Sedulius, Thomas, Luther, and others of our side, as well as Calvin, Beza, Zwingli, the Belgian, Crocius, etc., explain it.

For the Lord is the avenger of all these things) Thus the Greeks: God has an avenging eye. See Rom. XII. 19, Heb. X. 30. Ἔκδικος is מתנקם.

As we also told you before and testified) Namely, when we were among you.

Latin:

Vers. 6. Τὸ μὴ ὑπερβαίνειν καὶ πλεονεκτεῖν ἐν τῷ πρά- γματι τὸν ἀδελφὸν) Cum Thessalonicenses magni merca- tores fuerint, ut diximus supra I. 8. merito illis Apostolus ea inculcat præcepta, quæ & Ephesiis inculcavit Eph. IV. v. 11. ὒπερβαίνειν עבר est violare pacta, Deut. XVII. 2. & alibi, πλεονεκτεῖν vero עשק, in contractibus plus sibi sumere quam patitur rei cum re, aut pretii cum re æqua- litas. Ἐν τῷ πράγματι melius forte ἔν τινι πράγματι, in negotio aliquo. Negotii vox satis generalis est, sed proprie de mercatu dicitur, unde πραγματεύομαι nego- tior: πραγματεία negotiatio in Glossario; Vide Levit XXV. v. 14. 17. & ad eum locum à nobis dicta. Est ibi אחיך quod hic ἀδελφόν.

Reprobata illa non satis religiosa correctione loquutionis Spiritus Sancti (melius forte ἔν τινι πράγματι: Cur enim non ἐν τῷ πράγματι ex- ponas, in negotio scilicet quocunque, verbi gra- tia, in emptione, venditione, locatione, con- ductione & permutatione) non improbamus annotationem Grotii. Nec enim de adulterio hæc, quod censent Cajetanus, Erasmus, Sal- mero, Cornelius à Lapide, Ludovicus de Dieu cum Hieronymo, Chrysostomo & Theodoreto intel- ligenda, è quibus Chrysostomus τὸ ὑπερβαίνειν sic explicat: Unicuique Deus suam uxorem dedit, terminos naturæ posuit consuetudinem illam cum una. Itaque quæ cum altera fit, trans- gressio est, latrocinium & fraus, imo quovis la- trocinio pejor & gravior. Theodoretus vero πλεονεξίαν plura habendi cupiditatem hic pariter vocari adulterium notavit. Qui enim, quod ad se non pertinet, attingit, qui alienum violat matrimonium, & quod alium pertinet cubile, vim affert. Nam πλεονεκτεῖν proprie est frau- dare & fraude expilare, 2. Cor. cap. VIII, v. 2. cap. XII. v. 18. (ut illic explicant Chrysostomus & Theophylactus,) unde πλεονεξία avaritia est. Et ὑπερβαίνειν dicitur, qui transcendit regulas justi- tiæ, qui fratrem quasi pedibus calcat, quo pacto explicant Ambrosiasier, Anshelmus, Sedulius, Thomas, Lutherus, & alii nostrates necnon Calvinus, Beza, Zvinglius, Belga, Cro- cius &c.

Διότι ἔκδικος ὁ Κύριος περὶ πάντων τύτων) Sic Græci: Ἔχοι Θεὸς ἔκδικον ὄμμα. Vide Rom. XII. 19. Ebr. X. 30. Ἔκδικος מתנקם .

Καθὼς καὶ προείπομεν ὑμῖν καὶ διεμαρτυράμεθα) Nem- pe cum apud vos essemus.

## 4:7
Vers. 7. For God has not called us unto uncleanness, but unto holiness) That is, unto uncleanness, but unto holiness. For our writers often mix these particles. Ἀκαθαρσία, however, is taken here generally, as above II. 3, and extends as widely as that which is opposed to it, ἁγιασμός. See what we said above II. 3.

As he terrified the wicked with the gravity of wrath and divine vengeance: so he calls the faithful away from such things by the tenor of the divine calling. Not to impurity, which is both in foul lust and in base avarice, by which not indeed the body, yet the soul is defiled, God has called us, but to sanctification, Conf. 1 Tim. 6, 9. 10. For neither, says he, with Theophylact as interpreter, will God afflict you with torture, so that he may take vengeance on one who has suffered evil, but that he may vindicate himself. For when to cleanliness and purity be convicted of an injury brought upon him, who has bestowed the Holy Spirit upon you. If we listen to Flacius, impurity and sanctification encompass the whole just and unjust life. And therefore he wishes the Apostle to argue from the end of the calling, that all sins are to be fled, and virtues are to be pursued, both those previously enumerated, and others as well, because God has called us to holiness. But because the Apostle is about to admonish specifically concerning brotherly love later, it is better to understand these things specifically in the sense we have stated.

Latin:

Vers. 7. Οὐ γὰρ ἐκάλεσεν ἡμᾶς ὁ Θεὸς ἐν ἀκαθαρσίᾳ, ἀλλ̓ ἐν ἁγιασμῷ) Id est, εἰς ἀκαθαρσίαν, ἀλλ̓ εἰς ἁγιασμὸν. Has enim particulas sæpe permiscens nostri Scriptores. Ἀκαθαρ- σία autem hic generaliter sumitur, ut supra II. 3. & tam late patet, quam quod ei opponitur ἁγιασμὸς. Vide quæ dixi- mus supra II. 3.

Ut scelestos terruit ira & vindictæ divinæ gravitate: Ita fideles avocat à talibus voca- tionis divinæ tenore. Non ad impuritatem, quæ & in fœda libidine, & in turpi avaritia, qua non quidem corpus, anima tamen conta- minatur, vocavit nos Deus, sed ad sanctifi- cationem, Conf. 1. Timoth. 6, 9. 10. Neque enim te, inquit Theophylacto interprete, cru- ciatu afficiet Deus, ut eum, qui male perpessus sit, ulciscatur, sed seipsum ut vindicet. Nam cum ad munditiam te & puritatem vocasset, cum inquinatior fueris, illatæ in se argueris injuriæ, qui Spiritum sanctum tibi contulerit. Flacium si audiamus, impuritas & sanctificatio totam ju- stam & injustam vitam complectitur. Ideoque vult argumentari Apostolum à fine vocationis, fu- gienda esse peccata omnia, sectandasque esse virtu- tes, tum prius enumeratas, tum & alias, quia Deus nos vocavit ad sanctimoniam. Quia vero peculiariter de charitate fraterna postea monitu- rus est Apostolus, hæc specialiter intelligere præ- stat eo, quo diximus sensu.

## 4:8
Vers. 8. τοιγαροῦν ὁ ἀθετῶν) He who despises these precepts. Thus ἀθετεῖν is taken for מאס, as we said at Luke 10, 6.

οὐκ ἄνθρωπον ἀθετεῖ, ἀλλὰ τὸν θεὸν) A similar opposition Acts 5, v. 4.

τὸν καὶ δόντα τὸ πνεῦμα αὑτοῦ τὸ ἅγιον εἰς ἡμᾶς) Which Spirit, those who act otherwise, afflict with grief, Eph. 4, 30. nay, and extinguish, below c. 5, 19. He must be treated gently, so that such a great guest may be retained. καὶ is absent from the Manuscript. εἰς ἡμᾶς for ἡμῖν לנו.

Latin:

Vers. 8. τοιγαροῦν ὁ ἀθετῶν) Qui præcepta ista con- temnit. Sic ἀθετεῖν sumitur pro מאס, ut ad Luc. 10, 6. diximus.

οὐκ ἄνθρωπον ἀθετεῖ, ἀλλὰ τὸν θεὸν) Similis oppositio Act. 5, v. 4.

τὸν καὶ δόντα τὸ πνεῦμα αὑτοῦ τὸ ἅγιον εἰς ἡμᾶς) Quem Spiritum, qui aliter agunt, mœrore afficiunt, Eph. 4, 30. imo & extinguunt, infra c. 5, 19. Molliter habendus est, ut retineatur tantus hospes. καὶ abest à Manuscripto. εἰς ἡμᾶς. pro ἡμῖν לנו.

## 4:9
περὶ δὲ τῆς φιλαδελφίας) Namely, how it is to be exercised in individual circumstances.

οὐ χρείαν ἔχετε γράφειν ὑμῖν) Namely ἐμέ. There is no need for me to write to you about that matter in detail. The Rabbis would say: לא חשיהין אנחין.

Αὐτοὶ γὰρ ὑμεῖς θεοδίδακτοί ἐστε εἰς τὸ ἀγαπᾷν ἀλλήλους) The same sense as 1 John 2, v. 27. The anointing itself (the Holy Spirit) teaches you concerning all things, namely, those to be done. The greater the Spirit is, the fewer the prescriptions needed, Jerem. 31, v. 33. 34. Therefore, understand ἀγαπᾷν ἀλλήλους here not as a general precept, but as special determinations, as each matter and person and time requires. θεοδίδακτοι, δίδακτοὶ τοῦ θεοῦ, John 6, v. 45. where see the remarks.

Θεοδίδακτος according to Flacius is said in this place of one whose heart the preached word penetrates with a living sense through the grace of the Holy Spirit, and by that very work, which he has learned, he strives to perform. But he who knows what he ought to do, and does not do it, has not yet learned from God inwardly in the heart: but only outwardly in the senses and speculation: not according to the spirit, but according to the letter alone, which is dead. Let us therefore be admonished by this saying, that in Christianity idle speculations are not required, but living and industrious; and practical knowledge, whether they concern faith or the decalogue. This is Flacius. He who knows what it is that ought to be done, and does not do it, has not yet learned from God according to grace, but according to the law, not according to skill, but according to gain, says Augustine in the book on the grace of Christ, chapter 13.

Latin:

περὶ δὲ τῆς φιλαδελφίας) Quomodo scilicet ea exer- cenda sit in singulis circumstantiis.

οὐ χρείαν ἔχετε γράφειν ὑμῖν) Nempe ἐμέ. Non opus est, ut ea de re vobis particulatim scribam. Rabbini dicerent: לא חשיהין אנחין.

Αὐτοὶ γὰρ ὑμεῖς θεοδίδακτοί ἐστε εἰς τὸ ἀγαπᾷν ἀλλήλους) Idem sensus qui 1. Joh. 2, v. 27. Ipsum unguentum (Spiritus sanctus) de omnibus, agendis scilicet, vos do- cet. Quo major est Spiritus, eo minoribus præscriptis opus, Jerem. 31, v. 33. 34. Itaque ἀγαπᾷν ἀλλήλους intel- lige hic non de generali præcepto, sed de determinationi- bus specialibus, prout res quæque & personæ & tempora exigunt. θεοδίδακτοι, δίδακτοὶ τοῦ θεοῦ, Joh. 6, v. 45. ubi dicta vide.

Θεοδίδακτος juxta Flacium is hoc loco dicitur, cujus cor verbum prædicatum vivo sensu per gra- tiam Spiritus sancti penetrat, eoque opere ipso, quod didicit, præstare satagit. Qui vero novit, quid facere debeat, nec facit, nondum à Deo intus didicit in corde: Sed foris tantum in sensi- bus & speculatione: non secundum spiritum, sed secundum solam mortuamque literam. Admo- neamur igitur hoc dicto, in Christianismo non re- quiri otiosas speculationes, sed vivas ac operosas; practicasque notitias, sive illæ fidem, sive deca- logum spectent. Hæc Flacius. Qui novit, quid est, quod fieri debeat, & non facit, nondum à Deo didicit secundum gratiam, sed secundum le- gem, non secundum peritiam, sed secundum lu- crum, inquit Augustinus libr. de grat. Christi cap. 13.

## 4:10
Vers. 10. καὶ γὰρ ποιεῖτε αὐτὸ) That αὐτὸ here refers to the matter, you do this, that is, you show love.

εἰς πάντας τοὺς ἀδελφοὺς τοὺς ἐν ὅλῃ τῇ Μακεδονίᾳ) Not only in your city, but throughout all of Macedonia, as great as it is.

Latin:

Vers. 10. καὶ γὰρ ποιεῖτε αὐτὸ) Illud αὐτὸ hic ad rem refertur, facitis hoc, id est, dilectionem ostenditis.

εἰς πάντας τοὺς ἀδελφοὺς τοὺς ἐν ὅλῃ τῇ Μακεδονίᾳ) Non in urbe tantum vestra, sed per totam, quanta est, Ma- cedoniam.

## 4:11
Vers. 11. Παρακαλοῦμεν δὲ ὑμᾶς, ἀδελφοὶ, περισσεύειν μᾶλλον) That you may progress more and more, above verse 1. Rom. 15, 13. 1 Cor. 14, 12. chap. 15, 58. 2 Cor. 8, 7. c. 9, 8. Coloss. 2, 7.

καὶ φιλοτιμεῖσθαι ἡσυχάζειν) And to devote effort to tranquility. We had φιλοτιμεῖσθαι in this sense in 2 Corinthians 6, 9. ἡσυχάζειν שאן to study tranquility. See 2 Thessalonians 3, v. 12.

and to do your own business) And to be kept in one's own skin. Those who act otherwise are called ἀλλοτριοεπίσκοποι, 1 Pet. 4:15, busybodies, 2 Thess. 3:11, in Greek πολυπράγμονες; a vice in which the Greeks labored greatly, especially those who sought a soft life in leisure, parasites, buffoons, and those like them.

and to work with your own hands) Not to seek a living by fawning upon others, but by assiduous labor, 2 Thess. 3:10, 11, 12.

Theophylact indeed refers this 'to aspire' to the preceding remarks about benevolence. Although, he says, I am by no means unaware that charity toward a brother is maintained by you, we ask, however, that you abound more and more in benevolence, and that you strive for it with all zeal. He notes, however, that it can also be understood thus: That the following should immediately ensue, devote effort that you may conduct yourselves more quietly, and that each of you may perform his own business. From these things, however, he reproves those (so Theophylact continues) who are vacant in leisure, and devote themselves entirely to quiet, and curiously inquire into everything, disturbing all things. But indeed, he says, by working with your own hands, he reproves those who remove the exercise of the body, and demand only spiritual things, and are far deceived. For one does not work with the hands at fasting or sleeping on the ground, but with the Spirit. Whence it is given to be understood that the Apostle did not speak in this place of spiritual exercise, but of bodily. For it is the office of the Holy Spirit to impart a living to others from the work of the hands: the Spirit, I say, is a certain more certain work. For at that time, Christians, since they were a prey to infidels on account of the faith they had undertaken, with all their family property and goods of fortune exhausted, were living in the greatest scarcity of things, and therefore he teaches them to work, so that they might be able to be a protection both to themselves and to others. If, therefore, the Apostle enjoins them to sweat at the work of the hands, he nevertheless excludes nothing from those whose property still remained intact. Let begging monks and other lazy bellies, who are vacant in leisure under the pretext of spiritual exercises, note these things.

As we commanded you) Namely, when we were among you, as above v. 6. We say nothing new. It is Paul's custom to touch particularly upon those vices which were most prevalent in any given place.

Latin:

Vers. 11. Παρακαλοῦμεν δὲ ὑμᾶς, ἀδελφοὶ, περισσεύειν μᾶλλον) Ut magis magisque proficiatis, supra vers. 1. Rom. 15, 13. 1. Cor. 14, 12. cap. 15, 58. 2. Cor. 8, 7. c. 9, 8. Coloss. 2, 7.

καὶ φιλοτιμεῖσθαι ἡσυχάζειν) Et operam dare tranquil- litati. φιλοτιμεῖσθαι hoc sensu habuimus 2. Corinth. 6, 9. ἡσυχάζειν שאן tranquillitati studere. Vide 2. Thessal. 3. v. 12.

καὶ πράσσειν τὰ ἴδια) Propriaque in pelle teneri. Aliter qui agunt, vocantur ἀλλοτριοεπίσκοποι, 1. Petr. 4, 15. πε- ριεργαζόμενοι, 2. Thessal. 3, 11. Græcis πολυπράγμονες; quo vitio Græci plurimum laborabant, ii maxime, qui vitam in otio mollem quærebant, parasiti, scurræ, iisque similes.

καὶ ἐργάζεσθαι ταῖς ἰδίαις χερσὶν ὑμῶν) Non aliis affen- tando vitam quærere, sed labore assiduo, 2. Thessal. 3, v. 10. 11. 12.

Refert quidem hæc Φιλοτιμεῖσθαι Theophylactus ad præcedentia de benevolentia. Etsi, nequa- quam sim nescius, ait, per vos in fratrem chari- tatem servari, rogamus tamen, ut abundetis magis ac magis benevolentiam, ad eamque & omni stu- dio enitamini. Monet tamen, posse & ita in- telligi: Ut statim illud sequatur, date operam, ut vos quietius habeatis, & vestrum quisque ne- gotia propria peragat. Ex his autem eos arguit (ita pergit Theophylactus) qui otio vacant, & quieti se totos addicunt, curiosiusque aliena dis- quirunt omnia perturbare. Quin vero cum ma- nibus, inquit, propriis operamini, illos vituperat, qui corporis tollunt exercitationem, & spiritualia tantum deposcunt, & longe falluntur. Non enim jejunium vel humicubationem manibus quis opera- tur, sed Spiritu. Unde intelligi datur, non de spi- rituali exercitatione hoc loco dixisse Apostolum, sed de corporali. Est namque Spiritus sancti officium, ex manuum opera victum aliis impertiri: Spiritus inquam id certius quoddam est opus. Nam ea tem- pestate Christiani, tum Christi ob fidem susceptam infidelibus prædæ essent, re omni familiari & fortu- næ bonis exhausti, in summa rerum penuria dege- bant vitam, eoque ut operentur edocet, quatenus quirent, cum sibi tum aliis præsidio esse. Si itaque his injungit Apostolus operi manuum insudare, ni- hil tamen eos excludit, quibus res adhuc integra manebat. Hæc monachi mendicantes & alii ven- tres pigri, spiritualium exercitationum prætextu otio vacantes notent.

Καθὼς ὑμῖν παρηγγείλαμεν) Nempe cum apud vos esse- mus, ut supra v. 6. Nihil novi dicimus. Mos est Paulo, pe- culiariter ea vitia tangere, quæ quoque in loco vigebant maxime.

## 4:12
that you may walk becomingly toward those outside) Rom. 13:13, 1 Cor. 14:40. 'Toward those outside,' that is, in all the business which you have with those who are strangers to the faith, Col. 4:5.

He could have brought forward various things against restlessness, leisure, and curiosity or meddlesomeness, but he says that regard must be had primarily for the Gentiles, lest they be offended. Restless dispositions are hateful to all. No one loves a busybody. Idleness and leisure are hateful even to the Gentiles themselves. Cf. Sir. 3:21, Eph. 4:18, 1 Pet. 2:12, ch. 4:10, 15.

and that you may lack nothing) So that you do not lack necessities. Concerning this expression, see Acts 2:45, Eph. 4:26.

Theophylact explains these things with the preceding ones thus: That you may not act too impudently among those who wander outside the court of the faith by begging for alms. Which, however, he said more modestly, so as not to offend them, just as if he were saying: If the faithful themselves, when they see some believer begging in the best of bodily health, are greatly offended, and accuse a man of that kind of trafficking under the pretext of Christ, how much more are the infidels themselves going to disparage that kind of begging. Indeed, he adds two reasons to his exhortation: The one from public honesty, the other from private utility. Public honesty is that which adorns the profession of religion, if Christian men are said to be quiet, to attend to their own function, and to labor strenuously, and to provide a living for themselves by honest work and just reason, whereas on the contrary it is shameful to be sluggish in leisure and to covet the goods of others. Private utility is that you may provide a living for yourself and yours without begging by some honest labor, and furthermore bring help to others who are in need, so that as Flacius has in his Gloss. Furthermore, if the faithful ought not to seek out indigence directly, nor summon it, but rather avert it with all their might; therefore, indigence or poverty that is summoned is not a state of perfection: Nor is it to be vowed. The Papist monks therefore wrongly vow mendicancy: Which rightly infers and defends against Bellarmine.

PART II. Admonitions concerning the moderation of grief for the deceased.

Latin:

ἵνα περιπατῆτε εὐσχημόνως πρὸς τὺς ἔξω) Rom. 13, v. 13. 1. Corinth. 14, v. 40. πρὸς τὺς ἔξω, id est, in omnibus negotiis, quæ habetis cum iis, qui à fide alieni sunt Col. 4, v. 5.

Poterat varia contra inquietudinem, otium, & curiositatem vel πολυπραγμοσύνην afferre, sed im- primis gentium rationem habendam esse dicit, ne offendantur. Inquieta ingenia sunt omnibus exosa. Curiosus nemo amat. Ignavia & otium est ipsis gentibus invisum. Conf. Sir. 3, 21. Ephes. 4, 18. 1. Petr. 2, 12. cap. 4, 10. 15.

καὶ μηδενὸς χρείαν ἔχητε) Ita ut vobis non desint ne- cessaria. De hac locutione vide Actorum 2, v. 45. Ephes. 4, v. 26.

Explicat hæc cum præcedentibus ita Theo- phylactus : Ne quid impudentius apud illos aga- tis, qui extra fidei aulam divagantur stipem effla- gitando. Quod tamen modestius dixit, ne illos of- fenderet, perinde ac si dicat: Si fideles ipsi, cum fide- lem quempiam conspiciantur, optima corporis vale- tudine mendicantem, maxime offenduntur, & istiusmodi hominem sub Christi prætextu mercimo- nia factitare incusant, quanto magis sunt infideles ipsi id mendicandi genus obtrectaturi. Nimirum duas addit adhortationi rationes: Alteram ab ho- nestate publica, alteram ab utilitate privata. Publica honestas est, ornans professionem religio- nis, si dicantur Christiani homines esse quieti, suæ functioni vacare, & strenue laborare, & ho- nesto opere, justaque ratione sibimet victum pa- rare, cum contra turpe sit, otio torpere, & alienis bonis inhiare. Propria utilitas est, ut ipse tibi tuis- que sine mendicitate honesto aliquo labore vi- ctum pares, & insuper aliis egentibus opem feras, ut habet Flacius in Glossa. Porro si fideles non de- bent indigentiam expetere directe, non accer- sere, sed pro virili avertere; ergo indigen- tia seu paupertas accersita non est status perfe- ctionis: Nec vovenda. Male igitur mona- chi Papistici vovent mendicitatem: Quæ re- cte infert & contra Bellarminum tuetur Cro- cius.

PARS II. Monitoria de mæroris ob defunctos modera- tione.

## 4:13
Verse 13. ὐ θέλομεν δὲ ὑμᾶς ἀγνοεῖν, ἀδελφοὶ, περὶ τῶν κε- κοιμημένων) Concerning the dead. Regarding this manner of speaking, see Matt. 9:24, John 11:11. The Rabbis say שכבי, Daniel ישנים ch. 12:2. In the Manuscript περὶ τῶν κοιμωμένων, not badly. For it is not only a matter of those already dead, but also of those dying daily.

He does not want them to be ignorant, if any perhaps were less firm in that faith. For it is a meiosis. I want you to know this certainly, to believe it firmly. For faith is accustomed to be described through knowledge, Isa. 53:11, John 17:3. For the resurrection of the dead could not have been unknown, which is reckoned among the first rudiments or elements of the faith, which there is no doubt the Apostle had delivered to them, Heb. 6:2, just as it is evident from Acts 17:3 that Paul had preached to them about the resuscitation of Christ, and it is read that he preached to the Athenians the Gospel of Jesus and of the resurrection, from which he seemed to have announced new gods to them. It is therefore not only probable that the Thessalonians were not ignorant of the resurrection, but it is certain that they believed it, even if they seem to have raised certain doubts about the circumstances of the resurrection. For he opposes Christians to the Gentiles in that the former have the faith of the resurrection, while the latter do not, thus describing them in antithesis, οἱ μὴ ἔχοντες ἐλπί- δα. He calls the dead sleeping, not by reason of the soul, as the Psychopannychites dreamed of a sleep of souls, which by their opinion would not even be a sleep, but rather a cessation of all operation, since they imagine it to be devoid of every vital function in the state of separation, contrary to open scripture, Matt. 22:32, Luke 16:25, Rev. 6:10. But by reason of the body, because it rests in its bed, Isa. 57:2, sleeps under the earth, Isa. 26:19, in which it is buried, in the dust of the earth, Dan. 12:2 (note here that Grotius takes this passage concerning the resurrection of the dead differently than he had interpreted it in Daniel), namely in its monument, Job 5:29. He who sleeps is by no means extinguished, nor does his soul rest entirely, but the body rests only from labor, so that upon waking it may rise from the bed. As sleep is the image of death, so the bed is the image of the sepulcher. This appellation of death is frequent in the Holy Scriptures, see Deut. 31:26, 2 Sam. 7:12, 1 Kings 2:10, Isa. 26:20, ch. 56:14, Dan. 12:2, Matt. 9:24, Job 11:11, Acts 13:36, 1 Cor. 11:30, ch. 15:20. But concerning the death of the pious, as Hilary has it in Psalm 126, God most frequently calls the death of the saints sleep.

ἵνα μὴ λυπῆσθε, καθὼς καὶ οἱ λοιποὶ) We have warned above concerning the redundant καὶ in verse 5. Namely, just as the rest of your countrymen, not yet converted to Christ, and indeed the Jews as well. For these too were great show-offs in mourning. Thus we have οἱ λοιποὶ in Eph. 2:3 and 4:17, and below in ch. 5:6. Charondas in his laws saw more in this matter than the rest: ὡς ἀχαρίστης οὔσης πρὸς δαίμονας χθονίως λύπης ὑπὲρ τὸ μέτρον γενομένης. Thus the prophecy of Jeremiah 31:13 is fulfilled.

οἱ μὴ ἔχοντες ἐλπίδα) Either none, like the Epicureans and Sadducees, or not supported by sufficiently solid foundations, like the Pharisees and Platonists. See what has been said by us in Book II concerning the truth of the Christian religion.

The particle καὶ couples the unconverted with those among the converted who were mourning too much for the dead. It does not forbid grief or sorrow. For it is natural to grieve when friends are snatched away by death, since faith does not extinguish natural affection. Whence even the saints mourned their own, as Abraham mourned Sarah, Gen. 23:2, Joseph mourned Jacob, Gen. 50:1, Mary, and indeed Christ himself, mourned Lazarus, John 11:35, but [it forbids] the excess of sorrow, Sir. 28:16 ff. I do not forbid mourning at all, says Chrysostom in Homily LXI on John, but I forbid mourning ἀμέτρως, without due moderation. I am not inhuman and cruel. I see that nature grieves and requires daily custom. Weep, but gently and prudently and with the fear of God. If you shed tears in this way, you will not be accused of distrust of the resurrection, but you will be seen to bear the separation of a loved one with difficulty. We do not blame the affection, says Bernard in Sermon XXVI on the Song of Songs, unless it exceeds the measure. It is necessary that you be saddened, the ordinary gloss has from Aug. lib. X. de verbis Apostoli serm. XXXII. But when you are saddened, let hope console you. For he also calls them sleeping for that reason. Which custom is most true, so that when we are about to wake the sleeping, we do not despair at all. We are saddened, therefore, in the deaths of our own by the necessity of dying, but we are raised up by the hope of receiving them back. And in that sense must be accepted that of Isidore lib. III. de summo bono: Although piety commands us to weep for the deceased faithful: faith nevertheless forbids us to mourn for them. A limitation is therefore added by the Apostle, that we should not mourn as those who have no hope, namely of the resurrection, Acts 26, 6, and of eternal life, Eph. 2, 12. Therefore, one must not mourn in the manner of the Gentiles, lest we be recognized as taking away the hope of the resurrection along with them, because we mourn those whom we say live with God as if they were extinct and lost, and we reject by the testimony of our heart and breast the faith which we bring forth by speech and voice, as Cyprian speaks, serm. IV. de mortal. This also Chrysostom and Constantine of Antioch, serm. IV. in epist. ad Ebræos: When I see mourning in the streets and lamentations over those who have migrated from this life, and howlings and other ineptitudes, believe me, I blush, and the pagans, and the Jews, and the heretics seeing these things, and all who mock us. And for this cause it was also forbidden to the Jews in the Old Testament, in mourning for the deceased, to imitate the rites of the infidel nations, for example, that they shaved their heads, cut their flesh, made figures or marks upon themselves, Lev. 19, 27. Deut. 14, 1. 2.

Latin:

Vers. 13. ὐ θέλομεν δὲ ὑμᾶς ἀγνοεῖν, ἀδελφοὶ, περὶ τῶν κε- κοιμημένων) De mortuis. De hoc loquendi genere vide Matth. 9, 24. Joh. 11, 11. Rabbini dicunt שכבי Daniel ישנים c. 12, 2. In Manuscripto περὶ τῶν κοιμωμένων, non male. Non enim tantum de jam tum mortuis agitur, sed & de quotidie morituris.

Non vult eos ἀγνοεῖν, si qui forte minus firmi fuere in ista fide. Nam μείωσις est. Volo ut hoc certe sciatis, firmiter credatis. Nam fides per scien- tiam describi solet, Esa. 53, 11. Johan. 17, 3. Non enim ignota esse potuit resurrectio mortuorum, quæ inter prima fidei, quam Apostolum ipsis tra- didisse dubium non est, rudimenta vel elementa refertur, Ebr. 6, 2. quemadmodum ex Actor. 17, 3. constat, Paulum ipsis de Christi resuscitatione prædicasse, & Atheniensibus prædicasse legitur Evangelium de Jesu & de resurrectione, inde visus novos Deos illis annunciasse. Non ergo pro- babile tantum est, non ignorasse Thessalonicen- ses resurrectionem, sed certum est, eosdem il- lam credidisse, etsi dubia quædam de circumstan- tiis resurrectionis movisse videantur. Opponit enim Christianos gentilibus in eo, quod illi fidem resurrectionis habeant, hi non habeant, sic eos in ἀντιθέσει describens, οἱ μὴ ἔχοντες ἐλπί- δα. Dormientes autem dicit mortuos, non ra- tione animæ, ut Psychopannychitæ animarum dor- mitionem somniarunt, quæ ne quidem dormitio fuerit, eorum sententia, sed potius cessatio o- mnis operationis, quum in statu separationis o- mnis vitalis functionis expertem fingant contra apertam scripturam, Matth. 22, 32. Luc. 16, 25. Apoc. 6, 10. Sed ratione corporis, quia id in cu- bili suo quiescit, Esa. 57, 2. sub terra dormit, Esa. 26, 19. in qua conditum est, in pulvere terræ Dan. 12, 2. (quem locum nota hic Grotium de resurre- ctione mortuorum accipere secus, quam in Da- niele interpretatus erat) in monumento nempe suo Job. 5, 29. Qui dormit minime extinguitur, nec anima ejus prorsus quiescit, sed corpus quiescit tantum à labore, ut evigilans è lecto ex- surgat. Somnus ut est mortis, sic lectus imago sepulchri. Crebra est hæc mortis appellatio in sacris literis, Vid. Deut. 31, 26. 2. Sam. 7, 12. 1. Reg. 2, 10. Esa. 26, 20. cap. 56, 14. Dan. 12, 2. Matth. 9, 24. Job. 11, 11. Actor. 13, 36. 1. Cor. 11, 30. cap. 15, 20. Sed de morte piorum, ut habet Hilarius in Psal. 126. mortem sanctorum Deus frequentissime somnum nuncupat.

ἵνα μὴ λυπῆσθε, καθὼς καὶ οἱ λοιποὶ) De καὶ superabun- dante monuimus supra v. 5. Sicut cæteri nempe populares vestri, nondum ad Christum conversi, imo & Judæi. Nam & hi in luctu erant magni ostentatores. Sic οἱ λοιποὶ habe- mus Ephes. 2, 3. & 4, 17. & infra c. 5, 6. Charondas in le- gibus plus hac in re, quam cæteri, vidit: ὡς ἀχαρίστης οὔσης πρὸς δαίμονας χθονίως λύπης ὑπὲρ τὸ μέτρον γενομένης. Sic impletur vaticinium Jerem. 31, 13.

οἱ μὴ ἔχοντες ἐλπίδα) Aut nullam, ut Epicurei & Saddu- cæi, aut non satis solidis subnixam fundamentis, ut Pharisæi & Platonici. Vide quæ dicta à nobis ad librum II. de verita- te religionis Christianæ.

Particula καὶ copulat non conversos cum illis, qui è conversis nimium lugebant ob mortuos. Non prohibet luctum aut mœrorem. Nam hoc na- turale est, dolere, cum amici morte abripiuntur, quum στοργὴν non extinguat fides. Unde etiam sancti suos luxerunt, ut Abraham Saram, Gen. 23. v. 2. Josephus Jacobum, Gen. 50, 1. Maria, imo ipse Christus, Lazarum Johan. 11, 35. sed mœroris exces- sum Sir. 28, 16. seqq. Minime lugere, inquit Chry- sostomus homil. LXI. in Johannem, sed ἀμέτρως sine debita moderatione lugere veto. Non sum imma- nis atque crudelis. Video naturam dolere, & quoti- dianam requirere consuetudinem. Lacrymare, sed leniter & prudenter & cum Dei timore. Si hac ra- tione lacrymas fundes, non resurrectionis diffiden- tia argueris, sed ægre ferre charissimi sejunctionem videberis. Non culpamus affectum, inquit Bern- hardus Serm. XXVI. in Cantic. nisi cum excedit mo- dum. Necesse est, ut contristēris, habet glossa or- dinaria ex August. lib. X. de verbis Apostoli serm. XXXII. Sed ubi contristaris, soletur te spes. Nam & ideo dormientes eos appellat. Quæ consuetudo verissima, ut cum dormientes evigilaturus mi- nime desperemus. Contristamur ergo in nostrorum mortibus necessitate moriendi, sed spe recipiendi eos erigimur. Atque eo sensu accipiendum illud Isi- dori libr. III. de summo bono: Etsi pietas pro de- functis fidelibus flere jubeat: fides tamen pro iis luge- re vetat. Limitatio itaque additur ab Aposto- lo, ne ita lugeamus, ut illi, qui spem non habent, re- surrectionis scilicet, Actor. 26, 6. & vitæ æternæ, Ephes. 2, 12. Non ergo more gentilium lugendum, ne cum ipsis spem resurrectionis tollere agnosca- mur, quod, quos vivere apud Deum dicimus, ut extinctos & perditos lugemus, & fidem, quam ser- mone & voce depromimus, cordis & pectoris te- stimonio reprobemus, ut loquitur Cyprian. serm. IV. de mortal. Id & Chrysostomus & Constantinus Antiochenus serm. IV. in epist. ad Ebræos: Cum vi- deo luctus in plateis & lamentationes super eos, qui ex hac vita migrarunt, & ululationes & ineptias a- lias, credite mihi erubesco, & paganos, & Judæos, & hæreticos ista videntes, & omnes, qui nos irrident. Atque ex hac causa prohibitum etiam Judæis in Veteri Testamento fuit, in luctu ob defunctos imitari gentium infidelium ritus, exempli gratia, quod caput radebant, carnem incidebant, figuras aut stigmata sibi faciebant, Lev. 19, 27. Deut. 14, 1. 2.

## 4:14
Vers. 14. εἰ γὰρ πιστεύομεν, ὅτι Ἰησοῦς ἀπέθανε) Truly, which the Apostles construct with great effort, Matt. 27, 50. John 19, 30. 34.

καὶ ἀνέστη) And these truly: which likewise the Apostles construct in all ways, Luke 23, 53. John 19, 41. and in the following chapters. Paul himself 1 Cor. 15.

οὕτω καὶ ὁ θεὸς τοὺς κοιμηθέντας διὰ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ ἄξει σὺν αὐτῷ) διὰ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ, that is ἐν χριστῷ, as is said shortly after v. 16. For διὰ is accustomed to be taken for ἐν, as Rom. 4, 11. 1 Tim. 5, 14. namely because the Hebrew ב, which the Syriac uses here, is placed for both. In Christ, that is, obedient to Christ even to the end. ἄξει σὺν αὐτῷ, he will lead them into the part of his glory, John 14, 3. There is, moreover, an argumentation similar to that which is in 1 Cor. 15.

The Apostle constructs the resurrection not in general, but the blessed one, namely of the faithful, which the Apostle calls better, Heb. 11, v. 35, because by the hope of the resurrection, which does not fall to the infidels, and by the leading to Christ, he was consoling and commanding to relieve the mourning of those weeping for their own. Therefore, not only the truth of the death and resurrection of Christ is to be looked at here, but also the cause, namely that he died for our sins, and rose again for our justification, Romans IV, verse 25. For this is our faith, through which we have our only hope of a blessed death and resurrection. Διὰ τῆς Ἰησᾶ is indeed in Jesus in this passage, (cf. 1 Cor. 15:18), but through faith, since we fall asleep by faith in the resurrection and death of Christ, Rev. 14:13, and not truly through obedience. For just as we are constituted righteous not by our own, but by that one man's obedience, Rom. 5:17; so we attain life and salvation not through our own obedience or righteousness, but through faith in Christ, because he has been made righteousness for us by God, 1 Cor. 1:30, John 3:16, Eph. 2:8, Tit. 3:5, 7. Theophylact, although he notes that that 'through Jesus' can be referred to the bringing, namely that he is going to bring us through Jesus, who is the Mediator of this resurrection: nevertheless he also praises our explanation, which is joined with the word 'those who sleep,' and thus teaches that this passage deals with the resurrection of the faithful. Sleeping through Jesus, that is, the faithful, as those who, having Christ in themselves, sleep through Jesus. He is now discussing the principal resurrection, that is, that glorious raising of the faithful from the dead, which is to be with the Lord. For he will lead with him, that is, he will snatch and take us up into the clouds from every side. Regarding the consequence of the resurrection of the faithful to be concluded from the resurrection of Christ, it was said in 1 Cor. 15. But Christ, as the ordinary gloss observes, he calls dead, the faithful sleeping, so that they might more readily believe in the resurrection: he calls Christ dead, so that while we hear that he was dead and has risen, we too may hope that we shall rise through the power of his divinity. He calls the elect sleeping for this reason, that no one can so easily rouse a companion from sleep as easily as men will be roused from the sleep of death. For Theophylact wishes it to be noted how the Apostle said here that Jesus died all the more confidently because the resurrection had already happened and followed: but because we are to be raised, he called us sleeping here, arguing that it will come to pass that we shall one day be awakened from such a sleeping and sleep. But what he judges, that the Thessalonians were indeed made certain about the universal resurrection, but that the glory of the resurrection of the faithful was not established for them in those fates, does not deserve to be counted. For this is the principal article of faith, eternal life, which the faithful could not be ignorant of, which indeed does not look only to souls, but to men consisting of soul and body. Therefore they could not be ignorant of a blessed resurrection, or one to eternal life. He proposes to them the order of the bringing to Christ as a singular mystery, but not the blessedness of the resurrection, concerning which it follows now.

Latin:

Vers. 14. εἰ γὰρ πιστεύομεν, ὅτι Ἰησοῦς ἀπέθανε) Vere, quod magno molimine adstruunt Apostoli, Matth. 27, 50. Johan. 19, 30. 34.

καὶ ἀνέστη) Et hos vere: quod itidem Apostoli omnibus modis adstruunt, Luc. 23, 53. Johan. 19, 41. & capitibus se- quentibus. Paulus ipse 1. Cor. 15.

οὕτω καὶ ὁ θεὸς τοὺς κοιμηθέντας διὰ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ ἄξει σὺν αὐτῷ) διὰ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ, id est ἐν χριστῷ, ut mox dicitur v. 16. Nam διὰ pro ἐν sumi solet, ut Rom. 4, 11. 1. Tim. 5, 14. nempe quia Ebræo- rum ב, quo hic Syrus utitur, pro utroque ponitur. In Chri- sto, id est obedientes Christo ad finem usque. ἄξει σὺν αὐτῷ, ducet eos in partem gloriæ suæ, Joh. 14, 3. Est autem argu- mentatio similis ei, quæ est 1. Cor. 15.,

Adstruit Apostolus resurrectionem non in genere, sed beatam, fidelium nempe, quam Apostolus meliorem vocat Ebr. 11. v. 35. quia spe resurrectionis, quæ in infideles non cadit, & adductione ad Christum solabatur, ac leva- re jubebat luctum suos deflentium. Non ergo tantum veritas mortis & resurrectionis Christi hic spectanda, sed etiam causa, quod nempe mortuus est propter peccata nostra, & resurrexit propter justitiam nostram Roman. IV. vers. 25. Hæc enim fides nostra est, per quam unice spem habemus beatæ mortis & resur- rectionis. Διὰ τῆς Ἰησᾶ est quidem in Jesu hoc lo- co, (conf. 1. Cor. 15, 18.) sed per fidem, cum nempe fide in resurrectionem & mortem Christi obdor- miscimus, Apoc. 14, 13. non vero est per obedien- tiam. Ut enim non nostra, sed unius illius obe- dientia justi constituimur, Rom. 5, 17; ita non per nostram obedientiam vel justitiam, sed per fidem in Christum, quia nobis à Deo factus est justitia, 1. Cor. 1, 30. vitam & salutem consequimur, Joh. 3, 16. Eph. 2, 8. Tit. 3, 5. 7. Theophylact. etsi illud per Je- sum referri posse notet ad adductionem, quod nempe adducturus nos sit per Jesum, qui resurre- ctionis hujus Mediator: tamen nostram etiam laudat explicationem, quæ cum dormientium voce jungitur, adeoque de fidelium resurrectione hoc loco agi docet. Dormientes per Jesum, hoc est, fide- les, ut qui Christum in se habentes per Jesum dor- miunt. De præcipua autem resurrectione nunc dif- ferit, hoc est, de gloriosa illa fidelium à mortuis exci- tatione, quæ futura cum Domino est. Deducet enim secum, hoc est, & in nubes undequaque nos ille corripiet tolletque. De consequentia vero resurre- ctionis fidelium concludendæ è resurrectione Chri- sti dictum, 1. Cor. 15. Christum autem, observante glossa ordinaria, dicit mortuum, fideles dormientes, ut magis credant resurrectionem: Christum mor- tuum appellat, ut dum audimus, illum mortuum fuisse ac resurrexisse, nos quoque speremus resurre- cturos per virtutem divinitatis ejus. Electos autem ideo dicit dormientes, quod nemo tam facile po- test socium excitare à somno, quam facile homi- nes excitabuntur à somno mortis. Theophylactus enim adverti vult, quomodo Apostolus eo fiden- tius hic Jesum mortuum dixerit, quia facta jam & subsequuta sit resurrectio: nos vero quia suscitandi sumus, dormientes hic dixerit, futurum arguens, ut ab ejusmodi dormitione & somno excitemur nos ali- quando. Quod vero censet, Thessalonicenses de resurrectione quidem universali certiores redditos, non autem de gloria resurrectionis fidelium iis fatis constitisse, calculum non meretur. Nam hic præci- puus fidei articulus est, vita æterna, quam ignora- re non poterant fideles, quæ vero non ad animas tantum spectat, sed ad homines anima & corpore constantes. Ideo nec resurrectionem beatam, vel ad æternam vitam poterant ignorare. Adductio- nis ad Christum ordinem ceu mysterium singulare ipfis proponit, non vero resurrectionis beatitu- dinem, de qua jam sequitur.

## 4:15
Ver. 15. For this we say to you by the word of the Lord) By the command of Christ.

He notes the Word of Christ, although he must be considered to have written everything by the command of Christ and the inspiration of his Spirit. But he did not have this Word from the sermons of Christ because it is called κυρίε, which seemed so to Calvin, for it is contained in no sermon of Christ. Furthermore, he appeals here specifically to the Word of the Lord, because he was about to indicate something singular, not that faith would not be given to him as an Apostle simply saying something, but so that it might be observed all the more. For since they seemed to be distressed about their own who had already died, as if the survivors could be considered happier in that they would precede the dead at the coming of the Lord, whom they were expecting daily: and they could have arrived at the thought that perhaps they would be raised from their tombs only long after them, with others already snatched away to meet Christ and enjoying eternal glory, or whatever other anxious thoughts were theirs, for that reason the Apostle explains this mystery as if revealed by Christ, just as they used to prefix only that, 'thus says the Lord,' to their prophecies. Something wonderful, says Theophylact, he was about to say, and for that reason he gives assurance to this matter by the word of the Lord, as if saying: I have brought forth nothing truly from myself, but taught by Christ.

That we who are alive) Paul altogether thought that it could happen that he himself would be alive at the time of the general Judgment, and that is clear not only from these words which are sufficiently plain, but also from 1 Cor. 15:31, 52, 53 and 2 Cor. 5:1, 2. This was a condescension in that, as about the journey to Corinth and Ephesus, and many other things of that kind, such as the sayings of Samuel, 1 Sam. 10:16, and Nathan, 2 Sam. 7:3. Therefore, because he says there will be a future distinction between pious men, it is certain that this was revealed to him by Christ, not that he himself would be in one class. For what Paul had preferred in that matter, and had rather opined, did not happen, yet without any loss to him. A communion cannot have a place here. For that has use where we communicate the faults of others to ourselves or our own virtues to others out of modesty. Here it is a matter of events, and they become distinct members, in which no communion has a place.

But that does not seem consistent, that Paul thought it could happen that the last day would arrive while he himself was living.
