For he predicted in the later letter to the Thessalonians (which Grotius made the first) the coming of the Anti-Christ, and refuted the opinion of those who had spread the rumor that the day of the Lord was imminent; chap. 2:1 ff. He also predicted other things about the last times, which he was not ignorant would happen not in his own time, but only in the time that would follow, 1 Tim. 4:1, 2, 3, 2 Tim. 3:1 ff. Finally, that the day of the Lord, on which he hoped he would receive the crown of righteousness laid up for him, would arrive while he was living, does not fit the passage 2 Tim. 4:7. Therefore, it must be said with Theodoret that the Apostle is not speaking of himself in his own person, but of those whom the day of Christ will find alive, transferring their person to himself, and those who were living with him at that time, as St. Augustine advises in book XX of The City of God, chap. 20, and presenting these things hypothetically, as Erasmus in 1. 1 Cor. 15 noted that it can be understood in such a way that Paul, in the first person, designated whoever the coming of the Lord might find. We who are alive, that is, if the coming of the Lord were to happen now, what would happen to us will happen to them, whoever they may be. He seems to have used this form of speaking first because of the uncertainty of the day of the Lord, so that we may believe that that day is always imminent, the day which everyone is always ignorant of as to who or when it will be, and so that we may always prepare ourselves for it. For one day is hidden so that all days may be observed; then, because of the mystical unity of the faithful, on account of which that which happens to one member is judged to pertain also to the rest in its own way, as the blessed Hunnius holds here, whether you call it κοινοποίησιν or not: although that can also have a place in other things, not only in mighty works and vices. Thirdly because of the certainty, so that indeed they may persuade themselves that this, which is about the survivors not preceding, is so certain that if the Apostle himself, who had heard Christ in the third heaven, were to survive, he would not precede the dead. Therefore Salmero wrongly applies that which Paul joins himself with the living at the coming of the Lord to his own fiction, that by those living are understood those living by the common life of grace. For he feigns first that the saints who have died peculiarly in Christ and for Christ will rise again, with a perfect resurrection before the judgment has begun, and will be found with Christ the judge and the Blessed Virgin in the air to judge, yet segregated from others who are to be left under judgment, namely those living by the common life of grace, to whom the Apostle out of humility counts himself. But the blessed Gerhard refutes that fiction in his work on the resurrection of the dead, § 120. by many arguments; urging this among others; that Scripture is ignorant of a double resurrection of the pious, or that the pious who are to judge with Christ are to rise before the pious who are to be judged by Christ, nay rather that it teaches that the universal resurrection will be instantaneous: and that it is very harsh to understand by ζῶντας those living the life of grace, and that they are distinguished from those who will judge with Christ, since they themselves also live by the life of grace, and to understand by τοὺς νεκροὺς ἐν χριστῷ the Apostles themselves who are to judge with Christ, and finally to exclude the Apostle Paul from them, contrary to 2 Cor. 12:4. But it is too manifest from the opposite, and clearer than light, that by the living are understood those who will be living in this earthly life at the coming of the Lord, and will be found surviving in the world, just as the Apostle explains it immediately in the following words.

Those who are left unto the coming of the Lord) He explains what he understands by that ζῶντας, namely those who will be surviving at the coming of Christ: In the Glossary περιλειπτικόμενοι means survivors. we shall not prevent those who have fallen asleep) We shall not enter into the heavenly ark before those who have died in the faith and obedience of Christ.

The words of the Apostle are clear, that those surviving at the coming of the Lord will not precede others who have slept and died in the Lord, so that these latter are to be caught up to meet the Lord in time or order. Which words of the Apostle, as if written by the rays of the sun, it is a wonder that they could have been snatched away into far different senses; 1. For Methodius in his discourse on the resurrection in the Greek scholia of Oecumenius interpreted it thus: We who live, who are left: that is, immortal souls will not precede bodies in the resurrection, but the body together with the soul will rise to immortal life. But the Apostle is not speaking of separated souls, but of men living on earth, nor does he compare them with bodies to be resurrected, but the faithful survivors with those who have died in the Lord. 2. Augustine, book XX on the City of God, chapter 20. and Justinianus says that the living will not precede those who have fallen asleep, because they also are to depart from mortal bodies, or are to undergo death, before the dead rise, then having been resurrected together with the others they are to have immortal bodies. But the Apostle expressly distinguishes the living, who are survivors on the day of the Lord, from those who have fallen asleep: He does not, however, say that they also will fall asleep. For either they will fall asleep before the day of the Lord, and thus the day of the Lord does not find them living: or they will do so on the day of the Lord itself, and thus all will rise together, because the resurrection is to be on the day of the Lord. But if all are to rise together, how are those who died in the Lord said to rise first: Then the living, who are to be the remainder, are to be caught up together to meet the Lord. Theodoret's exposition tends almost to the same point: Those who have long since died and rotted many centuries ago will rise so easily and suddenly that they will precede those who will be found surviving and living at that time. For these must die before they rise. Therefore, as these die, those who were long since dead will rise, and consequently will precede these in the resurrection. But the Apostle does not assert that those living will be preceded by those sleeping, nor does he say that they will die, much less that they will rise, nay rather the contrary 1 Cor. 15:52, πάντες μὲν οὐ κοιμηθησόμεθα, we shall not all indeed fall asleep. Salmero makes a double resurrection, the former of those who are to judge with Christ, the latter of those of the pious who are to be judged, and that these are indicated by the name of the living, about which figment we have already spoken. We pass over other things with a dry foot.

Latin:

Vers. 15. τοῦτο γὰρ ὑμῖν λέγομεν ἐν λόγῳ κυρίου) Ex Chri- sti mandato.

Verbum Christi notat, etsi mandato Christi & Spiritus ejus inspiratione omnia scripsit, scripsisse censendus omnino sit. Non autem Verbum hoc, quia κυρίε dicitur, ex concionibus Christi habuit, quod Calvino visum, nam in nulla Christi concio- ne id habetur. Cæterum peculiariter hic pro- vocat ad Verbum Domini, quia singulare quid in- dicaturus erat, non quod sibi tanquam Apostolo simpliciter aliquid dicenti fides non adhiberetur, sed ut eo magis id observaretur. Quam enim angi de necessariis suis jam defunctis viderentur, quasi in eo feliciores censeri possint superstites, quod præventuri sint in adventu Domini, quem quoti- die expectabant, defunctos: & in eam cogitatio- nem devenire potuerint, forte longe demum post eosdem è monumentis suis resuscitatum iri, aliis jam in occursum abreptis Christo, æternaque glo- ria fruentibus, aut quæ aliæ solicitæ eorum fuere cogitationes, idcirco mysterium hoc explicat A- postolus, tanquam à Christo revelatum, quasi vaticiniis suis solum illud, sic dicit Dominus, præ- mittebant. Mirandum aliquid, inquit Theo- phylactus, erat dicturus, eoque ex Domini verbo rei huic & fidem facit, tanquam id inquiens : Ni- hil profecto à me, sed à Christo edoctus protule- rim.

Ὅτι ἡμεῖς οἱ ζῶντες) Omnino putavit Paulus, fieri posse, ut ipse viveret Judicii generalis tempore, idque non ex his tantum verbis satis apertis liquet, sed & ex 1. Cor. 15, 31. 52. 53. & 2. Cor. 5, 1. 2. 2. Hoc fuit in illo συγκατάβασις, ut de iti- nere ad Corinthios & Ephesum, & multa alia ejusmodi, qualia sunt & dicta Samuelis, 1. Samuel. 10, 16. & Nathan? 2. Sam. 7, 3. Ergo quod futurum discrimen inter homines pios ait, certum est, id à Christo ipsi patefactum, non item in una classe ipse futurus esset. Nam quod ea in re Paulus maluisset, magisque opinatus est, id non evenit, nullo ta- men ipsius damno. κοίνωσις hic locum habere non potest. Ea enim usum habet ubi aliena vitia nobis aut nostras vir- tutes aliis per modestiam communicamus. Hic de even- tis agitur, & fiunt membra ἀντιδιῃρημένα, in quibus nulla κοίνωσις locum habet.

Id vero non videtur consentaneum, Paulum putasse fieri posse, ut ipse vivente dies novissimus ad- veniat. Nam prædixit in posteriori ad Thessalo- nicenses (quam Grotius primam fecit) adventum Anti-Christi, ac profligavit eorum sententiam, qui sparserant, imminere diem Domini; cap. 2, 1. seqq. prædixit & alia de temporibus postremis, quæ non suo, sed sequuturo tempore demum e- ventura non ignorabat, 1. Tim. 4, 1. 2. 3. 2. Tim. 3, 1. seqq. Denique diem Domini, qua coronam justi- tiæ repositam se accepturum sperabat, se vivente adventurum, non congruit loco 2. Tim. 4, 7. Id- circo cum Theodoreto dicendum, non de se loqui Apostolum in propria persona, sed de iis, quos vi- vos offendet dies Christi, illorum personam in se transferens, & illos, qui tunc cum ipso vivebant, ut monet S. Augustinus libr. XX. de Civit. Dei cap. 20. & hypothetice hæc ita proferens, ut Erasmus in 1. Cor. 15. notavit, ita posse intelligi, ut Paulus sub prima persona designarit quosvis, quos ad- ventus Domini sit reperturus. Nos, qui vivimus, id est, si nunc incidat adventus Domini, quod in nobis accideret, idem accidet in illis; quicunque e- runt. Qua forma loquendi usus videtur primo ob diei Domini incertitudinem, ut nempe diem il- lum semper imminere credamus, quem quis vel quando futurus sit, semper ignoramus : & nun- quam non ad eundem nos præparemus. Latet enim unus dies, ut observentur omnes dies; deinde propter mysticam fidelium unitatem, propter quam id, quod uni evenit membro, ad reliqua etiam suo modo pertinere judicatur, ut hic habet B. Hunnius, sive jam id dicas κοινοποίησιν, seu non: quanquam illa etiam in aliis, non virtutibus, & vitiis solum, locum habere possit. Tertio propter certitudinem, ut nempe hoc, quod de non præ- venturis superstitibus tam certum esse sibi persua- deant, ut si ipse etiam Apostolus, qui in tertio cœlo Christum audiverat, superesset, non esset præventurus defunctos. Perperam ergo Salmero illud, quod Paulus se cum vivis sub adventum Do- mini conjungat, suo commento adhibet, per vivos illos intelligi viventes communi vitæ gratiæ. Fin- git enim primum resurrecturos sanctos, qui peculiariter in Christo & pro Christo mortui sint, resurrectione perfecta ante inchoatum ju- dicium, & cum Christo judice, & B. Virgi- ne inventum iri in aëre ad judicandum, se- gregatos tamen ab aliis, qui relinquendi sub judicio, viventes scilicet communi gratiæ vi- ta, quibus sese præ humilitate Apostolus ac- censeat. Sed commentum illud refellit B. Ger- hardus de resurrectione mortuorum §. 120. pluribus argumentis; id inter alia urgens; quod duplicem piorum resurrectionem, vel quod pii cum Christo judicaturi prius resurrecturi sint, quam pii à Christo judicandi, scriptura ignoret, imo momentaneam universam resurrectionem fore, doceat: quodque perquam durum sit, per ζῶντας intelligere viventes vitæ gratiæ, eosque distingui ab illis, qui cum Christo judicabunt, quum ipsi quoque vita gratiæ vivant, ac per τοὺς νεκροὺς ἐν χριστῷ intelligere ipsos Apostolos cum Christo judicaturos, denique ab illis Apostolum Paulum excludere, contra 2. Cor. 12, 4. Nimis autem manifestum ex adverso est, ac luce clarius, per vivos intelligi eos, qui sub adventum Domini in hac terrena vita vivent, & superstites in mundo invenientur, quemadmodum statim id exponit Apostolus verbis sequentibus.

Οἱ περιλειπόμενοι εἰς τὴν παρουσίαν τοῦ κυρίου) Explicat quid intelligat per illud ζῶντας, nempe eos, qui in adventu Christi erunt superstites: In Glossario περιλειπτικόμενοι superstites. οὐ μὴ φθάσωμεν τοὺς κοιμηθέντας) Non prius in cœlestem arcam introibimus, quam illi, qui in fide & obedientia Christi decesserint.

Luculenta sunt verba Apostoli, non præventuros esse superstites in adventu Domini alios, qui dormierunt & defuncti sunt in Domino, ita ut hi posteriores tempore aut ordine in occursum rapiendi sint Domino. Quæ verba Apostoli, utpote radiis solis exarata, mirum, in alios longe sensus abripi potuisse; 1. Methodius enim sermone de resurrectione in scholiis Græcis Oecumenii ita interpretatus est: Nos qui vivimus, qui residui sumus: id est, animæ immortales non prævenient corpora in resurrectione, sed corpus simul cum anima ad vitam immortalem resurget. Atqui Apostolus non de animabus separatis, sed de hominibus in terra viventibus loquitur, nec illas cum corporibus propriis resuscitandis comparat, sed fideles superstites cum iis, qui in Domino defuncti sunt. 2. Augustinus libr. XX. de civit. Dei cap. 20. & Justinianus, vivos non præventuros eos, qui obdormierunt ait, quod illi etiam mortalibus corporibus exituri, vel mortem obituri sint, antequam mortui resurgant, tum una cum cæteris resuscitati immortalia corpora habituri. Sed Apostolus diserte vivos, qui superstites sunt in die Domini, ab iis, qui obdormierunt, distinguit: Non autem illos etiam obdormituros ait. Nam aut ante diem Domini obdormiscent, & ita dies Domini non invenit eos vivos: aut in ipso die Domini, & ita resurgent omnes simul, quia in die Domini futura est resurrectio. Si autem omnes simul resurgent, quomodo resurrecturi primum dicuntur, qui mortui in Domino: Deinde vivi, qui reliqui futuri, in occursum Domini simul abripiendi. 3. Fere eo etiam abit Theodoreti expositio: Tam facile ac subito resurgent illi, qui jam olim ante multa secula mortui & putrefacti, ut præveniant eos, qui tum temporis superstites & vivi invenientur. Hi enim prius mori debent, quam resurgant. His ergo morientibus, illi jam olim scilicet mortui resurgent, & consequenter hosce in resurrectione prævenient. Sed illos viventes præventum iri à dormientibus, non asserit Apostolus, nec illos obituros, nedum resurrecturos dicit, imo contrarium 1. Cor. 15, 52. πάντες μὲν οὐ κοιμηθησόμεθα, omnes quidem non obdormiemus. Salmero geminam resurrectionem facit, priorem illorum, qui cum Christo judicaturi sunt, alteram eorum, qui judicandi sunt, ex piis, & hos viventium nomine indicari, de quo commento jam diximus. Alia sicco pede præterimus.

## 4:16
Verse 16. For the Lord himself with a command) Tertullian translates it as 'in a command', but it is truly 'by his own command'. For Christ has authority both over the Angels and

over the Archangels, Col. 2:16, Eph. 1:20, 21. See also John 5:25. With the voice of the Archangel and with the trumpet of God) It is a hendiadys, for 'with the voice of the Archangel through the trumpet of God'. See what we have said on Matt. 24:31. Thus 'Voices and trumpets', Exod. 19:13, the same as קול שופר 1 Chron. 15:28. Among the ancient Hebrews, Greeks, and Latins, the people were summoned by a trumpet call. Following that example, when God summons men, he is said to do it by a trumpet, Ps. 47:6, Isa. 27:13, Jer. 4:5, ch. 6:1, ch. 51:27, Hosea 5:8, Joel 2:1, Zech. 9:14. Therefore in the Apocalypse, in all the judgments of God, trumpets are given to the Angels, because since this judgment is the last of all, it is therefore the greatest and most general, so here the trumpet is given not to an Angel, but to one of the Princes of the Angels, such as Michael the great prince, Dan. 12:1.

The Vulgate also has 'in a command', which Haymo and Lombard understand as the Father's mandate. Κέλευσμα is the shouting of sailors or even of those inciting one another, whence B. Luther rendered it with a field-cry. To which some refer that shout in Matt. 25:6, Behold the bridegroom comes, go out to meet him. Photius in the Greek scholia attributes this κέλευσμα to the Lord, by which the dead are to be awakened. Furthermore, some prefer to distinguish the voice of the Archangel from the trumpet of God. Theodoret says the voice of the Archangel will be this: Let the dead rise! Others from Jerome bring forward this: Rise you dead and come to judgment! Theophylact assigns this: Prepare yourselves all, the judge is at hand. But by the Archangel, Ambrosiaster understands Christ, as does Hyperius. But the Lord is clearly distinguished here from the Archangel, because it is said that the Lord is to descend with a command, with the voice of the Archangel. Augustine and Haymo wish for all the angelic powers to be noted. This pleases Calvin and Crocius so much that they make it a common cry of the angels, yet they appoint one of them as the precentor. But Grotius quite confidently designates Michael, along with Thomas and Lyranus. Cornelius à Lapide wavers, judging that either Michael or certainly Gabriel is to be understood. B. Gerhard notes that some understand Gabriel, since he also announced the first coming to the Blessed Virgin Mary. Oecumenius, regarding the command, voice, and trumpet, has it thus: At the command, as soon as He has commanded, and the Archangel has uttered a voice, and the trumpets have sounded, He will descend. For the Lord commands, and the Archangel utters the Lord's command with his voice, and the other celestial orders, whom he figuratively calls trumpets, emit the sound, just as he also says to utter. But the Lord indeed commands, while the angel announces the Lord's command to those subject to him; furthermore, these administer it, and they thunder it forth to the ends of the world, and the dead, as many as there are, rise from the whole world and are gathered together. Photius takes the trumpet of God, which is called the last in 1 Cor. 15, as referring to several trumpets, and by them he understands the angelic powers. Others take it metaphorically. Gregory the Great takes it as the spiritual empire of Christ; Calvin and Tossanus as authority and majesty. I do not see why these things, which the Apostle brings forward distinctly in the explanation of λόγῳ κυρίου, should not be taken distinctly, or why one should depart entirely from the literal meaning. It is said 1. ἐν κελεύσματι, that is, in a cry as if military, namely of the holy angels. For because the coming of Christ to judgment is wont to be described in the Holy Scriptures as the coming of a King descending into battle to defeat his enemies, 2 Thess. 2:8, and to free his subjects from captivity, Luke 21:28. Therefore the Apostle joins the κέλευσμα, the military exhortation or military cry, and the Archangel as the leader of the celestial militia, and the trumpet as the announcer of war, says B. Gerhard on the resurrection of the dead §. 66. 2. Ἐν φωνῇ Ἀρχαγγέλου, which signifies the voice of one angel, and indeed an Archangel, whoever he may be, if it is taken properly, just as other voices of the angels are wont to be taken properly when mention is made of them in the scriptures. For the fact that Justinian argues that there will not be a voice which can be grasped by bodily ears, because neither can corpses perceive, nor souls separated from bodies, since they cannot receive a bodily sound us little. For there will still remain those living on earth, whom the day of the Lord will surely find surviving and alive, who may hear the voice; which also the angels, and the rest of the heavenly host, and the blessed souls will hear in their own way. And why should not the dead also be about to hear? If this voice of the Archangel be said to be indeed διακονικῶς or ministerially, but that of the Son of God κυρίως and principally, John 5, 38. 3. Ἐν σάλπιγγι Θεοῦ, with the trumpet of God. This is distinguished by the Apostle from the κελεύσματι, and also from the Φωνῇ Ἀρχαγγέλου. It is called, however, the trumpet of God, not because God himself is about to produce the voice or sound immediately by a trumpet, but because that will be great, just as the voice of God is wont to be added for the sake of signifying magnitude, according to the Hebrew idiom. Therefore Christ calls the voice of the trumpet great, Matt. 24, 31. Crocius indeed leans toward that opinion which Grotius has embraced. Perhaps, he says, you would not wrongly say that the voice of the Archangel and the trumpet are one and the same, that is, a trumpet-like voice, that is, sonorous, and indeed most highly so, for that is what the voice of God indicates. Yet he does not seem to deny altogether that a trumpet can be understood. I do not know, however, he says, since the voice of the Archangel has preceded, whether or not something sensible will be future? Nor, however, would I think, as Anselm hands down, that there will be a real trumpet properly so called: much less would I approve the boldness of Francis Suarez, asserting that it will be made of brass, which his colleague Cornelius à Lapide does not dare to approve: nay, he acknowledges it is uncertain of what material it will be, meanwhile he doubts not that it will be properly so called. There is no firm reason for either them or others. I confess that no other firm reason is found, except that one should not depart from the propriety of the letter, especially where some mystery is handed down. Blessed Gerhard brings forward in Harmon. Evangel. chap. CLXI. concerning the trumpets of the angels Matt. 24, 11. several reasons why they are to be understood properly, which can also be urged here: That the Apostle 1 Cor. 15, v. 52. repeats the voice of the trumpet twice, so as to hint that one must remain in the propriety of the word, ἐν ἐσχάτη σάλπιγγι, σαλπίσει γάρ (2.) That in the promulgation of the law the blast of a trumpet sounding vehemently was heard Exod. 19, v. 16. Therefore it is likely that the sound of a trumpet will also be heard when the execution of the law is instituted in judgment. (3.) That in the destruction of Jericho the voice of a trumpet sounded by divine command Josh. 6, v. 5. Therefore it is likely that, when the Jericho of this world is destroyed, some blast similar to the sound of trumpets, to be formed by the angels in the air, will likewise be heard. (4.) That John in the spectacle of the last judgment says that he heard the blast of a trumpet Apoc. 4, v. 1. c. 8, v. 6. c. 9, v. 1. c. 11, v. 15. etc. But of these, the τὸ ῥητὸν moves us especially, from which one must not depart in such things as consist only of divine revelation. For otherwise nothing certain will be had. Therefore we see Crocius wavering, now he wishes the sonorous voice of the Archangel, by whom he understands a created angel, to be the trumpet of God; now, distinguishing it from the voice of the Archangel, he thinks with Haymo, Lombard, and Calvin that the remaining angels will produce the sound when the Archangel sounds, because the Lord is about to send the angels with the voice of a great trumpet, Matt. 24, 31. nor does he doubt that the coming of the Lord to judgment must be heralded with some terrible sound, just as the Lord came with the blast of a trumpet to promulgate the law, Exod. 19; now he wishes the very voice of Christ to be designated. Christ, he says, calls this trumpet the voice of the Son of God John 5, 28. But if, indeed, so that the letter may not be left altogether, we understand the trumpet analogically, as the very strong blast of a trumpet heard in the promulgation of the law, Exod. 19, 16: which, whatever it may have been in the end, was certainly distinct from the voice of the Son of God, who promulgated the law ἀμέσως καὶ αὐτοπροσώπως. Thus, therefore, the sounding trumpet of God seems here to be distinguished not only from the voice of the Archangel, but also from the voice of the Son of man, John 5, 28, since the Archangel is distinguished here from the Lord, by whose power the dead are to be resurrected. Concerning which Blessed Hunnius has this in this place: Paul makes mention, however, of the voice of the Archangel. For although the Son of man will send his angels with the voice of a great trumpet, Matt. 24. In species, however, nay in individual, mention is made of one certain Archangel. He, however, is not Christ himself: the Lord is openly discerned from his Archangel, just as Christ is not accustomed to be called by such veiled names in the scripture of the New Testament any longer. That Archangel, however, according to the explanation of the Prophets and Apostles, is Michael, whom alone out of all the host of heavenly angels canonical scripture expressly calls an Archangel, under whom as leader his angels fight, as is read in Apoc. c. 12. In which apocalyptic passage, however, most understand Christ by the Archangel Michael.

Thus, therefore, those things seem to be only preparatory and preceding: first the shout, whether of all the heavenly host or of the angels: then the voice of the Archangel, finally that great trumpet, whether of a principality, or a throne, or some heavenly dominion: which huge sound, pleasant to the faithful, very horrible to the unfaithful, rushes in like the blast of a trumpet; as Apoc. 1, 10. I heard a great voice ὡς σάλπιγγος, as of a trumpet, speaking with me. The principal act will then follow, when the voice of the Son of man will resound: Arise, you dead, by which the dead will be awakened. For Paul here clearly hints that those things will precede this awakening (which, by the testimony of Christ, is to be performed by his own voice, just as he resurrected the dead in the days of his flesh by his own voice, Lazarus, come forth, Talitha kumi, damsel arise). Regarding the voice of the trumpet, Theodoret says on this passage: "For the Lord of all Himself shall appear descending from heaven, with the powers that do not fall under sight preceding Him, and He shall indeed command the Archangel to cry out, and the dead to rise again. But the trumpets shall resound on every side with a great and wondrous clangor." He says this also in the epistle to the Corinthians: "We shall not all sleep, but we shall all be changed, in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet. For the trumpet shall sound, and the dead shall rise incorruptible: and we shall be changed." If, however, when the sound was issued on Mount Sinai, accommodated to those who were present, the people could not bear the immense terror, but said to the great Moses: "Speak thou to us, and let not God speak with us, lest we die": who shall bear the voice that shall resound then? Where, however, he thinks that the dead are to be raised by the voice of the Archangel: but that is attributed to the voice of the Son of man, Joh. 5, but nowhere to the voice of the Archangel. This, he says, in the command, in the voice of the Archangel, signifies that some one of the Archangels, having been commanded, will order the dead to rise again. They, however, will immediately rise. Theophylact, by κέλευσμα, through which he likewise understands the command of God, distinguishes both the voice of the Archangel and the trumpet of God in the same place. For, he says, these are to be the commands of the Lord. But how is He to enjoin these things? In the voice of the Archangel presiding over the other Angels, and repeatedly calling out, prompt And be you all prepared: for the judge is now present. For just as the Father on Sinai, the mountain of Arabia, used trumpets and ministering Angels, so too will the Son, as Emperor, use these very things. He adds also another explanation: Either because the earth will be compelled by this command of God, which had received the bodies, to restore them, having been soon transformed to incorruption. But that they are to assemble from all sides into one place, the Archangel will effect by his voice, yet one by the ministry of other Angels. The Hebrews, as Schindler reports in his Pentaglot Lexicon under the word שׁופר, the feast of trumpets, Levit. 23, 24, also give this reason, that we may remember the day on which the dead will return to life. For these will rise again with the blast of a trumpet, and will be gathered no otherwise than when the people hear the voice of a trumpet, as it is said: All inhabitants of the world and dwellers of the earth, when the banner of the mountains is raised, you shall see, and when the trumpet sounds, you shall hear. And Isa. 27, 13. And it shall be in that day, it shall be sounded בשׁופר with a great trumpet, and those perishing in the land of Assur shall come, etc. Now the trumpet was accustomed to be used not only at the feast of trumpets, but also at other feasts: and not only at feasts, but in the convocation of the whole assembly, and in the setting out for war, as one may read in Num. 10. Now all the elect are to be called then to the eternal festival, Isa. 66, 23, the whole multitude of men is to be gathered to the Lord, and the Lord will rise up for battle against the impious, just as the day of judgment is called the day of the trumpet and of the blast, Ephes. 1, 16, and in the Johannine apocalypse the seven trumpets, with which the angels sound, ch. 8, ch. 9, ch. 10, intimate the judgments of God. Finally, as a trumpet is also accustomed to be sounded at the entry of a King: So will the trumpet of God sound at the arrival of the King of Kings. When they see, says Chrysostom, the tumult, then also the voice of the Archangel commanding and crying out to the remaining Angels will be heard, then also the trumpets will be heard, or rather the sound of trumpets. Concerning the last trumpet, Chrysostom says the same there: What is the last trumpet? He shows here that there will be many trumpets, and that the judge will descend at the last one. Those who metaphorically understand lightnings and thunders by the trumpet of God do not notice that they are distinguished, Exod. 19, 16, in the Apocalypse, and elsewhere; nor does it seem sufficiently convenient that thunders and lightnings be called a trumpet, since the sound of thunder is far different from that of a trumpet. Furthermore, this trumpet seems likewise to be distinguished from the voice of the great trumpet, or the trumpet of the great voice of the Angels, of which Matt. 24, 31. This will follow the awakening voice of the Son of man, which that former one, of which the Apostle speaks in this place, precedes the awakening of the dead. For the trumpet of the Angels deputed to that task from the assembly, of which Christ speaks, will be used for the gathering of the elect, but the present trumpet is to be used for the intimation of the coming of the Lord. Concerning which Chrysostom, homil. 8 on this passage, p. 1370. But what does he say about them being gathered, he says indeed that they will rise again everywhere simply, but that they are to be gathered by the Angels. Therefore, the resurrection is indeed the work of divine power, in that God will command the earth placed under it to depart, and no minister will do this, just as he once called out to Lazarus: Lazarus, come forth. But the bringing together will be the work of the ministers. Some of the ancients say that the Angels will appear in visible form to be seen by those who will still be survivors on the earth: because the judge will be visible, therefore it also seems plausible to our blessed Gerhard, l. c., that the companions and ministers of the judge will be visible, just as they for the most part appeared in visible form when they were sent to men still living in the body, Gen. 19, etc. But the day of the Lord will reveal these and other things more exactly, which it is better to await with pious preparation and joy than to pry into them too curiously, provided that we reverently accept those things which scripture hands down, and captivate our reason under the obedience of faith. He will descend from heaven, Acts 1, 11, Matt. 24, 30. Locally, says Crocius with Lombard, by reason of the body. But if Christ will descend by local motion from the highest heaven, which they place above the firmament, how many years or centuries will be needed for him to complete that interval as far as the clouds! The same Crocius notes a certain fanatic without a name, who said that Christ would descend through a vicar: Perhaps from Calvinistic principles, so that he might not be moved from the august place of heaven, and leave his seat on the throne of Majesty at the right hand of God at the time of the descent and in the highest place. And the dead in Christ) The dead who, namely, have died in Christ. Thus the Syrian and Latin have understood it here. Thus in the adjective dead is understood a participle of similar meaning, having fallen asleep. We have already said before what it is to die in Christ. Thus those dying in the Lord, Apoc. 14, 13. They will rise first) Namely, so that they may be able to ascend together with the living, not after them. Not a few of those dead in Christ, as Salmero wishes, that those will rise first who will sit with Christ the judge, but all who have died piously in Christ: nor first by reason of dignity, as Sedulius; but by reason of time, not regarding the order of the pious and the impious, for that is not the matter here, and both the impious and the pious will be awakened at the same time by the voice of the Son of man, John 5, 28, as Chrysostom and Theophylact explain. The dead in Christ, that is, the faithful, as those who are to be lifted up into the clouds, as those who are to rise first, but the others last, that is, the damned, since they are neither to be lifted up, nor to go to meet Christ in the air. For the first does not set an order among those who are dead, as if some were to rise sooner than others; but between those deceased in the Lord, and the survivors, and those the faithful, because those will rise first, he says, namely with glorified bodies, then, the living, who will remain, will be caught up together with them, to be changed in that rapture. Whence Aretius thinks that an argument of consolation is insinuated here in this way: The meaning of the narrative is, in the last judgment the first care will be had for the deceased. Whence it follows: Therefore they are not to be deplored too much. For they are in many respects happier than we, because they have already crossed this stormy strait, and have reached the harbor, and are nearer to perfection, and will be the first in the resurrection, etc. Verse 17. then we who are living, who are left over) Who will then be survivors. We, he says, because he thought it possible that he might be among them, as we just said. Ἅμα σὺν ἀυτοῖς) together with them, before the dead, but then resurrected Joh. 5, 28. ῾Αρπαγησόμεθα ἐν νεφέλαις) As if in a triumphal chariot, for clouds are the chariot of God, Psal. 104, 3. and of Christ Matth. 24, 30. Acts 1, 9. 11. Dan. 7, 13. We shall be caught up, however, changed 1. Cor. 15, 42. into the air 2. Cor. 5, 2. Εἰς ἀπάντησιν τῦ κυρίυ εἰς ἀέρα) That is, to Christ exercising judgment, in the middle place between the highest heaven and the earth, which space the Greeks call the air. Ἔπειτα the Apostle says, then, that is, after those who have died in the Lord have risen, we who are living, who will remain, will be caught up together with them. Therefore we shall not die first, he says, and then also rise again. But we who are living will be caught up together with those who have been resurrected. Anshelm. The dead in Christ will rise first, namely, before they are caught up to meet Christ in the air: Then we, who are living, will be caught up together with those who have risen from the dead to meet Christ. Those who are dead, says Chrysostom, will rise first, and thus the meeting will take place at the same time. Abel, who died before everyone else, together with those who then will live, he will meet. Therefore, as far as this is concerned, they will have nothing more, but he who had been corrupted, and lay buried in the earth for so many years, will meet both them and the living, and all the rest together. But since they are to be resurrected with glorified bodies, if it is asked whether those still living on earth, or rather those who are to obtain such bodies in the very rapture into the air, most people assume the latter. But the wicked seem indeed to be left on earth, both those who have been resurrected and those whom the day of the Lord will find living, until the judgment has been completed, but the elect will be caught up into the air together with those who have risen. Although the dead, says Theophylact, are to rise first, nevertheless we also, who will be in this life, will be caught up, worthy indeed to be carried up into the clouds, just as the clouds also received the Lord. But why, when he is about to descend, will he snatch up the faithful? He will do this, of course, for the sake of honor. For just as when any Emperor is about to enter a city, those who are preeminent in honors and dignity go out to meet him, but the harmful and those condemned to death, having been thrown into the inner prison, await this very judge: So at that time of judgment, sinners indeed and those bound by wicked deeds await him who is to judge on earth, even if they have obtained the name of Christian: But the just will be lifted on high. Thus, finally, they are to enjoy Christ himself, who is the head of all good things, and they are to remain with him forever. But if the Angels, says Chrysostom, will gather, and will run about, how will these be caught up? They will be caught up after the descent of the Lord, after they have been gathered. But how will they be caught up together in the clouds, unless those who live, having obtained glorious bodies like those who have been resurrected, are to have bodies that are agile and subtle, and therefore πνευματικὰ and glorified: Or will some be received by the clouds with immortal bodies, others with mortal ones and only then to be changed: Wherefore it seems to be said that, while the clouds lower themselves to receive the elect, they will be changed in an instant and in a moment, so that they can be received together with the resurrected and caught up to meet Christ. But they will not die first, but only be changed, which change will not be a separation of soul and body, but it is the perfection of that same bodily dwelling, with the soul remaining in the body, and the substance of the same also remaining, which will be endowed with πνευματικαῖς gifts, with the imperfect qualities destroyed, and it will be transformed from animal to spiritual, as far as the qualities are concerned. Theologians posit something analogous to death here, not true death, which brings about the dissolution of soul and body. Ambrosiaster indeed seems to establish that death will intervene in this place. Death will forestall the very rapture, and as if through sleep, the soul having departed, it is rendered in a moment. For when they are taken, they are warned that, arriving at the Lord, they receive their souls, because they cannot be dead with the Lord. But that opinion cannot be reconciled with the Apostle. Augustine also seemed to lean somewhere toward the fact that the living will also die on the day of the Lord. To this sense, he says in book 20 of The City of God, chapter 20, that we might think that even those whom the Lord will find living here will, in that very small space, both see death and receive immortality, the Apostle himself seems to urge us. And afterwards: If, therefore, we believe that the saints who will be found living when Christ comes, and who will be caught up to meet him, will depart from mortal bodies in the same rapture, and will soon return to the same immortal ones, we will suffer no difficulties in the words of the Apostle: Whether where he says: You, what you sow, is not made alive unless it dies, or where he says: We shall all rise or we shall all sleep: because neither will they be made alive through immortality unless they die, however briefly: and by this they will not be alien to the resurrection, which sleep precedes, although most brief, yet not none. It is believed, however, that Augustine handed down another opinion in book 2 of On the Merit and Remission of Sins, chapter 31. This GOD will grant to some at the end, that they do not feel death through such a sudden change, but are caught up together with those rising in the clouds to meet Christ in the air. But when I weigh his words more diligently, I do not discover another opinion of the Saint in any of them, but the same. For he ascribes death even to those who are dead on the day of the Lord, but such a death as they will NOT FEEL. THIS DEATH, he says, they will not FEEL because of a sudden change. But in the book on the eight questions of Dulcitius, question 3, Augustine fluctuates greatly regarding this question. He acknowledges that the present passage cannot easily be explained otherwise than that those who will be survivors on the day of the Lord will not die. But in truth, as far as the words of the Apostle are concerned, he seems to assert that some at the end of the age, when the Lord arrives, when the resurrection of the dead is to be, are not to die, but being found alive are to be suddenly changed into that immortality which is given to the other saints as well, and are to be caught up together with them in the clouds, and nothing else has seemed so to me, as often as I have wanted to think about these words. Yet because of the passage 1 Cor. 15. and its strange reading, he hesitates, nor does he find what to say. But I would rather hear the more learned on this, lest the Apostle be found to say even to those who think that some, without death preceding, will be made alive and pass to eternal life: Fool, what you sow is not made alive unless it first dies. For even that which is read in most codices, we shall all rise, how will it be able to happen unless we all die? For there is no resurrection unless death has preceded. And what some codices have, we shall all sleep: it makes that understood much more easily and clearly: And if anything else of that kind is found in the holy books, it seems to impel one to think that no humans will obtain immortality unless death has preceded. But again he inclines toward that opinion, that the survivors are seen to be exempted from death here on the day of the Lord: If, however, no other sense can be found in these words of the Apostle, and it shall have become clear that he wished this to be understood, which the words themselves seem to proclaim, that is, that there will be those at the end of the age and the second coming of the Lord who will not be stripped of the body, but will be clothed upon with immortality, so that the mortal may be swallowed up by life: it will without doubt be consistent with this opinion that we confess in the rule of faith, that the Lord will come to judge the living and the dead, so that we do not understand here the living as the just and the dead as the unjust, although the just and the unjust are to be judged, but the living as those whom his coming will find not yet to have departed, and the dead as those who have already departed from their bodies. Nor did he have certainty about this problem when he wrote his books of Retractations. For thus he speaks in book II, chapter 33. Either they will not die, or by a most rapid change from this life into death, and from death into eternal life, as if passing in the twinkling of an eye, THEY WILL NOT FEEL DEATH. Other Fathers, however, acknowledge with great consensus that they will not die, which is also entirely consistent with this passage and the parallel in 1 Corinthians 15. Tertullian, in his book on the resurrection of the flesh, chapter 41, teaches that by the shortening of death through transformation they will concur with those rising again. Jerome in epistle 152 to Minerius and Alexander brings Theodore of Mopsuestia to this opinion, whose words he alleges as follows: The saints, who are to be found in their bodies on the day of judgment, together with other saints who are to rise from the dead, shall be caught up in the clouds to meet Christ in the air, Lord, the most grievous necessity of death having been trampled underfoot. He also praises Apollinaris, who asserted the same things, namely that some are not to die, and are to be caught up from the present life into the future. Jerome also made this opinion his own, and explained it in his own words in epistle 148 to Marcella: This from the place itself of 1. Thess. IV. can be known from the context, that the saints who shall be found in the body at the coming of the Savior, shall meet the same in those same bodies, yet so that the inglorious and corruptible and mortal shall be transformed by glory, and incorruption, and immortality, so that the bodies of the living shall also be transformed into such a substance as the bodies of the dead are to rise in. Compare what we have said about these things at 1 Cor. XV.

And so we shall always be with the Lord) John XIV. 2. XVII. 24. always, without any end. With the Lord, that is, as sharers of his glory, kingdom, and joy 2 Tim. II. 12. Rom. VIII. 17.

Augustine, book XX of The City of God, ch. 20. When Paul says, and so we shall always be with the Lord, it is not to be understood as if he said we shall always remain with the Lord in the air, because he himself will certainly not remain there, because he is coming to pass through, for one will go to meet him who is coming, not one who is remaining: But we shall be with the Lord in this way, that is, we shall be thus always having eternal bodies, wherever we shall be with him. But whether something will intervene between the rapture into the air and that perpetual παρουσία, or whether that rapture to meet the Lord will precede the final judgment, opinions vary. It seems likely that something will intervene. For just as those who died in the Lord are to be resurrected first in glorified bodies: So the surviving faithful are to be changed, so that they may be caught up together with them. But both are to be caught up to meet the Lord who is about to appear for judgment in the air, and to be stationed there at his right hand, so that they may hear the sentence of acquittal in the assembly of Angels and men. But a session on thrones also seems likely to intervene, so that as assessors of Christ they may judge the world and the evil Angels, 1 Cor. VI. 1, 3. Marcus Monachus in the catena of Nicetas on the Symbols at Matthew XIII, p. 488, also raises a doubt about the order to be observed in these matters. This also needs investigation, how he says here that those doing iniquity are first to be cast into the furnace of fire, then the just are to attain splendor and righteousness, but elsewhere says that the just are to be caught up first? He answers as follows: The first are indeed caught up, but after Christ's coming, these are handed over to punishment, and then those enter into the kingdom of heaven. For since it is fitting that they be in heaven, but he himself is to come hither, and to judge all men, as some King rises with his friends leading them to that blessed rest, do you see, that the punishment is twofold, both to be burned, and to fall short of that glory?

Latin:

Vers. 16. ὅτι αὐτὸς ὁ κύριος ἐν κελεύσματι) In jussu vertit Tertullianus, id vero est, suo jussu. Nam & in Angelos &

in Archangelos Christus imperium habet, Coloss. 2, 16. Eph. 1, 20. 21. Vide & Joh. 5, 25. Ἐν φωνῇ Ἀρχαγγέλου καὶ ἐν σάλπιγγι Θεοῦ) Est ἓν διὰ δυοῖν, pro ἐν φωνῇ Ἀρχαγγέλου διὰ τῆς τοῦ Θεοῦ σάλπιγγος. Vide quæ diximus ad Matth. 24, 31. Sic Φωναὶ καὶ σάλπιγγες, Exod. 19, 13. idem quod קול שופר 1. Par. 15, 28. Apud Ebræos, Græcos & Latinos veteres populus convocabatur classico. Ad id exemplum cum Deus homines convocat, dicitur id facere per tubam, Psal. 47, 6. Esa. 27, 13. Jerem. 4, 5. cap. 6, 1. c. 51, 27. Oseæ 5, 8. Joel. 2, 1. Zach. 9, 14. Ideo in Apoca- lypsi in omnibus Dei judiciis dantur Angelis tubæ, quia ve- ro hoc judicium omnium est ut postremum, ita maximum atque generalissimum, ideo hic tuba datur non Angelo, sed alicui Angelorum Principi, qualis Michael השר הגדול Dan. 12, 1.

Vulgata etiam habet in jussu, quem de Patris mandato intelligunt Haymo & Lombardus. Κέ- λευσμα est conclamatio nautarum vel etiam sese mutuo excitantium, unde B. Lutherus mit einem Feld-Geschrey reddidit. Quo referunt nonnul- li clamorem illum Matth. 25, 6. Ecce sponsus venit, exite in occursum ejus. Hoc κέλευσμα tribuit Pho- tius in scholiis Græcis Domino, quo excitandi sint mortui. Porro vocem Archangeli nonnulli à tuba Dei distinguere malunt. Vocem Archangeli Theodoretus hanc dicit fore: Resurgant mortui! Alii ex Hieronymo hanc afferunt: Surgite vos mor- tui & venite ad judicium! Theophylactus hanc affignat: Apparate vos omnes, judex præsto est. Per Archangelum vero Ambrosiaster Christum in- telligit, ut & Hyperius. Sed distinguitur hic aperte Dominus ab Archangelo, quia dicitur Dominus ἐν κελεύσματι ἐν φωνῇ Ἀρχαγγέλου descensurus. Augu- stinus & Haymo omnes virtutes Angelicas notari vo- lunt. Quod Calvino & Crocio ita placet, ut commu- nem quidem Angelorum clamorem faciant, unum tamen ex illis præcentorem constituant. Sed Gro- tius satis confidenter Michaëlem designat cum Thoma & Lyrano. Cornelius à Lapide titubat, vel Michaelem vel certe Gabrielem intelligi censens. B. Gerhardus notat, quosdam Gabrielem intelli- gere, siquidem ille B. Virgini Mariæ etiam pri- mum adventum annuntiarit. Oecumenius de jus- su, voce, & tuba sic habet: In jussu simul ut ipse jusserit, & Archangelus vocem emiserit, ac tubæ sonuerint, descendet. Jubet quippe Dominus, & voce edit Archangelus jussum Dominicum, sonum- que emittunt cæteri ordines cælestes, quos figurative appellat tubas, quemadmodum etiam edere dicit. Sed Dominus quidem jubet, Angelus vero Domini- cum jussum nunciat sibi subditis, porro hi admini- strant ipsum, & usque ad mundi terminos intonant, & mortui, quotquot sunt, ex universo orbe resur- gunt ac congregantur. Tubam Dei, quæ 1. Cor. 15. postrema dicitur, de pluribus tubis accipit Pho- tius, & per eas intelligit potestates Angelicas. Alii metaphorice accipiunt. Gregorius M. de spirituali imperio Christi; Calvinus & Tossanus de autori- tate & majestate. Non video, cur non distincte hæc accipienda, quæ distincte in explicatione λό- γε κυρίε Apostolus adducit, aut cur à proprietate literæ penitus discedendum sit. Dicitur 1. ἐν κε- λεύσματι, hoc est, in clamore quasi militari, san- ctorum nempe Angelorum. Quia enim adventus Christi ad judicium in scripturis sacris describi solet, quasi adventus Regis in prælium descendentis ad de- bellandos suos hostes, 2. Thess. 2. v. 8. & liberandos ex captivitate suos subditos, Luc. 21. v. 28. Ideo con- jungit Apostolus τὸ κέλευσμα hortamen classicum, si- ve clamorem militarem, & Archangelum velut Du- cem cælestis militiæ & tubam belli denunciatricem, ait B. Gerhard. de resurrectione mortuorum §. 66. 2. Ἐν φωνῇ Ἀρχαγγέλου, quæ vocem unius Angeli, & quidem Archangeli, quisquis ille sit, significat, si proprie accipiatur, prout alias voces Angelo- rum proprie accipi solent, cum in scripturis ea- rum mentio fit. Quod enim Justinianus dispu- tat, non fore vocem, quæ auribus corporeis ca- piatur, quia nec cadavera percipere possint, ne- que animæ à corporibus separatæ, quippe quæ so- num corporeum absque sensu corporis nequeant sus- cipere, id nos parum movere debet. Nam super- erunt adhuc viventes in terris, quos nempe dies Domini superstites & vivos deprehendet, qui vocem audiant; Quam etiam Angeli, quam cœlites reliqui, & animæ beatæ suo modo au- dient. Et quidni audituri etiam mortui? si di- catur hæc vox Archangeli quidem διακονικῶς vel ministerialiter, Filii vero Dei κυρίως & princi- paliter, Johan. 5, 38. 3. Ἐν σάλπιγγι Θεꭣ, in tuba Dei. Hæc distinguitur ab Apostolo à κε- λεύσματι, nec non à Φωνῇ Ἀρχαγγέλε. Dicitur autem tuba Dei, non quod Deus ipse immedia- te vocem vel sonum tuba editurus sit, sed quod magna illa futura sit, quemadmodum vox Dei so- let addi magnitudinis significandæ causa ex idio- tismo Ebræo. Ideo dicit Christus vocem ma- gnam tubæ, Matth. 24, 31. Crocius quidem pro- pendet in eam sententiam, quam Grotius am- plexus est. Fortassè, inquit, non male dixeris, vo- cem Archangeli, & tubam esse unum idemque, id est, vocem tubalem, id est, sonoram, & quidem ma- xime, Id enim vox Dei indicat. Non tamen omni- no negare videtur, tubam intelligi posse. Nescio tamen, inquit, cum vox Archangeli præcesserit, an- non aliquid sensibile futurum? Neque tamen putem, quod Anshelmus tradit, fore tubam realem proprie dictam: multo minus probem audaciam Francisci Soarez, ex ære factum iri asserentis, quam socius Cornelius à Lapide non audet approbare: imo in- certum agnoscit, ex qua materia sit futura, interim proprie dictam fore nullus dubitat. Nulla vel illis vel aliis firma ratio. Fateor aliam firmam ratio- nem non reperiri, nisi quod à proprietate literæ non sit recedendum, imprimis ubi traditur ali- quod mysterium. Affert B. Gerhardus Harmon. Evangel. cap. CLXI. de tubis Angelorum Matth. 24, 11. plures rationes, quod proprie intelligendæ sint, quæ etiam hic urgeri possunt: Quod Apostolus 1. Cor. 15, v. 52. bis repetat vocem tubæ, ut in ver- bi proprietate permanendum esse innuat, ἐν ἐσχάτη σάλπιγγι, σαλπίσει γάρ (2.) Quod in promulga- tione legis clangor buccinæ vehementer perstrepentis auditus fuerit Exod. 19. v. 16. Ergo verisimile est, etiam tubæ sonum auditum iri, quando executio le- gis in judicio instituetur. (3.) Quod in Hierichuntis excidio vox tubæ divino mandato insonuerit Jos. 6. v. 5. Ergo verisimile est, quando Hiericho hujus mundi destruetur, clangorem aliquem similem buc- cinarum sono ab Angelis in aëre formandum itidem auditum iri. (4.) Quod Johannes in ultimi judicii spectaculo clangorem tubæ se audivisse dicit Apoc. 4, v. 1. c. 8. v. 6. c. 9, v. 1. c. 11, v. 15. &c. Sed ex hisce τὸ ῥητὸν præcipue nos movet, à quo non disceden- dum in talibus, quæ nonnisi revelatione divina constant. Alias enim nihil certi habebitur. Ideo fluctuare Crocium videmus, modo vocem sonoram Archangeli, per quem creatum Angelum intel- ligit, per tubam Dei vult; modo à voce Archan- geli eam distinguens, Archangelo clangente re- liquos Angelos sonum edituros cum Haymone, Lombardo, Calvino, putat, quia missurus est Do- minus Angelos cum voce tubæ magnæ, Matth. 24, 31. nec dubitat, quin aliquo terribili sono prænun- ciandus sit adventus Domini ad judicium, sicut Dominus cum tubæ clangore venit ad legem pro- pro- mulgandam, Exod. 19; modo ipsam Christi vocem designari vult. Christus, inquit, hanc tubam vocat vocem Filii Dei Joh. 5, 28. Quod si vero, ne omni- no relinquatur litera, intelligamus tubam analogi- ce, uti clangor valde fortis tubæ, Exod. 19, 16. in legis promulgatione auditus: qui qualis qualis tandem fuerit, à voce Filii Dei certe distinctus fuit, qui ἀμέσως ̀ ἀυτοπροσώπως legem promulgavit. Sic ergo distinguenda hic videtur tuba clangens Dei à voce non tantum Archangeli, sed etiam à voce Filii hominis, Johan. 5, 28. quum Archangelus à Do- mino hic distinguatur, cujus virtute resuscitan- di sunt mortui. Quo de B. Hunnius hoc loco habet: Meminit autem Paulus vocis Archange- li. Quamvis enim mittet Filius hominis Angelos suos cum tubæ voce magna, Matth. 24. In specie tamen, imo individuo, unius cujusdam Archan- geli mentio fit. Is vero non est Christus ipse: discer- nitur aperte Dominus ab Archangelo suo, quem- admodum neque in scriptura Novi Testamenti Chri- stus hujusmodi tectis nominibus amplius appellari consuevit. Est autem Archangelus ille secundum explicationem Prophetarum & Apostolorum Mi- chael, quem solum ex omni militia cælestium An- gelorum canonica scriptura expresse Archangelum appellat, sub quo tanquam duce militant Angeli ejus, ut Apoc. c. 12. legitur. In quo tamen Apocalypti- co loco per Archangelum Michaelem plerique Christum intelligunt.

Sic ergo illa tantum παρασκευαστικὰ & προηγύ- μένα videntur fore primum κέλευσμα sive cæli- tum universorum, sive Angelorum: tum vocem Archangeli, denique tubam illam magnam sive principatus, sive throni, sive dominationis ali- cujus cælestis: Qui sonus ingens fidelibus ju- cundus, infidelibus valde horribilis instar clan- goris tubæ inruitur; ut Apoc. 1, 10. audivi vocem magnam ὡς σάλπιγγος, tanquam tubæ, loquentis mecum. Sequctur deinde actus princeps, cum resonabit vox Filii hominis: Surgite mortui, qua excitabuntur mortui. Nam hanc excitationem (quæ teste Christo voce ipsius peragenda, uti voce sua, Lazare, veni foras, Talitha kumi, puella surge, in diebus carnis mortuos resuscitavit) antecessu- ra illa Paulus hic luculenter innuit. De voce tu- bæ Theodoretus in hunc locum: Ipse enim primus universorum Dominus apparebit de cælo descen- dens, quæ sub aspectum non cadunt potestatibus cum præcedentibus, & jubebit quidem Archangelum cla- mare, & mortuos resurgere. Tubæ autem ma- gno & mirabili clangore undique personabunt. Hoc autem dicit etiam in epistola ad Corinthios: Omnes quidem non obdormiemus, sed omnes immutabimur in momento, in ictu oculi, in ultima tuba. Tuba e- nim clanget, & mortui resurgent à corruptione alie- ni: & nos immutabimur. Si autem in monte Sina cum editus esset sonus iis, qui aderant, commoderatus, non tulit populus ingentem terrorem, sed dixit ma- gno Mosi: Loquere tu nobis, & non loquatur Deus nobiscum, ut non moriamur: Quis feret vocem, quæ tunc resonabit? Ubi tamen voce Archangeli re- suscitatum iri mortuos censet: Sed id voci Filii hominis tribuitur, Joh. 5. nuspiam autem voci Archangeli. Hoc autem, inquit, in jussu, in voce Archangeli, hoc significat, quod jussus aliquis ex Arch- angelis jubebit mortuos resurgere. Illi autem statim resurgent. Theophylactus κέλευσμα, per quod iti- dem jussum Dei intelligit, & vocem Archangeli & tubam Dei ibidem distinguit. Nam Domini, inquit, hæc futura sunt jussa. Verum quomodo ille hæc est injuncturus? In Archangeli voce cæteris An- gelis præsidentis, & identidem inclamantis, prompti Paratique estote omnes : adest enim jam judex. Ut enim Pater in Sina, Arabiæ monte, tubis est usus & Angelis ministrantibus, sic & Filius tanquam Imperator his ipsis utetur. Addit & aliam expli- cationem : Vel quia Dei terra hac jussu cogetur, quæ exceperat corpora restituere, ad incorruptionem mox transformata. Quod autem unum in locum undique sint conventura, voce Archangelus opera- bitur, unus tamen aliorum ministerio Angelorum. Ebræi, referente Schindlero in lexico pentaglotto in voce שׁופר, festi tubarum, Levit. 23, 24. causam etiam hanc reddunt, ut recordemur diei, quò in vi- tam redibunt mortui. Hi enim resurgent cum clan- gore tubæ, & congregabuntur non aliter, ac cum au- dit populus vocem tubæ, sicut dicitur : Omnes incolæ orbis & habitatores terræ, cum elevabitur vexillum montium, videbitis, & cum clanget tuba, audie- tis. Et Esa. 27, 13. Et erit in die illo, clangetur בשׁופר in tuba magna, & venient pereuntes in ter- ra Assur &c. Adhiberi autem tuba solebat non tantum in festo tubarum, sed etiam in aliis festis : nec in festis solum, sed in convocatione totius cœtus, & in profectione ad bellum, ut Num. 10. le- gere est. Vocandi autem tum sunt omnes electi ad festivitatem æternam, Esa. 66, 23. congre- ganda universa hominum multitudo ad Domi- num, & consurget Dominus in prælium adversus impios, quemadmodum dies judicii dicitur dies tubæ & clangoris, Ephes. 1, 16. & in apocalypsi Jo- hannæa septem tubæ, quibus clangunt angeli cap. 8. c. 9. c. 10. judicia Dei intimant. Denique uti tu- ba etiam cani solet in ingressu Regis : Ita sonabit in Regis Regum adventu tuba Dei. Quando vi- derint, inquit Chrysostomus tumultuationem, tunc & vox audietur Archangeli Angelis reliquis impe- rantis & clamantis, audientur tunc & tubæ, imo tubarum sonitus. De tuba postrema ita ibidem Chrysostomus : Quid est postrema tuba? Osten- dit hic multas fore tubas, & ad postremam descen- surum judicem. Qui metaphorice per tubam Dei fulgura & tonitrua intelligunt, non advertunt ea distingui, Exod. 19, 16. in Apocalypsi, & alias; nec commodum satis videtur, tonitrua & fulgara dici tubam, quum longe alius sonus sit tonitrui, quam tubæ. Porro hæc tuba itidem distinguenda videtur à voce magnæ tubæ, vel tuba vocis magnæ Angelorum, de qua Matth. 24, 31. Hæc vocem Filii hominis excitatricem sequetur, quam prior illa, de qua Apostolus hoc loco, antecedat excitationem mortuorum. An- gelorum enim ad id, è cœtu deputatorum tuba, de qua Christus, adhibebitur ad electorum con- gregationem, tuba autem præsens adhibenda ad intimationem adventus Domini. Quo de Chry- sostomus homil. 8. in h. l. p. 1370. Quid vero dicit congregandos esse, resurrecturos quidem ubique sim- pliciter dicit, congregandos vero ab Angelis. Est itaque resurrectio quidem divinæ virtutis opus, eo quod Deus impositæ telluri, ut discedat, mandabit, & nullus ministrorum hoc faciet, quemadmodum ali- quando evocavit Lazarum : Lazare veni foras. Adductio vero ministrorum opus erit. Nonnulli veterum Angelos in forma visibili apparituros di- cunt conspiciendos iis, qui adhuc superstites e- runt in terra : quia judex visibilis erit, ideo verisi- mile etiam videtur B. Gerhardo nostro l. c. judicis comites & ministros visibiles fore, quemadmo- dum plerumque in visibili forma apparuerunt, quando ad homines in corpore adhuc viventes ablegati fuerunt, Gen. 19. &c. Sed hæc, & alia exa- ctius dies Domini revelabit, quam cum pia præ- paratione & gaudio præstolari, quam illa curiosius rimari præstat, dum ea modo, quæ scriptura tra- dit, reverenter suscipiamus, & rationem nostram sub obsequium fidei captivemus. At si locali motu è supremo cæ- lo, quod collocant supra firmamentum, descendet Christus, quot annis opus erit vel seculis, ut διά- στημα illud usque ad nubes absolvat! In Christo mori quid sit jam ante diximus. Sic οἱ ἐν κυρίῳ ἀποθνήσκοντες Apoc. 14, 13. ᾿Αναστήσονται πρῶτον) Nempe ut una cum vivis possint ascendere, non post eos. Non pauci quidam è mortuis in Christo, ut Salmero vult, eos primum resurrecturos, qui Christo judici assidebunt, sed omnes, qui pie in Christo decesserunt: nec πρῶτον ratione digni- tatis, ut Sedulius; sed ratione temporis, non quoad ordinem piorum & impiorum, de eo e- nim hic non agitur, & simul voce Filii hominis tam impii, quam pii excitabuntur, Joh. 5, 28. ut Chrysostomus & Theophylactus exponunt. In Christo mortui, id est, fideles, ut qui in nubes sint sublevandi, ut priores resurrecturi, cæteri vero postremi, id est, damnandi, quippe qui neque attollendi sint, nec Christo in aëra obviam processuri. Τὸ πρῶτον enim non ordinem ponit inter eos, qui mortui sunt, quasi alii citius aliis resurrecturi sint; Sed inter defunctos in Domino, & superstites, eosque fideles, quia resurgent illi primum, inquit, corporibus nempe glorifica- tis, ἔπειτα, deinde viventes, qui reliqui erunt cum illis simul rapientur, in raptu illo commu- tandi. Unde argumentum consolationis insi- nuari hic censet Aretius hoc modo: Sententia narrationis est, in novissimo judicio prima cura habebitur defunctorum. Unde sequitur: Ergo non nimium sunt deplorandi. Sunt enim mul- tis partibus nobis feliciores, quod æstuosum istud fretum priores jam trajecrint, & portum appre- henderit, & viciniores sint perfectioni, & prio- res futuri in resurrectione, &c. Actor. 1, 9. 11. Dan. 7, 13. Rapiemur autem mutati 1. Cor. 15, 42. super aëra 2. Cor. 5, 2. Εἰς ἀπάντησιν τῦ κυρίυ εἰς ἀέρα) Id est ad Christum judi- cium exercentem, medio loco inter cœlum summum & ter- ram, quod spatium Græci aëra vocant. Ἔπειτα dicit Apostolus, deinde, hoc est, post- quam resurrexerint, qui in Domino mortui sunt, nos viventes, qui reliqui erimus, simul cum illis ra- piemur. Non ergo prius moriemur, inquit, deinde etiam resurgemus. Sed simul cum illis resuscitatis viventes rapiemur. Anshelm. Mortui in Christo re- surgent primum, antequam scil. Christo obviam in aëra rapiantur: Deinde nos, qui vivim9, simul cum illis, qui ex mortuis resurrexerunt rapiemur obvi- am Christo. Qui mortui sunt, inquit Chrysostomus, exurgent prius, atque ita simul fiet occursus. Abel, qui ante omnes mortuus est, simul cum illis, qui tum- vivent, occurret. Itaque quantum ad hoc attinet, nihil amplius habebunt illi, sed qui corruptus fue- rat, & tot annos in terra sepultus jacuit, cum ipsis tum viventibus occurret, & simul reliqui omnes. Quum vero illi corporibus glorificatis resuscitan- di sint, num & viventes adhuc in terris, an vero in ipso raptu in aërem talia corpora consequuturi sint, si quæratur, plerique posterius adsumunt. At videntur impii quidem in terris relinquendi, tum qui resuscitati sunt, tum quos viventes of- fendet dies Domini, donec judicium peractum fuerit, electi autem in aërem rapientur simul cum illis, qui resurrexerunt. Etsi mortui, inquit Theophylactus, sint priores resurrecturi, nihilo- minus & nos, qui in hac vita erimus, rapiemur, digni videlicet, ut subvehamur in nubes, sicuti & Dominum nubes suscepit. Cur vero, cum sit descensurus, fideles ille arripiet? Id utique hono- ris gratia facturus est. Nam quemadmodum Im- peratori cuiquam urbem aliquam inituro, honori- bus quique & dignitate præstantes, obviam pro- deunt, noxii vero & capitis damnati in carcerem interiorem conjecti judicem hunc ipsum opperiun- tur: Sic eo judicii tempore peccatores quidem & pravis facinoribus obstricti, in terris judicaturum illum expectant, vel si Christianum sortiti sint no- men: Justi vero in sublime tollentur. Sic demum & Christo eodem sunt fruituri, qui est bonorum omnium caput, & perpetuo sunt apud hunc per- mansuri. At si Angeli, inquit Chrysostomus, colli- gent, & discursabunt, quomodo isti rapientur? Post descensum Domini rapientur, posteaquam congre- gati fuerint. Sed quomodo simul rapientur in nu- bibus, nisi pariter illi qui vivunt, cum resuscitatis corpora gloriosa adepti, ut illi, agilia & subtilia, adeoque πνευματικὰ & glorificata habituri sunt corpora: An alii corporibus immortalibus à nu- bibus suscipientur, alii mortalibus & adhuc de- mum immutandis: Quapropter videtur dicen- dum, dum nubes sese ad electos suscipiendos de- mittent, actutum in momento immutatum & vi- ventes iri, ut cum resuscitatis simul suscipi & in occursum Christo rapi possint. Non autem morituros primum, sed immutandos tantum, quæ immutatio non separatio animæ & corporis erit, sed anima in corpore manente, ejusdem illius habitaculi corporis, manente etiam ejus- dem substantia, perfectio est, quod dotibus πνευμα[τικαῖς instruetur, destructis imperfectis qualitatibus, & ex animali in spirituale trans- formabitur, quantum ad qualitates. Aliquid ana- logum morti hic ponunt Theologi, non veram mortem, quæ dissolutionem animæ & corporis infert. Ambrosiaster quidem mortem statuere vi- detur interventuram in hunc locum. Ipso raptu mors preveniet, & quasi per soporem ut egressa a- nima in momento reddatur. Cum enim tollentur, monentur, ut pervenientes ad Dominum recipiant animas, quia cum Domino mortui esse non pos- sunt. Sed ea sententia cum Apostolo conciliari non potest. Propendere quidem alicubi visus est etiam Augustinus eo, quod morituri quoque sint vivi in die Domini. Ad hunc sensum, inquit libr. XX. de civit. Dei cap. 20. quo existimemus etiam illos, quos hic vivos inventurus est Domi- nus in ipso parvo spatio & visuros mortem, & ac- cepturos immortalitatem, ipse Apostolus videtur nos urgere. Et postea: Si ergo sanctos, qui repe- rientur Christo veniente viventes, eique obviam rapientur, crediderimus in eodem raptu de mor- talibus corporibus exituros, & ad eadem mox im- mortalia redituros, nullas in verbis Apostoli pa- tiemur angustias: Sive ubi dicit: Tu quod semi- nas, non vivificatur, nisi moriatur, sive ubi di- cit: Omnes resurgemus aut omnes dormiemus: quia nec illi per immortalitatem vivificabuntur, nisi quamlibet tamen paulummoriantur: ac per hoc à resurrectione non erunt alieni, quam dormitio præ- cedit, quamvis brevissima, non tamen nulla. Cre- ditur tamen aliam sententiam tradidisse Augusti- nus libr. II. de peccat. merit. & remiss. cap. 31. Hoc quibusdam DEUS in fine largietur, ut mor- tem tam repentina commutatione non sentiant, sed simul cum resurgentibus rapiantur in nubibus obviam Christo in aëre. Sed ubi diligentius ver- ba ejus expendo, non deprehendo in ullis aliam Sancti sententiam, sed eandem. Nam mortem adscribit etiam illis, qui mortui sunt in die Do- mini, sed talem, quam non SENSURI sint. MORTEM ISTAM, inquit, repentina com- mutatione non SENTIENT. In libro vero de octo quæstionibus Dulcitii quæst. III. valde flu- ctuat de hac quæstione Augustinus. Agnoscit, non facile aliter locum præsentem explicari pos- se, quam quod morituri non sint, qui superstites erunt in die Domini. Sed revera, quantum ad ver- ba Apostoli attinet, videtur asserere, quosdam in fine seculi adveniente Domino, cum futura est resurrectio mortuorum, non esse morituros, sed vivos repertos in illam immortalitatem, quæ sanctis etiam cæteris datur, repente mutandos, & simul cum illis rapiendos in nubibus, necali- quid aliud mihi visum est, quoties de his verbis volui cogitare. Ob locum tamen 1. Cor. XV. & alienam ejus lectionem, hæsitat, nec invenit, quid dicat. Sed vellem hinc potius audire doctio- res, ne illis etiam, qui putant aliquos morte non præcedente vivificatos, ad vitam transituros per- petuam, dicere inveniatur Apostolus, stulte tu quod seminas, non vivificatur, nisi prius moriatur. Nam & illud, quod in plerisque codicibus legitur, omnes resurgemus, unde fieri poterit, nisi omnes moria- mur? Resurrectio quippe, nisi mors præcesserit, nulla est. Et quod nonnulli codices habent, omnes dormiemus: multo facilius & apertius id cogit intel- ligi: Et si quid aliud tale in sanctis libris reperitur, ad id videtur impellere, ut nullos hominum existi- memus immortalitatem, nisi mors præcesserit, ade- pturos. Rursus autem in eam propendet senten- tiam, quod hic à morte videantur eximi supersti- tes in die Domini: Si autem in his verbis Apostoli nullus alius sensus poterit reperiri, & hoc cum in- telligi voluisse claruerit, quod videntur ipsa verba clamare, id est, quod futuri sint in fine seculi & secundo adventu Domini, qui non expolientur cor- pore, sed superinduantur immortalitate, ut absor- beatur mortale à vita: huic sententiæ procul dubio conveniet, quod in regula fidei confitemur, ventu- rum Dominum judicaturum vivos & mortuos, ut non intelligamus hic vivos justos, mortuos autem injustos, quamvis judicandi sint justi & injusti, sed vivos, quos nondum exiisse, mortuos autem, quos jam exiisse de corporibus, adventus ejus inveniet. Nec certitudinem de hoc problemate habuit, cum libros retractationum scripsit. Ita enim loquitur lib. II. cap. 33. Aut non morientur, aut devita ista in mortem, & de morte in æternam vitam celerri- ma commutatione, tanquam in ictu oculi transeun- do MORTEM NON SENTIENT. Alii au- tem Patres magno consensu agnoscunt non mori- turos, quod & huic loco & parallelo 1. Cor. XV. prorsus consentaneum est. Tertullianus libr. de resurr. carnis cap. 41. docet, quod compendio mor- tis per demutationem EXPUNCTÆ concurrent cum resurgentibus. Hieronymus in epist. CLII. ad Minerium & Alexandrum eam in sententiam adducit Theodorum Hemcleotum, cujus haec allegat verba: Sancti, qui in die judicii in corporibus reperiendi sunt, cum aliis sanctis, qui ex mortuis resurrecturi sunt, rapientur in nubibus obviam Christo in aëre, & non gustabunt mortem, eruntque semper cum Domino, gravissima mortis necessitate calcata. Laudat & Apollinarium, qui eadem asseruerit, videlicet quosdam non esse morituros, & de praesenti vita rapiendos in futurum. Quam sententiam suam etiam fecit, atque verbis propriis ita exposuit Hieronymus epistola CXLVIII. ad Marcellam: Hoc ex ipsius loci 1. Thess. IV. continentia sciri potest, quod sancti, qui in adventu Salvatoris deprehensi fuerint in corpore, in iisdem corporibus eidem occurrant, ita tamen, ut inglorium & corruptivum & mortale gloria, & incorruptione, & immortalitate, ut qualia corpora mortuorum surrectura sunt, in talem substantiam etiam vivorum corpora transformentur. Conf. quae de his diximus ad 1. Cor. XV.

Καὶ ὕτω πάντοτε σὺν κυρίῳ ἐσόμεθα) Joh. XIV. 2. XVII. 24. πάντοτε, sine ullo fine. Cum Domino, id est, consortes gloriae, regni gaudiique ipsius 2. Tim. II. 12. Rom. VIII. 17.

Augustinus lib. XX. de civitate Dei c. 20. Quando Paulus inquit, & sic semper cum Domino erimus, non sic accipiendum est, tanquam in aëre nos dixerit semper cum Domino mansuros, quia nec ipse utique ibi manebit, quia veniens transiturus est, venienti quippe ibitur obviam, non manenti: Sed ita cum Domino erimus, id est, sic erimus semper habentes corpora sempiterna, ubicunque cum illo fuerimus. An autem inter raptum in aëra & παρουσίαν illam perpetuam interventurum, an vero raptum illum in occursum Domini antecessurum sit extremum judicium, variant sententiae. Interventurum videtur verisimile. Nam ut prius resuscitandi sunt defuncti in Domino corporibus glorificatis: Ita immutandi superstites fideles, ut cum iis simul rapiantur. Rapiendi autem utriq; in occursum Domino ad judicium apparituro in aëre, & illic sistendi ei ad dextram, ut audiant absolutotiam sententiam in panegyri Angelorum & hominum. Sed & interventurus videtur consessus in thronis, ut tanquam assessores Christi judicent mundum & Angelos malos, 1. Cor. VI. 1. 3. De ordine in hisce observando etiam dubium movet Marcus Monachus in Nicetae catena in Symbolorum ad Matthaei XIII. p. 488. Hoc etiam inquisitione opus est, quomodo hic quidem dicat, primo facientes iniquitatem projiciendos in caminum ignis, deinde justos splendorem ac justitiam consecuturos, alibi vero dicat, prius justos esse rapiendos? Respondet autem ut sequitur: Rapiuntur quidem primi, post Christi vero adventum, hi traduntur supplicio, & tunc illi in regnum caelorum ingrediuntur. Cum enim eos in caelo esse oporteat, huc autem ipse venturus sit, omnesque homines judicaturus, ut Rex aliquis exsurgit cum amicis suis ad beatam illam quietem eos deducens, videsne, duplex esse supplicium, & comburi, & illa gloria excidere?

## 4:18
ver. 18. Therefore comfort one another) Friends, comfort friends who are in mourning, therefore, as 1 Corinthians XIV. 40. In these words) In the sermons about the resurrection, toward which all our hope tends. in is added here in the Hebrew manner. The purer Greeks express the instrumental cause with the Dative alone.

Augustine, sermon XXXIII on the words of the Apostle. Let sadness perish, where there is such great consolation: Let mourning be wiped away from the mind, let faith expel grief. In such great hope it is not fitting for the temple of God to be sad. There dwells the good consoler, there he who is a promiser who does not deceive.

The Apostle warns that because of the unexpected and sudden day of the Lord we should be vigilant, clothed with the breastplate of faith and love, and the helmet of hope, as if placed for salvation, and that we should build one another up, and respect those who are over us in the Lord; and he prescribes how we ought to conduct ourselves toward our neighbor with benevolence and long-suffering, toward ourselves with joy, toward God with devotion, as far as prayers and the Word of GOD are concerned, and to avoid every appearance of evil: Finally, having added a vow of sanctification, he seeks the prayers of the Thessalonians, commands them to greet the brothers, and grants them permission to read the epistle, and prays for the grace of Jesus.

There are two parts: I. Concerning preparation for the day of the Lord, to v. 10. II. Concerning mutual admonition, and the veneration of the Ministers of the Word, and various duties of piety. All of which are concluded with a vow and a salutation, to v. 28.

PART I. Exhortation concerning constant preparation for the day of the Lord.

Latin:

vers. 18. Ὥστε παρακαλεῖτε ἀλλήλους) Amici amicos, qui in luctu sunt, consolamini, ὥστε propterea, ut 1. Corinth. XIV. 40. Ἐν τοῖς λόγοις τύτοις) Sermonibus de resurrectione, ad quam omnis spes nostra tendit. ἐν hic additur Ebraeo more. Graeci puriores solo Dativo causam instrumentalem exprimunt.

Augustinus serm. XXXIII. de verb. Apost. Pereat contristatio, ubi tanta est consolatio: Detergatur luctus ex animo, fides expellat dolorem. In tanta spe non decet esse triste templum Dei. Ibi habitat bonus consolator, ibi qui non fallit promissor.

Monet Apostolus ob inopinatum subitumque diem Domini vigilemus, induti thorace fidei, & charitatis, ac galea spei, ceu ad salutem positi, & ut mutuo nos ædificemus, illosque, qui nobis in Domino præsunt, veneremur; ac præscribit, quomodo erga proximum bene- volentia & longanimitate, quoad nos lætitia, erga Deum devotione, quantum ad preces & Verbum DEI, nos exhibere debeamus, omnemque mali speciem vitare: Denique addito voto sanctificationis, preces Thessa- lonicensium expetit, fratres salvere, iisque epistolam legendam concedere jubet, ac gra- tiam Jesu precatur.

Partes duæ sunt: I. De præparatione ad diem Domini, ad v. 10. II. De mutua commonitione, ac Ministrorum Verbi veneratione, variisque pietatis officiis. Quæ omnia voto ac salutatione conclu- duntur, ad v. 28.

PARS I. Parænesis de jugi ad diem Domini præpa- ratione.

## 5:1 Argument
v. 1. But concerning the times and the seasons brothers) Such is the curiosity of the human mind, that it desires to know most of all those things which are most hidden. Thus many at that age desired to know when that judgment was to come. times are larger spans of time, such as years: seasons are smaller, such as months and days. You have these thus distinguished in Dan. VII. 12 in the Greek and Acts I. 7.

Οὐ χρείαν ἔχετε ὑμῖν γράφεσθαι) see above IV. 9. οὐ χρείαν ἔχετε γράφειν ὑμῖν. The sense is the same, there is no need for me to write to you, or there is no need for it to be written to you.

Latin:

v. 1. περὶ δὲ τῶν χρόνων καὶ τῶν καιρῶν ἀδελφοὶ) Est ea hu- mani ingenii curiositas, ut quæ maxime latent, ea maxime scire cupiat. Sic multi ea ætate scire cupiebant, quando venturum esset illud judicium. χρόνοι sunt majora tempo- rum spatia, ut anni: καιροὶ minora, ut menses & dies. Ha- bes hæc sic distincta Dan. VII. 12. in Græco & Actor. I. 7.

Οὐ χρείαν ἔχετε ὑμῖν γράφεσθαι) supra IV. 9. ἐ χρείαν ἔχετε γράφειν ὑμῖν. Idem est sensus, non opus est, vobis me scri- bere, aut non opus est vobis scribi.

## 5:2
vers. 2. Αὐτοὶ γὰρ ἀκριβῶς οἴδατε) You learned it long ago, when I and my assistants were teaching.

Ὅτι ἡ ἡμέρα τοῦ κυρίε, ὡς κλέπτης ἐν νυκτὶ, ὕτως ἔρχεται) That is, it will arrive unexpectedly. The same simile is in Matt. XXIV. 43. Luke XII. 39. ἔρχεται, as we have said elsewhere, is present in sound, but future in sense.

Theophylact, along with Chrysostom, wishes the day of the Lord to be understood both as the end common to all and as the private end of each individual. Lyranus explains it as the day of death. But the context is about the day of the Lord's coming to judgment, because he had previously been speaking about the resurrection of the dead and the bringing of the faithful to the Lord, which pertain to the final day of the world. Just as the day of the Lord is accustomed to be called a time of memorable divine judgment, Jer. XLVI. 10. Ezech. XIII. 5. Am. V. 18. So in the New Testament, the day of the Lord mostly and commonly denotes the day of the final judgment 1. Cor. I. 8. V. 5. 2. Cor. I. 14. Phil. I. 6. 10. II, 6. 2. Thess. II. 2. 2. Pet.
