III. 10. which is also called that great day Jude v. 6. Acts XVI. 4. and ἡ ἡμέρα, the day absolutely, Heb. X. 25. ἡ ἐκείνη ἡμέρα, Matt. VII. 22 XXIV. 36. XXVI. 29. Luke XXI. 34. 2. Thess. I. 10. 2. Tim. I. 18. except that the day of the Lord is also called the day of the first advent, John VIII. 56. and that it occurs regarding the day dedicated to the memory of Christ's resurrection, which is commonly called the day of the sun, Rev. I. 10. However, I do not find in the scriptures that the day of the Lord is said of any man's last day. But the day of the Lord is called the final day, not so much because he will appear in it as Lord, whereas in the first he appeared as a servant, which pleased Lyra. For that day is also called the great day of God Almighty, Rev. XVI. 14. nor so much as it seemed to Thomas, because in it he will fully perform his will in the good and the bad, as because it becomes the day of the Lord's final advent, the day of the Lord's universal judgment, the day of the Lord by way of excellence, because it is called the day of the Lord, just as whatever is great is accustomed to be called the Lord's: but primarily it can be called the day of the Lord, which the Lord is especially about to make, not by the rising of the sun, but by his own admirable splendor and glorious light, just as Malachi described that day, which the Lord of Hosts is about to make, ch. III. 17, which he also called a great and most venerable day, ch. IV. 5. Add that this day is the end of all days and the beginning of the everlasting age, which God will spend with his elect, that day which has no end but lasts for ages of ages: in which not the sun will shine, nor the moon, but the glory of the Lord will illuminate all things for all eternity. But how had the Apostles known about that day, that it was about to come like a thief? It is said in the commentaries of Jerome that the Thessalonians knew this by Evangelical election: But whence is it established that they had read the Gospel of Matthew, in which this is contained, ch. XXIV. 43. They could certainly have had it from Apostolic doctrine, or from the tradition of Christ's preaching, the memory of which remained with the saints; ὡς κλέπτης ἐν νυκτὶ, says the Apostle, looking not to the time of the Lord's coming, but to the manner, that it is to be sudden and unexpected at that time when no one could expect him, because the time of the coming is known to no one, which Theophylact says was perhaps known to Paul alone. For it is not for you to know the χρόνους ἢ καιροὺς, ὃς ὁ Πατὴρ ἔθετο ἐν τῇ ἰδίᾳ ἐξουσίᾳ, said Christ to the Apostles, Acts I. 7, and who would believe that the Apostle was superior to them in that part? And not unless ἀνακολούθως did some collect from this similitude of the nocturnal thief that the Lord would come by night, because, as we have said, the comparison is made only by reason of the manner of a sudden and unexpected coming, which both the context of the Apostle and the parallel passage, Matt. XXIV. 42, 43, clearly teaches. Compare also 2 Pet. III. 10. Apoc. III. 3. XVI. 15. Theodoret: He compared, he says, the sudden coming of the Lord to a thief. For he tries to lie hidden, but he who guards the house senses the arrival of the thief: but he who neglects and sleeps, to him the house is plundered. Thus he who is sober knows the signs of the Lord's coming. Oecumenius on 2 Pet. III: He signified, he says, the uncertainty of the Lord's coming, like assaults, when it will be least expected, by means of a thief and the night. By night indeed because of the uncertainty. For uncertain are all things that are in the night: but by a thief, because he is not expected. For no one will be plundered who expects a thief, but those who least expect him, they will be plundered.

Latin:

vers. 2. Αὐτοὶ γὰρ ἀκριβῶς οἴδατε) Didicistis pridem, me & adjutoribus meis docentibus.

Ὅτι ἡ ἡμέρα τοῦ κυρίε, ὡς κλέπτης ἐν νυκτὶ, ὕτως ἔρχεται) Id est, improviso aderit. Eadem similitudo Matth. XXIV. 43. Luc. XII. 39. ἔρχεται, ut alibi diximus, sono est præsens, sensu futurum.

Domini diem Theophylactus cum Chrysostomo & communem omnibus finem & privatum cujusque intelligi vult. Lyranus de die mortis explicat. At sernto est de die adventus Domini ad judicium, quia de resurrectione mortuorum, & adductione fide- lium ad Dominum antea nactum erat, quæ ad diem mundi novissimum pertinent. Uti dies Domini vo- cari solet tempus memorabilis judicii divini, Jer. XLVI. 10. Ezech. XIII. 5. Am. V. 18. Ita in N. Test. dies Domini plerumque & comuniter diem extre- mi judicii notat 1. Cor. I. 8. V. 5. 2. Cor. I. 14. Phil. I. 6. 10. II, 6. 2. Thess. II. 2. 2. Pet. III. 10. quæ etiam dies ille magnus dicitur Jud. v. 6. Act. XVI. 4. & ἡ ἡμέρα dies absolute Ebr. X. 25. ἡ ἐκείνη ἡμέρα, Matt. VII. 22 XXIV. 36. XXVI. 29. Luc. XXI. 34. 2. Thess. I. 10. 2. Tim. I. 18. nisi quod dies Domini etiam dicatur dies adventus primi, Joh. IIX. 56. quodq; de die re- surrectionis Christi memoria dicata, quæ dies solis vulgo dicitur, occurrat, Apoc. I. 10. Diem autem Do- mini dici de cujusvis hominis die ultimo, non in- venio in scripturis. Dicitur autē dies Domini dies novissim9, non tam, quod in eo apparebit ut Domi- nus, cum in primo apparuerit ut servus, quod Lyre placuit. Nam & dies ille magn9 Dei omnipotentis vo- catur, Apoc. XVI. 14. nec tam quod Thomæ visum, quia in eo voluntatem plene perficiet in bonis & malis, quā quod fit dies advent9 Domini novissimi, dies judicii Domini universalis, dies Domini κατ' ἐξοχὴν, quia dies Domini dicitur, quemadmodum quicquid magnum est, Domini esse dici solet: sed imprimis dies Domini dici potest, quàm peculia- riter facturus est Dominus non ortu solis, sed splen- dore suo admirando, & luce gloriosa, quemad- modum Malachias diem illum descripsit, quem fa- cturus est Dominus Zebaoth, cap. III. 17. quem et- iam diem magnum & venerabilem maxime dixit, c. IV. 5. Adde quod hic dies omnium dierum finis, & principium est ævi sempiterni, quod Deus cum electis suis aget, dies ille, qui non habet finem, sed in secula seculorum durat: quo non sol lucebit, nec luna, sed Domini gloria illustrabit omnia in o- mnem æternitatem. Unde autem sciverant Apo- stoli de illa die, quod venturus sit instar furis? Ele- ctione Evangelica id scivisse Thessalonicenses, in commentariis Hieronymi dicitur: Sed unde con- stat, Evangelium Matthæi eos legisse, in quo id ha- betur, c. XXIV. 43. Poterant utique id habuisse ex Apostolica doctrina, vel ex traditione concionis Christi, cujus memoria sanctis manserit; ὡς κλέπτης ἐν νυκτὶ, inquit Apostolus, non tempus adventus Domini, sed modum respiciens, quod subitus & in- opinato futuro sit eo tempore, quo nemo expecta- re eum poterat, quia nemini notum adventus tem- pus, quod temere Theophylactus Paulo fortasse so- li innotuisse ait. Nam vestrum non est, nosse χρόνους ἢ καιροὺς, ὃς ὁ Πατὴρ ἔθετο ἐν τῇ ἰδίᾳ ἐξουσίᾳ, dixit Christus Apostolis Act. I. 7. quibus ea parte supe- riorem fuisse Apostolum, ecquis credat? Nec nisi ἀνακολούθως ex hac similitudine de fure nocturno collegerunt nonnulli, Dominum noctu venturum, quia, ut diximus, comparatio fit tantum ratione modi subiti, & inexpectati adventus, quod tum con- textus Apostoli, tum locus parallelus Matth. XXIV. 42. 43. luculenter docet. Conf. & 2. Petr. III. 10. Apoc. III. 3. XVI. 15. Theodoretus: Repentinum, in- quit, Domini adventum furi comparavit. Is enim conatur latere, sed qui custodit domum, sentit furis adventum: qui autem negligit & dormit, ei domus diripitur. Ita qui est sobrius, novit signa adventus Domini. Oecumenius in 2. Pet. III. Incertitudinem, inquit, adventus Domini, tanquam insultus, cum mi- nime expectabitur, per furem & noctem significavit. Per noctem quidem propter incertitudinem. Incer- ta enim sunt, quæcunque in nocte sunt: per furem vero eo, quod non expectetur. Nullus enim expilabi- tur, qui furem expectat, sed qui hunc minime expe- ctant, illi expilabuntur.

## 5:3
vers. 3. Ὅταν γὰρ λέγωσιν, εἰρήνη κὴ ἀσφάλεια) Supply 'it is', which is understood in the Hebrew manner. A similar locution 2 Kings XI. 15. εἰρήνη κὴ ἀσφάλεια שלום ובטח, λέγουσι, εἰρήνη, you have in Ezek. XIII. 10. בטח ἀσφάλεια is translated in Lev. XXVI. 5. Deut. XII. 10. Prov. XI. 15. He speaks of the wicked, as also Christ in Matt. XXIV. 38, where see the things said.

Τότε αἰφνίδιος αὐτοῖς ἐφίσταται ὄλεθρος) ὄλεθρος, that is, punishment, as 1 Thess. I. 2. 1 Tim. VI. 9. שאון or בהלה. Αἰφνίδιος as in Luke XXI. 34 and Wisd. XVII. 15. To the Hebrews פתאם. The figure of this thing in the flood: in King Belshazzar Dan. V. in the captured Babylon of Isaiah XXI. 5.

Ὥσπερ ἡ ὠδὶν τῇ ἐν γαστρὶ ἐχούσῃ) The same similitude in Is. XIII. 8. Jer. XIII. 21. Hosea XIII. 13. Concerning the locution ἐν γαστρὶ ἔχειν we have spoken at Matt. I. 18. חבלים כיולדה Ezech. XLIX. 24.

Καὶ ὀὐ μὴ ἐκφύγωσιν) Thus Homer: Μηδ' ὃς φύγοι αἰπὺν ὄλεθρον.

The pains of the wicked are compared to the pains of childbirth on the day of the Lord's coming, because just as a pregnant woman is often unexpectedly oppressed by the pains of childbirth, when she thinks the time for giving birth is not yet present. Thus the wicked will be oppressed by the pains of a sudden coming. And just as those are very intense: so these will be by far the most grievous. A woman conceives with pleasure, she gives birth with pain: thus the pleasures of sin beget a birth full of pain, James I. 14. An example, says Theodoret, quite opposite. For what pregnant woman knows she has a fetus in her womb, but does not know the time of giving birth: So we also know indeed that the Lord of all is about to come: But we have by no means learned the time itself. For which reason that day is always to be expected. As pregnant women, through play and jest, are for the most part suddenly tormented by unspeakable pains at the same time: So also the souls of those who lead this life through delights and luxury in the present age, when that day has arrived, are by no means about to escape death and destruction, says Theophylact.

Latin:

vers. 3. Ὅταν γὰρ λέγωσιν, εἰρήνη κὴ ἀσφάλεια) Supple est, quod subauditur more Ebræo. Similis locutio 2. Reg. XI. 15. εἰρήνη κὴ ἀσφάλεια שלום ובטח, λέγουσι, εἰρήνη, habes Ezech. XIII. 10. בטח ἀσφάλεια vertitur Levit. XXVI. 5. Deut. XII. 10. Prov. XI. 15. Loquitur de improbis, ut & Chri- stus Matth. XXIV. 38. ubi dicta vide.

Τότε αἰφνίδιος αὐτοῖς ἐφίσταται ὄλεθρος) ὄλεθρος, id est, pœna, ut 1. Thess. I. 2. 1. Tim. VI. 9. שאון vel בהלה. Αἰφνίδιος ut Luc XXI. 34. & Sap. XVII. 15. Ebræis פתאם. Figura hujus rei in diluvio: in Rege Balthasare Dan. V. in capta Babylone Esaïæ XXI. 5.

Ὥσπερ ἡ ὠδὶν τῇ ἐν γαστρὶ ἐχούσῃ) Eadem similitudo Es. XIII. 8. Jer. XIII. 21. Oseæ XIII. 13. De locutione ἐν γαστρὶ ἔχειν diximus ad Matth. I. 18. חבלים כיולדה Ezech. XLIX. 24.

Καὶ ὀὐ μὴ ἐκφύγωσιν) Sic Homerus: Μηδ' ὃς φύγοι αἰπὺν ὄλεθρον.

Doloribus partus comparantur dolores impio- rum in die adventus Domini, quia sicut mulier prægnans sæpe ex improviso doloribus partus op- primitur, cum tempus pariendi nondum adesse opinatur. Sic impii repentini adventus doloribus opprimentur. Et sicut illi valde intensi sunt: Ita hi erunt longe gravissimi. Mulier cum voluptate co- cipit, cum dolore parit: Sic voluptates peccati par- tum dolore plenum gignunt, Jac. I. 14. Exemplum inquit Theodoretus, admodum oppositum. Quæ est enim gravida, scit se habere fœtum in utero, nescit autem tempus pariendi: Ita nos etiam esse quidem venturum universorum Dominum scimus: Ipsum autem tempus nequaquam didicimus. Qua de causa illa dies semper est expectanda. Ut mulieres gravidae per lusum plerumque & jocum derepente ineffabil- bus simul doloribus cruciantur: Sic & illorum ani- mae, qui praesenti seculo per delitias ducunt & luxum hanc vitam, cum dies ille advenerit, nequaquam mortem sunt & interitum evasurae, inquit Theo- phylactus.

## 5:4
vers. 4. Ὑμεῖς δὲ ἀδελφοὶ οὐκ ἐστὲ ἐν σκότει, ἵνα ἡ ἡμέρα ὑμᾶς ὡς κλέπτης καταλάβῃ) I think the Manuscript has it better: ὡς κλέπτας. It is not the same comparison that preceded: but another born from the occasion of it, such as we observed in John 17. Night covers thieves, Job XXIV. 14. Jer. XLIX. 8. Obadiah I. 5. Thus robbers rise by night, Horace. The same: And cover the night with furies and frauds with a cloud. But if they do not retreat before light, they are accustomed to be caught: John III. 20. Darkness signifies ignorance of divine things, light signifies knowledge.

The Manuscript is rashly preferred to all codices. Why should the comparison not be repeated in the application? That day certainly apprehends all who are in the darkness of ignorance, John XII. 3. Rom. II. 19. 1 Pet. IV. 18, and of sins or impiety of life, Rom. XII. 13. 1 John II. 11, and they do not arrive at the light of truth and justice, not as thieves, which kind of similitude nowhere occurs, but like a thief, because it apprehends them unexpectedly and with the highest damage, just as thieves bring nothing good, but snatch away good things from men. For whatever good things they will still have, granted until now by divine patience, all that will be snatched away from them, when, like a nocturnal thief, it will oppress those who are engaged in darkness. He persisted, says Theodoret, in the parabolic figure, and indeed calls darkness ignorance, but day knowledge. He says therefore, you who have received the ray of the knowledge of God, flee the pursuit of darkness, lest the sentence of punishment be suddenly brought upon you. Thus also Theophylact: But you are not in darkness, that is, you do not lead a dark and impure life. Someone will say: What then? Shall an uncertain end invade even these, even if they are affected by no stain? It will indeed invade, but it will cover them with no sorrow. For to those who are vigilant and living in the light, if some robber finds an entrance and attacks unexpectedly, he will be able to devastate nothing that is theirs: But if he catches them sleeping in the darkness, he will depart with the spoils carried off with impunity.

Latin:

vers. 4. Ὑμεῖς δὲ ἀδελφοὶ οὐκ ἐστὲ ἐν σκότει, ἵνα ἡ ἡμέρα ὑμᾶς ὡς κλέπτης καταλάβῃ) Puto melius habere Manuscri- ptum: ὡς κλέπτας. Non est eadem, quae praecessit compa- ratio: sed occasione ejus enata alia, quale quid observavi- mus Joh. 17. Nox fures tegit, Job. XXIV. 14. Jer. XLIX. 8. Abdiae I. 5. Sic surgunt de nocte latrones, Horatius. Idem: Et noctem furiis, & fraudibus obtege nubem. Quod si non recipiunt se ante lucem, deprehendi solent: Joh. III. 20. Tenebrae significant ignorantiam rerum divi- narum, lux cognitionem.

Temere praefertur Manuscriptus omnibus co- dicibus. Comparatio cur non eadem repetatur in applicatione? Apprehendit utique dies illa omnes, qui in tenebris sunt ignorantiae, Joh. XII 3. Rom. II. 19. 1. Pet. IV. 18. & peccatorum vel impietatis vitae, Rom. XII. 13. 1. Joh. II. 11. nec ad lucem veritatis & justitiae perveniunt, non ut fures, qualis similitu- do nuspiam occurrit, sed instar furis, quia inopi- nato & cum damno summo eos apprehender, quemadmodum fures nihil boni afferunt, sed ho- minibus bona eripiunt. Nam quicquid adhuc bo- norum habebunt, à divina patientia hactenus concessorum, id omne eripietur ipsis, cum ceu no- cturnus fur, illos, qui in tenebris versantur, oppri- met. Perstitit, inquit Theodoretus, in figura parabo- lica, & tenebras quidem vocat ignorationem, diem autem cognitionem. Dicit ergo, vos qui Dei cognitio- nis radium suscepistis, fugite studium tenebrarum, ne in vos repente inferatur sententia supplicii. Sic & Theophylactus: Vos autem non estis in tenebris, hoc est, non tenebrosam & impuram ducitis vitam. Di- cet aliquis: Quid ergo? Num & hos, etsi nulla sint labe affecti vel incertus invasurus est finis? Invadet quidem, sed nullo eos obducet maerore. Vigilantibus namque & in luce versantibus, si praedo aliquis ad- itum nactus de improviso incumbat, nihil poterit, quod horum sit, devastare: At si in tenebris dormi- tantes deprehendat, relatis spoliis abscedet impune.

## 5:5
vers. 5. Πάντες ὑμεῖς ὑιοὶ φωτός ἐστε καὶ ὑιοὶ ἡμέρας) You commit nothing that seeks darkness. You cannot be caught at a time foreign to you. See the parable in Matt. XXV. 1. and following. This is the mystical explanation of the lamp in the temple מנורה.

Οὐκ ἐσμὲν νυκτὸς, ὐδὲ σκότυς) See how he often repeats the same thing, so that by praising them he may excite the Christians. Cf. Rom. XIII. 12.

Chrysostom, in that manner, says, they are called both sons of the day and sons of light, who do the things that are of the light, that is, who walk in the light of heavenly truth and true piety, believing in the true light, clothed in the armor of light, teaching a pure life. For Christ says, while you have the light, believe in the light, that you may be sons of light, John XII. 36. Similarly Theophylact: Just as those are asserted to be sons of Gehenna who have committed things worthy of Gehenna, and sons of dissidence who distrust the words of the Apostles. So also they will be sons of light who have done those things which are of the light.

Latin:

vers. 5. Πάντες ὑμεῖς ὑιοὶ φωτός ἐστε καὶ ὑιοὶ ἡμέρας) Nihil committitis, quod tenebras quaerat. Non potestis deprehen- di alieno vobis tempore. Vide parabolam Matth. XXV. 1. & sequentibus. Haec est explicatio mystica lychni in templo מנורה.

Οὐκ ἐσμὲν νυκτὸς, ὐδὲ σκότυς) Vide, quae saepe idem re- petat, ut Christianos laudando excitet. Conf. Rom. XIII. 12.

Chrysostomus ad eum modum, inquit, dicuntur & filii diei, & filii lucis, qui, quae lucis sunt, faciunt, id est, qui in luce veritatis coelestis & verae pieta- tis incedunt, in veram lucem credentes armis lu- cis induti, vitam puram docentes. Christus enim ait, dum lucem habetis, credite in lucem, ut filii lu- cis sitis, Joh. XII. 36. Similiter Theophylactus: Quemadmodum gehennae filii asseruntur, qui gehen- na condigna patrarint, & dissidentiae filii, qui Apo- stolorum dictis diffidunt. Sic & filii lucis erunt, qui ea, quae lucis sunt, fecerint.

## 5:6
v. 6. Ἄρα ἓν μὴ καθεύδωμεν ὡς καὶ οἱ λοιποὶ) Let us not be negligent, such as are said to snore in Latin. Thus also the Hebrews speak Jer. V. 27. Nah. III. 18. Prov. X. 5. καὶ is absent in the Manuscript.

The sleep is understood not of the body but of the soul, concerning which St. Augustine in Psalm LXII. The sleep of the soul is bad, the sleep of the body is good. Moreover, the sleep of the soul is to forget its God. The soul that forgets its God sleeps, namely with the sleep of negligence, of sloth, of security. Λοιποὶ are the unfaithful and reprobate, to whom the ignorance of God and the love of carnal things, like the night, have taken away sense and reason.

But let us watch and be sober) You have these two joined in 1 Pet. 5:8. Just as γρηγορεῖν (to watch) signifies by metaphor being attentive, as ἀγρυπνεῖν (to be wakeful) in Luke 21:35, so νήφειν (to be sober) signifies being free from disturbances, which are compared to drunkenness. Thus Epicharmus: Be sober and remember to distrust. These are the sinews of the mind.

Vigilance is opposed to sleep, which is likewise twofold: both of the body, Neh. 7:3, Matt. 26:40, Mark 14:37, 1 Thess. 5:10, and of the soul or mind, which is clearly understood from the opposite, sleep, and the parallel passage, Luke 21:36, where it is added, watch AT ALL TIMES, and also 1 Pet. 5:8, where we are commanded to watch against the snares of the Devil, which is done by the vigilance of the mind, not of the body, as also from the more common acceptance of this word in the New Testament: because it occurs more frequently metaphorically for the vigilance of the soul, see Matt. 25:13, Luke 12:37, Acts 20:31, 1 Cor. 16:13, Col. 4:2, Rev. 3:2, 3, 16:16. Which indeed brings about attention, as the Syrian explained: Be mindful, namely of a constant and perpetual memory of the last day, Luke 12:36, but also preparation for the same, and the flight from security and sins, Rev. 16:15, and also prudence in avoiding the snares of Satan, and the solicitous custody of body and soul, 1. Pet. 5:8, implying. Which metaphor seems to be taken from military sentries, who must watch and be ready against the invasion of an enemy. We must always watch, says Ambrose in book 1 of On the Faith, ch. 8, so that, while we do not know the certain moments of the future judgment, we may always, as if stationed on watch and placed on a certain watchtower of virtue, decline the habit of sin, lest the day of the Lord overtake us among vices. But Τὸ νήφειν (to be sober) denotes here bodily sobriety rather than freedom from disturbances of the soul, because it is opposed to gluttony in Luke 21:36. And sobriety is required by the Apostle so that we may be able to resist the Devil, 1 Pet. 5:8, to whom not a window, but a double-folding door is opened through drunkenness. Therefore, Blessed Huss rightly interpreted these things there: Be sober in body, watch in soul. Theophylact: Let us watch and be sober, that is, let us by no means show ourselves more negligent in good works, but let us be sober. For sobriety itself and abstinence increase vigilance, just as if he were saying: Through continence, let us perform diligently and cautiously those things which are good. Grotius himself, verse 7, explained this passage concerning bodily drunkenness.

Latin:

v. 6. Ἄρα ἓν μὴ καθεύδωμεν ὡς καὶ οἱ λοιποὶ) Ne negligentes simus, quales stertere dicuntur Latinis. Sic & Ebraei loquun- tur Jer. V. 27. Nah. III. 18. Prov. X. 5. καὶ abest in Manuscripto.

Somnus non corporis sed animae intelligitur, quo de S. Augustinus in Psalm. LXII. Malus est so- mnus animae, bonus somnus corporis. Somnus autem animae est oblivisci Deum suum. Anima, quae obli- viscitur Deum suum, dormit, nempe somno negli- gentiae, desidiae, securitatis. Λοιποὶ sunt infideles & reprobi, quibus ignorantia Dei & amor carna- lium, instar noctis, sensum & rationem ademerunt.

Ἀλλὰ γρηγορῶμεν καὶ νήφωμεν) Hæc duo juncta habes 1. Petr. V. 8. Sicut γρηγορεῖν per translationem significat attentum esse, ut ἀγρυπνεῖν Luc. XXI. 35. ita νήφειν vacare à perturbationibus, quæ ebrietati comparantur. Sic Epicharmus: Νᾶφε καὶ μέμνασ' ἀπιστεῖν. Νεῦρα ταῦτα τῶν φρενῶν.

Vigilantia opponitur somno, quæ pariter duplex est, tum corporis, Neh. VII. 3. Matth. XXVI. 40. Marc. XIV. 37. 1. Thess. V. 10. tum animi vel mentis, quam intelligi patet ex opposito somno, & loco parallelo, Luc. XXI. 36. ubi additur, vigilate OMNI TEMPORE, nec non 1. Petr. V. 18. ubi contra insidias Diaboli vigilare jubemur, quod fit mentis non corporis vigilantia, ut & ex usitatiori hujus vocis in Novo Testamento acceptione: quia metaphorice pro animi vigilantia frequentius occurrit, vid. Matth. XXV. 13. Luc. XII. 37. Act. XX. 31. 1. Cor. XVI, 13. Col. IV. 2. Apoc. III. 2. 3. XVI. 16. Quæ attentionem quidem infert, ut Syrus exposuit: Memores estote, jugem nempe ac perpetuam memoriam diei novissimi, Luc. XII. 36. sed & præparationem ad eandem, ac securitatis & peccatorum fugam, Apoc. XVI. 15. nec non prudentiam in cavendis Satanæ insidiis, & solicitam corporis & animæ custodiam, 1. Petr. V. 8. inferens. Quæ metaphora à castrensibus excubitoribus desumpta videtur, qui vigilare ac parati esse debent, adversus hostis invasionem. Vigilare semper nos oportet, inquit Ambrosius libr. I. de fide cap. 8. ut, dum certa futuri judicii momenta nescimus, semper, tanquam in excubiis constituti, & in quadam virtutis specula collocati, peccati consuetudinem declinemus, ne nos inter vitia dies Domini deprehendat. Τὸ νήφειν vero sobrietatem corporis hic potius, quàm vacationem à perturbationibus animi notat, quia crapulæ opponitur Luc. XXI. 36. Et ab Apostolo requiritur sobrietas, ut resistere Diabolo possimus, 1. Petr. V. 8. cui per ebrietatem non fenestra, sed bipatens janua aperitur. Ideo illic B. Hussius recte hæc interpretatus est: Sobrii estote corpore, vigilate animo. Theophylactus: Vigilemus & sobrii simus, hoc est, nequaquam in bonis operibus negligentiores nos ipsos præstemus, sed sobrii simus. Auget namque vigilantiam sobrietas ipsa & abstinentia, perinde ac si dicat: Per continentiam, quæ bona sunt, diligenter & caute peragamus. Grotius ipse vers. 7. hunc locum de ebrietate corporis exposuit.

## 5:7
verse 7. For those who sleep sleep at night) He pursues the comparison begun.

And those who get drunk are drunk at night) At untimely banquets.

The same person also explains the protasis of the comparison, Crocius: But the protasis is only hinted at. They are said to be at night who are under the power of darkness; they are not children of light, as the opposition indicates, v. 8. But they sleep while they are overwhelmed by the sleep of security and sins; and in that spiritual night they also indulge in drunkenness, whether that happens by day or by night. Here he shows, as Chrysostom has it, that to be in the day is ours. For this day and night here is not ours, but night comes even against our will, and sleep is present even when we do not want it. But in that night and sleep it is not so: But it is permitted to watch perpetually, it is permitted to lead the day perpetually. For to close the eyes of the soul, and to induce sleep from vice, is not of nature, but of free will. He speaks here of drunkenness, not only that which is from wine, but also that which is from all evils. For the drunkenness of the soul is riches, and the desire for money, and the love of bodies, and whatever you might say is a drunkenness of the soul. He calls them sleepers, says Theophylact, here, who are captured by a certain sleep of wickedness, as if inert and sluggish toward virtues, and always imagining something as if through sleep. For such is this present life, nothing different from a stupor. But he calls drunkenness not only that which is vinous, and born from Bacchus, but the intoxication which arises from any vices whatsoever, as that which exceeds the limits and boundaries of nature itself, and darkens the mind itself. Therefore he by no means says that you should show yourselves of this kind. For you are not fashioned from night and darkness, but from day and light, born by the grace of baptism and divine traditions. The opposite member could have taught this sense to Crocius, since he himself establishes such an antithesis to the following verse: As if he were saying: The children of the night sleep at night, let them be drunk at night, let them do their own things negligently. For us all, as many as have been illuminated from heaven through Christ, in such light of the Gospel, other manners are fitting. Let us strive to do all our things attentively in our whole life. For I would not want to restrict it to bodily sobriety. But why he called vice sleep, Chrysostom explains thus: Because first, indeed, he who is of such a kind lacks every action of virtue. Then he apprehends by vision and fantasy, he sees nothing true, but is full of dreams. But if he has seen any good, he has nothing firm or solid. Such is the present life: It is full of dreams and vision: Riches are a dream and glory, and whatever things are of this kind. He who sleeps does not see the things that are, and that truly consist. But the things that are not, he apprehends by vision as if they were. Such is vice, and the life that is led in vice. He does not see the things that are, that is, the things that are spiritual, heavenly, remaining: But the things that flow and fly away, and quickly rebound from us. And afterwards: Vice is darkness, O beloved, it is death, it is night. We see nothing of the things that are necessary, we do nothing of the things that are fitting. Just as the dead are deformed and foul, so the soul of those who are in vice is full of much filth. Their eyes are closed, the mouth is compressed, they remain immobile in the bed of vice. Indeed, they are more miserable than those to whom these things have happened. For those are dead to both. But these are endowed with no sense toward virtue, while living toward vice.

Latin:

vers. 7. Οἱ γὰρ καθεύδοντες νυκτὸς καθεύδουσι) Persequitur cœptam comparationem.

Καὶ οἱ μεθυσκόμενοι νυκτὸς μεθύουσι) Conviviis intemperivis.

Id. de προτάσει comparationis etiam explicat Crocius: Sed πρότασις subinnuitur tantum. Noctu esse dicuntur, qui sub potestate tenebrarum sunt, non sunt filii lucis, ut oppositio indicat, v. 8. Dormiunt autem illi, dum somno securitatis & peccatorum obruuntur; & in illa etiam spirituali nocte ebrietati indulgent, sive interdiu id contingat, sive noctu. Hic ostendit, ut habet Chrysostomus, quod in die esse sit nostrum. Nam hic quidem in hoc die & nocte non est nostrum, sed vel nobis invitis venit nox, & nobis nolentibus adest somnus. In illa autem nocte & somno non est ita: Sed licet perpetuo vigilare, licet perpetuo diem agere. Nam animæ claudere oculos, & à vitio somnum inducere, non est naturæ, sed liberi arbitrii. Ebrietatem hic dicit, non eam solùm, quæ est à vino, sed eam etiam, quæ est ab omnibus malis. Ebrietas enim animæ sunt divitiæ, & pecuniæ cupiditas, & amor corporum, & quodcunque dixeris est ebrietas animæ. Dormientes eos, inquit Theophylactus, hic dicit, qui somno quodam nequitiæ capiuntur, tanquam ad virtutes inertes & torpidi, & semper aliquid quasi per so- mnum imaginantes. Talis est enim praesens haec vita, à sopore nihil aliena. Ebrietatem autem dicit non modo vinaticam illam, & à Baccho progenitam, sed quae à quibusvis vitiis oritur temulentia, tanquam quae ipsius naturae limites & metas excedat, & men- tem ipsam obtenebret. Haudquaquam itaque ait istiusmodi vos ipsi praestetis. Non enim conflati ex nocte & tenebris, sed ex die ac luce, baptismi & di- vinarum traditionum gratia orti. Docere hunc sensum poterat Crocium membrum oppositum, quum ipse ejusmodi antithesin constituat ad se- quentem versum: Quasi dicat: Filii noctis dormiunt noctu, sint ebrii noctu, agant sua negligenter. Nos omnes, quotquot caelitus illuminati per Christum sumus, in tanta Evangelii luce alii decent mores. Studeamus attente agere omnia nostra in tota vita. Nolim enim ad corporalem sobrietatem restringere. Cur autem vitium vocarit somnum, ita explicat Chrysostomus: Quoniam primum quidem, qui est ejusmodi, caret omni actione virtutis. Deinde visio- ne & phantasia apprehendit, nihil verum videt, sed est plenus somniis. Si quid autem boni viderit, ni- hil habet firmum nec solidum. Talis est vita praesens: Est plena somniis & visione: Divitiae sunt somnium & gloria, & quaecunque sunt hujusmodi. Qui dor- mit, ea quae sunt, & quae vere consistunt, non videt. Quae autem non sunt, tanquam quae sunt, visione apprehendit. Tale est vitium, & quae in vitio agi- tur vita. Non videt, quae sunt, hoc est, quae sunt spiritualia, caelestia, manentia: Sed quae fluunt & avolant, & cito à nobis resiliunt. Et postmodum: Tenebrae est vitium, ô dilecte, mors est, nox est. Nihil videmus eorum, quae oportet, nihil agimus eo- rum, quae convenit. Quomodo mortui sunt defor- mes & faetidi, ita anima eorum, qui sunt in vitio, sunt plenae multa immunditia. Clausi sunt eorum oculi, os est compressum, immobiles manent in lecto vitii. Imo vero sunt miserabiliores iis, quibus haec ac- ciderunt. Nam isti quidem ad utraque sunt mortui. Illi autem ad virtutem quidem nullo sunt sensu prae- diti, viventes autem ad vitium.

## 5:8
verse 8. But we who are of the day) We are like those nations to whom the light shines perpetually.

Νήφωμεν) We are free from every vicious effect.

Here the word νήφωμεν implies that the children of light should strive to be immune not only from every vice, but also from drunkenness: just as τὸ νήφειν is taken for the vigilance and sobriety of the mind, 1 Pet. 1 v. 13, chap. IV. 7. Therefore, both the temperance and sobriety of the body are indicated, as well as the sobriety of the mind, which brings about prudence, attention, and abstinence from vices.

Ἐνδυσάμενοι θώρακα πίστεως κὴ ἀγάπης) Protected in the breast, by faith within, by love without: which is the perfection of justice, cf. Eph. 4, 14.

Καὶ περικεφαλαίαν ἐλπίδα σωτηρίας) Ephes. VI. 17, where see the things said.

It is rightly said that the breast is protected within by faith, and without by love: but it is not rightly said that love is the perfection of justice. For the justice which is apprehended by faith is by far the most perfect, namely the justice of Christ, which it is injurious to the justice and obedience of Christ to claim is perfected by our love. He alone has been made justice for us by God, 1 Cor. I. 29, and He is Jehovah our justice, Jerem. XXIII. 6. The Apostle wishes us to be clothed with arms when we watch against the snares of Satan. An armed man easily brings an unarmed man into his power, despoils him, and slaughters him: Cf. Eph. VI. 1. Rom. XIII. 12. He assigns the arms of light to the children of light; by which the breast and the head are especially to be protected. For it is not enough, says Theophylact, that we keep sobriety and vigilance, unless we are also surrounded by arms. For if someone is more vigilant and alert, but lacks the arms by which he can protect himself, most quickly by robbers he will both be captured and slaughtered. B. Luther on 1 Pet. 5:8: Such is our life, as if a stranger were to come into an inn in which all the inhabitants were robbers; there he would certainly keep watch, arm himself, and fortify himself. By faith and love, however, Theophylact understands any more upright decrees and the best actions of life. We do not disapprove of the latter, but the former does not fit so well. For dogmas pertain to the Word, which in spiritual armor is conferred as a sword, not a breastplate. The faith by which one believes, not that which is believed, is to be understood. For the former is joined with love and hope. By the latter, the Devil is resisted, 1 Pet. 5:8, which is from Salmeron on the Petrine passage. The Apostle wants them to be strong in faith, or the confidence of divine mercy, and which embraces Christ himself fighting for us. William Estius on 1. Pet. 5 teaches: Blessed Peter [teaches] that the Devil's machinations, whether open or hidden, must be resisted with the firmness of faith, by which, clearly, we not only undoubtedly believe the promises of God, but also stir up in ourselves the confidence of obtaining them through the power, truth, and mercy of God set before our eyes through Christ. For grace and truth came through Christ, John 1:17, and this is the victory that overcomes the world, our faith, 1 John 5:4. If the world, then also the Prince of the world. Thus the Papists themselves are forced to leave this glory to confidence. Concerning the helmet of the hope of salvation, Theophylact, following Chrysostom: Just as the helmet itself, covering the head, which is the principal part in us, renders it more secure and safe, so also hope itself preserves the mind, and is argued to be salutary to it, since it allows nothing external to slip into it. Especially, the hope of victory inflames a soldier for battle, sustains him when pressed, encourages him when in danger, so that, neglecting every danger, he may persevere in the battle line and fight bravely, and prepare all his things to obtain victory. Thus, with the joyful hope of eternal blessedness that awaits the victors, the Thessalonians ought to fortify, support, and animate themselves, so that they might await the imminent enemy fearlessly, receive the rushing one bravely, repel the pressing one strenuously, and among the flying missiles not look around at temporal things by which they could be recalled from the fight, but, thinking solely of the sweetest enjoyment of God and heavenly joys, they might refer all their things to the victory which eternal salvation would certainly receive, as Crocius has on this passage.

Latin:

vers. 8. Ἡμεῖς δὲ ἡμέρας ὄντες ὑοὶ) Sumus tanquam illae gentes, quibus lux allucet perpetua.

Νήφωμεν) Liberi sumus ab omni vitioso effectu.

Hic verbum νήφωμεν uti ab omni vitio, ita etiam ab ebrietate, ut immunes sint studere filios lucis, innuit: quemadmodum τὸ νήφειν pro mentis vi- gilantia & sobrietate sumitur, 1. Pet. 1. v. 13. cap. IV. 7. Indicatur ergo tum temperantia & sobrie- tas corporis, tum etiam mentis sobrietas, quae prudentiam, attentionem, & abstinentiam à vitiis infert.

Ἐνδυσάμενοι θώρακα πίστεως κὴ ἀγάπης) Pectus muniti, fide intus, extra dilectione: quae justitiae perfectio, conf. Eph. 4, 14.

Καὶ περικεφαλαίαν ἐλπίδα σωτηρίας) Ephes. VI. 17. ubi dicta vide.

Recte pectus dicitur intus muniri fide, extra di- lectione: Sed non recte dilectio dicitur justitiae perfectio. Nam justitia, quae fide apprehenditur, longe perfectissima est, Christi nempe justitia, quam dilectione nostra perfici injuriosum est in Christi justitiam & obedientiam. Solus ipse nobis à Deo factus est justitia, 1. Cor. I. 29. estque Jeho- vah justitia nostra, Jerem. XXIII. 6. Armis autem indui nos vult Apostolus, cum vigilamus adversus Satanae insidias. Inermem facile armatus in pote- statem redigit, spoliat, trucidat: Conf. Eph. VI. 1. Rom. XIII. 12. filiis lucis arma lucis assignat; quibus pectus & caput cumprimis muniatur. Neque enim sat habet, inquit Theophylactus, ut sobrietatem & vigilantiam servemus, nisi & armis circumduca- mur. Nam si vigilantior quispiam & excitus fuerit, armis autem careat, quibus tutari se queat, celerrime à prædonibus & capietur & trucidabitur. B. Lutherus in 1. Pet. V. 8. Talis vita nostra, ac si peregrinus veniret in hospitium, in quo omnes incolæ essent latrones, ibi certe vigilaret, sese armaret & muniret. Per fidem autem & dilectionem intelligit Theophylactus rectiora quævis decreta, & optimas vitæ actiones. Quod posterius non improbamus, sed prius non adeo convenit. Nam dogmata pertinent ad Verbum, quod in armatura spirituali gladio confertur, non loricæ. Fides qua creditur, non qua creditur, intelligenda. Nam illa cum dilectione ac spe conjungitur. Illa Diabolo resistitur, 1. Pet. V. 8. quod de Salmero in locum Petrinum. Apostolus fortes vult esse in fide, sive fiducia divinæ misericordiæ, & quæ Christum ipsum complectitur pro nobis pugnantem. Guilielmus Estius in 1. Petr. V. docet: B. Petrus Diaboli tractationibus sive apertis sive occultis resistendum esse firmitate fidei, quâ videlicet non solum indubitanter credimus promissionibus Dei, verum etiam fiduciam in nobis excitemus eas consequendi proposita nobis ante oculos Dei potentia, & veritate, & misericordia per Christum. Nam gratia & veritas per Christum facta est, Joh. I. 17. & hæc est victoria, quæ vincit mundum, fides nostra, 1. Joh. V. 4. Si mundum, igitur & mundi Principem. Ita Papistæ ipsi fiduciæ hanc gloriam relinquere coguntur. De galea spe salutis Theophylactus præeunte Chrysostomo: Quemadmodum quod principale est in nobis, caput, galea ipsa obtegens securius reddit & tutum, sic & spes ipsa mentem conservat, & salutaris illi esse arguitur, cum nihil externum in hanc sinat delabi. Imprimis spes victoriæ militem accendit ad prælium, sustentat pressum, periclitantem animat, ut omni periculo neglecto perseveret in acie ac fortiter depugnet, omniaq́ue sua ad victoriam referendam comparet. Sic læta spe æternæ beatitudinis, quæ victores manet, Thessalonicenses se munire, fulcire, animare debebant, ut imminentem hostem expectarent intrepide, irruentem exciperent fortiter, prementem pellerent strenuè, inter volitantia tela non circumspicerent temporalia, quibus à pugna revocari possint, sed dulcissimam Dei & cælestium gaudiorum fruitionem, unice cogitantes omnia sua referrent ad victoriam, quam æterna salus certo exciperet, ut Crocius in hunc locum habet.

## 5:9
ver. 9. (For God has not appointed us to wrath) He did not prepare us for this through his word, indeed, so that he might destroy us.

From this it should not be gathered, with Crocius, that others have been appointed by God to wrath. For this consequence is not legitimate, but a corpse of a consequence: He did not appoint us to wrath. Therefore, he appointed others to wrath. He does not deny, says Crocius, that some are ordained to wrath: indeed, he not obscurely hints that those who remain in darkness are appointed to it, while he denies it of the children of light. He does not hint at that in any way, not even obscurely. Crocius will admit that it does not follow: God did not appoint us by an absolute decree to eternal death. Therefore, some are appointed to death by an absolute decree of God. For he protests that he is alien to this opinion. Or: God did not call us to impurity, 1 Thess. 4:7. Therefore, he called some to impurity.

But to the obtaining of salvation) To acquire salvation. Thus, for the obtaining of glory, 2 Thess. 2:14; for the obtaining of the soul, Heb. 10:39, which is to find the soul, Matt. 20:39; to gain the soul, Luke 21:19. And briefly, peripoiesis is said for the obtaining of the soul, 2 Chron. 14:13, machiah, which elsewhere is translated as vivification.

Through our Lord Jesus Christ) Through that doctrine which Christ brought to us, not the Rabbis, not the Philosophers.

Latin:

vers. 9. Ὅτι οὐκ ἔθετο ἡμᾶς ὁ Θεὸς εἰς ὀργὴν) Non ad hoc nos paravit per verbum nempe suum, ut nos perderet.

Ex hoc colligi non debet cum Crocio, alios positos esse à Deo ad iram. Non enim hæc consequentia legitima est, sed cadaver consequentiæ: Non posuit nos ad iram. Ergo alios ad iram posuit. Non negat, inquit Crocius, aliquos ad iram ordinatos: imo non obscure innuit, qui manent in tenebris, ad eam esse positos, dum de filiis lucis negat. Nullatenus id innuit, ac ne obscure quidem. Non sequi admittet Crocius: Deus non posuit nos absoluto decreto ad mortem æternam. Ergo quidam absoluto Dei decreto positi sunt ad mortem. Ab hac enim sententia se alienum esse protestatur. Aut: Deus non vocavit nos ad impuritatem, 1. Thess. IV. 7. Ergo aliquos vocavit ad impuritatem.

Ἀλλ’ εἰς περιποίησιν σωτηρίας) Ad acquirendam salutem. Sic εἰς περιποίησιν δόξης, 2. Thess. II. 14. εἰς περιποίησιν ψυχῆς, Ebr. X. 39. quod εὑρίσκειν ψυχὴν Matth. XX. 39. κτᾶσθαι ψυχὴν Luc. XXI. 19. Et breviter περιποίησις dicitur, pro περιποίησις ψυχῆς, 2. Par. XIV. 13. מחיה quod alibi vertitur ζωοποίησις.

Διὰ τοῦ κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ χριστοῦ) Per doctrinam eam, quam Christus nobis attulit, non Rabbini, non Philosophi.

## 5:10
Who died for us) Let us not doubt that he wished what was best for us, who for our sake did not refuse even death, Rom. 5:6.

ver. 10. (That whether we wake, or sleep) Here he repeats waking and sleeping, but in another sense. For just as those who have died are said to sleep, so those who have not reached that sleep of death are said to wake. Similar to Rom. 14:8.

Together with him we might live) It matters nothing whether we live here for a long time or a short one. The outcome of both things is the same, that we may live eternally with Christ.

These things do not deal with salvation to be acquired through the doctrine of Christ, but with salvation already acquired through the merit of Christ apprehended by faith to be obtained. For acquisition concerns all commonly, just as the application and attainment of salvation is proper to the faithful. That it is about merit and not about doctrine, the appended periphrasis teaches: For how do we obtain salvation through Jesus Christ our Lord? Because and insofar as he himself died for us, and by death endured in our stead, he freed us from the punishment of death and acquired life for us. Wherefore, says Chrysostom, he did not incline to this, that he might destroy, but that he might save. But whence is it evident that he wills this? He gave his own Son for us. He so desires that we be saved that he gave his own Son, and not only gave him, but even gave him unto death. From these thoughts and considerations, hope is born. For do not despair of yourself, O man, coming to God, who for your sake did not even spare His own Son. Do not lose heart because of present evils. He who gave His only-begotten, that He might save you and snatch you from hell, whom will He spare henceforth for your salvation? Wherefore it is necessary to hope for all good things. For if we were going to a Judge who was about to judge us, and who had shown such love for us that He would sacrifice His own Son, we would not be terrified. Let us therefore hope for good and great things. For we have received the head and the sum, if we believe.

PART II.

Concerning mutual admonition and various duties of piety.

Latin:

Τοῦ ἀποθανόντος ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν) Ne dubitemus, quin nobis optime consultum voluerit, qui nostri causa nec mortem recusavit, Rom. V. 6.

vers. 10. Ἵνα εἴτε γρηγορῶμεν, εἴτε καθεύδωμεν) Hic γρηγορεῖν & καθεύδειν repetit, sed sensu alio. Nam sicut dormire dicuntur, qui mortem obiere, ita vigilare, qui ad eum mortis somnum non pervenerunt. Simile Rom. XIV. 8.

Ἅμα σὺν αὐτῷ ζήσωμεν) Nihil refert, diu hic vivamus; an parvo. Utriusque rei idem exitus, ut cum Christo æternum vivamus.

Non de acquirenda per doctrinam Christi salute, sed de acquisita salute per meritum Christi fide apprehensum consequenda hæc agunt. Acquisitio enim comuniter omnes concernit, ut applicatio & consequutio salutis fidelium est propria. Quod de merito non de doctrina agatur, periphrasis subjuncta docet: Quomodo enim per Jesum Christum Dominum nostrum consequimur salutem? Quia & quatenus ipse mortuus est pro nobis, & morte nostri vice exantlata nos à pœna mortis liberavit, nobisq; vitam acquisivit. Quamobrem, inquit Chrysostomus, non ad hoc inclinavit, ut perderet, sed ut servaret. Quod autem hoc velit, undenam constat? Filium suum dedit pro nobis. Adeo desiderat, ut nos salvi simus, ut Filium suum dederit, & non solùm dederit, sed etiam dederit in mortem. Ex his cogitationibus & considerationibus spes nascitur. Ne de te enim desperes, ò homo, ad Deum veniens, qui propter te ne Filio quidem suo pepercit. Ne propter mala præsentia animum despondeas. Qui unigenitum dedit, ut te servaret, & eriperet à gehenna, cuinam de cætero parcet pro tua salute? Quamobrem oportet omnia bona sperare. Si enim iremus ad Judicem nos judicaturum, & qui pro nobis tantam ostendisset dilectionem, ut Filium suum mactaret, non extimesceremus. Bona ergo speremus & magna. Caput enim & summam accepimus, si credimus.

PARS II.

De mutua commonitione, variisque pietatis officiis.

## 5:11
ver. 11 Διὸ παρακαλεῖτε ἀλλήλες, κὰι οἰκοδομεῖτε εἷς τὸν ἑνα) εἷς τὸν ἑνα is the same as what the Hebrews would say as ἀλλήλους: איש את איש or איש איש אחיו: admonish with words, build up with example.

καθὼς κὰι ποιεῖτε) He employs exhortations and praises alternately: as if he were saying: I urge one who is already hastening. See above IV.

Theodoret here fixes the conclusion of the first part, and explains παρακαλεῖτε as consolation: But these things are more conveniently explained by others as concerning admonition. For the Apostle exhorts and teaches how they ought to conduct themselves toward others, and first indeed toward equals or even generally, v. 11: then also toward Teachers, v. 12, 13: then specifically toward different kinds of people—the unruly, the faint-hearted, the weak, the adversaries, v. 14, 15: and how they ought to conduct themselves toward themselves, v. 16, and how toward God and His Word, v. 17, 18, 19, 20, 21. Finally, that they should abstain from every form of evil, v. 22. Not only Ambrose and B. Luther, along with our theologians, but also Calvin and most of the Reformed, [interpret this] as concerning exhortation. B. Hunnius: He says, the Apostle wishes that by meditation on the last day, each person should not only live piously and holily for himself, but also rouse others to the pursuit of the holiness of life by pious and salutary admonitions, and so each should build up each other, so that they may make progress more abundantly in the practice of piety. The Apostle added praise to his admonition, writing that the Thessalonians were doing this very thing, but nevertheless, lest they should remit anything in this duty of Christian piety, he wished to add the goad and spur of exhortation to those who were already running of their own accord.

Latin:

vers. 11 Διὸ παρακαλεῖτε ἀλλήλες, κὰι οἰκοδομεῖτε εἷς τὸν ἕνα) εἷς τὸν ἕνα idem, quod ἀλλήλυς Ebræi dicerent: איש את איש vel איש איש אחיו: monete verbis, ædificate exemplo.

καθὼς κὰι ποιεῖτε) Alternis adhibet hortamenta & laudes: quasi diceret: σπέυδοντα κὰι αὐτὸν ὀτρύνω. Vide supra IV.

Theodoretus hic figit conclusionem primæ partis, & παρακαλεῖτε de consolatione exponit: Sed convenientius ab aliis hæc explicantur de commonitione. Hortatur nempe ac docet Apostolus, quomodo sese erga alios gerere debeant, & primo quidem erga æquales vel etiam communiter, v. 11. tum etiam erga Doctores, v. 12. 13: tum specialiter erga diversi generis homines inordinatos, pusillanimes, infirmos, adversarios, v. 14. 15. & quales per se, v. 16. quales erga Deum ejusq; Verbum v. 17. 18. 19. 20. 21. sese exhibere debeant. Deniq; ut ab omnibus etiam specie malis abstineant, v. 22. De adhortatione non tantum Ambrosius & B. Lutherus cùm nostris Theologis, sed etiam Calvinus & pleriq; Reformati. B. Hunnius: Vult, inquit, Apostolus, ut meditatione novissimi diei non pro se tantum quisque pie sancteq́ vivat, sed etiam alios ad vitæ sanctimoniam sectandā piis & salutaribus admonitionibus exsuscitet, adeoq́ singuli singulos ædificent, quo in pietatis cultu uberius subinde progressus faciant. Admonitioni suæ adscripsit Apostolus laudationem, scribens, Thessalonicenses hoc ipsum facere, nihilominus vero, ne in hoc officio pietatis Christianæ aliquid remitterent, stimulum exhortationis & calcar addere voluit sponte currentibq.

## 5:12
Ἐρωτῶμεν δὲ ὑμᾶς ἀδελφοὶ) See above IV.

Εἰδέναι τὺς κοπιῶντας ἐν ὑμῖν) To look upon, that is, to regard. Here נירע Prov. XXXI, 22. is περιβλεπτός. Thus also the Latins say spectabilem (respectable/notable). Τὺς κοπιῶντας, understand, ἐν λόγῳ from 1 Tim. V. 17. This is a description of those who were leaders of the assemblies, and by a common term used by way of excellence were called ἐπίσκοποι. For the proper duty of Bishops is to teach, [that of] Presbyters is only as they are empowered by the Bishops.

κὰι προϊσταμένυς ὑμῶν) προϊστάμενοι or προεστῶτες are presbyters, as appears in 1 Tim. V. 17, ποιμένες in Eph. IV, 11, to the Hebrews פרנסים. For פרנס to shepherd is προϊστασθαι.

κὰι νοθετῦντας ὑμᾶς) Which is indeed the duty of all Christians, Rom. XV. 14, Coloss. III. 16, but by an exceptional right it pertains to presbyters, as masters of morals.

Latin:

Ἐρωτῶμεν δὲ ὑμᾶς ἀδελφοὶ) Vide supra IV.

Εἰδέναι τὺς κοπιῶντας ἐν ὑμῖν) Spectare, id est, respicere. Hic נירע Prov. XXXI, 22. περιβλεπτός ἐστι. Sic & Latini dicunt spectabilem. Τὺς κοπιῶντας, intellige, ἐν λόγῳ ex 1. Tim. V. 17. Hæc descriptio est eorum, qui cœtus erant principes, & vocabulo communi κατ’ ἐξοχὴν usurpato dicti sunt ἐπίσκοποι. Nam Episcoporum munus proprium docere, Presbyterorum non nisi qua sufficiuntur ab Episcopis.

κὰι προϊσταμένυς ὑμῶν) προϊστάμενοι sive προεστῶτες sunt presbyteri, ut apparet 1. Tim. V. 17. ποιμένες Eph. IV, 11. Ebræis פרנסים. Nam פרנס ποιμαίνειν est προϊστασθαι.

κὰι νοθετῦντας ὑμᾶς) Quod omnium quidem Christianorum est, Rom. XV. 14. Coloss. III. 16. sed eximio jure ad presbyteros pertinet, ut morum Magistros.

## 5:13
verse 13. And to esteem them exceedingly in love) He said to esteem exceedingly in this way, just as Isocrates and others say to esteem more highly. Ambrose does not translate it badly as to hold in honor, nor does the Syrian mean anything else. For in the Syrian and Rabbinic languages, חשוב means honored. He added, however, in love, because this reverence proceeds not from fear, but from love. For priests exercise the rights of no power: it is not their forced by fear, as Chrysostom says. See, if anyone has time, our work on the Law of War and Peace, II, XXII, § 14.

Because of their work) He understands here by work the ministry which they perform, which is certainly to be venerated, מעשה.

Be at peace among yourselves) among one another, just as the same sense is expressed here in Mark 9:50. Concerning this phrase, see Philippians 2:3, Colossians 3:13, 16. Be at peace, שלמו.

That by those who labor, Bishops are understood to be distinct from Presbyters, that it is not the duty of Presbyters to teach, except insofar as they are supplied by Bishops, but that presbyters are called such leaders or presiding ones, shepherds, and that the duty of admonishing, which belongs to Christians, pertains to them by special right, as teachers of morals, are purely arbitrary hypotheses, resting on no testimony of either scripture or better antiquity, which are rejected with the same ease with which they are brought forward. The office of Bishops and Presbyters is nowhere distinguished in the scriptures. And that it is the duty of Presbyters by special right to admonish, but not to teach, is said without theology. For ministerial doctrines and admonitions, or those which are appropriate to persons divinely called to that task, cannot be separated. Therefore, ancient and recent interpreters do not discriminate by duties or degrees of office, much less by Ecclesiastical power, those who labor in the Word, and who preside in the Lord, and who admonish for the sake of duty, but they acknowledge that these are parts of the Teachers of the Word: to labor in the Church, to preside in the Lord, and to admonish. Although I may have permitted mutual edification among you (so the paraphrase of Theophylact has it), I beseech you, however, that you hold in honor those who teach and instruct you. For Teachers are compelled to undergo many heavy things, which the honors bestowed upon them make easier to bear. Thus concerning those who labor in the Word; whom he also teaches to preside in the Lord, and furthermore makes them those who admonish: In those things which are of the Lord, he who has been placed in charge will not only pray for you, but will care more attentively that you may be born again through the washing of baptism, and he will chastise and heal. Even if you should wake him in the dead of night, he will be ready at once. You see what kind of leadership in the Lord is. Similarly, long before him, Chrysostom says that those who labor, those who preside, those who admonish are teachers. It is necessary, he says, that he who presides should have many occasions for depressing and casting down the spirit, just as physicians must necessarily be troublesome to the suffering in many things, preparing both foods and medicines, which indeed have no pleasure, but much utility. And just as Fathers are frequently troublesome to their children: So also are Teachers, and much more so. And furthermore, he teaches that all those are Priests. But the Apostle demands 1. the knowing, that we should acknowledge them, that is, not only that we should understand their labor, as the commentary inscribed to Jerome has it, but that we should have regard and respect for them, that we should esteem them, and treat them with their due honor. 2. to esteem them exceedingly in love, which Erasmus indeed explains as that you should hold them in the highest price through charity, with the agreement also of Bullinger and Hyperius; yet Chrysostom, Theophylact, Oecumenius, Beza, and others prefer, with Blessed Luther, to interpret it as a singular love, to be shown above other Teachers of the Word. He does not say, says Chrysostom, love absolutely, but more abundantly, just as Fathers love their children, for through them you were generated by an eternal generation. Through them you have attained the kingdom. Through their hands all things are done. Through them the heavenly gates are opened to you. Let no one stir up sedition, let no one contend. He who loves Christ, of whatever kind a Priest may be, will love him, because through him he has attained venerable sacraments. Oecumenius: That you ought to lead them in your charity, that is, consider them worthy to be loved, and not in a small way, but vehemently and beyond measure. But there is a great intensification in the word exceedingly because of the double preposition, namely the preposition over and out. 3. To be at peace, to cultivate peace, where some codices read among yourselves, as Theophylact and Oecumenius have it, others among them, as most of the ancient Latins, Blessed Luther, Calvin, and others have interpreted. The matter comes to almost the same thing, except that in the former way a mutual obligation is inferred. But because this is an admonition directed to the hearers, as to how they ought to conduct themselves toward their Teachers, the latter reading is perhaps to be preferred. For Satan objects many things, by which he strives in every way to alienate the minds of the hearers from their pastors, so that they might not, either because of calumnies devised by enemies, or because of the severity of their pastors in taxing vices, sins, or errors, pursue them with some hatred, but rather cultivate concord and peace with them, as our Blessed Hunnius does here.

Latin:

vers. 13. Καὶ ἡγεῖσθαι αὐτοὺς ὑπὲρ ἐκπερισσοῦ ἐν ἀγάπῃ) Sic dixit ἡγεῖσθαι ὑπὲρ ἐκπερισσοῦ, quomodo περὶ πλείονος ἡγεῖ- σθαι Isocrates, & alii. Honorem habere non male vertit Am- brosius, nec aliud vult Syrus. Nam חשוב Syris & Rabbi- nis est honoratus. Addidit autem ἐν ἀγάπῃ, quia hæc reve- rentia non ex timore, sed amore proficiscitur. Sacerdotes enim nullius potestatis jura exercent : non est eorum ἀναγ- κάστη φόβῳ, ut ait Chrysostomus. Vide, si cui vacat, nostra ad II. de Jure Belli ac Pacis XXII. §. 14.

Διὰ τὸ ἔργον αὐτῶν) ἔργον hic intelligit διακονίαν, qua fun- guntur, quæ certe veneranda est מעשה.

Εἰρηνεύετε ἐν ἑαυτοῖς) ἐν ἀλλήλοις, quomodo idem hic sen- sus effertur Marci IX, 50. De hac loquutione vide Philipp. II. 3. Coloss. III. 13, 16. Εἰρηνεύετε שלמו.

Per τοὺς κοπιῶντας Episcopos à Presbyteris distin- ctos intelligi, Presbyterorum non esse docere, nisi qua ab Episcopis sufficiuntur, dici autem presbyteros e- jusmodi προϊσταμένους vel προεστῶτας, ποιμένας, & ad eos τὸ νουθετεῖν, quod Christianorum est, eximio jure pertinere, ut morum magistros, hypotheses mere arbitrariæ sunt, nullo neque scripturæ neque melioris antiquitatis nitentes testimonio, quæ ea- dem facilitate rejiciuntur, qua adducuntur. Epi- scoporum & Presbyterorum munus nuspiam in scripturis distinguitur. Et admonere quidem Pres- byterorum esse eximio jure, non autem docere, ἀθεο- λόγως dicitur. Nam doctrinæ & admonitiones mi- nisteriales, vel quæ personis divinitus ad id voca- tis conveniunt, separari non possunt. Ideo inter- pretes veteres & recentiores eos, qui in Verbo la- borant, & qui præsunt in Domino, & qui admonent officii causa, non discriminant muneribus vel gra- dibus officium, nedum potestate Ecclesiastica, sed has esse partes Doctorum Verbi agnoscunt labo- rare in Ecclesia, præesse in Domino, & monere. Etsi mutuam (ita habet Theophylacti paraphrasis) vo- bis ædificationem permiserim, obsecro tamen, ut qui vos edocent atque instituunt, in honore habeatis. Co- guntur enim gravia multa subire Doctores, quæ dela- ti his honores toleratu faciunt leviora. Ita de illis, qui in Verbo laborant; quos etiam præesse in Domi- no docet, ipsosque porro νουθετοῦντας facit: In his, quæ Domini sunt, qui fuerit præfectus, pro vobis non solum orabit, sed curabit attentius, ut per baptismi lavacrum iterato nascamini, castigabitque & mede- bitur. Etsi nocte hunc intempesta vos excitaveritis, præsto mox erit. Vides qualis sit in Domino præfectu- ra. Similiter longe ante ipsum Chrysostomus: τοὺς κοπιῶντας, τοὺς προϊσταμένους, τοὺς νουθετοῦντας dicit esse διδασκάλους. Necesse est, inquit, ut qui præest, multas habeat occasiones deprimendi & dejiciendi animi, sicut medici necesse habent in multis esse molesti laborantibus, & cibos & medicamenta parantes, quæ voluptatem quidem non habent, sed multā utilitatē. Et sicut Patres crebro filiis sunt molesti: Ita etiam Doctores, & multo magis. Et porro omnes illos Sa- cerdotes esse docet. Postulat autem Apostolus 1. τὸ εἰδέναι, ut agnoscamus eos, hoc est, non tantum intelligamus laborem eorum, ut habet commen- tarius Hieronymo inscriptus, sed ut eorum ratio- nem & respectum habeamus, eos æstimemus, & ho- nore suo afficiamus. 2. ἡγεῖσθαι αὐτοὺς ἐκπερισσοῦ ἐν ἀγάπῃ, quod Erasmo quidem etiam exponit, ut ha- beatis illos in summo pretio per charitatem, annuente quoque Bullingero & Hyperio; Chrysostomo tamen, Theophylactus, Oecumenius, Beza & alii malunt cum B. Luth. de amore singulari, præ aliis Docto- ribus Verbi exhibendo, interpretari. Non dicit, in- quit Chrysostomus, absolute diligite, sed abundantius, sicut Patres filios, Per eos enim generati estis æterna ge- neratione. Per ipsos estis regnum assequuti. Per manus ipsorum fiunt omnia. Per ipsos vobis portæ cælestes a- periuntur. Nemo seditionem agitet, nemo contendat. Qui Christum diligit, cujusmodicunque sit Sacerdos, eum diliget, quod per eum veneranda sit assecuutus sacramenta. Oecumenius: Ducatis illos in charita- te vestra esse debere, hoc est, ducite ipsos dignos esse, qui diligantur, neque id exiguo modo, sed ve- hementer & supra modum. Πολλὴ δὲ ἡ ἐπίτασις τῷ ὑπὲρ κῃ τῷ ἐκ. Magna autem est intensio in di- ctione ἐκπερισσῶ propter geminam præpositio- nem, nempe præpositionem ὑπὲρ & ἐκ. 3. Εἰρη- νεύειν pacem colere, ubi nonnulli codices legunt ἐν ἑαυτοῖς, ut Theophylactus & Oecumenius habent, alii ἐν αὐτοῖς, ut Latini veteres plerique, B. Lu- therus, Calvinus, aliique interpretati sunt. Res eo- dem fere recidit, nisi quod priori modo mutua ob- ligatio inferatur. Sed quia hæc ad auditores di- recta est admonitio, quales se erga Doctores exhi- bere debeant, posterior lectio fortassis præferen- da. Etenim multa Satanas objicit, quibus animos auditorum à suis pastoribus quoquo modo nititur abalienare, ne vel ob calumnias, ab hostibus excogi- tatas, vel ob severitatem pastorum suorum in taxan- dis vitiis, peccatis, aut erroribus illos odio aliquo prosequantur, sed potius concordiam atque pacem cum iis colant, ut hic B. Hunnius noster.

## 5:14
verse 14. And we beseech you, brethren) It is the custom of Paul after general admonitions to append those things which were most necessary for those times and places.

Admonish the unruly) That is, those walking in a disorderly manner, 1 Thessalonians 3:6, 11, those acting in a disorderly manner, 2 Thessalonians 3:7. Thus unruly is a Platonic term, which exceeds the rule, just as a vast, uncultivated land, void, unruly according to Aquila, Deuteronomy 32:10. On the contrary, those who do all things rightly and in order are called orderly. In the Glossary: Orderliness is temperance. Cicero says that is orderliness, in which the preservation of order is understood.

Παραμυθεῖσθαι τὲς ὀλιγοψύχως) Those who are dejected in spirit during adversities, Isa. 58:15. דַּכָּא in Greek ὀλιγόψυχος. In the same way עֲצוּב רוּחַ is translated, Isa. 54:6, and שְׁפַל רוּחַ, Isaiah 57:15, and נְכֵאָה, Prov. 18:14. In the Glossary ὀλιγοψυχία, pusillanimity. Horace: - - inopiæ me quodque pusilli Finxerunt animi.

Ἀντέχεσθε τ ἄθενῶν) Tolerate those who do not fully understand Christian liberty. For they are ἀθενεῖς or ἀσθενῶντες, Rom. 14:1, 2; 1 Cor. 8:7, 11, 12. But ἀντέχεσθαι is to sustain as if grasped by the hand. Thus it is translated מַחֲזִיק & תֹמֵךְ, help the weak; Ambrose is not bad here.

Theophylact and Lombard wish these things to be said to teachers, but they are more correctly held by most others to be common precepts, not only accommodated to those times as Grotius wishes. For there are always found in the Church some unruly ones, some faint-hearted ones, some weak ones. He wishes those not to be held in hatred, but to be admonished. By the word νυθετεῖτε it is implied that they are not endowed with a sufficiently sound mind, and therefore there is a need that they be recalled to a sound mind. He wishes these to be raised up by consolation, but a firm one, so that they may be established by just reasons. He commands these to be supported in faith and in life, not to be further prostrated, consumed, and rejected, Rom. 14:1. Admonish the disorderly ἀτάκτως, that is, as B. Hunnius interprets, who do not live according to τάξιν, the order, norm, and form of Evangelical discipline, but live dissolutely, or even flagitiously. He wishes these to be admonished, so that, having abandoned that disorderly manner of living, they may compose themselves to the prescribed rule of Christian life. Comfort the faint-hearted, ὀλιγοψύχες, that is, anxious consciences, terrified by the sense of sins and the wrath of God, and dejected by other temptations or calamities. He commands these to be raised up by the consolation of the Gospel. Support the weak, who are weak in faith regarding some part of doctrine, or the use of indifferent things; he commands these to be supported and established by necessary and gentle instruction and their infirmities to be tolerated.

Μακροθυμεῖτε πρὸς πάντας) As much as possible, hope for better things from everyone. See 1 Cor. 13:4.

Those whom he had mentioned seem to be regarded, and long-suffering, as the word implies, and patience are required, if admonition, consolation, and support should not immediately find their place among the disorderly, the faint-hearted, and the weak. Thus Theophylact: This is to support the dissolute, the faint-hearted, and the weak. For that is in the highest degree appropriate for teachers, that by tolerating even the most savage they may convert them to good. In general, however, all can be understood, as the blessed Hunnius interprets. Since no one in this life is perfect in every way, but that some infirmities always cling to him, he advises that all be tolerated with equanimity, and that the repentance of even impious men be patiently awaited.

Latin:

vers. 14. Παρακαλῶμεν δὲ ὑμᾶς ἀδελφοὶ) Mos Pauli post generalia monita attexere illa, quæ temporibus illis ac locis maxime erant necessaria.

Νυθετεῖτε τὲς ἀτάκτες) Id est περιπατῶντας ἀτάκτως, 1. Thess. III. 6. 11. ἀτακτῶντας 2. Thess. III. 7. Sic ἄτακτος אָפַרְ- תִישׁ Platonica, quæ regulam excedit, sicut terra vasta, incul- ta, תֹהוּ ἄτακτος Aquilæ, Deut. XXXII. 10. E contrario qui recte atque ordine cuncta faciunt, dicuntur εὐτακτοι. In Glossario: Εὐταξία temperantia. Cicero illam esse ait εὐτα- ξίαν, in qua intelligitur ordinis conservatio.

Παραμυθεῖσθαι τὲς ὀλιγοψύχως) Eos, qui in adversis animo sunt dejecto, Es. LVIII. 15. דַּכָּא in Græco ὀλιγόψυχος. Eo- dem modo vertitur עֲצוּב רוּחַ Es. LIV. 6. & שְׁפַל רוּחַ Esaiz LVII. 15. & נְכֵאָה Prov. XVIII. 14. In Glossario ὀλι- γοψυχία, pusillanimitas. Horatius: - - inopiæ me quodque pusilli Finxerunt animi.

Ἀντέχεσθε τ ἄθενῶν) Tolerate eos, qui libertatem Chri- stianam non plane intelligunt. Illi enim ἀθενεῖς vel ἀσθενῶν- τες, Rom. XIV. 1. 2. 1. Cor. VIII. 7. 11. 12. Ἀντέχεσθαι vero est sustentare velut manu prehensum. Sic vertitur מַחֲזִיק & תֹמֵךְ, opitulamini infirmis, Ambrosius hic non male.

Doctoribus hæc dici volunt Theophylactus & Lombardus, sed rectius ab aliis plerisque habentur communia præcepta, non tantum ut Grotius vult ad ista tempora accommodata. Semper enim in Ec- clesia inveniuntur nonnulli ἄτακτοι, nonnulli ὀλιγό- ψυχοι, nonnulli ἀσθενεῖς. Illos non odio haberi, sed moneri vult. Verbo νυθετεῖτε innuitur, eos non sa- tis sana mente præditos, opus ergo esse, ut ad men- tem sanam revocentur. Istos solatio vult erigi, sed firmo, ut justis rationibus constituantur. Hosce sublevari jubet in fide & in vita, non ulterius pro- sterni, affumi & rejici, Rom. XIV. 1. Monete inordi- natos ἀτάκτως, hoc est, interprete B. Hunnio, qui non vivunt secundum τάξιν, ordinem, normam ac formam disciplinæ Evangelicæ, sed vivunt dissolute, vel etiam flagitiose. Hos vult moneri, ut omissa illa inordinata ratione vivendi se ad præscriptam vitæ Christianæ regulam componant. Consolamini pu- sillanimes, ὀλιγοψύχες, id est, conscientias anxias, sensu peccatorum & iræ Dei perterrefactas, & aliis tentationibus vel calamitatibus dejectas. Has jubet erigi consolatione Evangelii. Sublevate infirmos, qui in fide circa aliquam doctrinæ partem, aut rerum indifferentium usum infirmi sunt, hos præcipit sub- levari & stabiliri necessaria ac mansueta institutione & illorum infirmitates tolerari.

Μακροθυμεῖτε πρὸς πάντας) Quantum fieri potest, de omnibus sperate meliora. Vide 1. Cor. XIII. 4.

Videntur illi, quos dixerat, respici, & longani- mitas, ut vox infert, ac patientia requiri, si non sta- tim monitio, consolatio, susceptio penes inordi- natos, pusillanimes & infirmos locum suum inve- niat. Ita Theophylactus: Hoc est dissolutos, pusillani- mes & infirmos sustinere. Id namq; maximum in mo- dum congruit Praeceptoribus, ut vel efferatissimos to- lerando ad bonum convertant. In genere tamen omnes intelligi possunt, ut B. Hunnius interpreta- tur. Cùm nemo in hac vita sit undiquaq; perfectus, quin aliquae semper ei infirmitates adhaereant, monet, aquanimiter tolerari omnes, & hominum impiorum quoque resipiscentiam patienter expectari.

## 5:15
V. 15. See that no one renders evil for evil to anyone. The same words are in Rom. XII. 17, which are explained in the same place XII. 19. See also Matth. V. 38 and following. It is not for servants to avenge themselves, but to permit the Lord the vengeance of their injuries.

But always pursue what is good. Be zealous for the advantages of others. Thus agathon is taken in Matth. VII. 11, Luc. I. 53, XII. v. 18, 19, 25, Gal. VI. 6.

The word diōkein implies singular zeal: Follow what is good; that is, strive intensely to do good, says Theophylact. We pursue a fugitive with the intention and effort of catching him, cf. Rom. XII. v. 13, 1 Cor. XIV. v. 1, 1 Tim. VI. 1, Heb. XII. 14.

And towards one another) towards Christians.

And towards all) even towards those outside the faith.

Latin:

V. 15. Ὁρᾶτε, μή τις κακὸν ἀντὶ κακῶ τινι ἀποδῶ) Eadem verba Rom. XII. 17. quæ exponuntur ibidem XII. 19. Vide & Matth. V. 38. & seqq. Servorum non est, se ulcisci, sed Domino ultionem injuriarum suarum permittere.

Ἀλλὰ πάντοτε τὸ ἀγαθὸν διώκετε) Alienis commodis stu- dete. Sic ἀγαθὸν sumitur Matth. VII. 11. Luc. I. 53. XII. v. 18. 19. 25. Gal. VI. 6.

Verbum διώκειν singulare studium infert: Se- ctamini quod bonum est; id est, impensè studete be- nefacere, inquit Theophylactus. Fugientem perse- quimur cum intentione & contentione ipsum ap- prehendendi, conf. Rom. XII. v. 13. 1. Cor. XIV. v. 1. 1. Tim. VI. 1. Ebr. XII. 14.

Καὶ εἰς ἀλλήλες) erga Christianos.

Καὶ εἰς πάντας) etiam erga extraneos à fide.

## 5:16
Vers. 16. Always rejoice) Be of equable mind, Rom. XII. v. 12, 2 Cor. VI. 10, 1 Pet. IV. 13, Matth. V. 12.

Always, that is, even in the midst of and urgent evils be affected with joy, as if he were saying: Tolerate all things for Christ with an equable mind. Note, however, how after he had said that evil is not to be rendered for evil, he immediately enjoined that one should also rejoice in these things. For he who has been taught to avenge no injuries, but has rather become accustomed to conferring benefits, and to doing good to those who have brought evils, whence will he be able to receive the stings of sorrow, says Theophylact.

Latin:

Vers. 16. Πάντοτε χαίρετε) Æquo este animo, Rom. XII. v. 12. 2. Cor. VI. 10. 1. Pet. IV. 13. Matth. V. 12.

Semper, hoc est, vel in mediis & urgentibus malis gaudio afficiamini, tanquam id dicat: Æquo animo pro Christo omnia tolerate. Adverte autem quemad- modum postquā malum minus esse pro malo redden- dum dixisset, mox & gaudendum his esse injunxerit. Qui enim edoctus nullas ulcisci injurias, sed confe- rendis beneficiis potius insuevit, & his benefacere, qui mala intulerint, unde hic poterit mæroris acu- leos excipere, inquit Theophylactus.

## 5:17
V. 17. Pray without ceasing) Thus above II. 13, adialeiptōs, that is, en panti kairō Eph. VI. 18, pantote Col. I. 2.

Not indeed that because of the assiduity of continuous prayers it is not permitted to be free for other parts of divine worship as well, or even for the labors of one's ordinary vocation, or furthermore for honest and lawful joys. But they are said to pray unceasingly who do not intermit any day without praying at set hours, and who, while they enjoy other labors and sometimes even external joys, yet ones permitted by the word of God, nevertheless retain a mind always prepared for praying, and even in their own joys, labors, and works of vocation, they intermix prayers from time to time, if not always with the mouth, yet with the spirit and mind, as the blessed Hunnius rightly says in this place. In vain, therefore, did the Euchites in Augustine, heresy LVII, contend from this passage that Christians ought to do nothing else than pray always.

Latin:

V. 17. Ἀδιαλείπτως προσεύχεσθε) Sic supra II. 13. ἀδια- λείπτως, id est, ἐν παντὶ καιρῷ Eph. VI. 18. πάντοτε Col. I. 2.

Non quidem quod præ assiduitate precum conti- nuata non liceat vacare aliis quoq; divini cultus par- tibus, vel etiam laboribus ordinariæ vocationis, vel gaudiis insuper honestis atq; licitis. Sed indesinenter orare dicuntur, qui diem nullum intermittunt, quin statise horis precentur, & qui, dum aliis laboribus et- iam ac nonnunquam externis, sed verbo Dei concessis gaudiis fruuntur, nihilominus animum retinent ad precandum semper paratum, & suis etiam gaudiis, laboribus & operibus vocationis preces subinde admi- scent, sinon semper ore, attamen spiritu atque men- te, ut recte hoc loco B. Hunnius. Frustrà ergo Eu- chetæ apud Augustinum hæres. LVII. contende- bant ex hoc loco, Christianos nihil aliud agere debere, quàm ut semper orent.

## 5:18
Vers. 18. In everything give thanks) Give thanks to God for all things: even for adverse ones. For these too are good, if they are taken rightly. The same sense is in Eph. V. 20.

For this is the will of God in Christ Jesus toward you) Clarius in the Manuscript: For this is the will of God toward you in Christ Jesus. But it is a Metonymy of the cause placed for the effect. This, he says, is what God requires of you through Christ. We have this θέλημα in Eph. VI. 6. Col. IV. 12. But that τῦτο is to be referred not only to thanksgiving, but also to prayers. Concerning thanksgiving, see the Examples of Christ, Matt. XV. 36. ch. XXVI. 27. Mark VIII. 6. ch. XIV. 23. Luke XVII. 16. ch. XVIII. 11. XXII. 17. 19. John VI. 11. 23. 41. Concerning prayers, we have very many of his precepts and examples in Luke XVIII. 1.

Indeed, this reason pertains not only to prayers and thanksgiving, but also to the other duties of piety, about which the Apostle had warned. For God wills and commands all these things, and even the law of nature divinely inscribed, which requires that as you wish others to show you, you also show those things to others: Bullinger, Hyperius, and Cornelius à Lapide refer to all those things.

Latin:

Vers. 18. Ἐν παντὶ εὐχαριστεῖτε) De rebus omnibus Deo gratias agite: etiam de adversis. Nam & hæc bona sunt, si dextrè sumantur. Idem sensus Eph. V. 20.

Τῦτο γὰρ θέλημα Θεὲ ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησῦ εἰς ὑμᾶς) Clarius in Manuscripto: Τῦτο γάρ ἐστι θέλημα Θεῦ εἰς ὑμᾶς ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησῦ. Est autem Μετωνυμία causæ positæ pro effectu. Hoc, ait, est, quod Deus à vobis exigit per Christum. Hic θέλημα habemus Eph. VI. 6. Col. IV. 12. Illud autem τῦτο referen- dum non ad gratiarum tantum actionem, sed & ad preces. De gratiarum actione vide Christi Exempla, Matth. XV. 36. cap. XXVI. 27. Marci VIII. 6. cap. XIV. 23. Luc. XVII. 16. c. XVIII. 11. XXII. 17. 19. Joh. VI. 11. 23. 41. De precibus præcepta ejusdem habem9 plurima & exempla Luc. XIIX. 1.

Imo non ad preces tantùm & gratiarum actio- nem, sed ad cætera etiam officia pietatis, de quibus monuerat Apostolus, hæc ratio pertinet. Hæc enim omnia Deus vult ac præcipit, & vel lex na- turæ divinitus insculpta, quæ vultis, ut alii vobis exhibeant, exhibere & vos ista aliis requirit: Ad omnia illa refert Bullingerus, Hyperius, Cornelius à Lapide.

## 5:19
V. 19. Do not quench the Spirit) The Spirit here are the gifts of healings and tongues, which, just as they were given in the form of fire, are rightly compared to fire, and therefore are said both to be stirred up, 2 Tim. 1. 6, and on the contrary to be quenched. They are stirred up by prayers, thanksgiving, and the perpetual pursuit of piety: they are quenched by the opposites. For in the New Testament, especially after the Churches were established, God does not wish to give or preserve those gifts, unless to those who believe and live piously. See Mark XVI. 17.

Why the gifts of healings and tongues? Which are only ministering [gifts], and were suitable only for certain persons at a certain time, and it is doubtful whether they flourished then in the Church of the Thessalonians? Why then should we not rather understand the sanctifying gifts, as most interpreters do, which are common to all the faithful? For all are warned not to quench those in themselves through unbelief and voluntary sins committed against conscience, but rather to strive to preserve them. So that it may be a litotes. Devote effort, so that you do not quench that torch and light of the grace of the Holy Spirit kindled in your hearts, either by sins against conscience, or by neglect of the Word and Sacraments, or even by the omission of prayer..., but that by the hearing of the Word and the use of the Sacraments this flame of the divine Spirit may be nourished and cherished, and that you may seek, in addition, by pious prayers to be confirmed in the grace of the Holy Spirit once received, as the Hunnian paraphrase has it. In the word of quenching there is a metaphor taken from a lamp, which is extinguished by a lack of oil, or by the throwing in of dust of the earth or mud, or by the blowing of the wind. Therefore, Theophylact beautifully says: Since this life is to be considered in the place of night, and God has brought us the torch of the Holy Spirit, which many have indeed rendered more splendid, just as the saints. But some have allowed themselves to be extinguished, just as those virgins who had allowed their lamp to lack oil. And no differently, he who was committing fornication at Corinth cast mud upon this same torch. He says, therefore, do not quench the Spirit, that is, the grace of the Spirit. Block up, therefore, the windows, or these bodily senses, so that wickedness may not invade that spirit, and thus that torch will not be able to be extinguished. Do not sprinkle dust or earthly cares. For thus it will remain unquenchable. There are indeed those who explain [it] concerning the ministering gift, but [concerning] prophecies with Theodoret and some among Chrysostom and Theophylact, as also with Ambrosiaster, who interprets it thus: It is not easily forbidden to anyone speaking through the Spirit: But the following admonition commands concerning the gift of prophecy not being despised, but being held reverently.

Latin:

V. 19. Τὸ πνεῦμα μὴ σβέννυτε) Spiritus hic sunt dona sa- nationum & linguarum, quæ sicut in ignis forma data erant, ita igni recte comparantur, ac proinde dicuntur & fufcitari, 2. Tim. 1. 6. & contra exstingui. Sufcitantur precibus, gratia- rum actione, ac perpetuo studio pietatis: exstinguuntur per contraria. Nam in N. T. maxime post constitutas Ecclesias Deus illa dona non vult dare aut servare, nisi credentibus & pie viventibus. Vide Marc. XVI. 17.

Cur dona fanationum & linguarum? Quæ mini- strantia tantum sunt, & certo tempore certis perso- nis solum conveniebant, dubiumq; est, an in Eccle- sia Thessalonicensium tum viguerint? Quidni ergo potius dona sanctificantia cum plerisq; interpreti- bus intelligamus, quæ omnibus fidelib9 sunt com- munia? Monentur enim omnes, ne illa in se extin- guant per incredulitatem, ac peccata voluntaria co- tra conscientiam admissa, sed poti9 conservare stu- deant. Ut λιτότης sit.
