Date operam, ut illam facem atq; lucem gratiæ Spiritus S. accensam in cordibus ve- stris non extinguatis, vel per peccata contra conscien- tiam, vel neglectu Verbi & Sacramentorum, vel etiam omissione preci …, sed ut auditu Verbi & usu Sacra- mentorum hæc flamma divini Spiritus alatur ac fo- veatur, & piis insuper precibus confirmari vos in gra- tia Spiritus S. semel accepta petatis, ut habet Hun- niana paraphrasis. In verbo extinguendi metapho- ra est à lampade desumpta, quæ extinguitur olei defectu, vel injecto pulvere terræ aut luto, vel ven- ti flatu. Pulchre itaq; Theophylactus: Cum noctis lo- co sit hæc vita habenda, & facem nobis detulit Deus Spiritum S. quam sanè splendidiorem reddidere ple- riq;, quemadmodum sancti. Nonnulli verò extinguî sunt passi, quemadmodum virgines illæ, quæ lucer- nam oleo carere permiserant. Nec secus & qui Co- rinthi fornicaretur, eandem hanc facem luto offudit. Dicit itaq;, Spiritum nolite restinguere, hoc est, Spi- ritus gratiam. Obstruite ergo fenestras, sive sensus hos corporales, ne nequitia spiritus ille invadat, & sic fax illa extingui non poterit. Non pulverem inspergas vel curas terrenas. Sic enim inextinguibilis perma- nebit. Sunt quidem, qui de dono ministrante, sed prophetias explicant cum Theodoreto ac nonnullis apud Chrysostomum & Theophylactum, ut & Ambro- siastro, qui ita interpretatur: Non facile alicui per Spiritum loquenti interdicitur: Sed de prophetiæ dono non contemnendo, sed reverenter habendo sequens monitum præcipit.

## 5:20
V. 20. Do not despise prophecies) It is a litotes. For he wishes prophecy to be valued most highly among all things, 1 Cor. XIV. 5.

But by prophecies he does not understand predictions of future events: For who knows that such Prophets were there? But the interpretation of Scripture, which is named thus for the sake of honor, and let dignity and authority be reconciled to good interpreters of Scripture, not that they are held in an equal place with Prophets, who by the impulse of the Holy Spirit predict future things, or even deliver divine mysteries through divine inspiration, such as the extraordinary Prophets of both kinds were, for those shone with divine authority: But because the prophecies of sacred Scripture are to be explained by the same Spirit by which they were brought and inspired. Prophecy, says the blessed Hunnius, here signifies the interpretation of Scripture. He does not wish this to be despised, or an interpretation brought forth by another to be immediately rejected out of prejudice, but he advises that it be weighed, so that, if it is consonant with the analogy of faith, it may be admitted.

Latin:

V. 20. Προφητείας μὴ ἐξουθενεῖτε) Est λιτότης. Vult enim inter omnia maximi fieri prophetiam, 1. Cor. XIV. 5.

Per prophetias autem non intelligit prædictiones futurorum: Quis enim scit, tales Prophetas ibi fuisse? Sed interpretationem scripturæ, quæ hono- ris causa ita nominatur, & dignitas & autoritas bonis interpretibus Scripturæ concilietur, non quod parili loco cum Prophetis, Spiritus Sancti impulsu futura prædicentibus, aut etiam mysteria divina per afflatum divinum tradentibus, quales utriusque generis Prophetæ erant extraordinarii, habeantur, illi enim divina fulgebant autoritate: Sed quod eodem Spiritu explicandæ sint prophe- tiæ Scripturæ sacræ, quo allatæ sunt & inspiratæ. Prophetia, inquit B. Hunnius, hic interpretationem scripturæ significat. Hanc non vult contemni, vel ex præjudicio statim rejici interpretationem ab alio pro- latam, sed expendi monet, ut, si analogiæ fidei conso- na sit, admittatur.

## 5:21
V. 21. Testing all things, hold fast to what is good) This pertains to the discernings of spirits, 1 Cor. XII. 10. XIV. 29, where see the things said. Thus 1 John IV. v. 1. test the spirits. Therefore, all things here must be restricted from the preceding to those things which are said by those who claim to be Prophets.

Because false prophets were mingling themselves with true Doctors or Prophets, some seem to have despised the whole ministry of the Word because of that, [and] others to have rashly given credence to anyone whatsoever: therefore, just as the Apostle taught that prophecies were not to be opposed; so not everything that is sold as prophecy is to be received, but to be tested against the touchstone of Scripture, so that nothing is admitted unless it is analogous to the faith, and that what the word κατέχετε demands may be held firmly and constantly, Rom. XII. 6.

Latin:

V. 21. Πάντα δοκιμάζοντες τὸ καλὸν κατέχετε) Hoc pertinet ad διακρίσεις πνευμάτων, 1. Cor. XII. 10. XIV. 29. ubi dicta vide. Sic 1. Joh. IV. v. 1. δοκιμάζετε τὰ πνεύματα. Ergo πάντα hic restringendum ex antecedente ad ea, quæ dicun- tur ab eis, qui se Prophetas dictitant.

Quia veris Doctorib9 vel Prophetis Pseudopro- phetæ se immiscbant, nonnulli videntur inde totum ministerium Verbi contempsisse, alii quibusvis te- mere fidem adhibuisse: ut ergo prophetias no op- ponendas docuit Apostolus; sic non recipienda o- mnia, quæ venditatur ceu prophetiæ, sed explora- da ad lydium scripturæ lapidem, ut nō nisi analoga fidei admittantur, & quod verbum κατέχετε postu- lat, firmiter & constanter teneantur, Rom. XII. 6.

## 5:22
V. 22. Abstain from every form of evil) Christians ought to abstain not only from evil things, but also from those which have the appearance of evil. Εἶδος πονηρὸν is the דומה רע of the Rabbis. See an example in 1 Cor. VIII, 10.

Calvin and Hyperius also refer this to doctrine: but Crocius more correctly says that it is subjoined as a summary of the whole of piety in the place of a concluding flourish. It simultaneously comprises, says Theodoret, those things which pertain to dogmas and those which pertain to morals: for he does not enjoin abstinence from this or that, as Theophylact teaches, but from every thing entirely, whether from any false and fictitious prophet, or from any wicked deeds whatsoever. Moreover, he wishes one to abstain not only from evil, but also from that which has the appearance of evil, so that, namely, no one may be affected by scandal. He does not say from this or that, but from every appearance of evil, says Chrysostom.

Latin:

V. 22. Ἀπὸ παντὸς εἴδες πονηρῦ ἀπέχεσθε) Christiani non à rebus malis tantum, sed ab iis, quæ speciem habent mali, abstinere debent. Εἶδος πονηρὸν דומה רע Rabbinis. Ex- emplum vide 1. Cor. VIII, 10.

Ad doctrinam etiam referunt Calvinus & Hype- rius: sed rectius Crocius id velut totius pietatis sum- marium coronidis vice subjici ait. Simul compre- bendit ea, inquit Theodoret9, quæ ad dogmata & quæ ad mores pertinent: Neque enim hoc illove, docente Theophylacto, abstinendŭ indicit, sed omni re prors9, sive propheta quovis falso & commentitio, sive pravis quibusvis facinoribus. Abstineri autem vult non tantùm à malo, sed etiam ab eo, quod speciem mali habet, ne sc. quis scandalo afficiatur. Non ait ab illa, ab ista, sed ab omni specie mali, inquit Chrysostomus.

## 5:23
Vers. 23. And may the God of peace himself sanctify you wholly) It is not enough for us to do our duty by admonishing; there is also need of the inspiration of God for holiness. He called him the God of peace, because peace is no small part of this holiness. So also Rom. 15, 33. 16, 20. 1 Cor. 14, 33. 2 Cor. 13, 11. Phil. 4, 9. Ὁλοτελεῖς means from every part.

After admonitions and prayers he introduces [this], says Theophylact, so that they may be safer on both sides. He calls him the God of peace, not only because he is the author of concord among us, but because he primarily works peace and internal tranquility of the soul, which is called the peace of God, Phil. IV. 7, and peace with God, Rom. V. 1. This epithet fits well not only because of the perpetual joy in the Lord, which the Apostle had requested, v. 16, which is nothing without the interior peace of the heart, Rom. XIV. 17, but also because of the rules which he had prescribed for the sake of external peace, and also because of the prayer for holiness, which is not true without a zeal for concord and peace.

And may your whole spirit, and soul, and body be preserved blameless in the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ) There is a zeugma here. For ὁλόκληρον means entire, solid in the Glossary, well-constituted in all its parts. And ἐν τῇ παρουσίᾳ is used for εἰς τὴν παρουσίαν, as also above III. 13, to be preserved, namely, by GOD. Man consists of two parts, soul and body, Matth. X. 28, and the soul is sometimes called πνεῦμα. But to the Rabbis, נפש is the vital soul, רוח is the sentient soul, and נשמה is the intelligent soul. But πνεῦμα in this place is that Holy Spirit dwelling in the souls of Christians, and if it is solicitously preserved, it adheres to the souls even until death, and indeed even after death until the resurrection. See what we said at 1 Cor. XV. 44, and Jerome at Gal. V. All the Greeks explain spirit in this place as a gift (χάρισμα). Philo [explains it] by allegories: That which breathes is God, that which receives is the mind, and that which is breathed into is the spirit. Irenaeus V. 6. But if the spirit is lacking to the soul, he who is such is truly animal, and being left carnal, he will be imperfect, having indeed the image in the formation, but not assuming the likeness through the spirit. And afterwards: And for this reason the Apostle, explaining himself, clarified the perfect and spiritual salvation of man in the first [epistle] to the Thessalonians, saying: And may the God of peace sanctify you perfect, that your whole spirit and soul and body may be preserved without complaint unto the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ. And what reason indeed did he have to pray for the entire and perfect preservation of these three, that is, soul, and body, and spirit, at the coming of the Lord, unless he knew that the salvation of them all was one and the same, through the integration and union of the three? For which reason he also calls them perfect who exhibit the three without complaint to the Lord. They are perfect, therefore, who have both the Spirit of God persevering in them, and have preserved their souls and bodies without complaint. Tatian: For the soul did not save the spirit itself, but it was saved by it, and the light overcame the darkness. The Word is the light of God, but the unillumined soul is darkness. For this reason, when it dwells alone, it inclines toward matter, dying together with the flesh. But having acquired the union of the Divine spirit, it is not helpless. It ascends to those places to which the spirit leads it. For the one is the dwelling place above, but the other is the generation from below. Clem. Strom. VI, after enumerating the nine faculties of the soul, adds: And the tenth is the characteristic property of the Holy Spirit, which comes through faith. Tertullian: The spirit, which approaches the soul of God or of a demon. And note in these words of Paul, blamelessly (ἀμέμπτως), just as blamelessly (ἀμέμπτως) above III. 13.

Grotius's opinion is perplexed; especially let the notes on 1 Cor. XV. 10 be compared. For who is that Holy Spirit dwelling in the souls of Christians, if not the third person of the Most Holy Trinity, whose temple the faithful are? But who would admit that he is reckoned among the parts of man? However, Grotius distinguishes the Holy Spirit in 1 Cor. XV from that spirit in man, which he says is in the place of the soul in the glorious body, and of which he constitutes the Spirit, who is given to Christians in this life, as the earnest. Which I confess I am unable to understand. Perhaps Grotius himself did not understand it either, so intricate are they. Others, however, understand those three in this place, either as man is viewed according to his nature, or according to the grace of regeneration. But as for nature, there are not three natural parts in man, since, besides those two, the rational soul and the organic body, man, physically considered, has no substantial parts, as Scripture and sounder philosophy testify. Although, therefore, some understand by those three designated by Paul a triple soul, or rather faculties of the soul, just as Theophylact reports concerning the exposition of Greg. Nyss.: Since man is composed of every species of soul, namely that which is in plants, then the sentient, and the intellectual, when the Apostle says Spirit, he surely expressed the intellectual: when soul, the sensibility itself: when body, he shows that life is in us, which is also found to be in plants. Which, however, has no place, since the body of man is not a faculty of the soul, but is distinguished from the soul as another substantial part, and is expressly named here. By that very fact, however, three substantial parts of man are not established. This must also be held regarding the opinion of those who call the πνεῦμα (spirit) the rational soul, but by ψυχὴν (soul) understand the sentient and vegetative soul. They certainly do not make three substantial parts of man, but retain those two which we have mentioned, and wish the soul of man to be designated only distinctly with regard to its higher faculty and with regard to its lower, in which way Calvin, Beza, Zanchius, and Piscator—as Crocius notes, with them in agreement—take the spirit as the higher part of the soul, by which we are wise and understand, which is wont to be called the mind; the soul as the lower faculties; and the body as the common dwelling place, not because the Apostle establishes two souls, but they interpret it as multiple faculties of one soul in one body. This is also the explanation of the blessed Hunnius: By spirit he understands the most noble power of the human soul, which distinguishes men from brutes, namely the mind and the will. By soul he understands the remaining faculties of the soul, which themselves also need to be sanctified and subjected to the Holy Spirit. Therefore, he prays that the whole man, sanctified and blameless in mind, soul, and body, or immune from external crimes, may be preserved on the day of the coming of the Lord Jesus: as also the ministry of Lübeck, Hamburg, and Lüneburg in the detailed report on the new prophets §. 326. Man must be considered according to a twofold state; one according to the natural, thus he has no more than body and soul: but if one wished to change the usual way of speaking, and as Luther in the fourth volume Part reports fol. 16, that he is accustomed to lead Moses; by the soul they understand the mere life, which fish, birds, and other animals have in common with man; but they call the powers of the human soul, such as understanding and will, the spirit; thus man has indeed body, soul, and spirit, but the spirit would not be an essential piece, but only the powers which are not given to other animals: according to which consideration St. Paul prays 1 Thess. 5:23, that God may preserve the body and life, high and low powers of the Christians, blameless until the day of the Lord Jesus. Since, however, man can also be viewed with regard to the grace of regeneration or in theological consideration according to this trichotomy, some understand by spirit the grace and gifts of the Spirit, with Chrysostom and Theophylact, as they acknowledge that the substantial parts of man themselves are designated by soul and body, or they take spirit as that which is found in man, insofar as he is a new creature, according to that saying of Christ in John 3:6: 'That which is born of the Spirit is spirit.' Aretius has it thus:

There are three integral parts of a reborn man: πνεῦμα, ψυχὴ & σῶμα. The spirit is ἡγεμονικὸν, that is, the leader and governor, forming new motions in the reborn, subjecting the will to the will of God. The ψυχὴ is ἐπιθυμητικὸν, to which are added τὰ πάθη in general: likewise the sensitive faculty: judgment, reason not purged by the Holy Spirit. The body is the organ of these: for it provides an instrument for diverse actions, and is as it were σῆμα, the prison and sepulcher of the soul. These integral parts belong to the reborn man, whereas of the physical man there are at least two, ψυχὴ & σῶμα. Hence is born the twofold man: ψυχικὸς, who is σαρκικὸς, who lives the life of an un-reborn man: and πνευματικὸς, who is reborn, and adorns his profession with life and morals, in whom reigns the Holy Spirit, the dictator of life, 1 Cor. II. So he. The Tripolitan ministry, recently praised in a public writing opposed to the fanatics (whose author was the blessed Dr. Nicolaus Hunnius), §. 326. regarding this later consideration of man, delivered the following explanation, which he left in the middle with the former: 'Afterwards man is considered according to his spiritual state; there he has body and soul, but also above these the powers of the Holy Spirit, which dwell in man, which are called the Spirit. In which sense a reborn man has three pieces in himself: body, soul, and spirit, of which the first two are natural, but the third is supernatural. And in this sense St. Paul wished that Christians be preserved until the end not only according to body and soul, but also in and with the gifts of the Spirit.' Our Luther’s interpretation, inasmuch as he refers not only the spirit to the renewal of man, but also the soul and body, and considers these three in man not physically, but theologically, namely under the reason and state of regeneration and renewal. I will add the words of the Great Man ἰδιογλώττως, which are as follows, Tom. I. Altenb. on the Magnificat p. 758: "The first part, the spirit, is the highest, noblest part of man, by which he is fitted to grasp incomprehensible, invisible, eternal things, and is in short the house where faith and God’s Word dwell. The second, the soul, is the very same spirit according to nature, but yet in another work, namely in that as it makes the body alive and works through it, and is often taken in Scripture for the life. For the spirit may well live without the body, but the body not without the spirit." 'This piece we see, how it also lives and works in sleep and without ceasing, and its nature is not to grasp incomprehensible things, but what reason can know and measure, and namely reason is here the light in this house, and where the spirit is not enlightened with faith as with a higher light, this light of reason rules, so it can never be without error. The third is the body with its members, whose work are only exercises and use, after the soul knows and the spirit believes.' We acquiesce to the former interpretation, as it seems the simplest, according to which Crocius did not poorly render the sense of this passage in this way: I pray and desire uniquely, not that any part, but that your whole mind, whole will, all faculties, all your senses, and all the powers of your body be preserved in holiness, so that the whole body may be subjected to the soul, the whole soul to the spirit, the whole spirit to God, and perfectly obeying in all things, so that your spirit may not be wounded by any depraved thought, false opinion, any error, any heresy, doubt, diffidence, or any consent to sin, so that it is not truncated in any article of faith, hope, charity, or another virtue, but may be perfect in the parts and numbers of hope, faith, charity, and all other virtues; so that the soul may not succumb to any lusts of the flesh, so that the affections and senses, both external and internal, immune from every stain, finally the whole body may be preserved intact from all pollution, so that you may incur no reproach before God and men.

Latin:

Vers. 23. Αὐτὸς δὲ ὁ Θεὸς τῇς εἰρήνης ἁγιάσαι ὑμᾶς ὁλοτελεῖς) Non satis est, nos monendo officium facere, Dei afflatu et- iam ad sanctitatem opus. Deum autem pacis dixit, quia pax non minima pars hujus sanctitatis. Sic & Rom. 15, 33. 16, 20. 1. Cor. 14, 33. 2. Cor. 13, 11. Phil. 4, 9. Ὁλοτελεῖς ex omni parte.

Post monita & vota inducit, inquit Theophylact. ut utrinq; sint tutiores. Deum autem pacis dicit, non tantum, quòd concordiæ inter nos autor sit, sed quòd imprimis pacem & tranquillitatem internam animæ operetur, quæ pax Dei dicitur, Phil. IV. 7. pax cum Deo, Rom. V. 1. congruit probe hoc epi- theton non modo ob gaudium perpetuum in Do- mino, quod requisiverat Apostolus, v. 16. quod si- ne pace interiori cordis nullum est, Rom. XIV. 17. sed etiam ob regulas, quas pacis externæ causapræ- scripserat, nec non ob votum sanctitatis, quæ sine concordiæ & pacis studio vera non est.

Καὶ ὁλόκληρον ὑμῶν τὸ πνεῦμα, καὶ ἡ ψυχὴ, κὶ τὸ σῶμα ἀμέμ- πτως ἐν τῇ παρουσίᾳ τῦ Κυρίε ἡμῶν Ἰησῦ Χρισῦ τηρηθείη) Est hic πρόσζευγμα. Nam ὁλόκληρον integrum, solidum in Glossa- rio, omnibus suis partibus bene constans. Et ἐν τῇ παρουσίᾳ pro εἰς τὴν παρουσίαν, ut & supra III. 13. servetur, nempe à DEO. Homo duabus constat partibus anima & corpore, Matth. X. 28. & vocatur anima interdum πνεῦμα. Rabbinis verò נפש est anima vitalis, רוח vero Spiritus est anima sentiens, נשמה est anima intelligens. At πνεῦμα hoc loco est Spiritus ille Sanctus in animis Christianorum habitans, & si solicite servetur ad mortem, imò & post mortem ad resur- rectionem usq; animis adhærens. Vide quæ dixim9 ad 1. Cor. XV. 44. & Hieronymum ad Gal. V. Græci omnes spiritum hoc loco exponunt χάρισμα Philo allegoriis: Τὸ μὲν εἶν ἐμ- πνέον ἐστιν ὁ Θεὸς, τὸ δὲ δεχόμενον ὁ νῦς, τὸ δὲ ἐμπνεόμενον τὸ πνεῦμα. Irenæus V. 6. Si autem defuerit animæ spiritus, ani- malis est vere, qui est talis, & carnalis derelictus, imperfectus erit, imaginem quidem habens in plasmate, similitudinem ve- rò non assumens per spiritum. Et postea: Et propter hoc Apo- stolus seipsum exponens explanavit perfectam & spiritualem salutem hominis in prima ad Thessalonicenses dicens: Deus au- tem pacis sanctificet vos perfectos, ut integer vester spiritus & anima & corpus sine querela in adventum Domini Jesu Chri- sti servetur. Et quam utique causam habebat his tribus, id est, anima, & corpori, & spiritui integram & perfectam perseve- rationem precari in adventu Domini, nisi deintegrationem & adunitionem trium unam & eandem ipsarum sciebat salutem. Propter quod & perfectos ait eos, qui tria sine querela exhibent Domino. Perfecti igitur, qui & Spiritum in se perseverantem habent Dei, & animas, & corpora sine querela servaverint. Tatianus: ψυχὴ γὰρ ἐκ αὐτὴ τὸ πνεῦμα ἔσωσεν, ἐσώθη δὲ ὑπ’ αὐτῶ καὶ τὸ φῶς τὴν σκοτίαν κατέλαβεν. ὁ λόγος μέν ἐστι τὸ τῦ Θεῦ φῶς, σκότος δὲ ἡ ἀφώτιστος ψυχή. Διὰ τῦτο μό- νη μὲν διαιτωμένη πρὸς τὴν ὕλην νεύἑ κάτω, συναποθνήσκεσα τῇ σαρκί Συζυγίαν δὲ κεκτημένη τὴν τῦ Θείο πνεύματος, ἐκ ἔστιν ἀβοήθητος. Ἀνέρχεται δὲ πρὸς ἅπερ αὐτὴν ὁδηγεῖ χωρία τὸ πνεῦμα. Τὸ μὲν γάρ ἐστιν ἄνω τὸ οἰκητήριον, ἡ δὲ κάτωθέν ἐστιν ἡ γένεσις. Clem. Strom. VI. post enumeratas novem animæ facultates addit: Καὶ δέκατον τὸ διὰ τῆς πίστεως προσ- γενόμενον ἁγίο πνεύματος χαρακτηριστικὸν ἰδίωμα. Tertullia- nus: Spiritus, qui accedit animo Dei vel Dæmonis. Et nota in his Pauli verbis ἀμέμπτως, sicut ἀμέμπτως sup. III. 13.

Perplexa est Grotii sententia, imprimis anno- tata ad 1. Cor. XV. 10. conferantur. Ecquis enim san- ct us ille Spiritus in animis Christianorum habi- tans, nisi tertia persona SS. Trinitatis, cujus tem- plum sunt fideles? Quem verò partibus hominis accenseri quis admittat? Spiritum autem Sanctum in 1. Cor. XV. distinguit Grotius ab illo spiritu in ho- mine, quem vice animae dicit esse in corpore glo- rioso, & cujus arrhabonem constituit Spiritum, qui in hac vita Christianis datur. Quae fateor me intelligere non posse. Forte nec Grotius ipse intel- lexit, adeo intricata sunt. Intelligunt autem hoc loco alii tria illa, vel prout homo spectatur quoad naturam, vel quoad regenerationis gratiam. Quod ad naturam autem tria in homine non sunt tres na- turales partes, quum praeter duas illas animam ra- tionalem & corpus organicum nullas substantiales partes homo physice consideratus habeat, teste scriptura & saniori philosophia. Licet itaque per tria illa a Paulo designata nonnulli intelligant tri- plicem animam, vel potius facultate animae, quem- admodum de Greg. Nyss. ἔκθεσις refert Theophylactis: Cum homo ex omni sit animarum specie commixtus, ea scilicet qua plantis inest, mox sensibili & intellecti- va, cum Spiritum dicit Apostolus, profecto intellecti- vam expressit: cum animam, sensibilitatem ipsam: cum corpus, vita nobis inesse ostendit, qua & in plan- tis esse comperitur. Quae vero locum non habet, cum corpus hominis non sit animae facultas, sed ab anima, tanquam pars altera substantialis distin- guatur, & hic expresse nominetur. Eo ipso tamen non constituuntur tres hominis partes substantiales. Quod etiam habendum de illorum sententia, qui πνεῦμα Spiritum vocant animam rationalem; per ψυχὴν autem intelligunt animam sentientem & ve- getantem. Qui utique non tres faciunt hominis par- tes substantiales, sed duas illas, quas diximus, reti- nent, & animam hominis tantum distincte quoad facultatem superiorem designari volunt, & quoad inferiorem, quo pacto Calvinus, Beza, Zanchius, Piscator Spiritum de superiore anima parte, notan- te Crocio ipsis ὁμοψήφως, qua sapimus, & intelligi- mus, qua mens vocari solet, animam de inferioribus facultatibus, at corpus de communi domicilio acci- piunt, non quod Apostolus duas animas constituat, sed unius animae plures facultates in uno corpore in- terpretantur. Quae etiam est explicatio B. Hunnii: Per Spiritum intelligit nobilissimam animae humanae potentiam, quae homines a brutis disterminat, nimirum mentem & voluntatem. Per animam reliquas animae facultates intelligit, quae ipsa quoque sanctificari, & Spiritui S. subjugari indigent. Proinde totum homi- nem mente, anima & corpore sanctificatum & incul- patum, seu ab externis sceleribus immunem servari, optat in die adventus Domini Jesu: ut & ministerii Lubec. Hamburg. & Luneb. im ausführlichen Bericht von den neuen Propheten §. 326. Der Mensch muß nach zweyerley Zustand betrachtet werden; Eines nach dem natürlichen/ also hat er nicht mehr denn Leib und Seele: wolte man aber die gewöhnliche Art zu reden verändern/ und wie Luther. im vierdten Ten. Theil berichtet fol. 16. daß sie Moses zu führen pflege; durch die Seele das blosse Leben/ welches die Fische/ Vögel/ und an- dere Thiere mit dem Menschen gemein haben; verstehen: die Kräffte aber der menschlichen Seelen/ als Verstand und Willen/ den Geist nennen; so hat der Mensch zwar Leib/ Seel und Geist/ aber der Geist wäre nicht ein we- sentliches Stück/ sondern nur die Kräffte/ welche andern Thieren nicht gegeben sind: nach welcher Betrachtung S. Paulus båtet 1. Thess. 5/23. daß GOtt der Christen Leib und Leben hohe und niedrige Kräffte/ biß auf den Tag des HErrn JEsu unstråflich bewahren wolle. Quum autem homo etiam quoad regenerationis gratia vel Theo- logica consideratione juxta hanc τριχοτομίαν spectari possit, per Spiritum nonnulli gratiam & dona Spi- ritus intelligunt cum Chrysostomo & Theophylacto, uti per animam & corpus ipsas substantiales par- tes hominis designari agnoscunt, vel Spiritum de eo, quod in homine, qua nova creatura est, re- peritur juxta illud Christi Joh. III. v. 6. Quod na- tum est ex Spiritu, Spiritus est. Aretius ita habet:

Hominis renati tres sunt partes integrales, πνεῦμα, ψυχὴ & σῶμα. Spiritus est ἡγεμονικὸν, hoc est, du- ctor & gubernator, formans in renatis novos motus, voluntatem Dei subjiciens voluntati. ψυχὴ est ἐπι- θυμητικὸν, cui adduntur τὰ πάθη in genere: item sen- sitiva facultas: judicium, ratio non repurgata à Spi- ritu S. Corpus organum est illorum: Præbet enim instrumentum ad diversas actiones, & est quasi σῆμα carcer & sepulchrum animæ. Hæ partes integrales sunt renati hominis, quū hominis physici duæ saltem sint ψυχὴ & σῶμα. Hinc nascitur duplex homo ψυ- χικὸς, qui est σαρκικὸς, qui vitam vivit hominis non renati: & πνευματικὸς, qui renatus est, & professio- nem suam ornat vita ac moribus, in eo regnat Spiri- tus S. dictator vitæ, 1. Cor. II. Hæc ille. Tripolitanu ministerium modo laudatum in scripto publico fanaticis opposito, (cujus autor fuit B. D. Nicolaus Hunnius) §. 326. quoad hanc posteriorem conside- rationem hominis sequentem tradidit explicatio- nem, quam cum priori in medio reliquit: Dar- nach wird der Mensch betrachtet nach dem geist- lichen Zustand/ da hat er Leib und Seel/ aber auch über dieselbe des H. Geistes Kräffte/ die im Men- schen wohnen/ die der Geist genennet werden. In welchem Verstande ein wiedergebohrner Mensch drey Stück in sich hat/ Leib/ Seele und Geist, deren zwey erste natürlich sind/ das dritte aber überna- türlich. Und in diesem Verstande hat S. Pau- lus gewünschet/ daß die Christen nicht allein dem Leibe und der Seelen nach/ sondern auch in und mit des Geistes Gaben biß ans Ende erhalten werden. Paululum diversa est B. Lutheri nostri in- terpretatio, utpote qua non tantum Spiritum ad renovationem hominis refert, sed etiam animam & corpus, nec physicè, sed Theologicè hæc tria in ho- mine spectat, sub ratione nempe ac statu regene- rationis ac renovationis. Addam Megalandri ver- ba ἰδιογλώττως, quæ sic habent, Tom. I. Altenb. su- per Magnificat p. 758. Das erste Stück/ der Geist ist das höchste/ edelste Theil des Menschen/ damit er geschickt ist/ unbegreiffliche/ unsichtige/ ewige Dinge zu fassen/ und ist kürtzlich das Haus/ da der Glaub und GOttes Wort innen wohnet. Das an- dere die Seele ist eben derselbe Geist nach der Na- tur/ aber doch in einem andern Wercke, nemlich in dem/ als er den Leib lebendig macht/ und durch ihn wircket/ und wird offt in der Schrifft für das Leben genommen. Denn der Geist mag wohl ohne den Leib leben/ aber nicht der Leib ohne den Geist. Diß Stück sehen wir/ wie es auch im Schlaff und ohn Unterlaß lebet/ und wircket/ und ist seine Art/ nicht die unbe- greiffliche Dinge zu fassen/ sondern was die Ver- nunfft erkennen und ermessen kan, und ist nemlich die Vernunfft hie das Licht in diesem Hause/ und wo der Geist nicht mit Glauben/ als mit einem höhern Licht erleuchtet/ diß Licht der Vernunfft re- gieret/ so mag sie nimmer ohne Irrthum seyn. Das dritte ist der Leib mit seinen Gliedern/ wel- ches Werck sind nur Ubungen und Brauch/ nach- dem die Seele erkennt/ und der Geist glaubt. Nos acquiescimus priori interpretationi, utpote quæ videtur simplicissima, juxta quam sensum hujus lo- ci non male reddidit Crocius hoc modo: Id oro & opto unicè, non ut pars aliqua, sed ut vestra tota mens, voluntas tota, facultates omnes, omnes vestri sensus, & vestri corporis vires omnes conserventur in san- ctimonia, ut corpus totum animæ, anima tota spiri- tui, spiritus totus Deo subjiciatur, & perfectè obse- quens in omnibus, ne spiritus vester ulla prava cogi- tatione, opinione falsa, errore ullo, ulla hæresi, dubita- tione, diffidentia, ulloq́; peccati consensu vulneretur, ita ut aliquo fidei, spei, charitatis, patientiæ, alterius- ve virtutis articulo truncetur, sed spei, fidei, chari- tatis, aliarumque omnium virtutum partibus & nu- meris sit perfectus; ne anima ullis cupiditatibus car- nis succumbat, ut affectus & sensus tum externi, tum interni, ab omni labe immunes, deniq; totū corpus ab omni pollutione intactum ita conservetur, ut nullam incurratis reprehensionem coram Deo & hominibus.

## 5:24
Verse 24. Πιστὸς ὁ καλῶν ὑμᾶς) He who called you to perseverance, he will also give the powers necessary for it. We have similar things in 1 Cor. I. 9, ch. X. 13, 2 Thess. III. 3, the faithful holy one of Israel, who chose you, Is. XLIX. 7.

ὃς κί ποιήσει τὴν ἐλπίδα ὑμῶν βεβαίαν) I do not deceive you: but as he ordered you to hope for heavenly life, so he will also perform it. Βέβαιον is called that which is fulfilled in reality, as Rom. IV. v. 16, 2 Cor. I. 7, Heb. II. 2, 2 Pet. I. 10.

Since what the Apostle vows is not of human powers, therefore, lest they doubt the fulfillment of the vow, he lifts their minds to the consideration both of the faithfulness of God, by whom they were called to the inheritance of eternal salvation, and of the divine power, which is easily able to make that hope valid: Indeed, in the place of God he promises the fulfillment of this hope. For if he called you to salvation, he is surely faithful, that is, truthful, and he is so going to act according to his will, that he also renders you saved, as Theophylact has it.

Latin:

Vers. 24. Πιστὸς ὁ καλῶν ὑμᾶς) Qui vos vocavit ad perseve- rantiam, is & vires dabit ad eam necessarias. Similia habe- mus 1. Cor. I. 9. c. X. 13. 2. Thess. III. 3. fidelis sanctus Israȩ- lis, qui elegit te, Es. XLIX. 7.

ὃς κί ποιήσει τὴν ἐλπίδα ὑμῶν βεβαίαν) Non fallo vos: sed vitam cœlestem sicut sperare vos jussit, ita & præstabit. Βέβαιον dicitur, quod reipsa impletur, ut Rom. IV. v. 16. 2. Cor. I. 7. Ebr. II. 2. 2. Pet. I. 10.

Cum quod vovet Apostolus, non sit humana- rum virium, idcirco ne de impletione voti dubi- tent, attollit mentes eorum ad considerationem & fidelitatis Dei, à quo vocati sunt ad salutis æternæ hæreditatem, & potentiæ divinæ, quæ facile spem illam ratam præstare valet: Imò Dei loco promit- tit spei istius impletionem. Nam si ad salutem vos ille vocavit, fidelis est sane, hoc est, verax, & ita est pro voluntate sua facturus, ut & salvos vos reddat, ut habet Theophylactus.

## 5:25
Verse 25. Ἀδελφοὶ προσεύχεσθε περὶ ἡμῶν) as Col. IV. 13, where see the things said.

Note, as Theophylact warns, how humble and abject he shows himself, when he says that he is in need of their prayers.

Latin:

Vers. 25. Ἀδελφοὶ προσεύχεσθε περὶ ἡμῶν) ut Col. IV. 13. ubi dicta vide.

Adverte, monente Theophylacto, quam humi- lem se & abjectum præstet, quum dicat, se horum precibus indigere.

## 5:26
Verse 26. Ἀσπάσασθε τὸς ἀδελφὺς πάντας ἐν φιλήματι ἁγίῳ) Rom. XVI. 16, and elsewhere at the end of the Epistles.

From this discourse, as Origen teaches, and from some other similar ones, a custom was handed down to the Churches, that after prayer the brothers should receive one another with a kiss. Concerning which Justin prays in his oration to the Emperor Antoninus: 'When the prayers are finished, we greet one another with a kiss.' Yet this was not held as necessary, as if it had been commanded by the Apostles, but as a free ceremony. The Apostle commands a greeting with a kiss of peace, which was a symbol of reconciliation and concord; he does not command that they should kiss one another in the assembly after prayer or the Eucharist.

Latin:

Vers. 26. Ἀσπάσασθε τὸς ἀδελφὺς πάντας ἐν φιλήματι ἁγίῳ) Rom. XVI. 16. & alibi in fine Epistolarum.

Ex hoc sermone, Origene docente, & aliis simi- libus nonnullis mos Ecclesiis traditus est, ut post orationem osculo se invicem suscipiant fratres. Quo de Justinus orat. ad Antonin. Imp. Precibus finitis mutuo nos invicem osculo salutamus. Non ta- men hoc habitum pro necessario, quasi ab Apo- stolis id præceptum esset, sed pro ceremonia libe- ra. Salutationem præcepit Apostolus cum pacis osculo, quod symbolum erat reconciliationis & concordiæ, non jubet, ut in conventu post oratio- nem aut Eucharistiam se mutuo osculentur.

## 5:27
V. 27. Ὁρκίζω ὑμᾶς (I adjure you) = ὁρκίζω ὑμᾶς השבעתי אתכם, Cant. V. 7. Then there is here an ἐπιτίμιον (adjuration). For Κύριον is said for διὰ τὸν Κύριον or νὴ τὸν Κύριον. The same is ἐξορκίζω in Mark V. 7 and Acts XIX. 13. In the same sense it is said ὁρκίζειν or ἐξορκίζειν κατὰ τῦ Κυρίυ, or κατὰ τῦ Θεῦ, 1 Kings II. v. 13, 2 Chron. XXXVI. 13, Matthew XXVI. 63, where see the things said. Thus also Irenaeus speaks at the end of his book. Moreover, it is the very same thing that John said as μαρτύρομαι at the end of the Apocalypse, which the Latins call 'obtestari' (to adjure). The Latins say 'obtestari per Deos' (to adjure by the gods) no less than the Greeks, as Cicero to Atticus II. 11, and 'Deos obtestari' (to adjure the gods), as Livy book VI. The manuscripts have ἐνορκίζω instead of ὁρκίζω: thus we have ἐνόρκισιν in Num. V. 25.

Ἀναγνωσθῆναι τὴν ἐπιστολὴν πᾶσι τοῖς ἁγίοις ἀδελφοῖς (That the epistle be read to all the holy brothers): I think not only the Ephesians are understood, but also those who were in the neighboring places of Asia. See a similar case in Colossians IV. 16.

Many others understand this adjuration as being about the Epistle being read to all in the Thessalonian Church, not just to some few, not only to the perfect, as a certain gloss in Lombard has it, but to all the sanctified and faithful. For it was inscribed to the whole Church. If he had wished it to be read in other Churches, he would undoubtedly have named them, as was done in Colossians IV. 16.

Latin:

V. 27. Ὁρκίζω ὑμᾶς τὸν Κύριον) ὁρκίζω ὑμᾶς השבעתי אתכם, Cant. V. 7. Deinde est hic ἐπιτίμιον. Nam Κύριον dicitur pro διὰ τὸν Κύριον aut νὴ τὸν Κύριον. Eadem ἐξορκίζω Marc. V. 7. & Act. XIX. 13. Eodem sensu dicitur ὁρκίζειν vel ἐξορκίζειν κατὰ τῦ Κυρίυ, aut κατὰ τῦ Θεῦ, 1. Reg. II. v. 13. 2. Paral. XXXVI. 13. Matth. XXVI. 63. ubi dicta vide. Sic & Irenæus loquitur in fine libri. Est autem idipsum, quod μαρτύρομαι dixit Johannes in fine Apocalypseos, Latini obte- stari. Dicunt autem Latini non minus quàm Græci obte- stari per Deos, ut Cicero ad Attic. II. 11. & Deos obtestari, ut Livius lib. VI. Manuscripta pro ὁρκίζω habent ἐνορκίζω: Sic ἐνόρκισιν habemus Num. V. 25.

Ἀναγνωσθῆναι τὴν ἐπιστολὴν πᾶσι τοῖς ἁγίοις ἀδελφοῖς) Puto non Ephesios tantùm intelligi, sed & eos, qui in vici- nis erant Asiæ locis. Simile vide Coloss. IV. 16.

Alii plerique de legenda omnibus in Ecclesia Thessalonicensi, non quibusdam tantùm paucis, E- pistola, obtestationem hanc intelligunt, non per- fectis solum, ut glossa quædam apud Lombardum habet, sed omnibus sanctificatis & fidelibus. Inscri- pta enim erat toti Ecclesiæ. Si in aliis Ecclesiis legi voluisset, sine dubio easdem nominasset, ut Coloss. IV. 16. factum.

## 5:28
Vers. 28. Ἡ χάρις τῦ Κυρίε ἡμῶν Ἰησῦ χρισῦ μεθ' ὑμῶν (The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you): Thus Romans XVI. 24 and elsewhere at the end of the Epistles.

The thing signified by that one word embraces the whole of salvation, Acts XV. 11, and is worth more than the entire world. He wishes grace in the Lord Jesus Christ, because outside of Him there is neither grace nor salvation, Eph. I. v. 6, Acts IV. v. 12. He had wished grace and peace to the Church from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ at the beginning of the Epistle, chap. I. v. 1. Now, at the end, he wishes the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ to the same, and seals it with the seal of the word AMEN: because that grace embraces peace at the same time, since it is a saving grace, Titus II. v. 11, and it is that of both the Father and Jesus Christ, because the Father and the Son

Latin:

Vers. 28. Ἡ χάρις τῦ Κυρίε ἡμῶν Ἰησῦ χρισῦ μεθ' ὑμῶν) Sic Rom. XVI. 24. & alibi in fine Epistolarum.

Res una voce illa significata totam salutem com- plectitur, Act. XV. 11. & plus valet, quàm orbis uni- versus. In Domino Jesu Christo gratiam vovet, quia extra illum nec gratia est, nec salus, Eph. I. v. 6. Actor. IV. v. 12. A Deo Patre & Domino Jesu Christo voverat Ecclesiæ gratiam & pacem sub ini- tium Epistolæ, cap. I. v. 1. Jam sub finem Domini Jesu Christi gratiam eidem vovet, & signaculo vo- cis AMEN obsignat : quia gratia illa complectitur simul pacem, quum sit gratia σωτήριος, Tit. # 2 Thessalonians

## 1:1 Introduction
[Abraham Calov, Biblia Novi Testamenti Illustrata (Vol. 2, Part 1). English: machine translation, The Faith Received (Mere Orthodoxy); the original follows each comment.]
GROTIUS'S PREFACE.

are one, I said in my dissertation published heretofore on a part of this Epistle, that I judged this epistle to be the first of the Pauline ones that have come down to us. A great argument for this matter is at the end of the epistle, where he wishes those to whom this epistle is written to observe that he makes the sign of his own hand in subscribing letters, which he would by no means have done if any Epistle to the Thessalonians had already come from him.

I said furthermore, that this epistle was not written to those whom Paul converted from the Gentiles after he himself came to Thessalonica, but to certain Jews who, having embraced Christ among the first, upon the persecution that arose after the death of Stephen, had withdrawn first into Syria, Act. 8. 4. c. 11. 19. and then also into Cyprus and other places, in which Macedonia was, the old nurse of Jewish business. That this is true is taught by those words II. 13. ὅτι ἀπ' ἀρχῆς ὁ Θεὸς ἀπ' ἀρχῆς εἰς σωτηρίαν. For that phrase ἀπ' ἀρχῆς shows that it concerns the Jews, who are called προηλπικότες, Eph. 1. 12. Among these Jews who embraced the Christian religion was the chief Jason, that is, Jesus (for the name is the same, as Silas and Silvanus), a kinsman of Silas and Timothy, who afterwards received Paul, Silas, and Timothy into his hospitality when they had come to Thessalonica. But it seems that the ancestors of Timothy also once lived in Thessalonica, whence Timothy is added to the Thessalonians, Act. 20. 4. And because this group from among the Jews living in Thessalonica was small, and therefore had no presbytery, those who did not live according to the rule of Christ are ordered to be avoided by others, whereas if a presbytery had been there, they would have been to be excommunicated, like that Corinthian. Since these things are so, and Paul's prophecies, which are in the second chapter of this Epistle, ought to look to matters that could happen within the span of one life, because we have already seen in three places that Paul thought that the last and universal judgment could happen in his own lifetime, I concluded from thence, when the history is compared with the prophecies, that it treats of nothing else there than of Gaius the Emperor and of Simon Magus, whose deeds correspond exactly to the words of the prophecy.

According to the most accurate Chronologers, among whom I hold in the first place the man of true erudition and piety, Dionysius Petavius, Saul, who is also Paul, was converted to Christ in the thirty-sixth year of Tiberius. After that, Tiberius presided over Roman affairs for three years. But since the things said here about Gaius happened partly in the third and partly in the fourth year of his reign, and it is said that Gaius had already then agitated in secret those designs which afterwards broke out: hence I concluded that this epistle was written in the second year of the reign of Gaius.

But we ought not to wonder if this Epistle was long hidden by those to whom it was written, since it could not be published without grave danger, while the house of the Caesars reigned, for the reason that after that attempt of Gaius to place himself in the very temple of God, it could be doubtful to no one that he himself was being designated by those black names, the man of sin, the son of perdition, and what follows, which there is no doubt would have been taken very ill by Gaius's uncle Claudius, and by Nero, who was grafted into the family of Claudius. Finally, when Vespasian reigned, the Jewish race having been overthrown, it was safe and useful for this Epistle to be published to all, and to be seen how all events from the first to the last corresponded to the predictions. And we said that this is the reason why this epistle, among those which were written to the Churches (for those written to individuals hold their own proper place), is the last, not in the order of writing, but in the arrangement. Therefore it is commonly called the second to the Thessalonians, just as the third Maccabees is called, which in the order of writing had been the first.

Grotius had handed down these things in his annotations on the New Testament in his commentary heretofore on II. chapter 2 to the Thessalonians, which, lest they should perchance be missed in the Grotian works, it is pleasing to subjoin, just as it is pleasing to insert those commentaries of his into any place of his annotations, and by the same work to bring them back under the anvil. The preface of those commentaries is thus.

Neither does the order of the epistles which is now received follow the order of time, nor are those things ancient which were added at the end to signify whence and by whom they were sent. For that order is placed according to the dignity of the cities, for which reason also the Epistles to individuals hold the last place, and those little annotations at the end are late, from conjecture or slight report. Both Chrysostom and others of the ancients note that the epistles to the Thessalonians are among the first that Paul wrote. Which is certainly most true of this one.

But since we hold that this Epistle was written during the principate of C. Caesar, who was called Caligula as a boy, around his second year, I see that it can be objected that this is said to be the latter [Epistle] to the Thessalonians, and that Paul first came to Thessalonica after the times of Gaius. I answer, that the latter could be placed in order, not because it was not written before the other, but because it later came to the knowledge of other Churches; written to a few, who had not yet formed an assembly, and therefore kept not in any archives of the Church, but by private faith. No light argument for this matter is that the Apostle here did not command men not living according to the rule to be excommunicated, which he had commanded where there was an assembly, as in the former [Epistle] to the Corinthians, but to be avoided, which is the right of individuals. Then truly nothing stands in the way of Paul's having written to Thessalonica much earlier than he came into that city, namely to Christians, who after suffering the most bitter things in Judaea had first withdrawn into Syria, and there also, being vexed by the same evils and perils, had taken refuge in Macedonia, with the sea crossed nearby. See here I. 4., comparing Act. VIII. 4. & XVIII. 18. Moreover Paul believed these Christians, tossed about by long miseries, ought to be warned, lest they should believe certain things that the Apostles had predicted of things to come, as predicted by them as imminent from near at hand, since if that had not come to pass, that alone would have been enough to shake the faith of the Apostles, and thereby of the Gospel itself. To this is added, that this Epistle, containing such things, could not become common without grave harm while Gaius reigned, or his uncle Claudius, or Claudius's son Nero, and for that reason too it became known later.

Latin:

PRÆLOQUIUM GROTII.

Dixi in mea ad partem hujus Epistolæ dissertatione edita antehac, ita me arbitrari, epistolam hanc esse Paulinarum, quæ quidem ad nos pervenere, primam. Ejus rei magnum argumentum est in fine epistolæ, ubi vult eos, ad quos scripta hæc epistola est, observare, quod fit manus suæ signum in subscribendis literis, quod minime fecisset, si jam ante aliqua ab ipso Epistola Thessalonicen. venisset.

Dixi præterea, scriptam hanc epistolam non ad eos, quos ex gentibus Paulus convertit, postquam Thessalonicæ ipse venit, sed ad Judæos quosdam, qui inter primos Christum amplexi, orta post Stephani mortem persecutione, concesserant in Syriam primum, Act. VIII. 4. c. XI. 19. deinde & in Cyprum & in alia loca, in quibus erat Macedonia, Judæorum negotium vetus nutrix, Id verum este docent illa II. 13. ὅτι ἀπ' ἀρχῆς ὁ Θεὸς ἀπ' ἀρχῆς εἰς σωτηρίαν. Nam illud ἀπ' ἀρχῆς ostendit de Judæis agi, qui προηλπικότες dicuntur, Eph. I. 12. Inter hos Judæos Christianam amplexus religionem præcipuus Jason, id est, Jesus, (idem enim est nomen, ut Silz & Silvani) propinquus Silæ & Timothei, qui postea Paulum, Silam, & Timotheum, cum Thessalonicam venissent, hospitio excepit. Videntur autem & majores Timothei olim habitasse Thessalonicæ, unde Thessalonicensibus additur Timotheus, Act. XX. 4. Et quia hæc ex Judæis Thessalonicæ habitantibus exigua erat, ideoque presbyterium non habebat, ideo ii qui eorum non ex Christi regula viverent, jubentur vitari ab aliis, cum si presbyterium ibi fuisset, excommunicandi illi essent, ut ille Corinthius. Hæc cum ita se habeant, & Pauli prophetiæ, quæ sunt capite hujus Epistolæ secundo, spectare debeant ad res, quæ intra unius vitæ spatium poterant contingere, quia jam tribus locis vidimus opinatum esse Paulum, se vito posse evenire judicium illud ultimum & universale, inde collegi, historia cum vaticiniis collata, non de aliis ibi agi quam de Cajo Imperatore & de Simone mago, quorum res actæ verbis prophetiz ad amussim congruunt.

Secundum accuratissimos Chronologos, in quibus præcipuo loco habeo virum veræ eruditionis ac pietatis Dionysium Petavium, conversus est ad Christum Saulus, qui & Paulus, anno Tiberii XXXVI. Post id tres annos rebus Romanis præfuit Tiberius. Cum verò quæ hic de Cajo dicuntur, evenirent anno imperii ejus partim tertio, partim quarto, dicaturque jam tum consilia ista, quæ postea erupere, in arcano agitasse Cajus: hinc collegi scriptam hanc epistolam anno altero Cajani Principatus.

Mirari autem non debemus, si diu occultata fuit hæc Epistola ab iis, ad quos scripta erat, cum fine gravi periculo vulgari non potuerit, regnante Cæsarum domo, ideo quod post conatum illum statu Caji collocandæ in ipso Dei fummi templo, dubium esse nemini poterat, quin is ipse designaretur atris illis nominibus, ὁ ἄνθρωπος τῆς ἁμαρτίας, ὁ υἱὸς τῆς ἀπωλείας, & quæ sequuntur, quod non dubium, quin ægerrimè laturi fuerint & patruus Caji Claudius, & in familiam Claudii insitus Nero. Vespasiano demum imperante, eversa Judæorum gente tutum & ex usu fuit edi omnibus hanc Epistolam, & conspici, quam eventus omnes à primo ad ultimum usque prædictis congruerent. Et hanc esse causam diximus, cur epistola hæc inter ea, quæ Ecclesiis scripta sunt, (nam quæ ad fingulos, proprium sibi locum obtinent) postrema fit, non scribendi ordine, sed digestu. Propterea vulgo dicitur secunda ad Thessalonicenses, sicut Maccabaicus tertius dicitur, qui scribendi ordine fuerat primus.

Hæc in annotatis ad N.T. familia tradiderat Grotius in comm. antehac ad II. cap. 2. ad Thessal. quæ, ne forte in Grotianis desiderentur, subjungere, quemadmodum & commentationes illas ino quasvis loco annotatis ejus inferere, eàdem-que opera sub incudem revocare placet. Ita autem habet commentationum istarum προαύλιον.

Neque ordo, qui nunc receptus est epistolarum, sequitur ordinem temporis, neque antiqua sunt illa, quæ sub finem sunt addita ad significandum, unde & per quos missæ sint. Nam ordo il le ex dignitate urbium est positus, qua de causa & ad singulos postremum obtineunt locum Epistolæ, & illæ in fine annotationculæ feræ sunt, ex conjectura aut tenui fama. Utramq; ad Thessalonicenses inter primas esse, quas scripsit Paulus, & Chrysostomus & veterum notant alii. Quod de hac certe verissimum est.

Sed nobis C. Cæsaris, eis qui, puer cum esset, Caligula vocabatur, principatu circa annum ejus secundum, scriptam hanc Epistolam cenfentibus, objici posse video, quod posteriore hæc ad Thessalonicenses dicatur, & quod post Caji tempora Thessalonicam primum pervenit Paulus. Respondeo, potuisse posteriorem poni ordine, non quod non ante alteram scripta sit, sed quod feriis ad aliarum Ecclesiarum notitiam pervenerit, ad paucos scripta, qui coetum nondum fecerant, ac propterea non ullis Ecclesiæ archivis custodita, sed privata fide. Cujus rei non leve argumentum est, quòd homines non ex regula viventes Apostolus hic non excommunicari præcepit, quod jussi cœtus fuerat, ut in priore ad Corinthios, sed vitari, quod jus fingulorum est. Tum verò nihil obitare, quo minus Thessalonicam scripserit Paulus, multò priùs, quàm in eam urbem veniret, nempe ad Christianos, qui in Judæa acerbissima quæque passi, in Syriam primum concesserant, & ibi quoque iisdem vexantibus malis & periculis, mari proximo trajecto se receperant in Macedoniam. Vide hic I. 4. collatis locis Act. VIII. 4. & XVIII. 18. Monendos autem hos agitatos longis miseriis Christianos credidit Paulus, ne quædam, quæ futura Apostoli predixerant prædicta ab iis tanquam à proximo imminentia crederent, cùm si id non evenisset, id vel unum satis futurum fuisset, ad labefactandum Apostolorum, ac per hoc ipsius Evangelii fidem. Accedit hoc, quod vulgari hæc Epistola, talia continens, fine gravi malo non potuit imperante Cajo, aut patruo ejus Claudio, aut Claudii filio Nerone, & ea quoque de causa ferius innotuit.

## 1:1 Introduction: Animadversions on the Preface
ANIMADVERSIONS ON THE PREFACE.

That the way in which Grotius has depraved this divine Epistle for the sake of the Roman Anti-Christ may be placed before the eyes at the very threshold, it will be worth the effort to examine the title, inscription, occasion, scope, argument, time, publication, and order of this Epistle, all of which are perverted in an unheard-of manner. But it is pleasing to premise to these the summaries or arguments of the Epistle of one or another of the ancients, so that it may be made plain how much he deviates from antiquity, which he is perpetually wont to harp upon. For those things are evident from the mere reading of the Epistle, and interpreters agree about them by consent. But the Grotian inventions, as they have no appearance of truth, of which there is no trace in antiquity nor in the Apostle's text itself, so they could never, as far as I know, have come into the mind of anyone, nor could the Polyhistor himself have taught them, until these times. Let us first hear the holy Athanasius, whose Synopsis has it thus: The argument of the epistle is such: In Thessalonica certain idle and disorderly living persons were going about, and seducing the brethren, as if the day of the Lord were already then at hand. They were seducing the hearers under this pretext as if they had heard this from the Apostle himself manifesting it and from the Holy Spirit himself. When the Apostle learned this, he wrote this Epistle to them. And first, indeed, he praises their growing faith, and boasts in them, because they were bravely enduring afflictions for Christ's sake: he also comforts them, because there will be vengeance from God for them, and for those by whom they were undeservedly afflicted; then, indeed, he inst ructs them concerning the coming of the Savior, so that they might not believe anyone, nor be troubled, whether by the Spirit, or as if he himself had written anything about that matter, nor in any way think that he is already at the doors, or about to be, before the falling away comes, and after this the Anti-Christ, that son of perdition, whose coming he signifies will be in signs and lying wonders according to the working of Satan: after these things, having exhorted them to stand firm, and to hold fast the traditions which they had learned from him, he warns them not to have communion with those who were living inordinately, but rather to repudiate them. For he shows that such curious persons are also wanderers. Moreover, he commands them that if anyone is disobedient to his words, they should cast him out of the synagogue. Finally, having prayed for peace for them, he finishes the epistle, with a salutation subscribed by his own hand, which he judges to be the sign of each of his Epistles. These things are clearer than light from the epistle itself.

Now Theodoret, who is quite like-minded: When the divine Apostle had learned of the benefit which the Thessalonians had derived from his former letters, and that, having been gravely attacked for the faith, they were bearing the assaults of their adversaries with a brave and generous spirit, he also wrote the second Epistle to them, comforting them toward virtue and greatness of soul and the hope of future things. But since some had also attempted to persuade them, to inflate the time of the consummation, saying that the Apostle had said these things: he writes also concerning these, teaching those things which are fitting, that it is necessary first for the enemy of truth to be, saying the Anti-Christ: Then for Christ our God and Savior to appear. He also persuades them to those things which are conducive to those who wished to lead a life in leisure. But the understanding of each of these things is derived from the interpretation of the context of the words. It is so entirely, from the context all things are clear.

Which that recent advocate of the Roman Anti-Christ has tried in vain to obscure with his glosses. Nor does Theophylact, or anyone else, depart from those ancients, as far as the sum of the matter is concerned. Grotius alone perverts everything, mixes the heavens with the underworld, and changes squares into circles.

De Titulo He strives first to change, nay, to invert the title, so that what has hitherto been believed by all to be the later Epistle to the Thessalonians, may henceforth be held as the former by Grotian authority.

Concerning which we have already spoken at the beginning of the first Epistle.

That this is the first of all Paul's Epistles is said precariously and without any witness. That it is necessary to assume many things, so that we may understand the former epistle to have been written later, and the later earlier, was also advised by Grotius's friend in his notes on the Grotian commentary, Jonas Schlichtingius the Socinian, upon whom, however, the interpretation of the entire second chapter rests. Yet he thinks he has found a great argument at the end of the Epistle, namely that the Apostle added the sign of his hand in writing the letters, because he would have been least likely to do that if any Epistle from him had already come to Thessalonica.

But why not? Could there not have been a reason for him to establish a certain sign, which did not yet exist at the time of the first writing of the epistle? That is certainly evident from the epistle itself. For the Doctors were not afraid to suppose that after that former one, another epistle was sent, as if it had proceeded from the hand of Paul, which is evident from chap. II. v. 2: Which danger, having then arisen, had to be met by giving a certain sign of his own hand, chap. III. v. 17.

But whence will it be taught that in the first to the Thessalonians there was no indication of Pauline writing, when that final adjuration, chap. V. v. 27, or the salutation, v. 26, or the last votive line could have been written by Paul's hand. It is certainly altogether probable that the first epistle, which is commonly believed to be the Apostolic one, was known, if not from the hand of Paul himself, which they did not ignore from the conversation had with the Apostle at Thessalonica, then from those things which are recounted in the epistle, concerning the sending of Timothy, and his report, and other contents of the Epistle, so that they had no need of a peculiar sign in that epistle. But for what there was need of later, when forgers arose, pretending to be Pauline Epistles, which they certainly could not have pretended if no epistle at all had been written by holy Paul before, and it had not been established to them that Paul sometimes addressed them by his letters. But every reason for doubt is cut off, that this which is before our hands is not the former, but the later Epistle, since in chap. II. v. 15 the Thessalonians are commanded to persist in the traditions which they had received from Paul, Silvanus, and Timothy, whether by word or by EPISTLE. For what is more certainly gathered from this, than that this epistle is not the first of all the Pauline Epistles, or the first which he wrote to the Thessalonians, but that he had already sent a former one to them, and indeed with Silvanus and Timothy, which is none other than that which has hitherto been believed by all to be the former, and bears that title before it.

Moreover, Grotius does not wish the inscription, which is directed to the Church of the Thessalonians, to remain intact. For that Church had been gathered for the most part from the Gentiles, as Luke taught, Acts XVII. Against this Grotius alleges that the same, when this Epistle was written, did not consist of Gentiles converted by Paul while he was at Thessalonica, but of Jews long before, and at almost the very first beginnings of the Christian Church, not converted by Paul, but by other Apostles, not at Thessalonica, but in Judaea; and he invents that they had crossed by ship into Syria and Macedonia because of the persecution that arose after Stephen's death, induced to this by no testimony or document whatsoever. Whereas on the contrary Paul found no converts at his arrival in Thessalonica, much less any Church of the Lord, Acts XVII. It is added that it is plainly indicated that the Apostle was already at Thessalonica when he wrote this Epistle to the Thessalonian Church, chapter II. v. 5. & μνημονεύετε, ὅτι ἔτι ὢν πρὸς ὑμᾶς ταῦτα ἔλεγον ὑμῖν, & v. 14. Let it be taught that the Thessalonians were then converted, and vers. 15. informed that they themselves were instructed through the Word preached by them. What of the fact that he also reminds them chapter III. v. 6. of the traditions which they had received, when they were present with them, and furnished an example of conduct which they were to imitate, and teaches that he had not accepted bread gratis from them, but had labored night and day so as not to be a burden to anyone at Thessalonica, that they might exhibit themselves to them as a pattern, vers. 17. seqq. By what clearer document could it be shown that the Apostle was with these men, and with others, at Thessalonica before this Epistle was written? By what more powerful means could the contrary fable of Grotius have been refuted?

What is brought forward from chapter II, verse 13, savors of Grotian ψευδερμηνείαν (false interpretation), such as is not easily observed by him himself without any passage, which others have accepted either concerning election ἀπ' ἀρχῆς, that is, made from eternity, or concerning their election as the firstfruits among the nations, but not that they themselves were among the first of the Jews converted to the faith of Christ. For how could those be among the Jews the first, and ἀπ' ἀρχῆς from the beginning of the primitive Church converted, who were converted through the Gospel of Paul, Silvanus, and Timothy, who did not even preach the Gospel from the beginning? For Paul indeed was the first to pursue that. But Timothy was only taken up into Paul's company later, Acts XVI. v. 1, nor had they seen the Thessalonian Church except after Paul had gone there, which it is confessed did not happen before the 50th year from the birth of Christ, and finally after the times of Gaius. There is no reason for us to speak here of the meaning of the word προηλπικότες in Eph. I. v. 12. It has been spoken of the same thing at that passage. Nor, even if the Jews were converted first, does it follow that the Thessalonian Church was constituted not from the Gentiles, but solely from the first converted Jews. The things about Jason, that he was among those who were converted in the time of Stephen, and that he was a relative of Silas and Timothy, are merely arbitrary hypotheses, just as is that one, that the ancestors of Timothy lived in Thessalonica, to which the passage Acts XX. 4 gives no support, if it does not contradict it entirely. For Aristarchus and Secundus are called Thessalonians there, but Gaius is called a Derbean, to whom Timothy is joined, perhaps because he was a Lystran, and from the vicinity of the Derbeans, which were only twelve miles apart; Acts XV. 24, he would have to be joined to Aristarchus and Secundus if he had been a Thessalonian.

Thirdly, Grotius changes the name of the Church, and feigns that only a few persons converted to the faith acted at Thessalonica, from Judea from the persecution after the slaughter of Stephen, when the epistle is inscribed on the contrary to the whole Church, just as the preceding one: Τῇ ἐκκλησίᾳ Θεσσαλονικέων, as the inscription has it in both places: and not to a few persons acting there in exile without a teacher, without a ministry: For it is placed beyond the hazard of controversy that the other epistle was directed to the whole Church by that very title. That argument is very trivial, that there was no presbytery there, because, forsooth, those who do not live according to the rule of Christ are ordered to be avoided by others, not excommunicated; for not all ἄτακτοι (disorderly) are immediately to be excommunicated, nor does that avoidance exclude excommunication, and avoidance is enjoined even there, where the whole Church with a presbytery is held, as Rome is an example, chapter XVI. 17. And Corinth also, 1 Cor. V. 9, 11.

Fourthly, if we look at the occasion of the Epistle, it was the ἑτεροδοξία (heterodoxy) of certain people, who were spreading it, as if revealed by the Spirit, or handed down by Paul either by word or by letter, that the day of Christ was at the door: of which they seem to have seized a πρόφασιν (pretext) or handle from the former epistle, which beat back the security of those who were saying about the coming of the Lord: There is peace, there is no danger, 1 Thess. IV. v. 2, 3. Thence therefore the Apostle had the cause in this latter epistle to inform the Thessalonians that the Anti-Christ must come first, to whose impiety and seduction Christ will bring an end by the glorious apparition of His coming to judgment. All of which are likewise perverted by Grotius. For he contends that those things which were predicted in chapter II to happen before the end of the world, look to matters which could happen within the space of one life: that Paul thought that the final judgment could happen while he was alive. That such an opinion was held by Paul is supported by no document, nor is it certain that it can be gathered except from wrongly understood passages of the Apostle. For neither the present prophecies, nor others which he predicted, 1 Tim. IV. 1, 2, 3, 2 Tim. III. 1, seqq., allow us to believe that such an erroneous opinion clung to Paul.

Fifthly, therefore, as far as the scope of the Apostle is concerned, his primary scope was to destroy that rumor about the final day being already imminent; to which he would have truly poured cold water, if he had hinted that Christ could not only arrive within the space of one life, but also that those things which he had warned would precede the final judgment would certainly happen in a short time, and within the interval of one or two years, so that it would not be believed that it was so near and at the door. Which is that not to pervert or rather to completely overturn the Apostolic scope? Thus the other scope was to confirm the Church of the Thessalonians in the acknowledged faith, to recall to their memory both what Paul had preached with his colleagues at Thessalonica, and what he had commended to them in the former Epistle, and to admonish them to perseverance in those things, and also to restrain them, and to teach how they ought to be restrained in that Church. But whom Grotius utterly destroys again, denying that the whole Church was there, denying that a presbytery was there, denying that Paul, Silvanus, and Timothy, when they wrote these things, had ever taught at Thessalonica, denying that the same men had sent letters to the Thessalonian Church, and that the former Epistle was written to them first.

Sixthly, it has hitherto been agreed among all interpreters, both ancient and modern, that the primary argument of the Epistle is the coming and description of the Anti-Christ, who was to emerge openly and be manifested before the supreme coming of Christ. Grotius, on the contrary, so as not to be lacking to the Roman Anti-Christ, has invented all other things, namely, that chapter II deals with nothing other than the Emperor Gaius and Simon Magus, although it is clearer than light that neither the time nor the words of the Apostle agree—of which in their proper place—so much so that no one hitherto, even in a fever, has dreamed of a prediction about Gaius from them, and all acknowledge that at the time these prophecies were recorded, Gaius was already dead, and at that time Simon Magus had already been confounded by Peter, Acts VIII. 20.

Seventhly, Grotius does not fear to confuse the chronology as well, calling Petavius to his aid, but against the mind of Petavius. Since this has already been shown in the preface to the first Epistle to the Thessalonians, there is no need to show it again. The opinion of Petavius is that Paul was converted to the Christian faith in the third year after Christ and the death of Stephen, part I, book V, Ration. temp. c. 1, near the end, namely in the year of Christ 37, in which year Petavius teaches that both the death of Tiberius and the beginning of the reign of Gaius Caligula fell, part II, book IV, cap. 5, p. 229, as also in part I, in the cited place. Therefore, the third and fourth years of Gaius were the 40th and 41st of Christ, just as the second year of the reign of Gaius, in which Grotius pretends this epistle was written, falls in the year of Christ 39, which is also the second year of Paul's conversion. But that Paul wrote this epistle to the Thessalonians immediately in the second year after his conversion, in which he λευκάδι Φωνῇ, chapter II, relates how he was at Thessalonica and there spread the Gospel, is a dream without a dream. But that it was written long after the passing of Gaius, as all interpreters and doctors agree ὁμοθυμαδὸν, not even excepting the Papists, so that the Apostle would have wished to predict those things which had already happened long ago—anyone who affirms this, all sane men will judge that he is in need of hellebore.

What Grotius trifles about in the eighth point concerning the long concealment of this epistle is more vain than Sicilian nonsense. How could it have been concealed, or how ought it to have been, when it was inscribed to the whole Church, when it was to be read publicly, so that they might be on guard against all seducers, and that false prophets might be avoided in their disorder, and other admonitions of the Apostle might be observed.

But we have already spoken of this fabrication in the cited place. Ninth cause, that this epistle holds the last place among all those which are inscribed to the Church, is not because it was published only when Vespasian was finally emperor: which Grotius affirms rashly and without any authority, but because it is later in the time of writing to the Thessalonians, and points out the former with a finger, and is the shortest among all the Pauline ones. For those longer ones to the Romans and to the Corinthians were placed before, and then the shorter ones were subjoined, and among these the first place was assigned to that which concerned the faithful throughout all Galatia, subjoined to the same was that to the Ephesians, equally long, and written to a most noble Church, afterwards that to the Philippians, and that to the Colossians, of which the former is earlier in the time of writing. Finally, as the Thessalonians were later in time, as far as their conversion is concerned, so they also obtained the last place for the epistle inscribed to them, which also consists of fewer words.

The tenth state of the epistle is now by no means obscure, namely that it is Paranetic-Didactic. For he exhorts to constancy in faith against persecutions, and dehorts from the seduction of false teachers, concerning the now imminent advent of Christ: and thus he informs them concerning the Anti-Christ who is to come first and to rule in the Church, and concerning his detention, and manifestation, and killing, and end. Finally, he exhorts to prayers, observance, and the avoidance of those who walk inordinately, and of the idle.

There are three parts according to the three chapters: The first is epenetic, which by the praises of the Thessalonians, the attestation of divine judgment, and a pious vow, insinuates an exhortation to constancy in persecutions, chap. I. The second is Didactic-Paranetic, in which he teaches concerning the last advent of Christ, not yet to come until the Anti-Christ emerges and is manifested, and warns concerning the guarding of Apostolic doctrine, chap. II. The third is Paranetic concerning prayer, and avoiding and pointing out those who live inordinately, chap.

III. PARS I. EPISTOLAE PARANETICA.

Latin:

ANIMADVERSIONES AD PRÆLOQUIUM.

Ut in ipso limine, qua κωλεία divinam hanc Epistolam in gratiam Anti-Christi Romani depravarit Grotius, ob oculos ponatur, titulum, inscriptionem, occasionem, scopum, argumentum, tempus, publicationem & ordinem hujus Epistolæ, quæ omnia inaudito more pervertuntur, dispicere operæ pretium erit. Quibus verò præmittere lubet unius alterius è veteribus summaria, vel argumenta Epistolæ, quo quantopere ab antiquitate, quam perpetuo crepare solet, divaricetur, palam fiat. Ea enim ex sola Epistolæ lectione patent, & ex affe de iisdem inter interpretes convenit. Grotiana verò commenta, uti nullam veri speciem habent, quorum nec in antiquitate, nec in ipso Apostoli textu ullum indicium reperire est, ita nemini, quod sciam, aut docere Poly-histor ipse potuerit, unquam in mentem venire ad hæc usque tempora. Sanctum Athanasium primum audiamus, cujus Synopsin ita habet: Argumentum epistola tale est: In Thessalonicam quidam epistola otiosi & inordinate viventes circumibant, ac fratres seducebant, quasi jam tum dies Domini præfomabus esset. Seducebant autem andientes eo prætex- eu, quasi hoc ab Apostolo id manifestante & ab ipso Spiritu S. audivissent. Quod ubi cognovit Apostolus, hanc ad eos Epistolam scripsit. Et primum quidem crescentem eorum fidem laudat, & gloriatur in ipsis, quod afflictiones fortiter tolerabant propter Christum: consolatur eos etiam, quod futura sit à Deo ultio eorum, & quibus immerito affligebantur, deinde verò & de adventu Servatoris eos instruit, ne cuiquam credant, neve turbentur, sive per Spiritum, sive tanquam ipse quicquam de ea re scripserit, nec allo modo putent, eum jam prae foribus esse, aut futurum, priusquam defectio veniat, & post hanc Anti-Christus, filius ille perditionis, cujus adventum in signis & prodigiis mendacibus secundum operationem Satanae futurum esse significat: post ista adhortatus eos, ut fortiter persistant, & traditiones, quas à se didicerant, fervent, denunciat illis, ne quam iis, qui inordinate vivebant, communio-nem habeant, sed magis repudient eos. Ostendit enim hujusmodi curiosos esse & errones. Prorsus autem praecipit eis, ut si quis sermonibus immorigerus sit, hunc è synagoga ejiciant. Ceterum pacem illis apprecatus finit epistolam, salutatione propria manu subscripta, id quod cujusque Epistolae suae signum esse judicat. Haec luce clarius constant ex ipsa epistola. Secundum Theodoretum

Jam Theodoretum admodum ὁμόφρονον: Cum rescivisset divinus Apostolus utilitatem, quam repererant Thessalonicenses ex prioribus literis, & quod graviter pro fide oppugnati forti & generoso animo ferrent adversariorum impetus, ad eos quóque scripsit secundam Epistolam, ad virtutem & animimagnitudinem & spe futurorum consolans. Quomiam autem nonnulli etiam tentaverant, eis persuade-re, inflare tempus consummationis, dicentes hec dixisse Apostolum: De iis quoque scribit, docens ea quae convenit, quod oportet prius visu esse inimicum veritatis, dicens Anti-Christum: Deinde apparere Christum Deum & Servatorem nostrum. Suadet etiam ea, quae sunt conducibilia iis, qui in otio agere vitam volebant. Uniuscujusque autem horum intelligentiam afflectur ex verborum contextus interpretatione. Sic omnino est, è contextu luculenta omnia sunt.

Quae nequicquam obfuscare glossis suis conatus est advocatus ille nuperus Romani Anti-Christi. Nec ab antiquis illis abit Theophylactus, aut quisquam alius, quod ad summam rei. Solus Grotius omnia pervertit, supera inferis miscet, quadrata rotundis commutat. De Titulo

Primum titulum immutare, imo invertere satagit, ut quae hactenus ab omnibus posterior ad Thessalonicenses credita est, deinceps auctoritate Grotiana habeatur prior.

Quo de diximus jam sub initium primae Epistolae.

Omnium Pauli Epistolarum hanc primam esse, precario & fine ullo teste dicitur. Adhuc multa fumere necesse esse, ut priorem epistolam posterius, posteriorem prius scriptam intelligamus, monuit etiam Grotii Amicus in notis ad commentationem Grotianam, Jonas Schlichtingius Socinianus, cui tamen rei totius capitis secundi interpretatio innixa est. Magnum tamen argumentum se invenisse putat in fine Epistolae, quod scilicet Apostolus signum manus suae in scribendis literis adjecerit, quia id facturus minimè fuisset, si jam ante aliqua ab ipso Epistola Thessalonicam venisset.

Cur verò non? Num causa ipsi esse non potuit signi certi jam constituendi, quae in prima epistolae scriptione nondum extitit? Id sane patet ex ipsa epistola. Nam supponere post priorem illam falli Doctores aliam veriti non sunt epistolam, ceu à manu Pauli profectam, quod è cap. II. v. 2. constat: Cui periculo tum enato occurrendum erat, signo certo manus propriae dato, cap. III. v. 17.

Unde vero docebitur, in prima ad Thessalonicenses nullum fuisse indicium Paulinae scriptionis, quum potuerit illa finalis obtestatio, cap. V. v. 27. vel salutatio, vers. 26. vel ultima linea votiva exarata esse Paulina manu. Id utique probabile omnino est, cognitam primam epistolam, quae communiter creditur, Apostolical, si non ex manu ipsa Pauli, quam e conversatione cum Apostolo Thessalonicae habita non ignorabant, ex illis, quae in epistola recensentur, de ablegatione Timothei, ejusdemque relatione, aliisque contentis Epistolae, ut non opus haberent signo peculiari in illa quidem epistola. Quo vero postmodum opus erat, cùm exorirentur falsarii, Epistolas Paulinas praetendentes, quas profecto non potuissent praetendere, si ante nulla plane epistola à sancto Paulo exarata fuisset, nec constitisset ipsis, Paulum quandoque literis suis compellare. Sed omnis dubitatio ratio praescinditur, non esse hanc, quae praemanibus nobis est priorem, sed posteriorem Epistolam, cum cap. II. v. 15. jubentur Thessalonicenses persistere in traditionibus, quas sive sermonem, sive per EPISTOLAM acceperant à Paulo, Silvano & Timotheo. Quid enim hinc certius colligitur, quàm quòd haec epistola non sit prima omnium Epistolarum Paulinarum, aut prima, quam ad Thessalonicenses exaravit, sed quod priorem jam ad illos miserit, & quidem cum Silvano & Timotheo, quae nulla alia est, quàm quae hactenus ab omnibus prior credita, eumque titulum prae se fert.

Porro inscriptionem, quae directa est ad Ecclesiam Thessalonicensem, salvam haud relinquere vult Grotius. Ecclesia enim illa collecta erat magnam partem ex gentibus, quod Lucas docuit, Actor. XVII. Contra praetendit Grotius, eandem, cum haec Epistola scriberetur, non constistisse ex gentibus, à Paulo, cum Thessalonicae esset, conversis, sed ex Judaeis longe ante, & sub prima fere initia Ecclesiae Christianae non à Paulo, sed aliis Apostolis, non Thessalonicae, sed in Judaea conversis, qui ob persecutionem exortam post Stephani mortem in Syriam & Macedoniam navigio trajecisse comminiscitur, nullo ad id inductus ulla testimonio, sive documento. Quum ex adverso Paulus fab adventum suum Thessalonicae nullos invenerit conversos, nedum Ecclesiam aliquam Domini, Act. XVII. Accedit, quod Apostolum, cum hanc Epistolam scriberet Ecclesiae Thessalonicensi, jam Thessalonicae fuisse palam indicetur cap. II. v. 5. & μνημονεύετε, ὅτι ἔτι ὢν πρὸς ὑμᾶς ταῦτα ἔλεγον ὑμῖν, & v. 14. Doceatur, Thessalonicenses dem conversos esse, ac vers. 15. informatos ipsos esse per Verbum ab ipsis praedicatum. Quid quod moneat etiam cap. III. v. 6. de traditionibus, quas acceperant, cum ipsis praesto essent, & exemplum conversationis praeberent, quod imitarentur, doceatque, se non accepisse gratis ab iisdem sanem, sed noctes atque dies laborasse, ne molesti essent ulli Thessalonicae, ut typum sese ipsis exhiberent, vers. 17. fegg. Quo documento quodnam clarius esse potest, Apostolum cum hisce, cumque aliis, Thessalonicense, antequam haec Epistola scriberetur, quonam potentius contraria Grotii fabula profligari potuisset?

Quod è cap.
