The Apostles taught in two ways, by words and by epistles. See toward the end of this chapter.

Others understand Λόγον not as rumor, but as the Word handed down by the Apostle, and that more correctly. For he removes those three modes, both of immediate revelation, and of Apostolic preaching, and of apostolic writing. He commands, says Theodoret, not to believe those who say that the time of the consummation is at hand, nor if they pretend that they are prophesying and predicting. For this is what he says, neither by the Spirit, nor if they produce a finished epistle as if written by him, nor if they assert that he said it without epistles. Epistle can also be understood commonly, so that it may refer either to that which he had written to them, the first to the Thessalonians, as if he had indicated some such thing in it, or any other whatsoever peddled by those seducers. Thus Beza explains it concerning writings that are either forged or falsely interpreted, since it is likely, in his own judgment, with others also concurring, even from among our own, that some from the former epistle took the occasion to spread this dogma concerning the imminent advent of CHRIST, as for instance from chap. IV, ver. 17.

Ὡς ὅτι ἐνέστηκεν ἡ ἡμέρα τῦ χριστῦ) Namely, in this year. For ἐνέστηκεν is used here of the present, as in Rom. VIII. 38, 1 Cor. III. 22, Gal. I. 4, Heb. IX. 9, קרוב. However, things that are clearly very near are accustomed to be announced as present, as we have said regarding Matt. XXVI. 28, where we brought forward many examples.

In the commentary he had thus handed down concerning these matters:

Ὡς ὅτι ἐνέστηκεν ἡ ἡμέρα τῶ χριστῶ) as if the day of the Lord were imminent. Ἐνεστώς is said to be imminent, because it is already present, Rom. VIII. 38, 1 Corinth. III. 22 & VII. 36, Galat. I, 4, Ebr. IX. 9. However, things that are just about to be are accustomed to be reckoned as present, and to be announced in the same way, as appears in Matt. III. vers. 10 & 11, V. vers. 23, VI. vers. 6, XX. vers. 22, Mark IX. 31, Luke XVII. 12, XXIII. v. 54, XXIV. vers. 48, John IV. 21. The great day, or ἡμέρα τῦ κυρίε ἡ μεγάλη, is the day of the destruction of Jerusalem, Acts II. vers. 20. We showed above why the same day is called Christ's as judge.

But that word ἐνέστηκεν by no means implies that for this reason something is impending in that very same year, neither by the force of the etymology, nor by the usage of Scripture, for which the cited passages do nothing, as inspection itself teaches. And how will Grotius persuade us that the Thessalonians were convinced that CHRIST was to come for judgment in that very year? Doubtless he devised this gloss in order to insinuate his own invention about a preceding sign that would happen within the space of two years. Of which later. Why would he warn the Macedonians about the day of the advent to the destruction of Jerusalem? Let this also be in his dissertation, Marckius page 43, to which Grotius replied nothing: Those Christians were not so eagerly expecting that particular judgment upon the Jews, as they were in some way fearing the return of CHRIST in their own time for the universal judgment, lest they should become spectators of the ruin of the universe, to which the prayers for the delay of the end, used by the ancients, looked, as found in Tertullian: therefore the Apostle, intending to free the Christians from this anxiety, and at the same time to close the mouths of the profane, who mocked the final return of Christ as if it would never happen, whence that voice in Peter 2. III. vers. 4, where is the promise τῆς παρεσίας αὐτῦ of his advent, wished to deal with that, as certainly to happen after the completion of his prophecies, yet not so near as some imagined. He did not dare to repeat here again that invention previously handed down in his commentary. It is too clear that the day of the Lord is understood, of which in the 1st epistle. IV. v. 2. 4. that it owes the παρεσίαν, which is designated below in v. 8. Crusius here notes the rashness of a certain recent Mathematician of Jena, who in the seventy-eighth year of the present century affirmed that the final day was at hand. Who that may be is not certain. Christ informed his disciples otherwise, Acts 1. 7.

Latin:

Vers. 2. Εἰς τὸ μὴ ταχέως σαλευθῆναι ὑμᾶς ἀπὸ τοῦ νοὸς) Ne facile dimoveamini ab illa sententia, nempe quam me docente imbibistis, aliquas res magnas debere præcedere, priusquam DEUS in Judæos, deinde & in humanum ge- nus ultionem suam exerceat. Νοῦς hic expono sententiam, ut Rom. XIV. 5. 1. Cor. I. 10. Sic & Job. VII. 19. XXXIII. 16. & alibi. Σαλεύειν est עֶרֶץ. Vide Act. XVII. 13.

De eo ita in commentatione:

Vers. 2. Εἰς τὸ μὴ ταχέως σαλευθῆναι ὑμᾶς ἀπὸ τοῦ νοὸς) ut non cito moveamini a sensu. Νοῦς hic intelligo eam sen- tentiam, quam ab Apostolis jam acceperant, non adeo vicinum esse, quam putabatur excidium gentis. Sic vox νοῦς sumitur Rom. XIV. 5. 1. Cor. I. 10.

Quomodo vero Thessalonicenses Apostolo docente imbiberant eam sententiam, si nec Paulus Thessalonicæ viva voce ipsos informavit, nec epistolam ad eosdem exaravit, quod utrumque Grotius inficiatur? Voce ταχέως indicat, vix eos à Paulo & συνεργοῖς esse de veriori sententia edoctos, ideoque inconstantiæ ac levitatis fore, si cito dimoveri se patiantur. Vox σαλεύεσθαι Metaphorica est à navi, quæ fluctibus hinc inde jactatur, soluta anchora, non absque periculo.

Μήτε θροεῖσθαι) Sic & Matth. XXIV. v. 6. Marci XIII. 7. Hoc ideo additur, quia si quid improvisum adveniat, magis terret.

Μήτε διὰ πνεύματος) πνεῦμα vocatur omnis prophetia, sive vere illa à DEO sit, sive talis esse dicatur, 1. Cor. XII. 22. 1. Joh. IV. 1. 2. 3. Nulla autem prophetia recipienda erat, quæ adversaretur dictis aut Christi, aut Apostolorum, quos pro se audiri Christus voluerat.

Μήτε διὰ λόγε) rumoribus de nobis, quasi aliud nunc diceremus, quam antehac diximus. Subintelligendum enim hic, ὡς δι’ ἡμῶν, ex membro sequente.

Μήτε δι ἐπιστολῆς ὡς δι’ ἡμῶν) Multi enim epistolas fabricabant sub Apostolorum nomine. Unde ista Apostoli cautio infra III. 17.

In commentatione sic habet:

Μήτε θροεῖσθαι) neque terremini. Solent quibus nondum expectata pericula subito ingruunt, gravius terreri.

Μήτε διὰ πνεύματος,) neque per Spiritum. Si quis, Prophetam se dicens, contra quam nos diximus, vaticinetur. Quia enim quidam falso sibi induebant Prophetarum nomen, ideo jubentur Christiani explorare talia, quæ prophetiarum nomine ipsis afferuntur 1. Corinth. XII. v. 10. 1. Thess. V. v. 21. 1. Joh. IV. v. 1. Optima autem exploratio erat collatio eorum dictorum cum dictis Christi ipsius aut Apostolorum, quos Spiritus ducebat in omni veritate, ad quorum autoritatem omnes Christianos respicere Christus ipse voluerat.

Μήτε διὰ λόγε) neque per sermonem. Est ὑπόζευγμα. Intelligendum enim ὡς δι ἡμῶν, tanquam per nos, neque per rumores allatos, quasi nos nunc alia hac de re doceamus, quam docuimus antehac. Nam multi falsa docentes Apostolorum autoritatem suis dictis præfcribebant. Sic Petri nomine contra Paulum quidam abutebantur, & suis commentis Gnostici præscribebant dicta Matthiæ & aliorum.

Μήτε δι’ ἐπιστολῆς ὡς δι’ ἡμῶν,) Neque per epistolam tanquam per nos missam. Etiam epistolas nomine Apostolorum subjiciebant falsarii, quæ causa est, cur tam sollicite Paulus sua manu aliisque notis muniebat epistolas suas, ut à falsis dignoscerentur, infra III. versu 17. Duobus modis docebant Apostoli verbis & per epistolas. Vide sub finem hujus capitis.

Λόγον non de rumore, sed de Verbo ab Apostolo tradito alii intelligunt, idque rectius. Tres enim illos modos removet, tum immediatæ revelationis, tum Apostolicæ prædicationis, tum apostolicæ scriptionis. Præcipit, inquit Theodoretus, non credere iis, qui dicunt, instare tempus consummationis, nec si præ se ferant, se vaticinari, & prophetare. Hoc enim dicit, neque per Spiritum, nec si confectam tanquam ab ipso scriptam epistolam proferant, nec si sine epistolis eum dixisse asserant. Epistola etiam communiter intelligi potest, ut respiciatur vel illa, quam ad eosdem exararat, prior ad Thessalonicenses, quasi tale quid in illa indicarīt, vel alia quæcunque à seductoribus istis venditata. Ita Beza explicat de scriptis vel ementitis, vel falso expositis, quum verisimile sit ipso judice, suffragantibus aliis, etiam è nostris, è priori epistola quosdam hujus dogmatis de instante adventu CHRISTI spargendi occasionem sumsisse, utpote è cap. IV. ver. 17.

Ὡς ὅτι ἐνέστηκεν ἡ ἡμέρα τῦ χριστῦ) Nempe hoc anno. Nam ἐνέστηκεν hic dicitur de præsenti, ut Rom. VIII. 38. 1. Cor. III. 22. Gal. I. 4. Ebr. IX. 9. קרוב. Solent autem quæ plane proxima sunt, velut præsentia enuntiari, ut diximus ad Matth. XXVI. 28. ubi multa attulimus exempla.

In commentatione sic de hisce tradiderat:

Ὡς ὅτι ἐνέστηκεν ἡ ἡμέρα τῶ χριστῶ) quasi instet dies Domini. Ἐνεστώς instare dicitur, quod jam præsens est, Rom. VIII. 38. 1. Corinth. III. 22. & VII. 36. Galat. I, 4. Ebr. IX. 9. Solent autem, quæ jamjam futura sunt, accenseri præsentibus, & eodem modo enuntiari, ut apparet Matth. III. vers. 10. & 11. V. vers. 23. VI. vers. 6. XX. vers. 22. Marci IX. 31. Luc. XVII. 12. XXIII. v. 54. XXIV. vers. 48. Johan. IV. 21. Dies magna, aut ἡμέρα τῦ κυρίε ἡ μεγάλη est dies excidii Hierosolymorum, Actor. II. vers. 20. Eadem dies cur Christi ut judicis dicatur, supra ostendimus.

Id vero verbum ἐνέστηκεν nequaquam infert, διὰ τοῦτο eodem ipso anno aliquid imminere, neque vi ἐτυμι, neque ex usu scripturæ, pro quo nihil facere loca allegata, ipsa inspectio docet. Et persuasum id fuisse Thessalonicensibus de CHRISTO illo ipso anno adventuro ad judicium, quomodo persuadebit Grotius? Nimirum glossam hanc excogitavit, ut ingereret commentum suum de signo prævio intra biennii spatium eventuro. Quo de postea. De die adventus ad excidium Hierosolymitanum cur moneret Macedonas? Utsit & hoc in dissertatione sua Marckius pag. 43. ad quod nihil reposuit Grotius: Judicium illud particulare in Judæos non tam avide expectabant Christiani illi, quam aliquo modo metuebant reditum CHRISTI suo tempore ad judicium universale, ne fierent spectatores ruinæ universi, quo spectabant apud Tertullianum preces pro mora finis, veteribus usurpatæ: Christianos ergo hac solicitudine liberaturus Apostolus, ac simul ora occlusurus profanis, qui ultimum Christi reditum, ut nunquam futurum, subsannabant, unde vox illa apud Petrum 2. III. vers. 4. ubi est promissio τῆς παρεσίας αὐτῦ adventus ipsius, de illo agere voluit, tanquam certe futuro post vaticiniorum suorum complementum, nec tamen tam proximo, ut nonnulli imaginabantur. Non ausus est, id commentum, in sua commentatione antea traditum, hic denuo repetere. Nimis luculentum, illum Domini diem intelligi, de quo 1. epist. IV. v. 2. 4. debere παρεσίαν, quæ infra v. 8. designatur. Notat hic Crusius temeritatem nuperi cujusdam Mathematici Jenensis, qui anno præsentis seculi septuagesimo octavo diem extremum instare apud se affirmavit. Quis ille sit, non constat. Aliter discipulos suos informavit Christus, Act. 1. 7.

## 2:3
Vers. 3. Μήτις ὑμᾶς ἐξαπατήσῃ κατὰ μηδένα τρόπον) In order that they might not be deceived, he repeats to them what he had said in person concerning the two great temptations which were bound to precede that time.

We add what is read in the commentary:

Vers. 3. Μήτις ὑμᾶς ἐξαπατήσῃ κατὰ μηδένα τρόπον) let no one seduce you in any way. Lest the Christians be deceived by an overly hasty expectation, not content with having said generally that that time was not too near, he predicts two notable temptations which were bound to precede that destruction, joined with the ruin of many, of which the former would proceed from the power of the empire, the latter from a false, eminent Teacher.

Everything, says Theodoret, of the kinds of deception he expelled. But he teaches them, and through them, all of us, the very greatest sign of the advent of the Lord. What Grotius dreams about two great temptations, no one before him ever dreamed, even in a fever. Nor is it to be believed that it will be approved by anyone hereafter. That he was not a good Advocate for the Roman Pontiff here, the Papists themselves will confess far and wide. The inventions of the Great Man are so inept that he could not have pleased any of those whom he wished to please.

Ὄτι ἐὰν μὴ ἔλθῃ ἡ πρῶτον ἡ ἀποσασία) There is an ἀποσιώπησις here. For either at the beginning or at the end of the passage, that will not happen is missing. Ἡ ἀποσασία, that is, that impiety of which I spoke to you. For ἀποσασία here signifies a certain eminent impiety, and corresponds to the Hebrew words מעל & סרה, for which ἀσέβεια is also accustomed to be placed, and it is also called of those who have not known the true God. For it is sufficient for ἀποστασίαν (apostasy), that they ought to have acknowledged him. Thus the Chaldeans in the song of the three children are called ἀποσάται (apostates), who had never worshipped the true God, but had been extremely injurious toward him. Thus to Antiochus, who had been a type of Gaius, of whom Paul begins to treat here, is attributed פשע, a name derived from a verb which is translated by ἀφίσασθαι (to depart), Jer. XXXIII. 8. Ezech. XX. 38. Elsewhere indeed by ἀσεβεῖν (to act impiously). Augustus and Tiberius had done nothing harmful to the temple or the synagogues of the Jews. Nay, they had even incurred expenses to offer sacrifices for themselves and the Roman empire, and by many edicts had confirmed the liberty of worshipping the one and supreme God for the Jews, as appears from Philo and Josephus in many places. Gaius fell away from the good institutions of these men in this regard, and indeed with the utmost impiety, which is depicted in the following verses clearly as if it were a present matter, so that it is difficult to find any prophecy to which the outcome corresponds more exactly.

He had proposed similar things in his commentary: Ὅτι ἐὰν μὴ ἔλθῃ ἡ ἀποσασία πρῶτον) For unless the falling away comes first. Ἀποσασία (apostasy), a falling away, corresponds to the Hebrew סרה, which signifies a defection from the true God, Deut. XIII. 5. Of the same signification is פשע. Dan. VIII. 12. in the prophecy concerning Antiochus the Illustrious, who is clearly a παράλληλος (parallel) and equal to this Gaius. However, it is to be understood here not as any kind of defection, but a full defection, ἀσεβημάτων χαλεπώτατον, the greatest of impieties, as Philo speaks when dealing with this matter. Augustus and Tiberius had indeed worshipped the Roman gods, but they had so far from opposed the God, the maker of the world, whom the Jews and Christians worshipped, that they even permitted free assemblies to the Jews everywhere, and free collections for the temple: nay, they themselves even sent gifts into the temple, and dedicated perpetual revenues to it, so that from thence daily burnt offerings might be made τῷ ὑψίσῳ Θεῷ, to the most high God, a bull and two lambs, as Philo teaches in his embassy, not in one place, thus indeed thinking, to use the words of the same Philo, ὅ, τι ἀναγκαῖόν ἐστιν ἐν τοῖς περιγείοις ἐξαίρετον ἀπονενεμῆσθαι τόπον τῷ ἀοράτῳ Θεῷ, μηδὲν ὁρατὸν ἀπεικόνισμα περιέξοντα πρὸς μετουσίαν ἐλπίδων χρησῶν, that it is necessary on earth that some one place be set apart for the invisible God, which should contain no visible image, namely for the participation of good hopes.

Ἀποσασία (apostasy) is not simply ἀσέβεια (impiety), but denotes a defection from the faith. Nor is it taken otherwise in Acts XXI. 21. Outside of which place it occurs nowhere else in the New Testament, the word is likewise used concerning a defection from the faith, 1 Tim. IV. 1. ἀποστήσονταί τινες τῆς πίστεως (some shall depart from the faith), as also Heb. III. 12. Καρδία πονηρὰ ἀπισίαν ἐν τῷ ἀποστῆναι ἀπὸ Θεοῦ ζῶντος (an evil heart of unbelief in departing from the living God). Add Luke VIII. 13. The noun ἀποστασίας (of apostasy) is also used concerning a defection from the faith among the LXX Interpreters 2 Chron. XXIX. 19. Jerem. XXIX. 32. chap. II. 19. as also in the Maccabees 1. II. 15. and also the concrete noun ἀποστάτης (apostate), 2 Maccab. V. 8. The verb ἀφίσασθαι (to depart) also occurs concerning a defection from the true religion and worship of God, Jerem. XXXIII. 8. Ezech. XX. 38. etc. And although the name ἀποστάτης (apostate) might be used once in an Apocryphal writing concerning the Chaldeans in a sense other than defection (which, however, can there also be taken concerning those who among the Jews at Babylon defected from the worship of GOD), yet the signification of defection is most common. However, it makes nothing to the point that the Hebrew words מעל and סרה, which are rendered by ἀποστασίαν (apostasy) in some places, are also sometimes explained by ἀσέβειαν (impiety). For nothing is more absurd than to interchange the significations of various Greek words because one Hebrew word encompasses those several Greek ones in its meaning. The question is not concerning the Hebrew, but the more famous signification of the Greek word, which cannot be denied to imply a defection, whether you look at the etymology or the use of the word. And Grotius himself acknowledges that ἀποστασίαν (apostasy) corresponds to סרה, which signifies a defection from the true God, and that פשע does not properly denote ἀποστασίαν (apostasy), but contumacy and impiety toward God. Whence the LXX Interpreters render that word as ἀνομίαν (lawlessness), ἀδικίαν (injustice), ἀδίκημα (wrongdoing), ἀνόμημα (transgression), ἁμάρτημα (sin), ἁμαρτίαν (sin), ἀσέβημα (act of impiety), ἀθέτημα (violation), παράπτωμα (trespass), ἀπώλειαν (destruction), πλάνην (error), never ἀποστασίαν (apostasy). In the passage of Daniel, however, they interpret it as ἁμαρτίαν (sin). Also, that Antiochus was a type of Gaius, no one, so far as I know, has said besides Grotius.

They commonly constitute him a type of the Anti-Christ. The Rabbis call an apostate מומר as if changed, Gregor. Tholosan. in Syntagm. Juris book II. chap. 2. h. 5. An apostate is called a deserter and traitor of the faith, who has altogether receded from the Catholic faith and from the religion of the true God; Becanus chap. XIV. on faith q. 3. apostasy is infidelity, through which one altogether recedes from the true faith received in baptism, as when a Christian becomes a Jew or a pagan. Conf. Tit. IX. l. V. decretal. which is concerning Apostates and the reiteration of baptism. In which manner Julian was called an Apostate: But also heretics are said to apostatize from the faith, and are called apostates. L. si qui sanctam C. de Apost. How, however, ἀποστασία (apostasy) in the proper sense fits Gaius, Grotius could not explain. What he says, that he fell away from good institutions, makes nothing to the point. For here the discourse is concerning a notable ἀποστασίᾳ (apostasy) and defection from the true religion: But was Gaius ever addicted to the true religion, so that he could be said to have defected from the same? Gaius surpassed the impiety of Augustus and Tiberius, but he was no more an apostate than they; if anyone is called an apostate who is impious toward God, even if he never obeyed GOD, and thus did not even defect from God, all the Caesars up to Constantine the Great are to be called apostates. Why therefore did Paul attribute ἀποστασίαν (apostasy) to Gaius as something singular? For the term from which the ἀποστασίας (of apostasy) is, is the faith, as is explained 1 Tim. IV. 1. The Spirit expressly says, that in the latter times some shall depart from the faith, giving heed to seducing spirits, and doctrines of devils, speaking lies in hypocrisy, and having their conscience seared, forbidding to marry, commanding to abstain from meats, etc. Which sense the following description also proves, when the mystery of iniquity is attributed to this apostate, when his coming is said to be according to the working of Satan, in power, signs and wonders, to persuade a lie, and the punishment of those who follow him is assigned as the efficacy of error, for the reason that they did not love the truth.

Therefore, the interpretation of those who have explained it as an apostasy from obedience to the Roman Empire is not to be approved: Tertullian, book on the resurrection of the flesh; Jerome to Algasia, question XI; Sedulius, Haymo, Cornelius à Lapide, Becanus, and others. But although the Antichrist may fall away from obedience or territorial subjection and the recognition of superiority, it is clear from what has been said that this is not what is being discussed here, but rather that a falling away from the faith is being designated. And therefore, we cannot approve the interpretation of those who join both that falling away from the faith and from the Roman Empire, ecclesiastical and civil, such as Bullinger, Hyperius, Aretius, Quirinus, Reuter in the continuation of Zanchius's commentary, etc., but we understand it solely as an apostasy from the faith, with the Greek Fathers Chrysostom, Damascene in book IV on the orthodox faith, chapter 28, Theodoret, and Theophylact. Chrysostom: He calls the Antichrist, he says, ἀποστασίαν, a falling away, ὡς πολλοὺς μέλλοντα ἀπολλύναι καὶ ἀφιστᾶν, so that he may deceive, if it were possible, even the elect. Theodoret explains ἀποστασίαν thus: He called the Antichrist himself a falling away, the name being imposed upon him from the thing itself, for he attempts to lead away from the truth and to cause them to fall away. Theophylact similarly: The Lord, he says, will by no means come unless the falling away also appears, that is, the Antichrist. He calls him the falling away for this reason, because in reality it will be so, that he will cause many to fall away from Christ, or even the elect themselves if it is possible. To this opinion also subscribe most of the Reformed: Calvin, Beza, Tossanus, Pareus, Piscator, Whitaker, Sutcliffe, the Belgian Interpreters, Crocius, Maresius; and among the Papists, Lyra, Arias Montanus, Adrichomius in his Chronicle, fol. 285, the Anglo-Rheims version, Scyanus, Justinianus, who openly professes that a defection from the Roman empire matters little.

But those among the Papists who wish for the dissolution or defection of the Roman empire to be understood here, so that they are not forced to admit that the Anti-Christ has already come and that the Roman Pontiff is the Anti-Christ, are by no means to be listened to. For apostasy does not denote the defection or dissolution of any kingdom; nor has the dissolution of the Roman empire been designated by any word, nor can it be expected before the end of the age by the force of Daniel's prophecies, since the mystery of iniquity had already begun secretly in Paul's time and was destined to break out into strength and be revealed, until at length the Anti-Christ is slain by the Spirit of Christ's mouth and destroyed by His most recent coming. The Apostle, however, implies not a small but a notable defection of the Anti-Christ, not a private one of one or a few, but a public one: not a particular one, but a general one of many Churches, provinces, and kingdoms in the whole world, when he says simply ἡ ἀποσασία, and adds a note of time, unless the falling away shall have come first, by which very thing a new and singular apostasy is predicted, since not a few had previously defected from the truth of the faith, John VI. 66, 2 Tim. I. 15, ch. II. 14, 18, Tit. I. 11. See also concerning the breadth of the apostasy and the multitude of apostates, Apoc. XIII. 4, 16. But there was never such a one in any sect as that of the Roman Pontiff, which has prevailed everywhere in the whole world. Concerning which apostasy of the Roman Church from the Christian faith, not a few have written. See the special treatise of the blessed Nicolaus Hunnius on the Roman apostasy. Church, as also that of the blessed Hieronymus Kromayer on the apostasy of the Roman Church accomplished in mystery, as well as that of the blessed Gerhard in his Catholic confession, etc. The quality of the Roman apostasy from the Apostolic faith is clear to the eye from a comparison of the profession of faith prescribed in the Council of Trent, and the worship which is exhibited in the Missals and Marials, with the profession of faith and worship existing in the Holy Scripture and the Oecumenical Symbols. Also, no sect besides the Roman ever aspired to such a height of civil power that it could, in such a breadth of kingdoms and provinces (of living, trading, buying, selling, etc.), interdict those who do not exhibit the sign of the Roman confession made, rosaries, and the Pater noster, nor was any ever so formidable in arms as this beast, Apoc. XIII. 4, ch. XVII. 1, 2, 8.

Καὶ ἀποκαλυφθῇ ὁ ἄνθρωπος τῆς ἁμαρτίας) Gaius uncovers his own character. For at the beginning of his reign, by feigning goodness, he had excited the hope of all. Ἀποκαλύπτεσθαι is גלה, as also below in verse 8, meaning to appear suddenly, as we have already said in verse 7. Ἁμαρτία sometimes corresponds to the Hebrew חטאה, sometimes in a more eminent sense to the noun רשע. And so here you may rightly translate it איש רשע, a man who is plainly wicked, being defiled by both incests and parricides. See Suetonius. Tertullian translates it: A man of delinquency.

Ὁ Υἱὸς τῆς ἀπωλείας) Which title is given to Judas, John XVII. 12, where we said it is the same as בן מות, 2 Sam. XII. verse 15, and signifies a man who is worthy to perish most miserably, which also happened to Gaius.

Which he had delivered more fully in a commentary in this manner:

Καὶ ἀποκαλυφθῇ ὁ ἄνθρωπος τῆς ἁμαρτίας) And the man of sin shall have been revealed. Gaius was indeed already Prince, but he had not yet uncovered his villainous character. Suetonius: Having thus obtained the empire, the most desired Prince made the Roman people, or if I may so say, the human race, possessors of their wish, for the greatest part of the provincials and soldiers. Then: He himself also inflamed the zeal of men with every kind of popularity. Of which kind, when the same Suetonius had narrated many things, he adds: Thus far as if about a Prince, the rest must be narrated as if about a monster. Philo: For no one remembers there to have been such joy of one region or one nation for the safety and establishment of a leader,

ὅση ἐπὶ Γαΐῳ συμπάσης τῆς οἰκουμένης, καὶ παραλαβόν- τῳ τὴν ἀρχὴν, καὶ ῥωσθέντι ἐκ τῆς ἀσθενείας. ᭭σπερ γὰρ ἐκ νομάδος βίου καὶ θηριώδους νῦν πρῶτον ἀρχόμενοι με- ταβάλλειν πρὸς τὸ σύννομον ἠὲ ὁμοδίαιτον, κᭀκ ἐξ ἐρημίας σκηνῶν καὶ ὑπαιθρείων ἀποικίζεσθαι πόλεσι τειχήρεσι, κᭀκ ἐξ ἀνεπιτροπεύτου ζωῆς ὑπὸ ἐπιτρόπῳ τάττεσθαι τομεῖ τινι ἠὲ ἀγελάρχῳ τῆς ἡμετέρας ἀγέλης. ἐγεγήθεσαν ἀγνοίᾳ τῆς ἀληθείας. Τυφλώττει γὰρ ὁ ἀνθρώπινος νοῦς πρὸς τὴν τοῦ συμφέροντος ὄντως αἴσθησιν εἰκασμῷ καὶ στοχασμῷ μᾶλ- λον, ἢ ἐπιστήμῃ χρῆσθαι δυνάμενος. Εὐθὺς γοῦν ἐκ τοῦ μακρὰν ὁ σωτὴρ καὶ εὐεργέτης εἶναι νομισθεὶς, καί τινας ἀγαθῶν πηγὰς νέας ἐπομβρήσειν Ἀσίατε καὶ Εὐρώπῃ πρὸς εὐδαιμονίαν ἀκαθαίρετον, ἰδίατε ἑκάστῳ ἠὲ πᾶσι κοινῇ τὸ λεγόμενον δὴ τοῦτο ἀφ' ἑστίας ἤρξατο, μεταβαλὼν πρὸς τὸ ἀτίθασσον, μᾶλλον δὲ ἣν συνεσκίασεν ἀγριότητα τῷ πλά- σματι τῆς ὑποκρίσεως, ἀναφήνας. For there is no memory of there having been such joy of one region or nation only in the safety or elevation of any Prince, as there was over Gaius, both when he first obtained the principate and when he recovered from sickness. For they rejoiced out of ignorance of the truth, as if they were now beginning to pass from a nomadic and wild life to another that was gentle and civil, or to migrate from solitary tents and open fields into walled cities, or to be transferred from a life needing guardianship into the guardianship of him who was to be the shepherd and leader of the human flock. For the human mind is accustomed to be blind regarding the sense of what is expedient for it, as it is led more by conjecture and opinion than by certain knowledge. For little time passed when he, who was hoped to be the savior and giver of benefits, who was thought to be about to irrigate Asia and Europe with new fountains of goods for perpetual and private happiness, starting from the very hearth, as they say, turned himself to ferocity, or rather, uncovered the ferocity which he had hidden under a fallacious mask. What ἀποκαλυφθῆναι is to reveal for Paul in the prediction, the same is ἀναφαίνειν for Philo in the history of the event through which the prediction is fulfilled; thus ἀποκαλύπτεσθαι is taken in Luke II. verse 35, 1 Corinthians III. 13, and soon twice in this same passage. Dion: Δημοκρατι- κώτατος γὰρ εἶναι τὰ πρῶτα δόξας, μοναρχικώτατος ἐγέ- νετο, when he seemed most popular at the beginning, he became most imperious, and what follows there.

The man of sin) The man of sin. A Hebrew manner of speaking, by which is signified he who is notably wicked, such as Gaius showed himself to be, not only by the slaughters of very many innocent people, and by debaucheries and adulteries, but by those crimes beyond which hardly anything can be conceived, parricides and incests. Suetonius records his saying, which is consistent with his deeds: Remember that I have the right to do anything to anyone. Whoever wishes to know fully this inhumanity of his, let him read Philo, Suetonius, Dio, and Josephus at the beginning of the 19th book of his Antiquities. The Apostle speaks secretly, however, because he is speaking of the Emperor, as he does of Nero in 2 Timothy 4:17.

The son of perdition) The son of perdition. בֶּן מָוֶת 2 Samuel 12:15. This expression occurs in John 17:12, and ἔθνος ἀπωλείας, a nation of perdition, in the book of Sirach 16:10. The Apostle signifies that Gaius, just as he was notably criminal, was also destined by GOD for a notable destruction, than which nothing could be said more truly. Philo says of him in Josephus: ὡς χρὴ θαῤῥεῖν, Γαΐου λόγῳ μὲν αὐτοῖς ὠργισμένου, ἔργῳ δὲ ἤδη τὸν Θεὸν ἀντιπαρεξάγοντος: that they ought to be of good cheer, since Gaius in words indeed showed anger toward them, but in the deed itself was setting God against himself as an enemy. Dio says of his end: Τοῖς ἔργοις ὡς οὐκ ἦν Θεὸς ἔμαθεν: By his end he learned that he was not God. It had been predicted to him that he should beware of Cassius. He could not beware. Many other things had preceded which openly signified the divine decree concerning his notable slaughter. See Suetonius and Dio. That memorable thing which is narrated in Josephus, that Minutianus said concerning his death: Καὶ νῦν λόγῳ μὲν εἴπαι τέτυς, οἳ ἀνῃρήκασι Γαΐον, ἔργῳ δὲ αὐτὸν ὑφ' ἑαυτοῦ κεῖσθαι διολωλότα, that they indeed have the reputation as if they had killed Gaius, but in reality Gaius was laid low by himself.

To these melodious trifles Maresius has already replied. 2. That after Gaius obtained the empire he had not been in his right mind for so long, that the revelation of his very wicked spirit had to be awaited for a long time. For it was immediately established concerning him that there had never been a better slave, nor a worse master, as it is in Suetonius, chapter 10. Indeed, Gaius already, when these were being written according to Grotius, in the second year of the reign, had sufficiently shown what kind of person he was. For since he did not complete a full four-year period in the empire, but actually spent three whole years in crimes of various kinds, as Sextus Aurelius Victor expressly asserts regarding him, it is necessary that he had revealed his criminal nature reign was completed, even if perhaps he did not begin to harass the Jews until the following year. What other reply could Grotius make than that Philo's credibility is undeservedly rendered suspect? But it is not rendered suspect. On the contrary, the same Philo had said in the words cited by Grotius himself that Caligula had hidden his nature for a short time. A little time, he says, intervened, when he revealed the ferocity which he was hiding under a deceptive mask. Add to this that, as Suetonius testifies in chapter 11, not even then could Gaius restrain his savage and shameful nature, when he deserved the praise of being an excellent slave, so much so that Tiberius, having perceived these things, would sometimes predict that Gaius was living for his own destruction and that of all, and that he was raising a viper (a serpent of that kind) for the Roman people and a Phaethon for the world: And that Dio in book 59 taught with what crimes Gaius consecrated the very beginnings of his reign: for which he had also made a way for himself by parricide, having suffocated Tiberius, as testified in the same book 58 and by Suetonius in chapter 12. Grotius wants the 'being revealed' predicted by Paul to be the 'manifesting' in the history of the event by which the prediction is fulfilled, according to Philo. But the things which Philo relates there pertain to the first year of Gaius, according to the same author. Paul, however, determined that these things were written in the second year of Gaius. Therefore, it must be that those things were fulfilled before they were predicted. The 'man of sin,' according to Theodoret, Chrysostom, and Theophylact, is the Anti-Christ, who did not even dream of Gaius.

But it was not enough for the Apostle to say 'sinner': He says 'man of sin,' because he will be entirely immersed in sins, a whirlpool of impiety, a sink of wickedness, a slave and at the same time an author of sin. For he does not mean one or two sins, but sins committed against both tables of the Decalogue. Moreover, he also calls this same person the 'man of sin,' says Theophylact, just as if he were to be the perpetrator of all crimes, and one who would seduce others to commit them as well. Therefore, he denotes not only one who is exceptionally wicked, but one who also induces others to wickedness, both by doctrine, as he sits as a Doctor in the temple of God, and by practice and example. The 'son of perdition,' according to Theodoret, is said to be one who both perishes himself and causes destruction for others. Maresius had replied to Grotius: 'Man of sin' indeed denotes someone notably wicked, but here it denotes one whose marks do not by any means fit Caligula. Nor were Heliogabalus, Domitian, or Nero himself—to whom Tiberius succeeded, whose malice was no less because it was more hidden—inferior to Gaius regarding the depravity of their morals: and it is even more detestable in him that he named as his successor Gaius, whom he knew would be the worst, so that he might, by this artifice, bring about the memory of his own crimes and leave the people longing for him. And further: Let Gaius be, as the Commentator observes, notably criminal, and for that reason destined by GOD for a notable destruction, it does not follow from that, however, that he could be called 'the son of perdition' by way of excellence, of whom mention is made here. For he who is adorned with this title must not only bring destruction upon himself, but also be a guide and a leader for others, leading them to destruction, as is observed in Acts 1:16 and Job 18:3, concerning Judas the traitor, who is also marked with this same title as a type and forerunner of the Anti-Christ, nor does 'son of death' (2 Samuel 12:5) mean the same thing, as the Commentator thinks. For every person guilty of death by the judgment of the magistrate is not, before God and the Church, a son of perdition: while the latter properly denotes guilt or the obligation to punishment, the former denotes vices and crimes. Do these things not fit far more easily the one who introduced such a defection into the Church from the purity of faith, specifically that which concerns foods and marriages, of which Paul speaks in 1 Timothy 4, and who, even if he leads countless peoples in droves with him to the first slave-pen of Gehenna, to be whipped forever with him with many stripes, would be subject to no one's reproof, as the Canon Law speaks of the Roman Pontiff in Canon 'Si Papa,' dist. 40? How many, I ask, have occupied that seat who were worse than the Caligulas and Neros themselves? Let the complaint of Baronius himself regarding the tenth century of Christ be seen, and the testimony of Genebrard concerning nearly fifty Pontiffs succeeding one another in that century who fell away from the virtue of their ancestors, 'apotactici' (renouncers) or rather 'apostatic' (apostates) than 'Apostolic.' These are called monsters and portents by Platina in Benedict IV, no less than Gaius by Suetonius. Mantuan also carps at the Romulean citadels and Pontifical roofs—a sink of crimes. Marcellus II himself, according to Onuphrius, thought that no Pontiff could be saved. I spare the names of individuals. But that which the Commentator commemorates as most foul regarding Gaius: 'Remember that all things are permitted to me and against all,' is far below that fullness of power in spiritual and temporal matters which the Roman Pontiff arrogates to himself, that spiritual man, if it pleases the gods, who judges all things and is judged by no one. Finally, the flatterers and admirers of that seat could not have been ignorant that writers have written more shameful things about their own Pontiffs than Suetonius, or Tacitus, or Philo, who was specifically hostile to him, wrote about Gaius, from which the 'marks' of the son of perdition can be deduced far more certainly than those which he himself assigns to Gaius. Grotius found nothing to reply to those points.

But how the doctrine of the Roman Anti-Christ induces sins of every kind and undermines the entire pursuit of piety, our blessed Gerhard demonstrates synoptically and learnedly in his special disputations. That Grotius maintains that no one was more wicked than Gaius neither serves the truth nor contributes anything to the matter, since it is sufficient that there were equally wicked people afterwards, so that it is rashly appropriated to Gaius by way of antonomasia: and this title fits Nero rather than Gaius, and most of all the Roman Pontiff, since there is no doubt that some of the Pontiffs were far superior to Gaius in impiety and crimes. All labor to this very end, that they may teach and defend impiety, justify parricides against Kings and Princes, absolve subjects from the oath of fidelity, subject supreme powers to themselves, maintain that treaties are not to be kept, permit and ratify incests, make illicit marriages licit, and according to the word of God, make pure and uncontaminated things impure and profane, and six hundred such notorious proofs of Papal impiety could be noted. Who therefore will deny that he, by way of eminence and with excellent right, is called the man of sin even before Gaius? He who thinks that all things are permitted to him against all men and in all things, that spiritual man, according to the Papal Gloss, who judges all things and is judged by no one.

To this effect is the fact that Grotius himself, at Job IX. verse 16, interprets ἄνθρωπον ἁμαρτωλὸν as one who falsely proclaims himself sent by God. For such, he says excellently, are called sinners. Thus ὁ ἄνθρωπος τῆς ἁμαρτίας, 2 Thess. II. 3. Who would attribute this to Gaius, who never proclaimed himself sent by God? Who does not see that in this way the Roman Pontiff is called ἄνθρωπος τῆς ἁμαρτίας by Grotius himself, not yet hired by the Anti-Christ, then called? Whom he also says is called the son of perdition above others, because by teaching heresies of perdition, he brings upon himself and countless others the swiftest perdition; 2 Pet. 2:1, 2. There can be no doubt, since at Trent several heresies were sanctioned by the Roman Pope. To whom, even if the countless papacy leads with it in droves to the first possession of hell, to be beaten with many stripes forever, no one ought to say: Pope, what are you doing? As observed before from can. Si papa. dist. 40.

Nor indeed must a singular individual be inferred because he is called ὁ ἄνθρωπος and ὁ υἱὸς. The article is also used where the discourse is not about a singular person, Matt. 5:7, 9; ch. 13:2, 27, 35; ch. 15:20; Mark 2:27; Luke 4:4. Therefore the Apostle calls him the man of sin, not because he was to be a singular man, but because a human kingdom was to be in the Church, which whoever occupies, that man is the sinner. Thus the daughter of Zion and the daughter of Babylon are used not of a certain person, but of a kingdom and a people. Nor indeed does Daniel otherwise understand many Kings by the singular names of the bear, the lion, and the leopard, joined into one body of a monarchy. For that man of sin, who has already begun secretly, is finally to be cut off on the last day. Whom we do not deny to exist for a time under an individual unity, or as a single one, just as there is one Roman Emperor, one King of the French; but that he is absolutely unique, just as Christ is one, or that the Anti-Christ ends with the death of one individual, or lacks a successor, this is what we deny. For that man of sin lasts until the day of the final judgment, which cannot be said of one individual. Whatever the Papists, the authors of a utopian Anti-Christ, may pretend here, that he is to reign for no more than three years and a half.

Moreover, the revelation of the Anti-Christ is taken in two ways: 1. When he openly revealed what he previously fostered secretly, when he began to exercise his tyranny openly. 2. When he himself was manifested by the works of others, with the opinion of truth and holiness stripped from him, and his impiety, both of doctrine and of life, brought into the light. This latter revelation is to be understood here: since that former one was not so public, when the impudent Anti-Christian tyranny was rather publicly directed against the piety and propagation of the kingdom of Christ, nor was it apparent to be noticed by any but a few, until it was manifested openly by the Spirit of the Lord. The Apostle here hints at this public and open manifestation which will be before the coming of the Lord, as most Interpreters, and of our own Osiander, Hunnius, the Vinarienses, and others have explained.

Latin:

Vers. 3. Μήτις ὑμᾶς ἐξαπατήσῃ κατὰ μηδένα τρόπον) Quo minus falli possent, repetit illis, quæ coram dixerat de duabus magnis tentationibus, quæ præcedere id tempus debebant.

Addimus, quæ in commentatione leguntur:

Vers. 3. Μήτις ὑμᾶς ἐξαπατήσῃ κατὰ μηδένα τρόπον) ne quis vos seducat ullo modo. Ne fallerentur Christiani nimium propera expectatione, non contentus generaliter dixisse, haud nimis propinquum esse id tempus, duas prædicit notabiles tentationes, quæ præcedere id excidium debebant, conjunctas cum multorum ruina, quarum prior à vi imperii proficisceretur, altera à falso Doctore eximio.

Omnia, inquit Theodoretus, deceptionis genera expulit. Docet autem ipsos, & per ipsos, omnes nos, vel maximum adventus Domini signum. Quæ Grotius de duabus magnis tentationibus somniat, nemo ante ipsum vel per febrim somniavit unquam. Nec credendum, à quoquam deinceps ea probatum iri. Non bonum hic fuisse Romani Pontificis Advocatum, ipsimet Papistæ ambiguo procul fatebuntur. Adeo inepta sunt Viri Magni commenta, ut nec eorum, quibus ille placere voluit, ulli placere potuerit.

Ὄτι ἐὰν μὴ ἔλθῃ ἡ πρῶτον ἡ ἀποσασία) Est hic ἀποσιώπησις. Nam aut initio, aut fine περικοπῆς deest, illud non eveniet. Ἡ ἀποσασία, id est, illa impietas, de qua loquutus vobis fui. Nam ἀποσασία hic impietatem quandam eximiam significat, respondetque Ebræis vocibus מעל & סרה, pro quibus & ἀσέβεια poni solet, diciturque etiam de iis, qui Deum verum non cognoverunt. Sufficit enim ad ἀποστασίαν, quod agnoscere eum debuerant. Itaque Chaldæi in cantico trium puerorum dicuntur ἀποσάται, qui Deum verum nunquam coluerant, sed summe in eum fuerant injuriosi. Sic Antiocho, qui typus fuerat Caji, de quo hic agere incipit Paulus, tribuitur פשע, nomen de- ductum à verbo, quod per ἀφίσασθαι vertitur, Jer. XXXIII. 8. Ezech. XX. 38. Alibi vero per ἀσεβεῖν Augustus & Ti- berius neque templo neque synagogis Judæorum quicquam hocuerant. Quin & sumptus fecerant ad victimas pro se & imperio Romano offerendas, & multis edictis libertatem unius ac summi Dei colendi Judæis firmaverant, ut ex Phi- lone & Josepho multis locis apparet. Ab horum bonis hac in parte institutis defecit Cajus, & quidem summa cum impietate, quæ in sequentibus depingitur plane velut in re præsente, ita ut difficile sit ullam reperire prophetiam, cui exitus exactius respondeat.

Similia proposuerat in commentatione: Ὅτι ἐὰν μὴ ἔλθῃ ἡ ἀποσασία πρῶτον) Quoniam nisi venerit discessio primum. Ἀποσασία discessio respon- det Ebræo סרה, quæ defectionem à Deo vero signifi- cat, Deut. XIII. 5. Ejusdem significationis est פשע. Dan. VIII. 12. in vaticinio de Antiocho illustri, qui Ca- jó huic plane παράλληλος compar est. Intelligenda autem est hic non qualiscunque, sed plena defectio, ἀσε- βημάτων χαλεπώτατον, impietatum maxima, ut hac de re agens Philo loquitur. Augustus & Tiberius Deos qui- dem coluerant Romanos, sed Deum opificem mundi, quem colebant Judæi & Christiani, adeo non oppugna- verant, ut & liberos ubique cœtus Judæis permiserint, liberasque in templum collationes: quin & ipsi dona in templum miserint, & perpetuos reditus in id dicaverint, ut inde quotidiana holocausta fierent τῷ ὑψίσῳ Θεῷ, Deo summo, taurus & agni duo, ut Philo in legatione docet, non uno in loco, ita scilicet existimantes, ut ejus- dem Philonis verbis utar, ὅ, τι ἀναγκαῖόν ἐστιν ἐν τοῖς πε- ριγείοις ἐξαίρετον ἀπονενεμῆσθαι τόπον τῷ ἀοράτῳ Θεῷ, μη- δὲν ὁρατὸν ἀπεικόνισμα περιέξοντα πρὸς μετουσίαν ἐλπίδων χρησῶν, opus esse in terris, unum aliquem seponi locum Deo conspicuo, qui nullam habeat aspectabilem effi- giem, nimirum ad bonæ spei participationem.

Ἀποσασία non simpliciter ἀσέβεια est, sed defe- ctionem à fide notat. Nec aliter accipitur Actor. XXI. 21. extra quem locum nuspiam alibi occurrit in Novo Testamento, verbum itidem de defectio- ne à fide adhibetur, 1. Timoth. IV. 1. ἀποσήσονταί τινες τῆς πίσεως, ut & Ebr. III. 12. Καρδία πονηρὰ ἀπισίαν ἐν τῷ ἀποσῆναι ἀπὸ Θεῦ ζῶντος. Adde Luc. IIX. 13. De defectione à fide usurpatur quoque nomen ἀποσασίας apud LXX. Interpretes 2. Pa- ral. XXIX. 19. Jerem. XXIX. 32. cap. II. 19. ut & in Maccabaicis 1. II. 15. nec non concretum ἀποσά- της, 2. Maccab. V. 8. Verbum etiam ἀφίσασθαι de defectione à vera religione ac cultu Dei occurrit, Jerem. XXXIII. 8. Ezech. XX. 38. &c. Et licet de Chaldæis semel nomen ἀποσάτης in scripto Apo- crypho alio quàm defectionis sensu adhiberetur (quod vero ibi etiam de iis, qui Babylone à DEI cultu ex Judæis defecerint, accipi potest) usita- tissima tamen est defectionis significatio. Nihil autem ad rem facit, quod voces Ebrææ מעל & סרה, quæ per ἀποσασίαν alicubi redduntur, etiam per ἀσέβειαν exponantur quandoque. Nam nihil ab- surdius, quam variarum vocum Græcarum signi- ficationes permutare, quia vox una Ebræa plures illas Græcas significatu suo complectitur. Non de Ebræa, sed Græcæ vocis significatione famosio- ri quæstio est, quam defectionem inferre negari non potest, sive etymon sive usum vocis respicias. Et agnoscit ipse Grotius, ἀποσασίαν respondere סרה, quod defectionem à Deo vero significat, & פשע non proprie ἀποσασίαν, sed contumaciam impietatemque in Deum notat. Unde LXX. In- terpretes eam vocem reddunt ἀνομίαν, ἀδικίαν, ἀδίκημα, ἀνόμημα, ἁμάρτημα, ἁμαρτίαν, ἀσέβημα, ἀθέτημα, παράπτωμα, ἀπώλειαν, πλάνην, ἀπο- σασίαν nunquam. In loco autem Danielis ἁμαρ- τίαν interpretantur. Antiochum etiam typum fu- isse Caji, præter Grotium nemo, quod sciam, dixit.

Anti-Christi eum typum comuniter constituunt. Apostatam Rabbini מומר quasi mutatum dicunt, Gregor. Tholosan. in Syntagm. Juris libr. II. cap. 2. h. 5. Apostata dicitur desertor & proditor fidei, qui omnino à fide Catholica, & à Dei veri religione re- cessit; Becano cap. XIV. de fide q. 3. apostasia est in- fidelitas, per quam quis omnino recedit à vera fi- in baptismo suscepta, ut quando ex Christiano fit Ju- dæus vel paganus. Conf. Tit. IX. l. V. decretal. qui est de Apostat. & reiter. baptism. Quo pacto Julianus Apostata dictus: Sed & hæretici apostatare à fi- de dicuntur, & apostatæ vocantur. L. si qui sanctam C. de Apost. Quomodo autem Cajo ἀποστασία sen- su proprio conveniat, Grotius explicare non po- tuit. Quod ait, eundem à bonis institutis defecisse, nihil ad rem facit. Nam hîc de insigni ἀποστασίᾳ & defectione à vera religione sermo est: Num au- tem Cajus unquam veræ religioni addictus fuit, ut ab eadem defecisse dici possit? Superavit Cajus Augusti & Tiberii impietatem, sed non magis apo- stata fuit, quam isti; si apostata quis dicitur, qui impius in Deum, etsi nunquam paruerit DEO, adeoque nec defecerit à Deo, omnes Cæsares us- que ad Constant. M. apostatæ vocandi. Qui ergo Paulus Cajo ἀποστασίαν ceu aliquid singulare tri- buit? Terminus enim à quo ἀποστασίας fides est, ut explicatur 1. Tim. IV. 1. Spiritus manifeste dicit, quod in novissimis temporibus discedent quidam à fide, attendentes spiritibus erroris, & doctrinis Dæ- monum, in hypocrisi loquentium mendacium, & cauteriatam habentium conscientiam, prohiben- tium nubere, jubentium abstinere à cibis &c. Quem sensum etiam probat sequens descriptio, cum tri- buitur huic apostatæ mysterium iniquitatis, cum adventus ejus futurus dicitur secundum operatio- nem Satanæ, in virtute, signis & prodigiis, ad men- dacium persuadendum, & pœna ipsorum, qui eun- dem sequuntur, assignatur efficacia errorum, ideo quod veritatem non dilexere.

Ideo probanda non est ipsorum interpretatio, qui de apostasia ab obsequio imperii Romani expo- fuere Tertullian. libr. de resurr. carn. Hieron. ad Algas. quæst. XI. Sedulius, Haymo, Cornelius à La- pide, Becanus alii. Sed quanquam Anti-Christus ab obsequio vel subjectione territoriali, & recogni- tione superioritatis deficiat; id tamen hîc non agi, sed defectionem à fide designari, ex dictis patet. Ideoque nec eorum, qui utramque illam defectio- nem à fide, & ab imperio Romano, Ecclesiasticam & civilem conjungunt, utpote Bullingeri, Hyperii, Aretii, Quirini, Reuteri in continuatione com- mentarii Zanchiani &c. interpretationem appro- bare possumus, sed unice de apostasia à fide intelli- gimus cum Græcis Patribus Chrysostomo, Dama- sceno libr. IV. de orthod. fide cap. 28. Theodoreto, Theophylacto. Chrysostomus: Anti-Christum, in- quit, vocat ἀποστασίαν defectionem, ὡς πολλοὺς μέλ- λοντα ἀπολλύναι καὶ ἀφιστᾶν, ut fraudalizentur et- iam, si fieri posset, electi. Theodoretus ἀποστασίαν sic explicat: Defectionem ipsum vocavit Anti-Christum, à re ipsa ei nomine imposito, conatur enim à veritate abducere, & efficere, ut deficiant. Theophylactus si- militer: Haudquaquam, inquit, adveniet Domi- nus, nisi & discessio prodeat, hoc est, Anti-Christus. Quem eo discessionem appellat, quia reipsa ita futu- rum sit, ut multos faciat à Christo desciscere, vel ele- ctos ipsos si fieri potest. Cui sententiæ etiam subscri- bunt è Reformatis plerique, Calvinus, Beza, Tos- sanus, Pareus, Piscator, Witakerus, Sutlivius, Bel- gici Interpretes, Crocius, Maresius; & inter Ponti- ficios, Lyra, Ariasmontanus, Adrichomius in Chron. fol. 285. Anglo-Remens. Scyanus, Justinia- nu, qui aperte profitetur, defectionem à Roma- no imperio parum ad rem facere.

Qui vero è Papistis dissolutionem vel defectio- nem Romani imperii hic intelligi volunt, ne có- gantur fateri, Anti-Christum jam venisse, Ro- manumque Pontificem Anti-Christum esse, nul- lo modo audiendi sunt. Nam nec apostasia defe- ctionem vel dissolutionem alicujus regni notat; nec ullo verbo designata est imperii Romani disso- lutio, nec illa ante consummationem seculi vi va- ticiniorum Danielis expectari potest, quum my- sterium iniquitatis Pauli tempore jam occulte cœperit, ac postmodum in nervum erumpere de- buerit, ac revelari, donec tandem Anti-Christus Spiritu oris Christi interficiatur, ac destruatur ad- ventu ejus novissimo. Non autem exiguam, sed insignem defectionem Anti-Christi fore, non pri- vatam unius aut paucorum quorundam, sed pu- blicam: Non particularem, sed generalem plurium Ecclesiarum, provinciarum, regnorum in toto orbe innuit Apostolus, cum simpliciter dicit ἡ ἀποσασία, & temporis notam addit, nisi prius ve- nerit, quo ipso nova & singularis apostasia præ- dicitur, quum à veritate fidei antea non pauci de- fecerint, Joh. VI. 66. 2. Tim. I, 15. c. II. 14. 18. Tit. I. 11. Vide & de latitudine apostasiæ & de multitudi ne apostatarum Apoc. XIII. 4. 16. Nulla autem un- quam tanta fuit in ulla secta, quanta Romani Pon- tificis, quæ passim in toto orbe prævaluit. De qua Romanæ Ecclesiæ apostasia à fide Christiana non pauci egerunt. Vid. peculiaris tractatus B. Nico- lai Hunnii de apostasia Rom. Eccles. ut & B. Hie- ronymi Kromayeri de Ecclesiæ Rom. apostasia in mysterio peracta, nec non B. Gerhardi in confess. Catholic, &c. Qualitas apostasiæ Romanæ à fide Apostolica patet ad oculum ex collatione profes- sionis fidei in Concilio Tridentino præscriptæ, & cultus, qui in Missalibus & Marialibus exhibetur, cum professione fidei & cultus exstantis in scri- ptura sacra & Symbolis Oecumenicis. Nulla etiam unquam secta præter Romanam ad tantum fastigium potestatis civilis aspiravit, ut potuerit in tanta latitudine regnorum & provinciarum (habi- tandi, negotiandi, emendi, vendendi &c.) inter- dicere iis, qui signum factæ exomologeseos Ro- manæ, rosaria, & Pater noster non exhibent, ne- que ulla ab armis tam formidabilis unquam fuit, quam hæc bestia Apoc. XIII. 4. cap. XVII. 1. 2. 8.

Καὶ ἀποκαλυφθῇ ὁ ἄνθρωπος τῆς ἁμαρτίας) Denudet in- genium suum Cajus. Nam initio principatus bonum se si- mulando spem omnium excitaverat. Ἀποκαλύπτεσθαι גלה ut & infra 8. est subito apparere, ut jam diximus l. vers. 7. ᾙμαρτία modo respondet Ebræo חטאה, modo in sensu eminentioni nomini רשע Et ita hic recte vertas איש רשע homo plane improbus, quippe & incestis & parrici- diis inquinatus. Vide Suetonium. Tertullianus vertit : Homo delinquentiæ.

Ὁ Υἱὸς τῆς ἀπωλείας) Qui titulus Judæ datur, Johan. XVII, 12. ubi diximus idem esse, quod בן מות, 2. Sam. XII. vers. 15. & significari hominem, qui dignus sit pessime perire, quod & Cajo evenit.

Quæ plenius tradiderat in commentatione ad hunc modum:

Καὶ ἀποκαλυφθῇ ὁ ἄνθρωπος τῆς ἁμαρτίας) Et reve- latus fuerit homo peccati. Erat jam quidem Princeps, sed facinorosum ingenium nondum detexerat Cajus. Suetonius : Sic imperium adeptus populum Romanum, vel ut ita dicam, hominum genus voti compotem fecit exoptatissimus Princeps maximæ parti provincialium ac militum. Deinde: Incendebat & ipse studia homi- num omni genere popularitatis. Cujus generis, cum multa narrasset idem Suetonius, subjungit : Hactenus quasi de Principe, reliqua ut de monstro narranda sunt. Philo: Μίμνηται γὰρ ὀδείς τοσαύτην χώρας μιᾶς ἡ̓ ἑνὸς ἔθνυς γενέσθαι χαράν ἐπὶ σωτηρίἀ κὰι καταστάσει ἡγεμόνος,

ὅση ἐπὶ Γαΐῳ συμπάσης τῆς οἰκουμένης, καὶ παραλαβόν- τῳ τὴν ἀρχὴν, καὶ ῥωσθέντι ἐκ τῆς ἀσθενείας. Ὥσπερ γὰρ ἐκ νομάδος βίου καὶ θηριώδους νῦν πρῶτον ἀρχόμενοι με- ταβάλλειν πρὸς τὸ σύννομον ἠὲ ὁμοδίαιτον, κᾀκ ἐξ ἐρημίας σκηνῶν καὶ ὑπαιθρείων ἀποικίζεσθαι πόλεσι τειχήρεσι, κᾀκ ἐξ ἀνεπιτροπεύτου ζωῆς ὑπὸ ἐπιτρόπῳ τάττεσθαι τομεῖ τινι ἠὲ ἀγελάρχῳ τῆς ἡμετέρας ἀγέλης. ἐγεγήθεσαν ἀγνοίᾳ τῆς ἀληθείας. Τυφλώττει γὰρ ὁ ἀνθρώπινος νοῦς πρὸς τὴν τοῦ συμφέροντος ὄντως αἴσθησιν εἰκασμῷ καὶ στοχασμῷ μᾶλ- λον, ἢ ἐπιστήμῃ χρῆσθαι δυνάμενος. Εὐθὺς γοῦν ἐκ τοῦ μακρὰν ὁ σωτὴρ καὶ εὐεργέτης εἶναι νομισθεὶς, καί τινας ἀγαθῶν πηγὰς νέας ἐπομβρήσειν Ἀσίατε καὶ Εὐρώπῃ πρὸς εὐδαιμονίαν ἀκαθαίρετον, ἰδίατε ἑκάστῳ ἠὲ πᾶσι κοινῇ τὸ λεγόμενον δὴ τοῦτο ἀφ' ἑστίας ἤρξατο, μεταβαλὼν πρὸς τὸ ἀτίθασσον, μᾶλλον δὲ ἣν συνεσκίασεν ἀγριότητα τῷ πλά- σματι τῆς ὑποκρίσεως, ἀναφήνας. Neque enim memo- ria est unius regionis aut gentis tantum fuisse gaudium in salute aut evectione Principis alicujus, quanta super Cajo fuit totius orbis, & cum primum principatum adeptus fuit, & ubi ex morbo convaluit. Tanquam enim ex vita sylvestri & ferina inciperent jamjam trans- ire ad alteram mansuetam atque civilem, aut ex tento- riis solitariis arduisque montium migrare in munitas urbes, aut ex vita tutelæ egente transferri in tutelam ejus, qui pastor & Dux futurus esset humano gregi, læ- tabantur ex veri ignorantia. Cæcutire enim solet hu- mana mens circa sensum ejus, quod sibi expedit, ut quæ conjectura magis & opinione ducatur quam scientia certa Parum enim intercessit temporis, cum ille, qui conservator & beneficiorum largitor fore sperabatur, qui bonorum fontibus novis irrigaturus putabatur A- siam atque Europam ad felicitatem perpetuam atque privatam, ab ipso lare, quod dicitur, exorsus ad feri- tatem se convertit, aut potius, quam sub fallaci persona tegebat feritatem, detexit. Quod ἀποκαλυφθῆναι reve- lari est Paulo in prædictione, idem Philoni in historia rei, per quam prædictio impleta est, ἀναφαίνειν, sic ἀπο- καλύπτεσθαι sumitur Luc. II. vers. 35. 1. Corinth. III. 13. & mox bis in eadem hac pericopa. Dion: Δημοκρατι- κώτατος γὰρ εἶναι τὰ πρῶτα δόξας, μοναρχικώτατος ἐγέ- νετο, cum initio maxime popularis videretur, factus est maxime imperiosus, & quæ ibi sequuntur.

Ἄνθρωπος τῆς ἁμαρτίας) Homo peccati. Loquen- di genus Ebræum, quo significatur is, qui insigniter est sceleratus, qualem Cajus se ostendit, non cædibus tan- tum plurimorum innocentium, stuprisque & adulteriis, sed iis criminibus, supra quæ cogitari vix quidquam potest, parricidiis & incestis. Memorat dictum ejus Sue- tonius factis congruens: Memento mihi omnia & in omnes licere. Hanc illius immanitatem plene cogno- scere qui volet, legat Philonem, Suetonium, Dionem, & Josephum initio XIX. antiquæ historiæ. Occulte au- tem loquitur Apostolus, quia de Imperatore, uti de Ne- rone 2. Timoth. IV. vers. 17.

Ὁ υἱὸς τῆς ἀπωλείας) Filius perditionis. בֶּן מָוֶת 2. Sam. XII. vers. 15. Occurrit hæc loquutio Joh. XVII. v. 12. & ἔθνος ἀπωλείας gens perditionis libro Sirac. XVI. vers. 10. Significat Apostolus Cajum, sicut infi- gniter facinorosus fuit, ita insigni etiam exitio a DEO fuisse destinatum, quo nihil dici potuit verius. Philo de eo apud Josephum : ὡς χρὴ θαῤῥεῖν, Γαΐου λόγῳ μὲν αὐτοῖς ὠργισμένου, ἔργῳ δὲ ἤδη τὸν Θεὸν ἀντιπαρεξάγον- τος : bonam spem sumendam, quando Cajus verbis quidem in ipsos iram ostenderet, re autem ipsa Deum sibi hostem faceret. Dion de ejus exitu: Τοῖς ἔργοις ὡς οὐκ ἦν Θεὸς ἔμαθεν: Exitu didicit, quam ipse non esset Deus. Prædictum ei fuerat, ut Cassium caveret. Ca- vere non potuit. Multa alia præcesserant, quæ divinum de ipsius nece insigni decretum aperte significarent. Vi- de Suetonium & Dionem. Memorabile illud, quod apud Josephum narratur, de ejus morte dixisse Minu- tianus: Καὶ νῦν λόγῳ μὲν εἴπαι τέτυς, οἳ ἀνῃρήκασι Γαΐον, ἔργῳ δὲ αὐτὸν ὑφ' ἑαυτοῦ κεῖσθαι διολωλότα, illos quidem famam habere, quasi Cajum interemissent, at reipsa Ca- jum a semetipso postratum.

Ad has canoras nugas respondit jam Maresius 2. Cajum post adeptum imperium tamdiu inge- nium suum recte non habuisse, ut multum fue- rit expectanda animi pessimi renudatio. De illo enim statim constitisse, nec servum meliorem ul- lum, nec deteriorem Dominum fuisse, ut est apud Suetonium cap. X. Imo Cajum jam, cum hæc scriberentur juxta Grotium, anno altero regni, satis ostendisse, qualis esset. Nam cum quadrien- nium integrum non expleverit in imperio, totum vero triennium consumpserit, in facinoribus varii generis, uti diserte asserit Sext. Aur. Victor in ipso, necesse est, eum facinorosum ingenium retexisse ante primum imperii sui annum exactum, etsi for- te Judæos non nisi sequente vexare cœperit. Quid reponere aliud potuit Grotius, quam quod imme- rito fides Philonis suspecta reddatur? At non reddi- tur suspecta. Imo idem Philo dixerat in verbis ab ipso Grotio adductis, tempore exiguo occultasse in- genium Caligulam. Parum, inquit, intercessit tem- poris, cum, quam sub fallaci persona tegebat, ferita- tem detexit. Adde, quod, Suetonio cap. XI. teste, ne tum quidem Cajus naturam sævam atque probro- sam inhibere potuerit, quando optimi servi elogium merebatur, adeo ut Tiberius ea perspecta aliquoties prædiceret, exitio suo omniumque Cajum vivere, & senatricem (serpentis id genus) populo Romano, Phaëtontern orbi terrarum educare : Quodque Dio l. 59. quibus sceleribus ipsas imperii sui primitias consecrarit Cajus, docuerit: ad quod etiam parri- cidio viam sibi fecerat, suffocato Tiberio, eodem l. 58. & Suetonio cap. XII. teste. Grotius vult τὸ ἀποκαλύπλεσθαι à Paulo prædictum Philoni in histo- ria rei, per quam prædictio impleta est, esse ἀποφαί- νειν. At, quæ refert Philo ibi, ad annum Caji pri- mum juxta eundem pertinent. Paulum autem hæc anno Caji secundo scripsisse, statuit Grotius. Prius ergo impleta illa, quam prædicta esse oportet. Ὁ ἄνθρωπος τῆς ἁμαρτίας Theodoreto, Chrysostomo, Theophylacto, Anti-Christus est, qui de Cajo ne somniarunt quidem.

Parum autem erat Apostolo dicere ἁμαρτωλόν: Dicit ἄνθρωπον τῆς ἁμαρτίας, quia totus immer- sus erit peccatis, gurges impietatis, sentina flagi- tiorum, mancipium simul & autor peccati. Nec enim peccatum unum aut alterum intelligit, sed peccata in utramque tabulam decalogi patrata. Insuper & peccati hominem eundem hunc dicit, in- quit Theophylactus, perinde ac si scelerum omnium futurus sit patrntor, seducturusque & alios ad patran- dum. Non ergo tantum eximie scelestum, sed qui alios etiam ad scelera inducat, tum doctrina, qui 'ceu Doctor sedet in templo Dei, tum praxi & exemplo denotat. Ὁ υἱὸς ἀπωλείας, Theodore- to autore, dicitur, qui & ipse pereat, & aliis interi- tum procuret. Maresius Grotio id reposuerat: Ho- mo peccati equidem insigniter scelestum notat, sed hic eum, cujus notæ omnes neutiquam in Caligulam cadant. Nec Cajo, quoad morum improbitatem, in- feriores fuerunt Heliogabalus, Domitianus, Nero ipse, cui successit Tiberius, cujus malitia non minor, quia tectior: & vel in eo magis detestanda, quod Ca- jum, quem pessimum norat futurum, successorem dixerit, ut scilicet scelerum suorum memoriam hac arte induceret, & sui desiderium populo relinqueret. Et porro: Fuerit Cajus, ut observat Commentator, facinorosus insigniter, & ob id insigni etiam exitio à DEO destinatus, non tamen inde sequitur, quod potuerit dici κατ' ἐξαίρετον ὁ υἱὸς τῆς ἀπωλείας filius ille perditionis, cujus hic fit mentio. Qui enim hoc elogio decoratur, non sibi modo debet exitium accer- sere, sed & aliis quoque, in exitium abducendis, esse ὁδηγὸς & antesignanus, ut Act. I. 16. & Job. XVIII. vers. 3. de Juda proditore observatur, qui & eodem hoc insignitur elogio, tanquam typus & prodromus Anti-Christi, neg; בן מות filius mortis 2.Sam. XII. v. 15. idem sonat, ut Commentator arbitratur. Omnis enim reus mortis ex magistratus judicio, non est, quoad Deum & Ecclesiam, filius perditionis : dum illud reatum proprie sive obligationem ad pœnam denotat, hoc vero vitia & crimina. Annon longe facilius hæc ei conveniant, qui tantam defectionem invexit in Ecclesiam à puritate fidei, eam speciatim, quæ cibos & conjugia spectat, de qua Paulus 1.Tim. IV. quique etsi innumerabiles populos catervatim se- cum ducat primo mancipio gehennæ, cum ipso pla- gis multis in æternum vapulaturos, nullius redar- gutioni esset obnoxius, ut loquitur jus Canonicum de Romano Pontifice Can. Si Papa. dist. 40. Quot, quæso, illam sedem obtinuerunt, ipsis Caligulis & Neronibus deteriores? Videatur Baronii ipsius que- rela ad decimum Christi seculum, & Genebrardi testimonium, de Pontificibus fere quinquaginta, sibi mutuo succedentibus eo seculo, qui à majorum virtute defecerunt, apotactici, apostaticive potius, quam Apostolici. Hi monstra & portenta Platina dicuntur in Bened. IV. non minus, quam Suetonio Cajus. Carpit etiam Mantuanus Romuleas arces & Pontificalia tecta, -- colluviem scelerum. Ipse Marcellus II. apud Onuphrium nullum Pon- tificem servari posse existimavit. Parco nominibus singulorum. Id vero, quod Commentator tanquam teterrimum de Cajo commemorat: Memento, mihi omnia & in omnes licere, est longe infra illam ple- nitudinem potestatis in spiritualibus & temporali- bus, quam sibi arrogat Pontifex Romanus, homo ille spiritualis, si Diis placet, qui omnia judicat, & à nemine judicatur. Illius denique sedis adulatores & admiratores turpiora de suis Pontificibus scripsisse, quam de Cajo, vel Suetonium, vel Tacitum, vel Philonem ei speciatim infensum, nescire non potuit Commentator, ex quibus adeo certiora desumi pos- sint filii perditionis γνωρίσματα, quam quæ ipse Cajo deputat. Grotius ad illa non invenit, quod reponeret.

Quomodo vero doctrina Romani Anti-Chri- sti ad omnis generis peccata inducat, ac univer- sum pietatis studium labefactet, synoptice atque erudite demonstrat B. Gerhardus noster disputa- tionibus peculiaribus. Quod ante Cajum scele- stiorem neminem fuisse pertendit Grotius, neque veritati litat, neque ad rem quicquam facit, quum sufficiat, æque scelestos postea fuisse, ut Cajo id temere approprietur κατ' ἀντονομασίαν: & Neroni potius hoc elogium, quam Cajo, convenire, maxi- me autem Pontifici Romano, quum nonnullos è Pontificibus, Cajo multo superiores fuisse im- pietate ac sceleribus, dubium non sit. Omnes in id ipsum laborant, ut impietatem doceant & pro- pugnent, parricidia in Reges & Principes justifi- cent, subditos à juramento fidelitatis absolvant, potestates summas sibi subjiciant, fœdera non servanda pertendant, incestus permittant & ratos habeant, conjugia illicita licita, juxta Dei ver- bum pura & incontaminata, impura & profana faciant, & quæ sexcenta talia impietatis Papalis notoria documenta annotari possent. Ecquis er- go eum κατ' ἐξοχὴν jure eximio hominem peccati etiam præ Cajo nuncupari inficietur? Qui sibi pu- tat omnia in omnes licere & in omnia, homo ille spiritualis, juxta Glossam Papalem, qui omnia ju- dicat, & à nemine judicatur.

Quo facit, quod Grotius ipse ad Job. IX. verf. 16. ἄνθρωπον ἁμαρτωλὸν interpretetur, qui se falso à Deo missum prædicat. Tales enim, inquit excellenter peccatores vocantur. Sic ὁ ἄνθρωπος τῆς ἁμαρτίας, 2. Thessal. II. 3. Quis hoc Cajo tribuat, qui nunquam se à Deo missum prædicavit? Quis non videt, ita Pontificem Romanum ἄνθρωπον τῆς ἁμαρτίας ab ipso Gretio, nondum ab Anti-Christo conducto, tum vocatum? Quem etiam præ aliis ὑὸν ἀπωλείας dici eximiē, quod αἱρέσεις ἀπωλείας docendo, sibi & aliis innumeris ταχίσην ἀπώλειαν adducat; 2. Petr. II. 1. 2. dubium esse nequit, quúm Tridenti à Papa Romano hæreses complures sancitæ sint. Cui, etiamsi innumerabiles papatus catervatim se- cum ducat primo mancipio gehennæ secum pla- gis multis in æternum vapulaturos, nemo dicere debeat: Papa, quid facis? Ut è can. Si papa. dist. 40. ante observatum.

Nec vero singulare individuum inferendum, quod ὁ ἄνθρωπος, & ὁ υἱὸς vocetur. Articulus etiam adhibetur, ubi non de singulari persona sermo est, Matth. V. 7. 9. c. XIII. 2. 27. 35. c. XV. 20. Marc. II. 27. Luc. IV. 4. Vocat ergo Apostolus hominem pec- cati, non quod futurus esset homo singularis, sed quod futurum regnum humanū in Ecclēsia, quod quicunque occupat, homo ille peccator est. Sic filia Zion & filia Babylon non de certa persona, sed de regno & populo usurpatur. Neque vero aliter Daniel singularibus ursi, leonis, pardi nominibus multos Reges intelligit, in unum monarchiæ cor- pus junctis. Homo enim ille peccati, qui jam oc- culte cœpit, demum in die novissimo exscindendǫ est. Quem pro tempore sub unitate individuali, sive unicum, existere non negamus, ut unus est Imperator Romanus, unus Rex Gallorum; abso- lute vero unicum esse, sicut Christus unus est, vel cum morte unius individui terminari, aut successore ca- rere Anti-Christum, hoc est, quod inficiamur. Du- rat enim homo ille peccati usque ad diem extremi judicii, quod de uno individuo dici nequit. Quic- quid etiam hic prætendant Papistæ, utopici Anti- Christi autores, quod non nisi per tres annos & dimidium regnaturus sit.

Cæterum revelatio Anti-Christi bifariam acci- pitur, 1. cum, quod occulte prius fovebat, aperte prodidit, cum tyrannidem suam palam exercere cœpit. 2. Cum manifestatus ipse fuit aliorum ope- ra, opinione veritatis & sanctitatis ipsi detracta, & impietate cum doctrinæ, tum vitæ ejus, in apri- cum producta. Quæ posterior revelatio hic intel- ligenda: Siquidem prior illa non adeo publica fue- rit, quum contra publice recta potius sit pietatis & propagationis regni Christi proterva tyrannis Anti-Christiana, nec nisi à paucis animadverti ea patuerit, donec palam per Spiritum Domini ma- nifestaretur. Quam publicam & apertam manife- stationem ante adventum Domini futuram hic in- nuit Apostolus, ut plerique Interpretes, & è nostris Osiander, Hunnius, Vinarienses, alii exposuere.

## 2:4
Verse 4. Ὁ ἀντικείμενος) שָׂטָן, that is, the adversary of God, as the Devil is especially called, and those who imitate him. For שָׂטָן is explained by ἀντικείμενος in Aquila and Symmachus, Gen. 26:21; in Origen, tenth book on Romans; in Chrysostom, on the 12th of the second to the Corinthians. Tertullian translates it enemy. But where nothing is added, it is understood as the enemy of GOD, as in Theodotion, Job 1. It fits Gaius best, who, as Philo speaks: ἄγος τὸν Θεὸν ἀντιπαρεξῆγε, by his deeds made God his enemy.

In the commentary, Grotius says this about this epithet:

Verse 4.

Ὁ ἀντικείμενος) who opposes, that is, שָׂטָן. Thus what is in the Hebrew in 3 Kings, or as others number it, ch. 11:14, ויקם יהוה שטן לשלמה, and in the Greek: Ἐξήγειρε Κύριος Σατὰν τῷ Σολομῶντι. Tertullian explains against Marcion, book 3: He will raise up a Satan for him, that is, an enemy. And Chrysostom in ch. 12 of the second to the Corinthians, citing 3 Kings v. 4, Ὄυκ ἦν Σατὰν ἐν ἡμέραις αὐτῶ, explains it as meaning ἀντικείμενος. Thus in Luke 13:17, 21:15, 1 Cor. 16:9, Phil. 1:28, 1 Tim. 5:14, the word ἀντικείμενος is used, but with an adjunct or addition, or easily understood from what precedes. But when it is placed absolutely, it signifies him who opposes God in any way, in which sense the Hebrew word is read in Matt. 16:23 and the places in Mark and Luke which correspond to that passage. But it is applied with the highest right to him who, not once or by mistake, but with a perpetual and determined purpose, opposes God, which Gaius did, a peer in this to the Devil, to whom that name is especially attributed. For the same reason, παράλληλος, a peer to Gaius, is called Antiochus Diabolus, 1 Macc. 1:38.

It is the unanimous opinion of all that by that great Anti-Christ, who was to surpass Antiochus, who was to surpass the impiety of Gaius, who was to surpass the impiety of all the impious as the first-born of the Devil, is to be understood. He who was to oppose Christ, not only in life and practice, but in public doctrine: not only regarding morals, but also regarding dogmas: not only regarding the worship of GOD and the duties to be shown to one's neighbor, and thus regarding both tables of the divine law, but also regarding the Gospel and the preaching of grace: not only regarding the principle, the Word of God, but also regarding the conclusions deduced from the principle of religion: not only by himself, but with his whole retinue, just as the Devil with all the power of darkness, and his whole kingdom, opposes Christ. He who by antonomasia is ὁ ἀντικείμενος (the adversary), because he opposes himself to God in all things; for example, he does not admit the Word of God to be the Word of God, unless his own authority is added: he does not leave the Word of God its perspicuity and perfection, he superadds his own traditions: he does not permit the Word of God to all, but to those whom he wishes: he does not want the Word of God to be expounded, except as he himself wishes: he dispenses against the Word of God and divine laws, he takes upon himself the power of mutilating and instituting sacraments, he snatches the cup from the laity, he prohibits marriage to the clergy, against the Word of God he converts the sacrament into a sacrifice, by feigning purgatory and liberation from it through the suffrages of the living and sacrifices, the treasury of the merits of the saints, indulgences, etc. Furthermore, he opposes himself to God in new divine worships, and in various interdictions to be enacted without the Word of God, and in ordering manifold idolatry? by either permitting or establishing contrary divine precepts: He opposes himself to GOD and Christ by defining another method of our justification and salvation, other means of justification and salvation, and there are countless others of this kind, by which he demonstrates himself to be the ἀντικείμενον, the adversary to GOD. If anyone, with Grotius, wishes to deny this regarding the Roman Pontiff, he might with the same rashness deny that the sun shines at midday.

He who is ὁ ἀντικείμενος, opposing himself and acting as an adversary to God, is also called ὁ Ἀντίχριςος, by which word John explains the present, 1 Epist. II. Some, even Maresius, explain both words not only as an enemy and adversary, opposing himself to God and Christ, but also as one who would make himself the vicar of Christ, and an ἀντίστροφον κὶ ἀντιτάλαντον (counterpart and counterweight) to him. But we easily agree that the former meaning alone has place, just as Origen in book X to the Romans and Theophylact to Matthew XII, as well as Aquila and Symmachus, Gen. XXVI. 21, explain the word שטן by the word ἀντικειμένη. Moreover, an enemy of God is to be understood, because that word has that meaning where it is placed absolutely, and the following words demand the same, as Grotius admits in the Appendix.

However, Maresius rightly notes in Anti-Christo Revel. part I. page 315, that ἀντικείμενος is always not some outsider and Gentile Emperor, but someone domestic within the very temple of God, inducing apostasy from the truth of Christ, and thus resisting Christ and His truth. For just as Christ κεῖται εἰς σημεῖον ἀντιλεγόμενον (is set for a sign that is spoken against), Luc. II. 34, so ὁ ἀντικείμενος, who most of all ἀντιλέγει τῷ χρισῷ (speaks against Christ), while he constitutes himself Head, King, and Monarch of the Church without His authority and command, just as he ἀντιλέγει τῷ Καίσαρι (speaks against Caesar) who makes himself King, Joh. XIX. 12, that is, as the great man interprets in the same place, taking upon himself the role of the Roman Emperor claims, who wishes to reign without his authority. Thus ἀντικείμενοι, Luke 21:15, are those who, as much as in them lies and with all their strength, ἀνθίσανται τῇ ἀληθείᾳ, resist the truth, and attempt to overcome it with every art, which is the phrase of Paul in 2 Timothy 3:8. In the same sense in Luke 13:17, ἀντικείμενοι αὐτῷ are those who contradict Christ and his truth, and no differently are the ἀντικείμενοι πολλοὶ, 1 Corinthians 16:9, Philippians 1:28; indeed, for this reason, whatever is contrary to sound doctrine is rejected by Paul, 1 Timothy 1:10, and what strikes more closely, 1 Timothy 5:14, he wishes younger widows to marry and manage domestic affairs, so that no occasion is given for slandering τῷ ἀντικειμένῳ.

And who exalts himself above every so-called God) As often as Christ or the Apostles take the very words from some place in the Old Testament, we must understand that it concerns a similar or even greater matter. These words are taken from Daniel, where he speaks of Antiochus Epiphanes, chapter 11:36, ויתגדל על־כל־אל: In Greek κὶ μεγαλυνθήσεται ἐπὶ πάντα Θεόν: Where μεγαλυνθήσεται, like ὑπεραιρόμενος here, is passive in sound, but reciprocal in sense, as appears from the Hebrew, he exalted himself above every God. Paul, lest anyone should believe that those of whom he is treating here were Gods, added for the sake of caution, λεγόμενον, by which mark he also designates the gods of the nations elsewhere, 1 Corinthians 8:5. Antiochus had notably despised all the gods of the nations: For ἱεροσυλήσας τὰ πλεῖστα τῶν ἱερῶν, as Polybius says of him in an excellent fragment which is in Athenaeus. Through these steps he arrived at the contempt of the true GOD. Thus also Gaius preferred himself to all the gods of the nations, even to Jupiter Olympius and Capitolinus: and if any doubted whether he was greater than Jupiter, he treated them most cruelly: he said the Moon was his concubine: the Castors his doorkeepers: concerning which matters we have brought forward testimonies elsewhere at length.

Ἡ σέβασμα) We have said that σέβασμα is everything through which God is worshipped, in which sense Jerome not badly translates σεβάσματα in Acts 17:23 as 'objects of worship': Severus and Theophylactus interpret this as images here. Philo in the history of the matter predicted here calls them σεβάσματα. Gaius surpassed the worship of all gods by the institution of his own worship, because he also took away the insignia from Hercules, Apollo, Liber, Venus, Mercury, the Castors, and others: and furthermore he wished sacrifices to be made to him at much greater expense, as Dion testifies. Those were not true Gods, but Gaius wanted them to be held as Gods, and yet he preferred himself to them. His own opinion bound him to guilt, as Seneca speaks somewhere. The Hebrews at Leviticus 24:15 say that a pagan man sins gravely if he curses his own Gods.

He had proposed similar things in his commentary, which, however much they are vainer than fig-leaf trifles, he did not fear to repeat here. For thus Grotius has it there:

And who exalts himself above every so-called God, and is exalted above everything that is called God) Taken from Daniel, where the discourse is about Antiochus, to whom Gaius did the like, Daniel 11:36. Paul added λεγόμενον only for the sake of interpretation. There are many λεγόμενοι Θεοὶ, who are called Gods, as the same Apostle says here, 1 Corinthians 8:5, namely those who were commonly believed to be such. Tertullian against Marcion, book 1: For the idols of the nations are also commonly called gods, but no one is a god by the fact that he is called a god. Paul rightly gathers the impiety of Gaius, who opposed himself to the true God, from this, that he not only equaled himself to those whom he himself held as Gods, but even preferred himself to them. Jupiter was held to be the highest of the gods. He accused him because he had occupied the Capitol. Even when he had wished to change the statue of Jupiter Olympius into his own likeness, and could not because of the thunderbolts which had destroyed the ship, he threatened him. At other times also, with machines made for that purpose, he would make a noise with thunder and imitate lightning: He even said that Homeric line to Jupiter: Ἤ μ᾽ ἀνάειρ᾽, ἢ ἐγὼ σε, either lift me up, or I you. Dion has all these things, and Suetonius many. Nor do I doubt that in chapter 22 of Suetonius the same Greek words that are in Dion, although they were uttered toward Jupiter Capitolinus, are to be restored, and all the more so because Seneca placed the same ones near the end of the first book of his work On Anger, where, commemorating those terrible and tumultuous sayings of Gaius Caesar, he says: He challenged Jupiter to a fight, and indeed without quarter, exclaiming that Homeric line: Ἤ μ᾽ ἀνάειρ᾽, ἢ ἐγὼ σε. Nor should that be omitted from Suetonius, that when, standing by the statue of Jupiter, he had consulted Apelles the tragedian as to which of them seemed greater, he whipped him when he hesitated. Josephus in book 19, at the beginning, narrates that when he was asked whether he was greater or Jupiter, he left it in the middle as if out of modesty. He said that he slept with the Moon. Moreover, he had made the Castors his doorkeepers, as Dion narrates: nor did he treat other gods more reverently, as will now appear. Thus Antiochus had despised the Elymaean Diana and other gods of pagan superstition.

˝Η σέβασμα) or object of worship. Σεβάσματα are called those things which serve the worship of God or of those who are thought to be Gods. In that sense this word exists in Acts 17:23, where Jerome translates it as 'objects of worship'. Philo called them σεβασμὺς in the same sense in this very matter.
