Such are temples, images, the insignia of the gods, and sacrifices. He envied Jupiter for the most august temple of the Roman empire, which was the Capitol. He ordered the statue of Jupiter Olympius to be brought from Greece so that he might change it into his own likeness, which Dion narrates. He had attributed to himself the insignia of the gods snatched from the gods: at one time he proceeded holding a thunderbolt, at another a trident, at another a caduceus, and he was even seen in the attire of Venus, says Suetonius. But Dion: And he often became Hera, and Artemis, and Aphrodite. For indeed, for the changing of the names, he took on all the other appearance appropriate to them, and at one time he appeared effeminate and held a mixing bowl and a thyrsus, and at another he wore a masculine club and a lion's skin. Leiogeneios and again, and upon this he imagined himself bearded, he is a trident-bearer, when he was in power, and he would brandish a thunderbolt again, and he would liken himself to a warlike virgin. He often made himself Juno, often Diana, often Venus, and just as he had changed his name, so he also assumed the habit appropriate to the name, sometimes putting on women's clothing and carrying a goblet and a thyrsus; at other times with a manly countenance he would take up a club and the skin of a lion, appearing now smooth, now bearded. There was a time when he held a trident: at another time he would extend a thunderbolt, and would show himself like a warlike virgin. But Philo sets forth most extensively all these insignia of the Gods, which Gaius had transferred to himself: the lion skins taken from Hercules, the caps from the Castors, the ivy, thyrsus, fawn-skin, caduceus, winged sandals, and cloak from Father Liber, the radiated crowns, bow, arrows, and thanks from Apollo, the sword, helmet, and shield from Mars. In the same place Philo calls these insignia parasēma, periapta, proskosmēmata, xoanois kai agalmasi prosidrymena, signs, accessories, ornaments placed upon statues and images, and as I just said, sebasmos. Dion indeed [calls them] prostheta ē prostheta. Not content with those sacrifices which were accustomed to be offered to the accepted Gods, he ordered birds of rare and immense value to be slaughtered, as Dion testifies. Thus he had either snatched away all the objects of worship of the Gods, or was surpassing them by the institution of his own cult.

That Daniel 11:36 does not treat of Antiochus, which Maresius and Crocius concede to Grotius, but of the Anti-Christ, we have shown in that place. Theodoret also explains it here concerning the Anti-Christ: The divine Daniel also predicted these things. For he said: He shall not understand the Gods of his fathers, and he shall glorify the God Maozim in his place. For that which is, he shall call himself a strong God. But that Antiochus was a type of Gaius, and that the latter was much worse than the former, which Grotius rashly asserted, we consider to have been sufficiently shown by Maresius in his response to the appendix of Grotius. See part I, Anti-Christ. Revel. chapter XVIII, page 326.

By panta legomenon Theon, or pan to legomenon Theon, which reading Beza introduced against the faith of all the Codices, the Old Interpreter, along with Jerome to Algasia, renders the sense, not the words, which was also done by the Blessed Luther; Grotius understands only the gods of the nations, and proves this sense from a comparison with 1 Cor. 8:6. But neither in that passage are the legomenoi Theoi only the idols of the nations, for many are also said TO BE GODS, just as many are called LORDS, not only said to be so: in which way both Angels and Magistrates are Gods not only kata to legesthai, but kata to einai, not indeed by nature, but by office, nor in this passage, when the Apostle pointed out panta legomenon Theon, is it necessary to restrict it either to the idols of the nations, since both Angels and Magistrates, to whom that name is also attributed in the scriptures, and God himself are included under that common name, when the Anti-Christ is said to be exalting himself not expressly, as Cornelius à Lapide perverts it, but by power above every one who is named God. Nor are there lacking Interpreters who take it generally, so that it embraces both the true God and the reputed ones, which is the explanation of Erasmus, Titelmann, and Cornelius à Lapide. To which also Jerome to Algasia tends: He shall be exalted above everything that is called God, so that he may trample under his foot the Gods of all nations, and every approved and true religion.

What most befits the Roman Pontiff, who exalts himself above God, since he pretends that the Word of God has its authority, meaning, and light from his infallible definition, and sets himself against the institutions of the law, and dispenses divine Sacraments, above all the gods of the gentiles, to whom they divided their empires, assigning heaven to Jupiter, the sea to Neptune, and the underworld to Pluto, with the Pontiff on the contrary seizing for himself the empire of heaven, earth, and the underworld: Above Kings and magistrates, to whom he decrees that he can give power and take it away: Above Angels, whom he dares to command; Above Saints, whom he constitutes as gods at his pleasure, and commands to be worshipped as gods.

Haymo, Lombard, and the Cardinal distinguish τὸ σέβασμα from the former, by 'everything that is called God,' the gods of the gentiles, as well as the elect (to whom, however, scripture never attributes the name of GOD), but by 'that which is worshipped,' they understand the most holy Trinity. But it is more correctly taken as an explanatory addition: 'Above everything that is called God or a Divine Being,' as Maresius had said in his dissertation, partly Kings and Caesars, who are also denoted here as σεβασοὶ, above whom the Roman Pontiff raises himself with intolerable arrogance, and partly whatever can be held as holy and to be worshipped, over which he arrogates to himself every haughty authority, because nothing is worshipped or adored in the Roman communion except dependently upon the Pope's canonization, declaration, consecration, ordination, and jurisdiction. To Grotius, σέβασμα is 'cultivation,' by which he understands the instruments of sacred worship, temples, images, and the insignia of the gods. But 'cultivation' is not used in Latin for sacred worship, and it is offensive to Latin ears that the instruments of farming and cultivation, e.g., a plow or a harrow, should be expressed by the name of 'cultivation.' And what would this be: 'The man of sin will exalt himself above every instrument in sacred worship'? Did Gaius exalt himself above these while he used them and dedicated them to his own worship, which he wanted to be sacred? Is it not sufficiently clear that σέβασμα denotes the sacred thing itself which is worshipped, or the object of worship, and not the act of worshipping or the instrument of worship? Among the LXX Interpreters it is not read, but in the book of Wisdom ch. XIV, v. 20, ch. XV, v. 17, and in the history of the Dragon added to Daniel, com. 26, where it occurs regarding the object of worship: in which way also here σέβασμα is rendered by the Syriac and in the Vulgate version as 'that which is worshipped.' Theophylact interprets it as idols. Erasmus says that σέβασμα is properly called that which we adore and venerate with the highest reverence, and which excels in majesty, and it could have been translated as 'Divine Being.' In his paraphrase, he explained it as a divine being to be religiously worshipped. Therefore, Grotius is wrong to say that σεβασμὸν in Philo and σέβασμα here in Paul have the same meaning. According to Henri Estienne and Jean Scapula, σέβασμα is that by which we venerate that in which God is worshipped: σεβασμὸς is veneration, adoration, worship. Therefore, σέβασμα also befits Kings and Caesars, who are accustomed to be called σεβασοὶ. For σεβασὸς, according to Suda, is προσκύνητὸς, to be venerated, worthy of adoration. 'Σεβασὸν,' says Dio, 'the Greeks translated as Augustus, as if you were to say worthy of veneration.' To this point contributes what Miletier, praised by Grotius, a Henoticist and flatterer of the Pope, says: that he truly adorns and clothes him with the epithets of the Anti-Christ in that horrible figure under which St. Paul pointed out with his finger to the faithful Thessalonians the son of perdition, by these characteristics, that he would exalt himself above everything that is called God, and Augustus, Θεὸν καὶ σέβασμα. For that is the name by which Emperors were called σεβασοὶ, Augusti. For that which is called God, that Kings and Caesars are, and that the ordinary name of the Emperor was 'Augustus,' formed from these two words which the Apostle gives as indicators, Θεὸς καὶ σέβασμα. There is nothing in the appendix that Grotius objects, that the Apostle would thus tacitly approve of the custom of the world, which sinned most gravely in the worship of the Roman Emperors: because not according to that custom, but in a true sense, Emperors could be referred to among 'those who are called Gods and objects of worship.' And what of it? Is he to be considered as having approved of the worship of idols by the very fact that he called them so? No one would say that. Although Princes do not name themselves gods, they are nevertheless called so even in scripture itself. Although Emperors, Theodosius and Valentinian, called our Divinity 'our Divinity' in book III of the Code on the most high Trinity, and likewise Honorius and Theodosius in book I and book II of the Code on the most holy Churches, they called it 'our Divine Being.'

So that he may finally place himself in the temple of GOD. Καθίσαι is very often transitive, Eph. I, v. 20, ἐκάθισεν ἐν δεξιᾷ αὐτοῦ. The Latin: 'he constituted at his right hand.' Beza: 'He placed at his right hand.' We have brought forward other places in great number in our appendix on the Anti-Christ. Whence it follows that either ἁυτὸν must be written here, which is free for us, since the ancient codices did not have those marks of spirits, as they are called, or αὐτὸν must be taken for ἑαυτὸν, which change Beza truly said is frequent even among suitable writers at Romans IV, v. 6. Among our own writers, however, it is less fitting to wonder at this, because among the Hebrews this meaning is expressed by the same suffix. But it is rightly said that Gaius placed himself into the temple, or in the temple of GOD (for both these expressions come to the same thing) because he ordered his image to be placed there. For to give to an image the name of him whom the image represents is accepted among all nations. Tacitus: 'Ordered by Gaius Caesar to place his effigy in the temple.' He wanted this statue of his to be called his temple itself. Thus Philo several times and Jerome: The temple of God in the holy scriptures is the Jerusalem temple, ναὸς Θεοῦ Matt. XXVI, v. 61, ναὸς Κυρίου Luke I, v. 9, ἱερὸν τοῦ Θεοῦ Matt. XXI, v. 12, בית יהוה in countless places of the Old Testament. Josephus in the history of the matter predicted here: 'To set up his statue in the temple of God.' And Jerome, Augustine, and others, whose passages we have produced before, accept this place concerning the Jerusalem temple. This proposal of Gaius did not indeed have its full effect in the temple (for he had it in the synagogues): but he is nevertheless said to have done it rightly, because he omitted nothing in order to do it. Thus it is said to Christ that he committed adultery who acted so that he might obtain adultery. Thus Micah II, v. 1. פָּעַל ἐργά- ζουσαι signifies thinking, as the following things manifestly show. Thus he is said to offer, who wishes to offer, Matt. V. v. 23. Heb. XI. v. 7. James II. v. 21. But this has place especially in crimes, by which the Majesty of God, who looks into hearts, is directly injured. Therefore in the ancient oracle, which Herodotus recites in Erato, we have τὸ πειρηθῆναι τοῦ Θεοῦ, καὶ τὸ ποιῆσαι ἶσον δύνασθαι. But that attempt to profane the temple, and indeed with such great violence, could not pass without the greatest grief of the Jews, even of those who had already embraced Christ, for the reason that they knew that temple to be dedicated to that God whom they themselves also worshipped, because they themselves also, as often as the situation required, would go to that temple for the sake of prayers or sacrifices, as can be seen in Acts II. v. 46. III. v. 1. V. v. 47. XXI. v. 23. 24.

Ἀποδεικνύντα ἑαυτὸν, ὅτι ἐστὶ Θεὸς) Here also ἀποδεικνύν- τα is put for ἀποδεικνύοντα, that is, the name of the effect is given to the intention: Πειρώμενον ἀποδεικνύναι, says Chrysostom here. For he wanted to show that he was God. Σπουδά- ζων Θεὸς νομίζεσθαι, says Philo. Ἠξίου ὑπὲρ ἄνθρωπον νομί- ζεσθαι, says Philo.

Addimus quæ in commentatione Grotiana pe- culiari tradita sunt: "Ὥστε ἀυτὸν εἰς τὸν ναὸν τοῦ Θεοῦ καθίσαι) So that he places himself in the temple of God. Not content with having despised those who were called Gods, and their worship, he wished to be insulting also εἰς τὸν ὄντως ἀληθῆ Θεὸν against the truly real God, as Philo speaks in this history, just as Antiochus spoke marvelous things against the God of Gods himself Dan. XI. v. 36. Ναὸς Θεοῦ, what can it be to pious writers other than the Jerusalem temple, which was accustomed to be visited even at that time by the Apostles themselves for the sake of prayer, Acts II. v. 46. Acts III. v. 1. V. 42. XXI. 26. who did not even abstain from sacrifices in that temple, as appears in Acts XVIII. 18. XXI. 23. 24. if you compare the law Num. VI. v. 13.

14. 15. 16. 17. 18. Wherefore the Romans, as Sulpicius Severus relates, later decreed that the temple should be overturned, so that the religion of the Jews and Christians might be more fully abolished. And its most common name was בית יהוה 1 Kings VI. 1. VIII. 63. 2 Chron. III. verse 1. ναὸς Θεῦ, Matt. XXVI. 61. as Josephus also for the most part speaks, ναὸς Κυρίου, Luke I. verse 9. ἱερὸν τῦ Θεῦ Matt. XXI. 12. and deservedly so. For it was the one temple in all the world consecrated to the true God by His own command, ἱερὸν τῷ ἀοράτῳ Θεῷ, a temple to the invisible God. Thus Philo calls it, and presently πε- ρίβολον καθιερωθέντα καθεσιμώτοις χρησμοῖς κὴ λογίοις θεοφάτοις, an enclosure dedicated and consecrated by oracles and divine responses. There had indeed been a temple consecrated to the same GOD on Mount Gerizim, but by human institution against the law of God. And that very temple did not exist in the time of Paul, having been destroyed long before by Hyrcanus, and never restored. See Josephus. The other temples everywhere were neither commanded by God, nor consecrated to the true God. But Gaius commanded, with great penalties added, and repeated the command ἰσᾶν ἀυτῷ ἀνδριάντα ἐν τῷ ναῷ τῶ Θεῦ, that a statue be placed for him in the temple of God, says Josephus. Philo: Ἀνδριάντα Κολοσσαῖον ἐἴσω- τάτω τῶν ἀδύτων ἀναθετῆναι Γάϊος προσέταξε, διὸς ἐπί- κλησιν ἀυτῷ: Gaius ordered a statue of colossal size to be placed in the innermost sanctuary of the temple, having assumed for himself the name of Jupiter. Then shortly after: Ἀναθιτῆναι πάλιν κελεύει τὸν ἀνδριάντα ἐν τῷ ἱερῷ, he again orders the statue to be placed in the holy city in the temple itself. Then: Τὸν δὲ ἐν τῇ ἱεροπόλει νεὼν ὡς λοιπὸς ἦν ἄψαυστος ἀσυλίας ἠξιωμένος τῆς πάσης, καθεημέζετο, κὴ μετεσχημάτισει εἰς ὀικεῖον ἱερὸν, ἵνα Διὸς ἐπιφανᾶς νέυ χρηματίζῃ Γαΐυ. The temple which is in the holy city, having been untouched until then and endowed with every right of sanctity, he violated and transformed into his own temple, so that it might be called the temple of the new, illustrious Jupiter, namely Gaius himself. Jerome in the Eusebian Chronicle: Gaius ordered Petronius, prefect of Syria, to place his own statue in Jerusalem under the name of Jupiter Optimus Maximus. Although Gaius, being forestalled, did not carry out his impious designs, it is rightly said both to Paul and to Philo himself, as we have already heard, that he did that for the doing of which he omitted nothing. For as in other atrocious matters, so especially in those which rightly offend the divine Majesty, everyone does as much as he intended, as Seneca says. Δύναται γάρ ἴσον τῷ δρᾷν τὸ νοεῖν; here to intend and to do are the same thing. Therefore Juvenal, having narrated the history that is also found in Herodotus, everywhere perjured in thought, and having added the most sorrowful outcome, added: Has patitur pœnas peccandi sola voluntas. Then indeed, what Paul here chiefly regards, the greatest sorrow and fear took full effect upon both the Jews and the Christians, by so many letters of Gaius, by such great efforts for the fashioning and placing of the statue, and indeed also by the example already given in very many synagogues, which, after Philo, was noted by Eusebius in the cited passage of the Chronicle. Furthermore, words in the Hiphil often signify only command. Orosius says of this deed of Caligula: "He commanded that that ancient sanctuary in Jerusalem be profaned by the sacrifices of the Gentiles and filled with statues and images, and he wished himself to be worshipped there as a God." Moreover, such is καθίζειν here, and it does not signify to sit, but to place, as in 1 Cor. VI. 4. For you may very often find in these books ἀυτὸν for ἑαυτόν, or with only the breathing changed, which formerly was not accustomed to be written, ἀυτὸς. Whence it happened that many codices have ἑαυτὸν here in the same sense. It would not be new if εἰς τὸν ναὸν (into the temple) were placed here for ἐν τῷ ναῷ (in the temple), since a similar expression appears in Mark II. 1. and elsewhere. But there is no need to resort to this, since καθίζειν τινὰ εἰς τὸν θρόνον (to seat someone into the throne), to place someone on the throne, is both a pure and frequent expression for the Greeks, which Plutarch also uses in his Romulus, just as Plato in Laws IX said καθίζειν εἰς χωρίον (to seat into a place). ᾿Αποδεικνύντα ἑαυτὸν, ὅτι ἐστὶ Θεός) Showing himself, as if he were GOD. Displaying himself by words and deeds as God. For here ὅτι is explanatory, as in Matt. XXVI. 24, 1 Cor. XI. 17 and 23, and often elsewhere. Ἠξίου ὑπὲρ ἄνθρωπον νομίζεσθαι, he wished to be believed greater than a man, says Dio: And shortly after: Ταῦτα μὲν οὖν τὰ σχήματα ὁπότε τις Θεὸς ἐπλάττετο εἶναι, ἐλάμβανε, καὶ αὐτῷ καὶ ἱκετεῖαι, καὶ εὐχαὶ, καὶ θυσίαι τὰ πρόσφορα προσήγοντο. Such forms, therefore, he assumed when he pretended to be some god, and prayers, supplications, and sacred rites suitable to such a deity were performed to him. Josephus: Προϊὼν ἐξίσατο τῶ ἀνθρωπίνε Φθονοῖν ὑπὸ μεγέθες τῆς ἀρχῆς ἐκ- θειάζων ἀυτὸν, κὴ τὰ πάντα ὑπ᾿ ἀτιμίᾳ τῦ Θεῖυ πολίτευειν ἤρετο. Finally, he ceased to conduct himself in a human manner, making himself a god on account of the magnitude of his empire, and began to do everything in contempt of God. Philo: ᾿Ουκ ἔτι ἠξίυ μένειν ἐν τοῖς τῆς ἀνθρωπίης Φύσεως ὅροις, ἀλλ᾽ ὑπερέκυπτε σπεδάζων Θεὸς νομίζεσθαι. He was no longer willing to keep himself within the permitted bounds of human nature, but exalted himself to such a degree that he desired to be believed a god. Soon after: Καὶ ἐπειδὴ ἅπαξ

ἐθρασύνετο κὴ ἀπετόλμησεν ὡς εἰς τὸ κοινῶς ἐξενεγκεῖν τὴν ἀθεωτάτην ἐκθέωσιν ἀυτῦ τὰ συνῳδὰ πράττειν ἐπεχείρει. After he had once laid aside all shame and dared to publish his impious deification, he began to act in a manner consistent with that claim. Then: Ἐνόμισε τὰ νομίζεσθαι παρ' Ἀλεξανδρεῦσι Θεόν: He thought that he was believed to be a god by the Alexandrians.

There is no need to dispute here whether the Greek words should be translated as "he places himself in the temple of God, or into the temple of God," as Grotius contends, or indeed, as Maresius with most others says, "so that he himself sits in the temple of God"? For either version stands consistent with the true opinion concerning the Anti-Christ. But because the latter in no way agrees with the Grotian commentary, he therefore labors to support the former. Concerning which, one may compare the *Concordia discors* of Maresius with the Appendix of Grotius. To defend his own translation, Grotius contends that *ἀυτὸν* is put for *ἑαυτὸν* or that *ἀυτὸν* should be read, contrary to the testimony of the manuscripts. And he wishes *καθίσαι* to mean not "to sit," but "to place." On the contrary, Maresius contends, (1) that no example can be brought forward from the writers of the New Testament where demonstrative pronouns are used for reciprocal ones. (2) That all manuscripts and all interpreters have read and understood it demonstratively, not reciprocally. (3) That it cannot be taken as a reciprocal, unless καθίζω has a transitive meaning; and that this is assumed gratuitously by Grotius, and not proven. (4) Nor should one depart from the proper usage of words, unless analogy, or the text, or the faith necessarily leads us to an improper one. Nor does the passage 1 Cor. 6:4 prove that καθίζειν means to place, or can it prejudice all others that occur in the New Testament, in which, with that one exception of Eph. 1:20, that verb signifies to sit, namely in twenty-six places.

However, it does not help Grotius if it is said that the man of sin places himself in the temple of God, or, if he prefers it so, into the temple of God. For that still differs as much as heaven from earth from what he brings forward about Gaius, namely that he had it in his mind and plan to place his own statue into the temple of God. For a proposal and a plan are one thing, the deed itself is another. Paul is not prophesying about a mere proposal or plan, but about that which was truly to come to pass. Furthermore, Gaius himself is one thing, the statue of Gaius is another. Did Gaius wish to place himself into the temple of God, when he wished to place his statue into the temple of God? The chief end of prophecies is, as Grotius says on Matt. 23:10, as later, when the event happens, the certainty of divine foreknowledge may appear. But that would not appear here, but would waver, if what Paul predicted about an effect had to be understood later as a mere affection. What is brought forward from Amos, or more correctly Micah 2:1, is vain. For there, to devise iniquity (upon their beds) and to work evil (as soon as it is morning) are clearly distinguished.

Nor indeed can the temple of Jerusalem be understood by the temple of God, as Grotius understands it along with the Papists, as also with some of the ancients, who seem to have been seduced by the Jews, who expect the restoration of the temple through the Messiah. For both those ancients and the Papists interpret it concerning the temple of Jerusalem being raised up again in the time of the Antichrist: which, however, not even the Jews believe consistently, namely that a third temple is to be raised up after the second destruction: as is evident from Seder Olam and Galatinus, book 5, on the hidden truth of the Catholic faith, chapter 10. Among the Papists, even after Galatinus, Lyranus on Matt. 13, Villalpandus, Pererius book 10 on Daniel, Baronius at the year 72, number 28, denied it, as did also Cornelius à Lapide on Ezekiel chapter 40 and in this place, p. 506, who cited Jer. 7:4 for this. And as they are truly dreams concerning the new Jerusalem temple after the final house, Hagg. II. 10. which was never to be restored, Dan. IX. 27. to be left eternally devastated, Matth. XXIII. 38. that were handed down: Yet no one has been found, except for Grotius, to whom it has occurred even in a dream that in this place, that Jerusalem temple which was destroyed by the Romans: Which after Christ's death was never called ναὸς τῶ Θεῶ in the New Testament, when by the veil being torn in the middle, Matth. XXVII. 51. the swift and perpetual desolation of the temple was signified, as Chrysostom and Jerome observed on that passage, and the Apostles, after the ascension of Christ, were entirely in the mystical temple of GOD, being built up from Jews and Gentiles. Therefore, by the name of the temple of GOD, the faithful come in the Apostolic writings; but not a material temple, 1. Cor. III. 15. Eph. II. 20. 1. Petr. II. 9. Nor does the temple of God occur anywhere else in the prophetic passages of the New Testament, such as the one here, than mystically. See Apoc. III. 12. ch. VII. 19. ch. XI. 1. 2. 19. ch. XIV. 15. ch. XV. 5. 6. 8. ch. XVI. 1. 17. But this prophecy can in no way be drawn to the times of the Jerusalem temple still standing, much less to the times of Gaius, unless the greatest violence is done to it, since that man of sin is to be destroyed only by the final coming of Christ. Therefore it must necessarily be explained concerning the Church; which is called the temple of the Lord, Eph. II. 21. 2 Cor. VI. 16, concerning which it is explained by Jerome: For he has it thus: Either at Jerusalem, as some think, or in the Church, which is more true: By Ambrose; who has it thus: That he may sit in the house of the Lord, in the seat of Christ; by Theodoret, who says he called the Churches the temple of GOD, in which (the Antichrist) seizes the first seat (which is that, if not the Roman one), attempting to show himself as God: By Chrysostom: he will sit in the temple of God, not that which is at Jerusalem, but in the temple of the Church: By Oecumenius, who seems to have expressed the words of Chrysostom, εἰς τὸν ναὸν, οὐ τὸν ἐν ἱεροσαλὲμ λέγει, ἀλλ’ εἰς τὰς Ἐκκλησίας τοῦ Θεοῦ: By Anselm, who says, or rather, he will sit in the temple of God, that is, in the minds of Christians, whom he will seduce, who had been the temple of GOD. Nor do most of the Papists deny that the Churches are understood here, although some join the other explanation concerning Jerusalem to our sense, Haymo, Lombard, Thomas, Hugo Cardinalis, Cajetan, Salmero, Cornelius à Lapide, Gregorius de Valentia Tom. IV. col. 2380. Suarez book V. on the Anti-Christ ch. XV. §. 5. Guilhelmus Estius on this passage n. 4. The doubt here is, of which temple of God the Apostle speaks? Some understand the Jerusalem temple. For although that which was in the time of Paul has been destroyed; yet they say another is to be rebuilt in its place at some time, either by the Jews, or by the Anti-Christ himself, so that he may be worshipped in it. But if the Anti-Christ will build a temple for himself as God: the Apostle would not call that the temple of God, no more than he would deem the temple of Jupiter and Diana worthy of that name. Cajetan thinks that no specific temple is signified, but that the sense is that the Anti-Christ will sit in whatever temple is dedicated to GOD, as if that were dedicated to him. But indeed Jerome in the letter cited long ago judges more truly that the Apostle signified the Church by the temple of GOD. Which interpretation, after the interlinear gloss, St. Thomas also receives, nor does St. Augustine reject it; Chrysostom also and Theodoret, and the other Greeks explain the Apostle as speaking of the Churches of GOD (for they speak in the plural), which comes to the same thing. For the Church of GOD consists of many particular Churches.

To Grotius himself, certainly, the people, the multitude, the Christian Church, and the temple of God are synonyms at Matth. XVI. 18. Not to mention that some copies here read λαὸν instead of ναὸν, as noted by Cornelius à Lapide, which can in no way be taken of a material temple. That which is in Greek εἰς τὸν ναὸν τοῦ Θεοῦ, Grotius himself concedes can be explained as ἐν τῷ ναῷ, Mark II, 1.

Augustine, while also retaining the meaning of the session, retains the usual force of the preposition, book XX. on the City of GOD ch. XIX. explaining it thus: That the Anti-Christ will sit in the Church, as if he himself were the true Church, who will arrogate the title of the Church to himself and his own. But because in the Greek text it is not said nakedly that he sits, but that he sits as God, it is better to explain it as in the temple of GOD, than to retain the usual meaning. But others explain that sitting as the session of the Anti-Christ, as a Doctor, who wants to be considered the Doctor of Doctors, an infallible Doctor, the Bishop of Bishops, and thus even the Archbishop of souls, Christ himself, in which way Doctors are said to sit, Matth. XXIII. 2. Luke II. 46. others explain it as the session of the same, as Lord, dominating in the Church, since to sit is to reign 1. Cor. XV. 25. (Psal. CX. 1.) in which sense the session is attributed to the great harlot and Babylon, Apoc. XVII. verse 1. ch. XIIX. 7. In both ways the Roman Anti-Christ sits in the Church of GOD, whence his seat is also called Rome, in which seat he usurps the man of both the supreme and infallible Doctor, and the head and ruler of the Church, so that by the very naming of the Roman seat the fulfillment of this prophecy may be more openly discerned.

That which Grotius contends to the contrary in the appendix, that it is without example and completely absurd for a gathering of idolaters, such as we judge those who adhere to the Roman Pope to be, to be called the temple of GOD, he has from the Papists, and it has already been refuted among them quite often. And Maresius rightly replied: The Anti-Christ sits in the Church of GOD, not in the composite sense, as if the true Church of GOD remains, which the Anti-Christ sits in, and which adheres to him, but in the divided sense, insofar as that which had once been the Church of GOD has admitted the Anti-Christ, and the faithful city has become a harlot, Isa. I. 21. yet so that it has not entirely stripped off every face of the Church, but has retained certain ruins and traces of that which was before, in name, profession, baptism, and if there are others, which God did not wish to be completely obliterated, the remnants of Christianity in the papacy. Add that by the name of the Church not only the faithful are called, but in the common assembly of Christians, even if hypocrites and the impious and infidels are mixed in, with the denomination made partly from the profession, partly from the nobler part, as is evident from the example of the Corinthian Church; and especially, that he exercises his tyranny, as much as is in him, not only upon that Christian multitude which is subject to him, but also upon that which is properly called the Church of GOD, and comes under the name of the people of God, and wishes to be held the head of the universal Church of Christ, and decrees that it is of the necessity of salvation for every creature to be subject to him. The Roman Antichrist sits in the temple of GOD, in that, having erected a dominion in the Church, he has infected a part of it with his poison, while the part that remained sounder, and was truly the temple of GOD, he has long oppressed, and all but crushed, with his tyranny, persecution, and corruptions, and even now strives to press and oppress in every way.

The Apostle says to sit ὡς Θεὸν, which, although neither the Vulgate, nor the Syriac, nor Beza's Claromontanus codex has, the Greek Interpreters nevertheless read, Chrysostom, Theophylact, Oecumenius, as also

B. Luther, whom almost all more recent writers follow, since the Antichrist is predicted to obtain not a common kingdom, but as it were a divine one in the Church: which is explained by what is added, ἀποδεικνύντα ἑαυτὸν, ὅτι ἐςὶ θεὸς, that he is about to demonstrate, not so much by explicit profession as by the deed itself, that he is God. For the Apostle did not say, as Chrysostom observes, that he says he is God, but that he attempts to show it. Which Theophylact also repeated, and Theodoret previously hinted at, trying to show himself to be God. While therefore he says, ἀποδεικνύντα, he declares that, even if he is not about to confess it in words, he will nevertheless demonstrate clearly enough by his deed what he seeks, namely, that he may be held as a divinity. He will conduct himself as Lord of the kingdoms of this world, he will arrogate to himself power over heaven, earth, and hell, authority over the consciences of men, he subjects all to his tribunal, he will wish to be subject to no one, as Crocius rightly says. Although we judge that the boasting of words is not to be entirely excluded, and thus we do not disapprove of Grotius's explanation, showing himself by words and deeds to be God.

What that man of sin was about to do in the temple of God or the Church, according to the Apostle, neither Gaius did there, nor did any other except the Roman Antichrist. Gaius also, even if he wished to be worshipped as a divinity, which was done by others also both before him and after him, could not be recognized by that character, in the way the Antichrist can, to whom this is proper to him alone and solely in the Church, who can bear neither equal nor partner in that matter: Who in Canon Law is called Our Lord God, canon Satis, dist. 96. gloss. ad extr. cum inter. In the Lateran Council, sess. IX, it is said that that is to be fulfilled in the Pope: All the kings of the earth shall adore him, all nations shall serve him. Sess. X, it was said to the Pontiff: All power has been given to you in heaven and on earth. Which also exists in the Ceremonial, book 1, tit. VII, sect. 7. In the same council, sess. VI, Leo X was called the Lion of the tribe of Judah, and the root of David. Bellarmine, preface in III. Controv. Gener. applies to the Pontiff that of Isaiah XXIX: Behold I will place in the foundations of Sion a cornerstone, etc. Franciscus Panigarola said in book II, part 1, that the Pope is that one Lord of whom Paul speaks in Ephesians IV. In the books of the Canonists it is read everywhere that the Pope has heavenly judgment, that he has the same consistory as God, the same tribunal as Christ, that his power extends to heavenly, earthly, and infernal things, that the whole spiritual machinery has been committed to the Pope, that the Pope is everything, that he can act against law, and above law, and outside of law, change the form of the sacraments, that he can derogate from the words of the Apostle, and decree against the epistles of Paul, etc.

Chrysostom and Theophylact refer to this ἀπόδειξιν the miracles by which the Antichrist tries to defend his own, which Gaius never wished to show. But Grotius acknowledges in the appendix that the Apostle here looks primarily to this, not that he wished to be held for God, but that he sits in the very temple of the true and supreme God: What need is there, therefore, to bring forward testimonies from Dio, Philo, Josephus, and others, which say nothing more than that Gaius wished to be believed greater than a man, and to be held as God, and thought that he was in truth held as such by the Alexandrians? But to whom does this apply more than to the Roman Pontiff, who seizes all authority in the Church of God to himself, and exalts himself above Princes, above the Word of God, above the sacraments, above consciences, above the faith of the Church, and who wantonly and impudently transfers to himself the things that are God's? And this profanation of the mystical temple, through the apostasy of the Antichrist, the Christians ought to have feared, not the Jerusalem temple made by hands, through the statue of Caligula; the destruction of which, as Grotius said before, the Christians eagerly awaited, not only as a document of a truthful Teacher, but also as a comfort for the many calamities they had suffered from the Jews. Add that those Jewish rites, according to Grotius himself at John V. 23, were already to be rooted out, as standing in the way of the true faith, which was done in the destruction of the temple. Nor is it likely that the Thessalonian Christians would conceive any sadness concerning the Jerusalem temple, which they knew was shortly to be polluted by the abomination of desolation and to be utterly overturned, nor did they know it to be the temple of God any longer, properly speaking, after the veil was torn, especially since, with the temple and the Republic destroyed, Christians professed Christ more freely without the change of Jewish rites, as Grotius admits.

Latin:

Vers. 4. Ὁ ἀντικείμενος) שָׂטָן, id est, Dei adversarius, quomodo eximie vocatur Diabolus, & qui eum imitan- tur. Nam שָׂטָן, per ἀντικείμενος explicatur Aquilæ & Symmacho Genes. XXVI. vers. 21. Origeni decimo libro ad Romanos, Chrysostomo in XII. secundæ ad Corinthios. Hostem vertit Tertullianus. Ubi autem nihil additur, in- telligitur DEI hostis, ut Theodotioni Job. I. optime id Cajo convenit, qui, ut Philo loquitur: ἄγος τὸν Θεὸν ἀντι- παρεξῆγε, factis Deum sibi fecit hostem.

In comentatione ita de hoc epitheto Grotius:

Vers. 4.

Ὁ ἀντικείμενος) qui adversatur, id est, שָׂטָן. Sic quod in Ebræo est 3. Reg. aut ut alii numerant cap. XI. v. 14. ויקם יהוה שטן לשלמה, & in Græco: Ἐξή- γειρε Κύριος Σατὰν τῷ Σολομῶντι. Tertullianus expli- cat adversus Marcionem III. Suscitabit eum illi Satan, id est, hostem. Et Chrysostomus in cap. XII. secundæ ad Corinth. citans 3. Reg. v. 4. Ὄυκ ἦν Σατὰν ἐν ἡμέραις αὐτῶ, explicat τουτέστιν ἀντικείμενος. Sic Luc. XIII 17. XXI. 15. 1. Cor. XVI. 9. Phil. I. 28. 1. Tim. V. 14. sumitur vox ἀντικείμενος, sed cum apposito aut addito aut ex supe- rioribus facile intellecto. At absolute cum ponitur, eum significat, qui Deo quoquo modo adversatur, quo sensu vox Ebræa legitur Matth. XVI. 23. & locis Marci & Lucæ, qui ei loco respondent. Summo autem jure ei aptatur, qui non semel aut per errorem, sed perpetuo destinatoque proposito Deum oppugnat, quod Caju fecit par in hoc Diabolo, cui id nomen eximie tribuitur. Eadem causa παράλληλος compar Cajo Ἀντίοχος Διάβολος vocatur, 1. Maccab. I. 38.

Anti-Christum illum magnum, qui Antiochum, qui Caji, qui omnium impiorum impietatem Dia- boli primogenitus superaturus erat, intelligi, omnium unanimis est sententia. Qui Christo ad- versaturus erat, non vita tantum & praxi, sed do- ctrina publica: non tantum quoad mores, sed etiam quoad dogmata: non tantum quoad cultum DEI ac officia proximo exhibenda, adeoq; quoad utram- que tabulam legis divinæ, sed etiam quoad Evan- gelium & concionem gratiæ: non tantum quoad principium, Dei Verbum, sed etiam quoad conclu- siones è principio religionis deductas: non per se tantum, sed cum toto suo satellitio, quemadmodum, Diabolus cum omni tenebrarum potestate, toto- que suo regno, Christo repugnat. Qui κατ' ἀντονο- μασίαν est ὁ ἀντικείμενος, quia in omnibus se op- ponit Deo; Exempli gratia, Verbum Dei non ad- mittit esse Dei Verbum, nisi sua accedat autoritas: Verbo Dei non relinquit perspicuitatem, & per- fectionem, superaddit suas traditiones: Verbum Dei non permittit omnibus, sed iis, quibus vult: Verbum Dei non vult exponi, nisi prout ipse vult: Contra Verbum Dei & leges divinas dispensat, sa- cramenta mutilandi & instituendi potestatem sibi sumit, calicem laicis eripit, matrimonium clericis prohibet, contra Dei Verbum sacramentum in sacrificium convertit, purgatorium & liberatio- nem ex eodem per suffragia viventium & sacrifi- cia, thesaurum meritorum sanctorum, indul- gentias fingendo &c. adhæc opponit se Deo in no- vis cultibus divinis, variisque interdictionibus citra Verbum Dei fanciendis, & idololatria multiplici ordinanda? contrariis præceptis divinis vel per- mittendis, vel statuendis: Opponit se DEO & Christo aliam justificationis & salutis nostræ ra- tionem definiendo, alia justificationis & salutis media, & quæ sunt ejus generis innumera alia, quibus se ἀντικείμενον adversarium DEO demon- strat. Quæ si quis cum Grotio de Romano Ponti- fice negare velit, eadem temeritate solem in me- ridie lucere neget.

Qui ὁ ἀντικείμενος, opponens se & adversans Deo, idem & ὁ Ἀντίχριςος dicitur, qua voce Jo- hannes præsentem explicat, 1. Epist. II. Nonnulli, etiam Maresius, vocem utramque non tantum de hoste & adversario, Deo & Christo sese opponen- te, sed etiam de eo, qui se Christi vicarium, eique ἀντίστροφον κὶ ἀντιτάλαντον esset facturus, exponunt. Sed facile annuimus, priorem tantum significatio- nem locum habere, uti vocem שטן per vocem ἀν- τικειμένη explicant Origenes libr. X. ad Roman. & Theophylactus ad Matth. XII. necnon Aquila & Symmachus, Gen. XXVI. 21. Hostem autem intelli- gendum Dei, quod eum sensum habeat ea vox, ubi ponitur absolute, eundem exigant verba sequen- tia, fatente Grotio in Appendice.

Id tamen recte notat Maresius in Anti-Christo Revel. part. I. pag. 315. quod ἀντικείμενος semper sit non extraneus quidam & Ethnicus Imperator, sed domesticus aliquis in ipsomet Dei templo, apostasiam à veritate Christi inducens, adeoque Christo resistens, & ipsius veritati. Ut enim Christus κεῖται εἰς σημεῖον ἀντιλεγόμενον, Luc. II. 34. Ita ὁ ἀντικείμενος, qui maxime ἀντιλέγει τῷ χρισῷ, dum seipsum sine illius autoritate & jussu Caput, Regem, & Monarcham Ecclesiæ constituit, prout ἀντιλέγει τῷ Καίσαρι, qui seipsum Regem facit, Joh. XIX. 12. id est, interprete ibidem Viro magno, partes Imperatoris Romani sibi vendicat, qui sine ejus autoritate vult regnare. Ita ἀντικείμενοι, Luc. XXI. 15. sunt ii, qui, quantum in se est, & totis viribus, ἀνθίσανται τῇ ἀληθείᾳ, resistunt veritati, & eam omni arte debellare conantur, quæ est phrasis Pauli 2. Tim. III. 8. Eodem sensu Luc. XIII. v. 17. ἀντικείμενοι αὐτῷ sunt, qui Christo & ipsius veritati contradicunt, nec aliter ἀντικείμενοι πολλοὶ, 1. Cor. XVI. 9. Philipp. I. 28. imo Paulo ideo rejicitur, quicquid sanæ doctrinæ ἀντίκειται, 1. Tim. I. v. 10. & quod magis stringit, 1. Tim. V. 14. vult juniores viduas nubere, & domestica administrare, ne detur occasio maledicendi τῷ ἀντικειμένῳ.

Καὶ ὑπεραιρόμενος ὑπὲρ πάντα λεγόμενον Θεὸν) Quoties Christus aut Apostoli verba ipsa sumunt de loco aliquo Vet. Test. intelligere debemus agi de re simili, aut etiam majore. Hæc verba de Daniele sumpta sunt, ubi de Antiocho Epiphane loquitur cap. XI. 36. ויתגדל על־כל־אל: In Græco κὶ μεγαλυνθήσεται ἐπὶ πάντα Θεόν: Ubi μεγαλυνθήσεται, uti hic ὑπεραιρόμενος, sono est passivum, sensu reciprocum, ut ex Ebræo apparet, extulit se supra omnem Deum. Paulus, ne quis illos, de quibus hic agitur, Deos esse crederet, cautionis ergo addidit, λεγόμενον, qua nota & alibi designat gentium Deos, 1. Cor. VIII. 5. Antiochus omnes gentium Deos egregie spreverat: Nam ἱεροσυλήσας τὰ πλεῖστα τῶν ἱερῶν, ut ait de eo Polybius in fragmento egregio, quod est apud Athenæum. Per hos gradus ad veri DEI contemptum pervenit. Sic & Cajus omnibus se Diis gentium prætulit, etiam Jovi Olympio, & Capitolino: ac si qui dubitarent, an major Jove esset, eos pessime tractavit: Lunam sibi dixit concubinam: Castores janitores: de quibus rebus testimonia alibi large protulimus.

Ἡ σέβασμα) Σέβασμα diximus omne id, per quod Deus colitur, quo sensu σεβάσματα Act. XVII. 23. culturas non male vertit Hieronymus: imagines hic interpretantur Severus & Theophylactus. Philo in historia rei hic prædictæ σεβάσματα vocat. Omnium Deorum culturas, sui cultu instituto, supergressus est Cajus, quia & insignia abstulit Herculi, Apollini, Libero, Veneri, Mercurio, Castoribus & aliis: ac præterea sacrificia sibi fieri voluit multo majoris impendii, ut testatur Dion. Non erant illi veri Dii, sed Cajus eos pro Diis haberi volebat, & tamen iis se præferebat. Opinio illum sua obligabat culpæ, ut alicubi Seneca loquitur. Ebræi ad Levit. XXIV. 15. peccare ajunt graviter hominem paganum, si suis Diis maledicat.

Similia proposuerat in commentatione, quæ utut gerris ficulis vaniora, hic repetere veritus non est. Ita enim habet illic Grotius:

Καὶ ὑπεραιρόμενος ἐπὶ πάντα λεγόμενον Θεὸν, & extollitur supra omne, quod dicitur Deus) Sumptum ex Daniele, ubi sermo de Antiocho, cui paria fecit Cajus, Dan. XI. 36. Tantum interpretationis causa addidit Paulus λεγόμενον. Multi sunt λεγόμενοι Θεοὶ, qui dicantur Dii, ut ait idem hic Apostolus, 1. Cor. VIII. 5. nimirum qui vulgo tales credebantur. Tertullianus adversus Marcionem libr. 1. Nam & idola gentium Dei vulgo, sed Deus nemo ea re, quod Deus dicitur. Recte Paulus Caji, qui vero Deo se opposuit, impietatem hinc colligit, quod etiam iis, quos ipse habebat Deos, se non æquavit modo, sed & prætulit. Summus Deorum habebatur Jupiter. Eum accusavit, quod capitolium occupasset. Etiam cum Jovis Olympii simulachrum in suam effigiem commutare voluisset, neque per fulmina, quæ navem absumpserant, potuisset, minatus ei est. Aliis etiam temporibus, machinis ad id factis, obstrepebat tonitribus, ac fulmina imitabatur: Dicebat etiam Jovi Homericum illud: Ἤ μ᾽ ἀνάειρ᾽, ἢ ἐγὼ σε, aut me perime, aut ego te. Hæc omnia Dion habet, multa & Suetonius. Nec dubito, quin capite XXII. Suetonii eædem, quæ apud Dionem sunt voces Græcæ quamquam ad Capitolium Jovem prolatæ sint reponendæ, eoque magis, quod easdem posuerit Seneca circa finem libri de ira primi, ubi ejus Caji Cæsaris dicta terribilia & tumultuosa commemorans ait: Ad pugnam vocavit Jovem, & quidem sine missione Homericum illud exclamans: Ἤ μ᾽ ἀνάειρ᾽, ἢ ἐγὼ σε. Nec omittendum ex Suetonio illud, quod cum, assistens simulachro Jovis, Apellem Tragœdum consuluisset, uter ille major videretur, cunctantem flagellis discidit. Josephus libr. XIX. initio narrat, cum interrogaretur, utrum major ille esset, an vero Jupiter, eum velut per modestiam in medio reliquisse. Cum Luna se concumbere dicebat. Castores autem sibi fecerat janitores, Dione narrante: neque reverentius tractabat Deos alios, ut jamjam apparebit. Sic Antiochus Dianam Elymaicam, aliosque paganicæ superstitionis Deos contempserat.

˝Η σέβασμα) aut cultura. Σεβάσματα dicuntur, quæ cultui Dei aut eorum, qui Dii putantur, inferviunt. Eo sensu extat hæc vox Act. XVII. 23. ubi culturas vertit Hieronymus. Philo σεβασμὺς eodem sensu dixit hac ipsa in re. Talia sunt templa, simulachra, Deorum insignia, sacrificia. Templorum Romani imperii augustissimum, quod erat Capitolium, Jovi invidit. Simulachrum Jovis Olympii è Græcia jussit afferri, ut id suam in effigiem commutaret, quæ Dion narrat. Deorum insignia erepta Diis sibi attribuerat: modo fulmen tenens processit, modo fuscinam, modo caduceum, etiam Veneris cultu conspectus est, ait Suetonius. At Dion: ˝Ηρα τε, καὶ ἄρτεμις, καὶ ἀφροδίτη πολλάκις ἐγίγνετο. Πρὸς γὰρ δὴ τῶν ὀνομάτων μετάθεσιν, καὶ τὸ ἄλλο σχῆμα πᾶν προσῆκον σφίσιν ἐλάμβανε, καὶ ποτὲ μὲν θηλυδριῶδες ἀράτο, καὶ κρητῆρα καὶ θύρσον εἶχε, ποτὲ δὲ ἀῥῥενοποιὸν ῥόπαλον καὶ λεοντῆν ἐφόρει. Λειογένειός τε αὖ κάπιτὰ τῦτο πωγωνίας ἐφαντάζετο, τριαίναντέ ἐστιν, ὅτε ἐκράτει, καὶ κεραυνὸν αὖθις ἀνέτεινε, παρθένω τε πολεμικῇ ὡμοίωτο. Sæpe fecit se Junonem, sæpe Dianam, sæpe Venerem, & prout nomen mutaverat, ita & convenientem nomini habitum sumebat, interdum muliebre induens craterem thyrsumque gerebat; alias virili cum vultu clavam sumebat & leonis exuvias, modo lævis, modo barbatus apparebat. Fuit cum tridentem teneret: alio tempore fulmen protendebat, virginiq; bellatrici similem se exhibebat. Sed latissime omnia hæc insignia Deorum, quæ ad se transtulerat Cajus, Philo exequitur, leoninas exuvias ab Hercule sumptas, à Castoribus pileos, à Libero patre hederam, thyrsum, nebrida, caduceum, talaria, chlamydem à Mercurio, coronas radiatas, arcum, sagittas & gratias ab Apolline, gladium, galeam, clypeum à Marte. Hæc insignia ibidem Philo vocat παράσημα, περίαπτα, προσκοσμήματα, ξοάνοις καὶ ἀγάλμασι προσιδρύμενα, signa, accessiones, ornamenta statuis & simulacris apposita, & ut modo dixi σεβασμός. Dion vero πρόσθετα ἡ πρόσθετα. Sacrificiis non contentus iis, quæ Diis receptis tribui erant solita, aves sibi raras & immensi pretii jubebat mactari Dione teste. Ita omnia Deorum σεβάσματα aut eripuerat Diis, aut instituto sui cultu supergrediebatur.

Non agi Danielis XI. 36. de Antiocho, quod Maresius & Crocius concedunt Grotio, sed de Anti-Christo, isthic loci ostendimus. De Anti-Christo etiam hic explicat Theodoretus: Hæc divinus etiam prædixit Daniel. Dixit enim: Super Deos Patrum suorum non intelliget, & Deum Maozim in loco suo glorificabit. Pro eo, quod est, Deum fortem seipsum nominabit. Antiochum vero Caji typum, & hunc illo multo pejorem fuisse, quam temere dixerit Grotius, à Maresio in respons. ejus ad append. Grot. satis ostensum censemus. Vid. part. I. Anti-Christ. Revel. cap. XVIII. pag. 326.

Per πάντα λεγόμενον Θεὸν, vel πᾶν τὸ λεγόμενον Θεὸν, quam lectionem contra omnium Codicum fidem intulit Beza, Vetus Interpres cum Hieronymo ad Algasiam, sensum reddit, non verba, quod etiam à B. Luthero factum; Grotius solum Deos gentium intelligit, & è collatione 1. Cor. VIII. 6. hunc sensum probat. Sed neque in isto loco λεγόμενοι Θεοὶ sunt idola solum gentium, nam & multi dicuntur ESSE DII, ut multi DOMINI, non tantum ita dici: quomodo & Angeli & Magistratus non tantum κατὰ τὸ λέγεσθαι, sed κατὰ τὸ εἶναι, non quidem natura, sed officio Dii sunt, neq; hoc loco, cum πάντα λεγόμενον Θεὸν indigitavit Apostolus, necesse est id restringere vel ad idola gentium, quum & Angeli & Magistratus, quibus id nominis etiam tributum est in scripturis, & Deus ipse comprehendatur sub illo communi nomine, quando Anti-Christus se elaturus non professione, ut Cornelius à Lapide pervertit, sed potestate dicitur supra omnem, qui nominatur Deus. Nec desunt Interpretes, qui generaliter id accipiunt, quod & verum Deum & putatitios complectatur, quæ Erasmi, Titelmanni, & Cornelii à Lapide explicatio est. Quo etiam abit Hieronymus ad Algasiam: Extolletur supra omne, quod dicitur Deus, ut cunctarum gentium Deos, & probatam omnem & veram religionem pede suo calcet.

Quod maxime convenit Romano Pontifici, qui se effert super Deum, cum Verbum Dei abs se au- toritatem ac sensum & lucem ab infallibili sua de- finitione habere prætendit, ac se adversus legis instituta ponit, & Sacramenta divina dispensat, supra omnes gentilium Deos, quibus illi sua impe- ria diviserunt, Jovi cœlum, Neptuno mare, Plu- toni infernum assignantes, Pontifice ex adverso ad se cœli, terræ, & inferni imperium rapiente: Supra Reges & magistratus, quibus se potestatem dare, & abrogare posse decernit: Supra Angelos, quibus præcipere audet; Supra Sanctos, quos Deos pro lubitu constituit, & ut Deos coli præ- cipit.

Τὸ σέβασμα distinguunt à priori Haymo, Lom- bardus, Cardinalis, per omne, quod dicitur Deus, Deos gentilium, ut & electos, (quibus vero nun- quam nomen DEI tribuit scriptura) at per id, quod colitur, sacrosanctam Trinitatem intelligen- tes. Rectius autem κατ' ἐπεξήγησιν accipitur: Supra omne, quod dicitur Deus aut Numen, ut Maresius in dissertat. sua dixerat, partim Reges & Cæsares, qui & σεβαςοὶ hic denotentur, supra quos intolerabili fastu se attolit Pontifex Roma- nus, partim quicquid pro sancto & colendo potest haberi, in quod omne superciliosum sibi arrogat imperium, quia nihil colitur vel adoratur in com- munione Romana, nisi dependenter à Papæ ca- nonisatione, declaratione, consecratione, ordi- natione & jurisdictione. Grotio σέβασμα est cul- tura, per quam intelligit instrumenta cultus sacri, templa, simulacra, Deorum insignia. Sed nec Latinis dicitur cultura de cultu sacro, & insolens auribus Latinis est, ut instrumenta rusticationis & culturæ e. g. aratrum, occa, culturæ nomine exprimantur. Et quid hoc esset: Hominem pecca- ti se elaturum supra omne instrumentum in cultu sacro? An Cajus supra hæc se extulit, dum iis usus est, & ea suo cultui, quem sacrum esse volebat, addixit? Annon satis constat, σέβασμα ipsam rem sacram, quæ colitur; vel objectum cultus notare, non vero vel actum colendi, vel instrumentum cul- tus. Apud LXX. Interpretes id non legitur, sed in libro Sapientiæ cap. XIV. vers. 20. cap. XV. v. 17. & in historia Draconis addita ad Dan. com. 26. ubi de objecto cultus occurrit: Quo pacto etiam hic σέβασμα à Syro & in Vulgata versione redditur, id, quod colitur. Theophylactus interpretatur idola. Erasmus, σέβασμα inquit proprie dicitur id, quod adoramus, & summa reverentia venera- mur, & quod majestate præcellit, idque verti po- terat Numen. In paraphrasi exposuit numen re- ligiosse colendum. Perperam ergo Grotius σεβα- σμὸν apud Philonem, & σέβασμα hic apud Paulum ejusdem esse significationis dicit. Σέβασμα juxta Henricum Stephanum & Johannem Scapulam est, quo veneramur id, in quo Deus colitur: σεβασμὸς veneratio, adoratio, cultus. Ideo σέβασμα, Regi- bus & Cæsaribus quoque convenit, qui σεβαςοὶ di- ci solent. Σεβαςὸς enim juxta Suidam est προσκύ- νητὸς, venerandus, adoratione dignus. Σεβαςὸν, inquit, Dio, Græci Augustum interpretati sunt, quasi venerandum dicas. Quo facit, quod Mile- terius, laudatus Grotio, Henoticus, Papæ adula- tor, illum revera Anti-Christi elogiis, ait, ornare ac vestire horrida illa figura, sub qua S. Paulus di- gito ostendebat fidelibus Thessalonicensibus filium perditionis, per hos characteres, quod sese extolleret super id omne, quod dicitur Deus, & Augustum, Θεὸν καὶ σέβασμα. Esse enim id nomen, quo Impe- ratores vocabantur σεβαςοὶ Augusti. Id enim, quod Deus dicitur, Reges esse & Cæsares, & nomen ordi- narium Imperatoris fuisse dictum Augustum, ex bis duobus vocabulis formatum, quæ dat Apostolus pro indicibus, Θεὸς καὶ σέβασμα. Nihil est, quod in append. obvertit Grotius, ita Apostolum tacite approbaturum mundi, qui gravis- sime in Imperatorum Romanorum cultu peccavit, morem: quia non secundum morem illum, sed sensu vero poterant Imperatores inter τοὺς λεγομέ- νους Θεοὺς ϰ͵ σεβάσματα referri. Et quid? Num ido- lorum cultum approbasse eo ipso censendus, quod eos sic vocavit? Id nemo dixerit. Etsi vero Prin- cipes se Deos ipsi non nominent, ita tamen vo- cantur in ipsa etiam scriptura. Quanquam & Im- peratores, Theodos. & Valent. nostram Divinita- tem libr. III. Cod. de summ. Trin. nec non Hono- rius & Theodosius l. B. & l. II. Cod. de SS. Eccles. nostrum Numen dixerunt.

Ὥστε αὐτὸν εἰς τὸν ναὸν τοῦ Θεοῦ, ὡς Θεὸν, καθίσαι) Ita ut tandem se collocet in templo DEI. Καθίσαι sæpissime est transitivum, Eph. I. vers. 20. ἐκάθισεν ἐν δεξιᾷ αὐτοῦ. La- tinus: constituerit ad dextram suam. Beza: Collocavit ad dextram suam. Loca alia magno numero attulimus in no- stra appendice de Anti-Christo. Unde sequitur aut scri- bendum hic ἁυτὸν, quod liberum nobis, cum veteres co- dices istas spirituum, quos vocant, notas non habuerint, aut αὐτὸν sumendum pro ἑαυτὸν, quam mutationem fre- quentem esse etiam apud idoneos scriptores, vere dixit Beza ad Roman. IV. vers. 6. Apud nostros autem scripto- res eo minus mirari id convenit, quia apud Ebræos per idem affixum sensus hic exprimitur. Recte autem dici- tur Cajus semet posuisse in templum, vel in templo DEI, (utraque enim hæc loquutio in idem recidit) quia simula- crum suum ibi collocari jussit. Nam simulacro nomen dare ejus, quem simulacrum refert, receptum est apud omnes gentes. Tacitus: Jussi à Cajo Cæsare effigiem ejus in templo locare. Hanc statuam suam ipsum tem- plum suum dici voluit. Ita Philo aliquoties & Hierony- mus: Templum Dei in sacris literis est templum Hieroso- lymitanum, ναὸς Θεοῦ Matth. XXVI. vers. 61. ναὸς Κυρίου Luc. I. vers. 9. ἱερὸν τοῦ Θεοῦ Matth. XXI. vers. 12. בית יהוה innumeris locis Testamenti veteris. Josephus in rei hic prædictæ historia: Ἱστᾷν αὐτοῦ ἀνδριάντα ἐν τῷ ναῷ τοῦ Θεοῦ. Et de templo Hierosolymitano hunc locum acce- pere Hieronymus, Augustinus & alii, quorum loca produ- ximus antehac. Non habuit quidem in templo (nam in synagogis habuit,) plenum effectum hoc Caji propositum: sed tamen recte fecisse dicitur, quod ut faceret, nihil omi- sit. Sic Christo dicitur adulterium commisisse, qui id egit, ut adulterio potiretur. Sic Mich. II. vers. 1. פָּעַל ἐργά- ζουσαι significat cogitantes, ut sequentia manifeste, osten- dunt. Sic offerre dicitur, qui offerre vult, Matth. V. v. 23. Ebr. XI. vers. 7. Jacob. II. vers. 21. Maxime vero id locum habet in criminibus, per quæ directe læditur Majestas Dei, corda introspicientis. Itaque in oraculo vetere, quod He- rodotus in Erato recitat, habemus τὸ πειρηθῆναι τοῦ Θεοῦ, καὶ τὸ ποιῆσαι ἶσον δύνασθαι. Non poterat autem conatus ille profanandi templi, & quidem tanta cum violentia, abire sine maximo Judæorum, etiam eorum, qui Christum jam amplexi erant, dolore, ideo, quod scirent illud templum esse ei Deo dicatum, quem & ipsi colerent, quia & ipsi, quoties ita res ferret, adirent templum illud precum aut sacrificiorum causa, ut videre est Actor. II. vers. 46. III. v. 1. V. v. 47. XXI. v. 23. 24.

Ἀποδεικνύντα ἑαυτὸν, ὅτι ἐστὶ Θεὸς) Hic quoque ἀποδεικνύν- τα positum est pro ἀποδεικνύοντα, id est, nomen effectus datur consilio: Πειρώμενον ἀποδεικνύναι ait hic Chrysosto- mus. Volebat enim ostendere, se esse Deum. Σπουδά- ζων Θεὸς νομίζεσθαι ait Philo. Ἠξίου ὑπὲρ ἄνθρωπον νομί- ζεσθαι, ait Philo.

Addimus quæ in commentatione Grotiana pe- culiari tradita sunt: "Ὥστε ἀυτὸν εἰς τὸν ναὸν τοῦ Θεοῦ καθίσαι) Ita ut in tem- plo Dei se collocet. Non contentus, spreviffe eos, qui dicebantur Dii, eorumque cultum, contumeliosus esse voluit etiam εἰς τὸν ὄντως ἀληθῆ Θεὸν in verum Deum, ut Philo loquitur in hac historia, sicut Antiochus mira loquutus est contra ipsum Deum Deorum Dan. XI. v. 36. Ναὸς Θεοῦ piis scriptoribus quid esse potest aliud quam templum Hierosolymitanum, quod ab ipsis Apostolis etiam eo tempore precum causa adiri solebat, Actor. II. vers. 46. Actor. III. vers. 1. V. 42. XXI. 26. qui ne sacri- ficiis quidem in eo templo abstinebant, ut apparet Act. XVIII. 18. XXI. 23. 24. si conferas legem Num. VI. v. 13.

14. 15. 16. 17. 18. quapropter Romani narrante Severo Sulpitio postea evertendum templum censebant, quo plenius Judæorum & Christianorum religio tolleretur. Nomenque ejus usitatissimum erat בית יהוה 1. Reg. VI. 1. VIII. 63. 2. Paral. III. vers. 1. ναὸς Θεῦ, Matth. XXVI. 61. quomodo & Josephus plerumque loquitur, ναὸς Κυρίου, Luc. I. vers. 9. ἱερὸν τῦ Θεῦ Matth. XXI. 12. & merito. Erat enim id unum in omni orbe templum Deo vero sacratum ipsius jussu, ἱερὸν τῷ ἀοράτῳ Θεῷ, templum Deo inspectabili. Sic vocat Philo, & mox πε- ρίβολον καθιερωθέντα καθεσιμώτοις χρησμοῖς κὴ λογίοις θεοφάτοις, septum dedicatum consecratumque oraculis & responsis divinis. Fuerat quidem eidem DEO sacra tum templum in monte Garizitano, sed humano insti- tuto contra Dei legem. Et idipsum templum Pauli tem- pore non exstabat, dirutum pridem ab Hircano, nec unquam repositum. Vide Josephum. Cætera ubique templa nec Dei jussu, nec Deo vero sacrata. Jussit autem Cajus magnis additis pœnis, jussumque repetiit ἰσᾶν ἀυτῷ ἀνδριάντα ἐν τῷ ναῷ τῶ Θεῦ poni sibi statuam in Dei templo, ait Josephus. Philo: Ἀνδριάντα Κολοσσαῖον ἐἴσω- τάτω τῶν ἀδύτων ἀναθετῆναι Γάϊος προσέταξε, διὸς ἐπί- κλησιν ἀυτῷ: Colosseæ molis statuam in intimis templi adytis poni jussit Cajus sibi adscito Jovis nomine. Deinde mox: Ἀναθιτῆναι πάλιν κελεύει τὸν ἀνδριάντα ἐν τῷ ἱερῷ, iterum jubet in sacra urbe poni statuam in ipso templo. Deinde: Τὸν δὲ ἐν τῇ ἱεροπόλει νεὼν ὡς λοιπὸς ἦν ἄψαυστος ἀσυλίας ἠξιωμένος τῆς πάσης, καθεημέζετο, κὴ μετεσχημάτισει εἰς ὀικεῖον ἱερὸν, ἵνα Διὸς ἐπιφανᾶς νέυ χρηματίζῃ Γαΐυ. Templum quod in sacra urbe est inta- ctum hactenus, & omni jure sanctimoniæ donatum, mutavit, transformavitque in templum suum, ut novi Jovis egregii, Caji scilicet ipsius, diceretur. Hierony- mus in Chronico Eusebiano: Cajus Petronio præfecto Syriæ præcepit, ut in Hierosolymis statuam suam sub no- mine Jovis optimi Maximi poneret. Quanquam autem præventus destinata impia Cajus non implevit, recte ta- men & Paulo & ipsi, ut jam audivimus, Philoni dicitur id fecisse, ad quod faciendum nihil omisit. Nam cum in aliis rebus atrocibus tum maxime in iis, quæ recte divi- nam lædunt Majestatem, fecit quisque quantum voluit, ut Seneca loquitur. Δύναται γάρ ἴσον τῷ δρᾷν τὸ νοεῖν hic tan- tundem velle & facere est. Itaque Juvenalis, ubique per- jure cogitari historiam narrasset eam, quæ & apud He- rodotum est, adjecisserque tristissimum eventum, addidit: Has patitur pœnas peccandi sola voluntas. Tum vero quod hic maxime respicit Paulus, mœror, metusque maximus & Judæorum & Christianorum ple- num habuit effectum, tot Caji epistolis, tantis ad fabri- candam ponendamque statuam molitionibus, imo & ex- emplo jam in plurimis Synagogis dato, quod post Phi- lonem notatum Eusebio dicto Chronici loco. Præterea verba in Hiphil sæpe solum imperium significant. Oro- sius de hoc Caligulæ facto, Antiquum illud in Hieroso- lymis sacrarium profanari sacrificiis gentilium, ac reple- ri statuis, simulacrisque imperavit, seque ibi ut Deum coli voluit. Est autem tale hic καθίζειν, neque sedere si- gnificat, sed collocare, ut 1. Cor. VI. 4. Nam ἀυτὸν pro ἑαυτόν, aut mutato solum spiritu, qui olim non solebat adscribi, ἀυτὸς sæpissime in his libris reperias. Unde fa- ctum ut multi Codices eodem sensu hic habeant ἑαυτὸν. Non novum esset, si hic positum esset εἰς τὸν ναὸν in tem- plum pro ἐν τῷ ναῷ in templo, cum similis loquutio ap- pareat Marc. II. 1. & alibi. Sed nihil opus, huc decurrere, cum καθίζειν τινὰ εἰς τὸν θρόνον, collocare aliquem in thronum, & pura & frequens Græcis sit loquutio, quam & Plutarchus in Romulo usurpat, quomodo & Plato le- gum IX. dixit καθίζειν εἰς χωρίον. ᾿Αποδεικνύντα ἑαυτὸν, ὅτι ἐσὶ Θεός) Ostendens se, tan- quam sit DEUS. Verbis factisque ostentantem se pro Deo. Est enim hic ὅτι εἰδικὸν, ut Matth. XXVI. 24. 1. Cor. XI. 17. & 23. & alibi sæpe, Ἠξίυ ὑπὲρ ἄνθρωπον νομίζεσθαι, voluit major homine credi, ait Dio: Et mox: Ταῦτα μὲν ἐν τὰ σχήματα ὁπότε τις Θεὸς ἐπλάττετο εἶναι, ἐλάμ- βανε κὴ ἀυτῷ κὴ ἱκετεῖναι, κὴ ἐυχαὶ κὴ θυσίαι τὸ πρόσφοροι προσήγοντο. Tales igitur formas, cum Deum aliquem se simulabat, sumebat, ipsique convenientes tali numini preces, supplicationes ac sacra fiebant. Josephus: Προϊὼν ἐξίσατο τῶ ἀνθρωπίνε Φθονοῖν ὑπὸ μεγέθες τῆς ἀρχῆς ἐκ- θειάζων ἀυτὸν, κὴ τὰ πάντα ὑπ᾿ ἀτιμίᾳ τῦ Θεῖυ πολίτευειν ἤρετο. Postremo desiit humano se modo tenere, ob ma- gnitudinem imperii Deum se faciens, cunctaque ad Dei contemptum cœpit facere. Philo: ᾿Ουκ ἔτι ἠξίυ μένειν ἐν τοῖς τῆς ἀνθρωπίης Φύσεως ὅροις, ἀλλ᾽ ὑπερέκυπτε σπεδάζων Θεὸς νομίζεσθαι. Noluit se tenere ultra intra concessos naturæ humanæ terminos, sed extulit se eo usque, ut Deus credi cuperet. Mox: Καὶ ἐπειδὴ ἅπαξ

ἐθρασύνετο κὴ ἀπετόλμησεν ὡς εἰς τὸ κοινῶς ἐξενεγκεῖν τὴν ἀθεωτάτην ἐκθέωσιν ἀυτῦ τὰ συνῳδὰ πράττειν ἐπεχείρει. Poftquam semel depofito pudore ausus est in publicum edere impiam suam Deificationem, etiam ei rei congruentia cœpit agere. Deinde: Ἐνόμισε τὰ νομίζεσθαι παρ' Ἀλεξανδρεῦσι Θεόν: Putabat se ab Alexandrinis Deum credi.

Non opus hic disputare, anne verti debeant Græca, ita ut in templo Dei, vel in templum DEI se collocet, quod Grotius contendit, an vero ut Marefius cum aliis plerisque ait, adeo ut in templo Dei ipse sedeat? Utraque enim versio salva in vera de Anti-Christo sententia consistit. Sed quia Grotiano commento nullatenus convenit posterior, ideo pro sustinenda priori laborat. Quo de vero conferri poterit cum Appendice Grotij Maresii concordia discors. Ut suam tueatur translationem Grotius, ἀυτὸν pro ἑαυτὸν poni vel ἀυτὸν legendum esse contra Codicum fidem dimicat. Et καθίσαι vult non sedere, sed collocare esse. Ex adverso Maresius contendit, (1) nullum exemplum e scriptoribus novi Testamenti proferri posse, quod pronomina demonstrativa adhibeantur pro reciprocis. (2) Omnes codices, omnesque Interpretes legisse, ac intellexisse demonstrative non reciproce. (3) Non posse pro reciproco sumi, nisi καθίζω habeat significationem transitivam; atque id gratis affumi à Grotio, non probari. (4) Nec à proprio vocum usu esse recedendum, nisi quando analogia vel textus, vel fidei, necessario nos ad improprium abducit. Neque locus 1. Cor. VI. 4. probat, καθίζειν esse collocare, aut præjudicare potest aliis omnibus, qui in Novo Testamento occurrunt, in quibus, unico illo Ephes. 1. vers. 20. excepto, verbum istud sedere significat, locis nempe viginti sex.

Nihil autem juvat Grotium, si dicatur, hominem peccati seipsum collocare in templo Dei, vel, si ita malit, in templum Dei. Nam id toto cœlo adhuc differt ab eo, quod de Cajo affert, quod nempe is in animo atque consilio habuerit, statuam suam in templum Dei collocare. Nam aliud est propositum atque consilium, aliud factum ipsum. Paulus non vaticinatur de nudo proposito, aut consilio, sed de eo, quod revera futurum erat. Aliud porro est Cajus ipse, aliud statua Caji. Num Cajus semetipsum in templum DEI collocare voluit, cum voluit in templum Dei collocare statuam suam? Vaticiniorum præcipuus finis est, dicente Grotio ad Matth. XXIII. 10. ut postea, cum res evenit, divina præscientiæ certitudo appareat. Illa vero hic non appareret, sed vacillaret, si, quod de effectu prædixit Paulus, de mero affectu debuerit postea intelligi. Quod ex Amoso, rectius Mich. II. 1. affertur, vanum est. Ibi enim cogitare iniquitatem (super cubilibus suis) & operari malum, (quamprimum diescat) aperte distinguuntur.

Nec vero per templum Dei potest intelligi templum Hierosolymitanum, quemadmodum cum Pontificiis intelligit Grotius, ut & cum nonnullis veterum, qui à Judæis, templi restitutionem per Messiam expectantibus, seducti videntur. Nam & veteres illi, & Papistæ de templo Hierosolymitano, Anti-Christi tempore iterum excitando, interpretantur: quod tamen ne Judæi quidem constanter credunt, nimirum post secundum excidiu tertium excitandum templum: ut è Seder Olam, & Galatino libr. V. de arcan. cath. verit. cap. 10. constat: E Pontificiis etiam post Galatinum Lyranus in Matth. XIII. Villalpandus, Pererius l. X. in Dan. Baronius ad ann. 72. num. 28. negavit, ut & Cornelius à Lapide in Ezech. cap. XL. & h. l. p. 506. qui eo adduxit Jer. VII. 4. Et ut vere somnia sunt, quæ de novo Hierosolymitano templo post domum ultimam, Hagg. II. 10. quæ nunquam restauranda, Dan. IX. 27. æternum vastata relinquenda, Matth. XXIII. 38. tradita sunt: Ita nemo tamen repertus, cui præter Grotium vel per somnium in mentem venerit, hoc in loco, templum illud Hierosolymitanum, quod à Romanis destructum: Quod post Christi mortem nunquam in Novo Testamento ναὸς τῶ Θεῶ vocatum, quando velo per medium scisso, Matth. XXVII. 51. significata fuit cita & perpetua templi desolatio, ut Chrysostomus & Hieronymus ad istum locum observarunt, & Apostoli, post ascensionem Christi, toti fuerunt in templo DEI mystico, è Judæis & gentibus extruendo. Nomine itaque templi DEI veniunt in scriptis Apostolicis fideles; non vero templum materiale, 1. Cor. III. 15. Eph. II. 20. 1. Petr. II. 9. Nec aliter templum Dei in Propheticis Novi Testamenti locis, cujusmodi hic habetur, uspiam occurrit, quam mystice. Vide Apoc. III. 12. cap. VII. 19. cap. XI. 1. 2. 19. cap. XIV. 15. cap. XV. 5. 6. 8. c. XVI. 1. 17. Hæc vero prophetia nullatenus ad tempora Hierosolymitani templi adhuc stantis, nedum ad Caji tempora trahi potest, nisi vis ei summa fiat, quum homo ille peccati demum per adventum Christi novissimum destruendus sit. Ideo necessario de Ecclesia explicanda; quæ templum Domini vocatur, Eph. II. 21. 2. Cor. VI. 16. de qua explicatur ab Hieronymo: Sic enim habet: Vel Hierosolymis, ut aliqui putant, vel in Ecclesia, quod verius: Ab Ambrosio; qui ita habet: Ut in domo Domini, in sede sedeat Christi; à Theodoreto, DEI templum, inquiente, appellavit Ecclesias, in quibus primam sedem, (quæ illa est, nisi Romana) arripit (Anti-Christus) seipsum Deum conans ostendere: A Chrysostomo: sedebit in templo Dei, non quod est Hierosolymis, sed in templo Ecclesiæ: Ab Oecumenio, qui Chrysostomi verba expressisse videtur, εἰς τὸν ναὸν, ᾈ τὸν ἐν ἱεροσαλὲμ λέγει, ἀλλ’ εἰς τὰς Ἐκκλησίας τῶ Θεῶ: Ab Anshelmo, qui, vel potius, inquit, in templo Dei sedebit, id est, in mentibus Christianorum, quos seducet, qui fuerant templum DEI. Neque abnuunt è Pontificiis plerique, Ecclesias hic intelligi, etsi alteram explicationem de Hierosolyma sensui nostro quidam conjungant, Haymo, Lombardus, Thomas, Hugo Cardinalis, Cajetanus, Salmero, Cornelius à Lapide, Gregorius de Valentia Tom. IV. col. 2380. Suarez libr. V. de Anti-Christo cap. XV. §. 5. Guilhelmus Estius in h. l. n. 4. Dubium hic est, de quo Dei templo loquatur Apostolus? Quidam templum Hierosolymitanum intelligunt. Quamvis enim destructum sit illud, quod erat tempore Pauli; aliud tamen ejus loco aliquando rædificandum dicunt, sive à Judæis, sive ab ipso Anti-Christo, ut ipse in eo colatur. Verum si Anti-Christus sibi tanquam Deo construet templum: non illud Apostolus templum Dei vocaret, nihilo magis quam templum Jovis & Dianæ eo nomine dignaretur. Cajetanus putat, non aliquod determinatum templum significari, sed sensum esse, quod in quocunque templo, DEO dicato, sessurus sit Anti-Christus, tanquam illud sibi dicatum esset. At vero Hieronymus in epistola dudum citata verius arbitratur, Apostolum per templum DEI Ecclesiam significasse. Quam interpretationem post glossam interlinearem etiam S. Thomas recipit, nec S. Augustinus rejicit, Chrysostomus quoque ac Theodoretus, & cæteri Græci de Ecclesiis DEI (pluraliter enim loquuntur) Apostolum exponunt, quod in idem recidit. Nam Ecclesia DEI ex multis particularibus constat Ecclesiis.

Grotio certe ipsi Synonyma sunt populus, mul- titudo, Christiana Ecclesia, templum Dei ad Matth. XVI. 18. Ut taceam, quod hic exemplaria nonnul- la pro ναὸν legant λαὸν, notante Cornelio à Lapi- de, quod nullatenus de templo materiali accipi potest. Quod in Græco est εἰς τὸν ναὸν τοῦ Θεοῦ, explicari posse pro ἐν τῷ ναῷ, Marci II, 1. con- cedit ipse Grotius.

Augustinus, retento etiam sessionis significatu, retinet vim præpositionis usitatam, libr. XX. de Civit. DEI cap. XIX. ita explicans: Quod sessu- rus sit Anti-Christus in Ecclesia, quasi ipse sit vera Ecclesia, qui sibi & suis titulum Ecclesiæ arrogabit. Sed quia in textu Græco non nude dicitur sedeat, sed tanquam Deus sedeat, præstat explicare in templo DEI, quam usitatum signifi- catum retinere. Sedere autem illud alii explicant de sessione Anti-Christi, ut Doctoris, qui vult Doctor Doctorum, Doctor infallibilis, Episco- pus Episcoporum, adeoque Archiepiscopus etiam animarum, Christus ipse, haberi, quomodo sede- re Doctores dicuntur, Matth. XXIII. 2. Luc. II. 46. alii de sessione ejusdem, ut Domini, in Ec- clesia dominantis, quum sedere sit regnare 1. Cor. XV. 25. (Psal. CX. 1.) quo sensu sessio tribuitur magnæ meretrici & Babyloni, Apoc. XVII. vers. 1. cap. XIIX. 7. Utroque modo sedet Anti-Christus Romanus in Ecclesia DEI, unde etiam sedes ejus vocatur Roma, in qua sede & Doctoris sum- mi, atque infallibilis, & capitis ac rectoris Ec- clesiæ hominem usurpat, ut sedis etiam Romanæ nuncupatione prophetiæ hujus complementum apertius dignoscatur.

Quod contra pertendit Grotius in appendice, sine exemplo & perabsurdum esse, cœtum idolola- trarum, qualem esse, qui Papæ Romano adhæret, censemus, vocari templum DEI, à Pontificiis ha- bet, & in illis jam sæpius profligatum est. Ac re- cte respondit Maresius: Anti-Christum sedere in Ecclesia DEI, non in sensu composito, quasi ma- neat vera DEI Ecclesia, quam insidet Anti-Chri- stus, & quæ ei adhæret, sed in sensu diviso, quate- nus ea, quæ olim Ecclesia DEI fuerat, admisit An- ti-Christum, & meretrix facta est civitas fidelis, Esa. I. 21. sic tamen, ut non omnem omnino Ec- clesiæ faciem exuerit, sed rudera quædam & ve- stigia ejus, quæ fuit ante, retinuerit in nomine, professione, baptismo, ac si quæ sunt aliæ, quas Deus noluit plane obliterari, in papatu Christia- nismi reliquiæ. Adde quod Ecclesiæ nomine non soli fideles, sed in communi cœtu Christianorum vocentur, etsi admixti sint hypocritæ & impii at- que infideles, denominatione facta partim à pro- fessione, partim à nobiliori parte, ut exemplo con- stat Ecclesiæ Corinthiacæ; & imprimis, quod ty- rannidem suam exerceat, quantum in ipso est, non in illam tantum multitudinem Christianam, quæ ei subjecta, sed etiam in illam, quæ Ecclesia DEI proprie dicitur, & nomine populi Dei venit, & haberi caput velit universæ Christi Ecclesiæ, ac decernat, de necessitate salutis esse, subesse sibi uni- versam creaturam. Sedet in templo DEI Anti- Christus Romanus, quatenus, erecto in Ecclesia dominatu, illius partem infecit veneno suo, par- tem vero, quæ sanior restabat, & vere templum DEI erat, tyrannide, persecutione, ac corruptu- lis suis diu pressit, & tantum non oppressit, atque etiamnum omnibus modis premere atque oppri- mere satagit.

Sedere dicit Apostolus ὡς Θεὸν, quod etsi nec Vulgata, nec Syrus, nec Claromontanus Bezæ co- dex habeat, Græci tamen Interpretes legerunt, Chrysostomus, Theophylactus, Oecumenius, ut &

B. Lutherus, quos sequuntur plerique omnes re- centiores, quum non vulgare regnum, sed quasi divinum in Ecclesia obtenturus prædicatur An- tichristus: quod explicant, quæ adduntur, ἀποδει- κνύντα ἑαυτὸν, ὅτι ἐςὶ θεὸς, quod demonstraturus sit, non tam diserta professione, quam reipsa, se Deum esse. Non enim dixit Apostolus, obser- vante Chrysostomo, dicens seipsum esse Deum, sed ostentare tentans. Quod & Theophylactus repetiit, & antea Theodoretus innuit, seipsum conans Deum ostendere. Dum igitur ait, ἀποδεικνύντα, declarat, etsi verbis non sit fassurus, facto tamen aperte satis demonstraturum esse, quid quærat, ut videlicet in- star numinis habeatur. Geret se Dominum regno- rum hujus mundi, potestatem sibi arrogabit in cæ- lum, terram & infernum, autoritatem in homi- num conscientias, omnes suo subjicit tribunali, nul- li volet subjici, ut recte Crocius. Quanquam ja- ctantiam verborum non omnino excludendam censeamus, & ita Grotii explicationem, verbis fa- ctisque semetipsum ostentantem pro DEO, non reprobemus.

Quod in templo DEI vel Ecclesia homo ille peccati facturus erat secundum Apostolum, nec Cajus illic, nec ullus alius fecit præter Romanum Anti-Christum. Cajus etiam, etsi Numinis in- star coli voluerit, quod ab aliis quoque tum ante ipsum, tum post eundem, factum, eo charactere agnosci non potuit, quemadmodum Anti-Chri- stus, cui hoc uni, & soli proprium in Ecclesia est, qui nec parem vel socium ea in re ferre potest: Qui in jure Canonico Dominus Deus noster vo- catur, canon. Satis, dist. 96. gloss. ad extr. cum in- ter. In concilio Lateranensi sess. IX. in Papa im- plendum dicitur illud: Adorabunt eum omnes Re- ges terræ, omnes gentes servient ei. Sess. X. dictum est Pontifici: Tibi data est omnis potestas in cælo & in terra. Quod etiam extat in Cæremoniali libr. 1. tit. VII. sect. 7. In eodem concilio sess. VI. Leo X. dictus est Leo de tribu Juda, & radix Da- vid. Bellarminus præfat. in III. Controv. Gener. Pontifici applicat illud Esa. XXIX. Ecce ego po- nam in fundamentis Sion lapidem angularem &c. Franciscus Panigarola dixit l. II. part. 1. Papam esse unum illum Dominum, de quo loquitur Pau- lus Eph. IV. In Canonistarum libris passim legi- tur, quod Papa habeat cæleste arbitrium, quod habeat idem cum Deo consistorium, idem cum Chri- sto tribunal, quod potestas ejus se extendat ad cælestia, terrestria, & infernalia, quod Papæ com- missa sit tota spiritualis machina, quod Papa sit omnia, quod possit contra jus, & supra jus, & ex- tra jus, formam sacramentorum immutare, quod possit Apostoli verbis derogare, & contra episto- las Pauli statuere &c.

Chrysostomus & Theophylactus ad hanc ἀπόδειξιν referunt miracula, quibus sua tueri conatur An- ti-Christus, quæ ostentare nunquam voluit Cajus. Sed agnoscit Grotius in appendice, id præcipue hic spectare Apostolum, non quod se pro Deo habe- ri voluit, sed quod in ipso veri summique Dei tem- plo sedeat: Quid ergo opus ex Dione, Philone, Jo- sepho, aliisque proferre testimonia, quæ nihil am- plius dicunt, quam voluisse Cajum majorem ho- mine credi, & Deum haberi, & putasse, quod re- vera pro tali ab Alexandrinis haberetur. Eccui vero potius id competat, quam Pontifici Roma- no, omnem in DEI Ecclesia autoritatem ad se ra- pienti, & sese supra Principes, supra DEI Verbum, supra sacramenta, supra conscientias, supra fidem Ecclesiæ efferenti, & quæ DEI sunt, proterve & impudenter in se transferenti? Atque hanc templi mystici profanationem, per Antichristi ἀποστασίαν, metuere debuerunt Christiani, non Hierosolymitani χειροποιήτου, per Caligulæ statuam; cujus potius excidium, quod antea dixit Grotius, avide expectarunt Christiani, non tantum ut documentum veracis Magistri, sed & ut calamitatum, quas ab Judæis multas pertulerant, solatium. Adde quod ritus illi Judaici, secundum ipsummet Grotium, ad Joh. V. 23. evellendi jam fuerint, ut veræ fidei obstantes, quod in destructione templi factum. Neque verisimile est, Christianos Thessalonicenses ullam concepturos mœstitiam, de Hierosolymitano templo, quod brevi & abominatione desolationis polluendum, & funditus evertendum noverant, nec amplius, proprie loquendo, templum DEI esse sciebant, post velum discissum, imprimis quum exciso templo ac Republica Christiani Christum liberius sine Judaicorum rituum immutatione professi sint, fatente Grotio.

## 2:5
V. 5. Do you not remember that when I was with you I told you these things? Again πρὸς for apud, as in John I, 1. But that happened in Syria. For Paul was there when he was going from Caesarea to Cilicia, Acts IX. 30. And those who were driven out of Judea lived first in Syria, but when persecution arose there too, they went to more distant places.

Which Grotius had thus proposed in his commentary before:

Remember that when I was still with you I told you these things.) I do not say these things now for the first time, lest you think I am inventing them now for the sake of gaining time. Already then, when we were together in Syria, I said the same things. Thus you see how I am consistent with myself.

But to pass over the contradiction of the Chronology, who will admit that things were said by Paul to the Jews fleeing into Syria, which he himself so openly testifies he said to the Thessalonian Church, collected for the most part from the Gentiles, in Macedonia? Or shall we believe that the Apostle told those fleeing Jews at that time about Gaius, that he had it secretly in mind to place his statue in the temple, even though he could never execute it, and is now writing it again to those living in Thessalonica? For what causes would have moved him to that? What comfort would have redounded from that to the exiled Jews, concerning their fellow citizens expelled from Judea?

Latin:

V. 5. Οὐ μνημονεύετε, ὅτι ὢν πρὸς ὑμᾶς ταῦτα ἔλεγον ὑμῖν. Iterum πρὸς pro apud, ut Joh. I, 1. Factum autem id in Syria. Nam ibi fuit Paulus, cum à Cæsarea iret in Ciliciam, Actor. IX. 30. Et illi è Judæa ejecti primum in Syria vixere, sed ibi quoque orta vexatione, longinquiora adierunt loca.

Quæ ita in commentatione antea proposuerat Grotius:

Μνημονεύετε, ὅτι ἔτι ὢν πρὸς ὑμᾶς ἔλεγον ὑμῖν, meministis, quod cum essem apud vos, hæc dicebam vobis.) Non nunc primum hæc dico, ne nunc me ista comminisci putetis lucrandi temporis causa. Jam tum, cum in Syria una essemus, dixi eadem. Ita videtis, ut mihi constem.

Sed ut taceam Chronologiæ pugnantiam, ecquis admittet, dicta à Paulo in Syriam profugis Judæis, quæ ipse tam palam testatur se Thessalonicensi Ecclesiæ, maximam partem è gentilibus collectæ, in Macedonia dixisse? Aut num credemus, illa de Cajo, quod clam in animo habeat, statuam suam collocare in templum, etsi nunquam id exequi potuerit, profugis illis tum dixisse Apostolum, ac jam denuo Thessalonicæ agentibus perscribere? Quænam enim causæ eum ad id movissent? Quid solatii inde ad exules Judæos, de civibus suis è Judæa expulsos, redundasset?

## 2:6
Vers. 6. And now you know what restrains) The neuter 'what restrains' is the same as the masculine 'he who restrains' shortly after, just as a neuter noun is often used even for persons, insofar as those persons are things. See Col. 1:20. You know what delays him. 'Κατέχω' corresponds to the Hebrew 'אחר', Gen. 24:56, and 'אסר', Gen. 39:20, 42:19, and 'עצר', Ruth 1:13, all of which have the meaning of delaying and detaining. So also Luke 4:43, Rom. 1:18. L.
