Vitellius, when Paul was saying these things and writing them, was holding Syria and Judea, a man influential among the Jews and commanding great armies, for which reason it would have been easy for him, if Gaius had so gravely exasperated the minds of the Jews, to undertake their protection and make the province subject to his own jurisdiction. Therefore Gaius, before he carried out his purpose, was waiting for the time when L. Vitellius would depart from the province and receive Petronius as his successor, who did not have equal authority.

So that he might be revealed in his own time) Here too is a passive used for a reciprocal. That he might reveal himself, that is, betray his own mind, in his own time, namely after a year or two from when these things were written: and this not without the providential dispensation of God, as John 7:30, 8:20, Luke 22:53. What is 'to be revealed' here, Philo called 'to bring to light what he had overshadowed.' That 'in his own time' is for 'בעתו' in Psalm 1:3 and elsewhere.

Concerning which the commentary of Grotius has this:

And now you know what restrains, and now, you know what detains. I have also added this, what it was that was delaying Gaius from publishing what he had conceived in his mind. What that is, will now appear.

So that he might be revealed in his own time, that he might be revealed in his own time) That is, that he might not lay bare his most wicked character before it shall have seemed good to GOD to permit it. See John 7:30 and 8:20, Luke 22:53. 'To be revealed' is to betray one's thoughts by one's deeds, 'to bring to light what he had overshadowed,' to open what he had covered, as we just heard Philo speaking.

But τὸ ἀποκαλυφθῆναι αὐτόν does not mean to reveal a very wicked character previously hidden, but to emerge, to be made manifest, to come forth from darkness into light, and for the Antichrist to appear in such a way that he is recognized by the pious as such, just as Christ is also said to be revealed when he is manifested to be known by men through the light of the Gospel. Which word is taken passively here by all interpreters, nor does it occur otherwise in Luke 2:35 and 1 Corinthians 3:13. And what, I ask, did it matter to the Thessalonians that Vitellius was standing in the way, preventing Gaius from exalting himself above God or bringing his statue into the temple? Furthermore, Vitellius was not particularly formidable to Gaius. For at his command, he left Syria and immediately gave way to his successor, Petronius. Nor is it likely that he himself would have stood much in Gaius's way, since, being of a wondrous talent for flattery, he was the first to institute that Gaius Caesar be worshipped as a god, and when the senate was dead, he erected a statue before the rostra with this inscription: 'Of immovable piety toward the Prince,' as Suetonius testifies in A. Vitellius, chapters II and III. Theophylact also notes that the Apostle by no means says this revelation will happen shortly, but IN HIS OWN TIME. Crocius says that Philo's ἀναφαίνειν denotes the same thing as Paul's ἀποκαλυφθῆναι. The man of sin was therefore revealed when, according to Philo, Caligula uncovered the cruelty of his mind, which he had previously concealed under a deceptive mask, which happened, according to Philo, when he killed his cousin Tiberius. Which slaughter indeed occurred at the beginning of Gaius's reign. But this Pauline epistle was written only when Gaius was secretly agitating that insolent plan concerning the statue, namely, after Macro and Silanus had been removed, as Grotius maintains. Who, therefore, in the slaughter of Tiberius, already revealed his wicked mind, Caligula—that is, according to Grotius's interpretation, was the man of sin revealed? How did Paul predict that revelation as something future, which had already taken place?

Maresius notes here a great oversight of Grotius in 'The Revealed Antichrist,' part 1, chapter XXII, page 438. For he had previously said, citing a praised but false witness, Dionysius Petavius, and directly against evangelical truth, that Stephen was stoned in the year 31 after the birth of Christ, Paul was converted in the year 33, and came to Caesarea in the year 36, after which time Tiberius ruled over the Romans for three years. That was to say that the year 39 of Christ was the last of Tiberius, and 40 the first of Gaius. How, therefore, can Macro be imagined, who died in the second year of Gaius, to have been killed in the year 38 of Christ? He had likewise said that the dispersion after the death of Stephen was eight years prior to the reign of Gaius. But if the death of Stephen preceded the beginnings of Gaius by eight years, and the second year of Gaius, in which Macro perished, coincides with the year 38 of Christ, Stephen must have undergone martyrdom for Christ in the year 28 of Christ, two full years before Christ was baptized.

But, setting aside entirely groundless inventions, let us examine the meaning of the Apostle's words. What in reality is τὸ κατέχον in this place? Augustine, in book XX of 'The City of God,' chapter XIX, confesses that he is entirely ignorant of it. Severianus and certain others once understood it as the grace of the Holy Spirit, which, because of the wickedness of men, being taken out of the way, the Antichrist would have a place; which Theodoret, understanding it as ordinary grace, refutes on the grounds that the grace of the Spirit is never to cease. Chrysostom took it as extraordinary grace, rejecting that interpretation on the grounds that the Antichrist would have had to arrive in his own time, and that the Apostle would have expressed it not so obscurely, but more openly, if he had intended to mean the Holy Spirit. Theodoret brings forward two other impediments. The first, which he says was also brought forward by others, is the decree of God, which established that he should appear at the very time of the consummation, but no such decree can be brought forward from the scriptures. The other is that the worship of idols must first be overturned, and the preaching of the Gospel must shine everywhere, and then the adversary of truth will appear. Theophylact also cites this opinion, that idolatry was the obstacle. But not without reason he prefers Chrysostom's explanation, that τὸ κατέχον is the Roman Empire. For unless that Roman Empire, he says, is overturned, the Antichrist will have no way to be able to accomplish what he wishes according to his desire, and for that reason Paul also spoke of this matter in an adumbrated way, and did not express it openly. For he did not want to rashly invite the enmity of the Romans upon himself, or expose himself to dangers in vain. For if he had said that the Roman Empire was soon to be taken away, they would have immediately buried him alive in the ground as one threatening the destruction of their Republic, and they would have destroyed other believers who followed him, as those for whom the overthrow of such a great dominion would have brought joy. Which he later explains further according to the opinion of Chrysostom on the words: 'Only he who holds, let him hold now, until he is taken out of the way, and then that wicked one will be revealed,' that is, when the Roman Empire is taken out of the way, then he will be present. But as long as the fear of this holds men, no one will easily subjugate himself to any other. But when that has been overturned, this one will invade the other dominion, and as if he had gained control of affairs, he will pervert human and divine things alike. For just as before the supreme monarchy of the Romans other empires were taken away, just as it is established that the empire of the Medes was destroyed by the Babylonians, that of the Babylonians by the Persians, that of the Persians by the Macedonians, and that of the Macedonians by the Romans: so also this Roman kingdom will be taken away by the Antichrist, and Daniel himself testifies that it will indeed happen in that way.

Theodoret indeed raises a doubt that the Roman Empire is not to be succeeded by another empire. But in the Roman Empire, signified by the fourth beast in Daniel, a little horn is to emerge, which will wage war with the saints, chapter VII:21. This, however, is that very one of whom the divine Apostle treats here. But neither Chrysostom, nor Theophylact, nor anyone else wishes to refer to the abolition of the Roman Empire, because it is to last until the end of the age, but only to a certain diminution, so that it can no longer restrain the breaking-forth of the Antichrist, when the strength of the empire will pass over to the Antichrist, according to Chrysostom, with the second beast exercising the power of the first, Revelation 13:12. In which way also that passage of Cyril's Catechesis XV is to be explained: 'That Antichrist will come when the times of the Roman Empire have been fulfilled.' And thus do many others of the ancients interpret these words of the Apostle concerning the Roman empire: Tertullian, Jerome, Ambrose, Oecumenius; among the Reformed, Bullinger, Beza, Hyperius, Tossanus, Piscator, the Belgian, Grotius, along with most of our own; among the Papists, Lombard, Hugo, Thomas, Justinianus in his paraphrase, Bellarmine in book III of De Romano Pontifice, chapter 5, and Cornelius a Lapide on this passage, who also says it is a tradition of the Fathers, as witnessed by Jerome in chapter VII of Daniel, and as it seems, an Apostolic one, to which he also says the passage in Daniel VII. 21 et seqq. pertains.

But as for the fact that the Papists add to this explanation that the Roman monarchy must first be destroyed and utterly cut off before the Anti-Christ comes, Theodoret rightly taught that this is repugnant to the oracle of Daniel, and it has been devised so that the work they may have to acknowledge; that the Anti-Christ has already arrived, and that they are ignorant of their own utopian Anti-Christ, whom they expect only at the end of the world (perhaps with the masked Messiah of the Jews?), just as they also trifle that that Antichrist will be received by the Jews as the Messiah.

Although our blessed Hunnius refers more impediments to the τὸ κατέχον [that which restrains], since in reality more things stood in the way of the Antichrist being revealed: yet he did not omit this regarding the Roman Empire: about which it is helpful to hear him himself. From the event, he says, it is easy to gather what that thing is which inhibited and retarded the Devil's attempts at that time. For first, it was hindered by the singular and almost incredible care of the holy Apostles, and the ardent zeal and tireless study of many faithful Doctors in the primitive Church, by which they bravely opposed themselves to the errors and corruptions of the heavenly doctrine, and either immediately repressed the rising heresies, or at least inhibited them so that they would not, having acquired strength, grow strong and creep further. Next, that first fervor of the Christian Church toward the more sincere doctrine of the Gospel stood in the way. Thirdly, the persecutions of the primitive Church hindered the attempt of the Anti-Christ, which repressed that pride of the Doctors, so that they would not exalt themselves in this manner: or if the Devil should ever inspire certain ones with a spirit of pride, yet because of the supreme power and majesty of the Roman Empire, they were not able to accomplish what they wanted, and to rise to such a height: These were those impediments which detained and delayed the thoughts and planned counsels of Satan and his instruments for some time, so that he would not suddenly pour out all his malice into the world. However, we do not doubt that the last impediment is properly looked to here, and that it was already more clearly explained to the Thessalonians by the Apostle, and is here at least obscurely insinuated, to be illustrated in its own time by the event: Concerning which Chrysostom on verse 7: When the Roman Empire shall have been taken from the midst, then he will come. And not without reason. For as long as there was fear of that empire, no one was immediately subjected. But when that empire shall have been dissolved, he will invade the principate of the empire, and will attempt to seize for himself the empire of both men and God. Indeed, the majesty of the old Roman empire and the power of the Caesars stood in the way, so that Anti-Christian iniquity would not break out among Christians. But when the majesty of the empire was torn away by the Saracens and Mahometans in the East, and by other barbarian peoples in the West, iniquity began to break out little by little. To which it contributes that Grotius himself in his annotations on Cassander, art. VII, acknowledges that it is possible that the Pope might fly into the rights of Bishops and Kings, and that it was in fact done, especially since the laceration of the Roman empire into many Kings occurred: and that in the appendix he says that the Roman empire remains partly in the Prince, partly in the Emperor. Concerning which, see what Maresius disputed against Grotius, part II, Antichrist. Revel. cap. III. §. 10. p. 87.

Latin:

Vers. 6. Καὶ νῦν τὸ κατέχον οἴδατε) Τὸ κατέχον idem, quod mox ὁ κατέχων, sicut sæpe neutrum nomen etiam de personis ponitur, quatenus eæ personæ res sunt. Vide Col. I, 20. Scitis quid eum moretur. Κατέχω respondet Ebræo אחר, Gen. XXIV. 56. & אסר Gen. XXXIX. 20. XLII, 19. & עצר Ruth. I. 13. quæ omnia morandi ac detinendi habent significationem. Sic & Luc. IV. 43. Rom. I. 18. L. Vitellius, cum Paulus ista diceret & hæc scriberet, Syriam & Judæam tenebat, vir apud Judæos gratiosus, & magnis exercitibus imperans, cui propterea facile fuisset, si tam graviter Judæorum animos exasperasset Cajus, eorum tutelam suscipere, & provinciam sui facere juris. Ideo Cajus, antequam propositum exequeretur, tempus expectabat, quo L. Vitellius è provincia decederet, & successorem acciperet Petronium, cui non erat par autoritas.

Εἰς τὸ ἀποκαλυφθῆναι αὐτὸν ἐν τῷ ἑαυτοῦ καιρῷ) Est & hic passivum pro reciproco. Ut se aperiat, id est animum suum prodat, suo tempore, post annum nempe unum atque alterum, ex quo hæc scripta sunt: idque non sine provida Dei dispensatione, ut Joh. VII. 30. VIII, 20. Luc. XXII. 53. quod hic est ἀποκαλυφθῆναι, id Philo dixit ἀναφαίνειν ἃ συνεσκίασε. Illud ἐν τῷ καιρῷ ἑαυτοῦ est pro בעתו Psalm. I. 3. & alibi.

Quo de commentatio Grotiana sic habet:

Καὶ νῦν τὸ κατέχον οἴδατε, & nunc, quæ detineat, scitis. Hoc etiam addidi, quid esset quod Cajum moraretur, quo minus id, quod animo conceperat, evulgaret. Id quid sit, jam apparebit.

Εἰς τὸ ἀποκαλυφθῆναι αὐτὸν ἐν τῷ ἑαυτοῦ καιρῷ, ut reveletur in suo tempore) Ut scilicet pessimum ingenium non ante denudet, quam DEO id visum erit permittere, Vid. Joh. VII. 30. & VIII. 20. Luc. XXII. 53. Ἀποκαλύπτεσθαι est factis cogitata prodere, Ἀναφαίνειν ἃ συνεσκίασεν, aperire, quæ obtexerat, ut Philonem loquentem modo audivimus.

At τὸ ἀποκαλυφθῆναι αὐτὸν non est renudare pessimum antea latens ingenium, sed emergere, pa- tefieri, ex tenebris in lucem prodire, & sic apparere Anti-Christum, ut à piis pro tali agnoscatur, pro- ut & revelari dicitur Christus, cum hominibus per lucem Evangelii cognoscendus manifestatur. Quod verbum ab omnibus interpretibus hic ac- cipitur passive, nec aliter Luc. II. 35. 1. Cor. III. 13. occurrit. Et quid quæso ad Thessalonicenses hoc pertinebat, Vitellium obstare, quo minus Cajus se supra Deum efferet, vel statuam suam templo in- ferret? Adhæc non admodum formidabilis Cajo fuit Vitellius. Eo enim jubente, excessit Syria, & statim locum dedit Petronio successori. Neque verisimile ipsum multum obstituram fuisse Cajo, cum, miri in adulando ingenii, primus Cajum Cæsarem adorari, ut Deum, instituerit, & mor- tuo senatu statuam pro rostris erexerit, cum hac inscriptione, Pietatis immobilis erga Principem, teste Suetonio in A. Vitellio cap. II. & III. Ad- vertit & Theophylactus, quod Apostolus hanc re- velationem nequaquam dicat brevi futuram, sed SUO TEMPORE. Dicit Crocius Philonis ἀναφαίνειν idem denotare, quod ἀποκαλυφθῆναι Pauli. Revelatus ergo homo peccati fuit, cum apud Philonem Caligula sævitiam animi detexit, quam antea sub fallaci persona dissimulaverat, quod juxta Philonem factum, cum Patruelem suum Tiberium occidit. Quæ vero cædes sub initia Caji contigit. At hæc epistola Paulina scri- pta tum demum fuit, cum insolens illud de statua consilium Cajus clam agitavit, sublatis nempe Macrone & Silano, ut vult Grotius. Qui ergo in cæde Tiberii jam sceleratam renudavit mentem Caligula, hoc est, interprete Grotio, revelatus fuit homo peccati? Qui Paulus prædixit revela- tionem eam, tanquam futuram, quæ jam facta erat?

Magnam hic notat Maresius in Anti-Christo revelato parte 1. cap. XXII. pag. 438. Grotii ἀβλε- ψίαν. Nam antea dixerat, laudato teste, sed falso, Dionysio Petavio, & directe contra veritatem Ev- angelicam, Stephanum lapidatum anno post Chri- stum natum XXXI. Paulum conversum anno XXXIII. Cæsaream venisse anno XXXVI. post quod tempus Romanis imperasse Tiberium per annos tres. Id erat dicere annum Christi XXXIX. fuisse Tiberii ultimum, XL. primum Caji. Qui ergo potest fingi Macro, qui occubuit secundo Caji, occisus XXXVIII. Christi? Dixerat pariter dispersionem post Stepha- ni mortem octennio fuisse priorem Cajano princi- patu. Quod si Stephani mors initia Caji præcessit octo annis, & concurrat Caji secundus, quo Macro periit, cum XXXVIII. Christi, debuit Stephanus XXVIII. Christi biennio integro, antequam Christus baptizaretur, martyrium pro Christo adiisse.

Sed, missis commentis prorsus ἀσυστάτοις, de sensu verborum Apostoli dispiciamus. Quidnam revera τὸ κατέχον hoc loco? Augustinus libr. XX. de civit. Dei cap. XIX. fatetur, se prorsus id igno- rare. Severianus & alii quidam olim intellexere Spiritus S. gratiam, qua, propter hominum mali- tiam, è medio sublata, locum habiturus sit Anti- Christus, quod Theodoretus, de ordinaria gratia in- telligens, ex eo refutat, quod nunquam gratia Spi- ritus sit cessatura. Chrysostomus de extraordinaria accepit, inde id reprobans, quod oportuisset suo tempore jam advenisse Anti-Christum, quodque Apostolus non tam obscure, sed apertius id ex- pressisset, si Spiritum Sanctum intelligere voluis- set. Theodoretus duo alia impedimenta adfert. Prius quod ab aliis etiam allatum dicit, Dei decretum, quod statueret, ut appareret in ipso tempore con- summationis, sed tale decretum e scripturis ad- duci nullum potest. Alterum quod prius ever- tendus cultus idolorum, & ubique fulgere debeat prædicatio Evangelii, & tunc appariturus sit ve- ritatis adversarius. Quam sententiam etiam alle- gat Theophylactus, quod idolatria obstiterit. Sed non immerito præfert Chrysostomi explica- tionem, quod τὸ κατέχον Romanum imperium sit. Nam nisi Romanum illud imperium, ait, ever- tatur, nullam Anti-Christus habiturus est viam, ut queat pro ejus cupiditate, quæ velit, perficere, eoque & Paulus rem hanc adumbrate dixit, nec palam expressit. Non enim temere volebat Roma- norum sibi inimicitias vendicare, vel sese periculis frustra objicere. Nam si dixisset, paulo post subla- tum iri Romanum imperium, mox eum, ut Rei- publicæ suæ interitum minantem, vivum suffodis- sent in terram, perdidissentque & alios, qui se secta- rentur, fideles, ut quibus tanti dominatus eversio lætitiam peperisset. Quod postea ex sententia Chry- sostomi porro sic explicat ad verba: tantum qui tenet, nunc teneat, donec de medio fiat, & tunc re- velabitur ille iniquus, hoc est, cum Romanum imperium tolletur e medio, tunc affuturus est ille. Quamdiu vero hujus formido tenuerit homines, se nemo facile alteri cuiquam subjugabit. At ubi illud fuerit eversum, invasurus hic alterum domi- natum, & tanquam rerum potitus, humana simul ac divina pervertet. Quemadmodum enim ante Romanorum summam omnium monarchiam fuere alia sublata imperia, sicuti Medorum constat a Babyloniis, Babyloniorum a Persis, Persarum a Macedonibus, Macedonum a Romanis fuisse de- leta: Sic & Romanum hoc regnum ab Anti-Chri- sto tolletur, & id quidem ita futurum Daniel ipse testificatur.

Movet quidem Theodoretus dubium, quod im- perium Romanum non sit excepturum aliud impe- rium. In Romano autem imperio, per quartam bestiam a Daniele significato, proditurum sit par- vum cornu, quod bellum gesturum cum sanctis, cap. VII. 21. Hoc autem esse illum ipsum, de quo hic agit divinus Apostolus. Ast nec Chry- sostomus, nec Theophylactus, aut alius quisquam Romani imperii abolitionem respici volunt, quod usque ad consummationem seculi duraturum, sed solum imminutionem quandam, ut cohibere pro- rumpentem Anti-Christum amplius nequeat, quum transiturum sit imperii robur in Anti-Chri- stum, secundum Chrysostomum, secunda bestia potestatem prioris exercente, Apocal. XIII. 12. Quomodo etiam illa Cyrilli Catech. XV. expli- canda: Veniet Anti-Christus ille, cum Romani imperii tempora impleta fuerint. Atque ita de Ro- mano imperio interpretantur hæc Apostoli ple- rique alii veteres Tertullianus, Hieronymus, Am- brosius, Oecumenius, e Reformatis Bullingerus, Beza, Hyperius, Tossanus, Piscator, Belga, Grotius cum plerisque nostratibus; e Pontificiis Lom- bardus, Hugo, Thomas, Justinianus in paraphrasi, Bellarminus libr. III. de Rom. Pontif. cap. 5. Cornelius a Lapide in hunc locum, qui etiam ait esse communem Patrum, teste Hieronymo in cap. VII. Dan. traditionem, & ut videtur, Apostolicam, quo pertinere etiam dicit locum Dan. VII. 21. seqq.

Quod vero Papistæ huic explicationi affuunt, monarchiam Romanam prius destruendam & ex- scindendam prorsus, antequam Anti-Christus ve- niat, id Danielis oraculo repugnare recte Theo- doretus docuit, & excogitatum est, ut ne opus- habeant agnoscere; quod jam pridem Anti-Chri- stus advenerit, utque utopicum suum Anti-Chri- stum ingorant, quem sub finem mundi demum, (fortasse cum Judaeorum larvato Messia?) expe- ctant, quemadmodum etiam nugantur, Antichri- stum illum pro Messia a Judaeis receptum iri.

Quanquam vero B. Hunnius noster ad τὸ κατέχον plura impedimenta referat, quum revera plura obstiterint, quo minus Antichristus revele- tur: Non tamen hoc de Romano imperio praeter- misit: quo de ipsum audire juvat. Ex eventu, in- quit, colligere promptum est, quidnam sit illud, quod Diaboli conatus eo tempore inhibuit & retardavit. Primo enim obstabat ei singularis ac pene incredi- bilis sanctorum Apostolorum cura, & multorum in primitiva Ecclesia fidelium Doctorum ardens ze- lus, indeffessumque studium, quo se erroribus & cor- ruptelis doctrinae coelestis fortiter opponebant, & exo- rientes haereses vel reprimebant statim, vel certe sic inhibebant, ne acquisitis viribus invalescerent ser- perentque latius. Deinde obstabat primus ille fervor Christianae Ecclesiae erga sinceriorem Evangelii do- ctrinam. Tertio impediebant Anti-Christi conatum persecutiones primitivae Ecclesiae, quae fastum illum Doctorum reprimebant, ne sese hunc in modum ef- ferrent: aut si maxime Diabolus quosdam superbia afflaret spiritu, tamen ob summam Imperii Romani potestatem & majestatem perficere, quod vellent, & ad ejusmodi celsitudinem assurgere non valebant: Haec erant impedimenta illa, quae Satanae & organo- rum ipsius cogitata consiliaque detinebant aliquan- diu & remorabantur, ne subito omnem malitiam suam in orbem terrarum effunderet. Postremum tamen impedimentum proprie hic respici, illudque clarius expositum jam Thessalonicensibus ab A- postolo hic obscure saltem insinuari, suo tempo- re ab eventu illustrandum non ambigimus: Quo de Chrysostomus ad v. 7. Quando e medio sublatum fuerit Romanum imperium, tunc veniet ille. Et non abs re. Donec enim imperii illius timor fuit, nemo statim subditur. Quando vero istud dissolutum fue- rit imperium, imperii principatum invadet, & ten- tabit ad se rapere & hominum & Dei imperium. Nimirum veteris imperii Romani majestas, & Caesarum potentia obstitit, ne Anti-Christiana in- ter Christianos erumperet iniquitas. Verum cum e Saracenis & Mahumetanis in Oriente, & ab aliis barbaris populis in Occidente majestas imperii convelleretur, iniquitas paulatim erumpere coe- pit. Quo facit, quod Grotius ipse in annot. ad Cassandr. art. VII. agnoscat, fieri posse, ut Papa in jura Episcoporum & Regum involet, & revera fa- ctum fuisse, maxime ex quo laceratio contigit im- perii Romani in plures Reges: quodque in appen- dice dicat, remanere imperium Romanum par- tim in Principe, partim in Imperatore. De quo vide, quae Maresius adversus Grotium disputavit part. II. Antichrist. Revel. cap. III. §. 10. p. 87.

## 2:7
Vers. 7. Τὸ γὰρ μυστήριον ἤδη ἐνεργεῖται τῆς ἀνομίας [For the mystery of iniquity is already at work]) Now the motions of that secret impiety are set forth, namely through Helicon and other Egyptians. It is called a mystery, whatever is secret: that which is unknown, according to the interpreter Chrysostom. Thus in Isaiah 24:17, רָז which signifies a secret, Theodotion translates as mystery, which word is also in the version of Daniel several times. The secrets of Kings are called by this name in Tobit 12:6, and others, Sirach 22:24, 27:16, 17, 21, 2 Maccabees 13:21. This is called the mystery of iniquity, because it pertains to impiety, which is חָמָס to the Hebrews, iniquity elsewhere, and elsewhere impiety to the Greeks translating the Hebrew. I shall take ἐνεργεῖται here passively, that is, it is being forged. Thus it is taken in 2 Cor. 1:6, 2 Cor. 4:12. Hesychius: ἐνεργεῖται means it is being constructed.

Μόνον ὁ κατέχων ἄρτι ἕως ἐκ μέσυ γένηται [Only he who now restrains will restrain until he is taken out of the way]) There is here an ellipsis of the word to be expected. And it ought to have been constructed as ἕως ὁ κατέχων ἄρτι γένηται ἐκ μέσου, until he who thus far delays is removed, namely from the province: That is, that plan: ἐκ μέσου γενέσθαι is said not only of those who perish, but also of those who are removed, especially those who were previously an impediment, as ἐξαρθῇ ἐκ μέσου, 1 Cor. 5:2. Thus you have it also in Isaiah 57:2. In the Greek ἦρται ἐκ τοῦ μέσου; Demosthenes also said it thus, ἐκ μέσου ἀνελεῖν.

Twin to these are the things which he had handed down in the commentary on this passage:

Vers. 7. Τὸ γὰρ μυστήριον ἤδη ἐνεργεῖται τῆς ἀνομίας [For the mystery of iniquity is already at work]) For the mystery of iniquity is already working. Now in secret that impiety is preparing itself, namely with Helicon and other Egyptian scoundrels persuading it, whom Philo describes. Such is that of Tacitus: Within the Alban villa the opinion of Messalinus was resounding. He shows both what was to be, and what was already being built in secret, revealed to him by GOD, and that he was not speaking of things that would arise after him and those to whom he was writing, but of things whose causes, although most hidden, were being born. Thus Chrysostom notes on Rom. 11:25 and 1 Cor. 15:51 that by the word mystery is signified that which is unknown. The same man, in his second sermon on almsgiving, rightly senses that these words concern some one of the Emperors, but he is deceived to such an extent that he takes Nero for Gaius.

Mόνον ὁ κατέχων ἄρτι ἕως ἐκ μέσου γένηται [Only he who now restrains will restrain until he is taken out of the way]) Only that he who holds, may now hold, until he is made out of the way. The evil will not be deferred longer than until Lucius Vitellius, who now holds Syria and with it Judea, shall have departed from there and received a successor. Gaius, as Philo notes, σφόδρα τοὺς ἐν ἡγεμονίαις ηὐλαβεῖτο, τὰς πρὸς νεωτεροποιίαν ἀφορμὰς ἀφαιρῶν ἔχοντας ἐν ἑτοίμῳ, καὶ μάλιστα τοὺς ἐν μεγάλαις καὶ μεγάλοις ἐπιτάττοντας στρατοπέδοις, ἡλίκα τὰ πρὸς Εὐφράτῃ κατὰ Συρίαν ἐστίν: he greatly feared those who were in the provinces, and for that reason was removing the opportunities for innovation that they had in readiness, and especially those who were both in great provinces and commanded great armies, such as the Syrian ones at the Euphrates. Vitellius, however, to speak in the words of Dio, was οὔτε ἀγενὴς, οὔτε ἄφρων, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἐκ τῆς ἐν τῇ Συρίᾳ ἀρχῆς ὀνομαστὸς γενόμενος [neither ignoble, nor foolish, but also having become famous from his command in Syria]. For he governed other matters brilliantly, and he struck down Artabanus, who was plotting against him even there, neither degenerate nor foolish, but he had gained for himself a great name from the province of Syria, both by many other matters excellently administered, and by the slaying of Artabanus, who was threatening Syria, and more things that are there. Tacitus concerning him: 'Of ancient virtue in governing provinces.' Under the command of this Vitellius, Pontius Pilate had gone to Rome, ταῖς ἐτελῖε πειθόμενος ἐντολαῖς, ὐκ ὄν ἀντειπεῖν, obeying the commands of Vitellius, against which it was not permitted to go, says Josephus, Book XVIII. Furthermore, Vitellius was favorable to the Jews, as appears from the remitted taxes and the Pontifical robe given to the priests for safekeeping, which things Josephus says were done by him ἐπὶ ἐυεργεσίᾳ τῦ ἔθνες, so that he might bind the nation to himself with benefits. Wherefore it is no wonder if, with such a man holding that province, Gaius dared to innovate nothing there.

First, one must look into the mystery of iniquity here. By the word 'mystery,' Grotius wishes to denote only a secret. But in the Scriptures it contains more than a mere secret, and it is a religious and sacred name, Matt. 13:11 (at which place Grotius's annotations should be compared), Mark 4:2, Luke 8:10, 1 Cor. 4:1, ch. 15:51, 1 Tim. 3:16, where it is called the mystery of godliness: 'God manifest in the flesh,' which certainly did not cease to be a mystery from the time it was manifested to us, it does not remain hidden any longer; thus Dan. 2:18, 19, 27, ch. 4:6, Rev. 1:19, ch. 17:9, these are mysteries which have a sacred and mystical significance. The name of mystery, therefore, since it implies something religious and sacred, is applied here to Antichrist with the best right, not only so that it may be opposed to the mystery of godliness in the coming of Christ 1. Tim. 3:15, the mystery of iniquity is to appear in the revelation of the Antichrist, but also because it began to creep in secretly, and under the pretext of the mysteries of religion this mystery succeeded, as is abundantly evident from the Pontifical, Ritual, and Papistic Ceremonials. It commends even the most trivial and insipid trifles as sublime mysteries. Nor is it inconsistent with this matter that Cornelius à Lapide says the mystery of iniquity is iniquity, secret and mystical, that is, cloaked under the title of piety and legitimate dominion and authority. Which in no way fits the counsel of Gaius, but fits perfectly the rise of the Roman Papacy, and exhibits the nature of him who, under the pretext of piety and the title of legitimate dominion, arrived at the peak of his power. The ordinary gloss in this place interprets the mystery of iniquity as iniquity cloaked under the name of piety. Hypocrisy, therefore, is noted by the word mystery, because that man of sin must present a semblance of truth and holiness; by which art the Roman Pontiff surpasses all other seducers, as is evident to the eye from the pretext of traditions, from the boasting of antiquity and Councils, from the variety of rites, from the multitude of superstitions, and from the definition and quality of sins and religions, from a specious humility and sanctity, from discipline, penance, satisfactions, flagellations, pilgrimages, mass-worships, Canonical hours, and formulas of beads, Rosaries, and Marian prayers, and other innumerable things of that kind. Compare 1 Tim. IV. 1. 29. Apoc. XIII. 11, where the Antichrist is said to be about to wear the horns of a lamb, and to speak like a Dragon; c. XVIII. 4. 5. 7. concerning the golden cup, with which he is said to be about to intoxicate the Kings of the world with the Spirit of fornication (spiritual), and concerning the harlot, who bears the mystery of holiness on her forehead. Caligula never had anything mystical, which would present a presumption of the veneration of a mystery, or of some divine revelation made to him from outside the order of things, who in the time of his empire certainly presented neither piety nor any mystical communion with GOD or the Gods, nor yet did he ever deign to cloak his public impiety with a charm. 2. That ἤδη ἐνεργεῖται concerning the mystery of iniquity is not indeed badly explained as, already in secret this impiety is preparing itself, but it is ineptly snatched away to the secret railings of Helicon and other scoundrels against Gaius, who was already suffering his punishments in hell when these things were written, and therefore could not stir up counsels, nor if we imagine these things written in the second year of Gaius, do these things fit those counsels of Gaius. For it would not be a prophecy here, if only those things were indicated which were already being done in secret at that time. On the contrary, the Apostle predicted here things that would not happen until long after those times, so that it might be clear to the Thessalonians that the day of the Lord was not so near; as some wished them to be persuaded. And since the Apostle joins the mystery of iniquity with a notable apostasy from the faith, and attributes it to him whose coming is to be in signs and lying wonders, and it is said to be already being performed even then, how will this be referred to the counsels of Gaius and Helicon with him in secret? The Syrian implies that this mystery was already effective in the time of Paul, even if it was not to be revealed until its own time. How can that fit the counsel of Gaius, which was then still hidden and immature, and not yet fully concocted according to Grotius? That ἐνεργεῖται is to be understood passively, that it had already begun to be performed and to creep secretly then, not in counsel, but through the occult machinations of Satan, and nascent heresies, just as fire, as Cornelius à Lapide says, secretly exerts its force among wood, and burns what is near, and gradually creeps forward, until it breaks out into a flame and a conflagration. He implies thus that that mystery of iniquity is also in the seed and would come forth in its own time into the harvest, for the ripening of which, since there was still need of some centuries, the faithful ought not to be disturbed, as if the day of the Lord were already pressing; which could not be so clear to the Ancients before the event, therefore it is no wonder that Chrysostom and Theophylact understand Nero, whom however they make a type and figure of the Antichrist, with this difference, that the Antichrist will act more covertly than Nero; just as it is also clear from Theodoret that there were those who said that Nero was called the mystery of iniquity, as one who was an artificer of impiety; which some of the ancients also believed to be the Antichrist himself, such as Victorinus in Apoc. XVII, Severus Sulpitius l. II. histor., and certain ones in Augustine book XX. de Civit. Dei cap. 19, and Jerome in Dan. XI, which Baronius reckons among monstrous errors at the year of Christ 70, n. 3. But no one ever dreamed of Gaius in this place: all interpreted Paul as speaking of the Antichrist.

Chrysostom has it thus: He speaks of Nero here as bearing the type of the Antichrist. For he wanted to be reputed as God. And yet he said mystery, that is, he does not do this openly, as he is about to do, nor with such a brazen face and impudently. To which Bellarmine, Cornelius à Lapide, and others accede. But chronology contradicts this. For the epistle was written while Claudius was emperor, not Nero. How then could the Apostle have said that the mystery was already being performed in his own time, when he was writing these things? Nor does that overly crude affectation of divinity fit the word mystery. Furthermore, this mystery is attributed to the Antichrist, not to the type of the Antichrist. The discourse is about the same subject, not about different ones. About one sitting in the Church, such as Nero was not. Rightly, therefore, does Guilhelmus Estius reject this sense: This entire commentary about Nero, although it has these and other authors, is overturned by the observation of the time in which Paul wrote this epistle, just as it was subtly observed by Cardinal Baronius at the year of the Lord 70, and can easily be gathered from those things which we have said in the argument of both epistles. For this epistle was not written under the Prince Nero, so that the saying of the Apostle, the mystery of iniquity is already working, could be understood of him, but about three years before his empire, while Claudius was still reigning. Although not even in the first years of his empire did Nero conduct himself in such a way that this sentence of the Apostle could be verified of him. Theodoret rejected it long ago: Some have said that Nero was called the mystery of iniquity, as one who was an artificer of impiety. But I think that the Apostle signifies the heresies which have arisen. For through them, many having been led away from the truth, the Devil prepares the destruction of deception. He called them the mystery of iniquity, as those who had the snare of iniquity concealed. For he himself openly leads men away from God. Which interpretation of Theodoret is approved by most of our people and the Reformed. He touched upon the matter better, says Crocius, than the others. For the heresies of Simon, Cerinthus, and others pertain entirely to this, not absolutely, but as the seed of that horrendous monster to be brought to light in its own time, as the foundation of the huge mass which Satan was contriving. Indeed, the Apostle notes Anti-Christianism itself, the seeds of which the Devil was scattering and the foundations of which he was laying. For although he does not say by whom it is performed, there is no doubt, however, that it was performed by the same one from whose efficacy he says the coming of the Anti-Christ is, v. 9. A mystery on account of the secret contrivance, not noticed by all, being indeed disguised not openly but secretly with the appearance of holiness and the title of piety. With which Estius agrees: I answer that the mystery of iniquity is understood as secret and latent iniquity, which is at some time to be brought into public and to rage openly, namely through him whom he calls shortly after that wicked one. But this mystery was already being acted out even then in the time of the Apostles through the forerunners of that wicked one, the heretical seducers of men, so that the sense of Paul is, although the Anti-Christ has not yet come in person, yet he is already present in his emissaries and precursors. For his iniquity, of which I have spoken, is now being carried out secretly, as if in a mystery, and is exercised through heretics. That iniquity is to oppose Christ and his kingdom with all one's might, and in imitation of the Devil to seize his divinity for oneself. To this business the heretics of all ages are subservient, while under the pretext of Christ's name they oppose Christ and his Church, and pave the way for the Anti-Christ to his manifest impiety. Theodoret and Gaignaeus favor this interpretation, but it is confirmed most of all by the doctrine of the Apostle John concerning the Anti-Christ and his heretical precursors, whom he also calls by name, together with their common Prince, Anti-Christs, that is, adversaries of Christ. Little children, he says in chapter III of his first epistle, it is the last hour: And as you have heard that the Anti-Christ comes, now many Anti-Christs have been made. And in chapter IV, every spirit that dissolves Jesus is not of God, and this is the Anti-Christ, of whom you have heard that he comes, and now he is already in the world. In both places it is clearly signified what Paul said more obscurely here, namely, that the Anti-Christ would indeed come and be revealed in his own time, just as the faithful had been taught, but that he was already present then in his precursors, through whom the mystery of his iniquity was being carried out, to be openly manifested in his person at some future time. To this also pertains that statement of the same Apostle John, that many false prophets and many seducers have gone out into the world, 1 Epist. IV, and in the II epistle, as if he were saying with Paul: These are they through whom the mystery of iniquity is now being carried out.

3. Therefore, as for those words μόνον ὁ κατέχων ἄρτι ἕως ἐκ μέσου γένηται, no one has ever understood them as referring to Lucius Vitellius departing from Judea so that Petronius might have his successor; almost everyone agrees that they understood them as referring to the Roman Empire, which was to endure for some time yet, which still restrained the Anti-Christ, and from whose ruins the mystery of iniquity would later openly erupt. See Tertullian, On the Resurrection, c. 24; Jerome to Algasia; Augustine, in the cited book; Chrysostom, Theophylact, and Oecumenius on this passage. This fits the Roman Anti-Christ perfectly, whose authority grew only from the ruin of the empire, as history testifies. Grotius thinks that Gaius dared to change nothing in Judea for fear of Vitellius. But Vitellius himself was not so great that he should be feared, nor was he so opposed to the impiety of Gaius, to whom, while he was still acting in Syria, Petronius was sent as a successor, and of whom Suetonius speaks in the life of his son, c. II. The same man, he says, of a wonderful talent for flattery, was the first to institute that Gaius Caesar be worshipped as a God. And whom, I ask, will one convince that τὸ ἐκ μέσου γίνεσθαι, to be made or taken from the midst, means to be recalled from a province and to receive a successor, when everyone understands that it means to be abolished and destroyed, which in no way fits Vitellius, as he by no means held that province until his death? Calvin refers these things to the Anti-Christ himself, and resolves the participle ὁ κατέχων into the future tense, so that it might be added for the consolation of the faithful that he is to be taken from the midst. But Crocius rightly refutes this. Yet, he says, the kingdom of the Anti-Christ and his end are described only in the following verse, nor is it probable that the end is indicated before the revelation. Secondly, he had said τὸ κατέχον οἴδατε, here he says ὁ κατέχων, without doubt about the same thing. But in the preceding verse it is not fitting to understand the Anti-Christ or his kingdom by τὸ κατέχον. Therefore, neither here. Crocius therefore retains the interpretation of the ancients concerning the Roman Empire, along with Lombard, Hugo, Thomas, Bullinger, Hyperius, and the Dutch, to whom our own people also agree. William Estius does not wish to admit it, but rather confesses that he is ignorant of τὸ κατέχον, v. 6. But in this place he invents another sense for the word κατέχων than what it signifies there, namely to detain or delay, which is to hold: In this way: The mystery of iniquity is now being carried out, to erupt someday into open apostasy. Meanwhile, however, while it is being carried out, whoever holds Christ and his true religion, let him hold firmly, until the apostasy of which I spoke above is made from the midst of the Church, that is, that great falling away by which kingdoms and peoples will recede from the Church. But Cornelius a Lapide has refuted that interpretation in Augustine himself. Truly, he says, this sense tears apart the words which Paul joins together. For Paul joins 'to be made from the midst' with that which is immediately preceding, 'he who holds, let him hold.' Therefore, both must be referred to the same thing. St. Augustine, however, refers 'he who holds, let him hold' to the pious faithful and to the faith of Christ. But he refers 'to be made from the midst' to the Anti-Christ and the assembly of the impious. It must be noted, therefore, that these words depend on the preceding verse and explain what it is that detains the coming of the Anti-Christ, namely, that Nero and the Roman Emperors hold the empire until it is overturned and taken from the midst. Thus Chrysostom, Theophylact, and the Fathers generally, as I have said, indeed Erasmus and Beza. Whence the Syrian here translates 'only' (namely, this is what detains the coming of the Anti-Christ) 'that he who now detains (the empire of the world) may be taken from the midst, and then that wicked Anti-Christ will be revealed.' The Greek words are thus: Μόνον ὁ κατέχων ἄρτι ἕως ἐκ μέσου γένηται, that is, 'only he who detains now, until he is made from the midst.' Where necessarily either is missing or is to be understood (as Erasmus and Beza confess) κατεχέτω, that is, 'let him detain,' as our author translates. This is Cornelius a Lapide. The Apostle therefore says that the majesty of the Roman Empire, which stands in the way so that that son of perdition might not emerge and occupy the kingdom, will henceforth perish, until it has been taken from the midst, not as to the name, but in reality. For he does not say, 'until his name is taken away,' but 'until he is taken away,' namely, as to the thing itself. So it happened. The majesty of the old Roman Empire and the power of the Caesars stood in the way so that Anti-Christian iniquity might not erupt among Christians. But when the majesty of the empire was torn apart by the Saracens and Mahometans in the East, and by other barbarian peoples in the West, iniquity began to erupt little by little. If the Roman infidels had known that it was believed by Christians, they would undoubtedly have been more exacerbated. For they were persuaded that it would be an eternal kingdom. Although indeed the holy Apostle did not fear for himself, inasmuch as he was prepared to die for Christ, he nevertheless wished to hint at the witness, not to write more openly, lest he should stir up unnecessary enmities and expose the Church to more serious dangers, as Crocius does here. And afterwards p. 320. Desolation is referred either to the Majesty or to the name. Paul did not predict concerning the name, but concerning the thing itself or the Majesty. Let him who contends concerning the abolition of the name prove it from the Apostle; we adhere to his words, we are not moved by the gloss of men. He predicts that that which stood in the way, preventing the Antichrist from breaking forth, would be taken away. Did the name stand in the way? Nay, the majesty and power and the fear of it. That the majesty and power of the Roman empire have long since collapsed is evident from the thing itself and from witnesses. Where you should remember that the Apostle is speaking of the ancient Roman empire, which was flourishing in his own time. Count the provinces which were then subject to Rome. Africa, Asia, Macedonia, Armenia, Egypt, Gaul, Spain were obedient. Do they still obey? Rome was the part and head of the Roman empire. Today it is not a part. It has therefore perished. Nor has the name remained to the Romans, but it has been transferred to the Germans. We have Papists as witnesses: Faber Stapulensis on 2 Thess. II. Where, he says, I ask, is the monarchy now? Where is he who holds the reins of the world in it? Since we also see the head of the monarchy failing from it. To which I beseech you, does Rome offer obedience to its King, to its Monarch? And at what times could a greater defection have appeared? Salmero on 2 Thess. II: That Roman Empire has long since been overturned, and dissipated into many kingdoms, and as it were extinguished. For he who now is, and is called the Roman Emperor, is a very thin shadow of the ancient empire, to such an extent that he does not even possess the city of Rome itself, from which he is named, and for many years the Roman Emperors have failed. Baronius at the year 476, n. 1: The Eastern empire has completely collapsed and devolved to the barbarians. From the same time, he says on p. 325, when the old empire failed, the Pontiff established himself, turning the fall of the empire to his own advantage. Under Maurice, Gregory I disapproved of the title of universal Bishop, as a mark of the imminent Antichrist. But his successor Boniface III. obtained it from the parricide Phocas, from which time he began to establish an Ecclesiastical monarchy, and gradually sought temporal dominion. The Emperor indeed still had Exarchs for some time in Ravenna in Italy; but the authority was gradually diminished, until Stephen II shook off the Exarchate of Italy from the Greek Emperors through Pepin, and Leo III snatched away the Empire of the whole West through Charlemagne. See Bullinger in Comment. on this passage, Foxe in Apocalypse. This fits the Roman empire best, says Maresius, with respect to the Anti-Christ, which, since it retarded Anti-Christianism with its splendor and authority, had to finally depart from its place, be broken, and be changed, and submit its fasces to him, as the lean cows devouring the fat and plump ones, as in Pharaoh's dream. Flacius in the gloss to v. 7. He who hinders or restrains, signifies that the Roman Emperor or the empire, then still flourishing, hindered him, so that he could not seize such great power. When that shall have been removed, then the Anti-Christ will emerge, which experience itself will prove. He who hinders, therefore, understand: he will still hinder. For such repetitions are customary for the Apostle. From this, however, it can be understood at the same time that, just as the hinderer himself, although he is named under the person of one man, nevertheless was not one man, but the whole empire: so also the Anti-Christ is that whole body of that Babylonian abomination or tyranny. Furthermore, from this it appears that that kingdom of the Anti-Christ will be long-lasting, not for the age of one man only. This verse ought not to be excluded here by a parenthesis. Until he shall have been taken out of the way, that is, until the Roman Emperor shall have been both weakened and, without doubt, removed from Constantinople, with his seat of empire and government: so that at last the Pope could reign at his own discretion and bear both swords. He predicts, therefore, here that, with the Roman empire removed, that monarchy of impiety is to follow, having occupied the citadel or seat of the Roman empire, and also in some part its power and wealth. B. Balduinus summarizes the history here epitomically on p. 1210: The majesty of the Roman empire stood in the way of the Pope's Tyranny, since no one submitted himself as long as the fear of it existed: Meanwhile, it was working its own secrets in hidden places, and even then, in the time of the Apostle, the mystery of iniquity was working: because then the foundations of Papistic dogmas were being laid by Pseudo-Apostles, in the article on justification, on marriage, fasting, and similar things, as is evident from Gal. II & III, Phil. III, Col. II, 1 Cor. VII. And thus, little by little, the kingdom of the Anti-Christ was propagated, and after some centuries finally placed itself in the citadel of the city of Rome, and in the seat of the Roman Pontiffs, when the terror of the Roman empire was somewhat diminished. This happened first of all around the second century of Christ, as Victor cut off from communion those Greeks dissenting from the Latins regarding the day of Easter, to whom Irenaeus opposed himself, as witnessed by Eusebius, book V, ch. 24; afterwards Stephen I threatened the thunderbolt of excommunication against all the Doctors of Cilicia, Cappadocia, and Galatia. Zosimus, Boniface, Celestine, through falsified canons of the Nicene council, attempted to extort the primacy; around the fifth century the Roman Popes invaded superiority among all Bishops; but because the power of the Roman empire had not yet been diminished, they were therefore repeatedly repressed, and there were two humble Bishops of Rome, Pelagius III and Gregory M. who affected no dominion, and rebuked those who wished to do this. Finally, after the death of Gregory M., around the year of the Lord 606, Boniface III boldly usurped the title of Oecumenical Bishop, helped by the Caesaricide Phocas, whom he confirmed in the empire, which he had obtained through crime, around the year of Christ 606, and in turn obtained from him the title of Oecumenical Bishop. But that Boniface was an Anti-Christ still an infant, recently emerged from the womb, whose limbs had not yet hardened for battle, so that he might force Emperors and Princes into his obedience: for at that time the Roman Popes did not yet have the fullness of power in temporal matters. For until the seventh century of Christ they were forced to obey the Emperors, and Benedict II was the first who was created Pontiff without the Emperor around the year 684, with Constantine Pogonatus granting him this privilege. On which occasion the Pontiffs began proudly to use both the temporal and spiritual sword, and subjected the highest heads of the empire to their power, which began to happen around the times of the Emperor Henry IV, and was afterwards continued with great effort. After the forces of the empire were more and more diminished, and its highest heads, demented by the superstitions of that century, submitted their fasces before this idol.

Latin:

Vers. 7. Τὸ γὰρ μυστήριον ἤδη ἐνεργεῖται τῆς ἀνομίας) Jam arcanae impietatis istius motiones ponuntur, per Helico- nem nempe & Aegyptios alios. Μυστήριον vocatur, quicquid arcanum est: τὸ ἀγνοόμενον interprete Chrysostomo. Sic Esaiae XXIV. 17. רָז quod arcanum significat, Theodo- tion vertit μυστήριον, quae vox & in Danielis versione est aliquoties. Vocantur hoc nomine Regum arcana Tob. XII. 6. & aliorum, Sirac. XXII. 24. XXVII. 16. 17. 21. 2. Maccab. XIII. 21. Dicitur hoc μυστήριον ἀνομίας, quia ad impietatem pertinet, quae חָמָס Ebraeis ἀνομία alibi, ali- bi ἀσέβεια Graecis Ebraea vertentibus. Ἐνεργεῖται sumam hic passive, id est, cuditur. Sic sumitur 2. Cor. I. 6. 2. Cor. IV. 12. Hesychius: Ἐνεργεῖται κατασκευάζεται.

Μόνον ὁ κατέχων ἄρτι ἕως ἐκ μέσυ γένηται) Est hic ἐλ- λειψις vocis expectandum. Et construi debuit ἕως ὁ κατέ- χων ἄρτι γένηται ἐκ μέσυ, donec amoveatur, nempe a pro- vincia, is, qui hactenus moratur: Illud nempe consilium: Ἐκ μέσε γενέσθαι non tantum dicitur de iis, quæ inter- eunt, verum etiam de iis, quæ amoventur, præsertim quæ antea impedimento fuere, ut ἐξαρθῇ ἐκ μέσε, 1. Cor. V. 2. Sic habes & Esaiæ LVII. 2. In Græco ἦρται ἐκ τῦ μέσε; Etiam Demosthenes sic dixit, ἐκ μέσε ἀνελεῖν.

His gemella sunt, quæ tradiderat in commen- tatione ad hunc locum:

Vers. 7. Τὸ γὰρ μυσήριον ἤδη ἐνεργεῖται τῆς ἀνομίας) Nam mysterium jam operatur iniquitatis. Jam in ar- cano impietas ista se præparat, nimirum id jam sua- dente Helicone, atque aliis Ægyptiis nebulonibus, quos describit Philo. Tale est illud Taciti: Intra Albanam villam sententia Messalini strepebat. Ostendit & quæ futura erant, & quæ in abdito jam struebantur, sibi à DEO revelata, nec de rebus se loqui post se & eos, quibus scribebat, orituris, sed quarum, causæ, quan- quam maxime latentes, nascerentur. Sic voce μυστη- ρίε significari τὸ ἀγνούμενον, quod ignoratur, ad Rom. XI. 25. & 1. Corinth. XV. 51. notat Chrysostomus. Idem in sermone secundo de eleemosyna his verbis de Imperatorum aliquo agi recte sentit, in tantum de- cipitur, quod pro Cajo accipiat Neronem.

Mόνον ὁ κατέχων ἄρτι ἕως ἐκ μέσυ γένηται) Tan- tum ut qui tenet, nunc teneat, donec de medio fiat. Non longius differetur malum, quam donec Lucius Vitellius, qui nunc Syriam & cum ea Judæam tenet, inde discesserit, successoremque acceperit. Cajus ut no- tat Philo σφόδρα τὺς ἐν ἡγεμονίαις ὐυλαβεῖτο, τὰς πρὸς νεωτεροποιίαν ἀφορμὰς ἀφαιρῶν ἔχοντας ἐν ἑτοίμῳ, καὶ μάλισα τὺς ἐν μεγάλαις καὶ μεγάλοις ἐπιτάττοντας στρα- τοπέδοις, ἡλίκα τὰ πρὸς Ἐυφράτῃ κατὰ Συρίαν ἐσίν : mul- tum metuebat eos, qui in provinciis erant, ac ob id ad res novas multas habebant opportunitates, præci- pue vero eos, qui & in magnis erant provinciis, & magnis exercitibus præerant, quales sunt Syriaci ad Euphratem. Vitellius autem, ut Dionis loquar verbis, erat, ὕτε ἀγενὴς, ὕτε ἄφρων, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἐκ τῆς ἐν τῇ Συ- ρίᾳ ἀρχῆς ὀνομασὸς γενόμενος. Τάτε γὰρ ἄλλα λαμπρῶς ἡγεμόνευσε, καὶ τὸν ᾿Αρτάβανον καὶ ἐκείνῃ ἐπιβυλεύοντα κα- τέπληξε, neque degener, neque stultus, quin & ma- gnum nomen ex provincia Syria sibi pepererat, & mul- tis aliis rebus egregie administratis, & cæso Artabane, qui Syriæ imminebat, & quæ ibi sunt plura. Tacitus de eo: Regendis provinciis virtute prisca. Hujus Vi- tellii imperio Pontius Pilatus Romam iverat, ταῖς ἐτελῖε πειθόμενος ἐντολαῖς, ὐκ ὄν ἀντειπεῖν, parens Vitellii jussis, quibus contra ire non licebat, ait Jose- phus XVIII. Erat præterea Vitellius favens Judæis, ut apparet ex remissis vectigalibus, & stola Pontificali sacerdotibus in custodiam data, quæ facta ab eo ait Jo- sephus ἐπὶ ἐυεργεσίᾳ τῦ ἔθνες, ut beneficiis sibi gen- tem obstringeret. Quare non mirum, si viro tali eam provinciam obtinente nihil ibi novare ausus est Cajus.

Primum hic de mysterio iniquitatis dispicien- dum. Mysterii voce Grotius arcanum tantum no- tari vult. Sed ea in Scripturis plus continet, quam merum arcanum, estque nomen religiosum & sacrum, Matth. XIII. 11. (quo loco conferen- da Grotii annotata) Marci IV. 2. Luc. VIII. 10. 1. Cor. IV. 1. cap. XV. 51. 1. Tim. III. 16. ubi my- sterium pietatis dicitur: Φανέρωσις Θεῦ ἐν σαρκὶ, quæ certe non desiit esse mysterium ex quo ma- nifestata nobis est, non amplius occulta manet; Ita Dan. II. 18. 19. 27. cap. IV. 6. Apoc. I. 19. cap. XVII. 9. mysteria sunt, quæ sacram & mysti- cam significationem habent. Mysterii ergo no- men, quum religiosum quid & sacrum inferat, optimo jure Antichristo hic adhibetur, non tan- tum ut mysterio pietatis in adventu Christi 1. Tim. III, 15. opponatur mysterium iniquitatis in reve- latione Anti-Christi appariturum, sed etiam quia clam serpere cœpit, & prætextu mysterio- rum religionis successit hoc mysterium, ut è Pontificalibus, Ritualibus, Ceremonialibus pa- pisticis abunde constat. Levissimas etiam & in- fulsissimas nænias ceu sublimia commendat my- steria. Nec inconveniens huic rei est, quod Cor- nelius à Lapide mysterium iniquitatis dicit esse iniquitatem, arcanum & mysticam, id est pietatis & legitimi dominii ac imperii titulo palliatam. Quæ nullatenus in Caji consilium, optime autem in Papatus Romani ortum quadrant, ejusque natu- ram exhibent, qui sub pietatis prætextu, & legi- timi dominii titulo ad ἀκμὴν potentiæ suæ perve- nit. Glossa ordinaria hoc loco mysterium iniqui- tatis interpretatur iniquitatem pietatis nomine pal- liatam. Hypocrisis ergo notata voce mysterii, quod veritatis & sanctitatis specimen præ se ferre debeat homo ille peccati, qua arte omnes alios se- ductores superare Romanum Pontificem è præ- textu traditionum, ex antiquitatis & Conciliorum jactantia, è varietate rituum, è multitudine super- stitionum, & definitione & qualitate peccatorum & religionum speciosa humilitate ac sanctimonia, è disciplina, pœnitentia, satisfactionibus, flagella- tionibus, peregrinationibus, cultibus missaticis, horis Canonicis, precularum, Rosariorum, Ma- rialium formulis, & id genus aliis innumeris ad oculum patet. Conf. 1. Tim. IV. 1. 29. Apoc. XIII. 11. ubi Anti-Christus dicitur gestaturus agnina cornua, & loquuturus sicut Draco c. XVIII. 4. 5. 7. de poculo aureo, quo inebriaturus dicitur Reges mundi Spiritu fornicationis (spiritualis), & de meretri- ce, quæ gerit mysterium sanctitatis in fronte. Ca- ligula nihil unquam mystici, quod venerationem mysterii, aut divinæ cujusdam extraque ordinem divinitus sibi factæ revelationis præsumptionem præ se ferret, qui tempore imperii sui profecto nec pietatem, nec mysticam quandam cum DEO Diisve consuetudinem præ se tulit, nec tamen impietati publicæ fascinum unquam prætexere di- gnatus est. 2. Illud ἤδη ἐνεργεῖται de mysterio ini- quitatis non male quidem explicatur, jam in ar- cano impietas ista se præparat, sed inepte abripi- tur ad clancularia Heliconis & aliorum nebulonum cum Cajo convitia, qui tum in inferno jam pœnas suas patiebatur, cum hæc scriberentur, ideoque consilia agitare non poterat, neque si fingamus se- cundo anno Caji hæc scripta, illis Caji consiliis hæc conveniunt. Non enim vaticinium hic habe- retur, si ea duntaxat indicarentur, quæ jam tum in occulto fiebant. Ex adverso res non nisi longe post illa tempora eventuras hic prædixit Aposto- lus, ut constaret Thessalonicensibus, non ita pro- pe esse diem Domini; ut illis persuasum nonnulli cupiebant. Et quum Apostolus mysterium ini- quitatis conjungat cum insigni apostasia à fide, idq; tribuat illi, cujus adventus futurus in signis & pro- digiis mendacibus, ac jam tum dicatur peragi, quomodo ad Caji, Heliconisque cum eo consilia clancularia hoc referetur? Syrus innuit, jam tum efficax fuisse tempore Pauli hoc mysterium, etsi non nisi suo tempore post revelandum. Quomodo id Caji consilio potest convenire, quod tum adhuc latens fuit & immaturum, necdum plene conco- ctum secundum Grotium? Illud ἐνεργεῖται passive intelligendum, quod jam tum clanculum peragi ac serpere cœperit non in consilio, sed per occultas Satanæ machinationes, & subnascentes hæreses, sicut ignis, Cornelio à Lapide dicente, inter ligna vim suam occulte exerit, & vicina adurit, sensimq; proserpit, donec in flammam & incendium erum- pat. Innuit ita & in semine esse mysterium illud iniquitatis & suo tempore proditurum in messem, cui maturandæ cum adhuc aliquot seculis opus esset, non debere fideles conturbari, ac si instaret jam dies Domini; quod ante eventum ita con- stare non potuit Veteribus, ideo non mirum, Chrysostomum & Theophylactum Neronem intelli- gere, quem tamen typum & figuram Anti-Christi faciunt, cum hoc discrimine, quod Anti-Chri- stus tectius acturus sit Nerone; quemadmodum etiam ex Theodoreto constat, fuisse, qui dixerint Neronem esse vocatum mysterium iniquitatis, ut qui fuerit impietatis artifex; quem Anti-Chri- stum ipsum fuisse etiam nonnulli veterum credi- dere, utpote Victorinus in Apoc. XVII. Severus Sulpitius l. II. histor. & quidam apud Augustinum libr. XX. de Civit. Dei cap. 19. & Hieronymum in Dan. XI. quod portentosis erroribus accenset Ba- ronius ad ann. Christi 70. n. 3. Gajum vero nemo unquam hoc loco somniavit: De Anti-Christo omnes Paulum interpretati sunt.

Chrysostomus ita habet: Neronem hic dicit tan- quam typum Anti-Christi gerentem. Nam ille vo- lebat reputari Deus. Et tamen dixit mysterium, hoc est, non aperte hoc agit, sicut ille acturus est, neque adeo perfricta fronte & impudenter. Cui Bel- larminus, Cornelius à Lapide aliique accedunt. Sed repugnat chronologia. Scripta enim est epi- stola Claudio imperante, non Nerone. Quomodo ergo dixisset Apostolus, jam peragi mysterium suo tempore, quum hæc scriberet? Neque voci mysterii convenit illa nimis crassa divinitatis affe- ctatio. Adhæc Anti-Christo hoc mysterium tri- buitur, non typo Anti-Christi. De eodem subje- cto sermo est, non de diversis. De sedente in Ec- clesia, qualis non erat Nero. Merito itaque reje- cit hunc sensum Guilhelmus Estius: Universus hic de Nerone commentarius, quamvis hos aliosque au- tores habeat, evertitur observatione temporis, quo Paulus hanc epistolam scripsit, quemadmodum sub- tiliter animadversum est à Cardinale Baronio ad annum Domini 70. & facile colligi potest ex iis, quæ nos in argumento utriusque epistolæ diximus. Non enim sub Nerone Principe scripta est hæc epi- stola, ut de illo dictum intelligi possit, mysterium jam operatur iniquitatis, sed ante ejus imperium annis circiter tribus, Claudio adhuc regnante. Quan- quam nec primis imperii sui annis Nero ita se gessit, ut de eo verificari possit hæc Apostoli sententia. Re- jecit jam pridem Theodoretus: Nonnulli dixerunt, Neronem esse vocatum iniquitatis mysterium, ut qui fuerit impietatis artifex. Ego autem existimo, Apostolum significare hæreses, quæ exortæ sunt. Per illas enim multis à veritate abductis præparat Dia- bolus exitium deceptionis. Eos autem appellavit my- sterium iniquitatis, ut qui habêrent celatum ini- quitatis laqueum. Ipse enim aperte à Deo abducit homines. Quæ Theodoreti interpretatio plerisque nostratium & Reformatorum probata. Rem me- lius tetigit, inquit Crocius, quam cæteri. Hæreses enim Simonis, Cerinthi, aliorum huc omnino perti- nent, non absolute, sed ut semen horrendi illius mon- stri suo tempore in lucem edendi, ut fundamentum ingentis molis, quam moliebatur Satanas. Nempe notat Apostolus ipsum Anti-Christianismum, cujus semina spargebat & jaciebat fundamenta Diabo- lus. Etsi enim non dicat, à quo peragatur, dubium tamen non est, ab eodem peractum esse, ex cujus efficacia adventum esse dicit Anti-Christi v. 9. my- sterium propter molitionem occultam, non omnibus animadversam, fucatam quippe non aperte sed oc- culte specie sanctitatis atque titulo pietatis. Cui con- sonat Estius: Respondeo mysterium iniquitatis in- telligi iniquitatem arcanam & latentem, quæ ali- quando sit in publicum proferenda & palam gras- satura, nimirum per eum, quem paulo post vocat illum iniquum. Agebatur autem hoc mysterium jam tum Apostolorum tempore per illius iniqui præ- cursores, hominum seductores hæreticos, ut sensus Pauli sit, etsi nondum venerit Anti-Christus in per- sona, jam tamen adest in emissariis ac præcursoribus suis. Nam iniquitas ejus, de qua loquutus sum, nunc occulte, velut in mysterio, agitur, & exercetur per hæreticos. Ea iniquitas est Christum & regnum ejus totis viribus oppugnare, atque ad imitationem Diaboli divinitatem illius ad se rapere. Cui negotio subserviunt omnium seculorum hæretici, dum prætenso Christi nomine Christum & Ecclesiam ejus oppugnantes, Anti-Christo ad manifestariam ejus impietatem viam sternunt. Favent huic interpretationi Theodoretus & Gaignæus, sed eam confirmat maxime Johannis Apostoli doctrina de Anti-Christo, & ejus prænunciis hæreticis, quos etiam nomine cum suo Principe communi Anti-Christos vocat, id est Christi adversarios. Filioli, inquit cap. III. epistolæ prioris, novissima hora est: Et sicut audivistis, quia Anti-Christus venit, nunc Anti-Christi multi sunt facti. Et cap. IV. omnis Spiritus, qui solvit Jesum, ex Deo non est, & hic est Anti-Christus, de quo audivistis, quoniam venit, & nunc jam in mundo est. Quo utroque loco clare significatur id, quod Paulus hic dixit obscurius, scil. Anti-Christum venturum quidem, ac revelandum suo tempore, sicut edocti erant fideles, sed jam tum adfuisse eum in suis præcursoribus, per quos agebatur mysterium iniquitatis ejus, olim in persona palam manifestandæ. Quo pertinet etiam illud ejusdem Johannis Apostoli, quoniam multi Pseudo-Prophetæ & multi seductores exierunt in mundum 1. epist. IV. & in II. epistola, quasi cum Paulo dicat: Hi sunt, per quos nunc agitur iniquitatis mysterium.

3. Quod ergo ad illa μόνον ὁ κατέχων ἄρτι ἕως ἐκ μέσου γένηται, nemo unquam de Lucio Vitellio intellexit discessuro è Judæa, ut successorem habeat Petronium, omnes fere consentiunt de Romano imperio aliquandiu adhuc duraturo, quod continuerit adhuc Anti-Christum, è cujus ruinis postea palam erupturum sit mysterium iniquitatis, acceperunt. Vid. Tertullianus de resurrectione c. 24. Hieronymus ad Algasiam, Augustinus l. cit. Chrysostomus, Theophylactus, Oecumenius ad hunc locum. Quod apprime convenit Antichristo Romano, cujus autoritas non nisi ex ruina imperii accrevit, teste historia. Putat Grotius, Vitellii metu Cajum nihil ausum fuisse in Judæa novare. Sed nec tantus ipse Vitellius erat, ut eum metueret, nec adeo adversus fuit Caji impietati, cui adhuc in Syria agenti successor missus est Petronius, & de quo Suetonius agens in vita filii ejus c. II. Idem, inquit, miri adulando ingenii primus C. Cæsarem adorari ut Deum instituit. Et cui, obsecro, persuadebitur, τὸ ἐκ μέσου γίνεσθαι, ex medio fieri aut tolli, esse ex provincia revocari, & successorem accipere, quum nemo non intelligat, id esse aboleri & interimi, quod nullatenus Vitellio convenit, utpote qui nequaquam provinciam illam usque ad mortem retinuit. Calvinus refert hæc ad Anti-Christum ipsum, & participium ὁ κατέχων in futurum tempus resolvit, ut in consolationem fidelium additum sit, eum è medio tollendum. Sed id merito refellit Crocius. Atqui, inquit, primo sequente versu demum regnum Anti-Christi ejusque finis describitur, nec quidem probabile est, finem indicari ante revelationem. Secundo dixerat τὸ κατέχον οἴδατε, hic dicit ὁ κατέχων sine dubio de re eadem. Atqui versu præcedente per τὸ κατέχον Anti-Christum vel ejus regnum intelligere non convenit. Ergo nec hic. Crocius ergo veterum interpretationem de Romano imperio retinet cum Lombardo, Hugone, Thoma, Bullingero, Hyperio, Belgis, quibus etiam nostrates annuunt. Guilielmus Estius non vult admittere, sed fatetur potius, se ignorare τὸ κατέχον, v. 6. Hoc vero loco alium vocis κατέχων, quam il- lic significare detinere seu remorari agnovit, sen- sum fingit, quod scil. sit tenere: Hoc modo: My- sterium iniquitatis nunc agitur, erupturum aliquan- do in apertam apostasiam. Interim vero dum agi- tur, quicunque tenet Christum & veram ejus religio- nem, firmiter retineat, donec de medio Ecclesia fiat apostasia, de qua supra loquutus sum, id est, magna illa defectio, qua regna & populi ab Ecclesia recedent. Sed illam interpretationem profligavit Cornelius a Lapide in ipso Augustino. Verum, inquit, hic sen- sus divellit verba, quæ Paulus conjungit. Tò enim de medio fiat conjungit Paulus cum eo, quod præ- proxime, qui tenet, teneat. Utrumque ergo eodem referendum est. S. Augustinus autem τό qui tenet teneat refert ad pios fideles, & ad fidem Christi. Tò vero de medio fiat refert ad Anti-Christum & cœ- tum impiorum. Notandum ergo hæc verba pendere à versu præcedenti, & explicare quid sit, quod deti- neat adventum Anti-Christi, scil. ut Nero & Romani Imperatores teneant imperium donec illud everta- tur & è medio tollatur. Ita Chrysostomus, Theophy- lactus, & passim Patres, ut dixi, imo Erasmus & Be- za. Unde Syrus hic vertit solum, (scil. hoc est quod detinet adventum Anti-Christi) ut qui nunc detinet (orbis imperium) tollatur de medio, & tunc reve- labitur ille iniquus Anti-Christus. Græca sic habent: Μόνον ὁ κατέχων ἄρτι ἕως ἐκ μέσυ γένηται, id est, tantum qui detinet nunc, donec de medio fiat. Ubi necessario vel deest vel subauditur, (ut fatentur Erasmus & Beza) κατεχέτω, id est, detineat, ut ver- tit Noster. Hæc Cornelius à Lapide. Dicit igitur Apostolus majestatem imperii Romani, quæ obstet, quo minus filius ille perditionis emergat, regnumque occupet, deinceps oblituram esse, donec è medio sub- lata fuerit non quoad nomen sed reipsa. Non enim ait, donec nomen ejus tollatur, sed donec tolla- tur, scilicet quoad rem ipsam. Sic factum. Ve- teris imperii Romani majestas & Cæsarum po- tentia obstitit, ne Anti-Christiana inter Christianos erumperet iniquitas. Verum cum à Saracenis & Mahumetanis in Oriente, & ab aliis barbaris popu- lis in Occidente imperii majestas convelleretur, ini- quitas erumpere paulatim cœpit. Si cognovissent in- fideles Romani à Christianis credi, sine dubio magis exacerbati fuissent. Æternum enim regnum fore persuasi erant. Etsi vero sanctus Apostolus sibi non metueret, quippe qui paratus esset pro Christo mori, teste tamen voluit innuere, non apertius scribere, ne inimicitias non necessarias excitaret, atque Ecclesiam gravioribus periculis objiceret, ut hic Crocius. Et postmodum p. 320. Desolatio refertur vel ad Ma- jestatem, vel ad nomen. De nomine non prædixit Pau- lus, sed de reipsa seu Majestate. De abolitione nomi- nis qui contendit, probet ex Apostolo, illius verbis inhæremus, non movemur hominum glossa. Illud sub- latum iri prædicit, quod obstabat, quo minus Anti- Christus erumperet. Num obstabat nomen? Imo ma- jestas & potentia ejusque metus. Majestatem & po- tentiam imperii Romani jampridem collapsam esse, patet à reipsa & testibus. Ubi memineris, Aposto- lum loqui de veteri Romano imperio, quod ipsius tempore florebat. Numera provincias, quæ tum erant Romæ obnoxiæ. Africa, Asia, Macedonia, Armenia, Ægyptus, Gallia, Hispania parebant. Num adhuc parent? Imperii Romani pars & caput erat Roma. Hodie non est pars. Interiit igitur. Nec nomen Ro- manis mansit, sed ad Germanos translatum est. Testes habemus Papistas: Faber Stapulensis in 2. Thessal. II. Ubi, inquit, nunc quæso monarchia? Ubi qui in ea mundi regit habenas? Cum & vi- deamus monarchiæ caput ab ea deficere. Quam obsecro Roma suo Regi, suo Monarchae prabet obe- dientiam? Et quibus temporibus potuit major de- fectio apparere? Salmero in 2. Thessal. II. Imperium illud Romanum jampridem eversum est, & in mul- ta regna dissipatum & quasi exstinctum. Nam qui nunc est, & vocatur Imperator Romanus, tenuissi- ma quadam umbra est imperii antiqui, usque adeo ut ne ipsam quidem urbem Romam, à qua denomi- natur, possideat, & per multos annos defecerunt Imperatores Romani. Baronius ad ann. 476. n. 1. Orientale imperium penitus collapsum est & devo- lutum ad barbaros. Ex eodem tempore, inquit p. 325. quo imperium vetus defecit, stabilivit Pontifex impe- rii casum in rem suam vertens. Sub Mauritio Gre- gorius I. titulum universalis Episcopi improbabit, velut notam imminentis Antichristi. At successor ejus Bonifacius III. à parricida Phoca eam impetra- vit, à quo tempore monarchiam Ecclesiasticam sta- bilire cœpit, & paulatim dominatum temporalem quæsivit. Exarchos quidem aliquandiu adhuc ha- buit Imperator Ravennæ in Italia; Verum autoritas paulatim minuebatur, donec Stephanus II. Exar- chatum Italiæ Græcis Imperatoribus per Pipinum excussit, & Leo III. per Carolum M. totius Occi- dentis Imperium eripuit. Vid. Bullinger. in Com- ment. in h. l. Foxum in Apocal. Optime hoc, in- quit Maresius, respectu Anti-Christi convenit im- perio Romano, quod cum sui splendore & autori- tate retardaret Anti-Christianismum, debuit tan- dem de loco decedere, infringi, & immutari, & fa- sces suos illi submittere, vaccis macilentis pingues & obesas, ut in Pharaonis somnio, devorantibus. Flacius in glossa ad v. 7. Qui obstat aut continet, significat, quod Romanus Imperator aut imperium tunc adhuc florens obstiterit ei, ne tantam potentiam arripere posset. Cum illud erit sublatum, tum Anti-Christus emerget, quod experientia ipsa com- probabit. Qui obstat ergo, subintellige, obstabit adhuc. Tales n. repetitiones sunt usitatæ Apostolo. Hinc vero simul intelligi potest, quod sicut ipse obstans licet sub unius hominis persona nominetur, tamen non unus homo fuerit, sed totum imperium: Sic etiam An- ti-Christus est totum illud corpus Babylonicæ illius abominationis aut tyrannidis. Præterea hinc appa- ret, illud regnum Anti-Christi diuturnum fore, non ad unius tantum hominis ætatem. Non debet hic ver- sus per parenthesin excludi. Donec è medio sublatus fuerit, id est, donec Imperator Romanus tum debili- tatus, tum procul dubio Constantinopoli amotus fue- rit, cum sua imperii sede ac regimine: ut tandem Pa- pæ pro arbitrio regnare, & utrumque gladium gestare posset. Prædicit igitur hic, quod Romano imperio sub- lato sequutura sit ista impietatis monarchia, occupa- ta imperii Romani arce aut sede, & etiam aliqua ex parte potentia opibusque. Historiam ἐπιτομικῶς hic complectitur B. Balduinus p. 1210. Majestas imperii Romani obstitit Tyrannidi Papæ, cum nemo se sub- misit, quamdiu timor illius fuit: Interim in occulto- res suos agebat, & jam tum Apostoli tempore myste- rium iniquitatis operabatur: quia tunc Papisticorum dogmatum fundamenta ponebantur per Pseudo-Apo- stolos, in articulo de justificatione, de conjugio, jejunio & similibus, ut constat ex Gal. II. & III Phil. III. Col. II. 1. Cor. VII. Et sic paulatim Anti-Christi re- gnum propagatum est, & post aliqua demum secula se in arce urbis Romæ, & in sede Pontificum Romano- rum collocavit, cum terror imperii Romani nonnihil minueretur. Factum hoc est primum omnium circa secundum seculum Christi, ut Victor per Græcos à Latinis dissentientes circa diem paschatis à commu- nione rescidit, cui se opposuit Irenæus teste Eusebio l. V. c. 24. postea Stephanus I cunctis Ciliciæ, Cappa- dociæ, & Galatiæ Doctoribus excommunicationis fulmen minatus est. Zozimus, Bonifacius, Cœlestinus, per falsatos Niceni concilii canones primatum extor- quere conati sunt, circa seculum quintum superiori- tatem inter omnes Episcopos invaserunt Papæ Ro- mani; sed quia nondum imminuta erat potestas Ro- mani imperii, ideo subinde repressi sunt, & fuerunt duo humiles Episcopi Romæ Pelagius III. & Gregor. M. qui nullum affectarunt dominium, eosque, qui hoc facere voluerunt, reprehenderunt. Tandem post obi- tum Gregorii M. circa ann. Dom. 606. Bonifacius III. Episcopi Oecumenici titulum audacter usurpa- vit, adjutus à Phoca Cæsaricida, quem circa annum Christi 606. in imperio, quod per scelus adeptus erat, confirmavit, & ab eo vicissim œcumenici Episcopi ti- tulum obtinuit. Erat autem iste Bonifacius Anti- Christus adhuc infantulus, recens ex utero egressus, cujus membra nondum obduruerant ad pugnam, ut Imperatores & Principes sibi in obsequium cogeret: nondum enim tunc temporis habebant Papæ Romani plenitudinem potestatis in temporalibus. Nam usque ad septimum seculum Christi Imperatoribus obsequi cogebantur, & Benedictus II. fuit primus, qui absque Imperatore fuit creatus Pontifex circa ann. 684. privilegium hoc concedente ei Constantino Pogo- nato. Qua occasione utroque gladio temporali & spirituali superbe cœperunt Pontifices, summaque imperii capita potestati suæ subjecerunt, quod circa tempora Imperatoris Henrici IV. fieri cœpit, & post- ea magno cum conatu continuatum fuit. Postquam vires imperii magis magisque imminutæ, & summa ejus capita superstitionibus illius seculi dementatæ, fasces suos coram hoc idolo submiserunt.

## 2:8
V. 8. And then shall that wicked one be revealed.) Then, that is, two or three years later. For 'then' is accustomed to convert times even much more distant, as Matt. II. 7, III. 13, IV. 11, XV. 12, XVII. 10, XIX. 3, 27, XXIV. 3, 14, 30, Zephaniah III. 9, Amos IX. 11, and often elsewhere. 'Shall be revealed' is again for 'will betray himself,' 'will uncover himself,' 'the wicked one,' namely that other one, of whom I have likewise spoken to you in Syria. Thus far he has described the impious Prince, now he comes to the impious Teacher, the other temptation of the Christians, and especially of those who were from Judea. But Simon Magus is rightly called impious, who came to Rome a little after the beginning of the Claudian principate, in order to lead men away from Christ and enslave them to himself, providing a supply for all the lusts to which the Romans were addicted, in that he said that the law 'thou shalt not commit adultery' and similar ones were not from God, but from the Angels of God without command: and that men are saved by faith without righteous works. We have explained these things more broadly elsewhere from Justin, Irenaeus, Philastrius, Cyril, Theodoret, and others.

Grotius had previously proposed these assertions in his commentary in almost the same way, but more copiously.

And then.) And then. Not before that which I have said has happened will the great impostor give himself to be seen, with no less danger. 'Then' is often accustomed to be placed for the signification of a time even at some interval distant, Matt. II. 7, IV. 5, XXIV. 14, and 30, and elsewhere. Therefore that 'then' is to be understood of the beginning of the principate of Claudius, who succeeded Prince Gaius. For in the second year of Claudius, Peter went to Rome to occupy Simon Magus, as Jerome teaches us concerning ecclesiastical writers.
