They too could be saved through the Gospel, God seriously intending it, even if these things are most true according to the Word of God: These things I say to you, that you may be saved, John V. 34. He feigns that by an absolute decree, the Gospel behaves toward some ONLY preceptively, whence it happens that it tends toward their destruction. For it is to those who are perishing an odor of death unto death, 2 Cor. II. 15, 16. Toward others, to whom it becomes an odor of life, it behaves even effectively, insofar as God through it works faith in those who are his own, 2 Tim. II. 19, John VIII. 47. That God seriously intends the salvation of both through the Gospel, but of the former conditionally, of the latter absolutely. To which Grotius deservedly says: It is well said that God seriously intends the salvation of those also who are not going to believe, but conditionally. But it must be added: that an impossible condition is held as nothing. From the same source also it is that the Grotian explanation does not satisfy him, that God sends the efficacy of errors by a wise permission and direction; but he wishes it should have been added that God thus often punishes prior sins with subsequent ones, as Rom. I. 28, nor does he say that God behaves merely negatively and idly, but also positively and directively. All of which are discussed more laboriously in the disputes against the Calvinists. In this, however, he easily deserves assent, that by the words that all might be judged who did not believe the truth, it is not a matter of the conviction of malice, but it is said to refer to punishments, and the just penalty of their incredulity, and that to consent is not simply to be delighted by the allurements of pleasures, but to assent to the doctrines of the lie, and to cherish and retain them, because they are more plausible to the flesh and human wisdom, and more accommodated to increasing or preserving their fortunes and affairs, which, how much it obtains in the communion of the Papacy, there is no one who does not know, so much so that many to this very day, even with a reluctant conscience, undertake the patronage of the otherwise most desperate cause of the Anti-Christ. And these things are especially against the Grotian comments concerning Caius and Simon Magus, which I conclude with the words of Grotius, but concerning Grotius: I fear that he does violence to his own conscience who defends such incredible things. Which is not so much my opinion as that of all Doctors concerning those matters.

PART II. OF CHAPTER II. EXHORTATORY. On thanksgiving, and perseverance in the recognized truth.

Latin:

Ἵνα κριθῶσι πάντες οἱ μὴ πιστεύσαντες τῇ ἀληθείᾳ) ut judicentur omnes, qui non crediderant veritati. Ut con- vincantur suæ malitiæ. Cum enim talibus credant ho- minibus ob præstigias quasdam, cur non Christo ejus- que Apostolis potius crediderunt, qui tanta tam solida vereque divina miracula ediderunt? Vide conferentem hæc Theodoretum.

Ἀλλ' εὐδοκήσαντες ἐν τῇ ἀδικίᾳ) Sed consenserunt ini- quitati. Hæc vera causa est, cur Simoni potius, quam Christo crediderint, quod Simonis dogma commeatum ipfis faceret fruendi quibuscunque voluptatibus, etiam iniquissimis, qua de re jam egimus. Quorum actiones malæ sunt, ii tenebras falsorum dogmatum luci Evan- gelicæ præferunt, Joh. III. 18. Is vero, qui facere vult voluntatem Patris, recte de Christi dogmate judicat, Joh. VII. 17. Lactantius libr. VII. divinarum institutio- num capite I. de hominibus ejusmodi: Malunt id esse fictum, quo desideriis suis renuntiare coguntur. Item: Qui libidinum furiis incitati, ut ait Poeta, in furias ignemque ruunt, utique incredibilia nos afferre dicunt, qua illos à voluptatibus suis prohibent, quibus animam suam cum corpore adjudicaverunt. Clemens Romanus de Simone: Quidam cum essent illius pernicie digni, remanserunt in ejus disciplina.

Hæc, si demas Simonem, recte se habent, ideo immerito censura notantur à Maresio, cui non probatur, ἀγάπην τῆς ἀληθείας notare summum Dei beneficium in patefacienda veritate Evangelica, mavult significari amorem & studium veritatis (ubi tamen, si quis ἀγάπην τῆς ἀληθείας exponat amabilem veritatem, ut Eph. 1. 18. Col. 1. 27. divitiæ gloriæ, id est, dives gloria, & 2. Thessal. 1. 4. ignis flammæ, hoc est ignea flamma, non refragabimur) non probantur, quæ de voluntate antecedente ac consequente dicuntur; quod temere ac falso Socinianum dicit, & alienum à Dei immutabilitate. Contrarium Tom. II. System. Theol. ostendimus. Non probantur illa de iis, qui pereunt. Poterant & illi servari per Evangelium, serio id agente Deo, etsi verissima sint juxta Dei Verbum: Hæc dico vobis, ut salvemini, Johan. V. 34. Fingit yi absoluti decreti, erga nonnullos Evangelium se habere TANTUM præceptive, unde fit, ut vergat in eorum exitium. Est enim τοῖς ἀπολλυμένοις odor mortis ad mortem, 2. Cor. II. 15. 16. Erga alios, quibus fit odor vitæ, sese habere etiameffective, quatenus Deus per illud fidem operatur in iis, qui sui sunt, 2. Tim II. 19. Joh. VIII. 47. Utrorumque salutem Deum serio intendere per Evangelium, sed priorum conditionaliter, posteriorum absolute. Ad quæ merito Grotius: Bene dicitur Deus serio intendere salutem eorum etiam, qui credituri non sunt, sed conditionaliter. Sed addi debet: conditionem impossibilem pro nulla haberi. Ex eodem etiam fonte est, quod non satisfaciat ipsi Grotiana explicatio, quod Deus immittat efficaciam errorum sapiente permissu, & directione; sed vult adjici debuisse, sic Deum sæpe peccata priora ulcisci posterioribus, ut Rom. I. 28. nec se habere Deum mere negative ait, & otiose, sed etiam positive & directive. Quæ omnia in disputationibus adversus Calvinianos operosius excutiuntur. In eo tamen facile assensum meretur, quod verbis ἵνα κριθῶσι πάντες οἱ μὴ πιστεύσαντες τῇ ἀληθείᾳ, non de convictione malitiæ agatur, sed pœnas referre dicatur, & justum supplicium suæ incredulitatis, quodque consentire non sit simpliciter delectari voluptatum illecebris, sed mendacii doctrinis assentiri, easque fovere ac retinere, quod carni & sapientiæ humanæ sint plausibiliores, ac fortunis & rebus suis vel augendis vel conservandis magis accommodatæ, quod quantum obtineat in Papatus communione, nemo est, qui nesciat, adeo ut desperatissimæ alias Anti-Christi causæ multi in hunc usq; diem quamvis reluctante conscientia patrocinium suspiciant. Atque hæc maxime adversus Grotiana commenta de Cajo & Simone Mago, quæ verbis Grotii, sed de Grotio concludo: Metuo, ne conscientiæ suæ vim faciat, qui tam incredibilia defendit. Quæ non tam mea, quam omnium Doctorum de istis sententia.

PARS II. CAPITIS II. PARÆNETICA. Ad gratiarum actionem, & perseverantiam in veritate agnita.

## 2:13
v. 13. But we are bound to give thanks to God always for you, brethren beloved by the Lord) See above I. 3. He says that he not only gives thanks, but also that he ought to.

Lest they be too much disturbed by the prophecy concerning the calamitous state of the Church, he now asserts for the sake of consolation that thanks are owed to God for the grace shown to the Thessalonians, he exhorts to perseverance, and adds a prayer for the same. Furthermore, when he has spoken of the unbelief and love of injustice of those who perish and are condemned, he proclaims the Thessalonians, on the contrary, chosen in the sanctification of the Spirit, in the faith of the truth, with a grateful mind, and he admonishes them to persist in the acknowledged truth, and he prays for divine corroboration for them. When he had explained, says Theophylact, certain horrible things, and such as might disturb the mind of the hearer, he now softens and calms these, thus admonishing: These things are indeed a horror to others, to those, I say, who are lost, over whom the demons also have the greatest dominion, but to us, thanks are to be given to God for you, since he himself chose you and embraced you with love. But if we ourselves give thanks to God for you, you ought much more to do the same, and to render thanks to God for your own benefit.

Because God chose you from the beginning for salvation) That phrase 'from the beginning' shows that these things are written to the Jews, who are the firstfruits of those who believe, Rom. XI. 16. Eph. I. 2. 'Eἵλετο' chose, that is, separated for himself. It is treated here of that election which follows faith, as in Matt. XXII. 14. It was said to the Israelites of old: 'The Lord chose you today to be a people,' Deut. XXVI. 18. namely, for temporal benefits. But here is added 'for salvation,' namely, for eternal salvation, which is truly reserved for Christians, Coloss. I. 5. 2. Tim. IV. 8.

In sanctification of the Spirit, and faith of the truth) Here the former genitive is of the efficient cause, but the latter is of the object, as also in Philipp. I. v. 27. How did God separate them? By sanctifying them through his Spirit. See 1. Cor. I, 2. Acts XX, v. 32. XXVI. v. 18. And how is that Spirit attained? Through faith held in the Gospel.

Not to the Jews only, but especially to the Gentiles. For the greater part of the Thessalonian Church, to whom these things were written, was from the Gentiles. But that phrase 'from the beginning' does not denote the firstfruits, as the Vulgate wrongly renders it, as if it were 'ἀπαρχὰς', but from the beginning, that is, from eternity, 1. John I. 1. For election to eternal salvation was made from eternity, Eph. I. 4. which follows faith, and is in the divine 'προγνώσει' (foreknowledge). For it was made 'κατὰ πρόγνωσιν' according to the foreknowledge not of works, but of faith, through the sanctification of the Spirit, through the faith of the truth, whether you interpret it as held toward the Evangelical truth, or as true, not feigned, it is the same, provided it is conceded that it denotes not faith actually existing, but faith viewed in the divine intuition and foreknowledge. For God did not choose without the intuition of the merit of Christ, because we are said to have been chosen in Christ, Ephes. I. verse 4. and to have predestined through Christ verse 5, in whom he loved us as his beloved Son, 'ἐχαρίτωσεν ἡμᾶς ἐν τῷ ἠγαπημένῳ', verse 6. But we are not in Christ except through faith. Theophylact says that God chose us, and predestined us to salvation, inasmuch as he foreknew us to be worthy. But if he understood this concerning dignity in Christ, his righteousness being imputed through faith, it would not be to be disapproved. But in that he understands our own proper dignity, and adds that we also contributed something to our own salvation, and that for that reason the faith of the truth is added here, he is mistaken, and wanders from the truth. But election was made out of the grace of grace. But if out of grace, not out of works, Romans XI. 5. 6. He does not have this from Chrysostom, whom he otherwise follows step by step. Chrysostom handed down the contrary in this place. How to salvation? That he might sanctify us through the Spirit. For these are the things which contain our salvation; 'μηδαμῶς ἀπὸ ἔργων', nowhere, or rather by no means from works; 'μηδαμῶς ἀπὸ κατορθωμάτων', nowhere, (by no means) from right actions, 'ἀλλὰ διὰ πίστεως ἀληθείας', but through the faith of the truth. 'ἰδὲ τὸ ἐν πάλιν διά ἐστι.' Behold, the 'in' is again 'THROUGH'. And immediately after: 'Ὁρᾷς πῶς οὐδὲν αὐτῶν δείκνυσιν ὂ, ἀλλὰ τὸ πᾶν τοῦ Θεοῦ.' You see how he shows that nothing is of them, but the whole is of God. For the same reason also the sanctification of the Spirit is placed before the faith of the truth. Which the Greek scholia observed along with Chrysostom: 'Διὰ τοῦτο δὲ πρῶτον εἶπε τὸν ἁγιασμὸν τοῦ Πνεύματος, δηλῶν ὡς οὐδὲ ἐπιστεύσαμεν, εἰ μὴ ἡ χάρις τοῦ Πνεύματος ἠγίασατο.' For this reason he said the sanctification of the Spirit first, showing that we would not even have believed, if the grace of the Spirit had not sanctified us.

He proceeds from election to vocation, not that it is posterior in the order of nature, but that he may confirm the same, as having been made from eternity, by that grace which happens to them in time. For whom he predestined, them he also called; and whom he called, them he also justified; and whom he justified, them he also glorified, Rom. VIII. 30. From vocation, therefore, and justification, which glorification follows, is gathered the predestination to glory made from eternity by God. Crocius wishes vocation, the sanctification of the Spirit, and the faith of the truth to be introduced as means of divine election. But he fosters a 'ὕπουλον' (a hidden sore). For it is a 'Πρῶτον ψεῦδος' (a primary falsehood) that election is absolutely feigned without the foreknowledge of the sanctification of the Spirit and the faith of the truth, or even of the vocation to the Gospel, through which the Holy Spirit sanctifies us, by kindling in us faith first of all, by which our hearts are purified, Acts XV. 9. But those things which precede in the divine mind in a sign of reason, equally as Christ with his merit, Eph. I. 4. 5. 6. For how could he have chosen any according to Christ, since we were all concluded under sin and the wrath of God, and propitiation and redemption were made only through Christ. How could he have chosen those in whom he could have had no good pleasure, that is, who were without faith. For without faith it is impossible to please God, Heb. XI. 6. But how could anyone have had faith in Christ without the 'ἁγιασμῷ' or sanctification of the Holy Spirit through the Word and sacraments. How could he sanctify through the Word, if they were not called to the communion of the Gospel. In the divine mind, therefore, these things follow one another in a sign of reason: redemption, vocation, sanctification, which is also regeneration, and faith, and finally election, which was made according to the 'πρόγνωσιν' (foreknowledge) of faith. A decree indeed, inasmuch as it is eternal, is followed by execution, which is temporal, if we consider the moments of time, so that it may be permitted to explain these, but the decree is not prior in the order of nature and causality to those temporal things, the redemption of Christ, the calling, and the sanctification or regeneration of the Holy Spirit and faith: But these are rather prior in the order of nature to the divine decree, inasmuch as it was made according to the foreknowledge of these: Blessed Menzer, therefore, who by ἁγιασμὸν πνεύματος understands the ministry of the Gospel, is rashly attacked here by Crocius, because he points out the operation of the Holy Spirit through the ministers of the Word, for He does not operate immediately, but through the ministry: such is regeneration, inasmuch as through it faith is begotten in us. Crocius wishes these to cohere, not with the word εἵλετο, but with the phrase εἰς σωτηρίαν. But in truth, this whole thing had to be taught, how GOD chose us for salvation. The Apostle teaches this: Namely, through sanctification of the Spirit and faith in the truth. He also proves and confirms that whole thing, namely that GOD chose us through sanctification of the Spirit and faith in the truth for salvation or eternal life, who called us through the Gospel to actually attain the same, to which He had predestined us from eternity. Theophylact and the Greek scholia explain glory concerning the glory of Christ thus, that GOD called us so that He might acquire glory for His Son, but because our election to salvation had to be confirmed, more correctly concerning glory, which

Christ has obtained for us by his merit, and which we attain uniquely through Christ, or through the faith of Christ, even if there is no doubt that it contributes to the glory of Christ himself. In which sense Chrysostom says: This is not a small thing either, if Christ says that our salvation is his own glory, for it is the glory of the benevolent and merciful one (δόξα γὰρ τοῦ φιλαθρώπου) that there are many to whom salvation is given. Great is therefore our Lord. Εἰς περιποίησιν is for possessing or attaining the glory of Christ through appropriation. For we have not received eternal glory by our own merits or works, but we appropriate to ourselves the glory acquired for all men by the merits of Christ through faith. For he has called us to the glory prepared for us, to be attained in act, which is done through faith, just as Christ is about to say, possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundations of the world, Matt. XXV. verse 34. Περιποίησις is an assertion, when we claim and assert something for ourselves; in Suidas it is the possession of acquired things.

Latin:

v. 13. Ἡμεῖς δὲ ὀφείλομεν εὐχαριστεῖν τῷ Θεῷ πάντοτε περὶ ὑμῶν, ἀδελφοὶ ἠγαπημένοι ὑπὸ Κυρίου) Vide supra I. 3. Gratias non tantum se agere dicit, sed & debere.

Ne vaticinio de calamitoso Ecclesiæ statu perturbentur nimium, jam solatii causa de gratia Thessalonisensibus exhibita Deo gratias deberi, asserit, ad perseverantiam hortatur, & votum subjungit pro eadem. Porro cum de eorum, qui pereunt, & condemnantur, ἀπιστίᾳ & amore injustitiæ dixerit, Thessalonicenses contra electos in sanctificatione Spiritus, in fide veritatis grata mente deprædicat, & ut in agnita veritate persistant, mo- net, ac corroborationem divinam ipsis precatur. Cum horribilia quædam, inquit Theophylactus, ex- plicasset, & quæ possint auditoris animum conturba- re, nunc horum lenit & cords, ita commonefaciens: Sunt quidem aliis ista horrori, his, inquam, qui per- diti sunt, in quos & plurimum habent Dæmones ditionis, nobis vero gratiæ sunt Deo pro vobis agen- dæ, quandoquidem vos ipse elegerit, & charitate complexus sit. Si vero ipsi pro vobis Deo habemus gratias, longe magis idipsum faclitare debetis, & in proprium commodum Deo grates referre.

Ὅτι εἵλετο ὑμᾶς ὁ Θεὸς ἀπ᾽ ἀρχῆς εἰς σωτηρίαν) Illud ἀπ᾽ ἀρχῆς ostendit ad Judæos hæc scribi, qui primitiæ creden- tium, Rom. XI. 16. Eph. I. 2. Ἑἵλετο elegit, id est, sibi se- paravit. Agitur hic de ea electione, quæ fidem sequitur, ut Matth. XXII. 14. Israëlitis dictum olim: Κύριος εἵλε- τό σε σήμερον γενέσθαι λαὸν, Deut. XXVI. 18. nempe ad be- neficia temporalia. At hic additur εἰς σωτηρίαν ad salutem nempe æternam, quæ vere Christianis reservatur, Coloss. I. 5. 2. Tim. IV. 8.

Ἐν ἁγιασμῷ Πνεύματος, καὶ πίστει ἀληθείας) Hic prior Ge- nitivus est causæ efficientis, alter vero objecti, ut & Philipp. I. v. 27. Quomodo eos separavit Deus? Sanctificando eos per Spiritum suum. Vide 1. Cor. I, 2. Actor. XX, v. 32. XXVI. v. 18. Et quomodo pervenitur ad illum Spiritum? Per fidem habitam Evangelio.

Non ad Judæos tantum, sed ad gentiles maxime. Major enim pars è gentilibus erat in Ecclesia Thessalonicensi, cui hæc scripta. Illud vero ἀπ᾽ ἀρχῆς non primitias notat, ut Vulgatus perperam reddit, quasi esse ἀπαρχὰς, sed ab initio, hoc est, ab æterno, 1. Joh. I. 1. Electio enim ad salutem æternam ab æterno facta est, Eph. I. 4. quæ fidem se- quitur, & in προγνώσει divina. Facta enim κατὰ πρόγνωσιν secundum prævisionem non operum, sed fidei, per sanctificationem Spiritus, per fidem veritatis, sive veritati Evangelicæ habitam inter- preteris, sive veram, non fictam, perinde est, dum- modo non actu existentem, sed in intuitu & præ- visione divina spectatam notari concedatur. Non enim elegit Deus sine intuitu meriti Christi, quia in Christo nos elegisse dicitur, Ephes. I. vers. 4. & prædestinasse per Christum vers. 5. in quo nos di- lexit ceu dilecto Filio suo, ἐχαρίτωσεν ἡμᾶς ἐν τῷ ἠγαπημένῳ, vers. 6. Non autem sumus in Christo nisi per fidem. Theophylactus dicit, nos elegisse Deum, & ad salutem prædestinasse, quippe quos dignos præsciret. At si de dignitate in Christo, imputata ejus justitia per fidem, intelligeret, non improbandum foret. Sed quam nostram propriam dignitatem intelligat, & addat, nos etiam ad no- stram salutem contulisse quicquam, eaque de cau- sa fidem veritatis hic adjectam, fallitur, & à veritate aberrat. Ex gratia autem facta est electio gratiæ. Si autem ex gratia, non ex operibus, Roman. XI. 5. 6. Non id à Chrysostomo habet, quem alias κατὰ πόδα sequitur. Chrysostomus contrarium tradidit hoc loc. Quomodo ad salutem? Ut nos sanctificaret per Spiritum. Hæc enim sunt, quæ nostram salutem continent; μηδαμῶς ἀπὸ ἔργων, nusquam, vel po- tius nequaquam ab operibus; μηδαμῶς ἀπὸ κατορ- θωμάτων, nusquam, (nequaquam) à recte factis, ἀλλὰ διὰ πίστεως ἀληθείας, sed per fidem veritatis. ἰδὲ τὸ ἐν πάλιν διά ἐστι. Ecce in rursus est PER. Et statim postea: Ὁρᾷς πῶς οὐδὲν αὐτῶν δείκνυσιν ὂ, ἀλ- λὰ τὸ πᾶν τοῦ Θεοῦ. Vides quomodo nihil ostendit esse eorum, sed totum Dei. Ex eadem etiam causa sanctificatio Spiritus prius ponitur, quam fides ve- ritatis. Quod cum Chrysostomo scholia Græca ob- servarunt: Διὰ τοῦτο δὲ πρῶτον εἶπε τὸν ἁγιασμὸν τοῦ Πνεύματος, δηλῶν ὡς οὐδὲ ἐπιστεύσαμεν, εἰ μὴ ἡ χάρις τοῦ Πνεύματος ἠγίασατο.

Ab electione ad vocationem progreditur, non quod posterior sit naturæ ordine, sed ut eandem firmet, ceu ab æterno factam, ab ea gratia, quæ ipsis in tempore contingit. Nam quos prædestinavit, eos vocavit, quos vocavit, eos justificavit, quos justificavit, eos vivificavit, Rom. VIII. 30. E vocatione ergo ac justificatione, quam glorificatio sequitur, colligitur prædestinatio ad gloriam ab æterno facta à Deo. Crocius vocationem, sanctificationem Spiritus, & fidem veritatis, ut media electionis divinæ introduci vult. Sed ὕπουλον fovet. Πρῶτον ψεῦδος enim est, electionem absolute fictam esse sine prævisione sanctificationis Spiritus & fidei veritatis, aut etiam vocationis ad Evangelium, per quod sanctificat nos Spiritus sanctus, fidem imprimis, qua purificantur corda nostra, Act. XV. 9. in nobis accendendo. Quæ vero in mente divina in signo rationis præcedunt, æque ut & Christus cum suo merito, Eph. I. 4. 5. 6. Nam quomodo elegisset juxta Christum ullos, quum omnes sub peccato & ira Dei conclusi fuerimus, nec nisi per Christum facta sit propitiatio & redemptio. Quomodo elegisset, in quibus nullum beneplacitum habere potuerat, hoc est, qui sine fide erant. Sine fide enim impossibile est Deo placere, Ebr. XI. 6. Fidem autem quomodo in Christum habere potuit quisquam sine ἁγιασμῷ vel sanctificatione Spiritus S. per Verbum & sacramenta. Quomodo per Verbum sanctificare poterat, si non vocati ad Evangelii communionem erant. In mente ergo divina hæc in figno rationis sese consequuntur, redemptio, vocatio, sanctificatio, quæ & regeneratio, ac fides, denique electio, quæ facta secundum fidei πρόγνωσιν. Decretum quidem, utpote æternum, sequitur exequutio, quippe temporaria, si temporis momenta respiciamus, ut hæc explicare liceat, sed decretum non est prius ordine naturæ & causalitatis illis temporariis, redemptione Christi, vocatione, & sanctificatione vel regeneratione Spiritus sancti & fide: Sed hæc potius ordine naturæ decreto divino priora sunt, utpote quod secundum horum prævisionem factum est: Beat. Menzerus igitur, qui per ἁγιασμὸν πνεύματος intelligit ministerium Evangelii, temere hic exagitatur à Crocio, quia operationem Spiritus sancti per Verbi Ministros, non enim immediate operatur, sed mediante ministerio, indigitat: qualis est regeneratio, utpote per quam fides in nobis gignitur. Crocius cohærere hæc vult, non cum verbo εἵλετο, sed cum voce εἰς σωτηρίαν. Verum enim vero docendum hoc totum erat, quomodo elegerit nos DEUS ad salutem. Id docet Apostolus: Nimirum per sanctificationem Spiritus & fidem veritatis. Totum id etiam probat ac confirmat, nimirum DEUM nos per sanctificationem Spiritus & fidem veritatis elegisse ad salutem vel vitam æternam, qui vocavit nos per Evangelium ad eandem actu consequendam, ad quam ab æterno nos prædestinarat. Gloriam Theophylactus & scholia Græca de gloria Christi sic explicant, quod vocarit nos DEUS, ut gloriam acquirat Filio suo, sed quia electio nostra ad salutem confirmanda erat, rectius de gloria, quam

Christus nobis peperit merito suo, quamque unice per Christum consequimur, vel per fidem Christi, etsi eam ad gloriam ipsiusmet Christi facere du- bium non sit. Quo sensu Chrysostomus: Non est hoc quoque parvum, inquit, si suam gloriam Christus nostram dicit esse salutem, benigni enim & clemen- tis est gloria, (δόξα γὰρ τοῦ φιλανθρώπου) esse mul- tos, quibus detur salus. Magnus est ergo Dominus nostar. Εἰς περιποίησιν est ad possidendam vel con- sequendam per appropriationem gloriam Christi. Non enim nos accepimus æternam gloriam nostris meritis aut operibus, sed meritis Christi omni- bus hominibus acquisitam nobis appropriamus per fidem. Vocavit enim nos ad gloriam nobis comparatam, actu consequendam, quod fit per fidem, sicut dicturus est Christus, possidete regnum vobis paratum ante jacta mundi fundamenta, Matth. XXV. vers. 34. Περιποίησις est assertio, quum nobis quid vindicamus & asserimus, Suidæ est rerum acquisitarum possessio.

## 2:15
Vers. 15.

Therefore then, brothers, stand fast) Persist, do not waver under the hardships of exile, 1 Cor. XVI. 13. Phil. IV. 1.

Concerning the exile or the hardships of the exile of the faithful Thessalonians, or of the Church to which this epistle was directed, neither anyone in this epistle, nor in the book of the Acts of the Apostles, has seen. Stand firm in the faith and in the acknowledged truth, do not be moved, do not waver, do not slip.

And hold fast the traditions) Every doctrine is called a παράδοσις, as we said at Matt. VII. v. 3. 5. κρατεῖτε here, which is κατέχετε, 1 Cor. XI. 2. traditions קבלות or לקחים.

As you were taught, whether by word or by our epistle) For the Apostles taught in two ways, by speaking and by writing: above 2. and the authority is equal in both. And the speaking came first, the writing followed. Many things indeed which the Apostles said, they also wrote: but not all, because it was enough that some things had been introduced for the use of the Churches, so that there was no need for them to be commanded also through epistles. In passing, however, mention is sometimes made of these as well.

Grotius here sails in favor of Papistic traditions, [saying] that not all things which the Apostles said were written, but why did he not bring forward the τὰς παραδόσεις [traditions] preached by word alone, and not reduced to the monuments of sacred letters, the number of which not even the Roman Pontiff himself has hitherto been able or dared to define? Why did he not bring forward at least some examples? But if certain things were indeed handed down to the Thessalonians which were not recorded in this or the previous epistle written to them, were they not therefore included in other later epistles of Paul (for these were the very first to the Thessalonians, as most Papists agree, Justinianus, Cornelius à Lapide, etc.)? Furthermore, it is known that the disjunctive particle εἴτε does not always distinguish different things, e.g., documents that are different in substance, but also only indicates different modes, just as the same thing could be handed down both by epistle and by living voice, as is evident from the example of those things which he had handed down by living voice concerning the Antichrist, which he here recalls to the memory of the Thessalonians and repeats in the present epistle. And Bellarmine admits in book IV de Verbo Dei c. II that all those things were written by the Apostles which are necessary for all, and which they themselves had openly preached to all the common people. But here those things are designated which the Apostle had preached to all the Thessalonians. For he enjoins that those things be kept by all. It is therefore necessary that all those things were written. What? That the particle εἴτε can be taken collectively, as in 1 Cor. XIII. 8. Col. I. 16. in this way, hold the traditions which you learned, both by word and by our epistle, which interpretation the context proves not obscurely. He is not speaking of rituals, but of dogmatics, in which they ought to stand firmly, so that they do not suffer themselves to be moved or seduced from them in any way.

Latin:

Vers. 15.

Ἄρα ὖν ἀδελφοὶ στήκετε) Perstate, ne labascite sub exilii incommodis, 1. Cor. XVI. 13. Phil. IV. 1.

De exilio aut incommodis exilii fidelium Thes- salonicensium, vel Ecclesiæ, ad quam epistola directa est, nec in epistola hac quisquam, nec in libro actuum Apostolicorum vidit. State in fide & veritate agnita immobiles, non dimoveamini, non vacilletis, non labamini.

Καὶ κρατεῖτε τὰς παραδόσεις) Omnis doctrina vocatur παράδοσις, ut diximus ad Matth. VII. v. 3. 5. κρατεῖτε hic, quod κατέχετε, 1. Cor. XI. 2. παραδόσεις קבלות aut לקחים.

Ὡς ἐδιδάχθητε, εἴτε διὰ λόγου, εἴτε δι᾽ ἐπιστολῆς ἡμῶν) Duo- bus enim modis docebant Apostoli, loquendo & scriben- do: supra 2. & par in utroque autoritas. Et præcessit lo- quutio, sequuta est scriptura. Multa quidem quæ dixere Apostoli, etiam scripsere: at non omnia, quia satis erat, quædam in usum Ecclesiarum esse introducta, ita ut nihil opus esset & per epistolas præcipi. In transcursu tamen & horum interdum fit mentio.

Velificatur hic Grotius Papisticis traditionibus, non omnia, quæ Apostoli dixere, scripta esse, sed cur non protulit τὰς παραδόσεις διὰ λόγου per ser- monem solum prædicatas, non vero in literarum sacrarum monumenta redactas, quarum numerum nec ipse Romanus Pontifex hactenus definire po- tuit vel ausus est? Cur non exempla tantum aliqua in medium produxit? Quod si omnino tradita quædam Thessalonicensibus, quæ in hac aut prio- re ad ipsos exarata epistola non confignata, num ideo in aliis Pauli epistolis posterioribus (nam hæ ad Thessalonicenses omnium primæ fuere consen- tientibus plerisque Papistis, Justiniano, Cornelio à Lapide, &c.) non comprehensa? Porro notum est, particulam disjunctivam εἴτε non distinguere sem- per diversa, v. g. documenta ratione substantiæ alia atque alia, sed diversos etiam solum modos innue- re, quemadmodum res eadem & per epistolam & per vivam vocem tradi potuit, ut constat exemplo eorum, quæ viva voce tradiderat de Antichristo, quæ Thessalonicensib. hic in memoriam revocat, & repetit præsente epistola. Et fatetur Bellarmi- nus l. IV. de Verbo Dei c. II. omnia illa esse ab Apo- stolis scripta, quæ omnibus necessaria sunt, & quæ ipsi palam omnibus vulgo prædicaverant. At hic de- signantur ea, quæ omnibus Thessalonicensibus præ- dicaverat Apostolus. Omnibus enim ea servanda injungit. Necessum itaque est, omnia illa scripta esse. Quid? quod particula εἴτε collective accipi possit, ut 1. Cor. XIII. 8. Col. I. 16. hoc modo, tenete traditiones, quas didicistis, & per sermonem & per epistolam nostram, quam expositionem haud ob- scure probat contextus. Non de ritualibus loqui- tur, sed de dogmaticis, in quibus firmiter persi- stare debebant, adeo ut non patiantur ab iisdem ullatenus se dimoveri aut seduci.

## 2:16
V. 16. May our Lord Jesus Christ himself and God and our Father, who has loved us) The prayer ascends. And that καὶ before ὁ Πατὴρ is an explanation of what preceded, as in Eph. I. 3. IV. 6. V. 20. Phil. IV. 20. Coloss I. 3. II. 2. III. 17. 1. Thess. I. v. 3. III. 11. 13. 1. Petr. I. 3. Concerning this love of God, see Rom. V. 7. VIII. 37. Eph. II. 4.

Who ascends in prayer, since the Father and Son are one, and it is not inferior to be the Lord, κατ' ἀντονομασίαν or that one Lord, through whom are all things, 1. Cor. IIX. 6. than to be God, or to be God than the Father? One truly divine work is attributed to the Lord, to God, and to the Father, the consolation of the heart and strengthening in the Word, as in a good work. From the unity of the work and of the infinite power of the operation, the unity of essence appears. Chrysostom observed that the prayer does not ascend, but that the order of the divine persons varies, so that a diversity of essence or dignity is not imagined. Where now are they, he says, who diminish the Son because he is named after the Father in the washing of baptism? For here the opposite is the case. Nor is it necessary that καὶ here be an exposition, since it can retain the ordinary force of conjunction, and the Holy Spirit be understood by God, so that he prays for this παράκλησιν & στήριξιν from the Lord Jesus Christ and God the Holy Spirit and the Father, and those three gifts are assigned to those three divine persons: to the Father, Jesus Christ, because he has loved us, Gal. II. v. 20. to God the Holy Spirit, because he has given eternal consolation. The Paraclete is specifically named, from whom is all παράκλησις, Act. IX. 31. Joh. XIV. 26. cap. XV. 26. c. XVI. 7. and to God the Father, because he has given good hope, 1. Petr. I. 3. But if anyone prefers to refer the word God here also to the Father, I will not object, provided that the Holy Spirit is not considered to be excluded, through whom we certainly have consolation and the hope of eternal life. Theophylact, however, not without reason notes here that under the guise of prayer he stirs their mind to God, indeed with more certain providence and care, produced in the place of an argument and a pledge. For he says that to you who are also laboring at nothing, he is about to give eternal goods for FAITH ALONE. Whence it is necessary that you also have the best hope. These things hold more correctly than the Grotians, which follow now, concerning eternal goods promised for brief obedience.

Καὶ διδοὺς παράκλησιν αἰώνιον) He calls it eternal consolation from the object of the promised eternal life: Thus διαθήκη αἰώνιος, Ebr. XIII. 20. εὐαγγέλιον αἰώνιον, Apoc. XIV. 6.

Καὶ ἐλπίδα ἀγαθήν) The hope of the best things. Thus κρείττων ἐλπὶς is said Ebr. VII. 19. ἐλπὶς ζῶσα, 1. Petr. I. 3.

Ἐν χάριτι) through his supreme goodness. For it is of immense goodness to promise eternal and heavenly things for brief obedience.

Latin:

V. 16. Αὐτὸς ὁ Κύριος ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦς χριστὸς καὶ ὁ Θεὸς καὶ ὁ Πατὴρ ἡμῶν ἀγαπήσας ἡμᾶς) Scandit oratio. Et καὶ illud ante ὁ Πατὴρ est explicatio ejus, quod præcessit, ut Eph. I. 3. IV. 6. V. 20. Phil. IV. 20. Coloss I. 3. II. 2. III. 17. 1. Thess. I. v. 3. III. 11. 13. 1. Petr. I. 3. De ista Dei dilectione vide Rom. V. 7. VIII. 37. Eph. II. 4.

Qui scandat orattio, quum Pater & Filius unum sint, nec inferius sit, Dominum esse, κατ' ἀντονομα- σίαν vel unum illum Dominum, per quem omnia, 1. Cor. IIX. 6. quam Deum, aut Deum esse, quam Patrem? Unum opus vere divinum tribuitur Do- mino, Deo, & Patri, consolatio cordis & corro- boratio in Verbo, ut opere bono. Ex unitate operis & operationis infinitæ virtutis unitas essen- tiæ apparet. Chrysostomus non scandere orationem, sed ordinem personarum divinarum variare obser- vavit, ne fingatur diversitas essentiæ vel dignitatis. Ubi nunc sunt, inquit, qui Filium propterea immi- nuunt, quod in baptismi lavacro post Patrem nomi- natur? Hic enim contrarium est. Neque necessum est, ut καὶ hic expositio sit, quum possit copulandi vim ordinariam retinere, ac per Deum Spiritus sanctus intelligi, ut à Domino Jesu Christo & Deo Spiritu S. & Patre hanc precetur παράκλησιν & στήριξιν, ac tribus illis divinis personis assignentur tria illa elo- gia, Patri, Jesu Christo, quod dilexerit nos, Gal. II. v. 20. Deo Spiritui S. quod dederit æternam con- solationem. Paracletus peculiariter nuncupatus, à quo omnis παράκλησις, Act. IX. 31. Joh. XIV. 26. cap. XV. 26. c. XVI. 7. & Deo Patri, quod dederit spem bonam, 1. Petr. I. 3. Si autem malit quis vo- cem Dei hic etiam referre ad Patrem, non refraga- bor, modo ne Spiritus S. excludi censeatur, per quem utique consolationem & spem habemus vi- tæ æternæ. Non abs re autem advertit hic Theophy- lactus, quod sub specie precationis excitet illorum mentem Dei certiori quidem providentia & cura in argumentum & pignoris loco producta. Ait namque vobis etiam nihil laborantibus, pro SOLA fide daturus est ille æterna bona. Unde & spem optimam habeatis necesse est. Quæ rectius se habent, quam Grotians, quæ jam sequuntur, de bonis æternis pro brevi obsequio promissis.

Καὶ διδοὺς παράκλησιν αἰώνιον) Consolationem æternam vocat ex objecto promissa vitæ æternæ: Sic διαθήκη αἰώνιος, Ebr. XIII. 20. εὐαγγέλιον αἰώνιον, Apoc. XIV. 6.

Καὶ ἐλπίδα ἀγαθήν) Spem rerum optimarum. Sic κρείτ- των ἐλπὶς dicitur Ebr. VII. 19. ἐλπὶς ζῶσα, 1. Petr. I. 3.

Ἐν χάριτι) per summam suam bonitatem. Ingentis enim bonitatis pro brevi obsequio æterna promittere ac cœlestia.

## 2:17
v. 17. Παρακαλέσαι ὑμῶν τὰς καρδίας) May he inscribe these comforts upon your hearts. See 2. Cor. I. 4. VII. 6. Eph. VI. 22.

Καὶ στηρίξαι ὑμᾶς) Rom. XVI. 25. 1. Thessal. III. 13. infra III. 3. 1. Petr. V. 10. 730

Ἐν παντὶ λόγῳ καὶ ἔργῳ ἀγαθῷ) that is, ὡς πάντα λόγον καὶ πᾶν ἔργον ἀγαθόν. So that you may speak and do those things which are right. In the Manuscript it is: καὶ στηρίξαι (namely τὰς καρδίας) ἐν παντὶ ἔργῳ καὶ λόγῳ ἀγαθῷ. The Latin Interpreter used a similar codex.

We append the explanation of Theophylact, which seemed worthy to be read here: He means that he may confirm you in right decrees, and in the best actions of life, so that in those things which happen to you, whether they be prosperous or adverse, you neither exceed the measure, nor be of too dejected a spirit. For that is what he intends, he says, when he exhorts and confirms. For he who has been best strengthened by God will surely bear with wonderful greatness of soul those things which must be tolerated, and will be firmer and stable. From the right observation of dogma, each one attains a firmer hope of those goods which are about to come to us as a reward. From the most praiseworthy morals of life, one is affected by a certain sweetness of soul. And when adversities are offered, he does not suffer some evil as a wrongdoer, but as a minister and servant of God.

PART III. PARENETIC EPISTLES. WITH A VOW AND AN EPISTOLARY SEAL.

Latin:

v. 17. Παρακαλέσαι ὑμῶν τὰς καρδίας) Inscribat ista sola- tia cordibus vestris. Vide 2. Cor. I. 4. VII. 6. Eph. VI. 22.

Καὶ στηρίξαι ὑμᾶς) Rom. XVI. 25. 1. Thessal. III. 13. infra III. 3. 1. Petr. V. 10. 730

Ἐν παντὶ λόγῳ καὶ ἔργῳ ἀγαθῷ) id est, ὡς πάντα λόγον καὶ πᾶν ἔργον ἀγαθόν. Ut quæ recta sunt, ea loquamini & aga- tis. In Manuscripto est: καὶ στηρίξαι (nempe τὰς καρδίας) ἐν παντὶ ἔργῳ καὶ λόγῳ ἀγαθῷ. Pari codice usus fuit Lati- nus Interpres.

Subjungimus Theophylacti explicationem, quæ digna visa, ut hic legatur: Id sentit, ut vos in rectio- ribus decretis confirmet, & vitæ optimis actionibus, ita ut in his, quæ vobis obtigerint, sive prospera fue- rint, sive adversa, neque modum excedatis, neque animo sitis abjectiori. Id enim prætendit, cum ex- hortetur inquit & confirmet. Nam qui optime fue- rit à Deo corroboratus, feret sane mira animi magni- tudine, quæ toleranda sunt, & firmior & stabilis. Ex recta autem dogmatis observatione eorum bonorum firmiorem spem quisque assequitur, quæ in præmium nobis sunt obventura. Ex vitæ vero laudatissimis moribus animi quadam suavitate afficitur. Et cum offeruntur adversa, non ut maleficus aliquid mali patitur, sed tanquam Dei minister & servus.

PARS III. EPISTOLÆ PARÆNETICA. CUM VOTO ET SIGILLO EPISTOLICO.

## 3:1 Argument
CHAPTER III. ARGUMENT, AND PARTITION.

The Apostle admonishes them to pray for him and for the course of the Word, to observe his precepts, to avoid those walking inordinately, to exhort them to avoid idleness, and to point out the disobedient by letter. Finally, having prayed for the peace of God and the gracious assistance of God for them, he establishes a sign of his letters by a salutation made with his own hand, and seals the epistle with a final vow.

There are two parts. I. It contains a threefold admonition concerning prayers, obedience, and labor, up to v. 15. II. It exhibits the Apostolic vow and seal, up to v. 18.

PART I. The Apostle's threefold admonition concerning prayers, obedience, and labor.

V. 1. Τὸ λοιπὸν) A word of one hastening to the end, as in 1 Thess. IV. 1, where see the remarks.

Προσεύχεσθε, ἀδελφοὶ, περὶ ἡμῶν) Thus also Coloss. IV. 3. 1. Thess. V. 25.

Ἵνα ὁ λόγος τῦ Κυρίυ τρέχῃ) An excellent translation, that is, that it may quickly become known.

Καὶ δοξάζηται) not only become known, but also be approved and praised נהדר.

Καθὼς καὶ πρὸς ὑμᾶς) πρὸς here again means 'among', as often elsewhere.

Just as the Apostle had prayed for the consolation and confirmation of the Thessalonians in the faith and in the Christian life toward the end of the chapter, so now he urges them to pray also for him, that the Word of the Lord may be glorified through his ministry, and that he himself may be delivered from wicked men along with his fellow-workers. To this exhortation, however, he interweaves a commendation concerning the course and glorification of the Gospel among them; not excluding, but tacitly implying, that his prayers are also to be poured out to the Lord for their sake. For as it is a matter of charity to pray silently for others, so it is a matter of necessity to pray for oneself. Thus, by a grateful mention, as Blessed Hunnus says, he effectively stimulates them by their own domestic example, both to perform the requested prayers devoutly and to persevere in obedience to the Gospel, inasmuch as they understand it to be so highly approved by their Apostle. When he had prayed for the upright, says Theophylact, that they might be established, he finally beseeches them to pray to God for him as well. Not that he might be removed from the dangers in which he was already involved, but that the preaching itself might run its course and attain its own glory. Nor is such a request devoid of praise for them, when he says, 'as also among you,' that is, that all may show themselves obedient to me, just as you were ready to obey. Therefore, the Apostle prayed for nothing in this way that concerned himself, but he prayed for all things that were of God. Τὸ λοιπὸν is not a particle of one hastening to the end, as is evident from parallel passages, but a kind of 'note well,' so that it may be signified that some things still remain that are necessary to be admonished and observed, and therefore not to be neglected. Moreover, it is a sign of humility that he asks for prayers for himself. He was certain of the assistance of God from the divine oracle, Acts XIII. 9, 10. Yet he solicits the prayers of others who are much inferior to him. Emphasis on the word τρέχῃ implies not only that the Word may quickly become known, but also that it may be propagated most swiftly, Ps. 147:15. That which is not propagated to others can also become known through fame. Nor does he wish them to pray only that it may run where Paul was active; but that it may be propagated everywhere throughout the whole world, not so that his own name, but that the Lord's name may be glorified. This happens when the Word of the Lord is received with glory, not as the word of men, but as what it truly is, the Word of God. The sermon is glorified in respect of the hearers, says Jerome. The conversion of men to Christ is the glory and glorification of the Gospel. The Thessalonians had received the Word of the Lord as the Word of God, 1 Thess. 2:13, and he bids them pray that it may be received everywhere. The faith of the Thessalonians was celebrated everywhere, just as it was celebrated in other churches, 1. Thess. 1:3 ff. He desires such faith as the fruit and glory of the Gospel also for others, and wishes it to be sought through prayers: The particle καὶ, just as 'also among you', implies that the word is already being glorified among others, so that he may confirm them by the example of others, and provoke them, as it were, to a contest with others.

Latin:

CAPUT III. ARGUMENTUM, ET PARTITIO.

Monet Apostolus, ut pro se, & cursu Verbi o- rent, præcepta sua observent, inordinate am- bulantes vitent, eosque ad vitandum otium hortentur, ac inobedientes per literas indi- cent. Denique pacem Dei & gratiosam Dei assistentiam ipsis precatus salutatione manu propria facta signum literarum suarum con- stituit, & finali voto epistolam obsignat.

Partes duæ sunt. I. Triplex monitum de preci- bus, obsequio & labore continet, ad v. 15. II. Votum & sigillum Apostolicum exhibet, ad v. 18.

PARS I. Triplex Apostoli monitum de precibus, ob- sequio & labore.

V. 1. Τὸ λοιπὸν) Vox properantis ad finem, ut 1. Thess. IV. 1. ubi dicta vide.

Προσεύχεσθε, ἀδελφοὶ, περὶ ἡμῶν) Sic & Coloss. IV. 3. 1. Thess. V. 25.

Ἵνα ὁ λόγος τῦ Κυρίυ τρέχῃ) Egregia translatio, id est, ut cito innotescat.

Καὶ δοξάζηται) non tantum innotescat, sed & appro- betur & laudetur נהדר.

Καθὼς καὶ πρὸς ὑμᾶς) πρὸς hic iterum apud, ut alibi sæpe.

Ut pro Thessalonicensium consolatione ac confirmatione in fide, ac vita Christiana preca- tus erat Apostolus sub finem capitis, ita jam hor- tatur ipsos, ut pro se etiam precentur, ut Verbum Domini glorificetur per ministerium suum, atque ipse cum συνεργοῖς suis à pravis hominibus libere- tur. Adhortationi autem immiscet commenda- tionem de cursu & glorificatione Evangelii inter ipsos; non excludens, sed tacite innuens, preces ejus gratia ad Dominum etiam fundendas. Ut enim tacite pro aliis orare charitatis: Ita pro se orare necessitatis est. Ita grata mentione, dicente B. Hunnio, exempli ipsorum domestici efficaciter eos estimulat, tum ad preces modo requisitas devote faciendas, tum vero ad perseverantiam in Evangelii obsequio, utpote quam suo Apostolo tantopere probari intelligunt. Cum probis, inquit Theophylactus, ut stabiliantur, orasset, obsecrat tandem, ut Deum pro se & ipsi precentur. Non ut periculis eximatur, in quibus jam versaretur, sed ut prædicatio ipsa decur- rat, suasque & gloriam assequatur. Nec illorum qui- dem laude vacat istiusmodi postulatio, cum inquit, sicut & apud vos, hoc est, ut omnes se mihi morige- ros præbeant, sicuti & vos faciles ad obtemperandum fuistis. Nihil itaque hoc modo, quod ad se attineret, orabat Apostolus, sed omnia, quæ Dei essent, depre- cabatur. Τὸ λοιπὸν non est ad finem properan- tis particula, ut è locis parallelis constat, sed quod- dam nota bene, ut significetur, restare adhuc non- nulla monitu & observatu necessaria adeoque non negligenda. Cæterum humilitatis est, quod pro se precari petit. Certus erat de assistentia Dei ex ora- culo divino, Act. XIII. 9. 10. Aliorum tamen se multo inferiorum preces solicitat. Emphasis in voce τρέχῃ non tantum id infert, ut cito innote- scat Verbum, sed etiam ut celerrime propagetur, Psal. CXLVII. 15. Innotescere per famam etiam potest id, quod non propagatur ad alios. Nec tantum, ut currat ibi, ubi agebat Paulus, precari eos vult; sed ut undiquaque propagetur per to- tum orbem, non ut suum, sed ut Domini nomen glorificetur. Quod fit, cum Verbum Domini cum gloria suscipitur, non ut Verbum hominum, sed quale revera est, Dei Verbum. Sermo glorifi- catur auditorum respectu, ait Hieronymus. Ho- minum ad Christum conversio est Evangelii glo- ria & glorificatio. Receperant Thessalonicenses Verbum Domini, ut Dei Verbum, 1. Thess. II. vers. 13. cum insigni fructu, ut ubique recipiatur, orare jubet. Celebrabatur fides Thessalonicen- sium passim, ut in aliis Ecclesiis celebraretur, 1. Thess. I. 3. seqq. ejusmodi fidem ceu fructum & gloriam Evangelii etiam aliis desiderat, & preci- bus exorari vult: Particula καὶ, sicut & apud vos, innuens, etiam apud alios verbum jam glorifica- ri, ut confirmet eos aliorum exemplo, & veluti ad contentionem cum aliis provocet.

## 3:2
Verse 2. And that we may be delivered from absurd and wicked men) Ἄτοπος is עול, Job 4:8, 11:11, 36:21, Prov. 30:20, Luke 23:41. Hence ἄτοποι are criminal, flagitious men, as that name is explained in the Glossary. Πονηροὶ are מרעים, malicious, as it is in the same Glossary. May we be delivered from these, that is, may God cause that they do not harm us either by calumnies or even by their example. Thus Rom. 15:31, ῥύῃ is ינצל.

Theophylact, along with Chrysostom, takes this concerning those who contradict the preaching and impugn the true dogmas, such as that Alexander the coppersmith was, because it is added, 'not all have faith', that is, not all believe; yet it can also be extended to others, so that those are noted at the same time who were providing scandals by their crimes and depraved morals, and were obstructing the course of the Word, or were even preparing a harsher winter for Paul and his co-workers with calumnies and other persecutions. Cf. 1 Thess. 3:7. Ἀτόπως, which the Vulgate rendered as 'importunate' and Ambrose as 'iniquitous', Crocius interprets as 'κατὰ πόδα', those who agree with no place, who rest in no harbor, who allow no one to be in peace, who contradict everyone, who disturb everything without reason. Πονηροὶ are those who have hardened their mind in malice, and therefore seduce others also to evil, nor do they bear those who call them back from evil, such as the Apostle encountered everywhere, and he knew that they would not be lacking in Jerusalem, where he had to contend. Therefore he wishes to be snatched from such, not indeed through death, to which Calvin extends these things, but through liberation from their snares. For he does not seek this for his own sake, but for the sake of the course of the Gospel, which he desired to be propagated also by his own ministry, Phil. 1:24, just as he did not seek the liberation of other fellow-workers through death, but their rescue from these absurd and wicked men in life and in the cultivation of the ministry. B. Hunnius designates three objects of the prayers: 1. that the word of the Lord may run, that is, that it may be propagated far and wide. 2. that it may be glorified, that is, that men may magnify the doctrine of the Gospel, and, bearing abundant fruit from it, may glorify God. 3. that they may be snatched away from absurd and perverse men, that is, that the Apostle and his fellow-mystics may be delivered from the importunity of those who oppose the Gospel and place various impediments in the way, so that it may not have a free course and success everywhere. Therefore they either oppose it in a hostile and open manner, or they mock it with a profane mind, or they involve and pervert the doctrine of truth with their own fanatical opinions.

For not all have faith) And yet all to whom the Gospel is announced are called to faith; so it is. But those who please themselves in their vices will not believe us, says Lactantius, even if we were to carry the Sun in our hands. They love the works of darkness. Therefore they shrink from the light, John 3:20. They do not wish to do the will of the Father, and therefore they do not judge rightly, John 7:17. A similar expression is found in Clement of Alexandria, Strom. 5, 'not all have knowledge'. Prudentius in his hymn on Rome:

Know that you are incapable of the sacrament, impious one, unable with blind senses to draw in our mystery: night does not grasp anything of the day.

Faith is not understood as fidelity or truthfulness, as Bullinger explains by an enallage of the thing for the person, as if he were saying, not all are faithful and truthful, but as in chapter I, v. 3, 4, 11, chapter II, verse 13, and in the former epistle this word is always understood as trust in Christ, which is not of all, not because it is denied by GOD to anyone, who is prepared to offer faith to all, Acts XVII. 31, but because most neglect the means of faith, and love darkness more than light, John III. 19. Which sentence, faith is not of all, is indeed added because of those troublemakers, but it is general, because it provides the reason why one must pray for the course of the Gospel, which is hindered by many, since faith is not of all, nor even of those who are called. For many are called, few are chosen, Matthew XX. 16. And therefore there is need for prayers, so that some may still be converted to the faith, even from among the troublemakers themselves. Faith is a gift and work of God, which He is indeed prepared to confer upon all, and denies to no one by an absolute good pleasure, 1 Tim. II. 4. But because it is conferred through the Word, which very many reject, God must be prayed to, so that both the Word of God may run, and through it men may be converted to the faith. Crocius wants the sense to be that it is not given to all to believe. But the Holy Spirit wants us to pray for all, that they may believe. He wants all to arrive at the knowledge of the truth: He gives the means of believing, the Word and the Sacraments, not only to those who believe, but also to those who reject them. Crocius therefore finally confesses that the malice of men hinders them from believing: yet he denies that this is the cause expressed here by the Apostle. But in the examples of the absurd and wicked it is entirely expressed. For whose sake this sentence is also added, even if it does not look here only at those who were around the Apostle, but also at similar ones whosoever and wheresoever. In which sense the explanation of the blessed Hunnius is not to be disapproved: For faith is not of all, that is, when they proudly resist the Evangelical doctrine, they declare in reality that they are faithless. For faith is not of all, since it is the work of God alone, who does not wish to confer it upon those stubborn and obstinate contemners (whether they be open enemies, or whether they oppose the Gospel secretly and by tunnels). Which, however, is to be understood only concerning the consequent and judiciary will according to the mind of the blessed Hunnius: and with a reduplication; insofar as they are stubborn and obstinate contemners of the Gospel. Crocius could not disapprove of that which Lombard brings forward here from Augustine in the sentences of Prosper: It must be known that to be able to have faith, just as to be able to have charity, is of the nature of men (namely, not as regards active power, as if man by his own strength could believe and love, but the capacity or faculty of receiving the gift, which is not in stones or brutes), but to have faith, just as also charity, is of the grace of the faithful: But since the will to believe is prepared for some by GOD, and for others is not prepared, it must be discerned what comes from His mercy, and what from His judgment.

Latin:

Vers. 2. Καὶ ἵνα ῥυσθῶμεν ἀπὸ τῶν ἀτόπων καὶ πονηρῶν ἀν- θρώπων) Ἄτοπος est עול, Job. IV. 8. XI. 11. XXXVI. v. 21. Prov. XXX. 20. Luc. XXIII. 41. Hinc ἄτοποι homines faci- norosi, flagitiosi, quomodo id nomen in Glossario exponi- tur. Πονηροὶ sunt מרעים, malitiosi, ut est in eodem Glossa- rio. Liberemur ab his, id est, faciat Deus, ne aut calumniis, aut etiam exemplo nobis noceant. Sic Rom. XV. 31. ῥύῃ est ינצל.

De contradicentibus prædicationi, & veræ do- gmata impugnantibus, qualis Alexander ille ὁ χαλ- κεὺς fuit, hæc accipit cum Chrysostomo Theophy- lactus, quod addatur, non omnium est fides, id est, non omnes credunt; potest tamen ad alios etiam extendi, ut notentur simul, qui flagitiis & pravis moribus scandala præbebant, & cursum Verbi sufflaminabant, vel etiam Paulo & cooperariis calumniis aliisque persecutionibus acriorem hye- mem parabant, Conf. 1. Thess. III. 7. Ἀτόπως, quos Vulgatus importunos, Ambrosius iniquos reddi- dit, Crocius, κατὰ πόδα interpretatur, qui nullo loco conveniunt, qui nullo in portu quiescunt, qui neminem sinunt esse in pace, qui omnibus contradicunt, qui omnia turbant sine ratione. Πονηροὶ sunt, qui animum suum in malitia obfir- marunt, ideoque alios etiam ad malum seducunt, nec ferunt eos, qui revocant à malo, quales passim Apostolus habuit, & Hierosolymis, quo conten- dendum erat, non defuturos noverat. Ideo eripi à talibus vult, non quidem per mortem, quo Calvi- nus hæc etiam extendit, sed per liberationem ab eorum insidiis. Non enim id sui causa expetit, sed ob cursum Evangelii, quod suo etiam ministerio propagari desideravit, Phil. I. 24. uti ne aliorum συνεργῶν liberationem per mortem, sed ereptio- nem ab istis ἀτόποις καὶ πονηροῖς in vita & cultu mi- nisterii expetebat. B. Hunnius tria precum objecta designat, 1. ut sermo Domini currat, hoc est, ut longe lateque propagetur. 2. ut glorificetur, hoc est, ut ho- mines Evangelii doctrinam magnifaciant, & ex eo copiosum ferentes fructum, Deum glorificent. 3. ut abripiantur ab absurdis & perversis hominibus, hoc est, ut Apostoli & illorum symmystæ liberentur ab im- portunitate eorum, qui obststunt Evangelio, varia- que impedimenta objiciunt, ne id liberum undiqua- que cursum successumque habeat. Itaque vel hostili- ter & aperte id oppugnant, vel profana mente rident, vel suis fanaticis opinionibus doctrinam veritatis in- volvunt, ac pervertunt.

Οὐ γὰρ πάντων ἡ πίστις) Atqui ad fidem vocantur omnes, quibus annuntiatur Evangelium; Sic est. Sed qui in vi- tiis sibi placent, non credent nobis, inquit Lactantius, etiam- si Solem manibus gestemus. Amant opera tenebrarum. Ideo lucem reformidant, Joh. III. 20. Nolunt facere vo- luntatem Patris, & ideo non recte judicant Joh. VII. 17. Par loquutio apud Clementem Alexandrinum Strom. V. ὁ πάν- των ἡ γνῶσις. Prudentius in Romam hymno:

Scia incapacem te sacramenti, impie Non posse cæcis sensibus mysterium Haurire nostrum: nil diurnum nox capit.

Fides non intelligitur de fidelitate vel veracita- te, ut per Enallagen rei pro persona Bullingerus explicat, quasi dicat, non omnes sunt fidi & ve- races, sed uti cap. I. v. 3. 4. 11. cap. II. vers. 13. & in priori epistola semper vox hæc accipitur de fi- ducia in Christum, quæ non omnium est, non quod denegetur cuiquam à DEO, qui omnibus fidem præbere paratus est, Act. XVII. 31. sed quod media fidei plerique negligant, & tenebras magis ament, quam lucem, Joh. III. 19. Quæ sententia, non omnium est fides, additur quidem ob turbones istos, sed ge- neralis est, quia rationem exhibet, cur orandum sit pro Evangelii cursu, qui à multis impeditur, cum ne omnium, ac ne eorum quidem, qui vocan- tur, fides sit. Multi enim sunt vocati, pauci electi, Matth. XX. 16. Ideoque precibus opus sit, ut ali- qui adhuc convertantur ad fidem, vel ex ipsis et- iam turbonibus. Donum & opus Dei est fides, quod omnibus quidem conferre paratus est, ne- mini absoluto beneplacito denegat, 1. Tim. II. 4. Sed quia per Verbum confertur, quod plurimi re- probant, orandus Deus est, ut & Verbum Dei cur- rat, & per illud homines convertantur ad fidem. Crocius vult, sensum esse, non omnibus datum esse, ut credant. At pro omnibus orare nos vult Spiritus sanctus, ut credant. Vult ut omnes ad agnitionem veritatis perveniant: dat credendi media, Verbum & Sacramenta, non saltem iis, qui credunt, sed etiam illis, qui ea rejiciunt. Fatetur itaque tandem Crocius malitiam hominum impedire, quo minus credant: negat tamen eam causam hic ab Apostolo expri- mi. At in exemplis τῶν ἀτόπων καὶ πονηρῶν omnino ea expressa est. Quorum causa etiam hæc sententia subjicitur, etsi non solos eos hic respiciat, qui circa Apostolum erant, sed similes etiam quoscunque & ubicunque. Quo sensu B. Hunnii explicatio non improbanda: Non enim omnium est fides, hoc est, cum superbe obsistant doctrinæ Evangelicæ, reipsa de- clarant se infideles. Nam fides non est omnium, quip- pe quæ solius Dei opus est, qui eam præfractis & ob- stinatis contemptoribus illis, (sive aperti sint hostes, sive occulte & per cuniculos Evangelium oppugnent) conferre non vult. Quod tamen de consequente ac judiciaria voluntate tantum intelligendum ex men- te B. Hunnii: & cum reduplicatione; quatenus præ- fracti & obstinati contemptores sunt Evangelii. Non potuit improbare illud, quod Lombardus hic ex Augustino in Prosperi sententiis affert, Crocius: Sciendum quia posse habere fidem, sicut posse habere charitatem, naturæ est hominum (scilicet non quo- ad potentiam activam quasi homo suis viribus pos- sit credere & diligere, sed capacitatem seu faculta- tem recipiendi donum, quæ non est in lapidibus aut brutis) habere autem fidem, sicut & charitatem, gratiæ est fidelium: Sed cum voluntas credendi aliis præparetur à DEO, & aliis non præparetur, discer- nendum est, quid veniat de misericordia ejus, & quid de judicio.

## 3:3
V. 3. But the Lord is faithful, who will strengthen you and guard you from the evil one) the same sense as 1 Cor. I. 8, 9, 1 Thess. V. v. 24. Take 'from the evil one' as in Matthew VI. 13. In the Manuscript: But God is faithful, who also will strengthen. And so the Latin reads.

Latin:

V. 3. Πιστὸς δέ ἐστιν ὁ Κύριος, ὃς στηρίξει ὑμᾶς καὶ φυλάξει ἀπὸ τοῦ πονηροῦ) idem sensus, qui 1. Cor. I. 8. 9. 1. Thess. V. v. 24. Ἀπὸ τοῦ πονηροῦ accipe ut Matth. VI. 13. In Manuscri- pto: Πιστὸς δέ ἐστιν ὁ Θεὸς, ὃς καὶ στηρίξει. Et ita legit Latinus.

## 3:4
V. 4. But we trust in the Lord concerning you) So also Gal. V. 10. I hope very well concerning you, God helping.

That what we command you, both you do, and will do) So also 1 Thess. IV. 10, V. 11.

Let there not be faith of all. But one is faithful, namely the Lord. Therefore the sequence and sentence of the Apostle is not incorrectly handed down by the blessed Hunnius: Lest he should provide an opportunity for the Thessalonians to doubt concerning their perseverance in the faith, because, namely, he removes that assent of faith from human powers and ascribes it to God alone working, for that reason he adds by way of consolation: The Lord is faithful, as if he were saying: Although faith is by no means either of all men or the work of human powers, yet do not for that reason doubt concerning your salvation. For He who once kindled faith in you will also confirm you in it, nor will He suffer it to be subverted or extinguished in you. And concerning this matter he makes his Thessalonians certain, having taken the argument from the constant fidelity of God, as if he were saying, your faith rests upon the faith of God. He is faithful and constant. Therefore He will not allow you to fall away from the gift of faith conferred, but will establish you in it, and will guard you from every evil, from Satan, and his fiery darts and snares, so that he may not be able to shake or weaken your faith with them. But lest, this consolation being less skillfully accepted, they might deflect too much to the other side and become secure, and determine that whatever they might do further, it could not be to their detriment, for that reason, just as on one side he has consoled them against the temptations of the Devil: So now on the other he fortifies their minds against the security of the flesh, so that they may walk and be kept in the middle and royal road with an unoffending foot. Therefore he subjoins: But we trust through the Lord, etc. This is, what I say with the intention of consoling concerning the fidelity of God, I would not have you accept as if it were permissible for you to do further whatever you please. But you shall know that you will be safe against the power and assaults of Satan only if you have persisted in the good begun, and have not yourselves turned away from the holy obsequies of God of your own accord. By the evil one, B. Luther, Calvin, Piscator, Crocius, and others also understand Satan, who is called the evil one by antonomasia, Matthew V. 37, c. XIII. v. 19, Eph. VI. 16, 1 John II. 13, 14, c. III. 12, c. V. 18. Hyperius understands all adversaries. But he who is guarded from that evil is guarded from every evil. Regarding the word 'you do and will do', Chrysostom: It is necessary indeed, he says, to cast everything upon God, but in such a way that we also may work, and undertake labors and struggles.

Latin:

V. 4. Πεποίθαμεν δὲ ἐν Κυρίῳ ἐφ᾽ ὑμᾶς) Sic & Gal. V. 10. Optime de vobis spero, Deo adjuvante.

Ὅτι ἃ παραγγέλλομεν ὑμῖν, καὶ ποιεῖτε, καὶ ποιήσετε) Sic & 1. Thess. IV. 10. V. 11.

Non sit omnium πίστις. At unus est πιστὸς, scili- cet Dominus. Itaque συνέχεια & sententia Aposto- li non inrecte traditur à B. Hunnio: Ne ansam præ- beret Thessalonicensibus de sua in fide perseverantia dubitandi, quia scilicet fidei assensum illum humanis derogat viribus, solique Deo operanti adscribit, id- circo consolationis loco subjicit: Fidelis est Dominus, quasi dicat: Etsi fides nequaquam vel omnium est hominum, vel opus humanarum virium, tamen haud- quaquam ideo dubitate de salute vestra. Is enim, qui fidem semel in vobis accendit, confirmabit etiam vos in illa, nec patietur eam in vobis subverti aut extin- gui. Et hac de re certos reddit Thessalonic. suos, sum- pto argumento a constanti fidelitate Dei, quasi dicat, fides vestra nititur Dei fide. Is fidelis est, & constans. Idcirco non sinet dono fidei collato vos excidere, sed stabiliet vos in eo, & custodiet ab omni malo, a sata- na, ejusque ignitis telis & insidiis, ne iis fidem vestram concutere vel labefactare possit. Ne autem hac con- solatione minus dextre accepta nimis ad alterum la- tus deflecterent, & securi evaderent, statuerentque, quicquid tandem porro facerent, id sibi fraudi esse non posse, idcirco sicut ex una parte contra tentationes Diaboli eos est consolatus: Sic nunc ex altera munit illorum animos adversus securitatem carnis, ut in media Regiaque via inoffenso pede ingrediantur ac serventur. Proinde subjungit: Confidimus autem per Dominum &c. Hoc est, quæ consolandi animo dico de fidelitate Dei, non sic velim accipiatis, quasi vobis integrum sit, porro facere, quicquid lubet. Sed ita demum contra potentiam & assultus Satanæ vos tu- tos fore noveritis, si in bono inchoato perstiteritis, ac non vos ipsi a sanctis Dei obsequiis sponte vestra defle- xeritis. Per πονηρὸν B. Lutherus, Calvinus, Pisca- tor, Crocius alii etiam intelligunt Satanam, qui An- tonomasitce vocatur πονηρὸς, Matth. V. 37. c. XIII. v. 19. Eph. VI. 16. 1. Joh. II. 13. 14. c. III. 12. c. V. 18. Hyperius omnes adversarios intelligit. Sed qui custoditur ab illo malo, custoditur ab omni malo. Ad verbum ποιεῖτε καὶ ποιήσετε Chrysostomus: O- portet quidem, inquit, totum in Deum projicere, sed ita, ut & ipsi operemur, & labores & certamina aggrediamur.

## 3:5
V. 5. And the Lord direct your hearts) Direct יַיְשֵׁר. The Lord, that is, Christ, through his Spirit, to be sure.

Into the love of God) that you may love God.

And into the patience of Christ) That patience, of which Christ is the cause, namely through the hope implanted in us 1 Th. I. 2.

Since there is no making of ours in spiritual matters, unless God directs our hearts, the Apostle adds a prayer to his admonition. By 'the Lord,' however, he does not understand Christ, for he names him expressly later, but the Holy Spirit, as Theophylact and Oecumenius observe with Basil the Great, thus exhibiting the three persons of the divinity. The Lord, that is, the Holy Spirit directing our hearts; God, into whose love; and Christ, in whose patience they are to be directed. For so Basil the Great, in his book on the Holy Spirit, ch. 21: 'Who is the Lord directing into the love of God, and into the patience for the afflictions of Christ? Let them answer us, who drive the Holy Spirit into servitude. For whether the discourse be about God the Father, it could altogether be said, The Lord direct you into the love of himself: Or about the Son, it could be added, into his own patience. Let them seek, therefore, what other person it is fitting to honor with the title of Lord.' He also compares a similar passage 1 Thess. III. 12. 13. Similarly Theodoret: 'The divine Apostle shows us the Trinity: but it is clear that he called the Holy Spirit the Lord. He wrote likewise to the Corinthians, "Now the Lord is the Spirit."' By the patience of Christ, however, he does not understand so much the patience which is from Christ, or that which endures on account of Christ and the persecutions to be exhausted for his sake, as, if ὑπομονὴ is explained as patience, that which relies upon the example or even the doctrine of Christ, so that we may be patient, and endure, after his likeness, or even according to his own prescription. Some, however, even Theophylact along with Chrysostom, asserting that explanation, prefer the interpretation of the word ὑπομονῆς as expectation, as Haymo, Erasmus, Beza, and Piscator have interpreted, as Bullinger, Calvin, Hyperius, and Crocius: who says that this sense is fuller, and comprehends the former. For no one can patiently bear adversities who does not patiently expect Christ, the coming judge. He who patiently expects him will bear all adversities with a calm mind for Christ's sake, and thus will strive to imitate his patience. Thus the Greek scholia: 'He says, that we may have patience, that is, that being prepared we may await him.' But simpler is the explanation of B. Hunnius, which is also that of B. Luther and others of our own: May he direct your hearts into the love of God, that you may thus pursue and revere God with sincere filial love; whereby this love for him may add sharp spurs to you to humbly obey his holy precepts. Then that he may direct your hearts εἰς ὑπομονὴν, into the patience of Christ, lest you allow yourselves to be disturbed from the right state of faith, piety, and obedience by the storms of adversities, but may persist unconquered with unbroken spirits, and that by the example of Christ himself, who goes before you in this matter.

Latin:

V. 5. Ὁ δὲ Κύριος κατευθύναι ὑμῶν τὰς καρδίας) Κατευ- θύναι יַיְשֵׁר. Dominus, id est, Christus, per Spiritum sci- licet suum.

Εἰς τὴν ἀγάπην τοῦ Θεοῦ) ut Deum diligatis.

Καὶ εἰς τὴν ὑπομονὴν τοῦ χριστοῦ) Eam patientiam, cujus causa est Christus, nempe per spem nobis insitam 1. Th. I. 2.

Quum nulla sit nostra ποίησις in spiritualibus, nisi Deus corda nostra dirigat, monitioni suæ vo- tum adjungit Apostolus. Per Dominum autem non Christum intelligit, hunc enim postea diferte no- minat, sed Spiritum S. ut cum Basilio M. Theophy- lactus & Oecumenius observant, exhibens ita tres personas divinitatis. Dominum, id est, Spiritum S. dirigentem corda nostra, Deum, in cujus amorem, & Christum, in cujus patientia illa dirigenda. Ita n. Basilius M. libr. de Spiritu S. c. 21. Quis est Do- minus dirigens in dilectionem Dei, & in patientiam pro afflictionibus Christi? Respondeant nobis, qui Spiritum sanctum in servitutem adigunt. Sive enim de Deo Patre fiat sermo, omnino dici poterit, Do- minus vos dirigat in dilectionem sui: Sive de Filio, addi poterit, in suam ipsius patientiam. Quærant igi- tur, quænam sit alia persona, quam Domini voca- bulo deceat honorari. Confert etiam similem locum 1. Thess. III. 12. 13. Similiter Theodoretes: Divinus autem Apost. nobis Trinitatem ostendit: Clarum est autem, eum Dominum vocasse Spiritum S. Ita etiam scripsit ad Corinthios, Dominus autem Spiritus est. Per patientiam vero Christi non tam patientiam, quæ a Christo est, aut eam, quæ ob Chri- stum ac persecutiones ejus causa exantlandas per- durat, intelligit, quam, si ὑπομονὴ de patientia ex- plicetur, eam, quæ exemplo aut etia doctrina Chri- sti nititur, ut patientes simus, ac sustineamus, illius- instar, vel ex praescripto etiam ipsius. Nonnulli ta- men, etiam Theophylactus cum Chrysostomo illam explicationem asserens praeferunt interpretatio- nem vocis ὑπομονῆς de expectatione, ut Haymo, Era- smus, Beza, Piscator interpretati sunt, ut Bulling. Calvinus, Hyperius, & Crocius: qui sensum hunc pleniorem esse, ac priorem comprehendere dicit. Nemo enim potest patienter ferre adversa, qui non patienter expectat Christum, venturum judicem. Hunc qui patienter expectat, ille aequo animo fe- ret propter Christum adversa omnia, adeoque ejus patientiam imitari studebit. Sic scholia Graeca: Ὑπομονὴν δέ, φησιν, ἵνα ὑπομείνωμεν, τουτέστιν, ἵνα ἐμπαράσκευοι ὄντες αὐτὸν προσδεχώμεθα. Sim- plicior autem est B. Hunnii explicatio, quae B. Lu- theri etiam, aliorumque e nostris: Dirigat corda ve- stra in dilectionem Dei, ut Deum sincero amore filiali sic prosequamini & revereamini; quo hic amor in ipsum contemptus acres stimulos vobis addat, sanctis praeceptis ejus humiliter obsecundandi. Deinde ut diri- gat corda vestra εἰς ὑπομονὴν, in patientiam Christi, ne adversitatum procellis de recto statu fidei, pietatis & obsequii vos deturbari patiamini, sed infractis animis persistatis invicti, idque ipsius Christi, praeeuntis vo- bis hac in re, exemplo.

## 3:6
V. 6. We command you, brethren, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ) That is, we command by Apostolic authority. Στέλλεσθαι ὑμᾶς ἀπὸ παντὸς ἀδελφοῦ ἀτάκτως περιπατοῦν- τος, καὶ μὴ κατὰ τὴν παράδοσιν, ἣν παρέλαβον παρ᾿ ἡμῶν) What παράδοσις is, see above II. 15. Ἀτάκτως περιπατοῦντες are the same as ἄτακτοι, 1 Thess. V. 14. He orders these to be avoided: for that is what στέλλεσθαι means here, ὑποστέλλειν in Gal. II. 13. If a presbytery had been there, he would have ordered them to be excommunicated. Now because there was no presbytery, he ordered such wickedly living persons to be avoided, that is, to shun their familiar company, which is a right that belongs to individual Christians. See what we said at Matt. XVIII. 17. In the Manuscript, for παρέλαβον it is παρελάβετε. By Boeotian inflection, concerning which see Rom. III, 13. Thus ἐξήλθοσαν Exod. XVI, v. 22. συνελάβοσαν Jer. XXVI, 8. But the construction is according to the meaning; for having spoken of individuals, he introduced the plural: which the Latin noted.

Why would he have ordered them to be excommunicated immediately? It concerns the idle. Ἄτακτος δὲ ἐστιν, ὁ δίχα τάξεως τῶν τοῦ Θεοῦ νόμων περιπατῶν, say the Greek scholia. But here it is restricted to those flowing away in idleness by Theodoret, which, however, I would not wish to take exclusively: Those not living according to the laws for public honesty and utility are designated: yet they are not manifestly flagitious, such as fornicators, thieves, etc. Estius: He understands, he says, one walking or conversing inordinately as him who does not do what is of his own order and duty, and disturbs those who do. Concerning such, it has already been said in the last chapter of the former epistle regarding that: Admonish the unruly, in Greek, the inordinate. B. Hunnius: That you abstain, he says, from the conversation of him who, while he is a brother by reason of his external profession, and a Christian by name, yet in his life and dissolute morals does not respond to so august a profession, nor allows himself to be restrained within the bounds of duty by the instruction which he received from us, but lives according to his own whim, given to slothful idleness, and from idleness flowing into other sins as well. Shall we immediately excommunicate them? That there was no presbytery there is gathered in vain from this command. Theophylact rightly: Withdraw from any man who lives inordinately, that is, through sloth and laziness, whether he be wealthy, or poor, or holy. I would call this one inordinate. In what way? Certainly even from inertia itself. For he will abstain even from crimes themselves, and will betake himself to jests or certain ravings and trifles. He adds: The tradition, namely that which I myself handed down to you by work and deeds, a form of living well for you. This is indeed true instruction. He had already denounced this before them, that each should mind his own business, which he recalled to their memory, 1 Thess. IV, 11, and here recalls again. There he had enjoined the Thessalonians to admonish the inordinate, c. V. 14; here, because the admonitions had not found a place, he orders that they avoid their company. If this does not profit, he commands that it be indicated even by letters, v. 14. Yet he says they are not to be treated as enemies, but to be admonished as brothers, v. 15. But those who are to be admonished as brothers are certainly not to be struck by the thunderbolt of excommunication. Concerning those who had sinned more gravely, a similar admonition exists in 1 Cor. V. 11, without mention of excommunication, even though there was no lack of a presbytery in the Corinthian Church. Estius explains the tradition thus: And not according to the doctrine and instruction handed down to them by me. The Greeks interpret this tradition as the example of Paul himself proposed to them for imitation. For he mentions this in the words immediately following. Others understand that sentence handed down to the Thessalonians by the Apostle, as he himself testifies below: If anyone does not wish to work, neither let him eat. It is simpler if we say that the Apostle speaks in general about the instruction of the Christian life, under which is primarily comprehended that everyone ought to be intent upon his own work, from which, if he is in need, he may provide himself a living. For that the Apostle had specially commanded this to the Thessalonians, he himself explicitly testifies in the former epistle, c. IV. He wishes to signify here the same kind of excommunication (as also 1 Cor. V. 11), namely such as is a medium between the greater and lesser excommunication, which we call them today. Which he understands concerning cloistral punishments. But Justinian denies that such were in use then, refuting Cajetan who explains it thus, whom Salmero also refutes here. Moreover, what he says in the name of the Lord, Chrysostom explains thus: We do not say so; but Christ. Similarly Theodoret: It is he who decrees these things through us.

Latin:

V. 6. Παραγγέλλομεν δὲ ὑμῖν ἀδελφοὶ ἐν ὀνόματι τοῦ Κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ) Id est, Apostolica autoritate praecipimus. Στέλλεσθαι ὑμᾶς ἀπὸ παντὸς ἀδελφοῦ ἀτάκτως περιπατοῦν- τος, καὶ μὴ κατὰ τὴν παράδοσιν, ἣν παρέλαβον παρ᾿ ἡμῶν) Quid sit παράδοσις vide supra II. 15. Ἀτάκτως περιπατοῦντες iidem sunt, qui ἄτακτοι, 1. Thess. V. 14. Hos jubet vitari: id enim στέλλεσθαι hic, ὑποστέλλειν Gal. II. 13. Si presbyterium ibi fuis- set, jussisset eos excommunicari. Nunc quia presbyterium non erat, jussit tales improbe viventes vitari, id est, familia- rem eorum consuetudinem defugi, quod jus singulis Chri- stianis competit. Vide quae diximus ad Matth. XVIII. 17. In Manuscripto pro παρέλαβον est παρελάβετε. Boeotica fle- xione, de qua vide Rom. III, 13. Sic ἐξήλθοσαν Exod. XVI, v. 22. συνελάβοσαν Jer. XXVI, 8. Est autem constructio κατὰ τὸ σημαινόμενον; nam de singulis loquutus intulit plurale: quod notavit Latinus.

Cur statim excommunicari jussisset? Agitur de otiosis. Ἄτακτος δὲ ἐστιν, ὁ δίχα τάξεως τῶν τοῦ Θεοῦ νόμων περιπατῶν inquiunt scholia Graeca. Sed hic restringitur ad otio diffluentes a Theodoreto, quod tamen exclusive accipere nolim: Non viventes se- cundum leges ad publicam honestatem & utilita- tem designantur: nec tamen ii manifeste flagitiosi, quales scortatores, fures &c. Estius: Ambulantem, inquit, seu conversantem inordinate intelligit eum, qui quod sui est ordinis atque officii, non facit, & fa- cientes turbat. De talibus jam dictum est ultimo ca- pite prioris epistolae ad illud: Corripite inquietos, Grae- ce, inordinatos. B. Hunnius: Ut abstineatis, inquit, a conversatione ejus, qui cum ratione externae profes- sionis sit frater, & nominetenus Christianus, vita ta- men & moribus suis dissolutis professioni tam augustae non respondet, nec intra officii cancellos se coerceri patitur per institutionem, quam accepit a nobis, sed ex suo vivit libitu, otio ignavo deditus, & ex otio in alia quoque peccata diffluens. Illosne actutum ex- communicabimus. Presbyterium ibi non fuisse, e praecepto hoc nequicquam colligitur. Recte Theo- phylactus: Secedite a quovis hominum, qui inordi- nate, id est, per ignaviam & segnitiem vitam dege- rit, sive opulentus, sive inops, sive sanctus sit ille. Inor- dinatum hunc dixerim. Quo pacto? Certe vel ex ipsa inertia. Nam & ab ipsis facinoribus abstinebit, & ad sales vel deliramenta quaedam & nugas se con- feret. Addit: Traditionem, eam videlicet, quam ipse vobis opere & factis tradiderim, forma vobis bene vivendi effectus. Haec utique vera est institutio. Co- ram id jam denunciaverat, ut quisque rem suam ageret, quod in memoriam ipsis revocavit, 1. Thess. IV, 11. ac denuo hic revocat. Ibi Thessalonicensibus injunxerat, ut monerent inordinatos, c. V. 14. hic quia locum non invenerant monitiones, jubet, ut consortium eorum vitent. Si hoc non proficiat, etiam per literas indicari præcipit, v. 14. Nec tamen ut inimicos ducendos, sed ut fratres monendos, dicit, v. 15. Qui vero ut fratres monendi, illi utique excommunicationis fulmine non sunt feriendi.
