De iis, qui gravius peccarant, simile monitum extat 1. Cor. V. 11. non facta excommunicationis mentio- ne, etsi in Ecclesia Corinthiaca non deesset pres- byterium. Traditionem Estius sic explicat: Et non secundum doctrinam & institutionem à me illis tradi- tam. Hanc traditionem Græci interpretantur ipsius Pauli exemplum propositum illis ad imitandum. Nam hujus meminit verbis proxime sequentibus. Alii in- telligunt sententiam illam Thessalonicensibus ab A- postolo traditam, ut ipse infra testatur: Si quis non vult operari, nec manducet. Simplicius est, si dica- mus, Apostolum loqui in genere de institutione vitæ Christianæ, sub qua illud imprimis comprehenditur, unumquemque operi suo intentum esse debere, ex quo, si egeat, victum sibi paret. Nam & hoc specialiter A- postolum Thessalonicensibus præcepisse, ipse diserte testatur in priori epist. c. IV. Idem hic genus aliquod excommunicationis significare vult (ut & 1. Cor. V. 11.) nimirum tale, quod medium sit inter excom- municationem majorem & minorem, quas hodie vo- camus. Quæ de pœnis claustralibus intelligit. Ta- les autem in usu tum fuisse negat Justinianus, Ca- jetanum sic explicantem refellens, quem etiam Salmero hic refutat. Cæterum quod in nomine Domini ait, Chrysostomus ita explicat: Non nos ita dicimus; Sed Christus. Similiter Theodoretus: ipse est, qui hæc per nos decernit.

## 3:7
V. 7. For you yourselves know how you ought to imitate us) That is, you know how you must live so that you may imitate us. See 1 Cor. IV. 16, XI. 1, Eph. V. 1, 1 Thess. I. 6. Ὅτι ἐκ ἠτακτήσαμεν ἐν ὑμῖν) Ἀτακτεῖν is ἀτάκτως περι- πατεῖν, not to do things rightly or in order. Plutarch uses this verb thus in Themistocles.

Latin:

V. 7. Αὐτοὶ γὰρ ὄιδατε πῶς δεῖ μιμεῖσθαι ἡμᾶς) Id est scitis, quomodo vobis vivendum sit, ut nos imitemini. Vide 1. Cor. IV. 16. XI. 1. Eph. V. 1. 1. Thess. I. 6. Ὅτι ἐκ ἠτακτήσαμεν ἐν ὑμῖν) Ἀτακτεῖν est ἀτάκτως περι- πατεῖν, non recte, neque ordine res agere. Utitur sic isto verbo in Themistocle Plutarchus.

## 3:8
V. 8. Neither did we eat bread for nothing from anyone) He lashes out especially at the hangers-on at tables, the freeloaders. But in toil and travail) 1 Thess. II. 2. Working night and day) This was Paul's custom everywhere, Acts XX. 34, 1 Thess. II. 9, IV. 12. That we might not burden any of you) & he repeats this 1 Thess. II. 7, 9. That we might not burden the Church of God, Clement, Constit. II. 33.

Latin:

V. 8. Ὀυδὲ δωρεὰν ἄρτον ἐφάγομεν παρά τινος) Mensarum asseclas maxime flagellat, τὲς ἀσυμβόλες. Ἀλλ' ἐν κόπῳ καὶ μόχθῳ) 1. Thess. II. 2. Νύκτα καὶ ἡμέραν ἐργαζόμενοι) Mos hic Paulo ubique Act. XX. 34. 1. Thess. II. 9. IV. 12. Πρὸς τὸ μὴ ἐπιβαρῆσαί τινα ὑμῶν) & hoc repetit 1. Thess. II. 7. 9. πρὸς τὸ μὴ ἐπιβαρῆσαι τὴν τῆ Θεῆ Ἐκκλησίαν, Clement. Constit. II. 33.

## 3:9
V. 9. Not that we do not have the authority) The right to live at your expense was not lacking to us, 1 Cor. IX. 6. But that we might give ourselves as a pattern to you to imitate us) That we might exhibit ourselves to you as an example for all the greatest things. Concerning the word τύπος in this sense, see Phil. III. 17.

He does not repeat 1 Thess. II. 7, 9. But here he repeats from that passage. But how could Paul, Silvanus, and Timothy live at the expense of exiles in Syria? How could they provide an example to the Thessalonian Church, to whom they had not yet been present? If I, he says, to whom it was permitted to abstain from manual labor and to be free for the ministry of the word alone, did not even use that permitted rest, but provided my own sustenance with my own hands so that I might spare others, then certainly others, outside of any calling, ought much less to live idly and be a burden to others. William Estius observes that the reason for the Apostle not accepting anything from the Thessalonians was not the same as from the Corinthians: for to the Thessalonians, among whom many were given to idleness and living off others, he wished to give an example of seeking sustenance by one's own labor. But he spared the wealthy and greedy Corinthians so that he might surpass in this glory their false apostles, who had hands ready for receiving, and for that reason might render his Gospel more commendable.

Latin:

V. 9. Ὀυχ ὅτι ἐκ ἔχομεν ἐξυσίαν) Jus nobis non deerat vivendi vestro sumptu, 1. Cor. IX. 6. Ἀλλ' ἵνα ἑαυτὲς τύπον δῶμεν ὑμῖν εἰς τὸ μιμεῖσθαι ἡμᾶς) Ut exemplar vobis nos ipsos exhiberemus ad maxima quæque. De voce τύπος in hoc sensu vide Phil. III. 17.

Non repetit 1. Thess. II. 7. 9. Sed hic repetit ex illo loco. Quomodo autem sumptu exulum in Syria vivere poterant Paulus, Silvanus, & Timo- theus. Quomodo exemplar Thessalonicensi Ec- clesiæ præbere, cui nondum adfuerant? Si ego, in- quit, cui licebat abstinere ab opere manuario, & vacare soli ministerio verbi, ne quidem concessa illa quidem sum usus requie, sed manibus meis mi- hi victum comparavi, ut parcerem aliis, multo profecto minus debent alii extra omnem vocatio- nem vivere otiosi, aliisque oneri esse. Guilielmus Estius observat, non eandem Apostolo causam fuis- se nihil accipiendi à Thessalonicensibus & à Corin- thiis: Nam Thessalonicensibus, apud quos multi erant otio dediti, & de alieno viventes, exemplum dare voluit, victum proprio labore quærendi. Corinthiis autem divitibus & avaris ideo pepercit, ut eorum Pseudo-Apostolos, qui manus habebant ad acci- piendum promptas, hac gloria superaret, atque ea ratione commendabilius redderet suum Evange- lium.

## 3:10
V. 10. For even when we were with you, we gave you this command) What preceded was of exhortation, but this is now of precept. That if any one will not work, let him not eat) This sentence exists in Bereschith Rabba & in Ohelmoed, as learned men have noted. There is also another not unlike it in the book Zeror: He who does not labor on the eve of the Sabbath, let him not eat on the Sabbath. The Apostles, like Christ, love to use good sentences which were in the mouths of the people or the wise. Similar is that of Homer in Odyssey T. -- For I will not endure an idle man, whoever touches my measure. And among the sayings of Pythagoras was: Do not sit on a measure. Which signifies, as Eustathius explains, not to be fed while idle. Demosthenes Olynthiaca IV. It is not possible for those who do nothing to have the things of those who do as a law requires. Alexis. -- For whoever delights in eating every day and does nothing worthy of his food, but leads a life of leisure, is the greatest evil to living. Clemens Constitut. II. If any one does not work, let him not eat among us, for the Lord, our God, hates the idle.

But why first of exhortation, and this now of precept? Is not the reason for both the same? Nay, here a new argument for the command is brought forward. The former was from example, but this is taken from equity, nay, from divine ordinance, and both concern the strengthening of the precept regarding those who walk inordinately. For even regarding the example, that word 'must' (δεῖ) is used, which belongs to a precept. Another reason, says B. Hunnius, is taken from the most just law which He had delivered to them when He was among them, namely, that if any one would not work, he should not eat. This rule, however, deals with those who have the bodily strength to work. Paul rightly ordained that food be denied to those who spend their time in idleness: establishing nothing new, but repeating the most ancient constitution of God Himself: In the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat thy bread, Gen. III. Baronius notes this ad ann. Christ. 52. n. XVII. Sœmahaja & Althalion relate that a certain common law was prescribed to the Rabbis who wished to profess the sacred letters, that they should learn some manual craft by which they might seek their living. For they were accustomed to read such institutions in the first reading of the first week of unleavened bread. R. Gamaliel also, in the doctrine of the brothers which is inscribed Haod, strongly recommends that those learning the sacred letters should exercise some manual work, and he affirms that those who have neglected to do this will be more prone to sin. Among other noble ancient Rabbis, it is read that Rabbi Johanan exercised the art of shoemaking, Rabbi Juda the art of baking, and others other arts of this kind. From such an institution, therefore, we think it came about that Paul, most learned in the sacred letters, learned some manual craft, which he exercised to provide himself with a living whenever he stayed in any place while he preached the Gospel. This is Baronius. Drusius l. VII. præterit. in h. l. p. 306. An old adage of the Hebrews, he says, is דאילא לעי לאנכים He who does not work, does not eat, which exists in Bresith Rabba, c. XIV. Whence I have found it cited by Nathan Justus in Baal Aruch under the word לע, & by Solomon, son of Abraham, grandson of Samuel, in Ohel Moed under the word רע.

Latin:

V. 10. Καὶ γὰρ ὅτε ἦμεν πρὸς ὑμᾶς τοῦτο παρηγγέλλομεν ὑμῖν) Quod præcessit, erat hortamenti, hoc vero jam præcepti. Ὅτι εἴτις ὀ θέλει ἐργάζεσθαι, μηδὲ ἐσθιέτω) Exstat hæc sen- tentia in Bereschith Rabba & in Ohelmoed, ut viri eruditi notarunt. Est & alia non dissimilis in libro Zeror: Qui non laboraverit in prosabbato, ne edat in sabbato. Amant Apostoli, ut & Christus, sententiis uti bonis, quæ in ore erant populi aut sapientum. Simile illud Homeri in Odysseæ T. -- Οὐ γὰρ ἀεργὸν ἀνέξομαι, ὅςκεν ἐμῆιο χοίνικος ἅπτηται. Et inter Pythagoræ dicta erat: Ἐπὶ χοίνικος μὴ καθίσθαι. quod significat, Eustathio exponente, μὴ τρέφεσθαι ἀργός. Demosthenes Olynthiaca IV. Οὐκ ἔστιν, ὅπω τοῖς μηδὲν ἑγὼ ποίησουσι τὰ τῶν ποικησάντων ἄποιοι ὡς δεῖ νόμον. Alexis. -- Ὅςις ἥδεται γὰρ ἐσθίων Ὁσημέραι ἀεὶ καὶ ποιεῖν τῶν σιτίων Ἐπάξιον μηδὲν, περιουσίαν δὲ σχολῆς Ἄγοντα, τῷ ζῆν πολεμώτατον κακόν. Clemens Constitut. II. Εἰ δέ τις μὴ ἐργάζεται, οὗτος παρ᾽ ἡ- μῖν μὴ ἐσθιέτω, ἀργὼς γὰρ μισεῖ ὁ κύριος, ὁ Θεὸς ἡμῶν.

Cur vero prius hortamenti, hoc vero jam præ- cepti? Annon ejusdem utriusque ratio? Imo vero hic novum profertur mandati argumentum. Prius erat ab exemplo, hoc vero est ab æquitate, imo ab ordinatione divina desumptum, utrumque autem ad firmandum præceptum, inordinate ambulantes concernens. Nam & circa exemplum adhibetur illud δεῖ oportet, quod præcepti est. Ratio alia, in- quit B. Hunnius, desumpta à justissima lege, quam tradiderat eis, cum apud eos versaretur, videlicet, ut si quis nollet operari, is nec èderet. Agit autem hæc regula de his, qui corporis viribus ad laborandum valent. Quibus ferias agentibus, recte cibum negari ordinavit Paulus: nihil novi constituens, sed anti- quissimam constitutionem ipsius Dei repetens: In su- dore vultus tui comedes panem tuum, Gen. III. Notat Baron. ad ann. Christ. 52. n. XVII. Sœmahaja & Althalion Rabbinis communem quandam legem præ- scriptam illis fuisse tradunt, qui sacras vellent literas profiteri, ut manuale quoppiam opificium addiscerent, quo victum quærerent. Legi enim consueverunt ejus- modi institutiones in prima lectione primæ hebdoma- dis azymorum. R. Gamaliel quoque in doctrina fra- trum, quæ inscribitur Haod, valde commendat, ut sacras literas addiscentes opus aliquod manuale exer- cerent, quod qui facere prætermisissent, procliviores ad peccandum futuros esse affirmat. Inter alios nobiles antiquos Rabbinos legitur Rabbi Johanna sutoriam, Rabbi Juda pistoriam artem exercuisse, & alios alia id genus. Ex ejusmodi igitur institutione provenisse existimamus, ut Paulus sacris literis exculsissimus ali- quod manuum opificium didicerit, quod ad victum sibi comparandum, cum Evangelium prædicaret, ubi- cunque locorum consisteret, exercuerit. Hæc Baro- nius. Drusius l. VII. præterit. in h. l. p. 306. Adagium, inquit, est Ebræorum vetus דאילא לעי לאנכים Qui non operatur, non comedit, quod extat in Bresith Rabba, c. XIV. Unde citatum inveni à Nathane Justo in Baal Aruch voce לע, & à Salomone, Abrabami filio, Samuelis nepote in Ohel Moed voce רע.

## 3:11
V. 11. For we hear that some are walking among you inordinately) (The trembling Judea eats a secret thing in the ear. (strange: Not working, but busy-bodying) In the Glossary: I am a busy-body, I inquire, a busy-body is curious. Regarding such a class of men, Horace says: Avoid the inquisitive man. For the talkative man is the same. And among Aeschines they are read joined: A busy-body and a slanderer. He understands, therefore, those who, by prying into the affairs of others and from there catching material for joking among others, would sustain themselves by this miserable way of life. Add 1 Tim. V. 13, where a similar vice of women is treated.

Latin:

V. 11. Ἀκούομεν γάρ τινας περιπατῶντας ἐν ὑμῖν ἀτάκτως) Ni- Arcanam Judæa tremens manducat in aurem. (mirum: Μηδὲν ἐργαζομένως, ἀλλὰ περιεργαζομένως) In Glossario: περιεργάζομαι sciscitor περίεργος curiosus. De tali homi- num genere Horatius: Percunctatorem fugito. Nam garrulus idem est. Et apud Æschinem juncta leguntur: Περίεργος καὶ συκο- φάντης. Eos ergo intelligit, qui aliena scrutando, & inde apud alios captando jocandi materiam hoc misero vitæ ge- nere se sustentarent. Adde 1. Tim. V. 13. ubi de simili vitio fœminarum agitur.

## 3:12
Vers. 12. But to such we command, and exhort by our Lord Jesus Christ) that is, by Christ's command, as above 6. That working with quietness they may eat their own bread) Well, 'their own bread'. For food belonging to another, among the Latin comic poet, 'another's dough', among the Greek comic poet, is a parasitic life. For 'bread' (ἄρτον), like 'bread' (לחם) among the Hebrews, is put for all food. And rightly 'with quietness', that is, to attend to their own affairs,

.) in which sense quietness (ἡσυχία) is taken also in 1 Tim. II. 12, this being the opposite of those who are running about and chattering.

He demands both, Theophylact saying, that those who have been inordinate or restless, and lazy and inert, should be quiet and silent, so that they may work and eat their own, not another's, bread. Nor should it be necessary that they hang from the hands of others and hope for a living. The Apostle, says B. Hunnius, excellently contrasts honest quiet with curiosity, and the work of a legitimate calling with shameful and lazy idleness, by antithesis, and opposes bread or food of one's own, obtained by labor and sweat, to another's (which those lazy drones were enjoying). For of the idle, according to Theodoret, the characteristics are trifles, futile talkativeness, and useless curiosity. In the words of the Apostolic exhortation, Estius notes an increase: As if he were saying, I do not only command but also beseech, and not just in any way, but by our Lord Jesus Christ, which is the way of one vehemently adjuring. For he could name nothing greater, nothing dearer, by which he might beseech.

Latin:

Vers. 12. Τοῖς δὲ τοιούτοις παραγγέλλομεν, καὶ παρακαλῶ- μεν διὰ τοῦ κυρίου ἡμῶν ἰησοῦ χριστοῦ) id est, Christi mandato, ut supra 6. Ἵνα μετὰ ἡσυχίας ἐργαζόμενοι τὸν ἑαυτῶν ἄρτον ἐσθίωσι) Bene τὸν ἑαυτῶν ἄρτον. Nam cibus alienus apud Comicum Latinum, ἀλλοτρία μάζα, apud Comicum Græcum, est vita parasitica. Ἄρτον enim ut לחם apud Ebræos pro omni cibo ponitur. Et recte μετὰ ἡσυχίας, id est, ad sua agenda,

.) quo sensu ἡσυχία sumitur & 1. Tim. II. 12. oppositum hoc discursantibus & garrientibus.

Utrumque deposcit, Theophylacto dicente, ut quie- scant & sileant, qui inordinati fuerint vel inquieti, & pigri & inertes, ut operentur, & suo non alieno pane vescantur. Neque oporteat, ut ab aliorum bi manibus pendeant, & victum sperent. Apostolus, inquit B. Hunnius, quietem honestam cum curiositate, opus le- gitimae vocationis cum turpi & ignavo otio per anti- thesin egregie contendit, & panem cibumve proprium victui parto labore ac sudore alieno, (quo ignavi illi fuci fruebantur,) opponit Otiosorum enim, secundum Theodoretum, propria sunt nuga, futilisque loquaci- tas & inutilis curiositas. In verbis adhortationis A- postolicae incrementum notat Estius: Quasi dicat, non praecipio tantum sed & obsecro, nec id quomodo- cunque, sed per Dominum nostrum Jesum Christum, quod est vehementer obtestantis. Nihil enim majus, nihil charius, per quod obsecraret, nominare potuit.

## 3:13
V. 13. But you, brothers, do not grow weary in doing good) Do not become fatigued in doing what is right. The same sense is in Gal. VI. 9, where 'doing good' (τὸ καλὸν ποιεῖν), which is here contracted to 'doing good' (καλοποιεῖν). A similar compound is 'doing good' (ἀγαθοποιεῖν), Mark II. 4, Luke VI. 9, 33, 34, & among Peter several times, & in the third of John. The opposite is 'doing evil' (κακοποιεῖν), both in those places of the New Testament & among the Greek Interpreters often for the Hebrew ערע.

Just as he wishes these things, which he has just written, to be said to those hateful and idle men: So now he passes from them to address the pious in the Church of the Thessalonians by way of apostrophe. He instructs them with this rule, that they should not cease to perform the works of their calling diligently and faithfully, nor, moved by the perverse example of the idle, become so weary that they themselves keep untimely holidays regarding their calling, as the blessed Hunnius says here. Similar things are read in Estius. Theophylact, along with Chrysostom, restricts that beneficence to the idle: See how immediately his fatherly heart is torn. For he immediately felt pity for them, as if to say: I would indeed concede that one must depart from these men, yet not so that you allow them to perish from hunger and starvation. But that explanation seems rather foreign. How these things act against monastic idleness, see the blessed Balduinus here.

Latin:

V. 13. Ὑμεῖς δὲ ἀδελφοὶ μὴ ἐκκακήσητε καλοποιοῦντες) Ne fatigamini recta agendo. Idem sensus Gal. VI. 9. ubi τὸ καλὸν ποιεῖν, quod hic contracte καλοποιεῖν. Simile com- positum ἀγαθοποιεῖν, Marc. II. 4. Luc. VI. 9. 33. 34. & apud Petrum aliquoties, & in tertia Johannis. Contrarium κα- κοποιεῖν & in illis Novi Testam. locis & apud Graecos Inter- pretes saepe pro Ebræo ערע.

Sicut hominibus odiosis illis atque otiosis haec, quae scripsit modo vult dicta: Ita nunc ab illis ad pios in Ecclesia Thessalonicensium per Apostrophen compel- landos transit. Quos hac regula instruit, ut ne desi- nant operas sua vocationis facere diligenter ac fideli- ter, nec otiosorum pravo exemplo permoti sic defati- gentur, ut & ipsi circa vocationem suam intempesti- vas ferias agant, ut hic B. Hunnius. Quibus gemina leguntur apud Estium. Theophylactus cum Chryso- stomo illam beneficentiam restringit ad otiosos: Vide ut confestim distracta paterna sint viscera. Nam statim illos commiseratus est, perinde ac si dicat: Con- cesserim equidem, fore ab his discedendum, haud ta- men ita, ut permittatis fame hos & inedia deperire. Sed ea explicatio alienior videtur. Quomodo haec faciant adversus otium Monachale, videatur hic B. Balduinus.

## 3:14
V. 14 If anyone does not obey our word) Those precepts which we give by Christ's command.

By this letter mark him) that is, in the letter written to me, depict him with your marks, so that I may then decide that which the Spirit shall dictate, 1 Cor. V. 3. in the Glossary: Σημειῦμαι I mark, I sign.

And do not associate with him) Namely, until I have decided something certain. Συναναμίγνυσθαι is to live together familiarly, 1 Cor. V. 9, 11. Συγχρᾶσθαι elsewhere.

Latin:

V. 14 Εἰ δέ τις ὐχ ὑπακύει τῷ λόγῳ ἡμῶν) Illis praeceptis, quae ex Christi mandato damus.

Διὰ τῆς ἐπιστολῆς τῦτον σημειῦσθε) id est, in epistola ad me scripta illum suis notis depingite, ut ego deinde statuam id, quod Spiritus dictaverit, 1. Cor. V. 3. in Glossario: Ση- μειῦμαι noto, signo.

Καὶ μὴ συναναμίγνυσθαι αὐτῷ) Nempe dum ego certi ali- quid statuerim. Συναναμίγνυσθαι est familiariter convivere, 1. Cor. V. 9. 11. Συγχρᾶσθαι alibi.

## 3:15
V. 15. That he may be ashamed) so that, touched by shame, he may return to a better mind. See what was said at Matt. XVIII. 17. You have the word ἐντρέπεσθαι in this sense also in Tit. II. 8. The Hebrew would be יכלם.

And do not regard him as an enemy) Namely, from the law of Levit. XIX. 17. But admonish him as a brother) that is, as one who has been a brother. The memory of former brotherhood ought to effect something. תוכחנה. See the cited passage of Leviticus, where in the Greek it is ἐλέγξεως. You have the word νυθετεῖν in Rom. XV. 14, Col. III. v. 16, 1 Thess. V. 14. Such an admonition is for the Rabbis נזיפה.

Estius wrongly says that this precept pertains to Prelates. Grotius did not see Prelates here. It seems doubtful whether the words 'by letter' should be referred to the preceding, that if anyone has not obeyed our word, delivered by letter—which sense the Syriac, Theophylact, Beza, the Dutch in their notes, Zepperus in his book on Ecclesiastical Polity, and Crocius embrace; as well as, among the Papists, Antonius Scaynus and Cornelius a Lapide—or whether they pertain to the following, that such persons ought to be indicated by letter, which pleases Thomas, Lombard, the blessed Luther, and most of our own, as well as Calvin, Bullinger, Hyperius, and Tossanus: which explanation we prefer. For λόγον denotes not only that which he delivered by the present letter, but also that which he had delivered by a previous letter, and that which he had delivered by word of mouth, and thus he wishes by letter such to be indicated, so that he may decide what is to be done with them. In this, however, Grotius does not deserve assent, because he wishes a brother to be understood, because he was a brother. For he still wishes him to be held as a brother, and teaches that he is to be received as a brother, not as an enemy: which name ἐχθρῶ is rashly explained from Lev. XIX. 17, where it is clearly not found. Estius is more correct: Rebuke him lovingly and kindly, as a brother, as one who is truly still your brother, even if he is to be avoided regarding the rest of his conversation on account of his offense. But the blessed Hunnius explained this whole passage very well in this way: Because the nature of men who conduct themselves in a disorderly manner was not unknown to the Apostle, and because they would not allow themselves to be brought into order by precepts alone, nor by bare exhortations, however serious, he therefore, judging that the almost final remedy of ecclesiastical severity should be applied, asks that if they see any such dissolute and idle man, they should both note him and report him to himself by letter or writing, so that he may consider what is to be determined about him, and in what way he is to be recalled to the path. Meanwhile, he wishes his association to be avoided, with this end noted, that he may be suffused with shame when he has seen that he is held unworthy of the company of the rest of the Christians, so that, having recognized his own perversity, he may repent. But lest anything be done wrongly in this part, he warns how the others ought to withdraw themselves from his familiarity, not that they should pursue him with hostility, but that they should labor to bring him back to the path with holy admonitions, and thus hate his sins, not hate his person, but strive to gain him for Christ. Theodoret also recognizes such as brothers: For they occupy the place of suffering members. For we are accustomed to apply a suitable remedy to those who are of this kind. Truly, says Theophylact here, it once seemed a most severe punishment to be separated from the conversation of men. For if one had to depart from him who led his life through laziness and sloth, how much more must one depart far from others who have been liable to greater offenses? Some Reformed, such as Beza, Piscator, Zepperus, and Crocius, warn that the word σημειῆσθε, mark, implies a public mark, and they explain these things regarding the mark of excommunication with Augustine, book after the conference with the Donatists, ch. IV, and thus they judge that the form of church discipline is prescribed here, which it should follow against the obstinate despisers of paternal admonitions and corrections. But in truth, since such men, about whom the Apostle speaks, are not to be held as enemies, but as brothers, excommunication has no place here. For excommunication, according to Crocius, is a public mark by which a stubborn despiser of laws is separated from the whole assembly, so that he may be held (no longer as a brother, but) as a Gentile and a tax collector, Matt. XVIII. 17.

PART II.

The Apostolic wish and seal.

Latin:

V. 15. Ἰνα ἐντραπῇ) ut pudore tactus ad mentem melio- rem redeat. Vide quae dicta ad Matth. XVIII. 17. Verbum ἐν- τρέπεσθαι habes hoc sensu & Tit. II. 8. Ebræum esset יכלם.

Καὶ μὴ ὡς ἐχθρὸν ἡγεῖσθε) Nempe ex lege Levit. XIX. 17. Ἀλλὰ νυθετεῖτε ὡς ἀδελφὸν) id est, ut qui frater fuerit. Aliquid operari debet pristinae fraternitatis memoria. Nus- tate תוכחנה. Vide dictum Levitici locum, ubi in Graeco ἐλέγξεως. Verbum νυθετεῖν habes Rom. XV. 14. Col. III. v. 16. 1. Thess. V. 14. Talis admonitio est Rabbinis נזיפה.

Perperam hoc praeceptum ad Praelatos spectare ait Estius. Non hic Praelatos vidit Grotius. Dubium videtur, an verba per epistolam ad praecedentia re- ferenda, quod si quis non obedivit verbo nostro, per epistolam tradito, quem sensum Syrus, Theo- phylactus, Beza, Belga in notis, Zepperus libr. de po- lit. Eccles. & Crocius amplectuntur; nec non e Pontificiis Antonius Scaynus, & Cornelius a Lapi- de, an vero ad sequentia spectent, quod nempe per epistolam tales indicari debeant, quod placet Tho- mae, Lombardo, B. Luthero, & plerisque nostris, Calvino item, Bullingero, Hyperio, & Tossano: Quam explicationem praeferimus. Nam λόγον notat non illum tantum, quem per epistolam praesentem, sed etiam, quem per superiorem epistolam, & quem viva voce tradiderat, adeoque vult per epistolam tales indicari, ut quid cum ipsis agendum sit, de- | cernat. In eo autem Grotius assensum non mere- | tur, quod fratrem intelligi velit, quia frater fuit. | Nam etiamnum pro fratre haberi vult, & ut fratrẽ | accipiendum esse docet,non ut hostem: Quod no- | men ἐχθρῶ temere explicatur è Lev. XIX. 17. ubi | plane non habetur. Rectius Estius: Corripite eum | amanter & benigne, tanquam fratrem, ut qui vere | adhuc frater vester sit, etsi quoad reliquam conver- | sationem vitandus propter delictum. Optime autem | totam hanc pericopam exposuit B. Hunnius hoc | modo: Quia D. Apostolo non ignotum erat ingenium | hominum, inordinate se gerentium, quod neque solis | præceptis, neque nudis obtestationibus, quantumvis | seriis se in ordinem redigi paterentur, ideo remedium | Ecclesiasticæ severitatis pene ultimum adhibendum | censens petit, si quempiam talem viderint hominem | dissolutum & ignavum, & illum notent, & per | epistolam seu literas sibi indicent, ut quid de illo sta- | tuendum, & quo pacto in viam revocandus ille sit, | despiciat. Interim vult illius vitari commercium, | annotato fine hoc, ut pudore suffundatur, quando sci- | licet viderit, se reliquorum Christianorum consortio | haberi indignum, ut agnita protervia sua resipiscat. | Ne autem hac in parte perperam quid fiat, submonet, | quomodo se ab illius familiaritate subducere debeant | cæteri, non ut hostiliter eum insectentur, sed ut san- | ctis admonitionibus in viam reducere laborent, atq; | sic peccata illius oderint, personam non oderint, sed | Christo lucrificare contendant. Fratres etiam agno- | scit tales Theodoretus: Ii enim laborantium mem- | brorum locum obtinent. Iis enim, qui sunt ejusmodi, | solemus convenientem medelam adhibere. Acerri- | mum sane, inquit hic Theophylactus, olim suppli- | cium videbatur, ab hominum conversatione sejungi. | Si n. erat ab eo, qui per inertiam & segnitiem vitam | duceret, abscedendum, quanto magis ab aliis procul | est abeundum, qui majoribus fuerunt delictis obno- | xii? Reformati nonnulli, utpote Beza, Piscator, | Zepperus, Crocius, monent, verbum σημειῆσθε, si- | gnate, notam inferre publicam,& de excommuni- | cationis nota hæc explicant cum August. libr. post | collat. cum Donat. c. IV.adeoque censent,præscri- | bi hic Ecclesiæ formam disciplinæ, quam sequatur | adversus obstinatos monitionum & correptionum | paternarum contemptores. Verum enim vero | quum non habendi sint tales, de quibus Apostolus | agit, ut hostes, sed ut fratres, excommunicatio hic | locum non habet. Excommunicatio enim, juxta | Crocium, est nota publica, qua præfractus legum | contemptor à toto cœtu discernitur, ut habeatur | (non pro fratre amplius, sed) pro Ethnico & pu- | blicano, Matth. XVIII. 17.

PARS II.

Votum & sigillum Apostolicum.

## 3:16
v. 16. Now the Lord of peace himself) שׂר־שׁלום Is. 9, 6. - Grotius therefore acknowledges that in Is. IX. 6 the discourse is about Christ, which is to be noted against his σρεβλότητα in the Isaian passage, where he twists the prophetic prediction toward Hezekiah.

May he give you peace) Paul loves word-plays, such as this one is. For peace in the former place signifies peace, in the following it signifies all prosperous things.

At all times) at every time, as Mark 5, 5. Luke 24, 53. Acts 11, 2. ch. 24, 16. Rom. 11, 10.

In every way) I approve the reading which the Latin interpreter and certain Greeks followed, in every place, as 1 Cor. I. 2. May God give you good things, whether you will be at Thessalonica, or will return to Judea or Syria, or will migrate elsewhere.

But why should the meaning of peace not be retained? For that wish fits the present subject matter perfectly. And thus Theodoret: That you may have peace both with yourselves and among one another, and be freed from the attack of adversaries. For this is what that signifies: in every way. And Theophylact: But here, since the matter itself required that contentions and dissensions of this kind should arise from the causes, since those who were removed from the fellowship of the brothers were more sharply embittered, and those who were enjoying the goods of fortune would no longer willingly forgive their own things to them, he deservedly prays for peace for them, not for a short time, but perpetual. For that is especially desired, that we may enjoy this peace perpetually and in any place, that is, that no occasion for altercation may be offered from any side, so that they may not dissent even by a word or by deeds. For thus you will render them better and more amended. For nothing contributes so much to accomplishing any matter according to one's will as to enjoy this peace, and to be free from perturbation of mind, and not to seem to rebuke anyone out of hatred. But there is not sufficient cause to depart from the more received reading because of the Vulgate's interpretation. For it very frequently wanders from the truth. Since he has already said always at every time, he has at the same time included that in every place. But that was a necessary wish, that they might also have peace in every way. The Greek scholia explain it as, in every business, in all opinions, words, and deeds, so that no occasion for contention may be left to them from any side, neither by word nor by work. That withdrawing into Judea or Syria is from Grotius's fabricated hypothesis about the Jewish exiles.

Ὁ Κύριος μετὰ πάντων ὑμῶν) May Christ be your helper. See Matt. 28, v. 20. In both Greek and Latin liturgies this is very ancient: Ὁ Κύριος μεθ' ὑμῶν: The Lord be with you. This succeeded to the place of that priestly blessing, of which mention is made in Num. 6, 22.

The passage in Matt. 28. 20 does not only imply the presence of grace without ἀδιαστασίᾳ (inseparability), but promises that Christ the God-man will be present to the disciples on earth by a true and substantial presence, just as he is said to have worked with them, being present to them everywhere, and certainly not absent, even after his assumption into heaven, Mark 16: Nor is the presence of divine power to be imagined without the presence of the subject. Concerning which see vol. I of the System of Theology regarding divine omnipresence.

Latin:

v. 16. Αὐτὸς δὲ ὁ Κύριος τῆς εἰρήνης) שׂר־שׁלום Es. 9, 6. - Agnoscit ergo Grotius, Es.IX.6. de Christo ser- | monem esse, quod contra ejusdem σρεβλότητα in | loco Esaiano notandum, ubi ad Hiskiam detor- | quet Propheticum vaticinium.

Δώη ὑμῖν τὴν εἰρήνην) Amat Paulus πλοκὰς, qualis & hic | est. Nam εἰρήνη priori loco pacem, sequente res omnes | prosperas significat.

Διὰ παντὸς) omni tempore, ut Marc. 5, 5. Luc. 24, 53. | Act. 11, 2. c. 24, 16. Rom. 11, 10.

Ἐν παντὶ τρόπῳ) Probo lectionem, quam sequutus est | Latinus Interpres & Græci quidam, ἐν παντὶ τόπῳ, ut 1. | Cor. I.2. Deus vobis det res bonas, sive Thessalonicæ eritis, | sive in Judæam aut Syriam redibitis, sive alio migrabitis.

Cur vero non retineatur pacis significatio? Nam | id votum apprime convenit, materiæ præsenti. | Atque ita Theodoretus: Ut & cum vobis ipsis, & in- ter vos invicem pacem agatis, & ab adversariorum impetu liberemini. Hoc enim significat illud: in omni modo. Et Theophylactus: Hic autem cum res ipsa exigeret, ut contentiones & dissidia ejusmodi decau- sis orirentur, cum hi, qui à fratrum essent consortio ablegati, acrius exacerbarentur, & quibus bonis po- tirentur fortunæ, haud ultra his sua libenti animo condonarent, merito pacem illis precatur, non ad breve, sed perpetuam. Id enim præcipue concupisci- tur, ut pace hac perpetuo & quovis loco fruamur, hoc est, ut nulla ex parte offeratur altercationis occasio, ita ut nec verbo quidem nec factis dissentiant. Sic enim meliores illos & emendatiores reddetis. Nam nihil adeo ad rem aliquam pro voluntate conficien- dam conducit, quam pace hac frui, & animi per- turbatione vacare, nec increpare quempiam videri præ odio. Cur autem à receptiori lectione absce- damus, satis causæ non est Vulgatæ interpretatio. Ea enim frequentissime aberrat à veritate. Quum πάντοτε omni tempore jam dixerit, illud ἐν παντὶ τό- πῳ simul complexus est. Id autem voti erat neces- sarii, ut ἐν παντὶ τρόπῳ etiam pacem habeant. Græ- ca scholia exponunt, in omni negotio, in omnibus sententiis, dictis, factis, ut nulla ex parte contentio- nis eis occasio relinquatur, neq; ex verbo, neq; ex opere. Illud secedite in Judæam aut Syriam est à conficta Grotii hypothesi de exulibus Judæis.

Ὁ Κύριος μετὰ πάντων ὑμῶν) Christus vobis sit adjutor. Vide Matth. 28. v. 20. In Liturgiis & Græcis & Latinis est hoc pervetus: Ὁ Κύριος μεθ' ὑμῶν: Dominus vobiscum. Hoc successit in locum sacerdotalis illius benedictionis, cujus mentio Num. 6, 22.

Locus Matth. XXIX. 20. non tantum præsen- tiam gratiæ sine ἀδιαστασίᾳ infert, sed Christum θεάνθρωπον discipulis in terris præsto futurum ve- ra & substantiali præsentia, quemadmodum παν- ταχοῦ ipsis præsens, sane non absens cooperatus di- citur, etiam post assumptionem in cœlum, Marc. XVI. promittit: Neque fingenda est præsentia di- vinæ virtutis sine præsentia suppositi. Quo de tom. I. System. Theol. circa omnipræsentiam divinam.

## 3:17
v. 17. Ὁ ἀσπασμὸς τῇ ἐμῇ χειρὶ Παύλου, ὅ ἐστι σημεῖον ἐν πάσῃ ἐπιστολῇ, ὕτω γράφω) Up to this point Paul had used the hand of a scribe in writing the epistle; these he writes with his own hand, and gives us a manifest indication that other epistles had been sent by him elsewhere, many of which have perished, but that this is the first which he sent to the Thessalonians. Otherwise, if his hand had already been known, he would not have used these words, just as he does not use them in the second to the Thessalonians, who were gathered from Jews and Gentiles, which is called the first, when in reality it was, as we have said, the later one. Thus you have ἀσπασμὸς τῇ ἐμῇ χειρὶ Παύλου at the end of the first to the Corinthians, not at the end of the second. He calls a certain connection of letters, by which he wrote his name, a sign.

Whether he used the hand of a scribe up to this point is not entirely clear. For there is no need for the words of the Apostle to be understood exclusively, when they can be understood inclusively. But that other epistles were sent by the Apostle elsewhere before this one, which have perished, and that this is the first which he sent to the Thessalonians, does not appear from these words by even an obscure judgment, let alone a manifest one. Those are merely precarious hypotheses. For what is the consequence? Paul gives a certain sign of his letters in the epistle written to the Thessalonians. Therefore others sent elsewhere have perished. What does the sign designated in this epistle have to do with the loss of other epistles sent elsewhere? It has to do with the recognition of forged letters, not with the loss of genuine ones. And therefore that indeed could have been the cause of the certain sign being established: but this latter can neither be gathered from that sign, nor believed to be its cause. Therefore Theophylact on these words: Which is a sign in every epistle, so I write: Just as if he were to say: Lest perhaps my epistles be altered by some forgers. For that, as we said at the beginning, many were in the habit of doing, by this my hand I sign in every epistle which, to be sure, I am about to send to you in the future, or it will be sent to any others at some time. Furthermore, what kind of consequence is that, if Paul's hand had already been known, he would not have used these words? For could not some letter be peddled by impostors as Pauline, as if spoken by Paul, even if it did not bear Paul's hand? It is necessary, therefore, that Paul's hand was not unknown before these letters, otherwise, from those words, even if they were written by his own hand, it could not have been distinguished. And who, I ask, denies that it was known, since he had spoken to the Thessalonians? But it seemed that a peculiar sign should be added, which he himself had chosen with the ἰδιογραφίᾳ for that purpose, so that they would not be deceived by some supposititious letter. For whatever letter did not have this sign written by Paul's hand, if by chance the whole letter was not written by his own hand (as can be seen in the letter to the Romans, ch. XVI. 22), that was to be held as spurious. Finally, it is doubtful whether that σημεῖον was a certain nexus of letters by which Paul wrote his name, or indeed the solemn closing of the letters written by his hand. The latter, however, seems more likely. For that closing, which is added here: Ἡ χάρις τοῦ κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ μετὰ πάντων ὑμῶν. Ἀμήν: is also read in Rom. XVI. 24, Phil. IV. 23, and in all other Pauline letters, either more succinctly, as for instance 1 Cor. XVI. 22 and 1 Thess. V. 28, ἡ χάρις τοῦ Κυρίου Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ μεθ' ὑμῶν; Col. IV. 18, ἡ χάρις μεθ' ὑμῶν; Heb. XIII. 25, ἡ χάρις μετὰ πάντων ὑμῶν, ἀμήν; 1 Tim. VI. 21, ἡ χάρις μετὰ σοῦ ἀμήν; and 2 Tim. IV. 22, ἡ χάρις μεθ' ὑμῶν, ἀμήν; Tit. III. 15, ἡ χάρις μετὰ πάντων ὑμῶν. Amen: Or more fully, as for instance Philem. v. 25, ἡ χάρις τοῦ Κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ μετὰ τοῦ πνεύματος ὑμῶν; Gal. VI. 18, ἡ χάρις τοῦ Κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ μετὰ τοῦ πνεύματος ὑμῶν, ἀδελφοί. Ἀμήν. And Eph. VI. v. 24, Ἡ χάρις μετὰ πάντων τῶν ἀγαπώντων τὸν Κύριον ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦν Χριστὸν ἐν ἀφθαρσίᾳ. Ἀμήν. As also 2 Cor. XIII. 13, Ἡ χάρις τοῦ Κυρίου Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ, καὶ ἡ ἀγάπη τοῦ Θεοῦ, καὶ ἡ κοινωνία τοῦ ἁγίου πνεύματος μετὰ πάντων ὑμῶν. Ἀμήν.

But that other salutation clause, ὁ ἀσπασμὸς τῇ ἐμῇ χειρὶ Παύλου, is not read in all the letters, but only in two besides this one of ours, as for instance 1 Cor. XVI. 22 and Col. IV. 18. Theodoret says that the blessing itself, which is placed at the end, is called a salutation, and he makes it the same as that sign. He added this, he says, because of those who dared to circulate forged letters, teaching them to look for the subscription. For this, he says, is the sign of my letters. For in every letter I write a salutation. From this, therefore, we learn that he was accustomed to write this, 'the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you all, Amen,' in place of 'farewell.' Although Anshelmus takes those words, 'my salutation by the hand of Paul,' as that sign, he nevertheless adds another explanation, that this sign is understood as those words which are immediately added, which Estius confesses is far more probable. Since it is possible to see this in all the Pauline letters, even that which is written to the Hebrews, although not always in exactly the same words: and from this he judges it to be understood how distinguished a preacher and commender of divine grace (

this Apostle was, so that he appended this salutation to all his letters as if for a seal, so much so that he did not want any letter that lacked this sign to be acknowledged as his.

Latin:

v. 17. Ὁ ἀσπασμὸς τῇ ἐμῇ χειρὶ Παύλου, ὅ ἐστι σημεῖον ἐν πά- σῃ ἐπιστολῇ, ὕτω γράφω) Hactenus in describenda epistola manu scribæ Paulus usus fuerat, hæc scribit sua manu, ma- nifestumque nobis indicium dat, alias a se epistolas alio mis- sas, quales multæ interciderunt, sed hanc primam esse, quam Thessalonicam miserit. Alioqui si nota jam fuisset ejus ma- nus, his verbis usus non fuisset, sicut eis non utitur in al- tera ad Thessalonicenses ex Judæis & gentibus collectos, quæ prior dicitur, cum revera fuerit, ut diximus, posterior. Sic ἀσπασμὸς τῇ ἐμῇ χειρὶ Παύλου habes in fine prioris ad Corinthios, non in fine posterioris. Σημεῖον vocat certum quendam nexum literarum, quo nomen suum scribebat.

Anne manu scribæ hucusque usus sit, non omnino liquet. Non enim opus est, exclusive in- telligi verba Apostoli, quum intelligi possint in- clusive. Alias autem epistolas ante hanc alio missas ab Apostolo, quæ interciderint, & hanc primam esse, quam Thessalonicam miserit, ex his verbis ne obscuro quidem judicio constat, nedum manife- sto. Merè sunt precariæ illæ hypotheses. Quæ n. consequentia? Paulus certum dat signum litera- rum suarum in epistola ad Thessalonicenses exa- rata. Ergo aliæ alio missæ interciderunt. Quid signum in hac epistola designatum ad aliarum alio missarum epistolarum deperditionem facit? Ad dignotionem literarum supposititiarum facit, non ad deperditionem genuinarum. Ideoque illa quidem causa fuisse potuit signi certi constituti: hæc autem nec è signo illo colligi, nec causa ejus credi potest. Ideo Theophylactus ad hæc verba: Quod est signum in omni epistola, ita scribo: Perinde ac si dicat: Ne forsan à nonnullis falsariis mea immutentur episto- læ. Id namque, ut principio diximus, factitabant plerique, hac mea manu subsigno in omni epistola, quam scilicet ad vos imposterum sum transmissurus, vel ad quoscunque alios olim transmittetur. Porro quænam illa consequentia, si nota jam fuisset Pauli manus, his verbis usus non fuisset? Annon enim venditari poterat ab impostoribus epistola quæ- dam pro Paulina, quasi à Paulo dicta, etiamsi Pauli manum non referret? Non ignotam itaque fuisse Pauli manum oportet ante hasce literas, alioquin enim ex istis verbis, etsi manu ejus propria exara- tis, dignosci non potuisset. Et quis quæso negat, notam fuisse, quum apud Thessalonicenses dixe- rit? Addendum autem videbatur peculiare si- gnum, quod cum ἰδιογραφίᾳ ipse eo fine elegerat, ut ne per epistolam aliquam supposititiam illis im- poneretur. Quæ enim epistola hoc signum manu Paulina exaratum non habebat, si forte epistola tota ipsius manu propria conscripta non fuerit, (ut videre est in epistola ad Romanos cap. XVI. 22.) illa pro spuria habenda erat. Denique num ση- μεῖον illud fuerit certus nexus literarum, quo no- men suum Paulus scripserit, an vero manu ejus scri- pta solennis epistolarum clausula, dubium est. Po- sterius vero similius videtur. Nam ea clausula, quæ hic additur: Ἡ χάρις τοῦ κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ μετὰ πάντων ὑμῶν. Ἀμήν: legitur etiam Rom. XVI. 24. Phil. IV. 23. & in aliis omnibus epistolis Paulinis, sive succinctius, utpote 1. Cor. XVI. 22. & 1. Thessal. V. 28. ἡ χάρις τοῦ Κυρίου Ἰη- σοῦ Χριστοῦ μεθ' ὑμῶν; Col. IV. 18. ἡ χάρις μεθ' ὑμῶν; Ebr. XIII. 25. ἡ χάρις μετὰ πάντων ὑμῶν, ἀμήν; 1. Tim. VI. 21. ἡ χάρις μετὰ σοῦ ἀμήν; & 2. Tim. IV. 22. ἡ χάρις μεθ' ὑμῶν, ἀμήν; Tit. III. 15. ἡ χάρις μετὰ πάντων ὑμῶν. Ἀμήν: Sive plenius, ut- pote Philem. v. 25. ἡ χάρις τοῦ Κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ μετὰ τοῦ πνεύματος ὑμῶν; Galat. VI. 18. ἡ χάρις τοῦ Κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ μετὰ τοῦ πνεύμα- τος ὑμῶν, ἀδελφοί. Ἀμήν. Et Ephes. VI. v. 24. Ἡ χάρις μετὰ πάντων τῶν ἀγαπώντων τὸν Κύριον ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦν Χριστὸν ἐν ἀφθαρσίᾳ. Ἀμήν. Ut & 2. Cor. XIII. 13. Ἡ χάρις τοῦ Κυρίου Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ, καὶ ἡ ἀγάπη τοῦ Θεοῦ, καὶ ἡ κοινωνία τοῦ ἁγίου πνεύμα- τος μετὰ πάντων ὑμῶν. Ἀμήν.

Altera vero illa salutatoria clausula, ὁ ἀσπασμὸς τῇ ἐμῇ χειρὶ Παύλου non legitur in omnibus epi- stolis, sed tantum in duabus præter hanc nostram, utpote 1. Cor. XVI. 22. & Col. IV. 18. Theodoretus salutationem dicit appellari ipsam benedictionem, quæ in fine sita est, & eandem signum illud facit. Hoc autem adjecit, inquit, propter eos, qui fictas epistolas circumferre audebant, docens eos ut quære- rent subscriptionem. Hoc enim, inquit, est signum mearum epistolarum. In omni enim epistola ego scri- bo salutationem. Hinc ergo discimus, quod hoc, gra- tia Domini nostri Jesu Christi cum omnibus, Amen, pro eo, quod est vale, scribere consueverit. Etsi Anshelmus verba illa, salutatio mea manu Pauli, pro signo illo habeat, addit tamen alteram expli- cationem, hoc signum intelligi verba ea, quæ statim subjiciuntur, quod longe probabilius esse fatetur Estius. Siquidem id videre sit in omnibus Paulinis epistolis, etiam ea, quæ ad Ebræos est exarata, licet non semper iisdem omnino verbis: & ex eo intelligi censet, quam insignis gratiæ divi- sos (

næ prædicator & commendator fuerit hic Apostolus, ut omnibus etiam suis epistolis hanc salutationem velut pro sigillo appenderet, adeo ut cui epistolæ hoc signum deesset, nollet eam pro sua agnosci.

## 3:18
v. 18. Ἡ χάρις τοῦ Κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ μετὰ πάντων ὑμῶν) And this is the solemn closing of Paul's letters.

He had begun from grace, and he concludes the letter in grace, fortifying his statements on both sides as if with a certain mass of walls, as Theophylact says, and imposing a safer end as if by having laid firmer foundations. To divine grace must be attributed both the beginning of faith, and its completion, and its end, the salvation of souls, and indeed the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ: which includes the grace of both the Father and the Holy Spirit, or as it is held more explicitly in 1 Cor. 13 v. 13, the love of the Father, and the communion of the Holy Spirit. Neither is obtained outside of Christ or the grace of Christ. For outside of Christ there is no blessing, no salvation, Gen. XII. 3, Acts IV. 12. Therefore he sometimes names grace absolutely, as for instance Eph. VI. 24, Col. IV. 18, 1 Tim. VI. 21, 2 Tim. IV. 22, Tit. III. 15, Heb. XIII. 25. Which, however, he wishes to be understood as the grace of Christ, as is gathered from this place along with similar ones, Rom. XVI. 24, Phil. IV. 23, 1 Thess. V. 28. Gal. VI. v. 18, 2 Cor. XIII. 13, Phil. V. 25. For through Christ grace and truth came to be, John I. v. 17. Beautiful here is the observation of the Blessed Balduinus, which he made last: The vow, which Saint Paul subscribed to his letters with his own hand in v. 17, indicates the chief sum of the Pauline writings, and distinguishes them from the doctrine of the Pseudo-Apostles. For it embraces the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, which is the most precious treasure of the pious man, and the fountain of our salvation, which others seek in their works, but for us it is prepared in the gratuitous mercy of God; this is what the Apostle urges in all his letters. Whatever, therefore, in the business of our salvation mixes the works of men with divine grace, let it not be held as Apostolic, because outside of Christ given to us through the grace of God there is no righteousness, no salvation. From this grace, therefore, we must take care that we do not fall, and that we may taste its sweetness in all our needs, let us pray for one another with pious affection.

Amen) The Church used to add this when the letter had been read. And from there it began to be inscribed.

Whence, however, is it evident to Grotius that this was added by the Church, and not indeed written by Paul? Which should rather be said: both so that that little word may not be denied to be authentic and canonical; and because it is most fitting, as a seal of the vow by which the Apostle testifies to his desire and faith in obtaining every grace, and confirms it in the minds of the Thessalonians; and then especially because this little word could not have been added by the Church to that sign in the parallel passage Rom. XVI. 24, as Grotius wishes, inasmuch as it is placed in the Apostolic context, not at the end of the letters. We conclude this present epistle with the final words of Theodoret: Thus the Apostle was accustomed to write his greetings: We, however, plucking the Apostolic blessing, let us praise Christ, who spoke through him. With whom to God the Father with the most holy Spirit be glory and magnificence, now and always and for ever and ever. AMEN.

Latin:

v. 18. Ἡ χάρις τῦ Κυρίε ἡμῶν Ἰησῦ Χρισῦ μετὰ πάντων ὑμῶν) Et hæc solennis Pauli epistolarum clausula.

A gratia initium cœperat, & in gratia concludit epistolam, utrinque tanquam quadam parietum mole, Theophylacto dicente, ejus dicta communiens, & velut jactis firmioribus fundamentis finem tutiorem imponens. Gratiæ divinæ acceptum ferendum, & initium fidei, & complementum, ac finis ejusdem, salus animarum, & quidem gratiæ Domini nostri Jesu Christi: quæ & Patris & Spiritus Sancti gratiam includit, vel ut explicatius habetur 1. Cor. 13. v. 13. dilectionem Patris, & communicationem Spiritus Sancti. Neutra extra Christum vel gratiam Christi obtingit. Extra Christum enim nulla est benedictio, nulla salus, Gen. XII. 3. Act. IV. 12. Ideo absolute gratiam quandoque nominat, utpote Eph. VI. 24. Col. IV. 18. 1. Tim. VI. 21. 2. Tim. IV. 22. Tit. III. 15. Ebr. XIII. 25. Quam tamen Christi vult intelligi gratiam, ut ex hoc loco cum similibus Rom. XVI. 24. Phil. IV. 23. 1. Thessal. V. 28. Gal. VI. v. 18. 2. Cor. XIII. 13. Phil. V. 25. colligitur. Per Christum enim gratia & veritas facta, Joh. I. v. 17. Pulchra est hic B. Balduini observatio, quam ultimam fecit: Votum, quod Divus Paulus manu sua epistolis suis subscripsit v. 17. summam præcipuam scriptorum Paulinorum indicat, eaque à doctrina Pseudo-Apostolorum discriminat. Complectitur enim gratiam Domini nostri Jesu Christi, quæ pretiosissimus thesaurus est hominis pii, & fons salutis nostræ, quam alii in operibus suis quærunt, nobis vero in gratuita DEI misericordia parata est; id quod urget Apostolus suis omnibus in epistolis. Quicquid ergo in negotio salutis nostræ gratia divina opera hominum admiscet, id non habeatur pro Apostolico, quia extra Christum per gratiam Dei nobis donatum nulla est justitia, nulla salus. Ab hac ergo gratia ne excidamus, cavendum est, & ut ejus suavitatem in omnibus necessitatibus nostris gustemus, alter alteri ex pio affectu comprecemur.

Ἀμήν) Hoc addebat Ecclesia, cum lecta esset epistola. Et inde adscribi cœpit.

Unde vero id constat Grotio, additum hoc fuisse ab Ecclesia, non vero adscriptum à Paulo. Quod potius dicendum: tum ne vocula illa negetur authentica esse, ac canonica: tum quod ea conveniat maxime, ceu sigillum voti, quo desiderium suum & fidem obtinendæ omnis gratiæ Apostolus testatur, & in Thessalonicensium animis confirmat, tum imprimis quod ad illud signum vocula hæc in loco parallelo Rom. XVI. 24. addi ab Ecclesia, uti Grotius vult, nequiverit: utpote in contextu Apostolico, non in fine literarum positum. Concludimus hinc præsentem epistolam verbis extremis Theodoreti: Sic vale scribere consuevit Apostolus: Nos autem Apostolicam benedictionem decerpentes laudemus Christum, qui per eum loquutus est. Cum quo Deo Patri cum sanctissimo Spiritu gloria & magnificentia, nunc & semper & in secula seculorum. AMEN.

AMEN.
